units.la: SEX anni sunt cum in Evangelia Matthæi & Marci Commentarium edidi, qui subjectam verbis sententiam, eamque litteræ consentaneam aperte declararet. Ad hujus à me confectionem adhibitum & quod evolvendus iis, quæ Patres Ecclesiæ reliquerunt, monumentis animadverti, & quod observavi perlegendis & diligenter expendendis multis & variis scriptoribus tam antiquis, quam neotericis, & quod mihimet ipsi prudentiæ ac cognitionis impertivit Deus optimus. Erat appendicis loco, quod novi fœderis intelligentiam præbet non contemnendam, comprehensi animo ritus Hebræorum & idiomata, in quibus ego natus, institutus, & educatus sum. Id temporis in Academia Andegavensi, cujus è Doctoribus sum unus, explicabam publicè Theologiam. Putaram igitur partes esse meas, ut in hoc commentario meo bene multas intexerem disputationes exquisitas ad divinam illam doctrinam & Christianæ religionis historiam pertinentes. In eodem hoc Ecclesiæ Romanæ superstitiones & errores, quibus tum tenebar, ubi ubi locus erat defendendi, defendi quàm poteram acerrimè. Quo major, cùm me tetrus istis è tenebris eripuisset summâ benignitate Deus, danda mihi fuit opera, ut typis excuderetur denuò meus ille Commentarius, in quo palàm oppugnarem, quos in eodem propugnaveram errores, simul & momenta rationum, quibus ad discutiendam animi mei caliginem usus est Deus, breviter hîc illîc exponerem. Porrò autem in hac editione mutavi permulta, quæ non venerunt in controversiam, ut bonam magnámque libri partem novam & in editione superiore invisam liceat verè dicere. Jam quoscunque produco scriptores, laudo illos syncerè quidem: verum enim, quoniam nulla mihi res familiaris adhuc parta est, illos, quorum indigeo, libros omnes unde mihi comparem utique non habeo. Atqui nonnullos in collectanea mea Græcos scriptores ita retuleram, ut tamen ipsorum verba Græca non essent adscripta: hos igitur, cùm mihi
units.tr: Six years have passed since I published a commentary on the Gospels of Matthew and Mark, which set out clearly the meaning lying beneath the words and agreeing with the letter. In composing it I made use of what I had noted while going through the monuments left by the Fathers of the Church, and of what I had observed while reading and carefully weighing many and various writers, both ancient and modern, and of the wisdom and knowledge that the most good God had bestowed upon me. As an appendix, I added the customs and idioms of the Hebrews, among which I was born, brought up and educated, since these offer no small help to the understanding of the New Covenant. At that time I was publicly teaching theology in the Academy of Angers, of whose teachers I am one. I therefore thought it my task to weave into this commentary of mine a good many carefully chosen disputations pertaining to that divine doctrine and to the history of the Christian religion. In the same work I defended, as vigorously as I could, the superstitions and errors of the Church of Rome, by which I was then held, wherever there was occasion to defend them. The more so, since God, in his great kindness, had snatched me from those foul shadows, I was bound to see to it that that commentary of mine be printed again, in which I would openly attack the errors I had once championed in it, and at the same time briefly set out here and there the considerations by which God was pleased to dispel the darkness of my mind. Moreover, in this edition I have changed a great deal that was not in controversy, so that I may truly say that a good and large part of the book is new and was not seen in the earlier edition. Now, as to whichever writers I cite, I quote them faithfully indeed; but since no property of my own has yet been acquired, I by no means have all the books from which I might obtain those I need. Yet I had cited some Greek writers in my collections in such a way that their Greek words were not added; these, therefore, since to me...

units.la: mihi copia librorum consulendorum non suppeteret, feci latinè loquentes. Sacræ verò Scripturæ testimonia pleraque omnia profero videlicet ex interpretatione vulgata, quæ mihi omnium est maximè familiaris: sed enim quid ea differat à textu primigenio Hebræo, item & Græco moneo diligenter cùm ad sacri textûs intelligentiam opus esse videatur. Ac de nostro quidem instituto satis dictum est.
units.tr: Since I did not have at hand a supply of books to consult, I cited those who write in Latin. But for the most part I quote the testimonies of Holy Scripture from the Vulgate translation, which is the one I am most familiar with; yet I carefully point out where it differs from the original Hebrew and also the Greek text, since this seems necessary for understanding the sacred text. And enough has been said about my plan.

units.la: Explicatio Litteralis EVANGELII SECUNDUM MATTHÆUM.
units.tr: Literal Explanation of the Holy Gospel according to Matthew.

units.la: MATTHÆUS Evangelista factus ex Publicano Apostolus, eorum à Deo primus electus est, quos Christi Domini historia divino modo conscribenda statuerat; Divino inquam, ut pote qui semper, tum vero præcipuè verbis & animo Spiritus-sancti organa fuerint. Evangelium Hierosolymis, vel Neophytorum (ut author est divus Hieronymus) obsecratione, vel præcipuo quodam Apostolorum (ut Epiphanius arbitratur) jussu literis mandavit; non Graeco quidem idiomate, sed Hebræo vel Syrio, ut testis est Eusebius, Patrésque non pauci, quos inter addit Hieronymus Panthenum propagandæ fidei studio in Indias profectum Evangelium Matthæi Hebraicè scriptum ibi reperisse ad suam usque ætatem in Bibliotheca Cæsariensi diligenter servatum, quod secum Alexandriam reportavit. Hebræum illud exemplar periit, Græca versio superest, cujus author incertus est, eam licèt quidam è Sanctis Patribus, vel Sancto Jacobo, vel Sancto Joanni Apostolo ascribant. Matthæus (ut notat Augustinus libro primo de consensu Evangelistarum capite secundo) Incarnationem Domini secundum stirpem Regiam, & pleraque secundum hominum præsentem vitam facta & dicta ejus recensenda suscepit; unde quemadmodum divo Joanne (qui sæpe & Trinitatis & Christi Divinitatis mysteria pro usitata sua celsitate pertractat) paulo dimissior, sic etiam eo Christianis compluribus utilior est; ut pote qui ea Christi opera, consiliaque & præcepta præcipuo[?] quodam consilio referre studuit, in quibus hominem, quem gerebat, ad nostra imitationis temperavit exemplum.
units.tr: MATTHEW the Evangelist, made an Apostle from a tax collector, was the first of those whom God chose to write the history of Christ the Lord, which he had determined should be written in a divine manner; divine, I say, since he was always, and especially then, an instrument of the Holy Spirit in words and mind. He committed the Gospel to writing at Jerusalem, either at the entreaty of the new converts (as the author is the divine Jerome), or by a particular command of the Apostles (as Epiphanius thinks). He wrote it not in Greek but in Hebrew or Syriac, as Eusebius testifies, and not a few of the Fathers. Among them Jerome adds that Pantaenus, who went to the Indies out of zeal for spreading the faith, found there Matthew's Gospel written in Hebrew, carefully preserved in the library at Caesarea until his own time, and that he brought it back with him to Alexandria. That Hebrew copy has perished; the Greek version survives, whose author is unknown, although some of the holy Fathers ascribe it either to St James or to St John the Apostle. Matthew (as Augustine notes in book one of On the Harmony of the Evangelists, chapter two) undertook to recount the incarnation of the Lord according to the royal line, and most of the deeds and sayings of his life among men. Hence, just as he is somewhat plainer than the divine John, who often treats the mysteries of both the Trinity and the divinity of Christ with his usual lofty style, so he is also more useful to many Christians, since he took pains to relate those works, counsels and precepts of Christ in which he set before us, as a pattern for our imitation, the man whom he bore.

units.la: SANCTUM JESU CHRISTI EVANGELIUM SECUNDUM MATTHÆUM.
units.tr: The Holy Gospel of Jesus Christ according to Matthew.

units.la: Sensus huius tituli est idem ac si diceretur, liber à Matthæo conscriptus, qui continet bonum nuntium de redemtione generis humani per Christum facta.
units.tr: The sense of this title is the same as if it were said: a book written by Matthew, which contains the good news of the redemption of the human race accomplished through Christ.

units.la: CAPUT I. VERS. I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I. VERSE I.

units.la: Liber generationis. Id est, enarratio eorum omnium, quæ acciderunt Messiæ per Prophetas Judæis toties promisso. Est autem hic Hebraismus; generatio enim Hebræis, seu toleda, ut monet Aben-Ezra. Gen. 37. v. 2. non tantum nativitatem seu genealogiam, sed etiam eventus & casus denotat. Ita verbum תולדות Jalad gignere, unde תולדה toleda generatio, sumi notat Prov. 27. v. 1. Nescis quid pariet יום dies, id est, quid unius diei spatio accidet. Est itaque primus hic versus brevis epigraphe, seu inscriptio totius Evangelii secundum Matthæum: q. d. Vita Jesu Christi Fili David secundum carnem. Statuit enim Matthæus generationem humanam & quæ Christo Jesu cum hominibus conversanti acciderunt, enarrare.
units.tr: The book of the generation. That is, the account of all the things that happened to the Messiah, which the Prophets had so often promised to the Jews. This is a Hebraism. For the Hebrews use generatio, or toledah, as Aben Ezra observes (Gen. 37. v. 2.), to denote not only birth or genealogy but also events and occurrences. So the verb jalad [ילד], to beget, from which toledah [תולדה], generation, is derived, is used in Prov. 27. v. 1: You do not know what the day [יום] will bring forth, that is, what will happen within the span of one day. The first verse is therefore a short heading, or title, of the whole Gospel according to Matthew, as if to say: the life of Jesus Christ, Son of David according to the flesh. For Matthew intends to set out the human generation and the things that happened to Christ Jesus while he lived among men.

units.la: B. Irenæus libro 2. adversus hæreses c. 41. Jesus nomen israelitarum proprium linguam Hebraeorum Literarum est datum. arum & dimidii, sicut periit eorum dicunt, significans Dominum eum, qui fecit cælum & terram. Hæc dicit B. Irenæus, quia יהוה שמים וארץ, quomodo per apocopam à captivitate Babylonica Hebræis usitatissimam scribitur Hebraicé nomen Salvatoris nostri, secundùm figuram à Rabbinis nuncupatam Notaricon (quì dictio una literis suis singulis singulas diversas dictiones connotat) designat, יהוה שמים וארץ, id est, Deus cæli & terræ. Iod autem dicitur dimidia Littera ratione suæ parvitatis.
units.tr: The blessed Irenaeus, in book 2 of Against Heresies, chapter 41: The name Jesus, proper to the Israelites, was given in the letters of the Hebrew language, and of a half [letter], as they say of what has perished, signifying the Lord who made heaven and earth. Blessed Irenaeus says this because the name of our Saviour is written in Hebrew, by the abbreviation most common among the Hebrews since the Babylonian captivity, as YHWH shamayim va'aretz [יהוה שמים וארץ], according to the figure that the rabbis call Notaricon, in which one word signifies different words by each of its single letters. That is, God of heaven and earth. The letter Iod [יוד] is called a half letter because of its smallness.

units.la: Christi. Id est, unctì. Hoc nomine ab Hebræis designari solet quasi per antonomasiam ille, qui per Prophetas promissus erat Redemtor Israel. Unde Ioa. 1. v. 41. dicit Andreas Simoni: Invenimus Messiam (addit Evangelista) quod est interpretatum Christus. Et mulier Samaritana sic alloquitur Christum Ioa. 4. v. 25. Scio quia Messias venit, supple, jam jam. q. d. Prope est ut in Lege promissus veniat Messias, qui, ut ait ibidem Evangelista, dicitur; Græco scilicet vocabulo, Christus, qui nempe propter unionem in se divinæ naturæ cum humana, Spiritu-sancto unctus est præ omnibus participibus suis. Christum à Paganis dictum fuisse Chrestum, fidem facit inter ceteros Corn. Tacit.
units.tr: Christ. That is, anointed. The Hebrews usually designate by this name, as if by way of eminence, the one who was promised through the Prophets as the Redeemer of Israel. Hence John 1. v. 41: Andrew says to Simon: We have found the Messiah (the Evangelist adds), which is interpreted Christ. And the Samaritan woman addresses Christ thus, John 4. v. 25: I know that the Messiah is coming, understand, now at last. That is, the Messiah, who was promised in the Law, is about to come, who, as the Evangelist says in the same place, is called Christ in Greek [Χριστός], because, by the union of the divine nature with the human in himself, he was anointed with the Holy Spirit above all his partakers. That Christ was called Chrestus by the pagans is attested, among others, by Cornelius Tacitus.

units.la: Filii David. Hoc non est initium aut caput genealogiæ, quæ in præsenti capite instituitur, sed attributum Domini, de cujus stirpe agitur. Nam Filius David nota est, quâ perpetuò tum utebantur Judæi ad Messiam significandum, quem jam advenisse, eúmque esse Jesum Christum, cujus genealogiæ series hic texitur, indicandum aggreditur Matthæus. At que hinc est quod tam crebrò Messias nostèr Jesus Christus dicitur in Novo Testamento Filius David, ut Matth. 9. v. 27. Miserere nostri Fili David. 12. v. 23. Stupebant omnes turbæ & dicebant nunquid hic est Filius David? 15. v. 22. Miserere mei Domine Fili David. 22. v. 30. & 31. &c. Unde & illud ipsius Domini quærentis Matth. 22. Si Filius David Christus, quomodo ergo in Spiritu vocat eum Dominum?
units.tr: Son of David. This is not the beginning or head of the genealogy that is set out in the present chapter, but an attribute of the Lord whose line is in question. For Son of David is the title that the Jews constantly used to signify the Messiah, whom they already expected to have come, and Matthew sets out to show that he is Jesus Christ, whose genealogy is woven here. Hence it is that our Messiah Jesus Christ is so often called Son of David in the New Testament, as Matth. 9. v. 27: Have mercy on us, Son of David. 12. v. 23: All the crowds were amazed and said, is this not the Son of David? 15. v. 22: Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David. 22. v. 30 and 31, etc. Hence also that saying of the Lord himself, asking, Matth. 22: If Christ is the Son of David, how then does David in the Spirit call him Lord?

units.la: Filii Abraham. qui & dicitur Antiquis. Initium Dominicæ vel stirpis vel familiæ ab eo duxit Matthæus, à quo ipsa fides originem initiúmque duxit; ab Abraham scilicet patre non multorum modo, sed & maximo, ac maximorum: Sanctorum enim major in fide, quam in generatione semen est, ut eleganter loquitur Ambrosius. Cavebimus imprimis, ne postalios etiam ex Veteribus, qui naufragium non semel hic fecerunt, genealogiam anxiè excutiamus, cur Lucas in ordine & in nominibus genealogiæ infertis tantoperè à Matthæo discrepet; nos contenti summus illo Ambrosij : Fidei meæ finis Christus est, finis fidei meæ Dei Filius est. Non licet mihi scire generationis seriem, non licet tamen nescire generationis fidem. Indultriæ tamen eorum, qui hic operam & nostro tempore & olim posuerunt, unice favemus, idem enim & Veteribus tentatum, inter quos Augustinus lib. 2. quæst. Evang. c. 5. Aut, inquit, unus Evangelista patrem Josephi, a quo genitus est, nominavit, alter vero vel avum maternum, vel aliquem de majoribus cognatis posuit; aut unus erat huic Josephi naturalis pater, & alter eum adoptaverat; aut more Judæorum, cum sine filijs unus decessisset, ejus uxorem propinquus accipiens, filium, quem genuit, propinquo mortuo deputavit. Hanc ultimam causam veriorem existimat D. Th. 3. p. q. 31. a. 3. ad 2. utpote quæ apud Eusebium tradita est à Julio Africano, qui discrepantiam, quam in Salvatoris nostri genealogia à Matthæo Lucaque descripta nonnulli esse volunt, sufflulisse dicitur. Sed quantum sapio, quantum capio, verè in his locum habet illud Leonis Ser. 9. De Nativitate Domini : Nemo ad cognitionem veritatis magis propinquat, quam qui intelligit in rebus divinis, etiam si multum proficiat, semper sibi superesse quod quærat. Nam qui se ad id, in quod tendit, pervenisse præsumit; non quæsita reperit, sed in inquisitione deficit.
units.tr: Son of Abraham. Which is also called the Ancient. Matthew began the line of the Lord, both of stock and of family, from him, from whom faith itself took its origin and beginning: from Abraham, the father not only of many but also of the greatest, and of the greatest men. For, as Ambrose elegantly says, the holy ones are greater in faith than in generation. We shall above all take care not to examine anxiously the genealogy, as others among the Ancients also did, who suffered shipwreck here more than once, why Luke differs so much from Matthew in the order and in the names inserted in the genealogy; let us be content with that saying of Ambrose: The end of my faith is Christ, the end of my faith is the Son of God. I am not allowed to know the sequence of the generation, yet I am not allowed not to know the faith of the generation. Nevertheless we wholeheartedly favour the diligence of those who have laboured on this question both in our own time and formerly, for the same was attempted also by the Ancients, among whom Augustine, book 2 of the Questions on the Gospels, chapter 5: Either, he says, one Evangelist named the father of Joseph, from whom he was born, and the other either set down the maternal grandfather or some one of the more distant kinsmen; or one was the natural father of Joseph and the other had adopted him; or, according to the custom of the Jews, when one had died without sons, a kinsman took his wife, and the son whom he begot was reckoned to the deceased kinsman. St Thomas (3 p. q. 31 a. 3 ad 2) thinks this last cause the truer, as it is handed down in Eusebius from Julius Africanus, who is said to have removed the discrepancy which some wish to be described in the genealogy of our Saviour by Matthew and Luke. But as far as I understand, as far as I grasp, the saying of Leo in Sermon 9, On the Nativity of the Lord, applies truly here: No one draws nearer to the knowledge of the truth than he who understands that in divine things, however much he advances, something always remains for him to seek. For he who presumes that he has arrived at that to which he strives has not found what he sought, but has failed in the search.

units.la: 3. Aram. Hic vocatur. 1. Paralip. 2. v. 9. & 10. Ram, Sic etiam vocatur in textu Hebraeo Ruth. 4. v. 19. more Hebraeis familiari, quo abjiciunt passim in suis dictionibus Aleph in earum principio, vel medio occurrens.
units.tr: 3. Aram. He is called here, 1 Chron. 2. v. 9 and 10, Ram. He is so called also in the Hebrew text, Ruth 4. v. 19, in the manner familiar to the Hebrews, by which they often drop the Aleph [א] occurring at the beginning or in the middle of their words.

units.la: De Thamar. Illas tantum feminas intexuit Matthæus Christi genealogiæ, de quibus, vel de quarum cum viris conjunctione peculiare aliquid sacra Scriptura prodidit.
units.tr: Of Tamar. Matthew wove into Christ's genealogy only those women about whom, or about whose union with their husbands, Holy Scripture has related something particular.

units.la: 5. David Regem. Emphaticè bis consequenter dicitur David Rex, cui ut dicitur Ecclesiastici 47. v. 13. Dedit Deus Testamentum regni & sedem gloriæ in Israel; ipsi enim dixit Nathan jussus à Deo : Regnum tuum usque in æternum ante faciem tuam & thronus tuus erit firmus jugiter.
units.tr: 5. David the King. David is called King emphatically, twice in succession, to whom, as it is said in Ecclesiasticus 47. v. 13: God gave the covenant of the kingdom and the throne of glory in Israel; for to him Nathan, commanded by God, said: Your kingdom shall be for ever before your face, and your throne shall be firm continually.

units.la: 6. Ex ea quæ fuit Uriæ. Scilicet uxor. Hoc ita exprimitur, ne Salomon ex adulterio natus crederetur, vel propter adulterium Davidis & homicidium suspicaretur quis rescissam fuisse promissionem ipsi Davidi Regi factam.
units.tr: 6. From her who had been the wife of Uriah. That is, his wife. This is so expressed lest Solomon be believed to have been born of adultery, or lest anyone suspect, on account of David's adultery and murder, that the promise made to King David himself had been annulled.

units.la: 8. Foram genuit Oziam. Exclusit Matthæus secundum sententiam B. Hil. Can. 1. à genealogia Domini tres Reges inter Joram & Oziam, qui & Azarias dicitur, intermedios, scilicet Ochoziam, Joam & Amasiam; quia Joram Rex generi se miscuerat impiissimæ Jesabelis, unde quanta benedictio facta est super Jehu, qui vindictam fecerat super domum mum Achab & Jefabel, tanta fuit maledictio super domum Joram propter filiam iniqui Achab & Jefabel, ut usque ad quartam generationem eradantur filij ejus e catalogo Regum antecessorum Christi, sicut scriptum est Exod. 20. Reddam peccata parentum in filios usque ad tertiam, & (i. e. vel) quartam generationem. Consimili de causa Apoc. 7. in Signatorum catalogo tribus Dan praetermittitur, quia a cultu Dei ad idola jam olim defecerat, & se cum gentibus permiscuerat. Judic. 18. Non autem evertitur sententia Hilarij, quòd Ochosias non constituatur nepos Achabi, sed vt Amri Regis Israel ex ejus filia Athalia 4. Reg. 8. v. 26. Nam Athalia neptis Amri vocatur ipsius filia Hebraismo Scripturae familiari, cùm revera fuerit filia Achabi, qui erat filius Amri, ut quater dicitur, 3. Reg. 16. v. 28. 29. & 30. Joram autem diserte dicitur 4. Reg. 8. v. 18. filiam Achabi habuisse pro conjuge, & v. 27. idem Joram filius Josaphat Rex Juda vocatur gener domus Achab.
units.tr: 8. Begot Uzziah. Matthew excluded from the genealogy of the Lord, according to the opinion of St Hilary (Can. 1), the three kings who came between Joram and Uzziah, who is also called Azariah, namely Ahaziah, Joash and Amaziah. For King Joram had mingled himself with the most impious family of Jezebel, whence, as great a blessing as came upon Jehu, who had executed vengeance on the house of Ahab and Jezebel, so great a curse fell upon the house of Joram on account of the daughter of the wicked Ahab and Jezebel, that his sons were blotted out of the catalogue of the kings who were Christ's ancestors, to the fourth generation, as it is written in Exod. 20: I will repay the sins of the fathers upon the children, to the third, or (that is, or) fourth generation. For a similar reason, in Apoc. 7, in the catalogue of the sealed, the tribe of Dan is passed over, because it had long before fallen from the worship of God to idols and had mixed itself with the nations, Judg. 18. But Hilary's opinion is not overturned by the fact that Ahaziah is not made a grandson of Ahab but of Omri king of Israel through his daughter Athaliah, 4 Kings 8. v. 26. For Athaliah is called the granddaughter of Omri, though she is his daughter, in the Hebraism familiar to Scripture, since she was really the daughter of Ahab, who was the son of Omri, as is said four times, 3 Kings 16. v. 28, 29 and 30. But Joram is expressly said, 4 Kings 8. v. 18, to have had Ahab's daughter as his wife, and v. 27 the same Joram, son of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, is called son-in-law of the house of Ahab.

units.la: II. Jechoniam. Alio nomine dictum Joakim, seu Joacim & Eliacim ut videre est 4. Reg. 23. &c.
units.tr: II. Jechonias. Called by another name Joakim, or Joacim and Eliacim, as may be seen in 4 Kings 23, etc.

units.la: Fratres ejus. Nempe Joachaz & Matthaniam, & Johanan.
units.tr: His brothers. Namely Joachaz, Matthaniah, and Johanan.

units.la: In transmigratione. Id est, lub, seu circa transmigrationem Babylonis; nam omnes filij Josiae nati sunt & adulti ante transmigrationes tres, quae indicantur 2. Paralip. 36. v. 6. 10. & 18.
units.tr: At the transmigration. That is, at or around the transmigration to Babylon. For all the sons of Josiah were born and grew up before the three transmigrations, which are indicated in 2 Chronicles 36 vv. 6, 10 and 18.

units.la: 12. Post transmigrationem Babylonis. Id est, postquam populus Israel transmigrasset in Babylonem, Jechonias qui & Joachin praedicti Jechoniae seu Joakimi filius anno decimo nono aetatis in Babylonem abductus, in ipsa Babylonica captivitate genuit Salathiel. Ne autem hic Jechonias confunderetur cum patre suo Jechonia, videtur dixisse Matthaeus Josias genuit Jechoniam & fratres ejus, scilicet Johanan, Matthaniam, qui & Sedecias vocatur, & Joachaz seu Sellum. Nam Joachin, qui vocatur Jechonias. 1. Paralip. 3. v. 16. Joakimi filius, Josiae nepos, non habuisse legitur nisi unum fratrem nomine Sedeciam loco citato Paralip. ubi & dicitur de eo, quod genuit Salathiel. De hoc Jechonia seu Joachin dicitur Jerem. 22. Scribe virum istum sterilem: nec enim erit de semine ejus vir, qui sedeat super solium David, & potestatem habeat ultra in Juda. Huic prophetiae Christi ex stirpe ejus generatio & sessio super solium David non est contraria; Christus enim erat Deus, ut ait B. Hieronymus ad locum citatum Jeremiae, neque ejus regnum erat de hoc mundo: Nec saeculari honore regnavit, ut loquitur Ambrosius. Praeterea, inbuit Hieronymus, in diebus Jechoniae non successit ei Rex filius, sicut sicut ipse successerat patri, sed multo post tempore de semine ipsius natus est Christus, cui dedit Dominus Deus sedem David patris sui & regnabit super domum Jacob in aeternum, & regni ejus non erit finis. Huic B. Hieronymi solutioni favet veritas Hebraica & textus Vulgatus apud Jeremiam.
units.tr: 12. After the transmigration to Babylon. That is, after the people of Israel had been carried off to Babylon. Jechonias, who is also called Joachin, son of the aforementioned Jechonias or Joakim, was led away to Babylon in the nineteenth year of his age, and in the Babylonian captivity itself he begot Salathiel. Lest this Jechonias be confused with his father Jechonias, Matthew seems to have written Josiah begot Jechonias and his brothers, namely Johanan and Matthaniah, who is also called Zedekiah, and Joachaz or Shallum. For Joachin, who is called Jechonias (1 Chronicles 3 v. 16), son of Joakim and grandson of Josiah, is read to have had only one brother, named Zedekiah, in the cited place of Chronicles, where it is also said of him that he begot Salathiel. Of this Jechonias or Joachin it is said in Jeremiah 22: Write this man down as childless, for no man of his seed shall prosper who sits upon the throne of David and has power any more in Judah. Christ's descent from his stock, and his sitting upon the throne of David, is not contrary to this prophecy. For Christ was God, as Saint Jerome says on the cited place of Jeremiah, and his kingdom was not of this world. Nor did he reign with secular honour, as Ambrose puts it. Moreover, Jerome taught, in the days of Jechonias no son of his succeeded him as king, as he himself had succeeded his father; but long afterwards Christ was born from his seed, to whom the Lord God gave the throne of David his father, and he shall reign over the house of Jacob for ever, and of his kingdom there shall be no end. The Hebrew truth and the Vulgate text in Jeremiah favour this solution of Saint Jerome.

units.la: Zorobabel. Hic etiam apud Esdram & Aggaeum dicitur Salathielis filius, & alius est a Zorobabele filio Phadaiae fratris Salathielis, cujus mentio fit 1. Paralip. c. 3. v. 19. Seriem autem generationum a Zorobabele ad Joseph virum Mariae Matthaeus non ex veteri Instrumento, sed aliunde collegit; semper enim Judaei erant genealogiae suae curiosissimi. Vide 1. Esd. 2.
units.tr: Zerubbabel. Here too, in Ezra and Haggai, he is called son of Salathiel. He is a different man from Zerubbabel son of Pedaiah, brother of Salathiel, who is mentioned in 1 Chronicles 3 v. 19. But Matthew gathered the succession of generations from Zerubbabel to Joseph, husband of Mary, not from the Old Testament but from elsewhere, for the Jews were always most careful about their genealogies. See 1 Esdras 2.

units.la: 16. Joseph virum Mariae. Supple, secundum Legem Mosis. Etsi enim non prolis spe, sed ut haberet cujus sub tutela delitesceret sexus injuriis obnoxia, nuptum iret Virgo Maria, cum consensus in copulam carnalem repugnet propositio perpetuae virginitatis, quod ipsi haud improbabiliter adscribunt plerique Veteres, exipsius verbis ad Gabrielem Luc. 1. v. 34. agnato tamen proximo nubere voluit sanctissima virgo, ne videretur propositi sui insciis ἁμαρτάνω prævaricata in legem filiabus heredibus praescriptam Num. 36. v. 7. secundum quam Tobiae 6. v. 11. & 12. Angelus Tobiam juniorem instruit ipsi deberi uxorem filiam unigenitam Raguelis patrui ipsius, et Raguel ipse Tobiae senioris frater: Credo, inquit Tob. 7. quoniam ideo fecit vos venire ad me Deus, ut ita conjungeretur cognationi suae secundum Legem Moysi. Haec cum ita sint, facile nobis ex genealogia Josephi innotescit quomodo Filius Dei factus sit misericorditer filius hominis ex semine David secundum carnem, cum ut diximus & aperte asserit Theophilus, Josephus jure propinquitatis fuerit maritus Virginis, adeoque cognatus ex eadem tribu atque familia David. Ut autem constaret Christum non solum Dei promissione aut donatione, sed jure successionis esse legitimum regni Davidici haeredem, Josephi potius quam Mariae genealogia textitur, cum foeminis nullum sit jus ad regnum, quamdiu proles masculae superstunt. Christus itaque vera proles Josephi, non quidem ex eo genita, vel sola vulgi opinione, sed ex propria uxore tanquam caro sua & proprio fundo Spiritus-Sancti virtute nata, jure gentium in paternam haereditatem & jura Josephi succedebat. Vide Augustinum libro quinto in Julianum c. 9.
units.tr: 16. Joseph the husband of Mary. Supply: according to the Law of Moses. For although the Virgin Mary married not in hope of offspring, but so that she might have someone under whose protection she would be hidden from the injuries to which her sex was exposed, and although the vow of perpetual virginity is at odds with consent to carnal union (which most of the Ancients quite plausibly attribute to her, from her own words to Gabriel in Luke 1 v. 34), nevertheless the most holy Virgin wished to marry a kinsman. She did not want it to seem that, without knowing it, she had sinned [ἁμαρτάνω] by transgressing the law prescribed for heiresses in Numbers 36 v. 7. Under that law, in Tobit 6 vv. 11 and 12, the Angel instructs the younger Tobias that the only daughter of Raguel, his uncle, is owed to him as his wife; Raguel himself was the brother of the elder Tobias. I believe, says Tobit 7, that God has therefore brought you to me, so that she might be joined in marriage to her kinsman according to the Law of Moses. Since this is so, we can easily see from Joseph's genealogy how the Son of God was mercifully made son of man, from the seed of David according to the flesh. For, as we have said, and as Theophilus openly asserts, Joseph by right of kinship was the husband of the Virgin, and so was a relative of her, from the same tribe and family as David. But so that it might be established that Christ was the lawful heir of David's kingdom not only by God's promise or gift but by right of succession, the genealogy is traced through Joseph rather than Mary, since women have no right to the kingdom while male offspring survive. Christ, therefore, was the true offspring of Joseph. He was not indeed begotten of him, or by the mere opinion of the crowd, but was born of his own wife, as his own flesh, by the power of the Holy Spirit, in his own field. By the law of nations he succeeded to the paternal inheritance and the rights of Joseph. See Augustine, book 5 against Julian, c. 9.

units.la: 17. Omnes itaque generationes. Id est, omnes personae generantes & genitae ab Abraham usque ad David inclusive quatuordecim, a David exclusive usque ad Jechoniam seu Joakim inclusive, qui natus est circa tempus transmigrationis Israelitarum in Babyloniam, personae quatuordecim.
units.tr: 17. So all the generations. That is, all the persons who begot and were begotten from Abraham to David inclusive: fourteen. From David exclusive to Jechonias or Joakim inclusive, who was born about the time of the transmigration of the Israelites to Babylon: fourteen persons.

units.la: A translmigratione Babylonis. Id est, à Jechonia, seu Joachin patre Salathielis usque ad Christum inclusive generationes, seu personæ quatuordecim. In textu Hebræo, quem in Italia natus est Joannes Tilius Episcopus Briocensis superiori seculo, personæ sunt quindecim, quia ubi nos legimus: Abiud autem genuit Eliacim, ibi habetur: Abiud genuit Abner, Abner genuit Eliacim.
units.tr: From the transmigration to Babylon. That is, from Jechonias, or Joachin, the father of Salathiel, to Christ inclusive, the generations or persons are fourteen. In the Hebrew text which Johannes Tilius, bishop of Brieuc, of Italian birth, had in the last century, there are fifteen persons, because where we read Abiud however begot Eliakim, there it reads Abiud begot Abner, and Abner begot Eliakim.

units.la: 18. Christi autem generatio, sic erat. Hæc verba sunt præfatio sequentium, quibus narratur quà ratione Filius Dei factus sit filius hominis ex femine David secundum carnem provectione carnis, non defectione Deitatis; quæ sic potentiam suam bonitatémque moderata est, ut & nostra suscipiendo proveheret, & sua communicando non perderet.
units.tr: 18. Now the generation of Christ was as follows. These words are the preface to what follows, in which it is told by what means the Son of God was made son of man from the seed of David according to the flesh: by an advance of the flesh, not by any loss of his Godhead. He so tempered his power and goodness that by taking up ours he might advance them, and by communicating his own he would not lose them.

units.la: Cùm esset desponsata. Græcè μνηστευθεῖσης, id est, cùm esset promissa, seu cùm sponsalia contraxisset. Nam ante celebrationem solemnem nuptiarum fiebat desponsatio, quâ facta, nondum erat sponsa sub custodia viri, sed patris sui, ut habetur Deuteron. 20. v. 7. & 22. v. 25. Sic vox desponsata accipitur à B. Hilario, B. Basil. Hom. De humana Chr. generatione. B. Epiph. Hær. 78, Orig. Hom. 1. in diver. Evang. &c.
units.tr: When she was betrothed. In Greek μνηστευθεῖσης [mnēsteutheisēs], that is, when she was promised, or when she had entered into betrothal. For before the solemn celebration of the wedding came the betrothal, and once it was made the bride was not yet under the custody of her husband but of her father, as in Deuteronomy 20 v. 7 and 22 v. 25. In this sense the word betrothed is used by Saint Hilary, by Saint Basil in the homily On the Human Generation of Christ, by Saint Epiphanius (Heresy 78), by Origen (Homily 1 on various Gospels), and others.

units.la: Antequam convenirent. Scilicet, in eandem domum; nam in solemni nuptiarum celebratione sponsa & sponsus in unam domum conveniebant; traducebatur quippe sponsa è domo patris sui in domum viri, ut non modo ex Deuteron. 22. sed etiam ex Hebræorum hodiernis & antiquis ritibus certum est. Ita etiam exponunt hæc verba mox citati Autores.
units.tr: Before they came together. That is, into the same house. For at the solemn celebration of the wedding the bride and groom came together into one house; the bride was led from her father's house into her husband's. This is certain not only from Deuteronomy 22 but also from the present and ancient rites of the Hebrews. The authors just cited also explain these words in this way.

units.la: Inventa est in utero habens de Spiritu-sancto. Id est, deprehensa est gravida sine ullius concubitu, sed opera Spiritussancti. Notat itaque Evangelista causam efficientem gravitatis, quam Joseph deprehendit in beata Virgine, ignorans unde esset illa graviditas, ut satis constat ex serie sequentium. Vir ejus. Vir Mariæ virginis dicitur Joseph, licèt nondum nuptiæ essent celebratæ. Sic Deut. 22. v. 23. dicitur : Si puellam virginem desponderit vir. Vide ibidem textum LXX.
units.tr: She was found to be with child of the Holy Spirit. That is, she was discovered to be pregnant without anyone's intercourse, but by the work of the Holy Spirit. The Evangelist therefore names the efficient cause of the pregnancy, which Joseph found in the blessed Virgin, not knowing where that pregnancy came from; this is sufficiently clear from the sequence of what follows. Her husband. Joseph is called the husband of the Virgin Mary, although the wedding had not yet been celebrated. So Deuteronomy 22 v. 23 says: If a man should betroth a virgin. See the Septuagint text there.

units.la: Justus. Id est, moderatus seu benignus et beneficus. Donatus ad illud Terentii in Andria, Justa fuerit servitus, Justa, inquit, moderata. Certè justitia sumitur pro beneficentia, Ps. III. v. 9. Dispersit, dedit pauperibus, justitia ejus manet in seculum seculi, quem locum laudat Apostolus. 2. Cor, 9. v. 9. Vide infrà, Cap.6.v.1.quæ observamus in hanc vocem, justitiam.
units.tr: Just. That is, moderate, or kind and beneficent. Donatus, on the line of Terence in the Andria, Justa fuerit servitus, says: "Just means moderate." Certainly justice is taken to mean beneficence, as in Ps. 111 v. 9: He has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor; his justice endures for ever and ever, a passage which the Apostle cites in 2 Cor. 9 v. 9. See below, chapter 6 v. 1, where we note what concerns this word, justice.

units.la: Traducere. Græcè παραδιδόμενα, id est, exemplare, ut vertit. ertit beatus Augustinus Q. 7. seu, in exemplum statuere; ho sensu hæc vox Græca passim usurpatur in versione veteris Instrumenti, ut videre est Nahum 3. v. 6. Ezechiel 28. 17. &c. Extat autem lex Deut. 22. v, 23. de lapidanda virgine desponsata, quæ concubuerit cum aliquo in civitate, cui legi beata Virgo fuisset subjecta, si a Josepho prodita esset Judicibus, cum ipsa maneret in civitate Nazareth; eam autem Joseph misericordia commotus noluit prodere, sed occulte voluit sponsalia dirimere sine judicio publico, et non dicta causa; Unde Aug. Ep. 14. ad Macedonium, Joseph, cui mater Domini fuerat desponsata, cum eam comperisset esse prægnantem, qui se noverat non esse commixtum, et ob hoc nihil aliud quam adulteram credidisset, puniri tamen eam noluit, nec approbator flagitii fuit.
units.tr: To expose her. In Greek παραδιδόμενα [paradidomena], that is, to make an example of her, as Saint Augustine translates it (Q. 7), or to set her up as an example. In this sense the Greek word is used throughout the version of the Old Testament, as may be seen in Nahum 3 v. 6, Ezekiel 28 v. 17, etc. There is indeed the law of Deuteronomy 22 v. 23 on stoning a betrothed virgin who has lain with someone in the city, and the blessed Virgin would have been subject to that law if Joseph had betrayed her to the judges, since she remained in the city of Nazareth. But Joseph, moved by mercy, was unwilling to betray her, and wished to dissolve the betrothal secretly, without public judgement and without the case being heard. Whence Augustine, Letter 14 to Macedonius: Joseph, to whom the mother of the Lord had been betrothed, when he had found her to be pregnant, knowing that he had not lain with her, and therefore believing her to be nothing but an adulteress, was yet unwilling to have her punished, nor did he approve of the crime.

units.la: 20. Joseph fili David. Joseph suspicione tentatus mox ab Angelo sanatus est, quia in eo non erat malevola suspicio, quales Apostolus dicit malevolas suspiciones nasci inter fratres. 1. Tim. 6. Malevolæ suspiciones sunt calumniantium, benevolæ suspiciones sunt gubernantium; licet de filio male suspicari, sed de filio non licet calumniari: suspicaris malum, sed optas invenire bonum. Qui malevole non suspicatur, vinci cupit. Tunc enim bene lætatur, quando falsum inventum fuerit, quod male suspicabatur; sic erat Joseph circa conjugem suam, cui jam fide fuerat copulatus. B. Augustus, Serm. 2. inter undecim in Cartusia majori repertos.
units.tr: 20. Joseph, son of David. Joseph, troubled by suspicion, was soon set right by the angel, because in him there was no malicious suspicion of the kind the Apostle says arise among brothers. 1 Tim. 6. Malicious suspicions belong to slanderers; benevolent suspicions belong to those who govern. It is permitted to suspect wrong of a son, but it is not permitted to slander a son. You suspect evil, but you wish to find good. He who does not suspect maliciously desires to be overcome. For he rejoices all the more when what he suspected of wrong is found to be false. So was Joseph toward his wife, to whom he was already joined in faith. B. Augustine, Sermon 2, among the eleven found in the Charterhouse of Major.

units.la: Noli timere] accipere Mariam conjugem tuam. q. d. Non est quod timeas solemniter celebrare nuptias cum Maria jam tibi desponsata. Scias, inquit Balsamon ad Canonem 99. Synodi 6. in Trullo, quòd a Lege Mosaica sponsalia pro nuptijs reputabantur et sponsa uxor nominabatur ... Et vir qui eam ducebat, ut adulter puniebatur. Dicit enim lex antiqua: Et humiliavit uxorem proximi: ejus scilicet sponsam devirginavit. Porro sancta quoque Virgo et Dei Mater, itidem Joseph uxor appellata est; dicit enim sacrum Dei Evangelium: Ne timeas accipere Mariam uxorem tuam. Idem videre est apud B. Cyrillum Jerosolymitanum Catech. 12.
units.tr: Do not fear] to take Mary your wife. That is, there is no reason to fear solemnly celebrating the wedding with Mary, who is already betrothed to you. Know, says Balsamon on Canon 99 of the Sixth Synod in Trullo, that under the Mosaic Law betrothal was reckoned as marriage, and the betrothed woman was called a wife ... And the man who would take her was punished as an adulterer. For the ancient law says: "And he has humbled his neighbour's wife," that is, he has deflowered her betrothed. Moreover, the holy Virgin, the Mother of God, was likewise called the wife of Joseph; for the holy Gospel of God says: "Do not fear to take Mary your wife." The same may be seen in St. Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechesis 12.

units.la: Quod enim in ea natum est. id est, quod non secundum communem modum carnis per intervalla paulatim formatum, sed illico perfectum est, inquit Basilius.
units.tr: For what is conceived in her, that is, not formed gradually by stages in the common manner of flesh, but made perfect at once, says Basil.

units.la: De Spiritu-sancto est. Q. d. Non ex humano lapsu, sed divino, illapsu, non virili, quod non cognovit, femine, sed Spiritus-sancti, quo impletur, opere concepit.
units.tr: is of the Holy Spirit. That is: conceived not by human descent but by divine descent, not by a man, since she had not known one, but by the work of the Holy Spirit, by whom she was filled.

units.la: Vocabis nomen ejus Jesum. Ablata est suspicio, quia inventa est redemtio, inquit Augustinus, loco mox citato; Jesus enim Græcis est Σωτήρ quæ vox Latine reddi non potest, ut ait Cicero Act. 4. in Verrem. Christiani Salvatorem reddunt, quo vocabulo usi sunt Lactantius, Ausonius, aliíque sacri Scriptores.
units.tr: You shall call his name Jesus. "The suspicion is removed, because redemption is found," says Augustine, in the passage cited just above. For Jesus in Greek is Σωτήρ, a word that cannot be rendered into Latin, as Cicero says in the fourth speech against Verres. Christians render it Saviour, a word used by Lactantius, Ausonius and other holy writers.

units.la: 22. Vt adimpleretur. Vox ut, non sumitur causaliter, sed consecutive; incarnatio enim Verbi consecuta est ejusdem incarnationis prophetiam. Nihil autem refert utrum Evangelista dictum Propheticum historice an typice & allegorice laudet, cum & typis sacris sua constet veritas, et certum sit mentes Prophetarum fuisse divinitus motas, ut eorum dicta sic saepenumero aliis eventibus responderent, ut tamen per Christum longe insigniùs praestarentur. Scimus ut vocibus, ita et rebus prophetatum. Tertul.
units.tr: 22. That it might be fulfilled. The word that is not used causally but consecutively; for the incarnation of the Word followed upon the prophecy of that same incarnation. Nor does it matter whether the Evangelist praises the prophetic saying historically or typically and allegorically, since the truth stands both in sacred types and in the certainty that the minds of the prophets were moved by God, so that their words were often fulfilled in other events, yet were fulfilled far more remarkably through Christ. We know that things were prophesied as well as words. Tertullian.

units.la: 23. Ecce Virgo. Hic locus paulò aliter habetur apud Esaiam; unde observari potest, quòd Evangelistae non verba, sed sensum prophetiarum citare soleant, ut etiam aliàs observabimus; quamvis multi existiment salsissima perfuasione Apostolos in suis citationibus semper ad verbum usurpasse versionem Graecam Septuaginta interpretum, uti vocant, cùm manifesto constet id rarissimè à Matthaeo & Joanne praestitum fuisse.
units.tr: 23. Behold, a virgin. This passage is found somewhat differently in Isaiah. From this it may be observed that the Evangelists are accustomed to cite not the words but the sense of the prophecies, as we shall note elsewhere as well. Although many think, with a very mistaken persuasion, that the Apostles always used the Greek version of the Seventy Interpreters, as it is called in their citations, it is clear that this was very rarely done by Matthew and John.

units.la: Vocabunt nomen ejus Emmanuel. Hebraismus; sensus enim est, vocare poterunt nomen ejus Emmanuel. Cùm enim Hebraei rebus ex suis proprietatibus vel adjunctis significantia nomina semper indere soleant, & hoc nomen Emmanuel duplicem, quà Christus constat, naturam simul quàm aptissimè insinuet, Christus certè vocari potest Emmanuel; id est, Nobiscum-Deus. Sic Esaiae 62. de Ecclesia dicitur: Vocaberis voluntas mea in ea & terra tua inhabitata; sensus est, eris mihi gratissima, & numero fidelium frequentissima, ut merito appellari possis, Voluntas mea in ea; quaesita civitas & non derelicta. Eodem Hebraismo dicitur Esaiae 9. Vocabitur nomen ejus Admirabilis, &c. Id est, vocari poterit.
units.tr: They shall call his name Emmanuel. This is a Hebraism; the sense is, they may call his name Emmanuel. For since the Hebrews are accustomed always to give names signifying things from their properties or attendant circumstances, and this name Emmanuel most aptly indicates the two natures of which Christ consists at once, Christ can certainly be called Emmanuel, that is, God with us. So in Isaiah 62 it is said of the Church: You shall be called My delight in her, and your land shall be inhabited; the sense is, you will be most pleasing to me and most numerous in faithful people, so that you may rightly be called My delight in her, a city sought out and not forsaken. By the same Hebraism it is said in Isaiah 9: His name shall be called Wonderful, etc., that is, he may be called.

units.la: 24. Accepit Conjugem suam. Id est, nuptias solemniter celebravit & Mariam e domo patris in suam traduxit; hinc Vulgatus interpres quod hîc dicitur Graece παρέλαβε τὴν γυναῖκα Deuter. 22. v. 13. vertit, duxit uxorem. Nec valet contra hanc noltram explicationem objectio Maldonati, quà dicit, si sensus nosser germanus esset, Evangelistae fuisse dicendum, Accepit eam in Conjugem suam, ut Hebraismo responderet expressio; nam loco citato Deuteronomij habetur in textu Hebraeo acceperis uxorem, non in uxorem; & si hic locus non urgeat, quia in eo non fit mentio alicujus determinatae personae, quae in Conjugem accipiatur, urget tamen locus Deuter. 24. v. 11. ubi habetur in textu Hebraeo, Et acceperis eam tibi in uxorem. LXX. vertunt, Et acceperis eam tibi uxorem. Vulgat: Voluerisque habere uxorem. V. 13. Hebraice, Ipsa erit tibi tibi in uxorem. LXX. et Vulg. Erit uxor tua. Deuter. 20. v. 7. in Hebraeo, LXX. et Vulg. habent, Quis est homo qui despondit uxorem, & non accepit eam, vadat, &c. Nemo autem miretur Evangelistam dicere de Iosepho solemniter nuptias celebrante & beatam Virginem à domo patris in suam traducente, quam sibi jam pridem sponsaverat, Accepit conjugem suam, cum Iacob postulans ut sibi in conjugem traderetur, quam sibi septennij servitute desponsaverat, his socerum affetur verbis: Da mihi uxorem meam. Illud itaque ex Scripturis colligere possumus quod ab antiquo inter Hebraeos moris fuerit, primo sponsalia contrahere cum ea, quam conjugem ducere cupiebant; & hanc actionem significare solent per verbum שָׁמַר, desponsavit; deinde interposito aliquo temporis spatio nuptias, quas per sponsalia futuras pollicebantur, solemniter celebrare, quam actionem denotat verbum לָקַח, accepit. Post nuptiarum celebrationem propriissime uxor dicebatur sponsa, quae post contracta sponsalia ratione futuri conjugij minus proprie uxor saepe & conjux appellari coeperat; sicut & sponsus vir dicebatur proprie nuptijs celebratis, qui tamen post sponsalia ratione earundem nuptiarum futurarum, vir, maritus, & conjux minus proprie quandoque dicebatur. Tertia denique est actio, cujus passim meminit Scriptura tanquam immediate sequentis acceptionem conjugis, seu celebrationem nuptiarum, quam exprimere solet hujusmodi circumlocutionibus: Et ingressus est ad eam; Et cognovit eam. Hanc tertiam actionem excludit Evangelista a conjugio Iosephi, dum dicit: Et non cognoscebat eam, licet in eodem conjugio duae priores actiones, nempe desponsatio & nuptiarum celebratio pro more intervenissent.
units.tr: 24. He took his wife. That is, he solemnly celebrated the wedding and led Mary from her father's house into his own. Hence the Vulgate translator renders the Greek παρέλαβε τὴν γυναῖκα [took the wife] in Deuteronomy 22:13 as duxit uxorem [led home a wife]. Nor does Maldonatus's objection tell against our explanation, where he says that if our sense were the true one, the Evangelist ought to have written He took her into his wife, so that the expression would match the Hebrew idiom. For in the cited passage of Deuteronomy the Hebrew text has if you take a wife, not take her into a wife; and even if that place does not press, since no particular person is mentioned there whom one takes as wife, Deuteronomy 24:11 presses, where the Hebrew text has and you shall take her to yourself as a wife. The Septuagint renders it and you shall take her to yourself as wife; the Vulgate, and you shall wish to have her as wife. Verse 13 in Hebrew: She shall be to you for a wife; the Septuagint and Vulgate have she shall be your wife. Deuteronomy 20:7 in Hebrew, the Septuagint and Vulgate have: Who is the man who has betrothed a wife and has not taken her? Let him go, etc. No one should wonder that the Evangelist says of Joseph, who solemnly celebrated the wedding and led the blessed Virgin from her father's house into his own, whom he had long since betrothed, He took his wife; just as Jacob, asking that she be given to him as wife, whom he had betrothed by seven years of service, is addressed by his father-in-law with these words: Give me my wife. From the Scriptures we may therefore gather that it was long the custom among the Hebrews first to contract betrothal with the woman whom they wished to take as wife, and this action they usually signify by the verb שָׁמַר [shamar], betrothed; then, after some interval of time, to celebrate solemnly the wedding which had been promised by the betrothal, an action denoted by the verb לָקַח [laqach], took. After the wedding had been celebrated, the betrothed woman was most properly called a wife; but after the betrothal, with respect to the future marriage, she was often called wife and spouse in a less proper sense, just as the bridegroom was properly called a husband once the wedding was celebrated, yet after the betrothal, with respect to the future wedding, was sometimes called husband, man and spouse in a less proper sense. Finally, there is a third action, which Scripture mentions in many places as immediately following the taking of a wife, or the celebration of the wedding, and which it usually expresses by such circumlocutions as: And he went in to her; and he knew her. This third action the Evangelist excludes from Joseph's marriage when he says: And he did not know her, although in that same marriage the two earlier actions, namely the betrothal and the celebration of the wedding, had taken place in the customary way.

units.la: 25. Et non cognoscebat eam. Nempe, quia ut ait B. Fulgent. Lib. de Incarnat. & Grat. Domini, Iosephum virum non ad concubitum, corruptelamque carnis, sed ad testimonium, custodiamque sacrae virginitatis, & castissimae fecunditatis Mariae habuit. Hinc eleganter B. Epiph. Iosephum vocat αἰδοῖα ἀνάνδρου, vir enim erat Mariae, cum interceßissent inter eos verae nuptiae; sed non erat vir Mariae, in quantum nunquam ipsam cognovit.
units.tr: 25. And he did not know her. Namely because, as the blessed Fulgentius says in his book on the Incarnation and Grace of the Lord, He had Joseph as husband not for the sake of intercourse and corruption of the flesh, but as witness and guardian of the holy virginity and most chaste fruitfulness of Mary. Hence Epiphanius elegantly calls Joseph a venerable man without husbandly relations [αἰδοῖα ἀνάνδρου]: for he was Mary's husband, since true nuptials had taken place between them; but he was not her husband in so far as he never knew her.

units.la: Donec peperit. Licet vox donec temporis alicujus terminum circumscribere videatur, vere tamen infinitum prae se fert. Sic & a Domino verbum hoc memoratur: Ecce, inquit, vobiscum sum omnibus diebus usque ad consummationem seculi. Post hoc seculum dicere, non erat necesse, non enim cum sanctis unquam Dominus esse desinet, sed promissio perpetuitatem indicat praesentium, neque aufert spem futurorum; sic & nunc illud donec accipitur. Quod vero dictum est, primogenitum non omnino ad succedentem prolem relationem habet. Omne adaperiens primùm vulvam, in Lege primogenitum vocatur. Ita B. Basil. Hom. De humana Christi generatione.
units.tr: Until she bore. Although the word until seems to mark the limit of some period of time, it truly carries an unlimited sense. So also the Lord is recorded as saying: Behold, I am with you all days, even to the end of the age. It was not necessary to add anything about after this age, for the Lord will never cease to be with the saints; the promise indicates the permanence of the present, and does not take away the hope of the future. So also here until is to be understood. What is said, that firstborn does not wholly refer to the offspring that follows. Every male that opens the womb first is called firstborn in the Law. So Basil in his homily On the Human Generation of Christ.

units.la: CAPUT. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: I. CUM ergo natus esset Jesus. Graecè Ϙ ℕ Ιησοῦ γεννηθέντος. Illud primò observandum est usurpasse Evangelistam participium aoristum, non praeteritum, quia participii aoristi ea vis est, ut denotet actionem paulò ante perfectam, adhuc quasi pendentem; cùm praeteritum de perfecta multò etiam ante actione rectè usurpaveris. Hujus observationis vim auget particula mox sequens, Ecce. Caeterum Magos adorasse Christum ante diem Purificationis Augustinus tenet, & ab Ecclesia est receptum, quae hujus rei memoriam tertio-decimo die à Christi nativitate celebrat. De die Natali Christi parum inter se consentiunt qui rationem temporum investigatam ediderunt. Quod cùm vel Dei nutu vel vitio vetustatis evenial calumniâ carere debebit, inquit Sulpitius Severus. Christum itaque nobis in tempore natum Salvatorem adoremus, etsi in quo temporis puncto natus sit, ignoremus.
units.tr: I. "When therefore Jesus was born" [τοῦ Ἰησοῦ γεννηθέντος]. Here we must first observe that the Evangelist used the aorist participle, not the past tense, because the aorist participle has the force of denoting an action just completed and still, as it were, hanging in the air, whereas one may rightly use the past tense of an action completed long before. The following particle, Ecce, strengthens this observation. Augustine holds that the Magi worshipped Christ before the day of the Purification, and the Church has received this, celebrating the memory of the event on the thirteenth day after Christ's birth. Scholars who have investigated the chronology do not agree among themselves about the day of Christ's birth. Since this has come about either by the will of God or through the corruption of antiquity, it ought to be free from calumny, says Sulpicius Severus. Let us therefore worship Christ, born for us in time as Saviour, even though we do not know at what moment of time he was born.

units.la: Jesus. Tres hoc nomine veniunt in Novo Testamento; scilicet Salvator nostrer Jesus Christus passim, Jesus filius Nun, seu Jesus Nave, Act. 7. v. 45. Heb. 4. v. 8. & Jesus cognomine Justus, Col. 4. v. 11.
units.tr: Jesus. This name occurs three times in the New Testament: namely, our Saviour Jesus Christ, who appears everywhere; Jesus the son of Nun, or Joshua, Acts 7:45, Heb. 4:8; and Jesus surnamed Justus, Col. 4:11.

units.la: Magi. Benè monet Chrysostomus multis vigiliis ac precibus opus esse, ut qui fuerint ac unde & quomodo & cujus jussu venerint rectè intelligatur; nam quod plerique & quidem doctissimi credunt eos fuisse Persas, rationibus nihil minùs nititur quàm certis. Efficacissima enim, ut ipsis videtur ratio est, ipsa vox Magi. Sed hanc rationem nullius momenti esse inde constat, quòd negare nemo possit Graecos sacrae Scripturae interpretes & Evangelistas peregrinas passim ex Oriente voces eâ significatione adhibuisse, quâ in usu tùm erant. Extat autem apud Graecos interpretes Danielis hanc vocem & respondet dictioni Chaldaeae יַדְעִין; quam vocem non accipi in malam partem, vel hinc patet, quòd Cap. 2. v. 27. eos Daniel appellat sapientes, quos hac voce significat. Rectè igitur Hieronymus ad Daniel-em nielem: Magi dicuntur qui de signis philosophantur, consuetudo autem & sermo communis Magos pro maleficis accipit, qui aliter habentur apud gentem suam, quòd sint Philosophi Chaldæorum, &c. Patet igitur quód tempore Matthæi Magus non tantum dicebatur Persa de signis philosophans, sed & Chaldæus. Secunda ratio eorum est, quòd Magi dicuntur advenisse ab Oriente. Sed hæc ratio nihil evincit. Oriens enim dicitur primò respectu Solis, seu Oriens simpliciter, quem ut significarent LXX. Deuter. 4. v. 41. Hebraeorum instar appellarunt Orientem Solis; secundo dicitur Oriens secundum quid passim in Scripturis regio, quæ est in Oriente respectu totius Judææ. Tertiò dicitur Oriens respectu Jerosolymæ, ut Zachar. 14. v. 4. Mons olivarum dicitur è regione Jerosolymæ ad Orientem. Et in eodem versu, idem Vates semel usurpat Orientem pro Oriente simpliciter, & semel pro Oriente Urbis, & utrobique Orientem legas absolutè sine addito. Dubium igitur esse potest, an Magi venerint ab Oriente Solis, scilicet à Persia, an verò ab Oriente urbis Jerosolymitanæ, scilicet à Chaldæa, ab Aram, unde vocatus olim Balaam dicit se de montibus Orientis vocatum? Huic autem secundæ parti dubitationis favent multi Veterum, qui asseruerunt hos Magos prophetiâ Balaami motos fuisse, ut ductum stellæ sequerentur. Forte etiam neutrum intendit Matthæus, & ab Oriente non significat terminum à quo profectionis Magorum, sed locum ipsorum natalem, quasi diceretur, Magi Orientales; sic dicitur alibi in Evangelio, Venit Joseph ab Arimathæa, id est, Joseph Arimathæus. Sic & Joseph Historicus vocat Balaamum ab Euphrate, & Latinis dicitur, Pastor ab Amphryso, &c. Conjecturis itaque supersedeamus, & reponamus has quæstiones inter eas, quas Hebræi non nisi in adventu Eliæ, hoc est, sub finem mundi revelandas judicant. Tres autem numero fuisse hos, qui Christum invisère, Magos B. Maximo Taurinensi Hom. 3. in festo Epiphaniæ allipulante, recepta opinio habet, quam passim sequitur B. Leo magnus in Sermonibus De Epiphania.
units.tr: Magi. Chrysostom rightly observes that much watching and prayer is needed to understand rightly who they were, whence and how they came, and at whose command. For the view held by many, and indeed by the most learned, that they were Persians rests on reasons that are anything but certain. The most effective reason, as it seems to them, is the word Magi itself. But that this reason carries no weight is clear from the fact that no one can deny that the Greek interpreters of Holy Scripture and the Evangelists everywhere used foreign words from the East in the sense in which they were then current. Now the Greek interpreters of Daniel have this word, and it corresponds to the Chaldee word יַדְעִין; and that this word is not taken in a bad sense is clear from this, that in chapter 2, verse 27, Daniel calls those whom he designates by this word wise men. Jerome therefore rightly says in his commentary on Daniel: The Magi are said to be those who philosophize about signs; but common usage and speech take Magi to mean sorcerers, who are regarded otherwise among their own people, since they are philosophers of the Chaldeans, etc. It is evident, therefore, that in Matthew's time a Magus was called not only a Persian who philosophized about signs, but also a Chaldean. The second reason for their identity is that the Magi are said to have come from the East. But this reason proves nothing. For "East" is used first with respect to the sun, or the East absolutely; and to express this the Seventy, in Deut. 4:41, following the Hebrew manner, called the rising of the sun the East. Secondly, "East" in a qualified sense is used throughout Scripture of a region lying to the east of the whole of Judea. Thirdly, "East" is used with respect to Jerusalem, as in Zech. 14:4: "The Mount of Olives is said to lie opposite Jerusalem to the East." And in the same verse the same prophet uses East once for East absolutely and once for the East of the city, and in both places you will read East absolutely, without any addition. It may therefore be doubtful whether the Magi came from the East of the sun, namely from Persia, or from the East of the city of Jerusalem, namely from Chaldea, from Aram, whence Balaam, once called, says that he was summoned from the mountains of the East. Many of the Ancients favour this second part of the doubt, who maintained that these Magi were moved by the prophecy of Balaam to follow the leading of the star. Perhaps Matthew intended neither, and from the East does not signify the point from which the Magi set out, but their native place, as if it were said the Eastern Magi. So elsewhere in the Gospel it is said, Joseph came from Arimathea, that is, Joseph of Arimathea. So also the historian Josephus calls Balaam from the Euphrates, and in Latin one reads a shepherd from Amphrysus, etc. Let us therefore refrain from conjecture, and leave these questions among those which the Hebrews judge can only be revealed at the coming of Elijah, that is, at the end of the world. That there were three of these Magi who visited Christ is the accepted opinion, as St. Maximus of Turin, in his third homily on the feast of the Epiphany, suggests, and which St. Leo the Great follows throughout his sermons on the Epiphany.

units.la: 3. Omnis Jerosolyma. Id est, Jerosolymitæ Universi, ut loquitur Marcus capite primo, versu quinto. Fuit autem Jerusalem totius Judææ Metropolis, eúque munitissima Straboni, & omnium, teste Plinio, urbium Orientis clarissima. Dicitur verò Jerusalem secundum Eusebium quasi ἱερὸν σωτῆρ, secundum Hegesippum quasi ἱερὸν σηλύμων, secundum Augustinum Steuchum Eugubinum, quasi Jebus Salem; idem sentire videtur B. Hieron. De locis Hebraicis; secundum Aben-Esram Efram quasi יראו־שלם timete Salem. In Berefith Rabba traditur Jerusalem dici ab יראה videbit, quod est nomen illi loco impositum ab Abrahamo, & Salem, quod nomen eidem loco inditum erat à Melchisedech. Deinde abjecta Littera He & conversa Littera Aleph in Vav, coalescere coepit ורו pro יראה cum dictione Salem tum primùm, ut existimat Drufius Linguarum peritissimus, cùm locus à Melchisedecho dictus Salem, & locus ab Abrahamo dictus Dominus videbit seu יראה coalescere inciperent, sive cùm Mons Moria qui proprie appellatur יראה, urbi Salem includeretur. Unde duæ partes seu portiones ejusdem urbis forma nominis duali Ferufalaim coeperunt appellari, pro quo Chaldæi Ferufalem dixere, sicut pro Ephraim Ephrem.
units.tr: 3. All Jerusalem. That is, all the people of Jerusalem, as Mark says in chapter 1, verse 5. Jerusalem was the metropolis of all Judea, and by Strabo's account it was very strongly fortified, and, as Pliny testifies, the most famous of all the cities of the East. Jerusalem is said, according to Eusebius, to mean as it were "holy saviour" [ἱερὸν σωτῆρ]; according to Hegesippus, "holy of strangers" [ἱερὸν σηλύμων]; according to Augustine, Steuchus of Gubbio, "Jebus Salem"; and Jerome also seems to hold the same view in his book on Hebrew place names. According to Abraham ibn Ezra, Efram, it means "fear Salem" [יראו־שלם]. In the Bereshith Rabba it is handed down that Jerusalem is named from יראה, "he will see", which was the name given to that place by Abraham, and Salem, which was the name given to the same place by Melchizedek. Then, the letter He being dropped and the letter Aleph changed into Vav, the word ורו, in place of יראה, began to unite with the word Salem, as Drusius, most skilled in languages, supposes, when the place called Salem by Melchizedek and the place called "the Lord will see" by Abraham [יראה] began to be joined together; or when Mount Moriah, which is properly called יראה, was included in the city of Salem. Hence the two parts or portions of the same city began to be called by the dual form of the name, Ferufalaim, for which the Chaldeans said Ferufalem, just as they said Ephrem for Ephraim.

units.la: Principes Sacerdotum. Id est, Sacerdotalium familiarum; nam viginti quatuor classes seu familiæ Sacerdotum institutæ erant à Davide, quarum singulæ suum habebant Principem. 1. Par. 24.
units.tr: Chief priests. That is, of the priestly families; for twenty-four classes or families of priests were instituted by David, and each of them had its own chief. 1 Chron. 24.

units.la: Scribas. Id est, Doctores, seu Legis-peritos, ut eos vocat Lucas, qui gloriabantur se habere clavem scientiæ, ut dicitur Luc. 11. v, 52. Olim namque insigne Doctoratus apud Judæos erat clavis cum pugillaribus.
units.tr: Scribes. That is, teachers, or men learned in the Law, as Luke calls them, who boasted that they possessed the key of knowledge, as is said in Luke 11:52. For formerly the badge of the teacher's office among the Jews was a key together with writing tablets.

units.la: Nasceretur. Id est, nasciturus esset.
units.tr: Should be born. That is, was about to be born.

units.la: 5. Bethlehem Juda. Sic dicitur, ut distinguatur ab altera Bethlehem, quæ est in Galilæa in tribu Zabulon.
units.tr: 5. Bethlehem of Judah. It is so called to distinguish it from the other Bethlehem, which is in Galilee, in the tribe of Zebulun.

units.la: 6. Et tu Bethlehem. Magna est dissensio Prophetæ & Evangelistæ in hoc testimonio recitando. Quam enim Propheta Bethlehem Ephrata & parvulam vocat, Evangelista Terram Judæ nominat & nequaquam minimam in Principibus, quos nominat. Huic difficultati sic occurrimus dicendo quòd Evangelista Scribarum verba referat, qui Regi imperito non verba Prophetæ obscuriuscula protulerint, sed sensum. Propheta enim dixit: Et tu Bethlehem Ephrata, quia Bethlehem ut dicitur Gen, 48. v.7. alio nomine Ephrata vocabatur; Scribæ verò dixerunt explicationis causâ, Et tu Bethlehem Terra Juda, quia erat & alia Bethlehem in tribu Zabulon, ut patet Josue 19. v. 15. Propheta dixit interrogando: Parvula seu minima es? Id Scribæ stylo simplici expresserunt, Nequaquàm minima es. Propheta dixit: In millibus, seu chiliadibus, in quas divisa erat quæque tribus jam à temporibus Moysis juxta consilium Iethro Exod. 18. Scribæ dixerunt: In Principibus, seu Chiliarchis, qui præsunt millibus seu chiliadibus; & hac metonymia tangunt Scribæ causam cur Bethlehem non sit minima, ut poté quæ clara est natalibus Chiliarcharum, qui jam ex ipsa prodierant multi, Abesan nimirum, Booz, Isai, David, sed maxime nobilitanda erat ortu Messiæ; unde hoc explicantes Propheta & Scribæ addunt: Ex te enim exiet dux, ille videlicet expectatus, quem Messiam expressit Chaldæus paraphrastes, qui regnat; nempè cum benignitate adinstar pastoris, ut fert textus Græcus; & cum potestate ut dominator, ut fert textus Hebræus. Addit Propheta: Et egressus ejus ab initio, a diebus æternitatis, in quibus verbis Michæas æternam Christi nativitatem designat; nam Egredi Hebræis est nasci quandoque, ut videre est Gen. 17, v. 6. 25. v. 26. &c. Dicitur autem nativitas Christi æterna Egressus in plurali, ut patet ex textu Hebræo & Græco, quasi diceretur, egressio egressionum, id est, summa egressio, seu generatio ejus, Auxesi Hebraeis usitata, dum res amplificare & extollere volunt. Sic æterna illa Patris Sapientia dicitur Prov. 1. v. 20. & q. v. 1. sapientiae in plurali, quasi diceretur, sapientia sapientiarum, seu summa sapientia. Ab initio, id est, ante initium. Sic Ephes. 1. v. 4. dicitur Græcè & Latinè, Ante mundi constitutionem. 2 Tim. 1. v. 9, Ante tempora sæcularia, quod 2 Thes. 2. v. 13. dicitur [illegible, ~3 letters], Apocalyp. 13. v. 8. Ab origine (Gr. constitutione) mundi, quod inibi refertur ad quorum nomina scripta sunt. A diebus æternitatis, Hebr. [illegible, ~4 letters], quod Paulus dixerit, Ante tempora sæcularia.
units.tr: 6. And you, Bethlehem. There is a great discrepancy between the Prophet and the Evangelist in quoting this testimony. For the Prophet calls Bethlehem Ephrathah and little, whereas the Evangelist names it the land of Judah, and by no means least among the princes, whom he names. We meet this difficulty by saying that the Evangelist reports the words of the Scribes, who, speaking to an unskilled king, did not give the very words of the Prophet, which are rather obscure, but their sense. For the Prophet said: And you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, because Bethlehem, as is said in Gen. 48:7, was also called by another name, Ephrathah. But the Scribes, for the sake of explanation, said: And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, because there was also another Bethlehem in the tribe of Zebulun, as is evident from Josh. 19:15. The Prophet said, by way of question: Are you little or least? The Scribes expressed this in plain style: By no means least. The Prophet said: among the thousands, or clans, into which every tribe had been divided since the time of Moses, according to the advice of Jethro, Exod. 18. The Scribes said: among the princes, or chiliarchs, who preside over the thousands or clans; and by this metonymy the Scribes touch on the reason why Bethlehem is not least, namely because it is renowned for the birth of chiliarchs, of whom many had already come forth from it, Ibzan indeed, Boaz, Jesse, David; but it was to be made most illustrious by the birth of the Messiah. Hence, explaining this, the Prophet and the Scribes add: For out of you shall come a leader, namely that expected one whom the Chaldee paraphrast expressed as the Messiah, who reigns; that is, with kindness, like a shepherd, as the Greek text has it; and with power, like a ruler, as the Hebrew text has it. The Prophet adds: And his going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity, words in which Micah designates the eternal birth of Christ. For to go forth among the Hebrews is sometimes to be born, as may be seen in Gen. 17:6, 25:26, etc. Now the eternal birth of Christ is called goings forth in the plural, as is clear from the Hebrew and Greek text, as if it were said: the going forth of goings forth, that is, his supreme going forth or generation, by the figure of amplification commonly used by the Hebrews when they wish to magnify and exalt a thing. So that eternal Wisdom of the Father is called wisdom in the plural in Prov. 1:20 and 8:1, as if it were said: wisdom of wisdoms, or supreme wisdom. From the beginning, that is, before the beginning. So in Eph. 1:4 it is said in Greek and Latin, before the foundation of the world; 2 Tim. 1:9, before the secular times, which in 2 Thess. 2:13 is called [illegible, about three letters]; Rev. 13:8, from the foundation (Gr. constitution) of the world, which there is referred to those whose names are written. From the days of eternity, in Hebrew [illegible, about four letters], which Paul expressed as before the secular times.

units.la: Terra Juda. Id est, portio terræ ascripta tribui Juda. Sic infrà Cap. 4. v. 15. dicitur Terra Zabulon & Terra Nephthali.
units.tr: The land of Judah. That is, the portion of land assigned to the tribe of Judah. So below, in chapter 4, verse 15, we read "the land of Zabulon and the land of Nephthali."

units.la: 7. Diligenter didicit. Id est, accuratè perquisivit.
units.tr: 7. Diligently learned. That is, carefully inquired.

units.la: Tempus stellæ. Id est, quo tempore stella apparuisset.
units.tr: The time of the star. That is, the time at which the star had appeared.

units.la: 8. Interrogate diligenter, Id est, exquirite exactè.
units.tr: 8. Search diligently. That is, seek out exactly.

units.la: 9. Quam viderant in Oriente. Si hic in Oriente referetur ad Magos, quasi diceretur, Magi in Oriente constituti viderant stellam, non video quo nixi fundamento tot graves Autores afferant stellam toto itinere Magos præcessisse.
units.tr: 9. Which they had seen in the East. If in the East is here referred to the Magi, as if it said that the Magi, placed in the East, had seen the star, I do not see on what foundation so many weighty authors rest when they say that the star went before the Magi through the whole journey.

units.la: Usque dum veniens. Hinc manifeste colligitur quòd stella Christo secundùm carnem nato non ad decretum dominabatur, sed ad testimonium famulabatur; nec eum subjiciebat obsequio. Unde non ipsa Christum fecit mirabiliter vivere, sed ipsam fecit Christus mirabiliter apparere. Nec ipsa Christi mirabilia decrevit, sed ipsam Christus inter sua mirabilia demonstravit. Ipse enim natus ex matre de cœlo terræ novum sydus ostendit, qui natus ex Patre cœlum terramque formavit. Eo nascente lux nova est in stella revelata, quo moriente lux antiqua est in Sole velata. Eo nascente Superi novo honore claruerunt; quo moriente Inferi novo timore horruerunt, quo resurgente Discipuli novo amore exarserunt, quo ascendente coeli novo obsequio paruerunt. Vide Aug. lib. 2. contra Faustum & Serm. 34. de tempore Cap. 2.
units.tr: Until coming. From this it is clearly gathered that the star, after Christ was born according to the flesh, did not rule him by decree but served him as a witness, nor did it subject him to its obedience. Hence it was not the star that made Christ live wonderfully, but Christ who made the star appear wonderfully. Nor did the star decree Christ's wonders, but Christ displayed the star among his own wonders. For he himself, born of a mother, showed a new star from heaven to earth, he who, born of the Father, formed heaven and earth. At his birth a new light was revealed in the star; at his death the old light was veiled in the sun. At his birth the heavenly beings were glorified with new honour; at his death those below trembled with new fear; at his rising the disciples burned with new love; at his ascension the heavens obeyed with new service. See Augustine, book 2 against Faustus, and Sermon 34 on the time, chapter 2.

units.la: II. Et intrantes domum. Gr. εἰς τὴν οἰκίαν, in illam domum, nempe in qua Maria Christum pepererat; ut enim scribit Maldonatus ad Luc. 2. repugnat Scripturæ extra Bethlehem vel in agro vel spelunca vicina Christum fuisse natum. Lucæ enim Evangelistæ verba sunt; Reclinavit eum in præsepio, Græce ἐν τῇ φάτνῃ, quia non erat ei locus in diverso: Græce ἐν τῇ καταλύματι. Sciunt vero periti fermonis Græci, articuli vel adjectione vel omissione multùm fieri diversam horum verborum sententiam. Nam sine articulo, sensus esset Josepho & Mariæ nullum omninò patuisse diversorium, cùm essent Bethlehemi plura; & cum articulo dupliciter exponi poterit, vel fuisse unicum Bethlehemi diversorium, ad quod non sint admissi, quod vix fit verisimile: vel unum aliquod diversorium Bethlehemiticum ipsos adiisse, atque in eo quoad cetera fuisse exceptos, sed locum vacuum non esse ibi repertum, qui ipsis ad cubandum concederetur. Coacti igitur sunt in stabulum jumentorum secedere, quod erat, ut sit verisimile, diversorio conjunctum, aut saltem propinquum. Urgendus autem videtur articulus Græcus, quem Lucas iterum repetit, dum a Pastoribus ait Christum inventum in præsepio jacentem, q. d. in illo præsepio, quod Angelus dixerat, cùm Angelus alloquens Pastores articulum omiserit; id enim satis ostendit sermonis Græci proprietatem a Luca servatam esse. Verisimile est, inquit Maldonatus, publici hospitij stabulum fuisse, in quod se Joseph & Maria exclusi receperint; quod quia in saxo erat excisum, Epiph. Hæresi 51. Greg. Nyss. De sancta Nativitate speluncam vocant; nec id mirum, observat enim Strabo totam regionem circa Jerosolymam ad sexagesimum usque lapidem esse petrosam; Bethlehem autem quatuor millia passuum duntaxat distabat ab Urbe, ut ait Jacobus de Vitriaco, vel sex, ut dicit Arabs Geographus, qui eruditus scriptor observat esse in illo tractu multas domos saxis incisas, vel potius cellas, in quibus homines se incluserunt religionis causâ. Idem Arabs locum ubi natus est Messias commemorans, speluncam vocat, & fere Græci ac Latini omnes. Confecta itaque descriptione, & hospitio, quod occupatum erat, discessione turbarum, quæ ut describerentur, in vicum Bethlehem venerant, vacuefacto, Josephus & Maria relicto stabuo ad illud diversorium se atque infantem transtulerunt, in quo etiam Christum Magi invenerunt, & procidentes adora- verunt; quia præter illam stellæ speciem, quæ corporeum incita- vit obtutum, fulgentior veritatis radius eorum corda perdocuit.
units.tr: II. And entering the house. Greek εἰς τὴν οἰκίαν [εἰς τὴν οἰκίαν], that is, into that house, namely the one in which Mary had brought forth Christ. For, as Maldonatus writes on Luke 2, it is contrary to Scripture that Christ was born outside Bethlehem, either in a field or in a nearby cave. The words are those of the Evangelist Luke: She laid him in a manger, Greek ἐν τῇ φάτνῃ [ἐν τῇ φάτνῃ], because there was no room for them in the inn [ἐν τῇ καταλύματι]. Those skilled in the Greek language know that the sense of these words differs greatly according to the presence, addition or omission of the article. For without the article the meaning would be that Joseph and Mary found no inn at all, since there were several in Bethlehem; with the article it can be explained in two ways: either there was only one inn in Bethlehem, and they were not admitted to it, which is hardly likely; or they went to some one inn in Bethlehem and were received there for the rest, but no empty place was found there which might be granted them to lie in. They were therefore compelled to withdraw into a stable for the beasts, which was, as is likely, joined to the inn or at least near it. Yet the Greek article seems to be of weight, which Luke repeats when he says of the shepherds that they found Christ lying in the manger, that is, in that manger which the angel had mentioned; for the angel, addressing the shepherds, omitted the article. This sufficiently shows that Luke preserved the proper character of the Greek idiom. It is likely, says Maldonatus, that the stable was a public inn, into which Joseph and Mary, having been shut out, withdrew.
