Because it had been hewn out of rock, Epiphanius in Heresy 51 and Gregory of Nyssa in his sermon on the holy Nativity call it a cave; nor is this surprising, for Strabo observes that the whole region around Jerusalem is rocky as far as the sixtieth milestone. Bethlehem was only four thousand paces from the City, as Jacques de Vitry says, or six, as the Arab geographer says, who, a learned writer, observes that in that district there are many houses, or rather cells, cut into rock, in which men shut themselves up for the sake of religion. The same Arab, when he mentions the place where the Messiah was born, calls it a cave, and nearly all Greek and Latin writers do so too. Thus, the description having been made, and the inn being occupied, and the crowds having dispersed, who had come to Bethlehem to be enrolled, Joseph and Mary left the stable and moved themselves and the infant to that inn, where the Magi also found Christ, and falling down they worshipped him. For besides that appearance of the star, which stirred their bodily gaze, a brighter ray of truth taught their hearts.

units.la: Thesauris. Id est, thecis, in quibus munera habebant re- posita; thesaurus enim est quodvis receptaculum, seu quid- vis in quo aliquid repositum est, sive sit sarcina, sive pera, sive saccus, sive theca. Sic Deus dicitur educere ventos de thesauris suis, id est, e receptaculis suis. Basilius Seleucienfis Orat. in Jonam, Deum vocat vitæ thesaurum. Cicero, memoriam dicit rerum omnium thesaurum. Virgilius apothecas servati mellis thesauros appellat. Et beatus Epiphanius Magos ait aperuisse peras suas, seu thesauros suos. Quod autem res conditæ sint conditoriis suis nobiliores, ipsæ dictæ sunt thesaurus.
units.tr: Treasures. That is, boxes in which they had stored their gifts. For a treasure is any receptacle, or whatever thing something is kept in, whether it be a bundle, a bag, a sack or a chest. Thus God is said to bring the winds out of his treasures, that is, out of his receptacles. Basil of Seleucia, in his oration on Jonah, calls God the treasure of life. Cicero calls memory the treasure of all things. Virgil calls the honeycombs of preserved honey treasures. And blessed Epiphanius says that the Magi opened their bags, or their treasures. And because things stored are more noble than their storehouses, they themselves are called a treasure.

units.la: Obtulerunt, Incertum est an singuli aurum, thus & myrrham, an vero unusquisque non nisi unum horum detulerit, ut testaretur more Orientalium se suaque omnia Christo esse subdita.
units.tr: They offered. It is uncertain whether each one offered gold, frankincense and myrrh, or whether each brought only one of these, to attest, in the manner of the Orientals, that he and all his possessions were subject to Christ.

units.la: 12. Responso accepto. Græce, χρηματισθέντες, quod B. Justinus in Dialogo cum Tryphone interpretatur, arcanâ revelatione, seu declaratione jussi.
units.tr: 12. Having received an answer. Greek χρηματισθέντες [χρηματισθέντες], which blessed Justin, in the Dialogue with Trypho, interprets as: instructed by a secret revelation, or declaration.

units.la: 13. Qui cum recessissent, ecce. Hic modus loquendi, ut jam supra notavimus & aoristus Græcus ἀναχωρησάντων, satis innuit non multis diebus post recessum Magorum Jose- phum admonitum fuisse ab Angelo ut in Ægyptum fugeret. Id autem contigit teste B. Aug. de Consen. Evang. statim atque in die Purificationis perfecerunt Legalia in Templo circa puerum. Quod igitur Lucas dicit parentes Christi, ut in Jerusalem die Purificationis Legalia perfecerunt in Tem- plo circa puerum, reversos esse Nazareth, non intelligen- dum est immediate; sed post reditum ex Ægypto, ut satis constat ex causa fugæ, metu Joseph & admonitione Angeli in somnis in præsenti capite ordine descriptis. Hinc monet B. Aug. unamquemque Evangelistarum sic narrationem suam contexere, ut tanquam nihil prætermittentis series digesta videatur; tacitis enim quæ non vult dicere, sic ea quæ vult dicere, illis quæ dicebat adjungit, ut ipsa continuo sequi videantur; sed cum ea alter dicit, quæ alter tacuit, diligenter ordo consideratus indicat locum, ubi ea potuerit, a quo prætermissa sunt, transilire, ut ea, quæ dicere intenderat, ita superioribus copularet, tanquam ipsa nullis interpositis sequerentur.
units.tr: 13. When they had departed, behold. This manner of speaking, as we have already noted above, and the Greek aorist ἀναχωρησάντων [ἀναχωρησάντων], sufficiently indicate that Joseph was warned by the angel to flee into Egypt not many days after the departure of the Magi. This happened, as blessed Augustine testifies in On the Harmony of the Evangelists, as soon as they had completed the legal rites in the Temple concerning the child on the day of purification. Therefore, when Luke says that the parents of Christ, having completed the legal rites in the Temple at Jerusalem on the day of purification, returned to Nazareth, this is not to be understood as immediate, but as after the return from Egypt, as is clear enough from the cause of the flight, the fear of Joseph, and the warning of the angel in dreams, described in order in the present chapter. Hence blessed Augustine advises that each of the Evangelists so weave his narrative that it appears as an orderly sequence of one who omits nothing. For by keeping silent about what he does not wish to say, he joins what he wishes to say to what he was saying, so that these things seem to follow immediately. But when one relates what another has passed over, a diligently considered order indicates the place where the one who omitted them could have passed over them, so that he might link what he intended to say to what precedes, as though nothing had been interposed.

units.la: 14. Secessit. Fugit Christus in Ægyptum non form dine humani humana; sed dispensatione divina, fugit non necessitate, sed potestate, ut B. loquitur Fulgentius, ut cedat tempori, non Herodi, ut ait Chrysolog. Serm. 150.
units.tr: 14. He withdrew. Christ fled into Egypt not by human ordering but by divine dispensation: he fled not from necessity but from power, as blessed Fulgentius says, so that he might yield to the time, not to Herod, as Chrysologus says in Sermon 150.

units.la: In Aegyptum. Aegypto, inquit B. Leo Ser. 2. de Epiphania, Salvator illatus est, ut gens antiquis erroribus dedita jam ad vicinam salutem per occultam gratiam signaretur, & quae nondum ejecerat ab animo superstitionem, jam hospitio acciperet veritatem.
units.tr: Into Egypt. "The Saviour was brought into Egypt," says blessed Leo in Sermon 2 on the Epiphany, "so that a nation given over to ancient errors might be marked for near salvation by hidden grace, and so that what had not yet cast superstition out of its mind might now receive truth as a guest."

units.la: 15. Ut. Eventus notatur, non causa. Vide cap. I. v. 22.
units.tr: 15. That. The outcome is noted, not the cause. See chapter 1, verse 22.

units.la: Adimplerentur. Tribus modis impleri dicitur prophetia. Primo dum praesens exhibetur, quod ad litteram per prophetiam futurum praedicebatur. Secundo, dum quae τυπικῶς praecedunt in aliis, juxta veritatem & adimpletionem, ut loquitur Hieron. referuntur ad Christum; impletur enim quod de typo dictum est, ubi exhibetur veritas, cum ipsius typi hic sit usus, ut in veritate impleatur. Tertio, cum aliqua prophetia non minus apte, de aliquo dici potest, quam de quo litteraliter dicta fuerat. Secundum hunc tertium loquendi modum B. Epiph. Antidicomarianitas non satis, & Collyridianos nimium beatae Virgini tribuentes ex aequo errasse ait, ut in illis adimpleretur, quod a quibusdam Paganorum Philosophis decantatum fuit, extremitates aequales, αἱ ἀκρότητες ἰσότητες; neque enim vir summus ignorare potuit Paganos Philosophos nihil unquam de Collyridianis vel Antidicomarianitis somniasse. Hic autem a Matthaeo prophetia Osee impleri dicitur, non tertio tantum modo, ut putat Jansenius Gandavensis, sed & secundo, ut mox dicemus.
units.tr: Might be fulfilled. Prophecy is said to be fulfilled in three ways. First, when what was foretold by prophecy as future to be taken literally is present. Second, when things that go before in others as types [τυπικῶς] are referred to Christ according to truth and fulfilment, as Jerome says; for what was said of the type is fulfilled where the truth is displayed, since the type itself is used here so that it may be fulfilled in the truth. Third, when some prophecy can be said of someone no less aptly than of him of whom it was literally spoken. In this third way of speaking, blessed Epiphanius says that the Antidicomarianites, and the Collyridians who attribute too much to the blessed Virgin, erred alike, so that in them would be fulfilled what certain pagan philosophers sang: extremes are equal [αἱ ἀκρότητες ἰσότητες]. For so great a man could not be ignorant that the pagan philosophers had never dreamed anything about the Collyridians or the Antidicomarianites. Here, however, Matthew is said to fulfil a prophecy of Hosea not only in the third way alone, as Jansenius of Ghent thinks, but also in the second, as we shall say presently.

units.la: Ex Aegypto. Hunc locum, inquit B. Hieron. lib. 3. in Oseam, in septimo volumine Julianus Augustus, quod adversum nos, id est, Christianos, evomuit, calumniatur, & dicit, Quod de Israel scriptum est, Matthaeus Evangelista ad Christum transtulit, ut simplicitati eorum, qui de gentibus crediderant, illuderet. Cui nos breviter respondebimus, primum, Matthaeum Evangelium Hebraeis litteris edidisse, quod non poterant legere, nisi hi, qui ex Hebraeis erant, ergo non propterea fecit ut illuderet Ethnicis; sin autem Hebraeis illudere voluit, aut stultus, aut imperitus fuit: Stultus, si apertum finxit mendacium: Imperitus, si non intellexit de quo haec dicerentur. Stultitiam ipsum volumen excusat, quod prudenter, ordinateque compositum est; imperitum non possumus dicere, quem ex aliis testimoniis Scripturarum scientiam Legis habuisse cognoscimus. Superest ut illud dicamus, quod scriptum est: Ex Aegypto vocavi filium meum, hoc dici quidem de populo Israel, sed perfecte refertur ad Christum. Haec B. Hieron. Quod igitur de typico Dei filio, id est, de populo Israel, qui Exod. 4. dicitur filius Dei primogenitus, typicè dictum erat, impletum est verè, cum Christus Dei Filius ex Ægypto in Terram Israel revocaretur.
units.tr: Out of Egypt. Blessed Jerome, in book 3 on Hosea, says that Julian Augustus, in the seventh volume he vomited out against us, that is, the Christians, finds fault with this passage and says: What is written about Israel, the Evangelist Matthew transferred to Christ, in order to mock the simplicity of those from the Gentiles who had believed. To this we will reply briefly. First, Matthew published his Gospel in Hebrew letters, which none could read except those who were of the Hebrews. Therefore he did not do this in order to mock the Gentiles. But if he wished to mock the Hebrews, he was either foolish or ignorant. He was foolish if he invented a plain falsehood; he was ignorant if he did not understand what these words were about. The volume itself excuses him from folly, since it is prudently and orderly composed. We cannot call him ignorant, since from other passages of Scripture we know he had knowledge of the Law. It remains for us to say what is written: Out of Egypt I have called my son. This is indeed said of the people of Israel, but it is perfectly applied to Christ. So far Blessed Jerome. Therefore what was said typically about the typical son of God, that is, the people of Israel, who in Exodus 4 is called the firstborn son of God, was truly fulfilled when Christ, the Son of God, was brought back out of Egypt into the land of Israel.

units.la: Filium meum : Ita vertit B. Hieron. Osee 2. juxta veritatem Hebraicam. Hinc ibidem ait, Ergo qui detrahunt nostræ translationi videant apud LXX. Scripturam, è qua Evangelista hoc testimonium sumserit. Et cùm invenire non potuerint, desinant rugare frontem, adducere supercilium, crispare nares, digitis concrepare. Male igitur LXX. transtulerunt, filios ejus, sicut verso Græca, ut verbis Hieronymi in Mich. 2. utar, LXX. est; Josephus enim scribit proœm. Antiq. quinque tantùm libros Moßs ab iis translatos & Ptolomæo Regi contraditos. Idem videre est apud eundem proœm. quæst. Hebraic. in Gen. &c.
units.tr: My son: so Blessed Jerome translates Hosea 2 according to the Hebrew truth. Hence he says in the same place: Therefore let those who disparage our translation look at the Scripture of the Seventy, from which the Evangelist took this testimony. And when they cannot find it, let them stop wrinkling their brow, raising their eyebrows, curling their nostrils, and snapping their fingers. The Seventy therefore translated badly, his sons, as the Greek has it, to use the words of Jerome on Micah 2: so the Seventy have it. For Josephus writes in the preface to the Antiquities that only the five books of Moses were translated by them and delivered to King Ptolemy. The same can be seen in the same author's preface to the Hebrew Questions on Genesis, etc.

units.la: 16. Illusus. Solemne est Scripturæ loqui de rebus, interdum quales sunt, interdum quales apparent. Sic Luna dicitur magnum luminare præ ceteris omnibus post Solem. Dij Damascenorum dicuntur percussisse Achabum. Sic Herodes dicitur illusus à Magis non verâ, sed apparenti illusione, quæ fundamentum habebat in imaginatione Herodis, non in intentione Magorum, vel in rei veritate.
units.tr: 16. Mocked. It is customary for Scripture to speak of things sometimes as they are, sometimes as they appear. Thus the moon is called the greater light above all others after the sun. The gods of the Damascenes are said to have struck Ahab. So Herod is said to have been mocked by the Magi, not by a real mockery but by an apparent one, which had its basis in Herod's imagination, not in the intention of the Magi or in the truth of the matter.

units.la: A bimatu. Id est, à bimulis, ut transtulit Syrus.
units.tr: From two years old. That is, from the two-year-olds, as the Syriac translated.

units.la: Et infrà secundum tempus quod exquisierat à Magis. Id est, non modò bimulos occidit, sed & omnes pueros infra bimulos, qui nati erant usque ad tempus, quo primùm, ut à Magis diligenter didicerat, stella apparuit in signum Messiæ jam nati, non nasciturî. Voluit ergo Herodes cautionis & securitatis causâ, bimulos licet multò ante apparitionem stellæ in lucem editos, occidere, sicut eadem de causa omnes pueros in omnibus finibus Bethlehem natos occidit, licet scisciantî ubi Christus nasciturus esset, fuisset responsum, in Bethlehem Judæ, hoc est, in ipsa urbe Bethlehem civitate David, ut ex prophetia Michææ colligitur.
units.tr: And below, according to the time which he had learned from the Magi. That is, he killed not only the two-year-olds but also all the boys under two years old who had been born up to the time when, as he had carefully learned from the Magi, the star appeared as the sign of the Messiah already born, not yet to be born. Herod therefore wished, for the sake of caution and safety, to kill the two-year-olds, even though they had been brought into the light long before the star appeared, just as for the same reason he killed all the boys born in all the territory of Bethlehem, although, when he inquired where Christ was to be born, the answer had been given: in Bethlehem of Judah, that is, in the city of Bethlehem itself, the city of David, as is gathered from the prophecy of Micah.

units.la: 17. Tunc adimpletum est. Secundo scilicet ac tertio modo dicto v. 15. q. d. Tunc prophetia Jeremiæ, quamvis ad litteram de abductione decem tribuum in captivitatem dicta fuerit, multò aptius tamen de infantibus ab Herode cæsis, quàm de ipsis abeuntibus in captivitatem dici potuit; hi enim viri, isti infantes; hi meriti, isti immerentes, innocentésque; hi non sunt, id est, non inveniuntur, quia in captivitatem abducti, isti non sunt, id est, inter vivos esse desierunt, quia crudeliter trucidati, ut merito istos magis plorare debeat Rachel, id est, Bethlehem, quæ Metonymicè per Rachel intelligitur, quia non procul à Bethlehem sepulta est, ut dicitur Gen. 36. quàm ipsa Rachel avia Ephraim à Jeremia inducitur plorasse Ephraim, seu, decem tribus in captivitatem abductas per Ephraim significatas, quia primus earum Rex fuit Jereboam è tribu Ephraim oriundus. Citat autem Matthæus hanc Jeremiæ Prophetiam neque secundum veritatem Hebraicam, neque secundum LXX. Ex quo, inquit Hieron. perspicuum est Evangelistas & Apostolos non interpretationem alicujus secutos, sed tanquam Hebræos, quod legebant Hebraicè, suis sermonibus exprefisse.
units.tr: 17. Then it was fulfilled. Namely in the second and third manner mentioned in verse 15, as if to say: Then the prophecy of Jeremiah, although it was spoken literally of the carrying away of the ten tribes into captivity, could be said much more aptly of the infants slain by Herod than of those going into captivity. For these were men, those were infants; these deserved it, those were undeserving and innocent; these are not, that is, are not found, because they were led away into captivity; those are not, that is, have ceased to be among the living, because they were cruelly slaughtered. So Rachel, that is, Bethlehem, which is metonymically understood by Rachel because she was buried not far from Bethlehem, as is said in Genesis 35, ought rather to weep for them. Jeremiah introduces Rachel herself, the grandmother of Ephraim, as weeping for Ephraim; or the ten tribes led away into captivity are signified by Ephraim, because their first king, Jeroboam, was born of the tribe of Ephraim. Matthew, however, cites this prophecy of Jeremiah neither according to the Hebrew truth nor according to the Seventy. From this, says Jerome, it is clear that the Evangelists and Apostles did not follow the translation of anyone, but, as Hebrews, expressed in their own words what they read in Hebrew.

units.la: 18. In Rama. Id est, teste Hieronymo, in excelso. Familiare autem est Hellenistis voces prout scriptas ab Hebraeis invenerint, litteris iisdem Graecè exprimere. Aliis tamen probabilius Rama est civitas in tribu Benjamin non longè à Bethlehem ad occasum juxta Gabaa, in confinio tribus Judæ & Benjamin. Vide Judic. 16. Utervis sensus recipiatur, semper eleganti Metaphorâ magnitudo luctûs exprimitur.
units.tr: 18. In Rama. That is, according to Jerome, on high. It is, however, customary for the Hellenists to render in Greek, with the same letters, the words as they found them written by the Hebrews. For others it is more probable that Rama is a city in the tribe of Benjamin, not far from Bethlehem to the west, near Gibeah, on the border of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin. See Judges 19. Whichever sense is accepted, the greatness of the grief is always expressed by an elegant metaphor.

units.la: Rachel. Apud Jeremiam intelligitur ipsa Rachel, hic vero Bethlehem, qua, ut Hieronymus loquitur, ex materni corpusculi hospitio nomen accepit. Eleganti autem Prosopopœia Prophetis & Poetis familiari, & ad affectus movendos efficacissima nemora & urbes, mortuorum manes & eversarum urbium umbrae lamentantes inducuntur.
units.tr: Rachel. In Jeremiah it is understood to be Rachel herself, but here Bethlehem, which, as Jerome puts it, received its name from the hospitality of its mother's little body. By an elegant personification, familiar to prophets and poets and most effective for stirring the emotions, groves and cities, the shades of the dead and the shadows of overthrown cities are introduced as lamenting.

units.la: Consolari. Id est, consolationem accipere.
units.tr: To be comforted. That is, to receive consolation.

units.la: 20. Defuncti sunt. Pluralis pro singulari, nam de solo Herode loquitur. Nihil autem frequentius hac numeri Enallage in Scriptura. Sic Gen. 19. v. 29. Liberavit Lot de subversione urbium, in quibus, id est, in quarum una, habitaverat. Gen. 21. v. 7. in textu Hebraeo Sara dicitur lactare filios, cum unum Isaacum lactaret. Gen. 28. v. 11. Tulit de lapidibus, id est, lapidum unum. Gen. 46. v. 7. Jacob dicitur in Ægyptum deduxisse filias suas, id est, Dinam, quae Jacob erat unica. Exod. 4. v. 19. Moysi dicitur: Mortui sunt qui quarebant animam tuam, de solo Pharaone. Num. 26. v. 42. Filij Dan per cognationes suas Suham; qui Suham solus fuit filius Dan. Josue 7. v. 1. Filij Israel dicuntur praevaricati mandatum, id est, unus ex filiis Israel nomine Achan. Judic. 12. v. 7. in textu Hebraeo Jephte dicitur sepultus in urbibus Galaad, id est, in una urbium Galaad. 1 Reg. 9. v. 21. unica tribus Benjamin dicitur tribus in plurali in textu Hebraeo. 2 Paralip. 16. v. 14. in textu Hebraeo de Asa dicitur: Et sepelierunt eum in sepulchris suis, id est, in sepulchro suo. Psal. 104. v. 30. In penetralibus regum ipsorum, id est, unius Pharaonis, qui Mosis ævo regnum Ægypti solus obtinebat. Psal. 136. Super flumina Babylonis, id est, ad Euphratem. Daniel 3. v. 12, 14. & 18 Deos Regis Nabuchodonosor non colere dicuntur, qui unam statuam auream ab ipso erectam colere detrectant. Act. 7. v. 42. Scriptum est in libro Prophetarum, id est, in libro unius e Prophetis. Heb. 11. v. 37. de uno Esaia dicitur, Serti sunt, &c. B. tamen Hiero. ex praesentibus Matthaei verbis colligit non solum Herodem, sed & Sacerdotes & Scribas eodem tempore necem Domini fuisse meditatos. Idem sentit Aug. Orat. contra Judaeos, Paganos & Arrianos.
units.tr: 20. They are dead. A plural for a singular, for he speaks only of Herod. Nothing is more frequent in Scripture than this enallage of number. So Genesis 19:29: He delivered Lot from the overthrow of the cities in which, that is, in one of which, he had lived. Genesis 21:7: in the Hebrew text Sarah is said to be nursing sons, when she was nursing only Isaac. Genesis 28:11: He took of the stones, that is, one of the stones. Genesis 46:7: Jacob is said to have brought his daughters into Egypt, that is, Dinah, who was Jacob's only daughter. Exodus 4:19: it is said to Moses: Those who sought your life are dead, said of Pharaoh alone. Numbers 26:42: The sons of Dan according to their families, Shuham; Shuham alone was the son of Dan. Joshua 7:1: the sons of Israel are said to have transgressed the commandment, that is, one of the sons of Israel named Achan. Judges 12:7: in the Hebrew text Jephthah is said to have been buried in the cities of Gilead, that is, in one of the cities of Gilead. 1 Kings 9:21: in the Hebrew text the single tribe of Benjamin is called tribes in the plural. 2 Chronicles 16:14: in the Hebrew text it is said of Asa: And they buried him in their sepulchres, that is, in his sepulchre. Psalm 104:30: In the inner chambers of their kings, that is, of the one Pharaoh, who alone held the kingdom of Egypt in the time of Moses. Psalm 137: By the rivers of Babylon, that is, by the Euphrates. Daniel 3:12, 14, 18: they are said not to worship the gods of King Nebuchadnezzar, who refuse to worship the one golden statue erected by him. Acts 7:42: It is written in the book of the Prophets, that is, in the book of one of the Prophets. Hebrews 11:37: of Isaiah alone it is said: They were sawn, etc. Yet Blessed Jerome gathers from the present words of Matthew that not only Herod but also the priests and scribes at the same time planned the death of the Lord. Augustine holds the same view in his oration against the Jews, the Pagans and the Arians.

units.la: Animam. Id est, vitam, idiotissimus Hebraeis familiaris. Sic Job 2. v. 6. &c.
units.tr: Soul. That is, life, a Hebraism very familiar to the idiom of the Hebrews. So Job 2:6, etc.

units.la: 21. Venit in terram Israel. In ejus scilicet limites Ægypto proximos.
units.tr: 21. He came into the land of Israel. That is, into its borders, the ones nearest Egypt.

units.la: 22. Audiens autem quòd Archelaus regnaret in Judaea. Id est, Judaeae Regiâ potestate praeesset, licet non Regio nomine. Nam Herodes Magnus, seu, Ascalonita testamento reliquerat regnum Archelao; sed Caesar Augustus, cujus beneplacito Herodes testamentum subjecerat, nomen Regis Archelao denegavit, & constituit eum Ethnarcham, id est, gentis Principem, in dimidiam partem regni Herodis patris sui, hoc est, in Judaeam, Samariam, & Idumaeam. Alterum dimidium regni in reliquos duos filios Herodis partitus est, Antipam scilicet, qui postea Herodes cognominatus est, creans Tetrarcham Galilaeae & Peraeae, Philippum vero Batanea, Ituraea, Traconitidis, &c. Porro Archelaus tantae fuit crudelitatis, ut vulgo diceretur, si Hebraeis fides est adhibenda, Nobis melius esset esse sine Rege, quàm Regem habere Archelaum. Tandem propter suam crudelitatem, fuit à Caesare in Galliam relegatus, ut testatur Josephus, Antipas vero mitioris dicitur suisse ingenii, quàm Archelaus, at Philippus mitissimi. Vide Josephi 17. Antiquit.
units.tr: 22. But hearing that Archelaus reigned in Judaea. That is, he presided over Judaea with royal power, though not with the royal title. For Herod the Great, or the Ascalonite, had left the kingdom to Archelaus by his will. But Caesar Augustus, to whose pleasure Herod had submitted his will, denied Archelaus the name of king and appointed him ethnarch, that is, prince of the nation, over half of his father Herod's kingdom, namely Judaea, Samaria and Idumaea. He divided the other half among Herod's two remaining sons. He made Antipas, who was later called Herod, tetrarch of Galilee and Perea, and Philip received Batanea, Ituraea, Trachonitis, and so on. Archelaus was so cruel that it was commonly said, if the Hebrews are to be believed, It would be better for us to be without a king than to have Archelaus as king. At last, on account of his cruelty, he was banished to Gaul by Caesar, as Josephus testifies. Antipas is said to have been of a gentler disposition than Archelaus, but Philip of the gentlest. See Josephus, Antiquities 17.

units.la: Judaea. Scilicet, proprie dicta, quae est optima & amplissima pars Terrae Israel, sita cis Jordanem, & ad mare Mediterraneum; dicebatur autem Judaea à tribu Juda omnium nobilissima, & fortissima, cuius in partitione Terrae sorte obtigerat.
units.tr: Judaea. That is, Judaea properly so called, which is the best and largest part of the land of Israel, lying on this side of the Jordan and along the Mediterranean sea. It was called Judaea from the tribe of Judah, the most noble and strongest of all, whose lot had fallen to it in the division of the land.

units.la: Pro Herode. Latina vocula pro, quoties personis applicatur, significat alterum successisse in alterius locum.
units.tr: For Herod. The Latin word pro, whenever it is applied to persons, means that one succeeded into the place of another.

units.la: Timuit eò ire. Nempe ut ibi, id est, in Judaea habitaret. Alias enim per omnes annos, ut testatur Lucas, in die solemni Paschae in Jerusalem ascendebat. Non igitur necem timebat Christo; sciebat enim Archelaum non quaerere animam ejus, sed sub duro crudelis tyranni imperio vitam degere reformidabat. Mirum autem non est quòd Josephus jussus in Terram Israel redire ex Ægypto, eam sibi ejusdem Terrae regionem gionem incolendam primùm cogitaverit, in qua ab Angelis, à Pastoribus, à Magis, à Senioribus & Justis generatio Domini, quæ ibidem contigerat, testimonium acceperat. . . .
units.tr: He feared to go there. Namely, to live there, that is, in Judaea. For otherwise, as Luke testifies, he went up to Jerusalem every year at the solemn feast of the Passover. He therefore did not fear death for Christ; he knew that Archelaus was not seeking his life, but he dreaded living under the harsh rule of a cruel tyrant. It is not surprising, however, that Joseph, bidden to return from Egypt to the land of Israel, first thought of settling in that region of the same land where the Lord's birth had taken place and had been attested by Angels, Shepherds, Magi, elders and the just. . . .

units.la: In partes Galilææ. Galilæa regio celeberrima, & quæ Septentrionalem obtinet totius Judææ partem, quatuor amplexa tribus, Afer, Nephtalim, Zabulon & Ifachar, quarum primæ duæ Phœnicibus & Syris gentilibus immixtæ Septentrioni etiam viciniores, sub Galilæa gentium Matthæo, aliis sub Galilæa superiori; reliquæ sub inferiori ut plurimùm intelliguntur. Totius fines sunt: à Septentrione Syria, incerjacente Libano monte: à Meridie Samaria & Carmelus mons: ab Oriente Jordanis fluvius: Ab Occidente mare Mediterraneum. Dicitur autem Galilæa à גְּלִיל[?], Volvere, quòd maris littori adjaceat, propter sinuosos littorum recessus, vel quia fluctus illisi ventis aut æstu reciprocantur, illicque volutatim ludunt, vel denique propter congestos illic arenarum tumulos. Populos verò Galilææ, maximè superioris, seu Galilææ gentium præ ceteris contemtos, invisos, peccatoresque à Judæis habitos, non Talmudiftæ modò, sed & sacræ Paginæ testantur. Hos Isaias vocat sedentes in tenebris & in regione umbræ mortis. A Galilæa, aiunt Pharisæi Joan. 7. Propheta non surgit. Et Nathanael, Joan. 1. A Nazareth potest aliquid boni esse? Hinc & ipse Christus contemtim vocatus est Galilæus & Nazarenus. Matth. 26. Joan. 7. Hinc & illud Juliani Augusti, Vicisti, Galilæe, vicisti. Hinc & nos Christiani Galilæi olim & Nazareni dicebamur; & hoc ultimo nomine etiamnum à Judæis vocamur.
units.tr: Into the parts of Galilee. Galilee is a very famous region, occupying the northern part of all Judaea and embracing four tribes: Asher, Naphtali, Zebulun and Issachar. Of these, the first two, being mixed with the Phoenicians and the Gentile Syrians and lying nearer to the north, are understood by Matthew as "Galilee of the Gentiles", and by others as "Upper Galilee"; the remaining ones are for the most part understood as "Lower Galilee". Its borders are: on the north, Syria, with Mount Lebanon lying between; on the south, Samaria and Mount Carmel; on the east, the river Jordan; on the west, the Mediterranean sea. Galilee is said to take its name from galil [גְּלִיל], to roll, either because it lies by the shore of the sea, on account of the winding recesses of the coast, or because the waves dashed against it by the winds or the tide roll back and forth and play there in rolling motion, or finally because of the heaps of sand piled up there. That the people of Galilee, especially of Upper Galilee or Galilee of the Gentiles, were despised beyond others, hated, and regarded by the Jews as sinners, is attested not only by the Talmudists but also by Sacred Scripture. Isaiah calls these people those who sit in darkness and in the region of the shadow of death. "Out of Galilee," say the Pharisees in John 7, "no prophet arises." And Nathanael, in John 1: "Can anything good come out of Nazareth?" Hence Christ himself was contemptuously called "the Galilean and the Nazarene" (Matt. 26; John 7). Hence also that saying of Julian the Augustus, "You have conquered, Galilean, you have conquered." Hence we Christians too were once called Galileans and Nazarenes, and by this last name we are still called by the Jews.

units.la: 23. Veniens habitavit. Ex hoc loquendi modo satis patet, quod Evangelista dixerat, timuit eò ire, intelligendum, ut ibi habitaret, non ut illac iter faceret in civitatem suam Nazareth.
units.tr: 23. He came and lived. From this way of speaking it is quite clear that what the Evangelist had said, he feared to go there, must be understood as: to live there, not to make a journey there to his own city Nazareth.

units.la: Nazareth. Interpretatur flos, & scribitur B. Hieron. teste de nominibus Hebr. non per Zain, sed per Tzade. Favet autem B. Hieron, non modò Syrus, sed & ipse titulus crucis, teste Pagnino, & hodierna Judæorum hujus nominis scribendi ratio. Nusquam autem in veteri Testamento fit hujus civitatis mentio, quod satis indicat eam non fuisse hactenus valde celebrem.
units.tr: Nazareth. It is interpreted as flower, and, as Blessed Jerome testifies in his book on Hebrew names, it is written not with Zain but with Tzade. Blessed Jerome is supported not only by the Syriac but also by the title of the cross, according to Pagninus, and by the present-day Jewish way of writing this name. Nowhere in the Old Testament is this city mentioned, which sufficiently indicates that it had not hitherto been very famous.

units.la: Dictum est. Observat B. Chrysost. non uno loco duobus modis aliquid dici scriptum vel dictum per Prophetas; 1. quia verbis eisdem aut non dissimilibus scriptum reperitur; 2. quia διὰ τῶν προφητῶν πραγμάτων κείμενον[?], rebus ipsis, licet non verbis expressum reperitur. Hoc 2. modo verè dici potest prædictum fuisse ut Christus appellaretur Nazaræus, seu potiùs Nazarenus, ut etiam Græcè exprimitur apud Marc. Siquidem apud Esaiam c. 11. v. 1. sic appellatur
units.tr: It was said. Blessed Chrysostom observes that in more than one place something is said or written through the Prophets in two ways: 1. because it is found written in the same or in not dissimilar words; 2. because it is found lying in the things themselves [διὰ τῶν προφητῶν πραγμάτων κείμενον], expressed not in words but in the realities. In the second way it can truly be said that it was foretold that Christ would be called a Nazaraean, or rather a Nazarene, as is also expressed in Greek in Mark. For in Isaiah ch. 11 v. 1 he is so called,

units.la: Greek words in the line above are read with doubt; see notes. tur, voce scilicet Hebraicâ נֵצֶר, quam alii furculum, alii cum vulgato interprete florem interpretantur. Hinc Hieron. scribens ad Marcellam, Ibimus, inquit ad Nazareth, & juxta interpretationem nominis ejus, Florem videbimus Galilææ. Idem in Epist. ad Pammach. de optimo genere interpretandi c. 3. testimonium Matthæi, quoniam Nazaraeus vocabitur, sumtum putat ex loco citato Esaiæ. Idem in locum citatum Esaiæ hanc opinionem Eruditis tribuit. Hanc sententiam sequuntur Lyranus, Abulensis & Jansenius Gandavensis, & volunt locum citatum Isaiæ sic vertendum: Exibit virga de radice Jesse & Nazaraeus de radice ejus ascendet. Hanc expositionem admittit & B. Hieron. l. 1. in Matth. Rabbi Elias in Lexico semper Nazaraeum scribit per Tzade, & civitatem Nazareth ait appellari Netzer. Idem contendunt Pagninus & Cajetanus.
units.tr: by the Hebrew word netser [נֵצֶר], which some interpret as a twig and others, with the Vulgate translator, as a flower. Hence Jerome, writing to Marcella: "We shall go," he says, "to Nazareth, and according to the interpretation of its name we shall see the Flower of Galilee." The same, in his letter to Pammachius on the best way of translating, ch. 3, thinks that the testimony of Matthew, because he shall be called a Nazarene, was taken from the passage of Isaiah cited. The same author, on the passage of Isaiah cited, attributes this opinion to the learned. This opinion is followed by Lyranus, Abulensis and Jansenius of Ghent, who want the passage of Isaiah cited to be rendered thus: A shoot shall come out of the stem of Jesse, and a Nazarene shall spring up from his root. Blessed Jerome too admits this explanation, in book 1 on Matthew. Rabbi Elias in his Lexicon always writes Nazarene with Tzade, and says that the city Nazareth is called Netzer. Pagninus and Cajetan also maintain the same.

units.la: Per Prophetas. Nempe per Esaiam, ut mox diximus, est igitur pro singulari pluralis, ut supra v. 20.
units.tr: By the Prophets. Namely by Isaiah, as we have just said; so the plural is used for the singular, as above at v. 20.

units.la: CAPUT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: IN diebus illis. Scilicet, intra quos Nazarethæ vixit Dominus Jesus. Est autem hic loquendi modus, in diebus illis, Scripturæ familiaris, nec est semper certi, aut definiti temporis index.
units.tr: In those days. That is, during the days in which the Lord Jesus lived at Nazareth. This way of speaking, in those days, is familiar in Scripture, and it does not always indicate a certain or fixed time.

units.la: In deserto Judææ. Cafaubonus post Theodorum Bezam existimat desertum, in quo Joannes praedicavit, fuisse montana, in quibus pater ejus Zacharias & Elisabeth morabantur. Verum ne tantis viris assentiar obstat quod, ut Evangelistæ indicant, desertum Judææ, in quo Joannes baptizabat & poenitentiam praedicabat, erat circa Jordanem fluvium, in extrema parte Ennon & Salim. Montana autem à Jordane remotissima erat, unde Jeremiæ 32. v. 44. montana Judææ opponuntur campestribus, scilicet circa Jordanem, sicut Oriens Occidenti. Hic igitur Joannes ab officio poenitentes baptizandi divinitus sibi delegato dictus Baptista, toto vitæ tempore ab incunabulis desertum incoluit, non tecto, non lecto, non mensa, neque aliâ re indiguit, sed quandam vitam Angelicam in carne hac agebat, qui potuit frigus & æstum pati, cum tenero esset corpusculo, ac immaturâ ætate. Ita Chrysostomus Hom. 10. in Matth. cui subscribit tota Antiquitas. ¶ 2. Pœnitentiam agite. Gr. μετανοεῖτε, quod absolutè positum, proprie significat resipiscere, seu, duci pœnitentiâ factî cum consilio emendationis. Unde Tertullianus, lib 2. adv. Marc. In Græco sono pœnitentiæ nomen, non ex delicti confessione, sed ex animi demutatione compositum est. Est itaque, pœnitentiam agere hic et alibi passim idem ac pœnitudine duci; nec unquam; si bene memini, hac phrasi indicat Vulgatus interpres opera illa, ad quæ pœnitentes tenemur, non ut divinæ justitiæ faciamus satis, sed ut Ecclesiæ nostram internam pœnitentiam exterius testemur, nósque ad Deum ardentius invocandum instimulemus, & probibeamus ne exstimulemur ad ulterius peccandum. In prima hujus libri editione cùm adhuc Ecclesiæ Romanæ erroribus esset infectus, docueram hîc ex Scripturis malè intellectis ad peccatorum deletionem requiri præter resipiscentiam resipiscentis pœnalem actionem; verùm cùm humanum sit errare, gratiæ hóminem ab errore revocare, divinæ gratiæ deputo quod mihi tandem patuerint aures ad Apostolicam tubam clamantem, 1 Pet. 2. v. 24. Christum pertulisse peccata nostra super lignum in corpore suo, & ejus livore nos esse sanatos, proindeque didici tandem hanc veritatem toties in Scripturis inculcatam, Christum Jesum videlicet sine culpa pœnam subeundo, nos & à culpa & à pœna liberasse, et si post gratuitam peccatorum omnium condonationem, divinitùs nobis immittuntur pœnæ aliquæ temporales, hoc non fieri ut divinæ justitiæ satisfiat, sed ut ait Aug. Tract. 124. in Joan. Ad demonstrationem debitæ miseriæ, vel ad emendationem labilis vitæ, vel ad exercitationem necessariâ patientiæ. Vide Chrysost.Hom.6. in Genes. & Hom.2. in Ps. 50. & in Oratione de B. Philogonio. Marcum Eremitam lib. de Baptismo, &c.
units.tr: In the wilderness of Judea. After Theodore Beza, Casaubon thought that the wilderness where John preached was the mountainous country where his father Zacharias and Elizabeth lived. But I cannot agree with such great men, because the Evangelists make it clear that the wilderness of Judea, where John baptized and preached repentance, lay near the river Jordan, in the furthest part of Aenon and Salim. The mountains, however, were very far from the Jordan. That is why, in Jeremiah 32:44, the mountains of Judea are set against the plains, that is, the country around the Jordan, just as the East is set against the West. So John, who was called the Baptist because he had been divinely appointed to baptize penitents, lived in the desert from infancy throughout his whole life. He had no house, no bed, no table, and needed nothing else. He lived a certain angelic life in this flesh, and he was able to endure cold and heat while his body was still tender and his age immature. So Chrysostom, in Homily 10 on Matthew, and the whole of antiquity agrees with him. ¶ 2. Repent [μετανοεῖτε]. The Greek word, used absolutely, properly means to come to one's senses, or to be led by repentance of what has been done to a resolve of amendment. Hence Tertullian, in Book 2 against Marcion: The name of repentance, in the Greek sound, is formed not from the confession of a fault, but from a change of mind. So to repent here, and elsewhere throughout, means the same as to be led by regret. If I remember rightly, the Vulgate translator never uses this phrase to mean those works which penitents are bound to perform, not in order to make satisfaction to divine justice, but to bear outward witness to the inward repentance of the Church, and to stir us to call upon God more earnestly and to keep us from being spurred on to sin further. In the first edition of this book, when I was still infected with the errors of the Roman Church, I taught here, from Scripture wrongly understood, that for the blotting out of sins, besides the repentance of the one who repents, a penal action is required. But since it is human to err, and it is a grace of God to recall a man from error, I count it a gift of divine grace that my ears were at last opened to the apostolic trumpet which proclaims (1 Peter 2:24) that Christ bore our sins in his body on the tree, and that we are healed by his wounds. So I have at last learned this truth, which is so often impressed upon us in Scripture: that Christ Jesus, by undergoing punishment without fault, has freed us both from fault and from punishment. And if, after the free forgiveness of all sins, some temporal punishments are sent to us by God, this does not happen so that divine justice may be satisfied, but, as Augustine says in Tractate 124 on John, to demonstrate our owed wretchedness, or to amend our frail life, or to exercise a necessary patience. See Chrysostom, Homily 6 on Genesis, and Homily 2 on Psalm 50, and in his oration on the blessed Philogonius; Marcus the Hermit, in his book on Baptism, etc.

units.la: Appropinquavit enim regnum cœlorum. Id est, regnum Christi, quod dicitur regnum cœlorum, quia, ut ipse testatur Joan. 18. non est de hoc mundo; Quid est enim, inquit Augustinus Tractatu 115. in Joannem, regnum ejus, nisi credentes in eum, quibus dicit, Joan. 15. De hoc mundo non estis: De mundo enim est, quidquid hominum à Deo quidem creatum, sed ex Adam vitiatâ stirpe generatum est; factum est autem regnum non jam de mundo, quicquid inde in Christo regeneratum est: sic enim nos Deus eruit de potestate tenebrarum, & transtulit in regnum Filii charitatis suæ.
units.tr: For the kingdom of heaven is at hand. That is, the kingdom of Christ, which is called the kingdom of heaven because, as he himself testifies (John 18), it is not of this world. For what is his kingdom, says Augustine in Tractate 115 on John, except those who believe in him, to whom he says (John 15), You are not of this world? For whatever is of mankind, created indeed by God but born from the tainted stock of Adam, is of the world; but whatever is regenerated in Christ is no longer of the world. For thus God has rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love.

units.la: 3. Dictus. Id est, prædictus typice.
units.tr: 3. Spoken of. That is, foretold in a type.

units.la: Vox clamantis. Scilicet Verbi. Verbum enim, inquit Glossa, clamat in voce, id est, Christus in Joanne, clamat, ut diffantes auditu percipiant, & gravem habentes auditum sentiant immensitatem eorum, quæ dicuntur. Clamavit autem Deus & per alios, sic enim, ait Glossa, clamavit in omnibus, qui tům, nfilio Græco ti dealibi i,hac entes e noDee exri eftus, rum pœatiæ quod bam cata esses in ilpa t fi iviieri in nem ideone &c. ritur Auen De ex am eua. ofdienem qui à principio aliquid divinitùs dixerunt, & tamen Joannes solus est Vox, quia pœ eum præsens Verbum offenditur, quod alij è longè nuntiaverunt. Beatus Epiph. Hæref. 69. vocem ait esse præparativam auditûs hominum: primùm enim inarticulatam vocem sonantem reddere solent clamantes, è longinquo vocantes eos, qui aliquid ab ipsis audire debent: & ubi illi solam vocem audierint, & mentem ad audiendum converterint, aurësque præparaverint, tunc is, qui sonantem vocem emisit, de cetero distinguit sermonem, quem dicere voluit. Sic etiam Joannes Vox fuit aures hominum præparans: non enim erat ipse Verbum, sed post ipsum venit Verbum, propter quod præparativa Vox fuit.
units.tr: The voice of one crying. That is, of the Word. For the Word, says the Gloss, cries out in the voice, that is, Christ cries out in John, so that those who are hard of hearing may perceive it, and those who have dull hearing may feel the greatness of what is said. God also cried out through others, for he cried out in all, says the Gloss, who from the beginning spoke something divinely; and yet John alone is the Voice, because the present Word is found in him, which the others announced from afar. Blessed Epiphanius, in Heresy 69, says that the voice is a preparation for human hearing. For those who call from a distance, calling those who ought to hear something from them, usually first give out an inarticulate sound. And when those others have heard only the sound and have turned their minds to listening and prepared their ears, then the one who gave out the sound goes on to speak distinctly the word he wished to say. So John too was a Voice preparing the ears of men; for he was not himself the Word, but the Word came after him, and for that reason he was a preparatory Voice.

units.la: Parate viam Domini, rectas facite semitas ejus. LXX. Dei nostri. Sensus est idem atque si diceretur, pœnitentiam agite.
units.tr: Make ready the way of the Lord, make straight his paths. Septuagint. Of our God. The sense is the same as if it were said, repent.

units.la: 4. De pilis camelorum. Pilos Camelorum Hebræi vocant גְּמַלִּים[?], lanam camelorum. Pilos camelorum in Caspiis olim fuisse mollißimos, & ex iis confectas vestes ad delicias testatur Ælianus Hist. Lib. 17. cap. 34. & ex Ctefia Persicorum libro decimo refert Apollonius Mirabilium cap. 20. Ita in imperio magni Cham, in urbe Calacia, Metropoli Provinciæ Tanguth, inveniuntur panni, quos Zambilotte vocant, de lana alba & camelorum pilis contexti, quibus vix pulchriores in mundo inveniuntur, ait Paulus Venetus I.I.c.63. Et rursus c. sequenti, ubi de Terra Gog & Magog: Fiunt, inquit, ibi Zambilotti optimi de pilis camelorum. Hujusmodi pannos proprie significat vox Gallica camelot, quamvis sumatur hodie latiùs. Sed camelorum in Caspiis aut in Tartaria villi quàm sunt tenues, tam sunt asperi vulgares, quibus Joannes induebatur. Hinc vestimentum Joannis ab Anselmo & aliis vocatur cilicium camelinum; hinc & Paulinus ille, cujus extat Carmen de Joanne Baptista, elegantèr cecinit:
units.tr: 4. Of camels' hair. The Hebrews call camels' hair [גְּמַלִּים], camel's wool. Aelian, in his Histories, Book 17, chapter 34, testifies that the hair of camels in the Caspian regions was once very soft, and that garments made from it were luxuries. Apollonius, in his Marvels, chapter 20, reports the same from Ctesias, Book 10 of his Persica. So too in the empire of the Great Khan, in the city of Calacia, the metropolis of the province of Tangut, there are cloths, which they call zambelotti, woven of white wool and camels' hair, and hardly more beautiful ones are to be found in the world, says Marco Polo, Book 1, chapter 63. And again, in the following chapter, where he speaks of the land of Gog and Magog: There, he says, the finest zambelotti are made of camels' hair. The French word camelot properly signifies cloth of this kind, although today it is used more widely. But the hair of camels in the Caspian regions or in Tartary, however fine it is, is as coarse as the common kind with which John was clothed. Hence Anselm and others call John's garment a camel-hair shirt; and hence that Paulinus whose poem on John the Baptist survives sang elegantly:

units.la: Vestis erat curvi setis conserta cameliContra luxuriem molles duraret ut artus, Arcereétque graves compunctò copere somnos.
units.tr: The garment was woven of the bristles of the curved camel, so that it might harden his soft limbs against luxury, and keep away heavy sleep by pricking him awake.

units.la: Videtur autem vestis villosa sen cilicina Prophetarum suisse propria, ut videre est in Elia 4. Reg. 1. v. 8. in Esaia, Ef. 20. v. 2. in Pseudo-prophetis Zacha. 13. v. 4.
units.tr: It seems, however, that a rough hair or sackcloth garment was peculiar to the prophets, as can be seen in Elijah (4 Kings 1:8), in Isaiah (Isaiah 20:2), and in the false prophets (Zechariah 13:4).

units.la: Zonam pelliceam. Hiero. ad Demetriadem Ep. 8. Stupebat, inquit, ad conversationem Eliæ & Joannis Baptistæ, quorum uterque Zonâ pelliceâ astrinxit, ac mortificavit lumbos suos.
units.tr: A girdle of skin. Jerome, to Demetrias, Letter 8: He was astonished, he says, at the way of life of Elijah and John the Baptist, each of whom bound his loins with a leather girdle and mortified them.

units.la: Esca autem ejus erat. Supple, tantùm, ex iis quæ dicuntur Matt. 11. & Luc. 7. ubi & Joannes à Christo commendatur ob asperitatem vestitûs.
units.tr: His food, moreover, was. Supply, only, from what is said in Matthew 11 and Luke 7, where John is also commended by Christ for the roughness of his clothing.

units.la: Locusta. In Ebionæorum Evangelio de Joanne legebatur: Cibus ejus erat mel fylvestre sapore manna tanquam lagani in oleo fritto. Ad quem locum B. Epiph. illos asserit hoc sibi proposuisse, ut veritatis sermonem in mendacium mutarent, & αὐτὴ ἀκρίδες πωόμενοι ἐγκρίδες ἐν μέλιτι, ex locustis faceret lagana in melle fritta. Occasione hæc confingendi in eo sumta, quòd ἀκρίδες & ἐγκρίδες sunt voces simillimæ. Atque ut in Evangelio junguntur ἀκρίδες καὶ μέλι, ita de manna dicitur Exod. 16. v. 31. Ejus autem sapor erat ὡς ἐγκρίδες ἐν μέλιτι, ut lagani in melle, sive, cum melle fritti.
units.tr: Locusts. In the Gospel of the Ebionites there was read of John: His food was wild honey, with the taste of manna, like cakes fried in oil. On this passage Blessed Epiphanius asserts that they had this purpose, to change the word of truth into a lie, and that they might make cakes fried in honey out of locusts [αὐτὴ ἀκρίδες πωόμενοι ἐγκρίδες ἐν μέλιτι]. The occasion for this invention was taken from the fact that ἀκρίδες [locusts] and ἐγκρίδες [cakes] are very similar words. And just as in the Gospel locusts and honey [ἀκρίδες καὶ μέλι] are joined together, so of manna it is said in Exodus 16:31 that its taste was like cakes in honey [ὡς ἐγκρίδες ἐν μέλιτι], that is, like cakes fried with honey.

units.la: B. Isidorus Pelusiota lib. 1. Ep. 5. vult ut Monachus à Joanne Baptista edoctus contentus sit herbarum & foliorum extremis ad tenue alimentum. Et Ep. 132. ita mordicus hæret huic interpretationi, ut eois, qui ἀκρίδων nomine locustas intelligunt, ἀφαθῶς, imperitè sentire pronunciet. Pelusiotæ succinit Paulinus in carmine de Joanne Baptista:
units.tr: B. Isidore of Pelusium, book 1, letter 5, wants a monk taught by John the Baptist to be content with the tips of herbs and leaves as a thin diet. In letter 132 he clings so stubbornly to this interpretation that he declares those who take ἀκρίδων [akridōn] to mean locusts to be ἀφαθῶς [aphathōs], imperitè (foolish and inexpert).

units.la: Præcebant victum facilem sylvestria mella Pomaque, & incultis enatæ cautibus herbæ.
units.tr: Wild honey from the woods and fruit gave him an easy food, and herbs sprang up among the rough rocks.

units.la: Ita & Pantaleon Diaconus in Sermone de luminibus sanctis, Theophylactus, Euthymius, & Nicephorus Callistus lib. 1. Hist. c. 14. & superiore seculo Cajetanus. Hoc autorum torrente abreptus Baronius ad annum Domini 31. Quid, inquit, de his sententiam sit, definiendum nobis non est, sed totum relinquimus Lectoris arbitrio; nam constat Græcam ditionem ἀκρίδες, & locustam infecti genus infirmas habentes alas ad volandum, & summitates arborum significare. Verùm pace tanti viri dixero, id neutiquam constare; imo extra dubium esse apud scriptores verè Græcos ἀκρίδας & ἀκρίδυα multùm differre, nec usquam confundi.
units.tr: Pantaleon the Deacon, in his sermon on the holy lights, does the same, as do Theophylact, Euthymius, Nicephorus Callistus (book 1 of his History, ch. 14), and, in the last century, Cajetan. Swept along by this flood of authorities, Baronius, at the year of the Lord 31, writes: "What opinion to hold on this we need not settle, but leave entirely to the reader's judgement; for it is established that the Greek word akrides [ἀκρίδες] signifies a kind of insect, the locust, with weak wings for flying, and also the tops of trees." But with all due respect to so great a man, I say that this is by no means established. Indeed, it is beyond doubt among writers who were truly Greek that akridas [ἀκρίδας] and akridya [ἀκρίδυα] differ greatly and are nowhere confused.

units.la: Alij existimant ἀκρίδας herbas esse, quas etiam, ut ait Theophylactus, melagra vocant, ut alludatur ad μέλι ἀγρίων. Ita & Euthymius. In hac sententia idem sunt mel & locustæ, herbæ scilicet genus aliunde prorsus ignotæ, quæ tamen Joanni pro cibo sola suffecit. Hac sententia nihil absurdius fingi potuit, tamen sectatorem habuit Surianum monachum, à quo eam se didicisse profitetur Jacobus de Vitriaco c. 53. Hist. Jerof. Fortasse etiam Dionysium Carthusianum, qui nonnullos per locustas intelligere scribit herbas deserti, cùm non videatur probabile, quòd Joannes, qui nec pane vescebatur, carnes animalium, aut aliquid coctum comederit. Et Hermolaus in Discoridem Corollario 256. eam herbam ait intelligi, quæ vocatur Arabicè pes locustæ, id est, blitum, ut quidam volunt, aut, ut alij, rapunculum.
units.tr: Others think akrides [ἀκρίδας] are herbs, which, as Theophylact says, are also called melagra, so that there is an allusion to meli agrion [μέλι ἀγρίων], wild honey. Euthymius agrees. On this view honey and locusts are the same thing, a kind of herb otherwise entirely unknown, which nevertheless alone sufficed as John's food. Nothing more absurd could be invented for this opinion, yet it had a follower: the monk Surianus, from whom James of Vitry professes to have learned it (History of Jerusalem, ch. 53). Perhaps Dionysius the Carthusian also belongs here, who writes that some understand by locusts the herbs of the desert, since it does not seem probable that John, who did not even eat bread, ate the flesh of animals or anything cooked. And Hermolaus, in his Corollary on Dioscorides, 256, says that the herb meant is the one called in Arabic pes locustae, that is, blitum, as some want, or, as others say, rapunculum.

units.la: Christianus Druthmarus, qui in Matthæum scripsit nono post Christum seculo, De locustis, inquit, audivi quendam dicere quòd quod ista locusta avicula fuerunt parva cum rubris tibiis. Quibus verbis a Druthmaro fuisse veram avem intellectam patet ex eo quod hujus sententiae authorem refellit: Quare, inquit, laudaretur Joannes de abstinentia rigore, si volatilia ederet, quae desideraverunt Judaei? Eadem ratione refellit eos, qui volunt locustas esse pisces marinos, quos Joannes ex Jordane habuerit, cum ii pisces in deliciis habeantur. Praeterea non in fluviis sed ipso mari has locustas reperire est. Ut taceam locustas marinas a Graecis non dici ἀκρίδες, sed καράβους.
units.tr: Christian Druthmar, who wrote on Matthew in the ninth century after Christ, says: "About the locusts I heard someone say that they were little birds with red legs." From these words it is clear that Druthmar understood a real bird, since he refutes the author of this opinion: "Why," he says, "would John be praised for the rigour of his abstinence if he ate the winged creatures which the Jews longed for?" By the same reasoning he refutes those who want locusts to be sea fish, which John is supposed to have had from the Jordan, since those fish are counted as delicacies. Besides, these locusts are found not in rivers but in the sea itself. I say nothing of the fact that the Greeks do not call sea locusts akrides, but karabous [καράβους].

units.la: Quidam ἀκρίδες in ἀκρίδας, id est, squillas, mutant, quibus nihil in toto cancrorum genere est praestantius. Verum haec sententia perridicula est, cum Joannes in Evangelio ab abstinentia laudetur.
units.tr: Some change akrides into akridas, that is, squills (squillas), of which nothing in the whole crab family is more excellent. But this opinion is very ridiculous, since John is praised in the Gospel for his abstinence.

units.la: Nonnemo conjicit Evangelistas Matthaeum & Marcum scripsisse ἀκρίδ[?], id est, pyra sylvestria, & exigua mutatione hoc nomen deflexum esse in ἀκρίδες. Verum nihil opus est quidquam mutare, cum in receptam lectionem conspirent libri omnes, neque illa quidquam habeat, quo lector eruditus merito possit offendi. Certum enim est locustarum esum in iis quae vel ad Ortum, vel ad Austrum sunt, regionibus fuisse receptissimum, ut testatur B. Hieron. l. 2. in Jovinian. c. 6. & ab Alexandri aevo inter Aethiopum populos Graecia descripsit Acridophagos, a locustarum esu sic dictos, ut videre est apud Agatharchidem lib. 5. c. 27. & Diodorum lib. 3. Strabonem l. 16. Solinum & Plinium l. 6. c. 30. & l. 11. c. 29. & praeter Acridophagos omnibus notos, Nasamones etiam & Leptitanos & Graecos & Hebraeos locustas olim pro cibo habuisse, quomodo Arabes quoque & Numidas & Mauritanos & novos Palaestinae incolas jam inde a multis seculis, fuse probat clarissimus Bochartus Hierozoici p. 1. lib. 4. cap. 7. Lex Mosis Levitic. 11. v. 21. & 22. diserte in eum concedit quatuor locustarum species. Itaque quod locustas edebat Joannes, novum non fuit, nec inauditum, sed hoc in illo fuit singulare, quod in deserto solum locustis & agresti melle vescebatur, iisque forte oblatis, nec aliunde comparatis, ut virum illum Judaei scirent extraordinarium habere munus & attentiores essent ad ejus conciones. Quid autem sint hujusmodi locustae egregie explicat & describit venerabilis Beda De locis sanctis cap. 14. ubi tradit se accepisse a sancto Episcopo Archulpho, qui ad ea loca, peregrinatus erat, notissimas esse locustas in Palaestina, quae corpusculis in modum digiti manus exiguis & brevibus, in herbis facile captae, coctaque oleo pauperem victum parent. Euthymius etiam in Matth. ait usque ad hodiernum diem in illis par-tibus tibus plerosque illud infecti genus edere fumo siccatum: habere autem gravem odorem, malúmque gustum. Causa igitur non fuit cur Pelufiotes eos accusaret imperitiæ, qui locustas apud Evangelistas intelligunt, in quo numero multi fuerunt Sancti Ecclesiæ Doctores celeberrimi, ut Theophilus Antiochenus, Hilarius & Chrysost. in Matth. Ambro. in Luc. Clemens Alex. l. 2. Paedag. Hieron. l. 2. in Jovin. & Epist. 23. ad Marcellam. August. l. 10. Conf. c. 31. Scriptores denique quotquot sunt Pelusiote vetustiores, praeter unicum Paulinum in sacro Poëmate de Joanne Baptista, cui opponimus vetustiores Poëtas aliter sentientes; ita enim de Joanne Juvencus lib. 1. Hist. Evang.
units.tr: Some conjecture that the evangelists Matthew and Mark wrote akrid[?], that is, wild pears (pyra sylvestria), and that by a slight change this word was altered into akrides. But there is no need to change anything, since all the books agree on the accepted reading, and it contains nothing at which a learned reader could justly take offence. For it is certain that eating locusts was most widely accepted in the regions to the east and south, as St Jerome testifies (book 2 against Jovinian, ch. 6). From Alexander's time Greek writers described the Acridophagi, the "locust-eaters," among the peoples of Ethiopia, so called from their eating locusts, as can be seen in Agatharchides (book 5, ch. 27), Diodorus (book 3), Strabo (book 16), Solinus, and Pliny (book 6, ch. 30, and book 11, ch. 29). Besides the Acridophagi, who are known to everyone, the Nasamones, the Leptitani, the Greeks and the Hebrews also once had locusts for food, as the distinguished Bochart fully proves (Hierozoicon, part 1, book 4, ch. 7). So too have Arabs, Numidians and Mauritanians, and the recent inhabitants of Palestine for many centuries. The law of Moses (Lev. 11. vv. 21 and 22) expressly allows four kinds of locust. So John's eating locusts was not new or unheard of. What was singular in him was that in the desert he lived only on locusts and wild honey, and those things by chance offered to him, not bought elsewhere, so that the Jews would know that this man had an extraordinary office and would be more attentive to his sermons. What such locusts are is admirably explained and described by the venerable Bede (On the Holy Places, ch. 14), where he writes that he had it from the holy Bishop Arculf, who had travelled to those places, that "locusts, very well known in Palestine, which are easily caught in the herbs, have small short bodies like a finger of the hand, and when cooked in oil provide a poor meal." Euthymius also says, on Matthew, that to this very day in those parts most people eat that kind of insect, dried in smoke; that it has a strong smell and a bad taste. So there was no reason for Pelusiota to accuse of ignorance those who understand locusts in the Evangelists. Among these were many most celebrated saints and teachers of the Church: Theophilus of Antioch, Hilary and Chrysostom on Matthew, Ambrose on Luke, Clement of Alexandria (book 2, Paedagogus), Jerome (book 2 against Jovinian, and letter 23 to Marcella), and Augustine (Confessions, book 10, ch. 31). Finally, all the older writers, apart from the single Paulinus in his sacred poem on John the Baptist, whom we set against the older poets who think otherwise, since Juvencus writes of John thus in book 1 of his Evangelical History:

units.la: Arvis qui solitus ruralibus esse locustas.
units.tr: Who was used to have locusts from the rural fields as his food.

units.la: Prudentius Cathemerinon Hymno septimo: Parvum locustis & favorum agrestium Liquore pastum corpori suetus dare.
units.tr: Prudentius, in hymn 7 of the Cathemerinon: Accustomed to give a small body fed on locusts and on the liquid of wild honeycombs.

units.la: Et Amoenus in Enchiridio: Perfundit fluvio pastus Baptista locustis.
units.tr: And Amoenus in his Enchiridion: The Baptist, fed on locusts, bathes himself in the river.

units.la: Paulus Diaconus in Hymno de Nativitate Sancti Joannis Baptistæ: Præbuit hirtum tegimen Camelus Artubus sacris, strophium bidentes. Cui latex haustum sociata pastum Mella locustis.
units.tr: Paulus Diaconus, in his hymn on the Nativity of St John the Baptist: The camel gave a shaggy covering to the holy limbs, and the sheep a girdle. To him water, joined with drink, gave honey with locusts as food.

units.la: Mel. Mellis duo sunt genera, domesticum unum ex apibus, quæ domi aluntur, & alterum sylvestre, quali dicitur hic, &Marc. 1. v. 6. Joannes vixisse. Vult autem Theophylactus secundum quosdam Mel sylvestre hîc non esse verum Mel, sed herbas esse acridas, quas etiam melagra vocant; sed repugnat quod Græcè scribitur hîc μέλι ἄγριον. Nihilo magis placet quod afferunt Beda in lib. De locis sanctis & Thomas in Matth. ex Arnulpho, vel Arculpho, in deserto Joannis arbores fuisse latis & rotundis foliis, laćtei coloris & mellei saporis, quæ naturâ fragilia manibus confricentur, atque edantur, & hoc dici mel sylvestre. Nec Christiano Druthmaro assentior, cui mel sylvestre hoc loco est illud ipsum manna, quo filij Israel pasti sunt per quadraginta annos. Mannæ quidem sapor fuit, ut dicitur Exod. 16. v. 3. quasi similæ cum melle, unde à nonnullis manna vocabatur. & ἀερόμελι. Tamen aliud manna, aliud sylvestre mel, nec Scripturæ vocibus notiones sunt affingendæ novæ, cùm receptæ quadrare possunt. In præsenti igitur versiculo nihil aliud intelligimus, quàm locustas & mel sylvestre. Et locustas jam probavimus in illis locis esse frequentes, adeoque in cibis receptas. Idem de sylvestri melle ex ipsa Scriptura probare est obvium. Notum est illud Salomonis Proverb. 26. v. 16. Mel invenisti, comede quod sufficit tibi, ne forte satiatus evomas illud; quod haud dubie pertinet ad sylvestre mel, quod in agris passim reperiebatur. Ita cùm in agro Samson in leonem incidisset, eùmque dilacerasset, anno sequenti mel reperit, quod in ejus cadavere apes elaboraverant, Judic. 14. v, 8. Quale est quod legitur. 1 Reg. 14. v. 25. & 26. Vulgus venit in saltum, id est, in sylvam, in quo erat mel super faciem agri. Ingressus est itaque populus saltum & apparuit fluens mel, &c. Sequitur autem ibi v. 27. de Jonatha, qui in eadem sylva extendit summitatem virgæ, quam habebat in manu, & intinxit in favum mellis. Hinc favus mellis sæpe in Scriptura appellatur Hebraicè יַעַר, quod proprie sylvam significat. Scriptores prophani idem de Scythia & Moscovia testantur, nimirum quòd apes passim in agris aut sylvis ibi mellificent; & Maldonatus refert se pauperes homines in Bœtica vidisse, qui mel ex sylvis colligerent, eóque vendendo quæstum facilitarent. Idem videre est, apud Poëtas tum Græcos, tum Latinos. Virgilius enim lib. 4. Georg. ut alios amittam, disertè testatur apes in cavis arborum, vel in arundinetis, aut in antris nidificare. Tanta autem erat abundantia mellis in Judæa, ut passim dicatur melle fluere, torrentes mellis habere, favos distillare, &c. Videtur autem B. Isidoro Pelusiotæ Epist. 132. & Euthymio mel sylvestre, quo usus est Joannes, fuisse amarum & gustui prorsus ingratum; sed gratis hæc dicuntur, nec Scripturæ satis consonant, quæ Judæam à melle non tantoperè commendaret, si mel in ejus agris proveniens insuave & amarum esset; tradit quidem Dioscorides lib. 2. Galenus lib. 7. De simplici facultate medicamentorum, & Diodorus lib. 5. in certis locis mel amarum progenerari, puta Sardoum & Corsicum, sive causa sit in absinthio, quod depascantur apes, sive id à buxo fiat, quæ in Corsica plurima est, sive à taxis, ut suadere videtur Virgilius Eclogâ 5. sive à cicutæ pastu, ut Ovidius testatur Elegiâ 12. lib. 1. Amorum, sine à thymis mali saporis, ut docet Martialis, lib. 11. Epigramate 13. Similiter Plinius, Dioscorides, Aristoteles & multi alii meminere mellis venenati, quod comedentes ad insaniam adigit; at in Judæa mel amarum, aut ulla ex parte vitiosum gigni, ne per sommium quidem auditum est. Quin Genef. 43. mel est ex iis, quæ in Terra Chanaan laudantur & decantantur, & blasphemus ille Rabsaces Assyriam ex eo commendat, quòd instar Terræ Chanaan oleæ sit & mellis ferax 4 Reg. c. 18. v. 32. Unde mel è Judæa in alias terras deferebatur, ut ad Tyriorum nundinas Ezechiel. 27. v. 17. & in Ægyptum Gen. 43. v. 11. quamvis ipsa etiam Ægyptus melle abundasse legatur Numer. 16. v. 13. Nec est quòd quis hæc sibi fingat non nisi de domestico melle dici. Agrestè enim fuit mel illud, cujus dulcedinem Samson tam illustribus verbis deprædicavit Judic. 14. v. 14. & mel aliud, quo degustato, Jonathæ oculi aperti sunt 1 Reg. 14. v. 24. Agrestè etiam erat mel petræ, id est, ex petrarum fissuris manans, in quibus feræ apes mellificabant; tamen id censetur in deliciis, quas populo suo Deus obtulit, Deut. 31. & Psal. 80. Itaque tam in sylvestri, quàm in domestico melle fuit, quod palato placeret; at in B. Joanne Baptista magnæ id fuit abstinentiæ, quòd solis locustis & melle sylvestri vixerit: quia ut in locustis, ita etiam in melle parùm est alimenti, cum solùm & per se sumitur; nam ut testatur Hippocrates c. 50. de affectionibus: Τὸ μέλι, ξλω ἐτέρως ἐξιδύωον, καὶ τριγεί, καὶ ἀυχγοίαι ποιεῖ. Αὐτὸ δὲ ἑαυτῷ λεπτύνει μᾶλλον, ἢ κομίζει. Mel cum alii quidem comestum, & nutrit, & bonum colorem exhibet; ipsum autem per se ipsum magis attenuat, quàm reficit. Ariftoxeni Cyrenæi Philosophi abstinentiam ex eo celebrant Veteres, quòd lactucam in horto sub vesperam mulso irrigatam vesperè & manè fumens, dicebat se flavas habere placentas; Pythagoræ verò, quòd tam frugaliter viveret, ut sæpe solo melle contentus esset. Sed utrumque longè superat Joannes. Ariftoxenus enim melli vinum & lactucam addebat, à quibus abstinuit Joannes; & Pythagoras sæpè quidem, non tamen semper solo melle contentus fuit, & ut Laertius testatur, vinum, licet non interdiu, ad vesperam tamen gustabat. Præterea hi cibis emtis, Joannes forte fortuna oblatis vescebatur, Dei providentia ita fretus, ut in deserto ex ea sola penderet etiam in ipsis vitæ necessariis, inter quæ recensetur mel Eccli. c. 39. v. 41. quod etiam puerile alimentum censetnr in illo celebri Esaiæ loco c.7. v.15. ubi Emmanuel dicitur butyrum & mel comesturus: Ac si dicat, inquit Bern. Serm. 2. de Adv. Parvulus erit & infantilibus vescetur cibis. Addit Esaias ibid. Ut sciat reprobare malum & eligere bonum. Id est, donec fiat paulò adultior, seu, ut adolescat. Inde est, quòd in Baptismo, in quo fideles renascuntur, lac & mel prægustandum dabant Veteres. Tert. de corona militis c. 3. Inde suscepti lactis & melli concordiam prægustamus. Quò alludens B. Hier. adversus Luciferianos c.4. è lavacro egressos dicit lactis & melli prægustare concordiam ad infantiæ significationem; neque enim solo lacte, sed melle tum alebantur infantes. Sic ex antiquissimis Cretensium Historijs narrat Didymus Meliffea Cretensium Regem duas habuisse filias, Amaltheam & Melissam, quæ Jovem puerum caprino lacte & melle nutrierint. Vide Lactantium lib.1. De falsa religione c. 22. &c.
units.tr: Honey. There are two kinds of honey: the domestic kind, from bees that are kept in hives, and the wild kind, which is the kind meant here, since John is said to have lived on it, Mark 1.6. Theophylact, following some writers, holds that wild honey here is not real honey but a bitter herb that some call melagra. But this does not fit the Greek, which here reads wild honey [μέλι ἄγριον]. No more do I approve of what Bede in his book On the Holy Places and Thomas in his commentary on Matthew, following Arnulphus (or Arculphus), report: that in John's desert there were trees with broad, round leaves, of a milky colour and honeyed taste, which are brittle and are crushed in the hands and eaten, and that this is called wild honey. Nor do I agree with Druthmar the Christian, who takes wild honey in this place to be that very manna on which the children of Israel were fed for forty years. Manna did indeed have a taste, as Exodus 16.3 says, like wafers made with honey, and for this reason some called it manna and [ἀερόμελι]. Yet manna is one thing and wild honey another, and new meanings should not be attached to the words of Scripture when the accepted ones fit. In the present verse, then, we understand nothing other than locusts and wild honey. We have already shown that locusts were common in those regions and so were accepted as food. The same about wild honey may easily be proved from Scripture itself. Solomon's saying in Proverbs 26.16 is well known: You have found honey; eat what is enough for you, lest perhaps being satiated you vomit it up. This undoubtedly refers to wild honey, which was found everywhere in the fields. So when Samson had met a lion in a field and torn it apart, he found honey the following year in its carcass, which bees had made there, Judges 14.8. Similar is what we read in 1 Kings 14.25-26: The people came into the forest, that is, into a wood, in which there was honey upon the face of the field. So the people entered the forest, and behold the honey was flowing, etc. There follows in verse 27 the account of Jonathan, who in the same wood put forth the tip of the rod which he had in his hand and dipped it in the honeycomb. Hence a honeycomb is often called in Scripture by the Hebrew word [יַעַר], which properly means a wood. Profane writers attest the same of Scythia and Muscovy: that bees there make honey everywhere in fields and woods. Maldonatus reports that he saw poor men in Baetica who gathered honey from the woods and so made a living by selling it. The same can be seen in the poets, both Greek and Latin. For Virgil in the fourth book of the Georgics, to pass over others, clearly states that bees nest in hollow trees, or in reed beds, or in caves. Moreover, there was such abundance of honey in Judea that it is said everywhere to flow with honey, to have streams of honey, to drip with honeycombs, and so on. Yet Isidore of Pelusium (Letter 132) and Euthymius seem to think that the wild honey on which John lived was bitter and utterly unpleasant to taste. But these things are said without warrant, and they do not agree well with Scripture, which would not so highly commend Judea for honey if the honey produced in its fields were insipid and bitter. Dioscorides (book 2), Galen (book 7, On the Simple Faculties of Medicines) and Diodorus (book 5) do indeed report that bitter honey is produced in certain places, such as Sardinia and Corsica, whether the cause is the wormwood on which the bees feed, or the box tree, which is very abundant in Corsica, or the yew, as Virgil seems to suggest in Eclogue 5, or feeding on hemlock, as Ovid attests in Elegy 12 of book 1 of the Amores, or thyme of bad flavour, as Martial teaches in book 11, epigram 13. Likewise Pliny, Dioscorides, Aristotle and many others mention poisonous honey, which drives those who eat it to madness. But that bitter honey, or honey vitiated in any way, is produced in Judea has never been heard of, not even in a dream. Indeed, in Genesis 43.11 honey is among the things praised and celebrated in the land of Canaan, and that blasphemer Rabshakeh recommends Assyria on the ground that it is like the land of Canaan, abounding in olive oil and honey, 4 Kings 18.32. Hence honey was carried from Judea to other lands, as to the markets of Tyre in Ezekiel 27.17 and to Egypt in Genesis 43.11, although Egypt itself is also read to have abounded in honey, Numbers 16.13. Nor should anyone imagine that these things refer only to domestic honey. For that honey was wild whose sweetness Samson praised in such striking words, Judges 14.14, and the other honey, which when tasted opened Jonathan's eyes, 1 Kings 14.24, was also wild. Wild too was the honey of the rock, that is, flowing from the clefts of rocks, where wild bees made honey; yet this is counted among the delights which God offered to his people, Deuteronomy 31 and Psalm 80. So both wild honey and domestic honey were such as pleased the palate. But in St. John the Baptist it was a great abstinence that he lived only on locusts and wild honey; for, as in locusts, so also in honey there is little nourishment when it is taken alone and by itself. For as Hippocrates testifies in chapter 50 of On Affections: Honey, when mixed with other foods, both nourishes and gives a good colour; but taken by itself it rather thins the body than restores it [Τὸ μέλι, ξλω ἐτέρως ἐξιδύωον, καὶ τριγεί, καὶ ἀυχγοίαι ποιεῖ. Αὐτὸ δὲ ἑαυτῷ λεπτύνει μᾶλλον, ἢ κομίζει]. The ancients praise the abstinence of Aristoxenus the Cyrenaean philosopher, because, eating lettuce watered with mulsum in his garden at evening and in the morning, he said that he had yellow cakes; and that of Pythagoras, because he lived so frugally that he was often content with honey alone. But John far surpasses both. For Aristoxenus added wine and lettuce to his honey, from which John abstained; and Pythagoras, though often content with honey alone, was not always so, and, as Laertius attests, he tasted wine in the evening, though not during the day. Moreover, these men ate bought food, whereas John ate what was offered to him by chance, relying so much on the providence of God that in the desert he depended on this alone even for the necessities of life. Among these necessities honey is counted in Ecclesiasticus 39.41; and in the famous passage of Isaiah 7.15 it is considered childish food, where Immanuel is said to eat butter and honey. As if he were to say, says Bernard in Sermon 2 On Advent, He will be little and will feed on infants' food. Isaiah adds in the same place: That he may know to refuse evil and choose good. That is, until he grows somewhat older, or, as it were, comes to maturity. Hence it is that in Baptism, in which the faithful are born again, the ancients gave milk and honey to be tasted beforehand. Tertullian, On the Crown of the Soldier, chapter 3: Thence, having been received, we taste beforehand the harmony of milk and honey. Alluding to this, St. Jerome in his book against the Luciferians, chapter 4, says that those who come up from the bath taste beforehand the harmony of milk and honey, to signify infancy; for infants were then nourished not by milk alone but also by honey. So too Didymus Meliseus, in his very ancient history of the Cretans, relates that the king of the Cretans had two daughters, Amalthea and Melissa, who nursed the boy Jupiter with goat's milk and honey. See Lactantius, On False Religion, book 1, chapter 22, etc.

units.la: 5. Judæa. Scilicet, strictè sumta, quæ est sexta pars earum, in quas ætate Christi divisa erat Judæa latè sumta, quæ aliàs Terra Sancta, Terra Chanaan, Terra Promissionis, Terra Israel & Palæstina dicitur.
units.tr: 5. Judaea. That is, taken strictly, it is the sixth part of those divisions into which Judaea was split in the age of Christ. Taken broadly, it is otherwise called the Holy Land, the Land of Canaan, the Land of Promise, the Land of Israel and Palestine.

units.la: 6. Baptizabantur. Sylvester Sguropulus in Historia Concilii Florentini Sect. 9. Cap. 9. Narrat a Gregorio Hieromonacho Alexandrinæ Ecclesiæ primicerio, & Philothei Patriarchæ ad Florentinam Synodum Vicario atque Legato cum Petro quodam Calabrico in disputationem incidente de Baptismo, Latinos redargutos quòd per regenerationis lavacrum non essent rite initiati Christianæ religioni, cùm baptismatis vox non significet ut more Latinorum aqua in alicujus caput affatim effundatur, sed ut quis in fluentem descendat, & ascendat immersus undis. Certè mersatione baptizandi consuetudo ab Apostolis derivata est,ut indicant loca ad eum ritum delecta, Joan.3.v.23.&Act.8.v.28. & allusiones multæ Apostolorum, quæ ad effusionem vel aspersionem referrinon possunt, Rom. 6. v. 3, & 4. Col. 2. v. 12. Nec est quod quis miretur ab Apostolo Petro baptizari potuisse una die tria hominum millia per immersionem, siquidem Gregorius Armenorum Apostolus una die duodecim millia baptizavit in Euphrate per immersionem, ut habetur in authentica ejus vita, et confirmat Isaac ejusdem gentis Patriarcha in prima Invectiva. Serius nec nisi circa Clementis v. pontificis Romani morem invaluisse, ut etiam extra necessitatem et mortis periculum baptismus daretur per aspersionem, seu perfusionem, patet ex Synodo II. apud Ravennam sub eodem Clemente celebrata. Terrere ergo Michael Cerularius Cp. Patriarcha ritum baptizandi sine immersione Latinis tribuit, cum ipsius ætate nusquam omnino receptus fuerit mos aliter baptizandi quam per immersionem extra casum necessitatis, ut constat vel ex Petro Damiani lib 6. Ep. 25. qui Petrus Damiani fuit Cerulario æqualis. Imo et sub finem sæculi duodecimi Alexandro, III. R. P. in Synodo Casselensi apud Hibernos celebrata decretum est, ut testatur Regerius Hovedenius, ut pueri deferrentur ad Ecclesiam, et ibi baptizarentur in aqua munda sub trina mersione. Verum, ut optime monuit Cyprianus in Epistola LXXVI. ad Magnum baptismapotius est mentis per fidem, quam corporis per aquam lavacrum, ei[?]que solum invisibilis lautionis visibile symbolum, ideoque sola aspersione seu perfusione compleri potest.
units.tr: 6. Baptizabantur. Sylvester Syropulus, in his History of the Council of Florence, Section 9, Chapter 9, relates that Gregory, a hieromonk, first priest of the Alexandrian Church, and vicar and legate of Patriarch Philotheus to the Synod of Florence, got into a dispute about baptism with a certain Peter of Calabria. The Latins were refuted because they had not been properly initiated into the Christian religion through the bath of regeneration, since the word for baptism does not mean, as the Latins practise it, pouring water abundantly over someone's head, but going down into a flowing stream and coming up immersed in its waves.
