Certainly the custom of baptizing by immersion came down from the Apostles, as the places chosen for that rite show (John 3:23 and Acts 8:28), and as the many allusions of the Apostles show, which cannot refer to pouring or sprinkling (Rom. 6:3-4; Col. 2:12). Nor is there any reason for wonder that the Apostle Peter could have baptized three thousand people in one day by immersion. For Gregory, Apostle of the Armenians, baptized twelve thousand in the Euphrates in one day by immersion, as is recorded in his authentic life, and Isaac, Patriarch of the same people, confirms it in his first Invective. Later, and not until the time of Pope Clement V, the custom became established of giving baptism by sprinkling or pouring even outside necessity and danger of death. This is clear from the Second Synod at Ravenna, celebrated under the same Clement. Therefore Michael Cerularius, Patriarch of Constantinople, wrongly attributed to the Latins the rite of baptizing without immersion. In his own age the custom of baptizing other than by immersion, outside a case of necessity, had nowhere at all been received. This is clear even from Peter Damian, Letter 25 of Book 6, and Peter Damian was a contemporary of Cerularius. Indeed, near the end of the twelfth century, under Pope Alexander III, it was decreed at the Synod of Cashel celebrated among the Irish, as Roger of Hoveden testifies, that children should be brought to the Church and baptized there in clean water with threefold immersion. Yet, as Cyprian admirably observed in Letter 76 to Magnus, baptism is more a washing of the mind through faith than of the body through water. It is only the visible symbol of an invisible cleansing, and therefore it can be completed by sprinkling or pouring alone.

units.la: Jordanem. Jordanis est fluvius maximus & pene unicus totius Judææ, seu Terræ Israel, cum reliqui omnes potius torrentes, quàm fluvij sint dicendi. Oritur autem ad radices montis Libani, & habet duos fontes, ut lib. 3. in Matth. testatur B. Hieron. unum nomine Jor & alterum Dan, qui simul mixti Jordanis nomen efficiunt. Idem B. Hieron. lib. 8. in Ezechielem, & in libro De locis Hebraicis insinuat Jordanem dici quasi יַרְדֵּן, rivus Dan, quod scilicet fluvius ille erumpat a vīculo Dan in quarto a Panæade milliario euntibus Tyrum, qui usque hodie Dan vocatur, terminus Judææ provinciæ contra Septentrionem. Habet autem Jordanis duos lacus diversæ omnino naturæ, ut testatur Joseph. lib. 5. De bello Judaico c. 4. nempe lacum Asphaltiten, quem Josephus appellat ἀσφαλτ, id est, sterilem, eò quòd piscibus careat, imo ut testatur Hieron. in Ezechiel. 47. Si Jordanes auctus imbribus pisces illuc influens repuerit, statim moriuntur, & pinguibus aquis supernatant. Unde Ezechiel c. 47. v. 8. Evangelij vim vivificam figuratis verbis adumbraturus prædicit fore ut aliquando hæ aquæ salubres & piscosæ fiant. Quàm autem salsus & sterilis lacus Asphaltites, tam dulcis est & fœcundus alter juxta eundem Jordanem lacus Tiberiadensis, quem Evangelistæ vocant Mare Tiberiadis, Galilææ, & lacum Genezareth. Ad hujus lacus oram Bethsaida piscatione fuit celebris; quod & ipsum Urbis nomen & Apostolorum historia palàm indicat. Quin & ad Jordanis fontes tertius fuit lacus longus sexaginta stadia, latus triginta, quem a situ Josue Cap. 11. appellat aquas Merom, q. d. aquas superiores: Et Josephus Antiq. 1. 5. c. 4. & 1. 3. De bello Jud. c. 18. Σεμαχωνῖτις, vel Σεμιχωνῖτις λίμνην, q. d. piscosum lacum: Haud dubie ab ubertate piscium. Nempe Samachon vel Semechon Arabicè est piscis. Indidem Semechonitæ populi l. 4. Bell. Jud. c. 1. & regio Semechonitis l. 3. c. 2. ubi Peræam ad ortum terminari dicit Josephus Arabiá & Semechonitide, ubi perperam legitur in exemplaribus Græcis Σιμωνιτῖδι, & in versione, Silbonitide. Hinc passim Chaldæus Arabiæ nomen reddit סוֹמְכוֹנִית, ut videre est 3. Reg. 10. v. 15. & Jerem. 25. v. 20. & Ezech. 30. v. 15. Hinc corrigendum est quod legitur apud Kimchium in Psal. 24. enumerantem septem Maria Terræ Chanaan, סוּכְנִי מְא, quod eruditissimus Kimchij interpres Latinus Domnus Ambrosius Janvier Congregationis S. Mauri Monachus Benedictinus transtulit mare Sicaniæ. Omninò enim legendum יםמכנית ימא, Mare Semechonites, quod est lacus Samachonites, qui cùm fit in ipsis Jordanis fontibus, in enumerationis ordine præponitur à Kimchio ibidem Mari Tiberiadis, quod est in Jordanis medio, sicut & Mare Tiberiadis præponitur ab eodem ibidem Mari Salinarum,seu lacui Asphaltiti ,qui est in extremo Jordanis, & vocatur à Geographo Nubiensi clm. 3. part. 5. Mare Mortuum, Quia, inquit, in eo nihil est animatum, non piscis, neque reptile, neque aliud quicquam eorum, quæ generari moris est in aquis stagnantibus, aut currentibus.
units.tr: Jordanem. The Jordan is the largest and almost the only river of all Judaea, or the Land of Israel. All the others should rather be called torrents than rivers. It rises at the foot of Mount Lebanon and has two sources, as Saint Jerome testifies in Book 3 on Matthew: one called Jor and the other Dan, which, mixed together, make up the name Jordan. The same Saint Jerome, in Book 8 on Ezekiel and in his book On the Hebrew Places, suggests that the Jordan is called, as it were, יַרְדֵּן, the stream of Dan. This is because that river bursts forth from the village of Dan, which lies on the road from Paneas to Tyre four miles away, and which to this day is called Dan. It is the northern boundary of the province of Judaea. The Jordan has two lakes of entirely different nature, as Josephus testifies in Book 5 of The Jewish War, chapter 4. One is the Lake Asphaltites, which Josephus calls asphaltos [ἀσφαλτ], that is, barren, because it lacks fish. Indeed, as Jerome testifies on Ezekiel 47, if the Jordan, swollen by rains, flows in there and brings fish, they die at once and float on the heavy waters. Hence Ezekiel, in chapter 47, verse 8, prophesying in figurative words, foretells the life-giving power of the Gospel, that these waters will one day become healthful and full of fish. But as salt and barren as the Lake Asphaltites is, the other lake beside the same Jordan, the Lake of Tiberias, is sweet and fruitful. The Evangelists call it the Sea of Tiberias, of Galilee, and the Lake of Gennesaret. Bethsaida was famous for fishing on the shore of this lake, as the very name of the town and the history of the Apostles plainly show. Moreover, near the sources of the Jordan lay a third lake, sixty stadia long and thirty wide. From its position Joshua, chapter 11, calls it the waters of Merom, that is, the upper waters. Josephus, in Antiquities 5.4 and in The Jewish War 3.18, calls it the Semachonitid or Semichonitid lake, that is, the fish-rich lake, undoubtedly from the abundance of fish. For Samachon or Semechon means fish in Arabic. From the same root come the Semechonites, a people (War 4.1), and the region of Semechonitis (War 3.2), where Josephus says Perea ends to the east at Arabia and Semechonitis. Here the Greek copies wrongly read Simonitis, and the Latin version reads Silbonitis. Thus the Chaldee paraphrast everywhere renders the name Arabia as סוֹמְכוֹנִית, as may be seen in 1 Kings 10:15, Jeremiah 25:20 and Ezekiel 30:5. Hence what is read in Kimchi on Psalm 24, where he lists the seven seas of the land of Canaan, סוּכְנִי מְא, must be corrected. The learned Latin translator of Kimchi, Dom Ambrose Janvier, a Benedictine monk of the Congregation of Saint Maur, rendered it mare Sicaniae. But it must surely be read יםמכנית ימא, Mare Semechonites, which is the Lake Semachonites. Since it lies at the very sources of the Jordan, Kimchi, in the same list, places it before the Sea of Tiberias, which is in the middle of the Jordan. In the same way, the same author places the Sea of Tiberias before the Mare Salinarum, or Lake Asphaltites, which is at the lower end of the Jordan and which the Nubian geographer, in Part 5 of Chapter 3, calls Mare Mortuum, the Dead Sea. Because, he says, nothing living is in it, neither fish nor reptile nor anything else of the kind that customarily arises in stagnant or running waters.

units.la: Confitentes peccata sua. Id est, profitebantur se peccatores, & in signum quod pœnitentes essent, offerebant se abluendos à Joanne tanquam exterior ablutio esset quædam professio pœnitentiæ, & mundæ deinceps vitæ ducendæ, inquit vere ad hunc locum Cardinalis Cajetanus. Nam confiteri peccata sua ab Hebræis dicuntur, qui se modis omnibus peccatores esse profitentur, & veniam à Dei misericordia petunt, ut Dan. 9. v. 3; & seq. Quo sensu & Levit. 16. v. 21. jubetur summus Pontifex confiteri peccata totius Israelis. Erroneè autem hoc loco in priori hujus commentarii editione confessionis auricularis necessitatem stabilire conatus sum autoritate Basilii, et Leonis magni, cùm Basilius de Sacramentali confessione hodie Romanensibus præcepta, ne somniaverit quidem, sed volenti propter Dei timorem apud homines erubescere, autor est ut non omnibus, aut quibusvis aperiat peccata sua, sed iis dumtaxat, quibus credita est dispensatio mysteriorum Dei; his enim sinceritas pœnitentiæ nostræ debet esse nota, in quantum fragilitas humana posse finit, & ab iisdem consilium levationemque petere debemus. Hoc Reg. Brev. Interrog. 229. probat exemplo corporis, cujus vitia non aperimus nisi iis, qui rationem ea curandi non ignorant. Et Interrog. 288. idem probat exemplo eorum, qui hîc Joannis & Act. 19. v. 18. Apostolis, à quibus baptizabantur, antequam iis baptismus daretur, confitebantur peccata sua. Leo quoque Ep. 80. receptam à veteribus consuetudinem publicæ exomologesis in cœtu Ecclesiastico removet, declarans sufficere reatus conscientiarum indicari solis sacerdotibus. Verè itaque Rhenanus in Admonit. de Tertul. Dogmatis ait; De secreta confessione, tanquam de ea, quæ præcepta fuerit, qui loquantur, inter veteres, haud temerè reperies.
units.tr: Confitentes peccata sua. That is, they professed themselves sinners, and to show that they were penitent, they offered themselves to be washed by John, as if the outward washing were a kind of profession of repentance and of a clean life to be led afterwards, as Cardinal Cajetan rightly says on this passage. For the Hebrews are said to confess their sins when they profess in every way that they are sinners and seek pardon from the mercy of God, as in Daniel 9:3 ff. In this sense also, Leviticus 16:21 orders the High Priest to confess the sins of all Israel. In the earlier edition of this commentary, however, I wrongly tried to establish the necessity of auricular confession at this point, on the authority of Basil and Leo the Great. Basil, in his Shorter Rules, does not even dream of the sacramental confession now prescribed by the Romanists. Rather, he advises someone who, out of fear of God, wishes to be ashamed before men, not to reveal his sins to everyone or to just anyone, but only to those to whom the dispensation of the mysteries of God has been entrusted. For to these, he says, the sincerity of our repentance ought to be known, so far as human frailty allows, and from them we ought to seek counsel and relief. He proves this in Shorter Rules, Question 229, by the example of the body, whose ills we disclose only to those who know how to cure them. In Question 288 he proves the same by the example of those who here confessed their sins to John, and in Acts 19:18 to the Apostles, by whom they were baptized, before baptism was given to them. Leo also, in Letter 80, removes the custom received from the ancients of public exomologesis in the ecclesiastical assembly, declaring that it is enough for the guilt of conscience to be disclosed to the priests alone. Thus Rhenanus, in his Admonition on Tertullian's Dogma, rightly says: You will not rashly find among the ancients those who speak of secret confession as if it were a commanded thing.

units.la: 7. Videns autem, &c. Quomodo non pugnat cum hoc loco, quod scribit Lucas Cap. 7. Pharisæos & Legisperitos consilium Dei sprevisse in semetipsos, non baptizatos à Joanne? Quamvis enim fortasse non ex animo ut vitam corrigerent in melius, ( ut qui sibi prae aliis justi videbantur ) sed magis ut populo suum pietatis studium venditarent, plerique eorum ad Joannem baptizandi accesserint : verè tamen ab eo multos Pharisaeorum baptizatos, hic Evangelista testatur; quod negare videtur Lucas. An dicendum Lucam loqui non de omnibus Pharisaeis & Legisperitis, sed de multis, & maximè de iis, qui, Christo ea, quae Lucas ibi commemorat, in Joannis commendationem dicente, praesentes aderant? Neque enim pugnant haec duo, multos Pharisaeorum fuisse à Joanne baptizatos, atque item multos eorum à Joanne non fuisse baptizatos. Potest & sic exponi quod dicit Lucas; Pharisaei, & Legisperiti, qui à Joanne baptizati non fuerunt, spreverunt consilium Dei in semetipsos. Quâ expositione non dicitur, multine fuerint an pauci, sed tantum significatur aliquos fuisse.
units.tr: 7. Videns autem, &c. How does this passage agree with what Luke writes in chapter 7, that the Pharisees and lawyers rejected God's counsel against themselves, since they were not baptized by John? For although many of the Pharisees perhaps came to John to be baptized, not sincerely, in order to amend their lives (since they seemed righteous before others), but rather to display their zeal for piety before the people, this Evangelist nevertheless testifies that many of the Pharisees were baptized by him, which Luke seems to deny. Should we say that Luke speaks not of all Pharisees and lawyers but of many, and especially of those who were present when Christ spoke the words Luke records there in commendation of John? For these two statements do not conflict: that many Pharisees were baptized by John, and likewise that many of them were not baptized by him. Luke's words can also be explained this way: the Pharisees and lawyers who were not baptized by John rejected God's counsel against themselves. By this explanation it is not said whether there were many or few, but only that some were.

units.la: Pharisaeorum. Pharisaei dicti videntur B. Hieron. à פרש ecundum Fungerum à פרש Paras divisit; melius Epiphanius initio Panarij à פרש Parasch separavit; dicunter enim Hebraicè פרושים, separati, quasi suo vivendi modo à ceteris segregati. Conslat autem ex Josephi decimo tertio antiquitatum c. 9. & 18. jam inde à tempore Machabaeorum sectas Pharisaeorum & Saducaeorum fuisse formatas. Ut autem ipse Josephus testatur locis citatis, & 18. antiquit c. 2. haec Saducaeos inter & Pharisaeos erat differentia, quod Pharisaei profiterentur certiorem Legalium rituum notitiam, traditiones mordicus tenerent, agnoscerent fatum, ita tamen ut libertatem arbitrij in plerisque non titulum sine re facerent, animam faterentur esse immortalem, & bonam animam sentirent in alia migrare corpora, cùm mala perpetuis plectatur poenis; at Saducaei, sic dicti à sectae principe צדוק, fatum e medio tollebant cum praemiis & poenis animarum, corporum resurrectione, spiritibus omnibus & traditionibus, omniáque tribuebant hominis libertati. Pauci quidem erant Saducaei, sed iis divites adhaerebant, utpote ditioribus, cùm populus adhaereret Pharisaeis tam pertinaci animo, ut etiam siquis Pharisaeorum Pontifici aut Regi obloqueretur, ei tamen populus fidem haberet. Nam quidquid ad solemnes precationes & cultum divinum spectabat, juxta Pharisaeorum praescriptum fieri solebat, adeo ut cùm Saducaei Magistratum licet inviti susciperent, mox Pharisaeorum decretis assentirentur, quod nisi facerent, non ferendi erant à populo.
units.tr: Pharisaeorum. The Pharisees seem to have been named by St Jerome from פרש [Paras], to divide; Epiphanius at the beginning of the Panarion does better, deriving it from פרש [Parasch], to separate. For in Hebrew they are called פרושים [perushim], separated, as if set apart from others by their manner of life. It is clear from Josephus, Antiquities book 13, chapters 9 and 18, that the sects of the Pharisees and Sadducees had already been formed from the time of the Maccabees. As Josephus himself testifies in the passages cited, and in Antiquities 18, chapter 2, the difference between the Sadducees and Pharisees was this: the Pharisees professed a more precise knowledge of the legal rites, held tenaciously to the traditions, and acknowledged fate, yet in such a way that for most of them free will was not an empty title; they held that the soul is immortal, and that good souls pass into other bodies while bad ones are punished with eternal penalties. The Sadducees, so named from the founder of their sect, צדוק [Tsadoq], removed fate from the picture, along with rewards and punishments of souls, the resurrection of bodies, all spirits and traditions, and attributed everything to human freedom. The Sadducees were few, but the wealthy adhered to them, since they were the richer class; the people, however, clung so stubbornly to the Pharisees that if anyone spoke against a Pharisaic high priest or king, the people still gave him their trust. For whatever concerned solemn prayers and divine worship was customarily done according to the Pharisees' rules, so that when the Sadducees accepted a magistracy, even unwillingly, they soon assented to the Pharisees' decrees, for otherwise they would not have been tolerated by the people.

units.la: In libro Talmudico, qui מסכת inscriptus est, capite secundo, scriptum legitur, quod septem sectae Pharisaeorum sunt, nempe Pharisæus Sichimita, Pharisæus impingens, Pharisæus sanguinem effundens, Pharisæus mortariarius, Pharisæus quid debeo facere & faciam illud, Pharisæus ex amore, & Pharisæus ex timore. Sichimitam vocant, quòd religionem suam carnalis alicujus commodi causa suscéperat, sicut Sichimitæ olim circumcisionem ob nuptias Dinæ Jacobi filiæ impetrandas. Impingentem, quod pedibus subinde in lapides impingeret. Sanguinem effundentem, quòd caput crebrò parietibus aut columnis illideret, donec multo sanguine manaret. Mortariarium, quod capitio seu calyptra caput opertum haberet, ex qua, velut ex profundo mortario prospiceret: cujusmodi hodie alicubi Judæi, alicubi verò etiam Sophistarum discipuli, in Scholis publicis utuntur, nisi quòd eam raro capiti recte inducunt. Nam ea recte inducta, neque sursum, neque dextrorsum, neque sinistrorsum, sed tantùm prorsum, atque deorsum prospicere possunt. Pharisæum quid debeo facere & faciam illud hic vocant, quòd hæc verba, inanis gloriæ causa, subinde ejacularetur. Pharisæum ex amore vocant, quod amore præmij suam religionem sedaretur. Pharisæum autem ex timore, qui metu iræ Dei, in suam superstitionem incidisset. Atque hic perpendat lector velim, an Paulus, cum diceret Act. 26. v. 5. secundùm certissimam sectam se vixisse Pharisæum, hoc significarit, quòd secta Pharisaica in genere exquisitissima fuerit, si ad sectam Saducæorum, Essenorum & similium compararetur: an verò quòd ex septem prædictis Pharisæorum familiis, eam, quæ certissima visa sit, elegerit, cui se addiceret? Nam utroque modo non inepte accipi potest.
units.tr: In the Talmudic tractate entitled מסכת [Masekhet], chapter two, it is written that there are seven sects of Pharisees, namely: the Shechemite Pharisee, the stumbling Pharisee, the blood-letting Pharisee, the mortar Pharisee, the "what must I do and I will do it" Pharisee, the Pharisee from love, and the Pharisee from fear. They call him the Shechemite because he had taken up his religion for some carnal advantage, as the Shechemites once did when they submitted to circumcision to obtain the marriage of Dinah, Jacob's daughter. The stumbling one because he kept striking his feet against stones. The blood-letting one because he kept dashing his head against walls or pillars until it ran with much blood. The mortar one because he kept his head covered with a hood or cap, through which he looked out as if from a deep mortar; the Jews somewhere today, and somewhere even the pupils of the Sophists, use this in public schools, except that they rarely put it on properly. For when it is put on properly, they can look neither upward, nor to the right, nor to the left, but only straight ahead and down. They call the one who says "what must I do and I will do it" by this name because he kept uttering these words for the sake of empty glory. They call the one from love the Pharisee who sought his religion from love of reward. The Pharisee from fear is the one who, out of fear of God's wrath, fell into his superstition. Here I would have the reader consider whether Paul, when he said in Acts 26:5 that he had lived as a Pharisee according to the most exact sect, meant that the Pharisaic sect in general was the most exact when compared with the sects of the Sadducees, Essenes and the like; or whether he meant that from the seven aforementioned families of Pharisees he chose the one that seemed most exact, to which he might attach himself. Either sense can be understood without absurdity.

units.la: Progenies viperarum. Id est, de malis parentibus pejores generati liberi. Huc respiciens Proto-martyr Stephanus Judæos ita compellat Act. 7. v. 51. Durâ cervice & incircumcisis cordibus & auribus, vos semper Spiritui-Sancto resistitis, sicut patres vestri, ita & vos. Et multò ante David Psal. 77. v. 8. Ne fiant sicut patres eorum generatio prava atque exasperans. Siquis viperarum nomine dæmones intelligat, qui passim in Scripturis per serpentes significantur, eadem erit locutio hic, atque Joan. 8. v. 44. ubi Christus dicit: Vos ex patre diabolo estis, & desideria patris vestri vultis facere. Sic & Paulus Act. 13. v. 10. magum Elymam vocat filium diaboli.
units.tr: Progenies viperarum. That is, children born worse than their wicked parents. Looking to this, the first martyr Stephen addresses the Jews thus in Acts 7:51: You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit, as your fathers did, so do you. And long before, David in Psalm 78:8: That they may not be as their fathers, a stubborn and rebellious generation. If anyone understands by "vipers" the demons, who are everywhere in Scripture signified by serpents, the expression here will be the same as in John 8:44, where Christ says: You are of your father the devil, and you want to do the desires of your father. So also Paul in Acts 13:10 calls the magician Elymas a son of the devil.

units.la: Quis demonstravit, &c. Verba sunt Joannis increpantis male conversos ad se confluentes secundum B. Greg. lib. 6 in cap. 15. I Reg. q. d. Quis tam male docuit vos rationem sugiendi venturam peccatorum vindictam, ut vobis persuaserit contra veritatem oris confessionem ad hoc sufficere?
units.tr: Quis demonstravit, &c. These are the words of John rebuking those who came to him badly converted, according to St Gregory, Moralia book 6 on 1 Kings 15: Who has taught you so badly the way of escaping the coming vengeance for sins, that he has persuaded you, against the truth, that confession by mouth is sufficient for this?

units.la: 8. Facite ergo fructus dignos pœnitentiæ. Id est, convenientes & idoneos, non repugnantes pœnitentiæ, quam profitemini. Quasi dicat, Si vere vos pœnitet, sic vivite ut appareat vos respuisse, et ex animo pristinæ vitæ pœnitentia teneri. Arbor est bona voluntas, verba reatum pristinæ vitæ confitentia sunt folia, at opposita pristinis peccatis facta justitiæ sunt fructus. Folia autem non propter ipsa, sed propter fructum sunt expetenda. Unde & Dominus arbori foliis decoræ sed fructu sterili maledixit, quia confessionis ornatum non recipit, sine fructu emendationis vitæ in melius.
units.tr: 8. Facite ergo fructus dignos pœnitentiæ. That is, fitting and suitable fruits, not contradicting the repentance you profess. As if he said: If you truly repent, live so that it appears you have rejected your former life and hold repentance from the heart. Good will is the tree; words confessing the guilt of the former life are the leaves; but deeds contrary to the former sins are the fruits of righteousness. Leaves, however, are to be desired not for their own sake but for the fruit. Hence the Lord also cursed the tree adorned with leaves but barren of fruit, because it received the ornament of confession without the fruit of amendment of life for the better.

units.la: 9. Ne velitis. Id est, ne præsumatis.
units.tr: 9. Ne velitis. That is, do not presume.

units.la: Potens est Deus, supple, vobis pereuntibus, suscitare, &c.
units.tr: Potens est Deus, supply: to raise up, for you who are perishing, etc.

units.la: De lapidibus istis. Quos, scilicet, cernitis; dum enim hæc sermocinabatur Joannes, lapides quosdam digito monstrabat. Ex lapidibus autem, inquit Hieron. apud D. Thom. in catena, generari homines simile est ei, quod ex Sara sterili processit Isaac, unde & Esaiæ c. 51. dicitur: Aspicite ad petram de qua excisi estis: Hujus igitur prophetiæ nos memores faciens monstrat Joannes quod possibile est nunc etiam simile fieri.
units.tr: De lapidibus istis. Which, namely, you see; for while John was speaking these things, he pointed with his finger at certain stones. To generate men from stones, says Jerome, as quoted by St Thomas in the Catena, is like that by which Isaac came forth from barren Sarah; hence Isaiah 51 says: Look to the rock from which you were hewn. Therefore, reminding us of this prophecy, John shows that what is possible now may likewise come to pass.

units.la: Abrahæ. Supple, promissos. Est enim Dativus, ut patet ex textu Græco. Non enim, inquit B. Hilarius, successio carnis quæritur, sed fidei hæreditas: dignitasque originis in operum consistit exemplis, & prosapiæ gloria fidei imitatione retinetur. Filium esse Abrahæ nihil aliud declarat, quàm gratis electum esse, Rom. 9. v. 8. & vestigiis fidei Abrahæ insistere, Rom. 4. v. 12. & opera Abrahæ facere Joa. 8. v. 39. ex quibus recte colligitur certa futuræ salutis expectatio. Si, inquit Aug. lib. 22. contra Faust. c. 32. semen cujusque non appellaretur, nisi quod ejus carne nasceretur, nec nos appellaret Apostolus semen Abrahæ, qui certe originem carnis ab illo non ducimus, sed imitatione fidei semen ejus facti sumus, credentes in Christum, cujus caro ex illius carne propagata est.
units.tr: Abrahæ. Supply: promised. For it is the dative, as is clear from the Greek text. For, says St Hilary, what is sought is not succession of flesh, but the inheritance of faith; the dignity of origin consists in the examples of works, and the glory of descent is kept by imitating faith. To be a son of Abraham declares nothing other than to have been freely chosen (Romans 9:8), and to walk in the footsteps of Abraham's faith (Romans 4:12), and to do the works of Abraham (John 8:39); from these a certain expectation of future salvation is rightly gathered. If, says Augustine in book 22 against Faustus, chapter 32, the seed of each person were called only what was born of his flesh, the Apostle would not call us the seed of Abraham, for we certainly do not derive our origin of flesh from him, but by imitating his faith we have become his seed, believing in Christ, whose flesh was propagated from his flesh.

units.la: 10. Jam enim, &c. Probat Joannes ex imminente peccatorum vindicta nulli quidquam prodesse quod sit filius Abrahæ, nisi & opera Abrahæ faciat. Jam, inquit Joannes, quia tam longanimis est Deus videndo iniqua, & non puniendo, ut tamen cito sit futurum judicium. More quippe humanæ vitæ prolixum est, quod Deo breve est. Ex Adam multi anni evoluti sunt, multi anni fluxerunt, & deinceps fluent: non quidem tam multi, sed tamen usque in finem seculi transibunt anni, sicut & illi transierunt. Longum videtur quod restat, quanquam non erit tantum, quantum transactum est: & tamen ex transacto præterito tempore, sperandus est finis reliqui temporis. Fuit tunc quidem dies, qui diceretur hodiernus, ex illo usque ad hunc hodiernum, nonne quid quid fuit futurum, præteritum factum est? Tale habetur ac si non fuerit. Sic erit quidquid restat extremum. B. Aug. De decem chordis c. 2.
units.tr: 10. Now, etc. John proves from the impending vengeance on sinners that being a son of Abraham profits no one unless he also does the works of Abraham. Now, says John, since God is so patient in seeing iniquity and not punishing it, yet judgment will come quickly. Indeed, what is long in human life is short for God. Many years have unrolled since Adam, many years have flowed by, and more will flow on; not so many, perhaps, but still the years will pass until the end of the age, just as those others have passed. What remains seems long, though it will not be as much as what has passed; yet from the time already past, the end of the remaining time is to be hoped for. There was once a day which would be called today; from that day until this today, has not whatever was future become past? It is reckoned as if it had never been. So will be whatever remains at the end. Blessed Augustine, On the Ten Strings, ch. 2.

units.la: Omnis ergo arbor. Id est, omnis homo, sive sit filius Abrahæ secundum carnem, sive non sit. Hæc sententia evidenter ostendit, quia non solum malum fecisse, sed etiam bonum non egisse damnabile erit, inquit Autor Ser. 16. 1. 50. Hom. apud Augustinum.
units.tr: Every tree therefore. That is, every man, whether he is a son of Abraham according to the flesh or not. This sentence clearly shows that not only to do evil but also not to do good will be damnable, says the author of Sermon 16 (or 50) among the homilies attributed to Augustine.

units.la: In ignem mittetur. Supple ex v. 12. inextinguibilem. His dictis à Joanne, ut constat ex Luc. 3. interrogatus à turbis, Publicanis & Militibus respondit quid singulis esset faciendum, ne immedicabiliter ferirentur, & igni inextinguibili comburendi traderentur; tum suspicanti populo ipsum esse in Lege & Prophetis promissum Messiam, dixit ea, quæ hic mox sequuntur: Ego quidem baptizo, &c. Vide Luc. 3. Quæ autem Matthæus hic refert dicta ad Pharisæos, Lucas cap. 3. refert dicta ad turbas, quia fortasis turbis dicta sunt, sed præcipuè propter Pharisæos, quorum magna multitudo ad Baptismum Joannis venerat.
units.tr: Will be cast into the fire. Supply from v. 12, "unquenchable." When John had said these things, as appears from Luke 3, he was questioned by the crowds, and to the publicans and soldiers he answered what each must do, lest they be struck beyond cure and handed over to be burned in unquenchable fire. Then, as the people suspected that he himself was the Messiah promised in the Law and the Prophets, he said what follows here: I indeed baptize, etc. See Luke 3. What Matthew reports here as said to the Pharisees, Luke ch. 3 reports as said to the crowds; perhaps they were said to the crowds, but chiefly on account of the Pharisees, a great number of whom had come to John's baptism.

units.la: II. In pœnitentiam. Id est, in signum pœnitentiæ, quòd scilicet anteactæ vitæ pœnitentes cor mundum in vobis creari desideratis.
units.tr: II. Unto repentance. That is, as a sign of repentance, since you who repent of your former life desire that a clean heart be created in you.

units.la: Venturus est. Scilicet, mox, jam jam; Græcè enim dicitur ἐρχόμενος in præsenti, venit, ut etiam est Latinè apud Marcum. Sensus igitur est idem ac si diceretur, qui jam vicinus adest munus suum auspicaturus.
units.tr: Is coming. That is, presently, now at once; for in Greek it is said ἐρχόμενος [erchomenos] in the present, "comes," as also in Latin in Mark. The sense is therefore the same as if it were said: he who is already near at hand, about to begin his office. [ἐρχόμενος]

units.la: Fortior. Id est, dignitate major, ut patet ex Joan. 1. v. 15.
units.tr: Mightier. That is, greater in dignity, as is clear from John 1:15.

units.la: Calceamenta portare. Alij Evangelistæ dixerunt, corrigiam calceamentorum solvere. Itaque, inquit Aug. lib. 2. de cons. Evang. c. 12. si ad rem pertinet aliquid aliud intelligere ex eo quod dictum est, calceamenta portare, aliquid aliud ex eo quod dictum est, corrigiam calceamenti solvere, quid aliud accipiendum recte existimaveris, nisi Joannem utrumque dixisse, sive aliud alio tempore, sive contextim; potuit enim sic dicere: Cujus non sum dignus corrigiam calceamenti solvere, nec calceamenta portare: Ut unus Evangelistarum hinc aliud, alij verò aliud, omnes tamen verum narraverint; si autem nihil intendit Joannes cùm de calceamentis Domini diceret, nisi excellentiam ejus & humilitatem suam, quodlibet horum dixerit, sive de solvenda calceamentorum corrigia, sive de portandis calceamentis, eandem tamen sententiam tenuit, quisquis etiam verbis suis per calceamentorum commemorationem eandem significationem humilitatis expressit. fit. Utilis est igitur modus, & memoriae maximè commendandus, cùm de convenientia Evangelistarum dicimus, non esse mendacium, cùm quisque etiam dicens aliquid aliud, quod etiam ille non dixit, de quo aliquid narrat, voluntatem tamen ejus hanc explicat, quam etiam ille, qui ejus verba commemorat. Ita enim salubriter discimus, nil aliud esse quaerendum, quam quid velit ille qui loquitur. Haec. Aug.
units.tr: To carry the sandals. The other Evangelists said, to loosen the thong of the sandals. "Therefore," says Augustine in Book 2 of On the Harmony of the Evangelists, ch. 12, if it pertains to the matter to understand something else from what was said, "to carry the sandals," and something else from what was said, "to loosen the thong of the sandal," what else would you rightly judge should be taken, except that John said both, whether one thing at one time and another at another, or in continuous speech? For he could have said thus: "Whose thong of the sandal I am not worthy to loosen, nor to carry the sandals"; so that one of the Evangelists narrates one thing from this and another from that, yet all have told the truth. But if John intended nothing else when he spoke of the Lord's sandals than his excellence and his own humility, whichever of these he said, whether of loosening the thong of the sandals or of carrying the sandals, he held the same meaning, since whoever, by mentioning the sandals, expressed the same sense of humility in his words. A method is therefore useful and especially to be commended to memory, when we say of the agreement of the Evangelists that there is no lie, since each, even in saying something else which the other did not say, about which he narrates something, nevertheless explains his intention, which the other also who recalls his words explains. For thus we learn wholesomely that nothing else is to be sought than what he who speaks wishes. So far Augustine.

units.la: Baptizabit in Spiritu-Sancto. Sic Act. I. v. 5. Christus ipse opponit Joannis baptisma, quod per aquam fiebat, baptismo per Spiritumsanctum quem à se brevi accepturi erant Apostoli. Itaque hujus baptismi respectu dicit Joannes in futuro, Baptizabit, simul imnuens sese ut hominem habere ministerialiter, externam baptismi ceremoniam Dei jussu administrando in remissionem peccatorum, cùm ipsa peccatorum remissio fiat non vi ipsius ceremoniae externae, sed virtute Spiritus-Sancti, quem Christus, ut Deus-homo, dat ut agens principale. Ut enim autor epistolae ad Demetriadem apud Prosperum, in Sacramentis aliud est quod visibiliter agitur, aliud quod invisibiliter celebratur: Nec idem est in Sacramento forma quod virtus; cùm forma adhibeatur per humani ministerii obsequium, virtus autem per divini operis praestetur effectum. Magis succinctè Cyprianus de Baptismo, Solus Spiritus rem Sacramenti nobis confert. Praeclarè itaque pro more Witakerus lib. 8. De paradoxis: Non Joannes modò, sed ne Petrus quidem, aut quisquam Evangelii minister conferre in eos Sp. Sanctum potest, quos baptizat. Homines externum Sacramentum praebent, mentes intus Christus Spiritu-Sancto purgat. Jam verò quid de Joannis baptismo Patres senserint, non laboro. Rem enim Scriptura satis perspicuè expediunt, ut non sit necesse Patrum varias et incertas opiniones inquirere. Nec ignoro Aug. lib. 5. De baptismo contra Donatistas cap. 10. palam profiteri se non alterum pugnaciter, siquis in baptismo Joannis dimissa esse peccata contenderit. Etiam Cornelius Janssenius Gandavensis Antistes in Concordia Evangelica cap. 13. fatetur hanc fuisse sententiam B. Ambrosii, cujus haec verba lib. 1. de Sp. Sancto c. 3. Illi, qui negaverunt Act. 19. Se sive Spiritum-Sanctum, quamvis baptizatos dicerent se in Joannis baptismo, baptizati sunt postea; quia Joannes in remissionem peccatorum in adventientis Jesu, non in suo baptizavit nomine. Et ideo Spiritum nesciebant, quia nec baptismum in Christi nomine, sicut Joannes baptizare solebat, acceperant. Quod idem diserte tradit autor commentariorum in Epistolas Pauli sub Ambrosii nomine in cap. 3. Ep. ad Galatas, nimirum duodecim illos discipulos, de quibus Act. 19. Pauli jussu baptizatos, quia in adulterino baptismate sub nomine Joannis fuerant non tincti, sed sordidati. Similiter B. Basilius
units.tr: He will baptize in the Holy Spirit. So Christ himself, in Acts 1:5, sets over against John's baptism, which was done through water, the baptism through the Holy Spirit which the Apostles were soon to receive from him. Therefore with respect to this baptism John says in the future, he will baptize, at the same time indicating that he himself has the office of a minister, administering by God's command the external ceremony of baptism for the remission of sins; yet the remission of sins itself is not effected by the power of the external ceremony, but by the virtue of the Holy Spirit, whom Christ, as God-man, gives as the principal agent. For as the author of the letter to Demetrias, cited by Prosper, says: in the sacraments one thing is done visibly, another is celebrated invisibly; nor is the form in a sacrament the same as its virtue, since the form is applied through the service of human ministry, but the virtue is supplied through the effect of divine work. More briefly Cyprian, in On Baptism: The Spirit alone confers the reality of the sacrament upon us. Accordingly, as is his custom, Whitaker in Book 8 of On the Paradoxes brilliantly says: Not only John, but not even Peter, nor any minister of the Gospel can confer the Holy Spirit upon those whom he baptizes. Men offer the external sacrament; Christ cleanses the minds within by the Holy Spirit. Now what the Fathers thought about John's baptism I do not labour to determine. For Scripture sets the matter forth clearly enough that it is not necessary to inquire into the various and uncertain opinions of the Fathers. Nor am I unaware of Augustine, Book 5 On Baptism against the Donatists, ch. 10, where he openly professes that he does not stubbornly contend otherwise if anyone maintains that sins were forgiven in John's baptism. Even Cornelius Jansenius, bishop of Ghent, in his Harmony of the Gospels, ch. 13, admits that this was the opinion of Blessed Ambrose, whose words in Book 1 On the Holy Spirit, ch. 3, are these: Those who denied that they had heard whether there was a Holy Spirit (Acts 19), though they said they were baptized in John's baptism, were afterwards baptized; because John baptized for the remission of sins in the name of the coming Jesus, not in his own name. And so they did not know the Spirit, because they had not received baptism in the name of Christ, as John used to baptize. The author of the commentaries on the Epistles of Paul published under Ambrose's name says the same expressly, on ch. 3 of the Epistle to the Galatians, namely that those twelve disciples of Acts 19, baptized by Paul's command, because they had been in adulterine baptism under John's name, were not washed but defiled. Likewise Blessed Basil

units.la: Hom. r. 2. & 13. De baptismo docuit Joannis baptismum datum missionem peccatorum. Hinc non minus eleganter, quàm verè de Joanne cecinit Prudentius Cathemer.Hym. 7. Hortator ille primus, & doctor nova, Fuit salutis: nam sacrato in flumine Veterum piatas lavit errorum notas. Sed tincta postquam membra defecaverat; Cælo refulgens influebat Spiritus. Hoc ex lavacro labe demta criminum, Ibant renati; non secus quam-si rudis Auri recocta vena pulchrum splendeat, Micet metalli sive lux argentei, Sudum polito præmitens purgamine.
units.tr: Homilies 1, 2 and 13 On Baptism taught that John's baptism was given for the remission of sins. Hence no less elegantly than truly Prudentius sang of John in the Cathemerinon, Hymn 7: He was the first exhorter and the new teacher of salvation: for in the consecrated river he washed away the ancient stains of errors with purifying water. But after he had cleansed the bathed limbs, the Spirit, shining from heaven, poured in. From this bath, with the stain of sins removed, they went forth reborn; not otherwise than when a vein of raw gold, refined by fire, shines beautifully, or the light of silver gleams, the clear purgation of the polished metal going before.

units.la: Idem innuit Chrysologus, dum Serm. 13. ait Joannem dominibus dimisisse peccata.
units.tr: Chrysologus hints at the same thing when he says in Sermon 13 that John had forgiven sins to the lords [dominibus].

units.la: Et igni. Hebraismus &, pro, id est: ut enim ait B. Aug. Serm. 11. De verbis Domini cap. 12. Non ab re est Spiritum-Sanctum nomine ignis significatum videri. Propter quod & in adventu ejus dictum est Act. 2. Visæ sunt illis linguæ divisæ velut ignis, qui & insedit super unumquemque eorum. Hinc & ipse Dominus ait, Luc. 12. Ignem veni mittere in mundum. Hinc & Apostolus dicit, Rom. 12. Spiritu ferventes: Quoniam hinc fervet charitas. Diffunditur quippe in cordibus nostris per Spiritum-Sanctum qui datus est nobis. Rom. 5. cui fervori contrarium est quod Dominus ait Matth. 24. Refrigescet charitas multorum. Hæc Aug. Est ergo Spiritus-Sanctus ignis, ut loquitur Cyrillus apud D. Th. in catena, Luc. 12. salubris & utilis, quo habitatores terræ frigidi quodammodo & extincti propter peccatum incalescunt ad pietatis vitam.
units.tr: And with fire. A Hebraism: "and" for "that is." For as Blessed Augustine says in Sermon 11 On the Words of the Lord, ch. 12: It is not out of place that the Holy Spirit seems to be signified by the name of fire. On account of this, at his coming it is said in Acts 2: "There appeared to them divided tongues as of fire, which also sat upon each one of them." Hence the Lord himself says, Luke 12: "I came to send fire on the earth." Hence also the Apostle says, Rom. 12: "fervent in spirit," since love burns hot from this; for it is poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us, Rom. 5. To this warmth is contrary what the Lord says in Matt. 24: "the love of many will grow cold." So Augustine. The Holy Spirit is therefore fire, as Cyril speaks in the catena of Thomas on Luke 12, wholesome and useful, by which the inhabitants of the earth, cold and in some way deadened by sin, are warmed to a life of piety.

units.la: 12. Ventilabrum. Id est, discretio judicij. Græcè πτύον pala, ut Aug. legit in Ps. 92. Cypr. Ep. 51. & Tert. De fuga. Instrumentum est, quo frumenta ad ventum ventilata quassatáque à paleis expurgantur, à πτύω dictum, quod veluti expuat ea, quæ sunt inutilia.
units.tr: 12. Winnowing fan. That is, the discernment of judgement. In Greek it is πτύον [ptyon], a shovel, as Augustine reads it in Ps. 92, and as in Cyprian, Ep. 51, and Tertullian, De fuga. It is the instrument by which grain, winnowed in the wind and shaken free of chaff, is cleansed. It is called from πτύω [ptyō], because it spits out, as it were, those things that are useless.

units.la: Manu. Id est, potestate.
units.tr: In his hand: that is, in his power.

units.la: Area. Id est, Ecclesiam.
units.tr: Threshing floor: that is, the Church.

units.la: Triticum. Id est, electos virtutibus graves.
units.tr: Wheat: that is, the elect, weighty in virtues.

units.la: Horreum. Id est, cœlestè habitaculum.
units.tr: Barn: that is, the heavenly dwelling.

units.la: Paleas. Id est, reprobos, leves, & operum bonorum expertes; Qui, ut ait B. Basilius in Reg. Brev. interrog. 257. eo modo utiles sunt dignis regno cœlorum, quo paleæ tritico; neque id ex ullo charitatis in Deum, proximive instinctu faciunt, atque ita imperfectos seipsos relinquunt. Ps. 1. v. 4. secundum veritatem Hebraicam impii assimilantur glumæ, quam projicit ventus. Vide & Ps. 35. v. 5. Esa. 17. v. 13. in quibus tribus locis Vulg. pro gluma, habet dictionem pulvis.
units.tr: Chaff: that is, the reprobate, light and lacking good works. As St Basil says in the Longer Rules, question 257, they are useful to those worthy of the kingdom of heaven in the way chaff is to wheat, yet they do this from no impulse of love for God or neighbour, and so they leave themselves imperfect. Ps. 1:4: according to the Hebrew truth, the wicked are likened to husks that the wind drives away. See also Ps. 35:5 and Isa. 17:13, in which three places the Vulgate, for husk, has the word dust.

units.la: Igni inextinguibili. Non videtur ex hoc loco posse colligi poena ignis materialis, quia totus sermo est Metaphoricus, ut patet; cujus ventilabrum in manu sua, & permundabit aream suam, & congregabit triticum suum in horreum; paleas autem comburet igni inextinguibili. Non magis ergo materialis ignis datur intelligi, quàm ventilabrum, area, triticum, horreum, paleæ, materialia & proprie dicta. Dicens ergo ignem inextinguibilem; videtur tantùm significare voluisse supplicium seu poenam æternam. Vide Commentarium nostrum in Marci caput nonum, ubi conciliare tentabimus dicta sanctorum Patrum, qui negare videntur ignem materialem in inferno, cum dictis aliorum, qui diserte ignem materialem in inferno adstruunt.
units.tr: Unquenchable fire. It does not seem that the punishment of material fire can be inferred from this passage, since the whole discourse is plainly metaphorical: whose winnowing fan is in his hand, and he will thoroughly clean his threshing floor, and gather his wheat into the barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire. No more, then, is material fire to be understood than winnowing fan, threshing floor, wheat, barn and chaff, which are material things taken in their proper sense. Therefore, in speaking of unquenchable fire, he seems to mean only eternal punishment or torment. See our commentary on Mark, chapter 9, where we shall attempt to reconcile the sayings of the holy Fathers, who seem to deny material fire in hell, with the statements of others who expressly maintain that there is material fire in hell.

units.la: 13. Tunc. Cùm scilicet Joannes omnes ad poenitentiam excitasset, & baptizando in aqua obsignasset remissionem peccatorum viva in Christum jamjam venientem fide impetratam..
units.tr: 13. Then. That is, when John had roused everyone to repentance and, by baptising with water, had sealed the forgiveness of sins, obtained by living faith in Christ, who was just about to come.

units.la: A Galilæa. Id est, ut dicitur Marc, I.v.9. à Nazareth Galilæa, ubi hactenus privatus vixerat.
units.tr: From Galilee. That is, as Mark 1:9 says, from Nazareth in Galilee, where he had until then lived in private.

units.la: In Jordanem. Id est, ad eum Jordanis locum, ubi Joannes baptizabat.
units.tr: To the Jordan. That is, to that place on the Jordan where John was baptising.

units.la: 14. Prohibebat eum.Magna hic est difficultas cur Joannes Christum ad baptisimum suum accedere prohiberet, cùm ipse de se dicat. Joan. I.v.33. Ego nesciebam eum, sed qui misit me baptizare in aqua, ille mihi dixit, super quem videris Spiritum descendentem & manentem, hic est qui baptizat in Spiritu-Sancto? Respondet Chrysostomus: ante adventum Christi ad Joannis baptismum sciivisse Joannem, quòd Christus in mundum veniset & in Spiritu-Sancto baptizaturus esset; nesciviisse tamen quisnam esset ille Christus, quem nondum facie noverat; in ipso verò Christi ad baptismum accessu; Spiritûs revelatione secretâ indicatum fuisse Joanni, hunc esse Christum, qui ad suum baptismum modo accedit, & ideò à Joanne prohibitum fuisse ne accederet; eodemque tempore ad certiorem revelationis fidem signum externum Christi internoscendi esse datum: Super quem videris Spiritum, &c. ut per hoc signum posset Joannes de ipso aliis testimonium perhibere. Augustinus rem aliter expedit, censet enim Joannem novisse personam Christi, neque hoc signum ei propterea datum, sed nesciviisse qualitatem ipsam, quòd ipse esset qui per omnium ministrorum manus baptizaret in Spiritu-Sancto; nesciviisse, inquam, quòd in baptismo minister qui baptizat, exhibeat ministerium, sed ipse Christus det Spiritum-Sanctum. stum in ministerio etiam servorum suorum. Hoc ut disceret Joannes, qui misit eum baptizare in aqua, illi dixit, Super quem videris Spiritum descendentem & manentem, hic est qui baptizat in Spiritu-Sancto. Ita Aug. Tract.5.& 6.in Joan.&aliis diversis locis.Hinc illud ejusdemAugustini:Hic est qui baptizat:Paulus baptizet,hic est qui baptizat : Judas baptizet,hic est qui baptizat.
units.tr: 14. He tried to prevent him. There is a great difficulty here as to why John tried to prevent Christ from coming to his baptism, since he himself says (John 1:33): I did not know him, but he who sent me to baptise with water said to me, "On whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining, this is he who baptises with the Holy Spirit." Chrysostom answers that before Christ came to John's baptism, John knew that Christ would come into the world and would baptise with the Holy Spirit, but did not know who that Christ was, whom he had not yet seen face to face. But at the very approach of Christ to baptism, it was revealed to John by a secret inspiration of the Spirit that this was the Christ who was now coming to his baptism, and for this reason John was prevented from baptising him. At the same time, to make his faith in the revelation more certain, an external sign was given by which Christ could be recognised: On whom you see the Spirit, etc. so that by this sign John could bear witness of him to others. Augustine explains the matter differently. He holds that John knew the person of Christ, and that this sign was not given to him for that reason, but that he did not know the particular fact that it was he who would baptise with the Holy Spirit through the hands of all his ministers; that is, he did not know that in baptism the minister who baptises performs the ministry, but Christ himself gives the Holy Spirit, even through the ministry of his servants. So that John might learn this, the one who sent him to baptise with water said to him, On whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining, this is he who baptises with the Holy Spirit. So Augustine, in Tractates 5 and 6 on John, and in various other places. Hence that saying of the same Augustine: "This is he who baptises." Let Paul baptise, it is he who baptises; let Judas baptise, it is he who baptises.

units.la: Debeo baptizari. Id est, ego à te baptizari indigeo, ut patet ex textu Græco. Indigebat autem Joannes baptismo Christi ut membrum fieret Ecclesiæ Christi, cujus janua est baptismus.Vide B.Hier.Autor.op. imperf.Theophyl.&Euthym.
units.tr: I need to be baptised. That is, I need to be baptised by you, as the Greek text makes plain. John needed Christ's baptism in order to become a member of the Church of Christ, of which baptism is the door. See B. Hier. (author of the Opus imperfectum), Theophylact and Euthymius.

units.la: 15. Sine modo. Hoc verbo, sine, non tam improbat, quàm approbat prohibitionem Joannis; sed addens, modo, significat hoc fieri debere temporali quâdam dispensatione, ut observat B. Greg. Nazian. Orat. 39.
units.tr: 15. Suffer it now. By the word suffer he does not so much reject John's objection as approve it. But by adding now he signifies that this must be done by a certain temporary arrangement, as St Gregory Nazianzen observes in Oration 39.

units.la: Sic. Pœnitentiam scilicet profitendo.
units.tr: Thus. That is, by professing repentance.

units.la: Decet nos. Qui nimirùm aliis pœnitentiam profitendam indicimus.
units.tr: It becomes us. That is, we who, of course, call on others to profess repentance.

units.la: Adimplere omnem justitiam. Id est, perfectam justitiam. Sic B. Jacobus perfectum gaudium vocat omne gaudium, & B. Paulus omnem fidem vocat fidem integerrimam, plenissimam & perfectissimam. Hæc autem est perfecta justitia secundum B. Ambr. lib. 2. in Lucam, ut quod alterum facere velis, prior ipse incipias & tuo alios horteris exemplo. Christus igitur factus pro nobis in similitudinem carnis peccati, ad pœnitentiæ baptismum accessit, ut nos doceret suo exemplo, quod quinto post Christum natum seculo Augustinus dicere solebat, neminem, etsi nullius sceleris sibi conscius esset, committere debere ut sine pœnitentia migraret e vita.
units.tr: To fulfil all righteousness. That is, perfect righteousness. So St James calls all joy perfect joy, and St Paul calls all faith faith most entire, full and perfect. This is perfect righteousness, according to St Ambrose, book 2 on Luke: that you first begin yourself what you wish another to do, and urge others by your own example. Christ, therefore, having been made for us in the likeness of sinful flesh, came to the baptism of repentance, so as to teach us by his own example what Augustine used to say in the fifth century after Christ's birth: that no one, even if conscious of no crime, ought to depart this life without repentance.

units.la: Baptizatus, &c. Christum fuisse nudum, cùm a Joanne baptizaretur, satis innuunt verba Evangelistarum, disertéque scribunt Epiphanius in Ancorato cap. 117. & Joannes Damascenus in Oratione adversus imperatorem Constantinum Caballinum. Qui mos nudos baptizandi ab apostolicis temporibus ad initium usque duodecimi seculi in ecclesia perseveravit, ut liquet ex Hugonis Victorini Theologicæ eruditionis Summæ Tract. 5. cap 7. Rationem autem hujus nuditatis discimus ex Facundo Hermianensi antistite in lib. 4. ad Justinianum imperatorem Cap. 4. nimirum, ut non solâ voce, verùm etiam totius habitu corporis profiteamur exuisse nos veterem hominem cum actibus suis.
units.tr: Baptised, etc. That Christ was naked when he was baptised by John is sufficiently hinted at by the words of the Evangelists, and Epiphanius in the Ancoratus, chapter 117, and John Damascene in his oration against the emperor Constantine Caballinus, write it plainly. This custom of baptising naked persisted in the Church from apostolic times until the beginning of the twelfth century, as is clear from Hugh of St Victor's Summa of Theological Learning, Tract. 5, chapter 7. We learn the reason for this nakedness from Facundus, bishop of Hermiane, in book 4, to the emperor Justinian, chapter 4: namely, that we profess, not only with our voice but with the whole habit of our body, that we have put off the old man with his deeds.

units.la: 16. Confestim ascendit. Particula confestim non ad ascendit, sed ad ecce aperti sunt, refertur; unde Marc. I. v. 10. habetur : Statim ascendens de aqua vidit.
units.tr: 16. Immediately he went up. The word immediately refers not to went up but to behold, the heavens were opened. Hence Mark 1:10 reads: Immediately, coming up out of the water, he saw.

units.la: Aperti sunt cœli. Sensibili divisione in supremo aere vel aethere. Similiter & columba, & vox audita fuerunt sensibiles; sicque haec omnia contigere, ut è coelo proficisci viderentur.
units.tr: The heavens were opened. By a perceptible parting in the highest air or ether. Likewise the dove and the voice that were heard were perceptible, and so all these things happened in such a way that they seemed to proceed from heaven.

units.la: Ei. Scilicet, Christo & propter Christum.
units.tr: To him. That is, to Christ, and on account of Christ.

units.la: Sicut Columbam. Sunt è Patribus qui veram Columbam in Christum descendisse volunt. Ita Tertullianus in lib. De carne Christi cap. 3. sic scribit de Spiritu-Sancto in Christum descendente: Tam verè erat Columba, quam & Spiritus; nec interfecerat (forte, interceperat) substantiam propriam assumta substantiâ extraneâ. Et B. Aug. de Agone Christiano c. 22. Christi corpus cum hac Columba conferens ait: Neque hoc ita dicimus, ut Dominum Jesum dicamus solum verum corpus habuisse, Spiritum autem Sanctum fallaciter apparuisse oculis hominum, sed ambo illa corpora, vera corpora credimus. Sicut enim non oportebat ut homines falleret Filius Dei, sic non decebat ut homines falleret Spiritus-Sanctus; sed omnipotenti Deo, qui universam creaturam de nihilo fabricavit, non erat difficile verum corpus Columbae sine aliarum columbarum ministerio figurare; sicut ei non fuit difficile verum corpus inutero Mariae sine virili semine fabricare. B. Augustinum sequitur D. Thomas, 3. p. q. 39. art. 7. & Sixtus Senensis lib. 6. Bibliothecae Annot. 13. omnes fere Scholasticos Theologos idem sentire scribit. Tamen quatuor Evangelistae Columbam in Christum descendisse non dicunt, sed tanquam Columbam, & distertius Lucas dicit c. 3. v. 22. Spiritum-Sanctum descendisse corporali specie tanquam Columbam; ubi Syrus & Arabs habent, juxta similitudinem corporis Columbae, & Aethiops, in corpore tanquam Columbae; unde concludi posset juxta mentem Aethiopis corpus fuisse quod apparuit, non vero corpus verae Columbae, quod & Augustinum sensisse vult Maldonatus, licet ipsius verba citata repugnent; alii contra Possidii Indiculum & ipsum Augustinum librum de Agone Christi pro suo agnoscentem l. 2. Retract. c. 3. negant eum esse Augustini. Sed textui Evangelico concinit universa authoritas traditionis. Justinus in dialogo cum Tryphone Judaeo, Irenaeus l. 3. c. 19. Origenes in Luc. Serm. 27. Epiph. adversus Sabellianos Haeresi 62. Hilar. in Matth. can. 2. Chrysost. in Matth. Hom. 12. Isidor. Pelusiotes Ep. 106. Cyril. in Joan. Author libri de mirabilibus Scripturae sub Augustini nomine l. 3. c. 5. Author libri de Sacramentis sub Ambr. nomine l. 1. c. 5. Procopius Gazaeus in Genes. 18. Imo & in Tertulliani libro de Baptismo c. 8. legitur Spiritus-Sanctus in Columbae figura delapsus in Dominum, & B. Aug. lib. 2. de Trinitate c. 5. idem asserit, & distertius Ep. 102. ad Evodium dicit de hac Columba sub cujus specie descendit Spiritus-Sanctus, quod fit, sola specie corporali oculis reddita, tanquam nonnatura viventis animalis expressa. Juvencus Evang. Hist. l. 1. Corporeaque quoque gerens speciem, descendit ab alto Spiritus, acream simulans ex nube Columbam.
units.tr: As a dove. Some of the Fathers hold that a real dove descended upon Christ. Thus Tertullian, in his book On the Flesh of Christ, chapter 3, writes of the Holy Spirit descending upon Christ: It was as truly a dove as the Spirit was; nor had it, by taking on an alien substance, destroyed its own proper substance. And St Augustine, in On the Christian Struggle, chapter 22, comparing Christ's body with this dove, says: We do not say this so as to claim that the Lord Jesus had only a true body, while the Holy Spirit appeared falsely to the eyes of men; we believe both those bodies to be true bodies. For just as the Son of God ought not to deceive men, so the Holy Spirit was not fit to deceive men. But to almighty God, who made the whole creation out of nothing, it was not difficult to form a true body of a dove without the help of other doves, just as it was not difficult for him to form a true body in Mary's womb without male seed. St Thomas follows St Augustine, 3 p., q. 39, art. 7, and Sixtus of Siena, in book 6 of his Bibliotheca, annotation 13, writes that almost all the Scholastic theologians hold the same view. Yet the four Evangelists do not say that a dove descended upon Christ, but as a dove. Luke says more clearly, in chapter 3:22, that the Holy Spirit descended in bodily form as a dove. Here the Syriac and Arabic versions have according to the likeness of the body of a dove, and the Ethiopic has in a body as of a dove. From this it could be concluded, according to the mind of the Ethiopic version, that what appeared was a body, but not the body of a real dove. Maldonatus holds that Augustine thought so too, although the words of Augustine cited by him contradict this; others, on the other hand, deny that the work is Augustine's, relying on the Indiculus of Possidius and on Augustine himself, who in Retractations 2, chapter 3, acknowledges the book On the Christian Struggle as his own. But the whole weight of tradition agrees with the text of the Gospel. Justin, in his dialogue with the Jew Trypho; Irenaeus, book 3, chapter 19; Origen, on Luke, Homily 27; Epiphanius, against the Sabellians, Heresy 62; Hilary, on Matthew, canon 2; Chrysostom, on Matthew, Homily 12; Isidore of Pelusium, Ep. 106; Cyril, on John; the author of the book On the Wonders of Scripture, under Augustine's name, book 3, chapter 5; the author of the book On the Sacraments, under Ambrose's name, book 1, chapter 5; Procopius of Gaza, on Genesis 18. Indeed, in Tertullian's book On Baptism, chapter 8, we read that the Holy Spirit descended upon the Lord in the figure of a dove, and St Augustine, book 2 of On the Trinity, chapter 5, asserts the same. More plainly still, in Ep. 102 to Evodius, he speaks of this dove under whose form the Holy Spirit descended, saying that it was presented to the eyes by a bodily form alone, as if expressed by a living creature that was not of its own nature. Juvencus, in his Evangelical History, book 1: Also bearing a bodily form, the Spirit descended from on high, feigning an airy dove out of the bright cloud.

units.la: Sedulius carminum lib. 2. Conspicit patuero poli, Sanctisque Columba Spiritus in specie Christum vestivit honore.
units.tr: Sedulius, Carmen paschale, book 2: "He beholds from the open heaven, and the Holy Spirit, in the form of a dove, clothed Christ with honour."

units.la: Interim notandum est Tertullianum ea dicere de Spiritu-Sancto, quae vera esse non possunt, nisi fingatur Spiritus-Sanctus Columbam unione hypostatica sibi assumfisse, ut patet ex ipsius verbis citatis; unde alius enim natus est, nempe Spiritum-Sanctum tanto esse infra Christum, quanto columba est infra hominem. Ut Martialis columbam Stellae cum Catulli passere conferens, Stellam contendit Catullo tanto meliorem esse Poetam, quanto passere major est columba. Sed hunc errorem ita refellit Chrysostomus in Matth. Hom. 12. ὁ μὲν ἐν τῇ ἡμετέρᾳ φύσει, τὸ δὲ ἐν ὁμοίῳ, πνεῦμα ἐπὶ πνεῦμα. Item, ὁ μὲν ὑὸς τῆς ἀνθρωπότητος ἀνέλαβε τὴν σάρκα, τὸ δὲ πνεῦμα ἡ φύσιν ἀνέλαβε ἐπὶ τὴν ἀθανασίαν. Ἀλλὰ τοῦτο ἡ εὐαγγελιστὴς ἐν ἕλλησι ὅτι ἐν φύσει σάρκα, ἀλλ᾽ ἐν τῷ ἀληθινῷ φωτὶ ἐν τόπῳ τῷ ὑψηλῷ, ἀλλὰ τότε μένον. Christus quidem in natura nostra, sed Spiritus in Columbae specie apparuit; hominis quidem naturam suscepit Dei Filius, sed columbae naturam non suscepit Spiritus. Proinde non dixit Evangelista eum in natura Columbae, sed in specie Columbae descendisse. Neque postmodum in ea specie apparuit, sed tunc solum. Nos admimus quòd etsi Spiritus-Sanctus vere naturam columbae assumsisset, pessime tamen inde concluderetur quòd persona Spiritûs-Sancti sit minûs perfecta, quàm persona Filij, nisi intelligeretur secundum naturam assumtam; sic enim assumfisset naturam columbae, ut suam non dereliquisset, quâ unum est cum Patre & Filio, sicut nec Filius est minor Patre secundum personalitatem, vel secundum naturam suam Divinam, quia assumfit nostram naturam; sic enim nostram assumfit, ut suam non derelinqueret.
units.tr: Meanwhile it should be noted that Tertullian says things about the Holy Spirit that cannot be true unless we suppose that the Spirit took the dove to himself by a hypostatic union, as is clear from the words quoted above. From this another error arises, namely that the Holy Spirit is as far below Christ as the dove is below man. Martial, comparing Stella's dove with Catullus' sparrow, maintains that Stella is as much a better poet than Catullus as the dove is larger than the sparrow. Chrysostom refutes this error in Homily 12 on Matthew: "The one [was] in our nature, the other in a like one, spirit upon spirit" [ὁ μὲν ἐν τῇ ἡμετέρᾳ φύσει, τὸ δὲ ἐν ὁμοίῳ, πνεῦμα ἐπὶ πνεῦμα]. Likewise: "The Son of humanity took on flesh, but the Spirit did not take on the nature of a dove for immortality" [ὁ μὲν ὑὸς τῆς ἀνθρωπότητος ἀνέλαβε τὴν σάρκα, τὸ δὲ πνεῦμα ἡ φύσιν ἀνέλαβε ἐπὶ τὴν ἀθανασίαν]. But the evangelist did not say this in the Greek [ἐν ἕλλησι]; rather, the Spirit appeared in the true light, in a lofty place, and then remained there. Christ indeed appeared in our nature, but the Spirit appeared in the form of a dove. The Son of God took on the nature of man, but the Spirit did not take on the nature of a dove. Therefore the Evangelist did not say that he descended in the nature of a dove, but in the form of a dove. Nor did he afterwards appear in that form, but only then. We admit that even if the Holy Spirit had truly assumed the nature of a dove, it would still be a very poor inference that the person of the Holy Spirit is less perfect than the person of the Son, unless this were understood of the assumed nature. For he would have assumed the nature of a dove in such a way that he did not abandon his own, by which he is one with the Father and the Son, just as the Son is not less than the Father in personhood or in his divine nature, though he assumed our nature. For he assumed ours in such a way that he did not forsake his own.

units.la: Superest solvendum B. Aug. argumentum, quo in lib. de Agone Christi. probare nititur veram fuisse hanc Columbam, sub cujus specie apparuit Spiritus-Sanctus in baptismo Christi: Ambo, inquit, corpora, nempe Christi & SanctiSpiritûs, vera corpora credimus; sicut enim non oportebat, ut homines falleret Filius Dei, sic non decebat ut homines falleret Spiritus-Sanctus. Verum haec argumentatio parum habet virium. Quem enim haec Columbae species fefellisset, cùm ex Matth. 3. v. 19. Mar. 1. v. 10. & Jo. 1. v. 32. illam non constet quemquam vidisse praeter Christum ipsum, & Joannem Baptistam? In mediis quidem turbis Christus baptizatus est Luc. 3. v. 21. sed his Columbam apparuisse Evangelistarum nemo scripsit; imò præter Christum à nullo fuisse visam Columbam præterquàm à Joanne aperte docent hæc verba Joan. 1. v. 32. Et testimonium perhibuit Joan. nes dicens: Quia vidi Spiritum descendentem quasi Columbam de cœlo, & mansit super eum. Quid enim opus fuisset tanti viri testimonio ad id probandum, quòd alij quoque vidissent, adeóque omnes turbæ, quæ tum Christum & Joannem circumstabant? Hæc porro Columbæ species Christo non imposuit, qui erat erroris expers: Nec Joanni, qui à Deo præmonitus fore, ut Spiritus suus visibili specie descenderet & maneret super Filium suum, cùm hanc Columbæ speciem super Christum descendere & desidere vidit, pro comperto habuit hæc in visione fieri, prout prædixerat Deus: unde non dicit se vidisse Columbam, sed tanquam Columbam. Præterea dato, non concesso hoc Columbæ φαίσμα, ut rectè vocat Origenes, ab omnibus fuisse conspectum, & à plerisque fuisse creditum veram fuisse Columbam, ne sic quidem eos sefellisset Spiritus-Sanctus. Neque enim is verè fallit, qui ob oculos imaginem ponit, non fallendi animo, sed docendi. Talis autem fuit hæc visio, quâ ob oculos Columbæ species proposita est, non ut crederetur vera esse columba, sed per eam Sancti-Spiritûs præsentia significaretur, & quæ sint ejus virtutes. Hoc si putetur esse falsitas, abolebitur omnium visionum usus, in quibus aliud oculis, aliud animo exhibetur; neque solùm in Columbæ, sed & in linguarum ignearum visione sefellerit Spiritus-Sanctus, cùm hæ linguæ, veræ linguæ non essent, nec verus ignis. Proinde ut hic descendisse legitur tanquam Columba, ita Act. 2. v. 3. visæ linguæ dicuntur tanquam ignis, & paulò ante auditus dicitur esse sonus non venti, sed tanquam venti, seu ut habat Vulgata editio, tanquam advenientis spiritûs vehementis, quod etiam observat B. Chrysost. Serm. 1. De sancta Pentecoste, ut sciamus hæc omnia in visione obtigisse.
units.tr: There remains the argument of Blessed Augustine, by which, in his book on the Agony of Christ, he strives to prove that this dove, in whose form the Holy Spirit appeared at the baptism of Christ, was real. "We believe both bodies," he says, "that is, of Christ and of the Holy Spirit, to be true bodies; for just as the Son of God ought not to deceive men, so the Holy Spirit ought not to deceive men." But this argument has little force. For whom would this form of a dove have deceived, since it is not established from Matthew 3:19, Mark 1:10 and John 1:32 that anyone saw it except Christ himself and John the Baptist? Christ was indeed baptized in the midst of crowds (Luke 3:21), but no evangelist wrote that the dove appeared to them. Indeed, that the dove was seen by no one except Christ and John is clearly taught by the words of John 1:32: "And John bore witness, saying: 'I saw the Spirit descending like a dove from heaven, and it remained upon him.'" For what need would there have been of the testimony of so great a man to prove that others also saw it, and so all the crowds who then stood around Christ and John? Moreover, this form of a dove did not deceive Christ, who was free of error; nor John, who, having been forewarned by God that his Spirit would descend in visible form and remain upon his Son, when he saw this form of a dove descend and settle upon Christ, held it as certain that this happened in a vision, as God had foretold. Hence he does not say that he saw a dove, but as a dove. Furthermore, even granting, though it is not conceded, that this appearance of a dove (which Origen rightly calls a phantasm) was seen by all and believed by most to be a real dove, the Holy Spirit would not even so have deceived them. For he does not truly deceive who sets an image before the eyes, not with the intention of deceiving but of teaching. Such was this vision, in which the form of a dove was set before the eyes, not so that it would be believed to be a real dove, but so that through it the presence of the Holy Spirit and what his powers are might be signified. If this is judged to be falsehood, the use of all visions will be abolished, in which one thing is shown to the eyes and another to the mind. And the Holy Spirit would have deceived not only in the vision of the dove but also in the vision of the tongues of fire, since those tongues were not real tongues, nor real fire. Therefore, just as he is read to have descended here as a dove, so in Acts 2:3 the tongues that were seen are said to be as of fire, and a little before, the sound is said to be not of wind but as of a wind, or, as the Vulgate has it, as of a rushing mighty wind. Blessed Chrysostom also observes this in Sermon 1 on holy Pentecost, so that we may know that all these things happened in vision.

units.la: 17. Hic est. Marcus & Lucas variant verba, sed non sensum. Anne, inquit Hila. lib. 6. de Trinit. tibi in eo, quod dicitur, Hic est, non hoc significare videtur, alios quidem cognominatos ab eo in filios, sed hic filius meus est? Donavi adoptionis plurimis nomen, sed iste mihi filius est.
units.tr: 17. This is. Mark and Luke vary the words, but not the sense. "Does it not seem to you," says Hilary, book 6 on the Trinity, "that in what is said, 'This is,' is signified not that others are called sons from him, but 'this one is my Son'? I have given the name of adoption to many, but this one is my Son."

units.la: Dilectus. Familiare est Græcis authoribus, tum prophanis, tum sacræ Scripturæ interpretibus dilectum dicere pro unico, seu unigenito. Sic Homero Astyanax dilectus dicitur tur, non enim alium habebat Hectòr. Idem videre est apud Græcos interpretes Genef. 22, v. 12. Judic. 11. v. 34. Proverb. 4. v. 3. &c. ubi Hebræum ἀγαπητός redditur. Ita ergo Christus hïc dilectus Dei Filius dicitur, quòd unicus fit; Unus enim de uno, inquit Ruffinus in Symbolum, nascitur, quia splendor unus est lucis, & unum est verbum cordis. Nec in numerum pluralem defluit incorporea generatio; nec in divisionem cadit, ubi qui nascitur nequaquam a generante separatur. Unicus est, ut menti sensus, ut sapientia sapienti, ut cordi verbum, ut forti virtus. Nam sicut solus sapiens Pater ab Apostolo dicitur, ita & solus Filius sapientia nominatur. Unicus ergo Filius est, & cum sit gloria, sempiternitate, virtute, regno, potestate, hoc quod Pater est, omnia tamen hæc non sine authore sicut Pater, sed ex Patre, tanquam Filius, habet, & cum sit ipse omnium caput, ipsius tamen caput est Pater. Hæc Ruffinus. Dilectus igitur Dei Filius dicitur Christus eo sensu, quo Philosophorum Princeps oculum monoculi, ἀγαπητὸν dixit.
units.tr: Beloved. It is a familiar usage among Greek authors, both profane and the interpreters of sacred Scripture, to call someone "beloved" to mean "only" or "only-begotten." So in Homer Astyanax is called "beloved," since Hector had no other son. The same may be seen in the Greek interpreters at Genesis 22:12, Judges 11:34, Proverbs 4:3, etc., where the Hebrew is rendered [ἀγαπητός]. Thus Christ is called here the beloved Son of God because he is the only one. "For one is born of one," says Rufinus on the Creed, "because the splendour of light is one, and the word of the heart is one. Incorporeal generation does not pass into plurality, nor does it fall into division, since he who is born is by no means separated from the one who begets. He is unique, as sense is to the mind, wisdom to the wise, the word to the heart, virtue to the strong. For just as the Apostle calls the Father alone wise, so the Son alone is named Wisdom. The Son is therefore unique, and although he has glory, eternity, power, kingdom, and authority, which the Father has, yet he has all these not from himself as the Father does, but from the Father, as Son; and although he is the head of all, the Father is his head." Thus Rufinus. Christ is therefore called the beloved Son of God in the sense in which the Prince of Philosophers called the only eye of a one-eyed man [ἀγαπητόν] "beloved."

units.la: In quo mihi bene complacui. Id est, cujus causâ & propter quem omnem in genus humanum conceptam indignationem depono.
units.tr: In whom I am well pleased. That is, for whose sake, and because of whom, I lay aside the indignation conceived against the whole human race.

units.la: CAPUT IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: I. Tunc. Id est, statim post Christi baptismum, ut patet ex Marc. 1. v. 12.
units.tr: I. Then. That is, immediately after Christ's baptism, as is clear from Mark 1:12.

units.la: Desertum. Hoc dicitur vocari Quarentana, éstque inter Jerusalem & Jericho, ut ait Anfelmus.
units.tr: The desert. This place is said to be called Quarantana, and it lies between Jerusalem and Jericho, as Anselm says.

units.la: A Spiritu. Scilicet, suo. Illuc autem Jesum suus Spiritus duxit, ubi eum ad tentandum malignus spiritus invenīret. B. Greg. Hom. 16. in Evang.
units.tr: By the Spirit. That is, by his own Spirit. For his own Spirit led Jesus thither, to the place where the evil spirit would find him to tempt him. B. Greg. Hom. 16 in Evang.

units.la: Ut tentaretur. Non delectatione & consensu, sed sola fugg eftione, atque adeo omnis illa diabolica tentatio foris non intûs fuit. Ita B. Greg. ibid. Præbuit autem Christus semetipsum tentandum, ut ad superandas tentationes mediator effet, non solùm per adjutorium, sed etiam per exemplum, ut ait B. Aug. 4. de Trin. c. 13. Porrò ordinem, quo Christus fuerit tentatus, sequi Matthæum, indicare videntur hæc verba, tunc, iterum. Marcus autem c. 1. totam Christi tentationem compendio tantùm tetigit. Lucas vero. 1. generatim tractat Christi tentationem, quam postea sigillatim tim & per singula describens, duas ultimas tentationes, ordine inverso tradit.
units.tr: To be tempted. Not by delight and consent, but only by the flight of the temptation; so that all that diabolical temptation was external, not internal. Thus B. Greg., ibid. Christ, however, offered himself to be tempted so that he might be a mediator in overcoming temptations, not only by help but also by example, as B. Aug. says, De Trin. 4, c. 13. Moreover, these words, then and again, seem to indicate that Matthew follows the order in which Christ was tempted. Mark, in chapter 1, touched on the whole temptation of Christ only briefly. Luke, in chapter 4, treats Christ's temptation in general terms, and then, describing it particularly and item by item, gives the last two temptations in reverse order.

units.la: A diabolo. Cùm omnes creaturæ ministrent Deo, & eis Deus utatur secundum qualitates earum; sicut bonis Angelis utitur ad benefaciendum, sic malis ad male faciendum, & nunquam è conuerso. Quare cùm aliquid mali inferendum est hominibus, præter tenorem causarum consuetum, tunc patet esse articulum agendi dæmonibus, sive hoc malum sit proprie malum, sive tantùm dispositio ad majus bonum, sicut in B. Job. Nihil tamen repugnat Angelos bonos esse ministros pœnæ, quatenus bona est, sicut & Deus sub hac ratione mali pœnæ causa est, sed nunquam Angeli boni sunt ministri immediati pœnæ, sed mediantibus Angelis malis; atque ita Angeli boni, qui in Scripturis leguntur male fecisse hominibus, ut qui pestem intulit Jerosolymis, exercitum Sennacherib interfecit, tantùm imperio præsuerunt actioni, ut à Deo proficiscenti, non autem executionem ipsam exercuerunt. Hinc videas, cur dæmones quidquid mali possunt, operantur, etiamsi non lateat illos plus boni hominibus postmodum exinde eventurum. Cùm enim appetitus nocendi prævaleat in eis fulgori veritatis, etiam contra scientiam operantur, ut & animæ separatæ reprobæ. Et inde fit, ut ministerium eorum nunquam desit Deo ad judicia sua exercenda, nec opus sit ut impellat eos aliquo modo præter naturam & inclinationem eorum. Unde leguntur & in B. Job, & in visione Michææ, sponte se obtulisse.
units.tr: By the devil. Since all creatures minister to God, and God uses them according to their qualities, as he uses good angels to do good, so he uses evil ones to do evil, and never the reverse. Therefore, when some evil is to be inflicted on men beyond the usual course of causes, it is plain that there is a point at which demons act, whether this evil is properly evil or merely a disposition towards a greater good, as in the case of B. Job. Nothing prevents good angels from being ministers of punishment, insofar as it is good, just as God too is the cause of punishment under this aspect of evil; but good angels are never the immediate ministers of punishment, only through the mediation of evil angels. And so the good angels who, in the Scriptures, are read to have done harm to men, such as the one who brought the plague on Jerusalem and slew the army of Sennacherib, only presided over the action by command, as proceeding from God, but did not themselves carry out the execution. From this you may see why demons do whatever evil they can, even though it is not hidden from them that more good will afterwards come to men from it. For since the appetite for harm prevails in them over the brightness of truth, they act even against knowledge, as do separated reprobate souls too. And hence it happens that their ministry is never lacking to God in carrying out his judgments, nor is there any need for him to impel them in any way beyond their nature and inclination. Hence they are read, both in B. Job and in the vision of Micah, to have offered themselves willingly.

units.la: 2. Quadraginta noctibus. Addidit Evangelista noctes diebus, ne putaretur Christus jejunasse more Judæorum, qui per diem nihil cibi, potúsve sumentes, noctu vescuntur. Non autem ultra processit jejunando, quàm Moyses & Elias, ne incredibilis videretur carnis assumtio. Chrysost. Hom. 13. in Mat.
units.tr: 2. For forty nights. The Evangelist added nights to days, lest it be thought that Christ fasted in the manner of the Jews, who take no food or drink by day and eat at night. He did not, however, go further in fasting than Moses and Elijah, lest the assumption of flesh seem incredible. Chrysost. Hom. 13 in Matth.
