units.la: Posteà esuriit. Id est, completis & transactis in jejunio quadraginta diebus & noctibus, cessit Christus humanæ naturæ, ut ex ipsius veritate esuriret. Esurivit, quia & hoc dignum est, quia & hoc ad humilitatem pertinuit. Esurivit panis, sicut defecit via, sicut vulnerata est sanitas, sicut mortua est vita. Serm. 41. de verbis Domini.
units.tr: Afterwards he hungered. That is, when the forty days and nights of fasting were completed and past, Christ yielded to human nature, so that in truth he might hunger. He hungered, because this too is worthy, because this too pertains to humility. Bread hungered, just as the way failed, just as health was wounded, just as life died. Serm. 41 de verbis Domini.

units.la: 3. Tentator. Id est, observator, seu insidiator, qui vulgò dicitur diabolus. Idem videtur significari Gen. 3. vi. per vocem Hebraicam נָחָשׁ, quæ proprie observatorem, infidiatorem, seu tentatorem significat. Unde loco citato Genesis, ubi vertitur: Sed & serpens erat callidior cunctis animantibus: mantibus : verti posset : Et tentator erat callidior cunctis viventibus: ut sensus sit callidiorem fuisse tentatorem etiam ipso homine, qui ceteris animantibus praerat; quod plus satis ex eventu patuit. Quia vero ex inspectione serpentium olim auguria fieri solebant, factum est ut vox Nachasch, quae proprie Augurem significat, ad serpentem significandum transferretur, quia ex serpentibus auguria fumi solebant.
units.tr: 3. Tempter. That is, an observer or lurker, whom people commonly call the devil. The same seems to be signified in Gen. 3. vi. by the Hebrew word נָחָשׁ [nachash], which properly means an observer, a lurker, or a tempter. Hence, in the cited passage of Genesis, where it reads Now the serpent was more subtle than all the living creatures, it could be rendered: "Now the tempter was more subtle than all living creatures," so that the sense is that the tempter was more crafty even than man himself, who ruled the other animals; the outcome made this plain enough. And because omens were often formerly taken from the inspection of serpents, it came about that the word Nachasch, which properly means an augur, was transferred to signify the serpent, since omens were commonly drawn from serpents.

units.la: Si Filius Dei es. Id est, siquidem Filius Dei es. Quis enim sibi persuadeat diabolum ignorasse quae gesta sunt olim, cum Christus offerretur in Templo, vocem in baptismo Christi e caelo delapsam, & publicum de Christo Joannis Baptistae testimonium? Tanto autem amplius contra Christum machinatur diabolus, quanto sperat Deo se nociturum.
units.tr: If you are the Son of God. That is, since you are the Son of God. For who could persuade himself that the devil was ignorant of what happened long ago, when Christ was presented in the Temple, of the voice that came down from heaven at Christ's baptism, and of the public testimony of John the Baptist concerning Christ? Yet the devil schemes all the more against Christ the more he hopes to harm God.

units.la: Dic ut lapides isti, &c. Haec prima Christi tentatio analogiam habet cum his ejusdem tentatoris ad proto-parentem verbis Gen. 3. v. 1. Cur praecepit vobis Deus ut non comederetis de omni ligno paradisi? Heb. Etiam quod dixit Deus, ut non comederetis de omni ligno paradisi? Q. d. Non satis fuit Deo ad custodiendum hortum suum vos obligavisse, sed etiam non permittit vos manducare?
units.tr: Command that these stones become bread, &c. This first temptation of Christ has an analogy with these words of the same tempter to our first parent, Gen. 3:1: Why did God command you that you should not eat of every tree of the garden? In Hebrew: Did God really say that you should not eat of every tree of the garden? That is to say: Was it not enough for God to bind you to keep his garden, but he does not even allow you to eat?

units.la: 4. Respondens. Christus respondit tentatori, docens te respondere tentatori; ad hoc enim pugnat imperator, ut milites discant. Non fecit Christus de lapidibus panes, qui utique sic potuit facere, sicut de aqua vinum: ejusdem enim est potentiae facere de lapidibus panem; sed non fecit, ut, voluntatem contemneret tentatoris. Aliter tentator non vincitur, nisi contemnatur. Aug. Serm. 41. de verbis Domini.
units.tr: 4. Answering. Christ answered the tempter, teaching you to answer the tempter; for an emperor fights in order that his soldiers may learn. Christ did not turn stones into bread, though he could certainly have done so, just as he turned water into wine; for it is of the same power to make bread from stones; but he did not do it, so as to scorn the tempter's will. Otherwise the tempter is not overcome, unless he is despised. Aug. Serm. 41 de verbis Domini.

units.la: Scriptum est. Sanctarum scripturarum testimonia diabolo ingeruntur non ut incorrigibilis doceatur, sed ut impudens consutetur, ait B. Maxim. Taurinensis Hom. 2. de Jejunio Quadragesimae. Edosemur, inquit Abbas Theonas, ut fraudulentis suggestionibus inimici nos quoque similiter auctoritate Scripturarum debeamus obsistere.
units.tr: It is written. The testimonies of the holy Scriptures are thrown at the devil not so that an incorrigible one may be taught, but so that a shameless one may be confounded, says B. Maximus of Turin, Hom. 2 on the Lenten fast. Let us be taught, says Abbot Theonas, that against the deceitful suggestions of the enemy we too must in the same way resist with the authority of the Scriptures.

units.la: Non in solo pane &c. Q. d. Nihil est prorsus, quod non loco panis esse possit, ubi Deo placet. Hoc est dicere, inquit B. Maximus Taurinensis Antistes Hom. 1. in Dominic. 1. Quadragesimae, Frustra, diabole iterum per ecam supplantare conaris: sufficiat tibi suadendo cibos illicitos, in paradiso Adam perte fuisse deceptum. Nec esuries me vincit, nec tuis suasionibus cedo. Voluntas enim Dei cibus est meus; verbum Dei mihi est persecta refectio.
units.tr: Not by bread alone, &c. That is: there is absolutely nothing that cannot be in place of bread, where it pleases God. This is to say, says B. Maximus of Turin, bishop, Hom. 1 on the first Sunday of Lent, Devil, in vain do you again try to trip me up by this bait: it is enough for you to persuade men to illicit foods, since through them Adam was deceived in paradise. Hunger does not conquer me, nor do I yield to your persuasions. For the will of God is my food; the word of God is my perfect refreshment.

units.la: 5. Tunc. Id est, secundo.
units.tr: 5. Then. That is, the second.

units.la: Assumsit. Permisit se Christus a diabolo in sanctam civitatem, id est, Jerusalem (ubi agebantur sancta temporalia, scilicet sacrificia & hujusmodi alia) & in montem excelsum per aera rapi, qui pertulit etiam a membris illius crucifigi.
units.tr: He took him. Christ allowed himself to be carried by the devil into the holy city, that is, Jerusalem (where holy temporal things were done, namely sacrifices and other things of that kind), and onto a high mountain through the air; and he also allowed the devil to crucify his members.

units.la: Mitte te. Proponere præcipitium potest, præcipitare non potest diabolus.
units.tr: Throw yourself down. The devil can propose a precipice, but he cannot cast anyone down.

units.la: Angelis suis &c. Hæc tentatoris verba analogiam habent cum his ejusdem tentatoris Gen. 3. v. 4. ad mulierem verbis: Nequaquam morte moriemini.
units.tr: To his angels, &c. These words of the tempter have an analogy with those of the same tempter to the woman, Gen. 3:4: You will by no means die the death.

units.la: In manibus &c. Q. d. Erit tibi, quasi Angeli te gestarent, ne ad lapidem allidas pedem. Simile dicitur Job. 5. v. 23. Cum lapidibus regionum pactum tuum, & bestiæ terræ pacifiçæ erunt tibi.
units.tr: On their hands, &c. That is: it will be for you as though the angels were carrying you, so that you do not dash your foot against a stone. A similar thing is said in Job 5:23: For you will have a covenant with the stones of the field, and the beasts of the earth will be at peace with you.

units.la: 7. Non tentabis &c. Id est, ne præsumseris experimentum sumere Divinæ potentiæ, sapientiæ, aut alterius attributi Divini. Q. d. Quod suades, diabole, tentationis præsumtio est, non consilium sanitatis: Facultas vanitas, non virtutis exemplum. Inane est enim omne miraculum, quod utilitatem saluti non operatur humanæ. B. Maxi. loco mox laudato.
units.tr: 7. You shall not tempt, &c. That is: do not presume to make trial of the divine power, wisdom, or any other divine attribute. That is to say: What you urge, devil, is the presumption of temptation, not the counsel of health. Ability is vanity, not an example of virtue. Every miracle is empty which does not bring about a benefit for human salvation. B. Maxim., in the place just cited.

units.la: 8. Iterum. Id est, tertiò.
units.tr: 8. Again. That is, the third time.

units.la: Montem. Hic mons non creditur longè abesse Septentrionem versus à Jericho.
units.tr: A mountain. This mountain is not thought to be far from Jericho towards the north.

units.la: Ostendit. Supple, ex Luc. 4. in momento temporis; idque per artem Perspectivæ vel Opticæ, ut putat Francifcus Lucas.
units.tr: He showed. Supply, from Luke 4: in a moment of time; and this by the art of perspective or optics, as Francis Lucas thinks.

units.la: Et omnem gloriam eorum. Hebraismus. Q. d. Et quidquid in quovis regno esset præstantissimum.
units.tr: And all their glory. A Hebraism. That is, whatever would be most excellent in any kingdom.

units.la: 9. Hæc omnia tibi dabo. Hoc superbus mendaciter dicit, sicut jam mendax ab initio dixerat proto-parenti: Eritis sicut Dij.
units.tr: 9. All these things I will give you. The proud one says this falsely, just as the liar had said from the beginning to the first parent: You shall be as gods.

units.la: Si cadens adoraveris me. B. Hier. in Dan. 3. Omnem, inquit, Scripturam sanctam mente percurrens, nisi tamen me fallit oblivio, nunquam reperio quod Sanctorum quisquam Deum cadens adoraverit, sed quicunque idola & dæmones & rem illicita adoraverit, cadens dicitur adorare. Sanè fefellit B. Hier. oblivio. Nam Gen. 17. v. 3. Abraham Deum adorans cecidit pronus in faciem. Jos. 5. v. 13. legimus: Cecidit Josue pronus in terram & adorans ait. Supra c. 2. Magi procidentes adoraverunt Christum, &c.
units.tr: If you fall down and worship me. Blessed Jerome, on Daniel 3: Running through all of Holy Scripture in my mind, unless forgetfulness deceives me, I never find that any of the saints fell down and worshipped God. Rather, whoever worshipped idols and demons and unlawful things is said to have fallen down and worshipped. Certainly the forgetfulness of blessed Jerome misled him. For in Genesis 17:3 Abraham, worshipping God, fell face down. In Joshua 5:13 we read: Joshua fell face down on the ground and worshipped, and said. Above, in chapter 2, the Magi fell down and worshipped Christ, etc.

units.la: 10. Vade. Id est, apage, ut patet ex textu Græco.
units.tr: 10. Begone. That is, "away with you" (apage), as is clear from the Greek text.

units.la: Satana. Nomen Satan improprie sonat Hebraicè adversarium; unde & bonus Angelus, qui in gratiam fidelium Balaamo se opposuit, dicitur Num. 22. v. 22. fuisse satan ipsi, id est, ut etiam Vulgatus interpretatur, ut ipsi adversaretur. Antonomastice autem Satan dicitur Diabolus utpote qui Deo adversatur, & Fidelibus. Proprie Satan vocatur, qui, quoad potest, adversatur executioni divinæ voluntatis. Impropriessime Satan appellatur, qui adversatur inepto alicujus consilio propter ejus em utilitatem, cui se opponit; sic improprie dicitur adversarius furiosi, qui ei se opponit, cum in præcipitium ruiturus est. Ineptiunt Judæi, dum asserunt Diabolum Antonomastice dictum Satanam nihil in homines posse unâ propitiationum die singulis annis, quod litteræ numericæ nominis יהוה valent 364. quo numero aiunt significari, unâ die propitiationum excepta, Diabolum per reliquos anni dies 364. imperium suum exercere in homines.
units.tr: Satan. The name Satan means, in Hebrew, improperly, an adversary. Hence the good angel who opposed Balaam for the sake of the faithful is said in Numbers 22:22 to have been a satan to him, that is, as the Vulgate also translates it, to oppose him. Antonomastically, however, the devil is called Satan, inasmuch as he opposes God and the faithful. Properly, he is called Satan who, as far as he can, opposes the execution of the divine will. Most improperly, he is called Satan who opposes someone's ill-judged plan for that person's own good; thus a madman's friend who restrains him from rushing over a precipice is improperly called the madman's adversary. The Jews talk nonsense when they assert that the devil, called Satan antonomastically, has power over men on only one day of the year, the Day of Atonement, and that the numerical value of the letters of the name [השטן] is 364, by which number they say it is signified that, apart from the one day of atonement, the devil exercises his rule over men on the remaining 364 days of the year.

units.la: Scriptum est. Falsas de Scripturis Diaboli sagittas veris Scripturarum frangit clypeis, ut loquitur B. Hier.
units.tr: It is written. "He breaks the devil's false arrows, drawn from Scripture, with the true shields of Scripture," as blessed Jerome puts it.

units.la: Dominum Deum tuum &c. Sensum, non verba ex Deut. 6. citat Christus. Q. d. Qui te, Dæmon, adoraverit, non ei regna, sed infernâ debentur. Adorare namque Deum verum, eique servire, prærogativa regnandi est. Tu autem, qui honores mundi, expetitâ prævaricatione promittis, nec regnum dare te posse noveris. B. Maxim. loco mox citato.
units.tr: The Lord your God, etc. Christ quotes the sense of Deuteronomy 6, not the words. That is: "You, demon, who worship, shall not be given kingdoms, but hell is owed to you. For to worship the true God and serve him is the prerogative of reigning. But you, who promise the honours of the world at the price of a sought-after apostasy, should know that you cannot give a kingdom." Blessed Maximus, in the passage cited just above.

units.la: Soli. Hæc particula non extat in veritate Hebraica Deut. 6 v. 13, & 10. v. 20, unde hic versiculus depromatur; verùm necessariò in sensu inclusam expressere Christus, LXX, & Vulgatus interpres. Imò & 1 Reg. seu, Sam. 7. v. 3, in ipso textu Hebraeo exprimitur ועבדהו לבדו, & servite ei Soli. Hac Christi restrictione didici Soli Deo cultum religiosum esse deferendum, proindeque mihi secedendum esse ab Ecclesia Romana, in qua cultus religiosus manu-factis, mente-fictis, & sanctis impertitur.
units.tr: Only. This particle is not in the Hebrew text of Deuteronomy 6:13 and 10:20, from which this little verse is taken. Yet Christ, the Seventy and the Vulgate translator necessarily expressed what is included in the sense. Indeed, in 1 Kings (or 1 Samuel) 7:3 the Hebrew text itself has ועבדהו לבדו, that is, serve him only. From this restriction of Christ I have learned that religious worship is to be paid to the one God alone, and therefore I must withdraw from the Roman Church, in which religious worship is given to things made by hands, things fashioned by the mind, and saints.

units.la: Servies. Gr. λατρεύσεις. Illa tria vocabula λατρεύειν, δουλεύειν, & προσκυνεῖν promiscuè usurpari apud sacros & prophanos Scriptores, & si vocabulorum vis ac proprietas attendatur, eis non designari diversas cultûs species, sed ejusdem cultûs sive civilis, sive religiosi, diversos gradus pridem observarunt Eruditi. Nam προσκύνησις proprie est exhibitio illius observantiæ, cui vulgò nomen est homagium; λατρεία in rigore secundùm etymon est reverentia ejus, ad cujus potentiam contremiscimus; δουλεία denique secundum propriam acceptionem significat debitum domino obsequium & servitium. Hinc verè Augustinus vocum strictam significationem attendens q. 94. in Exod. 9. ait λατρείαν tribui Deo ut Deus est, δουλείαν, ut est Dominus, eo videlicet dominio, quod creaturæ est incommunicabile.
units.tr: You shall serve. Greek λατρεύσεις [λατρεύσεις]. The learned have long observed that those three words, λατρεύειν [λατρεύειν], δουλεύειν [δουλεύειν] and προσκυνεῖν [προσκυνεῖν], are used indiscriminately by sacred and profane writers, and that if the force and proper meaning of the words is considered, they designate not different kinds of worship but different degrees of the same worship, whether civil or religious. For προσκύνησις [προσκύνησις] properly means the rendering of that deference which is commonly called homage; λατρεία [λατρεία], strictly according to its etymology, is the reverence of one before whose power we tremble; and δουλεία [δουλεία], finally, according to its proper sense, signifies the obedience and service owed to a lord. Hence Augustine, attending carefully to the strict meaning of the terms, says in Question 94 on Exodus 9 that λατρεία [λατρεία] is ascribed to God as he is God, and δουλεία [δουλεία] as he is Lord, namely with that lordship which is incommunicable to a creature.

units.la: bile. At citra ullum prorsus idoneum fundamentum idem Aug. q. 61. in Gen. λατρείαν asserit non significare nisi servitutem soli Deo debitam, & adorationem religiosam, quæ Deo exhibetur tanquam nostræ creationis & beatificationis principio, cum adoratio civilis, quæ consistit in agnitione alicujus dominii, vel excellentiæ, & hominibus competat, eaque Gen. 23. Abraham honoraverit populum quendam gentium, ut loquitur ibid. Aug.
units.tr: incommunicable. But without any suitable foundation at all, the same Augustine, in Question 61 on Genesis, asserts that λατρεία [λατρεία] signifies nothing but the servitude owed to God alone and the religious adoration offered to God as the source of our creation and blessedness; whereas civil adoration, which consists in acknowledging some lordship or excellence, belongs also to men, and Genesis 23 says that Abraham honoured a certain people of the nations, as Augustine says in the same place.

units.la: 11. Tunc. Scilicet, consummatâ omni tentatione.
units.tr: 11. Then. That is, once every temptation had been completed.

units.la: Reliquit. Supple ex Luc. 4. v. 3. Usque ad tempus. Prima Domino nostro principi Martyrum tentamenta sunt blandimenta proposita. Ilia lata mundi sunt in pane, concupiscentia carnis; in promissione regnorum, ambitio seculi; in curiositatis tentatione, concupiscentia oculorum: Hæc omnia de seculo sunt, sed blandiuntur, non sæviunt. Restabat alia tentatio in asperis & duris; in sævis, in atrocibus atque immitibus restabat alia tentatio. Recessit itaque ab eo Diabolus insidians serpens, aliquamdiu post venturus rugiens leo, vincendus ab eo, qui conculcabit leonem & draconem. Aug. Hom. 1. inter undecim è Carthusia majori depromtas.
units.tr: He left him. Supply from Luke 4:3: until a time. "The first temptations to our Lord, the prince of martyrs, were enticements set before him. Those were the things of the world's breadth: in the bread, the lust of the flesh; in the promise of kingdoms, the ambition of the age; in the temptation of curiosity, the lust of the eyes. All these belong to the age, but they flatter rather than rage. Another temptation remained, in hardships and harshness; in cruelty, in atrocities and savagery another temptation remained. So the devil, the lurking serpent, withdrew from him, to come again after a while as a roaring lion, to be overcome by him who will trample the lion and the dragon." Augustine, Homily 1 among the eleven taken from the Greater Chartreuse.

units.la: 12. Cùm autem audiisset. Non immediate post tentationem; nam inter Christi tentationem & Joannis Baptistæ incarcerationem intercessere secundum Joannis testimonium de Christo, & tertium ad legatos Judæorum ad se missos, prima vocatio Petri & Andreæ, colloquium Christi cum Nathanaele, nuptiæ & miraculum in Cana Galilææ, prima vendentium ejectio è Templo, Christi colloquium cum Nicodemo & quartum Joannis Baptistæ de Christo testimonium, dum facta est quæstio, utrum baptismus discipulorum Christi superet baptismum ejusdem Joannis; hæc omnia videre est, Joan. 2. & 3.
units.tr: 12. When he heard. Not immediately after the temptation. For between Christ's temptation and the imprisonment of John the Baptist there intervened, according to John's testimony about Christ, a third testimony sent to the envoys of the Jews, the first calling of Peter and Andrew, Christ's conversation with Nathanael, the wedding and the miracle at Cana in Galilee, the first expulsion of the sellers from the Temple, Christ's conversation with Nicodemus, and John the Baptist's fourth testimony about Christ, when a question arose whether the baptism of Christ's disciples surpassed the baptism of John himself. All of this may be seen in John 2 and 3.

units.la: Traditus esset. Scilicet, per invidiam Pharisæorum, qui ex Mat. 17. v. 12. videntur fuisse autores Herodi, ut Joannem Baptistam comprehenderet.
units.tr: Had been handed over. That is, through the envy of the Pharisees, who, according to Matthew 17:12, seem to have been the authors of the plot with Herod, so that he would seize John the Baptist.

units.la: Secessit. Nimirum, ex agro tribus Judæ, in quo demorabatur, & discipuli ejus baptizabant, ut cederet Pharisæorum invidiæ, uti dicitur Joan. 4. v. 1.
units.tr: He withdrew. Namely, from the region of the tribe of Judah, where he had been staying and his disciples were baptising, so that he might yield to the envy of the Pharisees, as is said in John 4:1.

units.la: In Galilæam. In eam videlicet partem Galilææ maritimam, in qua Bethsaida & Capharnaum, quæ non Herodi, sed Philippo ejus fratri obvenerat, ut patet ex Josepho. 18. Antiq. c. 3.
units.tr: Into Galilee. Into that maritime part of Galilee, namely, in which lie Bethsaida and Capernaum, which had fallen not to Herod but to his brother Philip, as is clear from Josephus, Antiquities 18, chapter 3.

units.la: 13. Relicta. Id est, neglecta Nazareth (in qua civitate conceptus, educatus, & plurimam ætatis suæ partem egerat) quia Propheta in patria sua honorem non habet, ut diciturtur Joan. 4. v. 44. exceptus à Galilæis, qui viderant, quæ fecerat Jerosolymis in die festo; & ipsi enim venerant ad diem festum, cum priùs fermè latuissèt, cœpit in magno hominum concursu concionari, palamque se Messiam profiteri, & inde à B. Luca. c. 4. v. 14. dicitur in virtute Spiritús regressus in Galilæam.
units.tr: 13. Having left. That is, having neglected Nazareth (the city in which he had been conceived, brought up, and had spent the greater part of his life), because a prophet has no honour in his own country, as is said in John 4:44. He was received by the Galileans, who had seen what he had done at Jerusalem on the feast day, for they themselves had gone up to the feast day. Although he had until then remained largely hidden, he now began to preach to great crowds of people and openly to profess himself the Messiah. From this point the blessed Luke, chapter 4:14, says that he returned into Galilee in the power of the Spirit.

units.la: Venit. Nempe, post varias prædicationes; post sanitatem filio Reguli, qui Capharnaum infirmabatur, in Cana Galilææ redditam; post vocationem Petri & Andreæ, Jacobi & Joannis, ut patet ex collatione Joan. 4. v. 43. &c. Marc. 1. v. 14. &c. Luc. 4. v. 14. &c. cum iis, quæ hic dicuntur.
units.tr: He came. Namely, after various preachings; after the healing of the son of the royal official, who was sick at Capernaum, performed at Cana in Galilee; after the calling of Peter and Andrew, James and John, as is clear from comparing John 4:43 etc., Mark 1:14 etc., and Luke 4:14 etc., with what is said here.

units.la: Habitavit. Non diu, ut patet ex Marc. 1. v. 35. & Luc. 4. v. 42.
units.tr: He dwelt. Not for long, as is clear from Mark 1:35 and Luke 4:42.

units.la: Capharnaum. Civitas tribûs Nephtali juxta flagnum Generezareth, quo à meridie terminabatur tribus Nephtali, ab oriente tribus Zabulon; totius Decapoleos pene celeberrima & pulcherrima est, alluitúrque ab oriente fluvij Jordanis ostio; à meridie Mari Galilææ, seu flagno Generzareth, ubi Jordanis hoc flagnum seu mare influit.
units.tr: Capernaum. A city of the tribe of Naphtali, beside the lake of Gennesaret, the tribe of Naphtali being bounded on the south by that lake and on the east by the tribe of Zebulun. It is almost the most famous and most beautiful city of the whole Decapolis. It is washed on the east by the mouth of the river Jordan, and on the south by the Sea of Galilee, or lake of Gennesaret, where the Jordan flows into this lake or sea.

units.la: Zabulon. Tribus inter Mare occiduum & Mare Galilææ posita; nomen sortitur à Zabulon decimo filiorum Jacob, sed sexto & ultimo ex uxore Lia.
units.tr: Zebulun. A tribe situated between the Western Sea and the Sea of Galilee. It takes its name from Zebulun, the tenth of Jacob's sons, but the sixth and last by his wife Leah.

units.la: Nephthalim. Ef. 9. Nephthali. Tribus ad superiorem, eámque occiduam Jordanis ripam sita, sic nominata à Nephtali inter filios Jacob sexto, sed ex Bala Rachelis ancilla secundo & ultimo, vicina est tribui Zabulon.
units.tr: Nephthalim. Isa. 9. Naphtali. The tribe situated beside the upper, western bank of the Jordan. It is so named from Naphtali, the sixth of Jacob's sons, but the second and last by Bilhah, Rachel's maidservant, and it lies next to the tribe of Zebulun.

units.la: 14. Adimpleretur. Iest, veritas exhiberetur ejus, quod de figura dictum fuit per Esaiam Prophetam c. 9.
units.tr: 14. Adimpleretur. That is, the truth of what was said about the type by the prophet Isaiah in chapter 9 would be displayed.

units.la: 15. Terra Nephthalim. Supple, & cetera. Solemne est Hebræorum Scriptoribus in citandis Scripturæ locis ea Scripturæ verba proferre, quorum causâ Scripturæ citantur; quæ vero illa præcedunt, vel mediant, leviter delibare, & non raro omnino transilire. Sed cum Hebræis in more positum fit defectum verborum inter citata mediantium hac nota, &c. ⁊ⁱ, designare, eam novi Instrumenti Scriptores industriæ lectoris passim subintelligendam reliquere.
units.tr: 15. Terra Nephthalim. Supply "and the rest." It is the custom of Hebrew writers, when citing passages of Scripture, to give the words for whose sake the passage is cited, but to touch lightly on those that precede or come between, and often to skip them altogether. Since the Hebrews customarily mark an omission of words between quoted passages with this sign, &c. ⁊ⁱ, the writers of the New Testament left it to the diligence of the reader to supply these words throughout.

units.la: Via maris. Hac particula denotatur Zabulon, cujus terra terminatur Mari Galilææ. Græce, viam maris, qui Accusativus regitur apud Esaiam à verbo Hebræo הדרך, aggravari fecit, quod verbum hic omisit Matthæus de industria, ut properaret ad illa verba: Populus qui ambulabat in tenebris, &c. quæ vere nunc impleta esse dicit; ex iis verò quæ præcedunt, ea tantùm citat, quæ necessaria sunt, ut in
units.tr: The way of the sea. By this phrase Zebulun is denoted, whose land is bordered by the Sea of Galilee. In Greek it reads the way of the sea, an accusative governed in Isaiah by the Hebrew verb הדרך [hadrech], made heavy. Matthew deliberately left out this verb, so that he could hasten on to the words The people who walked in darkness, etc., which he says are now truly fulfilled. Of the verses that come before, he cites only those that are necessary, so that in

units.la: Trans Jordanem. Scilicet refpeẑu Assyriorum, de quibus dicit Efaias quod quasi primo levibus pœnis in diebus Phacee Regis Israel affecerint Zabulonios & Nephtalitas, tandem nono anno Ofee filij Ela horum regionem quasi oppressere gravi pondere multitudinis filiorum Israel, quos universos illac in Assyriam abduxere captivos.
units.tr: Beyond the Jordan. Namely, with respect to the Assyrians, of whom Isaiah says that, as it were, at first they inflicted light punishments on the Zebulunites and Naphtalites in the days of Pekah, king of Israel, but at last, in the ninth year of Hoshea son of Elah, they overwhelmed their region with the heavy weight of the multitude of the sons of Israel, all of whom they carried off captive into Assyria.

units.la: Galilæa gentium. Hac particula designatur Nephtali, qui Galilæam gentium incolebat.
units.tr: Galilæa gentium. By this phrase Naphtali is denoted, who inhabited Galilee of the Gentiles.

units.la: 16. Sedebat. Apud Efaiam legitur, ambulabat. Ambo hæc verba supplent vicem verbi substantivi erat; unde in eundem sensum recidunt.
units.tr: 16. Sedebat. In Isaiah it reads "walked." Both these words take the place of the substantive verb "was," and so come to the same sense.

units.la: In tenebris. Id est, ad litteram apud Efaiam, in tribulationibus; at Evangelista tenebras hïc vocat errorem & impietatem, ut testatur Chrysost. Hom. 10. in Mat.
units.tr: In tenebris. That is, literally in Isaiah, "in tribulations," but the Evangelist here calls darkness error and impiety, as Chrysostom testifies in Hom. 10 on Matthew.

units.la: Lucem Magnam. Id est, apud Efaiam ad litteram, diem confolationis. Hïc intelligitur lux vera, quæ illuminat omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum. Idem repetit hemistichio sequenti, more Hebræis usitato, eodem sensu Litterali & Allegorico.
units.tr: Lucem Magnam. That is, literally in Isaiah, "the day of consolation." Here is understood the true light, which enlightens every man coming into this world. He repeats the same in the following half-verse, in the manner usual among the Hebrews, with the same literal and allegorical sense.

units.la: Sedentibus. Esa. habitantibus, id est, existentibus.
units.tr: Sedentibus. Isaiah has habitantibus, that is, "existing."

units.la: Umbræ mortis. Umbra mortis dicitur tristissima rerum & quasi mortis impendentis imago.
units.tr: Umbræ mortis. "Shadow of death" is said of the most sorrowful state of things, as it were an image of impending death.

units.la: Lux orta eis. Scilicet, luce non quærentibus, ad luce non currentibus & in ultimis malisjacentibus. Porro hanc Efaiæ authoritatem Evangelista non ex textu Græco, sed Hebræo est interpretatus.
units.tr: Lux orta eis. Namely, light for those who do not seek light, who do not run to the light, and who lie in the worst evils. Moreover, the Evangelist has rendered this authority of Isaiah not from the Greek text but from the Hebrew.

units.la: 17. Exinde. Id est, ex quo traditus est Joannes.
units.tr: 17. Exinde. That is, from the time when John was delivered up.

units.la: Cœpit. Scilicet, in Galilæa.
units.tr: Cœpit. Namely, in Galilee.

units.la: Prædicare. Palàm videlicet, & assiduè & frequenter. Licèt autem ex Lege Mosaica, ut constat ex Josepho adversus Appionem, tum ex ipsis Scripturis munus docendi publicè fuerit solis Sacerdotibus & Levitis proprium, tamen ut doctissimus notat Genebrardus ad annum mundi 3983. Scribæ, id est, Legis Doctores una cum Pharisæis Cathedram Mosis vacuam invaserunt, dum Sacerdotes divitiis Ecclesiasticis abutentes desererent suum officium. Huc forsan alludit Christus Luc. 11. v. 52. dum dicit: Væ vobis Legis-peritis, quia tulistis (Gr. ...) claveṁ Scientiæ; quod Tertullianus exponit interpretationem Legis, seu, munus docendi Scripturam. Ubi Christus maledicit Scribis, quod potestate, quam rapuerant ac sibi minimè debitam ex Synagogæ indulgentia tulerant, in suam & aliorum perniciem abuterentur. Ex quo autem subsidiarii & adventij, tam Scribæ, quam Pharisæi Sacerdotibus & Levitis, in eorum scilicet defectum creati sunt, cuivis doctrinæ Legis instructo licitum erat docere in Synagogis. Unde Christus ex semine David secundum carnem de Tribu Juda, ex qua nullus erat sacerdos, palàm docebat in Synagogis; & similiter Paulus de Tribu Benjamin, ut videre elt in Actis Apostolorum.
units.tr: Prædicare. Openly, of course, and constantly and frequently. Although, according to the Mosaic Law, as is clear from Josephus against Apion, and from the Scriptures themselves, the public office of teaching belonged only to priests and Levites, nevertheless, as the most learned Genebrard notes at the year of the world 3983, the scribes, that is the doctors of the Law together with the Pharisees, seized the vacant Chair of Moses, while the priests, abusing ecclesiastical riches, abandoned their office. Perhaps Christ alludes to this at Luke 11:52 when he says: "Woe unto you, lawyers! for ye have taken away (Gr. ...) the key of knowledge." Tertullian explains this as the interpretation of the Law, or the office of teaching Scripture. There Christ curses the scribes, because they abused, to their own and others' ruin, a power they had seized, which was by no means due to them, but which they had obtained by the indulgence of the synagogue. But since the scribes and Pharisees were created as deputies and newcomers, alongside the priests and Levites, to make up for their lack, anyone instructed in the doctrine of the Law was permitted to teach in the synagogues. Hence Christ, according to the flesh a descendant of David and of the tribe of Judah, out of which no priest arose, openly taught in the synagogues; and likewise Paul, of the tribe of Benjamin, as can be seen in the Acts of the Apostles.

units.la: 18. Mare Galilææ. Hebraismus, id est, congregatio aquarum Galilææ proxima, quæ & Mare Tiberiadis dicitur vicina ab urbe Tiberiade, quæ urbs primùm Cenereth, aut Cenerooth, dein Genesar aut Genesareth, tum demùm ab Herode Antipa ampliata, in honorem Tiberij Cæsaris appellata est Tiberiades. Hujus Maris longitudo esse dicitur quindecim aut sexdecim millium passuum, latitudo septem aut octo millium passuum interfluente Jordane. Totum hoc mare amœnis est circumdatum oppidis, Capharnao & Corozaim à Septentrione Juliade, Gerasa & Gadara ab Oriente, Bethsaida & Tiberiade ab Occidente, Tarichæa à Meridie.
units.tr: 18. Mare Galilææ. A Hebraism, that is, the nearby gathering of waters of Galilee, which is also called the Sea of Tiberias from the neighbouring city of Tiberias. That city was first called Chinnereth, or Chinneroth, then Gennesar or Gennesaret, and finally, enlarged by Herod Antipas, it was named Tiberias in honour of Tiberius Caesar. The length of this sea is said to be fifteen or sixteen thousand paces, its breadth seven or eight thousand paces, with the Jordan flowing through it. The whole sea is surrounded by pleasant towns: Capernaum and Chorazin to the north, Julias likewise from the north, Gerasa and Gadara to the east, Bethsaida and Tiberias to the west, and Tarichaea to the south.

units.la: Vidit. Non oculo corporis tantùm, sed etiam mentis; visus enim Christi est respectus misericordiæ juxta illud Exod. 3. Videns vidi afflictionem populi mei,
units.tr: Vidit. Not only with the eye of the body but also of the mind, for the seeing of Christ is a regard of mercy, according to that passage of Exodus 3: "I have surely seen the affliction of my people."

units.la: Duos fratres. Observat Severianus Gabalorum Episcopus Orat. 1. De mundi creatione, quod quemadmodum in veteri Testamento prima Dei vocatio à fratribus cepit; primos enim præcones Moysem & Aaronem accepit; ita & in Evangelio primam Petri & Andreæ vocationem facit. Et illic quidem simplex gratia; hic autem duplo auctior. Illic enim duo fratres vocati, Moyses & Aaron: Hic autem bis gemini, Petrus & Andreas, Jacobus & Joannes; quòd enim Salvator charitate Sancti Spiritûs nos voluit informare, fratréque animi affectione ac spiritu præstare, naturam fundamentum sumsit, commisitque naturæ viscera, & in illa Ecclesiæ fundamentum superextruxit.
units.tr: Duos fratres. Severian, bishop of Gabala, in Oration 1 On the Creation of the World, observes that just as in the Old Testament God's first call began with brothers, for he took Moses and Aaron as his first heralds, so also in the Gospel he makes the first calling of Peter and Andrew. There the grace is simple, but here it is doubled. For there two brothers were called, Moses and Aaron; but here two pairs of brothers, Peter and Andrew, James and John. For since the Saviour willed to form us by the charity of the Holy Spirit, and to make us excel in brotherly affection and spirit, he took nature as the foundation, committed himself to the bonds of nature, and built the foundation of the Church upon them.

units.la: Simonem, qui vocatur Petrus. Id est, cui jam ante sibi vivo Christus nomen Petri imposuerat, vel imponendum prædixerat; in vocatione enim Petri & Andreæ duo veluti gradus observari possunt, præparatio nimirum, quam vocitant nonnulli vocationem ad fidem, & ipsa vocatio, quâ ita vocati sunt, ut omnibus relictis Christum perpetuò sequerentur. Præparatio sic contigisse narratur Joan. 1. Andreas à Christi Præcursore impulsus venit ad Christum, à quo benignè exceptus mox fratrem Simonem ad illum duxit; Simonem Christus pari benignitate excipit, & insuper nomen imponit, vel saltem ipsi imponendum prædicit. Hæc fuit prima Jesu Christi in Simonem & Andeam quasi manûs injectio, quâ sibi illos afferebat, nondum tamen ad sui sequelam vocatos, ut testantur Eucherius Lugdunensis in cap. I, Joannis, Aug. Tract. 7. in Joan. &c. Hinc patet quod qui primos Apoltolorum vocatos aiunt fuisse Petrum & Andream, attendunt ad primam eorum vocationem, qui Christus, ut se discipulos ejus profiterentur, ac saepe ipsum invitarent, vocavit eos; de qua vocatione loquitur solus Joannes Evangelista c. 1. Eucherius, vero laudatus, dum in vigilia sancti Andreae Philippum ante Apostolos omnes vocatum secundum Evangelium Joannis videri ait, attendit ad vocationem, qui Christus Petrum & Andream assumsit in continuum suum comitatum, de qua vocatione hic Mat. Marc. 1. & Luc. 5.
units.tr: Simonem, qui vocatur Petrus. That is, to whom Christ had already, while still living, imposed the name Peter, or had foretold that it would be imposed. In the calling of Peter and Andrew two stages can be observed, as it were: the preparation, which some call the calling to faith, and the calling itself, by which they were called so as to leave everything and follow Christ perpetually. The preparation is narrated as having occurred in John 1. Andrew, moved by Christ's Forerunner, came to Christ, by whom he was kindly received, and soon led his brother Simon to him. Christ receives Simon with equal kindness and moreover imposes a name on him, or at least foretells that one would be imposed. This was, as it were, the first laying on of hands by Jesus Christ upon Simon and Andrew, by which he brought them to himself, though they were not yet called to follow him, as Eucherius of Lyon on John chapter 1 and Augustine, Tract. 7 on John, etc., testify. Hence it is clear that those who say Peter and Andrew were the first of the Apostles called are looking to their first calling, by which Christ called them so that they might profess themselves his disciples and often invite him; of this calling the Evangelist John alone speaks, in chapter 1. Eucherius, cited above, when he says that on the vigil of St Andrew, Philip was seen, according to John's Gospel, to be called before all the Apostles, looks to the calling by which Christ took Peter and Andrew into his continual company, of which calling Matthew here, and Mark 1 and Luke 5, speak.

units.la: Petrus. Sic dictus, ut elegantèr Chrysost. Hom. 2. in titulum Psal. 50. quod immotae rupis instar in fide solidatus esset.
units.tr: Peter. So called, as Chrysostom elegantly says in Hom. 2 on the title of Psalm 50, because he was made firm in faith like an immovable rock.

units.la: 19. Ait illis. Scilicet, ut constat ex Luc. 5. postquam vidisset Petrum & Andream piscantes, & in eorum navim conscendisset, & pusillum progressus vidisset filios Zebedaei, edidisset miraculum capturae piscium in navi Petri, & Petro dixisset: Ex hoc jam eris homines capiens.
units.tr: 19. He said to them. That is, as appears from Luke 5, after he had seen Peter and Andrew fishing, had got into their boat, and had gone a little farther and seen the sons of Zebedee, he worked the miracle of the catch of fish in Peter's boat and said to Peter: From now on you will be catching men.

units.la: Venite post me. Hebraismus Scripturae familiaris, id est, sequimini me, supple ex mox dictis, perpetuo.
units.tr: Come after me. A Hebraism familiar in Scripture, that is, follow me, with the words "continually" supplied from what was said just before.

units.la: Faciam vos fieri piscatores hominum. Nempe, ut vitalis escae captu, ut hamo caelestis verbi, de mortis gurgite animas ad lucem tollatis sempiternam. Vide Chrysologum Ser. 28.
units.tr: I will make you fishers of men. That is, that by taking the living bait, by the hook of the heavenly word, you may draw souls up from the abyss of death into the eternal light. See Chrysologus, Serm. 28.

units.la: 20. Relictis retibus. Id est, Synechdochicè, omnibus, ut patet ex Luc. 5. v. 11.
units.tr: 20. Leaving their nets. That is, by synecdoche, leaving everything, as is clear from Luke 5:11.

units.la: 21. Procedens inde. Supple ex Marc. 1. v. 19. pusillum
units.tr: 21. Going on from there. Supply a little from Mark 1:19.

units.la: Reficientes retia sua. Scilicet, in ipsa navi, ut post Matthaeum hic notat Marc. c. 1. v. 19. dum alij, ut dicitur Luc. 5. v. 2. ejusdem navis piscatores descenderant & lavabant retia. Vocat autem Matthaeus reficientes, quos Marcus appellat componentes.
units.tr: Mending their nets. That is, in the boat itself, as Mark 1:19 notes here after Matthew, while others, as Luke 5:2 says, the fishermen had got out of the same boat and were washing their nets. Matthew calls them mending, which Mark calls putting in order.

units.la: Et vocavit eos. Nempe, statim post assumtos Petrum & Andream in familiam & continuum comitatum suum, ut patet ex Marci 1. v. 20.
units.tr: And he called them. That is, immediately after taking Peter and Andrew into his household and constant company, as is clear from Mark 1:20.

units.la: 23. Et circuibat. Nimirum postquam Christus vocasset Petrum & Andream, Jacobum & Joannem, venit & habitavit in Capharnaum maritima civitate Galilaeae, ubi per aliquot Sabbata docuit, & postquam inibi ejecisset daemonium immundum ex quodam homine in Synagoga. & surgens in domo Petri curasset, ei sunt oblati innumeri daemoniaci & infirmi, quos omnes in domo Simonis & Andreae curavit. Egressus ex illa domo valde diluculo desertum petiit; cumque requirentes eum usque ad ipsum venissent & detinerent, ne a se discederent, dixit se missum ut & aliis civitatibus evangelizaret. Hoc dicto circuibat, seu cir-cuire cuire incipiebat pro prima vice totam Galilæam, ut hic dicitur. Hæc omnia patent ex collatione eorum, quæ hic dicuntur, cum Marc. 1. v. 21. &c. Luc. 4. v. 31. &c.
units.tr: 23. And he went about. That is, after Christ had called Peter and Andrew, James and John, he came and lived in Capernaum, a city on the sea of Galilee, where for some Sabbaths he taught; and after he had cast out an unclean demon from a certain man in the synagogue there, and had healed Peter's mother-in-law in Peter's house, innumerable demoniacs and sick people were brought to him, all of whom he healed in the house of Simon and Andrew. Going out of that house very early in the morning, he sought a desert place; and when those seeking him came to him and tried to keep him from leaving them, he said he had been sent to preach the gospel to other cities also. With this saying he went about, or began to go about the whole of Galilee for the first time, as is said here. All this is clear from comparing what is said here with Mark 1:21 ff. and Luke 4:31 ff.

units.la: In Synagogis. Synagogæ dicuntur loca non ad sacrificium, sed ad publicam orationem, sacram concionem & Legis explanationem destinata. Jerosolymis erant plusquam 480. Synagogæ, sicque pro frequentia urbium in eis erant plures, aut pauciores Synagogæ.
units.tr: In the synagogues. Synagogues are places set apart not for sacrifice but for public prayer, holy preaching and the explanation of the Law. At Jerusalem there were more than 480 synagogues, and so, according to the size of the towns, there were more or fewer synagogues in them.

units.la: Evangelium regni. Supple ex Marc. 1. v. 4. Dei, id est, latum nuncium de regno cœlorum, quod scilicet jam appropinquaverit & intra nos sit.
units.tr: The gospel of the kingdom. Supply of God from Mark 1:4, that is, the glad news of the kingdom of heaven, which is now near at hand and within us.

units.la: Sanans. Quia tarda est humanæ ignorantiæ fides ad credenda quæ non videt & speranda quæ nescit, oportebat divinâ eruditione firmandos corporeis beneficiis & visibilibus miraculis incitari, ut cujus tam benignam experiebantur potentiam, non ambigerent salutarem esse doctrinam.
units.tr: Healing. Because human ignorance is slow to believe what it does not see and to hope for what it does not know, it was necessary that those to be confirmed by divine teaching should be moved by bodily benefits and visible miracles, so that, having experienced such kindly power, they would not doubt that the teaching was saving.

units.la: 24. Opinio. Græcè ἀκοή[?], auditio, fama.
units.tr: 24. Report. In Greek [akoē], hearing, rumour.

units.la: Syriam. Heb. Aram; unde rectè sensit Pollidonius apud Strabonem in calce lib. 16. Syros ab Homero dici Ἀριμαῖοι[?], quos & Ἀραμαῖοι[?] suo tempore vocatos idem Strabo lib. 13. testatur. Josephus eos appellat Aramæos. Est autem Syria omnis regio ab Euphrate usque ad Mare Magnum, & a Cappadocia usque ad Ægyptum, in qua regione est provincia Palæstinæ, quam inhabitabant filij Israel.
units.tr: Syria. In Hebrew Aram; whence Posidonius, quoted by Strabo at the end of book 16, rightly thought that the Syrians were called Arimaioi [Ἀριμαῖοι] by Homer, whom Strabo himself, in book 13, attests were also called Aramaioi [Ἀραμαῖοι] in his own time. Josephus calls them Arameans. Syria, however, is the whole region from the Euphrates to the Great Sea, and from Cappadocia to Egypt, and in this region is the province of Palestine, which the sons of Israel inhabited.

units.la: Lunatici. Medici per lunaticos intelligunt, comitiali, seu sacro morbo laborantes, quos existimant conceptos dubiæ per tempora Lunæ, ut loquitur Sammonicus apud Heinsium, id est, inter deficientem lunam & novilunium, licet id negat Valesius Sacræ Philosophiæ c. 71.
units.tr: Lunatics. Physicians understand by lunatics those suffering from epilepsy, or the sacred disease, whom they think are conceived at doubtful times of the moon, as Sammonicus says in Heinsius, that is, between the waning moon and the new moon, although Valesius denies this in Sacred Philosophy, ch. 71.

units.la: 25. Et secutæ sunt eum turbæ. Quod hic narrat Matthæus per anticipationem, contigisse creditur post secundum a baptismo Christi Pascha, de quo Joannes c. 6. post confricationem spicarum in sabbato & manum aridam sabbato curatam infrà cap. 12. proindeque post ea, quæ narrantur miracula & reprehensiones infrà c. 8. à versu 18. usque ad versum 35.capitis noni.
units.tr: 25. And great crowds followed him. What Matthew narrates here by anticipation is believed to have happened after the second Passover from the baptism of Christ, of which John speaks in ch. 6, after the plucking of ears of grain on the Sabbath, and the withered hand healed on the Sabbath, mentioned below in ch. 12; and therefore after the miracles and rebukes narrated below in ch. 8 from verse 18 to verse 35 of chapter 9.

units.la: Decapoli. Decapolis est regio, quæ, præter alias minores urbes plurimas, decem celeberrimas complectitur; inter quas Cæsarea Philippi, Corozaim, Capharnaum, Bethsaida, Gadara, &c. ea pæne tota ad Jordanis superioris & ad Maris Galilæi utramque ripam extenditur.
units.tr: Decapolis. Decapolis is a region which, besides very many other smaller cities, embraces ten very famous ones, among which are Caesarea Philippi, Chorazin, Capernaum, Bethsaida, Gadara, etc. It extends almost wholly along both banks of the upper Jordan and of the Sea of Galilee.

units.la: Trans Jordanem. Id est, ex ea regione, quæ ad Orientem Jordanis posita, trans Jordanem est respectu Terræ promissæ, cujus limites à Deo primùm fuerant assignati inter Mare Magnum, seu Mediterraneum ab Occidente; & Jordanem ab Oriente; attamen tribus Ruben & Gad & dimidia tribus Manasse trans Jordanem ipsis petentibus descriptæ sunt, reliquæ decem cis Jordanem.
units.tr: Beyond the Jordan. That is, from that region which, lying to the east of the Jordan, is beyond the Jordan with respect to the Promised Land, whose boundaries were first assigned by God between the Great Sea, or Mediterranean, on the west, and the Jordan on the east. Nevertheless, the tribes of Reuben and Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh were assigned beyond the Jordan at their own request, and the remaining ten on this side of the Jordan.

units.la: CAPUT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: 1. Montem. Hic Mons creditur non procul abesse a Capharnao, Bethsaida, & Mari Galilææ. Tra autem legitur Christus refugia habuisse, desertum, navim, & montem ad quorum alterum, quoties a turbis opprimebatur, conscendebat.
units.tr: 1. The mountain. This mountain is thought not to be far from Capernaum, Bethsaida, and the Sea of Galilee. Moreover, we read that Christ had places of refuge: the desert, a boat, and a mountain, and whenever the crowds pressed upon him, he climbed to one of these.

units.la: Cùm sedisset. Christus primùm ascendit in Montis cacumen, ubi in oratione pernoctavit; dein mane, cùm dies factus esset, vocavit ad se discipulos suos, & elegit ex ipsis duodecim, quos & Apostolos nominavit, & destinavit ut mitterentur ad prædicandum Evangelium Regni, ut patet ex Luc. 6. à versu 12. usque ad versum 17. Tum descendit cum discipulis è Montis cacumine in campestrem locum, hoc est, in ejusdem Montis locum inferiorem cacumine multò magis æquabilem & turbarum capacem, & ibi stetit, dum ægrotos curaret; postea verò sedens doctoris in morem concionem habuit, cujus præcipuæ partes ad discipulos pertinebant, quamvis & turbæ audirent, ut testatur Matthæus in fine hujus concionis vulgò dictæ Sermo Domini in Monte. Sic fere B. Aug. l. de consensu Evan. c. 19.
units.tr: When he had sat down. Christ first went up to the top of the mountain, where he spent the night in prayer. Then, when day had come, he called his disciples to him and chose twelve of them, whom he also named Apostles and appointed to be sent out to preach the Gospel of the Kingdom, as is clear from Luke 6, from verse 12 to verse 17. Then he came down with his disciples from the mountaintop to a level place, that is, to a lower part of the same mountain, much more even at the summit and able to hold crowds, and there he stood while he healed the sick. Afterwards, however, he sat down, as a teacher does, and gave a discourse, whose main parts were addressed to the disciples, although the crowds also listened, as Matthew testifies at the end of this discourse, commonly called The Sermon on the Mount. Thus, more or less, Augustine, On the Harmony of the Gospels, book 1, chapter 19.

units.la: 2. Aperiens os suum. Hebraismus Scripturæ familiaris, id est, incipiens loqui.
units.tr: 2. Opening his mouth. A Hebraism familiar in Scripture, that is, beginning to speak.

units.la: 3. Beati. Spe in via, re in patria. Neque ulla alia hujus verbo, cùm beatum dicimus, subjecta notio est, nisi secretis malis omnibus cumulata bonorum omnium complexio. Cic. in Tusculana.
units.tr: 3. Blessed. Hope on the way, reality in the homeland. When we call someone blessed, no other notion is attached to the word than a full collection of all good things with every evil removed. Cicero, in the Tusculan Disputations.

units.la: Pauperes spiritu. Id est, animo & affectu, qui nimirum corda non apponunt ad divitias; Multi enim pauperes sunt in substantiis, avarissimi tamen secundum affectum, quos non salvat pauperta, sed affectus damnat, ut ait B. Basil. in Psal. 33. Hinc ad id, quod Christus Luc. 6. v. 24. in hoc eodem Sermone dixit væ divitibus, egregie advertit Ambrosius non censum sed affectum in crimine esse.
units.tr: Poor in spirit. That is, in mind and affection, those who of course do not set their hearts on riches. For many are poor in their possessions yet most greedy in their affection; poverty does not save them, but their affection condemns them, as Basil says on Psalm 33. Hence Ambrose rightly observes that it is not wealth but the affection that is the sin, in relation to what Christ said in this same Sermon, Luke 6:24, Woe to the rich.

units.la: 4. Mites. Qui nempe cedunt improbitatibus & non resistunt malo, sed vincunt in bono malum. Aug. l. 1. de Ser. Domini in Monte c. 3. Terram Terram. De qua evelli non possunt; illam, inquam, terram possidebunt, haereditario scilicet jure, ut fert textus Graecus, hoc est sine labore ac molestia, quemadmodum haereditatem possidemus, quae obtingit nobis a patribus, de qua terra dicitur Psalm, 141. v. 6. Portio mea in Terra viventium. Significat enim quamdam stabilitatem haereditatis perpetuae, ubi anima per bonum affectum, tanquam in loco suo requiescit, sicut corpus in terra: ipsa est requies & vita Sanctorum. Aug. ibid.
units.tr: 4. Meek. Those who, of course, yield to wicked men and do not resist evil, but overcome evil with good. Augustine, On the Sermon on the Mount, book 1, chapter 3. They shall possess the earth. The earth from which they cannot be torn; that earth, I say, they will possess by hereditary right, as the Greek text has it, that is, without labour and trouble, just as we possess an inheritance that has come to us from our fathers. Of this earth the Psalm says, Psalm 142:6 [141], My portion in the land of the living. For this signifies a certain stability of an everlasting inheritance, where the soul rests through good affection as in its own place, as the body rests on the earth; this is the rest and life of the saints. Augustine, ibid.

units.la: 5. Qui lugent. id est, qui per lachrymas & pressuras ad gaudia aeterna contendunt, ut loquitur Alcuinus in cap. 16, Joannis.
units.tr: 5. Who mourn. That is, who through tears and afflictions strive toward eternal joys, as Alcuin says on John 16.

units.la: Consolabuntur. Id est, consolatione afficientur, seu ut loquitur Luc. c. 6. Ridebunt. Promittit autem flentibus risum, non quidem emissum per mandibulas sonum, sed meram & impermixtam cuiuslibet tristitiae alacritatem. Glossa ordinaria ex B. Basil. in Hom. de gratiarum actione.
units.tr: Shall be comforted. That is, they shall be given comfort, or, as Luke 6 puts it: They shall laugh. He promises laughter to those who weep, not indeed a sound let out through the jaws, but a pure and unmixed cheerfulness free from any sadness. The Ordinary Gloss, drawing on Basil, in his homily on giving thanks.

units.la: 6. Esuriunt. Esurie corporali, ut patet ex Luc. 6. v. 21. & 25. ubi his esurientibus opponuntur saturati, quibus dicitur ue, quae dictio, ut monet Chrysost. Hom. 17. in Gen. semper in Scripturis dicitur his, qui non possunt evadere a futuro supplicio.
units.tr: 6. Who hunger. With bodily hunger, as is clear from Luke 6:21 and 25, where those who hunger are set against the full, to whom is said woe. This word, as Chrysostom observes in Homily 17 on Genesis, is always used in Scripture of those who cannot escape future punishment.

units.la: Et. Hebraismus, id est, quia.
units.tr: And. A Hebraism, that is, because.

units.la: Sitiunt iustitiam. Id est, ardent virtutis desiderio; solent enim Scripturae non per famem, sed per sitim vehementem desiderium significare, ut Psal. 41. v. 2. Sitivit anima mea ad Deum fortem vivum. Psal. 62. v. 2. Sitivit in te anima mea. Cicero quoque in Orat. pro Plancio hoc sensu dixit: Sitientem me virtutis tuae deseruisti. Illos itaque dicit Christus beatos, qui abstinentiam indicunt corpori, ut a vitiis magis animam abstinere possint. Frenum enim quoddam est luxuriantis animae corpus exhaustum, inquit Ambrosius Serm. 13. Praeclare itaque Aug. De utilitate Jejunii cap. 5. Dic mihi quem cibum diligas, ut approbem quod ab ipso (carnis) cibo te abstineas. Diligis justitiam? Forte, inquis, diligo. Appareat ergo justitia tua, &c.
units.tr: Who thirst for righteousness. That is, who burn with a desire for virtue. For Scripture usually signifies longing not by hunger but by intense thirst, as in Psalm 42:2, My soul thirsts for the living God. Psalm 63:1, My soul thirsts for you. Cicero too, in his speech for Plancius, used it in this sense: You have forsaken me, thirsting for your virtue. Christ therefore calls blessed those who impose abstinence on the body, so that they may be able to abstain more from vices in the soul. For the body, emptied out, is a kind of bridle for the soul that runs riot, says Ambrose, Sermon 13. Augustine too rightly says in On the Usefulness of Fasting, chapter 5: Tell me what food you love, so that I may approve that you abstain from that very food of the flesh. Do you love righteousness? Perhaps, you say, I do. Let your righteousness then appear, etc.

units.la: Saturabuntur. Scilicet in patria, cum apparuerit eis gloria Dei, & viderint Deum sicuti est.
units.tr: Shall be satisfied. That is, in the homeland, when the glory of God shall have appeared to them, and they shall see God as he is.

units.la: 7. Misericordes. Id est, qui subveniunt miseris, quantum in ipsis est.
units.tr: 7. Merciful. That is, those who help the wretched as far as lies in them.

units.la: Misericordiam consequentur. Id est, ipsis subvenietur a Deo, ut de miseria liberentur. Ideo vero ipsum a Deo promissum operibus bonis praemium appellatur in Scripturis misericordia & gratia, quia cum Deus coronat bona opera nostra, quae καλα χρηστικως a PP, subinde merita dicuntur, Non solum solum domus fuit Deus dona sua reddit, sed etiam ibi tantum gratia divinæ retributionis exuberat, ut incomparabiliter & ineffabiliter omne meritum quamvis bonæ & à Deo datæ voluntatis atque operationis excedat, inquit Fulgentius lib. 1. ad Monim. c. 10. Porrò misericordia definitur à Cic. Tuf. 4. ægritudo ex miseria alterius injuriâ (id est, injustè) laborantis. Ic Aug. quoque in lib. de motibus Ecclesiæ Catholicæ. c. 27. ait: Quis ignoret ex eo appellatam esse misericordiam, quòd miserum cor faciat condolentis alieno malo? Hinc miserere dicitur Hebraeis רחם Racham, quasi dicas, invisceratí, hoc est, intimo affectu, qui visceribus inditus est, tangi & commoveri erga aliquem, intimo commiseratione affectu quempiam prosequi, quòd scilicet matrix, quæ Hebraicè dicitur רחם Rechem, foetum complectitur tuendo & fovendo. Non absimili Etymologia eodem sensu occurrit Mat. 9. v. 36. & Mar. 6. v. 34. in textu Græco σπλαγχνίζομαι; nam σπλάγχνα fœm. significat cor, & neut. σπλάγχνα significat viscera, exta: ut sunt cor, jecur & similia interanea præcipua & vitaliora, quæ in cæsis victimis Aruspices considerabant, siquid portenderent. In sacris litteris Metaphorice eodem hoc nomine significantur in textu Græco omnes teneri & materni affectus, ut videre est Luc. 2. in Ep. ad Philip. c. 1. & alibi. Hinc & Ephef. 4. v. 32. & in Epist. 1 Petri c. 3. v. 8. Christiani vocantur εὔσπλαγχνοι, misericordes. Hinc & illæ loquendi formulæ: Commota sunt viscera. Viscera misericordiæ. Viscera crudelia. Claudere viscera sua ab aliquo.
units.tr: Shall obtain mercy. That is, they shall be helped by God, so that they are freed from misery. The reward promised by God to good works is called mercy and grace in Scripture, because when God crowns our good works, which the Fathers often call merits, not only does God repay his gifts, but there, too, the grace of divine recompense so overflows that it incomparably and ineffably exceeds every merit of a good will and operation given by God, says Fulgentius, book 1 to Monimus, chapter 10. Moreover, Cicero, Tusculan Disputations 4, defines mercy as the distress caused by the misery of another who suffers unjustly (that is, undeservedly). Augustine too, in his book On the Morals of the Catholic Church, chapter 27, says: Who would not know that mercy is so called because it makes a wretched heart share in another's evil? Hence in Hebrew to show mercy is called rḥm [רחם] Racham, as if you were to say, to be moved in the bowels, that is, to be touched and stirred in the innermost affection which is placed in the bowels toward someone, to pursue someone with heartfelt compassion, because the womb, which in Hebrew is called rḥm [רחם] Rechem, embraces and cherishes the foetus. A similar etymology occurs in the same sense at Matthew 9:36 and Mark 6:34, in the Greek text splanchnizomai [σπλαγχνίζομαι]; for splanchna [σπλάγχνα], feminine, means heart, and neuter splanchna means the viscera, entrails: such as the heart, liver and similar principal and more vital internal organs, which the diviners examined in sacrificed victims, to see whether they portended anything. In sacred letters, in the Greek text, all tender and maternal affections are metaphorically signified by this same word, as may be seen in Luke 2, in the Epistle to the Philippians chapter 1, and elsewhere. Hence also in Ephesians 4:32 and 1 Peter 3:8, Christians are called eusplanchnoi [εὔσπλαγχνοι], merciful. Hence also those forms of speech: His bowels were moved. Bowels of mercy. Cruel bowels. To shut up one's bowels against someone.

units.la: 8. Mundi corde. Hos Psaltes vocat ברי־לב יושרי reflos corde. Id est, qui Deum sincere colunt, defæcato à rerum creatarum curis animo, quantum finit humana fragilitas, quà etiam satagentibus, vigilantibusque ne peccent, subrepunt quodammodo peccata, quamvis parva, quamvis pauca, non tamen nulla: & eadem ipsa fiunt magna & gravia, si eis superbia incrementum & pondus adjecerit: à Sacerdote quem habemus in cælis, si piâ humilitate perimantur, totâ facilitate purgantur, inquit Aug. lib. De Sancta virginitate cap. 50. Unde idem ibidem cap. 49. Quamdiu nondum est in cœlesti sublimitate perfectio, invituperabiles facit in humilitate confessio.
units.tr: 8. Pure in heart. The Psalmist calls these bere-lev yesharei [בְּרֵי־לֵב יְשָׁרֵי], upright in heart. That is, those who worship God sincerely, with the mind cleansed of the cares of created things as far as human frailty allows; into the very people who are busy and watchful lest they sin, sins creep in somehow, though they are small, few, yet not none; and these same sins become great and grave if pride adds increase and weight to them. They are cleansed with all ease by the Priest we have in heaven, if they are destroyed by pious humility, says Augustine, On Holy Virginity, chapter 50. Whence the same author, in the same place, chapter 49: As long as perfection is not yet in heavenly height, confession in humility makes us blameless.

units.la: Videbunt. Scilicet, quid est in patria, in via verò quid non est, ut exponit. D. Th. 22 q. 8. art. 7.
units.tr: Shall see. Namely, what is in the homeland; what is not in the way, as Thomas Aquinas explains, 2-2, question 8, article 7.

units.la: 9. Pacifici sunt, qui a dissensionis & discordiæ scandalo separati dilectionem Charitatis, & pacem Ecclesiæ sub Catholicæ fidei unitate custodiunt; & eos, qui à pace dissentiunt, ad Ecclesiæ charitatem, quantum in eis est, pacis ac fidei studio revocare nituntur. Ita Chromatius Aquilegiensis. Filij Dei vocabuntur. Q. d. Deo quàm simillimi erunt; non enim Deus dissentionis, sed pacis.
units.tr: 9. Peacemakers are those who, separated from the scandal of dissension and discord, keep the love of charity and the peace of the Church under the unity of the Catholic faith; and they strive, as far as in them lies, to call back to the Church's charity those who dissent from peace, with zeal for peace and faith. So Chromatius of Aquileia. They shall be called sons of God. That is, they will be most like God; for God is not the God of dissension but of peace.

units.la: 1c. Justitiam. Id est virtutem; justitia enim consuevit promni virtute animi poni. Chrysost. Hom. 15 in Mat.
units.tr: 1c. Righteousness. That is, virtue, for righteousness is customarily put for every virtue of the mind. Chrysostom, Homily 15 on Matthew.

units.la: Regnum Cælorum. Id est, beatitudo æterna. Hoc unum præmium in omnibus & singulis Beatitudinibus promittitur, licet alio & alio nomine & prædicato, prout cujusque propositionis subjecto congruit.
units.tr: The kingdom of heaven. That is, eternal blessedness. This one reward is promised in each and every Beatitude, though under different names and predicates, as suits the subject of each proposition.

units.la: 11. Beati estis. Supple, unde Luc. 6. v. 22. eritis. Dicit tamen Aug. I. 83. qq. q. 82. quod justi, etiam sequestrata ipsæ utut vitæ, jucundius & lætius præ amore veritatis torquerentur, quàm luxuriosi præ cupiditate ebrietatis epulentur.
units.tr: 11. Blessed are you. Supply from Luke 6:22, you will be. Augustine, however, says in his 83 Questions, question 82, that the righteous, even when separated from the pleasures of life, are tormented more joyfully and gladly for love of the truth than the luxurious feast on account of their craving for drunkenness.

units.la: Maledixerint. Id est, pro odio probro affecerint præsentes, quo lucas exprobraverint, textus Græcus ὀνειδίσωσιν dixit.
units.tr: Revile you. That is, they heap disgrace upon you present with hatred. Luke wrote reproach; the Greek text has ὀνειδίσωσιν [oneidisōsin].

units.la: Persecuti. Scilicet, factis, à Synagoga vos expellendo, & nomen vestrum tanquam malum ejiciendo, ut dicitur Luc. 6.
units.tr: Persecute. That is, by deeds, by expelling you from the synagogue and casting out your name as evil, as is said in Luke 6.

units.la: Dixerint omne malum adversum vos. Scilicet, absentes, vestiæ famæ [?] & honori detrahendo.
units.tr: Say every evil against you. That is, in your absence, by detracting from your reputation and honour.

units.la: Mentientes. Virus, in mendacio. Si enim in veritate, seu vera, cujus mala dicantur, ex hoc non erit beatus, sed duplicater miser. Præclare itaque B. Hier. Illud maledictum contemnendum est, quod beatitudinem creat, quod falso maledicentis ore profertur.
units.tr: Lying. That is, in falsehood. For if the evils spoken of were true, the person would not be blessed on this account but doubly wretched. Blessed Jerome rightly says: That curse is to be despised which creates blessedness, which is uttered by the mouth of a false slanderer.

units.la: Propter me. Q. d. Quia in me creditis & meis insistitis vestigiis. Pœna non facit martyrem sed causa, inquit ex Cypriano Aug. Ep. 61. Refertur autem hæc clausula propter me ad tria persecutionum genera mox dicta.
units.tr: For my sake. That is: because you believe in me and follow my footsteps. "It is not the punishment that makes the martyr but the cause," says Augustine, quoting Cyprian, Letter 61. This clause, for my sake, refers to the three kinds of persecution just mentioned.

units.la: 12. Gaudete. Supple ex Luc. 6. in illa die, quâ nempe talia propter me patiemini.
units.tr: 12. Rejoice. Supply from Luke 6, on that day, namely when you suffer such things for my sake.

units.la: Merces. Remunerat Deus secundum opera, non propter opera, ex promissione gratuita, non ex facto nostro meritorio. Hæc autem remuneratio merces dicitur καταχρῆσις, quia confertur post opus præactum ut laboris præmium, non ut operis pretium. Hinc Aug. in Ps. 32. conc. 1. Teneamus fidelissimum debitorem, quia tenemus miseri ordinissimum promissorem; neque enim aliquid ei commodavimus, aut mutuum commendavimus ut teneamus eum debitorem, cum ab illo habeamus, quicquid illi offerimus, & ex illo fit quicquid boni sumus: Omnia bona, quibus gaudemus ab illo sunt, quoniam ab ipso, & in ipso, & per ipsum sunt omnia. Ergo non ei aliquid dedimus, & tenemus debitorem? Unde debitorem? Quia promisserem. Non dicimus Deo, Domine, quod recepisti, redde, sed, redde quod promisisti. Similiter Bernardus prope finem libri De gratia & libero arbitrio; Est, quàm Paulus expectat, corona justitiæ, sed justitiæ Dei, non suæ. Justum quippe est ut reddat. reddat quod debet: debet autem quod pollicitus est: & hæc est justitia, de qua præsumit Apostolus, promissio Dei. Nec dubium est, quin à Deo sit velle & perficere pro bona voluntate. Deus igitur autor est meriti, qui et voluntatem applicat operi, & opus explicat voluntati. Alioqui, si proprie appellentur ea, quæ dicimus nostra merita, quæ sunt quædam seminaria, charitatis incentiva, occultæ prædestinationis indicia, futuræ felicitatis præsagia, via regni, non causa regnandi. Denique, quos justificavit, non quos justos invenit, hos & magnificavit.
units.tr: Reward. God rewards according to works, not on account of works, by a gratuitous promise and not by our meritorious deed. This remuneration is called a reward by catachresis [καταχρῆσις, katachrēsis], because it is bestowed after the work is done as the wage of labour, not as the price of the work. Hence Augustine on Psalm 32, sermon 1: Let us hold fast to the most faithful debtor, since we hold fast to the most orderly promiser of wretched us; for we have lent him nothing, nor have we committed anything to him so that we might hold him as a debtor, since from him we have whatever we offer him, and from him comes whatever good we are. All the goods in which we rejoice are from him, since all things are from him and in him and through him. Have we then given him anything, and hold him as a debtor? A debtor of what? Because he promised. We do not say to God, Lord, repay what you have received, but repay what you have promised. Similarly Bernard, near the end of his book On Grace and Free Choice: There is the crown of righteousness which Paul expects, but it is the righteousness of God, not his own. For it is just that he should repay: he repays what he owes, and he owes what he has promised; and this is the righteousness on which the Apostle relies, the promise of God. There is no doubt that both the willing and the performing come from God, who for good will attaches the will to the work and unfolds the work to the will. Otherwise, if those things which we call our merits were properly so named, they would be certain seedbeds, incentives of charity, hidden indications of predestination, presages of future happiness, the way to the kingdom, but not the cause of reigning. Finally, those whom he justified, not those whom he found righteous, these he also glorified.

units.la: Copiosa. Id est, magna, seu multa, ut dicitur Luc. 6. Non tanquam, inquit Basil. apud D. Th. in Catena. comparata ad ea, quæ penes nos sunt, sed in se multa existens. Quod enim, inquit Damascenus c. 49. Logicæ quadam excellentia transcendit omnem mensuram & numerum, indeterminate dicitur magnum & multum; puta quando dicimus multam esse Dei misericordiam. Nihil autem, inquit S. Eucherius, est magnum re, quod parvum tempore: nec longius dilatatur gaudium, quicquid ardito fine concluditur. Æterna ergo futura est Sanctorum merces.
units.tr: Abundant. That is, great or many, as is said in Luke 6. Not as, says Basil, quoted by Thomas in the Catena, compared with what is among us, but existing many in itself. For what, says Damascene, chapter 49 of the Logic, by a certain logical excellence transcends every measure and number, is called great and many indefinitely; for instance when we say that the mercy of God is great. Nothing, however, says St Eucherius, is great in reality which is small in time; nor is joy spread out more widely, whatever is concluded with a hasty end. Therefore the reward of the saints will be eternal.

units.la: In Cœlis. Non quod Sanctorum remuneratio sit in corporalibus cœlis, sed in contemplatione supercœlestis naturæ, scilicet, Dei gloriosi, cui esse in cœlo tribuitur, non quia corporalibus cœlis continetur, sed ut per hoc designetur Dei eminentia super omnem creaturam; sicut cœli eminent super omnem aliam creaturam corpoream, secundum illud Psalmi 112. Excelsus super omnes gentes Dominus, super cœlos gloria ejus. D. Th. in compendio Theologiæ. Idem 1. P. q. 68. ar. 4. in cor. sub finem. 12æ, q. 4. ar. 7. ad 3. & ante D. Th. S. Aug. lib. 1. de Sermone Domini in monte c. 9. &c.
units.tr: In heaven. Not that the reward of the saints is in corporeal heavens, but in the contemplation of the supercelestial nature, namely of glorious God, to whom being in heaven is attributed, not because he is contained by corporeal heavens, but so that through this the eminence of God above every creature may be designated; just as the heavens are eminent above every other corporeal creature, according to the saying of Psalm 112: The Lord is high above all nations, his glory above the heavens. Thomas, in the Compendium of Theology. The same, 1 P., q. 68, art. 4, in the body near the end; 1a 2ae, q. 4, art. 7, ad 3; and before Thomas, St Augustine, book 1, On the Sermon of the Lord on the Mount, chapter 9, etc.

units.la: Persecuti sunt. Scilicet, Patres eorum, ut supplet Lucas c. 6. His dictis, væ dicitur à Christo divitibus, qui consolationem, seu beatitudinem suam in divitiis ponunt; saturatis, quorum scilicet Deus venter est; ridentibus, qui hoc unum spectant, ut in rebus hujus mundi transitoriis gaudium capiant; denique his, qui hominum plausum sibi conciliant, vitia eorum demulcendo. Hæc omnia videre est Luc 6. v. 24. 25. 26.
units.tr: They persecuted. That is, their fathers, as Luke adds in chapter 6. After these words, Christ pronounces woe on the rich, who place their consolation, or blessedness, in riches; on the sated, whose god is their belly; on those who laugh, who look only to this, that they may find joy in the transitory things of this world; and finally on those who win the applause of men by flattering their vices. All of these may be seen in Luke 6:24–26.

units.la: 13. Vos estis sal terræ. Id est, a me estis electi, ut quod sal est cibis, sitis universo hominum generi, ut per vestram doctrinam exsiccentur humores carnalium operum, auferantur fœtores & putredines malæ conversationis, & vermis libidinosæ cogitationis, & ille, de quo dicitur Esaiæ 66. v. 24. Vermis eorum non moritur.
units.tr: 13. You are the salt of the earth. That is, you have been chosen by me so that, as salt is to food, you may be to the whole human race, so that through your teaching the moisture of carnal works may be dried up, the stench and putrefaction of a bad way of life removed, and the worm of lustful thought, of which it is said in Isaiah 66:24, their worm does not die.

units.la: Evanuerit. Seu, insulsum fuerit, ut dicitur Marc. 9. id est, si saporem suum amiserit. In quo salietur? Q. d. Nihil est, quo sapor amissus illi reftitui possit; non enim datur sal falis.
units.tr: Lose its savour. Or, becomes tasteless, as is said in Mark 9; that is, if it has lost its taste. With what will it be salted? That is: there is nothing by which lost savour can be restored to it, for salt cannot be salted again.

units.la: Ab hominibus. Hebraifmus, id est, à quovis.
units.tr: By men. A Hebraism, that is, by anyone.

units.la: 14. Lux. Non lucifica essentialiter, sicut Christus dicitur Lux Joan. 8. v. 13. sed ex accidentali dono, cujusmodi Lux proprie dicitur lucerna, quia non ex fe lucet, sed aliunde accenditur, scilicet, à Deo, & extingui potest. Aug. Trac. 23 in Joan.
units.tr: 14. Light. Not light-giving in essence, as Christ is called Light in John 8:13, but by an accidental gift, of the kind by which a lamp is properly called light, because it does not shine of itself, but is kindled from elsewhere, namely by God, and can be extinguished. Augustine, Tractate 23 on John.

units.la: Mundi. Id est, generis humani, ad effugandas ipsius tenebras.
units.tr: Of the world. That is, of the human race, to drive away its darkness.

units.la: Non potest civitas. Deest hic prima pars similitudinis. Sensus enim est: vos estis civitas in monte posita, seu, similes civitati in monte positæ, quæ abscondi non potest, quia ipse mons manifestat eam. Syrorum igitur more multas ejusdem rei similitudines congerit Christus, quas accuratius applicant & explicant duo versus sequentes. Hinc optime probat Aug. in lib. De unitate Ecclesiæ c. 16. veram Dei Ecclesiam non posse esse opertam. Nam licet ista in monte posita civitas sic possit nubibus & caligine obduci, ut aliquoties aspectum fugiat; nihilominus semper fit confpicua quærentibus eam in Scripturis, non vero in pompatico Superstitiosorum apparatu.
units.tr: A city cannot be hidden. The first part of the comparison is missing here. The sense is: you are a city set on a hill, or, you are like a city set on a hill, which cannot be hidden, because the mountain itself makes it manifest. Christ therefore, after the manner of the Syrians, heaps up many likenesses of the same thing, which the two following verses apply and explain more precisely. Hence Augustine, in his book On the Unity of the Church, chapter 16, rightly proves that the true Church of God cannot be hidden. For although a city set on a hill can be so covered by clouds and mist that it sometimes escapes sight, nevertheless it is always conspicuous to those who seek it in the Scriptures, not in the showy display of superstitious people.

units.la: 15. Neque accendunt lucernam. Ne Apostoli sibi aliquid tributum putarent, quod de solo Christo intelligendum effet, & ita lucernæ vento superbiæ extinguerentur, cum dixisset: Vos estis lux mundi, continuo subjunxit: Neque accendunt lucernam, &c. Sic luceat lux vestra, &c. Ut glorificent, non vos, sed Patrem vestrum lucernæ accenforem. His igitur verbis commonet Christus Apostolos, ne quavis de causa prædicare trepident, imo docet eos sibi ex officio incumbere, ut palam & in tectis prædicent verbum, instent opportune, importune, arguant, obsecrent, increpent in omni patientia & doctrina. Aug. in Ora. De quinque hæresibus c. 7. ait: Domus, totus est mundus, lucerna accenfio. Verbi est incarnatio, candelabrum autem crucis est lignum, lucerna in candelabro lucens, Christus in cruce pendens. Et secundum hanc expositionem præcipitur Apostolis hic, ut ubique palam prædicent Jesum & hunc crucifixum.
units.tr: 15. Nor do they light a lamp. Lest the Apostles should think that something was ascribed to them which must be understood of Christ alone, and so their lamps should be extinguished by the wind of pride, when he had said: You are the light of the world, he at once added: Nor do they light a lamp, etc. So let your light shine, etc. That they may glorify not you but your Father, the kindler of the lamp. By these words, therefore, Christ admonishes the Apostles not to tremble at preaching for any reason; rather he teaches that it falls to them by their office to preach the word openly and from the housetops, to press on in season and out of season, to convince, entreat, rebuke, in all patience and teaching. Augustine, in the sermon On the Five Heresies, chapter 7, says: The house is the whole world, the lamp is the kindling. The incarnation of the Word is the lamp, but the candlestick is the wood of the cross, the lamp shining on the candlestick is Christ hanging on the cross. And according to this exposition the Apostles are here commanded to preach Jesus, and him crucified, openly everywhere.

units.la: 16. Ut videant opera vestra bona. Q. d. Ut factis etiam adstruatis, quod verbis prædicatis.
units.tr: 16. That they may see your good works. That is, that by your deeds you may also confirm what you preach in words.

units.la: Glorificent &c. Id est, fidem vestram confiteantur muneris esse divini; ut enim Deus dicitur blasphemari, dum ipfius dona alteri tribuuntur, vel contemnuntur, ita dicitur glorificari, seu, clarificari, dum ab ipso agnoscuntur omnia & singula sancta desideria, recta consilia & justa esse opera. Nolite &c. Jam tradere incipit Christus quid Apostoli docere debeant, & qua ratione velit eos omnium aspectibus expositos, & in mundo quasi in theatro pugnantes, aliis prælucere.
