units.tr: Glorify &c. That is, that they may confess your faith to be a gift of God. Just as God is said to be blasphemed when his gifts are attributed to another or despised, so he is said to be glorified or made clear when all and each of the holy desires, right counsels and just works are acknowledged to come from him. Do not &c. Here Christ now begins to set out what the apostles ought to teach, and by what method he wants them, exposed to the gaze of all and fighting in the world as on a stage, to shine a light before others.

units.la: Veni solvere Legem. Ad intelligentiam verborum Christi omnino notandum Legem per Mosem datam dupliciter accipi; aut secundum id quod commune habet cum aliis legibus, quæ ab hominibus condi solent, quatenus scilicet graviora delicta pœnarum aspectabilium formidine coercet, ut dicitur Heb. 2. v. 2. & populum Hebræum hac ratione in statu civilis societatis continet, quo sensu dicitur Lex mandati carnalis Heb. 7. v. 16. & factorum Rom. 3. v. 27. aut secundum id quod Legis Divinæ est proprium, quatenus scilicet etiam mentis requirit puritatem, & actus aliquos, qui sine temporali pœna omitti possunt: quo sensu vocatur Rom. 7. v. 14. Lex spiritualis & Psal. 18. Convertens animas &c. Scribæ seu Legisperiti & Pharisæi priore illa parte contenti, secundam, quæ potior est, insuper habebant, neque inculcabant populo; quod verum esse non ex nostris duntaxat libris, sed ex Josepho quoque & Rabbinis Hebræorum oftendi potest. Non venit itaque Christus ut evertat, destruat, excindat Legem, nec ut pervertat eam, sive verum ejus sensum mutando, sive scopum abolendo, sive illam irritam reddendo, sive alio detorquendo, quam oportebat, sed ut tanquam potestatem habens mentem Legis aperiat, a perversis Pharisæorum & Scribarum glossematis vindicet, atque potiorem Legis partem ab iisdem Pharisæis et Scribis insuper habitam verbo & opere omnibus inculcet esse adimplendam.
units.tr: I have come to destroy the Law. To understand Christ's words, it must be carefully noted that the Law given through Moses is taken in two ways. Either it is taken according to what it shares with other laws, which men usually enact, in so far as it restrains the graver offences by fear of visible penalties (as Heb. 2:2 says), and by this means holds the Hebrew people within the state of civil society; in this sense the Law is called a law of carnal commandment (Heb. 7:16) and of works (Rom. 3:27). Or it is taken according to what is proper to the Law of God, in so far as it also requires purity of mind and certain acts which can be omitted without temporal punishment; in this sense it is called a spiritual law (Rom. 7:14), and in Ps. 18, converting souls &c. The scribes, or lawyers, and the Pharisees were content with the former part, and despised the second, which is the weightier, and did not impress it on the people. That this is true can be shown not only from our books but also from Josephus and from the rabbis of the Hebrews. Christ therefore did not come to overturn, destroy or cut off the Law, nor to pervert it, either by changing its true sense, or by abolishing its purpose, or by making it void, or by twisting it to some other meaning than it ought to bear. Rather, as one having authority, he came to open up the mind of the Law, to free it from the perverse glosses of the Pharisees and scribes, and to impress on all, by word and deed, that the weightier part of the Law, which the same Pharisees and scribes had despised, must be fulfilled.

units.la: Prophetæ. Prophetæ hic spectantur non tantum ut futurorum prædagi, verum etiam ut Legis interpretes, quo sensu a præcepto dilectionis dicuntur infra cap. 22. v. 40. pendere Lex & Prophetæ.
units.tr: The Prophets. The Prophets are here regarded not only as foretellers of future things but also as interpreters of the Law; in this sense, from the precept of love, it is said below (22:40) that the Law and the Prophets hang on it.

units.la: Amen. Id est, ver; unde quod Matthæus c. 24. v. 47. exprimit his verbis: Amen dico vobis, quoniam super omnia bona constituet eum. Lucas c. 12. v. 44. sic retulit. Vere dico vobis quoniam supra omnia, quæ possidet, constituet illum. SS. PP. volunt Amen esse juramentum. Origenes in Mat. 26. Jesus dixit de Juda confuto sibi jurejurando: Amen dico vobis unus ex vobis tradet me. Hier. in Gal. 6. & in Esa, 25. Chrysost. Hom. 10. in Mat. aiunt quod quomodo in veteri Testamento quadam jurandi consuetudine Deus sua verba confirmat dicens: Vivo ego dicit Dominus: ita Salvator noster in Evangelio per verbum Amen vera esse, quæ loquitur, ostendit. Autor operis imperfecti Hom. 23. in Mat. similiter pro juramento agnoscit Amen. S. Aug. Tractatu 41. in Joan. Quodammodo, si dici fas est, juratic ejus est: Amen, amen dico vobis. At secundum Doctores Hebraeos Amen non jurationem, sed simplicem affirmationem sonat; & dum precationi apponitur, ut sit ejus quasi signaculum, sonat affirmationem per modum optantis; unde iis in locis apte a LXX. Amen transfertur per vocem fiat. Siquis, inquiunt Hebraei in libro inscripto (Hebrew) (qui conscriptus dicitur anno Dom. 1104.) sol. 8. col. 1. juranti responderit Amen, perinde est ac si ipse juraret. Similiter cum judex adjurat aliquem, & ipse respondet Amen, idem est ac si ipsemet juraret ore suo, &c.
units.tr: Amen. That is, truly. Hence Matthew, in ch. 24:47, expresses it in these words: Amen I say to you, he will set him over all his goods. Luke, ch. 12:44, reports it thus: Truly I say to you, he will set him over all that he possesses. The holy Fathers hold that Amen is an oath. Origen, on Matthew 26, says that Jesus, having confuted Judas with an oath of his own, said: Amen I say to you, one of you will betray me. Jerome, on Galatians 6 and on Isaiah 25, and Chrysostom, Homily 10 on Matthew, say that just as God in the Old Testament confirms his words with a certain custom of swearing, saying As I live, says the Lord, so our Savior in the Gospel shows by the word Amen that what he says is true. The author of the unfinished work, Homily 23 on Matthew, likewise recognizes Amen as an oath. St. Augustine, Tractate 41 on John, says: In a certain way, if it is lawful to say so, it is his oath: Amen, amen I say to you. But according to the Hebrew teachers, Amen does not signify an oath but a simple affirmation; and when it is added to a prayer, as its seal, it signifies affirmation in the manner of one who wishes; hence in such places the Seventy translate Amen by the word let it be. If anyone, the Hebrews say, in the book entitled [Hebrew title lost in transcription], which is said to have been written in the year of the Lord 1104, folio 8, column 1, answers Amen to one who swears, it is just as if he swore himself. Likewise when a judge adjures someone and he answers Amen, it is the same as if he had sworn with his own mouth, &c.

units.la: Donec transeat. Graece, transierit. Est autem Hebraismus pro perierit. Sensus est facilius, ut dicitur Luc. 16. v. 17. seu citius tota mundi machina defecerit, quam irritum fiat vel minimum quid in Lege, quod designatur per Jod (cui respondet Iota) litteram totius Alphabeti Hebraei ab Esdrae temporibus in usum recepti minimam, & per apicem, quo proprie designatur minima litterae pars; unde proverbialiter dicitur, de apicibus disputare, qui de minimis contendit. Non potest itaque hoc ex loco probari coelum aliquando corruptum iri. Notet hic prudens lector quod Lex Mosis in sua propria significatione accepta tres habet partes; scilicet mandata cum summa exactione perfectissimae obedientiae conjuncta; promissiones multas tum bonorum temporalium, tum vitae aeternae; denique maledictiones contra Legis in aliqua parte transgressiores. Fundamentum autem omnium mandatorum fuit Decalogus in duabus tabulis descriptus, quarum primae addita fuit lex ceremonialis, secundae lex politica. Omnes vero hae Legis partes habent suum veluti corpus, suam & animam: corpus dicitur quod sensibiliter & exterius faciendum praecipiunt aut vetant; at anima dicitur vera pietas constans fide viva & efficaci in Deum, vera charitate in proximum, & propria cujusque mortificatione & vivificatione, seu vitae sanctitate. Lex Mosis fuit abrogata per Christum quoad corpus, seu opera externa; ita ut quaedam facere jam nullatenus liceat, ut circumcidere carnem praeputii, immolare victimas ex brutis animantibus, & cetera, quae figurabant Christum venturum; quaedam vero libera maneant Ecclesiae, ut pro libito eis utatur, aut non utatur, ad aedificationem. Eadem Lex Mosis quoad animam, substantiam, succum, quia aeterna fuit, & Christus aeternam esse voluit; unde semper tenemur ad circumcisionem cordis, ablutiones interiores, &c. Potest tamen Lex etiam quoad animàm dici per Christum abrogata secundum quid, in quantum per Spiritum vivificantem Legis substantiam in tabulis carneis cordis nostri transcripsit, adeo ut jam non egeamus litterâ occidente, quâ eadem Legis Mosaicæ substantia scripta erat in tabulis lapideis. Itaque Christus abrogavit Legem, non solvendo, sed absolvendo, sicut pictor inchoatæ & extremis tantum lineamentis adumbratæ imagini, dum extremam adhibet manum, novam inducit imaginem & priorem abolet, non dissolvendo, sed absolvendo, nori delendo, sed perficiendo.
units.tr: Until heaven and earth pass away. In Greek it reads has passed away. This is a Hebraism for has perished. The sense is that it is easier, as is said in Luke 16:17, or sooner, for the whole machinery of the world to fail than for the smallest thing in the Law to become void. That smallest thing is signified by Jod (to which iota corresponds), the smallest letter of the whole Hebrew alphabet as used since the time of Ezra, and by the apex, which properly denotes the smallest part of a letter. Hence the proverb to dispute about apices, that is, to quarrel over the smallest things. It cannot therefore be proved from this place that heaven will ever be corrupted. Let the prudent reader note that the Law of Moses, taken in its proper sense, has three parts: commandments joined with the strictest exactness of most perfect obedience; many promises, both of temporal goods and of eternal life; and finally curses against those who transgress the Law in any part. The foundation of all the commandments was the Decalogue, written on two tables; to the first was added the ceremonial law, to the second the political law. All these parts of the Law have, as it were, their body and their soul. The body is what they command or forbid to be done outwardly and sensibly; the soul is true piety, consisting in a living and effective faith in God, true love of neighbour, and the mortification and quickening of each person, that is, holiness of life. The Law of Moses was abrogated by Christ as to the body, or outward works, so that some things may no longer in any way be done, such as circumcising the flesh of the foreskin, offering victims from brute animals, and the rest which prefigured the coming of Christ; but some things remain free for the Church, to use or not use as it pleases, for edification. The same Law of Moses remains as to the soul, its substance and sap, because it was eternal and Christ willed it to be eternal; hence we are always bound to circumcision of the heart, inner washings, &c. Nevertheless the Law can also be said to be abrogated by Christ as to the soul in a certain respect, in so far as by the quickening Spirit he has written the substance of the Law on the fleshly tables of our heart, so that we no longer need the killing letter, by which the same substance of the Mosaic Law was written on stone tables. Thus Christ abrogated the Law not by dissolving it but by completing it, just as a painter, when he adds the final touch to an image begun and sketched only in its outlines, introduces a new image and abolishes the earlier one; not by dissolving but by completing, not by destroying but by perfecting.

units.la: Est etiam hìc observandum locutiones esse synonymas: Donec transeat cælum & terra: Cum sole & ante lunam. Coram Luna: In generationem & generationem: In generationem generationum: In seculum seculi: In secula: In jeculum: Donec auferatur Luna: Non erit Luna: Ante Solem: Coram Sole: In æternum. Ps. 101. Heb. 102. v. 29 Semen eorum stabilietur coram te. Vul. In seculum dirigetur. In eundem modum expônit Rabbi Salomon Decalogi præceptum Exod. 20. Non habebis alienos Deos coram me. Id est, inquit, quamdiu ego ero, in æternum.
units.tr: It must also be observed here that the expressions are synonymous: until heaven and earth pass away; with the sun and before the moon; before the moon; in the presence of the moon; to generation and generation; to generation of generations; to age of ages; for ages; to the age; until the moon is taken away; there will be no moon; before the sun; in the presence of the sun; for ever. Ps. 101; Heb. 102:29: The seed of them shall be established before you. The Vulgate: shall be directed to the age. In the same way Rabbi Solomon explains the precept of the Decalogue, Exod. 20: You shall have no other gods before me. That is, he says, as long as I shall be, for ever.

units.la: 19. Qui ergo, &c. Q. d. Tantum abest ut Legem aut prophetas præxi doctrinâve sim dissoluturus, ut contrà omni asleverationè affirmem ea etiam, mandata, quæ à Pharisæis & Scribis pro minimis habentur transgressa reos facere homines iræ divinæ.
units.tr: 19. Whoever therefore, &c. That is: so far is it from being the case that I shall dissolve the Law or the Prophets by my practice or teaching, that on the contrary I affirm with every assertion that even those commandments which the Pharisees and scribes regard as least make those who transgress them liable to the wrath of God.

units.la: Et docuerit sic. Id est, aut solvendum, seu posse licitè solvi docuerit; copula enim, Et, hìc est pro particula disjunctiva, aut, cujus Hebraismi innumera exempla apud Granmaticos congesta videre est, è quibus sufficiat unum, aut alterum apponere. Deuter. 27. v. 16. Maledictus qui non honorat patrem suum & matrem, id est, vel matrem. Ibid. v. 19. Maledictus qui pervertit judicium advenæ, pupilli, & viduæ, id est, vel viduæ.
units.tr: And teaches so. That is, either he teaches that they are to be loosed, or that they may lawfully be loosed. For the conjunction and here stands for the disjunctive particle or; countless examples of this Hebraism, gathered by the grammarians, may be seen, of which it is enough to cite one or two. Deut. 27:16: Cursed is he who does not honour his father and mother, that is, either father or mother. Ibid. v. 19: Cursed is he who perverts the judgment of the stranger, the orphan, and the widow, that is, either the widow.

units.la: Minimus vocabitur. Hebraismus, id est, nullus erit, seu nullum locum habebit.
units.tr: Minimus vocabitur. A Hebraism, that is, he will be no one, or will have no place there.

units.la: In regno Cælorum. Id est, in regnomeo, quod non est de hoc mundo. Vide quæ diximus supra c. 3. v. 2. Cùm igitur in quovis regno, alij præclaré gestis, alij præclarè dictis sibi existimationem concilient, monet Christus eos in regno suo doctrinâ suâ fore commendabiles, qui facienda docent, quæ ipse Legis mentem aperiens faciendâ præceperit, & è converso illos Doctores socci facientes, qui quovis modo præcepta sua licitè violari posse docuerint. Similiter qui secundum mandata sua vixerit, eum magno in pretio futurum; qui verò ea solverit, eum gestis fore contemtibilem.
units.tr: In regno Cælorum. That is, in my kingdom, which is not of this world. See what we said above on chapter 3, verse 2. Just as in any kingdom some win esteem by their notable deeds and others by their notable words, so Christ warns that in his kingdom those will be commended by his teaching who teach the things to be done, which he himself, opening the meaning of the Law, has commanded to be done. Conversely, those teachers who have taught that his precepts may be lawfully violated in any way will be despised. Likewise, the one who lives according to his commandments will be held in high regard, and the one who dissolves them will be held in contempt.

units.la: 20. Dico enim vobis. Reddit rationem cur dixerit: Qui solverit unum &c. Itaque idem est solvere mandata minima, & non majorem habere justitiam, seu, perfectionem, quam Scribæ & Pharisæi tempore Christi habebant. Videquæ diximus de Scribis & Pharisæis supra v. 17. in hæc verba: Non veni solvere Legem.
units.tr: 20. Dico enim vobis. He gives the reason for what he said: Whoever shall break one of these, and so on. Thus to break the least commandments is the same as not having a greater righteousness, or perfection, than the scribes and Pharisees had in Christ's time. See what we said about the scribes and Pharisees above on verse 17, in these words: I came not to destroy the Law.

units.la: Scribarum. Scribæ apud Judæos fuerunt à Davide & Esdra constituti; eorum erat publica instrumenta conficere, sacras Scripturas incorruptas servare, earumque sensum interpretari. Vide 4. Reg. 22. v. 8. 9. & 10. Esdræ 7. v. 10. & 11. Mat. 7. v. 29. 17. v. 16. 23. v. 2.
units.tr: Scribarum. Among the Jews the scribes were appointed by David and Ezra. Their task was to draw up public documents, to keep the sacred Scriptures uncorrupted, and to interpret their meaning. See 4 Kings 22:8–10; Ezra 7:10–11; Matthew 7:29; 17:16; 23:2.

units.la: Non intrabitis in regnum cælorum. Seu, meum regnum, id est regnum Dei non erit inter vos. Hoc regnum Christi seu Dei esse dicitur Rom. 14. v. 17. Justitia, quâ animus erga Deum, proximum & se ipsum afficitur ut debet, & pax, id est, vera tranquillitas mentis, & gaudium, quod habetur in Spiritu-Sancto, id est, per gratiam Spiritûs-Sancti ex contemplatione & dilectione divinorum. Illa sunt regnum cælorum, Dei, seu Christi, quia per illa Christus seu Deus in nobis regnat inchoative in via, plenè & perfectè in patria.
units.tr: Non intrabitis in regnum cælorum. That is, my kingdom, the kingdom of God, will not be among you. This kingdom is said to be the kingdom of Christ or of God in Romans 14:17: righteousness, by which the mind is rightly disposed toward God, one's neighbour and oneself; peace, that is, true tranquillity of mind; and joy, which is had in the Holy Spirit, that is, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, arising from the contemplation and love of divine things. These are the kingdom of heaven, of God, or of Christ, because through them Christ or God reigns in us, inchoately on the way and fully and perfectly in the fatherland.

units.la: 21. Dictum. Id est, præceptum, edictum.
units.tr: 21. Dictum. That is, precept, edict.

units.la: Antiquis. Id est, Patribus, qui Mosis tempore vivebant. Quæ autem citat Christus in hoc capite ut Veteribus dicta, non Scribarum & Pharisæorum sunt, sed Mosis, aut verbo tenus, aut sensu.
units.tr: "To the ancients": that is, the Fathers who lived in the time of Moses. The things Christ quotes in this chapter as said to the ancients belong not to the Scribes and Pharisees but to Moses, either in the words themselves or in their sense.

units.la: Reus erit judicio. Id est, deferetur ad judices, ut ipsorum edicto secundum legem latam Exod. 21. v. 12. Levit. 24. v. 17. &c. morte moriatur. Ut totus hic locus intelligatur, sciendum apud Judæos duplex tribunal fuisse, ubi capitalium criminum rei postulabantur; primum erat viginti trium Senatorum in singulis Palæstinæ oppidis, quæ saltem centum & viginti incolas haberent: in ipsa vero urbe Jerosolyma duplex fuit hujusmodi Senatus, quorum alter erat ad portam, quæ aperiebat aditum ad montem Templi, alter nobilior ad portam atrii sedebat. Secundum erat in ea Templi parte, quæ [?] dicta est, id est, conclave lapideum, quod ipsum à Joanne c. 19. v. 13. dicitur [?], quod est Latinè, lapidibus stratus. Erat autem hoc tribunal LXXI. Judicum à Moyse primitùs institutorum, qui omnes erant primariæ nobilitatis & saltem matre Judææ, senes non ætate modò, sed etiam curâ & experientiâ. Senatores hujus supremi Senatûs, quem Judæi Græco vocabulo [?] dicebant, creabantur impositione manuum, ad quam impositionem
units.tr: "Liable to judgment": that is, he shall be brought before the judges, so that by their sentence he is put to death according to the law laid down in Exod. 21:12, Lev. 24:17, etc. To understand this whole passage, one should know that among the Jews there were two tribunals before which those accused of capital crimes were tried. The first was the court of twenty-three senators in each town of Palestine that had at least 120 inhabitants. In the city of Jerusalem itself there were two such courts: one sat at the gate that opened the way to the Temple mount, and the other, more distinguished, sat at the gate of the court. The second tribunal sat in that part of the Temple which was called [?], that is, the "stone chamber", which John 19:13 calls [?], which in Latin is "paved with stones". This tribunal was the court of seventy-one judges first instituted by Moses. All of them were of the first nobility and of mature age, elders not only in years but also in wisdom and experience. The senators of this supreme council, which the Jews called by the Greek word [?], were installed by the laying on of hands. The laying on of hands was followed by the descent of the Holy Spirit into their hearts, so that they could judge matters far beyond human understanding, such as a woman accused of adultery without witnesses, who was tested by the cup called [מוטו].

units.la: F tionem sequebatur descensus Spiritûs-Sancti in ipsorum corda, ut judicare possent de rebus humanum captum longè excedentibus, puta de muliere adulterii sine testibus accusata, per poculum, quod appellabatur מוטו. In hoc Senatu unus erat omnium princeps, qui dicebatur נשיא בכר מקום, Princeps in omni loco; alter huic proximus qui dicebatur אב בית דין, Pater domûs judicii, ceteri Senatores erant inter se æquales. Porro ad Synedrion hoc pertinebat, per omnem Judæam] ire, conventúsque populi lustrare, in oppidis Magistratus condere, traditionesse rvare, de rebus sacris statuere, Legem exponere, seu potiûs, comminisci modos, quibus Lex exponeretur, senem refractarium ipsorum statuta sequi recusantem capite damnare, de vatibus, (hinc illud Salvatoris Luc. 13. v. 33. Non capit Prophetam perire extra Jerusalem; hoc est, fieri non potest, ut Propheta quispiam pereat extra Jerosolymam) gravis delicti insimulatis judicare, & cetera, quæ videri possunt in Talmude & Maimonide Tract. Sanhedrin. Cùm itaque gravissima quæque apud Synedrion agerentur, usus invaluerat tempore Salvatoris, ut quemadmodum cujusvis capitalis criminis conscium, reum judicio, id est, dignum, qui edicto viginti trium Senatorum secundùm Legem morte moriatur, dicebant, ita sceleris præter modum enormis conscium reum Synedrio dicerent; & reum gehenna, cujus scelus videbatur, nec humanis posse expiari suppliciis.
units.tr: In this council one was chief over all, called [נשיא בכל מקום], Prince in every place; the next to him was called [אב בית דין], Father of the house of judgment; the other senators were equal among themselves. Moreover, it was the business of this Sanhedrin to go through all Judea, visit the assemblies of the people, appoint magistrates in the towns, keep the traditions, decide sacred matters, and expound the Law, or rather devise the methods by which the Law would be expounded; to condemn to death the stubborn man who refused to follow their statutes; and to judge prophets accused of a grave offence. (Hence the Saviour's saying in Luke 13:33, "It cannot be that a prophet perish outside Jerusalem"; that is, it cannot happen that any prophet should perish outside Jerusalem.) And there were other matters which may be seen in the Talmud and in Maimonides, Tract. Sanhedrin. Since therefore the gravest cases were handled before the Sanhedrin, by the time of the Saviour the custom had prevailed that, just as they called a person guilty of any capital crime "liable to judgment", that is, deserving to be put to death according to the Law by the decree of the twenty-three senators, so they called a person guilty of a crime beyond measure enormous "liable to the Sanhedrin". And they called "liable to Gehenna" one whose crime seemed unable to be expiated by any human punishment.

units.la: Ego autem. Supple, genuinum Legis sensum aperiens, non vero, ipsam Legem reprobans quasi quædam præcepta injusta continentem, ut somniarunt Manichæi & Ptolemæitæ, quem errorem explodunt SS. PP. præcipuè Epiphanius Hær. 85. adversus Ptolemæitas. Chrysost. Hom. 16. in Mat. Aug. lib. 19. contra Faustum à cap. 18. usque ad finem libri. Horum vestigia secutus est D. Th. 12æ. q. 107. ar. 2. & 3. Scotus 3. d. 30. q. unica. Lyranus, Strabus, Cajetanus, Tostatus in hunc locum, Jansenius Gandavensis in cap. 40. Concord. Evan. &c.
units.tr: "But I say to you": supply, opening the genuine sense of the Law, not rejecting the Law itself as if it contained some unjust precepts, as the Manichaeans and Ptolemaeans dreamed. The Holy Fathers refute this error, especially Epiphanius, Heresy 85, against the Ptolemaeans; Chrysostom, Homily 16 on Matthew; and Augustine, book 19 against Faustus, from chapter 18 to the end of the book. St. Thomas followed in their footsteps, Prima Secundae q. 107 art. 2 and 3; so did Scotus, 3 dist. 30, q. unica; and Lyranus, Strabus, Cajetan and Tostatus on this place, Jansenius of Ghent in chapter 40 of the Concordia Evangelica, etc.

units.la: Qui irascitur. In hodiernis codicibus Græcis plerisque additur εἰκῆ, temerè, sine causa. Verùm hanc vocem Hier. eradendam censet; ut enim ait idem in lib. 2. adversus Pelagianos: In plerisque codicibus antiquis, sine causa, addinum non est, ut scilicet ne cum causa quidem debeamus irasci. Similiter Aug. lib. 1. retractationum c. 19. Codices Græci non habent, sine causa, sicut hic positum est. Ne tamen omnis ira existimetur esse peccatum mortale, sciendum ex D. Thoma in opusculo de decem præceptis c. 21. quòd ira dicitur tripliciter; primò appetitus vindictæ in solo rationis judicio sine commotione animi, qui magis proprie dicitur judicium, quam ira: hoc sensu accipitur ira Mich. 7. v. 9. Iram Domini portabo. Secundò appetitus vindictæ ut est passio in appetitu sensitivo, sed ratione ordinata, nimirum ut si quando, quantum & pro quo oportet, & dicitur ira per zelum, esque actus virtutis. Tertiò demique dicitur ira appetitus vindictæ ut est passio in appetitu sensitivo refugiens judicium rationis, & ista semper est peccatum, licet non mortale, nisi sit appetitus vindictæ ex genere suo mortaliter illicitæ, puta homicidij vel hujusmodi gravis nocumenti. Lubet hic exhibere iracundiæ mala ex Gregorio Magno. lib. 5. Moral. cap. 30. Per iram gratia vitæ socialis amittitur, concordia rumpitur, lux veritatis extinguitur, Spiritus-Sancti splendor excluditur, iræ stimulis accensum cor palpitat, corpus tremit, lingua se præpedit, facies ignescit, exasperantur oculi, & nequaquam recognoscuntur amici.
units.tr: Qui irascitur. In most present-day Greek manuscripts the word [εἰκῆ], rashly, without cause, is added. But Jerome judges that this word should be erased; as he says in Book 2 against the Pelagians: In many ancient manuscripts the words "without cause" are not added, so that we ought not even to be angry with cause. Likewise Augustine, Book 1 of the Retractations, chapter 19: The Greek codices do not have "without cause", as is written here. Lest, however, every anger be thought a mortal sin, one should know from St. Thomas, in his little work on the Ten Commandments, chapter 21, that anger is spoken of in three ways. First, a desire for vengeance in the judgment of reason alone, without disturbance of the mind, which is more properly called judgment than anger; in this sense anger is taken in Micah 7:9: I will bear the anger of the Lord. Second, a desire for vengeance as a passion in the sensitive appetite, but ordered by reason, namely when one is angry as much as, for as long as and at what it is right to be, and this is called anger through zeal, and is an act of virtue. Third and last, anger is called a desire for vengeance as a passion in the sensitive appetite which shrinks from the judgment of reason; and this is always a sin, though not a mortal one, unless the desire for vengeance is of its own kind mortally unlawful, as for homicide or any such grave harm. It is fitting here to set out the evils of anger from Gregory the Great, Book 5 of the Moralia, chapter 30: Through anger the grace of social life is lost, concord is broken, the light of truth is extinguished, the splendour of the Holy Spirit is shut out; the heart kindled by the goads of anger throbs, the body trembles, the tongue trips over itself, the face flushes, the eyes grow bloodshot, and friends are no longer recognised.

units.la: Fratri suo. Vitiis irasci licet, fratri nunquam, nec ulla esse potest causa propter quam liceat succensere fratri suo, quamvis succensendum sit fratris vitio. Unde D. Th. 22æ. q. 158. ar. 1. ad 3. Appetere vindictam propter malum ejus qui puniendus est, illicitum est: sed appetere vindictam propter vitiorum correctionem, & bonum justitiæ conservandum, laudabile est: & in hoc potest tendere appetitus sensitivus, in quantum movetur à ratione: & dum vindicta secundum ordinem judicij fit, à Deo fit; cujus minister est potestas puniens, ut dicitur Rom. 13. Ad illud autem Exod. 10 v. 23. Non videbat homo fratrem suum: Ait Aug. in libris locutionum, Notandum fratrem hominis quemlibet hominem dici.
units.tr: Fratri suo. One may be angry at vices, but never at a brother, and there can be no cause for which it is lawful to be angry with one's brother, although one ought to be angry at his vice. Hence St. Thomas, Summa 2a 2ae, q. 158, art. 1, ad 3: To desire vengeance on account of the wrong of the one who is to be punished is unlawful; but to desire vengeance for the correction of vices and the preservation of the good of justice is praiseworthy; and in this the sensitive appetite may tend, insofar as it is moved by reason; and when vengeance is carried out according to the order of judgment, it is carried out by God, whose minister is the punishing power, as is said in Romans 13. As for Exodus 10:23, No one saw his brother, Augustine says in his books on locutions: It should be noted that any man whatever is called the brother of a man.

units.la: Reus erit judicio. Q. d. Homicida est, & iisdem pœnis dignus coram Deo, quibus secundum Legem plectebatur ille, qui hominis innocentis cædem destinatam perpetraverat.
units.tr: He shall be liable to judgement. That is to say: he is a murderer, and before God he deserves the same punishments that the Law imposed on the man who carried out a premeditated killing of an innocent person.

units.la: Raca. Id est, vocem convitii; ponitur enim vox convitii tunc temporis usitata pro quavis convitii voce. Porro Raca רקא Syriacè sonat vanum, levem, cerebro vacuum, mente & judicio carentem, & temerarium. Talmudicis est familiare רקא, seu ריקא. ריקים dicuntur Judic. 9. v. 4. ij, quorum opera septuaginta fratres occidit Abimelech, & 2. Paral. 3. v. 7. ij, quorum opera Jeroboam suum schisma conflavit. Apud Rabbam in Gen. Sect. 31. Noë Rekim ריקים vocat sux generationis homines.
units.tr: Raca. That is, a word of abuse. For a word of abuse in use at that time is put in place of any word of abuse whatever. Now Raca [רקא] in Syriac means empty, light, empty-headed, lacking mind and judgement, and rash. The Talmudists commonly use רקא, or ריקא. In Judges 9:4 the men whose work Abimelech used to kill seventy brothers are called ריקים [reqim], and in 2 Chronicles 3:7 the men whose work Jeroboam used to set up his schism are called the same. In Rabbah on Genesis, section 31, Noah calls the men of his generation רקים [rekim].

units.la: Reus erit Concilio. Græcè συνεδρίῳ, id est, majus peccatum habet irascente fratri suo; quia ejus peccatum Deo judice tantum est, ut inter gravissima censeatur, quæ communiter tunc temporis dicebantur crimina Synedrii, ut paulo ante diximus. Synedrii autem ea fuit institutio ut, si fieri posset, e solis Sacerdotibus & Levitis constaret, unde in Scripturis & Josepho, appellatione Sacerdotum intelligitur quandoque ipsum Synedrium. Sin e numero Sacerdotum aut Levitarum non reperirentur qui definitum Senatorum numerum implerent, tum demum aliis Judæis aditus in Synedrium patuit, nulla habita tribus ratione, ut diserte testatur R. Moses Maimonides in summa Talmudica Trac. de Synedrio cap. 2. Totius celebris illius confessus, sapientissimo princeps in Synedrio locus deferebatur, & hic Mosen referens dicebatur Princeps, non summus Pontifex, ut exististimabat Baronius anno Christi 31. num. 10. ut videre est apud Maimonidem, loco præcitato. Huic Synedrii Principi erat vicarius, qui dicebatur Pater domus judicii, ut supra dictum est. Porro Concilium hoc de rebus quibusque gravissimis, de ipsis Pontificibus maximis, at non de Regibus judicabat, ut diserte traditur in Talmude Trac. de Synedrio c. 11. ubi jura Regum & summorum Pontificum accurate explicantur. Nec oppositum probat, quod narrat Josephus, Herodem ad causam dicendam jussum esse in Synedrium se sistere, atque illum vadimonium obiisse; nam Herodi dicta est dies, cum adhuc admodum juvenis & privatus esset, necdum spem regnandi haberet, cum Antipater illius pater adhuc viveret, & Hircanus regnum obtineret. Aiunt denique Rabbini quadraginta circiter annis ante excidium Templi secundi Senatui viginti trium virorum & ipsi Synedrio ultimam sententiam in judiciis capitalibus pronuntiandi jus fuisse ademtum. Hinc Joan c. 18. v. 31. dicunt Judæi, ut & ipse Chrysost. Hom. 12. in Joan. testatur, Nobis non licet interficere quemquam.
units.tr: He shall be liable to the council. In Greek, συνεδρίῳ [synedrio], that is, he has committed a greater sin than one who is angry with his brother. For the sin is judged by God to be so grave that it is counted among the most serious offences, which at that time were commonly called crimes of the Sanhedrin, as we said a little earlier. The institution of the Sanhedrin was such that, if it could be managed, it consisted only of priests and Levites. Hence in the Scriptures and in Josephus the title "priests" sometimes means the Sanhedrin itself. But if there were not enough priests or Levites to fill the prescribed number of members, then at last other Jews were admitted to the Sanhedrin, without any regard to tribe, as R. Moses Maimonides plainly testifies in his Talmudic summary, the treatise on the Sanhedrin, chapter 2. The most wise prince of the whole famous assembly was given the chief place in the Sanhedrin. He, representing Moses, was called Prince, not high priest, as Baronius thought in the year of Christ 31, number 10. This can be seen in Maimonides, in the passage cited above. This prince of the Sanhedrin had a deputy, who was called Father of the house of judgement, as was said above. This council judged the most serious matters of every kind, including the greatest high priests themselves, but not kings. This is plainly stated in the Talmud, in the treatise on the Sanhedrin, chapter 11, where the rights of kings and of the high priests are set out in detail. Nor does what Josephus relates prove the opposite, that Herod was ordered to appear before the Sanhedrin to answer a charge and that he gave surety. For the day was set for Herod when he was still quite young and a private man, and did not yet have any hope of reigning, since his father Antipater was still alive and Hyrcanus held the kingdom. Finally, the rabbis say that about forty years before the destruction of the second Temple the Senate of twenty-three men, and the Sanhedrin itself, lost the right to pronounce the final sentence in capital cases. Hence in John 18:31 the Jews say, as Chrysostom also observes in Homily 12 on John, It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death.

units.la: Fatue. Verbum contumeliosum definitum pro indefinito, seu quovis verbo graviter contumeliose, quo scilicet non modo frater despicitur, ut in præcedenti propositione, sed omnino dehonoratur, seu, honor fratri aufertur.
units.tr: Fool. A word of insult, stated in a definite form in place of an indefinite one, that is, any word of serious insult. By it a brother is not merely looked down upon, as in the previous clause, but is wholly dishonoured, or in other words his honour is taken away from him.

units.la: Reus erit gehenna ignis. Id est, gravissimum admisit facinus. Vide dicta v. 21. Constat autem ex Glossa quod per has tres voces, judicium, concilium, & gehenna, diversæ mansiones in æterna damnatione pro modo peccati significanter exprimuntur. Porro notandum est, quod vallis urbi Jerosolymæ vicina, amœna & Cedronis aquis irrigua, cujus Dominus fuit olim Hinnom, aut hujus filius, inde dicta est גיא בן הנם, vallis filii Hinnon, & unà dictione בנהנם, Græcis elisâ aspiratione γέεννα & γέενναι. In illa valle erat locus nomine תפת, ubi filios & filias offerebant idolo Moloch, sicut Ethnici Saturno, ita ut pater filium suum traduceret per duas pyras, donec combustus moreretur. Ad hanc idololatriam abolendam Josias rex locum illum Thopheth polluit, ut dicitur 4. Reg. 23. v. 11. praecipiendo ut in eum equorum & mulorum, aliorumque animalium cadavera insepulta & sordes projicerentur, ne quis amplius comburere ibi liberos suos cuperet. Erat que ibi ignis perpetuus, quo sordes & offa cadaverum comburebantur. Inde per Metaphoram locus supplicii impiorum post mortem, tanquam vilissimus, infernus videlicet, vocatur ab Hebraeis גהנם, & in novo Testamento Gehenna; & ad illum ignem allusit Christus Mar. 9. v. 42. Ire in Gehennam, in ignem inextinguibilem, & Joannes, supra c.3. Paleas comburet igni inextinguibili. Placet hîc subjicere quæ de Valle Hinnom in ילקוט Hebræo commentario mystico in universum vetus Testamentum leguntur in cap. 7. Jeremiæ, folio 61. col. 4. Quamvis omnia idolorum fana in ipsa urbe Jerusalem fuerint, Molochi tamen fuit extra urbem in loco separato. Quânam ratione Moloch erat formatus? Erat imago ærea intrinsecus excavata, faciem habens vituli & manus expansas instar hominis volentis ab alio aliquid accipere. Septem ipsi extructa fuere sacella, ante quæ hæc Molochi statua erat collocata. Avem sive pullum columbarum offerens primum sacellum ingrediebatur. Ovem aut agnum, secundum. Arietem, tertium. Vitulum, quartum. Juvencum, quintum. Bovem, sextum. Proprium Filium, septimum, quod qui ingrediebatur, osculabatur statuam Molochi, juxta illud Osee 3. v. 2. Sacrificatores hominum vitulum osculantur. (Vulgat: Immolate homines vitulos adorantes.) Sic autem fiebat filii oblatio. Ponebatur filius ante Molochi statuam, quæ igne suppositæ succendebatur, donec ignita fieret instar lucis. Tunc sacrificuli acceptum infantem candentibus Molochi manibus indebant, ac ne parens ejulatum & clamorem audiret infantis, tympano pulsabant. Inde locus ille dictus Thopheth תפת , nempe à תפים Tuphim, tympanis. Vallis verò Hinnom, quia vox pueri erat בנם rugiens, aut quia astantes sacrificuli dicebant parenti: יהנח לך, utile, dulce, condimentum erit tibi; Erant enim persuasi parentes, ut scribit Rabbi Bechai in Levitic. 18. omnes liberos unius immolatione sospites futuros, sequeque per totam vitam fortunâ secundâ usuros. 23. Ibi. Id est, stans in ipso altari.
units.tr: He shall be liable to the fire of gehenna. That is, he has committed a most grave crime. See what was said at verse 21. It is clear from the Gloss that by these three words, judgement, council, and gehenna, different dwelling-places in eternal damnation are signified, according to the measure of the sin. Now it should be noted that the valley near the city of Jerusalem, pleasant and watered by the waters of Kidron, whose lord was once Hinnom, or his son, was called גיא בן הנם [gay ben hinnom], the valley of the son of Hinnom, and by a single word בנהנם [ben-hinnom], which the Greeks, with the aspirate elided, rendered γέεννα [gehenna] and γέενναι [gehennai]. In that valley there was a place called תפת [tophet], where sons and daughters were offered to the idol Moloch, just as the heathen offered to Saturn, so that the father passed his son through two pyres until he died burnt. To abolish this idolatry King Josiah defiled that place Tophet, as is said in 2 Kings 23:11, by ordering that the carcasses of horses, mules and other animals, unburied, and filth be thrown into it, so that no one would want to burn his children there any more. There was also a perpetual fire there, in which the filth and bones of corpses were burnt. Hence, by metaphor, the place of punishment of the wicked after death, as the vilest of places, is called hell, namely גהנם [gehinnom] by the Hebrews, and in the New Testament Gehenna. Christ alluded to that fire in Mark 9:42, to go into Gehenna, into the unquenchable fire, and John, above in chapter 3, he will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire. It is fitting here to add what is read about the Valley of Hinnom in the Hebrew mystical commentary on the whole Old Testament, called Yalkut, on chapter 7 of Jeremiah, folio 61, column 4. Although all the temples of the idols were in the city of Jerusalem itself, Moloch's was outside the city in a separate place. By what means was Moloch made? It was a bronze image, hollowed out inside, having the face of a calf and hands stretched out like a man wanting to receive something from another. Seven shrines were built for him, in front of which this statue of Moloch was placed. The one who brought a bird or a young pigeon entered the first shrine. A sheep or a lamb, the second. A ram, the third. A calf, the fourth. A young bullock, the fifth. An ox, the sixth. His own son, the seventh; and whoever entered kissed the statue of Moloch, according to that saying in Hosea 13:2, "Those who sacrifice men kiss the calves." (Vulgate: Sacrifice men, adoring the calves.) The offering of a son was done in this way. The son was placed before the statue of Moloch, which was heated by fire placed under it, until it became like light. Then the little priests took the child and put him into the glowing hands of Moloch, and so that the parent would not hear the wailing and cry of the child, they beat a drum. Hence that place was called Tophet תפת, from תפים [tuphim], drums. But the Valley of Hinnom, because the voice of the boy was בנם [banam], roaring, or because the priests standing by said to the parent: יהנח לך [yehenah lakh], it will be useful, sweet, a seasoning for you. For the parents were persuaded, as Rabbi Bechai writes on Leviticus 18, that by the sacrifice of one child all their other children would be safe and would enjoy good fortune for the rest of their lives. Verse 23, There, that is, standing on the altar itself.

units.la: Habens aliquid adversum te. Id est, offensus est à te. Hæc phrasis etiam usurpatur Marc. 11. v. 25. & Apoc. 2. v. 4. & 14.
units.tr: Having something against you. That is, he is offended by you. This phrase is also used in Mark 11:25 and Revelation 2:4 and 14.

units.la: Saltem motibus animi, si non potes commodè pedibus corporis; frustra enim pacem ambit apud Deum, qui cum fratre pacem non colit.
units.tr: At least with the feelings of your mind, if you cannot do so readily with the feet of your body; for he vainly seeks peace with God who does not cultivate peace with his brother.

units.la: Græce, benevolus, sícque da operam, ut & ipsum tibi benevolum habeas.
units.tr: In Greek, well-disposed; so take care that you also have him well-disposed towards you.

units.la: Adversario tuo. Id est, fratri qui habet aliquid adversum te.
units.tr: Your adversary. That is, the brother who has something against you.

units.la: In via. Id est, in hac vita.
units.tr: On the way. That is, in this life.

units.la: Ne forte tradat te judici. Luc. 12. v. 58. Ne forte trahat te ad judicem, id est, ne coram judice te conveniat.
units.tr: Lest perhaps he hand you over to the judge. Luke 12:58: lest perhaps he drag you to the judge, that is, lest he bring you before a judge.

units.la: Judex. Scilicet Christus, Pater enim omne judicium dedit Filio. Joan. 5. v. 22.
units.tr: The judge. Namely Christ: For the Father has given all judgement to the Son. John 5:22.

units.la: Ministro. Luc. 12. exactori.
units.tr: To the officer. Luke 12: the bailiff.

units.la: In carcerem mittaris. A ministro videlicet, seu exactore, ut dicitur Luc. 12. Ministros & exactores Christi esse Angelos patet ex eo quòd dicitur supra c. 4. Angeli ministrabant ei: & infra c.13. Exibunt Angeli & separabunt malos de medio justorum & mittent eos in caminum ignis. Carcer iste infernus est, inquit B. Bruno Signiensis Antiltes.
units.tr: You are cast into prison. That is, by the officer, or bailiff, as Luke 12 says. That the ministers and bailiffs of Christ are angels is clear from what is said above in chapter 4, Angels ministered to him, and below in chapter 13, The angels will come out and separate the wicked from among the righteous, and will cast them into the furnace of fire. That prison is hell, says Bruno of Segni, the Antilles.

units.la: Luc. 12. v. 59. Novissimum minutum. Unde colligi posse videtur quòd cùm dicitur Marc. 12. v. 42. Misit duo minuta, quod est quadrans, id sic non debet intelligi, ut duo minuta unum consecerint quadrantem, ut sentit Syrus' interpres, qui vertit ibi: Quæ sunt ostavæ, supple, partes assis duodecim unciis constantis; sed ut unum quodque fuerit quadrans, ut sentit Euthymius, seu quarta pars assis, quæ quia continet tres uncias, alio nomine vocabatur teruncius, & à Plinio triunx. Posteriorem hanc Marci expositionem priori præfert etiam eruditissimus Theologus Parisiensis c. 120. Concord. Evang. quia Plutarcho in Cicerone quadrans minimum erat in nummorum genere. Intendit autem Christus hac locutione Metaphorica in præsenti loco nullum prorsus peccatum quantumvis leve impunitum fore. Carcere infernus designatur. Quemadmodum vero apud Apostolum 2 Cor. 15. intelligitur his verbis: Oportet eum regnare donec ponat inimicos suos sub pedibus suis, semper Christum regnaturum, quoniam illi semper erunt sub pedibus; ita hic accipi debet de quo dictum est: Non exies inde donec reddas novissimum quadrantem, dum semper poenas peccatis debitas solvit., nunquam persolvit. Magnum inquit in hunc locum B. Bruno Signiensis, est hoc debitum: infinita est & innumerabilis pecunia, ad cujus novissimum quadrantem nunquam venitur, qui semper solvitur, nunquam finitur.
units.tr: Luke 12:59, the last mite. From this it may seem that when Mark 12:42 says, He cast in two mites, which is a farthing, it should not be understood as though the two mites together made one farthing, as the Syriac translator thinks, who renders there Which are eighths, supplying parts of an as, which consisted of twelve ounces; but rather that each one was a farthing, as Euthymius thinks, that is, a quarter of an as, which, since it contained three ounces, was known by another name, teruncius, and by Pliny triunx. The most learned theologian of Paris, in chapter 120 of his Harmony of the Gospels, also prefers this latter explanation of Mark to the former, because in Plutarch's Cicero the farthing was the smallest of coins. In the present place Christ, by this metaphorical expression, intends that no sin, however slight, will go unpunished at all. The prison signifies hell. Just as in the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 15, the words He must reign until he has put his enemies under his feet are understood to mean that Christ will always reign, since they will always be under his feet, so here it must be understood of the one of whom it is said: You will not come out from there until you pay the last farthing, since, while he always pays the penalties owed to sins, he never finishes paying. The debt, says Bruno of Segni on this passage, is great: the money is infinite and innumerable; the last farthing is never reached, which is always being paid and is never finished.

units.la: 28. Ego autem. Veram Legis mentem tradens. Omnis qui viderit mulierem, &c. Quoniam putabant Iudæi tantummodò corporalem cum fœmina illicitam commixtionem vocari mœchiam, demonstravit Magister talem concupiscentiam nihil esse aliud. Ita Aug. l. 19. contra Faustum c. 23. Quod verò Christus de visu dixit, etiam alijs sensibus applicari debet, quia eadem in omnibus est ratio, sed visum potiùs nominavit, quia per visum frequentius in concubitum illicitum expetendum incenditur animus.
units.tr: 28. Ego autem. Setting out the true meaning of the Law. Everyone who looks at a woman, etc. Since the Jews thought that only bodily illicit union with a woman was called adultery, the Teacher showed that such desire is nothing else. So Augustine, Against Faustus, book 19, ch. 23. What Christ said of sight should also be applied to the other senses, since the reason is the same for all, but he named sight rather because the mind is more often kindled through sight to desire illicit intercourse.

units.la: Ad concupiscendum eam. Id est, ut eam concupiscat. Ecce sensum videndi à libidine sentiendi breviter aperteque discrevit Christus. Illud Deus condidit instruendo corpus humanum, ipsum Diabolus seminavit persuadendo peccatum. Aug. l. 4. contra Iul. c. 14. Præclare Ambrof. Serm. 16. in Pf. 118. Oculus nihil delinquit, ideoque Salvatoris sententia plena iustitiæ est. Qui viderit mulierem ad concupiscendum eam, iam adulteravit eam in corde suo. Non dixit, Qui viderit mulierem, sed ad concupiscendum viderit. Oculum abjolvit, mentem ligavit. Non dixit, Adulteravit eam in oculo, sed in corde: in oculo visus est, in corde peccatum.
units.tr: To lust after her. That is, that he desire her. Here Christ briefly and plainly distinguished the sense of seeing from the lust of feeling. God made that in forming the human body; the Devil himself sowed the sin by persuading. Augustine, Against Julian, book 4, ch. 14. Ambrose excellently, Sermon 16 on Psalm 118: The eye commits no sin, and therefore the Saviour's sentence is full of justice. Whoever looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart. He did not say, Whoever sees a woman, but whoever looks in order to lust. He absolved the eye, he bound the mind. He did not say, He committed adultery with her in the eye, but in the heart: in the eye there was sight, in the heart sin.

units.la: 29. Si oculus tuus dexter &c. Elegans est exaggeratio, à Chirurgis desumta, qui cùm per unum membrum totum periclitatur corpus, ne corpus pereat, illud membrum quantumvis charum præscindunt; hâc autem Parabolicâ exaggeratione significat Christus quodvis delectabile, charum & necessarium abijciendum esse & contemnendum, dum aliter peccatum effugere non possis; cùm vero integritas membrorum nunquam causa fit peccati, sed sola voluntas membrorum actibus utens, nunquam necessaria est membrorum præcisio ad evitandum peccatum, proindeque nec unquam licita est ejusmodi præcisio, ut peccatum vitetur. Scandalizat. Id est, præbet ruinæ occasionem.
units.tr: 29. If your right eye, etc. This is an elegant exaggeration, taken from surgeons, who, when the whole body is endangered through one member, cut off that member, however dear, so that the body does not perish. By this parabolic exaggeration Christ signifies that any delightful, dear and necessary thing must be cast off and despised when you cannot otherwise escape sin. But since the integrity of the members is never the cause of sin, but the will alone, using the members' acts, is, the cutting off of members is never necessary to avoid sin, and therefore such cutting off is never lawful in order to avoid sin. Causes offence. That is, provides an occasion of falling.

units.la: 31. Dictum est autem. Continuatur expositio præcepti mœchiæ, quatenus etiam respicit propriam uxorem. Det ei libellum. Dare libellum in præcepto erat volenti dimittere, ut in dissidium animus præceps libelli conscriptione refractus abstineret; dimittere verò tantùm permissum erat, ut dicitur infrà c. 19. & Marc. 10. ob duritiam cordis ejus, qui primævam matrimonii legem servare non posset. Vide Aug. lib. 1. de Sermone Domini in monte. Lib 19. contra Faustum c. 26. Hier. in Mat. 5. & 19. Autorem operis imperfecti apud Chrysost. Hom. 12. &c. Hinc mulier dimissa per libellum repudij, si alteri viro nupserit, pollula & abominabilis facta est coram Domino, ut dicitur Deuter. c. 24. v. 4.
units.tr: 31. It has been said. The exposition of the precept on adultery continues, insofar as it also concerns one's own wife. Let him give her a bill of divorce. Giving a bill was prescribed for one who wished to dismiss his wife, so that a mind hasty toward discord would be checked by the writing of the bill and refrain. Dismissal was only permitted, as is said below ch. 19 and Mark 10, because of the hardness of heart of one who could not keep the first law of marriage. See Augustine, book 1 On the Sermon of the Lord on the Mount; book 19 Against Faustus, ch. 26; Jerome on Matthew 5 and 19; the author of the Opus Imperfectum in Chrysostom, Homily 12, etc. Hence a woman dismissed by a bill of repudiation, if she married another man, has become defiled and an abomination before the Lord, as is said in Deut. 24, v. 4.

units.la: Repudij. Repudium & divortium aliquando promiscuè urfurpantur, aliquando vero·sic distinguuntur, ut repudium fit distractio matrimonii quoad subsistantiam seu vinculum conjugale, divortium vero ejusdem relaxatio. Adeò repudium à primordio non fuit, inquit Tertullianus in libro de Monogamia cap. 9. ut apud Romanos post annum sexcentesimum Urbis conditæ id genus duritiæ commissum denotetur. Idem in Apologetico cap. 6. Ubi est illa felicitas matrimoniorum de moribus ubique prosperata, quo per annos ferè sexcentos ab Urbe condita nulla domus repudium scripsit?
units.tr: Repudiation. Repudium and divortium are sometimes used interchangeably, but sometimes distinguished, so that repudium is the dissolving of a marriage as to its substance or conjugal bond, while divortium is the loosening of that same bond. Repudiation was not from the beginning, says Tertullian in the book On Monogamy, ch. 9, so that among the Romans this kind of hardness is recorded as committed only after the six-hundredth year from the founding of the City. The same in the Apology, ch. 6: Where is that happiness of marriages, prospering everywhere in morals, when for about six hundred years from the founding of the City no household wrote a bill of repudiation?

units.la: 31. Dimiserit. Id est, jure debiti petendi simpliciter privaverit. Quod autem dicitur hîc de viro respectu uxoris, similiter intelligendum esse de uxore respectu viri, patet ex I Cor. 7. v. 10. & 11.
units.tr: 31. Dismisses. That is, simply deprives her of the right of claiming the debt. That what is said here of the husband with respect to the wife is to be understood similarly of the wife with respect to the husband is clear from 1 Cor. 7, vv. 10 and 11.

units.la: Excepta fornicationis causa. Per fornicationem intelligitur hîc omnis illicitus concubitus.
units.tr: Except on account of fornication. By fornication is understood here every unlawful intercourse.

units.la: Facit eam mœchari. Dans ei occasionem secundarum nuptiarum, ut ait Origenes, tractatu 7. in Mat. cùm tamen permaneat conjux ipsius dimittentis. Vide infrà cap. 19. v. 9.
units.tr: Makes her commit adultery. Giving her occasion for a second marriage, as Origen says, Tractate 7 on Matthew, although the wife of the one dismissing remains his wife. See below ch. 19, v. 9.

units.la: 33. Non perjurabis, &c. Sensum non verba citat Christus ex Exod. 20. v. 2. Num. 30. v. 3.
units.tr: 33. You shall not forswear yourself, etc. Christ cites the sense, not the words, from Exod. 20, v. 2, and Num. 30, v. 3.

units.la: Juramenta. Id est, vota juramento confirmata.
units.tr: Oaths. That is, vows confirmed by an oath.

units.la: 34. Non jurare omnino. Intellectus Sacræ Scripturæ ex actibus sanctorum intelligitur; idem enim Spiritus, quo Sacræ Scripturæ sunt editæ, Sanctos viros ad operandum inducit. Ex hoc ergo quod Paulus jurasse invenitur, offenditur verbum Domini non sic esse intelligendum, quasi juramentum sit omnino illicitum, sed quia ad hoc homo niti debeat, ut quantùm ex ipso est, juramento non utatur tanquam quodam bono & per se appetibili, tum propter periculum, quod imminet ex frequenti juratione, ne homo labatur in perjurium propter labilitatem humanæ linguæ, tum etiam quia contra reverentiam Dei facere videtur, qui ipsum absque necessaria causa testem inducit. Unde nec Apostolus juravit invenitur nisi scribendo, quando homo cum majori deliberatione & cautela loquitur; est etiam quandoque necessarium juramentum, ut fides verbo dicentis adhibeatur, quod utile est etiam ei qui audit, & sic Apostolus propter utilitatem auditorum, quibus erat utile ut ei crederent, juravit, quasi non quærens quod sibi utile esset, sed quod multis ut salvi fierent. Hæc D. Th. in Ep. ad Rom. c. 1. Lec. 5. Eadem docet 22æ q. 89. a. 2 ad primum. Sic & B. Aug. in hunc locum & Ser. 28. alias 30. de Verbis Apostoli, & de mendacio ad Consentium c. 15. & Magistr. Sent. 3. Distinc. 39. Lit. D. Verba Augustini sunt. Intelligendum est illud quod positum est, omninò, ad hoc positum, ut quanquantum in te est non affectes, non ames, non quasi pro bono cum aliqua delectatione appetas jusjurandum. Ratio est quia falsa juratio exitiosa est, vera juratio periculosa est, nulla juratio secura est. Nihil autem aliud est jurare, nisi Deum testem invocare, seu, à Deo partis assertæ in re controversa probationem petere, quod vel per simplicem contestationem fit, sicut cum quis dicit; testis mihi est Deus, coram Deo loquor, &c. vel per execrationem, dum scilicet aliquis se vel aliquid ad se pertinens ad poenam obligat, nisi sit verum quod dicit.
units.tr: 34. Not to swear at all. The meaning of Holy Scripture is understood from the acts of the saints; for the same Spirit by whom the Holy Scriptures were published also moves holy men to act. Therefore, from the fact that Paul is found to have sworn, it is shown that the Lord's word is not to be understood as if an oath were altogether unlawful, but that a man ought to strive, as far as in him lies, not to use an oath as some good and desirable thing in itself, both on account of the danger that threatens from frequent swearing, lest a man fall into perjury through the slipperiness of the human tongue, and also because it seems to act against reverence for God, who calls him as a witness without necessary cause. Hence the Apostle is found to swear only when writing, when a man speaks with greater deliberation and caution. Sometimes an oath is also necessary so that faith is given to the word of the speaker, which is useful also to the hearer; and so the Apostle swore on account of the usefulness to his hearers, to whom it was useful that they believe him, seeking not what was useful to himself but what would save many. Thus Thomas Aquinas on Romans ch. 1, lecture 5. He teaches the same in 2a 2ae q. 89, a. 2, ad 1. So also Augustine on this passage and in Sermon 28 (alias 30) On the Words of the Apostle, and in On Lying, to Consentius, ch. 15; and the Master of the Sentences, book 3, distinction 39, letter D. The words of Augustine are: What is said absolutely must be understood as said to this end: that, as far as is in you, you do not desire, love, or seek an oath as a good with any delight. The reason is that a false oath is deadly, a true oath is dangerous, and no oath is safe. Now to swear is nothing other than to call God as witness, or to ask God for proof of the asserted party in a disputed matter. This is done either by simple attestation, as when someone says: God is my witness, I speak before God, etc.; or by execration, when someone binds himself, or something pertaining to himself, to punishment unless what he says is true.

units.la: Per Cœlum. Supple, juraveris; juramentum tam præsentium vel præteritorum assertorium, quàm futurorum promissorium dupliciter potest fieri per creaturas; primò per simplicem contestationem, in quantum in creaturis divina veritas manifestatur; secundò per execrationem, in quantum assignantur à jurante creaturæ, in quibus divinum judicium exerceatur, nisi verum ipse dixerit. Ideo autem Christus postquam dixisset, non jurare omninò, addidit, neque per cœlum, quia ut colligi potest ex cap. 23. infrà, Scribæ & Pharisæi non putabant se teneri juramento, si per ista juraffent; hunc igitur errorem redarguere volens Christus, declarat quòd qui jurat per cœlum, per Deum jurat, cujus thronus est cœlum; qui per terram jurat, per Deum jurat, cujus pedum scabellum est; qui per Jerosolymam jurat, jurat per Deū, cujus civitas est; imò qui Gentilium more jurat, per caput, quod maximè nostrum esse videtur, per Deum jurat, in cujus potestate est & caput, cùm ipse solus possit sine applicatione activorum passivis capillos facere albos aut nigros.
units.tr: By heaven. Supply: you have sworn. An oath, whether assertory of present or past things or promissory of future things, can be made through creatures in two ways: first by simple attestation, insofar as divine truth is made manifest in creatures; second by execration, insofar as the one swearing names creatures in which divine judgment is exercised, unless he has spoken the truth. Christ, after saying not to swear at all, added nor by heaven, because, as can be gathered from ch. 23 below, the scribes and Pharisees did not think they were bound by an oath if they swore by such things. Wishing therefore to refute this error, Christ declares that whoever swears by heaven swears by God, whose throne is heaven; whoever swears by the earth swears by God, whose footstool it is; whoever swears by Jerusalem swears by God, whose city it is; indeed, whoever swears in the manner of the Gentiles by his head, which seems most to be his own, swears by God, in whose power the head also is, since he alone can make hairs white or black without any active or passive application.

units.la: Thronus Dei est. Alludit ad illud Esaiæ 66. v. 1. Cœlum mihi sedes est, terra autem scabellum pedum meorum; Ut enim indicaret omnipotens Deus inferiorem se esse & superiorem omnibus, cœlum ipse sibi sedem & terram scabellum esse perhibuit. Ut verò ostenderet se omnia circumdare, cœlum metiri palmo, & terram sesquiafferit Esaiæ c. 4. pugillo concludere. Ipse est interior, ipse inferior & superior, regendo superior, portando inferior, replendo interior, circumdando exterior, sicque est intus ut portet, sic portat ut præsideat. Greg. Hom. 17. in Ezech.
units.tr: God's throne is heaven. He alludes to Isaiah 66, v. 1: Heaven is my seat, and the earth is my footstool. That Almighty God might show that he is lower than, and higher than, all things, he declared heaven to be his seat and the earth his footstool. But that he might show that he encompasses all things, he measures heaven with a span and closes the earth with a handful, as Isaiah ch. 4 says. He is within, he is below and above: ruling as the highest, bearing as the lowest, filling as the innermost, encompassing as the outermost; thus he is within so that he may bear, and bears so that he may preside. Gregory, Homily 17 on Ezekiel.

units.la: 35. Civitas magni Regis. Id est, Regis Regum cultui dedicata. Magnus Rex vocatur Deus cùm alibi, tum Malach. 1. v. 14. Heb. & Tob. 3. v. 17. Græco in textu.
units.tr: 35. The city of the great King. That is, dedicated to the worship of the King of kings. God is called the Great King both elsewhere and in Malachi 1:14 (Hebrew), and in Tobit 3:17 (in the Greek text).

units.la: 37. Sit autem sermo vester, est, est: non, non. Id est, quæcunque erunt vobis affirmanda, sine fuco, aut mendacio affirmate, nullo adhibito juramento voluntario; similiter abque que omni tergiverfatione quæ neganda sunt, negate. Itaque Christus hoc loco non præcipit modò ut à Juramento voluntario abstineamus, sed etiam ut semper vera loquamur; nec unquam veritatem adulteremus per æquivocationem, aut per mendacium destruamus. Vide Aug. Enchir. cap. 17. & 22.
units.tr: 37. But let your speech be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay. That is, whatever you are to affirm, affirm without deceit or lie, adding no voluntary oath. Likewise, whatever is to be denied, deny without any evasion. Thus Christ in this place does not only command us to abstain from voluntary oaths, but also that we always speak the truth, never corrupting the truth by equivocation or destroying it by lying. See Augustine, Enchiridion, chapters 17 and 22.

units.la: Quod autem, &c. Q. d. Quod enim cogimur expressè Deum testem nominare, inde est, quòd mali sumus, mendaces, alii aliis non fidentes & mutuò nos insimulamus mendacitatis.
units.tr: But as for what follows, etc. That is to say: the reason why we are compelled to name God expressly as witness is that we are evil and deceitful, that we do not trust one another, and that we mutually accuse one another of lying.

units.la: 38. Oculum pro oculo. Supple, reposcere liceat in judicio. Videmus leviter læsos homines mostri cædem, sitire sanguinem, vixque invenire in malis inimici unde satientur; huic immoderatæ & injustæ ultioni Lex modum figens pœnam Talionis instituit, hoc est, ut qualem quisque intulit injuriam, tale supplicium rependat, quod non fomes sed lines furoris est. Aug. lib. 19. contra Faustum c. 25.
units.tr: 38. An eye for an eye. Supply: it is permitted to demand this in judgment. "We see that men slightly injured thirst for the blood of the one who harmed them, and can scarcely find in their enemy's misfortunes anything to satisfy them. To this immoderate and unjust revenge the Law, setting a limit, instituted the penalty of retaliation: that each should repay such punishment as the injury he inflicted. This is not fuel for fury but a bridle on it." Augustine, Against Faustus, book 19, chapter 25.

units.la: 39. Ego autem. Noxiam Legis corruptelam & spurias falsorum doctorum glossas corrigens.
units.tr: 39. But I say. Correcting the harmful corruption of the Law and the spurious glosses of false teachers.

units.la: Dico vobis. Privatis scilicet, neque enim Magistratus hic alloquitur Christus, sed eos qui impetuntur. Deinde cùm Lex imperet Magistratibus ut reum pleƈtant, rei ipsi futuri apud Deum ni fecerint, iis si Christus interdixisset ne debitâ reos pœnâ punirent, omninò contrarium Legi præcepisset, eámque proinde solvisset, quam tamen diserte dixit se non venille solvere, sed adimplere. Hinc Constitutionum, quæ sub nomine Clementis R. P. circumferuntur, lib. 7. c. 3. Non omnis cædes illicita, sed ea quæ est innocentis: ita tamen ut quæ justa est, solis Magistratibus sit reservata. Quod hic autor de cæde dicit, locum habet in quavis pœna reis infligenda.
units.tr: I say to you. To private persons, of course; for Christ is not here addressing magistrates, but those who are attacked. Furthermore, since the Law commands magistrates to punish the guilty, and the guilty themselves will answer before God if they fail to do so, had Christ forbidden them to punish the guilty with the due penalty, he would have commanded something wholly contrary to the Law and thereby dissolved it, though he plainly said that he had come not to dissolve it but to fulfil it. Hence the Constitutions circulated under the name of Clement the Roman Pontiff, book 7, chapter 3: "Not every killing is unlawful, but only that of the innocent; yet so that the lawful kind is reserved to magistrates alone." What this author says about killing holds true of any penalty to be inflicted on the guilty.

units.la: Non resistere malo. Id est, non solùm non rependere malum, quod vobis fuerit irrogatum, sed etiam non resistere, quin aliud vobis iterum irrogetur ab eo, quem tamen misericorditer emendatoriam subire vindiƈtam desiderare debetis. Paratus itaque debet esse homo justus & pius patienter eorum malitiam sustinere, quos fieri bonos quærit, ut numerus potiùs crescat bonorum, non ut pari malitiâ se quoque numero addat malorum. Sunt ergo ista præcepta patientiæ ut semper teneatur in secreto animi patientia cum benevolentia, in manifesto autem id fiat, quod eis videtur prodesse, quibus bene velle debemus; agenda sunt enim multa etiam cum invitis benignâ quâdam asperitate pleƈtendis, quorum potiùs utilitati consulendum est, quàm voluntati. Aug. Epis. 5. ad Marcellinum.
units.tr: Do not resist evil. That is, not only not to repay the evil that has been done to you, but also not to resist another evil being inflicted on you again by him whom, nevertheless, you ought mercifully to wish to undergo corrective punishment. "The just and pious man ought therefore to be ready to bear patiently the malice of those whom he seeks to make good, so that the number of the good may rather grow, and not that he himself, by matching their malice, should add himself to the number of the evil. These precepts of patience therefore require that patience together with goodwill be always kept in the secret of the mind, while in outward action we do whatever seems to benefit those to whom we ought to wish well. For many things must be done even to unwilling persons, with a certain kindly sternness, and we must consult their advantage rather than their will." Augustine, Letter 5 to Marcellinus.

units.la: Si quis te percusserit in dexteram, &c. Christi oratio talis est, ut occultæ occurrat responsationi. Ita enim dicimus, Veterem ferendo injuriam invitas novam, percussit me in una mala & fero, mox me percutiet in altera. Imò, ait Salvator, hoc potius facias, quam à charitate & patientia discedas. Quæ inquit Aug. lib. de mendacio ad Consentium c. 15. in novo Testamento à sanctis facta sunt, ubi morum imitandorum evidentissima commendatio est, valent ad intelligentiam Scripturarum, quæ in præceptis digesta sunt, velut cùm legimus in Evang. Accepisti alapam, para alteram maxillam. Exemplum autem patientiæ nullum, quam ipsius Dei potentius & excellentius invenimus. At ipse cùm alapâ percussus esset, non ait, Ecce altera maxilla, sed, Si male dixi, exprobra de malo, si autem bene, quid me caedis? Ubi ostendit illam præparationem maxillæ alterius in corde faciendam. Quis enim negaret Christum paratum fuisse in alteram maxillam cædi pro salute omnium, qui paratus fuit etiam toto corpore crucifigi? Ergo, pergit Aug. lib. 1. de Sermone Domini in monte cap. 19. quod sequitur: Et qui voluerit tecum judicio contendere, &c. ad præparationem cordis, non ad ostensionem operis præceptum intelligitur.
units.tr: If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, etc. Christ's saying is framed so as to meet a hidden retort. For we say: "By bearing an old injury you invite a new one: he struck me on one cheek and I endured it; soon he will strike me on the other." But the Saviour says: rather do this than depart from charity and patience. "The things," says Augustine, in his book On Lying to Consentius, chapter 15, "that were done by the saints in the New Testament, where there is a most evident recommendation of morals to be imitated, are of value for understanding the Scriptures which are laid out as precepts, as when we read in the Gospel: 'You have received a blow; prepare the other cheek.' Yet we find no example of patience more powerful and excellent than that of God himself. But when he had been struck with a blow, he did not say, 'Behold, the other cheek,' but: 'If I have spoken evil, bear witness to the evil; but if well, why do you strike me?' Where he shows that the preparation of the other cheek is to be made in the heart. For who would deny that Christ was prepared to be struck on the other cheek for the salvation of all, he who was prepared even to be crucified in his whole body?" Therefore, Augustine goes on in book 1 of his work On the Sermon on the Mount, chapter 19: "What follows: 'And if anyone wishes to contend with you at law, etc.' is to be understood as a precept concerning the preparation of the heart, not the display of a deed."

units.la: 40. Tunicam tuam tollere, dimitte ei & Pallium. Luc. c. 6. v. 20. Ab eo qui aufert tibi vestimentum, Græcè ἱμάτιον [?] id est, pallium, noli prohibere etiam tunicam. Utriusque Evangelistæ hic unus & idem sensus est, qui tibi litem intendit ut vestem unam tollat, paratus sis animo, & alteram ei dimittere sine lite. Cum enim pro terrena re pax à corde cum proximo scinditur, apparet, quod plus res terrena, quam proximus amatur. B. Greg. lib. 31. Moral. cap. 10.
units.tr: 40. Let him have your cloak as well as your coat. Luke 6:20. From him who takes away your garment, in Greek [ἱμάτιον], that is, the cloak: do not forbid him the tunic also. Both Evangelists have one and the same meaning here: whoever brings a suit against you to take away one garment, be ready in mind to give him the other too, without litigation. "For when peace with a neighbour is torn apart for the sake of an earthly thing, it becomes clear that the earthly thing is loved more than the neighbour." Gregory the Great, Moralia, book 31, chapter 10.

units.la: 41. Angariaverit. Id est, currere coëgerit; angariare dicitur esse vox à Persis derivata apud quos publici cursores angari dicebantur. Ratio angariæ est, cùm aliquis aufert asinum hujus domino sequenti illum, & omnem asinum primum occurrentem aufert & restituit priorem ei cujus est; secundus autem sequitur asinum suum, donec obviam factus fuerit alius, & sic deinceps. Ita Isaac. Satisan ex Rabbi Salomone Jarchi.
units.tr: 41. Should compel you to go. That is, to make you run. The word angariare is said to be derived from the Persians, among whom public couriers were called angari. "The rule of angary is this: when someone takes a donkey, its owner follows it; and whatever first donkey he meets, he takes and restores the former one to its owner, while the second follows its own donkey until another is met, and so on." So Isaac Satisan, following Rabbi Solomon Jarchi.

units.la: Vade. Hoc monet Christus non tam ut pedibus agas, quam ut animo sis paratus, Aug. lib. 1. de Sermone Domini in monte c. 19.
units.tr: Go. Christ admonishes this not so much that you should go on foot as that you should be ready in mind. Augustine, On the Sermon on the Mount, book 1, chapter 19.

units.la: Alia duo. Vox alia abest à textu Græco; vult itaque nos Christus, ita immobiles in charitate fraterna permanere, ut ab ea, non quæ ignominiosè nobis à fratribus inferuntur non quæ patimur ab eis opum dispendia, non denique quæ tyrannicè nobis imponunt onera, nos separare possint. Vult Christus nos semper paratos esse animo ad majores illatis ferendas injurias, ne ob illatas à fratris dilectione excidamus, sed quoniam parum est non nocere, nisi & beneficium præste praefer, ut loquitur Aug. consequenter dicit:
units.tr: Two others. The word other is absent from the Greek text. Christ thus wills us to remain so unmoved in fraternal charity that neither the shameful wrongs done to us by brothers, nor the losses of goods we suffer at their hands, nor finally the burdens they tyrannically lay upon us, can separate us from it. Christ wills us always to be ready in mind to bear greater injuries that may be inflicted, lest we fall away from love of the brother because of the injuries done to us. But since it is little not to harm, unless one also bestows a benefit (as Augustine puts it), he consequently says:

units.la: 42. Qui autem petit, &c, Luc. 6. v. 30. Omni petenti te tribue. Omni petenti, inquit, non omnia petenti, ut id des, quod dare bonestè & justè potes. Quid si enim pecuniam petat, quâ innocentem conetur opprimere? Quid si postremò stuprum petat? Sed ne multa persequar, quæ sunt innumerabilia, id prosectò dandum est, quod nec tibi, nec alteri noceat, quantum sciri aut credi ab homine potest; & cui juste negaveris quod petit, indicanda est ipsa justitia, ut non eum inanem dimittas. Ita omni petenti te dabis, quamvis non semper id quod petit dabis, sed aliquando melius aliquid dabis, cum petentem injustè correxeris. Aug. loco mox citato. Vide ejusdem Epistolam 48. ad Vincentium.
units.tr: 42. To him who asks of you, etc. Luke 6:30. Give to everyone who asks you. To everyone who asks, he says, not to one who asks for everything, so that you give what you can give honestly and justly. For what if he asks for money by which he tries to oppress an innocent person? What if, finally, he asks for debauchery? But, not to pursue many cases, which are innumerable: whatever you give must surely be something that harms neither you nor another, so far as this can be known or believed by a human being. And when you have justly refused what he asks, justice itself must be pointed out to him, so that you do not send him away empty. Thus you will give to everyone who asks, although you will not always give what he asks; sometimes you will give something better, when you have corrected the one who asks unjustly. Augustine, in the passage cited just above. See his Letter 48 to Vincentius.

units.la: Ne avertaris. Id est, ne te avertas, voluntate aut vultu tetricum aut difficilem te exhibendo, vel usuras exigendo, unde Luc. 6. v. 25. Mutuum date, nihil inde sperantes.
units.tr: Do not turn away. That is, do not turn yourself away, showing yourself stern or hard to deal with in will or look, or exacting interest; whence Luke 6:35: "Lend, expecting nothing in return."

units.la: 43. Diliges proximum tuum. Si amas te, proximum dilige, quia nihil magis commodis tuis dabis, quam quod contuleris alienis. B. Euch. in Ep. ad Valerianum.
units.tr: 43. You shall love your neighbour. "If you love yourself, love your neighbour, for you will give nothing more for your own advantage than what you have contributed to others'." Blessed Eucherius, in his Letter to Valerian.

units.la: Odio habebis inimicum tuum. Nempe alienigenam; nam inimicos Judæos satis expresse jubentur diligere Judæi Exod. 23. v. 4. &c. Non tamen ad verbum legitur in veteri testamento: Odio habebis inimicum tuum seu alienigenam, sed horum verborum sensus quoad alienigenas colligitur ex eo quod jussit Deus Israelitas nunquam jungere amicitias cum populis Terræ sibi promissæ Exod. 34. jussit eosdem populos internecione deleri ab iisdem Israelitis, ita ut nec magno, nec parvo parcerent Deut. 20. jussit ab eisdem Amalecitas deleri de sub cœlo, Deuteron. 26. & quia Saul misertus est Regi eorum & reservavit pecora eorum, Deus iratus abstulit ei regnum. 1 Reg. 15. jussit Israelitas nunquam pacem inire cum Ammonitis & Moabitis, nec quærere eis bona cunctis diebus vitæ suæ Deuteron. 23. jussit denique, ut alia omittam, eosdem Israelitas hostiliter se gerere contra Madianitas, quos ipsi hostes prius erant experti, Num. 25. Audito igitur & non intellecto quod Antiquis dictum erat implicitè, non expressis verbis, Oderis inimicum tuum: ferebantur homines in hominis odium, cum non deberent odisse nisi vitium. Hos ergo corrigit Dominus, Legis mentem aperiens his verbis: Diligite inimicos vestros: Ut quorum execramur iniquitatem, optemus salutem. Profp. Sent. 354.
units.tr: You shall hate your enemy. That is, a foreigner; for the Jews are quite expressly commanded to love their enemies, Exod. 23. v. 4, etc. Yet the words You shall hate your enemy or foreigner are not read word for word in the Old Testament. The sense of these words as regards foreigners is gathered from the fact that God ordered the Israelites never to join in friendship with the peoples of the land promised to them, Exod. 34. He ordered those same peoples to be destroyed by the same Israelites, so that they should spare neither great nor small, Deut. 20. He ordered the Amalekites to be blotted out from under heaven, Deut. 26. And because Saul spared their king and kept their flocks, God in anger took the kingdom from him, 1 Kings 15. He ordered the Israelites never to make peace with the Ammonites and Moabites, nor to seek their good all the days of their life, Deut. 23.
