Finally, to omit other instances, he ordered the same Israelites to act with hostility against the Midianites, whom they had previously found to be enemies, Num. 25. Therefore, having heard, but not understood, what was said to the ancients implicitly, though not in express words, You shall hate your enemy, people were carried into hatred of a human being, when they ought to have hated nothing but vice. The Lord therefore corrects these people, unfolding the meaning of the Law in these words: Love your enemies, so that you may wish salvation to those whose wickedness you abhor. Prosper, Sentences 354.

units.la: Diligite inimicos vestros. Huic præcepto videtur oppositum illud Prov. 25. Si esurierit inimicus tuus cibo illum; si sitierit da ei aquam bibere, prunas enim congregabis super caput ejus.
units.tr: Love your enemies. The following saying from Prov. 25. seems opposed to this precept: If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him water to drink; for you will heap coals of fire upon his head.

units.la: Quomodo enim quis diligit, quemuardere vult carbonibus[?]? Nulla tamen erit oppositio, si advertatur Salomon loqui de illis vastatoribus carbonibus, qui dantur homini adversus linguam subdolam; cum enim quis benefecerit inimico, & non vultus malo ejus viceris in bono malum, plerumque illum inimicitiarum suarum poenitebit, & irascetur sibi, quod tam bonum hominem laeserit. Ipsa vero utilis poenitentia est, quae tanquam carbones ignis inimicitias ejus, malitiasque consumit. Aug. de diversis Serm. 26. c. 18. de Doctrina Christ. lib. 3. cap. 16.
units.tr: For how can anyone love the one whom he wishes to burn with coals? There will be no contradiction, however, if it is noted that Solomon is speaking of those scorching coals which are applied to a man against a deceitful tongue. For when someone has done good to an enemy, and has not looked on his evil, but overcome evil with good, that enemy will for the most part regret his hostility and be angry with himself that he has wronged so good a man. Indeed, that repentance is useful which, like coals of fire, consumes his enmity and malice. Augustine, On Diverse Sermons 26, ch. 18; On Christian Doctrine, book 3, ch. 16.

units.la: 44. Benefacite. Id est, parati sitis benefacere, & si commode potestis, reipsa benefacite his qui oderunt vos. Quae dixit Christus, huc pertinent; ut adversus omnes simus patientes, officiosi, minime iracundi, ut ait S. Justinus Apol. 2. non vero ut inter aemulum & necessarium nulla distinctio sit, ut loquitur S. Hier. Dial. 1. adv. Pelag.
units.tr: 44. Do good. That is, be ready to do good, and where you conveniently can, actually do good to those who hate you. What Christ said pertains to this: that we should be patient towards all, dutiful, and least of all quick to anger, as St Justin says in Apology 2; but not that there should be no distinction between a rival and a necessary person, as St Jerome says in Dialogue 1 against Pelagius.

units.la: Orate. Admonemur orare pro inimicis nostris, utique nolentibus pie vivere, ut Deus in illis operetur ut velint, cujus est averta & adversa corda convertere. Orare autem est de necessitate praecepti, sicut & inimicos diligere in communi; charitas enim neminem ex dilectione excludit, proindeque debemus & pro eis orare in communi, orando pro omnibus hominibus sine inimicorum exclusione, & optare eis bona spiritualia in communi, & peccamus mortaliter, si eis aliquod velimus malum spirituale, quod nempe eos prohibeat a salute aeterna. Hinc imprecationes, quae in sacra Scriptura inveniuntur factae a sanctis viris, uno ex tribus sequentibus modis intelligi debent; primo ut intelligantur factae, non optantium voto, sed spiritu praevidentium; 2o. per modum optationis, ut tamen desiderium optantis non referatur ad poenam hominis, sed ad justitiam punientis; quia nec ipse Deus puniens laetatur in perditione impiorum, sed in sua justitia, quia justus Dominus & justitias dilexit; 3o. ut desiderium referatur ad culpae expiationem vel terminationem, non ad ipsam poenam. Ita post SS. PP. docet D. Thomas 22ae.q.25 ar.6.ad secundum & 3m.& q.83.ar.7.ad 3m.
units.tr: Pray. We are bidden to pray for our enemies, since they are certainly unwilling to live piously, that God may work in them so that they will, for it belongs to him to turn hard and hostile hearts. Now praying is a matter of necessity under the precept, just as loving enemies is in general; for charity excludes no one from love, and so we ought to pray for them too in general, praying for all people without excluding enemies, and wishing them spiritual goods in general. We sin mortally if we wish them any spiritual evil, namely that which would keep them from eternal salvation. Hence the curses found in sacred Scripture, uttered by holy men, must be understood in one of three following ways. First, that they are understood to be uttered not by the wish of those who curse, but by the spirit of those who foresee. Second, by way of wish, yet so that the desire of the one wishing does not refer to the punishment of the man, but to the justice of the one punishing, because God himself, punishing, does not rejoice in the destruction of the wicked, but in his justice: for the Lord is just and has loved justice. Third, that the desire refers to the expiation or ending of the fault, not to the punishment itself. Thus after the holy Fathers, St Thomas teaches, 2a 2ae, q. 25, art. 6, ad 2, and 3a, q. 83, art. 7, ad 3.

units.la: 45. Ut sitis filii, &c. Hebraismus; sensus enim est: ut sitis similes Patri vestro, qui & bonos beneficiis fovet, & malos iisdem beneficiis ad poenitentiam provocat.
units.tr: 45. That you may be sons, etc. A Hebraism; for the sense is: that you may be like your Father, who both cherishes the good with benefits and by the same benefits provokes the wicked to repentance.

units.la: 46. Quam mercedem habebitis? Qui enim amicum ita diligit, ut inimicum oderit, non tantum inimici peccatum; hic impetu naturae, non coelesti charitate in amici amorem fertur, proinde nec mercede a Deo donabitur hujusmodi dilectio, cum Deo nihil placere possit, nisi quod ex fide viva, seu ex fide & charitate fiat.
units.tr: 46. What reward will you have? For one who loves a friend in such a way as to hate an enemy does not merely commit the sin of an enemy; he is carried towards love of a friend by the impulse of nature, not by heavenly charity, and therefore such love will not be rewarded by God, since nothing can please God except what is done from living faith, that is, from faith and charity.

units.la: Id est, qui Romanis, ex quo Judæa à Pompeio subjecta est & facta vectigalis, ad collectionem vectigalium & tributorum à Judæis quotannis appendendorum (quod aurum Judaicum Cicero appellat) operam locabant. Hoc autem hominum genus vulgo invisum, & pro perditis peccatoribus habitum, passim testantur Evangelistæ. Qui scilicet solo naturæ impetu ducuntur. In plerisque codicibus Græcis hic iterum habetur vox Publicani.
units.tr: That is, those who hired themselves out to the Romans, since Judea was subjected by Pompey and made tributary, to collect the taxes and tributes which were paid yearly by the Jews (which Cicero calls Jewish gold). That this class of men was commonly hated and regarded as lost sinners, the Evangelists bear witness everywhere. Of course, they are driven by the mere impulse of nature. In most Greek manuscripts the word Publicans appears here again.

units.la: Scilicet, Judæos.
units.tr: That is, the Jews.

units.la: Supple, in misericordia; unde Luc. 6. v. 38. dicitur: Estote misericordes, sicut & pater vester misericors est; nempe circa bonos & malos; nullus enim tam malus est, qui non aliquem divinæ misericordiæ effectum percipiat. Aug. Serm. 15. de verbis Domini sic exponit locum laudatum Lucæ, ut sensus Christi videatur esse hic: Quemadmodum Deus perfectus est in misericordia, & dum dimittit seu ignoscit, & dum dat seu tribuit beneficium, ita & vos persecti estote, & dimittendo injurias vobis illatas, & tribuendo beneficia mendicis vestris.
units.tr: Supply: in mercy; whence Luke 6. v. 38 says: Be merciful, as your Father also is merciful; namely towards the good and the bad; for no one is so wicked that he does not perceive some effect of divine mercy. Augustine, Sermon 15 on the words of the Lord, explains the cited passage of Luke in such a way that Christ's meaning here seems to be: Just as God is perfect in mercy, both when he forgives or pardons and when he grants a benefit, so you too be perfect, both in forgiving the injuries done to you and in bestowing benefits on your beggars.

units.la: CAPUT VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: Attendite. Id est, cavete, quomodo vertit S. Hier. l. 2. adversus Pelagianos c. 4. Hinc discimus quòd opus nostrum, cùm hominibus ostenditur, in cordis prius examinatione pensandum est, per ejusdem ostensionis studium quid quaeratur. Si enim dantis gloriam quaerimus, etiam publica nostra opera in conspectu illius occulta servamus; si vero per hæc nostram laudem concupiscimus, foras ab ejus conspectu jam fusa sunt, etiamsi à multis ignorentur. Sed valde perfectorum est sic ostensio opere autoris gloriam quaerere, ut de illata laude privata nesciant exultatione gaudere. Tunc solum namque innoxiè hominibus laudabile opus ostenditur, cùm per dejectum mentis veraciter laus impensa calcatur; quam quia infirmi quique perfectè contemnendo non superant, necesse est ut bonum hoc, quod operantur, abscondant. Sæpe enim ab ipso ostensionis exordio propriam laudem quærunt; sæpe vero in ostensione operis, autoris gloriam patefacere cupiunt, sed exceptis favoribus in laudis propriæ cupiditatem rapiuntur: cùmque semetipsos dijudicare interius negligunt, sparsi exterius ignorant quod agunt, gunt, ebrumque opus sua elationi militat, atque hoc se impendere obsequio largitoris putant. B. Greg. lib. 8. Moral c. 38.
units.tr: Take heed. That is, beware. So St Jerome translates it in book 2 of Against the Pelagians, chapter 4. From this we learn that our work, when it is shown to men, must first be weighed in the examination of the heart, and by the eagerness of that same showing it must be asked what is sought. For if we seek the glory of the Giver, we keep even our public works hidden in his sight; but if by these we covet our own praise, they have already been poured out from his sight, even if they are unknown to many. Yet it belongs only to the very perfect to show a work so as to seek the glory of its author, and to be unable to rejoice in a private exultation at praise received. For a work is shown to men without harm only when the praise given is truly trodden underfoot by a humbled mind. Since the weak do not perfectly overcome this by despising it, they must hide the good they do. Often from the very beginning of the showing they seek their own praise; often, when they display the work, they wish to reveal the glory of its author, but, caught by the favour shown them, they are carried off into desire for their own praise. And when they neglect to judge themselves inwardly, outwardly they are scattered and do not know what they are doing; their work serves their own pride, and they think they are offering this service to the giver. St Gregory, Moralia, book 8, chapter 38.

units.la: Justitiam. Id est, inquit Hieronymus lib. 2. adversus Pelagianos c. 4. eleemosynam. Familiare est Hebraeis vocabulum, צדקה, justitia, pro eleemosyna usurpare. Hinc & hodie Judaei cum eleemosynam in gazophylacium pauperum, quod in Synagogis singulis extat, mittunt, his utuntur verbis: In justitia videbo faciem tuam. Sic Prov. 10. v. 2. 11. v. 4. Justitia liberabit a morte.
units.tr: Justice. That is, as Jerome says in book 2 of Against the Pelagians, chapter 4, alms. It is a familiar usage among the Hebrews to employ the word for justice [צדקה, tsedaqah] for alms. Hence even today the Jews, when they put money into the poor-box that stands in each of their synagogues, use these words: In justice I shall see your face. So also Proverbs 10:2 and 11:4: Justice delivers from death.

units.la: Faciatis. Supple, hoc animo.
units.tr: Do. Supply: with this intention.

units.la: Ut videamini ab eis. Ut sit ipse finis operis vestri, videri ab eis. Non autem Deus jussit bona opera abscondi, sed in bonis operibus laudem humanam non quaerere, ait Aug. Ser. 17. lib. 17. Hom. Hinc Paulus: Si adhuc hominibus placerem, i. e. placere vellem, Christi servus non essem. Gal. 1. v. 10. Cetera vitia trefcunt vitiis, vanitas virtutibus.
units.tr: So that you may be seen by them. So that being seen by them is itself the purpose of your work. God did not command good works to be hidden, but not to seek human praise in good works, says Augustine, Sermon 17 (book 17 of the Homilies). Hence Paul: If I still pleased men, that is, if I wished to please them, I would not be a servant of Christ. Galatians 1:10. Other vices are shaken by vices; vainglory is shaken by virtues.

units.la: 2. Noli tuba canere. Id est, populum quaerere spectatorem. Alludit autem Christus ad morem Hebraeis usitatum, ut cum publice aliquid dicendum aut faciendum esset, quod attentionem mererentur, buccina in vicis aut plateis canerent ac signum darent. Hinc clangere buccina, seu canere tuba populos jubent Prophetae, quoties de re magna, quae confiderari maxime meretur, vel audiri, agunt.
units.tr: 2. Do not sound a trumpet. That is, do not seek the people as spectators. Christ alludes to a custom common among the Hebrews: when something had to be said or done publicly that deserved attention, they would sound a horn in the villages or squares and give a signal. Hence the prophets command the peoples to blow a trumpet or sound a horn whenever they treat of a great matter that deserves above all to be considered or heard.

units.la: Hypocritae. Id est, simulatores. Vox haec proprie de histrionibus personam aliquam in fabula sustinentibus, sed passim usurpatur de iis, qui aliud haberi volunt, quam sunt, seu ut loquitur D. Th. Qui ea intentione opera perfectionis assumunt, ut malitiam suam occultius exerceant & magis nocere possint.
units.tr: Hypocrites. That is, pretenders. The word properly refers to actors who take on some character in a play, but it is commonly applied to those who wish to be thought other than they are, or, as St Thomas says, those who take up works of perfection with the intention of practising their malice more covertly and of being able to harm more.

units.la: In Synagogis &c. Id est, in locis, in quibus est hominum confluxus.
units.tr: In the synagogues, etc. That is, in places where people gather.

units.la: Receperunt mercedem suam. Quam scilicet quaesierunt; laudati enim sunt ab hominibus, quorum causa exercuere eleemosynam.
units.tr: They have received their reward. Namely, the reward they sought; for they were praised by men, for whose sake they performed the almsgiving.

units.la: 3. Nesciat sinistra, &c. Hoc adagio significat Christus usque adeo nobis non esse appetendum, ut ab hominibus videamur eleemosynam facientes, ut, si fieri posset, etiam nobis ipsis celanda esset nostra eleemosyna; Nam celata virtus Deo judice gaudet, inquit Hieron. in Epitaph. Fabiolae. In hunc sensum Eccli. 29. v. 11. dicitur: Conclude eleemosynam in corde pauperis, & haec pro te exorabit in die malo.
units.tr: 3. Let not your left hand know, etc. By this proverb Christ signifies that we ought so little to aim at being seen by men when giving alms that, if it were possible, even our own alms should be hidden from ourselves. For a hidden virtue rejoices, with God as judge, says Jerome in the Epitaph of Fabiola. To this effect Ecclesiasticus 29:11 says: Shut up alms in the heart of the poor, and it will pray for you in the day of evil.

units.la: 4. Reddet tibi. In hodiernis Graecis codicibus additur in manifesto, sed in Graecis exemplaribus, quae Latinis antiquiora sunt, non inveniri luculenter testatur Aug. libro 2. de Sermone Domini in monte capite 1. Non autem ait, Dabit, sed reddet, quia Deus mera liberalitate suâ bonis operibus mercedem promittens, debitorem se facit non tantum si-bi, sed & Christo & nobis, ut illi dicere possimus, Redde quod promisisti, fecimus quod jussisti, inquit Aug. Ser. 16. de verbis Apost. Hinc & oratio licet sit gratiæ testificatio, ut ait August. Ep. 105. (quod enim prece petimus, factò testamur nobis non debitum;) tamen ex liberali Dei promisso: Petite & dabitur vobis: debitum fit, quod sicut oportet oratione petierimus. Vide dicta cap. 5. v. 12.
units.tr: 4. Will reward you. In present-day Greek manuscripts the words openly are added, but Augustine, in book 2 of On the Lord's Sermon on the Mount, chapter 1, clearly testifies that they are not found in the Greek copies, which are older than the Latin ones. He does not say will give but will reward, because God, promising rewards to good works out of pure generosity, makes himself a debtor not only to himself but also to Christ and to us, so that we can say to him, Pay what you have promised; we have done what you commanded, says Augustine, Sermon 16 on the words of the Apostle. Hence, although prayer is a testimony of grace, as Augustine says in Letter 105 (for by asking in prayer we show by our deed that we do not have a claim), yet from God's generous promise, Ask and it will be given you, it becomes a debt that, if we have asked in prayer as we ought, must be paid. See what was said at chapter 5, verse 12.

units.la: 5. Sicut hypocritæ. Hoc non refertur ad locum, nec ad exteriorem corporis compositionem; in conventu enim orare laudabile est, ut dicitur Ps. 67. In Ecclesiis benedicite Deum; similiter stans oravit Azarias, Daniel 3. v. 25. stans oravit Publicanus, Luc. 18. v. 13. & utrinsque oratio Deo placuit. Imo veteres ferè semper orabant stantes, unde apud Hebræos inter orationis nomina recensetur, statio. Id unum ergo hic vetat Christus ne hunc unum orationis nostræ scopum adinstar hypocritarum habeamus, videri ab hominibus, seu, placere hominibus.
units.tr: 5. Like the hypocrites. This does not refer to place, nor to outward posture of the body; for it is praiseworthy to pray in assembly, as Psalm 67 says: Bless God in the congregations; Azariah prayed standing, Daniel 3:25; the tax collector prayed standing, Luke 18:13; and the prayer of both pleased God. Indeed the ancients almost always prayed standing, whence among the Hebrews station is counted among the names for prayer. Christ therefore forbids only this one thing here: that we should make this single aim of our prayer like that of the hypocrites, to be seen by men, or to please men.

units.la: 6. Intra in cubiculum, &c. Q. d. Tibi sufficiat ut ille solus noverit orationem tuam, qui solus omnium cordium novit occulta; Sive enim in Synagoga, sive in vicis, & plateis eleemosynam facis, (aut orationem) in abscondito tamen facis, quicunque hoc faciens, non ab hominibus, sed à Deo videri desideras. E contra verò, qui in abscondito facit, & videri cupiens, laudem ex hoc & gloriam quærit, non in abscondito quidem facit, quoniam absconditum non vult quod facit, tantùmque ei valet ac si in publico faceret. Deus autem qui videt in abscondito, & cui nihil est absconditum, qui & corda scrutatur, & videt cogitationes, reddet unicuique secundum opera sua. B. Bruno Signiensis.
units.tr: 6. Enter into your closet, etc. As if to say: let it be enough for you that he alone, who alone knows the secrets of all hearts, knows your prayer. For whether you give alms in the synagogue, or in the villages and squares (or pray), you do it in secret if you desire to be seen not by men but by God. On the other hand, whoever does it in secret, but desires to be seen, seeks praise and glory from it; he does not truly do it in secret, since he does not want what he does to be hidden, and it is worth to him just as much as if he did it in public. But God, who sees in secret, to whom nothing is hidden, who searches the hearts and sees the thoughts, will repay each one according to his works. St Bruno of Segni.

units.la: 7. Nolite multum loqui. Græcè μὴ βατταλογήσητε, id est, vitate battologiam, seu cavete ne labia & lingua sine mente orent; quod vitium dicitur ab Hebræis, בַּל־תְּשַׁתַּחוּ futilitas labiorum, à radice, בָּטָה, effutivit; unde battologia videtur esse diɛtio Hebræo-Græca potiùs, quàm derivata à Batto Ovidiano, qui ineptis repetitionibus dicitur usus. Præclarè itaque S. Isidorus libro 3. de summo bono c. 8. Oratio cordis est, non labiorum; neque enim verba deprecantis Deus intendit, sed orantis cor aspicit.
units.tr: 7. Do not use many words. In Greek, mē battalogēsēte [μὴ βατταλογήσητε], that is, avoid babbling, or beware lest lips and tongue pray without mind. This fault is called by the Hebrews bal-tesattahu [בַּל־תְּשַׁתַּחוּ], the emptiness of lips, from the root batah [בָּטָה], to blurt out; so battalogia seems to be a Hebrew-Greek word rather than one derived from Batto of Ovid, who is said to have used pointless repetitions. St Isidore therefore rightly says in book 3 of On the Supreme Good, chapter 8: Prayer is of the heart, not of the lips; for God does not attend to the words of one who prays, but looks upon the heart of the one who prays.

units.la: Sicut Ethnici. Qui exercendæ linguæ potiùs, quàm mutando animo dant operam. In multiloquio. Id est, propter multiloquium.
units.tr: As the Gentiles. Who labour to exercise the tongue rather than to change the mind. In much speaking. That is, on account of much speaking.

units.la: Scit enim &c. Oratio igitur nostra non ordinatur ad immutationem divinæ dispositionis, quæ pœnitudine non flectitur, sed ut obtineatur quod Deus omnipotens ante secula disposuit donare, ut ait B. Greg. lib. 1. Dialogorum c.
units.tr: For he knows, etc. Our prayer, therefore, is not directed to changing the divine disposition, which is not turned by repentance, but to obtaining what Almighty God decided before the ages to give, as St Gregory says in book 1 of the Dialogues, chapter …

units.la: 8. Non est necessarium nos Deo preces porrigere, ut ei nostras indigentias vel desideria manifestemus, sed ut nosipsi consideremus in his ad divinum auxilium esse recurrendum. D. Th. 22æ. q. 83. a. 2. ad 1m. Addit Augustinus in Ep. 121. ad Probam c. 8. exerceri in orationibus desiderium nostrum, quo possimus capere quod præparat Deus; illud enim valde magnum est, sed nos ad accipiendum parvi & angusti sumus..... Tantò quippe illud, quod nec oculus vidit, quia non est color; nec auris audivit, quia non est sonus; nec in cor hominis ascendit, quia cor hominis illuc debet ascendere, sumemus capacius, quantò id & fideliùs credimus, & speramus firmiùs & desideramus ardentiùs.
units.tr: 8. It is not necessary for us to offer prayers to God in order to make our needs or desires known to him, but so that we ourselves may consider that in these matters we must have recourse to divine help. St Thomas, II-II, question 83, article 2, reply to objection 1. Augustine adds in Letter 121 to Proba, chapter 8: Our desire is to be exercised in prayers, so that we may grasp what God prepares; for that is very great, but we are small and narrow to receive it….. For the more we believe that which the eye has not seen, because it has no colour; nor the ear heard, because it has no sound; nor has it entered the heart of man, because the heart of man ought to rise thither, the more capacious we shall make ourselves, the more faithfully we believe it, the more firmly we hope and the more ardently we desire.

units.la: Sic ergo. Statas Liturgias, seu, certas orandi formulas in sacra functione, quæ publicè peragitur, modò sacris Litteris non repugnant, esse probandas patet ex hoc, quod ut Baptista Luc. 11. v. 2. discipulis dictaverat, ita & Christus suis dictavit fixam orandi formulam, quam ab Apostolis in suis conventibus observatam testatur Justinus Martyr Apol. 2a. Tertul. Apologet. cap. 30. &c. Porro nullum est membrum istius Dominicæ orationis, quod non sparsim in Psalmis reperiatur. Sic primæ duæ petitiones reperiuntur in omnibus iis Psalmis, quibus cunctæ gentes ad confitendum nomen Dei invitantur. Ad tertiam petitionem pertinet totus Psalmus octonarius, quo David frequenter petit, ut Deus ipsius voluntatem flectat ad statuta sua, quod nihil est aliud, quàm id quod hac petitione, fiat voluntas tua, continetur. Quartæ petitionis materia est Ps. 103. Heb. 104, & 143. Heb. 144. Ad quintam petitionem referri possunt, Ps. 31. Heb. 32, & 50. Heb. 51. Sextæ & septimæ petitionis mentio fit quoties in Psalmis, e tentationibus, morbis, angustiis, ipsa denique morte erui flagitatur.
units.tr: So then. That set liturgies, that is, fixed forms of prayer used in the public worship service, are to be approved, provided they do not conflict with Holy Scripture. This is clear from the fact that, just as John taught his disciples (Luke 11:2), so Christ dictated to his own a fixed form of prayer. Justin Martyr testifies that the Apostles observed it in their assemblies (Apol. 2). See also Tertullian, Apologeticus, ch. 30, etc. Moreover, no part of this Lord's Prayer is absent from the Psalms, where it appears scattered about. The first two petitions occur in all those Psalms in which all nations are invited to confess the name of God. The whole eighth Psalm pertains to the third petition, in which David often asks God to turn his will toward God's own decrees. This is nothing other than what is contained in this petition, Thy will be done. The matter of the fourth petition is Psalm 103 (Heb. 104) and Psalm 143 (Heb. 144). The fifth petition can be related to Psalm 31 (Heb. 32) and Psalm 50 (Heb. 51). Mention of the sixth and seventh petitions is made whenever, in the Psalms, deliverance is sought from temptations, sicknesses, distresses, and finally from death itself.

units.la: Pater Noster. Dei nos filii sumus, quos voluntate suâ filios fecit, non ex natura sua filios genuit. quomodo Christum, qui solus est Dei filius naturâ. Genuit quidem & nos, sed quomodo dicitur adoptatus ab adoptante generatus, beneficio non naturâ. Aug. Ser. 51. de verbis Domini. Quo autem sensu Deus dicatur esse in cœlis, diximus supra c. 5. v. 12.
units.tr: Our Father. We are sons of God, whom he made sons by his own will, not whom he begot as sons by his nature, as Christ, who alone is the Son of God by nature. Indeed he also begot us, but in what sense is one said to be begotten by the one adopting, by favour and not by nature, when he has been adopted. Augustine, Sermon 51 on the words of the Lord. In what sense God is said to be in heaven, we have explained above, at chapter 5, verse 12.

units.la: Sanctificetur nomen tuum. Hoc non sic petitur, quasi non sit Jansanctum nomen Dei, sed ut sanctum habeatur ab hominibus, id est, ita illis innotescat, ut non exististiment aliquid sanctum, quod magis offendere timeant. Aug. l. 2. de Sermone Domini in monte.
units.tr: Hallowed be thy name. This is not asked as if the name of God were not holy, but that it may be held holy by human beings; that is, that it may become known to them in such a way that they do not think anything holy which they fear to offend more. Augustine, book 2, On the Sermon of the Lord on the Mount.

units.la: 10. Adveniat regnum tuum. Scilicet illud, quod praestituto tempore est omnibus perfectis ac Dei filiis generaliter repromissum, in quo eis dicetur a Christo: Venite benediciti Patris mei, possidete paratum vobis regnum a constitutione mundi. Abbas Isaac Col. 9. c. 19. apud Cassianum.
units.tr: 10. Thy kingdom come. That is, that kingdom which, at the appointed time, is promised in general to all the perfect and to the sons of God, in which Christ will say to them: "Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world." Abbot Isaac, Conference 9, ch. 19, in Cassian.

units.la: Fiat voluntas, &c. Haec petitio a B. Luca. c. 11. praetermittitur, quia ut dicit Aug. in Enchiridio c. 116. Haec tertia petitio est duarum praemissarum quodammodo repetitio. Est enim sensus huius petitionis secundum S. Hil. in Psal. 134. Fac ut sicut voluntati tuae in caelis ab indefessis et caelestibus virtutibus paretur, ita et a nobis in terra pareatur, ne corporalis nos infirmitas ab exequenda tua voluntate deflectat. In caelis enim indefessis quotidie vocibus dicitur: Sanctus, Sanctus, Sanctus Dominus Deus Sabaoth, pleni sunt caeli et terra gloria tua. Fac ut nobis quoque nihil aliud in opere sit, nisi per quod sanctificetur nomen tuum: nihil aliud in ipse, nisi per quod etiam in nos tuum regnum praeramus: nihil aliud in voluntate, nisi per quod tibi Deo nostro aeternae a nobis laudes sunt deferendae.
units.tr: Thy will be done, etc. Luke, ch. 11, omits this petition, because, as Augustine says in the Enchiridion, ch. 116, this third petition is in some sense a repetition of the two preceding ones. According to Hilary on Psalm 134, the sense of this petition is: "Cause that, just as your will is obeyed in heaven by the tireless and heavenly powers, so it may also be obeyed by us on earth, lest bodily weakness turn us aside from carrying out your will. For in heaven, by tireless voices, every day it is said: 'Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth; heaven and earth are full of your glory.' Grant that for us too nothing else in work may be, except that through which your name is sanctified; nothing else in the Spirit, except that through which your kingdom also is extended over us; nothing else in will, except that through which eternal praises are to be offered by us to you, our God."

units.la: 11. Panem. Synecdoche Hebr is familiaris, hoc est, omne subsidium necessarium ad vitae conservationem nobis tribue.
units.tr: 11. Bread. A synecdoche, familiar in Hebrew; that is, grant us every help necessary for the preservation of life.

units.la: Nostrum. Ecce et nostrum dicimus, et tamen ut detur oramus; nostrer quippe fit cum accipitur, qui tamen Dei est, quia ab illo datur. Sic justitia nostra dicitur, non quae ex nostro nostra est, sed quae divina largitate fit nostra. B. Greg. l. 24. Mor. c. 7.
units.tr: Our. See, we say our and yet pray that it be given; for it becomes ours when it is received, although it is God's, because it is given by him. So also righteousness is called ours, not because it is ours from what is ours, but because by divine bounty it becomes ours. Gregory the Great, Moralia, book 24, ch. 7.

units.la: Supersubstantialem. Id est, substantiae superadditum, vel super substantiam adjectum ad roborandam illam, conservandam vel augendam; quod aptissime significatur & per Graecum ἐπιούσιον & per Latinum supersubstantialem. Suidas explicat ἡ ἐπὶ τὴν ούσίαν ἡμῶν ἀρμόζουσα, substantiae seu naturae nostrae conveniens. Hanc etymologiam videre est & apud Basilium Magnum in Ascet. & apud Theophylactum. ἐπιούσιον ἄρτον, inquit, Basilius, τοῦτο δὲ πρὸς τὴν ἐπιούσαν ζωὴν τὴν ἡμῶν χορηγίαν ... Hoc est, Musculo interprete, qui quotidianam vitae sustentationem, substantiae nostrae conducit. Theophylactus ἐπιούσιον, inquit, ἡ ἐπιοῦσα ἡμῖν οὐσία, hoc est, qui ad substantiam et constitutionem nostram sufficiens est. Sunt qui deducunt ἐπιούσιον ab ἐπιοῦσα, quae vox Act. 7. v. 26. ponitur pro die sequenti. quenti seu crastino; nam in Evangelio Hebraeo Nazaraeorum, teste B. Hier. legebatur : Panem crastini מָחָר. Addunt tamen ἐπιούσιον non tam futurum hîc, quàm continuum, מָחָר, ac singulis diebus definitum significare; hinc & Vulgat. Luc. 11. ἐπιούσιον vertit quotidianum, ut sensus sit : Da nobis hodie panem, quo singulis diebus egemus.
units.tr: Supersubstantial. That is, added to substance, or added above substance, to strengthen, preserve or increase it; and this is most aptly signified both by the Greek epiousion [ἐπιούσιον] and by the Latin supersubstantialem. Suidas explains it as the one suited to our substance [ἡ ἐπὶ τὴν οὐσίαν ἡμῶν ἀρμόζουσα], that is, fitting our substance or nature. This etymology may also be seen in Basil the Great, in the Ascetica, and in Theophylact. Basil says epiousion bread [ἐπιούσιον ἄρτον], and this is the provision for our coming life [τοῦτο δὲ πρὸς τὴν ἐπιούσαν ζωὴν τὴν ἡμῶν χορηγίαν]. That is, as Musculus interprets it, it leads to the daily sustenance of our substance. Theophylact says epiousion is the substance coming to us [ἡ ἐπιοῦσα ἡμῖν οὐσία], that is, what is sufficient for our substance and constitution. Some derive epiousion from epiousa, a word which in Acts 7:26 is used for the following day, that is, tomorrow; for in the Gospel of the Nazarenes, as Blessed Jerome testifies, it was read: bread of tomorrow [machar]. They add, however, that epiousion signifies here not so much what is future as what is continual and defined for each day. Hence also the Vulgate, in Luke 11, translates epiousion as daily, so that the sense is: Give us today the bread which we need every day.

units.la: Da nobis. Voluit Christus singulos orare pro omnibus, ut omnes pro singulis orarent, sicque singuli omnium orationis participes fierent. B. Ambr. l. de Cain c. 9.
units.tr: Give us. Christ willed that each should pray for all, so that all should pray for each, and thus each would become a sharer in the prayer of all. Ambrose, On Cain and Abel, book 1, ch. 9.

units.la: 12. Dimitte nobis. Per hanc petitionem voluit nobis Salvator ostendere, quantumlibet juste in hujus vitae caligine, atque infirmitate vivamus, non nobis deesse peccata, pro quibus dimittendis debeamus orare, & eis qui in nos peccant, ut & nobis ignoscatur, ignoscere. Augusl. l. 21. de Civit. Dei c. 22 & 27.
units.tr: 12. Forgive us. By this petition the Saviour wished to show us that, however justly we live in the darkness and weakness of this life, sins are not lacking to us, for whose forgiveness we ought to pray, and that we ought to forgive those who sin against us, so that we too may be forgiven. Augustine, The City of God, book 21, chs. 22 and 27.

units.la: Debita, Peccata nostra debita vocantur, quòd illis tanquam ære alieno obstricti teneamur divinae Justitiae. Unde Luc. c. 11. distertis verbis dicitur, Dimitte nobis peccata nostra. Est autem dimittere, seu ut quidam Latinius dicunt, remittere debita, Syriaca, & Chaldaica locutio. Quod enim Hebraicè dicimur סלח לעון, נשא עון, id est, ignos-cere iniquitati, perferre delictum, hoc Syrus, & Chaldaeus reddunt שבק לחובי, remittere debita. Vide Gen. 50. v. 17. 3. Heb. 1 Reg. 9. v. 34.
units.tr: Debts. Our sins are called debts because we are held, as if bound by a debt of money, to divine justice. Hence in Luke 11 it is said in plain words: Forgive us our sins. Now to forgive, or, as some say more Latinly, to remit debts, is a Syriac and Chaldee expression. For what the Hebrews say as to forgive iniquity, to bear sin [salach la-avon, nasa avon], that is, to pardon iniquity, to bear a fault, the Syrian and the Chaldee render as shebaq lechobai, to remit debts. See Genesis 50:17; 1 Samuel 3 (Heb.); 1 Kings 9:34.

units.la: Sicut. Exempla sumuntur non tantùm à rebus, quae sunt genere proximo eadem; sed & ab iis, quae aliquid habent similitudinis, praesertim cùm iis idem aliquod nomen ob similitudinem imponitur. Sic vetat nos Christus judicare, temere nimirum & immisericorditer, ne ipsi judicemur: addítque quâ mensura mensi fuerimus, eadem nobis remensum iri; ubi judicare illud prius ab altero distat toto genere: nam prius est judicium libertatis, alterum judicium est potestatis. Eodem modo longe aliud est in Deo atque in aliis rectoribus remittere peccata, aliud in privatis ab altero laesis; illi enim oppositum est punire, huic verò poenam postulare, optare, aut etiam conqueri. Distant ergo intrinsecus, sed extrinsecus quodammodo conveniunt; nam causa impellens ad utrumque est benignitas, & utriusque effectus est quod is qui peccavit ab incommodo aliquo liberetur, aut reipsâ, aut certè quantùm est in remittente : quae convenientia sufficit, ut exemplo sua vis constet.
units.tr: As. Examples are taken not only from things which are the same in their nearest genus, but also from those which have some likeness, especially when the same name is given to them because of the likeness. Thus Christ forbids us to judge, rashly and without mercy, lest we ourselves be judged; and he adds that by whatever measure we measure, the same will be measured back to us. Here the former judging differs from the other by an entire genus: for the former is a judgment of freedom, the other is a judgment of power. In the same way, it is one thing for God, and another for other rulers, to remit sins; and another for private persons to forgive one who has wronged them, for to the former the opposite is to punish, but to the latter it is to demand a penalty, to wish it, or even to complain of it. They differ, therefore, intrinsically, but in some way agree extrinsically; for the impelling cause in both is kindness, and the effect of both is that the one who has sinned is freed from some disadvantage, either in fact or at least as far as lies with the one forgiving. This agreement is enough for the example to establish its force.

units.la: Debitoribus, Id est, offensoribus. Qui Hebraicè nuncupatur ܢܒܝܐ peccator, Syriacè dicitur ܕܒܝܢ, debitor.
units.tr: Debtors, that is, offenders. In Hebrew this is called [nabyā], sinner; in Syriac it is called [dāḇīn], debtor.

units.la: 12. Inducas. Id est, induci permittas, seu patiaris; sæpe enim facere dicitur Deus, quæ facere permittit. Inducimur autem in tentationem, cùm à tentatione vincimur, quod tunc fit, cùm caremus aut luce, quâ peccatum, tentationisve fallaciam dignoscamus, aut justitiæ amore, quo peccati blanditiis cruciatibusve resistamus. Quamvis autem Augustinus passim in hunc sensum sextam orationis Dominicæ petitionem expoñat, idem tamen in libro de Bono perseverantiæ c. 6. putat simpliciter nos orare, ut omninò non tentemur, ea potissimum tentatione, quâ ad peccandum sollicitamur; quia nostræ infirmitatis memores, nec de nobis ipsis confidentes optamus potiùs liberari tentationibus, earumque periculis, quàm eis exponi. Licèt enim tentatio interdum utilis sit, semper tamen est periculosa, idèque humilitas Christiana illam declinare suadet. Neque obstant Scripturæ tentationem seu afflictionem fortiter & cum gaudio tolerandam præscribentes; tolerare enim eam jubent, non amare. Ut autem ait August. l. 10. Conf. c. 28. Nemo quod tolerat amat, etsi tolerare amet. Quamvis enim gaudeat se tolerare, tamen mavult non esse, quod toleret.
units.tr: 12. Lead us not. That is, permit us not to be led, or allow us not to suffer it; for God is often said to do what he permits to be done. We are led into temptation when we are overcome by temptation, which happens when we lack either the light by which we discern sin and the deceit of temptation, or the love of righteousness by which we resist the allurements or torments of sin. Although Augustine, in many places, explains the sixth petition of the Lord's Prayer in this sense, yet in his book On the Gift of Perseverance, ch. 6, he thinks that we pray simply that we may not be tempted at all, especially by that temptation by which we are enticed to sin; because, mindful of our weakness and not trusting in ourselves, we prefer to be delivered from temptations and their dangers rather than be exposed to them. For although temptation is sometimes useful, it is always dangerous, and therefore Christian humility advises us to avoid it. Nor do the Scriptures, which prescribe that temptation or affliction be borne bravely and with joy, stand in the way; for they command us to endure it, not to love it. As Augustine says, Confessions, book 10, ch. 28: No one loves what he endures, although he may love to endure it. For although he rejoices that he endures, yet he would rather not have anything to endure.

units.la: A malo. Id est, a diabolo, qui diĉus est supra cap. 4. v. 3. Tentator. Passim autem diabolus dicitur malus sine addito, quia in extremo malitiæ gradu constitutus, ab eo revocari nequit. Porrò satis de se humiliter sentit, nec salvari per se præsumit, qui ut à malo per Deum liberetur implorat. B. Chrysol. Serm. 68.
units.tr: From evil. That is, from the devil, who is spoken of above in chapter 4, verse 3. Tempter. The devil is often called simply "evil" without any addition, because he has reached the extreme degree of wickedness and cannot be called back from it. Moreover, he who asks God to deliver him from evil thinks humbly enough of himself and does not presume to save himself. St Chrysologus, Sermon 68.

units.la: Quod hîc sequitur in textu Græco, Quoniam tuum est regnum & potentia & gloria in secula, reperitur in Syriaco & Hebraico Evangelio, & apud Chrysostomum, Theophylactum & Euthymium, sed apud nullum Latinorum extat, abesséque & à nonnullis vetustissimis codicibus Græcis manuscriptis testatur Beza. Verùm cùm magnifica hæc & longè sanctissima doxologia extet, 1 Tim. 6. v. 15, & 16, & alibi passim in Scripturis, est haud dubiè Canonica.
units.tr: What follows here in the Greek text, For yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory for ever, is found in the Syriac and Hebrew Gospels, and in Chrysostom, Theophylact and Euthymius, but it is not found in any Latin writer. Beza testifies that it is also absent from some of the oldest Greek manuscripts. Yet since this magnificent and very holy doxology occurs in 1 Timothy 6, verses 15 and 16, and elsewhere throughout Scripture, it is undoubtedly canonical.

units.la: Amen. Hæc vox est quasi orationis signaculum & velut ratificatio, quâ testamur nos non perfunctoriè eà, quæ explicata sunt, flagitare.
units.tr: Amen. This word is, as it were, the seal of the prayer and its ratification, by which we testify that we do not ask for the things explained here in a perfunctory way.

units.la: 14. Si enim dimiseritis &c. Non dixit: Vade in Orientem, & quære justitiam; naviga usque ad Occidentem, ut accipias indulgentiam. Dimitte inimico tuo, & dimittetur tibi: indulge & induigebitur tibi: da & dabitur tibi: nihil à te extra te quærit, ad teipsum & ad conscientiam tuam te Deus dirigit. In te enim posuit quod requirit. Non enim medicamenta vulneribus tuis longè longè opus habès inquirere, peccatorum tuorum indulgentiam, si vis, intùs in cellario cordis tui poteris invenire. Autor Ser. 47. de Sanctis apud Aug.
units.tr: 14. For if you forgive, etc. He did not say: Go to the East and seek righteousness; sail as far as the West to obtain forgiveness. Forgive your enemy, and you will be forgiven; be merciful, and mercy will be shown you; give, and it will be given to you. God does not ask you for anything outside yourself; he directs you to yourself and to your own conscience. For he has placed within you what he requires. You do not need to search far and wide for remedies for your wounds; if you wish, you will be able to find the forgiveness of your sins within, in the storehouse of your heart. The author of Sermon 47 on the Saints, among the works of Augustine.

units.la: 16. Cùm jejunatis. Jejunandi religio à Priscis summo studio observabatur, ut videre est tam in novo, quàm in veteri Testamento, atque in adversitatibus veluti ad anchoram, ad jejunium & orationem fe convertebant. Sic Moses suscepturus Legem primus jejunasse legitur, fdquê quadraginta diebus; quod iterum fecit & totidem diebus dum pro peccato populi Israel orabat. Sic Jofaphat ab hostibus circumdatus jejunium indixit: Sic Judith, sicEsther, sic Apostoli, jejunasse leguntur. Unde patet jejunium bonum esse ad salutem medium, & hac de causa à Deo remunerandum Christus asserit, si non fiat more hypocritarum, hoc est, ad venandam gloriam humanam, sed ad castigationem corporis, ne saturitate aut desidiâ exstimuletur ad peccandum, ad externam testificationem internæ pœnitentiæ, & ad ardentiùs Deum invocandum. Ut enim ait Tertul. adversus Psychicos : Multò pollentioris mentis & vivacioris cordis sumus ad hæc spiritualia jejuni, quàm cùm illud domicilium interioris hominis escis stipatur & vinis inundatur.
units.tr: 16. When you fast. The religious practice of fasting was observed with the greatest zeal by the ancients, as can be seen both in the New Testament and in the Old. In adversity they turned to fasting and prayer, as to an anchor. Thus Moses, about to receive the Law, is read to have fasted first, and for forty days; and he did the same again, for the same number of days, while he prayed for the sin of the people of Israel. So too Jehoshaphat, surrounded by enemies, proclaimed a fast; and Judith, Esther and the Apostles are read to have fasted. Hence it is clear that fasting is a good means to salvation, and for this reason Christ affirms that it will be rewarded by God, provided it is not done in the manner of hypocrites, that is, to hunt for human glory, but for the chastening of the body, so that it is not stirred to sin by satiety or idleness, as an outward testimony of inward repentance, and to call upon God more ardently. As Tertullian says in his work against the Psychics: We are of a far more vigorous mind and a more lively heart for these spiritual fasts than when that dwelling of the inner man is crowded with food and flooded with wine.

units.la: Nolite. Id est, ne affestetis.
units.tr: Do not. That is, do not pretend.

units.la: Fieri tristes. Id est, tetrico vultu ostentare jejunium.
units.tr: Become sad. That is, to display the fast with a gloomy countenance.

units.la: Exterminant. Id est, illuvie & squalore fœdant. Gr. Ἀφανίζουσι, id est, deformant; nempe illúvie & squalore fœdi nativam formam quasi è medio tollunt.
units.tr: They disfigure. That is, they defile with dirt and squalor. Greek [Ἀφανίζουσι], that is, they deform: by filth and squalor they as it were remove the native form from view.

units.la: 17. Unge caput, &c. Juxta ritum provinciæ Palæstinæ loquitur: ubi diebus festis solent ungere capita. Præcepit igitur, ut quando jejunamus, lætos & festivos nos esse monstremus. B. Hier. Non itaque ut coma capitis illecebroso redundet unguento serius Magister injungit, nec faciem nitescere soluto vult lavacro, sed habitu prandentis vult celari jejunium Christiano, qui Christianum vindicare, id est, sibi arrogare, non vult artifice mœrore jejunium. Cbrysol. Ser. 7.
units.tr: 17. Anoint your head, etc. He speaks according to the custom of the province of Palestine, where people are accustomed to anoint their heads on festal days. He therefore commands that when we fast we show ourselves cheerful and festive. St Jerome. Therefore the Master does not enjoin, as a later teacher might, that the hair of the head should abound with alluring ointment, nor does he wish the face to shine after a washing with loosened hair; rather he wishes the Christian's fast to be concealed under the appearance of one who dines, for the Christian who does not wish to claim for himself, that is, to arrogate to himself, the fast through a contrived sorrow. Chrysologus, Sermon 7.

units.la: 18. In abscondito. Intùs sunt servanda quæ agimus, si ab interno arbitro vicem recipere nostri operis expectamus. B. Greg. 8. Mor. c. 37.
units.tr: 18. In secret. What we do must be kept within, if we expect to receive our reward from the inner judge. St Gregory, Moralia 8, chapter 37.

units.la: 19. Tinea. Hæc vox videtur deduci à φθεῖρ, quod est, consumi vel tabescere. Est autem tineæ proprium laneas vestes consumere, quæ cùm olim in thesauris fuerint, tinea dicitur hîc thesauros corrumpere.
units.tr: 19. Moth. This word seems to derive from Greek [φθεῖρ], meaning to be consumed or to waste away. It is the proper function of the moth to eat woollen garments; since these were once kept in storehouses, the moth is here said to corrupt treasures.

units.la: 20. In Cœlo. Id est, apud Deum, in firmamento spirituali, quod semper manet, & de quo dictum est: Cœlum cœli Domino. B. August. l. 2. de Serm. Domini in monte. Præcipit itaque Christus ne coelestium thesaurorum oblivisccentes thesauris terrestribus cor apponamus. Ut autem judicare possimus, utrum ordinatus divitiarum amor animum occupet, videndum an tota cordis cogitatio, omnis amor, spes & metus iis apponatur. Ubi enim cujusque est thesaurus, hoc est, ubi est id in quo quisque suam putat sitam felicitatem, ibi & cor ipsius est. Dum itaque homo divitiis non cor apponit, neque iis fidit, sed spem suam ponit in Deum vivum, facile tribuit, & dives est in bonis operibus: hic etsi terrenarum opum thesauros habeat, non tamen dicitur thezaurizare in terra, sed in coelis, ubi cordis affectus est defixus. Ut ergo in cœlis thesaurizemus, cœlestia diligamus. Vis nosse ubi thesaurizas? Attende quid amas. Vis nosse quid ames? Attende quid cogitas. Ita fiet ut thesaurum tuum ex tuo amore cognoscas, & amorem tuum indicio tuæ cogitationis intelligas. B. Fulg. Serm. de Confess.
units.tr: 20. In heaven. That is, with God, in the spiritual firmament, which always remains, and of which it is said: The heaven of heaven is the Lord's. St Augustine, On the Sermon of the Lord on the Mount, book 2. Christ therefore commands that we, forgetting heavenly treasures, not set our heart on earthly ones. But so that we may judge whether an ordered love of riches occupies the mind, we must see whether the whole thought of the heart, all love, hope and fear, is directed to them. For where each man's treasure is, that is, where he thinks his happiness lies, there his heart is also. Therefore, when a man does not set his heart on riches nor trust in them, but places his hope in the living God, he readily gives and is rich in good works; even if he has treasures of earthly wealth, he is not said to store up treasure on earth, but in heaven, where the affection of his heart is fixed. So, then, let us store up treasure in heaven by loving heavenly things. Do you wish to know where you are storing your treasure? Consider what you love. Do you wish to know what you love? Consider what you think about. In this way you will come to know your treasure from your love, and your love from the evidence of your thought. St Fulgentius, Sermon on Confession.

units.la: 22. Lucerna, &c. Q. d. Ut oculus est lucerna corporis, sic intentio est lucerna animæ. Græcè absunt pronomina tui & tuus tam hic, quam Luc. 11. v. 34.
units.tr: 22. The lamp, etc. The sense is: just as the eye is the lamp of the body, so the intention is the lamp of the soul. In the Greek the pronouns your and yours are absent here, as also in Luke 11, verse 34.

units.la: Simplex. Id est, purus, nec ullo infectus vitio.
units.tr: Single. That is, pure, and not tainted by any vice.

units.la: Lucidum erit. Hoc est, erit quasi oculatum, quia singula & omnia corporis membra oculi simplicis luce & directione prævia omnes actiones suas recte obibunt.
units.tr: Will be full of light. That is, it will be as it were full of sight, because each and every member of the body, by the light and direction of a single eye going before, will rightly perform all its actions.

units.la: 23. Nequam. Id est, male affectus.
units.tr: 23. Evil. That is, ill-disposed.

units.la: Tenebrosum erit. Id est, carebit luce sibi necessaria ad rite exercendas actiones suas.
units.tr: Will be full of darkness. That is, it will lack the light necessary for performing its actions properly.

units.la: Quod in tenebris est. Id est, esse debebat. Sic infra c. 8. Filii regni dicuntur, qui filii regni esse debebant. Filii sapientiæ Luc. 7. quos sapientiæ filios esse oportebat, &c.
units.tr: What is in darkness. That is, what ought to be. So below, in chapter 8, those are called sons of the kingdom who ought to be sons of the kingdom; and in Luke 7 sons of wisdom are those who ought to be sons of wisdom, and so on.

units.la: Ipsæ tenebræ quantæ erunt? Q. d. Alia ab oculo corporis membra, quæ naturâ suâ tenebræ sunt, & nullum ex se lumen habent, quantis tenebris obvolventur? Quod de oculo dicitur respectu corporis, id de intentione respectu animæ est dicendum. Namque si ipsa cordis intentio, quæ lumen est animæ, non fuscetur vitii caligine, lucis opera erunt, quæcunque operabitur anima; si autem perversa est intentio, pravum est, quicquid facit anima. Vide Venerabilem Bedam in Luc. vi.
units.tr: How great will that darkness be! The sense is: how great a darkness will envelop the other members of the body, which by their nature are darkness and have no light of their own? What is said of the eye with respect to the body must be said of the intention with respect to the soul. For if the intention of the heart itself, which is the light of the soul, is not clouded by the darkness of vice, then whatever the soul does will be works of light; but if the intention is perverse, then whatever the soul does is wicked. See the Venerable Bede on Luke 6.

units.la: 24. Nemo, &c. Adagiali locutione Christus aliam addit rationem, cur divitiis terrenis non sit cor apponendum, quia scilicet nos à Dei servitute separant.
units.tr: 24. No one, etc. In a proverbial manner of speaking, Christ gives another reason why the heart should not be set on earthly riches: namely, because they separate us from the service of God.

units.la: Duobus dominis. Supple, non subordinatis.
units.tr: Two masters. Understand: not subordinate to one another.

units.la: Aut enim, &c. Sensus est: Aut hunc odio habebit, & illum diliget, aut vice versa illum sustinebit, seu ut fert textus Græcus, illi adhærebit mordicus, scilicet dilectione, & hunc contemnet præ odio nimirum.
units.tr: For either, etc. The sense is: either he will hate the one and love the other, or conversely he will endure the one, or, as the Greek text has it, he will cling to the one tenaciously, namely in love, and will despise the other out of hatred, of course.

units.la: Mammona. Mammona sermone Syriaco divitiæ nuncupantur. Non potestis servire Deo & mammonæ. Audiat hoc avarus, audiat qui censetur vocabulo Christiano, non posse se simul divitiis Christoque servire. Et tamen non dixit, Qui habet divitias: sed, Qui servit divitiis. Qui enim divitiarum servus est, divitias custodit ut servus: qui autem servitutis excussit jugum, distribuit eas ut Dominus. B. Hier.
units.tr: Mammon. In the Syriac language riches are called mammon. You cannot serve God and mammon. Let the covetous man hear this; let him hear who is called by the Christian name that he cannot serve both riches and Christ at the same time. And yet he did not say: He who has riches; but: He who serves riches. For he who is a servant of riches guards them as a servant does; but he who has shaken off the yoke of servitude distributes them as a lord does. St Jerome.

units.la: Solliciti. Sollicitudo importat studium quod iam adhibitum ad aliquid consequendum; unde eo major est sollicitudo, quo major est timor deficiendi; eo minor, quo major securitas consequendi. Sic ergo sollicitudo temporalium rerum tripliciter potest esse illicita: primo si temporalia tanquam finem quæramus; secundo si superfluum studium adhibeamus ad temporalia procuranda, ita ut mens a debita spiritualium officiorum functione avocetur, vel superflue sollicitudo præoccupet tempus futurum; tertio denique si nimia fit sollicitudo, ita ut homo metuat ne faciendo quod debet, necessaria sibi deficiant; quam nimiam sollicitudinem Christus hic prohibet. Primo propter majora beneficia homini præstita divinitus præter suam sollicitudinem. Secundo propter subventionem, qui Deus animalibus & plantis homine longe vilioribus subvenit. Aves sine patrimonio vivunt, & in diem pecua pascuntur: & hæc nobis tamen nata sunt: quæ omnia, si non concupiscimus, possidemus, inquit Minutius Felix. Tertio propter divinam providentiam, ob cujus ignorantiam Gentiles circa temporalia bona quærenda principalius sollicitantur. Et ideo concludit quod nostra sollicitudo principaliter esse debet de spiritualibus bonis; sperantes quod etiam temporalia nobis provenient ad necessitatem, si fecerimus quod debemus. D. Th. 22æ. q. 55. ar. 6.
units.tr: Solliciti. Anxiety implies an eager effort already applied to obtain something. The more we fear falling short, the greater the anxiety; the more confident we are of obtaining what we want, the less it is. So anxiety about temporal things can be unlawful in three ways. First, if we seek temporal things as our end. Second, if we apply excessive zeal to procuring them, so that the mind is drawn away from the proper performance of spiritual duties, or anxiety anticipates the future uselessly. Third, and finally, if the anxiety becomes excessive, so that a person fears that, by doing what he ought, he will lack what is necessary; it is this excessive anxiety that Christ forbids here. Christ gives two grounds for this. First, God has bestowed on man greater benefits, apart from his own anxiety. Second, God provides for the needs of animals and plants, which are far inferior to man. Birds live without any inheritance, and the flocks are fed day by day; yet these things were born for us, and if we do not covet them, we possess them all, says Minucius Felix. Third, on account of divine providence, through ignorance of which the Gentiles are chiefly anxious about seeking temporal goods. And so he concludes that our anxiety should be chiefly about spiritual goods, hoping that temporal things will also come to us as we need them, if we do what we ought. Thomas, 2a2ae, q. 55, art. 6.

units.la: Nonne anima, &c. d. Nonne vita potior est, quam id quo vita alitur? Argumentatur Christus à majori ad minus. q. d. Deus dedit vobis majora, scilicet vitam & corpus, ergo dabit & minora, nempe cibum quo vita sustentetur, & vestimentum quo corpus tegatur. Qui ergo esuriam aut vestimentum pauperibus largitur, sed tamen animæ vel corporis iniquitate pollitur, quod minus est, justitiæ obtulit, & quod majus est, culpæ commisit; sua enim Deo dedit, se diabolo. Greg. Palt. 3. p. admon. 21.
units.tr: Nonne anima, &c. Is not life more excellent than that by which life is sustained? Christ argues from the greater to the less. As if to say: God has given you the greater things, namely life and body; therefore he will also give the lesser, namely food by which life is sustained and clothing by which the body is covered. Whoever gives alms of food or clothing to the poor, yet is himself defiled by iniquity of soul or body, has offered the lesser to justice, but has committed the greater to sin; for he has given his possessions to God, but himself to the devil. Gregory of Palthen, 3rd admonition, p. 21.

units.la: Nonne vos magis pluris estis illis? Græcè, πόλλῳ διαφέρετε; Comparativus μᾶλλον verbo διαφέρειν (cui et ipsa
units.tr: Nonne vos magis pluris estis illis? In Greek, pollō diapherete [πόλλῳ διαφέρετε]. The comparative mallon [μᾶλλον], joined with the verb diapherein [διαφέρειν] (in which the force of the comparative is also present), indicates the man's remarkable excellence

units.la: {y} Greek and Latin marginal reference as printed above. vis comparativi inest) conjunctus, insignem hominis præ- avibus, atque parili ratione præ ceteris animantibus ex- cellentiam indigitat, ut pote qui solus inter omnia animan- tia in corpore mortali animam sortitus est immorta- lem.
units.tr: {y} Greek and Latin marginal reference as printed above. over the birds, and by the same reasoning over the other living creatures, since he alone among all living beings has received an immortal soul in a mortal body.

units.la: 27. Cogitans. Supple, sollicitè, ut patet ex textu Græco. Est autem sollicitudo ex Cic. Tusc. 4. Ægritudo animi cum cogitatione.
units.tr: 27. Cogitans. Supply "anxiously", as is clear from the Greek text. Anxiety is, according to Cicero, Tusculan Disputations 4, a distress of the mind together with thought.

units.la: Cubitum unum. Id est, vel minimam partem; ponitur enim mensura definita pro quavis mensura, juxta vulgarem loquendi modum. Hanc argumentationem perficit B. Lucas 12. v. 26. Si ergo neque quod minimum est potestis, de ceteris quid solliciti estis ? Q. d. Cùm id quod minimum est, scilicet adjicere ad staturam suam cubitum unum, vestra anxietate non potestis, multò minùs totius vitæ conservationem præstabit vobis vestra sollicitudo.
units.tr: Cubitum unum. That is, even the smallest part; a fixed measure is put for any measure, according to ordinary usage. Saint Luke 12:26 completes this argument: If then you are not able even to do what is least, why are you anxious about the rest? As if to say: since you cannot, by your anxiety, do even what is least, namely add one cubit to your stature, much less will your anxiety secure the preservation of your whole life.

units.la: 28. Lilia agri. In Judæa & Syria lilia non coli in hortis, ut apud nos, sed in agris passim occurrere observavimus in Commentario nostro in Canticum Canticorum cap. 4. v. 5.
units.tr: 28. Lilia agri. We have observed in our commentary on the Song of Songs, chapter 4, verse 5, that in Judaea and Syria lilies are not cultivated in gardens, as with us, but occur everywhere in the fields.

units.la: 29. In omni gloria sua. Id est, in omni vestitu & amictu suo glorioso. Sic Ps. 44. Omnis gloria filiæ Regis, id est, vestis vel amictus gloriosus. Esth. 15. v. 4. Circumdata est gloriâ suâ: id est, veste gloriosâ & honoratâ.
units.tr: 29. In omni gloria sua. That is, in all his glorious clothing and attire. So Psalm 44: All the glory of the king's daughter, that is, glorious clothing or attire. Esther 15:4: She was clothed in her glory, that is, in glorious and honourable clothing.

units.la: 30. Si autem fænum agri, &c. Hinc patet non solùm totam istam mundi partem rebus mortalibus & corruptibilibus deputatam, verùm etiam viliffimas ejus, abjectasque particulas divinâ regi providentiâ.
units.tr: 30. Si autem fænum agri, etc. From this it is clear that not only this whole part of the world, assigned to mortal and corruptible things, but even its most worthless and abject particles, are governed by divine providence.

units.la: Modicæ fidei. Id est, ô homines modicæ fidei; est enim increpatio modesta, quâ Christus excitat auditores suos ad dictorum perfuasionem.
units.tr: Modicæ fidei. That is, O men of little faith; for this is a gentle rebuke, by which Christ stirs his hearers to be persuaded of what he has said.

units.la: 33. Primùm. Id est, præcipuè & propter se.
units.tr: 33. Primùm. That is, chiefly and for its own sake.

units.la: Regnum Dei. Id est, beatitudinem.
units.tr: Regnum Dei. That is, blessedness.

units.la: Justitiam ejus. Scilicet Dei, Græcè enim est masculinum ἀυτῆ. Vocatur autem Dei justitia, quam ipsius gratiâ consequimur, quæque via est, quâ pervenitur ad beatitudinem.
units.tr: Justitiam ejus. That is, of God; for in Greek the word is masculine, autēn. His righteousness is so called because we obtain it by his grace, and it is the way by which blessedness is reached.

units.la: Hæc omnia. Nempe, temporalia.
units.tr: Hæc omnia. Namely, temporal things.

units.la: Adjicientur. Supple, si ita expediat; Quandoquidem temporalia sicut adjutoria medicus ille, cui nos totos committimus, novit quando apponat & quando detrahat, sicut nobis judicat expedire, quos consolandos & exercendos in hac vita, & post hanc vitam in perpetua requie stabiliendos atque firmandos gubernat ac dirigit. Non enim & homo, cùm plerumque jumento suo cibaria detrahit, deserit illud curâ suâ, ac non potiùs curando hæc facit. Aug. l. 2. de Serm. Domini in monte c. 17.
units.tr: Adjicientur. Supply: if it is expedient. Since that physician, to whom we commit ourselves entirely, knows temporal things as helps, and knows when to apply them and when to withdraw them, as he judges to be expedient for us; he guides and directs those whom he wishes to comfort and exercise in this life, and to establish and strengthen in perpetual rest after this life. For a man, when he often withdraws food from his beast of burden, does not abandon it to neglect, but rather does this out of care. Augustine, On the Sermon on the Mount, book 2, chapter 17.

units.la: 34. Nolite, &c. Q. d. Nolite tempus sollicitudinis præoccupare; unicuique enim tempori propria competit sollicitudo.
units.tr: 34. Nolite, &c. As if to say: do not anticipate the time of anxiety; for each time has its own proper anxiety.

units.la: In crastinum. Crastinum in Scripturis sanctis futurum tempus significat, sicut & Jacob in Genesi loquitur: Exaudiet me cras justitia mea. Qui ergo de futuris nos cogitare prohibuit, concessit de præsentibus propter humanæ vitæ fragilitatem. B. Hier. in Ep. 147. ad Amandum.
units.tr: In crastinum. In the holy Scriptures, "tomorrow" signifies future time, as Jacob also speaks in Genesis: "My righteousness will answer for me tomorrow." He who forbade us to think about the future has permitted us to think about the present, on account of the frailty of human life. Jerome, Letter 147 to Amandus.

units.la: Sollicitus erit sibi ipsi. Id est, suam propriam follicitudinem habebit, quæ sufficiet ad animum affligendum. Præsentis versiculi sententiam aliis verbis protulit Apostolus, in Ep. ad Hebræos. c. 13. v. 5. Sint mores sine avaritia, contenti præsentibus: ipse enim dixit, Non te deseram, neque derelinquam.
units.tr: Sollicitus erit sibi ipsi. That is, he will have his own anxiety, which will be enough to afflict the mind. The Apostle expressed the sense of this little verse in other words, in Hebrews 13:5: Let your manners be without covetousness, content with what you have; for he himself has said, I will never leave you nor forsake you.

units.la: Sufficit diei malitia sua. Id est, secundum. Hier. loco mox laudato, sufficit nobis de præsentibus hujus seculi cogitare angustiis. Quid necesse est sensum ad incerta & futura extendere, quæ aut consequi non possimus, aut cito inventa perdamus? Κακία enim, quam Latinus vertit in malitiam, apud Græcos duo significat, & malitiam & afflictionem, quam κάκωσιν Græci dicunt, & hic magis pro malitia transferri debuit afflictio. Quod si contentiose quis ducitur, volens κακίαν afflictionem sonare & angustias, sed malitiam; illo sensu explicandum est, quo mundus in maligno. hoc est, in malo positus dicitur, & in Dominica oratione dicimus: Libera nos a malo; ut sufficiat nobis contra malitiam hujus seculi præsens habere certamen.
units.tr: Sufficit diei malitia sua. That is, in the same sense. Jerome, in the passage just cited: It is enough for us to think about the present troubles of this age. What need is there to extend our mind to uncertain and future things, which we either cannot attain, or, once found, quickly lose? For the Greek word kakia [κακία], which the Latin renders as malice, signifies two things among the Greeks: malice and affliction, which the Greeks call kakōsin [κάκωσιν]; and here affliction ought to have been translated rather than malice. But if someone, contentiously, insists that kakia should mean affliction and troubles, and not malice, it must be explained in the sense in which the world is said to be in evil, that is, placed in evil, and in the Lord's Prayer we say: Deliver us from evil; so that it is enough for us to have the present struggle against the malice of this age.

units.la: CAPUT.
units.tr: CHAPTER.

units.la: CAPUT VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: 1. Nolite judicare. Supple temerè & immisericorditer. Hoc loco nihil aliud nobis præcipi existimo, nisi ut ea facta, quæ dubium est quo animo fiant, in meliorem partem interpretemur; quod enim scriptum est: A fructibus eorum cognoscetis eos: de manifestis dictum est, quæ non possunt bono modo fieri. Sunt quædam facta media, quæ ignoramus quo animo fiant, quia in bono & malo fieri possunt, de quibus temerarium judicare, maxime ut condemnemus. Duo autem sunt, in quibus temerarium judicium cavere debemus, cùm incertum est quo animo quidque factum sit, vel qualis quisque futurus sit, qui nunc bonus vel malus apparet. Non ergo reprehendamus ea, quæ nec scimus quo animo fiant, neque ita reprehendamus quæ manifesta sunt, ut defferemus sanitatem. Aug. lib. 2. de Serm. Domini in monte c. 23. Optimum hac in re consilium sancti Bernardi Serm. 4. in Cant. Cave alienæ conversationis esse aut curiosus explorator, aut temerarius judex; etiamsi perperam actum quid deprehendas, nec sic judices proximum: magis autem excusa. Excusa intentionem, si opus non potes, puta ignorantiam, puta subreptionem, puta casum. Quod si omnem dissimulationem rei certitudo recusat; suade nihilominus ipse tibi, & dicito apud temetipsum: Vehemens fuit nimis tentatio: quid de me illa fecisset, si in me accepisset similiter potestatem.
units.tr: 1. Judge not. Supply: rashly and without mercy. In this place I think nothing else is enjoined on us than that we should interpret in the better sense those deeds whose intention is doubtful. For what is written, "By their fruits you shall know them," was said of manifest things, which cannot be done in a good way. There are certain intermediate deeds whose intention we do not know, because they can be done with good or bad intent, and it is rash to judge them, especially to condemn them. There are two cases in which we must guard against rash judgment: when it is uncertain with what intention something was done, or what sort of person someone who now appears good or bad will turn out to be. So we should not blame those things whose intention we do not know, nor should we blame manifest things so harshly that we lose soundness of judgment. Augustine, On the Sermon on the Mount, book 2, ch. 23. The best counsel of St Bernard on this matter is in Sermon 4 on the Song of Songs: Take care not to be either a curious spy or a rash judge of another's conduct. Even if you perceive that something has been done amiss, do not judge your neighbour so; rather make excuses for him. Excuse his intention, if you cannot excuse the deed: suppose ignorance, suppose surprise, suppose chance. But if certainty of the fact rules out every pretence, still persuade yourself and say within yourself: the temptation was very strong; what would it have done to me, if it had received similar power over me?

units.la: Ut non judicemini. Q. d. Ne in severissimum Dei judicium incidatis.
units.tr: That you be not judged. That is, lest you fall into the most severe judgment of God.

units.la: 2, In quo enim, &c. Q. d. Eò severius vel benigniùs à Deo judicabimini, quò severius vel benigniùs alios judicaveritis. Hoc Christus significavit duplici præsentis versiculi adagio.
units.tr: 2. For with what judgment, etc. That is: the more severely or the more kindly you have judged others, the more severely or kindly you will be judged by God. Christ signified this by the double proverb of this little verse.

units.la: 3. Quid autem, &c. Adagiali locutione redarguit eos Christus, quicquam ipsi mortali crimine teneantur obnoxii, minora peccata fratribus non concedunt, ut loquitur Hier. Hoc hominum genus simili schemate perstringit Horatius, cùm dicit i Serm. Sat. 3. Cùm tua pervideas oculis mala lippus inunctis, Cur in amicorum vitiis tam cernis acutum, Quàm aut aquila, aut serpens Epidaurius?
units.tr: 3. And why, etc. Christ rebukes them with a proverbial saying: while they themselves are bound by mortal guilt, they do not grant lesser sins to their brothers, as Jerome puts it. Horace also lashes this kind of man with a similar figure when he says in Satire 1.3: "While you, bleary-eyed, with eyes smeared with ointment, see your own evils, why do you see so sharply the faults of your friends, as keenly as an eagle or the serpent of Epidaurus?"

units.la: 4. Quomodo. Id est, quà fronte.
units.tr: 4. How. That is, with what face.

units.la: 5. Hypocrita. Accusare vitia officium est bonorum, quod cùm mali faciunt, alienas partes agunt, sicut hypocritæ, qui tegunt sub persona quod sunt, & ostendunt in persona quod non sunt. Aug. lib. 2. de Serm. Domini in monte c. 3.
units.tr: 5. Hypocrite. To accuse vices is the duty of good people; when the wicked do it, they play another's part, like hypocrites, who hide under a mask what they are, and show under the mask what they are not. Augustine, On the Sermon on the Mount, book 2, ch. 3.

units.la: Videbis et icere. Id est, perspicies ut educas, quomodo loquitur B. Lucas c. 6. v. 42.
units.tr: You will see to cast out. That is, you will look carefully so that you may draw out, as Blessed Luke speaks in ch. 6, v. 42.

units.la: 6. Nolite,&c. Docet Christus duplici adagio divina mysteria non esse tradenda eorum contemtoribus & oppugnatoribus. Eadem itaque divina mysteria vocat, Sanctum, quia divina sunt, quæ non debent corrumpi; margaritas vero quia pretiosa, quæ non debent contemni.
units.tr: 6. Do not, etc. Christ teaches, by a double proverb, that divine mysteries are not to be handed over to their despisers and opponents. So he calls the same divine mysteries holy, because they are divine and must not be corrupted; and pearls, because they are precious and must not be despised.

units.la: Canibus. Id est, veritatis oppugnatoribus per rebellem obla-trationem.
units.tr: To dogs. That is, to opponents of the truth, by rebellious barking.

units.la: Ne forte. Græcè, ne quando.
units.tr: Lest perhaps. In Greek: lest at any time.

units.la: Conculcent, &c. Id quidem apris convenit potiùs, quàm porcis domesticis, tamen etiam à suibus homines quandoque lacerari Veteres scribunt. Plin. lib. 10. c. 67. Fœminæ suffantes in tantum efferuntur, ut hominem lacerent, maximè candidâ veste indutum. Et de Belgarum suibus hæc tradit Strabo lib. 4. [Greek text omitted] Sues etiam in agris pernoctant, proceritate, robore & celeritate præstantes, ad quas nemo insuetus, nisi cum periculo accedit; ut neque lupus. Quod autem Dominus quædam dixisse invenitur, quæ multi, qui audierant, vel resistendo, vel contemnendo non receperunt, non putandus est Sanctum dedisse canibus, aut Margaritas ante porcos misisse. Dedit enim eis, qui capere poterant, & simul aderant, quos propter aliorum immunditiam negligi non oportebat. Aug. lib. 2. de Sermone Domini in monte c. 22.
units.tr: Trample them, etc. This fits boars rather than domestic pigs, yet the ancient writers record that men are sometimes torn by swine too. Pliny, book 10, ch. 67: Sows, when they snort, are so excited that they tear a man, especially one dressed in white. And Strabo, book 4, writes this about the swine of the Belgae: [Greek text omitted] The swine also spend the night in the fields, outstanding in size, strength and speed; no one unaccustomed to them approaches without danger, nor even a wolf. But that the Lord is found to have said certain things which many who heard them did not receive, either by resisting or by despising, should not be thought to mean that he gave what is holy to dogs or cast pearls before swine. For he gave them to those who could take them in and were present, and who ought not to be neglected because of the uncleanness of others. Augustine, On the Sermon on the Mount, book 2, ch. 22.

units.la: 7. Petite, &c. Operosè, inquit Aug. lib. 1. retract. c. 16. ista tria: Petite, quærite, pulsate: quid inter se differant, exponendum putavi; sed longè melius ad instantissimam petitionem omnia referuntur. Unde Dominus concludit dicens: Dabit bona petentibus se: & non addit: Quærentibus & pulsantibus.
units.tr: 7. Ask, etc. "Diligently," says Augustine, Retractions book 1, ch. 16, "I thought I should explain these three: Ask, seek, knock, and how they differ from one another; but it is far better to refer all of them to the most urgent asking. Hence the Lord concludes, saying: He will give good things to those who ask him; and he does not add: to those who seek and knock."

units.la: 8. Qui petit, accipit. Scilicet si bona spiritualia petat nihil haec tamen. Imo & temporalia, nisi eorum privatio nobis convenientior sit ad salutem. Fatendum igitur secundum Salvatoris sententiam gratiam dari petentibus, quærentibus, pulsantibus; sed cum Augustino in lib. De bono perseverantiæ c. 23. agnoscendum est etiam hoc divini muneris esse, ut petimus, hoc est, petamus, quæramus atque pulsemus; accipimus enim Spiritum adoptionis filiorum, in quo clamamus, Abba Pater. Quod vividit Beatus Ambrosius; ait enim, Et orare Deum gratiæ spiritualis est, sicut scriptum est : Nemo dicit Dominus Iesus, nisi in Spiritu Sancto. Præclarè itaque S. Bernardus in libello de gratia & libero arbitrio : Liberi arbitrii conatus ad bonum cassum, non adjuvantur, & nulli, si non excitentur.
units.tr: 8. Whoever asks, receives. Namely, if he asks for spiritual goods; nothing of this kind, however, is denied; indeed also temporal goods, unless their privation is more fitting for us for salvation. It must therefore be confessed, according to the Saviour's saying, that grace is given to those who ask, seek and knock; but with Augustine, in the book On the Gift of Perseverance ch. 23, it must be acknowledged that this too is a gift of God, that we ask, that is, that we ask, seek and knock; for we receive the Spirit of the adoption of sons, in whom we cry, Abba, Father. Blessed Ambrose also saw this; for he says: "To pray to God is also a gift of spiritual grace, as it is written: No one says, Lord Jesus, except in the Holy Spirit." So admirably St Bernard in his little book On Grace and Free Choice: The efforts of free choice towards good are in vain, and they are not helped, and no one is helped unless he is stirred up.

units.la: Accipit. Aliquando tardiùs, ne citò data vilescant & contemnantur.
units.tr: Receives. Sometimes more slowly, lest what is given quickly become cheap and despised.

units.la: 9. Aut quis homo. Græcè, an quis homo, supple, quamvis immitis & malus.
units.tr: 9. Or what man. In Greek: or what man, supply: however harsh and evil he may be.

units.la: 11. Cum sitis mali. Scilicet, tum naturali proclivitate in malum, quam contraxistis ex natura per peccatum corrupta, tum propria voluntate & vivendi ratione.
units.tr: 11. Since you are evil. Namely, both by the natural inclination to evil which you contracted from nature corrupted through sin, and by your own will and manner of living.

units.la: Nostis. Id est, consueviستis.
units.tr: You know. That is, you were accustomed.

units.la: 12. Omnia ergo. Incipit Epilogus & compendium omnium, quæ ab initio capitis quinti hucusque sunt à Christo præcepta.
units.tr: 12. Therefore all things. Here begins the epilogue and summary of all the things that Christ has commanded from the beginning of chapter five until now.

units.la: Quæcunque vultis. Id est, desideratis voluntate non libidine, atque ita significanter dicit vultis; nam inter voluntatem & libidinem hoc interest secundum Cic. 4. Tusc. Volantas cum ratione desiderat; quæ autem ratione adversi incitata est, ea libido est vel cupiditas effrenata. Ergo desiderium in bono voluntas dicitur, desiderium in malo libido vocatur. Hieronymus Ep. 14. ad Celantiam ait, Quasi compendiosum quoddam commonitorium illa tibi Evangelii electa sententia est, & superscribenda cordi tuo, quæ ad totius juxta breviarium dominico ore proferetur : Omnia quæcunque vultis ut vobis faciant homines, ita & vos facite illis : cujus præcepti vires exprimens jungit, Hoc enim Lex et Prophetæ. Ad omnem actum, verbum, cogitatum hæc sententia retractetur. Quæ tibi quasi speculum quoddam paratum, & ad manum semper positum, qualitatem tuæ voluntatis ostendat, ac etiam, vel de injusto opere redarguat, vel de justo lætificet.
units.tr: Whatever you wish. That is, whatever you desire with the will, not with lust; and so he says significantly wish. For between will and lust there is this difference, according to Cicero, Tusculan Disputations book 4: the will desires with reason; but what is stirred up against reason is lust or unbridled desire. So desire for good is called will, desire for evil is called lust. Jerome, Letter 14 to Celantia, says: That chosen saying of the Gospel is, as it were, a short reminder for you, and it should be written on your heart; it is the summary that is spoken by the Lord's mouth: Whatever you wish that men should do to you, do so to them as well.
