Stating the force of this precept, he adds: For this is the Law and the Prophets. This saying should be applied to every deed, word and thought. Let it be to you like a mirror, prepared and always set at hand, showing the quality of your will, and either rebuking you for an unjust work or gladdening you over a just one.

units.la: Hoc est enim, &c. Q. d. Dilectio proximi propter Deum, est summa omnium quæ in Lege Mosis & Prophetis præcipiuntur. Qui enim proximum propter Deum diligit, Deum magis diligit, proinde habet charitatem, quæ est finis omnis præcepti. Etenim omne præceptum est morale, vel ceremoniale, vel judiciale; ceremoniale ad dilectionem Dei, judiciale ad dilectionem proximi spectat; morale quoddam spectat ad dilectionem Dei, ut tria prima præcepta Decalogi : quoddam ad dilectionem proximi, ut præcepta secundæ tabulæ, seu, septem postrema Decalogi præcepta. Cùm ergo utrumque præceptum charitatis, scilicet præceptum de diligendo Deo, & præceptum de diligendo proximo, no, ita fit, ut neutrum sine altero possit impleri, quod Dominus dicit infra capite 22. In his duobus mandatis universa Lex pendet & Prophetæ : potest indiscriminatim vel de his simul sumtis, vel de utrolibet seorsim sumto intelligi.
units.tr: For this is, etc. That is: love of neighbour for God's sake is the sum of all that is commanded in the Law of Moses and the Prophets. For whoever loves his neighbour for God's sake loves God more, and so has the charity which is the end of every command. For every command is either moral, or ceremonial, or judicial. The ceremonial concerns love of God, the judicial concerns love of neighbour; the moral concerns partly love of God, as the first three commandments of the Decalogue, and partly love of neighbour, as the commandments of the second table, or the last seven commandments of the Decalogue. Since each of the two commandments of charity, namely the command to love God and the command to love neighbour, is so bound together that neither can be fulfilled without the other, as the Lord says below in chapter 22: "On these two commandments hang all the Law and the Prophets," it can be understood indiscriminately either of these two taken together, or of either one taken separately.

units.la: 13. Intrate. Id est, contendite intrare, ut loquitur B. Lucas, c. 13. v. 24.
units.tr: 13. Enter ye. That is, strive to enter, as St. Luke puts it, ch. 13, v. 24.

units.la: Per angustam portam. Per portam & viam intelligitur vivendi ratio, quæ si fit secundum Evangelium, arcta & angusta dicitur, quia unica est & ita terminis charitatis circumscripta, ut ne quidem latum unguem ad dexteram vel sinistram fas sit deflectere, ut ulli cupiditati fiat satis; unde & hæc via difficilis est incessu propter pronitatem naturæ corruptæ in carnalia, à quibus difficile refrenatur. Iam qui polt suas concupiscentias eunt & vivunt secundum carnem, dicuntur intrare per latam portam & spatiosam viam, quia in hanc vivendi rationem prona est natura corrupta & per diversissima vitiorum genera, sive per excessum, sive per defectum hæc via initur, multisque & alte impressis conspicitur calcata vestigiis.
units.tr: By the narrow gate. The gate and the way here mean a manner of living. If it follows the Gospel, it is called narrow and strait, because it is single and so bounded by the limits of charity that it is not lawful to turn aside even a little to the right or the left in order to satisfy any lust. For this reason the way is also hard to walk, because of the proneness of corrupt nature toward the fleshly things, from which it is hard to restrain oneself. Those who go after their own lusts and live according to the flesh are said to enter by the broad gate and the wide way, because corrupt nature inclines to this manner of living, and this way is entered by very diverse kinds of vice, whether by excess or by defect. It is seen trodden by many footprints, deeply impressed.

units.la: 14. Quam angusta Græcè, quoniam angusta.
units.tr: 14. How narrow: in Greek, because narrow.

units.la: Arcta via est, &c. Sed quod angusto initio incipitur, processu temporis ineffabili dilectionis dulcedine dilatatur; omnia sæva & immania, prorsus facilia & prope nulla efficit amor. Quæ dura sunt laborantibus, eisdem ipsis mitescunt amantibus, qui nec sentiunt quod laborant, & tunc plus ab eis laboratur, quando à labore prohibentur. Hinc dictum est : Iugum meum suave & onus meum leve : Præcepta ejus gravia non sunt : ut cui gravia sunt, consideret divinitus dici non potuisse, gravia non sunt, nisi quia potest esse cordis affectus, cui gravia non sunt, & petat quo destituitur, & impleat quod jubetur. Omnia fiunt facilia charitati, cui uni sarcina Christi levis est, aut ea una est sarcina ipsa, quæ levis est.
units.tr: The way is narrow, etc. But what is begun in a narrow beginning is, as time goes on, widened by the unspeakable sweetness of love. Love makes all harsh and monstrous things altogether easy and nearly nothing. Things that are hard for those who labour become gentle to those who love, who do not feel that they labour; and they labour more when they are kept from labour. Hence it is said: My yoke is easy and my burden light; his commandments are not grievous. Let anyone for whom they are grievous consider that God could not have said they are not grievous unless there can be a disposition of heart for which they are not grievous, and that it seeks what it lacks and fulfils what is commanded. Everything becomes easy for charity, to which alone Christ's burden is light, or the one burden that is light is itself charity.

units.la: 15. Attendite. Cùm dixisset Dominus paucos esse, qui inveniant angustam portam & arctam viam, ne Hæretici, qui se plerumque paucitate commendant, se hic supponant significatos nomine paucitatis, monet Christus ut quærentes viam quæ ducit ad vitam, ab his diligenter caveamus.
units.tr: 15. Beware. When the Lord had said that few are those who find the narrow gate and the strait way, lest the heretics, who commonly commend themselves by their fewness, should place themselves here as signified by the name of fewness, Christ warns us to be diligently on guard against them as we seek the way that leads to life.

units.la: A falsis Prophetis. Id est, à seductoribus, qui veritatem refutantes inducunt verba falsa, interpretatores mali eorum, quæ bene dicta sunt, similia quidem nobis loquentes, dissimilia vero sentientes, ut ait B. Iren. in præfatione operis sui
units.tr: Beware of false prophets. That is, of seducers, who, refuting the truth, bring in false words, interpreting badly what has been well said, speaking to us things that are like, but thinking things that are unlike, as St. Irenaeus says in the preface to his work.

units.la: Veniunt. Supple, nullum mandatum habentes prædicandi quæ docent. ii vestimentis ovium. Q2 d. Manente luporum feroci, deponunt lupinam speciem, se mansuetudinis simulatione & verborum blanditiis veluti quibusdam velleribus obvolvunt, ut cum quisque lanarum mollitiem praesenserit, nequaquam dentium aculeos pertimescat. Dicuntur autem vestimenta ovium uno verbo μηλωτή, quibus amiciebantur vulgo Prophetæ, ut de Elia legitur 3 Reg. 19. v. 13. & de Elisæo in textu Græco 4 Reg. 2. v. 13. ubi Vulgatus habet, pallium. Itaque in Christi verbis est duplex allusio, una ad Prophetarum vestes, quas imitabantur falsi Doctores, ut pro veris haberentur: altera ad ovium mansuetudinem, quam externa specie mentiebantur, cum revera essent lupis rapaciores; nam ut lupus toti gregi, ita toti Ecclesiæ falsus Doctor insidiatur, atque ut lupus inhiat ovium vitæ & sanguini, ita ille animabus, quas sanguine suo redemit Christus. Vide Ezech. 13. v. 18. Ut illum taceam vero pastori esse tam similem, quàm lupum cani, & quomodo per noctis tenebras grassatur lupus, & dum pastores dormiunt, gregem invadit, ita eum invadere Christi Ecclesiam, cum Pastorum negligentia ignorantiæ tenebræ ingruentes videntur grassanti malo latam fenestram aperire.
units.tr: They come. Supply: having no commission to preach what they teach. In sheep's clothing. Their ferocity remains that of wolves, but they put off the wolfish appearance and wrap themselves, as in certain fleeces, in a pretence of gentleness and the flattery of words, so that whoever perceives the softness of the wool should not at all fear the sting of the teeth. The garments of sheep are named in one word melōtē [μηλωτή], the sheepskins in which the prophets were commonly clothed, as is read of Elijah, 3 Kings 19, v. 13, and of Elisha in the Greek text, 4 Kings 2, v. 13, where the Vulgate has pallium (mantle). So there is a double allusion in Christ's words: one to the garments of the prophets, which false teachers imitated so that they might be held to be true; the other to the gentleness of sheep, which they feigned in outward show while in truth they were more rapacious than wolves. For as the wolf lies in wait for the whole flock, so the false teacher lies in wait for the whole Church, and as the wolf thirsts for the life and blood of the sheep, so he does for the souls that Christ redeemed with his own blood. See Ezek. 13, v. 18. Not to mention that the true minister is as like the wolf as a dog is to a wolf, and how the wolf prowls through the darkness of night and, while the shepherds sleep, attacks the flock, so the Church of Christ is attacked when, through the negligence of the ministers, the darkness of ignorance seems to press in and open a wide window for the prowling evil.

units.la: 16. A fructibus. Id est, ab operibus ipsorum doctrinam naturaliter consequentibus; simulatio enim, folia sunt, opera fructus; non autem arbor dignoscitur an bona vel mala sit ex foliis, sed ex fructibus.
units.tr: 16. By their fruits. That is, by their works, which naturally follow their doctrine. For pretence is the leaves, works are the fruit; and a tree is known to be good or bad not by its leaves but by its fruits.

units.la: Cognoscetis eos. Supple, infallibiliter: si enim ex doctrina alicujus sequitur, ut ipsi assentientes supercertent semel traditæ Sanctis fidei & in firma Scripturarum basi fundati nullis Novatorum dolis dimoveantur, doctrina illa bona est; sin vero natum sit sequi oppositum, ut nempe non adoretur Scripturæ plenitudo, & doctrina aliqua præter vel extra Scripturam tanquam ad salutem necessaria suscipiatur, certum est eos, quia talia docent nequaquam divino instinctu, sed proprio corde vaticinari, Dei Spiritum relinquentes, sequi spiritum suum, & propter fraudulentiam ac nequitiam vulpium similes decipere incautos simplicesque, & depopulari vineam Domini Dei Sabaoth, quæ est sancta Dei Ecclesia. Fructus, inquit autor operis impersecti apud Chrysost. Hom. 19. in Mat. 7. hominis est consessio fidei ejus, & opera conversationis ipsius. Si ergo videris hominem Christianum, tatim considera, si confessio ejus convenit cum Scripturis, verus est Christianus. Si autem non est, quemadmodum Christus mandavit, falsus est. Nihil reliquisse aut reticuisse Scripturam eorum quæ nobis conducibilia essent, vir videre est diuersis verbis apud Chrysost. Serm. de Pseudo-Prophetis, & falsis doctoribus. Traditio seu ecclesiae testimonium & ratio instrumenta fidei esse possunt, non fundamenta; sicut nec sensus.
units.tr: You shall know them. Supply: infallibly. For if from someone's doctrine it follows that those who assent to it contend earnestly for the faith once delivered to the saints, and, being founded on the firm base of the Scriptures, are not moved by any tricks of the innovators, then that doctrine is good. But if, on the contrary, it naturally follows that the fullness of Scripture is not adored, and that some doctrine beyond or outside Scripture is received as necessary to salvation, it is certain that they, because they teach such things, do not prophesy by divine impulse but from their own heart; leaving the Spirit of God, they follow their own spirit, and by the craftiness and wickedness of foxes they deceive the unwary and simple, and despoil the vineyard of the Lord God of Hosts, which is the holy Church of God. "The fruit," says the author of the unfinished work cited in Chrysostom, Homily 19 on Matthew 7, "of a man is the confession of his faith and the works of his conduct. So if you see a Christian man, consider at once whether his confession agrees with the Scriptures; if it does, he is a true Christian. But if it does not, as Christ commanded, he is false." That the Scripture has left out or passed over nothing that would be useful to us, one may see in various words in Chrysostom's sermon on false prophets and false teachers. Tradition, or the testimony of the Church, and reason can be instruments of faith, but not its foundations, nor can the senses.

units.la: 17. Arbor bona. Adagio Christus suam sententiam confirmat. Q. d. Ab effectu naturaliter consequente dignoscitur causae cujuivis bonitas. Vide infra cap. 23. v. 3.
units.tr: 17. A good tree. Christ confirms his saying by a proverb. That is: the goodness of any cause is known from the effect that naturally follows it. See below, ch. 23, v. 3.

units.la: 21. Non omnis, &c. Cum dixisset Christus quosdam non recipientes propter dogmatum nequitiam, jam addit nec fidei integritatem sufficere ad salutem, nisi quam lingua loquitur, etiam moribus vita fateatur. Q. d. Non omnes, quorum Spiritus-Sanctus movet corda ad confessionem nominis mei, non omnes qui moti à Spiritu-Sancto prophetant & prodigia operantur per invocationem nominis mei, non omnes illi beatitudinem consequuntur, sed ij duntaxat, quos Spiritus-Sanctus inhabitat. Itaque nemo Jesum confitetur nisi Spiritu Sancto movente, sed ij tantum, qui faciunt voluntatem Dei, qui servant mandata, qui non negant factis, quem ore confitentur, & corde reverentur, moventur à Spiritu-Sancto inhabitante. Ita D. Th. 1 Cor. 12. Lect. 1. in haec verba : Nemo potest dicere Dominus Jesus, nisi in Spiritu-Sancto.
units.tr: 21. Not everyone, etc. Having said that some are not received because of the wickedness of their teaching, Christ now adds that integrity of faith is not enough for salvation unless life also confesses by morals what the tongue speaks. That is: not all those whose hearts the Holy Spirit moves to confess my name, not all who, moved by the Holy Spirit, prophesy and work miracles by invoking my name, attain blessedness, but only those whom the Holy Spirit indwells. So no one confesses Jesus except by the moving of the Holy Spirit, but only those who do the will of God, who keep the commandments, who do not deny by their deeds the one whom they confess with their mouth and revere in their heart, are moved by the indwelling Holy Spirit. So St. Thomas, on 1 Cor. 12, Lecture 1, on these words: No one can say, Jesus is Lord, except in the Holy Spirit.

units.la: 22. In illa die. Quā scilicet venturus sum judicare vivos & mortuos.
units.tr: 22. In that day. That is, the day on which I shall come to judge the living and the dead.

units.la: 23. Confitebor. Signanter dixit, Confitebor : quia multo ante tempore dicere dissimulaverat. Hier.
units.tr: 23. I will confess. He said I will confess with emphasis, because for a long time before he had pretended not to speak. Jerome.

units.la: Nunquam novi vos. Id est, nunquam vos approbavi, ne tunc quidem dum prophetaretis, ejiceretis daemonia & multas virtutes in nomine meo faceretis. Sic Cicero de legibus lib. 1. Vereor ne istam causam nullus noscat : id est, probet. Sic ars dicitur nescire vitia, cum improbat vitia. Praeclare Greg. II. Moral. c. 7. Scire Dei aliquando cognoscere dicitur, aliquando approbare ; & scit iniquum, quia cognoscendo judicat ; & tamen iniquum nescit, quia ejus facta non approbat ; & novit ergo, quia deprehendit ; & non novit, quia in sapientia sua speciem non recognoscit ; sicut de veraci quolibet viro dicitur, quia salsitatem nesciat, non quia, cum vel ab aliis falsum dicitur, hoc reprehendere ignorat, sed eandem ipsam fallaciam & scit in examine, & nescit in amore, ut videlicet & ipse hanc non agat, quam actam ab aliis damnat. Paulo aliter hunc locum exponit Augustinus in Epistola 47. ad Valentinum : Quid est, Non novi vos, nisi, tales vos [illegible, ~1 letters] non feci ? Quemadmodum illud quod dictum est de ipso Domino Jesu Christo, Quia non noverat peccatum, quid est ( non noverat ) nisi quia non fecerat ? Ac per hoc quod dictum est : Vias quæ à dextris sunt novit Dominus : quomodo intelligendum est, nisi quia ipse fecit vias dextras, id est, vias justorum, quæ sunt utique opera bona, quæ præparavit Deus ( sicut dicit Apostolus ) ut in illis ambulemus. Vias autem sinistras perversas, id est, vias impiorum, non utique novit, quia non eas ipse fecit in homine, sed homo sibi. Propter quod dicit : Odivi autem ego perversas vias malorum, ipsa sunt à sinistris.
units.tr: I never knew you. That is: I never approved of you, not even when you were prophesying, casting out demons, and doing many mighty works in my name. So Cicero, On the Laws, book 1: I fear that no one knows this case, that is, approves it. So an art is said not to know vices when it disapproves of vices. Gregory admirably, Moralia II, ch. 7: To know of God is sometimes said to be to recognise, sometimes to approve. And he knows the wicked, because by knowing he judges; and yet he does not know the wicked, because he does not approve their deeds; and so he knows, because he apprehends; and does not know, because in his wisdom he does not recognise the appearance. In the same way one says of any truthful man that he does not know falsehood, not because when something false is said by others he is ignorant how to reprove it, but because he both knows the very deceit under examination and does not know it in love, so that he himself does not do what he condemns when others do it. Augustine explains this passage somewhat differently in Epistle 47 to Valentinus: What is "I do not know you," unless it means "I did not make you such" [illegible]? Just as what was said of the Lord Jesus Christ himself, that he had not known sin, what does "had not known" mean except that he had not committed it? And so what was said, "The Lord knows the ways which are on the right," how is it to be understood except that he himself made the right ways, that is, the ways of the just, which are surely good works, which God prepared, as the Apostle says, that we should walk in them? But the perverse, left-hand ways, that is, the ways of the impious, he certainly does not know, because he did not make them in man; man made them for himself. Therefore he says: "But I have hated the perverse ways of the wicked, which are on the left."

units.la: Discedite à me. Supple, in ignem æternum.
units.tr: Depart from me. Supply: into everlasting fire.

units.la: Qui operamini iniquitatem. Non dixit, Qui operati estis iniquitatem : ne videretur tollere pœnitentiam : sed, qui usque in præsentem horam cum judicii tempus advenerit, licet non habeatis facultatem peccandi, tamen adhuc habetis affectum. B. Hier.
units.tr: Who work iniquity. He did not say, "who have worked iniquity," lest it seem to remove repentance; rather, "who up to the present hour," so that when the time of judgment has come, although you no longer have the opportunity to sin, you nevertheless still have the inclination. B. Hier.

units.la: 24. Omnis ergo, &c. Q. d. Cum tanta sit necessitas faciendi voluntatem Patris mei ; concludite eum stulto labore consumi, qui verba mea audire satagit, & facere negligit ; nullam enim parit fides, quæ ex auditu est, utilitatem, si fœda fit conversatio ; eum vero lætari de labore suo, qui non solo auditu verba mea suscepperit sed etiam opere impleverit. Hic autem idem sensus aliis verbis hic, aliis Luc. 6, exprimitur.
units.tr: 24. "Everyone therefore," etc. The sense is this: since there is such a necessity of doing my Father's will, conclude that he labours in vain who strives to hear my words and neglects to do them; for faith that comes by hearing brings no profit if one's conduct is foul. But he rejoices in his labour who has received my words not only by hearing but has also fulfilled them in deed. This same sense is expressed here in one set of words and in Luke 6 in others.

units.la: 29. Potestatem habens. Q. d. Omnes in admirationem rapiebantur, cum Christus Legem in monte latam, in monte interpretaretur ; talem enim Christus sua in doctrina promulgandâ majestatem exhibebat, ut se plane ἐξουσίαν, id est, authoritatem Regis ad jubendum, & Doctoris ad persuadendum habere ostenderet. Sermo enim Christi, licet simplicissimus, vestitus erat majestate quadam regali, ac penitus divina. Nam animæ medullam penetrabat ad electorum conversionem, & malorum convictionem. Scribarum autem & Pharisæorum doctrina talis non erat ; sed ratione materia erat ut plurimum de rebus frivolis & infructuosis ; & ratione qualitatis, laxior, fucata, & ad ostentationem, aut blandiloquium composita.
units.tr: 29. "Having authority." The sense is this: all were carried away in admiration when Christ, on the mountain, was expounding the Law delivered on the mountain; for Christ, in proclaiming his doctrine, displayed such majesty that he plainly showed he had ἐξουσία [authority], that is, the authority of a King to command and of a Teacher to persuade. For the speech of Christ, though most simple, was clothed with a certain royal and wholly divine majesty. For it penetrated to the marrow of the soul, to the conversion of the elect and the conviction of the wicked. But the teaching of the scribes and Pharisees was not of this kind; rather, in respect of its subject matter, it was for the most part concerned with frivolous and unfruitful things, and in respect of its quality it was lax, varnished, and composed for display or for flattering speech.

units.la: CAPUT VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: ET ecce leprosus. Post prædicationem, inquit Hieron. atque doctrinam signorum offertur occasio, ut per virtutum miracula præteritus apud audientes sermo firmetur. Hæc autem eadem leprosi miraculose sanati historia narratur à Marco, c. 1. v. 40. & à Luca 5. v. 12. sed solus Matt. hujus miraculi tempus atque ordinem significat, his verbis: Cùm ascendisset de monte &c. Et ecce &c.
units.tr: And behold, a leper. After the preaching and teaching, says Jerome, an occasion of signs is offered, so that the word, passed over, is confirmed among the hearers by the miracles of the powers. This same story of the leper miraculously healed is told by Mark, ch. 1 v. 40, and by Luke 5 v. 12. But Matthew alone indicates the time and order of this miracle, in these words: When he had come down from the mountain, etc. And behold, etc.

units.la: Veniens. Nempe, cùm Jesus esset in una civitatum, ut dicit Lucas, hoc est, prope unam civitatem, nam Levitic. 13. prohibetur leprosis urbes ingredi. Colligitur autem ex v. 5. hujus capitis, prope Capharnaum leprosum fuisse mundatum. Christum quoque esse passum dicimus in urbe Jerusalem, quia passus est prope urbem Jerusalem. Hebr. 9. v. 4. in Arca fuisse leguntur urna aurea manni plena, & virga Aaronis, id est, prope Arcam; nam in ipsa Arca nihil fuit præter duas Legis tabulas, ut dicitur 1 Reg. seu Sam. 8. v. 9. Sic Josue 10. v. 10. in Gabaon, id est, prope Gabaon; neque enim in ipsa urbe pugnatum fuerat, ut in ea hostes contererentur. Judic. 18. v. 12. castrametati dicuntur in Cariathiarim, id est, prope Cariathiarim; sequitur enim ibidem mox: Qui locus, ex eo tempore, castrorum Dan nomen accepit, & est post tergum Cariathiarim, id est, ab occidente ejus.
units.tr: Veniens. Namely, when Jesus was in one of the cities, as Luke says, that is, near a city, for Leviticus 13 forbids lepers to enter cities. It is gathered from v. 5 of this chapter that the leper was cleansed near Capernaum. We also say that Christ suffered in the city of Jerusalem, because he suffered near the city of Jerusalem. Hebrews 9 v. 4 says that in the Ark were found a golden urn full of manna and the rod of Aaron, that is, near the Ark; for in the Ark itself there was nothing but the two tables of the Law, as is said in 1 Kings, or 1 Samuel 8 v. 9. So Joshua 10 v. 10 says in Gibeon, that is, near Gibeon; for the battle had not been fought in the city itself, so that the enemies were crushed in it. Judges 18 v. 12 says they encamped in Kiriath-jearim, that is, near Kiriath-jearim; for immediately after there follows: That place from that time received the name Camp of Dan, and it is behind Kiriath-jearim, that is, to its west.

units.la: Adorabat. Scilicet accidens ad genua & procidens in faciem, ut dicitur Mar. 1. Luc. 5. Nam adoratio, ut ait D. Th. 22æ. q. 84. ar. 2. ad 2m. principaliter quidem in interiori Dei reverentia consistit; secundario autem in quibusdam corporalibus humilitatis signis: sicut genu-flectimus, nostram infirmitatem designantes in comparatione ad Deum: prosternimus autem nos quasi profitentes nos nihil esse ex nobis. Est autem formatum adorandi verbum non ab ador, quod frumenti genus est, ut censet vulgus Grammaticorum, sed à veterum more, quod diis supplicantes admovebant oribus suis dextras, primo digito in erectum pollicem reflidente, ut expressit Apulejus lib. 5. Miletiarum. Unde Job 31. v. 26. & 27. Si vidi solem cùm fulgeret, & lunam incedentem clarè: & osculatus sum manum meam ore meo: id est, si lunam aut solem adoravi. Si vis. Cùm Deus non promiserit bona corporalia nisi conditionatè, si animæ saluti expediant, orantibus concedenda, benè leprosus lepræ sanationem petens, totum Christi beneplacito committit; ipse enim novit quid fit sanitati animæ magis opportunum.
units.tr: Adorabat. Namely, falling to his knees and prostrating himself on his face, as is said in Mark 1 and Luke 5. For adoration, as St Thomas says (22ae q. 84 art. 2 ad 2m), principally consists in the inner reverence of God; secondarily, however, in certain bodily signs of humility: as we bend the knee, showing our weakness in comparison with God; we prostrate ourselves as though professing that we are nothing of ourselves. The word adorare is formed not from ador, which is a kind of grain, as the common run of grammarians think, but from the custom of the ancients, who, when supplicating the gods, brought their right hands to their mouths, with the first finger bent back against the raised thumb, as Apuleius expresses in book 5 of the Milesian Tales. Hence Job 31 v. 26 and 27: If I beheld the sun when it shone, and the moon walking clearly, and I kissed my hand with my mouth, that is, if I adored the moon or the sun. If you will. Since God has promised bodily goods only conditionally, to be granted to those who pray if they are expedient for the health of the soul, the leper, rightly asking for the healing of his leprosy, commits everything to Christ's good pleasure; for he knows what is more fitting for the health of the soul.

units.la: 3. Tetigit eum. Verbum individuam se cum carne societatem habere persuasum volens, pleraque miracula & signa per corporis ministerium edidit. Victor Antiochenus in cap. 1. Marci. Unde Cyrillus in Catena Græcorum Patrum in Luc. 4. ait quòd sicut ignis appositus vasi æneo imprimit ei propriæ caliditatis effectum, sic omnipotens Dei Verbum cum templum sibi ex Virgine assumtum animatum & intellectuale veraciter univit, particeps illud suæ potestatis effecit. Quamvis autem Christus videatur Legem solvere, quæ contactum leprosi vetabat Levitic. 13. revera tamen non solvit; Lex enim vetuit tangere lepram, non ut leprosi non sanarentur, sed ut tangentes non inficerentur; Christus verò infici non potuit, ideo tetigit, ut tangendo lepræ infectum mundaret, simulque ostenderet non corporis sed animæ lepram esse fugiendam. Tetigit ut contra Manichæos humanæ naturæ, quam habebat, probaret veritatem. Tetigit & locutus est, ut omnibus constaret leprosum ab ipso fuisse mundatum.
units.tr: 3. He touched him. The Word, wishing to be persuaded that it has an indivisible fellowship with the flesh, performed most of its miracles and signs through the ministry of the body. Victor of Antioch on Mark ch. 1. Hence Cyril, in the Catena of the Greek Fathers on Luke 4, says that just as fire applied to a bronze vessel imprints on it the effect of its own heat, so the almighty Word of God, when it truly united to itself the animated and rational temple assumed from the Virgin, made that temple a partaker of its power. Although Christ seems to abolish the Law, which forbade contact with a leper (Leviticus 13), in truth he does not abolish it. For the Law forbade touching leprosy not so that lepers would not be healed, but so that those who touched them would not be infected. Christ, however, could not be infected; therefore he touched, so that by touching he might cleanse the one infected with leprosy, and at the same time show that it is not the leprosy of the body but that of the soul which must be fled. He touched in order to prove, against the Manichaeans, the truth of the human nature which he had. He touched and spoke, so that it would be clear to all that the leper had been cleansed by him.

units.la: Volo. Christus hac omnipotenti voluntate contra Photinum Syrmiensem Episcopum probat se non tantùm hominem esse, sed & Deum, cujus voluntate omnia fiunt.
units.tr: Volo. By this almighty will Christ proves, against Photinus, bishop of Sirmium, that he is not only a man but also God, by whose will all things come to pass.

units.la: Mundare. Id est, sis mundus: est enim in imperativo, ut patet ex textu Græco. Imperat Christus, ut contra Arrium se offendat non minorem Patre. Amb. 1. 5. in Luc.
units.tr: Mundare. That is, be clean; for it is in the imperative, as is clear from the Greek text. Christ commands, so that he shows himself against Arius to be not less than the Father. Ambrose, book 5 on Luke.

units.la: Confessim. Id est, citra moram.
units.tr: Confessim. That is, without delay.

units.la: 4. Nemini dixeris. Redemptor noster per mortale corpus, omne quod egit, hoc nobis in exemplum actionis præbuit, ut pro nostrarum virium modulo ejus vestigia sequentes inoffenso pede operis, præsentis vitæ carpamus viam; miraculum namque faciens, & tacere jussit, & tamen tacere non potuit, ut videlicet electi ejus, exempla doctrinæ illius sequentes, in magnis quæ faciunt, latera quidem in voluntate habeant, sed ut prosint aliis, prodantur invidi, quatenus & magnæ humilitatis sit, quod opera sua tacere appetunt, & magnæ utilitatis sit, quod opera eorum tacere non possunt. Non ergo Dominus voluit fieri quidquam, & minimè potuit, sed quid membra ejus velle debeant, quidve etiam de iis volentibus fiat, doctrinæ magisterio exemplum dedit. B. Greg. l. 1. Dialog. c. 9.
units.tr: 4. Tell no one. Our Redeemer, through his mortal body, offered everything he did as an example of action for us, so that, following his footsteps according to the measure of our strength, we might tread the path of this present life with an unstumbling foot in our work. For in performing a miracle he both ordered silence and yet could not keep silent, so that his chosen ones, following the examples of his teaching, may indeed wish in their hearts to hide the great deeds they do, but, in order to benefit others, are exposed to envy. Thus it is a mark of great humility that they seek to keep their works silent, and a mark of great usefulness that their works cannot be kept silent. The Lord therefore did not will that anything be done in secret, and by no means could; but by the teaching of his instruction he gave an example of what his members ought to will, and of what is done with those who will it. St Gregory, Dialogues, book 1, ch. 9.

units.la: Sacerdoti. Marc. 1. v. 44. Principi sacerdotum, id est, ei, qui tibi primus occurrerit, sacerdoti; nam apud Marcum ipsum ipsum in textu Græco habetur, sacerdoti, sicut hic & Luc. 5. v. 44. etiam in Vulgato; tum etiam ut patet ex Levitic. 13. quilibet sacerdos leprosum considerare poterat, ut an mundus immundusve esset, decerneret.
units.tr: Priest. Mark 1 v. 44: to the chief priest, that is, to the priest who first meets you. For in Mark himself, in the Greek text, it is to the priest, as here and in Luke 5 v. 44, also in the Vulgate; and also, as is clear from Leviticus 13, any priest could examine a leper to determine whether he was clean or unclean.

units.la: Offer &c Hoc Christus ideo jussit, quia nondum in cruce obtulerat sacrificium sanctum sanctorum, quod corpus ejus est; non enim oportebat auferri ceremonialia Legis præcepta, nisi exhibitis his, quæ per ipsa ceremonialia præcepta promittebantur futura.
units.tr: Offer, etc. Christ ordered this because he had not yet offered on the cross the holy of holies sacrifice, which is his body. For the ceremonial precepts of the Law were not to be taken away unless first the things promised by those ceremonial precepts as future had been exhibited.

units.la: - In testimonium illis. Q. d. Ut hoc fit illis testimonio, quoniam non veni solvere Legem, sed adimplere, & ipsa adimpletione auferre ea, per quæ adhuc promittitur implendum, quod jam a me fuerit impletum.
units.tr: - For a testimony to them. As if he said: so that this may be a testimony to them, because I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfil it, and by that very fulfilment to remove those things through which it is still promised that something is to be fulfilled, which has already been fulfilled by me.

units.la: 5. Centurio. Sic dicebatur, qui uni centuriæ præerat. Centuria centum homines continebat eosque pedites; turma vero sic dicta quasi terma aut terdena, triginta seu terdenos equites, quorum primi dicti sunt Decuriones. Gentilis hic Centurio erat, ut patet ex sequentibus & Luc. 7.
units.tr: 5. Centurion. So was called the one who commanded a single century. A century contained a hundred men, and these were foot soldiers; but a troop was so called as if terma or terdena, thirty or threefold, namely thirty horsemen, whose first were called decurions. This centurion was a Gentile, as is clear from what follows and from Luke 7.

units.la: Accessit. Non per seipsum, sed primo per Seniores Judæorum, deinde per amicos, ut patet ex Luc. 7.
units.tr: Approached. Not in person, but first through the elders of the Jews, then through friends, as is clear from Luke 7.

units.la: 6. Puer. Id est, servus, ut patet ex Luc. 7.
units.tr: 6. Boy. That is, servant, as is clear from Luke 7.

units.la: 7. Ait illi Id est, Judæis ejus nomine venientibus.
units.tr: 7. He said to him. That is, to the Jews coming in his name.

units.la: 8. Sub tectum meum. Id est, in domum meam.
units.tr: 8. Under my roof. That is, into my house.

units.la: Dic verbo. Hebraismus, id est, jube unico verbulo.
units.tr: Say the word. A Hebraism, that is, command with a single word.

units.la: 9. Nam & ego, &c. Q. d. Si ego alteri subditus multa unico verbulo efficio, quid tu non possis, cui omnes serviunt potestates?
units.tr: 9. For I also am, etc. As if he said: if I, being under another's authority, accomplish much with a single word, what can you not do, to whom all powers are subject?

units.la: 10. Miratus est. Admiratio est, quando aliquis & videt efsectum & ignorat causam. D. Th. in Ps. 8. sed Christus qui fidem in Centurione fecerat, illius fidei causam ignorare non poterat. Unde dicit Augustinus in 1. super Genesim contra Manichæos c. 8. Quod mirabatur Dominus, nobis mirandum esse significat, quibus adhuc opus est sic moveri. Omnes ergo tales motus ejus non perturbati animi signa sunt, sed docentis Magistri.
units.tr: 10. He marvelled. Wonder is when someone both sees the effect and does not know the cause. St Thomas on Psalm 8. But Christ, who had produced the faith in the centurion, could not be ignorant of the cause of that faith. Hence Augustine says in his first book on Genesis against the Manichaeans, ch. 8: That the Lord marvelled signifies that it is to be marvelled at by us, who still need to be moved in this way. All such emotions of his are therefore signs not of a disturbed mind, but of a teaching Master.

units.la: In Israel. Supple, secundum carnem; nam & Centurio jam Israelites erat secundum spiritum, ut ait Aug. Ser. 6. de verbis Dom. c. 1. Itaque non confertur Centurionis fides cum fide eorum, qui tunc erant paucissimi Israelitæ secundum spiritum; unde non poterat inferri, fidem Centurionis fuisse majorem fide B. Virginis, aut eorum, qui Christum sequebantur tunc temporis.
units.tr: In Israel. Supply according to the flesh; for the centurion too was already an Israelite according to the spirit, as Augustine says in Sermon 6 on the words of the Lord, ch. 1. Therefore the centurion's faith is not compared with the faith of those who at that time were very few Israelites according to the spirit. Whence it could not be inferred that the centurion's faith was greater than the faith of the blessed Virgin, or of those who followed Christ at that time.

units.la: 11. Ab oriente, &c. Id est, ex omnibus mundi partibus. Recumbent, &c. Recumbere, seu, discumbere est in aeterna requie refoveri; discumbere quippe nostrum, in regno quiescere est. Greg. Hom. 13. in Evang. Regnum coelorum comparatur convivio, in quo Abraham pater credentium primum locum tenet, ceteri vero convivae una cum Abrahamo recumbunt. Hinc putat doctissimus Camero, quod quemadmodum honoratissimi habebantur, qui convivarum in sinu recumberent, ita qui prae ceteris beati sunt, dicuntur in sinu Abrahae esse. Verum magis arridet sententia Capelli dicentis quod sinus Abrahae non a more accumbentium mensae dictus est, sed a puerulis, qui parentibus sunt charissimi, quos parentes in sinu, sive gremio fovent, in quo etiam suaviter interdum dormiunt. Pii nempe dormire dicuntur & quiescere a laboribus suis, dum moriuntur; ubinam autem quiescere & dormire potius dicentur, quam in sinu patris omnium credentium?
units.tr: 11. From the east, etc. That is, from all parts of the world. Recline, etc. To recline, or to sit at table, is to be refreshed in eternal rest; for our sitting at table is resting in the kingdom. Gregory, Hom. 13 on the Gospel. The kingdom of heaven is compared to a banquet, in which Abraham, the father of believers, holds the first place, while the other guests recline together with Abraham. Hence the most learned Cameron thinks that just as those were considered most honoured who reclined in the bosom of the diners, so those who are blessed above the rest are said to be in the bosom of Abraham. But I prefer the view of Cappel, who says that the bosom of Abraham is named not from the custom of those reclining at table but from little children, who are most dear to their parents, whom parents cherish in their bosom or lap, where they sometimes also sleep sweetly. Indeed the godly are said to sleep and rest from their labours when they die; and where would one more fittingly say that they rest and sleep than in the bosom of the father of all believers?

units.la: 12. Filii autem regni. Hebraismus, id est, qui ad regnum, seu, gloriam nati, destinatique erant.
units.tr: 12. But the sons of the kingdom. A Hebraism, that is, those who were born and destined for the kingdom, or glory.

units.la: Ejicientur. Quia jactantes se de semine Abrahae, semen Abrahae fieri noluerunt, ut essent filii promissionis, quia fidem novi Testamenti non receperunt, ubi justitiam Dei contemserunt, & suam constituere volentes, id est, tanquam de suis meritis & operibus praesidentes praeverunt esse filii promissionis, hoc est, filii gratiae, filii misericordiae, ut qui gloriatur in Domino glorietur, credens in eum, qui justificat impium, hoc est, qui ex impio facit pium, ut deputetur fides ejus ad justitiam, & impleatur in eo, non quod postulabat ejus meritum, sed quod a Domino promissum est beneficium. August. Ep. 120. c. 20.
units.tr: Will be cast out. Because, boasting that they were of the seed of Abraham, they were unwilling to become the seed of Abraham, that is, the sons of promise, since they did not receive the faith of the New Testament; they despised the righteousness of God, and wishing to set up their own, that is, relying on their own merits and works, they failed to become sons of promise, that is, sons of grace, sons of mercy, so that "he who glories, let him glory in the Lord" (1 Cor. 1), believing in him who justifies the ungodly, that is, who makes the impious godly, so that "his faith is reckoned to him for righteousness" (Rom. 4), and what is fulfilled in him is not what his merit demanded but what the Lord has promised as a benefit. Augustine, Ep. 120, c. 20.

units.la: In tenebras exteriores. Utitur Christus hac loquendi formula, quia agit hic de regno coelorum sub similitudine coenae convivialis, quae quia de nocte fit, solet copiosio taedarum lumine celebrari, quod non solum ad necessitatem & usum, sed etiam ad celebritatem & ambitionem adhibetur. Itaque qui in coenaculo sunt, in magno sunt lumine; qui extra, in magnis versantur tenebris. Sic qui in regno coelorum erunt, non egebunt lumine solis, neque lumine lucernae, quoniam Dominus Deus illuminabit eos; qui vero extra regnum coelorum erunt, quoniam non a Domino Deo illuminabuntur, respectu cujus lucis alia quaevis lux, quanta quanta fit, tenebrarum nomen obtinet, in tenebris exterioribus fore dicuntur, sicque opponuntur tenebrae exteriores luci domesticae, ex qua ejiciuntur.
units.tr: Into the outer darkness. Christ uses this manner of speaking because here he is treating of the kingdom of heaven under the likeness of a festive banquet. Such a feast is held at night, and is wont to be celebrated with the abundant light of torches, which is used not only for necessity and convenience but also for display and splendour. So those who are in the dining room are in great light; those outside are in great darkness. In the same way, those who will be in the kingdom of heaven will not need the light of the sun or of a lamp, since the Lord God will illuminate them; but those who will be outside the kingdom of heaven, since they will not be illuminated by the Lord God, in comparison with whose light any other light, however great, takes the name of darkness, are said to be in the outer darkness. Thus the outer darkness is set against the light of the house, from which they are cast out.

units.la: Villalpandus in Apparatu Urbis ac Templi Jerosolymitani libri secundi c. 8. observat 10 tenebrarum nomine carcerem compellari solitum in Scripturis, ut videre est Psal. 106. v. 10. Sedentes in tenebris & in umbra mortis, vinctos in mendicitate & ferro : quæ omnia eorum sunt, qui in carcere detinentur, quomodo intellexit Rabbi David Kimchi, & ante ipsum intellexisse videtur Chaldæus. Præterea apud Esaiam c. 49. v. 9. Qui vincti sunt, exite : qui in tenebris, revelamini : repetitio ejusdem facti est, quo de carcere educuntur vincti, & de tenebris ejus ad libertatem & lucem. Neque vero tantummodo carcer vocatur tenebræ, sed & tanta est tenebrarum & carceris similitudo, ut tenebras ipsas carcerem quemdam vocet Sapientia; sic enim de Ægyptiorum coercita arrogantia loquitur c. 17. v. 2. Dum enim persuasum habent iniqui posse dominari nationi sanctæ, vinculis tenebrarum & longæ noctis compediti, inclusi sub tectis, fugitivi perpetuæ providentiæ jacuerunt.
units.tr: Villalpando, in the Apparatus of the City and Temple of Jerusalem, book 2, c. 8, observes that in Scripture the name of darkness is often applied to a prison, as can be seen in Ps. 106:10: "Sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death, bound in misery and iron," all of which belongs to those held in prison. Rabbi David Kimchi understood it so, and the Chaldee seems to have understood it before him. Moreover, in Isaiah 49:9, "Those who are bound, come out; those in darkness, be revealed," is a repetition of the same thing: prisoners are led out of prison, and out of its darkness into liberty and light. Nor is the prison called darkness only; the likeness between darkness and prison is so close that Wisdom calls darkness itself a kind of prison. For thus it speaks of the restrained arrogance of the Egyptians, c. 17:2: "For while the wicked were persuaded that they could rule over a holy nation, they lay bound in chains of darkness and of long night, shut up under roofs, fugitives from eternal providence."

units.la: Observat 2ò. Fuisse quidem Jerosolymis, ut in quibusvis, aliis grandioribus urbibus multos carceres leviorum scelerum reis detinendis aptissimos; unum vero horridum, deterrimum & gravissimâ capitis poenâ multandis destinatum, extra pomœria civitatis situm, ne sceleratorum afflatu, quod forte cavendum populo maximè ducebant Hebræi, fœdaretur civitas. In hunc carcerem conjecti fontes, tenebris, frigore, nuditate, fame, siti, ac omnium malorum maximo, perpetuo mortis timore torquebantur. Hunc carcerem vocatum putat Villalpandus, Betifo, q.d. locum stercoris, quia malefactores qui urbium dicuntur sordes, illuc conjiciebantur; sic arbitrantur nonnulli Portam stercoris dictam, quæ monti Calvariæ erat proxima, in quo monte plectebantur ultimo supplicio scelesti homines.
units.tr: Second observation. Jerusalem, like other larger cities, certainly had many prisons very well suited for holding criminals of lesser offences; but there was one horrible and most wretched prison, reserved for those to be punished with the gravest capital penalty, situated outside the boundaries of the city, so that the city would not be defiled by the breath of criminals, which the Hebrews thought the people especially had to guard against. Those thrown into this prison were tormented by hunger, thirst, darkness, cold, nakedness, and, the greatest of all evils, a perpetual fear of death. Villalpando thinks this prison was called Betifo, that is, a place of dung, because the malefactors, whom they call the filth of cities, were thrown there. Likewise some think that the Dung Gate, which was near the hill of Calvary, on which wicked men were executed with the final punishment, was named for this reason.

units.la: Hinc Christus volens designare poenas infernales, queis in impietate perseverantium audacia est exercenda, ipsas designat per nomen Carceris, qui tunc temporis erat in maximo horrore, & ob densissimas ipsius tenebras vocabatur Tenebræ, & ob situm dicebatur Tenebræ exteriores, & ob mala, quæ in hujusmodi Carcere tolerabantur ab inclusis, addit Christus : Ibi fletus & stridor dentium. Perpetuas hujus Carceris tenebras significare videtur Lucas, dum Act. 12. ait : Ecce Angelus Domini astitit & lumen refulsit in habitaculo Carceris : quasi novum & inauditum quidpiam esse insinuat, quòd lumen in illo Carcere refulserit; ubi etiam observare est quòd ille Carcer extra civitatem situs erat. Hunc sensum secutus videtur Epiphanius in vita sua apud Metaphraftem his verbis Persarum Regem alloquens : Esto justus apud Deum universorum, ne forte judiceris in condemnatione, & custodiaris in tenebris exterioribus, & tunc meorum verborum recorderis. Porrò ipsas hujus tetri Carceris densissimas tenebras maximi supplicii loco habitas probat·illud Ps. 54. Formido mortis, id est, terror mortifer ( ecce fletus ) cecidit super me. Timor & tremor ( ecce stridor dentium ) venerunt super me. Et horum atque reliquorum omnium malorum quasi symbolum, imò quasi complementum & causa, contexerunt me tenebræ.
units.tr: Hence Christ, wishing to designate the infernal punishments, in which the audacity of those persisting in impiety is to be exercised, names them by the name of a prison, which at that time was in the greatest horror, and which, because of its very dense darkness, was called "darkness," and because of its position was called "outer darkness." And because of the evils endured by those shut up in such a prison, Christ adds: "There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth." Luke seems to indicate the perpetual darkness of this prison when he says in Acts 12: "Behold, the angel of the Lord stood by, and a light shone in the dwelling of the prison"; as if he hints that it was something new and unheard of that light shone in that prison, where it is also worth noting that the prison was situated outside the city. Epiphanius, in his life, as quoted by Metaphrastes, seems to follow this sense when he addresses the king of the Persians in these words: "Be just before God of all, lest perhaps you be judged in condemnation and be kept in the outer darkness, and then remember my words." Further, that the very dense darkness of this foul prison was regarded as the greatest punishment is proved by Ps. 55 [54]: "The terror of death," that is, deadly fear (behold, weeping), "has fallen upon me; fear and trembling" (behold, gnashing of teeth) "have come upon me." And as a kind of symbol of all these and the other evils, indeed as their completion and cause, "darkness has covered me."

units.la: Ibi erit fletus, &c. Id est, summa tristitia & rabies, quarum signa sunt fletus & dentium stridor. Si fletus oculorum est, & stridor dentium offa demonstrat : vera est ergo corporum & eorundem membrorum, quæ ceciderunt, resurrectio. B. Hieron. Ex hoc Scripturæ loco simul collato cum Job 24. v. 19. multi interpretes colligunt duplicem esse gehennam, scilicet nimii caloris & nimii frigoris. Tamen B. Greg. magnus illud Job ; Ad nimium calorem transeat ab aquis nivium, & usque ad inferos peccatum ejus, exponit de impiorum in omnibus immoderatione, qui à frigore infidelitatis transeunt frequenter ad calorem hæresis. Alii putant sensum Jobi esse, improbos à nimia frigiditate hujus vitæ transire ad calorem nimium infernalem, sive ut loquitur Emmanuel Sa, ab una calamitate transfrę in aliam. Textus Hebræus apud B. Job sic habet ad verbum : Siccitas & æstus rapiunt aquas nivis, sepulchrum peccarunt : Continent hæc verba πεῤῥασιν & ἁπᾶ̈ν , & deest utriusque nota, quod in Jobo & Proverbiis insolens non est. Sensum expressit Mercerus his verbis : Ut siccitas & calor quam citissimè absumunt aquas nivis, ita & mors rapit eos qui peccarunt. q. d. Non contabescunt lenia morte, ut magna ex parte probi, sed cùm totam vitam in sceleribus transegerint impunè, suaviter etiam moriuntur. Toto enim c. 24. sententiam Eliphasi, qui asserebat Deum in hac vita semper punire impios, refutat B. Job testimonio experientiæ, quòd pii illud non videant, & quòd peccatores non ita moriantur, ut sentiant se mori, sed citâ & facili suavíque morte expirent. Similia dicuntur de morte peccatorum Job 21. v. 13. Ps. 72. v. 4.
units.tr: There will be weeping, etc. That is, the greatest sorrow and rage, of which weeping and the gnashing of teeth are the signs. "If weeping is of the eyes, and gnashing of teeth demonstrates the bones, then the resurrection of bodies, and of those same members which have fallen, is true." Jerome. From this passage of Scripture, compared with Job 24:19, many interpreters gather that there are two hells, namely of excessive heat and of excessive cold. Yet Gregory the Great explains that saying of Job, "let him pass from the waters of snow to excessive heat, and his sin to the underworld," of the immoderation of the wicked in all things, who often pass from the cold of unbelief to the heat of heresy. Others think the sense of Job is that the wicked pass from the excessive coldness of this life to excessive infernal heat, or, as Emmanuel Sa puts it, "from one calamity into another." The Hebrew text of Job, as rendered word for word, reads: "Drought and heat seize the waters of snow; the grave has [sinned]." These words contain [πεῤῥασιν] and [ἁπᾶ̈ν], and the mark of each is absent, which is not unusual in Job and Proverbs. Mercer expressed the sense in these words: "As drought and heat most swiftly consume the waters of snow, so death also seizes those who have sinned; that is, they do not waste away by a gentle death, as the good mostly do, but, having spent their whole life in wickedness with impunity, they even die pleasantly." For throughout chapter 24 Job refutes the opinion of Eliphaz, who maintained that God always punishes the wicked in this life, by the testimony of experience: the godly do not see that, and sinners do not die in such a way as to feel that they are dying, but breathe their last by a swift, easy and sweet death. Similar things are said of the death of sinners in Job 21:13 and Ps. 73 [72]:4.

units.la: 13. Centurioni. Id est, nuntiis à Centurione missis.
units.tr: 13. To the centurion. That is, to the messengers sent by the centurion.

units.la: Vade. Hebraismus Scripturæ familiaris, quo concedi solet quod petitur.
units.tr: Go. A Hebraism familiar in Scripture, by which what is asked is usually granted.

units.la: Sicut credidisti. Scilicet, me absentem corpore, præsentem majestate solo verbo posse puerum sanare.
units.tr: As you have believed. That is, that I, absent in body but present in majesty, can heal the boy by a word alone.

units.la: In illa hora. Id est, in illo temporis puncto, quo hæc verba à Christo sunt prolata.
units.tr: In that hour. That is, at the very moment when these words were spoken by Christ.

units.la: 14. Et cum venisset. Scilicet ex Synagoga Capharnaitarum Bethsaidam civitatem in Decapoli ad mare Tiberiadis, quod & Galilææ dicitur. Vide Marc. 1. & Luc. 4. Quæ autem hinc deinceps narrantur usque ad versum 35. capitis sequentis contigisse ante Sermonem Domini in monte jam diximus.
units.tr: 14. And when he had come. That is, from the synagogue of the Capernaites into the city of Bethsaida in Decapolis, by the sea of Tiberias, which is also called Galilee. See Mark 1 and Luke 4. We have already said that what is narrated from here on, up to verse 35 of the following chapter, happened before the Sermon on the Mount.

units.la: In domum Petri. Marc. 1. v. 24. Simonis & Andreæ. Sic dicitur hæc domus, vel quia eorum fuerat, antequam reliquissent omnia, vel quia patris eorum erat, vel quia ad Simonis socrum pertinebat, & in ea solebant hospitari.
units.tr: Into the house of Peter. Mark 1. v. 24. Of Simon and Andrew. This house is so called either because it had belonged to them before they left everything, or because it was their father's, or because it belonged to Simon's mother-in-law, and they used to lodge in it.

units.la: 15. Tetigit manum ejus. Id est, elevavit eam, apprehensâ manu ejus, ut dicitur Marc. 1. v. 31.
units.tr: 15. He touched her hand. That is, he raised her up, taking hold of her hand, as is said in Mark 1. v. 31.

units.la: 16. Vespere autem facto. Id est, sabbato finito, ut patet ex Marc. 1. v. 32.
units.tr: 16. But when evening had come. That is, when the Sabbath was over, as is clear from Mark 1. v. 32.

units.la: 17. Infirmitates nostras. Scilicet tùm animi, tùm corporis; ut enim generatim loquitur Esaias, sic generatim accipiendus est de omnibus infirmitatibus. Quamvis autem Matthæus hoc Esaiæ vaticinium applicet ad morbos corporis, præsupponit tamen morbos animi, hoc est, ipsa peccata, eorúmque curam, ut sublatâ causâ effectum tolli demonstret.
units.tr: 17. Our infirmities. That is, both of the mind and of the body. For as Isaiah speaks generally, so the word must be taken generally, of all infirmities. Although Matthew applies this prophecy of Isaiah to bodily diseases, he nevertheless presupposes diseases of the mind, that is, sins themselves and their cure, so that by removing the cause he shows the effect is removed too.

units.la: Accepit. Id est, accipiendo abstulit; Christus enim anima & corpore poenas tùm animi, tùm corporis nobis debitas luit, nos ab iis liberaturus.
units.tr: He took. That is, by taking he removed. For Christ, in soul and body, paid the penalties both of mind and of body that we owed, so as to free us from them.

units.la: Portavit. Id est, portando asportavit. Christus enim portando miserias nostras ex uno peccati fonte derivatas, omnes à nobis sustulit, seu, meruit nobis omnium ablationem; non tamen omnes omnino aufert in præsenti vita, sed meritis passionum ipsius Christi auferentur à justis in resurrectione, quando mortale hoc induet immortalitatem, ut dicitur 1 Cor. 15.
units.tr: He bore. That is, by bearing he carried away. For by bearing our miseries, which flow from the single fountain of sin, Christ removed them all from us, or rather merited for us the removal of them all. Yet he does not take them all away entirely in the present life; they are removed from the righteous at the resurrection, by the merits of Christ's sufferings, when this mortal shall put on immortality, as is said in 1 Cor. 15.

units.la: 19. Accedens unus, &c. Quod Matthæus hic insinuat contigisse ambulantibus Jesu & discipulis in via, ut venirent ad fretum: hoc Lucas Capite 9. v. 57. insinuare videtur contigisse, dum Jesus ascenderet Jerusalem. Ut ut fit, aut Matthæus, aut Lucas ordinem temporis non servavit, licet uterque hanc historiam his, quæ mox antè à se dicta sunt, annectat, ut nihil medium evenisse videatur.
units.tr: 19. And a certain scribe came, etc. What Matthew here suggests happened while Jesus and the disciples were walking on the road to come to the lake; Luke seems to suggest in chapter 9, verse 57, that it happened while Jesus was going up to Jerusalem. Whichever it was, either Matthew or Luke has not kept the order of time, though both join this story to what they had said just before, so that nothing seems to have happened in between.

units.la: Sequar te. An sit secuturus interrogat, quasi verò Lege non hunc esse Christum, quem sequi esse utile, contineretur. Igitur infidelitatis affectum sub diffidentia interrogationis expressit, quia fidei assumtio non interroganda est, sed sequenda. Hilar. can. 7. in Mat.
units.tr: I will follow you. He asks whether he is going to follow, as though the Law did not contain that this is the Christ whom it is useful to follow. So by the question he expressed a state of unbelief under the guise of doubt, because the assumption of faith is not to be questioned but followed. Hilary, Canon 7 on Matthew.

units.la: 20. Vulpes, &c. Q. d. Interrogabo te & egö unum sermonem, quem si dixeris mihi, dicam tibi, an sis me secuturus. Potésne summam illam rerum omnium abdicationem profiteri, quam ego profiteor? Est autem vulpes animal solivagum, quódque ἀλώπηξ & ἀλωπεκιά dictum volunt ἀπὸ τῆς ἀλαλάζω, ab errando & divagando in solitariis locis. Inde Ezech. 13. v. 4. de Pseudo-Prophetis dicitur: Quasi vulpes in desertis Prophetæ tui Israël erant. Thren. 5. v. 18. Propter montem Sion quia disperiit, id est, desolatus est, vulpes ambulaverunt in eo. Quin ut lateant magis, in ipsis terræ visceribus lustra habent sua. Huc alludit Christus hîc in præsenti versu, & Luc. 9. v. 58. Vulpium foveæ uno verbo vocantur ἀλωπεκιά. Si Isidoro credimus apud Gesnerum, habitat vulpes in foveis, quas ipsa tamen non parat, sed à taxo seu mele effossas dolo occupat, fœdo stercoris sui odore illum inde pellens. At videtur id fabulosum, cùm vulpium lustra sæpe sint in locis, ubi nulli meles. Proinde vulpem alii scribunt ipsam sibi lustra alte fodere. Phædrus fabula 76.
units.tr: 20. Foxes, etc. That is, I will question you and put one matter to you: if you answer me, I will tell you whether you are going to follow me. Can you profess that complete renunciation of all things which I profess? The fox is a solitary animal, and they say it is called [ἀλώπηξ] and [ἀλωπεκιά] from wandering and roaming in lonely places. Hence Ezekiel 13. v. 4 says of the false prophets: Like foxes in the deserts were your prophets, O Israel. Lamentations 5. v. 18: Because of Mount Zion, which is destroyed, that is, laid waste, foxes have walked upon it. Moreover, so that they may hide better, they have their dens in the very depths of the earth. Christ alludes to this here in the present verse, and in Luke 9. v. 58. The foxes' dens are called by one word [ἀλωπεκιά]. If we believe Isidore as cited by Gesner, the fox lives in holes which it does not dig itself, but which it seizes by cunning after they have been dug out by the badger, driving the badger out with the foul smell of its own dung. But this seems fabulous, since fox dens are often in places where there are no badgers. Therefore others write that the fox digs its own dens deep. Phaedrus, Fable 76.

units.la: Vulpis, cubile fodiens, dum terram eruit, Egitque plures altius cuniculos, Pervenit ad draconis speluncam ultimam, Custodiebat qui thesauros abditos.
units.tr: The fox, digging out its lair, while it tore up the earth, and made many burrows deeper, came to the last cave of a dragon, which guarded hidden treasures.

units.la: Sed non in hoc tantùm se prodit vulpis astutia, verum etiam in eo quòd latibulo suo septem, ut Oppianus testatur, facit ostia, ne ipsam venatores circa ostium insidiantes conjiciant in laqueos. Imò & scilla lustrum suum ambire dicitur à Zoroastre in Geoponicis lib. 15. & Alkazuinio Arabe, ut lupum (quem vulpi hostem esse observat Philosophus Histor. lib. 9. capite 1. & Giahid apud Damiren Arabem) suget, qui scillæ contactu convellitur, aut moritur. Quod Ambrosius (Hexaem. libri 6. cap. 4.) cur turturi tribuat, nullus capio; quia pullis turturis nullum est à lupo periculum, cùm turtur in locis celsissimis nidificare soleat; unde Origenes in Cantic. Hom. 2. Semper in montium jugis, & in arborum verticibus commoratur, scilicet, turtur.
units.tr: But the cunning of the fox is revealed not only in this, but also in the fact that, as Oppian testifies, it makes seven openings to its lair, so that hunters lying in wait around the entrance cannot drive it into their snares. Indeed, the squill is said by Zoroaster, in the Geoponics book 15, and by the Arab Alkazuini, to surround its den, to suck in the wolf (which the Philosopher observes to be the fox's enemy in the History of Animals, book 9, chapter 1, and which Giahid, cited by Damiren the Arab, also says), and the wolf, touched by the squill, is convulsed or dies. I cannot grasp why Ambrose (Hexaemeron, book 6, chapter 4) ascribes this to the turtle-dove, since the young of the turtle-dove are in no danger from the wolf, as the turtle-dove is accustomed to nest in very high places; hence Origen on the Song of Songs, Homily 2: It always dwells on the ridges of mountains and in the tops of trees, namely, the turtle-dove.

units.la: Filius hominis. Hebraismus Scripturæ familiaris, quo indicari solet homo. Christus autem commendans nobis quid misericorditer dignatus sit esse pro nobis, nomen hoc sæpius auribus nostris insinuat.
units.tr: Son of man. A Hebraism familiar in Scripture, by which a man is usually meant. Christ, however, in commending to us what he has deigned to be for us out of mercy, often impresses this name upon our ears.

units.la: 21. Alius. Cui scilicet Christus dixerat, sequere me, ut dicitur Luc. 9. v. 59. Unde hîc dicitur de discipulis Christi.
units.tr: 21. Another. To whom, that is, Christ had said follow me, as is said in Luke 9. v. 59. Hence it is said here of the disciples of Christ.

units.la: Permitte me, &c. Discipulus hîc non petiit, quòd patrem jam defunctum sepeliret, sed adhuc viventem in senectute sustentaret usquequo sepeliretur: quod Dominus non concessit, quia erant alii, qui ejus curam habere poterant, lineâ parentelæ adstricti. Cyrillus apud D. Th. 22æ. q. 101. ar. 4. ad 1m.
units.tr: Allow me, etc. The disciple here did not ask to bury his father who had already died, but to support him in old age while still living until he should be buried; which the Lord did not grant, because there were others who could take care of him, bound to him by the ties of kinship. Cyril, cited by Aquinas, Summa II-II, question 101, article 4, reply to the first objection.

units.la: 22. Sequere me. Paterni funeris sepultura prohibetur, ut intelligas humana postbabenda divinis. Bonum studium, sed majus impedimentum: nam qui partitur studium, derivat, id est, distrahit, affectum, & qui dividit curam, differt profectum. Ergo prius obeunda quæ maxima sunt; nam & Apostoli ne occuparentur studio dispensandi, ministros pauperibus ordinarunt, & ipsis, cum a Domino mitterentur, neminem in via salutare præscriptum, non quo benevolentiæ displiceret officium, sed quo persequenda devotionis intentio plus placeret. Ambr. lib. 7. in Luc. 9.
units.tr: 22. Follow me. The burial of a father's funeral is forbidden, so that you may understand that human things are to be placed after divine ones. A good pursuit, but a greater hindrance: for he who divides his zeal diverts, that is, distracts, his affection, and he who divides his care defers his progress. Therefore the greatest things must be undertaken first; for the Apostles, so that they might not be occupied with the work of distributing, appointed ministers for the poor; and when they were sent out by the Lord, they were ordered to greet no one on the way, not because duty would displease kindness, but because the intention of the devotion to be pursued would please more. Ambrose, book 7 on Luke 9.

units.la: Dimitte mortuos. Scilicet, quantum ad animam. Scriptura passim inculcat eos, qui cupiditatibus serviunt, esse mortuos in peccatis. Si enim ex jure civili, Servus, dum vivit, reputatur pro mortuo, quidni ex jure divino servus peccati reputabitur pro spiritualiter mortuo, cum amiserit Deum, qui est vita animæ?
units.tr: Let the dead bury their dead. That is, as far as the soul is concerned. Scripture everywhere insists that those who serve their lusts are dead in sins. For if by civil law a slave, while he lives, is reckoned as dead, why should not a slave of sin by divine law be reckoned as spiritually dead, since he has lost God, who is the life of the soul?

units.la: Sepelire mortuos suos. Id est, sibi similes curare. Non revocatur ab officio patris filius, sed fidelis a perfidi communione secernitur. Ambr. loco mox citato.
units.tr: To bury their own dead. That is, to take care of those who are like themselves. The son is not called back from his father's duty, but the faithful man is separated from communion with the faithless. Ambrose, in the passage cited just above.

units.la: 24. In mari. Scilicet, Galilææ, seu Tiberiadis, seu in stagno Genezareth.
units.tr: 24. On the sea. That is, of Galilee, or of Tiberias, or on the lake of Gennesaret.

units.la: Dormiebat. Supple ex Marci. 4. v. 38. In puppi super cervical.
units.tr: He was sleeping. Supply from Mark 4. v. 38: in the stern, upon a cushion.

units.la: 26. Quid timidi estis. Supple, me præsente, cujus nutu fiunt & cessant procellæ.
units.tr: 26. Why are you fearful? Supply: while I am present, at whose nod the storms rise and cease.

units.la: Modicæ fidei? Hanc increpationem sic exprimit Marcus c. 4. Nondum habetis fidem? Luc. vero c. 8. Ubi est fides vestra?
units.tr: Of little faith? Mark in chapter 4 expresses this rebuke thus: Do you not yet have faith? But Luke in chapter 8: Where is your faith?

units.la: Imperavit. Nempe cum increpatione & minis, ut patet ex Mar. 4. & Luc. 8.
units.tr: He commanded. Namely, with rebuke and threats, as is clear from Mark 4 and Luke 8.

units.la: 27. Homines. Scilicet tam discipuli, ut dicitur Luc. 8. quàm ii, qui erant in aliis navibus, quas Marcus dicit affuisse cap. 4.
units.tr: 27. The men. That is, both the disciples, as Luke 8 says, and those who were in the other boats, which Mark says were present in chapter 4.

units.la: Venti & mare obediunt ei. Non quidem sentiendo, sed motum ex imperio impressum suscipiendo & sequendo.
units.tr: Winds and sea obey him. Not indeed by perceiving, but by receiving and following the motion impressed upon them by his command.

units.la: 28. Gerasenorum. Quamdiu stetit Judæorum Respub. in Judæa nulli erant sues. Hinc 1 Par. 27. v. 29. & 30. David legitur alios habuisse præpositos super boves [illegible, ~3 letters] על הבקר, alios super camelos, [illegible, ~3 letters] על הגמלים, alios [illegible, ~3 letters] על הצאן, super oves & capras, sed de subulcis nulla est mentio. Et Patriarcharum opes camelis, asinis, bobus, & capris constitis-se cum identidem memoret Moses, suum, quos habuerint, cum reliquo pecore, non meminit uspiam. Quin, in vicina Arabia, Job in tot pecudum millibus ne unum quidem suem possedisse legitur. Et cum e vicinis gentibus armenta & greges saepe abegerint Israelitae, sues in praeda bellica nusquam censentur. Quin Prophyrius in lib. De abstinentia a caede animalium ullos in Judaea nasci sues diserte negat. Οὐδ' ὄχως, ait, ἐν τοῖς πόλεσιν ἐφυτο ὑ. Unde in Parabola Luc. 15. v. 11. filius acolastus porcos in Judaea non pavit, sed in regione longinqua. Gergeseni autem, quomodo vocantur in praesenti Matthæi loco in textu Graeco, & in versione Arabica & Æthiopica tam hic, quam Marc. 5. & Luc. 8. Sive Gadareni, ut in textu Graeco vocantur locis laudatis Marci & Lucae, & a Syro interprete apud tres Evangelistas, & ab Epiphanio adversus Manichaeos, sive Gerasceni, ut habet constanter Vulgatus interpres apud tres Evangelistas, fuere Graeci, aut Syri, proinde porcis alendis eos contra morem Judaeorum operam dedisse mirum non est. Josephus Antiq. lib. 17. cap. 13. Γαδαρα καὶ Ἵππος, Ἑλληνίδες πόλεις. Gadara & Hippos, urbes graecae sunt. Unde idem lib. 13. cap. 23. inter urbes peregrinas a Judaeis tentas sub Rege Alexandro censet Gadara oppidum ab Alexandro post decem mensium obsidionem occupatum, ut habetur cap. 21. Et a Judaeis diruptum Pompeius in libertatem sui Demetrii Gadarensis gratiam restituisse narratur lib. 2. De bello Judaico cap. 5. Sed Augustus cum regno Herodis attribuisset lib. 15. Antiq. cap. 11. Herode fatis functo, Romanorum provinciae Syriae adjunxisse dicitur lib. 17. Antiq. cap. 14. Syrorum oppidum Gerasa distinguit Josephus lib. 2. Belli Judaici cap. 19. & 20. a Gadara. Sed cum Gadara & Gerasa vicina fuerint oppida, ab utrovis eadem regio potuit nunc Gerasenorum, nunc Gadarenorum nominari. Forte etiam subinde appellabatur Gergesenorum, seu Gergesenorum, regio eadem a prisci illius incolis e stirpe Chanaanis, in cujus filiis Moses censet Gen. 10. v. 16. הגרגשי, pro quo Lxx. habent Γεργεσαῖον. Itaque Gergesa pagus ibi offendebatur. Hiero. in Locis Gergesa, ubi eos, qui a daemonibus vexabantur, Salvator restituit sanitati. Et bodieque super montem viculus daemonstratur juxta stagnum Tiberiadis, in quod porci praecipitati sunt. Eugesippus in Tractatu de distantiis locorum Terrae sanctae, Decimo sexto millari a Nazareth contra Orientem supra mare Galilaeae, Gergesa viculus, &c. Jam si quis objiciat id parum videri verisimile, ut Christus excesserit extra Judaeae limites in Graecorum aut Syrorum regionem Gadarenam, Gerazenámue, aut Gergesenam, cùm ipse profiteatur infrà. c. 15. v. 24. Se non fuisse missum, nisi ad oves perditas domûs Israelis, facilis est responsio. Cùm enim ea ipsa verba protulerit Christus extra Judaeam in finibus Tyri & Sidonis infrà cap. 15. v. 21, & Marc. 7. v. 24, & 31, potuit similiter ire ad Gergesenos, Gerasenóßve, maxime cùm apud eos non fuerit nisi ad tempus brevissimum, & post patratum in ipso appulsu miraculum, quo edidit virtutis suae documentum, rogatus ab incolis statim excesserit, ad suos postliminio reditu- rus.
units.tr: 28. Of the Gergesenes. While the Jewish commonwealth stood in Judea, there were no swine there at all. Hence in 1 Chron. 27:29–30 we read that David had some officials set over the oxen [illegible, ~3 letters] על הבקר, others over the camels [illegible, ~3 letters] על הגמלים, others over the flocks [illegible, ~3 letters] על הצאן, over sheep and goats, but there is no mention of swineherds. And although Moses repeatedly records that the wealth of the patriarchs consisted of camels, asses, oxen and goats, he nowhere mentions swine among the herds they possessed. Indeed, in neighbouring Arabia, Job is said to have possessed not even one swine among so many thousands of animals. And although the Israelites often drove off herds and flocks from neighbouring nations, swine are nowhere counted among the spoils of war. Porphyry, in his book On Abstinence from Killing Animals, expressly says that swine were never bred in Judea at all: "Nor indeed," he says, "were they ever reared in the cities" [οὐδ' ὅλως, φησίν, ἐν ταῖς πόλεσιν ἐφύετο ὗ]. Hence in the parable of Luke 15:11 the prodigal son did not herd swine in Judea, but in a distant region. The Gergeseni, as they are called in the present passage of Matthew in the Greek text, and in the Arabic and Ethiopic versions here as well as in Mark 5 and Luke 8; or the Gadareni, as they are called in the Greek text of the cited passages of Mark and Luke, and by the Syriac interpreter in all three Evangelists, and by Epiphanius against the Manichaeans; or the Gerasceni, as the Vulgate translator constantly has them in the three Evangelists, were Greeks or Syrians, so it is no wonder that they devoted themselves to rearing swine, contrary to the custom of the Jews. Josephus, Antiquities book 17 chapter 13: Gadara and Hippos are Greek cities [Γάδαρα καὶ Ἵππος, Ἑλληνίδες πόλεις]. Hence in the same author, book 13 chapter 23, he counts Gadara among the foreign cities attacked by the Jews under King Alexander; it was taken by Alexander after a siege of ten months, as stated in chapter 21. And Pompey is reported (Jewish War book 2 chapter 5) to have restored Gadara, which the Jews had destroyed, to freedom for the sake of his freedman Demetrius of Gadara. But when Augustus had assigned it to the kingdom of Herod (Antiquities book 15 chapter 11), after Herod's death it is said (Antiquities book 17 chapter 14) to have been added to the Roman province of Syria. Josephus (Jewish War book 2 chapters 19 and 20) distinguishes the Syrian town Gerasa from Gadara. But since Gadara and Gerasa were neighbouring towns, the same region could be called now the region of the Gerasenes and now of the Gadarenes, by either name. Perhaps it was also sometimes called the region of the Gergesenes, or Gergesenes, the same region named after its ancient inhabitants of the stock of Canaan, among whose sons Moses reckons the Girgashite in Genesis 10:16, הגרגשי, for which the Seventy have Γεργεσαῖον. Thus a village called Gergesa was found there. Jerome, in his Onomasticon: Gergesa, where the Saviour restored to health those who were vexed by demons. And even today on the mountain a little village is pointed out near the lake of Tiberias, into which the swine were cast headlong. Eusebius in his treatise on the distances of places in the Holy Land: Sixteen miles from Nazareth towards the east, above the Sea of Galilee, is the village of Gergesa, etc. Now if anyone objects that it seems unlikely that Christ should have gone beyond the borders of Judea into the Greek or Syrian region of the Gadarenes, Gerasenes, or Gergesenes, since he himself declares below, chapter 15:24, that he was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, the answer is easy. For when Christ spoke those very words outside Judea, in the regions of Tyre and Sidon, below in chapter 15:21 and Mark 7:24 and 31, he could likewise go to the Gergesenes or Gerasenes, especially since he stayed among them only for a very short time, and after performing the miracle at his very landing, by which he gave proof of his power, he left at once when asked by the inhabitants, intending to return home by the right of return.

units.la: Duo daemonia habentes. Marcus, & Lucas non meminerunt nisi unius, vel quia unus erat saevior, ut ait Chrysost. Hom. 29. in Matth. vel quia ut ait Aug: lib. 2. de conf. Evang. cap. 24. unus erat clarior & famosior.
units.tr: Two demoniacs. Mark and Luke mention only one, either because one was fiercer, as Chrysostom says (Homily 29 on Matthew), or because, as Augustine says (On the Harmony of the Evangelists book 2 chapter 24), one was more notable and famous.

units.la: Saevi nimis. Id est, quàm saevissimi.
units.tr: Exceedingly fierce. That is, most fierce of all.

units.la: 29. Quid nobis & tibi. Locutio tam Hebraeis, quàm Graecis familiaris: Latine diceretur, Quid nobis tecum, & subauditur, rei?
units.tr: 29. What have we to do with you? An expression familiar to the Hebrews as well as the Greeks; in Latin one would say, "What have we to do with you?" with "of the matter" understood.

units.la: Jesu Fili Dei. Non voluntatis ista confessio est, quam premium sequitur confitentis, sed necessitatis extortio, quae cogit invitos. B. Hier.
units.tr: Jesus, Son of God. This is not a confession of the will, which a reward follows for the one confessing, but a wrung-out confession of necessity, which compels the unwilling. Blessed Jerome.

units.la: Torquere nos. Tanta est daemonum cupiditas nocendi, ut torqueantur, dum eis nocere non permittuntur, in quorum tortura delectantur. In die autem judicij daemonum potestas ita coarctabitur ad inferos, ut nulli prorsus extra nocere possint; ne autem hic dies jam instaret verebantur daemones ad praesentiam Christi.
units.tr: To torment us. So great is the demons' desire to harm that they are tormented while they are not allowed to harm, and they delight in the torment of those they cannot hurt. But on the day of judgment the power of the demons will be so restricted to the lower world that none at all will be able to harm anyone outside it; and the demons feared that this day was already at hand at the presence of Christ.

units.la: Ante tempus. Id est, antequam putabamus; nondum enim diem judicii expectabamus.
units.tr: Before the time. That is, before we thought; for we did not yet expect the day of judgment.

units.la: 30. Erat autem. Supple ex Marc. 5. partim circa montem, & ex Luc. 8. partim in monte.
units.tr: 30. Now there was. To be supplied from Mark 5, partly near the mountain, and from Luke 8, partly on the mountain.

units.la: Grex multorum porcorum. Nempe duorum circiter millium, ut indicatur Marc. 5. v. 13.
units.tr: A herd of many swine. Namely about two thousand, as indicated in Mark 5:13.

units.la: 31. Mitte nos &c. Super porcos potestatem non habet summa daemonum cupiditas nocendi, multò magis nullum habet contra homines factos ad imaginem Dei: oportet ergo solum Deum timere, contemnere autem illos. S. Athan. in vita S. Antonii.
units.tr: 31. Send us, etc. The utmost desire of the demons to harm does not have power over swine, much less does it have any over men made in the image of God: it is therefore necessary to fear God alone and to despise them. Saint Athanasius, in the Life of Saint Antony.

units.la: 32. Hoc. Haec vox non est jubentis, sed permittentis, ut.
units.tr: 32. Go. This word is not of commanding but of permitting, as in "that."

units.la: patet ex textu Graeco hic, & etiam ex Vulg, Mar. 5. v. 13. & Luc. 8. v. 32. Permisit autem hoc daemonibus Christus, ut eorum summa malitia & infirmitas innotesceret, ut mi-
units.tr: is clear from the Greek text here, and also from the Vulgate, Mark 5:13 and Luke 8:32. Christ, however, allowed this to the demons so that their extreme malice and weakness might become known, so that the report of the miracle might spread more widely, and so that the greatness of the benefit might be evident to the demoniacs who were freed.

units.la: raculi fama latius vagaretur, & constaret ipsis dæmoniacis liberatis beneficii magnitudo.
units.tr: miracle's fame might spread more widely, and so that the demoniacs themselves, once freed, would know the greatness of the benefit.

units.la: Per præceps. Id est, præcipitans fe ex abrupto loco Mari Genefareth imminente.
units.tr: Headlong. That is, throwing themselves down from the steep place overhanging the Sea of Gennesaret.

units.la: In Mare. Scilicet, Genefareth.
units.tr: Into the sea. Namely, of Gennesaret.

units.la: 34. Rogabant. Scilicet Gadareni, seu Gerafeni, seu Gergefeni, quia ut dicitur Luc.8.v.37, magno timore tenebantur, ne videlicet iterum damnum aliquod paterentur, sicut passi fuerant in fubmerfione porcorum.
units.tr: 34. Began to beseech. Namely the Gadarenes, or Gerasenes, or Gergesenes, because, as is said in Luke 8:37, they were held by great fear, lest they should suffer some further loss of the kind they had suffered in the drowning of the swine.

units.la: CAPUT. IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.
