units.la: 1. Transfretavit. Scilicet stagnum Genefareth, & rediit in oppositam ripam, unde ad regionem Gerafenorum, Gergefenorumve, seu Gadarenorum venerat.
units.tr: 1. He crossed over. That is, he crossed the lake of Gennesaret and returned to the opposite shore, from which he had come to the region of the Gerasenes, Gergesenes, or Gadarenes.

units.la: In civitatem suam. Hoc est, in Capharnaum, ubi sequens miraculum contigit; ut diserte tradit Marcus c. 2. v. 1. Tres enim patrias habuit Christus, Bethlehem in qua natus, Nazareth in qua educatus, & Capharnaum in qua frequentius versatus, postquam relicta Nazareth eo commigraffet.
units.tr: Into his own city. That is, into Capernaum, where the following miracle took place, as Mark plainly reports in chapter 2, verse 1. For Christ had three homelands: Bethlehem, where he was born; Nazareth, where he was brought up; and Capernaum, where he spent more time after he had left Nazareth and moved there.

units.la: 2. Offerebant ei paralyticum. Supple, à tecto demissum, quia præ turba undequaque circumfusa non poterat aliter offerri, ut aperte dicitur Marc. 2. & Luc. 5.
units.tr: 2. They brought him a paralytic. Supply: let down from the roof, since the crowd pressed in on every side and he could not otherwise be brought in, as is clearly stated in Mark 2 and Luke 5.

units.la: Videns, &c. Ex eo quod Christus fidem offerentium paralyticum mifericorditer respexit, ut alienæ fidei suffragio animam prius, deinde & corpus paralytici oblati curaret, optimè infertur à B. Ambrof. in Luc. 5. ambiendum esse peccatori Ecclesiæ suffragium, cujus contemplatione, quod illi Dominus negare posset, ignoscat. At pessime ego in priori hujus Commentarii editione tenebris errorum Ecclesiæ Romanæ obvolutus hïc scripseram duplex esse meriti humani genus, de congruo scilicet & de condigno, illud improprie, hoc esse meritum proprie dictum. Nam ut ait Durandus 2. Sent. Diftinct. 27. q. 2. Meritum de condigno stricte & proprie acceptum actio est voluntaria, propter quam debetur alicui merces ex justitia, sic quod si non reddatur, ille ad quem pertinet reddere, injustè facit, & est simpliciter & proprie injustus: & tale meritum de condigno inveniri inter homines, sed non est hominis ad Deum. Causa autem hujus est, & illud quod sumus, & quod habemus, sive sint boni actus, sive boni habitus, vel usus, totum est in nobis ex liberalitate divina gratis dante & conservante: & quia ex dono gratuito nullus obligatur ad dandum amplius, sed potius recipiens magis obligatur danti, ideo ex bonis habitibus, & ex bonis actibus sive-usibus nobis à Deo datis, Deus nobis non obligatur ex debito aliquo justitiae ad aliquid amplius dandum, ita quod si non dederit, sit injustus, sed potius nos sumus Deo obligati. Et sentire, seu dicere oppositum est temerarium, seu blasphemum. Verbum mereri seu mereri usurparunt Patres passim pro impetrare vel adipisci. Unde illud Fulgentii lib. De incarnatione & gratia Christi cap. 7. Ipsum Deum hominem factum & concipere, & parere Maria, non humanis meritis, sed concepti, nascentisque ex ea summi Dei dignatione meruit. Et celebre est illud Zozimi, P. O felix culpa, quae talem ac tantum meruit habere Redemtorem. Meritum nullum praesupponens Dei promissionem, quod vulgò Romanenses vocant de congruo absurdum impietatis figmentum est; cum enim nullum praemium Deus nobis rependat unquam propter condignitatem praestiti operis, sed ex mera liberalitatis suae promissione, & in servandis promissis constantia, clarum est quod quicquid non praesupponit Dei promissionem, non habet relationem ad praemium, proindeque nullam habet rationem meriti. Verum ut Scriptura καταχρηστικῶς Mercedem vocavit gratuito & liberaliter promissa à Deo bonis operibus justificationem nostram in Christo consequentibus praemia, ita PP. καταχρηστικῶς Merita vocavere ipsa opera bona, quae sunt fructus fidei, & justificantem sequuntur; at verfatiores erant PP. in lectione Scripturae, & religiosiores quàm ut vel somniaverint hanc blasphemiam, quâ ii dicuntur proprie mereri, seu mereri de condigno Dei respectu, quorum omnes justitiae tanquam pannus menstruatae mulieris, ut loquitur Vates, & omne meritum miseratio Domino, ut loquitur Bernardus Serm. 61. in Cant. Quis enim nostrum, exclamat Ambr. in Ps. 118: Octon. 20. sine divina miseratione potest subsistere? Quid possumus facere dignum praemiis caelestibus? Non ergo secundum merita nostra, sed secundum misericordiam Dei caelestium decretorum forma procedit. Neque enim, inquit Bernardus Serm. 1. in Annunt. B. Mariae, talia sunt hominum merita, ut propter ea vita aeterna debeatur ex jure, aut Deus aliquam injuriam faceret, nisi eam donaret. Nam ut taceam quod merita omnia dona Dei sunt, & ideo homo magis propter ter ipsa Deo debitor est, quàm Deus homini: quid suut merita omnia ad tantam gloriam? Denique quis melior est Propheta, cui Dominus ipse tam insigne testimonium perhibet dicens, Virum inveni secundum cor meum? Verumtamen & ipse necessum habuit dicere Deo, Non intres in judicium cum servo tuo Domine. Nemo itaque se seducat. Præclare itaque Cassiodorus lib. De anima cap. ultimo Deum sic alloquitur: Meritum nostrum indulgentia tua est: dona quod offeram, cuiusdam quod exigas, ut velis coronare quod præstas. Domine in nobis non est quod remunereris, sed in te semper est quod largiaris. Contra peccata nostra misericordia tua munimen insurgat. Petimus, quia jubes, o altitudo pietatis! Clementiæ incomprehensa, profunditas dimitte peccata, & concede non debita.
units.tr: Seeing, etc. From the fact that Christ mercifully regarded the faith of those bringing the paralytic, healing first his soul and then the body of the man brought to him, by the help of another's faith, the blessed Ambrose rightly infers in Luke 5 that a sinner should seek the help of the Church, by whose intercession the Lord may forgive what he might otherwise refuse. But in the earlier edition of this commentary I wrote here, wrapped most wretchedly in the darkness of the errors of the Roman Church, that there are two kinds of human merit, the one of congruity and the other of condignity, the first improperly so called and the second being merit properly speaking. For as Durandus says in 2 Sent., distinction 27, question 2: Merit of condignity, taken strictly and properly, is a voluntary action on account of which a reward is owed to someone from justice, so that if it is not paid, he to whom it belongs to pay acts unjustly and is simply and properly unjust; and such merit of condignity is found among men, but not of man towards God. The cause of this is that both what we are and what we have, whether good acts, good habits, or uses, is wholly in us from the divine liberality freely giving and preserving them; and because no one who has received a free gift is obliged to give more, but rather the recipient is more obliged to the giver, therefore God is not bound to us by any debt of justice to give anything further on account of the good habits and good acts or uses given us by God, so that if he did not give, he would be unjust; rather we are obliged to God. And to think or say the opposite is rash or blasphemous. The Fathers everywhere used the word to merit or to deserve for to obtain or to attain. Hence that saying of Fulgentius in his book On the Incarnation and Grace of Christ, chapter 7: That God himself, made man, should be conceived and born of Mary, he merited not by human merits, but by the favour of the highest God, conceived and born of her. And famous is that saying of Zosimus: O happy fault, which deserved to have such and so great a Redeemer. Merit that presupposes no promise of God, which the Romanists commonly call of congruity, is an absurd fiction of impiety; for since God never repays us any reward on account of the worthiness of the work done, but from the mere promise of his liberality and the constancy of keeping his promises, it is clear that whatever does not presuppose God's promise has no relation to a reward, and therefore has no character of merit at all. But just as Scripture catachrestically [καταχρηστικῶς] called rewards those good works freely and generously promised by God to follow our justification in Christ, so the Fathers catachrestically called good works themselves merits, namely the fruits of faith which follow justification. But the Fathers were too well versed in the reading of Scripture and too religious even to have dreamed of this blasphemy, by which those men are said to merit properly, or to merit of condignity with respect to God, of whom all our righteousnesses are as a polluted garment, as the prophet says, and every merit is the mercy of the Lord, as Bernard says in Sermon 61 on the Song of Songs. For who among us, cries Ambrose on Psalm 118, octonary 20, can stand without divine mercy? What can we do that is worthy of the heavenly rewards? Therefore the form of the heavenly decrees proceeds not according to our merits, but according to the mercy of God. For, as Bernard says in Sermon 1 on the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin Mary, human merits are not such that eternal life is due on account of them by right, or else God would do wrong unless he gave it freely. For, to pass over the fact that all merits are gifts of God, and therefore man is more indebted to God on account of them than God to man, what are all merits to so great a glory? Finally, who is a better prophet than the one to whom the Lord himself bore such notable witness, saying, "I have found a man after my own heart"? Yet even he had to say to God, "Enter not into judgment with your servant, O Lord." Let no one therefore deceive himself. Accordingly Cassiodorus, in the last chapter of his book On the Soul, addresses God well in these words: Our merit is your indulgence; what we offer is a gift of yours, what you require is of yours, so that you may choose to crown what you yourself grant. Lord, there is nothing in us for you to reward, but in you there is always something to bestow. Against our sins let your mercy rise up as a defence. We ask, because you command, O height of piety! O unfathomable depth of clemency, forgive our sins and grant what is not owed.

units.la: Confide, &c. Q. d. Cùm infirmitatis tuæ causa sint peccata tua, jam male animo, & spera tibi sanitatem restitutuam iri, quia remittuntur tibi peccata tua hoc ipso dicto meo, quo ea remitti pronuntio.
units.tr: Take courage, etc. That is: since your sins are the cause of your weakness, now be of good cheer and hope that your health will be restored to you, because your sins are forgiven you by this very word of mine, by which I declare them forgiven.

units.la: Fili. Luc. 5. v. 20. Homo. Sed in hoc nulla est Evangelistarum antilogia, quia pallam alter verba, alter sensum referre solet in his, quas recensent historias.
units.tr: Son. Luke 5, verse 20. Man. But there is no contradiction between the Evangelists here, since in these histories one usually reports the words and another the sense.

units.la: 3. Dixerunt intra se. Intra se atque in corde suo dicere est cogitando dicere. Aug. 15. Trin. c. 10.
units.tr: 3. They said within themselves. To say within oneself, or in one's heart, is to say by thinking. Augustine, On the Trinity, book 15, chapter 10.

units.la: 4. Ut quid cogitatis mala. Quod velis homines nescire, ne feceris; quod Deum, ne cogitaveris. B. Eucherius in Ep. De contemtu mundi. Parietibus oculi hominum submoventur, Dei autem divinitas nec visceribus submoveri potest, inquit Seneca apud Lactantium lib. 6. Divin. Institut. cap. 24.
units.tr: 4. Why do you think evil? What you want men not to know, do not do; what you want God not to know, do not think. Blessed Eucherius, in the Letter On Contempt of the World. The eyes of men can be kept off by walls, but the divinity of God cannot be kept off even from the inward parts, says Seneca, as quoted by Lactantius in book 6 of the Divine Institutes, chapter 24.

units.la: 5. Facilius. Id est, minori cum periculo famæ suæ. Tria Christus hic dicit paralytico: Remittuntur tibi peccata tua: sed hoc sine ullo periculo convincendæ falsitatis, cùm Deus solus noverit quorum remissæ sint iniquitates; Pharisæis & Scribis dixit. Ut quid cogitatis mala in cordibus vestris? Quod nisi esset Dominus scrutans corda & probans renes, dicere non potuisset, quin ab iisdem Scribis & Pharisæis mendacii argueretur; tandem paralytico dixit: Surge, tolle lectum tuum & vade in domum tuam: cujus dicti effectus cum deberet esse manifestusomnibus, ab omnibus mendacii suisset redargutus Christus, nisi statim coram omnibus ad ipsius Christi imperium surrexisset paralyticus, tulisset grabatum suum & abiisset in domum suam. Probat itaque Christus fidem sibi esse adhibendam in re, quæ palpabili effectu, probari non potest, ex veritate assertionis de re, quæ statim atque prolata est, palpabilem requirit probationem.
units.tr: 5. More easily. That is, with less danger to his reputation. Christ here says three things to the paralytic. Your sins are forgiven you: but this could be said without any danger of the falsehood being exposed, since God alone knows whose iniquities have been forgiven. He said to the Pharisees and scribes, Why do you think evil in your hearts? Unless the Lord were searching hearts and trying the reins, he could not have said this without being convicted of lying by the same scribes and Pharisees. Finally he said to the paralytic, Rise, take up your bed and go into your house. Since the effect of this word ought to have been plain to all, Christ would have been convicted of lying before everyone, unless at once, before all, the paralytic had risen at Christ's command, taken up his couch and gone away to his house. Christ therefore proves that faith is to be given to him in a matter which cannot be proved by a visible effect, from the truth of an assertion about a matter which, as soon as it is uttered, demands a visible proof.

units.la: 8. Timuerunt. Scilicet timore admirationi adjuncto, ut patet ex Marc. 2. v. 12. & Luc. 5. v. 26. Unde iu textu Græco habetur hic: Turbæ admiratæ sunt. Hoc sensu dicitur 3 Reg. c. 3. v. 28. Timuerunt Regem, videntes sapientiam Dei esse in eo ad faciendum judicium.
units.tr: 8. They were afraid. That is, with fear joined to wonder, as is clear from Mark 2, verse 12, and Luke 5, verse 26. Hence the Greek text here has: the crowds were amazed. In this sense it is said in 3 Kings chapter 3, verse 28: They feared the king, seeing that the wisdom of God was in him to do judgment.

units.la: 9. Cùm transfiret inde. Supple ex Marc. 2. v. 13. ad mare, scilicet, Galilææ.
units.tr: 9. When he passed on from there. Supply from Mark 2:13: to the sea, namely of Galilee.

units.la: In Telonio. Telonium locus est in quo colligitur vectigal, quod Græcis est τελώνης, unde & telonarius dicitur, qui vectigal colligit.
units.tr: At the tax office. A telonium is the place where the customs duty is collected. The Greek is telōnēs [τελώνης], and so the collector of the duty is called a telonarius.

units.la: Matthæum, &c. Ceteri Evangelistæ propter verecundiam & honorem Matthæi, noluerunt eum nomine appellare vulgato, sed dixerunt, Levi. Duplici quippe vocabulo fuit. Ipse autem Matthæus, secundum illud quod dicitur à Salomone: Justus accusator est sui in principio sermonis. Et in alio loco: Dic tu peccata tua, ut justificeris: Matthæum se & Publicanum nominat: ut offendat legentibus nullum debere salutem deferre, si ad meliora conversus sit: cùm ipse de Publicano in Apostolum sit repentè mutatus. Arguit in hoc loco Porphyrius & Julianus Augustus, vel imperitiam historici mentientis, vel stultitiam eorum qui statim secuti sint Salvatorem, quasi irrationabiliter quemlibet vocantem hominem sint secuti, cùm tantæ virtutes, tantaque signa præcesserint, quæ Apostolos, antequam crederent, vidisse non dubium est. Certe fulgor ipse, & majestas Divinitatis occultæ; quæ etiam in humana facie relucebat, ex primo ad se videntes trahere poterat aspectu. Si enim in magnete lapide & succinis hæc esse vis dicitur, ut annulos & stipulant, & festucas sibi copulent: quanto magis Dominus omnium creaturarum ad se trahere poterat, quos volebat? B. Hier.
units.tr: Matthew, etc. Out of modesty and regard for Matthew, the other Evangelists did not wish to name him by his common name, but said "Levi." He had a double name. Matthew himself, following what Solomon says, "The righteous man is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech," and in another place, "Tell your sins, that you may be justified," names himself Matthew the Publican, so that he may offend readers who think no one should be granted salvation if he has turned to better things, since he himself was suddenly changed from a publican into an apostle. In this passage Porphyry and the Emperor Julian argue either the ignorance of a lying historian or the foolishness of those who at once followed the Saviour, as though they had followed without reason any man who called them, when such great virtues and such great signs had gone before, which the Apostles undoubtedly saw before they believed. Surely the very splendour and majesty of the hidden Godhead, which even shone in the human face, could draw men to himself at the first glance. For if this power is said to be in the magnet stone and in amber, so that they join rings and straws to themselves, how much more could the Lord of all creatures draw to himself those whom he willed? B. Hier.

units.la: Sequere me. Id est, meo discipulatui indivulsè inhære
units.tr: Follow me. That is, cling inseparably to my discipleship.

units.la: Secutus est eum. Supple ex Luc. 5. v. 27. relictis omnibus.
units.tr: He followed him. Supply from Luke 5:27: having left everything.

units.la: 10. In domo. Scilicet Matthæi, ut patet ex Marc. 2. v. 15. & Luc. 5. v. 24.
units.tr: 10. In the house. Namely Matthew's, as is clear from Mark 2:15 and Luke 5:24.

units.la: Ecce multi Publicani. Forte à Matthæo invitati, vel Matthæi exemplo ad meliora conversi, & Christi humanitate tracti, erant enim multi qui inquit Marcus, & sequebantur eum.
units.tr: Behold, many publicans. Perhaps invited by Matthew, or turned to better things by Matthew's example, and drawn by the kindness of Christ; for there were many who, as Mark says, also followed him.

units.la: Peccatores. Id est, homines vitæ aperte improbæ.
units.tr: Sinners. That is, men of openly wicked life.

units.la: 11. Et videntes Pharisæi, Id est, cùm id Pharisæi post convivium audiissent; patet enim eos convivio non inter fuisse.
units.tr: 11. And when the Pharisees saw: that is, when the Pharisees heard this after the banquet; for it is clear they were not present at the feast.

units.la: Quare, &c. Lucas cap. 5. aliquanto differentius hoc videtur commemorasse secundum quem dicunt Pharisæi discipulis: Quare cum Publicanis & peccatoribus manducatis & bibitis? non tantum Christo, sed ipsi & discipulis ejus objectum insinuans, quod cum peccatoribus manducarent. Verum cum discipulis dicebatur, magistro magis objiciebatur, quem sectando imitabantur, unde Matth. & Marc. de Christo discipulis objectum narrant. Una ergo est sententia & tanto melius à tribus Evangelistis insinuata, quanto quibusdam verbis, manente veritate, variata. Ita fere B. Aug. lib. 2. de conf. Evang. cap. 27.
units.tr: Why, etc. Luke in chapter 5 seems to have recorded this somewhat differently, where the Pharisees say to the disciples, "Why do you eat and drink with publicans and sinners?" thus hinting that the objection was made not only to Christ but also to his disciples, that they ate with sinners. But when it was said to the disciples, the objection was aimed more at the Master, whom they imitated by following him; hence Matthew and Mark report it as objected to the disciples concerning Christ. There is therefore one meaning, and it is conveyed all the better by the three Evangelists, the more it is varied in some words while the truth remains. So nearly Blessed Augustine, On the Harmony of the Gospels, book 2, chapter 27.

units.la: 12. Non est opus, &c. Q. d. Medicus sum animarum, tolle animæ vulnera, tolle morbos, & nulla erit mei necessitas. Ovid 3. de Pont. Eleg. 4.
units.tr: 12. There is no need, etc. As if to say: I am a physician of souls; take away the wounds of the soul, take away the diseases, and there will be no need of me. Ovid, Tristia, book 3, elegy 4.

units.la: Firma valens per se nullúmque Machaonâ quærit, Ad medicam dubius confugit æger opem.
units.tr: The healthy man, strong in himself, seeks no Machaon; the sick man, uncertain, flies to the physician's help.

units.la: 13. Euntes autem discite. Id est, ite, discite. Est autem hic Hebraismus Scripturæ familiaris, ut Exod. 10. v. 8. Ite, sacrificate. Judic. 10. v. 14. Ite & invocate Deos, &c.
units.tr: 13. But go and learn. That is, go, learn. This is a Hebraism familiar in Scripture, as in Exod. 10:8, Go, sacrifice. Judg. 10:14, Go and call upon the gods, etc.

units.la: Quid est. Id est, quid sibi velit ista prophetica sententia.
units.tr: What is it. That is, what this prophetic saying means.

units.la: Misericordiam volo & non sacrificium. Id est, misericordiam magis volo, quam sacrificium, seu præfero interna misericordiæ sacrificia externo religionis sacrificio; Talibus enim hostiis promeretur (id est, delectatur) Deus, ut ait Apost. Hebr. 13. v. 16. Familiare autem est Scripturæ cum unum alteri præfert, prælatum omnino affirmare, & id, cui præfertur, omnino negare. Sic dicitur Joan. 7. v. 16. Mea doctrina non est mea, sed ejus qui misit me Patris: Id est, mea doctrina non est tam mea, quam Patris, &c.
units.tr: I will have mercy and not sacrifice. That is, I desire mercy rather than sacrifice; or I prefer the inward sacrifices of mercy to the outward sacrifice of religious worship. For with such sacrifices God is well pleased (that is, delighted), as the Apostle says, Heb. 13:16. It is a familiar feature of Scripture, when one thing is preferred to another, to affirm absolutely the thing preferred and wholly to deny that to which it is preferred. So it is said in John 7:16, My doctrine is not mine, but his who sent me, the Father: that is, my doctrine is not so much mine as the Father's, etc.

units.la: Non enim, &c. Reddit rationem ejus, quod dixerat v. 12. ut patet ex Marc. 2. v. 27. & Luc. 5. v. 32.
units.tr: For not, etc. It gives the reason for what he had said in verse 12, as is clear from Mark 2:27 and Luke 5:32.

units.la: Veni. Id est, naturam humanam assumsi, & cum hominibus conversatus sum.
units.tr: I came. That is, I took on human nature and lived among men.

units.la: Vocare justos. Hoc est, ut solvetem præmia justis; omnes enim peccaverunt, & egentes gloria Dei. Si vis curam, agnosce languorem. Si vis misericordiam, confitere peccatum. Chrysol. Ser. 30.
units.tr: To call the righteous. That is, to pay rewards to the just; for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God. If you want healing, acknowledge the sickness. If you want mercy, confess the sin. Chrysologus, Sermon 30.

units.la: Sed peccatores, supple ex textu Græco hic & Marc. 2. v. 17. & ex ipso textu Vulgato Luc. 5. 32. Ad pænitentiam. Hinc non minus vere, quàm eleganter & ad mentem Evan- gelii B. Prosper in insigni illo carmine de ingratis cap. 17.
units.tr: But sinners: supply from the Greek text here and from Mark 2:17, and from the Vulgate text itself at Luke 5:32, to repentance. Hence Blessed Prosper, no less truly than elegantly and in accordance with the mind of the Gospel, in that notable poem On the Ungrateful, chapter 17:

units.la: Vsque adeò donum est, quod credimus, & data gratis Gratia non merita ditat mercede vocatos: Nec justorum operum discernit facta, sed omnes Sola ex immundis mundos facit: utque legentem Lectus amet, non hoc studio, sed munere sumit. Nam si spectatrix meritorum est gratia, & illis Se tribuit, quorum est animus purgatior, & quos Per libertatem arbitrii sibi repperit aptos: Infontes tantùm, justóque adsumere solos Debuit, & veri cupidos, ac recta volentes. Perversos autem, & scelerum assuetudine turpes Deturbare procul, lucémque negare tenebris, Atqui Salvator mundi non præmia justis Solvere, necsanis venit conferre medelam: Sed quod dispersum exciderat, fractúmque jacebat, Quaerere, & inventum reparare, & reddere curæ.
units.tr: So much is it a gift, which we believe, that grace, given freely and not for merits, enriches those who are called with a reward they did not earn. It does not discern the deeds of just works, but alone makes the clean out of the unclean; and as a reader loves what he has read, so it takes them, not from zeal but as a gift. For if grace were the judge of merits, and bestowed itself on those whose minds are purer and whom it found fit through the free choice of the will, it ought to have taken only the innocent and the just, and those who desire truth and wish what is right. But to cast far away the perverse, and those foul through habit of crimes, and to deny light to darkness: yet the Saviour of the world did not come to pay rewards to the just, nor to bring a remedy to the sound; but to seek what had scattered and fallen, and lay broken, and to find it and restore it, and to return it to care.

units.la: 14. Tunc accesserunt. &c. Quòd Evangelistæ inducant in disceptatione de jejunio, nunc discipulos Joannis Christum interrogantes, ut Matth. nunc Pharisæos solos, ut Lucas, nunc verò utrosque ut Marcus, nulla dissonantia est. Satis ex contextu conjicere est Pharisæos præ invidia in Christum instigasse discipulos Joannis, & utrosque Christum interrogasse, diverso licet animo.
units.tr: 14. Then came, etc. That the Evangelists, in the dispute about fasting, introduce now the disciples of John questioning Christ, as Matthew; now the Pharisees alone, as Luke; and now both, as Mark, is no discrepancy. From the context it is enough to infer that the Pharisees, out of envy, stirred up John's disciples against Christ, and that both questioned Christ, though with different intentions.

units.la: 15. Filii sponsi. Marc. 2. v. 19. Filii nuptiarum. Est autem Hebraismus, quo significantur ii, qui Judic. 14. v. 20. vocantur amici ac pronubi; qui familiares sponsi sunt, qui vocati ad ejus nuptias, eas variis lætitiæ argumentis celebrant. Simili Hebraismo dicuntur filii lucis, regni, tenebrarum, superbiæ, iniquitatis, &c.
units.tr: 15. Sons of the bridegroom. Mark 2:19 has sons of the wedding. This is a Hebraism by which are meant those who in Judg. 14:20 are called friends and best men; they are the intimates of the bridegroom, who, invited to his wedding, celebrate it with various tokens of joy. By a similar Hebraism they are called sons of light, of the kingdom, of darkness, of pride, of iniquity, etc.

units.la: Lugere. Id est jejunare, ut patet ex Marc. 2. v. 19. & Luc. 5. v. 34. Luctus ergo dicitur jejunium, vel quia jejunium facit homines mœstos, vel quia lugentes cibo abstinere solebant, ut constat ex Judic. 20. v. 26. 1 Regum 7. v. 6. 31. v. 13.
units.tr: To mourn. That is, to fast, as is clear from Mark 2:19 and Luke 5:34. Mourning is therefore called fasting, either because fasting makes men sad, or because those who mourn were accustomed to abstain from food, as is clear from Judg. 20:26, 1 Kings 7:6, 31:13.

units.la: Quamdiu cum illis est sponsus. Joannes igitur jejunabat licèt amicus sponsi, ut dicitur Joan. 3. v. 29. quia cum illo non semper erat sponsus, sicut cum discipulis erat, qui eum sequebantur quocumque pergeret.
units.tr: As long as the bridegroom is with them. John therefore fasted although he was the friend of the bridegroom, as is said in John 3:29, because the bridegroom was not always with him as he was with the disciples, who followed him wherever he went.

units.la: Cùm auferetur. Per mortem scilicet vel assumtionem in cælos.
units.tr: When he is taken away. Namely by death, or by being taken up into heaven.

units.la: Tunc jejunabunt. Eventus hanc Christi sententiam declaravit ravit, ut videre est Act. 13. v. 2, & 3. 2 Cor. 6. v. 5.
units.tr: Then they will fast. The outcome declared this saying of Christ, as may be seen in Acts 13:2, 3, and 2 Cor. 6:5.

units.la: 16. Nemo autem. Probat exemplis prudenter à se imbecillitatis discipulorum habitam fuisse rationem in tradendo vitæ genere, ne ipsum relinquerent.
units.tr: 16. No one. He proves by examples that he had prudently taken account of the weakness of the disciples in prescribing their way of life, lest they leave him.

units.la: Immittit commissuram panni rudis. Id est, infuit fructum panni novi; hunc sensum his verbis expressit Lucas. 5. v. 36. Nemo commissuram a novo vestimento immittit.
units.tr: He puts a patch of raw cloth. That is, he sews in a piece of new cloth. Luke expressed this sense in these words, Luke 5:36, No one puts a patch from a new garment.

units.la: In vetus vestimentum. Supple, reparandum.
units.tr: Into an old garment. Supply: to be mended.

units.la: Tollit enim. Scilicet, commissura panni rudis rigore suo.
units.tr: For it takes away: namely, the seam of a raw cloth by its stiffness.

units.la: Plenitudinem ejus. Hebraismus, id est, integritatem suam.
units.tr: Its fullness: a Hebraism, that is, its integrity.

units.la: A Vestimento. Supple ex Marc. 2. v. 21. veteri.
units.tr: From the garment: supply from Mark 2:21, "old."

units.la: Pejor. Id est major, proindeque restauratu difficilior. Addit Lucas & aliud incommodum, nempe ruptionem novi panni, seu vestimenti, & indecentiam commissuræ panni rudis, seu ut Lucas loquitur, a vestimento novo, in vestimento veteri.
units.tr: Worse: that is, greater, and therefore harder to repair. Luke adds another inconvenience, namely the tearing of the new cloth or garment, and the unsightliness of the seam of the raw cloth, or, as Luke puts it, "from the new garment," on the old garment.

units.la: Princeps. Supple ex Luc. 8. v. 41. Synagoga, cui nomen Jairus. Hanc historiam Marcus & Lucas quoque narrant, sed quo præcisè tempore contigerit ex solis Matthæi verbis, Hæc illo loquente ad eos, ecce, &c. apparet.
units.tr: A ruler: supply from Luke 8:41, "a synagogue ruler whose name was Jairus." Mark and Luke also relate this story, but the exact time when it happened appears only from Matthew's words, "While he was speaking these things to them, behold," etc.

units.la: Adorabat eum. Supple ex Marc. 5. & Luc. 8. procidens ad pedes ejus.
units.tr: He worshipped him: supply from Mark 5 and Luke 8, "falling at his feet."

units.la: Filia mea. Supple ex Luc. 8. unica annorum duodecim.
units.tr: My daughter: supply from Luke 8, "her only daughter, about twelve years old."

units.la: Modò defuncta est. Quia Jairus unicam filiam unicè diligebat eamque graviter & periculosè laborantem reliquerat domi, poterat præ magno affectu utrumque dixisse Christo, scilicet filia mea moritur, & fere modò mortua est; vel verba Matthæi intelliguntur, ut plerumque fit, q. d. Mortua est nisi promte venias; vel denique quod probabilius est, Matth. brevitati studens ultimam tantum petitionem posuit, nuntiatâ filiæ morte.
units.tr: Has just died: Because Jairus loved his only daughter with singular affection, and had left her at home gravely and dangerously ill, he could, out of great feeling, have said to Christ both things: my daughter is dying, and is almost just now dead. Or Matthew's words are understood, as often happens, as if he had said, "She is dead unless you come quickly." Or finally, what is more probable: Matthew, aiming at brevity, gave only the last request, the daughter's death having been announced.

units.la: 20. Duodecim annis. Advertit B. Hieron. lib. 18. in Efaiam tunc hæmorrhoissam ægrotare coepisse quando nata est filia Archisynagogi, & quando ista sanata est, statim illam esse mortuam; Divinóque ingenio, ut Marianus loquitur, idem sanctus Doctor trahit hanc similitudinem ad duos populos, Judæorum scilicet & Gentilium: etenim surgentibus ad fidem Judæis gentes ægrotare coeperunt: sanatæ autem sunt istæ & ad fidem venerunt, cum Judæi fidem in qua nati erant perdiderunt. Et ita ubi unus desiit populus alter coepit.
units.tr: 20. Twelve years: Jerome, in book 18 on Isaiah, observes that the woman with the issue of blood began to be ill at the time the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue was born, and that as soon as the daughter was healed, the woman was dead. By a "divine ingenuity," as Marianus puts it, the same holy Doctor draws this likeness to two peoples, namely the Jews and the Gentiles: for while the Jews rose up to the faith, the Gentiles began to fall ill; but these were healed and came to the faith when the Jews lost the faith into which they had been born. And so where one people ceased, the other began.

units.la: Tetigit fimbriam vestimenti ejus. Fimbria vocantur fila dependentia in quatuor oris seu extremitatibus pallii, quæ jussit Deus Judæos portare, ut esset insigne distinctionis suæ à ceteris gentibus, & nota sanctitatis. Vide Num. 15. v. 38. & Zach. 8. v. 23. Hinc invictum argumentum pro Reliquiarum cultu desumitur, aiebam in prima hujus commentarii editione, superstitiosâ Romanensium praxi abreptus, nec attendebam quàm stupidè ex eo, quod Hæmorrhoissa colens Christum vestimento indutum, fideliter eum tetigit per fimbriam vestimenti, inferatur vestimentum à Christo exûtum esse adorandum, aut Reliquias Sanctorum esse colendas. Has tamen supidissimas sequelas non ut probabiles modò, sed etiam ut necessarias & invictas intuebar, priusquam Deus ineffabili benignitate suâ sedentem in tenebris Romanensium ad lucem Ecclesiarum ad Scripturæ normam reformatarum vocasset, quæ puritatem Evangelii sectantes unicè, sic Sanctos prædicant honorificà æstimaticne venerandos ob pietatem, ut tamen non fit nobis religio cultus Sanctorum, quomodo loquitur B. August. De vera religione c. 55. Corpora Sanctorum honorificè sepelienda, quomodo viri timorati Stephanum, & discipuli Baptistam sepelierunt, omnis Orthodoxus profitetur. At eadem corpora sepulta effodere, ut effossa in capsis serventur, & in processionibus circumferantur, osculis, prostrationibus, votis, oblationibus & supplicationibus colantur, non solùm improbamus, sed insuper dicimus esse μετάθεσιν τῆς προσκυνήσεως ἀπὸ τῆς πεποιημένοτ ἐπὶ τὰ κτίσματα, quomodo idololatriam definit Gregorius Theologus Orat. 33. à qua cultûs translatione abhorruit primitiva Ecclesia edocta ab Apostolo Rom. 1. v. 25. quàm severa fuerit Dei vindicta in eos, qui coluerunt & servierunt creaturæ potiùs, quàm creatori dicenti Ef.42.v.8. Ego Dominus, hoc est nomen meum: gloriam meam alteri non dabo, nec laudem meam sculptilibus.
units.tr: She touched the hem of his garment. The fringes are the threads hanging from the four corners or edges of the cloak, which God commanded the Jews to wear, so that it would be a distinguishing mark of their own from the other nations, and a sign of holiness. See Num. 15:38 and Zech. 8:23. "From this an unconquered argument is drawn for the cult of relics," I said in the first edition of this commentary, carried away by the superstitious practice of the Romanists, and I did not notice how stupidly it is inferred from the fact that the woman with the issue of blood, honouring Christ clothed in a garment, faithfully touched him by the fringe of the garment, that the garment that Christ put off is to be adored, or that the relics of the saints are to be venerated. Yet I regarded these most foolish consequences not merely as probable but as necessary and unconquerable, before God, in his ineffable kindness, called those sitting in the darkness of the Romanists to the light of the Churches reformed according to the norm of Scripture, which, pursuing the purity of the Gospel alone, so honour the saints as worthy of veneration on account of their piety, yet "the cult of the saints is not a religion to us," as Blessed Augustine says in On True Religion, chapter 55. That the bodies of the saints are to be buried with honour, as God-fearing men buried Stephen and the disciples buried the Baptist, every orthodox person professes. But to dig up the same bodies once buried, so that they may be kept in caskets when dug up and carried about in processions, and to honour them with kisses, prostrations, vows, offerings and supplications, we not only disapprove but moreover say that it is a transference of worship from the Creator to the creatures, as Gregory the Theologian defines idolatry in Oration 33, from which transference of worship the primitive Church shrank, taught by the Apostle in Romans 1:25. How severe God's vengeance was against those who "worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator," saying in Isaiah 42:8: "I am the Lord, that is my name: I will not give my glory to another, nor my praise to graven images."

units.la: 22. Fides tua te salvam fecit. Id est, fides, quam misericorditer in corde tuo sum operatus, tibi impetravit ut virtus mea te salvam faceret effectivè.
units.tr: 22. Your faith has made you whole: that is, the faith which I have mercifully worked in your heart has obtained for you that my power should make you whole effectively.

units.la: Et salva facta est mulier in illa hora. Quà scilicet simbriam vestimenti tetigerat, vel sensus verborum Matth. est, & confirmata est illi salus, quam consecuta erat per contactum fimbriæ ex illo momento, quo Christus illi dixit, Fides tua te salvam fecit. Vide Marc. 5. ubi præsens hæc historia fusius narratur, & accuratius explicatur.
units.tr: And the woman was made whole from that hour: namely, from the time she had touched the hem of the garment; or the sense of Matthew's words is: the health which she had obtained through touching the hem was confirmed to her from the moment Christ said to her, "Your faith has made you whole." See Mark 5, where this present story is told more fully and explained more accurately.

units.la: 23. Tibicines. A gentibus ad omne funus lamentatrices & tibicines adhibere solitis videtur hic mos ad Judæos permanasse. Vide Jerem. 9. v. 17. & 18. Lucianum in DiaDialogo de luctu. Ovid. 4. Fasto. B. Ambro. lib. 8. in Luc.
units.tr: 23. Flute-players: this custom of employing mourning women and flute-players at every funeral, which seems to have been practised by the nations, appears to have spread to the Jews. See Jeremiah 9:17–18; Lucian in the Dialogue on Mourning; Ovid, Fasti book 4; Blessed Ambrose, book 8 on Luke.

units.la: 24. Non est enim mortua puella, sed dormit. Id est, non excessit e vivis ut non resurgat, nisi in novissimo die, sed mox resurget, unde ipsius mors tam brevi temporis spatio duratura, non tam mors est dicenda, quàm somnus seu mortis imago.
units.tr: 24. For the girl is not dead, but sleeping: that is, she has not departed from the living so as not to rise again, except on the last day; but she will soon rise again. Hence her death, which would last for so short a span of time, is to be called not so much death as sleep, or an image of death.

units.la: Deridebant eum. Scilicet, quia non capiebant sensum verborum ejus. Porro ambiguis verbis usus est Christus eadem de causa, quà teste Marco præcepit puellæ parentibus & iis qui secum erant, id est, ut patet ex Luc. c. 8. Petro, Jacobo, & Joanni, ne alicui dicerent.
units.tr: They laughed him to scorn: namely, because they did not grasp the sense of his words. Moreover Christ used ambiguous words for the same reason for which, as Mark testifies, he ordered the girl's parents and those who were with him, that is, as is clear from Luke chapter 8, Peter, James and John, not to tell anyone.

units.la: 28. Venisset domum. Id est, in civitatem Capharnaum, ubi domicilium elegerat.
units.tr: 28. Had come home: that is, to the city of Capernaum, where he had chosen his dwelling.

units.la: Creditis. Qui cæcis reddere poterat visum, non ignorabat an crederent, sed ideo interrogavit, ut quam corde gestabant fidem ad justitiam, ore confiterentur ad salutem,
units.tr: Do you believe? He who could restore sight to the blind did not fail to know whether they believed, but he asked so that they might confess with their mouths unto salvation the faith they bore in their hearts unto righteousness.

units.la: Possum. Supple, mea authoritate.
units.tr: I am able: supply, by my authority.

units.la: 29. Secundum fidem, &c. Operatio miraculorum attribuitur fidei propter duo: Primò quidem, quia ordinatur ad fidei confirmationem: Secundò, quia processit ex Dei omnipotentia, cui fides innititur. D. Th. 22.æ. q. 178. ar. 1. ad 5m.
units.tr: 29. "According to your faith," etc. The working of miracles is ascribed to faith for two reasons: first, because it is ordered to the confirmation of faith; second, because it proceeds from the omnipotence of God, on which faith rests. Aquinas, 2a2ae, q. 178, art. 1, ad 5.

units.la: 30. Aperti sunt oculi eorum. Hebraismus, id est, coeperunt videre.
units.tr: 30. Their eyes were opened: a Hebraism, that is, they began to see.

units.la: 32. Hominem mutum. Apud Lucam ipsum dæmonium dicitur mutum, scilicet effectivè.
units.tr: 32. A dumb man: In Luke the demon itself is called dumb, namely effectively.

units.la: 34. In principe. Id est ope, seu invocatione principis.
units.tr: 34. By the prince: that is, by the power or invocation of the prince.

units.la: 35. Circuibat. Anticipat Matthæus secundam peragrationem Galilææ, & missionem Apostolorum à Christo factam, ut videre est apud Marcum cap. 6.
units.tr: 35. He went about: Matthew anticipates the second circuit of Galilee and the sending out of the Apostles by Christ, as may be seen in Mark chapter 6.

units.la: Omnem languorem. Id est languorem omnis generis. Sic Gen. 2. v. 16. Ex omni ligno Paradisi comede: id est ex omni fructuum genere; ubi & arbor seu lignum est pro fructu arboris. Exod. 9 v. 6. Mortuaque sunt omnia animantia Ægyptiorum, id est, ex omni animantium genere; sequitur enim ibidem v. 25. Et percussit grando in omni terra Ægypti cuncta quæ fuerunt in agris, ab homine usque ad jumentum. Similiter Apostolus dixit in Ep. ad Philip. c. 2. Omnes quæ sua sunt quærunt: Id est plerique omnes, seu plurimi, sive valde multi. Hanc signi universalis, Omnis, acceptionem esse Scripturis usitatam docent S. Hier. in cap. 1. Ep. ad Ephes. sub. finem, & S. Aug. in lib. de unitate Ecclesiæ. cap. 12. &c.
units.tr: Every sickness: that is, sickness of every kind. So Genesis 2:16: "Eat of every tree of the garden," that is, of every kind of fruit; where also tree or wood stands for the fruit of the tree. Exodus 9:6: "And all the livestock of the Egyptians died," that is, of every kind of animal; for in the same place, verse 25, follows: "And the hail struck in all the land of Egypt everything that was in the field, from man to beast." Likewise the Apostle said in Philippians 2: "All seek their own." That is, nearly all, or most, or very many. The Scriptures commonly use this sense of the universal sign "all," as Saint Jerome teaches at the end of his commentary on chapter 1 of Ephesians, and Saint Augustine in his book On the Unity of the Church, chapter 12, etc.

units.la: 36. Vexati. Id est, variis miseriis afflicti.
units.tr: 36. Harassed: that is, afflicted by various miseries.

units.la: Facentes sicut oves, &c. Nihil tam miserum est quàm oves sine pastore, quod Scriptura toties repetit in veteri & novo Testamento; cum enim oves neque astu valeant, neque viribus, neque pedum celeritate, omnium animalium injuriis patent, cùm a pastore deseruntur.
units.tr: Like sheep: Nothing is so wretched as sheep without a shepherd, which Scripture repeats so often in the Old and New Testaments; for since sheep have neither cunning, nor strength, nor speed of foot, they are exposed to the injuries of all animals when they are deserted by the shepherd.

units.la: 37. Messis quidem multa. Proverbialis locutio qua Christus significat populorum multitudinem & idoneorum magistrorum penuriam. Vide Aug. Serm.42. de Sanctis cap. 1.
units.tr: 37. The harvest indeed is plenteous: a proverbial saying by which Christ signifies the multitude of peoples and the scarcity of fit teachers. See Augustine, Sermon 42 on the Saints, chapter 1.

units.la: CAPUT X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: I. ET convocatis duodecim discipulis suis. Supple, quos jam antè, scilicet in monte priusquam prolixum Sermonem illum inciperet, qui Sermo Domini in monte dici solet, ex ceteris discipulis elegerat in Apostolos, seu ordinaverat ut non certo loco alligarentur, sed mitterentur à se immediatè per totum mundum prædicare Evangelium omni creaturæ, & Ecclesiam suam paulatim fundare ubique gentium. Hæc patent ex collatione eorum quæ hîc dicuntur v. 1. & 2. cum iis quæ dicuntur Marc. 3. v. 13, 14, 15. & 16. v. 7. Luc. 6. v. 12. & 13.
units.tr: I. And having called together his twelve disciples. Supply: whom he had already chosen from the other disciples as Apostles, namely on the mountain, before he began that long discourse commonly called the Sermon on the Mount. Or he had ordained that they should not be tied to a fixed place, but should be sent out by him at once to preach the Gospel throughout the whole world to every creature, and gradually to found his Church everywhere among the nations. These things are clear from comparing what is said here at vv. 1 and 2 with what is said at Mark 3:13, 14, 15, and 16:7, and Luke 6:12 and 13.

units.la: Dedit illis potestatem. Non suam, quâ physicè Christus, utpote Deus verus, operabatur miracula, Apostolis indidit potestatem, aut communicavit, sed externum ministerium loquendi, & externa signa adhibendi tradidit: quibus suam efficaciam Christus ut miraculorum autor addidit. Adeò ut verba Apostolorum, sicut & Prophetarum, ad quæ miracula facta esse dicuntur, instrumenta moralia tantùm fuerint, indicantia quid Deus ipsis præsentibus operaretur, secundum promissionem de miraculis per ipsos futuris à Christo factam.
units.tr: He gave them power. He did not bestow on the Apostles his own power, by which Christ, as true God, worked miracles physically. He handed them an external ministry of speaking and an external use of signs, to which Christ, as the author of miracles, added his own efficacy. So the words of the Apostles, like those of the Prophets, by which miracles are said to have been done, were only moral instruments, showing what God was doing through them in their presence, according to the promise made by Christ that miracles would be done through them.

units.la: 2. Apostolorum. Christus cùm Syriacè loqueretur, voce Syriacâ usus, שליחים duodecim ex discipulis suis appellavit, quos Evangelistæ Græcè scribentes Ἀπόστολος dixerunt. Gratis Baronius anno Domini 32. num. 5. Græcam vocem Ἀπόστολος vult civitate suisse donatam à Judæis tempore Christi, & usurpatam pro his qui versarentur af-
units.tr: 2. Apostles. Christ, speaking in Syriac, used the Syriac word shelichim [שליחים] for the twelve of his disciples, which the Evangelists, writing in Greek, called apostles [Ἀπόστολος]. Baronius, in the year of the Lord 32, no. 5, rashly claims that the Greek word Apostle was a term given by the Jews in Christ's time to those who were engaged

units.la: assiduè cum summo Pontifice consulendi gratiâ. Nec id evincit, ut existimat ille Cardinalis, quod narrat S. Epiphanius hæresi 27. Judæorum fui temporis partem aliquam Tiberiade habitasse & in aliis Palæstinæ locis, qui dispersionis suæ caput agnoscerent, quem Patriarcham nominabant: huic fuisse velut Assessores quosdam adjunctos, qui Apostoli dicerentur. Hic certè Ephiphanii locus non evincit intentum Baronii. Primò quia Epiphanius loquitur de Assessoribus Patriarcharum suæ ætatis, non vero de Assessoribus summi Pontificis ætate Christi, qui summus Pontifex nusquam legitur Patriarcha appellari, imò id nomen non nisi post deletam Jerosolymam à Judæis Hellenìstis tributum Archisynagogis legitur. Secundò non dicit Epiphanius Judæos suæ ætatis, dum Hebraicè inter se colloquerentur, uti solitos his vocibus, Patriarcha, Apostoli, quod ne verisimile quidem est, cùm nulla extent harum appellationum vestigia in veterum Rabbinorum scriptis. Mens ergo Epiphanii est Synagogæ Præsectum & ipsius Assessores his nominibus solitos appellari Hebraicè, quæ Græcis vocabulis Patriarcha & Apostoli, respondeant. Hoc sensu & Lucas dixit c. 6. v. 13. Quos & Apostolos nominavit.
units.tr: in constant consultation with the high priest. Nor does the argument of that Cardinal prove this, that St. Epiphanius relates in heresy 27 that some part of the Jews of his time lived at Tiberias and in other places of Palestine, who acknowledged the head of their dispersion, whom they called the Patriarch; that certain assessors were attached to him, who were called Apostles. Certainly this passage of Epiphanius does not prove Baronius's point. First, because Epiphanius speaks of the assessors of the patriarchs of his own age, not of the assessors of the high priest in the age of Christ; and the high priest is nowhere read to have been called Patriarch; indeed that name is read as given to the Archsynagogues by the Hellenist Jews only after Jerusalem was destroyed. Second, Epiphanius does not say that the Jews of his age, when they talked among themselves in Hebrew, were accustomed to use the words Patriarch and Apostles, which is not even likely, since no trace of these appellations survives in the writings of the ancient Rabbis. The meaning of Epiphanius, therefore, is that the head of the synagogue and his assessors were commonly called by Hebrew names corresponding to the Greek words Patriarch and Apostles. In this sense Luke also said, at ch. 6, v. 13: Whom he also named Apostles.

units.la: Primus. Petrus dicitur primus propter Apostolatus sui primatum, ut August. loquitur Tractatu 124. in Joan. quo ipsi hoc personale privilegium est concessum, ut primus post Spiritûs-Sancti descensum annuntiaret Evangelium tam Judæis, ut patet ex Act. 2, & 3, quàm Gentibus, ut constat ex Act. 10, 11, & 15. ut ex utrisque in Christo unitis coalesceret Ecclesia Catholica. Erasmus testatur in multis Codicibus manu-scriptis Græcis etiam apud Marcum c. 3. v. 16. Petrum cognominari primum, quos Codices clarissimus Calvini discipulus Beza in sua versione Latina est secutus.
units.tr: First. Peter is called first on account of the primacy of his apostleship, as Augustine speaks in Tractate 124 on John. To him this personal privilege was granted, that he should be the first, after the descent of the Holy Spirit, to announce the Gospel both to the Jews, as is plain from Acts 2 and 3, and to the Gentiles, as is clear from Acts 10, 11, and 15, so that the Catholic Church might be formed from both peoples united in Christ. Erasmus testifies that in many Greek manuscripts, even in Mark ch. 3, v. 16, Peter is surnamed first; and the most renowned disciple of Calvin, Beza, followed those manuscripts in his Latin version.

units.la: Simon qui dicitur Petrus. Apponitur cognomen ut distinguatur ab altero Simone, qui dicitur Cananæus à Cana vico Galilææ, ubi Dominus aquam in vinum convertit. Cana autem zelus interpretatur, unde hic Simon Cananæus dicitur Luc. 6. Zelotes. Scaliger tamen vult hunc Simonem Zelotem dictum, quia à secta Zelatorum, de quibus apud Josephum, ad Christum conversus fuit. Hic Simon Zelotes contra receptam sententiam ab Hegesippo & Eusebio creditur esse Simeon Jacobi fratris Domini in sede Jerosolymitana successor, qui cùm esset annorum 120. Trajano Imperatore, martyr occubuit.
units.tr: Simon who is called Peter. The surname is added to distinguish him from the other Simon, who is called the Canaanite, from Cana, a village of Galilee where the Lord turned water into wine. Cana, moreover, is interpreted as zeal, whence this Simon is called the Canaanite at Luke 6, the Zealot. Scaliger, however, holds that this Simon was called Zealot because he was converted to Christ from the sect of the Zealots, of whom Josephus speaks. This Simon the Zealot, contrary to the commonly accepted opinion, is believed by Hegesippus and Eusebius to be Simeon, brother of the Lord James, who succeeded him in the see of Jerusalem, and who, being 120 years old, died a martyr under the Emperor Trajan.

units.la: 3. Jacobus Zebedæi. Supple, filius. Addit Evangelista Jacobi hujus patrem, ut distinguatur à sequente Jacobo Alphæi, supple, filio, qui minor à Marco vocatur cap. 15.
units.tr: 3. James of Zebedee. Supply: son. The Evangelist adds the name of this James's father, to distinguish him from the following James the son of Alphaeus, who is called the Less by Mark in ch. 15.

units.la: Bartholomæus. Rupertus & alii non levibus conjecturis existimant Bartholomæum Apostolum eundem esse cum Nathanaële, cujus laus est in Joannis Evangelio cap. 1.
units.tr: Bartholomew. Rupert and others, on no slight conjectures, think that the Apostle Bartholomew is the same as Nathanael, whose praise is in the Gospel of John ch. 1.

units.la: Thomas & Matthæus. Ceteri Evangelistæ Matthæum præponunt Thomæ in conjunctione nominum, sed Act. 1. Matthæus conjungitur cum Bartholomæo cui postponitur, & utrique præponitur Thomas.
units.tr: Thomas and Matthew. The other Evangelists place Matthew before Thomas when the names are joined; but in Acts 1 Matthew is joined with Bartholomew, to whom he is placed after, and Thomas is placed before both.

units.la: Publicanus. Ceteri Evangelistæ Matthæum nominantes, Publicani nomen non adscribunt, ne antiquæ conversationis recordantes sugillare Evangelistam viderentur; Matthæus vero se nominat Publicanum, ut ubi abundavit iniquitas, superabundet & gratia. B. Hier.
units.tr: The publican. The other Evangelists, naming Matthew, do not add the name of publican, lest they should seem to upbraid the Evangelist by recalling his former way of life; but Matthew himself names himself a publican, so that where sin abounded, grace may much more abound. St. Jerome.

units.la: Thaddæus. Thaddæum Apostolum, Ecclesiastica tradit historia missum Edessam ad Abagarum Regem Chosdroenæ, qui ab Evangelista Luca Judas Jacobi dicitur, & alibi appellatur Lebbæus, quod interpretatur corculum; credendumque est eum fuisse trinomium, sicut Simon Petrus, & filii Zebedæi Boanerges & firmitate & magnitudine fidei nominati sunt. B. Hier.
units.tr: Thaddeus. Ecclesiastical history hands down that the Apostle Thaddeus was sent to Edessa to King Abgar of Osroene. He is called Judas of James by the Evangelist Luke, and elsewhere is named Lebbaeus, which is interpreted as "little heart." And it must be believed that he had three names, just as Simon Peter, and the sons of Zebedee, Boanerges, were named for their steadfastness and the greatness of their faith. St. Jerome.

units.la: 4. Iscariotes. Sic dicitur Judas proditor, qui de tribu Ephraim, & de vico ejusdem tribus Iscarioth, non longe a Samaria Orientem versus, ortus erat. B. Hier. in Esa. 28. v. 1.
units.tr: 4. Iscariot. Thus Judas the traitor is called, who was born of the tribe of Ephraim and of the village of that same tribe, Iscariot, not far from Samaria toward the east. St. Jerome on Isaiah 28, v. 1.

units.la: 5. In viam Gentium Hebraismus, id est, ad Gentes. Sic autem Apostolis præcepit Dominus ante resurrectionem suam, quia juxta altitudinem sapientiæ & scientiæ Dei oportebat Judæis primum prædicari verbum Dei, & cum repellerent illud, & indignos se judicarent vitæ æternæ, oportebat post Christi resurrectionem converti ad Gentes, ut dicitur Act. 3. v. 46. Rom. 15. v. 8.
units.tr: 5. Into the way of the Gentiles. A Hebraism, that is, to the Gentiles. The Lord gave this command to the Apostles before his resurrection, because according to the depth of the wisdom and knowledge of God it was fitting that the word of God be preached first to the Jews, and when they rejected it and judged themselves unworthy of eternal life, it was fitting that after Christ's resurrection the Gentiles be turned to, as is said in Acts 3, v. 46, and Romans 15, v. 8.

units.la: Samaritanorum. Samaritani dicuntur Gentes, quas e locis sinui Persico (qui pars est Maris Rubri) vicinis Asor-Haddan, ut vocatur 1 Esd. 4. v. 2. Seu Asbazareth, quomodo appellatur 3 Esd. 5. v. 69. Assyriorum rex collocavit in civitatibus Samariæ pro decem tribubus Israel inde a decessore suo Salmanasar in Assyriam translatis, 4 Reg. 17. v. 6. Hæ Gentes a ceteris distinguebantur propter nonnullum cultum veri Dei, & expectationem veri Messiæ. Regio autem pulcherrimo & uberrimo loco sita, licet nec Judææ, nec Galilææ magnitudine conferenda, a Regia urbe nominis ejusdem nomen arcessit, sed urbs ipsa appellationem trahit a Somer ejus agri domino, quem Amri Rex Israel emit duobus talentis argenti ad urbem hanc maximam, pulcherrimam & munitissimam, inter decem tribuum urbes extruendam. Vide 3 Reg. 16.
units.tr: Of the Samaritans. The Samaritans are said to be peoples whom the king of Assyria, Asor-Haddan, as he is called in 1 Esdras 4, v. 2, or Asbazareth, as he is named in 3 Esdras 5, v. 69, settled in the cities of Samaria, in place of the ten tribes of Israel, who had been carried into Assyria by his predecessor Shalmaneser, 4 Kings 17, v. 6. These peoples were distinguished from the others because of some worship of the true God and an expectation of the true Messiah. The region, placed in a most beautiful and fruitful location, though not to be compared in size with Judea or Galilee, takes its name from the royal city of the same name; but the city itself derives its name from Shemer, the lord of that field, whom King Omri of Israel bought for two talents of silver in order to build on it this very great, very beautiful and very well fortified city, among the cities of the ten tribes. See 3 Kings 16.

units.la: 6. Perierunt. Id est, a via salutis aberrarunt.
units.tr: 6. Have perished. That is, they have strayed from the way of salvation.

units.la: 8. Gratis date. Ille gratis præest, & pascit gregem, qui nec lucrandi, nec ditescendi animo id facit: quanquam victum sibi necessarium à grege, id est, ab Ecclesia accipit, quemadmodum docet & Christus versu decimo mox sequenti, & Paulus 1 Cor. 9. 2 Cor. 11.
units.tr: 8. Give freely. He rules and feeds the flock freely who does so without any desire for gain or enrichment, although he receives from the flock, that is from the Church, the sustenance necessary to him, as Christ also teaches in the tenth verse that follows, and Paul in 1 Corinthians 9 and 2 Corinthians 11.

units.la: 9. Nolite possidere aurum, &c. Id est, ne solliciti sitis possidere, seu, ut vertit Beza, Comparare aurum ceteráque ad iter quàm commodissime conficiendum requisita, sed nullà interpositâ morâ, abjectâque prorsus rerum omnium istarum curâ, ita ut estis, baculis videlicet, quos manu, & soleis, quas pedibus nunc gestatis, contenti, vos e vestigio in viam date. Quo d autem Dominus in hac profectione præcepit Apostolis, præcepit & aliis septuaginta duobus discipulis Luc. 10. v. 1. Itaq; apu l Matthæum & Lucam non interdicitur baculi aut solearum usus, qui apud Marcum permittitur cap. 6. v 8, & 9. sed vetatur ne solearum, baculive commodioris quærendi causâ vel temporis puncto iter differatur. Unde optime hic vertit Portus-Regius, Ne vous mettés point en peine d'avoir de l'or, &c. Quibus verbis satis indicatur non prohiberi possessionem auri, & ceterorum, quæ sequuntur, sed eorum sollicitam ambitionem, studiosamve comparationem, quâ præceptum iter tantisper retardetur.
units.tr: 9. Do not possess gold, etc. That is, do not be anxious to possess, or, as Beza translates it, to procure gold and the other things most convenient for completing the journey, but without any delay, and with all care for these things utterly laid aside, go out on the road just as you are, with the staves, namely, which you hold in your hands, and the sandals, which you now wear on your feet, content with them. What the Lord commanded the Apostles in this mission, he also commanded the seventy-two other disciples, Luke 10, v. 1. Therefore in Matthew and Luke the use of staff or sandals is not forbidden, which is permitted in Mark ch. 6, vv. 8 and 9, but it is forbidden that the journey be delayed, even for a moment, in seeking more convenient sandals or staves. Hence the Port-Royal translation renders this very well: Ne vous mettés point en peine d'avoir de l'or, etc. By these words it is sufficiently indicated that the possession of gold and the other things that follow is not forbidden, but their anxious pursuit and eager procurement, by which the commanded journey is for a while held up.

units.la: In Zonâ. Veteres pecuniam in zonis reconditam gestabant; unde apud Plautum in Mercatore adolescens jam jam profecturus ait: Zonam sustuli. Et in Truculento: Solve Zonas. Hinc & castrense proverbium, zonam perdidit, ufurpatur de iis, qui nihil habent nummorum.
units.tr: In the Belt. The ancients carried their money hidden in belts. Hence in Plautus's Merchant, a young man about to set off says, I have taken up the belt. And in Truculentus: Loose the belts. From this also comes the military proverb "he has lost his belt," used of those who have no money at all.

units.la: 10. Peram. Ponitur hic continens pro contento, Dignus est enim operarius cibo suo. Luc. 10. v. 7. mercede sua. q. d. Prohibui vobis sollicitam omnium vitæ sustentationi in itinere necessariorum provisionem, quia do vobis potestatem vivendi de Evangelio, qui Evangelium annuntiatis. Uni nostro operi duæ mercedes debentur, una in via, altera in patria: una quæ nos in labore sustentat, alia quæ nos in resurrectione remunerat. Merces itaque, quæ in præsenti accipitur, hoc in nobis debet agere, ut ad sequentem mercedem robustius tendatur. Verus ergo quisque prædicator non ideo prædicare debet, ut in hoc tempore mercedem recipiat: sed ideo mercedem recipere, ut prædicare subsistat. Quisquis namque ideo prædicat, ut hic vel laudis vel muneris mercedem recipiat, æterna â procul dubio mercede se privat. Quisquis verò vel ea quæ dicit, ideo placere hominibus appetit, ut dum placet quod dicitur, per eadem dicta non ipse, sed Dominus ametur: vel idcirco terrena stipendia in prædicatione consequitur, ne à prædicationis voce per indigentiam lassetur: huic proculdubio ad recipiendam mercedem nihil obstat. obstat in patria, quia sumtus sumsit in via. Greg. Hom. 17. in Evang.
units.tr: 10. Purse. Here the container stands for the thing contained, as in "The labourer is worthy of his food" (Luke 10:7), that is, of his wages. The sense is: I have forbidden you to make anxious provision for all the necessities of life on the journey, because I give you the power of living from the Gospel, since you proclaim the Gospel. Two wages are owed to our one work, one on the way and the other in our homeland: the one sustains us in our labour, the other rewards us in the resurrection. The wage received in the present life ought therefore to work in us so that we strive more vigorously toward the wage to come. Thus no true preacher ought to preach in order to receive a wage in this time; rather he should receive a wage so that he may continue to preach. For whoever preaches in order to receive here the reward of praise or of office undoubtedly deprives himself of the eternal reward. And whoever seeks to please men with what he says, so that while what is said pleases, it is not he but the Lord who is loved through those same words; or who gets worldly support from preaching, lest by poverty he be worn down from the voice of preaching: for such a person nothing stands in the way of receiving his reward. He will not be hindered in the homeland, because he has spent his expenses on the way. Gregory, Homily 17 on the Gospels.

units.la: 11. Interrogate, &c. Hospes famâ eligendus est populi & judicio vicinorum, ne prædicationis dignitas suscipientis infamiâ deturpetur. B. Hier.
units.tr: 11. Inquire, etc. The host must be chosen for his good name and by the judgement of his neighbours, so that the dignity of the preaching is not disfigured by the infamy of the one who receives it. Jerome.

units.la: 12. Dicentes, &c. Cùm hæc absint à textu Græco, videntur hîc addita ex Luc. 10. v. 5. ut sequentia meliùs cohærerent, in quibus fit mentio pacis. Salutatio autem apud Hebræos fit pacis precatione; unde hæc additio nihil mutat in sensu, cùm salutare idem sit, ac precari alicui pacem.
units.tr: 12. Saying, etc. Since these words are absent from the Greek text, they seem to have been added here from Luke 10:5, so that what follows, in which peace is mentioned, coheres better. Among the Hebrews, however, greeting is made by a prayer for peace, so this addition changes nothing in the sense, since to greet is the same as to pray peace for someone.

units.la: 13. Siquidem fuerit domus illa digna. Luc. 10. v. 6. Si ibi fuerit filius pacis, id est, aliquis pace dignus, requiescet super illum pax vestra. Nobis quidem tunc incipit esse quisque filius pacis, cum obedierit & crediderit Evangelio, & ex fide justificatus pacem ad Deum habere cœpe it: secundum autem prædestinationem Dei, jam filius pacis erat. Neque enim dictum est: Super quem requieverit pax vestra fiet filius pacis: sed, Ubi fuerit, inquit, filius pacis, requiescet super eum pax vestra. Jam ergo & antequam illi annuntiaretur hæc pax, filius pacis ibi erat, sicut eum noverat atque præscierat non Evangelista, sed Dominus. Ad nos ergo qui nescimus quisnam sit filius pacis, aut non sit, pertinet nullum excepturn facere, nullúmque discernere, sed velle omnes salvos fieri, quibus prædicamus hanc pacem; neque enim metuendum est, ne perdamus eam, si illi cui prædicamus non est filius pacis, ignorantibus nobis: ad nos enim revertetur, id est, nobis proderit hæc prædicatio, non & illi; si autem super eum pax prædicata requieverit, & nobis & illi. Aug. De correpi. & grat. cap. 15.
units.tr: 13. If that house is worthy. Luke 10:6: If there is there a son of peace, that is, someone worthy of peace, your peace will rest upon him. For us, indeed, each person begins to be a son of peace when he obeys and believes the Gospel, and, justified by faith, begins to have peace with God; but according to the predestination of God he was already a son of peace. For it is not said, "Upon whomever your peace shall rest, he shall become a son of peace," but, "Where there is a son of peace," he says, "your peace will rest upon him." So already, even before this peace was announced to him, the son of peace was there, just as the Lord, and not the Evangelist, knew and foreknew him. It is therefore not for us, who do not know who is or is not a son of peace, to make any exception or to make any distinction, but to wish all to be saved to whom we proclaim this peace. For we need not fear that we lose it if the one to whom we preach is not a son of peace, while we are ignorant of it: for it will return to us, that is, this preaching will profit us, and not him; but if the peace proclaimed rests upon him, it profits both us and him. Augustine, On Rebuke and Grace, chapter 15.

units.la: 14. Excutite pulverem de pedibus vestris. Marc. 6. additur, in testimonium illis: Hoc est, teste Origene Hom. 18. in Gen. ut illis ostendatis illum ipsum pulverem, quem ex itinere propter ipsos suscepto collegistis, in die judicii testem contra eos futurum, qui vos recipere, seu, sermones vestros audire noluerunt.
units.tr: 14. Shake off the dust from your feet. Mark 6 adds for a testimony against them. That is, as Origen says in Homily 18 on Genesis, so that you may show them that the very dust which you gathered on the journey for their sake will be a witness against those who were unwilling to receive you or to hear your words on the day of judgement.

units.la: 15. Tolerabilius, &c. Ratio hujus sententiæ patet ex cap. 11. v. 23. Porrò ea quæ deinceps sequuntur in hoc capite vel sæpius dicta sunt à Christo, vel Matthæus, ut passim solet, ob argumenti similitudinem, simul congessit, quæ, ut ex aliis videtur colligi Evangelistis, non simul à Christo dictata fuerunt.
units.tr: 15. More tolerable, etc. The reason for this sentence is plain from chapter 11, verse 23. Moreover, the things that follow in this chapter were either said by Christ more than once, or Matthew, as he often does, gathered them together because of the similarity of the subject; and, as may be gathered from the other Evangelists, they were not all spoken by Christ at the same time.

units.la: 16. Mitto vos sicut oves, &c. Id est, infirmos, inermes, & ab omnibus auxiliis humanis imparatos, nec lupi unius furori expositos atque obvios, sed plurimorum. Quot enim inter Judæos, quot inter Gentiles fuerunt veritatis ignari, tot hostes habuerunt primi Evangelii præcones, quorum conatibus bus quid opponerent nihil illis fuit præter Christi promissionem: Super hanc Petram ædificabo Ecclesiam meam & porta inferi non prævalebunt adversus eam: Ecce ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus usque ad consummationem seculi. Quod si unus lupus sufficit magno gregi perdendo & devastando, in medio tot luporum quomodo evasisset Christi pusillus grex, nisi illum servasset idem, qui Danielem inter leones?
units.tr: 16. I send you as sheep, etc. That is: weak, unarmed, and unprepared with any human aids, and exposed and opposed not to the fury of one wolf but of many. For as many as there were ignorant of the truth among the Jews and among the Gentiles, so many enemies did the first heralds of the Gospel have, and against their efforts they had nothing to set against them except Christ's promise: Upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; behold, I am with you all days, even to the end of the world. But if one wolf is enough to destroy and lay waste a great flock, how would Christ's little flock have escaped in the midst of so many wolves, unless the same one had preserved it who preserved Daniel among the lions?

units.la: Luporum. Hoc nomine hic & alibi sæpe intelliguntur tyranni & bonorum persecutores propter rabiem insitam & morum immanitatem, qua fit ut, luporum instar, sanguinem populi sitiant, neque eo satientur unquam. Metu luporum ejusmodi fugiunt pastores mercenarii, id est, qui avaritiâ ducuntur, non zelo gloriæ Dei, & oves per illorum defectionem rapiuntur & dissipantur. Tamen illos ipsos lupos quandoque mutat in oves, aut in pastores etiam, vis Spiritûs flexanima, ut patet ex Pauli exemplo; & tum impletur quod Esaias prædixerat, fore ut lupus & agnus una degerent, & simul pascerentur, hoc est, in eadem Ecclesia.
units.tr: Wolves. Under this name, here and often elsewhere, are understood tyrants and persecutors of the good, on account of the rage implanted in them and the savagery of their character, by which, like wolves, they thirst for the blood of the people and are never satisfied. From wolves of this kind hired ministers flee, that is, those who are led by greed and not by zeal for the glory of God, and through their desertion the sheep are seized and scattered. Yet the power of the flexible Spirit sometimes changes those very wolves into sheep, or even into shepherds, as is clear from the example of Paul; and then what Isaiah had foretold is fulfilled, that the wolf and the lamb would dwell together and feed together, that is, in the same Church.

units.la: Prudentes sicut serpentes. Prudentiæ serpentis quatuor argumenta profert S. Epiphanii Physiologus. Primum quod cum senium præsensit, quærit petram, & Παγιδευτικῶς περιελίξας δὲ ἑαυτὸν τῷ ὀπῇ ... ἐκτείνεται τὸ γῆς. in rimam se insinuat, pronúsque per foramen transfire nititur, & seneitutem exuit. Atque id omnes uno ore afferunt. Secundum, quod cum ab homine vestito fugiat, eundem nudum γυμνὸν ἀγγρεδιτur confidenter. Contrarium omninò diserte docent Eustathius in Hexaëmero, Autor Epistolæ ad Præsidium sub Hieronymi nomine, S. Isidorus Hispalensis lib. 12. Orig. cap. 4. & id se non raro expertum scribit Olaus Magnus, quod hominem nudum & dormientem non lædant serpentes. Tertium, quod ab homine appetitus solum caput servat illæsum, & reliquum corpus objicit. Quartum, quod cùm ad fontem venit ut bibat, virus ante deponit, atque ita aquam ex fonte bibit, ne eum venenum aquâ concretum occidat, ut loquitur autor Epistolæ ad Præsidium apud Hieronymum. His ex Plinio addi queat serpentem, hybernâ latebrâ visu obscurato, oculos marathro inungere, ac refovere; si vero squammæ obtorpuerunt, spinis juniperi scabere: & draconem vernam nauseam lactucæ succo restinguere.
units.tr: Wise as serpents. Saint Epiphanius, in the Physiologus, offers four arguments for the serpent's prudence. The first: when it senses old age, it seeks a rock, and coiling itself cunningly around the hole ... it stretches itself along the ground [Παγιδευτικῶς περιελίξας δὲ ἑαυτὸν τῷ ὀπῇ ... ἐκτείνεται τὸ γῆς], it insinuates itself into a crack, and striving to pass through the opening head first, it casts off its old age. And all agree on this. The second: that when it flees from a man clothed, it confidently attacks the same man when naked [γυμνὸν ἀγγρεδιτur]. Eustathius in the Hexaemeron, the author of the letter To Praesidius under Jerome's name, Saint Isidore of Seville in book 12 of the Origines, chapter 4, teach the exact opposite; and Olaus Magnus writes that he himself has often found that serpents do not harm a naked man who is asleep. The third: that when attacked by a man, it protects only its head and offers the rest of its body. The fourth: that when it comes to a spring to drink, it first lays down its poison, and so drinks the water from the spring, lest the poison, mixed with the water, kill it, as the author of the letter To Praesidius in Jerome says. To these, from Pliny, one may add that the serpent, in its winter hiding-place with its sight dimmed, anoints and restores its eyes with fennel; and if its scales have grown numb, it rubs itself against juniper thorns; and the dragon in spring quenches its nausea with the juice of lettuce.

units.la: Simplices. Græce ἀκέραιοι, quod à quibusdam vertitur, mites, quia secundum Grammaticos ἀκέραιον de animali dictum significat excorne, benignum, & innoxium, quæ Epitheta optimè quadrant in columbam, quæ, ut ait Cyrillus Alexandrinus in lib. 15. de adoratione, Περὶ ἀκεραίου πνεύματος μεγαλοπρεπὴς, suprêmum mansuetudinis fastigium attingit; unde & quidam mansuetudinem advertentes & vesicam fellis propè jecur non habere, tradiderunt eam felle carere, cùm tamen revera in tergo fel habeat intestino junctum, ut testantur Horus Hierogl. lib. 2. cap. 45. Plinius lib. 11. c. 37. & Galenus in lib. de atra bile post Philosophum Historiæ lib. 2. c. 15. Sed licèt verum sit columbam esse placidam, ut eam vocat Ovidius Metamorph. lib. 7. Fabula 12. tamen in præsenti loco Evangelistæ, non debet contra mentem SS. PP. & ipsorum Mahumetanorum Doctorum exponi ἀκέραιον de mansuetudine columbæ, maximè cùm nullus locus Prophetarum occurrat, ubi columba mitis vocetur, sed occurrat locus Osee 7. v. 11. ubi columba dicitur יוֹנָה simplex, sicut serpens dicitur עָרוּם prudens Genef. 3. v. 5. Maximè autem est advertendum quòd nec serpentis prudentia, nec columbæ simplicitas laudantur à Christo solæ & ab invicem divulsæ, sed tum demum laudantur, cùm simul conjunctæ sunt; ita ut una supplear quod deest in altera, aut corrigat quod excedit, quomodo ex duobus pharmacis, quæ separatim noxia, tertium componitur, quod utile est & salutare, quia se mutuò temperant. Unde B. Greg. Nazian. de patre suo Oratione 19. Τὸ γὰρ τῆς ὄφεως φρόνημα, πρὸς τὸ κακὸν τῆς ... Cùm serpentis ad malum prudentiam cum columbæ ad bonum simplicitate conjunxisset, itase comparavit, ut nec prudentiam in versutam improhibitam, nec simplicitatem in soliditatem degenerare sineret: verùm ex ambabus, quoad ejus fieri poterat, unam virtutis speciem efficeret numeris omnibus perfectam & absolutam. B. Hieron. ad Paulinum de institut. Monachi: Habeto, inquit, simplicitatem columbæ, ne cuiquam machinetis dolos, & serpentis astutiam, ne aliorum supplanteris insidiis. Hoc sensu etiam B. Paulus Apost. Rom. 16. v. 19. Volo, inquit, vos sapientes esse in bono, & simplices in malo. Sic Faustus Rhegien. de liber. arbi. lib. 2. c. ultimo: Faciamus, inquit, hominem simplicem, faciamus astutum: simplicem ne malum callidus inferat, astutum, ne incautus incurrat. Sic Martialis lib. 10. Epig. 47.
units.tr: Simple ones. In Greek unmixed, pure [ἀκέραιοι], which some render meek, because according to the grammarians ἀκέραιον [akeraion], said of an animal, means hornless, gentle and harmless. These epithets fit the dove very well. As Cyril of Alexandria says in book 15 on worship, the dove, magnificent in its unmixed spirit [Περὶ ἀκεραίου πνεύματος μεγαλοπρεπὴς], reaches the highest summit of meekness. Hence some, noticing its meekness and that its gall-bladder lies almost against the liver, have taught that it has no gall. Yet in truth it has gall in its back, joined to the intestine, as Horapollo attests (Hierogl. book 2, ch. 45), and Pliny (book 11, ch. 37), and Galen in his book on black bile, following the Philosopher's History of Animals (book 2, ch. 15). But although it is true that the dove is gentle [placidam], as Ovid calls it (Metamorphoses book 7, fable 12), still in the present passage the Evangelist's word ἀκέραιον [akeraion] should not, against the mind of the Holy Fathers and of the Muslim doctors themselves, be explained as the dove's mildness. This is especially so since no passage of the Prophets occurs where the dove is called meek, but there occurs Hosea 7:11, where the dove is called simple [יוֹנָה], just as the serpent is called prudent [עָרוּם] in Genesis 3:5. Moreover it must be noted that Christ praises neither the serpent's prudence nor the dove's simplicity when they are alone and separated from each other, but they are praised only when they are joined together, so that one supplies what is lacking in the other or corrects what is excessive in it. So, too, from two drugs which are harmful separately, a third is compounded which is useful and wholesome, because they temper each other. Hence Saint Gregory Nazianzen, in his Oration 19 on his father: For the mind of the serpent [Τὸ γὰρ τῆς ὄφεως φρόνημα, πρὸς τὸ κακὸν τῆς ...], since he had joined the serpent's prudence toward evil with the dove's simplicity toward good, arranged it so as neither to let prudence degenerate into unlawful cunning nor simplicity into dullness, but to make from both, as far as it could be done, one kind of virtue perfect and complete in all respects. Saint Jerome, to Paulinus on the institution of the monk: Have, he says, the simplicity of the dove, so that you do not devise tricks against anyone, and the cunning of the serpent, so that you are not supplanted by the snares of others. In this sense also Saint Paul the Apostle, Romans 16:19: I want you, he says, to be wise in good, and simple in evil. So Faustus of Riez, On Free Will, book 2, last chapter: Let us make, he says, a man simple, let us make him shrewd: simple, lest the crafty man inflict evil; shrewd, lest the unwary man run into it. Thus Martial, book 10, epigram 47.

units.la: Prudens simplicitas, pares amici.
units.tr: Prudent simplicity, equal friends.

units.la: Sicut columbæ. Simplicitatem columbæ & Arabes, & SS. PP. testantur in eo maximè apparere, quòd illa pullis sublatis non avolat, verùm in iisdem locis remanet, & B. Hieron. in Osee 7. v. 11. Aves, inquit, ceteræ pullos suos etiam cum periculo vitæ suæ protegere festinant, & cùm ad nidum suum accipitrem, colubrum, corvum, sive cornicem accedere viderint, huc illucque volitant, & immittunt se morsu, & unguibus lacerant, & dolorem parentis querulâ voce testantur; sola columba ablatos pullos non dolet, non requirit. Hoc licet verum sit in plerisque columbarum speciebus, non tamen in omnibus verum est. Nam Damir Arabs testatur quoddam columbæ genus tanto affectu fervere erga pullos suos, ut quandoque seipsam mater interimat, cum illos videt in manu aucupis.
