Imò & in genere Scriptores columbam commendant ab amore in prolem, ut videre est apud Plin. lib. 10. c. 34. Aristot. Hist. lib. 9. c. 7. Ælianum Hist. lib. 3. c. 45. Athenæum lib. 9. c. 11. &c. Hinc alii in eo patere afferunt columbæ simplicitatem, quod retia non evitat, neque laqueos sibi paratos, cum se demittit ad cibum. Ut ut sit, hanc columbæ simplicitatem, & Ethnici scriptores agnoverunt, unde ad illud Juvenalis, Vexat censura columbas, dicit vetus Scholiastes, columbas retulit ad simplicitatem.
units.tr: Like doves. Both the Arabs and the holy Fathers testify that the dove's simplicity shows itself chiefly in this: when its young are taken away, it does not fly off but stays in the same place. Blessed Jerome, on Hosea 7:11, says: "Other birds hasten to protect their young even at the risk of their own lives. When they see a hawk, a snake, a raven, or a crow approach their nest, they fly here and there, attack with beak and claws, and show their grief with a plaintive cry. Only the dove does not grieve for its young when they are carried off, and does not seek them." Although this holds true of most kinds of doves, it is not true of all. For the Arab Damir reports that a certain kind of dove burns with such love for its young that the mother sometimes kills herself when she sees them in the fowler's hand. Indeed, writers in general commend the dove for its love of its offspring, as can be seen in Pliny, Natural History 10.34; Aristotle, History of Animals 9.7; Aelian, Historical Miscellany 3.45; Athenaeus 9.11; and others. Hence some say that the dove's simplicity is shown in this, that when it comes down to feed it does not avoid the nets and snares set for it. Whatever the case, the pagan writers too recognised this simplicity of the dove. So the old scholiast on Juvenal's line, "Censure vexes the doves," says that "he referred the doves to simplicity."

units.la: 17. Cavete autem ab hominibus? Id est, nolite confidere in hominibus.
units.tr: 17. But beware of men. That is, do not put your trust in men.

units.la: Tradent enim vos. Scilicet, examinandos, judicandos, & puniendos.
units.tr: For they will deliver you up. Namely, to be examined, judged and punished.

units.la: In Conciliis. Scilicet, Synedriis. De iis egimus supra, c. 5.
units.tr: In councils. Namely, in the Sanhedrins. We discussed these above, in chapter 5.

units.la: 18. In testimonium illis & Gentibus. Id est, ut testes fitis Judæis & Gentibus veram esse fidem, pro qua acerbissima quæque supplicia subire estis parati, & juste eos aliquando esse damnandos, qui eam vobis prædicantibus recipere noluerint.
units.tr: 18. For a testimony to them and to the Gentiles. That is, that you may be witnesses to Jews and Gentiles that the faith is true, a faith for which you are prepared to undergo the most cruel punishments, and that those who refuse to receive it when you preach it will one day be justly condemned.

units.la: 19. Nolite cogitare, &c. Sacra ergo ad nos eloquia frustrà mandata sunt, qui repleti Spiritu verbis exterioribus non egemus? sed aliud est, quod angustiati persecutionis tempore absque dubitatione confidere, aliud quod in tranquillitate Ecclesiæ agere debemus; oportet enim nos per Spiritum hunc modò legendo percipere quæ possumus: si contigerit causa in nobis esse. etiam patiendo demonstrare. B. Greg. lib. 2. Epist. 37. ad Natalem Episcopum Salonitanum.
units.tr: 19. Do not think, etc. Are the holy oracles therefore given to us in vain, since we, filled with the Spirit, have no need of outward words? But it is one thing to trust without doubt in a time of persecution when we are distressed, and another thing to act in the tranquillity of the Church. For we must, through this Spirit, now perceive by reading what we can; if it happens that there is a cause, we must also demonstrate it by suffering. Blessed Gregory, Letters 2.37, to Natalis, Bishop of Salona.

units.la: 20. Non enim vos estis, &c. Hebraismus, id est, non enim tam vos estis, qui loquimini, quam Spiritus Patris vestri, & consequenter meus, qui loquitur in vobis; Neque enim, inquit August. Epist. 105. hoc ita fit de nobis tanquam nihil facientibus nobis; adjutorium igitur Spiritus-Sancti sic expressum est, ut ipse facere diceretur, quod ut faciamus facit.
units.tr: 20. For it is not you who speak, etc. This is a Hebraism: that is, it is not so much you who speak as the Spirit of your Father, and consequently my Spirit, who speaks in you. "For," says Augustine, Letter 105, "this is not done in us as if we did nothing ourselves." The help of the Holy Spirit is therefore so expressed that he is said to do what he does in us so that we may do it.

units.la: 22. Eritis odio omnibus. Est distributio pro generibus singulorum, non pro singulis generum. q. d. Eritis odio Gentibus & Judæis, viris, ac fœminis, nobilibus ac ignobilibus, cognatis & extraneis. Hinc Autor de voc. Gent. l. 2. c. 2. Apparuit, ut ait Apostolus, Tit. 2. v. 11. Gratia Salvatoris nostri Dei omnibus hominibus, & tamen ministri gratiæ odio erant omnibus hominibus; & cùm alii essent qui oderant, alii qui odiis persequentium premebantur, neutra tamen pars nuncupatione omnium hominum privabatur, habente quidem salutis suæ damnum, rebellium portione, sed obtinente plenitudinis censum Fidelium dignitate. Dicit enim Joann. Apost. Sed & si quis peccaverit, advocatum habemus apud Patrem, Jesum Christ. justum: & ipse est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris, non pro nostris autem tantùm, sed etiam pro totius mundi. B. Fulgent. lib. de Incar. & gratia, c. 31. Dicit, inquit, Propheta Psal. 85. v. 9. Omnes gentes quascunque fecisti, venient & adorabunt coram te, & glorificabunt nomen tuum in æternum. Dominus autem suis Fidelibus dicit: Eritis odio omnibus gentibus propter nomen meum. Numquid ergo contrariis sibi repugnat Scriptura divina sententiis? absit! Sed & illos omnes, & istos omnes veraciter dicit, id est, & omnes Fideles qui nomen Domini in omnibus gentibus glorificant, & omnes incredulos qui per easdem omnes gentes, in odio nominis Christi Fideliúmque ejus, mortiferâ impietate perdurant.
units.tr: 22. You will be hated by all. This is a distribution by kinds of individuals, not by individuals of kinds. The sense is: you will be hated by Gentiles and Jews, men and women, nobles and commoners, relatives and strangers. Hence the author of On the Calling of the Gentiles, book 2, chapter 2: "As the Apostle says in Titus 2:11, the grace of our Saviour God appeared to all men; yet the ministers of grace were hated by all men. And although some hated and others were oppressed by the hatred of their persecutors, neither party was deprived of the name of all men: the one party indeed suffered the loss of its salvation, as the portion of rebels, but the other obtained the fullness of its worth as the faithful. For John the Apostle says: 'And if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world.'" Blessed Fulgentius, On the Incarnation and Grace, chapter 31: "The Prophet says, Psalm 85:9: 'All the nations whom you have made will come and worship before you, and will glorify your name for ever.' But the Lord says to his faithful: 'You will be hated by all nations because of my name.' Does divine Scripture then contradict itself? Far from it! He speaks truly of both all of them: that is, of all the faithful who glorify the name of the Lord among all nations, and of all the unbelievers who, among those same nations, persist in deadly impiety, in hatred of the name of Christ and of his faithful people."

units.la: Qui autem perseveraverit. Supple, in patientia, unde Marc. 13. dicitur, Qui sustinuerit in finem, hoc est, qui ad mortem usque Christo constanti fide adhæserit, licet ab impiis habeatur perditus, & malè mulctetur.*
units.tr: But whoever endures to the end. Supply: in patience. Hence Mark 13 says: "He who endures to the end," that is, he who holds fast to Christ with constant faith even to death, although he is regarded as lost by the wicked and is punished badly.

units.la: 23. Fugite, &c. B. Hilarius Can. 10. in Matth. hæc interpretatur de secunda missione Apostolorum post Christi resurrectionem, ut sensus fit: fugite de civitate Judæorum, in civitatem gentium, prædico enim vobis quòd non sitis neque per vos, neque per successores vestros consummaturi, seu ad perfectionem Evangelii perducturi civitates Israel, antequam veniat Filius hominis, scilicet ad judicium, seu ante consummationem seculi. Quicunque isto modo fugit, ut Ecclesiæ necessarium ministerium illo persecutionem fugiente, non desit, facit quod Deus hîc præcepit, sive permisit; qui autem sic fugit, ut gregi Christi ea, quibus spiritualiter vivit, alimenta subtrahantur, mercenarius ille est, qui videt lupum venientem & fugit, & non est ei cura de ovibus, ita Aug. Epist. 180. ad Honoratum, ubi fusissimè, doctissimè, & quàm subtilissimè disputat quando pastores Ecclesiæ in persecutione fugere vel remanere debeant. Nam de privatis personis, certum est quòd possint ad periculum Christi negandi vitandum, quantùm potuerint, fugere.
units.tr: 23. Flee, etc. Blessed Hilary, Canon 10 on Matthew, interprets this as referring to the second sending of the Apostles after Christ's resurrection, so that the sense is: flee from the cities of the Jews into the cities of the Gentiles. For I tell you that you will not, either by yourselves or by your successors, bring to completion, that is, lead to the perfection of the Gospel, the cities of Israel before the Son of man comes, namely to judgement, or before the end of the age. Whoever flees in such a way that the Church's necessary ministry is not lacking while he flees from persecution does what God commands here, or permits. But whoever flees in such a way that the food by which the flock of Christ lives spiritually is taken away from it is that hireling who sees the wolf coming and flees, and has no care for the sheep. So Augustine, Letter 180 to Honoratus, where he disputes at length, learnedly and most subtly, when the ministers of the Church ought to flee or remain in persecution. For as for private persons, it is certain that they may flee, as far as they can, to avoid the danger of denying Christ.

units.la: Non consummabitis, &c. Id est, non percurretis omnes Israelitarum civitates de alia in aliam fugiendo, donec veniat Filius hominis, scilicet, ad judicium, hoc est, usque ad consummationem seculi. q. d. Non deerunt civitates quò fugiant sectatores mei, quandocunque persecutionem passi fuerint. Ita fere B. Aug. lib. 1. contra Epist. Gaudentii Donatiltæ Thamugadensis Episcopi c. 18.
units.tr: You will not finish, etc. That is, you will not run through all the cities of the Israelites, fleeing from one to another, until the Son of man comes, namely to judgement, that is, until the end of the age. The sense is: there will not be lacking cities to which my followers may flee, whenever they have suffered persecution. Blessed Augustine says much the same in book 1 against the letter of Gaudentius, Donatist Bishop of Thamugadi, chapter 18.

units.la: Civitates Israël. Sic vocat Christus eas, in quibus Deus Israël tutò, liberè, palàm, & ritè colitur, ubi, ut loquitur Aug. loco mox citato, tanquam in portu possint Fideles à persecutionum tempestate requiescere.
units.tr: The cities of Israel. Christ calls by this name those places in which God is worshipped by Israel safely, freely, openly and lawfully, "where," as Augustine says in the passage just cited, "the faithful may rest from the storm of persecution as in a harbour."

units.la: 24. Non est discipulus, &c. Proverbialibus locutionibus apud Rabbinos usitatis hortatur Christus sectatores suos suis ut insistant vestigiis: q. d. Nolite vos servos & discipulos putare melioris conditionis, quàm ego Magister & Dominus sui, qui pro vobis passus sum; vobis relinquens exemplum.
units.tr: 24. A disciple is not above his teacher, etc. By proverbial sayings in common use among the rabbis, Christ urges his followers to follow in his footsteps. The sense is: do not think that you as servants and disciples are in a better condition than I, your Master and Lord, who suffered for you, leaving you an example.

units.la: 25. Patrem-familias. Id est, Patrem meum, & illius familiæ, cujus sum caput, & in cujus virtute dæmonia ejicio.
units.tr: 25. The master of the house. That is, my Father, and of that household of which I am the head, and in whose power I cast out demons.

units.la: Beelzebub. Id est, principem dæmoniorum vocaverunt, dùm suprà cap. 9. v. 34. dicebant me in principe dæmoniorum ejicere dæmonia. Beelzebub, inquit Hier. idolum Accaron, quod vocatur in Regum volumine, idolum muscæ. Beel, ipse est Bel, sive Baal, Zebub autem musca dicitur; principem ergo dæmoniorum ex spurcissimi idoli vocabant vocabulo: qui musca dicitur propter immunditiam, quæ exterminat suavitatem olei. Probabilius tamen est Deum Accaronitarum dictum Beelzebub, quòd abigeret muscas ab æde sua, quod & Herculi tribuunt Plinius & Solinus. Fortè in hac parte diabolus fujit Dei veri simia, in cujus Templo, si creditur Talmudicis, nunquam conspecta est musca.
units.tr: Beelzebub. That is, they called me the prince of demons, since above, in chapter 9:34, they said that I cast out demons by the prince of demons. "Beelzebub," says Jerome, "is the idol of Ekron, which in the book of Kings is called the fly-idol. Beel is the same as Bel or Baal, and Zebub means fly. So they called the prince of demons by the name of this most filthy idol, which is called a fly because of its uncleanness, which spoils the sweetness of oil." It is more probable, however, that the god of the Ekronites was called Beelzebub because he drove flies away from his temple, which Pliny and Solinus also attribute to Hercules. Perhaps in this respect the devil copied the true God, in whose temple, if the Talmudists are to be believed, a fly was never seen.

units.la: Domesticos ejus. Supple, convitiis lacessient.
units.tr: Domesticos ejus. Supply: they will heap abuse on them.

units.la: 26. Ne ergo, &c. Id est, nihil ad persecutorum impetus paveatis; quidquid enim moliantur, non possunt nisi corpori vitam auferre, imò nec potestatem adversum corpus habent ullam, nisi detur eis desuper à Patre vestro cœlesti, Qui nec exigui, ut loquitur Aug. 5. de Civit. Dei c. 11. & contemtibilis animantis viscera, nec avis pennulam, nec herbæ flosculum, nec arboris folium sine suarum partium convenientia dereliquit. Quidquid moliantur, Evangelium quod à me docti estis occultè, ipsis invitis à vobis usquequaque prædicabitur.
units.tr: 26. Ne ergo, etc. That is: do not fear the assaults of persecutors at all. Whatever they plan, they can take away only the body's life. Indeed they have no power at all over the body unless it is given them from above by your heavenly Father, who, as Augustine says (De Civ. Dei 5.11), has not left unattended even the viscera of a contemptible little creature, nor a bird's small feather, nor a flower of grass, nor a leaf of a tree, without the proper harmony of their parts. Whatever they plan, the Gospel, which you have been taught secretly by me, will be preached everywhere by you, even against their will.

units.la: 27. In tenebris. Id est, in Allegoriarum obscuritatibus. B. Greg. Hom. 6. in Ezech.
units.tr: 27. In tenebris. That is, in the obscurities of allegories. Blessed Gregory, Hom. 6 on Ezekiel.

units.la: In lumine, Id est, aperte. B. Greg. ibid.
units.tr: In lumine. That is, openly. Blessed Gregory, ibid.

units.la: In aure. Id est, in occulto, seu privatim.
units.tr: In aure. That is, in secret, or privately.

units.la: Prædicate super tecta. Hinc. B. Epiph. hær. 45. exponit illud Christi Joan. 18. v. 20. In occulto locutus sum nihil; q. d. Nihil dixi quod occultatum vellem; cùm de seorsum enarratis dixe-rim; rim, Quod in aure auditis, prædicate super tecta: Supple, quamdiu aliqua spes successus affulget, & ii quibus prædicatis non sunt prorsus immorigeri. Ita fere & B. Aug. Tracta. 113. in Joan.
units.tr: Prædicate super tecta. Hilary. Blessed Epiphanius (Haer. 45) explains by this Christ's words in John 18:20, In secret I have said nothing; as if to say: I have said nothing that I wished to be kept hidden, since I spoke of things told apart: What you hear in the ear, preach upon the housetops. Supply: as long as some hope of success shines forth, and those to whom you preach are not wholly unwilling to obey. Blessed Augustine, Tract. 113 on John, says much the same.

units.la: 28. Animam autem non possunt occidere. Id est, animæ nec substantiam vivendi, nec qualitatem vivendi, seu nec vivere, nec beate vivere possunt auferre. Vide B. Greg. lib. 6. Epist. 31. ad Eulog. Alexand. sub finem.
units.tr: 28. Animam autem non possunt occidere. That is, they cannot take from the soul either its substance of living, or its quality of living, or indeed its living or living blessedly. See Blessed Gregory, Book 6, Letter 31, to Eulogius of Alexandria, near the end.

units.la: *In gehennam. Græcè, in gehenna. Anima itaque mortalis & immortalis esse intelligitur; mortalis, quia beatè vivere amittit; immortalis, quia essentialiter vivere nunquam desinit, & naturæ suæ vitam perdere non valet, nec cùm in perpetua fuerit morte damnata; illic enim posita beatè esse perdit, & esse non perdit; qua ex re semper cogitur ut & mortem sine morte, & defectum sine defectu, & finem sine fine patiatur; quatenus ei & mors immortalis sit, & desectus indeficiens, & finis infinitus. B. Greg. lib. 4. Dialog. cap. 45. Augusst. de verbis Apost. Serm. 18. Considerans timorem gehennæ hic apud Matthæum, & vehementius apud Lucam c. 12. v. 5. nobis incussum; Cùm, inquit, Dominus timorem incusserit, & vehementer incusserit, & repetendo verbum apud Lucam cap. 12. v. 5. comminationem geminaverit, dicturus ego sum male times? ista non dicam; plane time, nihil melius times, nihil est quod magis timere debeas. Sed interrogo te, si non te videret Deus, quando facis, nec quisquam te convinceret in iudicio illius, faceres? tu te vide; non enim potes ad omnia verba mea respondere, inspice teipsum, faceres? Si faceres, ergo pœnam times, castitatem nondum amas, charitatem nondum habes, servili-ter times, formido est mali, nondum dilectio boni, sed time tamen, ut ista formido custodiat te, ut perducat ad dilectionem. Timor enim iste, quo gehennam times, & ideo mala non facis, continet te: et sic volentem peccare animum interiorem non finit: est enim quidam custos timor, quasi pædagogus Legis, litera est minans, nondum gratia juvans. Custodiat tamen te timor iste, dum non facis timendo, & venit charitas; intrat in cor tuum, & quantum intrat illa, tantum timor exit. Timor enim id agebat ne faceres, charitas id agit, ne velis facere. etiam si impune possis admittere. Idem ibidem, Serm. 13. c. 3. Qui adhuc ideo bene agit, quia pœnam timet, Deum non amat, nondum est inter filios, utinam tamen vel pœnam timeat; timor servus est, charitas libera est. & ut sic dicamus, timor est servus charitatis. Ne possideat diabolus cor tuum, præcedat servus in corde tuo, & servet dominæ venturæ locum. Fac, fac, vel timore pœnæ, si nondum potes amore justitiæ, veniet domina, & servus abscedet, quia consummata charitas foras mittit timorem, non enim accepisti spiritum servitutis iterum in timore. Novum TestaTestamentum est, non vetus; vetera transierunt, & ecce nova facta sunt omnia, omnia autem ex Deo.
units.tr: *In gehennam. In Greek, in gehenna. The soul is therefore understood to be both mortal and immortal: mortal, because it loses the ability to live blessedly; immortal, because it never ceases to live in its essence, and cannot lose the life of its nature, not even when it is condemned to eternal death. For there, placed in that state, it loses being blessed, yet does not lose being; and for this reason it is always forced to suffer death without death, defect without defect, and end without end, inasmuch as for it death is immortal, defect unfailing, and end infinite. Blessed Gregory, Dialogues 4.45. Augustine, Sermon 18 on the words of the Apostle. Considering the fear of hell which is struck into us here in Matthew, and more forcefully in Luke 12:5, he says: Since the Lord has struck fear, and struck it hard, and by repeating the word in Luke 12:5 has doubled the threat, shall I say, "You are afraid wrongly"? I will not say that. Be plainly afraid; you cannot be afraid of anything better; there is nothing you ought to fear more. But I ask you: if God did not see you when you act, and no one could convict you at his judgment, would you do it? Look at yourself; for you cannot answer all my words. Examine yourself: would you do it? If you would, then you fear the punishment; you do not yet love chastity, you do not yet have charity; you fear as a slave, your fear is of evil, not yet delight in good. Yet be afraid, so that this fear may guard you and lead you to love. For that fear by which you fear hell, and so do not do evil, restrains you, and so does not let the inner mind wish to sin. It is a kind of guardian fear, like the schoolmaster of the Law: the letter threatens, grace does not yet help. Let that fear guard you while you do not act from fear; and charity comes; it enters your heart, and as much as it enters, so much fear goes out. For fear was working so that you would not do it; charity works so that you do not want to do it, even when you could sin with impunity. The same, Sermon 13, ch. 3: One who still does good only because he fears punishment does not love God; he is not yet among the sons. Yet would that at least he feared punishment! Fear is a slave, charity is free; and, so to speak, fear is the slave of charity. Lest the devil possess your heart, let the slave go before in your heart and keep the place for the mistress who is coming. Do it, do it, if not yet from love of righteousness, then at least from fear of punishment; the mistress will come, and the slave will depart, because perfect charity casts out fear; for you have not received again the spirit of bondage in fear. The New Testament, not the Old: the old things have passed away, and behold, all things have become new, and all things are from God.

units.la: 29. Nonne, &c. Providentiam Dei erga superiora & majora probat Christus ex eo quod infimarum & minimarum rerum curam gerit. Cùm ergo Apost. dicit 1 Cor. 9. quòd Deo non est cura de bobus, non simpliciter negat boves Deo curæ esse, sed tantùm vult Deum hanc legem de non ligando ore bovi trituranti, non tam propter boves, quàm propter homines condidisse, & hoc præcipuè respexisse, ut nos doceret unumquemque ex labore suo vivere oportere, ut manifestè patet ex eodem Apost. 1 Tim. 5. v. 17, & 18. Familiare autem est Hebræis dum unum alteri præferunt, prælatum simpliciter affirmare, & id cui præfertur simpliciter negare, ut suprà advertimus ad illud Prophetæ: Misericordiam volo & non sacrificium. Sic Philo Judæus Paulo coævus in lib. de sacrificiis, agens de lege, quæ præcipit ut Deo victimæ eximiæ, integræ, puræ, atque ab omni labe immunes offerantur, ait non de victimis, sed de offerentibus legem esse sollicitam, ne quod eis vitium insideat. Similiter R. Menachem Ricinensis ad illud Deuteron. 22. Non accipies matrem cum pullis; Intentio, inquit, præcipientis non est misereri avium, sed propter homines hoc voluit, quos ita voluit assuefacere ad mansuetudinem & commiserationem.
units.tr: 29. Nonne, etc. Christ proves God's providence toward higher and greater things from the fact that he takes care of the lowest and smallest things. When the Apostle says in 1 Cor. 9 that God is not concerned about oxen, he does not simply deny that oxen are God's concern; he means only that God laid down the law not to muzzle the ox while it treads grain not so much for the sake of oxen as for the sake of men, and chiefly had this in view: to teach us that each should live by his own labour, as is clear from the same Apostle in 1 Tim. 5:17–18. It is also a Hebrew habit, when they prefer one thing to another, to affirm simply the thing preferred and simply to deny that to which it is preferred, as we noted above on the prophet's words: I desire mercy and not sacrifice. So Philo the Jew, a contemporary of Paul, in his book On Sacrifices, speaking of the law that commands that choice victims, whole, pure, and free from every blemish, be offered to God, says that the law is concerned not with the victims but with the offerers, lest any fault cling to them. Likewise Rabbi Menahem of Rieti on Deut. 22, You shall not take the mother with the young: The intention of the commander, he says, is not to show mercy to birds, but he willed this for the sake of men, whom he wished to accustom to gentleness and compassion.

units.la: Duo passeres asse veneunt. Id est, nunquid passeres sunt res vilissimi pretii; unde Matth. non est contrarius Lucæ referenti cap. 12. Christum dixisse: Nonne quinque passeres venunt dipondio, id est, duobus assibus; nam eumdem sensum, licèt aliis verbis expressit Luc. ac Matth. contrarietas autem penes sensum, non penes verba attenditur.
units.tr: Duo passeres asse veneunt. That is: are sparrows things of the cheapest price? Hence Matthew is not contrary to Luke, who reports in ch. 12 that Christ said: Are not five sparrows sold for two farthings? that is, for two asses. For Luke and Matthew express the same sense in different words; contrariety is to be judged by sense, not by words.

units.la: Cadit super terram. Ἐπὶ γῆν. B. Epiph. adversus Marcionem & B. Chrysost. legerunt Εἰς παγίδα, in laqueum; hoc alicubi secutus videtur B. Hieron.
units.tr: Cadit super terram. [ἐπὶ γῆν]. Blessed Epiphanius against Marcion and Blessed Chrysostom read [εἰς παγίδα], into a snare; Blessed Jerome seems to have followed this somewhere.

units.la: Sine Patre vestro. Id est, sine Patris vestri ordinatione, decreto & voluntate. Huc facit locus, quem ex Talmude Jerosolymitano profert clarissimus Buxtorfius Lexici Talmudici pag. 113. Rabbi Simeon Ben Jochai latebat in quadam spelunca. Die quodam sedens ad ostium spelunca, & videns aucupem aves capientem, & rete extendentem, audivit filiam vocis (oraculum) quæ cùm diceret דימום (id est, liberatio) tum evadebat aves. Quando verò filia vocis dicebat סםיקולא (id est, sententia mortis,) tum avis capiebatur. Proinde dixit oraculum, צפור שבלבדי שמיא לא יבדא כל שכו בר נשא, Avicula sine cælo (id est, sine Dei voluntate, & providentia) non perit, Quanto minùs homo? Pro יבדא lege יאבד.
units.tr: Sine Patre vestro. That is, without the ordinance, decree and will of your Father. The passage which the most distinguished Buxtorf quotes from the Jerusalem Talmud, in his Lexicon Talmudicum p. 113, is relevant here: Rabbi Simeon ben Yochai was hiding in a certain cave. One day, sitting at the mouth of the cave, and seeing a fowler catching birds and spreading a net, he heard a daughter of a voice (an oracle) which, when it said [דימום] (that is, release), the birds escaped. But when the daughter of a voice said [סםיקולא] (that is, sentence of death), then the bird was caught. Accordingly the oracle said: [צפור שבלבדי שמיא לא יבדא כל שכו בר נשא], A little bird without heaven (that is, without the will and providence of God) does not perish; how much less man? For [יבדא] read [יאבד].

units.la: 30. Vestri autem capilli. Græcè, vestri etiam capilli, supple, qui abjici & contemni solent.
units.tr: 30. Vestri autem capilli. In Greek, your hairs also, supply: which are usually cast off and despised.

units.la: Numerati sunt. Hinc teste Aug. 2. de Civit. Dei c. 194 patet quòd illud Lucæ 21. v. 18. Capillus de capite vestro non peribit: aptiùs de numero quàm de longitudine capillorum intelligitur.
units.tr: Numerati sunt. Hence, as Augustine testifies (De Civ. Dei 2.19), it is clear that the saying in Luke 21:18, Not a hair of your head will perish, is better understood of their number than of their length.

units.la: Præclarè itaque Hilar. Can. 10. in Matth. In numerum, inquit, aliquid colligi diligentiæ ac sollicitudinis cura est, neque enim dignum negotium est peritura numerare. Ut igitur nihil ex nobis periturum esse cognosceremus, quia multò passeribus meliores sumus, ipso capillorum nostrorum supputatorum numero indicatur, salvis nobis ex solido futuris, cùm quod innumerabile in nobis sit, conservandi & affectu & potestate numeretur.
units.tr: Admirably, therefore, Hilary (Can. 10 in Matth.) says: "To count something into a number is a matter of care and concern, for it is not a worthy business to number things that will perish. So that we might know that nothing of us will perish, we are shown by the very number of our hairs, which have been counted, that we shall be safe in our entirety; since what is innumerable in us is counted in regard to both the care and the power of preserving us."

units.la: 32. Qui confitebitur me. Id est, me & verba mea quæ corde seu voluntate credit, ore & opere confiteri non erubuerit. Vide Marc. 8. v. 38. Luc. 9. v. 26. 12. v. 8. Ex hoc loco factum est ut professiones fidei, quæ non fuerunt morte sigillatæ, confessiones appellarentur, & qui eas ediderant, confessores. Hic autem mandatur nobis, ut fidem nostram testatam faciamus, non solùm coram bonis ac piis, verùm etiam coram ipsis veræ & puræ religionis professis hostibus.
units.tr: "32. Whoever shall confess me." That is, whoever has not been ashamed to confess me and my words, which he believes in heart or will, with mouth and deed. See Mark 8:38; Luke 9:26; 12:8. From this place it came about that professions of faith which were not sealed by death were called "confessions," and those who had made them "confessors." Here, however, we are commanded to make our faith witnessed, not only before the good and pious, but also before the very enemies of the true and pure religion who profess it.

units.la: Confitebor. Id est, ut patet ex locis mox cit. in die judicii palàm agnoscam pro meo.
units.tr: "I will confess." That is, as is clear from the places just cited, on the day of judgment I will openly acknowledge him as mine.

units.la: 33. Negaverit. Scilicet, verbis vel factis.
units.tr: "33. Shall deny." Namely, by words or deeds.

units.la: Me. Supple ex locis cit. vel verba, seu, præcepta mea.
units.tr: "Me." Supply from the cited places, either "my words" or "my precepts."

units.la: Negabo. Id est, non cognoscam esse de quibus meis.
units.tr: "I will deny." That is, I will not acknowledge him as among mine.

units.la: 34. Non veni pacem mittere. Id est, concordiam, quam solam mundus novit & æstimat pacem, quæ consistit in fruitione rerum caducarum sine molestia litium & bellorum.
units.tr: "34. I have not come to send peace." That is, concord, which alone the world knows and esteems as peace, consisting in the enjoyment of perishable things without the annoyance of quarrels and wars.

units.la: Sed gladium. Id est, discordiam, seu separationem, ut loquitur Lucas c. 12. v. 51. Conjunctio cœlestis, inquit Chrysolog. Serm. 104. est in ista separatione terrena, nemo potest connecti terræ & jungi cælo; grata ergo & chara sit ista terrena separatio, quæ nos sic à terrenis separat, ut inserat nos divinis.
units.tr: "But a sword." That is, discord, or "division," as Luke says in ch. 12:51. "Heavenly union," says Chrysologus (Serm. 104), "is found in this earthly separation; no one can be joined to the earth and united to heaven. Let this earthly separation, then, be welcome and dear, which separates us from earthly things so as to join us to divine things."

units.la: 35. Veni enim separare, &c. Hic locus prope iisdem verbis in Michæa Propheta scribitur c. 7. & notandum quod ubicunque de veteri Testamento testimonium ponitur, non refert utrum sensus tantùm an & verba conveniant. Hier. Sensus itaque Christi est q. d. Occasione Evangelii mei tale orietur dissidium inter filios & parentes, & alios sanguine junctos, quale fuit olim tempore Michææ Prophetæ apud Judæos; sicut enim tunc, ita etiam nunc impii conspirabunt in ruinam piorum; Infideles in eversionem Fidelium, nullo habito respectu, seu sanguinis, seu propinquitatis, solo odio virtutis, & opum extorquendarum cupidine impulsi. Hominem. Hebraismus, id est, filium.
units.tr: "35. For I have come to separate, etc." This place is written in nearly the same words in the prophet Micah, ch. 7; and it is to be noted that wherever a testimony is taken from the Old Testament, it does not matter whether only the sense or also the words agree. (Jerome.) The meaning of Christ, then, is as if he said: Through the occasion of my Gospel there will arise such a division between sons and parents, and others joined by blood, as once existed among the Jews in the time of the prophet Micah; for just as then, so now also the wicked will conspire for the ruin of the pious, unbelievers for the overthrow of the faithful, impelled by hatred of virtue and by the desire to extort wealth, with no regard had either to blood or to kinship. "A man": a Hebraism, that is, a son.

units.la: 37. Qui amat patrem, &c. Qui ante praemiserat: Non veni pacem mittere, sed gladium, & dividere homines adversus patrem, & matrem, & nurum & socrum: ne quis religioni pietatem anteferret, subjicit dicens: Qui amat patrem & matrem plus quam me. Ordo in omni affectu necessarius est. Ama post Deum, patrem, ama matrem ac filios, si autem necessitas venerit ut amor parentum ac filiorum Dei amori comparetur, & non posset utrumque servari, odium in suos, pietas in Deum sit. Non ergo prohibuit amare patrem aut matrem, sed signanter addidit, Qui amat patrem aut matrem plus quam me. B. Hier. Idem est sensus Lucæ 14. v. 26, licet alia adhibeat verba.
units.tr: "37. He who loves father, etc." He had said before: "I have not come to send peace but a sword, and to divide men against father and mother, and daughter-in-law and mother-in-law." Lest anyone should put piety before religion, he adds, saying: "He who loves father or mother more than me." Order is necessary in every affection. Love, after God, father; love mother and children; but if necessity should come, so that love of parents and children must be weighed against the love of God, and both cannot be kept, let there be hatred toward one's own and piety toward God. He therefore did not forbid loving father or mother, but he pointedly added: "He who loves father or mother more than me." (St Jerome.) The sense is the same in Luke 14:26, though it uses other words.

units.la: Non est me dignus. Supple, præceptore, unde Luc. loco mox citato additur: Non potest meus esse discipulus.
units.tr: "Is not worthy of me." Supply: "of the teacher"; whence in the Luke passage just cited it is added: "He cannot be my disciple."

units.la: 38. Qui non accipit crucem, &c. Luc. 14. v. 27. Qui non bajulat crucem suam. Duobus modis crux tollitur, cum aut per abstinentiam afficitur corpus, aut per compassionem proximi affligitur animus. Greg. Hom. 32. in Evang. & Hom. 37. D. Hieron. lib. 3. in Matth. 16. Qui deponit veterem hominem cum operibus suis, denegat semetipsum dicens; Vivo autem, non ego, vivit vero in me Christus: Tollit crucem suam & mundo crucifigitur; cui autem mundus crucifixus est sequitur Dominum crucifixum.
units.tr: "38. He who does not take up his cross, etc." Luke 14:27: "He who does not bear his cross." The cross is taken up in two ways: either the body is afflicted through abstinence, or the mind is afflicted through compassion for one's neighbour. (Gregory, Hom. 32 in Evang., and Hom. 37; St Jerome, bk. 3 in Matth. 16.) He who puts off the old man with his works denies himself, saying: "I live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me." He takes up his cross and is crucified to the world; and to him to whom the world is crucified, he follows the crucified Lord.

units.la: Et sequitur me. Bajulare crucem, & post Dominum ire, est vel carnis abstinentiam, vel compassionem proximo pro studio æternæ intentionis exhibere; nam quisquis pro temporali intentione hæc exhibet, crucem quidem bajulat, sed ire post Dominum recusat. Greg. Hom. 37. in Evang.
units.tr: "And follows me." To bear the cross and go after the Lord is either to practise abstinence of the flesh, or to show compassion to a neighbour for the sake of an eternal aim; for whoever shows these things for a temporal aim bears indeed a cross, but refuses to go after the Lord. (Gregory, Hom. 37 in Evang.)

units.la: 39. Qui invenit animam suam. Supple ex Joan. 12. v. 25. in hoc mundo, id est, in hac vita; dicitur autem in hoc mundo amare, invenire seipsum, seu phrasi Hebraicâ, invenire, amare animam suam, qui non nisi hujus mundi quærit sibi commoda, & fugit incommoda; perdere vero & odisse qui gravissimas hujus mundi calamitates, afflictiones & angustias propter Christum, propter Evangelium, propter justitiam fortiter tolerat. Confer hunc locum cum eo quod dicitur Joan. 12. v. 25.
units.tr: "39. He who finds his soul." Supply from John 12:25: "in this world," that is, in this life. He is said to love and find himself in this world, or, in the Hebrew phrase, to find and love his soul, who seeks only the conveniences of this world and flees its discomforts; but he loses and hates it who bravely endures the most grievous calamities, afflictions and distresses of this world for Christ, for the Gospel, for righteousness. Compare this place with what is said in John 12:25.

units.la: Perdet eam. Supple, in vita æterna, id est, vitæ æternæ jacturam faciet, seu morte æternâ multabitur.
units.tr: "Shall lose it." Supply: in eternal life; that is, he shall suffer the loss of eternal life, or he shall be punished with eternal death.

units.la: Qui perdiderit animam suam. Clarius Joan. loco citato, Qui odit animam suam in hoc mundo.
units.tr: "He who loses his soul." More clearly in the cited place of John: "He who hates his soul in this world."

units.la: Propter me. Martyrem Christi non facit poena, sed causa.
units.tr: "For my sake." Suffering does not make a martyr of Christ, but the cause does.

units.la: Inveniet eam. Supple, in vita æterna, ut patet loco cit. Joan. Porrò in hac & similibus sententiis anima synecdochicè usurpatur pro toto homine, phrasi apud Hebræos & in veteri TestaTestamento usitatissima. Hinc quod Matth. 16. v. 26. dicitur: Anima vero sua detrimentum patiatur, Lucas proprietatem Hebraicam explicans dicit c. 9. v. 25. Seipsum autem perdat, & detrimentum sui faciat.
units.tr: "Shall find it." Supply: in eternal life, as is clear from the cited place of John. Moreover, in this and similar sayings "soul" is used synecdochically for the whole man, a usage most common among the Hebrews and in the Old Testament. Hence, where Matthew 16:26 says, "but let him suffer loss of his soul," Luke, explaining the Hebrew idiom, says in ch. 9:25: "but lose himself and suffer the loss of himself."

units.la: 40. Qui recipit, &c. Ordo pulcherrimus: ad praedicationem Christus discipulos mittit, docet pericula non timenda, affectum subjicit religioni, aurum supra tulerat, as de zona excusserat; dura Evangelistarum conditio; unde ergo sumus, unde vitus necessaria? Auferitatem mandatorum spe temperat promissorum. Qui recipit, inquiens, vos, me recipit, ut in suscipiendis Apostolis unusquisque credentium Christum Jesum suscepisse arbitretur. Hieron. lib. 1. in Matth. 10.
units.tr: "40. He who receives, etc." A most beautiful order: Christ sends the disciples out to preach, teaches that dangers are not to be feared, and subjoins an incentive to religion; he had before set aside gold, and had shaken out the copper from the belt; hard is the condition of the Evangelists; whence then are we, whence the necessary sustenance? He tempers the austerity of the commands with the hope of the promises. "He who receives you," he says, "receives me," so that in receiving the Apostles each believer may think he has received Christ Jesus. (Jerome, bk. 1 in Matth. 10.)

units.la: Recipit eum qui me misit. Id est, Deum Patrem.
units.tr: "He receives him who sent me." That is, God the Father.

units.la: 41. In nomine Prophetae. Id est, ideo tantum, quia Propheta dicitur & existimatur; eodem penitus sensu in versu sequenti intelligitur, tantum in nomine discipuli, ut patet ex Marc. 9.
units.tr: "41. In the name of a prophet." That is, only because he is called and thought to be a prophet; in exactly the same sense in the following verse it is understood, "only in the name of a disciple," as is clear from Mark 9.

units.la: Mercedem Prophetae accipiet. Id est, qui aliquem hospitio accipit, non alia de causa, quam quia Propheta esse dicitur & existimatur, tunc etiamsi hospitio exceptus revera Propheta non fuerit, excipiens tamen eandem recipiet mercedem suae hospitalitatis, atque si verum Prophetam excepisset.
units.tr: "Shall receive a prophet's reward." That is, whoever receives someone into his hospitality for no other reason than that he is called and thought to be a prophet, even if the one received has in fact not been a prophet, the one receiving him will nonetheless receive the same reward for his hospitality as if he had received a true prophet.

units.la: 42. Uni ex minimis istis. Supple, qui in me credunt, ut exprimitur Matth. 18. vel, fratribus meis, ut Matth. 25. hoc est, ex infimis & contemptissimis Fidelibus. Hic indicatur quod, ut Apostolus docet Galat. 6. v. 10. quamvis ad omnes bonum operari debeamus, maxime tamen ad domesticos fidei.
units.tr: "42. One of these least." Supply: who believe in me, as is expressed in Matthew 18; or "my brothers," as in Matthew 25; that is, of the lowliest and most despised of the faithful. Here it is indicated that, as the Apostle teaches in Galatians 6:10, although we ought to do good to all, yet especially to the household of faith.

units.la: Calicem aquae frigidae potum dederit. Id est, vel abjectissimum ministerium exhibuerit; ponitur enim pro more Scripturae unum vile ministerium determinatum pro indeterminato.
units.tr: "Gives a cup of cold water to drink." That is, he has rendered even the most abject service; for by the custom of Scripture one determinate vile service is put for an indeterminate one.

units.la: CAPUT XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: 1. CUM consummasset, &c. Id est, cum Jesus finem faceret præcipiendi, seu officii Apostolici præscribendi tam præceptis, quam consiliis & prædictionibus.
units.tr: 1. When Jesus had finished, etc. That is, when Jesus had finished giving instructions, or laying down the office of the Apostles, both by precepts, counsels and predictions.

units.la: Transiit inde. Scilicet, ab Apostolis nunc primum à se ad prædicandum Evangelium missis se separavit; quid autem Apostoli sic à Christo dimissi fecerint narrat Marc. c. 6. v. 12. Lucas c. 9. v. 8.
units.tr: He went on from there. That is, he separated himself from the Apostles, whom he now first sent out from himself to preach the Gospel. What the Apostles did when thus dismissed by Christ is related in Mark 6:12 and Luke 9:8.

units.la: In civitatibus eorum. Id est, Apostolorum. Sic dicuntur civitates Galilææ, quia in eis nati, educati & ut plurimum Apostoli sunt conversati.
units.tr: In their cities. That is, the cities of the Apostles. The cities of Galilee are so called because the Apostles were born and brought up in them and for the most part lived in them.

units.la: 2. Joannes Baptista, &c. Quæ hic narrantur & Matth. 14. de Joanne contigerunt ante missionem Apostolorum; ut patet ex Luc. 7. v. 18. & opinione Herodis de Christo, quàm ipse Matthæus c. 14. testatur fuisse causam secessûs Christi in desertum cum Apostolis ex missione reversis. Vide Luc. 9. à v. 7. ad 11. Marc. 6. v. 3. & 31.
units.tr: 2. John the Baptist, etc. What is related here, and in Matt. 14 about John, happened before the sending out of the Apostles, as is clear from Luke 7:18 and from Herod's opinion about Christ. Matthew himself testifies in ch. 14 that this opinion was the reason Christ withdrew into the desert with the Apostles after their return from the mission. See Luke 9 from v. 7 to 11, and Mark 6:3 and 31.

units.la: 3. Tu es qui venturus es, &c. Joannes non suæ sed discipulorum ignorantiæ consulit; ipse enim venturum in remissionem peccatorum prædicavit. Sed ut scirent non alium à se prædicatum, ad opera ejus intuenda discipulos suos mittit: ut autoritatem dicti sui illius opera conferrent, neque alius Christus expectaretur, quàm cui testimonium opera præstitissent. Hilar. Can. 11. in Matth.
units.tr: 3. Are you the one who is to come, etc. John is not consulting his own ignorance but that of his disciples; for he himself had preached that the one to come would bring forgiveness of sins. But so that they might know that no other had been preached apart from himself, he sends his disciples to look at his works, so that they might compare his works with the authority of his words, and no other Christ might be awaited than the one to whom the works had given testimony. Hilary, Canon 11 on Matthew.

units.la: 4. Euntes renuntiate, &c. Non dicit eis expresse, Ego sum, sed ducit eos magis ad rei certitudinem, ut congruâ ratione sumentes fidem ipsius revertantur ad eum qui misit eos, unde non ad verba sed ad propositum mittentis responsum exhibuit. Q.d. Narrate Joanni quæ quidem audistis per Prophetas, consummari vero vidistis à me; ea enim tunc agebat, quæ prædixerant Prophetæ David Psal. 145. & Esaias c. 35. eum facturum.
units.tr: 4. Go and report, etc. He does not say expressly, "I am," but leads them rather to certainty of the matter, so that, taking up faith by a fitting line of reasoning, they might return to him who sent them. Hence he gave an answer not to the words but to the purpose of the sender. That is: Tell John what you have indeed heard through the Prophets, but what you have seen accomplished by me; for then he was doing those things which the Prophets David (Psalm 145) and Isaiah (ch. 35) had foretold he would do.

units.la: 5. Pauperes Evangelizantur. Vel pauperes spiritu, vel certè opibus pauperes, ut nulla inter divites & egenos in prædicatione distantia sit. Hæc magistri rigorem, hæc præceptoris comprobant veritatem; quando omnis apud eum, qui salvari potest, æqualis est. Hier. Alludit Christus ad illud Esaiæ 61. v. 1. Ad annuntiandum mansuetis misit me: pauperes enim à fastu & ferocitate divitum remotiores esse solent, & mansuetudini Evangelicæ aptiores & propinquiores. 6. Beatus.
units.tr: 5. The poor have the gospel preached to them. Either the poor in spirit, or certainly the poor in means, so that in the preaching there is no distinction between rich and needy. These things confirm the rigour of the teacher and the truth of the instructor, since with him who can be saved all are equal. Jerome. Christ alludes to Isaiah 61:1, He has sent me to preach to the meek; for the poor are usually further removed from the pride and fierceness of the rich, and are more fit for and closer to evangelical meekness. 6. Blessed.

units.la: 6. Beatus, &c. Tacitè notat Joannis discipulos, quos habuisse aliquid mordacitatis ex livore & invidia adversus Christum,patet ex Matth. 9. v. 14. & Joan 3. v. 26. ubi dicunt Joanni; Cui tu testimonium perhibuisti, ecce hic baptizat, & omnes veniunt ad eum. Q. d. Nos deserimur, hic raritas est, ad illum turba concurrit. Hier. lib. 1. in Matth. cap. 11. & Epist. 151. ad Algasiam quæst. 1.
units.tr: 6. Blessed, etc. He tacitly notes John's disciples, who had some biting spite, born of envy and jealousy against Christ. This is clear from Matt. 9:14 and John 3:26, where they say to John: He to whom you bore witness, behold, he baptizes, and everyone comes to him. That is: we are deserted, here is scarcity, while the crowd flocks to him. Jerome, book 1 on Matthew, ch. 11, and Letter 151 to Algasia, question 1.

units.la: Scandalizatus. Id est, scandalum passus. Scandalum proprie lapsus & offensio est pedis. In sacra Scriptura sæpè transfertur à corpore ad animum, & sumitur pro dicto aut facto ex se malo, vel mali speciem habente, quod alicui ruinæ spiritualis occasionem præbet, & dicitur scandalum activum, vel datum; vel sumitur pro ipsa ruina, quâ quis propter dictum aut factum alterius spiritualiter ruit, & dicitur scandalum passivum vel acceptum; quod scandalum passivum, si non ex infirmitate vel ignorantia, sed ex malitia ruentis oriatur, Pharisaicum dicitur, quia Pharisæi tale scandalum in vera Christi doctrina & bonis moribus passi sunt.
units.tr: Scandalized. That is, having suffered a scandal. A scandal is properly a stumbling and offence of the foot. In Holy Scripture it is often transferred from the body to the mind, and is taken for a word or deed evil in itself, or having the appearance of evil, which gives someone an occasion of spiritual ruin. This is called active or given scandal. Or it is taken for the ruin itself, by which someone falls spiritually because of another's word or deed, and this is called passive or received scandal. If this passive scandal arises not from weakness or ignorance but from the malice of the one who falls, it is called Pharisaic, because the Pharisees suffered such scandal at the true doctrine of Christ and at his good morals.

units.la: 7. Illis autem abeuntibus. Non enim, inquit Simeon in Catena Græcorum in Luc. 7. præsentibus Joannis discipulis proferre volebat Christus Joannis præconia, ne blandientis verba esse putarentur.
units.tr: 7. But when they had gone away. For, says Simeon in the Greek Catena on Luke 7, Christ did not wish to utter praises of John in the presence of John's disciples, lest his words be thought to be flattery.

units.la: Quid exiistis. Supple, toties.
units.tr: Why did you go out? Supply: so often.

units.la: Arundinem, &c. q. d. Numquid ob hoc exiistis toties in desertum ad Joannem, ut videretis hominem levem & instabilem, dapibus affluentem, mollibus vestitum?
units.tr: A reed, etc. That is: Did you go out so often into the desert to John for this, to see a light and unstable man, abounding in delicacies and dressed in soft clothing?

units.la: 8. In domibus Regum sunt. Offenditur rigidam vitam & austeram prædicationem vitare debere aulas Regum, & mollium hominum Palatia declinare. B. Hier.
units.tr: 8. They are in kings' houses. It is shown that a harsh life and austere preaching ought to avoid royal courts and shun the palaces of effeminate men. Jerome.

units.la: 9. Etiam. Nam ab ipso matris utero prophetavit, & positus in tenebris, lumen, quod jam venerat, non ignoravit, ut loquitur B. Isidorus Pelusiota in Ep. 33. ad Prunichium.
units.tr: 9. Yes. For from his mother's womb he prophesied, and placed in darkness he did not fail to know the light which had already come, as Saint Isidore of Pelusium says in Letter 33 to Prunichius.

units.la: Plusquam Prophetam. Tantus enim est Joannes inter Prophetas, ut de eo tanquam de nobilissimo Prophetarum ceteri Prophetæ prophetaverint; hic est enim de quo scriptum est, &c.
units.tr: More than a prophet. For John is so great among the Prophets that the other prophets prophesied about him as about the most noble of the prophets; for this is he of whom it is written, etc.

units.la: 10. Mitto Angelum. Angelum hic dici Joannem non putemus naturæ societate, sed officii dignitate: id est, nuntium: quòd venturum Dominum nuntiavit. B. Hier.
units.tr: 10. I send my messenger. We should not think that the angel here is John by community of nature, but by the dignity of his office: that is, a messenger, because he announced the coming Lord. Jerome.

units.la: Ante faciem tuam. Hebraismus, id est, ante te; sex enim mensibus ante Christum conceptus & natus est Joannes, & totidem circiter ante Christum prædicare coepit.
units.tr: Before your face. A Hebraism, that is, before you. For John was conceived and born six months before Christ, and began to preach about as many months before him.

units.la: Præparabit. Id est, Pervia reddet tibi corda auditorum, tæ itentiam prædicando & baptizando. D. Th. in Catena ex Glossa.
units.tr: Will prepare. That is, will make the hearts of the hearers open to you by preaching and baptizing repentance. Thomas, in the Catena, from the Gloss.

units.la: 11. Surrexit. Hebraismus Scripturæ familiaris, id est, extitit. Major.
units.tr: 11. Has arisen. A Hebraism familiar to Scripture, that is, has appeared. Major.

units.la: Supple ex Luc. 7. v. 8. Propheta; ut enim ait S. Maximus Taurinensis Hom. 3. in Nat. S. Joannis Bap. Joannes idcirco in hoc seculum superna dispensatione direetus est, ut non solum ipse prophetali sublimaretur gloria: sed ut & omnium etiam per eum Prophetarum præconia firmarentur, qui speciali quadam gratia, ob hoc Redemtorem mundi novissimus prophetavit, ut ostenderet eum primus. Neque obstat quod dicitur Deut. 34. Non surrexit ultra Propheta in Israël sicut Moyses; ut enim ait D. Th. 22. Q. 174. Ar. 4. ad 3. Joannes pertinet ad novum Testamentum, cujus ministri præferuntur etiam ipsi Moysi, quasi magis revelatè speculantes, ut habetur 2. Cor. 3.
units.tr: Supply from Luke 7:8: a prophet. For, as Saint Maximus of Turin says in Homily 3 on the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, John was therefore sent into this world by heavenly dispensation, not only so that he himself might be exalted with the glory of a prophet, but also so that the proclamations of all the Prophets might be confirmed through him. Who by a special grace prophesied of the Redeemer of the world, the last of them, so that he might point him out as the first. Nor does it stand in the way that it is said in Deut. 34: There arose no prophet again in Israel like Moses; for, as Thomas says (2a2ae, Q. 174, Art. 4, ad 3), John belongs to the New Testament, whose ministers are preferred even to Moses himself, as seeing more openly, as is found in 2 Cor. 3.

units.la: Scilicet, tum nativitate, ut intelligit Augustinus, tum hominum opinione, ut exponit Hilar.
units.tr: That is, both by birth, as Augustine understands it, and by the opinion of men, as Hilary expounds it.

units.la: Id est, in Ecclesia justorum sive militante, sive triumphante.
units.tr: That is, in the Church of the just, whether militant or triumphant.

units.la: Nimirum, potestate, Divinitate, majestate, charitate, ut exponit Aug. Tract. 13. in Joan & lib. 2. contra Adverf. Legis & Prophetarum cap. 5. Alludere videtur Christus ad illud: Qui post me venturus est, ante me factus est.
units.tr: Namely, in power, divinity, majesty and charity, as Augustine expounds in Tractate 13 on John and in book 2 against Adversarius of the Law and the Prophets, ch. 5. Christ seems to allude to the words: He who comes after me has been made before me.

units.la: Supple, prædicationis.
units.tr: Supply: of preaching.

units.la: 12. Usque nunc. Id est, usque ad præsens tempus, quo ego Joanni in prædicatione succedo.
units.tr: 12. Until now. That is, until the present time, in which I succeed John in preaching.

units.la: Regnum cœlorum, &c. Dominus ire Apostolos, ad oves Israël perditas jusserat, sed hæc omnis prædicatio profectum Publicanis & peccatoribus afferebat. Aliis Christus prædicatur, & ab aliis agnoscitur, aliis nascitur, & ab aliis diligitur. Sui eum repuunt, alieni suscipiunt. Proprii insectantur, complectuntur inimici. Hæreditatem adoptio expetit, familia rejicit. Testamentum filii repudiant, servi recognoscunt. Itaque vim regnum cælorum patitur, inferentesque diripiunt illud, quia gloria Israël patribus debita, à Prophetis nunciata, à Christo oblata, fide gentium occupatur, & rapitur. B. Hil. Can. 11. in Mat.
units.tr: The kingdom of heaven, etc. The Lord had ordered the Apostles to go to the lost sheep of Israel, but all this preaching brought profit to tax collectors and sinners. Christ is preached by some and acknowledged by some; he is born for some and loved by others. His own people reject him, strangers receive him. Those who are his own pursue him, enemies embrace him. Adoption seeks the inheritance, while the household rejects it. Sons repudiate the testament, servants recognize it. Thus the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it, because the glory of Israel, owed to the fathers, announced by the Prophets and offered by Christ, is taken up and seized by the faith of the Gentiles. Hilary, Canon 11 on Matthew.

units.la: 13. Omnes enim, &c. Lex dicitur duraffe usque ad Joannem, quia ab illo incepit doctrina clarior Lege & Prophetis; nam principium Evangelii à Joanne ducitur Marc. 1. v. 1. Luc. 1. v. 77. & hoc nomine major Prophetis est Joannes missus ad dandam scientiam salutis plebi Dei, & ad multa evangelizanda populo, ut dicitur Luc. 3. v. 18. Evangelium autem, seu Lex nova, regnum dicitur, quia Legem regni nomine appellare Hebræis mos est; dicitur autem regnum cœlorum, seu regnum Dei, quia per doctrinam Evangelii Deus regnat in Ecclesia, & vilescunt Fidelibus omnia, quæ habentur in terris. Hæc doctrina cœpit à præ-dicatione dicatione Joannis, & consummata est à Christo Salvatore diffundente charitatem in cordibus Fidelium per Spiritum Sanctum, qui datus est eis.
units.tr: 13. For all, etc. The Law is said to have lasted until John, because from him began a teaching clearer than the Law and the Prophets; for the beginning of the Gospel is taken from John (Mark 1:1; Luke 1:77). In this name John is greater than the Prophets, sent to give the knowledge of salvation to the people of God, and to preach the gospel to the people in many things, as is said in Luke 3:18. The Gospel, or new Law, is called the kingdom, because it was the custom of the Hebrews to call the Law by the name of kingdom. It is called the kingdom of heaven, or kingdom of God, because through the doctrine of the Gospel God reigns in the Church, and to the faithful all the things that are on earth become worthless. This doctrine began from the preaching of John, and was completed by Christ the Saviour, who pours out charity into the hearts of the faithful through the Holy Spirit, who was given to them.

units.la: Prophetaverunt. Id est, obscuris figuris praedixerunt, quae & quanta sint quae nobis promittuntur in superna felicitate.
units.tr: They prophesied. That is, they foretold in obscure figures what and how great the things are that are promised to us in heavenly happiness.

units.la: 14. Si vultis recipere. Hac locutione utitur Christus ad significandum improprium sensum sententiae sequentis.
units.tr: 14. If you are willing to receive it. Christ uses this expression to signal that the following sentence is to be taken in a figurative sense.

units.la: Ipse est Elias. Non persona, sed spiritu & virtute; quod enim ab Elia in Christi adventu faciendum praedixit Malachias cap. 4. v. 6. hoc à Joanne in spiritu & virtute Eliae faciendum interpretatus est Angelus Luc. 1. v. 17.
units.tr: He is Elijah. Not in person, but in spirit and power. What Malachi (ch. 4, v. 6) foretold Elijah would do at the coming of Christ, the angel interpreted (Luke 1:17) as something John would do in the spirit and power of Elijah.

units.la: 15. Qui habet, &c. Solet Christus hac uti phrasi, cum de re maxime seria, & quae maxime auditores attingit, verba facit, ut attentionem & studium auditorum excitet, simulque indicet, non omnes habere aures audiendi, id est, donum Dei, quo intelligitur id quod dicitur, dictoque obeditur, quia non omnibus datur ab eo, qui de se dicit Baruch 2. v. 31. Dabo eis cor & intelligent, aures & audient.
units.tr: 15. He who has ears, etc. Christ commonly uses this phrase when he speaks of a matter of the utmost seriousness that touches his hearers most closely. He does so to arouse the attention and zeal of his hearers, and at the same time to show that not everyone has ears to hear, that is, the gift of God by which what is said is understood and obeyed. This gift is not given to all by him who says of himself (Baruch 2. v. 31): I will give them a heart to understand, and ears to hear.

units.la: 16. Similem aestimabo. Id est, comparabo.
units.tr: 16. I will liken. That is, I will compare.

units.la: Generationem istam. Id est, istud hominum genus.
units.tr: This generation. That is, this kind of men.

units.la: Similis est, &c. Q. d. Simile quid accidit in hoc hominum genere, atque si pueri ludentes in foro coetaneis seu sodalibus suis morosis acclamarent: Nec cantu ad saltandum, nec planctu ad lamentandum, vos movere potuimus; nam Legisperitos & Pharisaeos neque Christi facilitas, neque Joannis austeritas ad poenitentiam adduxit.
units.tr: It is like, etc. The sense is: something similar happens with this kind of men as when children at play in the marketplace call out to their stubborn playmates: "We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not mourn." So in the same way, you Scribes and Pharisees were not moved to repentance either by Christ's kindly approach or by John's austerity.

units.la: 18. Neque manducans. Supple ex Luc. 7. v. 33. panem.
units.tr: 18. Neither eating. Supply "bread" from Luke 7:33.

units.la: Neque bibens. Supple ex Luc. 7. v. 33. vinum.
units.tr: Nor drinking. Supply "wine" from Luke 7:33.

units.la: Daemonium habet. Hoc est, daemonis virtute tam austeram vitam agit.
units.tr: He has a demon. That is, by the power of a demon he lives so austere a life.

units.la: Manducans & bibens. Id est, vulgari mensa & ratione vivens cum hominibus. Joannis ejcam & potum novimus; non enim dictum est quod omnino non biberet, sed quod vinum & siceram non biberet: bibebat ergo aquam; cibus autem ejus non omnino nullus erat, sed locustae & mel sylvestre. Unde ergo dictus est, non manducans neque bibens, nisi quia illo victu, quo Judaei utebantur, ille non utebatur: hoc ergo Dominus nisi uteretur, non in ejus comparatione manducans bibensque diceretur. Aug. contra Faustum, lib. 16. c. 30.
units.tr: Eating and drinking. That is, living among men with the ordinary table and manner of life. "We know John's food and drink: it is not said that he did not drink at all, but that he did not drink wine or strong drink; so he drank water. Nor was his food altogether absent, but locusts and wild honey. Why, then, was he said to be neither eating nor drinking, unless because he did not use the diet the Jews used? Had the Lord not used that diet, he would not have been described as eating and drinking in comparison with John." (Augustine, against Faustus, bk. 16, ch. 30.)

units.la: Et justificata est sapientia. q. d. Sed sapientissima Dei providentia & Joannis austeritate, & Christi comitate Judaeos ad poenitentiam revocantis probata & laudata, seu justa declarata est.
units.tr: And wisdom is justified. That is, but the most wise providence of God, both in the austerity of John and in the courtesy of Christ calling the Jews to repentance, was proved and praised, or declared just.

units.la: A filiis suis. Divina Scriptura operationum studiorumque, qui-
units.tr: From her children. Holy Scripture calls the activities and pursuits of which-

units.la: bus hus se homines impendunt, ipsos filios esse dicit ac proles. Sic sapientia filios vocat sapientes, & lucis filios, qui scientia veritatis ac virtutis operibus sunt illuminati. Quia etenim qui alicujus filii sunt a parente esse habent, quo exstant: quique adeo imbuti qualitate sunt, ex ea, quae illis accesserit, qualitate nancisscuntur ut tales sint; merito itaque sic imbuti qualitate, qualitatis filii nuncupantur ac nati. Didymus Alexandrinus contra Manichaeos.
units.tr: of the activities and pursuits to which people devote themselves, Scripture calls them sons and offspring. So Wisdom calls the wise its sons, and the sons of light are those who have been enlightened by the knowledge of truth and by the works of virtue. For those who are the sons of someone have from their parent the being by which they exist; and those who are thus imbued with a quality acquire, from the quality that has come to them, the state of being such as they are. Therefore, being thus imbued with a quality, they are rightly called and born sons of that quality. Didymus of Alexandria, against the Manichaeans.

units.la: 20. Tunc cæpit exprobare. Hanc exprobrationem inserit Lucas c. 10. Sermoni Christi ad LXXII. discipulos, forte quod illi in mentem venisset occasione verborum Christi pronuntiantis Sodomis remissius fore, quam illi civitati, quae discipulos suos non recepisset, quibus verbis similia in hac exprobratione hic v. 24. continentur. Cum autem, si exprobrationis verba apud Lucam a Christi ad discipulos Sermone demseris, antecedentia & consequentia optime inter se cohaerent, probabilius est hanc exprobrationem suo loco hic referri a Matthaeo, cum adhuc Dominus versaretur in Galilaea, & ut apparet Capharnai, ad quam urbem ideo specialiter sua verba dirigit.
units.tr: 20. Then he began to upbraid. Luke (ch. 10) inserts this rebuke into Christ's sermon to the seventy-two disciples, perhaps because it came to his mind on the occasion of Christ's words that it would be more tolerable for Sodom than for the city that did not receive his disciples; and similar words are found in this rebuke here at v. 24. However, if you remove the words of rebuke from Christ's address to the disciples in Luke, what precedes and follows coheres very well with one another. It is therefore more probable that Matthew reports this rebuke here in its proper place, while the Lord was still in Galilee, and apparently in Capernaum, to which city he therefore specifically directs his words.

units.la: Væ. Non est vox maledicentis, sed plangentis & futura praedicentis.
units.tr: Woe. This is not the voice of one cursing, but of one lamenting and foretelling what is to come.

units.la: Corozaim. Civitas est in Galilaea, una inter urbes Decapoleos sita in conspectu Capharnai, sed ad alteram eamque orientalem Jordanis ripam in dimidia tribu Manasse.
units.tr: Chorazin. A city in Galilee, one of the cities of the Decapolis, situated in view of Capernaum, but on the other, eastern, bank of the Jordan, in the half-tribe of Manasseh.

units.la: Bethsaida. Galilaeae civitas est in Decapoli, sita in tribu Zabulon ad mare Tiberiadis, quod & Galilaeae dicitur.
units.tr: Bethsaida. A city of Galilee, in the Decapolis, situated in the tribe of Zebulun by the Sea of Tiberias, which is also called the Sea of Galilee.

units.la: Quia si, &c. His verbis suis Dominus Jesus altius nobis mysterium praedestinationis offendit. Aug. de bono perseverantiae c. 9. Ex quo apparet habere quosdam in ipso ingenio divinum naturaliter munus intelligentiae quo moveantur ad fidem, si congrua suis mentibus vel audiant verba, vel signa conspiciant, & tamen si Dei altiore judicio a perditionis massa non sunt gratia praedestinatione discreti, nec ipsa eis adhibentur vel dicta divina vel facta, per quae possent credere, si audirent utique talia vel viderent. Idem. ibid. c. 14.
units.tr: For if, etc. By these words the Lord Jesus reveals to us the deeper mystery of predestination. (Augustine, On the Gift of Perseverance, ch. 9.) From this it appears that some have in their very nature a divine gift of understanding by which they are moved to faith, if they hear words or see signs suited to their minds; and yet, if by God's deeper judgment they are not set apart by grace and predestination from the mass of perdition, neither the divine words nor the deeds by which they could believe are given to them, even though they would surely believe such things if they heard or saw them. (Idem, ibid., ch. 14.)

units.la: In Tyro & Sidone. Tyrus & Sidon urbes sunt conterminae Galilaeae, nunquam a Judaeis possessae, ideoque Gentiles & Idololatrae in littore maris Mediterranei, mercimoniis totius orbis opulentissimae, deliciis Deique contemtu plenae. Hinc & Basilius Seleuciae Orat. 20, quae est in Chananaeam, animadvertit Tyrum & Sidonem unam & eamdem esse impietatis sedem, daemonum olim diverstia, idolorum cubilia, idololatriae sedes, accusationis Prophetarum argumentum. Diffabat autem Sidon à Tyro stadiis ferè ducentis, teste Strabone. Homerus plurimis in locis Sidonis & Sidoniorum, nunquam Tyri meminit, unde colligitur Sidonem esse vetustiorem. Trogus scribit Sidonem à piscium ubertate nomen habere; quòd non est improbabile, cùm Hebraei nos doceant Sidonem esse ad mare piscosissimum, & צידון, id est, piscatio, hodiéque dicatur, ut Galilææ oppidum Bethsaida, id est, domus piscationis.
units.tr: In Tyre and Sidon. Tyre and Sidon are cities bordering Galilee, never possessed by the Jews, and therefore Gentile and idolatrous, on the shore of the Mediterranean, very wealthy from the trade of the whole world, and full of luxury and contempt for God. Hence Basil of Seleucia also, in Oration 20, which is in Chananaea, observes that Tyre and Sidon are one and the same seat of impiety, once the haunt of demons, the den of idols, the seat of idolatry, and the subject of the Prophets' accusation. Sidon, according to Strabo, was about two hundred stadia distant from Tyre. Homer often mentions Sidon and the Sidonians, but never Tyre, from which it is inferred that Sidon is the older. Trogus writes that Sidon had its name from the abundance of fish, which is not improbable, since the Hebrews teach us that Sidon lies by a very fish-rich sea, and [צידון], that is, fishing, is still its name, just as Bethsaida, a town of Galilee, means "house of fishing."

units.la: Olim. Id est, jam diù, q. d. Simul ac prædicationem audivissent & signa apud se facta vidissent.
units.tr: Long ago. That is, long since: as soon as they had heard the preaching and seen the signs done among them.

units.la: In cilicio & cinere. Cilicium & cinis sunt arma pœnitentium, ut per asperitatem & compunctionem cilicii vindictam in se excerceant, & per aspersionem cineris in memoriam revocent mortis sententiam, quâ in pulverem redire tenentur.
units.tr: In sackcloth and ashes. Sackcloth and ashes are the arms of penitents: by the roughness and piercing of sackcloth they inflict punishment on themselves, and by sprinkling ashes they recall to memory the sentence of death, by which they are bound to return to dust.

units.la: Pœnitentiam egissent. Quærat prudens Lector & dicat: Si Tyrus & Sidon & Sodoma potuerunt agere pœnitentiam ad prædicationem Salvatoris, signorumque miracula, non sunt in culpa, quòd non crediderunt, sed vltium silentii in eo est, qui afluris pœnitentiam noluit prædicare. Ad quod facilis & aperta responsio est: ignorare nos judicia Dei & singularum dispensationum ejus sacramenta nescire, B. Hier. hic, cui succinit Aug. in lib. de bono perseverantiæ c. 11. Proinde sicut Apostolus ait: Non volentis neque currentis, sed miserentis est Dei: qui & parvulis quibus vult, etiam non volentibus neque currentibus subvenit, quos ante constitutionem mundi elegit in Christo, daturus etiam eis gratiam gratis, hoc est nullis eorum vel fidei vel operum meritis præcedentibus; & majoribus etiam his, quos prævidit si apud eos facta essent, suis miraculis credituros, quibus non vult subvenire, non subvenit, de quibus in sua prædestinatione occultè quidem, sed justè aliud judicavit; non enim est iniquitas apud Deum, sed inscrutabilia sunt judicia ejus, & investigabiles viæ ejus: Universæ autem viæ Domini misericordia & veritas. Itaque misericordiam ejus in his qui liberantur, & veritatem in his qui puniuntur sine dubitatione credamus: neque inscrutabilia scrutari neque investigabilia vestigare conemur.
units.tr: Would have repented. Let the prudent reader ask: if Tyre, Sidon and Sodom could have repented at the preaching of the Saviour and the miracles of his signs, they are not to blame for not believing; rather, the fault lies in the silence of him who was unwilling to preach repentance to those who would have repented. To this the answer is easy and plain: we do not know God's judgments, and we are ignorant of the mysteries of his individual dispensations. (Blessed Jerome here, to which Augustine agrees in his book On the Gift of Perseverance, ch. 11.) Therefore, as the Apostle says: "It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy" (Rom. 9:16). He helps even infants, whom he wills, though they neither will nor run; those whom he chose in Christ before the foundation of the world, and to whom he will give grace freely, that is, without any prior merits of faith or works on their part. And to those greater ones too, whom he foresaw would believe if his miracles had been done among them, he does not give help, because he has judged otherwise, secretly indeed but justly, in his predestination. For there is no unrighteousness with God, but his judgments are unsearchable and his ways past finding out (Rom. 11:33); yet all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth (Ps. 25:10). Thus let us believe without doubt his mercy towards those who are delivered, and his truth towards those who are punished, and let us not try to search out the unsearchable or to trace out the untraceable.

units.la: 22. Tyro & Sidoni remissius erit, &c. Quòd Tyrus & Sidon naturalem tantum Legem calcaverint: Corozaim verò & Bethsaida post transgressionem naturalis Legis & scriptæ, etiam signa, quæ apud eas facta sunt, parvi duxerint. B. Hier.
units.tr: 22. Tyre and Sidon will fare more tolerably, etc. That is, Tyre and Sidon trampled only the natural law, whereas Chorazin and Bethsaida, after transgressing both the natural law and the written law, made light of the signs performed among them. St Jerome.

units.la: 23. Et tu Capharnaum nunquid, &c. Græcè hic & in Vulg. Luc. 10. v. 15. sine interrogatione legitur: Usque ad cælum exaltata. Et est duplex intelligentia. Vel ideo ad inferna descendes: quia contra prædicationem meam superbissimè restitisti. Vel ideo, quia exaltata usque ad cælum meo bostitio, & meis signis atque atq; virtutibus, tantum habens privilegium majoribus plectendis suppliciis, quòd his quoque credere noluisti. B. Hier.
units.tr: 23. And you, Capernaum, will you not, etc. Here, and in the Vulgate at Luke 10:15, the Greek is read without a question: "Exalted up to heaven." It has a twofold meaning. Either you will therefore go down to hell, because you resisted my preaching most proudly; or else, because you were exalted up to heaven by my dwelling among you, and by my signs and mighty works, you had the privilege of greater punishments, because you refused to believe even in these. St Jerome.

units.la: Fortè manserint. Causæ indifferentis certa cognitio vocatur etiam conjecturalis notitia effectus, idcirco Deus sermone ad captum nostrum abjecto, quod de causa compertum habet, id sæpe veluti dubitabundus de effectu pronuntiat, ut Exod. 23. Non habitent in terra tua, ne forte te peccare faciant. Jerem. 2. Noli subtrahere verbum, si forte audiant, &c. Imò quæ ipse Deus facturus erat, ideoque indubitata erant, quasi dubitanter ipse disserit, ut volubilitatem creaturæ, vel libertatem illæsam significet. Sic loquitur Jerem. 6. Erudire Jerusalem, ne forte te ponam terram desertam. Sic hic dicit: Fortè manserint, &c. Itaque sæpè Deus loquitur secundum ordinem causarum secundarum, & non secundum suam præscientiam, quâ novit quid præter ordinem rerum fit eventurum ex ipsius decreto.
units.tr: Perhaps they would have remained. A certain knowledge of an undetermined cause is also called conjectural knowledge of the effect. Therefore God, setting aside language suited to our understanding, often speaks of an effect as if in doubt about it, when he knows the cause: as in Exodus 23, "They shall not dwell in your land, lest they make you sin," and in Jeremiah 2, "Do not withhold the word, if perhaps they may hear," etc. Indeed, even things God himself was going to do, and which were therefore certain, he speaks of as if doubtfully, in order to signify the mutability of the creature or the unimpaired freedom of the will. So he speaks in Jeremiah 6: "Be instructed, O Jerusalem, lest perhaps I make you a desolate land." So here he says, "Perhaps they would have remained," etc. Thus God often speaks according to the order of secondary causes, and not according to his foreknowledge, by which he knows what will come to pass beyond the order of things, by his own decree.

units.la: 25. In illo tempore. Quo scilicet ex missione reversi sunt ad Christum LXXII. discipuli, ut patet ex Luc. 10. v. 20.
units.tr: 25. At that time. Namely, when the seventy-two disciples returned to Christ from their mission, as is clear from Luke 10:20.

units.la: Respondens. Hebraismus, id est, in verba prorumpens, seu loqui incipiens.
units.tr: Answering. A Hebraism, that is, breaking out into speech, or beginning to speak.

units.la: Confiteor. Id est, gratias ago.
units.tr: I confess. That is, I give thanks.

units.la: Domine cœli & terræ. Audiant qui Salvatorem non natum, sed creatum calumniantur, quòd Patrem suum vocet cœli & terræ Dominum. Si enim & ipse creatura est, & creatura conditorem suum Patrem appellare potest: stultum fuit non & sui & cœli ac terræ Dominum vel Patrem similiter appellare. B. Hier.
units.tr: Lord of heaven and earth. Let those hear who slander the Saviour as created and not begotten, because he calls his Father the Lord of heaven and earth. For if he himself is a creature, and a creature can call its maker its Father, it would have been foolish not to call the Lord of himself, and of heaven and earth, likewise his Father. St Jerome.

units.la: Hæc. Scilicet, adventûs mei Sacramenta.
units.tr: These things. Namely, the sacraments of my coming.

units.la: A sapientibus, &c. Sapientes quidem superbos, & alta de se sentientes, parvulos verò dixit humiles. Quorum certè alia Scriptura meminit, dicens: Deus superbis resistit, humilibus dat gratiam. Resistit namque superbis, ne æterna bona intelligant, sed parvulis gratiam dat, ut eadem bona æterna, ipso revelante, cognoscant. B. Greg. lib. 4. in 1 Reg. cap. 4. Deus autem humiles, quibus dat gratiam, non ante datam humiles invenit, sed dando gratiam humiles facit. B. Fulgentius lib. 1. ad Monimum cap. 18.
units.tr: From the wise, etc. He called the wise proud, and those who think highly of themselves; but the little ones he called humble. Another Scripture certainly speaks of these, saying: "God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble." For he resists the proud, lest they understand the eternal goods, but gives grace to the little ones, so that, by his own revelation, they may know those same eternal goods. St Gregory, Book 4 on 1 Kings, ch. 4. "But God does not find the humble, to whom he gives grace, already humble before the grace was given; rather, by giving grace, he makes them humble." St Fulgentius, Book 1 to Monimus, ch. 18.

units.la: Parvulis. Qui non subjunxit, stultis, sed parvulis, tumorem se damnasse innotuit (id est, notum facit) non acumen. B. Greg. 27. Moral. cap. 7.
units.tr: Little ones. He who did not add "fools," but "little ones," made known (that is, shows) that he condemned the swelling, not the sharpness of wit. St Gregory, Morals 27, ch. 7.

units.la: 26. Ita Pater. Locutio Christo familiaris, qui aliquid vehementer confirmare solet. Vide Luc. 10. v. 21. 11. v. 51. &c.
units.tr: 26. Yes, Father. A locution familiar to Christ, who is wont to affirm something emphatically. See Luke 10:21 and 11:51, etc.

units.la: Quoniam sic fuit placitum ante te. Q. d. Tuo placito sunt id quod sunt, non suo merito; nec enim invenis merita, sed prævenis. B. Bern. Ep. 146. ad Burchard. Abbatem. Nemo ergo discuniat, curstame Judaico populo, dudum in infidelitate Gentilitas jacuit, & cur ad fidem Gentilitate surgente, Judaicum populum infidelitatis culpa prosravit. Nemo discuiat cur alius trahatur ex dono, alius repellatur ex merito. Consilium summa & occulta virtutis, satisfactio sit aperta rationis.
