Unde & in Evangelio Dominus cum de hujus rei causa loqueretur, ait: Confiteor tibi Pater, &c. atque mox tanquam rationem quandam absconsionis ac revelationis adjungens, ait: Quia sic fuit placitum ante te; quibus nimirum verbis exempla humilitatis accipimus ne temere discutere superna consilia de aliorum vocatione, aliorum vero repulsione praesumamus. Cum enim intulisset utrumque, non mox rationem reddidit, sed sic Deo placitum dixit: hoc videlicet offendens, quia injustum esse non potest, quod placuit justo; unde & in vinea laborantibus mercedem reddens, cum quosdam operarios inaequales in opere aequaret in praemio, & plus in mercede quaereret, qui labori amplius infudasset, ait: Non ne ex denario convenisti mecum, volo autem & huic novissimo dare sicut & tibi, an non licet mihi quod volo facere? In cunctis ergo, qua exterius disponuntur, aperta causa rationis est occulta justitia voluntatis. B. Greg. lib. 25. Moral. cap. 18.
units.tr: For so it seemed good in your sight. That is: "They are what they are by your pleasure, not by their merit; for you find no merits in them, but you forestall them." St Bernard, Letter 146 to Abbot Burchard. "Let no one, therefore, inquire why the Gentile world once lay in unbelief, and why, when the Gentiles rose to the faith, the Jewish people were cast down by the guilt of unbelief. Let no one inquire why one is drawn by gift, and another is rejected by merit. The counsel of supreme and hidden power, let the explanation of reason be open. Hence also in the Gospel, when the Lord spoke about the cause of this matter, he said, 'I confess to you, Father,' etc., and immediately, adding as a kind of reason for the hiding and the revealing, he said, 'For so it seemed good in your sight.' By these words we receive examples of humility, not to presume rashly to examine the heavenly counsels about the calling of some and the rejection of others. For when he had stated both, he did not at once give a reason, but said that it so pleased God, thereby indicating that what pleased the just one cannot be unjust. Hence also, in the vineyard, when rendering wages to the labourers, he made the unequal workers equal in reward, and when one who had laboured more demanded more wages, he said: 'Did you not agree with me for a denarius? I wish to give to this last one as to you. Is it not lawful for me to do what I wish?' In all things, therefore, which are arranged outwardly, the open cause is the reason, and the hidden cause is the justice of the will." St Gregory, Morals 25, ch. 18.

units.la: 27. Omnia mihi tradita sunt. Id est, mihi, per quem absque carne facta sunt omnia, in carne manifestato tradita sunt in tempore tanquam Mediatori omnia instauranda per & propter carnem assumtam & sanctificatam, qua opus erat pro sacrificio crucis.
units.tr: 27. All things have been delivered to me. That is, to me, through whom all things were made without flesh, all things have been delivered in time, when made manifest in the flesh, as to the Mediator, that all things are to be restored through and on account of the flesh assumed and sanctified, which was necessary for the sacrifice of the cross.

units.la: A Patre meo. Ideoque, & a me ipso, qua Deus sum.
units.tr: By my Father. Therefore also by myself, as I am God.

units.la: Novit Filium. Id est, Quis sit Filius, ut explicat Lucas c. 10 v. 22. Videtur autem Christus alludere ad illud Proverb. 30. v. 4. Quod nomen est ejus, & quod nomen Filii ejus, dic, si nosti?
units.tr: Knows the Son. That is, who the Son is, as Luke explains in ch. 10 v. 22. Christ seems to allude to Proverbs 30:4: "What is his name, and what is the name of his Son, tell me if you know?"

units.la: Nisi Pater. Supple, & cui voluerit revelare Pater. Sic Petrus novit quis esset Filius, quia quod secretum caro & sanguis revelare non potuit, Filii Pater qui in coelis est per gratiam coelitus inspiravit, ut dicitur infra c. 16. v. 17. Particula exclusiva, nisi, hoc loco minime a notitia Patris & Filii Spiritum-Sanctum excludit, sed tantum creaturas omnes, hoc est, quidquid ejusdem cum Patre & Filio essentiae non est; est autem Spiritus-Sanctus ejusdem essentiae cum Patre & Filio, unde & ab Apostolo ipsi Spiritui-Sancto tribuitur perfectissima Dei Patris cognitio, 1 Cor. 2. v. 11. quippe qui est in ipso Patre. Fallacia igitur esset ex ignoratione figurae dictionis, & phraseon Scripturae, si quis argumentaretur a particulis exclusivis in loco praesenti & in loco laudato Pauli ad personas sanctissimae Trinitatis; alioquin apud Paulum à notitia Dei Patris excluderetur Filius, quia ait Paulus: Nemo novit quæ sunt Dei, nisi Spiritus Dei; imò & hic & apud Lucam Filius & similiter Pater excluderetur à cognitione sui, quia dicitur: Nemo scit quis sit Filius, nisi Pater: & quis sit Pater, nisi Filius, & cui voluerit Filius revelare. Intentum itaque Scripturæ est particulis istis exclusivis, non omnia simpliciter, sed illa tantum excludere, quorum causa instituta est oratio, & quæ cum altera parte comparantur. Sic apud Paulum mortalium omnium causa institutus est sermo de sapientia Evangelii in mysterio abscondita; eam scilicet absconditam esse omnibus hominibus, ita ut nisi Spiritus-Sanctus eam revelet, ipsam percipere nequeant, quia solus Spiritus novit quæ sunt Dei. Quis ibi non videat hac dictione (nemo) non excludi Filium, qui non cum Spiritu confertur, cum de Deo nullus ibi sit sermo, sed de solis hominibus, qui ibi cum Spiritu Dei comparantur. Sic & Christus de hominibus proprie loquens, quorum causa in mundum venerat, ut illis Patrem, Patrisque voluntatem revelaret; hoc illis esse necessarium dicit, quia nemo, scilicet horum hominum novit Patrem, nisi per revelationem Filii. Non venit autem Christus ut doceret Spiritum-Sanctum, sed homines, proinde minimè Spiritus-Sanctus a notitia Dei excluditur. Est igitur semper spectandum quanam de re agatur, & quænam inter se conferantur. Quare certum est quotiescunque in Scripturis aliqua divinæ illius essentiæ persona creaturis, fictitiisve diis opponitur, tunc reliquas Deitatis personas minimè ab ea re, quà persona illa à creaturis distinguitur, sive ea res sit scientia, sive Deitas, sive aliud quidpiam ad essentiam Dei pertinens, excludi.
units.tr: Except the Father. Supply: "and to whom the Father wishes to reveal." So Peter knew who the Son was, because the Father who is in heaven, by grace, breathed from heaven what flesh and blood could not reveal, as is said below in ch. 16 v. 17. The exclusive particle "except" here by no means excludes the Holy Spirit from the knowledge of the Father and the Son, but only all creatures, that is, whatever is not of the same essence as the Father and the Son. The Holy Spirit, however, is of the same essence as the Father and the Son, and so the Apostle attributes to the Holy Spirit himself the most perfect knowledge of God the Father, 1 Cor. 2:11, since he is in the Father himself. It would therefore be a fallacy, arising from ignorance of the figure of speech and the idioms of Scripture, if anyone argued from exclusive particles in this place, and in the place of Paul cited, to the persons of the most holy Trinity. Otherwise, in Paul the Son would be excluded from the knowledge of God the Father, because Paul says: "No one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God." Indeed, here and in Luke the Son, and likewise the Father, would be excluded from the knowledge of himself, because it is said: "No one knows who the Son is except the Father, and who the Father is except the Son, and to whomever the Son wishes to reveal him." The intent of Scripture, therefore, in using such exclusive particles, is not to exclude all things simply, but only those things for whose sake the discourse was instituted, and which are compared with the other part. Thus in Paul the discourse was instituted for the sake of all mortals, concerning the wisdom of the Gospel hidden in mystery; namely, that it is hidden from all men, so that unless the Holy Spirit reveals it, they cannot perceive it, because only the Spirit knows the things of God. Who there does not see that by this word "no one" the Son is not excluded, since he is not compared with the Spirit, as there is no discourse there about God, but only about men, who there are compared with the Spirit of God? So also Christ, speaking properly of men, for whose sake he had come into the world, that he might reveal to them the Father and the Father's will, says that this is necessary for them, because no one (namely, of these men) knows the Father except by the revelation of the Son. But Christ did not come to teach the Holy Spirit, but men; therefore the Holy Spirit is by no means excluded from the knowledge of God. It must always be considered, therefore, what matter is being treated, and what things are being compared with one another. Hence it is certain that whenever in the Scriptures some one person of that divine essence is set over against creatures or fictitious gods, then the remaining persons of the Godhead are by no means excluded from that thing by which that person is distinguished from creatures, whether that thing be knowledge, or deity, or anything else pertaining to the essence of God.

units.la: 28. Venite. Nimirum non gressibus corporis, sed profectibus cordis. Ipse namque ait: Veniet hora quando neque in monte hoc, neque in Hierosolymis adorabitis Patrem. Et paulò post: Veri adoratores adorabunt Patrem in Spiritu & veritate. Nam & Pater tales quærit qui adorent eum. In corde ergo esse gressus insinuat, quando & ut veniamus vocat, & tamen motu corporis nequaquam nos ad alia transfire denunciat. B. Greg. 21. Moral. c. 4.
units.tr: 28. Come to me. Clearly not with the steps of the body, but with the progress of the heart. For he himself says: "The hour is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem." And a little later: "True worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth. For the Father also seeks such people to worship him." So he indicates that the coming takes place in the heart, when he calls us to come, and yet he nowhere announces that we must move from one place to another by bodily motion. B. Greg. 21. Moral. c. 4.

units.la: Ad me. Supple, cui soli est datum præstare quietem venientibus ad se, quam mundus dare non poterit.
units.tr: To me. Supply: to whom alone it has been given to grant rest to those who come to him, a rest the world cannot give.

units.la: Omnes. Ne quis dicat se non audere ad Christum unum mediatorem Dei & hominum accedere, & Romanensium instar ad Sanctos confugiat, Christus omnes ad se vocat.
units.tr: All. Lest anyone say that he does not dare to approach Christ, the one mediator between God and men, and flee instead to the saints in the manner of the Papists, Christ calls all to himself.

units.la: Qui laboratis & onerati estis. Scilicet, peccatis, ærumnis, sollicitudinibus, & Legalibus sarcinis, quas neque vos poteritis, neque patres vestri portare potuerunt. Reficiam vos. Id est, vos exonerabo & in perfecta quiete constituam.
units.tr: You who labour and are burdened. That is, with sins, troubles, anxieties, and the burdens of the Law, which neither you nor your fathers were able to bear. I will refresh you. That is, I will relieve you of these and establish you in perfect rest.

units.la: 29. Tollite jugum meum. Jugum Christi est ipsius Evangelium, quod Judæos & Gentes in unitate conjungit; hoc autem secundum Rabbanum jubemur tollere, seu super nos sumere, id est, in honore habere, ne forte subtus ponentes, Id est, illud prave contemnentes lutulentis pedibus vitiorum conculcemus.
units.tr: 29. Take my yoke upon you. The yoke of Christ is his Gospel, which joins Jews and Gentiles in unity. According to Rabbanus, however, we are commanded to take this up, or to put it upon ourselves, that is, to hold it in honour, lest, by setting it beneath us, that is, by despising it, we trample it under muddy feet of vices.

units.la: Discite à me. Id est, disciplinam meam subite, quia non tyrannus, sed benignus & mansuetus sum accedentibus ad me. Ita author operis imperfecti apud Chrysostomum. Communiùs tamen, à me, exponitur, exemplo meo. Signanter dicit, à me, quem Prophetæ & Apostoli & medius inter eos Præcursor Joannes sub agni typo exhibent. A me, cui licèt data sit omnis potestas in cœlo & in terra, & penes me habeam plusquam duodecim Angelorum legiones, quorum unus posset omnes hostes meos dissipare & perfundare, tamen non veni ut ministrer, sed ut ministrem & dem animam meam redemptionem pro multis. A me, qui sum leo tribus Juda, mirâ metamorphosi ex leone factus sum agnus innocentiâ, lenitate, humilitate & patientiâ. A me, in quo ænigma Samsonis abunde impletum est, De comedente exivit cibus, & de forti egressa est dulcedo: carne enim meâ vos alam, sanguine potabo, lavabo, redimam, lanaque meâ induam, imò me ipso vos induam. Hinc Christum induere dicitur Rom. 13. v. 14. & Gal. 3. v. 27. & vestes albas à Christo accipere, quibus nuditatis nostræ confusio obtegatur, Apoc. 3. v. 18.
units.tr: Learn from me. That is, undergo my discipline, because I am not a tyrant but kind and gentle toward those who come to me. So the author of the unfinished work quoted by Chrysostom. More commonly, however, from me is explained as: by my example. He says pointedly from me, whom the Prophets and Apostles, and John the Forerunner who stands between them, present under the type of the lamb. From me, to whom, although all power in heaven and on earth has been given, and although I have at my command more than twelve legions of angels, one of whom could scatter and destroy all my enemies, nevertheless I did not come to be ministered to but to minister, and to give my life as a ransom for many. From me, who am the lion of the tribe of Judah, yet by a wonderful metamorphosis have become a lamb in innocence, gentleness, humility, and patience. From me, in whom Samson's riddle is fully fulfilled: Out of the eater came forth meat, and out of the strong came forth sweetness. For I will nourish you with my flesh, give you my blood to drink, wash you, redeem you, clothe you with my wool, or rather clothe you with myself. Hence Christ is said to be put on (Rom. 13.14; Gal. 3.27), and the white garments received from Christ, by which the shame of our nakedness is covered (Rev. 3.18).

units.la: Humilis corde. Ad hoc unigenitus Dei filius formam infirmitatis nostræ suscepit, ad hoc invisibilis non solùm visibilis, sed etiam despectus apparuit, ad hoc contumeliarum ludibria, irrisionum opprobria, passionumque tormenta toleravit, ut superbum non esse hominem doceret humilis Deus. Quanta ergo humilitatis virtus est, propter quam solam veraciter edocendam, is qui sine æstimatione magnus est, usque ad passionem factus est parvus? Quia enim originem perditionis nostræ superbia præbuit diaboli, instrumentum redemptionis nostræ inventa est humilitas Dei. Hoc ipse noster magnus inter omnia conditus, videri super omnia voluit elatus. Redemptor autem noster magnus manens super omnia, fieri inter omnia dignatus est parvus. B. Greg. 24. Mor. cap. 22.
units.tr: Humble in heart. For this the only-begotten Son of God took on the form of our weakness; for this the invisible one appeared not only visibly but even despised; for this he endured the mockery of insults, the reproach of scorn, and the torments of suffering, so that God, being humble, might teach that man is not proud. How great, then, is the virtue of humility, for the sake of teaching which alone he who is great beyond all estimation was made small even to the point of suffering? For since pride provided the origin of our ruin in the devil, humility was found to be the instrument of our redemption in God. He who was created great above all things wished to appear exalted above all things. Our great Redeemer, who remains great above all things, deigned to become small among all things. B. Greg. 24. Mor. cap. 22.

units.la: Invenietis requiem animabus vestris. Id est, quietem, quam percipere in æternitate desideratis, in tempore per tranquillitatem mentis degustabitis.
units.tr: You will find rest for your souls. That is, the rest which you long to receive in eternity, you will taste in time through tranquillity of mind.

units.la: 30. Jugum enim meum suave est & onus meum leve. Jugum est instrumentum illud, quo boves alligantur, ad trahendum dum aratrum, aut currum: hic metaphoricè designat Legem Christi Evangelicam, quæ Christianis suavissima ac maximè commoda redditur, quia cordi inscribitur, & Spiritus-Sanctus vires præbet efficacissimas ad eam implendam, certáque præstat, ac ampla implentibus eam præmia.
units.tr: 30. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light. A yoke is the instrument by which oxen are fastened to draw a plough or a cart. Here it figuratively designates the Evangelical Law of Christ, which is made most sweet and most agreeable to Christians, because it is written on the heart, the Holy Spirit supplies most effective strength to fulfil it, and it gives certain and abundant rewards to those who fulfil it.

units.la: CAPUT. XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: I. Sabbato. Scilicet proprie dicto, sive die septimo hebdomadæ; nam illo tantum & expiationis die nihil operis facere, non solùm servilis, sed neque necessarii ad parandos cibos licebat Judæis, ut videre est Exod. 35. & Levit. 23. Hoc autem Sabbatum, quo præsens historia contigit, appellatur Luc. 6. v. 1. Δευτεροπρῶτον, secundo-primum, quod, ut docet Josephus Scaliger 6. de emendat. temp. cap. 6. Paschatis diem secundum proximè fit secutum, à quo secundo die numerabantur septem hebdomades usque ad Pentecosten, ita ut prima hebdomas vocaretur secundo-prima, & ejus Sabbatum secundo-primum; secunda hebdomas vocaretur secundo-secunda, & ejus Sabbatum secundo-secundum, & sic deinceps. Certum atque indubitatum Scaligeri fundamentum est in verbis Moßs Levit. 23. v. 15. ubi jubet Dominus intervallum, quod inter secundam Paschatis diem & sextam mensis interjectum est, & à Græcis Pentecoste dicitur, numerari. Quia verò secunda Paschatis die, ut dicitur Levitic. 23. v. 15. offerebatur Deo, id est, manipulus primitiarum, ipsa dies secunda Paschatis decima sexta mensis dicta est Omer, & numerum intervalli, quod inde ad festum Pentecostes numeratur, hodiéque Judæi vocant æram.
units.tr: I. Sabbath. That is, properly speaking, the seventh day of the week. On that day alone, and on the Day of Atonement, the Jews were forbidden to do any work, not only servile work but even the work needed to prepare food, as may be seen in Exod. 35 and Lev. 23. This Sabbath, on which the present history took place, is called in Luke 6:1 second-first [Δευτεροπρῶτον], that is, second-first. As Joseph Scaliger teaches (De emendatione temporum, bk. 6, ch. 6), this name comes from the day following the first day of Passover, from which seven weeks were counted up to Pentecost. Thus the first week was called second-first, and its Sabbath the second-first Sabbath; the second week was called second-second, and its Sabbath the second-second Sabbath, and so on in order. Scaliger's foundation is certain and beyond doubt, in the words of Moses at Lev. 23:15, where the Lord commands that the interval lying between the second day of Passover and the sixth day of the month, which the Greeks call Pentecost, be counted. Since on the second day of Passover, as Lev. 23:15 says, an offering was made to God, namely a sheaf of the firstfruits, that second day, the sixteenth day of the month, was called Omer, and the number of days counted from it up to the feast of Pentecost is still called by the Jews today the Omer.

units.la: Cæperunt vellere spicas. Hoc in agris alienis facere permittitur Deut. 23. v. 25.
units.tr: They began to pluck the ears. Deut. 23:25 permits this to be done in other people's fields.

units.la: 2. Dixerunt ei. Nempe, Christo. Luc. 6. v. 2. habetur: Dixerunt illis: nempe Christi discipulis. Verùm à diversis & ipsi Domino & discipulis hæc potuerunt objici, & cuicunque sint objecta, ad ipsum Dominum maximè respiciunt.
units.tr: 2. They said to him. That is, to Christ. Luke 6:2 has they said to them, that is, to Christ's disciples. But these charges could have been brought by different people, both against the Lord himself and against the disciples; and whoever made them, they aimed chiefly at the Lord himself.

units.la: 3. Quando esuriit. Marc. 2. v. 25. Quando necessitatem habuit, supple, similem necessitati meorum discipulorum.
units.tr: 3. When he was hungry. Mark 2:25 has when he had need, supply, similar to the need of my disciples.

units.la: Et qui cum eo erant. Hinc & ex Luc. 6. v. 4. patet David-dem dem in hoc non fuisse mentitum, quòd 1 Sam. seu, Reg. cap. 21. Achimelecho interroganti, Quare tu solus & nullus es tecum, responderit Pueris condixi in illum & illum locum.
units.tr: And those who were with him. From this, and from Luke 6:4, it is clear that David did not lie in this matter, when, in 1 Sam. (or 1 Kings) ch. 21, he answered Ahimelech who asked, Why are you alone, with no one with you?, I have appointed the young men to such and such a place.

units.la: 4. Intravit in domum Dei. Id est, in atrium Tabernaculi; nec enim laicis, qualis erat David, sed solis Sacerdotibus licebat ingredi Sanctum, & soli summo Pontifici semel in anno Sanctum Sanctorum. Porro Tabernaculum fuisse tum in civitate Sacerdotum Nobe patet ex 1 Sam. seu, Reg. 21. v. 7. Arca tamen tunc erat, non in Silo, ut putat Maldonatus, sed in domo Abinadab Cariathiarim, ut constat ex 1 Sam. seu, Reg. 7. Quòd autem Marc. 2. v. 26. David dicitur introiisse domum Dei sub Abiathar Principe Sacerdotum, id est, summo Pontifice, cùm tamen id sub Achimelecho contigisse narretur 1 Sam. seu, Reg. 21. cujus filius erat Abiathar; ratio est quia pater & filius binomines erant, ut colligi potest ex 2 Sam. seu, Reg. 8. v. 17. 1 Paralip. 18. v. 16. & 24. v. 6. ubi filius appellatur Achimelech, seu Abimelech, & pater Abiathar. Scribit doctissimus Iprensis Episcopus Jansenius, dum haec historia contigit, Arcam fuisse in Gabaa; sed Joannes Tarnovius in Exercit. Biblicis merito negat Arcam unquam substitisse in Gabaa. Nam Abinadab, in cujus domum translata est Arca ex oppido sacerdotali Bethsames, non habitabat in Gabaa, quae est civitas in tribu Benjamin, ut dicitur Judic. 19. & 1 Sam. seu, Reg. 22. sed in Cariathiarim, ut patet ex 1 Reg. seu, Sam. 6. v. 21. 7. v. 1, & 2. 1 Paralip. 13. v. 6. Cariathiarim autem (quae & alio nomine Josue 15. v. 60. & 18. v. 14. Cariathbaal, & 1 Paralip. 13. v. 6. in textu Hebraeo בעלה dicitur) sita erat in tribu Juda, ut diserte traditur in locis mox citatis; unde 2 Regum seu, Sam. 6. v. 2. appellatur בעלי יהודה, cujus proprii nominis ibi Vulgatus exhibet interpretamentum, vertens Hebraeum Mibaale-Juda, de Viris Juda: quod ne obscuritatem pariat, vocabulum Viris scribendum est ibi principe litera majuscula; atque ita David qui dicitur 1 Paralip. 3. v. 6. in textu Hebraeo contendisse cum toto Israele בעלתה, (Vulgat. ad collem) quae est Cariathiarim, ut Arcam inde in Sionem averheret, describitur 2 Regum seu, Sam. 6. v. 2. egrediens e Baala, adversus contenderat cum toto Israele, ut Arcam abduceret. Fine licet vox קרית יערים alibi fit nomen urbis, tamen 1 Regum seu, Sam. 7. v. 1. ubi viri Cariathiarim dicuntur intulisse Arcam in domum Abinadab בגבעה, & similiter 2 Reg. seu, Sam. 6. v. 3, & 4. ubi idem dicitur, juxta primariam suam significationem pro colle accipitur, unde & LXX. vertunt ἐν τῷ βουνῷ, sic & Chald. & alii. Germanus frater meus Ludovicus de Compiegne de Veil Doctor Artium, in notis suis ad Tractatum de ædificio Templi c. 1. existimat urbem Cariathiarim in clivo fuisse sitam, ex quo fiebat inquit, ut pars ejus superior, quæ fortassis arx erat, Gaba, seu Gabaa nominaretur; quippe quæ vox Hebraica collem, seu locum præcelsum atque eminentem sonat. In hac urbis superiori parte habitabat Abinadab, ad quem Arcam de Bethsamitis reportarunt incolæ Cariathiarim.
units.tr: 4. Entered into the house of God. That is, into the court of the Tabernacle. Laymen, such as David was, were not permitted to enter the Holy Place, but only priests, and only the high priest, once a year, the Holy of Holies. Moreover, that the Tabernacle was then in the city of the priests, Nob, is clear from 1 Sam. (or 1 Kings) 21:7. But the Ark was not then in Shiloh, as Maldonatus thinks, but in the house of Abinadab at Kiriath-jearim, as appears from 1 Sam. (or 1 Kings) 7. As for Mark 2:26, which says that David entered the house of God under Abiathar the chief priest, that is, the high priest, although the narrative of 1 Sam. (or 1 Kings) 21 places this event under Ahimelech, whose son Abiathar was, the explanation is that father and son had two names, as can be gathered from 2 Sam. (or 2 Kings) 8:17, 1 Chron. 18:16 and 24:6, where the son is called Ahimelech, or Abimelech, and the father Abiathar. The most learned Jansenius, bishop of Ypres, writes that when this history happened the Ark was at Gibeah; but Johannes Tarnovius, in his Biblical Exercises, rightly denies that the Ark ever stood at Gibeah. For Abinadab, into whose house the Ark was carried from the priestly town of Beth-shemesh, did not live in Gibeah, a town in the tribe of Benjamin, as is said in Judg. 19 and 1 Sam. (or 1 Kings) 22, but in Kiriath-jearim, as appears from 1 Sam. (or 1 Kings) 6:21, 7:1–2, and 1 Chron. 13:6. Kiriath-jearim (which is also called by another name, Kiriath-baal, Josh. 15:60 and 18:14, and in 1 Chron. 13:6 in the Hebrew text is called Baalah [בעלה]) lay in the tribe of Judah, as is plainly stated in the passages just cited. Hence 2 Sam. (or 2 Kings) 6:2 calls it Baale-Judah [בעלי יהודה], and the Vulgate there gives an explanation of this proper name, rendering the Hebrew Mibaale-Judah as of the men of Judah. So that this should not cause obscurity, the word Men must be written there with a capital letter. And so David, who in 1 Chron. 3:6 in the Hebrew text is said to have gone to Baalah [בעלתה] (the Vulgate: to the hill), which is Kiriath-jearim, to bring the Ark from there to Zion, is described in 2 Sam. (or 2 Kings) 6:2 as setting out from Baalah, having quarrelled with all Israel, in order to bring the Ark away. Although the phrase Kiriath-jearim is elsewhere the name of a city, nevertheless in 1 Sam. (or 1 Kings) 7:1, where the men of Kiriath-jearim are said to have brought the Ark into the house of Abinadab in Gibeah [בגבעה], and similarly in 2 Sam. (or 2 Kings) 6:3 and 4, where the same thing is said, the word is taken in its primary meaning as hill; hence the Seventy render it in the hill [ἐν τῷ βουνῷ], and so do the Chaldee and others. My German brother Louis de Compiègne de Veil, Master of Arts, in his notes to his treatise on the building of the Temple, ch. 1, thinks that the city of Kiriath-jearim was situated on a slope, from which it came about, he says, that its upper part, which was perhaps the citadel, was called Gaba, or Gibeah, since that Hebrew word means a hill, or a high and prominent place. In this upper part of the city lived Abinadab, to whose house the inhabitants of Kiriath-jearim brought the Ark from Beth-shemesh.

units.la: Panes propositionis. Sic vocati sunt, non quia ponebantur in mensa, sed quia ponebantur coram Domino; quos enim LXX. vocant panes propositionis, Hebraica veritas vocat [Hebrew: לֶחֶם הַפָּנִים], panem facierum, id est, ante faciem, seu conspectum Arcæ, quæ præsentiam Domini significabat. In epistola ad Hebræos 9. v. 2. per Hypallagen propositio panum vocantur panes propositionis. Rationem vero, quam dixi, Dominus ipse Moysi præcipiens assignat. Exod. 26. ubi enim Vulgat. Et pones super mensam panes propositionis in conspectu meo semper: Hebraicè habetur ad verbum: Et dabis super mensam panem facierum ad facies meas jugiter. Quod quidam volunt fuisse dictos panes facierum, eo quòd ordine duplici collocati se mutuò respicerent, præter Scripturam dicitur.
units.tr: Bread of the Presence. They are so called not because they were placed on the table, but because they were placed before the Lord. The Seventy call them loaves of the setting forth, but the Hebrew text calls them bread of the faces [לֶחֶם הַפָּנִים], that is, before the face, or sight, of the Ark, which signified the presence of the Lord. In the Epistle to the Hebrews 9:2, by hypallage, the setting forth of the loaves is called loaves of the setting forth. The reason I have mentioned is given by the Lord himself when he commands Moses, Exod. 26. For where the Vulgate has And you shall set upon the table the loaves of the setting forth in my sight always, the Hebrew reads word for word: And you shall give upon the table the bread of faces before my faces continually. Some want these to have been called bread of the faces because, placed in a double row, they faced one another, but this is said without warrant in Scripture.

units.la: Nisi solis Sacerdotibus. Id est, sed solis Sacerdotibus; sic enim passim particula (nisi) non sumitur exceptive, sed adversative. Sic, ut alia loca omittam, 4 Reg. 5. dicit Naaman Syrus ad Elifæum: Non faciet servus tuus holocaustum aut victimam diis alienis, nisi Domino: Id est, sed Domino. Cicero lib. 13. Epist. fam. epist. 73. De re nihil possum judicare, nisi (hoc est, sed) illud mihi certe persuadeo, te talem virum nihil temere fecisse. Jam ut ad seriem Evangelici contextûs redeamus, dicimus Christum quatuor argumentis purgare discipulos suos.
units.tr: Except only for the priests. That is, but only for the priests; for the particle (except) is in such places not used exceptively but adversatively. Thus, to omit other passages, in 2 Kings 5 Naaman the Syrian says to Elisha: Your servant will not offer burnt offering or sacrifice to other gods, except to the Lord: that is, but to the Lord. Cicero, Letters to Friends, bk. 13, letter 73: I can judge nothing about the matter, except (that is, but) I am certainly convinced of this, that such a man as you has done nothing rashly. Now, to return to the sequence of the Gospel text, we say that Christ clears his disciples by four arguments.

units.la: Primum est. Qui invicta necessitate legem violat positivam, à peccato excusatur, ut patet exemplo Davidis. Necessitas, inquit Seneca, magnum humanæ imbecillitatis patrocinium. Quicquid cogit, excusat: atqui discipuli mei invicta famis necessitate legem positivam de Sabbato violaverunt, ergo à peccato excusantur.
units.tr: The first is this. One who violates a positive law by unconquerable necessity is excused from sin, as the example of David shows. Necessity, says Seneca, is a great defence of human weakness. Whatever compels, excuses. But my disciples, by the unconquerable necessity of hunger, have violated the positive law about the Sabbath; therefore they are excused from sin.

units.la: Secundum est. Qui violat legem communem positivam, ut observare possit legem magis particularem ab eodem Legislatore sibi præscriptam, excusatur à peccato; sic Sacerdotes sine crimine violant Sabbatum in Templo, ut impleant ministerium sibi præscriptum, Num. 28. v. 9. Atqui discipuli mei violaverunt Sabbatum vellendo spicas, ut earum grana fame coacti comederent, sicque mihi, qui dignior ac sanctior Templo sum, præceptum illis ministerium in prædicando dicendo regno Dei possent exhibere, ergo à peccato excu-santur.
units.tr: The second is this. One who violates a general positive law so that he may keep a more particular law prescribed to him by the same Lawgiver is excused from sin. Thus priests, without guilt, violate the Sabbath in the Temple so that they may fulfil the ministry prescribed to them (Num. 28:9). But my disciples have violated the Sabbath by plucking ears, so that, compelled by hunger, they might eat their grains; and thus, since I am worthier and holier than the Temple, they could perform for me the ministry enjoined on them, namely preaching and proclaiming the kingdom of God. Therefore they are excused from sin.

units.la: Tertium est. In illa occasione legis positivæ violatio excusatur à peccato, in qua ejus observatio contraria est humanitati; Deo enim magis misericordia placet, quàm sacrificium, id est, quilibet cultus externus; atqui in hac occasione, cùm scilicet discipuli famelici per fata ambulârent Sabbato, non avellere spicas ut fami cogenti subvenirent, Sabbati observatio fuisset contraria humanitati, ergo in hac occasione Sabbati violatio excusatur à peccato.
units.tr: The third is this. On that occasion a violation of a positive law is excused from sin when observing it would be contrary to humanity. God is pleased by mercy rather than by sacrifice, that is, by any external worship. On this occasion, when the disciples were walking hungry through the fields on the Sabbath, not to pluck ears of grain to relieve their hunger would have been contrary to humanity in keeping the Sabbath. Therefore on this occasion the violation of the Sabbath is excused from sin.

units.la: Quartum est. Illa legis positivæ violatio est sine crimine; quæ fit ad servandam illius vitam, cujus causa lex lata est; atqui lex de Sabbato sanctificando lata est hominis causa, seu, ut Marcus loquitur cap. 2. v. 27. Sabbatum propter hominem factum est, & non homo propter Sabbatum: Itaque dominus est filius hominis etiam Sabbati, q. d. Unde homo, qui Hebraismo Scripturæ familiari vocatur ־ ־ ־ habet Sabbatum in sua potestate, ut possit pro vita sua conservanda illud violare, præferens, ut decet, legis ἀναγκαῖον τῷ ἁπλῶς. Ergo sine crimine discipuli mei fame pressi ad vitam suam servandam Sabbatum violarunt.
units.tr: The fourth is this. A violation of a positive law is without crime when it is done to preserve the life of the one for whose sake the law was given. But the law on sanctifying the Sabbath was given for man's sake, or, as Mark says in chapter 2, verse 27: The Sabbath was made for man, and not man for the Sabbath; therefore the Son of man is lord even of the Sabbath. That is to say, man, who in the familiar Hebraism of Scripture is called the son of man, has the Sabbath in his power, so that he may violate it to preserve his life, preferring, as is fitting, the necessity of the law to the law absolutely [ἀναγκαῖον τῷ ἁπλῶς]. Therefore my disciples, pressed by hunger, violated the Sabbath without crime in order to preserve their lives.

units.la: 7. Scitis. Id est, animo impressum habetis; non enim tam ignorantiæ speculativæ, quàm practicæ Pharisæos redarguit Dominus.
units.tr: 7. You have read. That is, you have it impressed on your minds. For the Lord rebukes the Pharisees not so much for speculative ignorance as for practical ignorance.

units.la: 9. Venit. Supple ex Luc. 6. v. 6. in alio Sabbato.
units.tr: 9. He came. Supply from Luke 6:6: on another Sabbath.

units.la: 10. Manum. Supple ex Luc. 6. v. 6. Dexteram. Præ-termittit Matthæus, quod Lucas & Marcus narrant Christum dixisse habenti manum aridam, Surge & sta.
units.tr: 10. A hand. Supply from Luke 6:6: the right. Matthew omits what Luke and Mark relate, that Christ said to the man with the withered hand: Rise and stand.

units.la: Licet Sabbatis curare? Christus ut propositam à Pharisæis quæstionem solveret, aliam eis quæstionem propositi, quam referunt Marc. 3. v. 4. & Luc. 6. v. 9. Licet Sabbatis benefacere, an male? innuens tacitè eum male facere, qui non benefecerit proximo, cùm possit & debeat.
units.tr: Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath? In order to resolve the question put by the Pharisees, Christ put another question to them, which Mark 3:4 and Luke 6:9 report: Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good, or to do evil? By this he tacitly implied that he does evil who does not benefit his neighbour when he can and ought to.

units.la: 11. Ipse autem. Supple ex Marc. 3. v. 4. Pharisæis tacentibus.
units.tr: 11. But he. Supply from Mark 3:4, the Pharisees being silent.

units.la: 12. Magis melior. Pleonasmus Scripturæ familiaris. Sic supra, c. 6. v. 26. magis pluris, &c.
units.tr: 12. How much better. A pleonasm familiar in Scripture. So above, chapter 6, verse 26: much more of more value, and so on.

units.la: Benefacere. Id est, beneficentiæ opera exercere; neque enim Pharisæi negabant quæcumque bona opera fieri posse die Sabbati, ut orare, sacrificare; sed ea quæ impendebantur proximis, quamvis officia beneficentiæ forent. Hæc autem fieri posse Sabbato probat Christus à minori ad majus, scilicet ex eo quòd ovem forte delapsam in foveam non dubitarent extrahere etiam in Sabbato. 13. Tunc. Supple ex Marc. 3. v. 5. Circumspiciens eos cum ira, contristatus super cæcitate cordis eorum. Vera fuit ira in Christo; & notandum aliter in nobis, aliter in Christo, aliter in Deo iram esse. In nobis ira est perturbatio obnubilans & præveniens frequenter rationem, mentisque quietem conturbans. In Christo est affectus appetitûs irascibilis plenè subjectus rationi, atque à ratione imperatus, quo insurgit contra peccatum hominis tanquam punitione & vindicta dignum. In Deo ira figuratè ponitur; irasci enim dicitur quando id facit, quòd homines irati solent, id est, cùm punit, & vindicat; sicut poenitentiâ duci dicitur, quando opus suum destruit, quod solent homines, operis poenitentiâ ducti.
units.tr: To do good. That is, to exercise works of beneficence. The Pharisees did not deny that any good works could be done on the Sabbath, such as praying or offering sacrifice; but they denied that those works which are rendered to neighbours could be done, although they were duties of beneficence. Christ proves that these can be done on the Sabbath from the less to the greater, namely from the fact that they did not hesitate to pull out a sheep that had perhaps fallen into a pit, even on the Sabbath. 13. Then. Supply from Mark 3:5: looking around at them with anger, grieved at the blindness of their hearts. The anger in Christ was real, and it should be noted that anger is one thing in us, another in Christ, and another in God. In us anger is a disturbance that often clouds and overrides reason and disturbs the calm of the mind. In Christ it is an affection of the irascible appetite, fully subject to reason and commanded by it, by which he rises against the sin of man as deserving punishment and vengeance. In God anger is expressed figuratively, for he is said to be angry when he does what angry men are wont to do, that is, when he punishes and avenges. Likewise he is said to be moved to repentance when he destroys his own work, as men moved by repentance are wont to do.

units.la: Ait homini. q. d. Non ego te tango, ne habeant Judæi quod calumnientur, ne attingere illum idem sit ac operari; quod si verbum opus efficiat, admirationi sit ille, qui hoc verbum dixit: Extende manum tuam. Athan. Hom. de Semente. In Evangelio (inquit hîc B. Hier.) quo utuntur Nazareni & Ebionitæ: quod nuper in Græcum de Hebræo sermone translatum & quod vocatur à plerisque Matthæi authenticum, homo ille qui aridam habebat manum commentarium scribitur ipsiusmodi vocibus auxilium precans: Cementarium erat manibus victum quæritans: precor te Jesu ut mihi restituas sanitatem, ne turpiter mendicem cibos.
units.tr: He said to the man. That is: "I do not touch you, so that the Jews have nothing to complain about; for to touch him would be the same as to work. But if a word can effect the work, let him who spoke this word be the object of wonder: Stretch out your hand." Athanasius, Homily on the Sowing. "In the Gospel (says Jerome here) which the Nazarenes and Ebionites use, which was recently translated from Hebrew into Greek and is called by most the authentic Gospel of Matthew, that man who had the withered hand is described as a mason, seeking his living by his trade, praying for help in such words: 'I was a mason, earning my living with my hands. I beg you, Jesus, restore my health to me, so that I need not shamefully beg for food.'"

units.la: 14. Exeuntes. Scilicet, è Synagoga.
units.tr: 14. Going out. That is, from the synagogue.

units.la: Pharisæi consilium faciebant. Supple ex Marc. 3. v. 6. cum Herodianis, quos aiunt fuisse corycæos & emissarios Herodis, qui quid à singulis diceretur sedulo explscarentur.
units.tr: The Pharisees took counsel. Supply from Mark 3:6: with the Herodians, whom they say were flatterers and spies of Herod, who diligently sought out what was said by each person.

units.la: Perderent. Id est, occiderent.
units.tr: Might destroy. That is, might kill.

units.la: Sciens. Id est, virtute divinâ secretas Pharisæorum cogitationes cognoscens.
units.tr: Knowing. That is, knowing by divine power the secret thoughts of the Pharisees.

units.la: Recessit inde. Supple, ad mare Galilææ. Vide Marc. 6. v. 7.
units.tr: He withdrew from there. Supply: to the sea of Galilee. See Mark 3:7.

units.la: Curavit eos omnes. Qui, scilicet, sanatione egebant, quos multos fuisse dicit Marc. 3. v. 10.
units.tr: He healed them all. Namely, those who needed healing, which Mark 3:10 says were many.

units.la: 18. Ecce puer. Id est, servus. Non solùm in præsenti loco, sed ubicumque de veteri Instrumento Evangelistæ & Apostoli testimonia protulerunt, diligentius observandum est non eos verba secutos esse, sed sensum, & ubi Septuaginta ab Hebraico discrepant, Hebræum sensum suis expressisse sermonibus. Puer igitur Dei omnipotentis juxta dispensationem carnis assumtæ, quâ ad nos mittitur, Salvator est appellatus, ad quem & in alio loco dicit Pater: Magnum mihi est vocari puerum meum, ut congreges tribus Jacob; hoc est vinea Sorec, quæ interpretatur, Electa; hic est Filius electissimus, in quo sibi bene complacuit anima Dei; non quòd Deus animam habeat, sed quòd in anima omnis Dei manifestum affectus; & non mirum nement si in Deo anima committetur, cum universa humani corporis membra secundum leges Tropologiae & discretionis intelligentiae habere dicatur. Hieron. Epist. 151. ad Algasiam q. 2.
units.tr: 18. Behold my servant. That is, my servant. Not only in this place, but wherever the Evangelists and Apostles have brought forward testimonies from the Old Testament, it must be observed with care that they followed not the words but the sense; and where the Septuagint differs from the Hebrew, they expressed the Hebrew sense in their own words. The child of almighty God, therefore, by the dispensation of the flesh he assumed, by which he is sent to us, is called Saviour. To him also the Father says in another place: It is a great thing for me to be called my child, that you should gather the tribes of Jacob; that is, the vineyard of Sorek, which is interpreted "chosen." This is the most chosen Son, in whom my soul is well pleased; not that God has a soul, but that in the soul the whole affection of God is made manifest. And it is no wonder if a soul is ascribed to God, since all the members of the human body are said to have one according to the laws of tropology and of discerning understanding. Jerome, Letter 151 to Algasia, q. 2.

units.la: Ponam Spiritum meum super eos. Q.d. Non super eum sicut super omnem carnem effundam de Spiritu meo, quasi ad mensuram, sed Spiritum meum, seu plenitudinem Spiritus, quasi principium quoddam universale, ut loquitur D. Th. ex quo procedit & profluit in membra Ecclesiae omnis varietas donorum Spiritus-Sancti.
units.tr: I will put my Spirit upon them. That is: not that I will pour out my Spirit on him as on all flesh, as if by measure, but my Spirit, or the fullness of the Spirit, as a certain universal principle, as St Thomas puts it, from which proceeds and flows into the members of the Church every variety of the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Judicium gentibus nuntiabit. Id est, omnes gentes judicabit; non enim Pater judicat quemquam per praesentiae suae manifestationem, sed omne judicium dedit Filio secundum visibilem judicis majestatem exercendum.
units.tr: He will declare judgment to the Gentiles. That is, he will judge all nations. For the Father does not judge anyone by manifesting his presence, but has given all judgment to the Son, to be exercised according to the visible majesty of the judge.

units.la: 19. Non contendet, &c. Significatur Christi mansuetudo, & in docendo lenitas, & benignitas. Hac autem de causa hoc Esaiae testimonium profert Matthaeus.
units.tr: 19. He will not strive, etc. Christ's meekness is signified, along with his gentleness and kindness in teaching. For this reason Matthew brings forward this testimony of Isaiah.

units.la: Neque audiet aliquis in plateis vocem ejus. Non est hoc contrarium ei quod Luc. 13. v. 26. dicitur quosdam dicturos Domino: In plateis nostris docuisti; non enim Esaias negat Christum in plateis docuisse, qui prout occasio ferebat passim docebat, vel in Templo, vel in Synagoga, vel in plateis, vel in deserto, vel in navi, vel in via; sed praedicit Christi mansuetudinem, animique moderationem & tranquillitatem, ut qui clamosus & contentiosus futurus non esset; talium enim vox, licet intus in domo sint, foris atque in plateis audiri solet.
units.tr: Neither shall anyone hear his voice in the streets. This is not contrary to what Luke 13:26 says, that some will say to the Lord: You taught in our streets. For Isaiah does not deny that Christ taught in the streets. He taught everywhere as occasion arose: in the Temple, in the synagogue, in the streets, in the desert, in a boat, or on the road. Rather, he foretells Christ's meekness and the moderation and tranquillity of his mind, so that he would not be clamorous or contentious. For the voice of such people, even when they are inside a house, is usually heard outside and in the streets.

units.la: 20. Arundinem quassatam. Id est, jam frangi coeptam. Linum fumigans. Id est, ellychnium lucernae extinctum proximum.
units.tr: 20. A bruised reed. That is, one already beginning to be broken. Smoking flax. That is, a lamp-wick nearly extinguished.

units.la: Non exstinguet. Supple, יכבה, &c. more Hebraeorum. Vide supra c. 4. v. 15. His autem adagialibus locutionibus incredibilis Christi humanitas, & in omnes lenitas experimitur.
units.tr: He will not quench. Supply [yikbeh], and so on, after the manner of the Hebrews. See above, chapter 4, verse 15. By these proverbial expressions the incredible humanity of Christ and his gentleness towards all are shown.

units.la: Donec ejiciat ad victoriam judicium. Id est, donec proferat judicium illud ultimum, quo adversarios suos vincat. Quasi diceret, usque ad consummationem seculi. In textu Esaiae cap. 42. v. 2. habetur: Donec ponat in terra judicium.
units.tr: Until he brings forth judgment to victory. That is, until he brings forth that last judgment by which he overcomes his adversaries. As if he were saying: until the consummation of the age. In the text of Isaiah chapter 42, verse 2, it reads: until he sets judgment in the earth.

units.la: 21. In nomine ejus gentes sperabunt. Id est, in Christo Salvatore omnes spes suas collocabunt. Apud Hebraeos (inquit Hier.) legitur: In lege ejus sperabunt insulae: sed Matthaeus sensum potius quam verba interpretans, pro lege & insulis nomen posuit & gentes. Hanc autem Esaiae Prophetiam tam Chaldaeus Paraphrastes, quam caeteri Judaei de Christo, seu de Messia acceperunt, soli LXX. de Jacob exposuerunt, unde Evangelista, dimissâ eorum interpretatione, quasi Hebræus ex Hebræis, & in Lege Domini doctissimus, ea gentibus protulit, quæ in Hebræo legerat. Ita Hieron. Epist. ad Algasiam 151. q. 2.
units.tr: 21. In his name the Gentiles will hope. That is, in Christ the Saviour they will place all their hopes. Among the Hebrews (says Jerome) it is read: In his law the islands will hope. But Matthew, interpreting the sense rather than the words, put "name" for "law" and "Gentiles" for "islands." Indeed, this prophecy of Isaiah was understood of Christ, or of the Messiah, by the Chaldee paraphrast as well as by the other Jews, while the Seventy alone explained it of Jacob. Hence the Evangelist, setting aside their interpretation, like a Hebrew among Hebrews and most learned in the Law of the Lord, gave to the Gentiles what he had read in the Hebrew. So Jerome, Letter 151 to Algasia, q. 2.

units.la: 22. Tunc. Hæc vox non pertinet hìc ad tempus rei proximè narratæ, non enim in secessu, sed in domo coram Pharisæis contigit sequens historia, ut colligitur ex Marc. 3. v. 20, 21, & 22. simul collatis. Licèt autem Marcus non faciat mentionem daemoniaci cæci & muti, & Luc. c. 11. v. 14. reticeat daemoniacum fuisse cæcum, ex iis tamen verbis, in quibus Matthæus, Marcus, & Lucas conveniunt, sicut in historiam consequentibus, patet eandem historiam ab illis tribus enarrari.
units.tr: 22. Tunc. This word does not here refer to the time of the event just narrated. The following story did not happen in a secluded place but in a house, before the Pharisees, as can be gathered from Mark 3:20, 21 and 22 read together. Although Mark does not mention the blind and dumb demoniac, and Luke in chapter 11, verse 14, passes over the fact that the demoniac was blind, it is nonetheless clear from the words in which Matthew, Mark and Luke agree, as well as from what follows in the narrative, that all three relate the same history.

units.la: Ab hoc insigni miraculo redit Matthæus ad continuandam narrationem eorum quæ post secundum Christi e Judæa in Galilæam reditum contigerunt, cùm horum pleraque anticipasset; Lucas verò idipsum serius narrat, nimirum post missionem septuaginta discipulorum, ita verò ut nullam cohærentiam significet.
units.tr: Having finished this notable miracle, Matthew returns to continue his account of what happened after Christ's second return from Judea to Galilee, although he had anticipated many of those events. Luke, however, relates this same incident later, namely after the sending out of the seventy disciples, and does not indicate any connection between them.

units.la: Cæcus & mutus. Non naturæ vitio, sed dæmonis maleficio; unde Luc. 11. v. 14. ipsum daemonium dicitur mutum, scilicet effectivé.
units.tr: Blind and dumb. Not from a defect of nature but from the sorcery of a demon; hence in Luke 11:14 the demon itself is called dumb, that is, in its effect.

units.la: Curavit eum. Supple ex Luc. 11. v. 14. à daemonio.
units.tr: He healed him. Supply from Luke 11:14: from the demon.

units.la: 23. Stupebant omnes. Quia ut dicitur Marc. 1. in potestate spiritibus immundis imperabat, & obediebant ei.
units.tr: 23. All were amazed. Because, as Mark 1 says, he commanded unclean spirits with authority, and they obeyed him.

units.la: 24. Beelzebub. Deum Accaronitarum, sic dictum volunt Græci Patres, quasi Deum muscæ habuerit imaginem; sed multò probabiliùs Beelzebub dictus est, ut Latini Patres volunt, quasi Princeps muscarum, adeo ut, Zebub, non fit in Nominativo, sed Genitivo casu; quòd nimirum, hic Deus muscas abigeret à suo Templo. In textu autem Græco idem appellatur in Evangelio Beelzebul, quasi Dominus stercoris, seu Deus stercoreus, quod probabiliter est nomen interpolatum à posterioribus Judæis contemptus causâ. Illud autem maximè notandum est, Pharisæos hìc & Luc. 11. v. 15. Beelzebub, seu Beelzebul daemonum Principem afferere, qui Hebraeorum aliis est Afmodau.
units.tr: 24. Beelzebub. The Greek Fathers hold that he was so called as the god of Accaron, as if the god had the image of a fly; but it is much more probable, as the Latin Fathers hold, that he was called Beelzebub as the prince of flies, so that Zebub is not in the nominative but in the genitive case, the idea being that this god drove the flies away from his temple. In the Greek text of the Gospel the same name is written Beelzebul, as if it meant lord of dung, or dung-god, which is probably a name altered by later Jews out of contempt. But this above all must be noted: here and in Luke 11:15 the Pharisees assert that Beelzebub, or Beelzebul, is the prince of demons, who is called Asmodeus by some Hebrews.

units.la: Principe daemoniorum. Quatuor sunt daemonum principis nomina in Scripturis, draco, serpens antiquus, diabolus, & Satanas, & à Scripturæ consuetudine recedunt, qui omnes daemones, quos Scriptura passim daemonia vocat, diabolos appellant. Multi etiam è veteribus diabolum, hoc est, daemoniorum principem, vocant zabolum, à verbo ζαβάλλειν, quod idem est ac διαβάλλειν, unde diabolus, id est, decipere, calumniari. Scičns cogitationes. Nempe, ex quibus prodiret sinistra illa interpretatio Pharisæorum, quibus Dominus non ad dicta, sed ad cogitata respondit: ut vel sic compellerentur credere potentiæ ejus, qui cordis videbat occulta. B. Hier.
units.tr: Prince of demons. There are four names of the prince of demons in the Scriptures: dragon, ancient serpent, devil, and Satan. They depart from the usage of Scripture, which elsewhere calls all demons demons, by calling them devils. Many of the ancients also call the devil, that is, the prince of demons, zabolus, from the verb [ζαβάλλειν], which is the same as [διαβάλλειν], whence devil, that is, one who deceives or slanders. Knowing their thoughts. Namely, the thoughts from which that sinister interpretation of the Pharisees arose. The Lord answered them not in words but in their thoughts, so that they might be compelled, even in this way, to believe in his power, since he saw the hidden things of the heart. Blessed Jerome.

units.la: 26. Si satanas satanam ejicit, adversus se divisus est. In his verbis non significantur diversi dæmones, quorum alter alterum ejiciat, sed unus & idem dæmonum princeps qui seipsum ejiciat, unde dicitur: Adversus se divisus est: & apud Lucam habetur, Si autem & satanas in seipsum divisus est. Dicitur autem se ipsum ejicere, si suos ministros, per quos exequitur sui regni negotia, ejicit; sicut Rex seipsum ejiceret, si ministros suos, sine quibus populum in officio continere non potest, ejiceret. Itaque ex hoc loco non potest statui quòd nomen satanæ inferioribus etiam dæmonibus in Scriptura tribuatur, & non soli dæmoniorum principi.
units.tr: 26. If Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself. In these words there is meant not different demons, one of whom casts out another, but one and the same prince of demons who casts out himself; hence it is said, he is divided against himself, and in Luke it is found, If Satan also is divided against himself. He is said to cast out himself if he casts out his own ministers, through whom he carries out the business of his kingdom; just as a king would be casting out himself if he cast out his own ministers, without whom he cannot keep the people in obedience. Therefore from this passage it cannot be concluded that the name Satan is given in Scripture also to the lesser demons and not only to the prince of demons.

units.la: 27. Filii vestri, &c. Non Apostoli hîc intelliguntur, qui à Pharisæis unà cum Christo accusabantur, sed Exorcistæ Pharisæorum discipuli, qui ex more ad invocationem Dei ejiciebant dæmonia. Altissimi & omnipotentis appellationi omnia subjecta sunt: & hujus invocatione etiam ante adventum Domini nostri salvabantur homines, & à spiritibus nequissimis, & à dæmoniis universis.... Et propter hoc Judæi usque nunc hac ipsa advocatione dæmonas effugant, quando omnia timent invocationem ejus, qui fecit ea. B. Irenæus lib. 2. cap. 5.
units.tr: 27. Your sons, etc. Not the apostles are meant here, who were accused by the Pharisees together with Christ, but the exorcists, the disciples of the Pharisees, who in the customary way cast out demons by calling upon God. All things are subject to the name of the Most High and Almighty, and by the invocation of him men were saved even before the coming of our Lord, both from the most wicked spirits and from all demons... And for this reason the Jews to this day drive out demons by this very invocation, since all things fear the invocation of him who made them. Blessed Irenaeus, book 2, chapter 5.

units.la: 28. In Spiritu Dei. Lucas digitum Dei dicens, ubi Matthæus Spiritum Dei dixit, docet quemadmodum intelligamus, ubicunque in Scriptura legerimus digitum Dei.
units.tr: 28. By the Spirit of God. Luke, saying the finger of God where Matthew said the Spirit of God, teaches us how we should understand wherever we read of the finger of God in Scripture.

units.la: Igitur pervenit in vos regnum Dei. q. d. Ergo verum esse testatur miraculis Spiritus-Sanctus appropinquasse & venisse regnum Dei, sicut ego, Joannes Baptista, & Apostoli mei prædicavimus.
units.tr: Then the kingdom of God has come upon you. That is: therefore the Holy Spirit bears witness through miracles that the kingdom of God has truly drawn near and come, just as I, John the Baptist, and my apostles have preached.

units.la: 29. Aut. Id est, alioquin, nisi hæc vera sint.
units.tr: 29. Or. That is, otherwise, unless these things are true.

units.la: Vasa. Hebraismus, id est, quidquid est supelleċtilis.
units.tr: Goods. A Hebraism, that is, whatever belongs to household furniture.

units.la: Alligaverit fortem. Id est, refrænaverit ejus potentiam & vires imminuerit. Alludit autem Christus ad illud Esaïæ 49. v. 24. Numquid tolletur à forti præda, &c. Nisi ergo priùs vincat diabolum, & alliget, quomodo vasa ejus, id est, à diabolo, quoad animam, vel quoad corpus possessos diripiet & direptos Deo ejusque Ecclesiæ adunabit? Hinc præclarè Aug. Ep. 107. Mediator intrat in domum fortis, id est, in hoc seculum mortalium sub potestate diaboli, quantùm ad ipsum pertinet, constituitur. De ipso quippe scriptum est, quòd potestatem habeat mortis: intrat in domum fortis, id est, in suo dominatu habentis genus humanum, & priùs alligat eum, id est, eius coërcet & cohibet potestatem potestatis suæ fortissimus vinculis, & sic eripit vasa ejus quæcunque prædestinavit eripere, arbitrium eorum ab ejus potestate liberans, ut illo non impediente credant in ipsum libera voluntate.
units.tr: Binds the strong man. That is, restrains his power and diminishes his strength. Christ here alludes to Isaiah 49:24: Shall the prey be taken from the mighty, etc.? Unless, therefore, he first conquers the devil and binds him, how shall he plunder those who are the devil's goods, that is, those possessed by the devil in soul or in body, and gather the plundered to God and his Church? Hence Augustine excellently says, Letter 107: The Mediator enters the house of the strong man, that is, he is established in this mortal world, which, as far as it concerns him, is under the power of the devil. For it is written of him that he has the power of death: he enters the house of the strong man, that is, the human race which he holds in his dominion, and first binds him, that is, restrains and curbs his power, with the most mighty bonds of his own power, and so snatches away his goods, whomsoever he predestined to snatch, freeing their will from his power, so that, with it no longer hindered, they may believe in him by free will.

units.la: 30. Qui non est mecum, &c. Id est, qui mihi per fidem non conjungitur, is mihi contrarius est. Hac sententia Christus Pharisæos nec miraculis suis, nec doctrinæ suæ credentes sugillat. Huic sententiæ è diverso respondet alia Christi sententia Luc. 9. v. 50. Qui non est adversum vos, pro vobis est, vel ut Græca & Latina multa exemplaria habent nos, nobis; sensus est; Quicunque non est nobis seu vobis contrarius, is per fidem nobis seu vobis conjungitur, etiamsi corporaliter non adunetur. Quibus verbis Christus innuit neminem sine aliqua fide in ipsum posse in ipsius nomine dæmonia ejicere, vel alia miracula facere, unde Marc. 9. v. 38. Nemo, inquit, est, qui faciat virtutem, id est, aliquod miraculum, in nomine meo, & possit cito, id est, facile, male loqui de nomine meo, id est, de authoritate mea detrahere, mihi seu prædicationi Evangelii mei adversari. Et in Actis Apostolorum, filii Sceuæ principis Sacerdotum, tentabant ejicere dæmonia invocato Jesu, quem Paulus prædicabat, ut dicitur Act. 19. v. 13. & 14. Constat autem ex utraque Christi sententia, nihil esse medium inter hæc duo, esse cum Christo, & esse contra Christum. Non est ullus illi locus medius ut possit esse nisi cum diabolo, qui non est cum Christo, inquit Aug. lib. 1. de peccatorum meritis & remissione, cap. 28.
units.tr: 30. He who is not with me, etc. That is, whoever is not joined to me through faith is against me. By this saying Christ rebukes the Pharisees, who believed neither his miracles nor his teaching. To this saying there corresponds, on the other side, another saying of Christ, Luke 9:50: He who is not against you is for you, or as many Greek and Latin copies have it, against us, for us; the sense is: whoever is not contrary to us, or to you, is joined to us, or to you, through faith, even if he is not united with us bodily. By these words Christ indicates that no one can cast out demons in his name or do other miracles without some faith in him; hence Mark 9:38: No one, he says, is there who does a mighty work, that is, some miracle, in my name, and can quickly, that is, easily, speak evil of my name, that is, detract from my authority, and oppose me or the preaching of my Gospel. And in the Acts of the Apostles, the sons of Sceva, a chief priest, tried to cast out demons by invoking Jesus, whom Paul preached, as is said in Acts 19:13 and 14. It is clear from both of Christ's sayings that there is no middle ground between these two: to be with Christ and to be against Christ. There is no middle place for anyone, so that he can be anywhere but with the devil, who is not with Christ, says Augustine, book 1, On the Merits and Remission of Sins, chapter 28.

units.la: Qui non congregat mecum. Id est, qui congregat homines, sed non mecum, seu non ita, ut mihi adhærent, sed sibi; ut Pharisæi & Hæretici omnes.
units.tr: He who does not gather with me. That is, he who gathers men, but not with me, or not in such a way that they cling to me but to himself; as all Pharisees and heretics do.

units.la: Spargit. Ut enim, ait Aug. lib. 2. de baptismo contra Donatistas, c. 31. Spargunt oves Christi, qui eas ad mortem suorum habent pravâ imitatione perducunt.
units.tr: Scatters. For, as Augustine says, book 2, On Baptism against the Donatists, chapter 31: They scatter the sheep of Christ, whom they lead to death by their wicked imitation.

units.la: 31. Ideo, q. d. Cùm constet me non diaboli virtute, sed in Spiritu Dei, ejicere dæmonia; primo quidem per hoc quod Satanas contra seipsum non dividitur; deinde exemplo aliorum qui dæmonia ejiciebant per Spiritum Dei: tum quia dæmonium expellere non possem, nisi ipsum vicissem virtute divina; postremo quia nulla convenientia in operibus nec in effectu est mihi & Satanæ, cum Satanas dispergere cupiat, quos ego collecturus adveni.
units.tr: 31. Therefore, that is: since it is clear that I cast out demons not by the power of the devil but by the Spirit of God, first indeed because Satan is not divided against himself; second, by the example of others who cast out demons by the Spirit of God; third, because I could not expel a demon unless I had overcome it by divine power; last, because there is no agreement between me and Satan, either in works or in effect, since Satan wishes to scatter those whom I have come to gather.

units.la: Dico vobis. Id est, aperte declaro.
units.tr: I say to you. That is, I declare plainly.

units.la: Blasphemia remittetur. Id est, verbum in contumeliam Dei prolatum, est remissibile, quia utcunque excusabile. Spiritus autem blasphemia. Id est, blasphemia, quâ quis contra veritatem intus in animo sibi à Spiritu-Sancto (cui veluti proprium officium tribuunt Scripturæ docere omnem veritatem) patefactam, ex destinata malitia adinstar Pharisæorum impie dicere audet ea esse à diabolo, quæ persuasus & convictus in conscientia cognoscit esse opera Spiritus-Sancti, hoc est, opera divinæ bonitatis, quæ Spiritui-Sancto appropriantur. Hunc esse genuinum hujus loci sensum patet ex Marc. 3. v. 30.
units.tr: Blasphemy will be forgiven. That is, a word spoken in contempt of God can be forgiven, because it can in some way be excused. But the blasphemy against the Spirit. That is, the blasphemy by which someone, out of settled malice like the Pharisees, impiously dares to say that those things come from the devil which he, persuaded and convicted in his conscience, knows to be works of the Holy Spirit. The truth has been revealed to him inwardly by the Holy Spirit, to whom the Scriptures assign, as it were, the proper office of teaching all truth. That this is the genuine sense of the passage is clear from Mark 3:30.

units.la: Non remittetur. q. d. Irremissibilis est, seu, non habet in se unde remittatur, quia nullâ ratione excusari potest; unde rarissimè Deus talibus gratiam poenitentiæ impertit.
units.tr: Will not be forgiven. That is, it is unforgivable, or it has in itself no ground for forgiveness, since it can be excused on no reasoning. Hence God very rarely grants the grace of repentance to such people.

units.la: 32. Quicunque dixerit, &c. Clarius mox à se dicta explicat Christus.
units.tr: 32. Whoever shall speak, etc. Christ explains more clearly what he has just said.

units.la: Verbum. Supple, contumeliosum.
units.tr: A word. Supply: insulting.

units.la: Qui autem dixerit. Scilicet, sciens & volens ex destinata malitia.
units.tr: But whoever shall speak. Namely, knowingly and willingly, out of settled malice.

units.la: Contra Spiritum-Sanctum. Supple, in cujus virtute Filius hominis operatur.
units.tr: Against the Holy Spirit. Supply: in whose power the Son of man works.

units.la: Neque in hoc seculo neque in futuro. Hoc est, in aeternum, ut loquitur Marcus c. 3. v. 29. Ut enim ait Aug. Ser. 11. De verbis Domini c. 8. Aliis verbis, & alio loquendi modo eadem ipsa est expressa sententia. Proverbialem locutionem à Matthæo usurpatam Drusius sub Lege natam eenslet, dum Hebraei Legis tempus vocarunt hoc, id est, præsens, seculum, & tempus Messiæ futurum seculum, quo credebant remissum iri omnia peccata. Hinc ab Angelo dictum supra c. 1. v. 21. Vocabis nomen ejus Jesum; ipse enim salvum faciet populum suum à peccatis eorum.
units.tr: Neither in this age nor in the age to come. That is, for ever, as Mark says in chapter 3, verse 29. For as Augustine says, Sermon 11, On the Words of the Lord, chapter 8: In other words, and in another manner of speaking, the same meaning is expressed. Drusius considers the proverbial expression used by Matthew to have arisen under the Law, since the Hebrews called the time of the Law this age, that is, the present age, and the time of the Messiah the age to come, in which they believed all sins would be forgiven. Hence the angel said above, in chapter 1, verse 21: You shall call his name Jesus, for he shall save his people from their sins.

units.la: 33. Aut facite. Reprehendit hic Christus Pharisæorum hypocrisin, quòd cùm arbor bona videri vellent, malos tamen fructus facerent: aut cùm mala arbor essent, bonos videri vellent fructus facere, jubétque aut aperte malos, aut aperte bonos esse. q. d. Non oportet esse tepidos in negotio pietatis: aut ferò cum Deo esse agendum, aut planè abeo discedendum; non enim habet opus hypocrisi, non amat tepidos illos, oportet esse calidum, aut planè frigidum: proinde vobis optionem offerens dico, Estote ingenui, & palam boni; sin id non placeat, aperte praestat esse malos. Quid opus ista claudicatione? Simile est Eliæ dictum ad Israëlem, 3 Reg. 18. v. 21. Usque quo claudicatis in duas partes? Si Dominus est Deus, sequimini eum: si Baal, sequimini illum. Et quod Angelo Laodiceæ Ecclesiæ scriptum, Apoc. 3. v. 15, & 16. Scio opera tua, quia neque frigidus es, neque calidus: utinam frigidus frigidus esses, aut calidus: sed quia tepidus es, & nec frigidus, nec calidus, incipiam te evomere ex ore meo.
units.tr: 33. Either make. Here Christ rebukes the hypocrisy of the Pharisees, who, wishing to seem a good tree, nevertheless bore bad fruit, or, being a bad tree, wished to seem to bear good fruit. He bids them be either openly bad or openly good. That is: one must not be lukewarm in the business of piety. Either one must deal with God in earnest, or depart from him altogether; for hypocrisy has no place here, and he does not love those who are lukewarm. One must be hot or plainly cold. So, offering you a choice, I say: be honest and openly good; but if that does not please you, it is better to be openly wicked. Why this limping? Similar is Elijah's saying to Israel, 3 Kings 18:21: How long will you limp between two parts? If the Lord is God, follow him; if Baal, follow him. And what was written to the angel of the church of Laodicea, Revelation 3:15-16: I know your works, that you are neither cold nor hot. I would that you were cold or hot. But because you are lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will begin to spew you out of my mouth.

units.la: Pharisaos ostendit arborem malam, & tales afferre fructus blasphemiæ redundantes, qualia habeant semina diaboli. B. Hier.
units.tr: He shows the Pharisees to be a bad tree, and such that they bring forth fruits of overflowing blasphemy, such as have the seeds of the devil. St Jerome.

units.la: Quomodo potestis. Supple, facile; magis enim difficultatem, quam impossibilitatem significat Christus, & familiari proverbio confirmat. Nam, ut ait Sanctus Prosper in responsione ad sextam objectionem Vincentianam, Multorum hominum talis est malitia, qualis & daemonum; sed hoc inter malos homines distat & daemones, quod hominibus etiam valde malis superest, si Deus misereatur, reconciliatio: daemonibus autem nulla est in aeternum servata conversio.
units.tr: How can you. Supply: easily. For Christ signifies difficulty rather than impossibility, and confirms it with a familiar proverb. As Saint Prosper says in his reply to the sixth objection of Vincentius: Many men have a malice such as that of the demons; but between wicked men and demons this differs, that for men even very wicked, if God shows mercy, reconciliation remains; but for demons no conversion is preserved for eternity.

units.la: Ex abundantia enim cordis. Cor in Scripturis figurate, sed usitatissimè nunc intellectum, nunc voluntatem, ut hic, significat, quod facile dignoscitur per adjuncta.
units.tr: For out of the abundance of the heart. In the Scriptures the heart is spoken of figuratively, but it is most commonly understood now as the understanding and now as the will, as here. This is easily recognised from the context.

units.la: Loquitur. Id est, loqui solet.
units.tr: Speaks. That is, is accustomed to speak.

units.la: q. d. Homines id quod maximè ipsis intus allubescit, libenter ex cordis penu reconditum depromunt: & quidem si boni sint, bona; si verò mali sint, mala.
units.tr: That is: men willingly bring out of the store of the heart whatever most pleases them inwardly; and indeed, if they are good, good things, and if they are evil, evil things.

units.la: Ostendit Christus argumento a minori ad majus, quale judicium de Pharisaeorum blasphemiis contra Spiritum-Sanctum sit ferendum.
units.tr: Christ shows, by an argument from the less to the greater, what judgment is to be passed on the blasphemies of the Pharisees against the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Omne verbum otiosum, &c. Syntaxis Hebraica, quæ nominativus redundat. Judæorum Doctores eò procedebant fastus & arrogantiæ, ut pronuntiare auderent etiam otiosum sermonem Doctoris profecturum discipulis. De hoc inter cæteros Kimchius ad Pf. 1. Definitur autem verbum otiosum à B. Hier. hic, Quod sine utilitate & loquentia dicitur & audientis. A B. Greg. Mag. Hom. 6. in Evang. Quod aut utilitate rectitudinis, aut ratione justæ necessitatis caret; & 3. p. Pastoralis admon. 15. Quod aut ratione justæ necessitatis, aut intentione piæ utilitatis caret. Denique à B. Bern. in Serm. de triplici custodia manus, linguæ, & cordis, verbum otiosum definitur, Quod nullam rationabilem causam habet.
units.tr: Every idle word, etc. A Hebrew construction, in which the nominative is redundant. The teachers of the Jews went so far in pride and arrogance that they dared to say that even the idle word of a teacher would profit the disciples. Kimchi discusses this among others on Psalm 1. An idle word is defined by Jerome here as that which is spoken without usefulness, both to the speaker and to the hearer. Gregory the Great, Homily 6 on the Gospel: that which lacks either the usefulness of rectitude or the reason of just necessity. And in part 3 of the Pastoral Admonition, chapter 15: that which lacks either a reason of just necessity or the intention of a pious usefulness. Finally, Bernard, in his sermon on the threefold guard of hand, tongue and heart, defines an idle word as that which has no reasonable cause.

units.la: Ex verbis enim tuis. q. d. Non ex operibus tantum, sed etiam ex verbis tuis justus aut reus declaraberis in die judicii, prout judicis examen de te feret.
units.tr: For by your words. That is: not by your works alone, but also by your words, you will be declared righteous or guilty on the day of judgment, as the judge's examination of you shall determine.

units.la: Justificaberis. Varia est in Scripturis justificationis acceptio. 1. Justificari dicitur proprie, qui ex injusto fit justus, & justificare qui ex injusto facit justum. Hinc verbale justificatio, est motus seu transitus ab injustitia ad justitiam.
units.tr: You will be justified. The meaning of justification in Scripture is varied. (1) To be justified is properly said of one who is made just from unjust, and to justify is to make a just man from an unjust one. Hence the noun justification is the movement or transition from injustice to justice.

units.la: 2. Justificari est justitiam conservari, augeri, perfici, quod vocari solet justificatio secunda; hinc & bona opera & Dei præpraecepta, quorum exercitio solet augeri & conservari justitia, justificationes in Scripturis dicuntur. 3. Justificari est justum ostendi, praedicari, declarari; quo sensu in praesenti versiculo accipitur. Ab hac significatione non longe recedit, dum quandoque significat defendi, excusari; unde & justificatio Job. 27. pro apologia sumitur.
units.tr: (2) To be justified is to have righteousness preserved, increased or perfected; this is usually called second justification. Hence both good works and God's precepts, by the exercise of which righteousness is usually increased and preserved, are called justifications in Scripture. (3) To be justified is to be shown, proclaimed or declared just; it is in this sense that the word is taken in the present verse. This meaning does not depart far from the sense in which it sometimes means to be defended or excused; hence also justification in Job 27 is taken for a defence.

units.la: Condemnaberis, id est, reus pronuntiaberis, seu punie-ris.
units.tr: You will be condemned, that is, you will be pronounced guilty, or punished.

units.la: 38. Tunc, &c. Multo magis cohaeret narratio Matthaei, quam Lucae; verisimilius enim est hanc primam signi petitionem contigisse eo ordine, quo à Matthaeo narratur, nempe post gravem Pharisaeorum reprehensionem de blasphemia, quàm ante, ut legitur apud Lucam cap. 11. Item cùm dixi-ssset Christus Jonam fuisse signum Ninivitis, potiùs videtur primo subjecisse comparationem Ninivitarum, ut apud Matthaeum, quàm Reginae Austri, ut apud Lucam legitur.
units.tr: 38. Then, etc. Matthew's narrative fits much better than Luke's. For it is more likely that this first request for a sign happened in the order in which Matthew relates it, namely after the severe rebuke of the Pharisees about blasphemy, than before, as read in Luke chapter 11. Likewise, when Christ had said that Jonah was a sign to the Ninevites, he seems to have first added the comparison with the Ninevites, as in Matthew, rather than with the Queen of the South, as read in Luke.

units.la: Quidam. Diversi scilicet ab iis, quorum jam calumniam confutarat, ut patet ex Luc. 11. v. 15, & 16.
units.tr: Some. Namely, people different from those whose calumny he had already refuted, as is clear from Luke 11:15-16.

units.la: Signum. Supple ex Luc. 11. de caelo. Vel in morem Eliae, ignem de sublimi venire cupiebant: vel in similitudinem Samuelis, tempore aestivo contra naturam loci mugire tonitrua, coruscare fulgura, imbres ruere, quasi non possint & illa calumniari, & dicere ex occultis & variis acris passionibus accidisse. Nam qui calumniari ea quae oculis vides; manu tenes, utilitate sentis: quid facturus es de his quae de caelo venerint? utique respondebis, & Magos in Aegypto multa signa fecisse de caelo. B. Hier.
units.tr: A sign. Supply from Luke 11: from heaven. Either they wanted fire to come from on high in the manner of Elijah, or thunder to roar in the summer, contrary to the nature of the place, in the likeness of Samuel, and lightnings to flash and showers to pour down, as if they could not also calumniate these and say that they came from hidden causes and the various passions of the air. For those who calumniate what you see with your eyes, hold in your hand and perceive by use, what will they do with things that come from heaven? Surely you will answer that the Magi in Egypt also performed many signs from heaven. St Jerome.

units.la: 39. Generatio mala & adultera. q. d. Natio adulterina & degener à fide & moribus Patriarcharum; illi enim in Christum crediderunt venturum, qui hi praesentem & tot miraculis se probantem agnoscere nolunt. Similem sensum expressit Daniel, c. 13. v. 56. hac phrasi, Semen Chanaan, & non Juda.
units.tr: 39. An evil and adulterous generation. That is: a nation adulterous and degenerate from the faith and morals of the Patriarchs. For they believed that Christ would come, whereas these refuse to acknowledge him present and proving himself by so many miracles. Daniel, chapter 13, verse 56, expressed a similar sense in this phrase: The seed of Canaan, and not of Judah.

units.la: Signum quaerit. Supple, ex Luc. 11. v. 16. tentans. Duplici modo tentatur Deus; nonnunquam infirmitate fidei, quae sentiens se labascere, confugit ad miracula quibus fulciatur & sublevetur: quomodo qui titubat baculum petit quo fustentetur. Nonnunquam etiam infitia animi pervicacia tentatur Deus ab his, qui non solùm increduli sunt, sed & prorsus infideles, nec miraculum petunt ut credant, sed ne credant: quia de Dei potentia & providentia quicquid dicitur inter fabulas rejiciunt, & verbo ejus non acquiescunt, quin ut futile & absurdum irrid={ent}. Priorum exemplum nonnulli statuunt Gedeonem, Judic. 6. v. 36, 37, & 39. Ezechiam, 4 Reg. 20. v. 8. Posteriorum exemplum sunt Scribae & Pharisaei, qui signum à Christo petebant, quem omnino rejiciebant; neque illis signis contenti, quæ multa & valde illustria in terris ediderat, alia petebant edi cœlitus quæ ut priora despexissent & insuper habuissent. Venerant enim ad eum tentantes, id est, sperantes sic se aliquid in eo reperturos, unde justæ reprehensionis occasionem acciperent.
units.tr: Seeks a sign. Supply from Luke 11:16: tempting. God is tempted in two ways. Sometimes it is through weakness of faith: feeling itself faltering, faith flees to miracles by which it may be propped up and supported, as one who staggers seeks a staff to lean on. Sometimes God is also tempted through the obstinacy of a mind that is not only unbelieving but utterly faithless. Such people seek a miracle not that they may believe, but that they may not believe; for whatever is said about God's power and providence they reject as fables, and they do not assent to his word, but mock it as futile and absurd. Some hold Gideon (Judges 6:36, 37, 39) and Hezekiah (4 Kings 20:8) as examples of the former. The examples of the latter are the Scribes and Pharisees, who sought a sign from Christ whom they utterly rejected. Not content with the signs he had shown on earth, many and very illustrious, they sought others to be performed from heaven, so that they might despise and disregard the former. For they came to him tempting, that is, hoping that they would thus find something in him from which they might take an occasion of just rebuke.
