units.la: Nisi. Hæc particula hic & alibi passim in Scripturis non exceptivam, sed adversativam vim habet, éstque idem, atque, sed tantum. Petebant enim signum de Cœlo, quale non erat signum Jonæ, sed magis de mari in Jona, vel de terra in Christo. Sensus itaque præsentis versiculi est, Hæc generatio quærit signum de cœlo, at non dabitur ei signum de cœlo, sed tantum dabitur ei signum in Jona Propheta præfiguratum, quale non quærunt, quia erit eis ingratum. Per id enim manifeste confundetur, & redarguetur eorum ambitio. Signum illud fuit resurrectio Filii hominis. Eundem sensum Marc. expressit c. 8. v. 12. oratione ecliptica juxta phrasim Hebraeis usitatissimam, his verbis; Amen dico vobis, si dabitur generationi isti signum!
units.tr: Nisi. Here, and elsewhere throughout the Scriptures, this particle has not an exceptive but an adversative force, and it is the same as but only. For they were asking for a sign from heaven, not the sign of Jonah, which was rather from the sea in Jonah, or from the earth in Christ. The sense of the present verse, therefore, is: this generation seeks a sign from heaven, but no sign from heaven will be given to it, only the sign foreshadowed in the prophet Jonah, which they do not seek, because it will be unwelcome to them. For by that sign their ambition will be plainly confounded and refuted. That sign was the resurrection of the Son of man. Mark expressed the same sense in chapter 8, verse 12, with an elliptical form of speech, most usual in the Hebrew idiom, in these words: Amen I say to you, if a sign shall be given to this generation!

units.la: 40. In ventre ceti. Cetum Hebraei iisdem nominibus appellant, quibus draconem, nempe ײַן & תַּנִּין, aut ob formæ similitudinem, aut ratione molis, & quia cetus in aquatilibus tantum præstat, Oppiano teste. Halieut. lib. 1.
units.tr: 40. In the belly of the whale. The Hebrews call the whale by the same names by which they call the dragon, namely [ײַן] and [תַּנִּין], either because of a likeness of form, or because of its bulk, and because the whale surpasses all other sea creatures, as Oppian testifies, Halieutica, book 1.

units.la: Ὅσων ἀεισύιων ἐν ἐμπυσήσῃ ἀρχοντες. Quantum in reptilibus præstant virtute dracones.
units.tr: Ὅσων ἀεισύιων ἐν ἐμπυσήσῃ ἀρχοντες [Of all creatures that swim, the whales are the lords]. That is, as far as dragons excel among reptiles in strength.

units.la: Cetus vel proprie dicitur, vel improprie. Cetus proprie dictus est viviparus, non oviparus ut pisces. In ceto insuper corium durum est, caro firma & compacta, ossa solidissima, pulmo etiam & guttur, & vera vox, virga denique maribus, & lac & mammæ fœminis, quibus omnibus caret piscis. Ceti papillæ in mammis receptæ tanquam in vaginis conduntur: unde illas educunt ut lactent catulos suos, ut observavit Scaliger, Exercit. 104. Quo procul dubio respexit Jeremias Thren. 4. v. 3. ubi secundum veritatem Hebraicam habetur, Etiam cete mammam educunt, ut lactent catulos suos. Vulgat. Sed & lamia nudaverunt mammam, lactaverunt catulos suos; ubi minus commode pro cete legitur lamiæ, cum lamia piscis mammam non habeat, lamia autem fera, vel fœmina fabulosa sit. Sed & inter se cete multum differunt; minora sunt. phoca (quæ, licet sit quadrupes, dicitur ab Homero Odyss. 4. sine pedibus, quod exiguos pedes habeat: ita in avibus Cypselli dicti sunt apodes à brevitate pedum) hippopotamus, (quem sub nomine Behemoth describi, Job. 40, & 41. egregie probat doctissimus Bochartus) & delphin; majora, priscis, orca, & balæna; rursus phoca & hippopotamus pilos pedésque & collum habent: at balæna & delphin corium glabrum, & pinnas pro pedibus, & pro collo fistulam in fronte, quæ de superiori parte trahunt aërem. Porro quia ingens est cetorum moles, qui in vulgo piscium sunt reliquis majores cetacei dicuntur, & in iis qui sunt multo maximi, ut lamiæ, maltha (pro quo corrupte Æmilius Portus edidit apud Suidam) zygæna (quæ caput jugi, aut, quod idem est, vectis instar habet ex transverso situm, & leviathan dicitur improprie, quomodo cetus à Græcis, Esa. 27. v. 1.) thynnus (cujus nomen videtur factum ab Hebræo תנין, quo cetus significatur, ut valde sit verisimile, hanc thynnis appellationem venisse à Phoenicibus, quos thynnorum piscatione celebres cum alii testantur, tum maxime Aristoteles in lib. Mirabilium) & alii maximi quique cetaceorum piscium ex usu apud probatissimos autores recepto, licet improprie, solent tamen dici cete sine addito. Sic Jonas hic dicitur fuisse in ventre ceti, cum tamen non fuerit in ventre ceti proprie dicti; ut enim ceti vastæ sint belluæ, tamen gulæ meatus habent angustiores, quam ut possint solidum hominem transglutire; nempe quotquot animalia pulmone spirant, iis gulæ meatus coarctari necesse est, quomodo collum in follibus, ut ex iis angustiis spiritus per fauces majore nisu erumpat. Itaque cetus in cujus ventre fuit Jonas dicitur, Jonæ 2. v. 1. piscis grandis; nempe is fuit verus piscis, sed ita ingens, ut ratione molis suæ cetis adscribi meruerit, hincque probat doctissimus Bochartus fuisse ex ea canis marini specie, quam carchariam alii vocant ab asperitate dentium & acumine, alii lamiam & lemnam λαμίαν ἢ ψῶρον, à gulæ vastitate etc.
units.tr: The whale is spoken of either properly or improperly. The whale properly so called is viviparous, not oviparous like fishes. Moreover, the whale has a tough hide, firm and compact flesh, very solid bones, lungs and a throat, a true voice, and finally, in males, a penis, and in females, milk and teats, all of which the fish lacks. The whale's teats are received into the breasts as if into sheaths, and so they draw them out in order to suckle their young, as Scaliger observed, Exercitations 104. Jeremiah undoubtedly had this in mind, Lamentations 4, verse 3, where according to the Hebrew truth we read: Even the whales draw out the breast, that they may suckle their young. The Vulgate has: But the lamias have bared the breast, they have suckled their young; where, less fittingly, lamiae is read for whales, since the lamia, being a fish, has no breast, while the lamia is a wild beast, or a fabulous female. Moreover, whales differ greatly among themselves; the smaller ones are the phoca (which, although it is a quadruped, is called by Homer, Odyssey 4, "without feet", because it has small feet; so among birds the swifts are called apodes from the shortness of their feet), the hippopotamus (which, under the name Behemoth, is well shown by the most learned Bochart to be described in Job 40 and 41), and the dolphin; the larger are the porpoise and the balaena. Again, the phoca and the hippopotamus have hair, feet and a neck; but the balaena and the dolphin have a smooth hide, fins in place of feet, and, in place of a neck, a blowhole on the forehead, through which they draw air from the upper part. Furthermore, because the whales are of huge bulk, the larger cetaceans among those which are commonly called fishes are, and among those which are by far the largest, such as the lamia, the maltha (for which Aemilius Portus in his edition of Suidas wrongly printed another word), the zygaena (which has its head in a yoke, or, what is the same, situated across like a bar, and is improperly called leviathan, as the Greeks call the whale cetus, Isaiah 27, verse 1), the tunny (whose name seems to be derived from the Hebrew תנין, by which the whale is signified, so that it is very likely this name for the tunny came from the Phoenicians, who are said to have been famous for tunny fishing, as others attest, and above all Aristotle in his book of Wonders), and all other largest cetaceans, by the usage received among the most approved authors, although improperly, are nevertheless commonly called whales without any addition. So Jonah is here said to have been in the belly of a whale, although he was not in the belly of a whale properly so called; for although whales are vast beasts, yet the passage of their throat is too narrow to swallow a full-grown man whole. Indeed, all animals that breathe with lungs must have the passage of the throat narrowed, as the neck is in bellows, so that the breath may burst out through the jaws with greater effort from those narrow places. Therefore the whale in whose belly Jonah was is called, Jonah 2, verse 1, a great fish; that is, it was a true fish, but so huge that, because of its bulk, it deserved to be counted among the whales. Hence the most learned Bochart proves that it was of that species of sea dog which others call the carcharias, from the roughness and sharpness of its teeth, and others the lamia and the lemna, lamian or psoron, from the vastness of its gullet, and so on.

units.la: Tribus diebus & tribus noctibus.
units.tr: Three days and three nights.

units.la: Supple, ut postea vivus evomeretur. Est autem Hebraica hæc Scripturæque frequens periphrasis dierum trium naturalium, qui die & nocte, seu luce & tenebris constant.
units.tr: Supply: so that afterwards he might be vomited out alive. This is a Hebrew periphrasis, frequent in Scripture, for three natural days, which consist of day and night, that is, of light and darkness.

units.la: In corde terræ. Hebraismus, id est, intra terram. Sic Ezech. 27. v. 3. Tyrus, quæ non procul abest à littore, dicitur sita in corde maris.
units.tr: In the heart of the earth. A Hebraism, that is, within the earth. So Ezekiel 27, verse 3, Tyre, which is not far from the shore, is said to lie in the heart of the sea.

units.la: Tribus diebus & tribus noctibus. Supple, ut inde vivus resurgat. Fuit autem Christus in sepulchro per tres dies naturales Synecdochicé. Synecdochen hanc explicat S. Leo Ser. 7. De resurrectione Domini, dicens de Christo: Ne turbaret discipulorum animos longa multitudo cruciaret, denunciatam tribulationem tam mira celeritate breviavit, ut dum ad integrum secundum dum diem pars primi novissima & pars tertii prima concurrit, & aliquantùm temporis spatio decederet, & nihil dierum numero deperiret.
units.tr: Three days and three nights. Supply: so that he might rise again alive from there. Christ was in the tomb for three natural days, by synecdoche. St. Leo explains this synecdoche in Sermon 7 on the Resurrection of the Lord, saying of Christ: "So that the long delay should not trouble the minds of the disciples or torment them, he shortened the announced suffering with such wonderful speed that, while the last part of the first day and the first part of the third day coincided as if they made up a whole day, a little time was lost and none of the number of days was lost."

units.la: 41. Condemnabunt. Non sententia potestate, sed comparationis exemplo. B. Hier. Sic Sap. 4. Condemnat justus mortuus vivos impios, & juventus celerius consummata longam vitam injusti. Sic inquit B. Hilarius in Pf. 2. Sancti quique intelligendi sunt esse judices terræ, quorum vita atque fides infidelium iniquorumque judicii vice sit ...... cum per meritum adepta beatitudinis, criminosorum vitam, sanctitas comparata condemnet.
units.tr: 41. They will condemn. Not by the power of sentence, but by the example of comparison. Saint Jerome. So Wisdom 4: The righteous who is dead condemns the living ungodly, and youth quickly brought to completion condemns the long life of the unrighteous. So Saint Hilary says on Psalm 2: All the saints are to be understood as judges of the earth, whose life and faith stand in the place of the judgment of unbelievers and wicked men ... when, having attained blessedness by merit, their holiness, thus acquired, condemns the life of the guilty.

units.la: 42. Regina Austri. Periphrasis est Reginæ Sabæ; nam Sabæa regio, quæ à Romanis Scriptoribus Arabia aromatifera vulgò vocatur, Arabicè dicitur ימן jeman, & cum articulo הימן aljeman, id est, austrum, ut testantur Aben-Ezra in Dan. 11. v. 6. Nubiensis Geographus Clim. 1. part. 6. Rabbi Benjamin Tudelensis in Itinerario nuperæ editionis pag. 73. & 82. & Rabbi Abraham Zacuth in libro שלשלת sol. 14. B. & 135. A. Est autem regnum Saba situm ad Austrum Judææ, longòque dissitum terrarum intervallo, Arabiæ adeóque terrarum extima occupans versus Mare Rubrum. Quare merito Sabæorum gens longinqua vocatur à Domino apud Joelem Prophetam, cap. 3. v. 8.
units.tr: 42. The queen of the south. It is a periphrasis for the Queen of Sheba; for the region of Sheba, commonly called by the Roman writers Arabia the Fragrant, is called in Arabic ימן jeman, and with the article הימן aljeman, that is, the south, as Aben Ezra attests on Daniel 11, verse 6, the Nubian geographer, Climate 1, part 6, Rabbi Benjamin of Tudela in his Itinerary, in the recently published edition, pages 73 and 82, and Rabbi Abraham Zacuto in the book Sheshelet, folio 14 verso and 135 recto. The kingdom of Sheba lies to the south of Judea, far distant by a long stretch of land, occupying Arabia and so the furthest parts of the lands towards the Red Sea. Therefore the Sabaean people is rightly called distant by the Lord through the prophet Joel, chapter 3, verse 8.

units.la: Surget in judicio. Ergo ibi erit diversitas. Nec mirum, quia ubi vera caro, ibi distinctio membrorum & personarum; ubi verò talis distinctio, procul dubio & Joannes Joannes est, & Maria Maria est. B. Ambr. in Symb. cap. 43.
units.tr: Will rise in judgment. Therefore there will be a difference there. Nor is this surprising, because where there is true flesh, there is a distinction of members and persons; and where there is such a distinction, undoubtedly John is John, and Mary is Mary. Saint Ambrose on the Creed, chapter 43.

units.la: Hic. Adverbium loci, non pronomen intelligas, q. d. In præsentiarum, inter vos. B. Hier. similiter supra v. 6. & 41. Hic, adverbium est loci non pronomen.
units.tr: Here. You should understand it as an adverb of place, not a pronoun, as if to say: at present, among you. Saint Jerome likewise above, on verses 6 and 41. Here is an adverb of place, not a pronoun.

units.la: 43. Cùm autem, &c. Q. d. Cùm quis à diaboli obsessione liberatus est, diabolus, cui unica quies est hominem lædere, instar hominis in exilium terræ aridæ & desertæ relegati frustrà locum ubi quiescat quærit. Atque ita statuit reverti in hominem, quem obsederat, eúmque inveniens virtutibus vacuum, & deturpatum peccatis, (quæ diabolo propter ejus pravitatem sunt instar nitoris & ornatûs, quo delectatur, sicut porci luto, aliísque sordibus) justo Dei vindicis judicio permittitur regredi, eum constanter obsessurus cum plenitudine vitiorum, quæ plus nocet homini obsessio, quàm ipsa diaboli obsessio, ideóque deterior illius viri conditio est, quàm fuerat ante ipsius liberationem à diaboli obsessione, propter ingratum illius liberationis contemtum.
units.tr: 43. But when, etc. That is: when someone has been freed from the possession of a devil, the devil, whose only rest is to harm a man, like a man banished into a dry and desert land, seeks in vain a place where he may rest. And so he resolves to return into the man he had possessed, and finding him empty of virtues and defiled by sins (which to the devil, because of his wickedness, are like the brightness and adornment in which he delights, as pigs delight in mud and other filth), he is permitted, by the just judgment of God the avenger, to return, to possess him constantly, with a fullness of vices; for the possession harms a man more than the very possession by the devil, and therefore that man's condition is worse than it was before his liberation from the devil's possession, on account of his ungrateful contempt for that liberation.

units.la: 44. Septem alios Spiritus. Sic septem spiritus dixit Joannes de Spiritu Dei, Apoc. 1. v. 4. Nempe quicquid in suo genere ad plenam mensuram pervenit, eo numero significatur, ut I Sam. seu, Reg. 2. v. 5. Ef. 4. v. 1. Septem spiritus Glossa Ordinaria hic interpretatur plenitudinem vitiorum. Sic venerabilis Beda in Luc. II. v. 26. Per septem malos spiritus, universa vitia designari ait: Universitas enim hoc numero aliquoties comprehenditur, inquit B. Ambrof. in Luc. II. Porro totum hoc exemplum Judæos, aut Judæorum Pharisæos & Scribas spectare declarat sequens clausula:
units.tr: 44. Seven other spirits. Thus John spoke of the seven spirits of God, Rev. 1:4. Indeed, whatever in its kind has reached its full measure is signified by that number, as in 1 Sam. or 1 Kings 2:5, Eph. 4:1. The Ordinary Gloss here interprets "seven spirits" as the fullness of vices. Likewise the venerable Bede, on Luke 11:26, says: "By the seven evil spirits all vices are designated," for "the totality is sometimes comprehended by this number," says St. Ambrose on Luke 11. Moreover, that the whole example concerns the Jews, or the Pharisees and Scribes of the Jews, is shown by the following clause:

units.la: Sic erit generationi huic pessimæ. Q. d. Sic pejora erunt Pharisæorum & Scribarum, quos supra v. 39. merito nominavi generationem malam & adulteram, novissima, quàm priora; multò quippe magis rei sunt Scribæ & Pharisæi in Spiritum-sanctum blasphemi, ex destinata malitia opera, quæ à me in Lege & prophetis promisso Messia in Spiritu Dei fieri, intùs in animo convicti agnoscunt, Beelzebub dæmoniorum principi ascribentes, quàm si veritatis lumen eis in peccatorum suorum poenam nunquam illuxisset; melius enim est non agnoscere viam justitiæ, quàm agnitam detinere in injustitia, & falsitatis damnate. Vide 2 Pet. 2. v. 21.
units.tr: So it will be for this evil generation. That is, the state of the Pharisees and Scribes will be worse, whom above, at v. 39, I rightly called an evil and adulterous generation, worse at the last than at the first. For the Scribes and Pharisees are far more guilty of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, since with settled malice they inwardly recognise, convinced in their own minds, that the works which I do in the Spirit of God are those promised of the Messiah in the Law and the Prophets, yet they ascribe them to Beelzebub, the prince of demons. It would have been better for them had the light of truth never shone on them, to their punishment for their sins; for it is better not to know the way of righteousness than, having known it, to hold to unrighteousness and to falsehood once condemned. See 2 Pet. 2:21.

units.la: 46. Adhuc eo loquente. Scilicet mulieri, quæ audiens Christum exclamaverat: Beatus venter qui te portavit, &c. ut narratur Luc. II. v. 27.
units.tr: 46. While he was still speaking. That is, to the woman who, hearing Christ, had cried out, "Blessed is the womb that bore you," etc., as is related in Luke 11:27.

units.la: Ecce mater, &c. Hunc adventus matris & fratrum, id est, cognatorum Christi Lucas non servans ordinem temporis refert, c. 8. v. 19. post parabolam seminantis.
units.tr: Behold, your mother, etc. Luke, not keeping the order of time, reports this arrival of the mother and brothers, that is, of Christ's kinsfolk, at ch. 8:19, after the parable of the sower.

units.la: Stabant foris. Quia non poterant prae turba ad eum adire in domum, in qua ei oblatus est daemoniacus mutus & caecus curandus, ut patet ex iis quae hic sequuntur, & ex Marc. 3. v. 20. & Luc. 8. v. 19.
units.tr: They stood outside. Because, on account of the crowd, they could not approach him in the house in which a dumb and blind demoniac had been brought to him to be healed, as is clear from what follows here, and from Mark 3:20 and Luke 8:19.

units.la: 48. Quae est mater mea, &c. Si matrem & fratres eos fecit qui non erant, quomodo negavit eos, qui erant? Sed in semetipso docuit qui patrem aut matrem aut fratres praeponeret verbo Dei, non esse dignum discipulum. Nihil magnum, si fidem sanguini (id est, sanguinis affectui) praeposuit, quem non habebat. Tert. lib. 4. adversus Marcionem c. 19. Solet id adimplere Christus, quod alios docet. Quale ergo erat, si docens non tanti facere matrem aut fratres, quanti Dei verbum, ipse Dei verbum nunciatâ matre & fraternitate desereret? Negavit itaque parentes, quomodo docuit negandos pro Dei opere. Idem in lib. de carne Christi. c. 6.
units.tr: 48. "Who is my mother?" etc. If he made mother and brothers of those who were not, how did he deny those who were? But in his own person he taught that one who puts father or mother or brothers before the word of God is not worthy to be a disciple. Nothing great if he preferred faith to blood (that is, to the affection of blood), which he did not have. Tertullian, Against Marcion, bk. 4, ch. 19. Christ usually fulfils what he teaches others. What then would it have been, if, teaching that mother and brothers are not to be valued as highly as the word of God, he himself, when told of his mother and kinsfolk, had deserted the word of God? So he denied parents, just as he taught they must be denied for the sake of God's work. The same, in his book On the Flesh of Christ, ch. 6.

units.la: 49. Extendens, &c. Formam se ipsum universis agendi sentiendique constituit Christus.
units.tr: 49. Stretching out, etc. Christ set himself up as the pattern for all action and feeling.

units.la: 50. Quicunque fecerit, &c. In quo numero profecto etiam ipsam sanctam Mariam benignus inclusit, faciebat enim & illa voluntatem Patris ejus. Ita optimus magister atque divinus & maternum nomen quod ei quasi privatum propriumque nunciavarant, quia terre-
units.tr: 50. Whoever does, etc. In that number the kindly one surely included even holy Mary herself, for she too did the will of his Father. So the best and divine Teacher, since they had announced to him a maternal name as if it were private and his own, because it was earthly, set it beside the closer kinship of heaven, among his disciples...

units.la: num. mum erat, in comparatione cœlestis propinquitatem, in discipulis suis ... versum consorti generis cum cæteris fa- ... officiendit. Et ne ipso salubriimo magistro ... affectum in parentibus docuit, admonuit ... matrem habuisse à quibusdam negatur, ... se patrem in terris dicant habere, ut ... habuisse patres, sic se habuisse matrem ... terrena cognatione contempta, contemnat ... mum discipulis præberet exemplum. B. ... contemtu mundi, quæ epistola à nom ... tino.
units.tr: ...num. ...in comparison with heavenly kinship, in his disciples ... to share a bond of kind with the rest ... and so not to hinder. Nor did that most wholesome Teacher ... taught affection in parents, and admonished ... it is denied that he had a mother ... they say they have a father on earth, as ... had fathers, so he had a mother ... earthly kinship despised, he might despise ... and offer an example to his disciples. St. Bernard, On the Contempt of the World, which letter is ascribed to ... Tinus.

units.la: Ipse meus frater & soror & mater est. ... tates in populo quem redemit spiritualiter e... haber sanctos viros & sanctas feminas, qu... reditate cohæredes. Mater est ejus tota ... id est, fideles ejus per Dei gratiam ipsa ... ejus est omnis anima pia, faciens voluntatem ... mu charitate, in iis quos parturit donec ... ria ergo faciens voluntatem Dei, corpo... mater est, spiritualiter autem & soror & ... mina, non solum spiritu, verùm etiam c... Et mater quidem spiritu, non capitis ... ex quo illa magis spiritualiter nata est, qu... derint in quibus & ipsa est, rectè filii spo... mater membrorum ejus quod nos sumus, ... ut fideles in Ecclesia nascerentur, qui i... corpore verò mater ipsius capitis: oportebi... ter insigne miraculum secundum carnem na... caret membra sua de Virgine Ecclesia se... Sola ergo Maria & spiritu & corpore ... Christi & Virgo Christi: Ecclesia verò tu... suris, spiritu quidem tota mater Christi est ... pore autem non tota, sed in quibusdam ... mater, sed non Christi. Et conjugatæ qui... gines Deo dicatæ, sanctis moribus & cher... scientia bona & fide non sicta, quæ ... Christi spiritualiter matres sint. Quæ ... poraliter pariunt, non Christum, sed Ad... runt ut Sacramentis imbuti Christi membra ... niam quid peperierint norunt. B. Aug. i... nitate c. 5, & 6. inquisitis abjecit, & eandem ius commemorans, quo sibi ...
units.tr: He himself is my brother and sister and mother. ... the people whom he redeemed spiritually ... holy men and holy women, who are co-heirs in grace. The whole Church is his mother ... that is, his faithful, by the grace of God; every pious soul is his mother, doing the will of God, in charity, in those whom she bears until Christ is formed in them. Therefore, doing the will of God, she is mother of the body ... and spiritually both sister and ... not in spirit only but also in ... And indeed a mother in spirit, not of the head ... by which she is more spiritually born, who ... in whom she herself is; rightly the sons of the spouse ... mother of his members, which we are ... that the faithful might be born in the Church, who ... but in body the mother of the head itself. It must be ... an extraordinary miracle, according to the flesh born ... his members lacking ... from the Virgin, the Church ... Mary alone, both in spirit and in body, is mother of Christ and Virgin of Christ; but the Church, indeed, is wholly mother of Christ in spirit, yet not wholly in body, but in some of her members ... mother, but not of Christ. And married women and virgins dedicated to God, by holy conduct and sincere love, by good knowledge and unfeigned faith, are spiritually mothers of Christ. Those who bear physically do not bear Christ, but ... they know what they have borne. St. Augustine, On Holy Virginity, chs. 5 and 6, rejected the questioners and, recalling the same ...

units.la: CAPUT XIII.
units.tr: Chapter 13.

units.la: I. Mare, Scilicet, Galilææ.
units.tr: I. The sea, namely of Galilee.

units.la: 3. In parabolis. Luc. 8. v. 4. per similitudinem. Parabola ab eo vocatur, quod alteri παραβολὴ , hoc est, assimilatur, & quasi umbra prævium veritatis est. B. Hier. Ep. 151. ad Algasiam q. 6. Quod cæteri Evangelistæ parabolam dicunt seu similitudinem, ab uno Joanne dicitur ubique μυθοιμα, hoc est, celebre dictum, seu ut habet Vulgat. proverbium.
units.tr: 3. In parables. Luke 8. v. 4. By way of likeness. A parable is so called because it is set alongside another (παραβολὴ [parabolē]), that is, it is compared with it, and it is as it were a shadow going before the truth. St Jerome, Ep. 151, to Algasia, q. 6. Where the other Evangelists call it a parable or likeness, John alone everywhere calls it μυθοιμα [mythoima], that is, a famous saying, or as the Vulgate has it, proverb.

units.la: 10. Et. Supple, ex Marc. 4. v. 10. cum esset singularis.
units.tr: 10. And. Supply, from Mark 4. v. 10: when he was alone.

units.la: Discipuli. Id est, qui cum eo erant duodecim, ut loquitur Marcus loco citato, utique quia hæ parabolæ dictæ sunt post constitutum Apostolorum numerum; quare quod idem Marcus post parabolas narraturus sedatam maris tempestatem, subdit: & ait illis in illa die cum sero esset factum: Id intelligi non potest de die dictarum parabolarum, hæc enim tempestas sine dubio contigit ante vocationem Matthæi, nec ullus in lectione Evangelistarum est adeo hospes, ut id ignorare possit.
units.tr: The disciples. That is, those who were with him, the twelve, as Mark says in the passage cited. This is certainly because these parables were spoken after the number of the Apostles had been fixed. Hence, since the same Mark, after the parables, is about to narrate the calming of the storm at sea, and adds: and he said to them on that day, when evening had come, this cannot be understood of the day on which the parables were spoken. For this storm certainly happened before the calling of Matthew, and no one who reads the Evangelists is so much a newcomer that he could be ignorant of this.

units.la: II. Vobis datum est. Singulari Dei dono. Christus hac manifesta responsione donum gratiæ cœlestis aperuit, ut B. Fulgentius loquitur, lib. 1. de ver. præd. c. 22.
units.tr: II. To you it has been given. By a singular gift of God. Christ by this plain answer disclosed the gift of heavenly grace, as St Fulgentius puts it, book 1 On the Truth of Predestination, ch. 22.

units.la: Nosse. Supple, clare & distincte.
units.tr: To know. Supply: clearly and distinctly.

units.la: Mysteria regni Dei. Id est, arcana ad regnum Dei pertinentia; non enim hic agitur de præceptis Evangelicis, quæ cum nemini debeant esse ignota, coram turbis in Sermone Domini in monte, clarissime ab ipso fuerunt exposita.
units.tr: The mysteries of the kingdom of God. That is, the hidden things pertaining to the kingdom of God. For the evangelical precepts are not what is meant here, since these ought to be known to no one, and were most clearly expounded by him in the Sermon on the Mount before the crowds.

units.la: Illis. Addit Marcus c. 4. v. 11. qui foris sunt, id est, phrasi Talmudicis familiari, qui non sunt de populo Dei; cum enim filiis Israël ex promissione Domini in sortem obtigisset terra Chanaan, omnes Gentiles signare solebant hac phrasi, qui foris sunt, scilicet extra Terram sanctam, nec ullum in eam jus habent.
units.tr: To those. Mark adds, ch. 4 v. 11, who are outside, that is, in a Talmudic phrase, those who are not of the people of God. For when the land of Canaan had fallen by the Lord's promise as a lot to the sons of Israel, all Gentiles were customarily marked by this phrase, who are outside, namely outside the Holy Land, and have no right in it.

units.la: 12. Qui enim habet. Id nempe, quod habere debet, usum videlicet bonum donorum Dei.
units.tr: 12. For whoever has. That is, what he ought to have, namely the good use of the gifts of God.

units.la: Dabitur ei. Magis atque magis in remunerationem. Quis autem habet cui dabitur, nisi cui datum est? Quis autem non habet, nisi cui non est datum? Quare ergo illi datum est, & illi non est datum? Non me piget dicere, hoc est profundum crucis. De profundo nescio quo judiciorum Dei, qua perscrutari contemplari-que non possumus, procedit omne quod possumus: de profunditate, inquam, nescio qua judiciorum Dei; quae inscrutabilia contemplari non possumus, perscrutari non valemus, procedit omne quod possu-mus. Quod possum video, unde possim non video, nisi quia & hoc hactenus video quod novi esse a Deo. Quare autem illum & non illum? Multum est ad me, abyssus est, profundum crucis est, admiratione exclamare possum, disputatione demonstrare non possum. Quid possum exclamare de ista profunditate? Quàm magnificata sunt opera tua Domine! Gentes illuminantur, Judaei excaecantur...... Quàm magnificata sunt opera tua Domine, nimis profunda facta sunt cogitationes tuae: & sequitur, Vir imprudens non cognoscit, & stultus non intelligit haec. Quid non intelligit stultus & imprudens? Quia vel profundum est. Nam si stultus non intelligit, & sapiens intelligit, non est nimis profundum. Sed si sapiens intelligit quia profundum est, stultus non intelligit quia vel profundum est. Ideo multi de isto profundo quaerentes reddere ra- tionem, in fabulas vanitatis abierunt. B. Aug. Serm. 7. de verbis Apostoli.
units.tr: It will be given to him. More and more, as a reward. But who has, to whom it will be given, unless to whom it has been given? And who does not have, unless to whom it has not been given? Why then has it been given to one and not given to another? I do not hesitate to say it: this is the depth of the cross. Everything we are able to do comes from the depth, I know not what, of the judgments of God, which we can neither search out nor contemplate. From the depth, I say, of I know not what judgments of God, which we cannot contemplate as unsearchable and cannot search out, comes everything that we are able to do. What I am able to do I see; whence I am able I do not see, except that I see this much, that I know it to be from God. But why this one and not that one? It is too much for me; it is an abyss, it is the depth of the cross. I can cry out in wonder, but I cannot demonstrate it by argument. What can I cry out about this depth? How magnified are your works, O Lord! The Gentiles are enlightened, the Jews are blinded... How magnified are your works, O Lord; your thoughts are exceedingly deep. And it follows: the unwise man does not know, and the fool does not understand these things. What is it that the fool and the unwise man do not understand? That it is deep. For if the fool does not understand and the wise man does, it is not too deep. But if the wise man understands that it is deep, the fool does not understand that it is deep. Therefore many, seeking to give an account of this depth, have gone off into the fables of vanity. St Augustine, Sermon 7, on the words of the Apostle.

units.la: Abundabit. Scilicet, incrementis profectûs sui, ut loquitur Hilarius.
units.tr: He will have abundance. Namely, by increases of his progress, as Hilary puts it.

units.la: Qui non habet. Nempe bonum usum donorum Dei.
units.tr: From him who does not have. Namely the good use of God's gifts.

units.la: Quod habet. Ipsa videlicet dona Dei.
units.tr: What he has. That is, the very gifts of God.

units.la: Auferentur ab eo. Supple, in poenam delicti, quòd videlicet donis Dei non fit bene usus.
units.tr: Will be taken away from him. Supply: as punishment for the offence, namely that the gifts of God are not put to good use.

units.la: 13. Videntes. Oculis corporis; quae ego facio miracula.
units.tr: 13. Seeing. With the eyes of the body: the miracles which I work.

units.la: Non vident. Oculis cordis.
units.tr: They do not see. With the eyes of the heart.

units.la: Audientes. Corporis sensu, quae ego profero oracula.
units.tr: Hearing. With the bodily sense: the oracles which I utter.

units.la: Non audiunt. Cordis assensu. Sensus itaque Matthaei est idem ac si diceret: Quia clarissimis miraculis quae vident, & sermonibus apertissimis quos audiunt, nolunt credere & obedire, justo judicio eis per parabolas loquor; qui enim videre nolunt cum possunt, Deo puniente, etiam cum volunt videre, non possunt. Unde Aug. in lib. De natura & gratia. c. 22, ait quòd praevaricatorem Legis digne lux deserit veritatis, quâ destitutus, utique fit caecus, & plus necesse est offendat, & cadendo vexetur, vexatúsque non surgat, ut ideò tantùm audiat vocem Legis, quò admoneatur implorare gratiam Salvatoris.
units.tr: They do not hear. With the assent of the heart. The sense of Matthew is therefore the same as if he said: because they are unwilling to believe and obey the most manifest miracles which they see and the most open words which they hear, I speak to them in parables by a just judgment. For those who are unwilling to see when they can, God punishing them, cannot see even when they wish to. Hence Augustine, in the book On Nature and Grace, ch. 22, says that the light of truth worthily forsakes the transgressor of the Law, and, deprived of it, he is of course made blind, and it is more necessary that he should stumble, and by falling he is troubled, and being troubled he does not rise, so that he hears only the voice of the Law, in order to be admonished to implore the grace of the Saviour.

units.la: Sed difficultas oritur ex Marco & Luca, qui per particulam finalem dicunt Christum eis in parabolis loqui, ut videntes non videant, &c. Cui respondetur Matthaeum causam supplicii meritoriam, alios Evangelistas non causam finalem, sed eventum exprimere, quamvis non desint, qui etiam causam finalem significari velint; sicut enim verum est Deum quosdam propter peccata velle damnare, & reipsa damnando nolle etiam ut salvi fiant: ita etiam verum est propter peccata Deum quibusdam obscure loqui, ne ipsius mysteria intelligant, idque in quibusdam quia illis dare non vult gratiam conversionis, in quibusdam vero ut convertantur & salvi fiant. Nam ex divina misericordia excæcatio ad tempus ordinatur medicinaliter ad salutem quorundam qui excæcantur, ut scilicet cæcitate sua sibi displicentes & se dolentes, & ex hoc humiliati atque commoti ad confitenda peccata sua & pie quærendum Dominum excitentur, sicut nonnullis usque ad Deicidium excæcatis post Christi passionem contigit. Quorundam enim superbia debet etiam ipsa cæcitate & peccatis inde consequentibus edomari ac frangi. Dici etiam potest Christum loquutum in parabolis ut videntes non videant, quia noverat illos quibus loquebatur contemtores esse veritatis, sicque si extra parabolas illos fuisset alloquutus, sanctum dedisset canibus, & margaritas projecisset ante porcos, qui ipsum Filium Dei conculcaverunt. Ne autem mirum videretur sic puniri populum, qui tanta aviditate Messiam promissum videre atque audire cupiebat, probat Evangelista hoc prædictum ab Esaia.
units.tr: But a difficulty arises from Mark and Luke, who by a final particle say that Christ speaks to them in parables so that seeing they may not see, and so on. To this it is answered that Matthew expresses the meritorious cause of the punishment, while the other Evangelists express not the final cause but the outcome. Yet there are not lacking those who wish the final cause to be signified as well. For just as it is true that God wishes some to be damned on account of their sins, and in actually damning them does not wish them to be saved either, so it is also true that on account of sins God speaks obscurely to some, so that they do not understand his mysteries. This is so in some because he does not wish to give them the grace of conversion, but in others so that they may be converted and saved. For by divine mercy blindness is ordained for a time, as a remedy for the salvation of some who are blinded: namely, that displeased with their own blindness and grieving over it, they may be humbled and moved by this, and stirred to confess their sins and to seek the Lord devoutly. This happened to some who were blinded, even to the point of deicide, after Christ's passion. For the pride of some must be tamed and broken even by blindness itself and the sins that follow from it. It can also be said that Christ spoke in parables so that seeing they might not see, because he knew that those to whom he spoke were despisers of the truth; and so, if he had addressed them outside parables, he would have given what is holy to dogs and cast pearls before swine, who trampled underfoot the Son of God himself. Lest it seem strange that a people who desired with such eagerness to see and hear the promised Messiah should be so punished, the Evangelist proves that this was foretold by Isaiah.

units.la: 14. Auditu audietis, &c. Esaias in textu Hebræo & in Vulgato vaticinium suum per imperativum exprimit, partim quia imperativus idiotismo Hebraico pro futuro usurpari solet, partim ad significandum quod cæcitas & obduratio sæpe ab irato Deo infligitur in pœnam peccati, sicque vaticinium Esaiæ est quasi prolatio justæ sententiæ. Præclare itaque Aug. lib. 1. contra Julianum. c. 3. Cæcitas cordis, quam solus removet illuminator Deus, & peccatum est, quo in Deum non creditur, & pœna peccati, quæ cor superbum digna animadversione punitur, & causa peccati, cum mali aliquid caeci cordis errore committitur, & lib. 1. Operis imperfecti, nunc perfecti: Eadem cæcitas, si peccati pœna non esset, non diceretur: Excæcavit illos malitia eorum. Quod si Dei judicio non veniret, non legeremus: Obscurentur oculi eorum ne videant, & dorsum eorum semper incurva. Itaque harum pœnarum inflictionem divina voluntate exprimit Esaias in textu Hebræo & Vulgato, & Joan. 12. v. 40. quarum causam meritoriam Matthæus dicit fuisse ipsos Judæos. Ad perfectiorem hujus intelligentiam sciendum quod excæcatio & obduratio duo important: quorum unum est motus animi humani inhærentis malo & aversio a divino lumine; & quantum ad hoc Deus non est causa excæcationis & obdurationis, sicut non est causa peccati. Aliud autem est subtractio gratiæ, ex qua sequitur quod mens dividivinitus non illuminetur ad recte videndum, & cor hominis non emolliatur ad recte vivendum: Et quantum ad hoc Deus est causa excæcationis & obdurationis. Est autem considerandum quod Deus est causa universalis illuminationis animarum secundum illud Ioan. 1. Erat lux vera quæ illuminat omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum; sicut sol est universalis causa illuminationis corporum. Aliter tamen & aliter: Nam sol agit illuminando per necessitatem naturæ: Deus autem agit voluntarie per ordinem suæ sapientiæ. Sol autem, licet quantum est de se, omnia corpora illuminet, si quod tamen impedimentum inveniat in aliquo corpore, relinquit illud tenebrosum; sicut patet de domo cujus fenestræ sunt clausæ: Sed tamen illius obscurationis nullo modo causa est sol, non enim suo judicio agit, ut lumen interius non immittat, sed causa ejus est solum ille qui claudit fenestram: Deus autem proprio judicio lumen gratiæ non immittit illis, in quibus obstaculum invenit: Unde causa subtractionis gratiæ est non solum ille, qui ponit obstaculum gratiæ, sed etiam Deus, qui suo judicio gratiam non apponit: & per hunc modum Deus est causa excæcationis, & aggravationis aurium, & obdurationis cordis: quæ quidem distinguuntur secundum effectus gratiæ, quæ & perficit intellectum dono sapientiæ, & affectum emollit igne charitatis: & quia ad cognitionem intellectus maxime deserviunt duo sensus, scilicet visus & auditus, quorum unus deservit inventioni, scilicet, visus, alius disciplinæ, scilicet auditus, ideo quantum ad visum ponitur excæcatio; quantum ad auditum, aurium aggravatio; quantum ad affectum, obduratio. D. Th. 122. q. 79. ar. 3.
units.tr: 14. By hearing you shall hear, etc. Isaiah, in the Hebrew text and in the Vulgate, expresses his prophecy by the imperative, partly because the imperative is commonly used in the Hebrew idiom for the future, and partly to signify that blindness and hardening are often inflicted by an angry God as punishment for sin; so Isaiah's prophecy is as it were the pronouncing of a just sentence. Well therefore does Augustine say, book 1 Against Julian, ch. 3: The blindness of heart, which God the illuminator alone removes, is both a sin, by which one does not believe in God, and the punishment of sin, by which the proud heart is worthily punished with retribution, and the cause of sin, when something evil is committed through the error of a blind heart. And in book 1 of the Unfinished Work, now Finished: The same blindness, if it were not the punishment of sin, would not be called: "Their malice has blinded them." And if it did not come by the judgment of God, we would not read: "Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see, and bend their back always." Thus Isaiah, in the Hebrew text and in the Vulgate, expresses the infliction of these punishments by the divine will, and so does John 12. v. 40; the meritorious cause of these, Matthew says, was the Jews themselves. For a fuller understanding of this, it must be known that blindness and hardening imply two things. One is a movement of the human mind clinging to evil and turning away from the divine light; and as regards this, God is not the cause of blindness and hardening, just as he is not the cause of sin. The other is the withdrawal of grace, from which it follows that the mind is not divinely illumined to see rightly, and the heart of man is not softened to live rightly; and as regards this, God is the cause of blindness and hardening. It must further be considered that God is the universal cause of the illumination of souls, according to John 1: "That was the true light which enlightens every man coming into this world"; just as the sun is the universal cause of the illumination of bodies. Yet they act in different ways: the sun acts by the necessity of its nature, but God acts voluntarily according to the order of his wisdom. The sun, although as far as it is in itself it illumines all bodies, if it finds some obstacle in a body, leaves that body dark, as is plain of a house whose windows are closed. Yet the sun is in no way the cause of that darkening, for it does not act by its own judgment so as to withhold the inner light; the only cause of it is he who closes the window. God, however, by his own judgment does not send the light of grace into those in whom he finds an obstacle. Hence the cause of the withdrawal of grace is not only he who places the obstacle to grace, but also God, who by his judgment does not apply grace. And in this way God is the cause of blindness, of dulling of the ears, and of hardening of the heart. These are distinguished according to the effects of grace, which both perfects the intellect with the gift of wisdom and softens the affection with the fire of charity. And because two senses serve chiefly the knowledge of the intellect, namely sight and hearing, of which one serves discovery, namely sight, and the other instruction, namely hearing, therefore blindness is named as regards sight, dulling of the ears as regards hearing, and hardening as regards the affection. St Thomas, 1a 2ae, q. 79, art. 3.

units.la: 15. Incrassatum est. Quæ Hebraice imperative exprimuntur, per præteritum vel futurum hic exprimuntur, ut lectori innotescat hujusmodi loquutiones, quæ imprecationes esse videntur, à Prophetis non optantis animo, sed prophetanis mysterio efferri. Est autem hic metaphora à crassitudine corporali; sicut enim crassitudo corporalis efficit corpus minus agile, minúsque mobile, sic crassitudo cordis, quæ est carnalitas, quâ quis terrenis voluptatibus totus inhiat, reddit animam veritatum cœlestium incapacem, acediosam ac tenebrosam. Dionys. Carth. in Act. 28.
units.tr: 15. Is made gross. Words that are expressed in Hebrew in the imperative are here expressed by the past or future tense, so that the reader may know that such expressions, which seem to be curses, are uttered by the Prophets not from a wish of their own mind but by the mystery of prophecy. The metaphor here is taken from bodily thickness. Just as bodily thickness makes the body less nimble and less mobile, so the thickness of heart, which is carnality, by which a man is wholly bent on earthly pleasures, makes the soul incapable of heavenly truths, sluggish and dark. Dionys. Carth. in Act. 28.

units.la: Oculos suos clauserunt. Græcè ἐκάμμυσαν. Familiare est sacris Scriptoribus hoc verbum Καμμύω pro Κατα μύω per Poeticam syncopen. Hujusmodi homines, qui ideo cæci sunt, quia sponte claudunt oculos ne videant, seu qui videre se diffimulant, quod vel inviti cernunt, vocantur. Job. 24. v. 13. Rebelles lumini. Esaiæ 33. v. 15. qui sic claudit oculos vocatur phrasi plane Gallica, qui, fermer, firmare, est claudere, עצם עינים, firmans oculos suos, id est, claudens. Cui simile id Apuleii lib. 7. Perica, quâ stabuli fores affirmari solebant, id est, claudi. Hujusmodi homo dicitur à B. Dionysf. lib. de Ecclesiastica Hierarchia c. 2. & à B. Pet. in Ep. 2. c. 1. v. 9. μυωπάζων, pro quo Vulgatus interpres & Æthiops vertentes manu-tentans, videntur legisse μυωπῶν, quasi ἀπὸ τῆς ὀπῆς τῶν μυῶν, à murium latibulo. Male etiam Syrus & Arabs vertunt, cæcus & lumine luscus, & alii, minus bene videns, seu proxima, & quæ fere sunt sub oculis videns; dicitur enim μυωπίζειν, oculis nictare, connivere, quasi μύειν τὰς ὄψεις, oculos claudere. Hinc μυωπῶ dicitur, qui cum infirmus est visu, palpebras in angustum cogit; Visus enim cum prodit confertus, magis videt, at diducto oculo, diffrahitur; ut ait Philosophus in Problematis. Hinc & aliud culicis genus, quo boves infestantur, μυωπῶ dicitur, quod in boum oculos involans ad continuas oculorum nictationes eos adigit.
units.tr: They have closed their eyes. In Greek [ἐκάμμυσαν]. Sacred writers commonly use this verb, kammyō [Καμμύω], for katamyō [Κατα μύω], by a poetic syncope. Men who are blind because they willingly close their eyes so as not to see, or who pretend not to see what they do in fact perceive, even against their will, are called such. Job 24:13. Rebels against the light. Isaiah 33:15. One who closes his eyes in this way is described by a phrase quite French: since fermer (to shut) means to make firm or to close, the Hebrew [עצם עינים], "firming his eyes," means closing them. Similar to this is the passage in Apuleius, book 7: Perica, by which the doors of the stable were usually fastened, that is, shut. Such a man is called by Dionysius in his book on the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, ch. 2, and by St Peter in 2 Ep. ch. 1 v. 9, one who is myōpazōn [μυωπάζων]. The Vulgate translator and the Ethiopic, rendering it as "holding by the hand," seem to have read myōpōn [μυωπῶν], as if from apo tēs opēs tōn myōn [ἀπὸ τῆς ὀπῆς τῶν μυῶν], from the hiding-place of mice. The Syriac and the Arab also translate it badly as "blind and one-eyed in the light," and others as "seeing less well," or "seeing what is near and almost under the eyes." For myōpizein [μυωπίζειν] means to blink, to wink, as if myein tas opseis [μύειν τὰς ὄψεις], to shut the eyes. Hence one is called myōpōn who, being weak in sight, narrows his eyelids. For, as the Philosopher says in the Problems: the sight, when it is gathered together, sees better, but when the eye is opened wide, it is scattered. Hence also another kind of gnat, by which oxen are troubled, is called myōpōn, because it flies into the eyes of oxen and forces them to blink continually.

units.la: Ne quando. Hebraicè & Act. 28. ne forte.
units.tr: Lest at any time. In Hebrew, and in Acts 28, lest perhaps.

units.la: Videant, &c. Esse quosdam homines usque adeo obcæcatos; ut nolint à suis concupiscentiis liberari, testatur illud Psaltis: Noluit intelligere, ut bene ageret: id est, ne beneageret; testatur & humillima illa Augustini de se confessio, lib. 8. confess. c. 7. At ego adolescens miser valdè, miser in exordio ipsius adolescentiæ, etiam petieram à te castitatem, & dixeram: Da mihi castitatem & continentiam, sed noli modò. Timebam enim, ne me citò exaudires, & citò sanares à morbo concupiscentiæ, quam malebam expleri, quam extingui.
units.tr: Let them see, etc. That some men are so blinded that they are unwilling to be freed from their lusts is shown by that saying of the Psalmist: He would not understand, that he might do well, that is, lest he might do well. It is also shown by Augustine's very humble confession about himself, book 8 of the Confessions, ch. 7: But I, a wretched youth, very wretched at the very beginning of my youth, had indeed asked you for chastity and had said: Give me chastity and continence, but not yet. For I feared that you would hear me too quickly and cure me too quickly of the disease of concupiscence, which I preferred to be satisfied rather than extinguished.

units.la: Sanem eos. Id est, ignoscam eis, ita ut ex peccati reatu tanquam ex morbo convalescant. Unde Marc. 4. v. 12. pro, & sanem eos, habetur; & dimittantur eis peccata. Ita etiam Psaltes ait: Sana animam meam: id est, ignosce mihi; hinc 2. Paralip. c. 30. Vulgatus vertit, placatus est populo, quod in textu Hebraeo est: & sanavit populum: id est, Dominus pii Regis Ezechiæ oratione pacatus ignovit verè conversis, qui ante esum agni Paschalis à legali immunditia sua se non purificaverant secundum ritus Lege ceremoniali præscriptos.
units.tr: And I should heal them. That is, I will forgive them, so that they may recover from the guilt of sin as from a disease. Hence in Mark 4:12 the words and I should heal them are given as and their sins should be forgiven them. The Psalmist also says: Heal my soul, that is, forgive me. Hence in 2 Chronicles 30 the Vulgate translates the people was appeased, which is what the Hebrew text has, and he healed the people, that is, the Lord, moved by the prayer of the pious King Hezekiah, pardoned those who were truly converted, who before the eating of the Passover lamb had not purified themselves from their legal uncleanness according to the ritual prescribed by the ceremonial Law.

units.la: 16. Vestri autem beati oculi. Scilicet in comparatione eorum, qui Christi venituri tantum obscuram habuerunt notitiam; sunt enim tres gradus notitiæ Christi considerandi, in quorum infimo consistit obscura notitia, quam habuerant de Christo Prophetæ ac ceteri priorum temporum justi. Secundum gradum tenet evidens ejusdem Christi per sensum notitia, qualis fuit Apostolorum & omnium eorum, qui Christum in carne assumta oculis corporeis videntes, in eum crediderunt. Tertius gradus est ejus notitiæ, quâ Christus cognos-ceitur. citur per præsentiam in vita immortali. Medius ergo gradus respectu primi infigne bonum erat, ac vehementer optabile, ut observat Augustinus in Conc. 20. in Psal. 118. Beati igitur dicuntur oculi Apostolorum, non quia meliores, quo sensu dicuntur beati qui non viderunt, & crediderunt, sed quia magnum bonum eis obtigit, quod antiquis Prophetis non obtigerat. Huic loco contrarium non est, quod Paulus dicit 2 Cor. 5. Etsi cognovimus secundum carnem Christum: sed nunc jam non novimus. Sensus enim Apostoli est se non gloriari de nobilitate generis, sicut Pseudo-Apostoli, quod Hebræi, quod Israëlitæ, quod semen Abrahæ essent, ut dicitur 2 Cor. 11. v. 22. hoc enim Apostolus ibidem v. 18. appellat gloriari secundum carnem. Dicit ergo Apostolus: Etsi cognovimus secundum carnem Christum: hoc est, etsi aliquando magnum & gloriosum putavimus gentilem & consanguineum esse Christi secundum carnem: sed nunc jam non novimus: id est, nunc ita penitus mortui sumus affectibus vitæ veteris, ut non amplius in hujusmodi re gloriandum censeamus, cum ipse dixerit matrem & fratrem ipsius esse, qui verbum Dei audit & facit. Similiter in Ep. ad Philip. c. 3. agens adversus Pseudo-Apostolos in carne fiduciam habentes, ait se quidem se habere unde confidere posset in carne, sed universam illam in carne gloriandi, seu in cognatione confidendi materiam æstimasse propter Christum ut detrimenta & stercora.
units.tr: 16. But blessed are your eyes. That is, in comparison with those who had only a dim knowledge of the coming Christ. For there are three degrees of knowledge of Christ to be considered. In the lowest stands the obscure knowledge which the Prophets and the other righteous of earlier times had of Christ. The second degree is the evident knowledge of the same Christ through the senses, such as that of the Apostles and of all those who, seeing Christ in the assumed flesh with their bodily eyes, believed in him. The third degree is the knowledge by which Christ is known through his presence in immortal life. The middle degree, therefore, compared with the first, was a remarkable good and greatly to be desired, as Augustine observes in Sermon 20 on Psalm 118. The eyes of the Apostles are therefore called blessed, not because they were better, in the sense in which blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed is said, but because a great good befell them which had not befallen the ancient Prophets. There is nothing contrary to this in what Paul says, 2 Cor. 5: Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him no longer. For the sense of the Apostle is that he does not glory in the nobility of birth, as the false apostles did, that they were Hebrews, Israelites, the seed of Abraham, as is said in 2 Cor. 11:22. The Apostle himself calls this, in the same place at v. 18, glorying according to the flesh. The Apostle therefore says: Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, that is, even if we once thought it great and glorious to be related to Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him, that is, now we are so completely dead to the affections of the old life that we no longer judge that there is any ground for glorying in such a thing, since he himself said that those who hear and do the word of God are his mother and brother. Similarly, in the Epistle to the Philippians ch. 3, arguing against the false apostles who put their trust in the flesh, he says that he indeed had grounds on which he could trust in the flesh, but that he counted all that matter of glorying in the flesh, or of trusting in kinship, as loss and dung for the sake of Christ.

units.la: 17. Cupierunt videre.
units.tr: 17. They desired to see.

units.la: Magnam jucunditatem habebant sancti Prophetæ, cùm ea videbant in Spiritu futura, quæ Apostoli videbant præsentia. Avidissimè tamen ac vehementissimè cupiebant ab origine generis humani usque ad manifestationem verbi incarnati oculis videre præsentia quæ à longè salutabant, hoc est, non exire de hac vita, priusquam viderent incarnatum, quem credebant incarnandum, teste sanctissimo sene Simeone, qui cùm Christum infantem accepisset in ulnas suas, benedixit Deum & dixit: Nunc dimittis servum tuum Domine secundum verbum tuum in pace: Quia viderunt oculi mei salutare tuum. Acceperat enim responsum Divinum non se moriturum, donec videret Christum Domini. Quale autem desiderium fuit in isto sene, tale fuisse credendum est in omnibus superiorum temporum sanctis. Aug. Conf. 20. in Psal. 118. Vide eumdem Serm. 20. De tempore c. 3.
units.tr: The holy prophets had great joy when they saw in the Spirit the things that the Apostles saw present. Yet they desired most eagerly and fervently, from the beginning of the human race until the manifestation of the incarnate Word, to see with their eyes the present things which they greeted from afar. That is, they did not wish to leave this life before they had seen the incarnate one, whom they believed was to be incarnated. The most holy old man Simeon bears witness to this. When he had taken the infant Christ into his arms, he blessed God and said: Now you let your servant depart, Lord, according to your word, in peace: for my eyes have seen your salvation. For he had received a divine answer that he would not die until he had seen the Christ of the Lord. Whatever desire there was in that old man, it must be believed that the same desire was in all the saints of earlier times. Augustine, Confessions 20, on Psalm 118. See also the same, Sermon 20 On Time, chapter 3.

units.la: 19. Omnis qui audit verbum regni.
units.tr: 19. Everyone who hears the word of the kingdom.

units.la: Q. d. Siquis audit prædicationem de regno cœlorum seu Evangelii. Redundat autem hîc nominativus omnis. Non intelligit. Id est, non curat intelligere.
units.tr: That is: if anyone hears the preaching about the kingdom of heaven, or the Gospel. The nominative omnis is redundant here. Does not understand: that is, does not care to understand.

units.la: Malus. Id est, diabolus qui immutabiliter malus est.
units.tr: Evil one. That is, the devil, who is unchangeably evil.

units.la: Hic est. Id est, significatur, scilicet per eum agrum, qui, ut sequitur, secus viam seminatus est.
units.tr: This is. That is, it is signified, namely by that field which, as follows, was sown beside the road.

units.la: Seminatus. Sic dicitur homo, non sicut semen dicitur se-minatum, sed sicut sata dicuntur agri, qui seruntur. & seminatus dicitur ager semine conspersus. Significatur itaque cor istius hominis esse instar viae publicae peccandi consuetudine induratum, nullo fructificandi desiderio velut aratro scissum & praeparatum, ideoque semen verbi Dei auribus, non animo recipiens.
units.tr: Was sown. A man is called "sown" in this way, not as seed is called sown, but as fields that are planted are called sown, and a field is called sown when it is scattered with seed. It is signified, therefore, that the heart of this man is like a public road, hardened by the habit of sinning, and, having no desire to bear fruit, is not ploughed open and prepared like a field cut by the plough. So he receives the seed of God's Word in his ears, not in his mind.

units.la: 2o. Qui autem super petrosa seminatus est. Id est, qui significatur per terram inter petras excipientem semen. Eodem sensu sequentia erunt exponenda: Qui autem seminatus est in pinis: qui in terram bonam seminatus est.
units.tr: 2. But he who was sown on rocky ground. That is, he who is signified by the ground that receives the seed among rocks. The following words are to be explained in the same sense: But he who was sown among thorns; he who was sown in good ground.

units.la: 21. Est temporalis. Id est, ad tempus credit, ut patet ex Luc. 8. v. 13. Idque fide evanida, quae specie differt, a radicata, ut plus satis ostendunt oppoliti effectus, qui ex eadem natura specifica non solent profluere.
units.tr: 21. He is temporary. That is, he believes for a time, as is clear from Luke 8:13. And this is a faith that fades away, which differs in kind from a rooted faith, as the opposite effects sufficiently show, which do not usually flow from the same specific nature.

units.la: Scandalizatur. Id est, scandalum accipit & corruit.
units.tr: He is offended. That is, he takes offence and falls.

units.la: 22. Audit. Scilicet, sensu corporis, & assensu cordis.
units.tr: 22. Hears. That is, with the sense of the body and with assent of the heart.

units.la: Sollicitudo seculi istius. Id est, rerum quarumlibet ad hoc seculum pertinentium.
units.tr: The cares of this age. That is, of whatever things pertain to this age.

units.la: Fallacia divitiarum. Hebraismus, id est, divitiae fallaces. Blanda enim sunt divitiae, & aliud agentes, & aliud pollicentes; lubrica est earum possessio, dum huc illucque circumferuntur, & instabili gradu, vel habentes deserunt, vel non habentes resarciunt. B. Hier.
units.tr: The deceitfulness of riches. A Hebraism, that is, deceitful riches. For riches are flattering, and say one thing while meaning another; their possession is slippery, since they are carried hither and thither, and with an unsteady step either desert those who have them, or make amends to those who do not. Jerome.

units.la: Suffocat verbum. Quia impertunis cogitationibus suis guttur mentis strangulant, & dum bonum desiderium intrare ad cor non sinunt, quasi aditum flatus vitalis necant. B. Greg. Hom. 15. in Evang.
units.tr: It chokes the word. Because by importunate thoughts they strangle the throat of the mind, and while they do not allow a good desire to enter the heart, they kill, as it were, the entrance of the vital breath. Gregory, Homily 15 on the Gospels.

units.la: 23. Qui audit verbum. Supple, ex Luc. 8. v. 15. in corde bono & optimo, seu ut habetur in textu Graeco, in corde bonetto & bono.
units.tr: 23. He who hears the word. Supply from Luke 8:15: in a good and excellent heart, or, as it is in the Greek text, in a heart that is good and noble [καλῇ καὶ ἀγαθῇ].

units.la: Fructum affert. Addit Lucas, in patientia scilicet, quae exercetur in expectando potius, quam in tolerando, juxta illud Rom. 8. Per patientiam expectamus. Et illud Jac. 5. Ecce agricola expectat pretiosum fructum terrae, patienter ferens, donec accipiat pluviam, &c. Sic semper apud LXX. ὑπομονή, patientia sumitur; ubique enim respondet Hebraeae dictioni, quae spem, expectationem, seu patientiam, ut aiunt, activam sonat: cum patientia, quam passivam vocant, propria voce non exprimatur in veteri Testamento, sed appelletur silentium Psal. 38. & Esa. 53. Hinc Deus & laboves dicuntur patientia nostra; Deus quidem ut & fructus, in quantum sunt id quod expectamus: labores vero, in quantum sunt id quod toleramus. Itaque dum dicitur Deo Psal.71. v. 6. Tu es patientia mea: sensus est: tu es ille, quem patienter expecto, tu es objectum patientis illius expectationis, qua tuum auxilium praestolor.
units.tr: Bears fruit. Luke adds in patience, that is, the patience that is exercised in waiting rather than in enduring, according to Romans 8: We wait for it through patience. And James 5: Behold, the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, bearing patiently until he receives the rain, etc. So the Seventy always take hypomonē [ὑπομονή] to mean patience. For it always corresponds to the Hebrew word, which, as they say, sounds like hope, expectation, or active patience. The passive patience, which they call that, is not expressed by a proper word in the Old Testament, but is called silence in Psalm 38 and Isaiah 53. Hence God and labours are both called our patience: God indeed as well as the fruit, insofar as they are what we wait for; labours, insofar as they are what we endure. So when it is said to God in Psalm 71:6, You are my patience, the sense is: you are he whom I wait for patiently; you are the object of that patient waiting by which I look for your help.

units.la: Aliud quidem centesimus, &c. Centesimus & sexagesimus & tricesimus fructus, quanquam de una terra, & de una semente nascatur, tamen multum differt in numero. Triginta referuntur ad nuptias, nam & ipsa digitorum conjunctio, quasi molli se complexans osculo & federans, maritum pingit & conjugem. Sexaginta vero ad viduas, eo quod in angustia & tribulatione sunt posita. Unde & superiori digito deprimuntur, quantoque major est difficultas expertæ quondam voluptatis illecebris abstinere, tanto majus est præmium. Porro centesimus numerus, diligenter quaso lector attende, de sinistra transfertur ad dextram, & eisdem quidem digitis, sed non eádem manu, quibus in læva nuptæ significantur & viduæ: circulum faciens, exprimit virginitatis coronam. B. Hier. l. 1. adversus Jovinianum.
units.tr: Indeed, one bears a hundredfold, another sixtyfold, another thirtyfold. Though the fruit grows from one land and one seed, it nonetheless differs greatly in number. The thirtyfold is referred to marriage, for the very joining of the fingers, embracing and clasping as in a soft kiss, depicts husband and wife. The sixtyfold refers to widows, because they are placed in distress and tribulation. Hence they are pressed down by the upper finger, and the greater the difficulty of abstaining from the allurements of a pleasure once experienced, the greater the reward. Moreover, the hundredfold number, I earnestly ask the reader to note carefully, is carried from the left hand to the right, with the same fingers but not the same hand, by which, on the left, married women and widows are signified. Making a circle, it expresses the crown of virginity. Jerome, Book 1 against Jovinian.

units.la: Aliter hanc parabolam interpretatur S. Greg. Hom. 17. super Ezech. eadem tamen allusione & similitudine, qua D. Hieron. usus est hunc in modum. Fructus terræ bonæ triginta affert: cùm mens perfectionem fidei, quæ est in Trinitate, conceperit. Sexaginta affert: cùm bonæ vitæ opera perfecte protulerit. Centum vero affert: cùm ad æternæ vitæ contemplationem profecerit. Sinistra enim nostra, est vita præsens: dextra vero, est vita venturæ. Et rectè per centenarium numerum æternæ vitæ contemplatio designatur: quia cùm post triginta ac sexaginta ad centesimum numerum computandum pervenimus, idem centenarius numerus in dextram transit. Fides atque operatio adhuc in sinistra est: quia hic adhuc positi & credimus quod non videmus, & operamur ut videamus. Cùm vero jam se animus in contemplationem æternæ vitæ suspenderit, quasi ad dextram manum computus pervenit.
units.tr: Gregory interprets this parable differently, though with the same allusion and comparison that Jerome used, in this way. The fruit of good land bears thirtyfold when the mind has conceived the perfection of faith, which is in the Trinity. It bears sixtyfold when it has brought forth the works of a good life perfectly. It bears a hundredfold when it has advanced to the contemplation of eternal life. For our left hand is the present life, and our right hand is the life to come. And rightly is the contemplation of eternal life designated by the number one hundred, because when after thirty and sixty we reach the hundredth number in counting, the same hundred passes to the right hand. Faith and works are still on the left, because while we are here we still believe what we do not see, and work so that we may see. But when the soul has now given itself to the contemplation of eternal life, the count arrives, as it were, at the right hand.

units.la: Ad horum intelligentiam sciendum ex libello venerabilis Bedæ, De computo vel loquela per gestum digitorum, quod veteres computum suum a sinistra ordiebantur usque ad decem. Cùm autem dicebant decem, unguem indicis in medio figebant artu pollicis; cùm dicebant triginta, ungues indicis & pollicis blando conjungebant amplexu adinstar conjugum se exosculantium. Cùm sexaginta numerabant, deflectebant indicem supra pollicem curvatum. Hinc numerus tricesimus significare dicitur matrimonium, ut sexagenarius viduitatem, viduarumque afflictionem. Tandem observat Beda numerum varie
units.tr: To understand these things, one must know, from the little book of the venerable Bede, On Counting, or Speech by Gesture of the Fingers, that the ancients began their counting on the left hand, up to ten. When they said ten, they fixed the nail of the index finger in the middle joint of the thumb. When they said thirty, they joined the nails of the index finger and thumb in a gentle embrace, like spouses kissing each other. When they counted sixty, they bent the index finger curved over the thumb. Hence the thirtieth number is said to signify marriage, as the sixtieth signifies widowhood and the affliction of widows. Finally, Bede observes that the number was expressed

units.la: varie variè exprimi solitum in sinistra, donec perventum fuit ad centenarium. Cùm vero centum significabant, transibant à sinistra ad dextram, & eodem utebantur gestu dextræ ut significarent centum, quo in lævalaeva decem demonstrabant. Hoc itaque circulo, qui indicis ungue in medio pollicis defixo inftar coronæ in dextra, exprimitur secundum Hieronymum Virginum corona. Centum verò, & qui deinceps sequuntur numeri, in dextra numerari solitos docent & illa Juvenalis de Nestore carmina: Felix nimirum, qui per tot secula mortem Difulit, atque suos jam dextra computat annos.
units.tr: in various ways on the left hand, until one reached the hundredth. When they signified a hundred, they passed from the left hand to the right, and they used on the right the same gesture that they used on the left to show ten. Thus, according to Jerome, the crown of virgins is expressed by this circle, formed by the index nail fixed in the middle of the thumb, like a crown on the right hand. Moreover, that the numbers from a hundred onward were customarily counted on the right hand is taught by those verses of Juvenal about Nestor: Happy indeed is he who has put off death through so many ages, and now counts his years on his right hand.

units.la: Prodit enim Homerus Nestorem trecentos annos, hoc est, tria hominum secula vixisse. Juvenalem imitatus Sidonius Apollinaris Faustò applaudens & grandævum significans, velut centenarium ait l. 9. Ep. 9. Quandoquidem tuos annos jam dextera numeraverit.
units.tr: For Homer tells that Nestor lived three hundred years, that is, three generations of men. Imitating Juvenal, Sidonius Apollinaris, praising Faustus and signifying an aged man, says in Book 9, Letter 9, as if of a centenarian: since his right hand has now counted your years.

units.la: 24. Simile factum est, &c. Id est, perinde Ecclesia ad regnandum in cœlis destinata se habet, atque si quis in agro suo bonum semen seminaverit, & aliquis ejus inimicus superseminet malum.
units.tr: 24. The matter is like this, etc. That is, the Church, destined to reign in heaven, stands in the same way as if someone had sown good seed in his field, and an enemy of his had oversown bad seed.

units.la: 29. Ne forte. Datur locus pœnitentia & monemur ne citò amputemus fratrem, quia fieri potest, ut ille qui hodie noxio depravatus est dogmate, cras resipiscat, & defendere incipiat veritatem. B. Hier.
units.tr: 29. Lest perhaps. Room is left for repentance, and we are warned not to cut off a brother hastily, because it can happen that one who today is corrupted by a harmful doctrine will tomorrow come to his senses and begin to defend the truth. B. Hier.

units.la: Sinite, &c. Modò tempus separationis non est, sed tolerationis. Videtur hoc contrarium illi præcepto. 1 Cor. 5. Auferte malum de medio vestrum, & nequaquam societatem habendam cum iis, qui fratres nominantur & sunt adulteri & fornicatores. Si enim prohiberetur eradicatio, & usque ad messem tenenda est patientia; quomodo ejiciendi sunt quidam de medio nostrum? Inter triticum & zizania quod nos appellamus lolium, quamdiu herba est, & nondum culmus venit ad spicam, grandis similitudo est, & in discernendo aut nulla, aut perdifficilis distantia. Præmonet ergo Dominus, ne ubi quid ambiguum est, citò sententiam proferamus, sed Deo judici terminum reservemus, ut cùm Dies judicii venerit, ille non sufficienem criminis, sed manifestum reatum de Sanctorum cœtu ejiciat. B. Hier.
units.tr: Suffer them, etc. The time for separation is not yet; it is a time for toleration. This seems to contradict that precept of 1 Cor. 5: "Put away the evil from among you," and that one must have no fellowship with those who are called brothers but are adulterers and fornicators. For if uprooting were forbidden, and patience must be kept until the harvest, how are some to be cast out from among us? Between the wheat and the tares, which we call darnel, while the plant is still grass and the stalk has not yet come to the ear, there is a great likeness, and in distinguishing them there is either no difference or a very hard one. The Lord therefore warns that where something is doubtful we should not pronounce judgment quickly, but should reserve the limit to God the judge, so that when the Day of Judgment comes he may cast out of the assembly of the saints not a mere suspicion of crime but a manifest guilt. B. Hier.

units.la: 31. Regnum cœlorum. Id est, Prædicatio Evangelii & notitia Scripturarum, qua ducit ad vitam. B. Hier.
units.tr: 31. The kingdom of heaven. That is, the preaching of the Gospel and the knowledge of the Scriptures, which leads to life. B. Hier.

units.la: 32. Minimum quidem est omnibus seminibus. Id est, unum est ex minimis omnium seminibus; nam semen rutæ & nonnulla alia minora sunt grano sinapis. Prædicatio Evangelii minimæ minima est omnibus disciplinis. Ad primam quippe doctrinam fidem non habet veritatis, hominem Deum, mortuum & scandalum crucis prædicans. Confer hujusmodi doctrinam dogmatibus Philosophorum & libris eorum, & splendori eloquentiæ, & compositioni sermonum: & videbis quanto minor sit ceteris feminibus semeniis Evangelii. Sed illa cum creverit, nihil mordax, nihil vividum, nihil vitale demonstrat, sed totum flaccidum marcidumque & mollitum ebullit in olera, & in herbas quæ citò arescunt & corruunt. Hæc autem prædicatio quæ parva videbatur in principio, cum vel in animà credentis, vel in toto mundo sata fuerit, non exurgit in olera, sed crescit in arborem: ita ut volucres cæli, quas vel animæ credentium, vel fortitudines Dei servitio mancipatæ, sentire debemus: veniant & habitent in ramis ejus. Ramos puto Evangelicæ arboris, quæ de grano sinapis creverit, dogmatum esse diversitas, in quibus suprædictarum volucrum unaquæque quiescit. B. Hier.
units.tr: 32. Indeed the least of all seeds. That is, it is one of the smallest of all seeds; for the seed of rue and some other things are smaller than the grain of mustard. The preaching of the Gospel is the least of all the teachings. For at first hearing it does not have the faith of truth, since it proclaims a God made man, dead, and a scandal of the cross. Compare such a doctrine with the doctrines of the philosophers and their books, with the splendour of eloquence and the polish of speeches, and you will see how much smaller the seed of the Gospel is than the other seeds. But when it has grown, it shows nothing biting, nothing lively, nothing vital, but puffs up wholly limp, withered and softened into herbs and greens which quickly dry up and fall. Yet this preaching, which seemed small at the beginning, when it has been sown either in the soul of the believer or in the whole world, does not rise up into herbs but grows into a tree, so that the birds of the heaven, which we ought to understand as the souls of believers or the powers given over to the service of God, come and dwell in its branches. I think the branches of the Gospel tree, which has grown from the grain of mustard, are the diversity of doctrines, in which each of the aforesaid birds rests. B. Hier.

units.la: Majus est omnibus oleribus. q. d. Unum est è maximis omnium oleribus.
units.tr: Greater than all herbs. That is, it is one of the greatest of all herbs.

units.la: Fit arbor. Id est, lignescit stipes ejus, & locis maximè calidis longè supra humanam statpram assurgit.
units.tr: It becomes a tree. That is, its stalk becomes woody, and in the hottest places it rises far above human stature.

units.la: Ut habitent in ramis ejus. Id est, ut obumbrentur sub ramis ejus, ut habet versio Arabica.
units.tr: So that they dwell in its branches. That is, so that they are sheltered under its branches, as the Arabic version has it.

units.la: 33. Regnum cœlorum. Id est, doctrina Evangelii.
units.tr: 33. The kingdom of heaven. That is, the teaching of the Gospel.

units.la: Fermento. Hoc nomen à fervore dici placet Grammaticis, quia fervendo crescit, ipsamque massam, cui inspergitur, turgidam reddit. Unde Plautus in Mercatore dixit in fermento jacere uxorem, cùm iratam significare vellet.
units.tr: Leaven. Grammarians are pleased to derive this word from fervour, because it grows by fermenting and makes the mass into which it is sprinkled swell up. Hence Plautus in the Merchant said "to lie in leaven" for a wife, when he wished to signify an angry one.

units.la: Mulier. Apud Hebræos erat & etiamnum est fere mulierum officium pinsere, ut etiam indicatur Levitic. 26. v. 26.
units.tr: Woman. Among the Hebrews it was, and still is, nearly the office of women to grind, as is also indicated in Lev. 26:26.

units.la: In farinæ satis tribus. Satum est tertia pars Ephi, & tantùm unicâ vice pinsi solebat, ut patet ex Gen. 18. v. 6. De hac & aliis quibusdam mensuris antiquis sic habetur in opere Rabbi Alphes Tract. de Pascha c. 5. Quadrans, sive quartarius Legis, id est, quarta pars mensuræ sacræ in liquidis, continet sesqui-ovum. sextarius, mensura liquidorum continet quatuor quadrantes, id est, sex ova. cabus, mensura frumentaria continens quatuor sextarios, seu viginti quatuor ova, mensura Hin quidorum continens duodecim sextarios, seu ova septuaginta duo. satum, mensura aridorum continens sex cabos, viginti quatuor sextarios, duo hin, nonaginta sex quadrantes, ova centum quadraginta quatuor. vulgo Ephi tantùm continens in aridis, quantùm Batus in liquidis, scilicet tria sata, cabos octodecim, sex hin, septuaginta duo sextarios, ducentos octoginta octo quadrantes, ova quadrin-genta triginta duo. Dnv vulgò Gomer mensura aridorum sit decima pars Ephi continens ova quadraginta tria & quinque tam partem ovi. Ut autem ad parabolam Evangelicam redeamus; aiunt nonnulli per mulierem significari Dei Sapientiam; per fermentum doctrinam Evangelicam; per tria sata tres facultates animae, scilicet, appetitum rationalem, irascibilem & concupiscibilem; hoc enim tres appetitus doctrinae Evangelicae conformat Dei Sapientia. Dicitur & alia de hac parabola, quae omittimus brevitatis causa, quia ut monet hic B. Hier. Numquam Parabolae & dubia aenigmatum intelligentia potest ad auctoritatem dogmatum proficere.
units.tr: Into three measures of meal. A seah is the third part of an ephah, and it was usually ground only once, as is clear from Gen. 18:6. Concerning this and certain other ancient measures, the following is found in the work of Rabbi Alphes, Tract. on the Passover, ch. 5. A quarter, or quartarius of the Law, that is, the fourth part of the sacred measure for liquids, holds a ovum and a half. A sextarius, a measure of liquids, holds four quarters, that is, six eggs. A cab, a measure for grain holding four sextarii, or twenty-four eggs. A hin, a measure of liquids holding twelve sextarii, or seventy-two eggs. A seah, a measure for dry goods holding six cabs, twenty-four sextarii, two hin, ninety-six quarters, one hundred and forty-four eggs. The ephah, commonly, holds in dry goods as much as the bath does in liquids, namely three seahs, eighteen cabs, six hin, seventy-two sextarii, two hundred and eighty-eight quarters, four hundred and thirty-two eggs.
