The gomer, which is commonly called the measure for dry goods, is the tenth part of an ephah, holding forty-three eggs and five parts of an egg. But to return to the Gospel parable: some say that the woman signifies the Wisdom of God, the leaven the Gospel teaching, and the three seahs the three faculties of the soul, namely the rational appetite, the irascible and the concupiscible; for the wisdom of God conforms the teaching of the Gospel to these three appetites. Other things are also said about this parable, which we omit for brevity, since, as B. Hier. warns here, "the understanding of parables and doubtful riddles can never contribute to the authority of doctrines."

units.la: 34. Locutus est Iesus in parabolis ad turbas. Quia non erant digni nec idonei audire veritatem accipere, quam discipulis exponebat. D. Th. 3. p. q. 42. ar. 3. ad 3. hoc Marcus c. 4. v. 33. significat his verbis: Prout poterant audire.
units.tr: 34. Jesus spoke in parables to the crowds. Because they were not worthy or fit to hear and receive the truth, which he explained to his disciples. D. Th. 3 p. q. 42 a. 3 ad 3. Mark ch. 4 v. 33 signifies this in these words: "as they were able to hear."

units.la: Sine parabolis non loquebatur eis. Hoc secundum Chrysost. Hom. 48. in Matth. intelligendum est quantum ad illum sermonem, quamvis alios sine parabolis multa turbis locutus fuerit. Vel secundum Aug. in lib. De quaestionibus Evang. hoc dicitur, non quia nihil proprie locutus est, sed quia nullum fere sermonem explicavit, ubi non per parabolam aliquid significaret, quamvis in eo aliqua propria diceret. D. Th. loco mox citato.
units.tr: "Without a parable he did not speak to them." This, according to Chrysostom, Hom. 48 on Matthew, "must be understood with respect to that discourse, although he spoke to the crowds on many other occasions without parables." Or according to Augustine, in the book On the Questions of the Gospels, this is said not because he spoke nothing plainly, but because he explained almost no discourse in which he did not signify something by a parable, although in it he also said some things plainly. D. Th. in the place just cited.

units.la: 35. Ut impleretur, &c. q. d. Ex parabolicis Christi concionibus evenit, ut in eo vere impleretur, quod significabatur Allegorice per Prophetam parabolice loquentem in Psal. 77. Heb. 78.
units.tr: 35. That it might be fulfilled, etc. That is, from the parabolic sermons of Christ it came about that what was signified allegorically through the Prophet speaking in parables in Psalm 77 (Hebrew 78) was truly fulfilled in him.

units.la: In parabolis. Haec verba in Psalmo intelliguntur ad literam de parabolis in ipso contentis, ut scribit sapiens Rabbi Abraham filius Esrae: ex cujus quidem sententia verba ista: Mittentes in arcum: Parere mensam in deserto: Ignis accensus est in Jacob: Iamua coeli aperuit: Panem coeli dedit eis: parabolae sunt, & instar aenigmatis obscurae.
units.tr: In parables. These words in the Psalm are understood literally of the parables contained in it, as the wise Rabbi Abraham son of Ezra writes; according to his opinion these words: "They bent the bow; they prepared a table in the desert; a fire was kindled in Jacob; the gates of heaven opened; he gave them bread from heaven," are parables, and obscure like a riddle.

units.la: Eructabo. Id est, eloquar. Ructum solet vocare Scriptura doctrinam Prophetarum, quia ut ructus ex cocto cibo exhalatur, sic Dei verbum ex corde coelestis alimonia pleno depromi debet.
units.tr: I will utter. That is, I will speak. Scripture is accustomed to call the teaching of the Prophets a belch, because just as a belch is breathed out from cooked food, so the word of God ought to be brought forth from a heart full of heavenly nourishment.

units.la: Abscondita a constitutione mundi. Heb. aenigmata ab initio. Haec verba in Psalmo ad literam dicuntur de locutionibus aenigmatum instar obscuris in ipso contentis; ut enim alias omittamus, aenigma est ista locutio: Tradidit in captivitatem virtutem eorum: quâ significatur arca capta à Philistaeis. Aenigma est & omnino obscurum quonam de bello fit sermo, ubi dicitur in eodem Psalmo: Filii Ephraim intendentes arcum, &c.
units.tr: Hidden from the foundation of the world. Hebrew: riddles from the beginning. These words in the Psalm are said literally of expressions containing riddles, obscure like enigmas; for, to pass over other examples, this expression is an enigma: "He delivered their strength into captivity," by which the ark captured by the Philistines is signified. It is also an enigma, and wholly obscure, what war is being spoken of, where it says in the same Psalm: "The sons of Ephraim, bending the bow, etc."

units.la: 39. Messis. Hoc nomen hic significat tempus opportunum & à Deo destinatum judicio exercendo & secernendis impiis è medio justorum. Alias verò hoc idem nomen sumitur pro opportunitate & debita dispositione multitudinis animarum ad prædicationis suscoptionem.
units.tr: 39. Harvest. This word here signifies the time fitting and appointed by God for exercising judgment and separating the wicked from the midst of the righteous. Elsewhere, however, the same word is taken for the opportunity and due disposition of the multitude of souls to receive the preaching.

units.la: 41. Colligent. Messores [illegible, ~6 letters] Angeli Zizania ad comburendum in fasciculos ligant; cum pares paribus in tormentis similibus sociant, ut superbi cum superbis, luxuriosi cum luxuriosis, avari cum avaris, fallaces cum fallacibus, invidi cum invidis, infideles cum infidelibus ardeant. Cum ergo similes in culpa, ad tormenta similia deducuntur: quia eos in locis penalibus angeli deputant, quasi zizaniorum fasciculos ad comburendum ligant. B. Greg. 4. dialog. c. 35.
units.tr: 41. They will gather. The reapers [illegible] The angels bind the tares into bundles to be burned; they join like with like in similar torments, the proud with the proud, the lustful with the lustful, the greedy with the greedy, the deceitful with the deceitful, the envious with the envious, the unbelieving with the unbelieving, that they may burn. Therefore, since those alike in guilt are led to similar torments, because the angels assign them to places of punishment, they are bound as bundles of tares to be burned. B. Greg. 4 Dialogues ch. 35.

units.la: De regno ejus. Id est, de Ecclesia militante.
units.tr: Of his kingdom. That is, of the Church militant.

units.la: Scandala. Id est, malos, quos Christus vocavit zizania & filios nequam, atque oppositos filiis regni seu electis & prædestinatis.
units.tr: Offences. That is, the wicked, whom Christ called tares and children of the wicked one, and who are set against the children of the kingdom, that is, the elect and predestinated.

units.la: 42. In caminum. Id est, in fornacem. Καμίνῳ nominatus videtur à verbo Καίειν, quod accendere significat.
units.tr: 42. Into the furnace. That is, into the oven. It seems to be named [καμίνῳ] from the verb [καίειν], which means to set on fire.

units.la: 43. Justi fulgebunt sicut sol. Non quod omnes æqualiter fulgebunt, cùm scriptum sit. 1 Cor. 15. Alia claritas solis, alia lunæ, alia stellarum, sic erit resurrectio mortuorum. Sed significatur hic magna valdè excellentia fulgoris & claritatis in corporibus beatorum: unde assumitur comparatio à sole tanquam à corpore in hoc mundo fulgentissimo.
units.tr: 43. The righteous shall shine forth as the sun. Not that all will shine equally, since it is written: 1 Cor. 15: There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; so also is the resurrection of the dead. Rather, great and very surpassing brilliance and splendour in the bodies of the blessed is meant here, and so the comparison is taken from the sun, the most brilliant of bodies in this world.

units.la: 44. Regnum cœlorum. Id est, Evangelica doctrina.
units.tr: 44. The kingdom of heaven. That is, the evangelical teaching.

units.la: Abscondit. Id est, non jactanter inventum ostentat, sed ne surripiatur secretum servat, & ejus causâ libenter omnium jacturam facit.
units.tr: He hides it. That is, he does not display the treasure he has found boastfully, but keeps it secret lest it be stolen, and for its sake he gladly gives up everything.

units.la: 45. Simile est regnum cœlorum. Id est, Evangelii doctrina ab Apostolis mox ubique disseminanda: passim enim hæc doctrina vocatur regnum Dei. Unde non desunt qui exponant illud supra c. 3. v. 2. Appropinquavit regnum cœlorum. Q. d. Advenit tempus, quo omnibus prædicabitur Evangelium. Et illud cap. 11. v. 11. Qui autem minor est in regno cœlorum, major ipso est. Qui minimus est inter eos, quibus Evangelium prædicandi munus incumbet, major est Joanne. Hinc & infrà c. 21. v. 43. ait Christus Pharisæis: Auferetur à vobis regnum Dei, & dabitur genti facienti fructus ejus. Quod impletum legitur Act. 13. v. 46. cùm Paulus & Barnabas constanter Judæis dixerunt: Vobis oportebat primùm loqui verbum Dei: sed quoniam repellitis illud, & indignos vos judicatis æternæ vitæ, ecce convertimur ad Gentes. Hoc ergo Dei regnum, id est, Evangelii doctrina cum margarita confertur non immeritò. rito 1. Nam si margaritæ nobis è remotis locis, & ex ultimo Oriente afferuntur, hanc doctrinam e cœlis attulit, qui vocatur Luc. 1. v. 78. Oriens ex alto, ἀνατολὴ ἐξ ὕψους. 2. Si candor in margaritis magni fit, in doctrina Evangelii nobis offertur calculus candidus Apoc. 2. v. 17. per quem etsi fuerint peccata nostra ut coccinum, tanquam nix dealbabuntur. 3. Si lævor in margaritis placet, quodque ad amussim rotundæ sunt, nec quidquam habent inæquale, Evangelii gratia nihil est æqualius, cum omnes ex æquo admittat; Non enim est Iudæus, neque Græcus, non est servus neque liber, non est masculus neque fœmina; omnes enim vos unum estis in Christo Iesu. Gal. 3. v. 28. 4. Si in margaritis requiritur firmitas, quid firmius est & solidius Dei promissis, quæ in Christo sunt, est, &, amen.
units.tr: 45. The kingdom of heaven is like. That is, the teaching of the Gospel, to be spread at once everywhere by the Apostles; for this teaching is everywhere called the kingdom of God. Hence there are those who explain the verse above, ch. 3: 2, The kingdom of heaven is at hand, as if to say: the time has come when the Gospel will be preached to all. And that in ch. 11: 11, He who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he: whoever is least among those to whom the office of preaching the Gospel falls is greater than John. Hence also, below in ch. 21: 43, Christ says to the Pharisees: The kingdom of God shall be taken from you and given to a nation bringing forth its fruits. This is read as fulfilled in Acts 13: 46, when Paul and Barnabas said firmly to the Jews: It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles.* Therefore this kingdom of God, that is, the teaching of the Gospel, is not unjustly compared with a pearl. (1) For if pearls are brought to us from distant places and from the furthest East, this teaching was brought from heaven by him who is called Dawn from on high [ἀνατολὴ ἐξ ὕψους] in Luke 1: 78. (2) If brightness is greatly prized in pearls, the Gospel teaching offers us a white pebble, Rev. 2: 17, by which, though our sins be like scarlet, they shall be made white as snow. (3) If smoothness pleases in pearls, and they are perfectly round with nothing uneven, the grace of the Gospel is nothing more even, since it admits all on equal terms: There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus. Gal. 3: 28. (4) If firmness is required in pearls, what is firmer and more solid than the promises of God that are in Christ: they are yes, and amen.

units.la: 2 Cor. 1. v. 20. Cœlum & terra transibunt, verba autem mea non transibunt, inquit Christus Marc. 13. v. 31. 5. Si margaritæ sunt in pretio propter vires additas, Evangelium est Dei virtus in salutem omni credenti. Rom. 1. v. 16. Ab antiqui serpentis morsu nos sanat, nec solum ægros sublevat, sed & mortuos suscitat, quia venit hora & nunc est, quando mortui audient vocem Filii Dei, & qui audierint, vivent. Ioann. 5. v. 25. 6. Splendoris & ornatus ratione quæruntur uniones, ac proinde appenduntur auribus, collo & brachio ligantur; sed & mandata sua Deus jubet collo alligari. Prov. 3. v. 3. Nec quidquam auribus tam decorum est, quam Dei verbum audire, aut manibus, quàm illud exequi. 7. Ut margaritarum pretium latet Barbaros, qui rem tantillam mirantur à nobis tanti fieri: ita Evangelium nostrum, cui omnia desiderabilia non possunt æquari, in quibus pereunt, est opertum, in quibus Deus huius sæculi excæcavit mentes, ut non fulgeat illis illuminatio Evangelii gloriæ Christi. 2 Cor. 4. v. 3, & 4. Hinc forte & doctrina Evangelica assimilatur thesauro abscondito. Utraque autem parabola, scilicet, thesauri abscondíti & pretiosæ margaritæ, negat nos assequi posse doctrinam Evangelicam, seu eminentem scientiam Iesu Christi, nisi omnia omnino detrimentum faciamus, & ea quibus plerique ambitiosius inhiant, ut stercora arbitremur, quæ, quàm fieri potest studiosissime, procul amandamus.
units.tr: 2 Cor. 1: 20. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away, says Christ, Mark 13: 31. (5) If pearls are valued for the powers attributed to them, the Gospel is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes, Rom. 1: 16. It heals us from the bite of the ancient serpent, and not only relieves the sick but also raises the dead, for the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear shall live, John 5: 25. (6) Pearls are sought for their splendour and adornment, and therefore they are hung on the ears and tied on the neck and arm; but God also commands his precepts to be bound about the neck, Prov. 3: 3. Nothing is so becoming to the ears as hearing God's word, or to the hands as carrying it out. (7) As the price of pearls is hidden from barbarians, who wonder why we set such store by such a trifle, so our Gospel, which cannot be equalled by all the desirable things of the world, is hidden to those who perish, among whom the god of this age has blinded the minds, so that the illumination of the Gospel of the glory of Christ should not shine on them, 2 Cor. 4: 3–4. Hence perhaps the evangelical teaching is also likened to a hidden treasure. Both parables, namely of the hidden treasure and of the precious pearl, deny that we can attain the evangelical teaching, or the outstanding knowledge of Jesus Christ, unless we utterly suffer the loss of all things, and count as dung those things after which most people eagerly pant, and cast them away as far and as zealously as possible.

units.la: 47. Simile est regnum cœlorum sagenæ, &c. Sagena ista, prædicatio est Evangelica: quæ in mare, id est, in fluctuationem, & amaritudinem præsentis sæculi demissa congregat multitudinem piscium, id est, ex omni genere hominum trahit ad litus maris, id est, ad finem præsentis sæculi. Impletio sagenæ, consummatio prædicationis Evangelicæ. Congregat ex omni genere hominum; quia ex Iudæis, quibus prædicavit Christus: & ex Romanis, quibus prædica- dicadicaverunt Petrus & Paulus: & ex Indis quibus Thomas: ex Persis, quibus predicaverunt Simon & Judas, & ex hominibus minoris India, quibus Bartholomaeus: ex Syriis, quibus Philippus: ex Asianis, quibus predicavit Joannes: ex Achaicis, quibus Andreas: ex Æthiopibus, quibus Matthaeus: & ex Alexandrinis, quibus Marcus, & sic ex aliis nationibus, ad quas sive per Apostolos sive per Apostolorum discipulos & successores, pervenit sonus praedicationis. In omnem enim terram exivit sonus eorum. In eo namque quod praedicatio Evangelica ex omnibus nationibus assumit: ex omni genere piscium trahit. Aliter: Congregat ex omni genere piscium, quia congregat ex omni genere peccatorum. Congregat immundos peccatores, fornicatores, adulteros, incestuosos, foeneratores, & ex omnibus aliis qui minoribus, vel majoribus peccatis sunt a Deo divisi, & per multas iniquitates differsi. Et ex omnibus congregat, & congregatos justificat: & neminem expellit, qui, ipsa audita, eam intrare voluerit. Continet autem sagena illa pisces multos, & diversos, bonos, & malos: sed interim dum sagena ad litus trahitur: isti inimillos frequenter commiscentur. Boni etenim nonnunquam mali sunt per culpam, & mali aliquando boni sunt per gratiam, & nondum potest judicari, qui in vasa sint eligendi: qui foras proiciendi. Cum ad litus, id est, ad finem seculi ventum fuerit: tunc judicium verum secernendorum bonorum, & malorum patebit: quia Angeli eligent bonos in vasa, id est, in aeterna tabernacula: & malos foras mittent in aeterna tormenta.
units.tr: 47. The kingdom of heaven is like a net, etc. This net is the evangelical preaching, which, let down into the sea, that is, into the turmoil and bitterness of the present age, gathers a multitude of fish, that is, it draws men of every kind to the shore of the sea, that is, to the end of the present age. The filling of the net is the completion of the evangelical preaching. It gathers from every kind of men: from the Jews, to whom Christ preached; from the Romans, to whom Peter and Paul preached; from the Indians, to whom Thomas preached; from the Persians, to whom Simon and Jude preached, and from the people of Lesser India, to whom Bartholomew preached; from the Syrians, to whom Philip preached; from the Asians, to whom John preached; from the Achaeans, to whom Andrew preached; from the Ethiopians, to whom Matthew preached; from the Alexandrians, to whom Mark preached; and so from other nations, to which the sound of the preaching came, either through the Apostles or through the Apostles' disciples and successors. For their sound has gone out into all the earth. In that the evangelical preaching takes up men from all nations, it draws them from every kind of fish. Otherwise: it gathers from every kind of fish, because it gathers from every kind of sinner. It gathers unclean sinners, fornicators, adulterers, incestuous persons, usurers, and all others who are divided from God by lesser or greater sins and scattered through many iniquities. It gathers from all, and justifies those gathered, and it casts out no one who, having heard it, wishes to enter. Now that net holds many fish, of various kinds, good and bad; but meanwhile, while the net is being drawn to the shore, these are often mixed together. For the good are sometimes bad through fault, and the bad are sometimes good through grace, and it cannot yet be judged who are to be chosen as vessels, and who are to be thrown out. When the shore, that is, the end of the age, has come, then the true judgment separating the good from the bad will be made plain; for the angels will choose the good into the vessels, that is, into eternal tabernacles, and will cast the bad out into eternal torments.

units.la: Omnes autem, qui fidem Christianam recepturi non sunt, extra sagenam istam sunt: sicut Judaei, & Pagani. Et tales jam judicati sunt, non solum judicio secundum praescientiam & judicio secundum causam, sed etiam judicio secundum operationem, deinceps judicandi judicio secundum retributionem. Est autem judicium secundum praescientiam, quo judicati sumus antequam essemus. Judicium secundum causam: quo judicamur ex quo boni & mali sumus. Judicium secundum operationem: quo judicamur per manifestam operationem: quo judicamur per manifestam actionem esse boni, & mali, qui prius secundum causam eramus occulti. Judicium secundum retributionem est quo recipimus in premio secundum quod fuimus, & fecimus in merito.
units.tr: Now all who are not going to receive the Christian faith are outside that net, as are the Jews and the pagans. Such have already been judged, not only by the judgment according to foreknowledge and the judgment according to cause, but also by the judgment according to operation, and are yet to be judged by the judgment according to retribution. Now the judgment according to foreknowledge is that by which we were judged before we existed. The judgment according to cause is that by which we are judged in that we are good or bad. The judgment according to operation is that by which we are judged, through a manifest operation or action, to be good or bad, who before, according to cause, were hidden. The judgment according to retribution is that by which we receive a reward according to what we were and what we did in merit.

units.la: Ex his quatuor judiciis, duo sunt occulta, duo manifesta. Occulta, judicium secundum praescientiam, & judicium secundum causam. Manifesta, judicium secundum retributionem, & judicium secundum operationem. Duo quoque pertinent ad Deum, judicium videlicet secundum praescientiam, & judicium secundum retributionem. Duo ad hominem: judicium secundum causam, & judicium secundum operationem. Sed qui fidem Christianam prorsus repudiant: jam tribus praecedentibus judiciis, videlicet judicio secundum praescientiam, judicio secundum causam, & judicio secundum operationem sunt judicati: judicio autem secunsecundum retributionem judicandi. Hugo Victorinus lib. 2. Alleg. in Matth. c. 31.
units.tr: Of these four judgments, two are hidden and two are manifest. Hidden: the judgment according to foreknowledge and the judgment according to cause. Manifest: the judgment according to retribution and the judgment according to operation. Two also pertain to God, namely the judgment according to foreknowledge and the judgment according to retribution. Two pertain to man: the judgment according to cause and the judgment according to operation. But those who utterly reject the Christian faith have already been judged by the three preceding judgments, namely the judgment according to foreknowledge, the judgment according to cause, and the judgment according to operation; but they are yet to be judged by the judgment according to retribution. Hugo Victorinus, Allegories on Matthew, bk. 2, ch. 31.

units.la: 52. Omnis Scriba. Id est, peritus Legis, & interpres Judæis; nunquam enim Scriba in novo Testamento pro Evangelico Doctore sumitur.
units.tr: 52. Every scribe. That is, one skilled in the Law and an interpreter for the Jews; for in the New Testament the word scribe is never taken for a teacher of the Gospel.

units.la: Discipulus in regno cælorum. Græc. in regnum cælorum. His verbis indicat Christus se non de Scriba simpliciter loqui, sed de eo, qui cùm antea Legis peritus esset, hanc scientiam ad finem suum, hoc est, ad Evangelicam doctrinam didicit referre. Hujusmodi Scriba fuit ille, qui cùm Judæorum sapientiam ad pedes Gamalielis didicisset, factus est vas electionis.
units.tr: A disciple in the kingdom of heaven. Greek: into the kingdom of heaven. By these words Christ indicates that he is not speaking of a scribe in general, but of one who, although he was formerly skilled in the Law, has learned to refer that knowledge to its proper end, that is, to the Gospel teaching. Such a scribe was he who, having learned the wisdom of the Jews at the feet of Gamaliel, became a chosen vessel.

units.la: De thesauro. Id est, de conditorio suo aut promtuario.
units.tr: From his treasure. That is, from his storehouse or pantry.

units.la: Nova & vetera. Id est, abundè ex omni genere rerum; alludit enim Christus ad illud Levitic. 26. v. 10. ubi Deus inter ceteras benedictiones promittit tantam singulis familiarum patribus copiam, ut nihil unquam illis sit defuturum: quod his verbis Scriptura expressit: Comedetis vetustissima veterum & veteris novis supervenientibus projicietis. Cùm ergo tales optimè instructi sint, multò tamen copiosius ac largius, qui tempore eodem, ex eodem promtuario, & vetera, & nova depromit; hujusmodi patris-familias instar ait Christus Scribam ad Evangelicam doctrinam Legis peritiam prudenter referentem, abundè omnibus, quæ scire oportet, ac largissimè instructum esse.
units.tr: New and old. That is, abundantly, from every kind of thing. For Christ alludes to Leviticus 26:10, where God, among other blessings, promises to each head of a household so great an abundance that nothing will ever be lacking to them; Scripture expressed this in these words: You shall eat the very old store of the old, and you shall cast out the old because of the new coming in. Since, therefore, such men are excellently furnished, yet he who brings forth from the same storehouse at the same time both old and new things has far more copious and abundant supply; by the likeness of such a householder Christ says that the scribe who wisely refers his skill in the Law to the Gospel teaching is most richly and fully furnished with all that it is fitting to know.

units.la: 53. Inde. Hæc particula hic & Marc. 6. v. 5. significat tam urbem Capharnaum, quàm loca adjacentia, quæ circa mare erant, ubi parabolas enarrabat. Ab eo autem tempore non videtur amplius habitasse Capharnai, licet aliquoties illac transierit sicut per alias civitates, in quibus non habitavit. Porro Lucas c. 4. v. 16. præsentem historiam anticipat, ut obiter rationem reddat, cur Capharnai potius domicilium elegerit Christus, quàm in urbe Nazareth, ubi fuerat educatus. Hanc autem anticipationem ipse satis indicat loco citato v. 23. his verbis: Quanta audivimus facta in Capharnaum, fac & hic in patria tua; unde quod ibidem completa hujus historiæ narratione Lucas v. 31. dicit: & descendens in Capharnaum, &c. Hebraismus est, id est, & descenderat, &c. & est recapitulatio omissorum.
units.tr: 53. Thence. This particle here and in Mark 6:5 signifies both the city of Capernaum and the neighbouring places around the sea where he was telling parables. From that time, however, he does not seem to have dwelt any longer in Capernaum, although he passed through it several times, as he passed through other cities in which he did not dwell. Moreover, Luke in chapter 4, verse 16, anticipates the present narrative, so as to give in passing the reason why Christ chose Capernaum as his home rather than the city of Nazareth, where he had been brought up. This anticipation he himself sufficiently indicates in the cited place, verse 23, in these words: Whatever we have heard done in Capernaum, do here also in your own country. Hence what Luke says in verse 31, once the narrative of this history has been completed, and going down to Capernaum, etc., is a Hebraism, that is, and he had gone down, etc., and it is a recapitulation of what was omitted.

units.la: 54. Et veniens. Græcè, cùm venisset.
units.tr: 54. And coming. Greek: when he had come.

units.la: 55. In patriam suam. Id est, in Nazareth, ut patet ex Luc. 4. v. 16.
units.tr: 55. Into his own country. That is, into Nazareth, as is clear from Luke 4:16.

units.la: 55. Fabri filius. Id est, secundum Hilarium & Ericum fabri ferrarii; communiter tamen existimatur fuisse faber ligna-rius. Est autem verisimile dixisse Nazarenos, Nonne hic est faber, faber, ut habetur apud Marcum, & fabri filius, ut habetur hic, & filius Joseph, ut habetur apud Luc. nec in hoc est contradictio, cum alius Evangelista scripto mandat, quod alius omiserit.
units.tr: 55. The carpenter's son. That is, according to Hilary and Eric, a blacksmith's son; yet it is commonly thought that he was a carpenter. It is likely that the Nazarenes said, Is not this the carpenter, the carpenter, as found in Mark, and the carpenter's son, as found here, and the son of Joseph, as found in Luke; nor is there any contradiction in this, since one Evangelist writes what another has omitted.

units.la: Fratres. Id est, propinquitate, non natura, ut loquitur Hieronymus in lib. de perpetua virginitate B. Mariæ adversus Helvidium. Idem dicendum de Christi sororibus.
units.tr: Brothers. That is, by kinship, not by nature, as Jerome speaks in his book on the perpetual virginity of the Blessed Mary against Helvidius. The same must be said of Christ's sisters.

units.la: 57. Scandalizabantur. Id est, offendebantur educationis & prosapiæ humilitate.
units.tr: 57. Were offended. That is, they were scandalized at his humble upbringing and family.

units.la: 58. Non fecit ibi virtutes multas. Hoc Marc. c. 6. v. 5; Hebraismo Scrip. sacræ familiari expressit: Non poterat ibi virtutem ullam facere. Sic Deut. 2. v. 17. Non poteris comedere in oppidis tuis decimam frumenti, &c. Id est, non comedes in oppidis tuis, &c. sic Genef. 18. v. 17. Num celare potero Abraham quæ gesturus sum? id est, num celabo, &c. sic Marc. 9. Si potes credere, omnia possibilia sunt credenti: id est, si credis, &c. Joan. 5. v. 19. Non potest Filius a se facere quidquam: id est, non facit Filius, &c. Luc. 16. v. 2. Jam non poteris villicare: id est, non villicabis. Joan. 12. v. 39. Propterea non poterant credere, quia iterum dixit Esaias, &c. Id est, propterea non credebant; nam ibidem v. 37. eodem penitus sensu idem Evangelista dixerat simplicibus verbis: Non credebant in eum, ut sermo Esaiæ impleretur. B. Greg. Naz. Hom. 2. de Filio ait non posse in Scripturis sacris dupliciter sumi, cum non proprie sumitur. 1. Ut sit idem ac non velle, & sic inquit Christus dicitur non potuisse facere virtutes in patria sua. 2. Ut sit idem ac non convenire, dedecere, & sic dicuntur filii sponsi non posse lugere, quamdiu cum illis est sponsus. Hoc modo etiam potest exponi, quod de Christo dicit Marcus: Non poterat ibi virtutem ullam facere. Et hunc ultimum modum exponendi amplectitur B. Isidorus Pelusiota, & multis confirmat exemplis, ut explicet locum citatum ex Joan. 5. v. 19.
units.tr: 58. He did not do many mighty works there. Mark 6:5 expresses this in a Hebraism familiar to Holy Scripture: He could not do any mighty work there. So Deuteronomy 2:17: You cannot eat the tithe of the grain in your towns, etc., that is, you shall not eat in your towns, etc.; so Genesis 18:17: Can I hide from Abraham what I am about to do? that is, shall I hide, etc.; so Mark 9: If you can believe, all things are possible to him who believes: that is, if you believe, etc. John 5:19: The Son can do nothing of himself: that is, the Son does not do, etc. Luke 16:2: You can no longer be steward: that is, you shall not be steward. John 12:39: For this reason they could not believe, because Isaiah said again, etc. That is, for this reason they did not believe; for in the same place, verse 37, the same Evangelist had said in entirely the same sense, in plain words: They did not believe in him, so that the word of Isaiah might be fulfilled. Blessed Gregory Nazianzen, in Homily 2 on the Son, says that cannot in the sacred Scriptures may be taken in two ways, when it is not taken properly. 1. So that it means the same as not to will; and in this sense Christ is said not to have been able to do mighty works in his own country. 2. So that it means the same as not to agree or not to be fitting; and in this sense the sons of the bridegroom are said not to be able to mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them. In this way also can be explained what Mark says of Christ: He could not do any mighty work there. And Blessed Isidore of Pelusium embraces this last way of explaining, and confirms it with many examples, in order to explain the passage cited from John 5:19.

units.la: CAPUT XIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: 1. Herodes. Antipas scilicet, Herodis magni Filius ex Mathace Samaritide.
units.tr: 1. Herod. That is, Antipas, son of Herod the Great by Malthace the Samaritan.

units.la: Tetrarcha. Hunc Marcus c. 6. & ipse Matth. mox. v. 9. Regem appellat, quòd Rex diceretur, quicunque summâ potestate, licèt non regiâ, praeesset; sic & quod Cicero Tetrarchias dixit, Plinius regna vocavit.
units.tr: Tetrarch. Mark calls him so in chapter 6, and Matthew himself a little later, at verse 9, calls him king. He was called king because anyone who ruled with supreme power, though not with royal authority, was called that. So too Cicero spoke of tetrarchies and Pliny called them kingdoms.

units.la: - Famam Iesu. Id est, omnia quae fiebant ab eo, ut explicat Luc. c. 9. v. 7. Quaeritur qui fieri potuerit, ut Herodes tamdiu Christum, & edita a Christo miracula ignoraverit? Respondet Baronius, quia diu abfuit a domo ut bellum sibi intentum ab Arete Rege ob ejectam e domo filiam ipsius, quam prius uxorem duxerat, sustineret. Sed fallitur, nam ut omittam anachronismum, quem docte urget Casaubonus exercit 15. diserte tradit Iosephus lib. 18. hoc bellum utrinque per Legatos fuisse gestum. Vere itaque sentit Chrysostomus Hom. 49. in Matth. in causa tam diuturnae ignorationis fuisse incuriam rerum bonarum, quâ Princeps ut plurimum laborat; Tales enim, inquit, sunt viri potentes, & supercilia tumidi, ferò discunt talia, quia negligunt.
units.tr: - The fame of Jesus. That is, all the things that were done by him, as Luke explains in chapter 9, verse 7. It is asked how it could happen that Herod was so long ignorant of Christ and of the miracles he performed. Baronius answers that Herod was for a long time away from home, sustaining a war that Aretas the king had waged against him because of his divorced daughter, whom Herod had previously married. But he is mistaken. To pass over the anachronism, which Casaubonus rightly presses, Josephus clearly records in Antiquities book 18 that this war was conducted on both sides through envoys. Chrysostom therefore judges rightly, in Homily 49 on Matthew, that the cause of so long an ignorance was the carelessness about good things to which princes are for the most part prone: For such are powerful men, and haughty of brow; they learn such things late, because they neglect them.

units.la: 2. Et ait. Non affirmando, sed haesitando, & dubitando, ut patet ex loco citato Lucae. Haec autem Herodis haesitatio orta est ex variis vulgi de Christo sententiis, quas recensent Marcus, & Lucas locis citatis.
units.tr: 2. And he said. Not affirming, but hesitating and doubting, as is clear from the passage of Luke cited. Herod's hesitation arose from the various opinions of the crowd about Christ, which Mark and Luke recount in the passages cited.

units.la: Virtutes operantur in eo. Id est, potestates patrandi miracula vim suam exerunt in eo, quam ante, dum viveret, non exerebant.
units.tr: Powers work in him. That is, the powers of performing miracles exert their force in him, which they did not exert before, while he was alive.

units.la: Herodes enim, &c. Incarceratio Joannis, quam Lucas c. 3. v. 19. anticipavit; Matthaeus vero & Marcus decollationi junxerunt, quando contigerit, vide supra c. 4. v. 12. p. 47.
units.tr: For Herod, etc. The imprisonment of John, which Luke anticipated in chapter 3, verse 19; Matthew and Mark joined it to the beheading. When it happened, see above, chapter 4, verse 12, page 47.

units.la: - Propter Herodiadem. Filiam Aristobuli fratris sui. Josephus aliam causam affert, motum scilicet novationis rerum, quod verisimile est Pharisaeos suggessisse Herodi, & eorum invidia & authoritate captum Joannem; alioqui enim Herodes nec capere fuisset ausus; quod significat Dominus infra c. 17. v. 12. nisi suppleatur ibi nominativus, Iudaei, quae vox tam Herodem & Galilaeos proceres, quam Pontifices; Senatores, & Legis-peritos, illos Baptistæ, hos Christi interfectores comprehendat.
units.tr: - On account of Herodias. The daughter of Aristobulus, his brother. Josephus gives another cause, namely a movement toward political upheaval. It is likely that the Pharisees suggested this to Herod, and that John was seized through their hatred and influence; otherwise Herod would not have dared to arrest him. The Lord indicates this below, in chapter 17, verse 12, unless the nominative the Jews is supplied there, a word that embraces both Herod and the Galilean nobles as well as the high priests, senators and lawyers, the former as John's killers and the latter as Christ's.

units.la: Uxorem fratris sui. Addit Marc. Philippi. Is autem Philippus non Tetrarcha Trachonitidis filius Herodis magni ex Cleopatra, de quo Luc. c. 3. v. 1. sed alius Herodis item magni filius ex Mariamne Simonis Pontificis filia; quem Josephus lib. 1. de bello Judaico c. 18. Herodem nominat: quare Binominus fuerit necesse est; sicut & ipse Herodes, qui Joannem occidit, vocabatur Herodes, & Antipater, aut Antipas.
units.tr: His brother's wife. Mark adds, of Philip. This Philip was not the tetrarch of Trachonitis, the son of Herod the Great by Cleopatra, concerning whom see Luke chapter 3, verse 1, but another son, likewise of Herod the Great, by Mariamne, daughter of Simon the high priest, whom Josephus, in Jewish War book 1, chapter 18, calls Herod. So he must have had two names, just as Herod who killed John was called both Herod and Antipater or Antipas.

units.la: 4. Non licet tibi habere uxorem fratris tui. Dicitur enim Levitic. 18. v. 16. Turpitudinem uxoris fratris tui non revelabis: à qua Lege nulla datur exceptio, nisi Deuteron. 25. dum frater fuerit defunctus sine liberis; constat autem ex Josepho & Philippum seu Herodem adhuc fuisse superstitem, dum Herodes Antipas Herodiadem ejus uxorem in conjugium, & domicilium suum migrare jussit; insuper etsi Philippus fuisset defunctus, non licuisset tamen per Legem Herodi Antipæ eam ducere uxorem, cùm Philippus ex ea suscepisset filiam, quam ipse nominat Salomen, Evangelistæ cognominant saltatricem.
units.tr: 4. It is not lawful for you to have your brother's wife. For Leviticus 18, verse 16, says: You shall not uncover the nakedness of your brother's wife. No exception is given to this law except Deuteronomy 25, when the brother has died without children. It is established from Josephus that Philip, or Herod, was still alive when Herod Antipas ordered Herodias, his wife, to come into his marriage and into his home. Moreover, even if Philip had died, it would still not have been lawful for Herod Antipas to take her as wife under the Law, since Philip had had a daughter by her, whom Josephus names Salome and whom the Evangelists call the dancing girl.

units.la: 5. Volens illam occidere. Scilicet, ad placendum Herodiadi; ipse enim ut dicitur Marc. 6. v. 20. metuebat, id est, reverebatur Joannem, sciens eum virum justum & sanctum, & custodiebat, id est, tuebatur eum ab insidiis Herodiadis, & audito eo multa faciebat, & libenter eum audiebat.
units.tr: 5. Wanting to kill him. That is, in order to please Herodias. For as Mark says in chapter 6, verse 20, Herod feared, that is, he revered John, knowing him to be a just and holy man, and kept him, that is, protected him from the snares of Herodias, and when he heard him, he did many things and heard him gladly.

units.la: Timuit populum. Ne Herodiadi Herodes faceret satis & sanctitas Joannis, ut sidem faciunt verba, mox ex Marco citata, & metus populi, ut hîc testatur Matthæus, prohibebant. Facilè deviat à justitia, qui in causis non Deum, sed homines pertimescit. Hîc timor peccandi facultatem differre potest, auferre non potest voluntatem: unde etiam quos suspendit à crimine avidiores reddit ad crimen, & æstuat animo quoufquae perficiat, quod cogitat, malum. Solus est Dei timor, (filialis) qui mentes corrigit, fugat crimina, & innocentiam servat. B. Petrus Chrysologus Ser. 127.
units.tr: He feared the people. That Herod should not give satisfaction to Herodias, and the holiness of John, as the words quoted soon after from Mark make clear, and the fear of the people, as Matthew testifies here, restrained him. He easily turns aside from justice who fears men rather than God in his causes. Such fear may defer the opportunity of sinning, but it cannot remove the will; hence those whom it restrains from crime make them more eager for crime, and they seethe in mind until they carry out the evil they are planning. Only the fear of God, the filial fear, corrects minds, puts crimes to flight, and preserves innocence. Saint Peter Chrysologus, Sermon 127.

units.la: 9. Propter juramentum. Præpostera religio; nam juramenta ejusmodi generalia intelligi debent de licitis & possibilibus juranti: quin imò, licèt in animo jurantis ad illicita se extenderent, non tamen obligant, sed rescindenda est eorum fides. Vide B. Greg. lib. 5. in 1 Reg. 14. v. 45.
units.tr: 9. On account of the oath. A misguided scruple. For oaths of this kind, being general, ought to be understood as concerning what is lawful and possible for the one swearing. Indeed, even if in the mind of the one swearing they extended to unlawful things, they do not bind, but their pledge must be annulled. See Saint Gregory, book 5, on 1 Kings, chapter 14, verse 45.

units.la: Et eos. Q. d. Ne proceribus Galilæis simul recumbentibus inconstans aut perjurus videretur. Nullum alium invenimus obferoasse diem natalis sui, nisi Herodem & Pharaonem: ut quorum erat par impietas, esset & una solemnitas, observat hîc B. Hier.
units.tr: And those who reclined with him. That is, lest he should seem fickle or forsworn to the Galilean nobles reclining with him at the same time. Saint Jerome observes here: We find that no one else kept his birthday except Herod and Pharaoh, so that, since their impiety was equal, their festivity might also be one.

units.la: 10. Misitque, & decollavit. Q. d. misit qui decollaret; nam non ipse decollavit eum, sed spiculator, sive carnifex, quem ad eam rem miserat in carcerem, ut dicitur Marc. 6.
units.tr: 10. He sent and beheaded him. That is, he sent someone to behead him. For he did not himself behead him, but an executioner, or headsman, whom he had sent into the prison for this purpose, as Mark says in chapter 6.

units.la: 13. Quod cum audisset. Non ad mortem Joannis hoc referendum est; jamdiu enim contigerat; sed potius ad sermones, qui de Christo in aula Herodis habebantur; cum enim Matthaeus de illis sermonibus agere coepisset, illorum occasione interpositis incarceratione Joannis, ejusque decollatione, eo quod Christus crederetur a quibusdam Joannes redivivus, redit unde abierat- Cum audisset, inquit, Jesus quid de se Herodes exitimaret, secessit in desertum, non ob hanc solam causam, sed etiam ut Apostolis ab Evangelii munere redeuntibus & fatigatis, requiescendi spatium daret, quod narrant Marcus. c. 6. v. 31. & Lucas c. 9. v. 10.
units.tr: 13. When he heard this. This should not be referred to the death of John, for that had happened long before. It refers rather to the talk about Christ that was going on at Herod's court. For when Matthew had begun to deal with those reports, he inserted, on the occasion of them, the imprisonment of John and his beheading, since some believed Christ to be John risen from the dead, and he returns to where he had left off. When Jesus heard, says the text, what Herod thought of him, he withdrew into the desert, not for this reason alone, but also so that he might give the Apostles, returning and weary from the office of the Gospel, a space for rest, as Mark, chapter 6, verse 31, and Luke, chapter 9, verse 10, relate.

units.la: Secessit inde. Supple ex loco citato Lucae, assumtis discipulis.
units.tr: He withdrew from there. Supply from the passage of Luke cited: taking the disciples with him.

units.la: In locum desertum. Supple ex loco citato Lucae, qui est Bethsaida. Desertum autem dicebatur Bethsaidae, quod, interjecto mari Galilaeae, e regione esset, ut patet ex Joan. 6. v. 1. ideo satis perceperunt, qui Jesum abeuntem videbant, eum in desertum illud secedere, ad quod cum pedestre iter esset, nonnihil circumeundo, turbae undique illuc properarunt, multi currendo & praevenientes, ut ait Marc. c. 6. v. 33. & multi sequendo, ut Matth. hic & Luc. c. 9. v. 11. & Joan. c. 6. v. 2. narrant.
units.tr: To a deserted place. Supply from the passage of Luke cited: which is Bethsaida. The desert was called that of Bethsaida, because it lay opposite across the sea of Galilee, as is clear from John 6, verse 1. Therefore those who saw Jesus going away understood well enough that he was withdrawing into that desert. Since the way there was on foot, and they had to go round somewhat, the crowds hurried there from every side, many running ahead and outstripping him, as Mark says in chapter 6, verse 33, and many following, as Matthew here, and Luke, chapter 9, verse 11, and John, chapter 6, verse 2, relate.

units.la: 14. Et exiens. Scilicet, e navicula, subiit ut dicitur Joan. 6. v. 3. in montem, & ibi sedebat cum discipulis suis, deinde sublevans oculos vidit turbam multam ad se venientem, & misertus est eis, eósque benigne excepit & curavit languidos eorum usque ad vesperam, quâ imminente duodecim discipuli monuerunt Christum ut turbam in proximas villas dimitteret, ubi corpus cibo reficere possent; at Christus jussit ut ipsi discipuli darent turbae manducare: atque ut Philippo propria fidei imbecillitas innotesceret, explorans utrum deficientibus humanis mediis ad Magistri omnipotentiam & providentiam recurreret, dixit ad eum: Unde comparabimus pretium, ut emamus cibos multitudini reficiendae necessarios? Respondit Philippus frustra adhiberi hanc sollicitudinem, cum nec ducentorum denariorum panes tantae turbae alendae sufficerent. Suam autem mentem Philippus expressit, vel his verbis Joannis c. 6. v. 7. Ducentorum denariorum panes non sufficiunt eis, ut unusquisque modicum quid accipiat; vel his verbis quasi per ironiam dictis. Marc. 6. v. 37. Euntes emamus ducentis denariis panes, & dabimus illis manducare. Tum Jesus dixit discipulis; Quot panes habetis? ite & videte. Et cùm vidissent respondit omnium nomine Andreas, Est puer unus hîc, qui habet quinque panes hordeaceos, & duos pisces, sed hæc quid inter tantos, nisi nos eamus & emamus in omnem hanc turbam escas? Hoc audito, Jesus iussit sibi afferri panes, & pisces, quos eo modo multiplicavit, ut omnibus reficiendis non sufficerent modò, sed & duodecim cophini fragmentorum pleni superesset. Hoc modo ordinanda est praesens multiplicationis panum historia, & apparebit nullam prorsus esse inter quatuor Evangelistas dissonantiam.
units.tr: 14. And going out. That is, out of the little boat; he went up, as John 6, verse 3, says, into the mountain, and there sat with his disciples. Then, lifting up his eyes, he saw a great crowd coming toward him, had compassion on them, received them kindly, and healed their sick until evening. As evening drew near, the twelve disciples advised Christ to send the crowd away into the nearby villages, where they could feed their bodies with food. But Christ ordered the disciples themselves to give the crowd something to eat. And so that the weakness of Philip's own faith might be made known, testing whether, when human means failed, he would turn to the Master's omnipotence and providence, he said to him: Where shall we buy bread, so that we may buy food necessary for feeding such a multitude? Philip replied that this anxiety was useless, since not even bread worth two hundred denarii would suffice to feed so great a crowd. Philip expressed his mind either in these words of John, chapter 6, verse 7: Bread worth two hundred denarii is not enough for them, so that each may receive a little; or in these words, spoken as if by irony, Mark 6, verse 37: Let us go and buy bread for two hundred denarii, and give them something to eat. Then Jesus said to the disciples: How many loaves do you have? Go and see. And when they had seen, Andrew answered on behalf of all: There is one boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish, but what are these among so many? Unless we go and buy food for this whole crowd. Having heard this, Jesus ordered the loaves and fish to be brought to him, and he multiplied them in such a way that they not only sufficed to feed everyone, but twelve baskets full of fragments were left over. In this way the present history of the multiplication of the loaves is to be arranged, and it will appear that there is no discrepancy at all among the four Evangelists.

units.la: 19. Cùm iussisset turbam discumbere super fænum. Id est, cùm praecepisset discipulis ut accumbere facerent omnes secundum contubernia super viride fœnum in partes, per centenos & quinquagenos, ut dicitur Marc. 6. v. 39.
units.tr: 19. When he had commanded the crowd to recline upon the grass. That is, when he had instructed the disciples to have everyone recline in their companies upon the green grass, in groups, by hundreds and by fifties, as is said in Mark 6:39.

units.la: Aspiciens in cœlum benedixit. Nempe panibus, ut patet ex Luc. 7. v. 16. Hoc autem fecit Jesus Hebræorum more; solent enim Hebræi hodieque, cùm ad mensam accedunt, priusquam panes frangant, impositis manibus benedicere illis hac formulâ: Benedictus tu Dominus Deus noster Rex mundi, qui educis panem de terra. Hac formulâ si usus est Christus, nemo mirabitur Joannem his verbis usum: Cùm gratias egisset, pro eo quod alii tres Evangelistæ expresserunt per vocem benedixit; eadem quippe panum benedictio gratiarum actionem continet.
units.tr: He looked up to heaven and blessed. Namely the loaves, as is clear from Luke 7:16. Jesus did this in the manner of the Hebrews. For the Hebrews even today, when they come to the table, before they break the bread, lay their hands on it and bless it with this formula: Blessed are you, Lord our God, King of the world, who bring forth bread from the earth. If Christ used this formula, no one will be surprised that John, using other words, when he had given thanks, expressed what the other three Evangelists expressed by the word blessed; for the blessing of the bread contains the giving of thanks.

units.la: Dedit discipulis panes, & discipuli turbis. Quia per Apostolos erant divinæ gratiæ dona inferioribus hominibus reddenda, id est, communicanda, ut ait B. Hilar. can. 14. in Matth.
units.tr: He gave the loaves to the disciples, and the disciples to the crowds. Because through the Apostles the gifts of divine grace were to be given to, that is, shared with, people of lower rank, as Blessed Hilary says in his Canons on Matthew, canon 14.

units.la: 21. Fuit numerus quinque millia virorum. Supple, circiter, ut patet ex textu Græco hîc, & Marc. 6. v. 44. & ex ipso textu Latino Joan. 6. v. 10.
units.tr: 21. The number was five thousand men. Supply "about," as is clear from the Greek text here, from Mark 6:44, and from the Latin text itself in John 6:10.

units.la: Exceptis mulieribus & parvulis. Mulieres & parvuli, sexus fragilis & ætas minor, numero indigni sunt. Unde & in Numerorum libro quoties sacerdotes atque Levitæ, & exercitus vel turba pugnantium describuntur: servi, & mulieres, & parvuli, & vulgus ignobile absque numero prætermittitur. B. Hier.
units.tr: Besides women and children. Women and children, the weaker sex and the younger age, are unworthy of being counted. Hence also in the book of Numbers, whenever priests and Levites, or an army or a crowd of fighters, are listed, servants, women, children and the common rabble are passed over without being counted. Blessed Jerome.

units.la: 22. Statim. Postquam Christus in manibus suis multiplicasset quinque panes, quomodo Deus multiplicat de paucis granis segetes, agnitus est pro vero Messia à turba, ut testatur Joan. c. 6. v. 14. cùmque Jesus cognovisset, quòd iidem homines tanto miraculo commoti venturi essent ut raperent eum & facerent regem, compulit discipulos suos ascendere in naviculam, ut præcederent eum trans fretum ad Bethsaidam, donec dimitteret turbas, ut dicitur Marc. 6. v. 45. Joan. 6. v. 14, & 15. Ut autem fero factum est descenderunt discipuli ad mare, & cùm ascendissent navim, venerunt trans mare primò in terram Genefareth, quæ & Genefar, & Cenereth, & Ceneroth, & Tiberias dicitur; deinde aliquot miraculis ibi factis à Christo, appulerunt Capharnaum; ipse verò Christus cùm valedixisset turbæ, iterum rediit solus oraturus in montem, è quo descenderat ad turbam ante panum multiplicationem.
units.tr: 22. Immediately. After Christ had multiplied the five loaves in his hands, as God multiplies crops from a few grains, he was acknowledged as the true Messiah by the crowd, as John 6:14 attests. And when Jesus knew that these same men, moved by so great a miracle, were about to come and seize him and make him king, he made his disciples get into the boat and go ahead of him across the sea to Bethsaida, until he dismissed the crowds, as Mark 6:45 and John 6:14–15 say. When this was done, the disciples went down to the sea, and when they had got into the ship, they first crossed the sea to the land of Gennesaret, also called Genesar, Cinnereth, Cinneroth and Tiberias; then, after some miracles performed there by Christ, they arrived at Capernaum. Christ himself, having bid farewell to the crowd, went back alone up the mountain to pray, from which he had come down to the crowd before the multiplication of the loaves.

units.la: Vespere autem facto solus erat ibi. Cùm Matthæus ante panum multiplicationem dicat supra v. 13. vespere autem facto, quod tamen aliquot horis ante secundum illum Christi secessum in montem contigit, palam fit vespertinum tempus ab Hebræis dividi in duas vesperas; unam meridiei, alteram occasui propiorem, quarum initium est tempus, ut aiunt Talmudistæ Tract. de Pascha te c. 5. à quo sol incipit in occasum vergere: hoc est, ut ibidem exponit Glossa, primâ semi-horâ post meridiem; finis verò duarum vesperarum est solis occasus; cùm illud spatium, quod ambæ vesperæ complectuntur, intra quod die decimâ quartâ mensis primi immolari jubetur Pascha Exod. 12. Levit. 23. Num. 9. patet ex Deut. 16. v. 6. durasse usque ad solis occasum; siquidem agnus Paschalis, qui ex locis mox citatis immolandus est inter, seu intra duas vesperas, ibi legitur immolandus vespere, ad (id est, circa) solis occasum. Rabbini, & Chaldei duas vesperas alio nomine appellant inter-soles, seu, duos soles, & utrilibet horum duarum sesqui-horarum spatium assignant. Duplicem hanc vesperam agnoscit Eustathius in lib. 17. Odyss. Suidas addit Atticum esse hoc loquendi genus, ejusque proferuntur exempla ex Philemone. Eodem pertinet illud Varronis in Satyra Menippea, Nescis quid vesper ferus vehat. Vesper ferus, id est, δεῖλη ὀψία, cui ἑσπέρια opponitur apud Hesychium, & Eustathium loco mox laudato.
units.tr: And when evening had come, he was there alone. Since Matthew, before the multiplication of the loaves, says above in verse 15, and when evening had come, which nevertheless happened some hours before Christ's withdrawal to the mountain mentioned here, it is plain that the Hebrews divided the evening time into two evenings: one from midday, and the other nearer to sunset. The beginning of these is the time at which, as the Talmudists say in the tractate on the Passover, chapter 5, the sun begins to decline toward the west; that is, as the Gloss explains in the same place, the first half-hour after noon. The end of the two evenings is sunset. That the space covered by both evenings, within which on the fourteenth day of the first month the Passover is commanded to be sacrificed (Exod. 12; Lev. 23; Num. 9), lasted until sunset is clear from Deut. 16:6; for the Passover lamb, which by the passages just cited is to be sacrificed between, or within, the two evenings, is there read to be sacrificed in the evening, at (that is, about) sunset. The rabbis and the Chaldeans call the two evenings by another name, between-suns, or two suns, and assign a space of an hour and a half to each of these. Eustathius, in his commentary on book 17 of the Odyssey, recognizes this double evening. Suidas adds that this way of speaking is Attic, and examples are cited from Philemon. To the same point belongs Varro's line in the Menippean Satire: You do not know what the wild evening brings. "Wild evening" is the Greek deile opsia [δεῖλη ὀψία], which in Hesychius and in Eustathius, cited just above, is set against hesperia [ἑσπέρια].

units.la: 25. Quartâ autem vigiliâ noctis. Hebræi veteriores dividebant noctem in tres vigilias, quarum prima dicitur Thren. 2. v. 19. principium vigiliarum. Qui per hanc noctis partem vigilabant, ibant cubitum cùm secunda noctis pars inciperet, & alii vigiles è somno excitati his succedebant per secundam noctis vigiliam, quæ Judicum 7. v. 19. dicitur media, seu vigilia noctis media. Tertia denique vigilia dicitur Exod 14. v. 24. vigilia matutina. B. Lucas c. 12. v. 38. more veteri tertiam vigiliam videtur habere pro ultima. At Romanis demum temporibus pro tribus vigiliis, quatuor constitui coeperunt, unde in præsenti versiculo & Marc. 6. v. 48. quartæ vigiliæ mentio est.
units.tr: 25. In the fourth watch of the night. The older Hebrews divided the night into three watches. The first is called, in Lam. 2:19, the beginning of the watches. Those who kept watch during this part of the night went to bed when the second part of the night began, and other watchmen, roused from sleep, took their place during the second watch of the night, which in Judg. 7:19 is called the middle, or the middle watch of the night. Lastly, the third watch is called, in Exod. 14:24, the morning watch. Blessed Luke, in chapter 12, verse 38, seems by the old custom to take the third watch as the last. But only in Roman times did they begin to count four watches instead of three; hence in the present verse, and in Mark 6:48, there is mention of the fourth watch.

units.la: 26. Videntes eum. Adde ex Joan. c. 6. v. 19. cum remigassent quasi stadia viginti quinque aut triginta.
units.tr: 26. Seeing him. Add from John 6:19: when they had rowed about twenty-five or thirty stadia.

units.la: Phantasma. Id est, spectrum, quod melius dicitur Graece φάσμα.
units.tr: A phantasm. That is, an apparition, which in Greek is better called phantasma [φάσμα].

units.la: 27. Habete fiduciam. Scilicet, in me praesente.
units.tr: 27. Have confidence. Namely, in me, who am present.

units.la: 28. Si tu es. Non de Christi virtute dubitat Petrus, sed de persona, nam & spectrum poterat Christi effigiem & vocem ejus ementiri.
units.tr: 28. If you are he. Peter does not doubt Christ's power, but his person, for an apparition could also imitate Christ's likeness and voice.

units.la: Jube. Ita, scilicet, ut res ipsa sequatur; alias enim & spectrum hoc jubere poterat.
units.tr: Bid me. That is, so that the thing itself would follow; otherwise that apparition too could command this.

units.la: 30. Timuit. Cum Christo tamen jam esset propior; Haec enim est humana conditio naturae, ut difficilioribus nonnunquam superatis, in minoribus succumbat, ut praeclare observat Chrysostomus.
units.tr: 30. He was afraid. Yet he was already nearer to Christ. "For this is the human condition: having overcome the greater difficulties, we sometimes give way in lesser ones," as Chrysostom remarkably observes.

units.la: Clamavit. Nempe praesentia pericula sopitam excitant fidem & dilectionem.
units.tr: He cried out. Namely, present dangers rouse faith and love that had lain dormant.

units.la: 31. Modicae fidei. Increpat Christus Petrum, ut admoneretur non a vento valido, sed ab imbecilla fide periculum submersionis provenisse.
units.tr: 31. O you of little faith. Christ rebukes Peter so that he would be reminded that the danger of sinking came not from the strong wind but from weak faith.

units.la: 32. Et cum ascendissent. Nimirum Christus, & Petrus in naviculam, cessavit ventus. Alterum addit miraculum Joan. c. 6. v. 21. nempe statim atque cum Petro ascendisset Christus in naviculam: navim subito appulisse ad terram, cum discipuli vellent, ut solebant, una cum Christo navigare.
units.tr: 32. And when they had got into the boat. Of course, when Christ and Peter got into the boat, the wind ceased. John 6:21 adds another miracle: as soon as Christ had got into the boat with Peter, the ship suddenly reached the land, though the disciples had wished, as they usually did, to sail along with Christ.

units.la: Vere filius Dei es. Hac confessione non videntur Apostoli intellexisse Filium Dei naturalem, sed adoptivum ceteris praestantiorem, & Messiam promissum; nam ex c. 16. Matth. v. 16. & 17. manifeste colligitur Simonem Petrum primum fuisse, qui Christum Dominum ex revelatione Patris coelestis palam confessus fuerit esse Filium Dei vivi naturalem.
units.tr: Truly you are the Son of God. By this confession the Apostles do not seem to have understood the Son of God in the natural sense, but an adopted son, superior to the others, and the promised Messiah. For from Matt. 16:16–17 it is plainly gathered that Simon Peter was the first who, by revelation of the heavenly Father, openly confessed Christ the Lord to be the natural Son of the living God.

units.la: 34. Venerunt in terram Genesar. A qua terra Genesar, seu Genesareth deinde venerunt in Capharnaum, ut dicitur Joan. 6. v. 17.
units.tr: 34. They came to the land of Gennesar. From that land of Gennesar, or Gennesareth, they then came to Capernaum, as John 6:17 says.

units.la: Quicunque tetigerunt, &c. Non minus absurde hinc infertur, licitum esse Crucis Domini & Reliquiarum cultum, quam siquis inferret umbras Sanctorum esse religiose colendas, quia Petri umbra inumbrati liberabantur ab infirmitatibus suis, Act. 5. v. 15.
units.tr: Whoever touched him, etc. It is no less absurd to infer from this that the cult of the Cross of the Lord and of relics is lawful, than it would be to infer that the shadows of the Saints are to be venerated religiously, because by Peter's shadow the sick were freed from their infirmities, Acts 5:15.

units.la: CAPUT. XV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XV.

units.la: 1. SENIORUM
units.tr: 1. OF THE ELDERS

units.la: Sensus genuinus hujus loci est: id quo à me juvari possis, id omne est Corban, seu Deo devotum. Meritò itaque redarguit Christus Pharifæos absolventes eum à culpa violati præcepti de honorandis parentibus, qui fe non exhibuerit beneficium in egenos parentes, modò id, quo ipforum inopias sublevare posset, Deo devoverit; merito, inquam, Pharifæos sic sentientes redarguit Christus, quia qui Deo vovet quæ patri necefforia sunt, aliena vovet, non sua; nam pars bonorum; quâ pater eget, mea non est, sed patris; dicitur autem Proverb. 3. Honora Dominum de tua substantia: de injusto immolantis oblatio ridicula est, proindè David Areunæ Regis boves emit & solvit, Deóque tum demum obtulit. Emam, inquit David, pretio à te, & non osseram Domino Deo meo holocausta gratuita 2 Sam. seu Reg. 24. v. 24.
units.tr: The true sense of this passage is this: whatever you could be helped by me with, that is all Corban, that is, devoted to God. Christ rightly rebukes the Pharisees, who absolve a man of guilt for breaking the command to honour his parents if he has not given aid to his needy parents, provided that he has devoted to God what could have relieved their want. Christ rightly rebukes the Pharisees for thinking this, I say, because whoever vows to God what his father needs is vowing what belongs to another, not to himself. For the part of his goods of which the father is in need is not mine but my father's. It is said in Proverbs 3: Honour the Lord from your substance. The offering of one who sacrifices what he has gained unjustly is ridiculous. So David bought the oxen of King Araunah, paid for them, and only then offered them to God. I will buy them, said David, from you for a price, and I will not offer burnt offerings to the Lord my God that cost me nothing, 2 Sam. or Reg. 24. v. 24.

units.la: Queritur hîc Christus populum Dei abductum fuisse ab observatione mandatorum divinorum, dum toti incumbebant in traditiones Pharifeorum. Hoc ipsum Joannes Gerfon de vita Spirit. parte 3. reprehendit in colluvie ceremoniarum & traditionum Romanenfium: Supervacua, inquit, occupatio circa traditiones humanas gignit ignorantiam divinorum præceptorum.
units.tr: Here Christ complains that the people of God had been drawn away from keeping the divine commandments, because they devoted themselves entirely to the traditions of the Pharisees. John Gerson, in De vita spirituali, part 3, censures this very thing in the mass of Roman ceremonies and traditions: A superfluous preoccupation with human traditions, he says, breeds ignorance of the divine precepts.

units.la: Cor. Id est; voluntas.
units.tr: Heart. That is, the will.

units.la: frivolus enim est cultus exterior fine interiori, seu fine charitate: quia Deus charitate colitur.
units.tr: For external worship without inner worship, that is, without love, is empty, since God is worshipped with love.

units.la: Docentes doctrinas & mandata hominum. Rejicit hîc Christus illas Judæorum traditiones, quas deuterofes vocant, à Pharisæis excogitatas, præpostero pietatis studio, ut pote quæ ut plurimum repugnant Legi Dei, vel saltem nihil ad sincerum pietatis cultum conducunt, ut videre est, apud Hieronymum Ep. 151. ad Algasiam quæst. 10. & in commentariis in Esaiam. Non rejicit autem Dominus mandata Legi Dei non repugnantia, si præscribantur ab iis, qui legitimam potestatem habent, vel externi ordinis causâ, vel quatenus ad finem aliquem utilem referri possunt.
units.tr: Teaching doctrines and commandments of men. Here Christ rejects those Jewish traditions, which they call deuterosis, devised by the Pharisees with a perverse zeal for piety. Such traditions for the most part conflict with the Law of God, or at least contribute nothing to sincere worship of God, as can be seen in Jerome, Ep. 151 to Algasia, question 10, and in his commentary on Isaiah. The Lord does not, however, reject commandments that do not conflict with the Law of God, if they are prescribed by those who have lawful authority, either for the sake of external order or insofar as they can be referred to some useful end.

units.la: 11. Non quod intrat. Jam reddit Christus directè rationem turbis de discipulorum suorum facto.
units.tr: 11. Not what enters. Now Christ directly gives the crowd the reason for his disciples' action.

units.la: Coinquinat hominem. Clarius Marc. 7. v. 15. Nihil est extra hominem introiens in eum, quod possit eum coinquinare, sed quæ de homine procedunt (quod Matthæus ut antithesim servaret, Synecdochicè exprimit per hæc verba, ex ore) illa sunt quæ communicant, id est, inquinant, hominem. Advertit autem Aug. lib. 15. de Trinitate c. 10. ex hoc loco constare duo esse quædam hominis ora, unum corporis, alterum cordis.
units.tr: Defiles a man. More clearly in Mark 7. v. 15: Nothing that enters a man from outside can defile him, but the things that come out of a man (which Matthew, to keep the antithesis, expresses by synecdoche in these words, from the mouth) are the things that defile, that is, pollute, a man. Augustine, in De Trinitate book 15, chapter 10, notes that from this passage it is clear that there are two mouths of a man, one of the body and one of the heart.

units.la: 12. Scandalizati. Id est, offensi.
units.tr: 12. Offended. That is, taken offence.

units.la: 13. Omnis plantatio. Id est, planta. Intelligitur autem hic per plantationem reprobam & succidendam, genus illud hominum, quod per traditionem suam irritum fecit Dei mandatum; habet enim consuetudo Scripturæ, ut ipsos homines vocet palmites, genimina, germina, arbores & vineas. Hinc author de vocat. Gent. lib. 1. cap. 6. ait quòd quidquid non est eradicandum, manifestum est à Patre esse plantatum.
units.tr: 13. Every plant. That is, plant. Here the reprobate plant to be rooted out is understood to be that kind of people who by their tradition have made the command of God void. For it is the custom of Scripture to call men themselves branches, shoots, sprouts, trees and vines. Hence the author of De vocatione gentium book 1, chapter 6, says that whatever is not to be uprooted is clearly planted by the Father.

units.la: Sinite illos. Ecce magistra veritas ne in quorundam cordibus scandalum gigneretur, quod non debuit tributum dedit. Et rursum quia generari scandalum in quorumdam cordibus contra veritatem vidit, in suo eos scandalo remanere permisit. Ex qua re nobis considerandum est, quia in quantum sine peccato possumus, vitare proximorum scandalum debemus. Si autem de veritate scandalum sumitur, utilius permittitur nasci scandalum, quam veritas relinquatur. B. Greg. Hom. 7. in Ezech. Idem docet in Epistolarum lib. 9. Ep. 39. ad Theotistam Patritiam. Hinc D. Th. 22. q. 43. ar. 7. ad 2. propter nullum scandalum, quod sequi videatur, debet homo prætermissa veritate falsitatem docere.
units.tr: Let them alone. Behold, the teacher Truth, so that a stumbling block might not arise in the hearts of some, gave what ought not to have been given. And again, because she saw that a stumbling block was being produced in the hearts of some against the truth, she allowed them to remain in their stumbling. From this we must consider that, so far as we can without sin, we ought to avoid causing a stumbling block to our neighbours. But if the stumbling block is taken from the truth, it is more useful to allow the stumbling block to arise than for the truth to be abandoned. Blessed Gregory, Homily 7 on Ezekiel. He teaches the same in the Letters, book 9, letter 39, to Theotista the Patrician. Hence St. Thomas, II-II, question 43, article 7, reply 2: On account of no stumbling block that seems likely to follow, may a man, passing over the truth, teach what is false.

units.la: Cæci sunt. Cæcos appellat mentem non habentes illustratam à Patre luminum, nec scientes viam quæ ducit ad vitam, quos mox ratione malorum affectuum plantatos à Patre suo negavit, & proinde eradicandos affirmavit.
units.tr: They are blind. He calls blind those who do not have their mind illuminated by the Father of lights, and do not know the way that leads to life. Soon afterwards, on account of the evil affections, he declared that they had not been planted by his Father, and therefore affirmed that they must be rooted out.

units.la: Ambo in foveam cadunt. Pastorum imperitia meritis congruit tape subiectorum, qui quamvis lumen scientiæ suâ culpâ agente non habeant, dissimulo tamen Dei judicio agitur, ut per eorum ignoignorantiam hi etiam qui sequuntur offendant. Hinc namque in Evangelio per semetipsam veritas dicit: Si cæcus cæco ducatum præbeat, ambo in foveam cadunt. Hinc Psalmista non optantis animo, sed prophetantis ministerio denuntiat dicens: Obscurentur oculi eorum ne videant: & dorsum eorum semper incurva. Oculi quippe sunt, qui in ipsa honoris summi facie positi providendi itineris officium suscipiunt: quibus hi nimirum qui subsequenter inhærent dorsa nominantur. Obscuratis ergo oculis dorsum flectitur: quia cum lumen scientiæ perdunt qui præeunt; profecto cuncti ad portanda peccatorum onera curvantur qui sequuntur. B. Greg. Past. I. p. cap. I.
units.tr: Both fall into the pit. The inexperience of the teachers rightly matches the merits of their subjects. Although these have no light of knowledge through their own fault, nevertheless, by the judgement of God it happens that through their ignorance those who follow them also stumble. Hence in the Gospel Truth itself says: If a blind man leads a blind man, both fall into a pit. Hence the Psalmist announces, not with the wish of his mind but by the ministry of prophecy, saying: Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see, and bend their back always. For the eyes are those who, placed in the very face of the highest honour, take on the office of providing the way; these, of course, are the ones who cling to them afterwards and are called their backs. So when the eyes are darkened, the back is bent; for when those who go before lose the light of knowledge, surely all who follow are bowed down to carry the burdens of sins. Blessed Gregory, Pastoral Care, part 1, chapter 1.

units.la: Respondens autem Petrus. Scilicet, nomine omnium discipulorum, cum Christus introisset in domum dimissis turbis, ut patet ex Marc. 7. v. 17.
units.tr: Peter answering. That is, in the name of all the disciples, when Christ had entered the house after the crowds were sent away, as is clear from Mark 7. v. 17.

units.la: 16. Adhuc & vos sine intellectu estis? Quod aperte dictum suerat, & patebat auditui, Apostolus Petrus per parabolam dictum putat, & in re manifesta mysticam quærit intelligentiam: corripiturque a Domino, quare parabolicæ dictum putet, quod perspicue locutus est. Ex quo animadvertimus vitiosum esse auditorem qui aut obscura manifestè, aut manifesta dicta obscure velit intelligere. B. Hier.
units.tr: 16. Are you also still without understanding? Peter, the apostle, thinks that what had been plainly said, and was clear to the hearing, was spoken in a parable, and seeks a mystical understanding in a matter that is manifest. He is rebuked by the Lord for thinking that a thing said plainly was said in a parable. From this we notice that a hearer is at fault who wishes either to understand obscure things as if they were plain, or plain things as if they were obscure. Blessed Jerome.

units.la: 17. Quod in os intrat. Supple, immundum & sordium plenum, non potest communicare, id est, inquinare, hominem, quia non intrat in cor ejus, id est, in ipsius animam. Stultum est sanctitatem aut justitiam quærere in illis rebus caducis, terrenis & corruptibilibus, vel pollutionem aliquam & peccati contaminationem ab istis metuere; sunt enim hujusmodi omnia nec bona, nec mala in se, sed perinde sunt hominibus atque animi illorum sunt, qui eis utuntur.
units.tr: 17. What enters the mouth. Supply: what is unclean and full of filth cannot communicate, that is, defile, a man, because it does not enter his heart, that is, his soul. It is foolish to seek holiness or righteousness in those transient, earthly and corruptible things, or to fear from them any pollution or contamination of sin. For all such things are neither good nor evil in themselves, but they are to men exactly what the minds of those who use them are.

units.la: In secessum emittitur. Id est, quidquid immunditiæ & sordium cibo inest, homo per fæces ejicit & in secessum emittit, relicta in corpore puriori substantia. Unde Marcus cap. 7. v. 19. addit: purgans omnes esca: id est, hac sui emissione secernens quod impurum & fæculentum est in cibo, ab eo quod purum & mundum eidem inest. Origenes in præsentem Evangelii locum propugnat & Eucharistiam, juxta id quod habet materiale, in ventrem abire & in secessum ejici. Idem videntur sensisse Patres Conc. Tolet. XVI. vetant enim can. VI. Ne grande aliquid in altari proponatur benedictione sacerdotali consecrandum, sed tantum modica oblata, quæ non ventrem illius, qui sumserit gravis farciminis onere premat, nec in digestionem vadat, sed animam alimonia spirituali reficiat. Nempe in Eucharistia consideratur materiale, seu sacramentum, scilicet Panis & vini, quæ per consecrationem fiunt typi & symbola atque Christi corpus & sanguis: hoc materiale non suapte naturâ sanctificat utentem, in ventrem dbit, & in secessum ejicitur, ut loquitur Origenes. Consideratur & formale, seu res, & virtus sacramenti, scilicet proprium Christi corpus, propriusque sanguis post consecrationem præfens spiritualiter, id est, per vinculum Spiritûs, quo fit ut fideliter sumens typicum symbolicúmque Christi corpus & sanguinem, seu, quod idem est, panem & vinum consecratum, revera conjungatur cum ipso proprio corpore & sanguine Christi, licèt locis longè diflerminentur. Hoc formale Eucharistiæ, seu cœnæ Dominicæ nec consumitur, nec corrumpitur, nec in secessum abit, ut verè asserit Joannes Damascenus lib. 4. Orthodoxæ fidei cap. 14.
units.tr: Is cast out into the drain. That is, whatever uncleanness and filth is in food, a man expels through the bowels and sends into the drain, leaving the purer substance in the body. Hence Mark, chapter 7, verse 19, adds: purifying all food, that is, by this discharge separating what is impure and foul in the food from what is pure and clean in it. Origen, on the present passage of the Gospel, defends the view that the Eucharist, according to what it has as material, goes into the belly and is cast out into the drain. The Fathers of the Council of Toledo XVI seem to have held the same view, for in canon 6 they forbid that anything large be placed on the altar to be consecrated by the priestly blessing, but only small offerings, which do not weigh down the belly of him who has received them with the burden of a heavy mass, nor go into digestion, but refresh the soul with spiritual nourishment. Indeed, in the Eucharist what is considered is the material, or sacrament, namely the bread and wine, which by consecration become types and symbols, and the body and blood of Christ. This material does not of itself sanctify the one who uses it; it goes into the belly and is cast out into the drain, as Origen says. There is also considered the formal element, or thing, and power of the sacrament, namely the proper body of Christ and his proper blood present after consecration spiritually, that is, through the bond of the Spirit. The result is that the one who receives faithfully the typical and symbolic body and blood of Christ, or what is the same, the consecrated bread and wine, is truly joined with the very body and blood of Christ, although they are separated by a great distance in place. This formal element of the Eucharist, or of the Lord's Supper, is neither consumed, nor corrupted, nor goes into the drain, as John of Damascus truly asserts in book 4 of De fide orthodoxa, chapter 14.

units.la: 18. De ore. Id est, ab intus, seu de homine; ut enim intrare in os Matthæus dixit pro eo quod Marcus dixit extrinsecus introiens in hominem, sic idem Matthæus ut antithesim servaret procedere de ore dixit quod Marcus de homine exire, & ab intus procedere, pronuntiavit.
units.tr: 18. Out of the mouth. That is, from within, that is, from the man himself. For just as Matthew said to enter into the mouth where Mark said entering from outside into the man, so Matthew, to keep the antithesis, said to proceed out of the mouth where Mark said to go out of the man, and he expressed it as to proceed from within.

units.la: De corde. Id est, ex libero arbitrio.
units.tr: Out of the heart. That is, from free choice.

units.la: Coinquinant. Id est, coinquinare possunt, sicut & sanctificare. Hinc patet sicut & ex Apoltolo pronunciante omnia munda mundis, quòd animalia à Deo in lege interdicta, natura non erant immunda, sed significatione solùm, ut observat B. Aug. lib. 6. contra Faustum c. 7. ubi ait quòd fi de porco & agno requiratur, utrumque natura mundum est, quia omnis creatura Dei bona est, quàdam vero significatione agnus mundus, porcus immundus est; tanquam fi stultum & sapientem diceres, utrumque hoc verbum natura vocis & literarum & syllabarum, quibus conflat, utique mundum est: significatione autem unum horum verbum, quod dicitur stultus, immundum dici potest, non natura fui, sed quoniam quiddam immundum significat; & fortasse quod est in rerum figuris porcus, hoc est in rerum genere ftultus & tam illud animal, quàm ista duæ syllabæ, quod dicitur ftultus, quiddam unum idémque significat. Immundum quippe illud animal in Lege positum est, eo quòd non ruminet: non autem hoc ejus vitium, sed natura est. Sunt autem homines, qui per hoc animal significantur, immundi proprio vitio, non natura: qui cùm libenter audiant verba sapientiæ, postea de his omnino non cogitant. Quod enim utile audieris, velut ab intefino memoriæ, tanquam ad os cogitationis recordandi dulcedine revocate, quid est aliud, quàm spiritaliter quodammodo ruminare? quod qui non faciunt illorum animalium genere figurantur. Unde & ipsa à talibus carnibus abftinemia, tale vitium nos cavere pramonuit; cùm enim thesaurus desiderabilis sit ipsa sapientia, de hac munditia ruminandi, & immunditia non ruminandi scriptum est (Proverb. 21. v. 20. juxta editionem LXX.) Thesaurus desiderabilis requiescit in ore sapientis, vir autem stultus glutit illum. Hæ autem similitudines rerum in locutionibus & observationibus figuratis propter quarendi & comparandi exercitationem, rationales mentes utiliter & suaviter movent.
