Sed priori populo multa talia non tantum audienda, verum etiam observanda præcepta sunt. Tempus enim erat, quo non tantum dictis, sed etiam factis prophetari oporteret ea, quæ posteriori tempore fuerant revelanda. Quibus per Christum atque in Christo revelatis, fidei Gentium onera observationum non sunt impositia, prophetiæ tamen autoritas commendatur.
units.tr: Defile. That is, they are able to defile, just as they are able to sanctify. From this it is clear, as also from the Apostle declaring that all things are clean to the clean, that the animals forbidden by God in the law were not unclean by nature, but only by signification, as Blessed Augustine observes in Book 6 against Faustus, chapter 7, where he says: If one asks about the pig and the lamb, both are clean by nature, because every creature of God is good; but by a certain signification the lamb is clean and the pig unclean; just as if you were to call the word "fool" and the word "wise" both by nature of sound, letters and syllables, of which they are made up, clean; yet by signification one of these words, the one called "fool", can be called unclean, not by its own nature, but because it signifies something unclean. And perhaps what the pig is among the figures of things, the fool is among the kinds of men, and that animal and those two syllables called "fool" signify one and the same thing. For that animal was declared unclean in the Law because it does not chew the cud. But this is not its fault, it is its nature. Yet there are men who are signified by that animal, unclean through their own fault, not by nature: who, although they gladly hear the words of wisdom, afterwards do not think about them at all. For what useful thing you have heard, recalled from the inner store of memory, as if brought back up to the mouth of thought by the sweetness of recollection, what else is it than to chew the cud in a certain spiritual way? Those who do not do this are represented by the kind of those animals. Hence also abstinence from such flesh warns us to beware of such a fault; for since wisdom itself is a desirable treasure, it is written about this cleanness of chewing and the uncleanness of not chewing (Prov. 21:20, according to the edition of the LXX): A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise, but the foolish man swallows it. These likenesses of things in figurative speeches and observances, because of the exercise of seeking and comparing, move rational minds usefully and pleasantly. But for the former people many such precepts had to be not only heard but also observed. For there was a time when those things which were to be revealed in a later time had to be prophesied not only by words but also by deeds. These things having been revealed through Christ and in Christ, the burdens of observances have not been imposed on the faith of the Gentiles, yet the authority of prophecy is commended.

units.la: 21. Inde. Id est, ex Galilæa, quam Jesus perambulabat post multiplicationem panum supra relatam, post egressum e terra Genesar, & habitum Sermonem de cibo coelesti apud Capharnaitas, qui habetur, Joan. 6. non enim volebat, ut idem Joannes narrat c. 7. v. 1. in Judæam sciliet strictè sumtam ambulare, quia quærebant eum Judæi interficere.
units.tr: 21. Thence. That is, from Galilee, which Jesus was traversing after the multiplication of the loaves related above, after his departure from the land of Gennesaret, and after the discourse on heavenly food given at Capernaum, which is found in John 6. For he did not wish, as the same John relates in chapter 7, verse 1, to walk into Judea properly so called, because the Jews were seeking to kill him.

units.la: 22. Et ecce mulier. Hoc loquendi modo tacitè innuit Matthæus quod aperte dicit Marc. c. 7. v. 24. nempe quod Christus, ut advenit in fines Tyri & Sidonis, ingressus domum neminem voluit scire, & non potuit latere; mulier enim Gentilis & Syrophœnissa, cujus filia habebat spiritum immundum, intravit & procidit ad pedes ejus, &c. Porro quod Marcus dicit Christum voluisse latere, & non potuisse, intelligendum est de voluntate, ut Scholastici loquuntur, signi & præparationis, quia nempe Christus id faciebat, quod faceret homo volens latere, nam subducens se clanculum ingrediebatur domum. Sic Luc. c. 24. v. 28. dicit Christum finxisse se longius ire. Hoc sensu etiam Marc. 11. v. 13. dicitur: Cùm Christus vidisset à longè ficum habentem folia, venit, si quid forte inveniret in ea: non quòd Christus dubitaret an quid esset in ea, cùm nemo nesciret nullos tunc temporis in ficu esse fructus, etenim ut observat Evangelista, non erat tempus ficorum, sed quòd faceret ea, quæ facere solent homines quærentes & sperantes se fructus in arbore inventuros. Potuisset etiam Marcus his terminis uti: Venit Christus & voluit decerpere fructus, aut finxit se velle decerpere fructus, & tamen idem penitus esse sensus.
units.tr: 22. And behold, a woman. By this manner of speaking Matthew tacitly hints at what Mark says plainly in chapter 7, verse 24: namely that Christ, when he came into the regions of Tyre and Sidon, entered a house and wished no one to know it, and could not be hidden; for a Gentile woman, a Syrophoenician, whose daughter had an unclean spirit, came in and fell at his feet, etc. Further, what Mark says, that Christ wished to be hidden and could not, is to be understood of the will, as the Schoolmen put it, of sign and preparation, because Christ was doing what a man who wished to be hidden would do, for he entered the house secretly, slipping in unobserved. So Luke, chapter 24, verse 28, says that Christ pretended to go farther. In this sense also Mark 11:13 says: When Christ had seen from afar a fig tree having leaves, he came, if perhaps he might find anything on it: not that Christ doubted whether there was anything on it, since no one did not know that at that time there was no fruit on the fig tree; for, as the Evangelist observes, it was not the season of figs; but that he did what men are accustomed to do when seeking and hoping to find fruit on a tree. Mark could also have used these terms: Christ came and wished to pick fruit, or pretended to wish to pick fruit, and yet the sense would be entirely the same.

units.la: Chananæa. Sic dicitur, quia erat ex stirpe Chanaan, cujus Sidon erat primogenitus. A Marco vocatur Syrophœnissa, id est, ex Phœnicia Syriæ, nam erat & alia Phœnicia in Lybia. Gentilis denique dicitur, seu ut habetur in textu Græco apud Marcum, Græca, propter religionem prophanam. Clamavit. Valdé verisimile est mulierem primùm clamasse ante januam, & excitasse turbam, deinde etiam intrasse.
units.tr: Canaanite. She is so called because she was of the stock of Canaan, whose firstborn was Sidon. Mark calls her a Syrophoenician, that is, from Phoenicia of Syria, for there was also another Phoenicia in Libya. Finally she is called a Gentile, or, as is found in the Greek text of Mark, a Greek, on account of her profane religion. She cried out. It is very likely that the woman first cried out before the door, and roused the crowd, and then also came in.

units.la: Clamat. Supple, importune.
units.tr: She cries out. Supply: importunately.

units.la: Non sum missus, &c. Quid est, inquit Aug. Tract. 47. in Joan. non sum missus nisi ad oves, quae perierunt domus Israël, nisi quia praesentiam suam corporalem non exhibuit nisi populo Israël? Ad Gentes non perrexit ipse, ut qui contemnebant majus judicium sumerent, quia & praesentia illius est exhibita. Ipse Dominus ibi fuit, ibi matrem elegit, ibi concipi, ibi nasci, ibi sanguinem fundere voluit, ibi sunt vestigia ejus, modò adorantur, ubi novissimè stetit; unde ascendit ad coelum; ad Gentes autem misit. Sed forte aliqui arbitrantur quoniam non ipse ad nos venit, sed misit ad nos, non nos audiisse vocem ipsius, sed vocem eorum quos misit: Absit, pellatur ista cogitatio de cordibus vestris, & in his quos misit ipse erat. Ipsum Paulum audi quem misit, ad Gentes enim praecipuè Paulum misit Apostolum, & ait ipse Paulus, terrens non de se sed de illo: An vultis accipere experimentum ejus qui in me loquitur Christus? audite & ipsum Dominum: Et alias oves habeo, id est, in Gentibus, quae non sunt in hoc ovili, id est, de populo Israël, oportet me & illas adducere: ergo & per suos non alter adducit. Adhuc audi: Vocem meam audient, ecce & per suos ipse loquitur, & per eos quos misit, vox ejus auditur: Ut sit unum ovile & unus pastor. Duobus istis gregibus tamquam duobus parietibus factus est lapis angularis per similitudinem, non proprie. Non autem, ut monet B. Chrysost. Hom. 53. quia negligebat, sed ut repositum atque abscondisum in animo Chananaeæ virtutis thesaurum in lucem protraheret, Christus eam repellebat.
units.tr: I was not sent, etc. What is this? says Augustine, Tractate 47 on John. I was not sent except to the sheep which have perished of the house of Israel: is this not because he showed his bodily presence only to the people of Israel? He himself did not go to the Gentiles, so that those who despised might receive a greater judgment, because his presence was also displayed to them. The Lord himself was there, there he chose his mother, there he willed to be conceived, to be born, to shed his blood; there are his footprints, now they are adored where he last stood; thence he ascended to heaven; but to the Gentiles he sent. But perhaps some think that he did not come to us himself, but sent to us, and that we have not heard his own voice, but the voice of those whom he sent: far be it; let such a thought be driven from your hearts, for he was in those whom he sent. Hear Paul himself, whom he sent; for he sent Paul especially as Apostle to the Gentiles, and Paul himself says, not speaking of himself but of him: Do you seek proof of him who speaks in me, Christ? Hear the Lord himself too: I have other sheep, that is, among the Gentiles, which are not in this fold, that is, of the people of Israel; I must bring them too. Therefore he does not bring them by another through his own. Hear further: They will hear my voice; behold, he speaks himself through his own, and his voice is heard through those whom he sent: So that there may be one fold and one shepherd. Like two walls, these two flocks have been made into one by a corner stone, in a figurative, not a proper sense. But Christ repelled the Canaanite woman, as Blessed Chrysostom observes in Homily 53, not because he was neglecting her, but in order to bring into the light the treasure of her virtue that was laid up and hidden in her mind.

units.la: 25. Venit. Marc. 7. v. 25. intravit, sed in utriusque Evangelistæ textu Graeco habetur, ἐλθοῦσα, venit, seu cùm venisset.
units.tr: 25. She came. Mark 7:25 says entered, but in the Greek text of each Evangelist it is found: ἐλθοῦσα [elthousa], came, or when she had come.

units.la: 26. Adoravit eum. Hoc Marcus his verbis expressit, procidit ad pedes ejus.
units.tr: 26. She worshipped him. Mark expressed this in these words: she fell at his feet.

units.la: Ait. Hic supple ex Marc. 7. v. 27. sine prius saturari filios, non est enim bonum sumere, &c. Sic Apostoli Act. 13. Vobis, scilicet, tamquam filiis, oportebat primùm loqui verbum Dei, sed quia repellitis illud, & indignos vos judicatis aeternae vitae, ecce convertimur ad Gentes.
units.tr: He said. Here supply from Mark 7:27: Let the children first be filled, for it is not good to take, etc. So the Apostles in Acts 13: To you, namely as children, it was fitting that the word of God should first be spoken; but since you reject it, and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles.

units.la: 27. Etiam Domine. Suscepit mulier humiliter convicium, & meruit beneficium.
units.tr: 27. Yes, Lord. The woman humbly accepted the insult, and earned the blessing.

units.la: Catelli. Catellos hic intellige non praecisè melitaeos, quos habent mulieres in deliciis; hi enim plerumque micas panis sub mensa non colligunt, sed in ipso sinu dominae, iisdem cum illa ciborum deliciis lautè vescuntur. Catelli igitur hic sunt, quivis canes domestici infra molossos & vertagos; molossis enim & vertagis cadentes de mensa micæ non sufficiunt, sed majoribus ossibus opus est.
units.tr: Little dogs. Here by "little dogs" understand not precisely the Maltese lapdogs that women keep as pets; for these for the most part do not gather crumbs of bread under the table, but feed sumptuously on the same dainties as their mistress, in her very lap. The little dogs here, therefore, are any household dogs below the mastiffs and bulldogs; for crumbs falling from the table are not enough for mastiffs and bulldogs, which need larger bones.

units.la: De micis. Id est, de frustulis; neque enim canes colligunt micas proprie dictas, sed gallinæ, aut aves aliæ, quibus rostrum est acutius, aut minora animalcula.
units.tr: From the crumbs. That is, from the scraps; for dogs do not gather crumbs properly so called, but hens, or other birds whose beaks are sharper, or smaller creatures.

units.la: Qua cadunt. Sive forte fortunâ id fiat, sive à domino projiciantur.
units.tr: That fall. Whether this happens by chance, or they are thrown down by the master.

units.la: 28. Magna est fides tua. Credidit hæc mulier ex auditu, seu famâ miraculorum Christi; unde Marc. 7. v. 25. signanter dicit: Statim ut audivit de eo, &c. Fides enim ut est determinatio de credibili, est ex auditu, licèt fides ut est cordis inclinatio ad credendum, non fit ex auditu, sed ex dono gratiæ, ut loquitur D. Th. in Rom. 10. Lect. 2.
units.tr: 28. Great is your faith. This woman believed from hearing, or from the report of Christ's miracles; hence Mark 7:25 pointedly says: As soon as she heard of him, etc. For faith, as it is the determination of what is credible, comes from hearing; although faith, as it is the inclination of the heart to believe, does not come from hearing but from the gift of grace, as St Thomas puts it on Romans 10, lecture 2.

units.la: 29. Inde. Id est, de finibus Tyri & Sidonis, ut patet ex Marc. 7. v. 31. venit secus mare Galilææ. Supple, ex Marc. inter medios fines Decapoleos. Ibi autem Christus sanavit surdum & mutum, seu ut habet textus Græcus difficulter loquentem ad se adductum, ut narratur Marc. 7.
units.tr: 29. From there. That is, from the borders of Tyre and Sidon, as appears from Mark 7:31: he came by the sea of Galilee. Supply from Mark: through the midst of the coasts of Decapolis. There Christ healed a deaf man and a dumb one, or, as the Greek text has it, one who spoke with difficulty, who was brought to him, as is related in Mark 7.

units.la: 30. Claudos. Græcè, mutilos.
units.tr: 30. The lame. In Greek, the maimed.

units.la: 31. Claudos ambulantes. Græcè, mutilos sanos.
units.tr: 31. The lame walking. In Greek, the maimed made whole.

units.la: 34. Pisciculos. Græcè, hic est Marc. 8. v. 7. ἰχθύδια. Apud Joannem verò c. 6. & alibi, pascim pisciculi vocantur ὀψάρια, nempe cùm ὀψον fit opsonium quodvis, piscis id obtinuit, ut sibi hoc vocabulum aptaretur soli propter sapotis præstantiam, ut & diminutivum ὀψάριον. A multis hoc sensu usurpari testes sunt Athenæus, Suidas, Eustathius, & ceteri. Sic Terentius in Andria Act. 2. Sce. 2. paululùm opsonii, & pisciculos minutos pro eodem sumit.
units.tr: 34. Little fishes. In Greek, here in Mark 8:7, ἰχθύδια. In John 6 and elsewhere, however, the little fishes of the feeding are called ὀψάρια; for ὀψον is any relish whatever, but fish came to claim this word for itself alone because of its excellence as a delicacy, and so the diminutive ὀψάριον as well. That many have used it in this sense is attested by Athenaeus, Suidas, Eustathius and others. So Terence in the Andria, Act 2, Scene 2, takes a little opsonium and small fishes for the same thing.

units.la: 36. Gratias agens fregit. Gratias agens hic dixit Matthæus, quod supra expressit per verbum benedixit. Idem tum apud ipsum, tum apud ceteros Evangelistas observare licet passim; hæ autem expressiones synonymæ sunt ob rationem supra allatam cap. 15.
units.tr: 36. Giving thanks, he broke. Here Matthew said "giving thanks", which above he expressed by the verb "blessed". This may be observed everywhere, both in him and in the other Evangelists; these expressions are synonyms, for the reason given above in chapter 15.

units.la: 37. Sportas. Queritur unde in deserto tot sportæ, sed facilis est responsio, vel enim Evangelista per sportas mensuram tantùm significat, non verò quòd reipsa ibi fuerint sportæ; vel sportæ erant in deserto in quibus allatus erat panis turbis ad Christum venientibus vendendus, & in his collecta sunt fragmenta reliquiarum, ut jussit Christus.
units.tr: 37. Baskets. It is asked how there came to be so many baskets in the desert; but the answer is easy: either the Evangelist means by baskets only a measure, and not that baskets were really there; or baskets were in the desert, in which bread brought to be sold to the crowds coming to Christ was carried, and into these the fragments of the leftovers were gathered, as Christ commanded.

units.la: 39. In fines Magedan. Græce Μαγεδάν. Sed optimi Codices dicuntur habere Μαγαδὰν, & hæc fuit olim Græca lectio, ut colligere est ex Hier. & Aug. Marcus verò habet Dalmanutha, quia in eodem tractu vici Magedan, sive Magadan & Dalmanutha sunt, ita ut ab utrovis is tractus denominari potuerit. Potest etiam dici quòd Christus primò venerit in partes Dalmanutha, deinde in fines Magedan, vel e converso, quorum alterutrum ab utroque Evangelista omissum est.
units.tr: 39. Into the borders of Magedan. In Greek, Μαγεδάν. But the best manuscripts are said to have Μαγαδάν, and this was the Greek reading of old, as may be gathered from Jerome and Augustine. Mark, however, has Dalmanutha, because Magedan, or Magadan, and Dalmanutha are in the same region, so that the district could have been named from either of them. It may also be said that Christ first came into the parts of Dalmanutha and then into the borders of Magedan, or the reverse, and that one of the two names was omitted by each Evangelist.

units.la: CAPUT XVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI.

units.la: 2. Facto vespere, &c. Nubes densæ tectæ sole obliquo, qualis est quum jam occidit, nigrorem præ se ferunt: quæ vero sunt rubicundæ, cùm non sint adeo opacæ ac densæ, penetrantur lumine, ideóque in diem posterum nullum indicant tempestatis apparatum: serenitatem igitur præniuntiant. Cùm vero oriente sole, triste hinc inde, & nubilosum se cœlum exhibet: solent plerumque nubes ad occursum solis condensatæ in pluviam destillare, aut in ventos resolvi.
units.tr: 2. When it is evening, etc. Dense clouds covering the slanting sun, such as appear when it is already setting, show a darkness; but those that are reddish, since they are not so opaque and thick, let the light through, and therefore indicate no storm for the following day: they foretell fair weather. But when the sun rises and the sky shows itself gloomy and cloudy on every side, the clouds, gathered together at the sun's approach, usually either drip down as rain or dissolve into winds.

units.la: 4. Faciem ergo cœli, &c. Q. d. nostis ô Pharisæi & Sadducæi fallacia rerum futurarum signa discernere, & signa infallibilia Legis & Prophetarum oraculis consignata, quibus adventus meus jam præsens agnoscatur, observare non potestis? ô præpostera sapientia & ingenii subtilitas! Neque repugnat huic Christi dicto alterum ipsiusmet dictum Luc. 17. v. 20. Regnum Dei, quo scilicet Christus gloriosus dominabitur, non venit cum observatione; sensus enim illius dicti est, regnum Dei; seu tempus illud post resurrectionem futurum, quo Christus per secundum adventum suum regnum, quod intra nos per primum adventum inchoavit, consummabit, non longè antequam veniat, pompa, comitatu, aliisve signis præcedetur, quibus futurus observari possit, licèt non sint defutura signa à Christo promissa Luc. 21. v. 27. quibus & ille secundus adventus præsens declaretur.
units.tr: 4. The face of the sky, etc. In other words: "O Pharisees and Sadducees, you know how to discern the signs of future weather, yet can you not observe the infallible signs, sealed in the oracles of the Law and the Prophets, by which my coming, already present, might be recognised? O perverse wisdom and cleverness of mind!" Nor does another saying of Christ himself, Luke 17:20, The kingdom of God does not come with observation, contradict this saying. For the sense of that saying is this: the kingdom of God, that is, that time after the resurrection in which Christ, by his second coming, will complete the kingdom he began within us at his first coming, will not be preceded, shortly before it comes, by pomp, retinue or other signs by which it could be observed beforehand. This is so, although the signs promised by Christ at Luke 21:27 are not lacking, by which that second coming too will be declared present.

units.la: Generatio mala, &c. Hæc ut patet ex Marc. 8. v. 12. dixit Christus ingemiscens spiritu, id est, in semetipso; sic enim Jo. c. 11. quod v. 33. expressit his verbis infremuit spiritu, ibidem v. 38. exprimit istis fremens in semetipso; ille autem ingemiscit in semetipso, qui intimos doloris affectus intra semetipsum cohibet; & infremit spiritu seu in semetipso, qui sonum indignationis intra semetipsum cohibet ne foras erumpat. Fremitus enim est sonitus quidam indignantis, qui fit flatu oris repressio.
units.tr: An evil generation, etc. As is clear from Mark 8:12, Christ said this groaning in spirit, that is, within himself. For in John 11, what he expressed in verse 33 by the words he groaned in spirit, he expresses in verse 38 by groaning in himself. Now a man groans within himself who keeps his inmost feelings of grief shut up inside himself; and a man groans in spirit, or within himself, who keeps the sound of indignation shut up within himself, lest it break out. For a snorting is a certain sound of one who is indignant, produced by the mouth's breath being held back.

units.la: 5. Cum venissent. Id est, cum venire coepissent; nam patet ex Marc. 8. v. 14. quae hic sequuntur, in ipsa navi, cum transfretarent mare Galilaeae in Bethsaidam, contigisse.
units.tr: 5. When they had come. That is, when they had begun to come; for it is clear from Mark 8:14 that what follows here took place in the boat itself, as they were crossing the sea of Galilee to Bethsaida.

units.la: 7. Cogitabant, &c. Graece, disceptabant; nam & verbis eos inter se egisse indicat Marcus.
units.tr: 7. They thought, etc. In Greek, they disputed; for Mark also indicates that they argued with one another in words.

units.la: 8. Cogitatio. Graece, disceptatio.
units.tr: 8. Thought. In Greek, dispute.

units.la: 11. Cavete. Prudentem & sapiens informat & stultus; ille quid imitandum sit docet, ipse quid vitandum. B. Eucherius in Epistola de contemtu mundi.
units.tr: 11. Beware. The prudent and wise man instructs, and the fool too; the one teaches what is to be imitated, the other what is to be avoided. Blessed Eucherius, in his Letter on contempt for the world.

units.la: A fermento. Fermentum malitiae opponit Paulus 1 Cor. v. 8. cap. quinti azymis sinceritatis & veritatis. Alii dum de moribus dicitur, per fermentum superbiam intelligunt, quia massa fermentata statim intumescit. Alii odia & simultates quibus acescunt animi & exacerbantur. Secundum varias has fermenti acceptiones, varie exponitur illud Ps. 71. v. 4. quod David juxta veritatem Hebraicam liberari petit a manu impii, praevaricatoris & fermentati.
units.tr: Of leaven. Paul opposes the leaven of malice to the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth, 1 Cor. 5:8. Others, when it is spoken of morals, understand by leaven pride, because a leavened mass immediately swells up. Others understand hatreds and enmities, by which minds turn sour and are embittered. According to these various senses of leaven, the saying of Psalm 71:4 is variously explained, where David, following the Hebrew truth, asks to be delivered from the hand of the wicked, the transgressor and the leavened man.

units.la: 12. A doctrina Pharisaeorum & Sadducaeorum. Supple ex Luc. 12. v. 1. quae est hypocrisis; nam Pharisaei quaedam docebant Legi consentanea & ad pietatem conducentia, & haec omnia facienda & servanda praecipit Christus infra cap. 23. v. 2. Alia vero docebant Legi Dei adversantia, rescindentes verbum Dei, & haec est doctrina a qua suis cavendum Christus praecipit, ne irrita facientes praecepta Dei, ut traditiones hominum servent, adinstar Pharisaeorum sibi inurant notam hypocritarum, quibus ad amussim competit, ut ipse Christus testatur supra cap. 15. v. 7. quod in hypocritis aetatis suae perstrinxit Esaias dicens: Populus hic labiis me honorat, &c. Sicut autem Christus hic a fermento Pharisaeorum & Sadducaeorum, hoc est, a doctrina illorum hypocritica; item Marc. 8. v. 14. etiam a fermento Herodis, id est, ab hypocritica ipsius vitae conversatione cavendum praecipit. Nam Herodes Tetrarcha qui propter insignem astutiam a Christo vocatur vulpes Luc. 13. v. 32. erat compositus ad Romani tunc Imperatoris exemplum, qui nullam ex virtutibus suis magis, quam dissimulationem diligebat. Itaque videas Herodem magna arte & populo se commendasse quasi Judaicae religionis perquam studiosum, & Romano Imperatori adulatum serviliter quasi ei devotissimum, cum interim omnimode ipse res suas ageret.
units.tr: 12. Of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees. Supply from Luke 12:1, which is hypocrisy; for the Pharisees taught some things that agreed with the Law and conduced to piety, and Christ commands that all these be done and kept, below in chapter 23:2. But they also taught things opposed to the Law of God, setting aside the word of God; and it is this teaching that Christ commands his people to beware of, lest, making the commandments of God void in order to keep the traditions of men, they brand themselves, like the Pharisees, with the mark of hypocrites, which fits them exactly, as Christ himself testifies above in chapter 15:7, where Isaiah rebuked the hypocrites of his own age, saying: This people honours me with their lips, etc. Now just as Christ here commands them to beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees, that is, of their hypocritical teaching, so at Mark 8:14 he also commands them to beware of the leaven of Herod, that is, of his hypocritical manner of life. For Herod the tetrarch, who on account of his notable cunning is called a fox by Christ, Luke 13:32, had modelled himself on the example of the Roman emperor of that time, who loved dissimulation more than any of his virtues. So you may see Herod, with great art, commending himself to the people as a very zealous adherent of the Jewish religion, and servilely flattering the Roman emperor as his most devoted subject, while all the time he was pursuing his own affairs in every way.

units.la: 13. Venit. Scilicet à vico Bethsaida, postquam ibi illuminavit cæcum extra vicum, ut narratur Marc. 8.
units.tr: 13. He came. Namely from the village of Bethsaida, after he had there healed the blind man outside the village, as is related in Mark 8.

units.la: In partes Cæsarea Philippi. Cæsarea sine addito dicitur urbs maritima in medio totius Judææ littore, olim Turris Stratonis dicta; hanc Herodes Magnus maximam & munitissimam reddidit, & defectionis metu, Judæorum genti arcem imposuit,ædificiis ornavit, templum, theatrum, amphitheatrum, cloacas magnifice extruxit, portumque Pyrœo non minorem adjecit, quem Sebastum, id est, Augustum appellavit, ut refert Josephus l. 15. Antiq. Jud. qui testatur quoque hujus Cæsareæ incolas plerosque fuisse Græcos, id est, Gentiles. Altera est Cæsarea, quæ dicitur Philippi, ut pote quæ à Philippo Herodis Majoris filio Iturææ & Trachonitidis Tetrarcha fuit ampliata & in gratiam Cæsaris Augusti Cæsarea appellata, cum prius Paneas diceretur. Hæc civitas sita est prope Jordanis fontes & olim dicta Lais seu Lesem, postea Dan à Tribu illa, quæ hanc urbem occupavit: dein à Græcis Syriæ dominantibus, quibus notior erat Pan, quàm Dan, nominata est Paneas.
units.tr: Into the parts of Caesarea Philippi. Caesarea, without any addition, is the name of a maritime city on the coast in the middle of all Judaea, formerly called the Tower of Strato. Herod the Great made it very large and strongly fortified, and, fearing revolt, placed a citadel in it over the Jewish nation; he adorned it with buildings, and magnificently built a temple, a theatre, an amphitheatre and sewers, and added a harbour not smaller than the Piraeus, which he called Sebastus, that is, Augustus, as Josephus reports in book 15 of the Jewish Antiquities. Josephus also attests that most of the inhabitants of this Caesarea were Greeks, that is, Gentiles. There is another Caesarea, called that of Philip, since it was enlarged by Philip, son of Herod the Great and tetrarch of Iturea and Trachonitis, and named Caesarea in honour of the emperor Augustus, though it was previously called Paneas. This city lies near the sources of the Jordan, and was formerly called Laish or Leshem, then Dan, from the tribe that occupied this city; afterwards, under the Greek rulers of Syria, to whom Pan was better known than Dan, it was named Paneas.

units.la: 15. Vos autem, &c. Cum Discipuli opinionem vulgi Christo indicassent, tunc propria ab eis qualitas veræ fidei expetitur, ut erroris humani falsitas auferatur.
units.tr: 15. But you, etc. When the disciples had told Christ the opinion of the crowd, then their own qualification of true faith is sought from them, so that the falsehood of human error may be removed.

units.la: Me. Utique Filium hominis, inquit Fulgentius l. 3. ad Thrasym.
units.tr: Me. Surely the Son of man, says Fulgentius, book 3, to Thrasymund.

units.la: 16. Tu es Christus, &c. Divina sapientia, quæ ad sui fruitionem hominem fecerat, eum sui expertem esse non sinens, totam se in naturam humanam contulit, eamque sibi modo admirabili assumendo, ut erroneum hominem ad se totaliter revocaret. Hujus igitur sapientiæ claritatem nube mortalitatis velatam primus Apostolorum Princeps considere meruit, & eam constanter & plenarie absque errore confiteri. D. Th. in Epistola nuncup. aureæ sua Catenæ.
units.tr: 16. You are the Christ, etc. Divine wisdom, which had made man for its own enjoyment, not allowing him to be without it, gave itself wholly to human nature, and assumed it to itself in a wonderful manner, so that it might recall erring man wholly to itself. The first of the Apostles, therefore, was deemed worthy to behold the clarity of this wisdom, veiled by the cloud of mortality, and to confess it constantly and fully, without error. Thomas Aquinas, in the dedicatory letter to his Golden Chain.

units.la: Dei vivi. Vivus dicitur Deus, quia solus verè vivit, nos autem quod vivimus, per ipsum & in ipso vivimus; nec Deus verus adinstar deorum, quos Gentilitatis dementia, vel de mortuis hominibus, vel de opere manuum sibi instituit adorandos, mortuus est, ut sicut ipsi dii mortui dicuntur, & quæ ipsis offeruntur, sacrificia mortuorum, sic & ipse Deus verus mortuus nuncupetur; vivus denique dicitur Deus verus, quia perennis & æternus est, quo sensu aqua dicitur viva, & secundum nonnullos infrà cap. 22. v. 32. Deus dicitur non mortuorum sed viventium.
units.tr: Of the living God. God is called living because he alone truly lives, while we, in so far as we live, live through him and in him. Nor is the true God, like the gods whom the madness of the Gentiles set up for themselves to be worshipped, either of dead men or of the work of hands, dead, so that, just as those gods are called dead, and the sacrifices offered to them are sacrifices of the dead, so the true God too should be named dead. Lastly, the true God is called living because he is everlasting and eternal, in which sense water is called living; and according to some, below in chapter 22:32, God is called the God not of the dead but of the living.

units.la: 17. Beatus es. Ex hac Christi responsione ad Petri consessionem satis patet quod, licet alii ante Petrum iisdem fere verbis usi fuerint, dum Christum adorarent, non tamen eodem modo eum agnoverint Filium naturalem & unigenitum Dei.
units.tr: 17. Blessed are you. From this response of Christ to Peter's confession it is quite clear that, although others before Peter, when they worshipped Christ, used almost the same words, they did not nevertheless acknowledge him in the same way as the natural and only-begotten Son of God.

units.la: Bar Jona. Id est, filius Jona, ut habetur Jo. 1. v. 42. est autem Jona contractum à Johannan, unde Jo. 21. v. 11. B. Petrus appellatur Simon Joannis, supple, filius.
units.tr: Bar Jona. That is, son of Jonah, as is found at John 1:42. Now Jonah is a contraction of Johanan, whence at John 21:15 the blessed Peter is called Simon of John, that is, son of John.

units.la: Caro & sanguis. Haec locutio frequens est in SS. Scripturis pro homine, & apud Rabbinos, quoties homo cum Deo comparitur, ut vilitas mortalium declaretur. Non autem ex humana sapientia esse fidem, sed ex inspiratione divina, praesenti ipsius veritatis voce firmatur.
units.tr: Flesh and blood. This expression is frequent in Holy Scripture for a human being, and among the rabbis it is used whenever a man is compared with God, so that the frailty of mortals may be shown. That faith comes not from human wisdom but from divine inspiration is confirmed by the present voice of truth itself.

units.la: 18. Et ego dico tibi. Non sermone cassò, & nullum opus habente, sed dico tibi, quia meum dixisse, fecisse est.
units.tr: 18. And I say to you. Not an empty word with no work behind it, but "I say to you," because for me to have spoken is to have acted.

units.la: Tu es Petrus. Id est, tu es is, cui ego in primo ad me adventu novum nomen impositi, Cephas, id est, Petrus, vel potius me impositurum promisi, quod ecce nunc praesto.
units.tr: You are Peter. That is, you are the one to whom I gave the new name Cephas, that is, Peter, at my first coming to you, or rather, the one whom I promised I would name, and that promise is now fulfilled.

units.la: Super hanc Petram, &c. Quatuor sunt sententiae seu sententiarum classes apud SS. PP. de expositione horum verborum. In prima classe per Petram intelligitur B. Petrus. Secunda per Petram intelligit Apostolos & eorum successores. Tertia, quae celebrior est & ad litteram accommodatior, Petram hic vult dici fidem a Petro confessam. Quarta denique non longe recedens a tertia per Petram putat signisicari ipsummet Christum. Verum non rebus ipsis differunt inter se quatuor istae sententiae, sed modo tantum & loquendi ratione. Quemadmodum enim si quis dicat: Deus me sanavit, aut medicus me sanavit, aut rheubarbarum me sanavit, etsi diversis locutionibus, communem loquendi consuetudinem sequens utitur, idem tamen semper sentit, nempe sanatum esse à Deo tanquam à causa efficiente prima, à medico tanquam à causa secunda, à rheubarbaro tanquam ab instrumento. Sic prorsus SS. PP. quando dixerunt aedificatam esse Ecclesiam super Christum, super Petrum vel Apostolos & eorum successores, super fidem aut confessionem fidei, in re optime consenserunt, & ut Augustinus dicere solet, locutionum hae fuit diversitas, non sententiarum. Christus nempe aedificii Ecclesiae prima causa efficiens, à quo ceu sonte unico, vis omnis oritur, quae Ecclesiam instituit, tuetur & facit durare; ipse Christus est fundamentum quod positum est, & praeter quod aliud nemo potest ponere: ipse Christus est illud fundamentum, quod ut loquitur D. Thomas per se habet soliditatem, sicut rupes aliqua supra quam aedificium construitur. Petrus verò ut Apostolus & Apostolorum præcipuus & ꝏ erat causa secundaria efficiens; Apostoli enim, Paulo temte, cooperatores sunt Christi in Ecclesia ædificanda: ipse etiam Petrus est fundamentum sicut & ceteri Apostoli, quod habet soliditatem non ex se, sed ex alio solido subjecto, sicut lapides qui primò imponuntur Petræ solidæ; Apostoli enim primò superædificati sunt Christo per fidem & charitatem, ita ut Petrus qui primus ex persona omnium Apostolorum confessus est Christum Filium Dei vivi, ab hac confessione Petri appellationem sit sortitus. Ταῦτλω ὁμολογίαν Πέτρον ... Πέτρος ... ὁμολογήσαντος ... ἀληθείας ... Θεμέλιον ... ὃς ἐστὶν Ἰησοῦς Χριστός. Id est, Hanc confessionem Christus Petram cum vocasset, Petrum nominat eum, qui primò hanc confessus est, confessionis indicem appellationem donans. Hæc enim verè est petra pietatis, hæc salutis basis, hic fidei murus, hoc veritatis fundamentum; fundamentum enim aliud nemo potest ponere præter id quod positum est, quod est Christus Iesus. Basilius Seleucensis Antistes Hom. 25. Fidës in Christum Filium Dei vivi est causa instrumentalis Ecclesiæ ædificandæ, & super ejusdem fidei confessionem citra casus periculum formata est & fundata Christi Ecclesia, ut loquitur B. Cyrillus Alexandr. l. 4. de Trin. Unusquisque autem Fidelium est causa materialis templi Dei, quod ædificatur, ut ait Augustinus, ex diis quos facit non factus Deus.
units.tr: Upon this rock, etc. The Fathers have four opinions, or classes of opinion, about the interpretation of these words. In the first class, by the rock is understood Saint Peter. The second understands by the rock the Apostles and their successors. The third, which is the more common and better suited to the literal sense, holds that the rock here means the faith confessed by Peter. The fourth, not far removed from the third, thinks that Christ Himself is signified by the rock. These four opinions differ from one another not in the things themselves but only in the mode and manner of speaking. For if someone says, "God healed me," or "the physician healed me," or "rhubarb healed me," then, although he uses different expressions, following common usage, he always means the same thing: that he was healed by God as the first efficient cause, by the physician as the second cause, and by the rhubarb as the instrument. In exactly the same way, when the Fathers said that the Church was built upon Christ, upon Peter or the Apostles and their successors, or upon faith or the confession of faith, they agreed excellently in substance; and, as Augustine is accustomed to say, there was a diversity of expressions, not of opinions. Christ is, of course, the primary efficient cause of the building of the Church, from whom as from a single source flows all the power that founded the Church, preserves it and makes it endure. Christ Himself is the foundation that has been laid, and no one can lay another besides it; Christ Himself is that foundation which, as Thomas says, has solidity in itself, like a rock upon which a building is constructed. But Peter, as an Apostle and the chief of the Apostles, was a secondary efficient cause; for the Apostles, as Paul says, are fellow workers with Christ in building the Church. Peter himself is a foundation, as are the other Apostles, but he has his solidity not from himself but from another solid base, like the stones that are first laid upon a solid rock; for the Apostles were first built upon Christ through faith and love. Thus Peter, who first confessed, on behalf of all the Apostles, that Christ is the Son of the living God, received his name from this confession of Peter. [Ταύτῃ τῇ ὁμολογίᾳ Πέτρον ... Πέτρος ... ὁμολογήσαντος ... ἀληθείας ... θεμέλιον ... ὃς ἐστὶν Ἰησοῦς Χριστός.] That is: Since Christ called this confession a rock, He names Peter, who first made this confession, giving him a name that points to the confession. For this is truly the rock of piety, this is the basis of salvation, this is the wall of faith, this is the foundation of truth; for no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ. Basil, bishop of Seleucia, Homily 25. Faith in Christ the Son of the living God is the instrumental cause by which the Church is to be built, and upon the confession of this same faith the Church of Christ was formed and founded, without danger of falling, as Saint Cyril of Alexandria says in book 4 of his work on the Trinity. Moreover, each of the faithful is a material cause of the temple of God that is being built, as Augustine says, out of gods whom God, who was not made, has made.

units.la: Ædificabo Ecclesiam meam. Sicut architecti lapides quaerunt, inventos ad opus ædificii parant cædendo, poliendo, & aliis rationibus, deinde probè paratos conjungunt inter se, ut ex omnibus rectè compositis surgat opus ædificii; sic Dominus noster ex innumero mortalium numero quosdam eligit, electos erudit, eisque fidem infundit, totóque adeo immutat lavacro regenerationis, ut ab Apostolo novæ creaturæ dicantur; tum autem ita paratos & concinnatos vinculo charitatis, participatione eorumdem Sacramentorum, communione ejusdem spei, velut cæmento quodam conjungit invicem, ut è pluribus extruantur Ecclesiæ singulæ, ex omnibus Ecclesia Catholica, quam si gregem subditum cogites, Christus in ea est Pastor Pastorum, & si fabricam cogites, Christus fundamentum fundamentorum. Sunt Apostoli fundamenta; sed innituntur primo fundamento, quod est Christus Iesus, qui totum Ecclesiæ ædificium per propriam sibi firmifirmitatem & soliditatem sustentat; sic etiam Christus est principalis hujus aedificii architectus, sed Apostoli etiam hanc dignitatem & denominationem ut causae instrumentales communicantur 1 Cor. 3. v. 10. fides vero, quam Apostoli praedicant, & Christus Apostolorum eorumque successorum ministerio infundit, habet rationem instrumenti ab architectis adhibiti ad aedificii construction​em.
units.tr: I will build my Church. As architects seek stones, and when they have found them prepare them for the work of the building by cutting, polishing and other means, and then fit them together carefully so that the work of the building rises from all the rightly joined parts, so our Lord chooses some out of the countless number of mortals, instructs the chosen, infuses faith into them and changes them entirely by the bath of regeneration, so that the Apostle calls them new creatures. Then, having been so prepared and fitted, He joins them to one another with the bond of love, by sharing in the same sacraments and by communion in the same hope, as with a kind of mortar, so that the individual congregations are built up from many, and from all of them the Catholic Church. If you think of it as a flock under His care, Christ is in it the Shepherd of shepherds; if you think of it as a building, Christ is the foundation of foundations. The Apostles are foundations, but they rest upon the first foundation, which is Christ Jesus, who sustains the whole building of the Church by His own firmness and solidity. So also Christ is the principal architect of this building, but the Apostles share in this dignity and title as instrumental causes, as in 1 Cor. 3.10. The faith, however, which the Apostles preach, and which Christ infuses through the ministry of the Apostles and their successors, has the character of an instrument used by architects for the construction of the building.

units.la: Portae inferi. Id est, haereticorum mortifera lingua, inquit, V. Synodus Oecumenica Cp. II. Col. 8.
units.tr: Gates of hell. That is, the deadly tongue of heretics, says the Fifth Ecumenical Synod, Constantinople II, canon 8.

units.la: Non praevalebunt. Valebunt quidem sed non praevalebunt, premunt sed non opprimunt, oppugnabunt sed non expugnabunt. Pugnare, inquit Aug. l. 1. de Symbolo ad Catechumenos cap. 6. potest Ecclesia, expugnari tamen non potest. Haereses omnes de illa exierunt tanquam sarmenta inutilia de vite praecisa; ipsa autem manet in radice sua, in vite sua, in caritate sua. Portae inferorum non vincent eam. Non eradicabitur, nec cedet quibuslibet tentationibus. Vide eumdem Aug. in Ps. 66. B. Leonem Ser. 2. de suo anniversario.
units.tr: They shall not prevail. They will indeed assail, but they shall not prevail; they press upon it, but do not crush it; they attack it, but do not overthrow it. The Church, says Augustine in book 1 of his work on the Creed to Catechumens, chapter 6, can be fought against, but cannot be overthrown. All heresies have gone out from her like useless branches cut off from the vine; but she herself remains in her root, in her vine, in her love. The gates of hell shall not overcome her. She shall not be uprooted, nor yield to any temptations. See the same Augustine on Psalm 66, and Leo, Sermon 2, on his anniversary.

units.la: Adversus eam. Subaudi, Ecclesiam, ut patet ex locis mox citatis & ex Isidoro Peleusiota, Epiphanio & aliis.
units.tr: Against it. Supply "the Church," as is clear from the passages just cited and from Isidore of Pelusium, Epiphanius and others.

units.la: Tibi. Numquid, inquit Augustinus Ser. 26. de diversis, illas claves Petrus accepit & Paulus non accepit? Petrus accepit & Joannes, & Jacobus non accepit, & caeteri Apostoli? aut non sunt illae in Ecclesia claves, ubi peccata quotidie dimittuntur? sed quoniam in significatione personam Petrus gestabat Ecclesiae, quod illi uni datum est, Ecclesiae datum est. Ergo Petrus figuram gestabat Ecclesiae, Ecclesia corpus Christi est. Idem ibidem Ser. 108. Inter Apostolos pene ubique solus Petrus totius Ecclesiae meruit gestare personam. Propter ipsam personam, quam totius Ecclesiae solus gestabat, audire meruit: Tibi dabo claves regni coelorum: has enim claves non homo unus, sed unitas accepit Ecclesiae. Hinc ergo Petri excellentia praedicatur, quia ipsius universitatis & unitatis Ecclesiae figuram gessit, quando ei dictum est: Tibi trado, quod omnibus traditum est; nam ut noveritis Ecclesiam accepisse claves regni coelorum; audite in alio loco quid Dominus dicat omnibus Apostolis suis Joan. 20. Accipite Spiritum Sanctum, & continuo: Sicut dimiseritis peccata, dimittuntur ei, sicut tenueritis, tenebuntur. Hoc ad claves pertinet, de quibus dictum est: Quae solveritis in terra, soluta erunt & in coelo, & quae ligaveritis in terra, ligata erunt & in coelo. Sed hoc Petro dixit, ut sciatis quia Petrus universalis Ecclesiae personam tunc gerebat. Audi quid ipsi dicatur, quid omnibus fidelibus sanctis Matth. 18. Si peccaverit in te frater tuus, &c. Idem S. Doctor. in Ps. 108. lib. de agone Christiano c. 3. Tractatu 50. in Jo. & Tractatu 118, &c. clarè docet Petro datas esse regni cœlorum claves, quia Christus eas contulit Ecclesiæ, quam Petrus repræsentabat, cùm ei Dominus dixit: Tibi dabo claves regni cœlorum. Vide eumdem S. Doctorem Tractatu 124. in Jo. & l. 1. de Doctr. Christiana c. 18.
units.tr: To you. Did Peter, asks Augustine in Sermon 26, On Various Subjects, receive those keys, and Paul not receive them? Did Peter receive them, and John and James and the other Apostles not? Are not those keys in the Church, where sins are forgiven every day? But since Peter in signifying bore the person of the Church, what was given to him alone was given to the Church. Therefore Peter bore the figure of the Church, and the Church is the body of Christ. The same, in Sermon 108: Among the Apostles, almost everywhere, Peter alone deserved to bear the person of the whole Church. Because of that very person which he alone bore for the whole Church, he deserved to hear: "I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven." For it was not one man but the unity that received these keys of the Church. Hence Peter's eminence is proclaimed, because he bore the figure of the universality and unity of the Church, when it was said to him, "I give to you what has been given to all"; for that you may know that the Church received the keys of the kingdom of heaven, hear what the Lord says in another place to all His Apostles, John 20: "Receive the Holy Spirit," and immediately: "Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; whose you retain, they are retained." This pertains to the keys, of which it was said: "Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven." But He said this to Peter so that you may know that Peter then bore the person of the universal Church. Hear what is said to him, and what is said to all the holy faithful: Matthew 18: If your brother sins against you, etc. The same holy Doctor, in Psalm 108, in the book on the Christian contest, chapter 3, in Tractate 50 on John, and in Tractate 118, etc., clearly teaches that the keys of the kingdom of heaven were given to Peter because Christ conferred them on the Church, which Peter represented, when the Lord said to him: I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. See the same holy Doctor, Tractate 124 on John, and book 1 of On Christian Doctrine, chapter 18.

units.la: Dabo. In futurum pollicetur, scilicet se daturum claves, non hoc loco dedit, sed post resurrectionem, dum discipulis dixit Joan. 20. Accipite Spiritum Sanctum, quorum remiseritis peccata, &c.
units.tr: I will give. He promises for the future that he will give the keys; he did not give them at this place, but after the resurrection, when he said to the disciples, John 20: Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you remit, etc.

units.la: Claves. Id est, potestatem ex officio prædicandi Evangelium, Sacramenta administrandi, & speciatim discipulorum ecclesiasticam exercendi. Utitur autem Christus hac metaphorâ, ut Ecclesiæ præpositi noverint se esse dispensatores mysteriorum Dei, tanquam fideles servos, quos constituit Dominus super familiam suam, nec sint dominantes in Clero.
units.tr: Keys. That is, the power, from the office of preaching the Gospel and administering the sacraments, and especially of exercising ecclesiastical discipline by the disciples. Christ uses this metaphor so that those set over the Church may know that they are the stewards of the mysteries of God, as faithful servants whom the Lord has set over his household, and that they are not to lord it over the clergy.

units.la: Regni cœlorum. Non terrarum. Hinc Bernardus l. 1. de Consideratione ad Eugenium: In criminibus, non in possessionibus potestas vestra, quoniam propter illa & non propter hæc, accepistis claves regni cœlorum, prævaricatores utique exclusuri, non possessores. Ut sciatis, ait Matth. 9. quia Filius hominis habet potestatem in terra dimittendi peccata, &c. Quænam tibi major videtur & dignitas & potestas dimittendi peccata, an prædia dividendi? Sed non est comparatio. Habent hæc infima & terrena judices suos, Reges & Principes terræ. Quid fines alios invadiatis? Quid falcem vestram in alienam messem extenditis? Non quia indigni vos, sed quia indignum vobis talibus insistere, quippe potioribus occupatis. Hinc & Christus Luc. 12. v. 14. hominibus litigantibus pro terrena hæreditate, & flagitantibus à se judicium, dixit: Quis me constituit judicem aut divisorem super vos? Hæc Bernardus. Hinc & Prudentius sic Herodem alloquitur: Hostis Herodes impie Christum venire quid times? Non eripit mortalia, Qui regna dat cælestia.
units.tr: Of the kingdom of heaven. Not of the earth. Hence Bernard, book 1 On Consideration, to Eugenius: Your power lies in crimes, not in possessions, since you received the keys of the kingdom of heaven for the sake of those things and not of these, to exclude transgressors, not possessors. That you may know, he says in Matthew 9, that the Son of man has power on earth to forgive sins, etc. Which seems to you the greater dignity and power, to forgive sins or to divide estates? But there is no comparison. These lowest and earthly things have their own judges, the kings and princes of the earth. Why do you invade other people's boundaries? Why do you stretch your sickle into another's harvest? Not because you are unworthy, but because it is unworthy of you to busy yourselves with such things, since you are occupied with weightier matters.* Hence also Christ, Luke 12:14, when men quarrelling over an earthly inheritance demanded judgment from him, said: Who made me a judge or divider over you? So Bernard. Hence also Prudentius addresses Herod thus: Impious enemy Herod, why do you fear that Christ has come? He does not snatch away mortal things; he who gives heavenly kingdoms.

units.la: Et. Hæc particula hîc & alibi passim exegeticè sumitur pro, id est.
units.tr: And. This particle here and elsewhere throughout is taken explanatorily, for that is.

units.la: 19. Et quodcumque ligaveris super terram, &c. Jus ligandi atque solvendi à Christo Domino Ecclesiæ concessum, unum idemque est cum jure retinendi remittendique peccata, Quia cùm excommunicat Ecclesia, in cœlo ligatur excommunicatus: cùm cùm reconciliatur ab Ecclesia, in cœli solvitur reconciliatus, inquit Aug. Tract. 50. in Joan. Verùm hæc potestas ligandi & solvendi non omnino absoluta est Ecclesiæ concessa, sed ut pro cujusque merito & dispositione præpositi ea utantur; ut alioqui nec noceant ligando nec solvendo juvent. Hinc præclare Hier. Iflum locum Episcopi & Presbyteri non intelligentes aliquid sibi de Pharisæorum assumunt supercilio, ut vel damnent innocentes, vel solvere se noxios, arbitrentur: cùm apud Deum non sententia Sacerdotum, sed reorum vita quæratur. Legimus in Levitico de leprosis, ubi jubentur ut ostendant se Sacerdotibus: & si lepram habuerint, tunc à sacerdote immundi fiant: non quò Socerdotes leprosos faciant, & immundos, sed quo habeant notitiam leprosi & non leprosi, & possint discernere qui mundus, qui ve immundus sit. Quomodo ergo ibi leprosum Sacerdos mundum, vel immundum facit; sic & hic alligat vel solvit Episcopus & presbyter, non eos qui insontes sunt vel noxii; sed pro officio suo, cùm peccatorum audierit varietates, scit qui ligandus sit, (in foro externo authoritative, absolutè, & judicialiter publicâ censurâ & correptione, declarative verò conditionaliter, & ministerialiter quoad internum conscientiæ forum) quive solvendus.
units.tr: 19. And whatever you bind on earth, etc. The right of binding and loosing granted to the Church by Christ the Lord is one and the same as the right of retaining and remitting sins: For when the Church excommunicates, the excommunicated is bound in heaven; when he is reconciled by the Church, the reconciled is loosed in heaven, says Augustine, Tractate 50 on John. Yet this power of binding and loosing was not granted to the Church absolutely, but so that those set over it use it according to each person's merit and disposition; otherwise they would neither harm by binding nor help by loosing. Hence Jerome excellently: Bishops and presbyters, not understanding this place, assume for themselves something of the haughtiness of the Pharisees, so that they think they may condemn the innocent or absolve the guilty; whereas before God the judgment is not of priests but of the life of the guilty. We read in Leviticus about lepers, where they are commanded to show themselves to the priests; and if they have leprosy, then they are made unclean by the priest; not that the priests make the lepers unclean, but so that they may know the leper from the non-leper and may distinguish who is clean and who is unclean. Just as there the priest makes the leper clean or unclean, so here the bishop and presbyter bind or loose, not those who are innocent or guilty, but by virtue of their office, when they have heard the varieties of sins, they know who is to be bound (in the external forum authoritatively, absolutely and judicially by public censure and correction; but declaratively, conditionally and ministerially as regards the internal forum of conscience) and who is to be loosed.

units.la: 21. Offendere. Id est, claris verbis indicare.
units.tr: 21. To show. That is, to indicate in plain words.

units.la: Senioribus. Id est, Senatoribus.
units.tr: By the elders. That is, by the senators.

units.la: 22. Assumens. Id est, apprehendens, ut patet ex Marc. 8. v. 32.
units.tr: 22. Taking. That is, seizing, as is clear from Mark 8:32.

units.la: Increpare. Tanquam sui oblitum.
units.tr: Rebuke. As one forgetful of himself.

units.la: Absit à te Domine. Familiaris Hebræis locutio, quâ deprecari solent, ne quod dicitur, veniat.
units.tr: Far be it from you, Lord. A locution familiar to the Hebrews, by which they are accustomed to pray that what is said may not come to pass.

units.la: 23. Conversus. Vultu scilicet minaci in Petrum lateri suo adhærentem, & in discipulos ceteros, ut patet ex Marc. 8. v. 33.
units.tr: 23. Turning. That is, with a threatening look at Peter, who clung to his side, and at the other disciples, as is clear from Mark 8:33.

units.la: Vade post me. Id est, apage, facesse hinc.
units.tr: Get behind me. That is, begone, get away from here.

units.la: Satana. Obtinet apud Hebræos Proverbii locum effici alicui in Satan, pro eo quod est dare consilium malum & perniciosum alicui; Satan enim apud Hebræos adversarium sonat & inimicum. Extat exemplum lib. 2. Sam. seu Reg. c. 19. v. 22.
units.tr: Satan. Among the Hebrews it holds the place of a proverb to be made a Satan to someone, meaning to give that person bad and pernicious counsel; for among the Hebrews Satan means adversary and enemy. An example exists in 2 Samuel, or 2 Kings, chapter 19, verse 22.

units.la: Non sapis ea quæ Dei sunt, &c. Non divina sed humana, quæ caro & sanguis suggerere solet, sapis.
units.tr: You do not savour the things that are of God, etc. You savour not divine things but human ones, which flesh and blood are wont to suggest.

units.la: 24. Tunc. Supple ex Marc. 8. v. 34. convocatâ turbâ cum discipulis suis, dixit eis, id est, omnibus, ut patet ex Luc. 9. v. 23.
units.tr: 24. Then. Supply from Mark 8:34: having called the crowd together with his disciples, he said to them, that is, to all, as is clear from Luke 9:23.

units.la: Abneget semetipsum. Quid hoc nisi suum esse negare, quod perinde est ac si quisquam non sum, seu nihil sum diceret. Hoc etiam fatetur qui credit, sperat, & amat. Prorsus, non quia videt, sed quia Deum audit, credit; non in sua virtute, sed in Dei potentia & promissione spem collocat; nihil quia suum, sed quia divinum diligit; unde sibi quisque credendo veritatem, sperando potestatem, amando bonitatem abdicat ac si aperte diceret: Nihil est in me purae veritatis, potentiae, bonitatis, cui fides certa, fiducia secura, amor cassus, sive à nihili, sive à mali appetitione, ac proinde vitio, & labe integer inniti queat; neque ego, neque res alia creata, sed Deus solus verus, potens, bonus, imo solus Deus est, qui est, sive esse purum possidet. Ego igitur non sum, sive entis indolem non obtineo, nisi significatione quadam ab ea, quae Numinis proprium est nomen, diversissima; sic etenim aseitatem meram significat, cui nihil ullo modo simile in creaturae abalieitate sub entis notione conspicitur; nam Deus & creatura sunt differentiae purae nullius generis communione miscendae; illa mera aseitas, haec abalieitas mera cognoscitur, ut vox magis nusquam aequivocè reperiatur, quam ubi ens aseitati & abalieitati tribuitur, quae non sunt entis differentiae, sed ipsae per seipsas ab invicem totae differunt. Haec per Ecclesiam exigitur abnegatio, seu abrenuntiatio à baptizandis, cum baptismi suscepti fit solemnis professio sequelae Christi, seu voluntatis vivendi quomodo Christus vivendum verbo & exemplo docuit.
units.tr: Let him deny himself. What is this but to deny that one is one's own, which is just as if someone should say, I am not, or I am nothing? This also is confessed by one who believes, hopes and loves. Truly, he believes not because he sees but because he hears God; he places his hope not in his own virtue but in the power and promise of God; he loves not what is his own but what is divine; whence each person, by believing, renounces his own truth, by hoping, his own power, by loving, his own goodness, as if he were openly saying: There is nothing in me of pure truth, power, goodness, on which certain faith, secure trust, or pure love, free from the desire of nothing or of evil, and therefore from vice and stain, could rest; neither I nor any other created thing, but God alone is true, powerful, good; indeed God alone is he who is, or possesses being in its purity. I therefore am not, or I do not have the nature of being, except by a certain signification, which is most different from that which is the proper name of the Deity; for it signifies pure aseity, to which nothing at all similar is seen under the notion of being in the abaseity of a creature; for God and creature are pure differences, to be mixed with no common genus; the former is known as pure aseity, the latter as pure abaseity, so that the word is nowhere more equivocally found than where being is attributed to aseity and abaseity, which are not differences of being, but wholly differ from each other through themselves. This denial, or renunciation, is required of those to be baptized by the Church, since the solemn profession of baptism is the following of Christ, or the will to live as Christ taught by word and example to live.

units.la: 26. Quid enim, &c. Sensus est: Irreparabilis est quovis pretio seu lytro sui ipsius jactura. Alludit autem Christus ad belli seu humanorum judiciorum consuetudinem.
units.tr: 26. For what, etc. The sense is: the loss of oneself is irreparable at any price or ransom. Christ alludes here to the custom of war or of human judgments.

units.la: 28. Gustabunt mortem. Hebraismus, id est, morientur. Haec metaphorica locutio videtur desumta à potionibus, quarum sapor amarus est, unde & ipsa mors ab Amalecitarum Rege Agag, amara vocatur 1 Sam. seu Reg. 15.
units.tr: 28. They shall taste death. A Hebraism, that is, they shall die. This metaphorical expression seems to be taken from drinks whose taste is bitter, whence death itself is called bitter by Agag, King of the Amalekites, 1 Samuel, or 1 Kings, 15.

units.la: In regno suo. Cum hoc de ultimo adventu intelligi non possit, quidam impletum volunt in transfiguratione, quam Evangelistae mox subjungunt; nonnulli referunt ad adventum Christi in gloria post resurrectionem, quae usque ad Ascensionem omnibus discipulis manifestata est; alii denique ad regnum Christi per Evangelii praedicationem in toto orbe.
units.tr: In his kingdom. Since this cannot be understood of the last coming, some want it fulfilled in the transfiguration, which the Evangelists immediately add; some refer it to Christ's coming in glory after the resurrection, which was made manifest to all the disciples until the Ascension; others finally to Christ's kingdom through the preaching of the Gospel in the whole world.

units.la: CAPUT XVII.
units.tr: CAPUT XVII.

units.la: 1. Post dies sex. Supple, integros; unde Luc. 9. v. 28. dicitur: factum est post hæc verba fere dies octo: nempe quia hoc evenit post dies sex integros & duorum extremorum aliquam partem.
units.tr: 1. Post dies sex. Supply "whole days." So Luke 9:28 says: factum est post hæc verba fere dies octo ("about eight days after these words"). That is because it happened after six whole days and parts of the two extreme days.

units.la: Jacobum. Non fratrem Domini Jerosolymorum Episcopum & Catholicæ epistolæ scriptorem, ut Aug. putavit, sed Majorem, qui ab Herode est occisus, cum Matthæus ipsum appellet fratrem Joannis.
units.tr: Jacobum. This is not the Lord's brother, the Bishop of Jerusalem and writer of the Catholic epistle, as Augustine thought, but James the Greater, who was killed by Herod, since Matthew calls him the brother of John.

units.la: In montem excelsum. Est vetustissima in Ecclesia traditio per montem excelsum hic intelligi Thabor, qui sic vocatur in Paraphrasi Chaldaica Jonathæ κατ' ἐξοχὴν. Hunc montem Græci interpretes & Josephus Itabyrium appellant, & Hieronymus in Epistola ad Marcellam vocat Tabyrium. Est autem Thabor mons in Galilæa situs in campestribus, rotundus atque sublimis, & ex omni parte finitur æqualiter, inquit idem Hier. Quia vero hic mons Occidentem respiciebat, pro Occidente ponitur Psal. 88. Heb. 89. v. 13. ut Hermon pro Oriente. Idem mons Thabor nuncupatur mons Sanctus 2. Pet. 1 v. 18. à Polybio Atabyrius, & dicitur à Mafio in Josue abfuisse à Nazareth duarum horarum itinere. Idem mons à nonnullis dicitur mons nivis. Hujus altitudo triginta est stadiorum, & vertex habet planiciem viginti sex stadiorum, ut ait Josephus lib. 4. de bello Judaico c. 6. cum tamen Polybius in quinta historia tantum dicat hunc montem habere altitudinem stadiorum amplius quindecim; sed fieri potest ut de diversis partibus montis scripserint Polybius & Josephus, non enim solum ex una parte adiri solent magni montes. Testimonio Gemini in elementis astronomiæ cognoscimus hunc montem habere altitudinem ad perpendiculum stadiorum fere 14. ut non fit mirum quod Josephus ait de 30. stadiis, si accipiatur de viis & flexibus circa montem, per quos ascenditur. Joan. Damascenus inusitatæ altitudinis montem Thabor fuisse satis ostendit in Homil. de transfiguratione.
units.tr: In montem excelsum. There is a very ancient tradition in the Church that the high mountain here is Tabor, which is called par excellence [κατ' ἐξοχήν] by the Chaldee paraphrase of Jonathan. The Greek translators and Josephus call this mountain Itabyrium, and Jerome in his letter to Marcella calls it Tabyrium. Tabor is a mountain in Galilee, set in the plain, round and lofty, and it ends equally on every side, says the same Jerome. Because this mountain faces west, it stands for the west at Psalm 88 (Hebrew 89:13), as Hermon stands for the east. The same mountain Tabor is called the holy mountain at 2 Peter 1:18; Polybius calls it Atabyrius; and Masius says in his commentary on Joshua that it was two hours' journey from Nazareth. Some also call this mountain the mountain of snow. Its height is thirty stadia, and its summit has a plain of twenty-six stadia, as Josephus says in book 4 of the Jewish War, chapter 6. Yet Polybius, in his fifth history, says only that this mountain is more than fifteen stadia high. But Polybius and Josephus may have written about different sides of the mountain, since large mountains are not usually approached from only one side. From the testimony of Geminus in his Elements of Astronomy we learn that the mountain's perpendicular height is about fourteen stadia, so it is no wonder that Josephus speaks of thirty stadia if this is taken as the roads and turns around the mountain by which one climbs. John Damascene has sufficiently shown, in his homily on the Transfiguration, that Tabor was a mountain of unusual height.

units.la: 2. Transfiguratus est. Id est, facta est dum oraret species vultus ejus altera, ut habetur Luc. 9. v. 29. Et. Hæc particula exegetice hic sumitur, ut alibi passim, pro, id est.
units.tr: 2. Transfiguratus est. That is, his face's appearance became different while he was praying, as Luke 9:29 has it. Et. This particle is here taken explanatorily, as it often is elsewhere, to mean that is.

units.la: Facta sunt alba sicut nix. Græcè φῶς lumen, unde Marc. c. 9. v. 2. addit, qualia fullo non potest super terram candida facere; unde albor hic non est proprie albor, sed luminis transparentis fulgor, qualis fere est nubium soli subjectarum directé.
units.tr: Facta sunt alba sicut nix. In Greek it is light [φῶς]; therefore Mark 9:2 adds such as no fuller on earth can make white. So this whiteness is not properly whiteness but the brightness of transparent light, such as is roughly that of clouds lying directly under the sun.

units.la: 3. Moyses & Elias. Hi apparuerunt, quia Lex & Prophetæ in alto celsioris intelligentiæ cernuntur cum Evangelio, & concordant cum eo in dictis suis; unde in eo quod Petrus tria tabernacula facere quæsivit, nesciebat quid diceret, cum unum sit tabernaculum Evangelii, in quo Lex & Prophetæ recapitulantur, ut Hieronymi voce utar.
units.tr: 3. Moyses & Elias. These appeared because the Law and the Prophets are seen, in a higher and fuller understanding, together with the Gospel, and agree with it in what they say. Hence, when Peter sought to make three tabernacles, he did not know what he was saying, since there is one tabernacle, that of the Gospel, in which the Law and the Prophets are summed up, to use the words of Jerome.

units.la: Cum eo loquentes. Nempe de passione sua, quam Lucas excessum ejus vocat c. 9. v. 31. Loquebantur cum illo, quia locuti erant de illo, ostendebant quæ prædixerant, manifestabant quem prophetaverant. Loquebantur. Putas, quid loquebantur? Ut Judæi convincerentur, Pagani converterentur, Manichæi confunderentur, Hæretici comprimerentur, Catholici confirmarentur. Loquebatur Lex & gratia, lenitas & asperitas, terror & mansuetudo, præceptum & adjutorium, ferramentum & medicus, umbra & lux, præco & judex, sententia & misericordia. Aug. de quinque Hær. c. 7.
units.tr: Cum eo loquentes. Namely about his passion, which Luke calls his departure (Luke 9:31). They spoke with him, because they had spoken about him; they showed what they had foretold, they made plain whom they had prophesied. They spoke. Do you think what they spoke? So that the Jews might be convicted, the pagans converted, the Manichaeans confounded, the heretics restrained, the Catholics strengthened. The Law spoke, and grace; gentleness and severity; terror and meekness; command and help; the iron and the physician; shadow and light; herald and judge; sentence and mercy. Augustine, On the Five Heresies, chapter 7.

units.la: 4. Respondens. Hebraismus, id est, loqui incipiens.
units.tr: 4. Respondens. A Hebraism, that is, beginning to speak.

units.la: Petrus. Scilicet evigilans, gravatus enim erat somno, sicut & qui cum illo erant, ut testatur Luc. c. 9. v. 32.
units.tr: Petrus. Namely, waking up, for he was weighed down with sleep, as he and those with him were, as Luke 9:32 testifies.

units.la: - Dixit. Cum scilicet Moyses & Elias discederent à Christo, ut testatur Lucas c. 9. v. 33. Hæc autem dixit nesciens quid diceret, ut Marc. & Lucas testantur.
units.tr: - Dixit. Namely when Moses and Elijah were leaving Christ, as Luke 9:33 testifies. He said these things not knowing what he was saying, as Mark and Luke testify.

units.la: 5. Obumbravit. &c. Id est, velut umbra quædam texit Christum, Moysen & Eliam, ut patet ex Luc. 9. v. 33.
units.tr: 5. Obumbravit. Etc. That is, like a kind of shadow it covered Christ, Moses and Elijah, as is clear from Luke 9:33.

units.la: Ipsum audite. Præclare hinc infert B. Cyprianus lib. 2. epist. 3. ad Cæcilium, quæ est epistola 63. in editione Pameliana: Quare, si solus Christus audiendus est, non debemus attendere, quid aliquis ante nos faciendum putaverit; sed quid, qui ante omnes est, Christus prior fecerit. Neque enim hominis consuetudinem sequi oportet, sed Dei veritatem: cum per Esaiam prophetam Deus loquatur & dicat, sine causa autem colunt me, mandata & doctrinas hominum docentes. Et iterum Dominus in Evangelio hoc idem repetat, dicens: Rejicitis mandatum Dei, ut traditionem vestram statuatis.
units.tr: Ipsum audite. From this St. Cyprian draws a fine conclusion in book 2, letter 3, to Caecilius, which is letter 63 in Pamelius's edition: Therefore, if Christ alone is to be heard, we ought not to consider what anyone before us thought should be done, but what Christ, who is before all, did first. For we must follow not the custom of man but the truth of God, since God speaks through the prophet Isaiah and says: "In vain do they worship me, teaching the doctrines and commandments of men." And again the Lord in the Gospel repeats the same thing, saying: You reject the commandment of God so that you may establish your own tradition.

units.la: 7. Accessit Jesus. Qui scilicet inventus est solus dum fieret vox, ut testatur Luc. c. 9. v. 36.
units.tr: 7. Accessit Jesus. He was found alone when the voice came, as Luke 9:36 testifies.

units.la: 10. Quid ergo, &c. Q. d. Unde ergo tam constanter Legis-periti tradunt Eliam esse venturum, ut omnia emendet, populum doceat, Messiamque notum faciat?
units.tr: 10. Quid ergo, &c. That is: why then do the scribes so constantly teach that Elijah is to come, to restore all things, teach the people, and make the Messiah known?

units.la: Primum. Id est, ante Messiæ manifestationem.
units.tr: Primum. That is, before the manifestation of the Messiah.

units.la: 11. Elias quidem venturus est, &c. Q. d. Vera fuit vetus illa traditio de venturo Elia ante Messiæ manifestationem ad omnia emendanda.
units.tr: 11. Elias quidem venturus est, &c. That is: the old tradition about Elijah's coming before the manifestation of the Messiah, to restore all things, was true.

units.la: 12. Elias. Qui nempe ex recepta eruditorum sententia venire debebat.
units.tr: 12. Elias. Who, according to the accepted opinion of the learned, was bound to come.

units.la: Iam venit. Id est, jam functum est suo officio.
units.tr: Iam venit. That is, he has already completed his office.

units.la: 13. De Joanne Baptista. Supple, qui juxta Malachiæ & Angeli prædictionem Christum præcesserat in Spiritu & virtute Eliæ. Vide Luc. 1. v. 17.
units.tr: 13. De Joanne Baptista. Supply: who, according to the prediction of Malachi and the angel, had gone before Christ in the spirit and power of Elijah. See Luke 1:17.

units.la: 18. Secreto. Id est, privatim.
units.tr: 18. Secreto. That is, privately.

units.la: 19. Propter incredulitatem vestram. Id est, quia diffidentia non penitus abest ab animis vestris.
units.tr: 19. Propter incredulitatem vestram. That is, because distrust is not wholly absent from your hearts.

units.la: Si habueritis fidem sicut granum sinapis. Comparatio fit simul ratione quantitatis minimæ, & virtutis maximæ; unde Apostolus ad hunc locum alludens 1 Cor. 13. v. 2. talem fidem vocat omnem fidem, id est, integerrimam, plenissimam, ita ut per eam montes transferantur. Sic Jacobus omne gaudium appellat gaudium perfectissimum & plenissimum.
units.tr: Si habueritis fidem sicut granum sinapis. The comparison is made both in respect of the smallest quantity and the greatest power. Hence the Apostle, alluding to this passage in 1 Corinthians 13:2, calls such faith all faith, that is, most complete and full, so that by it mountains are moved. So James calls all joy the most perfect and full joy.

units.la: Dicetis monti huic, &c. Hoc ad literam factum traditur a B. Aniano primo Marci in cathedra Alexandrina successore & a B. Gregorio Thaumaturgo Neocæsareæ Ponti Episcopo.
units.tr: Dicetis monti huic, &c. It is handed down that this was literally done by St. Anianus, the first successor of Mark in the Alexandrian see, and by St. Gregory Thaumaturgus, bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus.

units.la: 20. Hoc autem genus. Id est, ut optime explicant Chrysost. & D. Th. omne dæmoniorum genus, quod pro diversitate tentationum & vexationum diversas appellationes & nomenclaturas sortitur; unde alius dicitur spiritus immundus vel spiritus fornicationis, alius spiritus superbiæ, alius spiritus vertiginis, alius pater mendacii, alius homicida ab initio, dæmonium mutum, &c.
units.tr: 20. Hoc autem genus. That is, as Chrysostom and Thomas explain very well, every kind of demon, which, according to the variety of temptations and vexations, receives different names and designations. Hence one is called an unclean spirit or spirit of fornication, another a spirit of pride, another a spirit of vertigo, another the father of lies, another a murderer from the beginning, a dumb demon, and so on.

units.la: Non ejicitur, &c. At, inquies, malus dæmon per Davidem expulsus est ex Saule vi musicæ? Nam medici Regis astantes Saüli de materia cantûs parum solliciti, hoc solum quæsierunt, ut vocaretur peritus citharædus, qui Regem a cacodæmone vexatum arte sua recrearet & liberaret. Quomodo inanis sonus dæmonem potuit pellere, qui Christo teste non pellitur nisi in jejunio & oratione? Respondeo musicam, quæ res est corporea, per se nihil posse in dæmonem, qui spiritus est; tamen aliquid posse per accidens, quia mitigatis affectibus, per quos in animos nostros diabolus se insinuat, & mœrore aut furore pulso, aut si quid aliud sit, quo in perniciem nostram humanæ salutis hostis abutatur, etiam ipse pellitur. In hanc rem diserta sunt Pauli verba Ephef. 4. v. 26, & 27. Sol non occidat super iracundiam vestram. Nolite locum dare diabolo: q. d. Ne detis locum diabolo. Ex his emicat per inordinatos affectus aditum patere diabolo, præcipuè si sint vehementes, qualis ira est, quæ furor brevis dicitur. Diabolus igitur excluditur eâ arte, quâ hi affectus demulcentur. Exemplo sint radii solis, qui neque gladio secari, neque flatu extingui, neque ullo conatu averti queunt, ita ut verè dicatur, nos in eos nihil posse: radios tamen clausâ fenestrâ ex cœnaculo excludimus; ita quamvis musica in dæmonem nihil directè possit, eum tamen excludit obstructo aditu, quo animorum arcem invadit; denique musica malum spiritum eodem modo abigit, quo bonum accersit: bonum autem spiritum accersit, dum perturbatum animum pacat & piâ voluptate permulcet, ne in mente nostra quidquam sit, quod Sanctum-Spiritum repellat, aut resistat ejus inspirationibus; unde Eliseus 4. Reg. cap. 3. fidicinem jussit advocari, quo pulsante fieret idoneus ad oracula fundenda. Hinc lunaticus vocatur à Matthæo, qui dæmonium habuit, quia idem erat obnoxius morbo, qui lunâ crescente intendebatur, quo morbo ita aucto, arripiebatur à diabolo. Itaque si medicus morbum illum sanasset, is ægrum eâdem operâ à dæmone liberasset; ita pari ratione musicus Saülis animum mitigando, potuit eum à spiritu liberare, cui vesaniâ suâ locum dederat. Sed extraordinariam musicæ peritiam Deum indulsisse Davidi, satis indicant Scripturæ, in quibus non modò habentur sacræ illæ cantiones ab ipso compositæ, quas hodie universus orbis Christianus canit, sed etiam præ ceteris musicis commendatur, & Amos Propheta cap. 6. v. 5. in textu Hebraeo testatur ipsum Davidem excogitasse & fabricasse quædam instrumenta musica; quod etiam habet Pseudo-Psaltes in editione Syriacæ Psal. 151.
units.tr: Non ejicitur, &c. But you will object: was not the evil demon driven out of Saul by David, by the power of music? For the king's physicians, standing by Saul, were not much concerned about the matter of the song, but asked only that a skilled harpist be summoned, who by his art might refresh and free the king, who was troubled by an evil demon. How could an empty sound drive out a demon, when, as Christ testifies, it is driven out only by fasting and prayer? I answer that music, being a corporeal thing, can do nothing by itself against a demon, who is a spirit; yet it can do something accidentally, because when the emotions through which the devil creeps into our minds are calmed, and sorrow or fury is dispelled, or whatever else it is that the enemy of human salvation uses for our ruin, then he himself is driven out too. The words of Paul in Ephesians 4:26–27 are clear on this: Let not the sun go down upon your wrath. Do not give place to the devil, that is, do not give room to the devil. From this it shines forth that through disordered emotions a way lies open to the devil, especially if they are violent, as anger is, which is called a brief madness. The devil is therefore shut out by that art by which these emotions are soothed. Take the rays of the sun as an example: they cannot be cut by a sword, extinguished by a breath, or turned aside by any effort, so that it is truly said that we can do nothing against them; yet we shut out the rays by closing the window of the room. So, although music can do nothing directly against a demon, it shuts him out by blocking the entrance by which he invades the citadel of the mind. Finally, music drives out an evil spirit in the same way that it summons a good one: it summons the good spirit when it calms a troubled mind and soothes it with a pious delight, so that nothing in our mind repels the Holy Spirit or resists his inspirations. Hence Elisha, in 4 Kings chapter 3, ordered a harpist to be called, so that by his playing the prophet might become fit to utter oracles.
