Hence Matthew calls the lunatic one who had a demon, because he was subject to a disease that grew worse as the moon waxed, and when the disease was thus increased he was seized by the devil. Therefore, if a physician had cured that illness, he would at the same time have freed the sick man from the demon. In the same way, by soothing Saul's mind, the musician could free him from the spirit to which he had given room by his madness. But that God granted David an extraordinary skill in music is sufficiently shown by the Scriptures, in which not only are those sacred songs composed by him, which the whole Christian world sings today, held up above all others, but also Amos the prophet, in Amos 6:5 in the Hebrew text, testifies that David himself devised and made certain musical instruments; the Syriac edition of Psalm 151 by the pseudo-Psalmist also has this.

units.la: 21. Conversantibus autem eis in Galilæa. Hinc patet quòd dum Marcus dicit Christum & discipulos profectos à monte, in quo contigit transfiguratio, prætergressos Galilæam, nihil aliud significare, quàm eos per Galilæam hac illac transiisse prædicando & sanando omnes pro more. Quod autem ibidem dicitur à Marco: nec volebat quemquam scire: refertur ad profectionem. Q. d. clàm autem profectus est Christus à monte, in quo est transfiguratus, unà cum discipulis, ut unà cum iis prætergrederetur Galilæam.
units.tr: 21. But while they were staying in Galilee. From this it is clear that when Mark says that Christ and the disciples departed from the mountain where the transfiguration took place and passed through Galilee, he means nothing more than that they travelled through Galilee here and there, preaching and healing everyone as usual. What Mark adds there, and he did not want anyone to know, refers to the journey. The sense is: Christ left the mountain where he had been transfigured secretly, together with his disciples, so that he might pass through Galilee with them.

units.la: 23. Didrachma accipiebant. Nempe, ad pensitationem à Deo Exod. 30. v. 13. institutam in usum tabernaculi aut Templi; hæc enim didrachma exiguntur quasi precario, non superbè & cum violentia, sicut solent exigi tributa à Principibus seculi imposita. Ita Hilar. can. 17. in Matth. Baronius anno Christi 33. Num. 31. &c.
units.tr: 23. They collected the didrachma. Namely, the levy instituted by God in Exodus 30:13 for the use of the tabernacle or Temple. For these didrachmas were demanded as a due request, not arrogantly and by force, as the taxes imposed by secular princes are usually exacted. So Hilary, on Matthew, canon 17; Baronius, in the year of Christ 33, no. 31, etc.

units.la: 26. Ut autem non scandalizemus eos. Noverat Christus aliud jus, quo tributum non debebat, sed eo jure tributum ille solvebat, quo ab omni non solum re, sed etiam specie maligna, quantum possumus, nos abstinere & custodire bonam famam dispensationi nostræ multum necessariam tenemur. Aug. Epist. 239. ad Alipium.
units.tr: 26. But that we may not offend them. Christ knew another right, by which he was not obliged to pay the tax, but by that right he paid it, by which we are bound, as far as we can, to abstain from every evil thing, not only from the act but even from its appearance, and to guard a good reputation, which is very necessary for our stewardship. Augustine, Letter 239, to Alypius.

units.la: Invenies saterem. In annotationibus ad B. Ambrosium ex Petri Nannii & aliorum scholiis, stateres dicuntur esse nummi Dorici, ejus ponderis, cujus didrachmum. Stater itaque idem est ac siclus, Hebraicè שקל Schekel à radice שקל Schakal quod est appendere & ponderare. Nimirum, ut observat germanus frater meus Ludovicus de Compiegne de Veil Doctor Artium in notis suis ad tract. De instrumento, apparatu & ministris rempli cap. 1. priscorum temporum nummi tam ex ære, quam ex argento non sic, ut nunc signati numerabantur, sed plane rudes ponderibus appendebantur. Jam id extra controversiam est siclum omninò numismatum omnium, quæ litteris consignata sunt, esse antiquissimum. Etenim Scriptum videmus Genes. 23. Ephron agrum suum illum, in quo erat spelunca duplex, æstimasse quadringentis siclis argenti, quos illi dicitur Abraham appendisse transeuntes per mercatores. Erat autem siclus, ut videre licet Exod. 30. v. 13. & Ezech. 45. v. 12. obolorum viginti. Majemonides tract. de siclis cap. 1. art. 2. asserit siclum ejusdem fuisse ponderis ac grana hordeacea vulgaria trecenta viginti. Flavius autem Josephus lib. 3. Antiq. cap. 10. testatur siclum fuisse drachmarum Atticarum quatuor. Unde sequitur ut duarum esset drachmarum Hebraicarum. Etenim pondera Hebraica, itemque Alexandrina erant altero tanto majora Atticis, ut cuivis ex Varrone cognoscere licet. Qua de causa LXX. siclum ubique reddiderunt non ταλαντον, sed διδραχμον; quia Legem interpretabantur Alexandriæ, cujus pondera ponderibus Hebraicis plane congruebant. Quæ cùm minùs perspecta fuissent nonnullis, commenti sunt duplicem fuisse siclum; unum sanctum, drachmarum Atticarum quatuor, & alterum communem, qui tamen nusquam & nunquam reperitur, duarum tantùm drachmarum. Non est ita. Sed enim quòd sicli passim in litteris sacris jubentur examinari pondere sicli sancti, vel, ut textus Hebraicus ad verbum habet, juxta siclum Sanctuarii, ea causa fuit, fuit, quia in Sanctuario servarentur cuncta pondera, quae erant reliquorum omnium certa & perpetua norma. Quod & apud Ethnicos usitatum esse, ut in delubris suis asservarent pondera mensurasque, atque adeo sacra putarent, ad quorum normam cetera exigerentur. Litteris proditum est. Haec germanus meus Ludovicus de Veïl.
units.tr: You will find a stater. In the annotations to Saint Ambrose, drawn from the scholia of Pierre Nannius and others, the staters are said to be Dorian coins of the same weight as the didrachm. The stater is therefore the same as the shekel, Hebrew שקל Schekel, from the root שקל Schakal, which means to weigh and to measure out. Indeed, as my German brother Louis de Compiègne de Veil, Master of Arts, observes in his notes on the treatise On the instrument, equipment and ministers of the temple, chapter 1: in early times coins, whether of bronze or of silver, were not counted as they are now stamped, but were simply weighed out as raw metal by weight. Now it is beyond dispute that the shekel is the oldest of all coins that have been recorded in writing. For we see in Genesis 23 that Ephron valued his field, in which was the double cave, at four hundred shekels of silver, which Abraham is said to have weighed out, as they passed through the merchants. Now the shekel, as may be seen in Exodus 30:13 and Ezekiel 45:12, was worth twenty obols. Maimonides, in the treatise on shekels, chapter 1, article 2, asserts that the shekel had the same weight as three hundred and twenty common barley grains. Flavius Josephus, in Antiquities book 3, chapter 10, testifies that the shekel was equal to four Attic drachmas. It follows that it was two Hebrew drachmas, for Hebrew weights, and likewise Alexandrian ones, were twice as large as Attic ones, as anyone may learn from Varro. For this reason the Seventy everywhere rendered the shekel not as talent [ταλαντον] but as didrachm [διδραχμον], because they interpreted the Law at Alexandria, whose weights agreed exactly with Hebrew weights. Since this was less well understood by some, they invented a double shekel: one holy, of four Attic drachmas, and another common one, which however is found nowhere and never, of only two drachmas. That is not so. For the reason why shekels are everywhere in the sacred writings commanded to be weighed by the holy shekel, or, as the Hebrew text has it word for word, according to the shekel of the Sanctuary, was this: all weights were kept in the Sanctuary, and they were the fixed and perpetual standard for all the rest. That the heathen too had the custom of keeping their weights and measures in their temples, and so regarded them as sacred, by whose standard the others were to be regulated, has been recorded in writing. So writes my German brother Louis de Veil.

units.la: CAPUT XVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVIII.

units.la: 1. IN illa hora. Hebraismus, id est, sub idem tempus.
units.tr: 1. At that hour. A Hebraism, that is, at about the same time.

units.la: Accesserunt discipuli, &c. Intraverat in discipulos cogitatio, quis eorum esset major, ut patet ex Luc. 9. v. 46. imo & hac de re, ut testatur Marcus c. 9. v. 43. in via inter se disputaverant; sed cum domi essent interrogati à Christo, quid in via tractassent, primum tacuerunt, deinde verecundiae causâ, non de se, sed in universum interrogaverunt Christum, ut Matthaeus hic narrat. Atque ita Lucas cogitationis, Marcus disputationis, Matthaeus interrogationis meminit.
units.tr: The disciples came, etc. The thought had entered the disciples' minds of which of them was the greatest, as is clear from Luke 9:46. Indeed, as Mark 9:43 testifies, they had argued among themselves about this matter on the way. But when Christ asked them at home what they had been discussing on the road, they first kept silent, and then, out of shame, asked Christ, not about themselves but in general, as Matthew here relates. So Luke mentions the thought, Mark the dispute, and Matthew the question.

units.la: Quis putas. Graecè Τίς ἄρα[?], quisnam? quis tandem.
units.tr: Who do you suppose? In Greek, τίς ἄρα [tis ara]: who then, who in the world?

units.la: In regno caelorum. Id est, in Ecclesia triumphante, ut patet ex versu tertio mox sequenti.
units.tr: In the kingdom of heaven. That is, in the Church triumphant, as is clear from the third verse immediately following.

units.la: 2. Advocans Jesus parvulum. Non tam statura, quàm aetate, unde Graecè παιδίον[?], quod puerulum significat.
units.tr: 2. Jesus called a little child. Not so much in stature as in age; whence the Greek παιδίον [paidion], which means a little child.

units.la: Statuit eum. Supple ex Luc. 9. v. 47. secus se. Anastasius Bibliothecarius in Scholiis ad octavam Synodum explicans cur in actione secunda ejusdem Synodi, quae est Constantinopolitana quarta, Thomas Tyriorum Metropolita Sedisque Antiochenae Vicarius & Legatus, ac Elias Presbyter Legatusque & Syncellus Theodosii Patriarchae Jerosolymitani Deiferum vocent sanctum Ignatium Martyrem & Antiochenae Ecclesiae tertium ab Apostolo Petro Episcopum, ait: Tradunt Graeci quòd quem Dominus advocatum statuit in medio dicens: Nisi conversi fueritis & efficiamini sicut hic parvulus: iste Ignatius fuit, & idcirco hunc Deiferum nuncupant. Unde nec Apostoli ausi[?] fuerunt ei, cum ad Ecclesiae Praesulatum promoveretur, amplius manus imponere: nimirum ore Dei laudatum & ipsius tactu sanctificatum cognoverunt.
units.tr: He set him. Supply from Luke 9:47, "beside himself" (secus se). Anastasius the Librarian, explaining in his Scholia on the Eighth Synod why, in the second session of that Synod (which is the Fourth Council of Constantinople), Thomas, Metropolitan of Tyre and Vicar and Legate of the See of Antioch, and Elias, presbyter, legate and syncellus of Theodosius, Patriarch of Jerusalem, call Saint Ignatius the Martyr, the third bishop of the Church of Antioch after the Apostle Peter, "God-bearer," says: The Greeks hold that the one whom the Lord called and set in the midst, saying, "Unless you are converted and become like this little child," was this Ignatius, and for this reason they name him God-bearer. Hence the Apostles did not dare to lay hands on him again when he was promoted to the leadership of the Church; they recognised that he had been praised by the mouth of God and sanctified by his touch.

units.la: 3. Nisi conversi fueritis. Ab ista Primatus ambitione. Et efficiamini sicut parvuli. Id est, efficiamini humiles per virtutem, sicut parvuli sunt perætatem.
units.tr: 3. Unless you are converted. From this ambition for primacy. And become like little children. That is, become humble in virtue, as little children are in age.

units.la: Non intrabitis in regnum cœlorum. Quia ut dicitur Apocal. 21. v. 27. Non intrabit in illud aliquid coinquinatum.
units.tr: You shall not enter the kingdom of heaven. Because, as Revelation 21:27 says, nothing defiled shall enter into it.

units.la: 5. Qui susceperit. Ponitur unum officium beneficentiæ definitum pro quovis beneficentiæ genere & officio. Q. d. Usque adeo humiles mihi placent, ut etiam qui benencus in eos extiterit, perinde à me remunerabitur, quasi in me ipsum se exhibuerit beneficum, & similiter, qui eos scandalizaverit, id est, qui eis offendiculum in via justitiæ sive contemtu, sive aliis modis posuerit, gravissimè punietur, ut potè qui inhonoret eos, quos in primis diligo. Amat Christus infantiam, quam primùm & animo suscepit & corpore. Amat Christus infantiam, quæ majorum dirigit mores, ad quam senum reducit ætates, & eos ad suum inclinat exemplum, quos ad regnum sublimat æternum. Amat Christus infantiam humilitatis magistram, innocentiæ regulam, mansuetudinis formam. Ut autem plenè valeamus cognoscere quomodo apprehendi possit tam mira conversio, & in puerilem gradum, quâ nobis imitatione redeundum sit, doceat nos B. Paulus & dicat: Nolite pueri effici sensibus, sed malitiâ parvuli essote. Non ergo ad lubrica infantiæ & imperfecta nobis primordia redeundum est, sed aliquid, quod graves annos deceat, inde sumendum est: velox à commotione transitus, citus ad pacem recursus, nulla sit offensionis memoria, nulla cupiditas dignitatis, amor socia dilectionis, æqualitas naturalis; magnum enim bonum est nocere non posse & ad maligna non sapere, quia inferre ac referre injuriam mundi hujus prudentia est: nemini autem malum pro malo reddere, christiana est æquanimitatis infantia. B. Leo. Ser. 7. in Epiph.
units.tr: 5. Whoever receives. One definite office of kindness is named for every kind of kindness and duty. As if to say: humble people are so pleasing to me that whoever shows kindness to them shall be rewarded by me just as if he had shown it to myself; and likewise whoever gives offence to them, that is, whoever places a stumbling-block in the way of justice for them, whether by contempt or by other means, shall be punished most severely, as one who dishonours those whom I love above all. Christ loves childhood, which he first embraced both in mind and in body. Christ loves childhood, which guides the conduct of its elders, to which he brings back the ages of the old, and whom he inclines to his own example, those whom he raises to the eternal kingdom. Christ loves childhood, the teacher of humility, the rule of innocence, the form of gentleness. But that we may fully understand how so wonderful a conversion may be grasped, and by what imitation we must return to the childlike state, the blessed Paul teaches us and says: "Brothers, do not be children in understanding, but in malice be babes." Therefore we must not return to the wavering and imperfect beginnings of infancy, but must take from it something that befits mature years: a swift passage from anger, a quick return to peace, no memory of offence, no desire for dignity, the love of a companion in affection, natural equality. For it is a great good not to be able to do harm and not to be wise in evil; for to inflict and repay injury is the wisdom of this world, but to return evil for evil to no one is the childhood of Christian equanimity. Blessed Leo, Sermon 7 on the Epiphany.

units.la: Parvulum talem. Qui nempè, ut Hilarius exponit, in infantium simplicitate collocatus circumfert speciem humilitatis mæ.
units.tr: Such a little child. Who, as Hilary explains, placed in the simplicity of infants, carries about the appearance of my humility.

units.la: 6. Expedit ei. Id est, bonum magis est ei, ut Marcus, seu, utilius est illi, ut Lucas loquitur.
units.tr: 6. It is better for him. That is, it is more good for him, as Mark puts it; or, it is more useful for him, as Luke says.

units.la: Mola asinaria. Id est, saxum prægrande. Erant autem molarum duo genera, asinariæ, & trusatiles; hæ minores erant, ut quæ manu truderentur, ut asinariæ majores, quas asinus oculis linteo velatis perpetuà gyratione circumagebat, ut tellantur Lucianus & Apuleius. Hinc Hilar. Can. 18. in Matth. Molæ, inquit, opus, labor est cacitatis, nam clausis jumentorum oculus aguntur. Per molam, inquit B. Greg. Pastoralis curæ 1. p. c. 2, asinariam secularis vitæ circuitus ac labor exprimitur, & per profundum maris extrema damnatio designatur. Qui ergo ad sanctitatis speciem deductus, vel verbo ceteros dejicit, vel exemplo, melius profecto ei fuerat, ut hunc ad mortem sui exteriori habitu terrena acta constringerent, quàm sacra officia cesris in culpa imitabilem demonstrarent, quia nimirum si solus cadsret, utcunque hunc tolerabilior inferni pœna cruciaret.
units.tr: A donkey's millstone. That is, a very large stone. There were two kinds of millstones: donkey millstones and hand millstones. The latter were smaller, being turned by hand, while the donkey millstones were larger, which a donkey, its eyes covered with a cloth, turned round in continual circles, as Lucian and Apuleius relate. Hence Hilary, Canon 18 on Matthew: The work of the mill is labour of blindness, for beasts are driven with their eyes closed. Blessed Gregory, Pastoral Care 1, part 1, chapter 2, says: "By the donkey's mill is expressed the round and toil of secular life, and by the depths of the sea is signified extreme damnation. Therefore, one who is led into the appearance of holiness and by word or example casts down others, it would certainly be better for him that, with a millstone round his neck, his earthly conduct should bind him to death, than that by his sacred office he should show others a fall to imitate; for if he alone fell, the punishment of hell would torment him more tolerably, whatever it may be."

units.la: 7. Væ mundo à scandalis. Transit Christus ad generalem doctrinam de scandalis. q. d. Cùm ita sit grave peccatum offendiculum ponere humilibus in via justitiæ, quàm ingentia mortalibus imminent mala à scandalis! Nam scandalizantibus certa & gravis impendet ultio, cunctis vero periculum ingens, ne à scandalis objectis offendantur.
units.tr: 7. Woe to the world because of offences. Christ passes to a general teaching about offences. As if to say: since it is a grave sin to place a stumbling-block before the humble in the way of justice, how great are the evils that hang over mortals because of offences! For a certain and grievous punishment awaits those who give offence, and a great danger threatens everyone, lest they be made to stumble by offences put in their way.

units.la: Necesse est enim ut veniant scandala. Hoc non est intelligendum de necessitate absoluta, sed de necessitate conditionali, quà scilicet necesse est præscita, vel prænuntiata à Deo venire, si tamen conjunctim accipiatur; vel necesse est evenire scandala necessitate finis, quia utilia sunt ad hoc, ut qui probati sunt, manifesti fiant; vel necesse est evenire scandala, secundum conditionem hominum qui sibi à peccatis non cavent: sicut si aliquis medicus videns aliquos indebitâ diætâ utentes dicat, necesse est tales infirmiri. D. Th. 22. q. 43. à 2. ad 1.
units.tr: For it must needs be that offences come. This is not to be understood of absolute necessity, but of conditional necessity: either it is necessary that offences come, foreknown or foretold by God, if they are taken together; or it is necessary that offences come by necessity of the end, because they are useful for this purpose, that those who are approved may be made manifest; or it is necessary that offences come according to the condition of those men who do not guard themselves from sins: just as if some physician, seeing some people using an improper diet, should say, "Such people must necessarily fall ill." Thomas Aquinas, Summa 2-2, q. 43, art. 2, ad 1.

units.la: 10. Angeli eorum. Id est, Angeli ad eorum tutelam & custodiam deputati.
units.tr: 10. Their angels. That is, the angels assigned to their guardianship and protection.

units.la: Semper vident. Sic videlicet parvulorum custodiæ deputati, ut non privati ullo modo beatitudine suâ. B. Bern. Ser. 5. in Dedic. Eccl.
units.tr: They always see. Thus assigned to the guardianship of little ones, that they are in no way deprived of their blessedness. Blessed Bernard, Sermon 5 on the Dedication of the Church.

units.la: Faciem Patris. Ac per hoc totius Trinitatis, quia per filium vident in Spiritu-Sancto. Aug. lib. 3. ad Bonifacium c. 7.
units.tr: The face of the Father. And thus of the whole Trinity, because through the Son they see in the Holy Spirit. Augustine, Book 3 to Boniface, chapter 7.

units.la: 11. Venit enim. Aliam reddit Christus rationem cur pusilli non sint contemnendi. q. d. Ne contemnatis pusillos, cùm ego grandis Deitate factus sim pusillus acceptâ servi formâ, ut quærerem & salvum facerem quod perierat in Adamo.
units.tr: 11. For the Son of Man came. Christ gives another reason why the little ones should not be despised. As if to say: do not despise little ones, since I, made great in Deity, have been made little by taking the form of a servant, in order to seek and to save what had perished in Adam.

units.la: 12. Quid vobis videtur. Q. d. Nonne vobis ipsis judicibus ita fieri solet inter homines, ut si fuerint alicui centum oves, & erraverit una ex eis, relictis nonaginta novem, perditam quærat, & de inventa magis gaudeat, quam super nonaginta novem, quæ non erraverunt? Nam in rebus humanis majus gaudium major molestia præcedit, ut fusè, & doctè disserit Aug. lib. 8. Confes. c. 1. Intendit ergo Christus se tanto studio & pietatis ardore errantes oves quæsitum advenire, ut etiam si nonnisi una ovis periisset, misericordiâ commotus venisset ipsam salvam facere.
units.tr: 12. What do you think? As if to say: does it not commonly happen among men, judges like yourselves, that if someone has a hundred sheep and one of them has gone astray, he leaves the ninety-nine and seeks the lost one, and rejoices more over the one found than over the ninety-nine which did not stray? For in human affairs great joy is preceded by great distress, as Augustine discusses at length and learnedly in Confessions, Book 8, chapter 1. Christ therefore intends to come, seeking straying sheep with such zeal and ardour of piety, that even if only one sheep had perished, he would have come, moved by mercy, to save it.

units.la: 15. Si autem, &c. Hactenus Christus egit de non scandalizandis aut lædendis iis, qui neminem lædunt; nunc de iis, à quibus nos ipsi lædimur, agit, ne tales aliquis putare posset vicissim impune lædi posse.
units.tr: 15. But if, etc. Hitherto Christ has spoken of not giving offence to or harming those who harm no one; now he speaks of those by whom we ourselves are harmed, lest anyone should think that such people may in turn be harmed with impunity.

units.la: 17. Dic Ecclesiæ. Id est, πῇς προεστῶσιν, præsidentibus, ut exponit Chrysost. Hom. 60. in Mat. Pastores enim, quorum est ex proprio officio gregem pascere, & gubernare, hic intelliguntur nomine Ecclesiæ. Ea quippe intelligitur Ecclesia, cui obedire & subjici oportet. Scriptura autem non populo, sed tantum pastoribus τῆς ἡγουμένοις ecclesiasticam deberi obedientiam subjectionem docet Heb. 13. v. 17. & pastorum collegio subjectus est quilibet de collegio. Idcirco enim, inquit Cyprianus epist. 67. seu lib. 3. epist. 13. ad Stephanum R. P. copiosum corpus est sacerdotum, concordiæ mutuæ glutine atque unitatis vinculo copulatum, ut siquis ex collegio nostro hæresim facere, & gregem Christi lacerare & vastare tentaverit, subveniant ceteri, & quasi pastores utiles & misericordes, oves Dominicas in gregem colligant ..... Nam etsi pastores multi sumus, unum tamen gregem pascimus, & oves universas, quas Christus sanguine suo & passione quæsivit, colligere & fovere debemus; nec pati supplices & dolentes fratres nostros crudeliter despici, & superbâ quorundam præsumtione calcari.
units.tr: 17. Tell the Church. That is, the Greek τοῖς προεστῶσιν [tois proestōsin], "those who preside," as Chrysostom explains in Homily 60 on Matthew. For those whose proper office is to feed and govern the flock are here understood by the name "Church," since it is that Church which ought to be obeyed and submitted to. Scripture, however, teaches that ecclesiastical obedience and subjection are owed not to the people but only to the ministers who lead (τοῖς ἡγουμένοις [tois hēgoumenois]), Hebrews 13:17; and each member of the college is subject to the college of ministers. For this reason, says Cyprian, Letter 67, or Book 3, Letter 13, to Stephen, our brother: the body of priests is a numerous one, joined together by the bond of mutual concord and the tie of unity, so that if anyone from our college tries to make a heresy and to tear and lay waste the flock of Christ, the others should come to help, and like useful and merciful shepherds gather the Lord's sheep into the flock ..... For although we are many ministers, we feed one flock, and we ought to gather and cherish all the sheep which Christ sought with his blood and suffering; nor should we allow our suppliant and grieving brothers to be cruelly despised and trampled under the proud presumption of certain men.

units.la: Sit tibi sicut Ethnicus & Publicanus. Id est, qui non morem gesserit Ecclesiæ pastoribus sit tibi sicut homo à communione ejusdem religionis alienus, & publicis peccatis infamis.
units.tr: Let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector. That is, whoever does not obey the ministers of the Church, let him be to you as a man alien to the communion of the same religion and infamous for public sins.

units.la: 18. Amen dico vobis. Supple, & successoribus vestris.
units.tr: 18. Truly I say to you. Supply: and to your successors.

units.la: Quæcunque alligaveritis. Ignoscendi misericors mansuetudo, propter quam dictum est, non solum septies, verum etiam septuagies septies fratri remittenda esse peccata, non ad hoc valet ut sit iniquitas impunita, aut torpens & dormiens disciplina, quod potius obsit, quam diligens vigilansque vindicta. Claves quippe regni cælorum sic dedit Christus Ecclesiæ, ut non solum diceret, Quæ solveritis super terram, erunt soluta & in cælis: ubi apertissimè bonum, non malum pro malo reddit Ecclesia: verum & adjungeret, Quæ ligaveritis in terra, erunt ligata & in cælo: quia bona est & vindicandi justitia. Illud enim quod ait: Si nec Ecclesiam audierit, sit tibi tanquam Ethnicus & Publicanus: gravius est, quam si gladio feriretur, si flammis absumeretur, si feris subrigeretur. Nam subjunxit: Amen dico vobis, quæ ligaveritis super terram, erunt ligata & in cælis: ut intelligeretur, quanto gravius sit punitus, qui velut relictus est impunitus ..... Ecce ab hominibus non reddentibus malum pro malo, alligatur homo amarius & infelicius Ecclesiæ clavibus, quam quibuslibet gravissimis & durissimis ferreis vel adamantinis nexibus. B. Aug. lib. 1. contra adversarium Legis & Prophetarum cap. 17. Vide quæ diximus supra cap. 16. v. 19.
units.tr: Whatever you bind. The merciful gentleness of forgiveness, for which it was said that sins are to be remitted to a brother not only seven times but seventy times seven, does not mean that wickedness should go unpunished, or that discipline should be slack and asleep, which would do more harm than a careful and watchful vengeance. Christ gave the keys of the kingdom of heaven to the Church in such a way that he did not only say, "Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven," where the Church very clearly returns good, not evil, for evil; he also added, "Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven," because the justice of punishing is also good. For what he says, "If he will not hear the Church, let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector," is more serious than if he were struck with the sword, consumed by flames, or thrown to the wild beasts. For he added, "Truly I say to you, whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven," so that it might be understood how much more severely he is punished who is, as it were, left unpunished. See, a man who does not repay evil for evil is bound by the keys of the Church more bitterly and unhappily than by any heaviest and hardest iron or adamantine chains. St Augustine, book 1, Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets, chapter 17. See what we said above, chapter 16, verse 19.

units.la: 19. Iterum dico vobis. Q. d. Imo etiam hoc affirmo.
units.tr: 19. Again I say to you. That is, indeed I affirm this too.

units.la: 20. Ubi enim sunt duo, &c. Corruptores Evangelii atque interpretes falsi extrema ponunt, & superiora prætereunt, partim memores, & partim subdolè corrumpentes. Ut ipsi ab Ecclesia sciissi sunt, ita capituli unius sententiam scindunt. Dominus enim cum discipulis suis unanimitatem suaderet & pacem: Dico, inquit, vobis, quoniam si duobus ex vobis convenerit in terra, de omni re quamcunque petieritis, continget vobis a Patre meo qui in cœlis est. Ubicunque fuerint duo aut tres collecti in nomine meo, ego cum eis sum. Offendens non multitudini, sed unanimitati deprecantium plurimum tribui. Si duobus, inquit, ex vobis convenerit in terra, unanimitatem prius posuit, concordiam pacis ante præmisit, ut conveniant nobis fideliter & firmiter docuit. Quomodo autem potest ei cum aliquo convenire, cui cum corpore ipsius Ecclesiæ & cum universa fraternitate non convenit? Quomodo possunt duo aut tres in nomine Christi colligi, quos constat à Christo & ab ejus Evangelio separari? Non enim nos ab illis, sed illi à nobis recesserunt. Et cum hæreses & schismata postmodum nata sint, dum conventicula sibi diversa constituunt, veritatis caput atque originem reliquerunt.
units.tr: 20. For where two are... The corrupters of the Gospel and false interpreters take the ends and pass over what comes before, partly from forgetfulness and partly by subtly corrupting it. Just as they have torn themselves away from the Church, so they tear the meaning of this one sentence. For when the Lord was urging unanimity and peace on his disciples, he said: "I say to you, that if two of you agree on earth concerning anything whatever that you ask, it will be granted you by my Father who is in heaven. For where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them." He shows that much is given not to the multitude but to the unanimity of those who pray. "If two of you," he says, "agree on earth," he first set down unanimity and sent ahead the concord of peace, teaching that they should come together faithfully and firmly to us. But how can one agree with someone with whom he does not agree with the body of the Church itself and with the whole brotherhood? How can two or three be gathered in the name of Christ when it is plain that they have been separated from Christ and from his Gospel? For it was not we who departed from them, but they who departed from us. And since heresies and schisms have afterwards arisen, while they set up separate conventicles for themselves, they have abandoned the head and origin of the truth.

units.la: Dominus autem de Ecclesia sua loquitur, ad hos qui sunt in Ecclesia loquitur, ut si ipsi concordes fuerint, si secundum quod mandavit & monuit, duo aut tres licet collecti unanimiter oraverint, duo aut tres licet sint, impetrare possint de Dei majestate quod postulant. Ubicunque fuerint duo aut tres collecti in nomine meo, ego, inquit, cum eis sum. Cum simplicibus scilicet atque pacatis, cum Deum timentibus, & Dei præcepta servantibus. Cum his duobus vel tribus licet, esse se dixit: quomodo & cum tribus pueris in camino ignis fuit, & quia in Deum simplices atque inter se unanimes permanebant, flammis ambientibus medios spiritu roris animavit. Quomodo Apostolis duobus in custodia clausis, quia simplices, quia unanimes erant, ipse affuit, ipse resolutis carceris clausris, ut verbum quod fideliter prædicabant, multitudini traderent, ad forum rursus impo suit.
units.tr: But the Lord speaks of his Church, he speaks to those who are in the Church, so that if they themselves are of one mind, if, according to what he commanded and advised, two or three, even though gathered together, pray with one accord, they can obtain from the majesty of God what they ask, though they be only two or three. "Where two or three are gathered in my name," he says, "I am with them." That is, with the simple and peaceable, with those who fear God and keep God's precepts. He said that he was with two or three of these, just as he was with the three boys in the furnace of fire; and because they remained simple before God and of one mind among themselves, he gave life to those in the midst with a spirit of dew while the flames surrounded them. So too he was present with the two apostles shut up in prison, because they were simple and of one mind; he himself loosed the bonds of the prison and sent them back to the forum, so that they might deliver to the multitude the word which they faithfully preached.

units.la: Quando ergo in præceptis suis ponit & dicit: Ubi fuerint duo aut tres collecti in nomine meo, ego cum eis sum: non homines ab Ecclesia dividit, qui instituit & fecit Ecclesiam, sed exprobans discordiam perfidis, & fidelibus pacem suâ voce commendans, offendit magis esse securum duobus aut tribus unanimiter orantibus, quàm cum diffidentibus plurimis, plúsque impetrari posse paucorum concordi prece, quàm discordi oratione multorum. S. Cyprianus Tract. de simplicitate Prælatorum.
units.tr: When therefore in his precepts he sets down and says: "Where two or three are gathered in my name, I am with them," he does not divide men from the Church, he who instituted and made the Church; rather, rebuking the discord of the faithless and by his own voice commending peace to the faithful, he shows that one is more secure with two or three praying in unanimity than with very many who distrust, and that more can be obtained by the concordant prayer of a few than by the discordant prayer of many. St Cyprian, treatise On the Simplicity of Prelates.

units.la: Sum in medio eorum. Speciali modo Deus in medio eorum esse dicitur, quos tuetur, & à malis eximit.
units.tr: I am in the midst of them. God is said to be in the midst of those whom he protects and delivers from evil in a special manner.

units.la: 22. Septuagies septies. Quocunque modo haec verba exponantur, sensus hic est, quotiescunque frater tuus in te peccabit, toties paratus eris ei ex animo dimittere, & eum recipere in gratiam, quod Christus confirmat parabolà mox sequenti; quia ut ait Hieronymus, Familiare est Syris & maxime Palaestinis ad omnem sermonem suum parabolas jungere: ut quod per simplex praeceptum teneri ab auditoribus non potest, per similitudinem exemplaque teneatur.
units.tr: 22. Seventy times seven. However these words are explained, the sense here is this: as often as your brother sins against you, so often you shall be ready to forgive him from the heart and receive him into favour, which Christ confirms by the parable that immediately follows; for, as Jerome says, it is familiar to the Syrians, and especially the Palestinians, to attach parables to every discourse of theirs, so that what cannot be held by the hearers through a simple precept may be held through a comparison and example.

units.la: 23. Assimilatum est regnum caelorum, &c. Scopus Christi in ista parabola est nos hortari ad remittendas aliis injurias in nos commissas. Argumentum autem petit ab exemplo Dei peccata nobis remittentis & severe punientis eos qui remittere aliis detrectant: atque hoc proponit sub typo Regis creditoris liberaliter remittentis debitum & severe punientis inhumanitatem alterius servi. Dei & creditoris actus conveniunt causa movente quae est benignitas; & effecto, quod est liberatio a miseria aut molestia: atque insuper in utroque praecedit jus aliquod, in Deo ad puniendum, in creditore ad exigendum creditum: utrinque etiam contingit dissolutio quaedam obligationis antea existentis; quanquam in ipsa obligatione & in dissolutione aliquid sit dissimile, quod cum ad eam rem, ad quam affertur id exemplum, proprie non pertineat, similitudinem sive parabolam vitiare non potest.
units.tr: 23. The kingdom of heaven is likened, etc. Christ's aim in this parable is to exhort us to remit the injuries committed against us by others. He takes his argument from God's example, who forgives us our sins and severely punishes those who refuse to forgive others; and he sets this forth under the type of a king who generously remits a debt and severely punishes the inhumanity of another servant. God's act and the creditor's act agree in their moving cause, which is kindness, and in their effect, which is deliverance from misery or distress; moreover, in both there precedes some right, in God the right to punish, in the creditor the right to exact the debt; in both too there occurs a certain dissolution of a previously existing obligation. Although in the obligation itself and in its dissolution there is something unlike, since this does not properly pertain to the matter for which the example is brought forward, it cannot spoil the comparison or parable.

units.la: 24. Decem millia talenta. Id est, ingentem pecuniae summam; ponitur enim summa certa pro quavis summa maxima, quae incomparabiliter major sit, ea quae servo debetur a conservo suo. Talentum autem valevat Siclis ter mille ut colligit Aben Ezra ex cap. 38. Exod. v. 25.
units.tr: 24. Ten thousand talents. That is, an enormous sum of money. For a definite sum is put for any very great sum, one incomparably greater than what a servant is owed by his fellow servant. Now a talent was worth three thousand shekels, as Aben Ezra gathers from Exodus 38.25.

units.la: 27. Debitum dimisit ei. Rex hic in parabola descriptus nequaquam Deo benignior est, quia Deus infinitam obligationem remittit, ille finitam. Disconveniunt quidem in eo Rex & Deus, quod Rex citra ullam satisfactionem, Deus non citra satisfactionem Christi, quae nobis applicatur per fidem vivam in Christum, remittit. Ratio est quia, cum jus repetendi creditum ad utilitatem privatam creditoris spectet, de eo statuendi quisque habet liberrimam potestatem: & quo minus exigit, eo est liberalior; exigendo autem nullum actum virtutis exercet. At justitiae virtus exigit ut nullum peccatum citra condignam satisfactionem a Deo & Rectoribus dimittatur. Hanc cum praestare pro offensis nostris Deo non possemus, ipse satisfactionis, quam exigebat justitia, modum invenit sapientiae & misericordiae suae testandae etiam convenientissimum, nobis nihil tale sperantibus aut cogitantibus; proprio enim Filio suo pro nobis incarnato non pepercit, sed pro nobis redimendis tradidit illum passioni & morti, morti autem crucis.
units.tr: 27. He forgave him the debt. The king described in the parable is by no means kinder than God, because God remits an infinite obligation, while the king remits a finite one. The king and God do differ in this: the king remits without any satisfaction, whereas God remits not without the satisfaction of Christ, which is applied to us through living faith in Christ. The reason is that, since the right to demand a debt concerns the private advantage of the creditor, each person has the freest power to decide about it; and the less he exacts, the more generous he is, whereas by exacting he exercises no act of virtue. But the virtue of justice demands that no sin be forgiven by God and by rulers without a fitting satisfaction. Since we could not render this for our offences to God, he himself found, for the satisfaction that justice demanded, a manner most suited to displaying his wisdom and mercy, though we were hoping for nothing of the kind nor thinking of it; for he did not spare his own Son, incarnate for us, but delivered him up to suffering and death for our redemption, the death of the cross.

units.la: 28. Debebat ei centum denarios. Non omnes conveniunt quid sit denarius; aliis enim idem est, ac drachma Attica: aliis idem ac drachma Judaica, quæ continebat duas Atticas seu Romanas. Qui tamen rem exactius expendunt non eundem esse denarium cum drachma evincunt, sed proximè eum ad hanc accedere probant, si Joanni Fungero credimus.
units.tr: 28. He owed him a hundred denarii. Not all agree on what the denarius is: for some it is the same as the Attic drachma, for others the same as the Jewish drachma, which contained two Attic or Roman ones. Those who weigh the matter more exactly, however, show that the denarius is not the same as the drachma, but they prove that it comes closest to it, if we believe John Fungerus.

units.la: 35. Sic Pater meus cœlestis faciet vobis, &c. Certum est peccata absolute dimissa non redire; quia hoc est donum Dei sine pœnitentia, neque potest hominum incredulitas fidem Dei evacuare. Sed est dimissio quædam conditionalis, quæ conditione non præstita fit inutilis, & pro non data jure censetur. Itaque Christus hic nos monet remissionem divinam habere annexam conditionem remissionis nostræ, proindeque remissionem nunquam fuisse acceptatam, atque adeo nec habitam ab iis, qui non remittunt fratribus.
units.tr: 35. "So shall my heavenly Father do to you," etc. It is certain that sins absolutely forgiven do not return, because this is a gift of God without repentance, and the unbelief of men cannot nullify the faith of God. But there is a certain conditional forgiveness, which, if the condition is not fulfilled, becomes ineffective and is judged in law as never given. Thus Christ here warns us that the divine remission has attached to it the condition of our remission, and therefore that the remission was never accepted, and indeed was not possessed, by those who do not forgive their brothers.

units.la: CAPUT XIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIX.

units.la: 1. Migravit à Galilæa. Nempe ut ascenderet in Jerusalem ad festum Scenopegiæ, ut patet ex Joan. 7. dum autem iret in Jerusalem, transibat per mediam Samariam, & in quodam castello decem viros leprosos jussit ostendere se Sacerdotibus, qui dum irent, mundati sunt, ut narratur à Luca cap. 17. tum in templum ascendit, & ibi prædicavit, ut narratur à Joanne cap. 7. à versu 11. ad finem; deinde pergens in montem Oliveti absolvit mulierem adulteram ad se adductam, ut narratur à Joanne cap. 8. usque ad versum 12. postea longam concionem habuit, quæ describitur per totum caput 8. ejusdem Joannis, quà finitâ prætereiens vidit hominem cæcum à nativitate, quem curavit & ejectum à Pharisæis edocuit Joan. 9. Quis pastor esset & fur, pastor bonus & mercenarius & quod sponte ipse pro ovibus moriatur declaravit Joan. 10. Circa idem tempus probabiliter contigit electio & missio septuaginta duorum discipulorum, quæ narratur Luc. 10. unà cum responsione Christi à Legisperito interrogati quid sibi esset faciendum, ut
units.tr: 1. He departed from Galilee. Namely, to go up to Jerusalem for the Feast of Tabernacles, as is clear from John 7. While he was going to Jerusalem, he passed through the middle of Samaria, and in a certain village he ordered ten lepers to show themselves to the priests, and as they went they were cleansed, as is related by Luke ch. 17. Then he went up into the temple and preached there, as related by John ch. 7 from verse 11 to the end. Then, going on to the Mount of Olives, he absolved the adulterous woman brought before him, as related by John ch. 8 to verse 12. Afterwards he gave a long sermon, which is described throughout the whole of ch. 8 of the same John. When this was finished, passing by, he saw a man blind from birth, whom he healed; and after he had been cast out by the Pharisees, he taught him, John 9. Who the shepherd and the thief are, the good shepherd and the hireling, and that he dies of his own accord for the sheep, he declared in John 10. About the same time there probably occurred the choosing and sending of the seventy-two disciples, which is related in Luke 10, together with Christ's answer to the lawyer who asked what was to be done, so that

units.la: Note: the right-margin notes are cut off and only partly legible; they are not transcribed. ut vitam æternam possideret. Etiam circa idem tempus videtur contigisse, quod eodem capite à Luca narratur de sollicitudine Marthæ, & Mariâ sedente secus pedes Domini.
units.tr: he might possess eternal life. Also about the same time it seems to have happened what is related in the same chapter of Luke about the anxiety of Martha and Mary sitting at the Lord's feet.

units.la: Venit in fines Judæa trans Jordanem. Nempe post Encænia celebrata in Jerosolymis, ut narratur Joan. 10. venit in Peræam quæ trans Jordanem erat respectu Judææ, & ditionis Herodis, unde ibi dictum est Christo à Pharisæis, ut Luc. testatur cap. 13. v. 31. Vade hinc, quia Herodes vult te occidere.
units.tr: He came into the regions of Judea beyond the Jordan. Namely, after the Feast of Dedication celebrated in Jerusalem, as related in John 10, he went into Perea, which was beyond the Jordan with respect to Judea, and in the realm of Herod. Hence the Pharisees said to Christ, as Luke testifies in ch. 13 v. 31, Go away from here, for Herod wants to kill you.

units.la: 4. Masculum & fœminam fecit eos. Id est, in gemino sexu creavit, unum marem, & alteram fœminam.
units.tr: 4. Male and female he made them. That is, he created them in two sexes, one male and the other female.

units.la: Dixit. Deus per os Adami tanquam Prophetæ divinitus inspirati, ut exponit Aug. lib. 9. de Genesi ad litteram cap. 19.
units.tr: He said. God, through the mouth of Adam as a divinely inspired prophet, as Augustine explains in book 9 of On Genesis according to the Letter, ch. 19.

units.la: 5. Erunt duo in carne una. Hebraismus, id est, erunt duo caro una, seu, ut Apostolus loquitur Ep. 1 Cor. cap. 6. v. 16. unum corpus, per conjugalem scilicet commixtionem corporum.
units.tr: 5. They two shall be one flesh. A Hebraism, that is, they shall be two, one flesh; or, as the Apostle puts it in 1 Cor. 6:16, one body, namely by the conjugal union of bodies.

units.la: 7. Quid ergo. Ex hac Pharisæorum instantia patet quàm verè dixerit Aug. Tract. 18. in Joan.* Non natæ sunt hæreses & quædam dogmata perversitatis illaqueantia animos, & in profundum præcipitantia; nisi cùm Scripturæ bonæ, intelliguntur non bene, & quod in eis non bene intelligitur, etiam temerè & audacter asseritur. Neque enim, pergit idem S. Doctor de Genesi ad litt. 7. cap. 9. non omnes hæretici Scripturas Catholicas legunt, nec ob aliud sunt hæretici, nisi quòd eas non rectè intelligentes, suas falsas opiniones contra earum veritatem pervicaciter asserunt.
units.tr: 7. Why then? From this objection of the Pharisees it is clear how truly Augustine said, in Tractate 18 on John: Heresies were never born, nor were certain dogmas of perversity born which ensnare minds and cast them into the depths, unless when good Scriptures are understood badly; and what is not well understood in them is also asserted rashly and boldly. For, the same holy Doctor continues, in On Genesis according to the Letter, book 7 ch. 9, not all heretics read the Catholic Scriptures, nor are they heretics for any other reason than that, not understanding them rightly, they stubbornly assert their false opinions against the truth of those Scriptures.

units.la: 8. Permisit. Hinc sumitur distinctio inter voluntatem permissivam & voluntatem præceptivam & propriè dictam, seu verè optativam.
units.tr: 8. He permitted. From this is drawn the distinction between the permissive will and the preceptive will, and the will properly so called, that is, truly optative.

units.la: 9. Quicunque dimiserit uxorem, &c. Vide quæ dicta sunt à nobis cap. 5. v. 31.
units.tr: 9. Whoever divorces his wife, etc. See what we have said on ch. 5 v. 31.

units.la: Nisi ob fornicationem. Prima Synodus Arelatensis ca. 10. Venetica (Gallice de Vanne) ca. 4. Agathensis ca. 2. Triburiensis apud Gratianum 32. quæstione 7. & ibidem Zacharias. I. R. P. ob legitimè probatum adulterium uxorem dimitti & aliam duci lucidè permittunt, & Evangelium hoc in loco sibi patrocinari omninò crediderunt. Augustinus contrà propugnat repetita conjugia post legitimum repudium esse adulterina duobus libris ad Pollentium, vúltque hanc locutionem, Quicunque dimiserit uxorem suam, nisi ob fornicationem, & aliam duxerit, mœchatur: Esse similem huic: Scienti bonum, & non facienti, peccatum est illi; ita ut quemadmodum scienter peccantes damnantes, ignoranter lapsos non expurgat Jacobus ApoApostolus, sic a Domino, dum citra fornicationis causam repudiantes ac alias nuptias attentantes damnat adulterii, qui dimissa ob adulterium uxore, aliam ducunt, non expurgentur. Hieronymus Epist. 30. ad Oceanum, 147 ad Amandum, & in Commentariis ad quintum & decimum nonum caput Matthæi exceptionem, nisi ob fornicationem, ad solam, quæ proximè antecedit, dimittendi licentiam restringit. Hæc Hieronymi explicatio si genuina est & litteralis, ut exîstimat Synodus Foro-Juliensis per Paulinum Aquileiæ Patriarcham sub Caroli Magni imperio celebrata, Qui causa fornicationis dimissis uxoribus, alias ducunt, Domini sententia adulteri esse notantur; quomodo loquitur Synodus Parisiensis VI. sub Ludovico Pio habita. Augustinus tamen, qui acriter novas nuptias post legitimum repudium initas contendit esse adulterinas, ac Evangelio repugnare; & oppositam sententiam ab omni Africana ecclesia proscribi a Generali ducentorum & quatuordecim Episcoporum Carthaginensi synodo obtinuit quinti sæculi anno decimo octavo, Zozymo. R. P. ipse, inquam, Augustinus postea scripsit in libro de fide & operibus. Cap. 19. Quisquis uxorem in adulterio deprehensam dimiserit: & aliam duxerit, non videtur æquandus eis, qui exceptâ causâ adulterii dimittunt & ducunt. Et in ipsis divinis sententiis ita obscurum est, utrum et ille, qui quidem sine dubio adulteram licet dimittere, adulter tamen habeatur si alium duxerit, ut quantum existimo, venialiter ibi quisque fallatur. Hinc mirum non est, quòd hac de re per omnes gentes & ætates variè statuerint Christiani Imperatores & Reges, variè definierint Synodi, varièque senserint Theologi & Patres. Imò & Augustinus Retract. lib. 20. cap. 57. profitetur quæstionem hanc esse difficillimam, & à se non posse plenè explicari. Hoc unum mihi certum videtur in hac quæstione, quòd ubi leges patriæ & recepti Canones non vetant, vir si alteram uxorem duxerit, aut mulier alteri viro nupserit, sacrarum litterarum autoritas, ab omni culpâ illos absolvit, neque ab Ecclesiâ aut æterna vita rejicit, sed propter imbecillitatem tolerandos existimat, ut loquitur vir inexhaustæ eruditionis Epiphanius Hæreʒ. 59. Quæ Catharorum, seu, Novatianorum apud Dionysium Petavium. Num. 4. Ὁ δὲ μὴ ἀνυπάνδρως τὴν μὲν ἀρχὴν ἀλλ᾽ ἀ ἐντολὴν τὴν πρὸς ἀφ᾽ ἐκ τὴν μοιχείας ... Vide ad hunc Epiphanii locum notas Petavii. Et aliam duxerit, Moechatur. Valentinianus Imperator, ut refert Socrates Hist. Ecclesiast. lib. 4. cùm uxorem haberet Severam, seu, Serenam, è qua susceptum Gratianum Augustum jam adolescentem creasset, retentâ illà, duxit & Justinam Justi filiam, formâ virginis captus, lege etiam lata, ut geminas simul uxores habere cuique liceret. Verum qui uxore dimissâ aliam ducit non moecharetur, si etiam illà retentâ liceret aliam ducere, ut optimè argumentatur Innocentius III. R. P. Extra de divortiis cap. Gaudeamus. Nec est quod quis regerat, Moechatur hîc positum pro eo quod dicitur supra cap. 5. v. 31. Facit eam moechari, quia mos est Hellenistarum verba formae Hiphil per activa exprimere, ut videre est Rom. 8. v. 26. Gal. 4. v. 6. &c. Quod enim hîc Matthaeus ait absolutè, Moechatur, suppletur a Marco cap. 10. v. 11. qui ait, Μοιχᾶται ἐπ' αὐτὴν, moechatur adversus eam, seu, ut Vulgatus vertit, adulterium committit super eam. Itaque qui dimittens uxorem, exceptâ fornicationis causâ, dicitur supra cap. 5. v. 32. facere eam moechari, dans ei occasionem ambiendi promiscuos concubitus, aut novas nuptias illicitas, cùm permaneat conjux dimittentis, hic si aliam duxerit uxorem, dimissâ superstite, propriâ moechiâ moechari dicitur testimonio veritatis.
units.tr: Except for fornication. The First Synod of Arles, canon 10; the Synod of Vannes (in French, de Vanne), canon 4; the Synod of Agde, canon 2; the Synod of Trebur, cited by Gratian, 32 q. 7, and there Zacharias. The Papists clearly permit that a wife may be dismissed for legitimately proven adultery and another taken, and they have wholly believed that this passage supports them. Augustine, on the other hand, strongly maintains in two books addressed to Pollentius that remarriages after a lawful divorce are adulterous, and he wants this expression, Whoever divorces his wife, except for fornication, and marries another, commits adultery, to be similar to this: To one who knows what is good and does not do it, it is sin; so that just as Saint James the Apostle does not cleanse those who sin knowingly and condemns them, but does not cleanse those who have fallen through ignorance, so by the Lord, those who repudiate without the cause of fornication and attempt other marriages are condemned for adultery, and those who, having dismissed a wife because of adultery, take another, are not cleansed. Jerome, in Epistle 30 to Oceanus and in Epistle 147 to Amandus, and in his Commentaries on the fifth and nineteenth chapters of Matthew, restricts the exception, except for fornication, to the permission to dismiss that immediately precedes it alone. If this explanation of Jerome is genuine and literal, as the Synod of Friuli judged, held under Paulinus, Patriarch of Aquileia, under the reign of Charlemagne, Those who, because of fornication, dismiss their wives and take others, are marked as adulterers by the sentence of the Lord; as the Synod of Paris VI, held under Louis the Pious, also says. Augustine, however, who vigorously contends that new marriages entered into after a lawful divorce are adulterous and contrary to the Gospel, and who secured the rejection of the opposite opinion by the whole African Church in the general Synod of Carthage of two hundred and fourteen bishops in the eighteenth year of the fifth century, in the time of Pope Zosimus, this same Augustine, I say, later wrote in his book On Faith and Works, ch. 19: Whoever dismisses a wife caught in adultery and takes another does not seem to be equated with those who dismiss for a cause other than adultery and take another. And in the divine sentences themselves it is so obscure whether he who, without doubt, may dismiss an adulterous wife, is nevertheless to be regarded as an adulterer if he takes another, that, as I think, each one may venially err there. Hence it is no wonder that Christian Emperors and Kings have judged this matter variously through all peoples and ages, that Synods have defined it variously, and that Theologians and Fathers have thought variously about it. Indeed Augustine, in Retractations book 2 ch. 57, declares that this question is most difficult and that he cannot explain it fully. One thing seems certain to me in this question: that where the laws of the country and accepted canons do not forbid it, a man who takes another wife, or a woman who marries another man, is absolved of all guilt by the authority of the sacred letters, and is not rejected by the Church or eternal life, but is judged to be tolerated because of weakness; as the man of inexhaustible learning, Epiphanius, says in Heresy 59, which is of the Cathari, or Novatians, as cited by Dionysius Petavius, n. 4. [Ὁ δὲ μὴ ἀνυπάνδρως τὴν μὲν ἀρχὴν ἀλλ᾽ ἀ ἐντολὴν τὴν πρὸς ἀφ᾽ ἐκ τὴν μοιχείας ...] See Petavius's notes on this passage of Epiphanius. And he who takes another commits adultery. The Emperor Valentinian, as Socrates reports in Ecclesiastical History book 4, when he had a wife Severa, or Serena, by whom he had begotten Gratian, now grown up as Augustus, kept her and also took Justina, daughter of Justus, captivated by her beauty as a virgin, a law having also been passed that each man might have two wives at once. But truly, he who dismisses a wife and takes another would not commit adultery if it were also permitted to take another while keeping her, as Innocent III argues well in the Decretals, On Divorces, ch. Gaudeamus. Nor can anyone reply that commits adultery is used here in the sense of what is said above in ch. 5 v. 32, causes her to commit adultery, because it is the custom of the Hellenists to express the forms of the Hiphil by active verbs, as can be seen in Rom. 8:26, Gal. 4:6, etc. For what Matthew here says absolutely, commits adultery, is supplied by Mark ch. 10 v. 11, who says, [Μοιχᾶται ἐπ' αὐτὴν], commits adultery against her, or, as the Vulgate translator renders it, commits adultery upon her. Therefore he who, dismissing his wife without the cause of fornication, is said above in ch. 5 v. 32 to cause her to commit adultery, giving her occasion to seek promiscuous intercourse or illicit new marriages, since the spouse of the one dismissing remains, is said here, if he takes another wife while the dismissed one is still living, to commit adultery by his own adultery, by the testimony of truth.

units.la: 10. Nubere. Id est, uxorem ducere, unde habetur Graecè γαμίσκω.
units.tr: 10. To marry. That is, to take a wife; whence in Greek the word is [γαμίσκω].

units.la: 12. Qui se ipsos Castraverunt. Non in corpore, ut Origenes & alii stultè intellexerunt, sed in ipsa concupiscentiae radice, ut exponit Aug. in lib. de S. Virgin. c. 24. hoc est, qui dono continentiae libidinis stimulo renuntiant.
units.tr: 12. Who have made themselves eunuchs. Not in the body, as Origen and others foolishly understood, but in the very root of concupiscence, as Augustine explains in his book On Holy Virginity, c. 24. That is, those who by the gift of continence renounce the goad of lust.

units.la: Propter regnum coelorum. Id est, ut liberiùs expeditiúsque cogitent quae Domini sunt, ut sint sancti corpore & spiritu, unicè solliciti quomodo placeant Deo.
units.tr: For the sake of the kingdom of heaven. That is, that they may think more freely and unencumbered about the things of the Lord, so that they may be holy in body and spirit, solely anxious how they may please God.

units.la: Qui potest capere capiat. Q. d. Qui coelitùs dono continentiae est instructus, ei permittitur a conjugio abstinere, ut rerum coelestium studio totus incumbat.
units.tr: He who is able to receive it, let him receive it. The sense is: he who has been equipped from heaven with the gift of continence is permitted to abstain from marriage, so that he may devote himself wholly to the study of heavenly things.

units.la: 13. Ut manus eis imponeret. More scilicet Judaeorum, qui benedicturi manus imponebant, ut patet ex Gen. 48. v. 14.
units.tr: 13. That he should lay his hands on them. Namely after the custom of the Jews, who laid on hands when about to bless, as is clear from Gen. 48:14.

units.la: Sinite parvulos. Hinc probat S. Bernardus in Ep. 240. ad Hildefonsum Comitem S. Aegidii quòd baptismus dandus sit parvulis, Salvatore pie clamante pro eis: Sinite parvulos venire ad me. Certè baptismi capaces sunt infantes aequè ac benedictionis, cùm in utroque se tantùm habeant passive.
units.tr: Suffer the little children. From this St Bernard proves, in Letter 240 to Hildefonsus, Count of St Gilles, that baptism is to be given to little children, the Saviour piously crying out for them: Suffer the little children to come to me. Certainly infants are capable of baptism just as they are of blessing, since in both they have only a passive part.

units.la: 17. Quid me interrogas de bono? Unus est bonus Deus. Hoc textus Graecus vulgaris hîc, & ipse textus Latinus Marc. 10. v. 18. sic exprimit: Quid me dicis bonum? Nemo bonus nisi unus unus Deus. Christum filium Dei vivi bonum esse patet ex eo quod ipse se appellet Joan. 10. Pastorem bonum, & infrà c. 20. dicat: An oculus tuus nequam est, quia ego bonus sum? Et Sap. 7. dicitur speculum sine macula claritatis Dei & imago bonitatis illius. Hinc præclare Hilarius lib. 9. de Trinit. Omnis responsionum ratio necesse est, ut ex interrogationum causis proficiscatur. Ad id enim respondetur, unde quæritur. Et primum requiro à disci hujus calumniatore, utrùmne id arguere Dominum existimet, cur bonus dictus sit, séque maluerit malum dici? Id enim significari videtur hoc dicto, Quid me bonum dicis? Non opinor quisquam tam vecors erit, ut malitiæ professionem ei velit ascribere, qui dixerit: Venite ad me omnes qui laboratis & onerati estis, & ego reficiam vos. Tollite jugum meum super vos, & discite à me quia mitis sum & humilis corde, & invenietis requiem animabus vestris: Jugum enim meum suave est, & onus meum leve est. Mitem se profitetur & humilem: & irasci creditur, cur bonus dictus sit? Professionum diversitas dissidet, ut bonitatis suæ testis nomen in se bonitatis accuset. Non ergo irasci intelligitur se bonum dici: & quærendum est, quam aliam de se professionem arguat, qui non credendus est nomen in se bonitatis arguere. Videamus itaque, quid præter bonum interrogans dixerit, ait enim: Magistre bone quid boni faciam? Duas igitur res communcupavit, & bonum, & magistrum. Et quia non arguit bonum se dici: hoc necesse est arguat, quòd magister bonus dictus sit: ita autem arguit se magistrum bonum dici, ut fidem interrogantis potiùs, quam vel magistri in se, vel boni nomen argueret. Juvenis enim infoliens per observantiam Legis, & finem Legis, qui Christus est, nesciens, & justificatum se in operibus existimans, & non intelligens venijse eum ad oves perditas domûs Israel, & impossibile esse Legi per fidem justificationis salvare credentes: tanquam communium præceptorum, & in Lege scriptorum magistrum interrogat Dominum Legis, & unigenitum Deum. Detestatus itaque Dominus hanc de se irreligiosa fidei professionem, quòd tanquam magister Legis interrogaretur, respondit: Quid me dicis bonum? Atque ut significaret quatenus intelligendum & profitendus bonus esset, subjecit: Nemo bonus nisi unus Deus. Non respuit bonitatis nomen, si sibi hoc tanquam Deo deputaretur. Denique offendens se magistri in se boni, per fidem ejus, qui tanquam hominem interrogabat, nomen arguere: post jactantiam juvenis & gloriam Legis impleta, ita respondit: Unum tibi deest: Vade, vende quæcunque habes, & da pauperibus, & habebis thesaurum in cœlo, & veni, sequere me. Non refugit bonitatis de se nomen, qui cœlestem thesaurum pollicetur: Nec magistrum se non vult videri, qui ducem se perfectæ hujus beatitudinis præstat. Terrenæ autem de se opinionis fidem arguit, bonitatem in solo Deo docens esse. Et ut se & Deum & bonum significaret, bonitatis est usus officiis, caelestes thesauros pandens, & se ad eos praevium tribuens. Ita & quae sibi tanquam homini tantum deferebantur, detestatur, neque se ab his, quae Deo deputabat, professus alienum est: cum unum Deum bonum confitens, ea ipse loqueretur atque ageret, quae unius Dei virtutis, bonitatis atque naturae sunt. Quam igitur non bonitatis nomen refugerit, sed neque magistri honorem recusaverit, sed fidem ejus, qui in se nihil nisi corporeum & carnale sapuisset, arguerit, hinc intelligitur, quod aliter ad Apostolos magistrum se confitentes locutus est, dicens: Vos me vocatis magistrum & Dominum & benedicitis, sum etenim. Et cum alibi dixisset: Ne vocemini magistri, quia magister vester Christus est. Ubi cum fide magister est, ibi adeo laudat, ut & profiteatur hoc nomen: hic vero boni magistri nomen non recognoscit, ubi nec Dominus intellectus est esse, nec Christus: solum unum Deum bonum praedicans, non se utique a Deo secernens, qui & Dominum se professus, & Christum, ducem caelestis thesauri offendat.
units.tr: 17. Why do you ask me about the good? There is one who is good, God. The common Greek text here, and the Latin text of Mark 10:18 itself, express this thus: Why do you call me good? No one is good but one, that is, God. That Christ is good, the Son of the living God, is clear from the fact that he calls himself the good Shepherd in John 10, and later in chapter 20 says: Is your eye evil, because I am good? And in Wisdom 7 he is called the unspotted mirror of the power of God and the image of his goodness. Hence Hilary well says in book 9 of On the Trinity: The whole reasoning of answers must necessarily proceed from the causes of the questions. For the answer is given to the point from which the question arises. And first I ask this calumniator of the passage whether he thinks the Lord was rebuking him for being called good, and whether he would rather have been called evil. For this seems to be what the words Why do you call me good? signify. I do not suppose anyone would be so mad as to attribute a confession of malice to one who said: Come unto me, all you who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me, for I am meek and lowly in heart, and you shall find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light. He professes himself meek and humble; is he thought to be angry at being called good? The professions differ and do not agree, if a witness to his own goodness were to accuse in himself the name of goodness. It is therefore not to be understood that he was angry at being called good; and we must ask what other profession of himself he is rebuking, since he is not to be believed to reject the name of goodness in himself. Let us see, then, what the questioner said besides "good," for he says: Good Master, what good shall I do? He therefore gave two titles together, both good and master. And since he does not rebuke being called good, it must be that he rebukes being called a good master; yet he rebukes being called a good master in such a way that he rebukes the faith of the questioner rather than the name of master or of good applied to himself. For the young man, puffed up by his observance of the Law and ignorant of the end of the Law, which is Christ, and thinking himself justified by works, and not understanding that he had come to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, and that it is impossible for those who believe to be saved by the Law without faith in justification, questioned the Lord of the Law and the only-begotten God as if he were a teacher of common precepts written in the Law. The Lord, therefore, detesting this irreligious profession of faith about himself, that he should be questioned as a teacher of the Law, answered: Why do you call me good? And so that he might signify in what sense and to what extent he was to be understood and professed as good, he added: No one is good but one, God. He does not reject the name of goodness if it is ascribed to him as to God. Finally, rebuking the profession of himself as a good teacher, which the young man made as to a mere man, after the young man's boasting and the glory of the Law had been fulfilled, he answered thus: One thing you lack. Go, sell whatever you have, and give to the poor, and you shall have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me. He does not shrink from the name of goodness concerning himself, who promises heavenly treasure; nor does he wish not to be seen as a teacher, who presents himself as the guide to this perfect blessedness. But he rebukes the faith of the earthly opinion about himself, teaching that goodness is in God alone. And so that he might signify both himself and God as good, he exercised the offices of goodness, opening up the heavenly treasures and presenting himself as the one who goes before to them. Thus he also rejects what was offered to him as to a mere man, and he does not profess himself foreign to those things which he ascribed to God, since, confessing the one God as good, he himself spoke and did those things which belong to the power, goodness and nature of the one God. Thus it is understood that he did not refuse the name of goodness, nor did he decline the honour of a teacher, but rebuked the faith of one who had savoured nothing in him but the bodily and the carnal. That he spoke otherwise to the Apostles, who confessed him as teacher, is shown by what he said: You call me Teacher and Lord, and you say well, for so I am. And when he had said elsewhere: Do not be called teachers, for your one Teacher is Christ. Where he is teacher with faith, there he so praises it that he even professes this name; but here he does not acknowledge the name of a good teacher, where he is not understood to be Lord, nor Christ. Proclaiming only the one God as good, he does not of course separate himself from God, though he professes himself Lord and Christ, the guide to the heavenly treasure, and takes offence at it.

units.la: Serva mandata. Turpiter itaque allucinantur, qui dicunt Legis praecepta nihil ad Christianos pertinere, aut Christum a Deo hominibus datum, ut Redemtorem cui fidant, non etiam ut Legislatorem cui obediant: aut denique hominem justificatum, & quantumlibet perfectum non teneri ad observandam mandatorum Dei.
units.tr: Keep the commandments. Therefore they wander shamefully who say that the precepts of the Law have nothing to do with Christians, or that Christ was given by God to men as Redeemer in whom they may trust, but not also as Lawgiver whom they should obey; or finally that a justified man, however perfect he may be, is not bound to observe the commandments of God.

units.la: 21. Si vis perfectus esse, &c. Praeceptum hoc personale erat ad hominem, & διαχειρισμὸν ad detegendum interrogantis latentem avaritiam, non generale, quod quisvis obligat, nisi in tali casu, ubi aut omnia sunt deserenda, aut Christus relinquendus. Erronee hinc Romanenses monachatus vota astruunt, quae non temeraria modo, sed & superstitiosa sunt, Scripturaeque adversantur.
units.tr: 21. If you wish to be perfect, etc. This precept was personal to that man, and a [διαχειρισμὸν] test to uncover the hidden avarice of the questioner; it is not a general precept binding everyone, except in such a case where either all things must be forsaken or Christ must be abandoned. Hence the Papists wrongly assert monastic vows, which are not only rash but also superstitious, and opposed to Scripture.

units.la: 24. Facilius est camelum per foramen acus transfire, &c. Multis visum est non agi hic de camelo animali, sed de camelo vel camilo, fune nautico; nam camelum vocari crassum rudentem, quo nautae utuntur ad jaciendas anchoras, habemus apud Theophylactum, Euthymium, & Phavorinum. Quamvis autem liberum sit lectori camelum hic sumere pro animali, ut suadet vocis acceptio usitatior, & similia Talmudicorum proverbia de elephante, & ita Christo camelus per foramen acus ingrediens, ut Talmudicis elephas per foramen acus immissus, seu intrans, videri potest fuisse symbolum rei impossibilis: quasi pro elephante camelum usurpaverit Christus; agi tamen hic de rudente potius suadet analogia major inter rudentem & filum, quod solet per foramen acus induci, & illud Hebraeorum non absimile adagium a doctissimô Buxtorfio ex Moëd katan laudatum: Gravis est exitus animæ è corpore, ut rudentum per foramen angustum. Itaque non immeritò Syri & Arabes non animal, sed rudentem per camelum hîc intellexere.
units.tr: 24. It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle, etc. Many have thought that the camel here is not an animal but a camel or camilus, that is, a ship's rope; for we find in Theophylact, Euthymius and Phavorinus that the thick cable sailors use for casting anchors is called a camel. Although the reader is free to take camel here as the animal, as the more usual sense of the word suggests, and as similar Talmudic proverbs about the elephant do, so that the camel passing through the eye of a needle, like the elephant put through or passing through the eye of a needle in the Talmudists, may seem to have been a symbol of an impossible thing, as if Christ had used camel for elephant; nevertheless a closer analogy between rope and thread, which is customarily drawn through the eye of a needle, suggests that the matter concerns a rope rather than an animal. So too that Hebrew saying, not unlike it, quoted by the most learned Buxtorf from Moëd katan: The departure of the soul from the body is hard, like ropes through a narrow hole. Therefore not without reason the Syrians and Arabs understood by camel here not the animal but a rope.

units.la: 26. Apud Deum autem omnia possibilia sunt. Quia nempè Deus potest facere suâ gratiâ ut divites, nec nimis solliciti sint de divitiis confervandis, & acquirendis, nec nimio earum amore teneantur, nec de ipsis superbiant, nimisve in iis confidant; divites enim ideò difficilè salvantur, quia ut plurimùm confidunt in pecuniis, ut patet ex Marc. c. 10. v. 23, & 24.
units.tr: 26. With God all things are possible. For God can by His grace bring it about that the rich are neither overly anxious about keeping and acquiring riches, nor held fast by an excessive love of them, nor proud of them, nor too confident in them; for the rich are therefore hard to save, because for the most part they trust in money, as is clear from Mark 10:23 and 24.

units.la: 27. Ecce nos reliquimus omnia. Q. d. Quæ à juvene modò exigebas, nos fecimus, ut tibi indivulsè adhæreremus, quid ergo erit nobis præmii?
units.tr: 27. Behold, we have left all things. That is: "What you now demand of the young man, we have done, so that we might cling to you without division; what then will be our reward?"

units.la: 28. In regeneratione. Regenerationem hoc loco, ambigente nullo, novissimam resurrectionem Christus vocat, quam Paulus quoque Apostolus Rom. 8. v. 23. & adoptionem & redemtionem nuncupat. Numquid non per lavacrum sacrum regenerati, adoptati & redemti sumus? Et tamen restat regeneratio, adoptio, redemtio, quam in fine venturam nunc patienter expectare debemus, ut tunc filii hujus seculi ex nulla parte jam simus. Aug. lib. 3. ad Bonifac. c. 3.
units.tr: 28. In the regeneration. Without any doubt Christ here calls the regeneration the final resurrection, which the Apostle Paul also calls adoption and redemption, Rom. 8:23. Have we not already been regenerated, adopted and redeemed through the holy washing? And yet the regeneration, adoption and redemption remain, which we must now patiently await to come at the end, so that then we who are now the sons of this age may be in no part so. Augustine, book 3 to Boniface, ch. 3.

units.la: Cùm sederet Filius hominis in Sede majestatis suæ. Id est, cùm apparuerit Filius hominis judiciariam potestatem sibi à Patre traditam exercens. Cùm enim Reges in solio sedentes, potissimùm regiam ostendant vel exerceant authoritatem, & judices sententiam sedentes proferant, inde sedere, sæpe significat regnare, & judicare, ut videre est hîc & Exod. 11. v. 5. 3 Reg. c. 2. v. 12. Apocal. c. 20. v. 4.
units.tr: When the Son of man shall sit in the throne of his glory. That is, when the Son of man shall appear exercising the judicial power given to him by the Father. For since kings sitting on a throne chiefly display or exercise royal authority, and judges sitting pronounce sentence, hence to sit often signifies to reign and to judge, as may be seen here and at Exod. 11:5, 3 Kings 2:12, and Revelation 20:4.

units.la: Sedebitis & vos, &c. Id est, & vos à me recipietis judiciariam potestatem, ut judicetis universas tribus Israël.
units.tr: You also shall sit, etc. That is, you too shall receive from me the judicial power to judge the twelve tribes of Israel.

units.la: 29. Centuplum accipiet. Hoc Marcus sic explicat. Accipiet centies tantùm, nunc in tempore hoc, domos & fratres, & sorores, & matres, & filios, & agros, cum persecutionibus, hoc est, quantumvis sæviant persecutionum procellæ. Præclarè B. Greg. Hom. 18. in Ezech. Per centenarium magna perfectio designatur; neque enim sanctus quisque ideo terrena deserit, ut hæc possidere in hoc mundo multiplicius possit: quia quisquis terreno studio terram relinquit, terram non relinquit, sed appetit, nec quem unam uxorem deserit, centum recepturus est; sed per centenarium numerum perfectio designatur, quia quisquis pro Dei nomine temporalia atque terrena contemnit, & hîc perfectionem mentis recipit, ut jam ea non appetat, quæ contemnit, & in sequenti seculo ad æterna vitæ gloriam pervenit. Centies itaque recepit, quod dedit, qui perfectionis spiritum accipiens, terrenis non indiget, etiamsi hoc non habet. Ille autem qui pauper est, eget eo, quod non habet. Nam qui & non habens habere non appetit, dives est; Paupertas quippe in inopia mentis est, non in quantitate possessionis. Nam qui in paupertate bene convenit, non est pauper.
units.tr: 29. He shall receive an hundredfold. Mark explains this thus: "He shall receive a hundred times as much, now in this time, houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and sons and fields, with persecutions, that is, however fiercely the storms of persecution rage." Blessed Gregory wrote admirably in Homily 18 on Ezekiel: "By the hundred a great perfection is designated; for no holy person forsakes earthly things so that he may possess these more abundantly in this world. For whoever leaves the earth with an earthly aim does not really leave it, but still desires it; nor is he who forsakes one wife going to receive a hundred. Rather, by the number hundred perfection is designated, because whoever for the name of God despises temporal and earthly things, and here receives perfection of mind, so that he no longer desires those things which he despises, attains in the following age the glory of eternal life." Thus he receives a hundredfold what he has given, who, receiving the spirit of perfection, does not need earthly things, even if he does not have them. But he who is poor lacks what he does not have. For he who, not having, does not desire to have, is rich; poverty indeed lies in a lack of mind, not in the quantity of possessions. For he who agrees well in poverty is not poor.

units.la: 30. Multi autem erunt, &c. Q. d. Multi qui primi sunt variis nominibus in hoc seculo, erunt novissimi in futuro, & e converso multi novissimi in hoc seculo, erunt primi in gloria. Hoc autem hic videtur dictum a Christo, ne Apostoli mirarentur quod ipsi & qui omnia desererent, judicaturi essent universas tribus Israel; id est, universam multitudinem judicandorum.
units.tr: 30. But many that are first shall be last, etc. That is: many who are first in this age in various respects will be last in the future, and conversely many who are last in this age will be first in glory. But this seems to have been said here by Christ so that the Apostles would not marvel that they themselves, who had given up everything, would judge the twelve tribes of Israel; that is, the whole multitude of those to be judged.

units.la: CAPUT XX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XX.

units.la: 1. Simile est regnum coelorum, &c. Id est, similiter se habet aequitas divinae dispensationis circa regnum coeleste, ac, si quis paterfamilias exiret summo mane conducere operarios in vineam suam, &c.
units.tr: 1. The kingdom of heaven is like, &c. That is, the fairness of God's dealing with the heavenly kingdom stands in the same relation as when a householder went out early in the morning to hire workers for his vineyard, &c.

units.la: 3. Circa horam tertiam. Id est, circa illam horam, quam nos nonam matutinam vocare consuevimus; dies enim apud Judaeos in horas duodecim dividebatur, quarum prima dicebatur sole oriente, duodecima eodem occidente, atque illae duodecim horae in quatuor partes aequaliter distantes distribuebantur, & hae partes appellebantur prima, tertia, sexta, & nona, quarum quaeque constabat tribus horis, & denominabatur ab hora, ad quam immediate sequebatur.
units.tr: 3. About the third hour. That is, about the hour which we are accustomed to call the ninth in the morning. For among the Jews the day was divided into twelve hours.
