The first began at sunrise and the twelfth ended at sunset. These twelve hours were distributed equally into four parts, and these parts were called the first, third, sixth and ninth. Each of them consisted of three hours and took its name from the hour with which it immediately began.

units.la: 6. Invenit alios stantes. Supple ex textu Graeco, otiosos.
units.tr: 6. He found others standing. Supply from the Greek text: idle.

units.la: 15. Non licet mihi quod volo facere? Graece additur: in rebus meis. Docet Christus hac sententia in iis quae Deus voluit & vult & agit ut liberrimus Dominus, ipsius voluntatem suam esse justitiam & regulam omnis justitiae; neque enim semper ideo aliquid vult Deus, quia illud justum nobis videtur, sed ideo aliquid justum nobis videri debet, quia illud vult Deus, qui nihil vult, nisi ex summa sapientia. Unde sicut voluntas Dei in Lege revelata ideo justa est, quia voluntas Dei est, ab illius infinita sapientia profecta, ita voluntas arcana Dei ideo semper justa est, quia voluntas Dei est cum immensa ejusdem sapientia semper conjuncta. Appositeque itaque Aug. lib. 2. de peccatorum meritis cap. 18. Quare Deus velit illos convertere, illos pro aversione punire, quanquam & in beneficio tribuendo nemo juste reprehendat misericordiam, & in vindicta exercenda nemo juste reprehendat veracem, sicut in illis Evangelicis operariis, aliis placitam mercedem reddentem, aliis etiam non placitam largientem, nullus juste culpaverit, consilium tamen occultioris justitiæ penes ipsum est.
units.tr: 15. Is it not lawful for me to do what I wish? The Greek adds: with my own things. By this saying Christ teaches, concerning those things which God has willed, wills and does as the most free Lord, that his own will is justice and the rule of all justice. For God does not always will something because it seems just to us; rather, something ought to seem just to us because God wills it, he who wills nothing except from supreme wisdom. Hence, just as the will of God revealed in the Law is just because it is the will of God, proceeding from his infinite wisdom, so the hidden will of God is always just, because it is the will of God, always joined with his immense wisdom. Accordingly Augustine well says, in book 2 of On the Merits of Sins, chapter 18: Why God wills to convert those, to punish others for their aversion, although no one justly finds fault with mercy in bestowing a benefit, and no one justly finds fault with the truthful one in exercising vengeance; just as in the parable of the Gospel workers, one who pays the agreed wage to some and gives a larger, unagreed wage to others, no one would justly blame him; nevertheless, the counsel of a more hidden justice rests with him.

units.la: 16. Sic erunt novissimi primi, &c. Q. d. Primi hominum judicio erunt coram Deo novissimi, & è converso novissimi hominum judicio erunt judicio Dei primi dignitate, sanctitate & merito. Novissimi autem judicio Dei dicuntur hic Judæi reprobi, qui receperunt denarium temporalem à Moyse promissum; primi vero Dei judicio dicuntur Gentiles electi, qui recipiunt denarium æternum, quem promittit gratia. Manifestum est autem ex Luc. 13. v. 28. per novissimos hic intelligi reprobos Judæos, qui foras expellentur. Sic & supra cap. 5. minimus in regno cœlorum dicitur, qui non erit in regno Dei, secundum alios qui in præsenti Ecclesia contemtibilis est, secundum utrosque, qui regno cœlorum indignus est. Simili phrasi infrà cap. 21. v. 31. Publicani & meretrices dicuntur à Christo præcessuri Pharisæos in regnum Dei, quòd crediderint Joanni, cùm Pharisæi, nec crediderint, nec pœnitentiam egerint; ubi certè significatur, quòd Publicani & meretrices erunt in regno Dei, cùm Pharisæi sint expellendi foràs. Quod autem dicitur in parabola, Redde illis mercedem incipiens à novissimis usque ad primos, hominum scilicet judicio: innuere potest, quòd in die judicii primò sint præmiandi, qui hominum judicio sunt novissimi, & ab ipsis in derisum habiti, deinde reprobi debito supplicio addicendi, ut satis indicat ipse Christus infrà cap. 25. v. 34, & 47. Simul etiam significat Christus non omnium in Ecclesia laborantium labores probari à patrefamilias, sed eorum tantùm, qui cùm sint electi in Christo ante mundi constitutionem, perseveranter sunt sancti & immaculati in conspectu ejus in charitate. Verissimè itaque & doctissimè Dionysius Petavius asserit præsentis parabolæ finem & scopum in eo situm, ut demonstretur regni cœlestis & adipiscendæ salutis modum & rationem non ex humanis æstimari judiciis, sed ex sola Dei gratuita voluntate ac pro ejus arbitrio, nec usu hominum & consuetudine totum illud administrari. Hunc esse præsentis parabolæ sensum, probat ipse Petavius ex parabolæ clausula: Multi enim sunt vocati, pauci vero electi: Hinc enim apparet solos electos opponi reprobis, nec de majori aut minori gloria electorum agi. Ceterùm non oportere omnia quæ parabolæ continent verbatim scrutari, sed scopum intelligere, ad quem instituræ sunt, eóque percepto, nihil amplius inquirere, monet B. Chrysostomus hanc nostram parabolam exponens Hom. 64. in Matth. Tertul. de pudicitia cap. 9. & elegantissime Aug. lib. 22. contra Faustum cap. 94. & lib. 16. de Civitate Dei cap. 11. unde Petavius ait ea, quæ parabolæ inseruntur de denario uno omnibus dato, de dispari mora laboris & operæ, de querela maturiùs conducto-rum, & id genus alia, adornandæ & instruendæ parabolæ inservire, quâ id unum quæritur, ut omnes intelligant, quod ab Apostolo traditum sæpe adversus Pelagianos & eorum reliquias inculcat Aug. Gratia salvati estis per fidem, & hoc non ex vobis, Dei enim donum est: non ex operibus ut nemo glorietur. Cùm enim bona ipsa vita, cui æterna vita redditur, Dei gratia fit, ut scribit Aug. lib. de grat. & lib. arb. cap. 8. & ipsa æterna vita gratis datur, quia gratis data est illa, cui datur. Verùm etsi Christus hac parabola docere intendat gratis salvari, quicunque beatam immortalitatem adipiscuntur, alludit tamen potissimùm ad Judæorum abdicationem, qui juxta ordinem vocationis primi fuere, & adoptionem Gentium in abdicatorum Judæorum locum, ita ut nec rejecti, nec asciti jure possint conqueri de Deo, apud quem non est iniquitas.
units.tr: 16. So the last will be first, &c. That is: those who are first in the judgment of men will be last before God, and conversely, those who are last in the judgment of men will be first in the judgment of God, in dignity, holiness and merit. Here, however, the reprobate Jews are called "the last in the judgment of God," those who received the temporal denarius promised by Moses; the Gentiles who are elect, who receive the eternal denarius which grace promises, are called "the first in the judgment of God." It is clear from Luke 13:28 that "the last" here means the reprobate Jews, who will be cast out. So also above, in chapter 5, he who is least in the kingdom of heaven is one who will not be in the kingdom of God, according to some; according to others, one who is contemptible in the present Church. According to both, he is unworthy of the kingdom of heaven. In a similar way, below in chapter 21:31, the tax collectors and harlots are said by Christ to go before the Pharisees into the kingdom of God, because they believed John, whereas the Pharisees neither believed nor repented. There it is certainly signified that the tax collectors and harlots will be in the kingdom of God, while the Pharisees are to be cast out. As for what is said in the parable, Pay them their wages, beginning from the last to the first, this may hint, in the judgment of men, that on the day of judgment those who are last in the judgment of men are to be rewarded first, and those who were held in derision by them, and then the reprobate are to be consigned to their due punishment, as Christ himself indicates sufficiently below in chapter 25, verses 34 and 47. At the same time Christ signifies that the labours of not all who labour in the Church are approved by the householder, but only of those who, being chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world, persevere in holiness and blamelessness before him in love. Therefore Dionysius Petavius rightly and most learnedly asserts that the end and aim of the present parable lies in this: that it is shown that the manner and reason of entering the heavenly kingdom and obtaining salvation are judged not by human judgments but by God's free will alone and at his pleasure, and that the whole matter is not administered by human custom and habit. Petavius himself proves that this is the sense of the present parable from the closing words of the parable: For many are called, but few are chosen. From this it appears that only the elect are set against the reprobate, and that there is no question of a greater or lesser glory of the elect. Moreover, Blessed Chrysostom, expounding this parable of ours in Homily 64 on Matthew, advises that one ought not to search out verbatim everything that the parable contains, but to understand the aim for which it was constructed, and once that is grasped, to inquire no further. See also Tertullian, On Modesty, chapter 9, and most elegantly Augustine, Against Faustus, book 22, chapter 94, and City of God, book 16, chapter 11. Hence Petavius says that the features the parable introduces, such as the single denarius given to all, the unequal length of labour and work, the complaint of those hired earlier, and other things of that kind, serve to adorn and furnish the parable, whose one purpose is that all should understand what the Apostle taught and what Augustine often urges against the Pelagians and their remnants: By grace you have been saved through faith, and this not of yourselves; it is the gift of God; not of works, so that no one may boast. For since the good life itself, to which eternal life is rendered, is by the grace of God, as Augustine writes in On Grace and Free Will, chapter 8, eternal life itself is also given freely, because that to which it is given was freely given. But although Christ intends in this parable to teach that all who attain blessed immortality are saved freely, he alludes chiefly to the rejection of the Jews, who by the order of calling were first, and to the adoption of the Gentiles in the place of the rejected Jews. Thus neither those who were rejected nor those who were received can justly complain about God, with whom there is no unrighteousness.

units.la: Vocati. Sc. à Deo ad fidem, charitatem, perfectionem Evangelicam & beatitudinem.
units.tr: Called. That is, by God to faith, love, evangelical perfection and blessedness.

units.la: Pauci. Supple, ex illis vocatis.
units.tr: Few. Supply: from among those who were called.

units.la: Electi. Id est; prædestinati secundum propositum ejus, qui operatur omnia secundum consilium voluntatis suæ. Hominibus, inquit Aug. in lib. de dono perseverantiæ, c. 8. videtur omnes, qui boni apparent Fideles, perseverantiam usque in finem accipere debuisse: Deus autem melius esse judicavit miscere quosdam non perseveraturos certo numero sanctorum suorum, ut quibus non expedit in hujus vitæ tentatione securitas, non possent esse securi; multos enim à perniciosa elatione reprimit quod ait Apostolus 1 Cor. 16. Qui videtur stare, videat ne cadat. Voluntate autem suâ cadit qui cadit, ac voluntate Dei stat qui stat. Potens est enim Deus statuere illum, Rom. 11. non ergo ipse se ipsum, sed Deus. Veruntamen bonum est non altum sapere, sed timere. In cogitatione autem sua cadit quisque vel stat. Sicut autem ait Apostolus 2 Cor. 3. Non sumus idonei cogitare aliquid ex nobismetipsis, sed sufficientia nostra ex Deo est. Quem secutus B. Ambros. lib. de fuga seculi. c. 1. addit & dicit, Non enim in potestate nostra est cor nostrum, & cogitationes nostræ: Quod omnis qui humiliter & veraciter pius est, esse verissimum sentit. Hæc Augustinus.
units.tr: Chosen. That is, predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will. It seems to men, says Augustine in the book On the Gift of Perseverance, chapter 8, that all faithful who appear good ought to have received perseverance until the end. But God judged it better to mix in a certain number of his saints who will not persevere, so that those for whom security in the temptations of this life is not expedient might not be secure; for the Apostle's words, 1 Cor. 10, restrain many from harmful pride: "Let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall." One who falls, falls by his own will, and one who stands, stands by the will of God. For God is able to make him stand, Rom. 11. It is not therefore he himself who stands by himself, but God. Nevertheless, it is good not to be high-minded but to fear. Each one falls or stands in his own thinking. As the Apostle says, 2 Cor. 3: "We are not sufficient to think anything of ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God." Following him, Blessed Ambrose, in On Flight from the World, chapter 1, adds and says: For our heart and our thoughts are not in our power, which every man who is humbly and truly pious feels to be most true. Thus Augustine.

units.la: 17. Et ascendens Iesus Ierosolymam. Nempe ex civitate Ephrem; nam ut Ioan. testatur c. 11. Christus biduo post auditam Lazari infirmitatem iterum ivit in Judaeam, ex qua post festum Encaeniorum exierat in Peraeam, ut supra diximus; quae respectu Judaeae sita est trans Jordanem; ut autem in Judaeam reversus advenit in civitatem Bethaniam ab Jerusalem stadiis quasi quindecim distantem Lazarum quatriduanum jam foetentem suscitavit; quod cum audissent Pontifices & Pharisaei, collegerunt Concilium primum adversus Christum; ipse vero secessit in regionem juxta desertum, in civitatem quae dicitur Ephrem, & ibi moratus est cum discipulis suis, donec inde ascenderet Jerosolymam Pascha ultimum vitae suae celebraturus, de quo ascensu hic loquitur Matthaeus. In hoc etiam ascensu contigisse credimus, quae Luc. c. 9. a v. 51, ad v. 57. narrat de Christo a civitate Samaritanorum repulso, propter haec Lucae verba, dum complerentur dies assumtionis eius, quae satis aperte significant profectionem illam non longe abfuisse a morte Christi, quod initium est assumtionis ejus; assumi enim ibi nihil aliud est, quam ad Deum recipi. Accedit etiam quod ait Lucas Jesum firmasse faciem suam, ut iret in Jerusalem, quod denotat firmam animi constantiam ad certam mortem proficiscentis. Fatendum tamen ex civitate Ephrem inter Jericho & Samariam sita, quo Christus ante concesserat, rectum iter non fuisse per Samariam; sed facile fieri potuit, ut varias ob causas a consueto itinere Christus deflecteret. Cur autem Lucas suo loco id non retulerit, causam affert vir eruditus: Nam cum duo, inquit, insignia Christi monita Lucas ante narrasset, quorum prius ad vitandam ambitionem, alterum ad vitandam invidiam Apostolos hortabatur, commodum locum esse credidit adjiciendae monitionis tertiae adversus ultionem.
units.tr: 17. And Jesus, going up to Jerusalem. Namely from the city of Ephraim. For, as John testifies in chapter 11, two days after hearing of Lazarus's sickness, Christ went again into Judea, from which he had gone after the feast of Dedication into Perea, as we said above, which lies beyond the Jordan with respect to Judea. But when he returned into Judea and came to the village of Bethany, about fifteen stadia from Jerusalem, he raised Lazarus, who had been dead four days and was already stinking. When the chief priests and Pharisees heard this, they gathered the first council against Christ. He himself withdrew into the region near the desert, to the city called Ephraim, and there he stayed with his disciples until he went up from there to Jerusalem to celebrate his last Passover in life. It is of this going up that Matthew speaks here. We believe that in this same journey happened what Luke relates in chapter 9, from verse 51 to verse 57, about Christ being repulsed by a city of the Samaritans. This is because of Luke's words, when the days of his being taken up were being fulfilled, which quite plainly signify that this journey was not far from the death of Christ, which is the beginning of his being taken up; for to be taken up there means nothing other than to be received by God. Add to this that Luke says Jesus set his face firmly to go to Jerusalem, which denotes the firm constancy of mind of one setting out toward a certain death. It must be admitted, however, that the direct road from the city of Ephraim, which lies between Jericho and Samaria, and from which Christ had earlier withdrawn, did not go through Samaria; but it could easily happen that Christ turned aside from the usual road for various reasons. Why Luke did not record this in its proper place, a learned man gives the reason: For since Luke had already related two remarkable warnings of Christ, of which the first urged the apostles to avoid ambition and the second to avoid envy, he believed it a suitable place to add a third warning, against revenge.

units.la: 18. Condemnabunt eum morte. Id est, reum mortis declarabunt, licet ultimam sententiam non sint pronuntiaturi; nam, ut ait B. Greg. Nyss. Orat. 1. in resurrec. Christi, non alio, quam crucis supplicio Christus affici volebat. Hoc autem Judaei afficere ipsum non poterant. Unde Joannes advertit Pilato Judaeis permittenti ut Christum secundum Legem suam judicarent & punirent, ipsos, qui nimirum mulierem adulteram, & Christum ipsum lapidare tentaverant, & Stephanum postea lapidaverunt, ipsos, inquam, respondisse: Nobis non licet interficere quemquam, ut sermo Jesu impleretur, quem dixerat significans qua morte esset moriturus.
units.tr: 18. They will condemn him to death. That is, they will declare him liable to death, although they will not pronounce the final sentence; for, as blessed Gregory of Nyssa says in his first oration on the resurrection of Christ, Christ wished to be subjected to no other punishment than the cross. The Jews, however, could not inflict this on him. Hence John notes that when Pilate allowed the Jews to judge and punish Christ according to their own Law, they answered, namely those who had tried to stone the adulterous woman and Christ himself, and later stoned Stephen: It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death, so that the word of Jesus might be fulfilled, which he had spoken, signifying by what death he would die.

units.la: 19. Tradent eum Gentibus, &c. Admonentur discipuli judicium, quo damnandus erit Christus, a Gentibus fore reddendum, quia clavis configendus erat cruci, quod non fuit Judaeis usitatum supplicium, ut Casaubonus Exercit. 16. adversus Baron. c. 77. tribus argumentis probat. Primum est Rabbinorum testimonium, qui verbis expressis crucem Romanis usitatam, fuisse genti suae ignotam affirmant. Secundum petitur ex ipso jure veteri populi Judaici, quod & Rabbini idem afferunt; ut sententiae suae fidem astruant. Nam ex antiquis fragmentis Doctorum, quae in Pandectis Talmudicis habentur, non nisi quatuor erant supplicium capitalium genera a populo Judaeorum usurpata; sc. lapidatio, vivicomburium, decollatio & strangulatio. Verum omnibus lapidatione jam extinctis poena ignominiae causa irrogabatur, ut suspenderentur ad paucas horas, & foli, & oculis hominum exponerentur; quod Judaeis erat quavis dira morte diriús propter horribile carmen vocis divinae Deuteron. 21. v. 23. Maledictus a Deo est qui pendet in ligno. Idem poenae genus irrogari solitum homicidis scribit Philo, licet secundum Rabbinos, homicidae non lapidatione, sed decollatione extinguerentur. Tertium denique argumentum sumitur ex eo quod nullum sit veteris linguae Hebraeorum vocabulum, quod crucem proprie dictam significet, nullum verbum actioni crucifigendi proprium, nullum denique in toto veteri testamento extet certum de eo supplicii genere in Hebraeorum Republica contra allata e commentariis Rabbinorum testimonia argumentum; nam suspendi in patibulo, & in cruce dicuntur omnes, qui in altum sublati acuta sude transfigebantur, vel laqueo strangulabantur, vel jam extincti, oculis hominum & soli ignominiae causa exponebantur: unde omnibus his vocibus, patibulum, crux, &c. in Vulgat. & aliis versionibus usurpatis, in textu Hebraeo respondet una vox ⁠, id est, lignum.
units.tr: 19. They will hand him over to the Gentiles, etc. The disciples are warned that the sentence by which Christ is to be condemned will be pronounced by the Gentiles, because he was to be fastened to the cross with nails, which was not a punishment customary among the Jews. Casaubon proves this in his Exercitationes against Baronius, chapter 77, by three arguments. (1) The first is the testimony of the rabbis, who state in express words that the cross, customary among the Romans, was unknown to their nation. (2) The second is drawn from the ancient law of the Jewish people itself, which the rabbis also cite to support their view. For from the ancient fragments of the teachers preserved in the Talmudic Pandects, there were only four kinds of capital punishment used by the Jewish people: namely stoning, burning alive, beheading and strangling. But once stoning had fallen out of use, a penalty of disgrace was imposed, so that the condemned were hanged for a few hours, exposed alone and before the eyes of men. This was more dreadful to the Jews than any cruel death, because of the terrible words of the divine voice in Deuteronomy 21:23: Cursed by God is he who hangs on a tree. Philo writes that the same kind of punishment was customarily inflicted on murderers, although according to the rabbis murderers were put to death not by stoning but by beheading. (3) Finally, the third argument is taken from the fact that there is no word in the ancient Hebrew language that properly means the cross, no verb peculiar to the act of crucifying, and indeed no certain mention of that kind of punishment anywhere in the whole Old Testament, in the Hebrew commonwealth. The testimonies from the rabbinical commentaries cited against this argument fail; for all who were lifted up on high and pierced through with a sharp stake, or strangled with a noose, or, when already dead, exposed alone before the eyes of men for disgrace, are said to be hanged on a gibbet and on a cross. Hence for all these words, gibbet, cross, and so on, used in the Vulgate and other versions, the Hebrew text has one word, namely wood.

units.la: Tertia die resurget. A vespere sepultura usque ad diluculum resurrectionis Christi triginta sex horae sunt, id est, nox tota cum die, & nocte tota. Aug. lib. 4. de Trinitate. c. 6.
units.tr: He will rise on the third day. From evening burial until the dawn of Christ's resurrection there are thirty-six hours, that is, a whole night with a whole day and a whole night.

units.la: 20. Accessit ad eum mater. Instigatione scilicet filiorum, unde Marc. 10. v. 35. ipsi accessisse dicuntur; accesserunt autem non per se, sed per matrem, ut petitio esset honestior, & impetratio facilior: hinc Christus non matri, sed filiis respondit.
units.tr: 20. His mother came to him. Evidently at the instigation of her sons; hence in Mark 10:35 the sons themselves are said to have come. They came, however, not in person but through their mother, so that the request might seem more becoming and be more easily obtained. Hence Christ answers not the mother but the sons.

units.la: 21. Dic ut sedeant. Petebant filii Zebedaei excellentiam habere prae aliis in participando judiciariam potestatem Christi: unde non petebant, quod sederent ad dextram vel sinistram Patris, sed ad dextram vel sinistram Christi. D. Thom. 3. part. q. 58. art. 4. ad 4.
units.tr: 21. Say that they may sit. The sons of Zebedee sought to have pre-eminence over the others in sharing Christ's judicial power. Hence they did not ask to sit at the right or left hand of the Father, but at the right or left hand of Christ. Thomas Aquinas, Summa 3, q. 58, art. 4, ad 4.

units.la: 22. Nescitis quid petatis. Cùm inordinatè petatis, triumphum scilicet ante victoriam.
units.tr: 22. You do not know what you ask. Because you ask in an disordered way, namely the triumph before the victory.

units.la: Potestis bibere calicem, &c. Adagiali sententiâ docet discipulos in hoc mundo non gloriam Christi, sed crucem esse ambiendam; qui enim compatitur, & conglorificabitur. Idem significat & alterum adagium in textu Græco hîc & etiam in Latino Marc. 10. v. 38. additum: Baptismo, quo ego baptizor, baptizari.
units.tr: Can you drink the cup, etc. By a proverbial saying he teaches the disciples that in this world it is not Christ's glory but the cross that is to be sought, for whoever suffers with him will also be glorified with him. The other proverb, added in the Greek text here and also in the Latin of Mark 10:38, has the same sense: to be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized.

units.la: 23. Calicem quidem meum bibetis. Calicem in Scripturis divinis intelligimus passionem juxta illud: Pater, si possibile est, transeat à me calix iste. Porro calicem martyrii bibit Jacobus filius Zebedæi, dum ab Herode fuit capite truncatus; Joannes autem bibit calicem confessionis, quem & tres pueri in camino ignis biberunt, licèt persecutor non fuderit sanguinem; legimus enim in Ecclesiasticis historiis, quòd & ipse Joannes propter martyrium sit missus in ferveнтis olei dolium, & inde ad suscipiendam coronam Christi athleta profecerit, statimque sit relegatus in Patmos insulam. B. Hier.
units.tr: 23. You will indeed drink my cup. By the cup in the divine Scriptures we understand suffering, according to that saying: Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me. Moreover, James the son of Zebedee drank the cup of martyrdom when he was beheaded by Herod. John drank the cup of confession, which the three boys also drank in the furnace of fire, although the persecutor did not shed their blood. For we read in the ecclesiastical histories that John himself was sent, on account of his martyrdom, into a vat of boiling oil, and from there, as an athlete, advanced to receive the crown of Christ, and was immediately banished to the island of Patmos. Blessed Jerome.

units.la: Non est meum dare vobis. Plures sunt hujus loci expositiones, sed omnium optima meo judicio est expositio Epiphanii Hær. 69. Ambrosii lib. 5. de fide, c 2. & Cyrilli Alexandrini lib. 10. Thesauri. c. 5. Hi dicunt vim præsentis loci non consistere in his verbis: non est meum, sed in hoc pronomine, vobis; neque enim facit Christus comparationem inter se & Patrem, quasi velit dicere se non posse dare & Patrem posse; quia si hoc dicere voluisset, dixisset: Non est meum dare vobis, sed Patris mei; sed comparationem facit Christus inter filios Zebedæi, & inter prædestinatos ad gloriam à filiis Zebedæi expetitam. q. d. Meum quidem est concedere quod petitis, sed non vobis, verùm quibus paratum est à Patre meo. Quòd autem paratum est, à Patre, inquit Aug. lib. 1. de Trinitate. c. 12. & ab ipso Filio paratum est, quia ipse & Pater unum sunt.
units.tr: It is not mine to give you. There are many explanations of this passage, but in my judgment the best of all is that of Epiphanius, Heresy 69, of Ambrose, On the Faith, book 5, chapter 2, and of Cyril of Alexandria, Thesaurus, book 10, chapter 5. These writers say that the force of the present passage lies not in the words it is not mine, but in the pronoun you. For Christ does not make a comparison between himself and the Father, as if he wished to say that he cannot give while the Father can; for had he wished to say this, he would have said: It is not mine to give you, but my Father's. Rather Christ makes a comparison between the sons of Zebedee and those predestined to glory, whom the sons of Zebedee sought. As if to say: it is indeed mine to grant what you ask, but not to you, rather to those for whom it has been prepared by my Father. That it has been prepared by the Father, says Augustine in On the Trinity, book 1, chapter 12, is also prepared by the Son himself, because he and the Father are one.

units.la: Quibus paratum est à Patre meo. Cum Patre se intelligi voluit parare sedes gloriæ, quibus vellet. Aug. ibid. Solet autem in Scripturis prædeparatio regni seu prædestinatio appropriari Deo Patri, quia pertinet ad providentiam, quæ appropriatur Deo Patri, quia patris est prospicere filiis. Hinc nunquam legimus in Scripturis Christum prædestinasse quempiam, sed solum Deum Patrem, quamvis prædestinatio in rei veritate fiat à tribus personis sanctissimæ Trinitatis.
units.tr: For those for whom it has been prepared by my Father. He wished it to be understood that he, together with the Father, prepares the seats of glory for whomever he wills. Augustine, ibid. In the Scriptures, however, the advance preparation of the kingdom, or predestination, is usually ascribed to God the Father, because it belongs to providence, which is ascribed to God the Father, since it is the father's part to provide for his sons. Hence we never read in the Scriptures that Christ predestined anyone, but only God the Father, although in the reality of the matter predestination is effected by all three persons of the most holy Trinity.

units.la: 25. Principes Gentium dominantur eorum. Id est, habent super eos dominatum, seu dominium illud ἐξουσίαν, sive supereminens, ut Aristoteles loquitur, quod provinciarum dispendio totius Reipublicæ salutem procurare permittit. Agit autem Christus de legitima Regum autoritate, non vero de tyrannica. cùm de iis Regibus loquatur, qui benefici vocantur à subditis, ut patet ex Luc.22. v.25. Ex quo etiam loco patet vocem Græcam κατακυριεύοντων non sumi à Matthæo in malam partem propter additam præpositionem κατ; cùm Lucas utatur simplici verbo κυριεύοντων.
units.tr: 25. The rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them. That is, they have dominion over them, or that lordship which Aristotle calls exousia [ἐξουσία], or supremacy, which permits the welfare of the whole commonwealth to be secured at the cost of the provinces. Christ, however, is speaking of the lawful authority of kings, not of tyrannical authority, since he speaks of those kings who are called benefactors by their subjects, as is clear from Luke 22:25. From this same passage it is also clear that the Greek word katakyrieuousin [κατακυριεύουσιν] is not taken by Matthew in a bad sense, despite the added preposition kata, since Luke uses the simple verb kyrieuousin [κυριεύουσιν].

units.la: 26. Non ita erit inter vos. Apostolis interdicitur dominatus, seu summum imperium, quod despoticum vocant, ab Ecclesia amovetur, cujus administratio aristocratico regimine temperata est ex sententia omnium Theologorum. Vehemens est B. Bernardus & fere totus in eo, ut hanc sententiam Eugenio R. P. persuadeat: Nec enim tibi ille (Petrus sc.) dare quod non habuit, potuit; quod habuit, hoc dedit, sollicitudinem, ut dixi, super Ecclesias. Numquid dominationem? audi ipsum: Non dominantes in Clero, sed forma facti gregis. Et ne dictum sola humilitate putes, non etiam veritate, vox Domini est in Evangelio: Reges gentium dominantur eorum, & qui potestatem habent super eos, benefici vocantur. Et infert: Vos autem non sic. Planum est Apostolis interdicitur dominatus. Ergo tu, & tibi usurpare aude, aut dominans Apostolatum, aut Apostolicus dominatum. Plane ab altero prohiberis. Si utrumque similiter habere velis, perdes utrumque. Hactenus Bernard. de Consid. lib. 2. c 6. Nec aliena est Bernardi explicatio à veterum sensu. Etenim Origenes Tract. 12. in Matth. hunc locum Evangelii sic edisserit: Principes Gentium non contenti tantum regere subjectos suos, violenter eis dominari nituntur. Inter vos autem, qui estis, non erunt hæc, ne forte qui videntur habere aliquem in Ecclesia principatum, dominentur fratribus propriis, vel potestatem in eos exerceant. Quoniam sicut omnia carnalia in necessitate sunt posita, non in voluntate; spiritualia autem in voluntate, non necessitate; sic & Principes spirituales. Principatus eorum in dilectione esse debet esse positus, non in timore corporali.
units.tr: 26. It shall not be so among you. Domination is forbidden to the apostles; supreme power, which they call despotic, is removed from the Church, whose government, according to the opinion of all theologians, is tempered by an aristocratic rule. Blessed Bernard is vehement, and almost entirely intent on persuading Pope Eugenius of this view: For he (Peter, that is) could not give you what he did not have; what he did have he gave, namely, as I have said, concern for the churches. Is it domination? Hear him: not lording it over the clergy, but being examples to the flock. And lest you think this is said only from humility, not also from truth, the word of the Lord in the Gospel is: The kings of the nations lord it over them, and those who have power over them are called benefactors. And he adds: But you, not so. It is plain that domination is forbidden to the apostles. So you, too, dare to usurp either the lordship of the apostleship or the apostolic dominion. Plainly you are prohibited from the one. If you wish to have both alike, you will lose both. Thus far Bernard, On Consideration, book 2, chapter 6. Nor is Bernard's explanation foreign to the sense of the ancients. For Origen, in Tractate 12 on Matthew, expounds this passage of the Gospel thus: The rulers of the Gentiles, not content merely to govern their subjects, strive to dominate them by force. But among you, who are, these things shall not be, lest perhaps those who seem to have some principate in the Church should lord it over their own brothers or exercise power over them. For just as all carnal things are subject to necessity, not to will, but spiritual things are subject to will, not necessity, so too spiritual rulers. Their principate ought to be founded in love, not in bodily fear.

units.la: 27. Erit vester servus. Interdicitur dominatio, indicitur ministratio, Præest Pontifex ceu fidelis servus, quem constituit Dominus super familiam suam, non ut eorum dominetur, sed ut det illis escam, ut dispenset, non ut imperet, inquit Bernardus. Hinc præclarè Chrysost. Hom. 25. in 1 Cor. Τῶν χρῶν ... κοινῷ συμμέτρως ζῆν. Hæc est Christiani mi regula, hæc illius exacta definitio, hic est vertex supra omnes eminens, publicæ utilitati consulere. Idem in Acta Apost. Hom. 3. Legibus ac mandatis omnia peraguntur, scilicet apud Principes, hic vero, id est, in regimine Ecclesiastico, nihil tale; neque enim licet ex authoritate præcipere. Quod Gregorius Nazianzenus conceptis verbis testatur in Apolog. Vel maximè id Lex nostra, & Legislator noster sanxit, ut grex non coacte sed sponte ac libenti animo pascatur. Hinc & Hieronymus in Epitaphio Nepotiani Regem nolentibus, Episcopum volentibus praesse scribit.
units.tr: 27. Erit vester servus. Lordship is forbidden and service is enjoined: The bishop presides as a faithful servant, whom the Lord has set over his household, not to lord it over them, but to give them food, to dispense and not to command, says Bernard. Hence Chrysostom excellently, Hom. 25 on 1 Cor.: Τῶν χρῶν ... κοινῷ συμμέτρως ζῆν. This is, my Christian friend, the rule, this is its exact definition, this is the summit that rises above all, to look to the public advantage. The same in Acts, Hom. 3: Everything is carried through by laws and commands, namely among princes; but here, that is, in ecclesiastical government, there is nothing of the kind; for it is not lawful to command by authority. Gregory Nazianzen bears witness to this in so many words in his Apology: Above all, our Law and our Lawgiver has ordained that the flock be fed not by compulsion but willingly and with a ready mind. Hence Jerome also writes in the Epitaph of Nepotianus that kings rule those who are unwilling, and a bishop those who are willing.

units.la: Itaque regium imperium a sacerdotali in eo maxime distat, quod illi non solae singulorum civium rationes commissae sint, sed totius Reipublicae salus; unde fit ut in cives, etiam invitos ad fovendum totius Reipublicae corpus jus illi competat. Quod aliter se habet in Episcopali ministerio, cui Ecclesiae sollicitudo ita est commissa, ut singulorum saluti praecipue invigilare debeat, nec curare possit universum corpus aliquorum membrorum pernicie; sed ad exemplum Magistri nonaginta novem oves deserendae illi sunt, ut centesimam ad causas reportet. Deinde in ipsa ratione legum ferendarum, quae singulorum civium controversias respiciunt, Principes quidem eorum utilitatibus consulere debent, adeo ut eos tacita conditione suis legibus obstringi nolint, nisi usu ipso confiterit eas leges Reipublicae commodas & utiles esse. Attamen si non jure ordinario, sed summo jure agere velint, earum constitutionum executionem urgere, quae de jure dubio feruntur, & ab invitis civibus obsequium extorquere possunt, sine ulla tyrannici imperii exprobatione. Etsi enim dura sint aliquando Regum imperia, ordo ille imperandi & parendi id exigit, ut subditi dominorum mandatis cedant, quemadmodum Apostoli difertissime docuerunt, Paulus Rom. 13. & Petrus 1 Ep. c. 2. Sed in legibus Ecclesiasticis, quae jus naturale aut divinum non exsequuntur, summum illud imperium locum non habet. Quo sensu accipienda sunt, quae adduxi testimonia e Gregorio Nazianzeno, Chrysostomo, & Bernardo ad textus Evangelii explicationem. Quin etiam magnum discrimen intercedit inter supplicia, quae leges publicae contumacibus irrogant, & excommunicationes, aut certas censuras, quibus utitur Ecclesia adversus sceleratos.
units.tr: Thus the royal power differs from the priestly chiefly in this: that the princely office is entrusted not only with the affairs of individual citizens but with the welfare of the whole commonwealth. Whence it follows that the prince has the right to bind citizens, even unwilling ones, in order to cherish the body of the whole commonwealth. It is otherwise in the episcopal ministry, to which the care of the Church is so committed that it must watch chiefly over the welfare of individuals, and cannot neglect the whole body for the destruction of some members; rather, after the example of the Master, the ninety-nine sheep must be left so that he may bring back the hundredth. Further, in the very principle of enacting laws, which concern the disputes of individual citizens, princes indeed ought to consult their advantage, so much so that they do not wish to bind them to their laws by a tacit condition unless experience itself has shown those laws to be useful and beneficial to the commonwealth. Yet if they wish to act not by ordinary right but by the highest right, they can insist on the execution of those enactments which are issued in doubtful right, and extract obedience from unwilling citizens, without any reproach of tyrannical rule. For although the commands of kings are sometimes harsh, the very order of commanding and obeying requires that subjects yield to the orders of their masters, as the Apostles taught most clearly: Paul in Rom. 13 and Peter in 1 Ep. ch. 2. But in ecclesiastical laws, which do not enforce natural or divine law, that supreme power has no place. In this sense must be understood the testimonies I have adduced from Gregory Nazianzen, Chrysostom, and Bernard in explaining the text of the Gospel. Indeed, there is a great difference between the punishments which public laws inflict on the obstinate, and the excommunications or certain censures which the Church uses against the wicked.

units.la: Principes enim adulterum, aut caedis reum, gladio plectit; id est, maleficum commerita poena afficit, in eoque vim imperii sui ostendit. Ecclesia vero non exigit poenam sed morborum curationem. Itaque non infligit excommunicationem, ut mactet, sed ut poenitenti salutem conciliet; quemadmodum diserte interpretatur Chrysostomus Hom. 15. in 2 Cor.
units.tr: For the prince strikes an adulterer or a murderer with the sword; that is, he visits the wrongdoer with deserved punishment, and in this shows the force of his power. The Church, however, does not demand punishment but the cure of diseases. Therefore it does not inflict excommunication in order to kill, but to win salvation for the penitent; as Chrysostom clearly explains, Hom. 15 on 2 Cor.

units.la: Unde Theodoretus in Praefat. ad Synagogen Canonum adnotavit aliam esse rationem legum Regiarum, & Canonum; quod illae severas poenas a reis exigant, hi autem errantes in vitam reducere, & aegris remedia parare conentur, quando peccatum est in leges Evangelicas, aut mores receptos.
units.tr: Hence Theodoret, in the Preface to the Synagogue of Canons, observed that there is a different rationale of royal laws and of canons: the former exact severe penalties from offenders, while the latter seek to lead the erring back to life and to prepare remedies for the sick, when sin has been committed against the Gospel laws or accepted customs.

units.la: 28. Filius hominis non venit ministrari, sed ministrare. Nempe, carnem suam in cibum, sanguinem in potum, animam in pretium, ut loquitur Bernardus Serm. 54. in Cantic.
units.tr: 28. The Son of Man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister. Indeed, his flesh as food, his blood as drink, his soul as the price, as Bernard says in Sermon 54 on the Song of Songs.

units.la: Dare animam suam redemtionem pro multis. Non dixit animam suam redemtionem dare pro omnibus, sed pro multis, id est, pro his qui credere voluerint. B. Hier. hîc; unde sanctus Leo Magnus in Ep. 81. ad Palaestinos, quae incipit, sollicitudini meae. Effusio, inquit, pro injustis sanguinis justi, tam potens fuit ad privilegium, tam dives ad pretium, ut si universitas captivorum in Redemptorem crederet, scilicet fide viva, nullum tyrannica vincula retinerent. Hinc & Ecclesia Smyrnensis in Epistola, quam anno Domini 169. de Polycarpi martyrio scripsit apud Eusebium lib. 4. Hist. Eccl. cap. 15. ait, οὐ γὰρ δυνησόμεθα ... Id est, Neque Christum unquam deserere poterimus, qui pro salute totius mundi eorum qui salvantur passus est.
units.tr: To give his soul as a ransom for many. He did not say that he would give his soul as a ransom for all, but for many, that is, for those who were willing to believe. Blessed Jerome here; whence Saint Leo the Great in Ep. 81 to the Palestinians, which begins sollicitudini meae: The effusion of the just man's blood for the unjust was so powerful for privilege, so rich for the price, that if the whole multitude of captives believed in the Redeemer, with living faith, tyrannical chains would hold none of them. Hence also the Church of Smyrna, in the letter it wrote about the martyrdom of Polycarp in the year of the Lord 169, as recorded in Eusebius, Church History book 4, ch. 15, says: οὐ γὰρ δυνησόμεθα ... That is: Neither will we ever be able to desert Christ, who suffered for the salvation of the whole world, of those who are saved.

units.la: 29. Egredientibus illis ad Jericho. In quam civitatem mox venerant, ut patet ex Marc. 10. v. 46. & ibi Zachaeum Publicanorum principem salvum facturus invisit, & parabolam de decem minis, quarum singulae, ut dicitur Ezech. 45. continent sexaginta siclos, coram omnibus dixit, ut narrat Luc. c. 19. Distat autem Jericho a Jerusalem decem parasangis, ut Talmudici loquuntur, seu ut Josephus lib. 5. de bello Judaico. c. 4. stadiis centum quinquaginta, id est, viginti milliaribus.
units.tr: 29. As they went out from Jericho. They had soon come into that city, as is clear from Mark 10:46, and there he visited Zacchaeus, the chief of the tax collectors, intending to save him; and in the sight of all he told the parable of the ten minas, each of which, as Ezek. 45 says, contains sixty shekels, as Luke relates in ch. 19. Jericho lies ten parasangs from Jerusalem, as the Talmudists say, or, as Josephus says in book 5 of the Jewish War, ch. 4, a hundred and fifty stadia, that is, twenty miles.

units.la: 30 Ecce duo caeci. Quia horum duorum caecorum alter altero nobilior erat, unius tantum meminerunt Marcus c. 10. & Lucas c. 18. cujus & nomen Marcus appellat Bartimaeum. Idem enim miraculum a tribus Evangelistis narrari, circumstantiae omnes satis declarant. Nec obstat quod Lucas ait miraculum contigisse, cum Christus appropinquaret Jericho, cum alii Evangelistae miraculum, quod narrant, contigisse affirment proficiscente Christo de Jericho; nam fieri potest, ut Lucas locum notaverit, unde primo inceperit caecus clamare, scilicet cum appropinquaret Jericho; sed cum esset dilata ejus sanitas, eundem iterum cum alio caeco viam obsedisse, egrediente Jesu ex urbe Jericho, & tunc utrumque vocatum ac sanatum esse. Alii fortasse melius respondent verbum ἐγγίζειν appropinquare, etiam cum praepositione εἰς ad, non semper motum ad locum, sed saepe distantiam tantum significare; sicut apud eundem Lucam c. 19. v. 29. ὡς ἤγγισεν εἰς Βηθφαγὴ καὶ Βηθανίαν, cum appropinquasset ad Bethphage & Bethaniam: hoc est, cum esset circa ea loca; nam Bethaniam jam transierat.
units.tr: 30 Behold, two blind men. Because one of these two blind men was more notable than the other, Mark in ch. 10 and Luke in ch. 18 mention only one, whom Mark also names Bartimaeus. That the same miracle is related by three evangelists is made plain by all the circumstances. Nor is there an objection in that Luke says the miracle happened as Christ was approaching Jericho, while the other evangelists affirm that the miracle they narrate happened as Christ was leaving Jericho. For it can be that Luke noted the place where the blind man first began to cry out, namely as Jesus was approaching Jericho; but since his healing was deferred, he again besieged the way with another blind man as Jesus went out of the city of Jericho, and then both were called and healed. Others perhaps answer better that the verb to approach [ἐγγίζειν] and especially with the preposition to [εἰς] does not always signify motion toward a place, but often only distance; as in the same Luke, ch. 19 v. 29: ὡς ἤγγισεν εἰς Βηθφαγὴ καὶ Βηθανίαν, when he drew near to Bethphage and Bethany: that is, when he was in the region of those places; for he had already passed Bethany.

units.la: CAPUT XXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXI.

units.la: I. Cum appropinquassent, &c. Præsens hæc historia, ut patet ex Joan. 12. v. 12. contigit postridie cœnæ Christi in vico Bethania in domo Simonis Leprosi, qua in cœna Maria soror Lazari unxit pedes Domini, ut per recapitulationem commemorant Matthæus cap. 26. & Marcus cap. 14. indicaturi causam proditionis Judæ indignantis sibi periisse lucrum, quod ex vendito unguento provenire potuisset. Joannes vero cap. 12. historiam cœnæ Christi in Bethania & unctionis in ea factæ suo tempore reddidit, & more suo quaedam notat ab aliis prætermissa. Cùm autem Joannes dicat sex diebus ante Pascha Christum venisse Bethaniam, & postero die (quem ab ultima usque antiquitate omnes Christiani crediderunt fuisse diem Dominicum, ut fidem faciunt quidam Augustini Sermones de tempore, & cujusdam Homiliæ S. Maximi Taurinensis, qui circa annum 420. floruit, titulus) multam turbam, quæ venerat ad diem festum, cùm audiissent Jesum venire Jerosolymam, accepisse termites palmarum & prodiisse ei obviam, patet Jesum venisse die Sabbati in vicum Bethaniam; qui si fuit sex diebus ante Paschale festum, festum illud die Veneris, non Sabbati celebratum est: ut citra idoneum fundamentum existimant Rupertus & Paulus Burgensis; sextus enim à Sabbato dies, non est Sabbatum, sed dies Veneris. Nec obstat quod Ruperti sententiæ fautores objiciunt de festo Pentecostes, quod omnis Christianitas, ut aiunt, ab ultima usque antiquitate credidit anno Passionis Christi in Dominicam incidisse, ut fidem faciunt Clementis Constitutiones, & Augustini Sermo de Tempore 154. & Leo passim: ergo, inquiunt, illo anno primus azymorum fuit Sabbatum, non dies Veneris. Nam à secunda die azymorum numerabantur septem hebdomades, id est, dies quadraginta novem, quibus pro colophone addebatur quinquagesima, unde Pentecoste dicta. Itaque si prima azymorum fuit Sabbatum, prout Rupertus & Burgensis contendunt, prima septem hebdomadum, adeóque sex reliquæ inceperunt die Dominicâ, & in Sabbatum desierunt. Et post Sabbatum septimæ hebdomadis dies Dominica secuta est, id est, Pentecoste. At, si prima azymiorum in diem Veneris incidit, in eandem Veneris diem omnes hebdomades desierunt, & Pentecoste, id est, quinquagesima fuit Sabbatum. Hæc adversariorum objectio nihil obstat contra veritatem nostræ sententiæ; duplici enim via solvi potest. Primo ex ipsa Lege dubium oboritur de vero die Pentecostes; ita enim habetur Deut. 16. v. 9. Septem hebdomadas numerabis tibi ab ea die, quâ falcem in segetem miseris. Falx autem in segetes immittebatur postridie festi primi azymorum, quod vocatur Sabbatum, Levit. 23. v. 15. ut ex demessis frugibus offerretur Deo manipulus. At, cum festum primum azymorum sequebatur Sabbati dies, manipulus ille frugum non postridie, sed perendie videtur fuisse oblatus, quia Sabbato non licebat salcem in segetes immittere. Quo dato nulla fuerit objectio adversoriorum, cum, quo anno Christus passus est, primo post festum azymorum die Sabbatum fuerit, unde sequetur frugum oblationem & septem hebdomadum enumerationem in diem Dominicam eo anno fuisse rejiciendam, adeoque Pentecosten in eandem diem incidisse. Secundo dici potest quod illa verba Lucæ Act. 2. v. 1. Cum complerentur dies Pentecostes, completantur Hebraismum, q. d. Cum impleti essent, seu, postquam impleti sunt dies Pentecostes. Quod non est sine exemplo; Hebræi enim sic loqui amant, ut videre est in veritate Hebraica Levit. 12. v. 6. Num. 6. v. 13. Esther 1. v. 5. Sic dato, non concesso, Judæorum Pentecosten in Sabbatum incidisse, quo anno Christus passus est, potest tamen intelligi Spiritus-Sanctus in Apostolos die Dominica descendisse, quia Lucæ cum complerentur, Hebraico loquendi more non solum significat impleri dies Pentecostes, sed & jam plene & plane impletos fuisse, ita ut descensus Spiritus-Sancti contigerit postridie Pentecostes Judæorum.
units.tr: I. When they drew near, etc. This story, as is clear from John 12:12, took place on the day after Christ's supper, in the village of Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, where at the supper Mary, the sister of Lazarus, anointed the feet of the Lord. Matthew (ch. 26) and Mark (ch. 14) recall it by way of recapitulation, to show the cause of the treachery of Judas, who was indignant that the profit which could have come from the sold ointment had been lost to him. John, however, in ch. 12, gives the account of Christ's supper in Bethany and of the anointing done there at its proper time, and in his own manner notes some things that the others passed over. Now John says that Christ came to Bethany six days before the Passover, and that on the next day (which all Christians from the most ancient times have believed to be the Lord's Day, as the titles of certain Sermons of Augustine on the time, and of a Homily of St. Maximus of Turin, who flourished about the year 420, bear witness) a great crowd, which had come for the festival, heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem, took palm branches, and went out to meet him. It is clear that Jesus came to the village of Bethany on the Sabbath day. If this was six days before the Passover feast, that feast was celebrated on a Friday, not a Sabbath. Rupert and Paul of Burgos think this, but without a sound foundation, for the sixth day from the Sabbath is not a Sabbath but a Friday. Nor is there any obstacle in what the supporters of Rupert's opinion object concerning the feast of Pentecost: they say that all Christendom, from the most ancient times, has believed that in the year of Christ's passion Pentecost fell on the Lord's Day, as the Constitutions of Clement, Augustine's Sermon on the Time 154, and Leo everywhere attest. Therefore, they say, in that year the first day of unleavened bread was the Sabbath, not a Friday. For from the second day of unleavened bread seven weeks were counted, that is, forty-nine days, to which the fiftieth was added as a crown, whence the name Pentecost. So if the first day of unleavened bread was the Sabbath, as Rupert and Burgensis contend, the first of the seven weeks, and therefore the other six, began on the Lord's Day and ended on the Sabbath; and after the Sabbath, the Lord's Day followed the seventh week, that is, Pentecost. But if the first of the unleavened bread fell on a Friday, then all the weeks ended on that same Friday, and Pentecost, that is, the fiftieth day, was the Sabbath. This objection of our opponents does nothing against the truth of our view, for it can be answered in two ways. First, from the Law itself a doubt arises about the true day of Pentecost. For it is written in Deut. 16:9: You shall number seven weeks to yourself from the day when you first put the sickle to the standing corn. The sickle was put to the corn on the day after the first feast of unleavened bread, which is called the Sabbath (Lev. 23:15), so that a sheaf of the harvested grain might be offered to God. But when the first feast of unleavened bread was followed by a Sabbath day, that sheaf of grain seems to have been offered not on the next day but on the day after that, because it was not lawful to put the sickle to the corn on the Sabbath. Granting this, there will be no objection from our opponents. For in the year Christ suffered, the first day after the feast of unleavened bread was a Sabbath; from which it follows that the offering of the sheaf and the counting of the seven weeks in that year had to be placed on the Lord's Day, and so Pentecost fell on that same day. Second, it can be said that those words of Luke in Acts 2:1, When the days of Pentecost were fully come, are a Hebraism, as if to say: when they had been fulfilled, or, after the days of Pentecost were fulfilled. This is not without precedent, for the Hebrews love to speak in this way, as may be seen in the Hebrew text of Lev. 12:6, Num. 6:13, and Esther 1:5. So, even if it be granted, which we do not grant, that the Jewish Pentecost fell on the Sabbath in the year Christ suffered, it may still be understood that the Holy Spirit descended upon the Apostles on the Lord's Day. For Luke's phrase when they were fully come, in the Hebrew manner of speaking, means not only that the days of Pentecost were being completed, but that they had already been fully and completely completed, so that the descent of the Holy Spirit happened the day after the Jewish Pentecost.

units.la: Venissent Bethphage. Marcus habet cap. II. v. I. Cum appropinquarent Jerosolymæ & Bethaniæ. Lucas vero cap. 19. v. 29. Cum appropinquassent ad Bethphage & Bethaniam. In hodiernis exemplaribus Græcis Marci habetur: Cum appropinquarent ad Jerusalem, ad Bethphage & Bethaniam. Verum Vulgatus interpres, ut & Origines Tractatu 14. in Matthæum, non legerunt in Marco Bethphage, sed solum Bethaniam. Distabat Jerosolymis Bethania quindecim stadiis, ut dicitur Joan. 11. v. 18. id est, duobus milliaribus. At Bethphage prope fuit sub ipsis Jerosolymorum mœnibus, si Hebræis credimus, secundum quos ibi coquebantur oblationes vespertinæ, ut probat doctissimus Buxtorfius ex Bartenora, & Bartenora ex Rabbi Mose Majemonide in tractatu Talmu-dico
units.tr: They came to Bethphage. Mark has in ch. 11:1: When they drew near to Jerusalem and Bethany. Luke, however, in ch. 19:29, has: When they drew near to Bethphage and Bethany. In the present Greek copies of Mark it reads: When they drew near to Jerusalem, to Bethphage and Bethany. But the Vulgate translator, and also Origen in Tractate 14 on Matthew, did not read Bethphage in Mark, but only Bethany. Bethany was fifteen stadia from Jerusalem, as is said in John 11:18, that is, about two miles. But Bethphage was close to the very walls of Jerusalem, if we believe the Hebrews, according to whom the evening offerings were cooked there. The most learned Buxtorf proves this from Bartenora, and Bartenora from Rabbi Moses Maimonides, in the Talmudic tractate

units.la: dico Menachoth cap. II. sol. 95. B. Bethphage, inquit, nomen erat loci extra Ierusalem, prope montem Templi, in quo coquebant oblationes. Quin glossa Talmudis in tractatu Sota sol. 45. A. & Bava Metsia sol. 90. A. ait, Quidquid est in ambitu exteriore Jerosolymorum vocari Bethphage, & hoc nomine significari cingulam. Aliis Phage non est cingula, sed caput lupati. Bochartus linguarum peritissimus Bethphage nomen habere ait à grossis, ut Olynthus urbs Thraciæ; grossi enim Chaldæis & Syris Pagge, vel Phage ἀςχαικως. Origenes & Hieronymus in Matthæum Bethphage explicant domum maxillarum. Bernardus in Sermone ad milites templi cap. 12. domum buccæ, quod effet Bethphaccha vel Bethphacche. Liber nominum, Bethphage, domus oris vallium, quod effet Beth-pi-ge. Tremellius exponit domum fontis, quod est, Bethphage; ita enim scribitur ab Hebraeis Graecum παγή. Ludovicus de Dieu, domum adulatoris, id est, Beth-phagia. Verum ex omnibus his interpretamentis magis arridet sententia Bocharti, ut Bethphage dicatur, quasi domus grossorum, ut hoc nomen sonat ad verbum citra ullam mutationem, utpote Hebraeo-Chaldaeum, seu Syrum. Jam quod res eadem ab uno Evangelista facta narratur in vico Bethphage, ab altero in Bethaniae pago, à tertio in utroque, facile est conciliare. Horum nempe vicorum agri confines erant, & quod factum est in confiniis, dici potest in alterutro, vel in utroque factum.
units.tr: Menachoth ch. 11, fol. 95 B: Bethphage, he says, was the name of a place outside Jerusalem, near the mountain of the Temple, where the offerings were cooked. Indeed, the gloss on the Talmud in the tractate Sota, fol. 45 A, and Bava Metsia, fol. 90 A, says that whatever is in the outer circuit of Jerusalem is called Bethphage, and that by this name a girdle is meant. Others say that Phage is not a girdle but the head of a lupatum (a bit or bridle). Bochart, the most skilled of the languages, says that Bethphage has its name from the grossi, as the city Olynthus of Thrace does; for the grossi are called Pagge or Phage by the Chaldeans and Syrians, [ἀρχαϊκῶς] archaically. Origen and Jerome in their commentary on Matthew explain Bethphage as house of the jaws. Bernard, in his Sermon to the Knights of the Temple, ch. 12, says house of the cheek, which would be Bethphaccha or Bethphacche. The Book of Names gives Bethphage, house of the mouth of the valleys, which would be Beth-pi-ge. Tremellius explains it as house of the spring, which is Bethphage, for the Hebrews so write the Greek [παγή]. Ludovicus de Dieu gives house of the flatterer, that is, Beth-phagia. But of all these interpretations, the opinion of Bochart pleases me most, that Bethphage is so called as house of the grossi, since the name sounds that way word for word without any change, being Hebrew-Chaldean, or Syriac. Now, that the same event is related by one Evangelist as having happened in the village of Bethphage, by another in the district of Bethany, and by a third in both, is easy to reconcile. The fields of these villages were, of course, adjacent, and what happened on the border may be said to have happened in one or the other, or in both.

units.la: 2. Ite in castellum quod contra vos est. Id est, e regione vestri. Sic infra c. 27. v. 61. sedentes contra sepulchrum dicuntur mulieres, quae prope sepulchrum sedebant. Sic Carthago sita dicitur Italiam contra, id est, e regione. Nugantur, qui castellum vobis adversarium interpretantur, id est, Jerosolymam Apostolis adversaturam; neque enim Jerosolyma castellum, seu vicus, ut habet Syrus, Arabs, & textus Graecus, sed urbs appellatur, ut certe urbs erat una e totius Asiae maximis. Et fortasse ob id ipsum in Marco quidam codices Graeci legunt in urbem, pro in vicum, nempe ut Jerosolymorum urbs significari putetur. Ego vicum intelligo qui oculis se offerebat, & Christus intento digito monstrabat. Quis is fuerit tacent Veteres. Solum in Nubiensi Geographo haec habentur Clim. 3. Part. 5. Ad duo milliaria e monte Olivarum pagus erat, ex quo adducta est asina, qua vectus est Dominus Christus, cum ingressus est Jerosolymam: sed pagus ille nunc desertus est, nec ullos habet incolas. Perdiccas Ephesius in lib. de Dominicis thematibus circa Jerosolymam, postquam egit de Bethphage & Bethania, ait:
units.tr: 2. Go into the village that is over against you. That is, opposite to you. So below, in ch. 27:61, the women are said to be sitting over against the sepulchre, that is, sitting near the sepulchre. So Carthage is said to lie over against Italy, that is, opposite it. Those who interpret a village hostile to you as meaning Jerusalem, which would oppose the Apostles, talk nonsense. For Jerusalem is not called a village or hamlet (as the Syriac, the Arabic, and the Greek text have it), but a city, as indeed it was one of the greatest of all Asia. And perhaps for this very reason some Greek manuscripts of Mark read into the city instead of into the village, namely so that the city of Jerusalem might be thought to be meant. I take the village to be the one that was visible to the eyes, and that Christ pointed out with his finger. The ancients are silent about what it was. Only the Nubian geographer has the following in Clim. 3, Part 5: Two miles from the Mount of Olives there was a village, from which the she-ass was brought on which the Lord Christ rode when he entered Jerusalem; but that village is now deserted and has no inhabitants. Perdiccas of Ephesus, in his book on the Lord's themes around Jerusalem, after treating of Bethphage and Bethany, says:

units.la: Τότε τὸ ὄρος ἀντικρυ πρὸς νοτον τὸ μέρος, Καὶ ἡ ἡ ἴνου ἄξαα ἡ πῶλον σμικρὸν χώϊων.
units.tr: Then, opposite the mountain on the southern side, and the village that brings an ass or a little colt [Τότε τὸ ὄρος ἀντικρυ πρὸς νοτον τὸ μέρος, Καὶ ἡ ἡ ἴνου ἄξαα ἡ πῶλον σμικρὸν χώϊων].

units.la: E regione hujus montis ad australem partem etiam vicus est parvus, qui asinam & pullum egit.
units.tr: Over against this mountain, on the southern side, there is also a small village, which supplied the ass and the colt.

units.la: Invenietis asinam alligatam & pullum cum ea. Matris cum pullo adductæ meminit solus Matthæus, alii Evangelistæ id prætereunt tanquam minus necesse, quia solum pullum Christus equitavit. Notanda est locutio Joannis, c. 12. v. 14. dum Jesum dicit invenisse asellum, quem non per se sed per discipulos à se missos invenerat. Observant Marcus & Lucas hunc pullum neminem unquam insedisse, quia ad honorem Christi pertinet, ut quod à Joanne observatur Christum in eo sepulchro fuisse positum, in quo nemo unquam positus fuerat. Non absimili exemplo Philistæi 1 Sam. seu Reg. 6. Arcam remiserunt in plaustro novo vaccis alligatis, quæ nunquam jugum tulerant. Sic & apud Gentiles in quibusdam sacrificiis injuges hostiæ immolabantur, id est, quæ nunquam sub jugo fuerunt, ut videre est apud Macrobium Saturnal. lib. 2. c. 5, &c. Addunt alii Christum ita significasse sibi parere etiam quæ maximè sunt indomita. Ceterum vectionem asini non fuisse vilem in Oriente constat ex Genes. 22. v. 3. Exod. 4. v. 20. Num. 22. v. 21. Josue 15. v. 18. Jud. 1. v. 14. c. 10. v. 4. c. 12. v. 14. 1 Reg. 25. v. 20. 2 Reg. 17. v. 23. c. 19. v. 26. 3 Reg. 13. v. 13, & 23. Quibus adde, quod Chrysostomus, in Titum Hom. 1, Constantinopolitano Episcopo, id est, sibi dicit objici tanquam argumentum nimii fastûs, quod servos habet, qui illi ministrent, & asino vehitur, ἐπὶ ὄνω ὀχεῖται. Mitto quod referunt Arabes de Arabum Magnatibus sic vehi solitis, & quod Leo Africanus testatur in Ægypto matronas hodieque sic vehi, quemadmodum olim Romæ, ut ex Lampridio colligere est in vita Heliogabali.
units.tr: You will find an ass tied, and a colt with her. Only Matthew mentions the mother brought with the colt; the other Evangelists pass this over as less necessary, since Christ rode only the colt. John's wording in chapter 12, verse 14, is to be noted, where he says that Jesus found a young ass, which he had found not by himself but through the disciples whom he sent. Mark and Luke observe that no one had ever sat on this colt, because it belongs to the honour of Christ, just as John observes that Christ was laid in a tomb in which no one had ever been laid. A similar example is found in the Philistines in 1 Samuel (or 1 Kings) 6, who sent back the ark on a new cart drawn by cows that had never borne the yoke; so too among the Gentiles, in certain sacrifices, unyoked victims were slaughtered, that is, those that had never been under the yoke, as may be seen in Macrobius, Saturnalia, book 2, chapter 5, etc. Others add that Christ thereby signified that even the most untamed things obeyed him. Moreover, that riding on an ass was not considered base in the East is clear from Genesis 22:3; Exodus 4:20; Numbers 22:21; Joshua 15:18; Judges 1:14; 10:4; 12:14; 1 Kings 25:20; 2 Kings 17:23; 19:26; 3 Kings 13:13 and 23. To these add that Chrysostom, in his first homily on Titus, says that the bishop of Constantinople, that is, himself, is objected to as an argument of excessive pride, because he keeps servants to attend him and rides on an ass [ἐπὶ ὄνω ὀχεῖται]. I pass over what the Arabs report of their great men, who were accustomed to be carried thus, and what Leo Africanus testifies, that in Egypt matrons are still carried thus today, just as formerly at Rome, as may be gathered from Lampridius in the life of Heliogabalus.

units.la: 3. Si quis vobis aliquid dixerit, &c. Non solum prædixit Christus fore ut asinus reperiretur, sed & asinus cum matre, isque nondum subactus, & ligatus, & in aditu pagi seu castelli, & quo momento discipuli ingrederentur, & tum, cum solveretur, dominos primò reclamaturos, atque assensuros postmodum, cum resciverint iis egere Christum Dominum. Quas rerum minutias nemo alius prædixerit, quam qui gerit & suo nutu administrat. Nempe non casu factum est, ut injugis asini pullus eo loco & momento reperiretur, quo prædixerat Christus, & à dominis suis tam facilè dimitteretur. Quin omnia hæc disposuit Dei providentia, & jumenti dominos ad assensum inclinavit illâ vi flexanimâ & vorticordiâ, quâ Regum etiam corda in manu habet ut rivos aquarum, & quocunque vult inclinat, ut dicitur Prov. 21. Neque ethnicos id latissime testantur apud Themistium Orat. 9. Assyriorum pisturæ, in quibus Regis animus in manu Dei servatur. Cùm autem quidquid nomine Dei geritur, sit primario actio Dei, & minister sacramentorum faciat actiones sacramentales & verba proferat nomine Dei, seu potius Deihominis, id est, Christi, sequitur actiones sacramentales & verba esse principaliter Christi, ideóque efficere quod significant, sicut cum Apostoli nomine Christi asinæ domino dicerent, Dominus his opus habet; & Christus leproso Mundare, &c.
units.tr: 3. If anyone says anything to you, etc. Christ foretold not only that an ass would be found, but also that it would be with its mother, and that it was not yet broken and was tied, and at the entrance of the village or town, and at the very moment the disciples entered, and that when it was untied the owners would at first object, but afterwards would consent, once they had learned that the Lord Christ had need of it. No one but one who governs all things and administers them by his will could have foretold such minute details. Certainly it did not happen by chance that a colt unbroken to the yoke was found in that place and at that moment, as Christ had foretold, and was so readily let go by its owners. Indeed, the providence of God arranged all these things and inclined the minds of the owners to consent by that powerful and heart-turning force, by which he holds even the hearts of kings in his hand like streams of water, and inclines them wherever he wishes, as it is said in Proverbs 21. Nor do the heathen bear wide witness to this in vain, in Themistius, Oration 9, on the paintings of the Assyrians, in which "the mind of the king is kept in the hand of God." Since whatever is done in God's name is primarily the action of God, and a minister of the sacraments performs sacramental actions and speaks words in God's name, or rather in the name of the God-man, that is, Christ, it follows that sacramental actions and words belong chiefly to Christ, and therefore they effect what they signify; so when the Apostles said to the owner of the ass, The Lord has need of it, and Christ said to the leper, Be clean, etc.

units.la: 4. Ut impleretur. Eventus significatur non finis. Nam si finem respiciamus, res non tam implentur, quia sunt prædictæ, quam prædicuntur quia implendæ.
units.tr: 4. That it might be fulfilled. The outcome is meant, not the purpose. For if we look to the purpose, the things are not fulfilled because they were foretold, but are foretold because they are to be fulfilled.

units.la: Per Prophetam. Quidam putant intelligi Esaiam. Itâ Nonnus in Paraphrasi Joannis ad hunc locum.
units.tr: By the prophet. Some think Isaiah is meant. So Nonnus in his paraphrase of John on this passage.

units.la: Fiat ut Esaias quidquid prædixerat olim.
units.tr: Let it happen as Isaiah had once foretold.

units.la: Et Matthæi Æthiops interpres, Et hoc fuit ut evenieret & compleretur dictum Esaiæ Prophetæ, quod dixerat. Nempe hæc habentur Esaiæ 62. v. 11. Dicite filiæ Sion, Ecce Salvator tuus venit: ad quæ Matthæus ita alludit, ut etiam bene multi velint verba quæ citat, ex parte saltem ex Esaia depromta esse. Alii tamen, quia Matthæus unum Prophetam laudat non plures, volunt per Prophetam, unum intelligi Zachariam cap. 9. v. 9. cujus sensus hic & Joan. 12. citatur, non verba; nam, inquiunt, hic Dicite filiæ Sion: & Joan. 12. v. 15. Noli timere filia Sion: idem sonat secundum sensum atque hæc Zachariæ verba: Exulta satis filia Sion, jubila filia Ierusalem. Nempe filia Sion sunt Jerosolymitani, qui viso Rege Christo, in quo uno salutis spes erat sita, cum lætitia & clangore dixerunt alii aliis verba plena fiduciæ.
units.tr: And the Ethiopic translator of Matthew: And this was that it might come to pass and be fulfilled what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah, who had said. Indeed, these words stand in Isaiah 62:11: Say to the daughter of Zion, Behold your Saviour comes; and Matthew alludes to them in such a way that many quite plausibly hold that the words he quotes are taken, at least in part, from Isaiah. Others, however, because Matthew names one prophet and not several, prefer to understand by "the prophet" one, Zechariah, chapter 9, verse 9, whose sense, not whose words, is quoted here and in John 12; for, they say, Say to the daughter of Zion here, and Fear not, daughter of Zion in John 12:15, mean the same as the words of Zechariah: Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; shout aloud, daughter of Jerusalem. Indeed the daughters of Zion are the people of Jerusalem, who, seeing the king Christ, in whom alone the hope of salvation lay, spoke to one another with joy and shouting words full of trust.

units.la: 5. Ecce Rex tuus. Cujus scilicet regnum non est de hoc mundo, sed ab hujus seculi Regum pompa maximè alienum.
units.tr: 5. Behold your King. Whose kingdom, that is, is not of this world, and is very far removed from the pomp of the kings of this age.

units.la: Venit tibi mansuetus. Alii vertunt, venit tibi pauper, quia vox Hebræa mansuetum, & pauperem sonat.
units.tr: He comes to you meek. Others translate, he comes to you poor, because the Hebrew word sounds both "meek" and "poor."

units.la: Sedens super asinam & pullum filium subjugalis. Subjugale & asinus in Græcis Scripturæ interpretibus sunt omninò synonyma & in usu promiscuo. Non immerito exclamat hic
units.tr: Sitting on an ass and a colt, the foal of a beast of burden. In the Greek translators of Scripture, "subjugalis" (yoke-animal) and "asinus" are wholly synonymous and used interchangeably. Not without reason does Chrysostom exclaim here:

units.la: Chrysostomus: 'Εφαπσον πίνυν ἡ 'Ιερουσαλὴμ, ὁ Ποῖ Βασιλεὺς ὀχύμιλυ ὅτι ὃν ἠλθεν 'Ιερουσαλὴμ, 'ᾳ' ἐκ ἂν ἔχοιεν εἰπεῖν 'ᾳ' ἢ τῆτην μόνον. Judæum interroga, Quisnam Regum asino vectus venerit Jerosolymam? Neminem profecto dicere poterunt præter hunc solum. Agi autem in hac Zachariæ Prophetia ad literam de Christo, patet ex his quæ laudata à Matthæo verba sequuntur de pace per illum Regem restituenda, & ita ut curribus, & equis, & armis bellicis amplius non sit opus & de imperio ejus à mari ad mare atque ad extrema terræ propagando; de captivis denique per sanguinem fœderis ab eo redimendis. Itaque Judæi veteres hunc locum ad Messiam referunt summo consensu, neque aliter sentiunt plerique recentiores. Quod hic obiter docere non videtur esse extra rem.
units.tr: Chrysostom: Ask the Jew: what king came to Jerusalem riding on an ass? They will be able to name no one except this one alone [Ἐφαπσον πίνυν ἡ Ἰερουσαλὴμ, ὁ Ποῖ Βασιλεὺς ὀχύμιλυ ὅτι ὃν ἠλθεν Ἰερουσαλὴμ, ᾳ' ἐκ ἂν ἔχοιεν εἰπεῖν ᾳ' ἢ τῆτην μόνον]. Ask the Jew, what king came riding on an ass to Jerusalem? They will certainly be able to name no one but this one alone. That this prophecy of Zechariah refers literally to Christ is clear from the words that follow the passage Matthew quotes, concerning peace to be restored by that King, so that there is no more need of chariots, horses and weapons of war, and concerning his dominion spreading from sea to sea and to the ends of the earth, and finally concerning the captives to be redeemed by him through the blood of the covenant. Therefore the ancient Jews refer this passage to the Messiah with the greatest unanimity, and most of the more recent writers think the same. This is not, I think, out of place to teach here in passing.

units.la: Rabbi Eliezer cap. 31. ubi de Abrahami asino ait: Hic quoque asinus erit ... Filius Davidis. Hinc dicitur Zach. 9. v. 9. Ex ... &c. Talmudici in Sanhedrin cap. 11. sol. 98. ... filius Levi objecit, Scriptum est de Messia Dan. ... Et ecce cum nubibus cæli quasi filius hominis venit ... v. 9. de eodem Scriptum est, Pauper & ascendens ... Respondit si Israelitæ digni sunt, veniet cum nubibus ... si non sunt digni, veniet pauper & asino insidens. Inde ibidem cavillus Saporis Regis Persarum. Dixit Rex Sapores Rabbino Samuelî, Dicitis Messiam super asinum venturum: ego mittam ipsi varium equum, quem habeo. Respondet Rabbi Samuel verbis semi-Persicis: An tibi est asinus mille colorum? Mens Rabbini est asinum illum, cui insessurus est Messias non fore asinum e vulgo, sed animal multiplici colorum mixtura ita insigne, ut quemvis equum forma & pretio longe superet, Nempe Regis cavillos aliter eludere non potuit, quàm hoc commento. Sed regerendum erat id quod res est, Christi regnum scilicet non esse de hoc mundo, sed pacificum & humile. Ibidem pagina sequenti Rabbi Josephus ait: Utinam veniat Messias, & sedere dignus sim in umbra fimi asini ejus. Ibidem sol. 99. A. Rabbi Hillel dicit, Non erit Israelitis Messias, quia jam eum consumserunt in diebus Ezechiæ. Regerit Rabbi Josephi, Ignosce Rabbino Hilleli, ô Domine ejus. Ezechias quando fuit? Tempore primi Templi. Porrò prophetavit Zacharias tempore Templi secundi, & de Messia tanquam adhuc futuro dixit, Exulta filia Sion, &c. Galatinus lib. 4. cap. 2. hæc citat ex Rabbi Osaia in libro Bereschith Rabba ad Genes. 49. v. 14. Hoc autem, quod scriptum est Es. 32. v. 20. Mittentes pedem bovis & asini. Mittentes, ipse est Elias, de quo scriptum est Mal. 3. v. 1. Ecce ego mitto Angelum meum. Pedem bovis, hic est Messias filius Josephi, sicut
units.tr: Rabbi Eliezer, chapter 31, where he speaks of Abraham's ass, says: This ass too will be ... the son of David. Hence it is said in Zechariah 9:9: Out of ... etc. The Talmudists in Sanhedrin, chapter 11, folio 98, ... the son of Levi objected: it is written of the Messiah in Daniel ... And behold, with the clouds of heaven, as a son of man, he comes ... verse 9: of the same it is written, Poor and riding ... He answered: if the Israelites are worthy, he will come with the clouds ... if they are not worthy, he will come poor and seated on an ass. From this there is also a jest of Sapor, king of the Persians, in the same place. King Sapor said to Rabbi Samuel: you say the Messiah will come on an ass; I will send him a dappled horse that I have. Rabbi Samuel answers in half-Persian words: Have you an ass of a thousand colours? The rabbi's meaning is that the ass on which the Messiah is to sit will not be an ordinary ass, but an animal of such marvellous mixture of many colours that it far surpasses any horse in form and price. Indeed, he could not evade the king's jest in any other way than by this contrivance. But he ought to have answered what is the truth: that Christ's kingdom is not of this world, but peaceful and humble. On the following page of the same, Rabbi Joseph says: Would that the Messiah might come, and that I might be worthy to sit in the shade of the dung of his ass. In the same place, folio 99 A: Rabbi Hillel says: there will be no Messiah for Israel, because they have already used him up in the days of Hezekiah. Rabbi Joseph replies: Forgive Rabbi Hillel, O Lord of him. When was Hezekiah? In the time of the first Temple. Moreover, Zechariah prophesied in the time of the second Temple, and spoke of the Messiah as still future: Rejoice, daughter of Zion, etc. Galatinus, book 4, chapter 2, cites these words from Rabbi Osaiah in the book Bereshith Rabba on Genesis 49:14: But that which is written in Isaiah 32:20, Sending forth the foot of the ox and the ass: "sending forth" is Elijah, of whom it is written in Malachi 3:1, Behold, I send my messenger. "The foot of the ox" is the Messiah son of Joseph, as

units.la: … sicut de Iosepho dictum est Deut. 33. v. 17. Primogeniti bovis decor est illi. Et asini, hic est Messias filius David, de quo scriptum est Zach. 9. v. 9. Pauper & asino insidens. Midras Kobeleth in hæc Eccles. 1. v. 9. Quid est quod fuit? Ipsum quod suturum est. Rabbi Barachias dixit in nomine Rabbi Isaac. Qualis fuit primus Redemtor (Moses) talis erit Redemtor ultimus (Messias.) Qualis fuit Redemtor primus? Qualis dicitur Exod. 4. v. 20. Tulit Moyses uxorem suam & filios suos & impositit eos super asinum. Ita erit Redemtor ultimus, de quo dicitur Zach. 9. v. 9. Pauper & ascendens super asinum. Hæc Hebraeorum scriptores vetustissimi, a quibus non differtiunt plerique recentiorum. Rabbi Saadias Gaon in Daniel 7. v. 13. An non de Messia scriptum est Zach. 9. v. 9. Pauper & ascendens super asinum? an non cum humilitate veniet, non cum equitatu & fastu? Rabbi Salomon in Zach. 9. v. 9. ait: Locus iste non potest exponi de ullo alio, quam de Messia; quia de eo dicitur, Et dominabitur a mari ad mare. Neque ullum reperimus Templi secundi tempore, qui ut ille in justitia regnaverit. Kimchius hæc eadem verba exponens ad Messiam ita refert. Justus erit & per justitiam suam servabitur a gladio Gog & Magog. item; 1JY, pauper hic idem est, quod 1JY, mitis, manuetus: atque ita explicat Ionathan. Quale est quod de eo dicitur Isa. 42. v. 2. Non clamabit, nec audietur vox ejus foris, calamum quassatum non conteret. Asino insidebit, non pra inopia, quia totus orbis erit sub illius ditione, sed prae humilitate, atque etiam ut doceat Israelii non opus fore equis & curribus. Proinde addit: Disperdam quadrigam ex Ephraim & equum de Ierusalem. Rabbinos Salomonem & Kimchium secutus Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel ait: Quia populi solent Regis ad exemplum se componere, cum videbit totus Israel Regem Messiam esse humilem & asino insidentem, nullus erit in Ephraim (quo nomine significatur regnum Israelis decem tribuum) neque Ierosolymis in regno Judæ, qui velit currui aut equo insidere. Unde est quod dicit: Et disperdam quadrigam ex Ephraim, &c.
units.tr: ...as it was said of Joseph, Deut. 33:17, "The firstling of his bullock, majesty is his." And the ass: this is the Messiah the son of David, of whom it is written, Zech. 9:9, "Lowly, and riding upon an ass." Midrash Kohelet on Eccles. 1:9, "What is that which hath been?
