It is that which shall be," says Rabbi Berechiah in the name of Rabbi Isaac: "As the first Redeemer (Moses) was, so shall the last Redeemer (the Messiah) be." How was the first Redeemer? As it is said, Exod. 4:20, "Moses took his wife and his sons and set them upon an ass." So shall the last Redeemer be, of whom it is said, Zech. 9:9, "Lowly, and riding upon an ass." These are the most ancient Hebrew writers, from whom most of the more recent ones do not differ. Rabbi Saadia Gaon on Daniel 7:13: "Is it not written of the Messiah, Zech. 9:9, 'Lowly, and riding upon an ass'? Will he not come in humility, not with cavalry and pomp?" Rabbi Solomon on Zech. 9:9 says: "This place cannot be explained of anyone other than the Messiah, because of what is said of him, 'And he shall have dominion from sea to sea.' Nor do we find anyone in the time of the second Temple who reigned in righteousness as he did." Kimchi, expounding these same words of the Messiah, reports: "He will be just, and through his righteousness he will be preserved from the sword of Gog and Magog." Again: the word for "lowly" (עני) is the same as "meek" and "gentle," and so Jonathan explains it. What is the meaning of what is said of him, Isa. 42:2, "He shall not cry, nor lift up, nor cause his voice to be heard in the street; a bruised reed shall he not break"? He will ride on an ass, not from poverty, since the whole world will be under his rule, but from humility, and also to teach Israel that horses and chariots will not be needed. Accordingly he adds: "I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem." Following Rabbi Solomon and Kimchi, Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel says: "Since peoples are wont to model themselves on the example of their king, when all Israel sees the Messiah the King to be humble and riding upon an ass, no one in Ephraim (by which name the kingdom of the ten tribes of Israel is signified) nor in Jerusalem, in the kingdom of Judah, will wish to ride in a chariot or upon a horse. Hence it is that he says, 'And I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim,' etc."

units.la: Huic consensui tam universo opponere se ausi sunt Rabbini duo celeberrimi, sed mala mente, malo animo, neque alia de causa, quam ut Christi manifestationis hoc argumentum nobis eriperent. Hi sunt Rabbi Moses Sacerdos & Rabbi Abraham Aben-Ezra, quorum primus in Nehemia, alter in Iuda Machabæo impletum esse contendit Zachariæ oraculum de Rege, qui pauper, atque humilis Ierosolymam erat ingressurus. At manifesti utrumque erroris, convincit clarissimus Bochartus, ut & recentiorem quendam inter Christianos (cujus nomini parcit) qui contra traditionem in Ecclesia clesia & Synagoga receptam, Zachariæ locum vult ad literam intelligi de Zorobabele. Rabbinos mox laudatos primò refellit Bochartus hunc in modum. Quidquid Rabbini illi asserant, Nehemiam & Judam Machabæum aut in Judæa regnasse, aut pauperes fuisse, aut asino insedisse, nunquam probabunt, nec in summa pace vixisse, nec imperasse à mari ad mare & usque ad extrema terrarum, quæ sunt criteria Regis illius, de quo agitur in Zacharia. Nehemias quidem dicitur Rex in Juda Nehem. 6. v. 7. Quod arripit Rabbi Moses Sacerdos, ut Regem fuisse probet, sed per summam imperitiam; neque enim verè Rex dicitur, sed Sanaballat scribit Nehemiam à Gosfem Arabe affectati regni accusatum. Sed hoc crimen Nehemias à se amolitur his verbis: Non est factum secundum verba hæc, quæ tu loqueris: de corde enim tuo tu componis hæc. Et c. 5. v. 14. ipse Nehemias diserte asserit sibi ab Artaxerexe Rege præceptum, ut esset dux eorum in terra Juda. Idem esto judicium de Juda Machabæo, & de fratribus ejus, qui ipsi successerunt, Jonathane, & Simone, & de Hyrcano Simonis filio, qui, ut ut Reges appellentur in Chronico Templi secundi, tamen nil quidquam fuere, quam Judæorum Pontifices & Ethnarchæ; unde sub illis res gerebantur ex communi totius populi consilio. Hinc 1 Mach. 4. v. 59. Et statuit Judas, & fratres ejus, & universa ecclesia Israël. Et ibid. 12. v. 6. Jonathas summus Sacerdos, & seniores gentis, & Sacerdotes, & reliquus populus Judæorum, Spartiatis fratribus salutem. Sed Hyrcani Filius Aristobulus principatu in regnum verso, diadema sibi primus imposuit, ut asserit Josephus 1 de bello Jud. c. 3. & 13 Antiq. c. 19. & ex Josepho Pseudo-Hegesippus lib. 1. c. 2.
units.tr: Two very famous rabbis have dared to oppose this whole consensus, and they did so with a wicked mind and a wicked purpose, and for no other reason than to snatch this proof of Christ's manifestation from us. They are Rabbi Moses the Priest and Rabbi Abraham Ibn Ezra. The first contends that the oracle of Zechariah about the King who was to enter Jerusalem poor and humble was fulfilled in Nehemiah, the second in Judas Maccabeus. But the most illustrious Bochart refutes both errors, as he also does a certain more recent writer among Christians (whose name I spare), who, against the tradition received in the Church and the Synagogue, wants the passage of Zechariah to be understood literally of Zerubbabel. Bochart first refutes the rabbis just praised in this way. Whatever those rabbis assert, they will never prove that Nehemiah or Judas Maccabeus either reigned in Judea, or was poor, or rode upon an ass, or lived in complete peace, or ruled from sea to sea and to the ends of the earth, which are the marks of that King of whom Zechariah speaks. Nehemiah is indeed called king in Judah, Neh. 6:7, and Rabbi Moses the Priest seizes on this to prove that he was king, but through great ignorance; for he is not truly called king, but Sanballat writes that Nehemiah was accused by Gashmu the Arab of aspiring to a kingdom. But Nehemiah himself rejects this charge in these words: It has not been done according to these words which you speak; for you invent these things out of your own heart. And in chapter 5:14 Nehemiah himself expressly declares that he had been commanded by King Artaxerxes that he should be their governor in the land of Judah. The same judgment holds for Judas Maccabeus, and for his brothers who succeeded him, Jonathan and Simon, and for Hyrcanus, the son of Simon, who, although they are called kings in the Chronicle of the second Temple, were nothing more than high priests and ethnarchs of the Jews; hence under them affairs were carried on by the common counsel of the whole people. Hence 1 Macc. 4:59: And Judas and his brothers and the whole church of Israel decreed. And ibid. 12:6: Jonathan the high priest, and the elders of the nation, and the priests, and the rest of the people of the Jews, to the brethren the Spartans, greeting. But Hyrcanus's son Aristobulus, when the principate had been turned into a kingdom, first placed a diadem upon himself, as Josephus asserts, Jewish War 1, ch. 3, and Antiquities 13, ch. 19; and from Josephus, Pseudo-Hegesippus, book 1, ch. 2.

units.la: Jam, sive Nehemiæ, sive Judæ asinus, quo Jerosolymam venerint, nusquam comparet. De Nehemia quidem dicitur Nehem. 2. v. 12, & 14. quòd jumento fuerit vectus, sed cujusnam speciei fuerit illud jumentum, fueritne equus, mulúsve, an camelus, an asinus non loquitur Scriptura. Pincerna Regis potentissimi erat Nehemias, & ipsi Susis discedenti Rex copiarum præfectos atque aliquot equites pro comitatu attribuit, ut dicitur Nehem. 2. v. 9. Dum Jerosolymorum mœnia instaurabantur, quotidie Nehemiæ mensæ assidebant Judæorum Magnates centum & quinquaginta, quibus illius impensis cædebantur in dies bos unus, arietes sex electi, exceptis volatilibus, & inter dies decem vina diversa & alia multa tribuebantur, ut dicitur Nehem. 5. v. 17, & 18. Idem in sacrum thesaurum contulit mille auri drachmas, phialas quinquaginta, tunicas Sacerdotales quingentas triginta, ut dicitur Nehem. 7. v. 70. Hic ille est quem Rabbi Moses Sacerdos habuisse negat unde equum aleret, dum in Israelis plebe septingenti & amplius erant equites, & alii, vel mulis, vel camelis instructi fere totidem, ut dicitur Nehem. 7. v. 68, & 69. Recte igitur Rabbi Mosem Sacerdotem refellens Aben-Ezra, Dux, inquit, erat Nehemias, nec petebat annonas Ducatus sui & quotidie multi ad mensam ejus admittebantur; ut dicitur Nehem. 5. v. 17, & 18. quomodo igitur caruisset equo? At, quae fuit Aben-Ezrae caecitas, non vidit idem de Juda Machabaeo posse objici. Judas Machabaeus Sacerdos fuit e stirpe Jojarib; ut dicitur 1 Mach. 2. v. 1. unde Sacerdotum primus fuit ordo 1 Paralip. 24. v. 7. itaque Judae patrem Mathathiam quidam a Rege missi sic allocuntur 1 Mach. 2. v. 17. Princeps & clarissimus & magnus es in hac civitate. Et Mathathiae successor Judas Machabaeus ipsius filius hostes plurimos fuderat, antequam veniret Jerosolymam, Apollonium puta Samariae & Seronem Coelesyriae Praefectos; Ptolemaeum, Gorgiam, & Nicanorem Duces a Lysia submissos: ipsum denique Lysiam, cui omnes imperii provincias, ab Ægypto usque in Euphratem commiserat Antiochus. In his Apollonii & Samaritanorum castra spoliaverat, ut dicitur 1 Mach. 3. v. 12. & e Ptolemaei, Nicanoris & Gorgiae castris diripuerat aurum multum & argentum & hyacinthum & purpuram marinam, & opes magnas; ut dicitur 1 Mach. 4. v. 23. Eo scilicet multi convenerant mercatores bene nummati, captivos e Judaeis polt victoriam, quae certa putabatur exercitui Lysiae, comparaturi, ut dicitur 1 Mach. 3. v. 41. & 2 Mach. 8. v. 10. His demum spoliis ditatus Judas Machebaeus Jerosolymam recuperavit, Dei cultum instauravit, Templum ab Antiocho profanatum repurgavit, & nova vasa in illud intulit, nempe, ut dicit Josephus lib. 12 Antiq. cap. 12. candelabrum, mensam, altare, ex auro conflata. Frontem etiam Templi ornavit coronis aureis & scutulis, ut dicitur 1 Mach. 4. v. 57. Restaurati Templi festum cum populo celebravit per octiduum, toto illo tempore, ut refert Josephus loco mox laudato, [Greek], nullum voluptatis genus omittens, sed sumtuosis & splendidis sacrificiis, tanquam epulis eos excipiens. Haec ab eo facta, quem inopia redegerit ab equis ad asinos, quis nisi mente caecus credat? Proinde ut Rabbi Mosem Sacerdotem refellit Aben-Ezra; sic Aben-Ezram refellit Abarbanel his verbis: Miror pravam intentionem, quae intellectum ejus excaecavit: cum Judas Machabaeus Regis nomen non habuerint toto vitæ suæ tempore, multò minùs Regis à Sion denominati, quam cepit David. Porrò, si de Machabæis, seu de Hasamonæis prophetavit Zacharias, quid ipsi fuit cum Ephraimitis, cùm regnum Ephraim non exiterit secundi Templi tempore? præterea Judas Hasamonæus seu Machabæus non locutus est pacem omnibus Gentibus, neque à mari ad mare dominatus est, nec diebus ejus firmatus est arcus regni Ephraim. Quin regnum decem tribuum, quod vocatur regnum Ephraim, non restitutum est hactenus. Omnia denique verba hujus sectionis sententiam ejus arguunt summi erroris. Hæc Abarbanel, in quibus, ut Zachariæ prophetiam probet nondum impletam, falsò supponit Prophetam meminisse regni Ephraim restituendi, cùm non loquatur nisi de arcu Ephraim, q. d. fore ut cum Juda etiam Ephraim bello Græcos adoriatur; quod verè impletum est sub Machabæis, quibus ducibus, Græcorum jugum excusserunt Judæi omnes, in quibus & Ephraim erat; neque enim Israelitas decem tribuum per Ephraim designatos abduxit omnes Salmanasar. Itaque annis ferè centum post abductos Israelitas, Josias eorum reliquias ad reformationem compulit, & ex eo numero multi pecunias alacriter contulerunt ad Templi restaurationem, & Pascha Jerosolymis celebrarunt cum tribubus Juda & Benjamin 2 Paralip. 34, & 35. Et sub Esdra & Nehemia Judæi Babylone reduces obtulerunt in oblationem pro peccato, pro toto Israele duodecim hircos & juvencos totidem pro numero tribuum Israëlis, Esd. 6, & 8. Rursus Act. 26. v. 27. asserit Paulus duodecim Judæorum tribus Deo nocte & die perpetuò servire.
units.tr: Now, the ass of Nehemiah or of Judas, on which they came to Jerusalem, appears nowhere. Of Nehemiah it is said, Neh. 2:12 and 14, that he was carried on a beast, but Scripture does not say what kind of beast it was: whether a horse, a mule, a camel, or an ass. Nehemiah was cupbearer to the most powerful king, and when he left Susa the king assigned him military commanders and some horsemen as an escort, as is said in Neh. 2:9. While the walls of Jerusalem were being restored, there sat daily at Nehemiah's table a hundred and fifty of the leading men of the Jews, at whose expense one ox and six choice rams were provided each day, besides birds, and within ten days various wines and many other things were supplied, as is said in Neh. 5:17 and 18. He also contributed to the sacred treasury a thousand gold drachmas, fifty bowls, and five hundred and thirty priestly tunics, as is said in Neh. 7:70. This is the man whom Rabbi Moses the Priest says had not the means to feed a horse, when among the people of Israel there were seven hundred and more horsemen, and others, equipped with mules or camels, nearly as many, as is said in Neh. 7:68 and 69. Rightly, therefore, Ibn Ezra, refuting Rabbi Moses the Priest, says: "Nehemiah was governor, and he did not ask for the provisions of his office, and many were admitted daily to his table, as is said in Neh. 5:17 and 18. How then could he have lacked a horse?" But what blindness was Ibn Ezra's, that he did not see the same objection could be raised about Judas Maccabeus! Judas Maccabeus was a priest of the family of Joiarib, as is said in 1 Macc. 2:1, whence the first order of priests was in 1 Chron. 24:7; so certain men sent by the king addressed Judas's father Mattathias thus, 1 Macc. 2:17: You are a prince and a most distinguished and great man in this city. And Mattathias's successor, Judas Maccabeus, his son, had routed very many enemies before he came to Jerusalem: Apollonius, the governor of Samaria, and Seron, the governor of Coele-Syria; Ptolemy, Gorgias, and Nicanor, commanders sent by Lysias; and finally Lysias himself, to whom Antiochus had entrusted all the provinces of the empire from Egypt to the Euphrates. In these battles he had plundered the camps of Apollonius and the Samaritans, as is said in 1 Macc. 3:12, and from the camps of Ptolemy, Nicanor, and Gorgias he had seized much gold and silver, hyacinth and sea-purple, and great wealth, as is said in 1 Macc. 4:23. Many well-off merchants had gathered there, intending to buy Jewish captives after the victory, which was thought certain for the army of Lysias, as is said in 1 Macc. 3:41 and 2 Macc. 8:10. Finally, enriched by these spoils, Judas Maccabeus recovered Jerusalem, restored the worship of God, cleansed the Temple profaned by Antiochus, and brought into it new vessels, namely, as Josephus says in Antiquities 12, ch. 12, a candelabrum, a table, and an altar, all cast in gold. He also adorned the front of the Temple with golden crowns and small shields, as is said in 1 Macc. 4:57. He celebrated the feast of the restored Temple with the people for eight days, throughout that whole time, as Josephus reports in the passage just cited, omitting no kind of pleasure, but receiving them as at a banquet with lavish and splendid sacrifices. Who but a man blind in mind would believe that these things were done by one whom poverty had reduced from horses to asses? Accordingly, just as Ibn Ezra refutes Rabbi Moses the Priest, so Abarbanel refutes Ibn Ezra in these words: I marvel at the perverse intention which has blinded his understanding: since Judas Maccabeus did not bear the name of king during the whole of his life, much less was he called a king from Zion, as David was. Moreover, if Zechariah prophesied of the Maccabees or Hasmoneans, what had he to do with the Ephraimites, since the kingdom of Ephraim did not exist in the time of the second Temple? Besides, Judas the Hasmonean or Maccabee did not speak peace to all the nations, nor did he rule from sea to sea, nor in his days was the bow of the kingdom of Ephraim established. Indeed the kingdom of the ten tribes, which is called the kingdom of Ephraim, has not been restored to this day. In short, all the words of this section prove that his opinion is a very great error. Thus Abarbanel; but in attempting to prove that Zechariah's prophecy is not yet fulfilled, he wrongly supposes that the prophet was speaking of restoring the kingdom of Ephraim, whereas he speaks only of the bow of Ephraim, that is, that together with Judah, Ephraim too would make war on the Greeks. This was truly fulfilled under the Maccabees, under whose leadership all the Jews, Ephraim among them, shook off the yoke of the Greeks; for Shalmaneser did not carry off all the Israelites designated by Ephraim, the ten tribes. So about a hundred years after the Israelites were carried away, Josiah compelled their remnants to reform, and from that number many eagerly contributed money for the restoration of the Temple, and celebrated the Passover at Jerusalem with the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, 2 Chron. 34 and 35. And under Ezra and Nehemiah the Jews returning from Babylon offered, as a sin offering for all Israel, twelve he-goats and as many bullocks, according to the number of the tribes of Israel, Ezra 6 and 8. Again, Paul, Acts 26:7, asserts that the twelve tribes of the Jews serve God night and day without ceasing.

units.la: Non minùs absurdè Zachariæ prophetia dicitur impleta in Zorobabele, quàm in Nehemia aut Juda Machabæo. Zorobabel enim neque re neque nomine Rex fuit. In Scriptura vocatur Mal. 1. v. 8. פחה, ut & Aggæi 1, &c. id est, Dux, Præfectus. Nempe Babylone Zorobabel Regis-fuerat στρατηγοφύλαξ, & captivorum Judæorum Dux, ut habetur in Josepho lib. 11 Antiq. cap. 4. uno verbo Æchmalotarcha. Unde primò à Cyro, deinde à Dario Hystaspis filio in Judæam missus est, ut provinciam regeret, & Regio nomine & sumtibus Jerosolymitanum Templum restauraret. Proinde Esd. 3. v. 2. nominatur post Josue Sacerdotem, quem tamen alibi præcedit, quia Prorex & summus Sacerdos apud Judæos erant dignitate pares, aut suppares. Frustrà autem objicitur Zorobabelem appellari Regem Jerem. 23. v. 5. & Ezec. 37. v. 22, & 24. His enim in locis nullatenus de Zorobabele, sed de Christo, seu Messia sermo est, ut fatentur ipsi Rabbini summo consensu, quod videre est in Talmude in Tractatu inscripto Bava Bathra cap. 5. sol. 75. & alios tum recentiores, tum veteres Rabbinos, qui hodieque Judæorum manibus teruntur; adeo ut mirum sit Theodoretum dixisse locum Jeremiæ laudatum à Judæis fulguritis (id est, tam stupidis atque attonitis, quam qui fulmine ictí sunt) ad Zorobabelem trahi. Sed optime hanc sententiam refellit Theodoretus ex eo quòd Jeremias agat de Rege, quod non quadrat in Zorobabelem, qui nunquam fuit Rex, sed Dux populi. Deinde addit Jeremias Regis illius nomen fore יְהוָה צִדְקֵנוּ, Dominus justitia nostra, quod unanimi consensu Synagoga & Ecclesia agnoscit non quadrare nisi in Messiam in Lege & Prophetis promissum. Locum autem ex Ezechiele objectum, non nisi ad Messiam pertinere abunde docet sola lectio. Ibi enim promittitur fore ut Rex unus & Pastor, David nomine, Israelitis omnibus in æternum imperet, cum Zorobabel solum Judæis illis præfuerit, qui è Babylone reduces erant, id est, hominum quatuor vel quinque myriadibus, idque in paucos annos. Proinde hic etiam de Messia rem esse agnoscunt Hebræi commentatores; imo maxime timent ne Zorobabel pro Rege habeatur: nempe ne promissiones factæ à Prophetis de restituendo regno Davidis posteris videantur in illo completæ, ita ut Rex alius jam non sit expectandus. Vide hanc in rem Chronicon Templi secundi fere statim initio.
units.tr: Zechariah's prophecy is no less absurdly said to have been fulfilled in Zerubbabel than in Nehemiah or Judas Maccabeus. For Zerubbabel was a king neither in fact nor in name. In Scripture he is called (Mal. 1:8) [פחה], as also in Haggai 1, that is, Leader, Governor. Indeed at Babylon Zerubbabel had been the king's strategophylax [στρατηγοφύλαξ] and leader of the Jewish captives, as Josephus reports in Antiquities book 11, chapter 4, in a single word, Aechmalotarch. Hence he was sent into Judea first by Cyrus and then by Darius, son of Hystaspes, to govern the province and, with the royal title and at royal expense, to restore the temple at Jerusalem. Accordingly, in Ezra 3:2 he is named after Joshua the priest, though elsewhere he is put before him, because among the Jews the viceroy and the high priest were equal or nearly equal in rank. It is futile to object that Zerubbabel is called king in Jeremiah 23:5 and Ezekiel 37:22 and 24. In these places the discourse is in no way about Zerubbabel but about Christ, or the Messiah, as the Rabbis themselves unanimously admit. This can be seen in the Talmud, in the tractate entitled Bava Bathra, chapter 5, folio 75, and in other Rabbis, both more recent and older, who are still handled today in the hands of the Jews. So it is astonishing that Theodoret said that the passage of Jeremiah cited by the Jews, who were thunderstruck (that is, as stupefied and dazed as men struck by lightning), is drawn to Zerubbabel. But Theodoret refutes this opinion very well on the ground that Jeremiah is speaking of a king, which does not fit Zerubbabel, who was never king but leader of the people. Further, Jeremiah adds that the name of that king will be Dominus justitia nostra [יְהוָה צִדְקֵנוּ], "the Lord our righteousness," which the Synagogue and the Church alike with one voice acknowledge fits none but the Messiah promised in the Law and the Prophets. As for the passage from Ezekiel that is objected, the reading alone sufficiently shows that it pertains only to the Messiah. For there it is promised that there will be one king and shepherd, named David, who will rule over all Israelites for ever; whereas Zerubbabel governed only those Jews who had returned from Babylon, that is, some four or five myriads of people, and that for a few years. Accordingly the Hebrew commentators also acknowledge that this matter concerns the Messiah here too; indeed they greatly fear that Zerubbabel might be taken for the king, namely that the promises made by the Prophets of restoring the kingdom to the posterity of David might seem fulfilled in him, so that no other king would any longer be expected. On this matter see the Chronicle of the Second Temple, almost at the very beginning.

units.la: Præterea dato, non concesso, Zorobabelem pro Rege suisse habitum, de illo non dixerit Zacharias, Exulta satis filia Sion, jubila filia Jerusalem, ecce Rex tuus veniet; nisi velimus Prophetam ut futuram prædixisse rem præteritam. Jam enim venerat Zorobabel, quo tempore scripsit Zacharias, qui anno Darii quarto hæc se scripsisse profitetur c. 7. v. 1. At Zorobabel, ut dicitur Esd. 1, & 2. Jerosolymam venerat anno primo Cyri Majoris, id est, eo anno, quo Cyrus, capta Babylone, imperii potestatem ad se transtulit; quod factum fuerat ante annos viginti quinque, ut patet ex Josepho 11 Antiq. 4. & Esd. 4. v. 24. & cùm Babylonem rediisset anno primo Darii, ut novo Regi gratularetur, statim in Judæam remissus est, ut Templi instaurationem sub Cyro coeptam, & sub Cambyse, qui Persis Artaxerxes, interruptam, de novo aggrederetur. Gratis autem dicitur Zachariam futuro uti pro præterito, maximè cùm omnia addita magis in Christum quadrent, quàm in Zorobabelem; dicit enim Propheta: Ecce Rex tuus venit tibi: id est, bono & commodo tuo, non suo. Christus Dominus non sibi venit, sed nobis. Hinc Esa. 9. v. 5. Parvulus natus est nobis, filius datus datus est nobis. Et Angelus Pastoribus Luc. 2. v. 11. Natus est vobis hodie Salvator, qui est Christus Dominus. Non ita Zorobabel, qui etiam sibi venerat; tam enim illius intererat, quàm reliquorum è populo, ut Templum instauraretur. Jam quòd Rex idem dicitur justus & Salvator, proprie Christo convenit, cùm de justitia Zorobabelis Scriptura nihil quidquam referat memorabile; Christum verò appellet Jer. 23. v. 6. Dominus justus noster, & secundum veritatem Hebraicam, Dominus justitia nostra, & Angelus testetur Mat. 1. v. 21. Christum vocatum esse Jesum, quod salvaturus esset populum suum à peccatis eorum. Praeterea potiori jure Christus dicitur Pauper, quàm Zorobabel, qui primò Cyri, deinde Darii opibus subnixus, Templum Jerosolymitanum extruxit magnis sumtibus. At Christus tam fuit pauper, ut è mulierculārum eleemosynis aegrè se sustentaverit, Luc. 8. v. 3. neque locum habuerit, Mat. 8. v. 20. ubi reclinaret caput. Et virtutes Christo tam propriae fuerunt mansuetudo & humilitas, ut eas à se, id est, exemplo suo, potissimùm nos velit Mat. 11. v. 24. edoceri, ad hunc ipsum, ut videtur, Zachariae locum alludens. Quid in Zorobabele simile occurrat non video.
units.tr: Moreover, granting for argument's sake that Zerubbabel was regarded as king, Zechariah would not have spoken of him in these words: Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; shout, daughter of Jerusalem; behold, your King will come, unless we want the prophet to have foretold a past event as future. For Zerubbabel had already come by the time Zechariah wrote, who professes in chapter 7:1 that he wrote these things in the fourth year of Darius. But Zerubbabel, as Ezra 1 and 2 say, had come to Jerusalem in the first year of Cyrus the Great, that is, in the year in which Cyrus, after taking Babylon, transferred the power of the empire to himself. This had happened twenty-five years earlier, as is clear from Josephus, Antiquities 11.4, and Ezra 4:24. And when he had returned to Babylon in the first year of Darius to congratulate the new king, he was at once sent back into Judea to take up again the restoration of the temple, which had been begun under Cyrus and interrupted under Cambyses, who is called Artaxerxes by the Persians. It is therefore gratuitous to say that Zechariah uses the future for the past, especially since all the additional details fit Christ better than Zerubbabel. For the prophet says: Behold, your King comes to you, that is, for your good and advantage, not his own. Christ the Lord did not come for himself but for us. Hence Isaiah 9:5: A child is born to us, a son is given to us. And the angel to the shepherds, Luke 2:11: To you is born today a Saviour, who is Christ the Lord. It is not so with Zerubbabel, who also came for himself; for it was as much in his interest as in that of the rest of the people that the temple be restored. Now, that the same king is called just and a Saviour properly suits Christ, since Scripture records nothing memorable about the righteousness of Zerubbabel, whereas it calls Christ Dominus justus noster in Jeremiah 23:6, and according to the Hebrew truth, Dominus justitia nostra, and the angel bears witness in Matthew 1:21 that Christ was called Jesus because he would save his people from their sins. Furthermore, Christ can be called poor with better right than Zerubbabel, who, supported first by the wealth of Cyrus and then of Darius, built the temple at Jerusalem at great expense. But Christ was so poor that he scarcely sustained himself on the alms of women, Luke 8:3, and he had no place, Matthew 8:20, where he might lay his head. And meekness and humility were so peculiarly Christ's virtues that he especially wishes us to learn them from himself, that is, from his example, Matthew 11:29, apparently alluding to this very passage of Zechariah. What similarity to Zerubbabel may occur here I do not see.

units.la: Denique quomodo de Zorobabele potest intelligi, quod Zacharias dicit Regem illum, de quo loquitur, asino vectum venturum Jerosolymam? Quandonam id fecit Zorobabel? Nec dicas his Zachariae verbis significari Zorobabelis modestiam & pacis studium; Sic enim & Salomon cum toto equitatu suo potuerit dici asino fuisse vectum, quia Rex nullus fuit pacis studiosior. Quomodo potuerit intelligi de Zorobabele, quod Zacharias, ut significet pacem spiritualem futuram in Ecclesia sub regno Christi, phrasi Prophetis familiari ait: Et disperdam quadrigam ex Ephraim, &c. Quomodo de Zorobabele potest intelligi, quod de eodem Rege in eumdem sensum dicit Zacharias, Loquetur pacem gentibus, &c. Neque haec Zachariae verba ad Jerusalem referri possunt, quasi illa civitas dicatur loqui pacem Gentibus eodem sensu, quo Mardochaeus dicitur in libro Esther c. 10. secundum veritatem Hebraicam, loquens pacem omni semini suo; quia civitas Jerusalem sub Machabaeis contraxit foedus cum Lacedaemoniis & Romanis. Nam verbum, loquetur, Hebraicè est masculini generis, & proinde necessariò ad Regem refertur, de quo egerat Propheta, non verò ad Jerusalem, cujus nomen Hebraeis est foemininum; similiter & pronomen, ejus, in sequenti phrasi, & potestas ejus à mari usque ad mare, & à fluminibus usque ad fines terrae, est affixum masculinum in textu Hebraeo. 7. Imposuerunt super eos vestimenta sua, & eum desuper sederũ fecerunt. Sunt qui hic agnoscant numeri Enallagen Scripturis perquàm familiarem, quâ pluribus indefinitè tribuitur, quod illorum uni convenit: ut Gen. 8. v. 4. dicitur arca Noë requievisse super montes Armeniæ, Hebraicè, Ararat, id est, super unum montium Armeniæ, seu Ararat. Gen. 23. v. 6. In electiu sepulchris nostris sepeli mortuum tuum, id est, in uno sepulchrorum nostrorum, quodcunque eligere yisum suerit, sepeli mortuum tuum. Matth. 26. v. 8. Videntes discipuli indignati sunt, id est, discipulorum unus, Judas scilicet Iscariotes. Et. 27. v. 44. Id ipsum ei exprobabant latrones, id est, latronum unus, ut patet ex aliis Evangelistis. Theophylactus tamen nullam hic agnoscens Enallagen ait: Sedit autem super illis, non super duobus jumentis, sed super palliis: aut primùm quidem asinæ, deinde etiam pullo insedit. Syrus interpres ait discipulos adduxisse ad Jesum asinam & pullum, & posuisse super pullum vestes suas, & super eum equitasse Jesum.
units.tr: Finally, how can it be understood of Zerubbabel what Zechariah says, that the king of whom he speaks will come to Jerusalem riding on an ass? When did Zerubbabel do this? Nor can you say that by these words of Zechariah the meekness and peaceableness of Zerubbabel is signified; for in that case Solomon, with all his cavalry, could be said to have ridden on an ass, since no king was more devoted to peace. How can it be understood of Zerubbabel what Zechariah, to signify the spiritual peace to come in the Church under the reign of Christ, says in a phrase familiar to the Prophets: And I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim, etc.? How can it be understood of Zerubbabel what Zechariah says of the same king in the same sense: He shall speak peace to the nations, etc.? Nor can these words of Zechariah be referred to Jerusalem, as if that city were said to speak peace to the Gentiles in the same sense in which Mordecai is said, in the book of Esther chapter 10, according to the Hebrew truth, to be speaking peace to all his seed; for Jerusalem under the Maccabees made a covenant with the Spartans and the Romans. For the verb he shall speak is in Hebrew of the masculine gender and therefore must necessarily refer to the king, of whom the prophet had been speaking, and not to Jerusalem, whose name is feminine for the Hebrews. Likewise the pronoun his in the following phrase, and his dominion from sea to sea, and from the rivers to the ends of the earth, is a masculine suffix in the Hebrew text. 7. They placed their garments upon them, and made him sit upon them. There are those who here recognize an enallage of number, a figure very familiar in Scripture, by which what belongs to one is attributed indefinitely to several: thus Genesis 8:4 says that Noah's ark rested upon the mountains of Armenia, in Hebrew Ararat, that is, upon one of the mountains of Armenia, or Ararat. Genesis 23:6: Bury your dead in the choicest of our sepulchres, that is, in one of our sepulchres, whichever you think fit, bury your dead. Matthew 26:8: Seeing this, the disciples were indignant, that is, one of the disciples, Judas Iscariot, namely. And 27:44: The robbers reproached him with the same thing, that is, one of the robbers, as is clear from the other evangelists. Theophylact, however, recognizing no enallage here, says: He sat upon them, not on two animals, but on the garments; or first indeed he sat on the she-ass, and then also on the colt. The Syriac interpreter says that the disciples brought to Jesus the ass and the colt, and placed their garments upon the colt, and that Jesus rode upon it.

units.la: 8. Cædebant ramos. Sic in Apophtegmatis PP. legitur quòd Macario ex Paneremo, quem solus inhabitabat, ad inferiorem eremum pergenti Fratres sumentes ramos palmarum obviam processerunt. Sic honoris causâ obviam B. Fulgentio Rufpensi Episcopo testatur ipsius vitæ autor cap. 29. his verbis; Per omnes prolixi itineris vias gaudia majora reperiens, in occursum suum populis tendentibus, cum lucernis & lampadibus, & arborum frondibus. Idem factum Eboni Rhemorum Antistiti ad tertium tumum conciliorum Galliæ observat Sirmondus ex narratione clericorum Rhemensium, verba sunt: Receptus est ab Episcopis suffraganeis suis, Rothaldo Episcopo, Simeone Episcopo, Lupo Episcopo, unà cum legatis omnium aliorum Episcoporum Remensis Diœceseos, qui variis detenti infirmitatibus illuc corporali præsentiâ occurrere non valentes, suam tamen per Ecclesiasticos legatos & excusatorias literas illi exhibuerunt præsentiam. Insuper etiam à Canonicis & Monachis, atque corregionalibus Presbyteris totius Diœcesis, atque infinitâ multitudine utriusque sexûs. Qui omnes cum ramis palmarum & cereis ardentibus, laudésque Deo intimis cordibus & excelsissimis vocibus proclamantes, longe ei ab Ecclesia obviaverunt, & usque ad Ecclesiam indesinenter psallentes deduxerunt. Vide commentarium nostrum in Marc. 11. v. 8.
units.tr: Cut branches. So in the Apophthegmata of the Fathers it is read that when Macarius, going from Paneremus, where he lived alone, to the lower desert, the brethren, taking palm branches, went out to meet him. So too, in honour, the author of his life attests that blessed Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, was met, in chapter 29, in these words: Along all the ways of his long journey he found greater joys, as the peoples hurried to meet him with lanterns and torches and leafy branches. Sirmond notes the same thing for Ebo, archbishop of Reims, at the third council of Gaul (tomus), from the account of the Reims clergy. The words are: He was received by his suffragan bishops, Rothald, Simeon and Lupus, together with the legates of all the other bishops of the diocese of Reims, who, held back by various infirmities, could not come in person but nonetheless showed their presence through ecclesiastical legates and letters of excuse. Moreover, the canons, monks and rural priests of the whole diocese came, with an infinite crowd of both sexes. All of them, with palm branches and burning candles, proclaiming praises to God with inmost hearts and loudest voices, met him far from the church and led him to the church, singing without ceasing. See our commentary on Mark 11:8.

units.la: 9. Turbæ autem, &c. Verisimile est Joannem c. 12. v. 13. per anticipationem eas ipsas acclamationes narrare, quas Matthæus hic & Luc. 19. v. 37. Fieri tamen potest ut diversæ sint, quod colligi posse videtur, ex eo quòd Joannes dicit turbas, audito quòd Jesus Jerosolymam veniret, & antequam pullo insideret, obviàm ei processisse & acclamasse. Similiter videtur de aliis turbis loqui Lucas loco citato, quàm ceteri tres Evangelistae; videtur enim Lucas loqui de iis, qui miraculis excitati è Galilaea Christum sequebantur.
units.tr: Verse 9, and the crowds, etc. It is likely that John, in chapter 12:13, narrates by anticipation the very acclamations that Matthew relates here and Luke in 19:37. It may be, however, that they were different, which seems to be gathered from the fact that John says the crowds, having heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem, went out to meet him and acclaimed him before he sat on the colt. Luke, in the passage cited, seems similarly to speak of different crowds from the other three Evangelists; for Luke seems to speak of those who, roused by the miracles, followed Christ from Galilee.

units.la: Hosanna Filio David. Author est Elias Levita in opere (quod inscripsit הושענא) Hosanna compendio sermonis dici solitum in acclamationibus pro הושיעה נא, salva obsecro. Ad perficiendum igitur sensum, subintelligenda sunt, quae hic, ut in omnium fere linguarum acclamationibus & statuarum inscriptionibus relinquuntur audientibus & legentibus supplenda; adeo ut haec locutio Hosanna Filio David sic accipienda sit, q. d. Salva quaeso, ô Deus, Filium David; nam verbum Hebraicum unde derivatur Hosanna, saepe construitur cum tertio casu, ut videre est Psal. 85. Heb. 86. v. 16. Potest etiam dictio Hosanna aliter accipi, quoniam (ut verissimè observavit doctissimus vir Angelus Caninius) in scriptis Rabbinorum fit nomen ex hac dictione ὡσαννὰ, cujus plurale extat in Ritualibus eorum, cùm dicunt Hoschannoth Lelucoth, id est, formulæ Hymnorum usitatæ in celebrando festo tabernaculorum, cujus singuli septem dies habent sibi proprias, quæ dicuntur הושענא Hoschana, seu Hosanna primæ diei, Hosanna secundæ diei, Hosanna tertiæ diei, & sic deinceps. Sic autem & nominantur frondes arborum, puta palmæ, oleæ, aut salicis, quas tenere manibus per illos dies solent Judæi, dum subinde repetitur ab eis ea formula, Hoschiah Na, & similes quidem versus intercalares, in quibus id vocabulum inest. Possumus igitur in præsenti locutione Hosanna Filio David, eam vocem sic interpretari, ut idem sit ac βαΐα, quod nomen in hac historia Joannes usurpavit. Tum autem supplendo locutionem imperfectam, Hosanna Filio David interpretabimur, q. d. Haec βαΐα, sive hos termites palmæ, oleæve aut salicis, aliarumve arborum in honorem Filii David gestamus & vibramus. Erat moris apud veteres, ut quorundam festorum pompas deducentes, olivæ termites gestarent, qui propterea σκιοφόροι dicebantur, quorum etiam meminit Chrysostomus Serm. in Annam. Aliquando è pluribus arborum frondibus & fructibus concinnabatur quasi fasciculus levis quem gestabant, ut fuit illa, quæ dicebatur Atheniensibus Ἐιρεσιώνη, quomodo & Josephus lib. 3 Antiq. c. 10. vocat Judæorum fasciculum (quem hodieque Judæi in festo tabernaculorum gestare & quatere solent in honorem Dei, & Hoschana seu Hosanna vocant) ubi ejus conficiendi è myrtho, salice, spadice-palmæ, & perfea rationem exponit. Videtur autem B. Epiphanius Sermone in die Palmarum habito alludere ad concinnationem hujus fasciculi Judaici, sicut ad concussionem harum frondium; has enim frondes & veteres in ducenda pompa quatiebant in honorem ejus, cui pompa ducebatur, ut Judæi solent in honorem Dei; ad quem morem alludit etiam Chrysostomus Hom. in magnam Septimanam.
units.tr: Hosanna to the Son of David. Elias Levita, in the work he entitled Hosanna, is the authority for saying that Hosanna was customarily said in acclamations as a shortened form of [הושיעה נא], save, I beseech. To complete the sense, therefore, the words that are left out here must be supplied, as in almost all languages' acclamations and inscriptions, where the hearers and readers are left to supply them. Thus this phrase Hosanna to the Son of David is to be taken as if it said: Save, we beseech you, O God, the Son of David. For the Hebrew verb from which Hosanna derives is often construed with the dative case, as can be seen in Psalm 85 (Heb. 86:16). The word Hosanna may also be taken otherwise, since (as the most learned man Angelo Caninio truly observed) in the writings of the rabbis a noun is formed from this word [ὡσαννά], whose plural is found in their rituals when they say Hoschannoth Lelucoth, that is, the forms of hymns customary in celebrating the feast of tabernacles. Each of its seven days has its own, called Hoschana [הושענא], or Hosanna, of the first day, Hosanna of the second day, Hosanna of the third day, and so on. The fronds of trees, namely palm, olive or willow, which the Jews customarily hold in their hands during those days, are also called by this name, while that formula is repeatedly recited, along with similar intercalary verses containing that word. In the present phrase Hosanna to the Son of David we can therefore interpret the word so that it means the same as [βαΐα], the term John used in this history. Then, supplying the incomplete phrase, we shall interpret Hosanna to the Son of David as: "These [βαΐα], that is, these branches of palm, olive or willow, or of other trees, we carry and wave in honour of the Son of David." It was customary among the ancients, when leading the processions of certain festivals, to carry olive branches, which for this reason were called [σκιοφόροι]; Chrysostom also mentions them in his sermon on Anna. Sometimes a light bundle was made of several tree fronds and fruits, which they carried, such as the one the Athenians called [Εἰρεσιώνη]. Josephus too (Antiquities 3.10) calls the Jewish bundle a bundle, which Jews still carry and shake at the feast of tabernacles in honour of God, and call Hoschana or Hosanna; he there explains how it is made from myrtle, willow, the spadix of the date palm, and the persea. Epiphanius, in a sermon delivered on Palm Sunday, seems to allude to the making of this Jewish bundle, and also to the shaking of these fronds; for the ancients too shook these fronds when leading the procession in honour of the one to whom the procession was led, as the Jews customarily do in honour of God. Chrysostom, in his homily on the Great Week, also alludes to this custom.

units.la: Hosanna in altissimis. Marc. II. v. 10. in excelsis, supple, audiatur, ut sit quasi ardentis populi exhortatio ad exclamandum magnis vocibus, Hosanna Messiæ suo. Præsenti historiæ non absimile est quod in Antonini Augusti itinerario Jerosolymitano legitur; Venerunt mulieres in occursum nobis cum infantibus, palmas in manibus tenentes, & ampullas cum rosaceo oleo: & prostratæ pedibus nostris, plantas nostras ungebant, cantabantque lingua Ægyptiaca psallentes Antiphonam; Benedicti vos a Domino, benedictusque adventus vester, Osanna in excelsis. Porrò tam ardenti populi voto commota est Pharisæorum invidia adversus Christum, & quidam ex iis Christum interrogavere, cur non increparet acclamantes, quibus ipse ait, quod si hi tacuerint, lapides clamabunt, ut Lucas refert c. 19. v. 40. Ut verò Christus proximè ad mœnia Jerusalem accessit, videns civitatem flevit super illam, & 20 prædixit ejus eversionem, ut ibidem narratur à Luca.
units.tr: Hosanna in the highest. Mark 11:10. In the highest: supply let it be heard, so that it is as if the ardent people were urging one another to shout with loud voices, Hosanna to their Messiah. Not unlike the present history is what is read in the Jerusalem itinerary of the emperor Antoninus: Women came to meet us with infants, holding palm branches in their hands and flasks of rose oil; prostrate at our feet, they anointed our soles, and singing in the Egyptian tongue they chanted an antiphon: "Blessed are you by the Lord, and blessed is your coming, Hosanna in the highest." But the envy of the Pharisees against Christ was stirred by such an ardent vow of the people, and some of them asked Christ why he did not rebuke those who were acclaiming him. He answered them: If these were silent, the stones would cry out, as Luke reports in 19:40. But when Christ drew near to the walls of Jerusalem, seeing the city, he wept over it and foretold its overthrow, as Luke relates there.

units.la: 10. Universa civitas. Id est, cives Jerosolymitani.
units.tr: 10. The whole city. That is, the citizens of Jerusalem.

units.la: 11. Populi. Scilicet, simplices & candidi.
units.tr: 11. The people. Namely, the simple and sincere ones.

units.la: Hic est Jesus Propheta. Quem nimirum Moses similem sui dixerat esse venturum & qui proprie apud Græcos scribitur cum [illegible, ~12 letters] , id est, cum articuli testimonio. Hier.
units.tr: This is Jesus the Prophet. The one whom Moses had said would come as like himself, and who in Greek is written properly with [illegible], that is, with the testimony of the article. Jerome.

units.la: 12. Intravit. Scilicet, hac eadem die, ut patet ex v. 15. mox sequenti; unde Marcus, qui cap. 11. ad diem sequentem videtur referre hanc secundam vendentium & ementium è Templo ejectionem, usus est recapitulatione ejus, quod pridie acciderat, ut ait Aug. lib. 2. de Cons. Evang. cap. 68.
units.tr: 12. He entered. Namely, on this same day, as is clear from verse 15 just below. Hence Mark, who in chapter 11 seems to refer this second expulsion of the sellers and buyers from the Temple to the following day, used a recapitulation of what had happened the day before, as Augustine says (De consensu Evangelistarum 2.68).

units.la: Ejiciebat, &c. Ne victimæ deessent, in prima Templi parte, quæ Heb. [Hebrew: פרבר] dicitur 1 Paralip. 26. v. 18. venditabantur oves & boves & columbæ. Unde à Majemonide in Tractatu de vasis Sanctuarii cap. 7. num. 9. inter Templi præfectos, quos Hebræi vocabant [Hebrew: ממוני המקדש], Vulgat. Luc. 22. v. 52. magistratus Templi recensetur præfectus super nidos, id est, super aves, cum quo pacificuntur, ut ad oblationes aves comparet, has vel istas pro siclo. Et quisquis tenebatur vel turtures offerre, vel pullos columbarum, pretium ad Sanctuarium afferebat. Et ipse præfectus dabat aves iis, quorum erat offerre, & cum quæstoribus eas æstimabat, & postquam de pretio convenerat, eas intra triduum dabant..... Et siqua avis profana erat, aut profana fiebat (per pollutionem ceremonialem) antequam offerretur, aliam pro ea dabat. Hæc Rabbi Moses Majemonides, quæ ad quæstum à lucripetis & avaris Sacerdotibus fuisse excogitata, luculenter in præsentem Evangelii locum docet Hier. his verbis: Juxta mandata Legis, augustissimo in toto orbe Templo Domini, & de cunctis penè regionibus Judæorum illuc populo confluente, innumerabiles immolabantur hostiæ, maximè festis diebus, taurorum, arietum, hircorum; pauperibus, ne absque sacrificio essent, pullos columbarum & turtures offerentibus: accidebat plerumque, ut, qui de longè venerant, non haberent victimas. Excogitaverunt igitur Sacerdotes, quomodo prædam de populo facerent, & omnia animalia, quibus opus erat ad sacrificia, vendebant, ut & venderent non habentibus, & ipsi rursum emta suscuperent. Hanc stropham eorum crebra venientium inopia dissipabat, qui indigebant sumtibus, & non solùm hostias non habebant, sed ne unde emerent quidem aves & vilia munuscula. Posuerunt itaque & nummularios, qui mutuam sub cautione darent pecuniam. Sed quia erat Lege præceptum ut nemo usuras acciperet, & prodesse non poterat pecunia fœnerata, quæ commodi nihil haberet, & interdum sortem perderet: excogitaverunt & aliam technam, ut pro nummulariis collybistas facerent: cujus verbi proprietatem Latina lingua non exprimit. Collyba dicuntur apud eos, quæ nos appellamus tragemata, vel vilia munuscula, verbi gratiâ, frixi ciceris, uvarumque passarum, & poma diversi generis. Igitur quia usuras accipere non poterant collybistæ, qui pecuniam fœnerati erant, pro usuris accipiebant varias species, ut quod in nummo non licebat, in his rebus exigerent, quæ nummis commutantur: quasi non hoc ipsum Ezechiel prædicaverit, dicens: Usuram & superabundantiam non accipietis. Istius modi Dominus cernens in domo Patris negotiationem, seu latrocinium, ardore Spiritûs concitatus, juxta quod scriptum est in sexagesimo octavo Psalmo: Zelus domûs tuæ comedit me: fecit sibi flagellum de funiculis, & tantam hominum multitudinem ejecit de Templo, dicens: Scriptum est: Domus mea, domus orationis vocabitur: vos autem fecistis eam speluncam latronum. Latro enim est, & Templum Dei in latronum convertit specum, qui lucra de religione sectatur, cultúsque ejus non tam cultus Dei, quàm negotiationis occasio est. Jungit autem hic Christus, ut & alibi passim, duorum Prophetarum sententias, quasi unius & ejusdem est; prima enim sententia est Esa. 56. v. 7. secunda verò est Jerem. 7. v. 11.
units.tr: He drove out, etc. So that the victims would not be lacking, sheep, oxen and doves were sold in the outer part of the Temple, which is called in Hebrew [פרבר] (1 Chron. 26:18). Hence Maimonides, in his treatise on the vessels of the sanctuary, chapter 7, paragraph 9, lists among the Temple officers, whom the Hebrews called [ממוני המקדש], the Vulgate, Luke 22:52: the magistrate of the Temple, the officer over the nests, that is, over the birds, with whom they reached agreement, so that for a shekel the birds were brought for offerings, these or those. Whoever was bound to offer turtle doves or young pigeons brought the price to the sanctuary. The officer himself gave the birds to those who were to offer them, and assessed them with the treasurers; and once the price was agreed, they gave them within three days... And if a bird was unclean, or became unclean (through ceremonial pollution) before it was offered, he gave another in its place. These are the words of Rabbi Moses Maimonides, which were devised to make a profit by greedy and avaricious priests. Jerome clearly illustrates this present passage of the Gospel in these words: According to the commands of the Law, in the most august temple of the Lord in the whole world, with the people flocking there from almost all the regions of the Jews, countless victims were sacrificed, especially on feast days: bulls, rams and goats; and for the poor, lest they be without sacrifice, pigeons and turtle doves were offered. It often happened that those who had come from afar had no victims. The priests therefore devised a way to make a prey of the people: they sold all the animals needed for sacrifice, so that they sold to those who had none, and bought back again what they had sold. Their scheme was undone by the frequent poverty of those who came, who needed money, and who had no means to buy not only victims but even birds and cheap little offerings. So they also set up money-changers, who would lend money on security. But since the Law commanded that no one take interest, and money lent at interest could not profit, and sometimes would even lose its principal, they devised another trick, namely to have collybists in place of the money-changers. The Latin language does not express the exact meaning of this word. Among them, [κόλλυβα] are called what we call sweetmeats, or cheap little gifts, for example fried chickpeas, raisins, and apples of various kinds. So since the collybists who had lent money could not take interest, they took various kinds of goods in place of interest, so that what was not permitted in coin they might exact in those things which are exchanged for coin; as if Ezekiel had not himself forbidden this, saying: "You shall not take usury or increase." The Lord, seeing such trading, or rather robbery, in his Father's house, roused with the zeal of the Spirit, according to what is written in Psalm 68: "The zeal of your house has consumed me," made for himself a whip of cords and drove out so great a crowd of people from the Temple, saying: "It is written, My house shall be called a house of prayer; but you have made it a den of robbers." For he is a robber, and turns God's Temple into a den of robbers, who seeks gain from religion, and whose worship is less worship of God than an occasion for trade. Christ here joins, as he does elsewhere too, the sayings of two prophets as if they were one and the same: the first saying is Isaiah 56:7, the second is Jeremiah 7:11.

units.la: 15. Videntes autem, &c. Plerique arbitrantur maximum esse signorum quod Lazarus suscitatus est, quod cœcus ex utero lumen acceperit, quod ad Jordanem vox audita sit Patris, quod transfiguratus in monte gloriam ostenderit triumphantis. Mihi interim alia signa quæ fecit hoc videtur mirabilius esse, quod unus homo illo tempore contemtibilis, & in tantum vilis, ut postea crucifigeretur, Scribis & Pharisæis contra se sævientibus, & videntibus lucra destrui, potuerit ad unius flagelli verbera tantam ejicere multitudinem, mensasque subvertere & cathedras confringere, & alia facere, quæ infinitus non fecisset exercitus. Igneum enim quendam atque sydereum radiabat ex oculis ejus, & Divinitatis majestas lucebat in facie. Cumque manum non audeant injicere Sacerdotes, tamen opera calumniantur, & testimonium populi atque puerorum, qui clamabant Hosanna Filio David, vertunt in calumniam, quod videlicet hoc non dicatur nisi Filio Dei. B. Hier.
units.tr: 15. Now when they saw, etc. Most people think the greatest of the signs was that Lazarus was raised, that the blind man received sight from birth, that the Father's voice was heard at the Jordan, and that on the mountain he showed the glory of one triumphing in his transfiguration. For my part, however, the other signs he worked seem more wonderful to me: that one man, at that time despised and so worthless that he was afterwards crucified, while the Scribes and Pharisees raged against him and saw their profits destroyed, could by the strokes of a single whip drive out so great a crowd, overturn the tables, break the seats, and do other things which an endless army could not have done. For a fiery and starry radiance shone from his eyes, and the majesty of his Godhead gleamed in his face. And although the priests did not dare to lay hands on him, they still slandered his works, and they turned into an accusation the witness of the people and of the children who cried "Hosanna to the Son of David", on the ground that, of course, this is said only of the Son of God. B. Hier.

units.la: 16. Nunquam legistis, &c. Q. d. Jam olim per os David Spiritus-Sanctus prophetavit Deum ex ore puerorum esse expressurum laudes, quas adulti ingrati canere deberent, & non canunt.
units.tr: 16. Have you never read, etc. As if to say: long ago the Holy Spirit prophesied through the mouth of David that God would bring forth praises from the mouths of children, which ungrateful adults ought to sing, but do not sing.

units.la: Perfectissimi laudem. Heb. Aquila & VI. Editio, fundasti hur, hoc est, veram ac solidam laudem.
units.tr: Of perfect praise. The Hebrew, as in Aquila and the Sixth Edition, is "you have founded strength" [fundasti hur], that is, true and solid praise.

units.la: 18. Mane. Sc. diei sequentis, ut patet ex Marc. 11. v. 12. Revertens in civitatem. Nempe, Jerusalem ex Bethania, ut patet ex v. 17. hic mox præcedenti, & Marc. 11. v. 12.
units.tr: 18. In the morning. That is, of the following day, as is clear from Mark 11.12. Returning into the city. Namely, Jerusalem, from Bethany, as is clear from verse 17 here, just before, and from Mark 11.12.

units.la: 19. Nunquam fructus ex te nascetur. D. Th. 3. p. q. 44. ar. 4. ad 2. ait quod sicut Chrys. dicit super Mat. Hom. 69. cum in plantis vel in brutis aliquid tale Dominus operatur, numquid quæras qualiter juste siccata est ficus, si tempus non erat? Hoc enim quærere est ultimæ dementiæ, quia scilicet in talibus non invenitur culpa & pœna: sed miraculum inspice & admirare miraculi factorem. Nec facit creator injuriam possidenti, si creatum suo arbitrio utatur ad aliorum salutem, sed magis ut Hilarius dicit super Matth. can. 21. In hoc bonitatis Dominicæ argumentum reperimus; nam ubi afferre voluit procuratæ per se salutis exemplum, virtutis suæ potestatem in humanis corporibus exercuit: ubi vero in contumaces formam severitatis constituebat futuræ speciem, damno arboris indicavit.
units.tr: 19. May no fruit ever grow from you. Aquinas, 3 p., q. 44, art. 4, ad 2, says: As Chrysostom says on Matthew, Homily 69: when the Lord does something of this kind to plants or to brute things, do you ask how the fig tree was justly dried up, when it was not the season? For to ask this is the height of folly, since no fault or punishment is found in such things. Rather, look at the miracle and marvel at the worker of the miracle. Nor does the Creator do wrong to the owner if he uses his creature at his own will for the salvation of others. Rather, as Hilary says on Matthew, canon 21: In this we find a proof of the Lord's goodness; for where he wished to offer an example of salvation obtained through himself, he exercised the power of his virtue on human bodies; but where he set up a form of severity against the obstinate, he showed in the loss of the tree a picture of what was to come.

units.la: 20. Mirati sunt. Quod nimirum tam cito non obstante humiditate naturali, quam, ut advertit Chrysost. præ ceteris plantis maximam habet ficulnea, exsiccata sit & usque ad radices arefacta.
units.tr: 20. They marvelled. That indeed it should be dried up and withered right down to the roots so quickly, despite the natural moisture which, as Chrysostom notes, the fig tree has in greater measure than other plants.

units.la: Dicentes, &c. Hæc non dicta sunt a discipulis eadem hora, qua ficulnea est arefacta, sed dicta sunt a Petro postridie, ut patet ex Marc. 11. v. 21.
units.tr: Saying, etc. These words were not spoken by the disciples at the same hour the fig tree withered, but were spoken by Peter the next day, as is clear from Mark 11.21.

units.la: 25. Baptismus Joannis. Baptismus non dicitur Joannis, quasi Joannem habuerit autorem, sed quia jussus à Deo primus promulgavit & administravit baptismum in remissionem peccatorum, cum Apostoli administrarint baptismum à Christo promulgatum, cui baptismus à Joanne promulgatus cedebat spiritualium donorum copia atque ubertate, quam ab Apostolis baptizati consequebantur.
units.tr: 25. The baptism of John. The baptism is not called John's as though John had been its author. Rather, it is called so because he was the first to proclaim and administer baptism for the remission of sins by God's command. The apostles administered the baptism proclaimed by Christ, and the baptism proclaimed by John gave way to it in the abundance and richness of spiritual gifts which those baptized by the apostles received.

units.la: 32. In via justitiæ. Supple, incedens.
units.tr: 32. In the way of righteousness. Supply: walking.

units.la: 33. Aliam parabolam audite. Hanc parabolam non ad eos solos dictam, qui Christum interrogaverant, In qua potestate hæc facis? sed etiam ad plebem, patet ex collatione Matthæi cum Luca eandem parabolam referente c. 20. ut observavit Aug. lib. 2. de Conf. Evang. c. 70.
units.tr: 33. Hear another parable. That this parable was spoken not only to those who had asked Christ, By what authority do you do these things? but also to the people, is clear from comparing Matthew with Luke, who reports the same parable in chapter 20, as Augustine observed in Book 2 of On the Harmony of the Gospels, chapter 70.

units.la: Plantavit vineam. Plantata est vinea, Lege datâ in cordibus Judæorum. Missi sunt Prophetæ, quærentes fructum, bonam viam eorum. Prophetæ ab eis contumeliis affecti & occisi sunt. Missus est Christus unicus Filius Patrisfamilias, & ipsum occiderunt heredem, & ideo perdiderunt hereditatem. In contrarium eis vertit malum consilium. Ut possiderent occiderunt, & quia occiderunt perdiderunt. Aug. Serm. 59. de verbis Domini.
units.tr: He planted a vineyard. The vineyard was planted when the law was given in the hearts of the Jews. Prophets were sent, seeking fruit, its good way. The prophets were treated with insults by them and killed. Christ, the only Son of the householder, was sent, and they killed the heir, and so they lost the inheritance. Their evil counsel turned against them. They killed in order to possess, and because they killed, they lost. Augustine, Sermon 59, on the words of the Lord.

units.la: Fodit in ea torcular. Id est, lacum recipiendo vino è torculari, in quo exprimitur, defluenti.
units.tr: He dug a winepress in it. That is, a vat to receive the wine flowing down from the press in which it is pressed out.

units.la: Peregrè profectus est. Non quia ex loco ad locum profectus est Dominus, qui ubique semper præsens est: sed quia est præsentior diligentibus, negligentibus abest. Multis temporibus abfuit, Luc. 20. v. 9. ne præpropera videretur exactio. Nam quo indulgentior, libertas, eò inexcusabilior pervicacia. B. Ambr. lib. 9. in Luc. c. 20.
units.tr: He went abroad. Not because the Lord, who is always present everywhere, went from place to place, but because he is more present to those who love him and absent from the negligent. He was absent for a long time, Luke 20.9, lest the demand seem too hasty. For the more indulgent the liberty, the less excusable the obstinacy. B. Ambrose, Book 9 on Luke, chapter 20.

units.la: 35. Lapidaverunt. In textu Græco, Marc. 12. v. 3. lapidantes in capite vulneraverunt.
units.tr: 35. They stoned. In the Greek text, Mark 12.3: stoning, they wounded in the head.

units.la: 38. Habebimus. Græce, occupemus.
units.tr: 38. We shall have. In Greek: let us seize.

units.la: 41. Aiunt illi. Sc. quidam de plebe Christo. Horum responsionem cum Christus confirmasset, Sacerdotes intelligentes ad se dirigi parabolam, dixerunt, ut habetur Luc. 20. v. 16.
units.tr: 41. They say to him. That is, some of the people to Christ. When Christ had confirmed their answer, the priests, understanding that the parable was aimed at them, said, as is found in Luke 20.16.

units.la: Absit. Sc. ut nos heredi necem paremus & consequenter male perdamur.
units.tr: God forbid. That is, lest we prepare death for the heir and consequently perish wretchedly.

units.la: Vineam suam locabit aliis agricolis. Non ait, Eradicabit, sed eandem ipsam locabit aliis agricolis. Eadem namque est sanctorum societate civitas Dei, & congregatio filiorum promissionis, mortalium decessione atque successione componenda, atque in fine seculi simul in omnibus immortalitatem recepura. Neque enim quia fracti sunt infideles & superbi, ac per hoc infructuosi rami, ut insereretur oleaster Gentium, ideo perire potuit ædix Patriarcharum & Prophetarum. Aug. in Orat. adversus Judæos c. 6.
units.tr: He will let out his vineyard to other husbandmen. He does not say, He will root it up, but he will let out that same vineyard to other husbandmen. For the city of God is one and the same fellowship of the saints, and the congregation of the sons of promise, to be composed by the death and succession of mortals, and at the end of the age all of them together are to receive immortality. For it was not because the unbelieving and proud were broken off, and thereby the unfruitful branches, so that the wild olive of the Gentiles might be grafted in, that the building of the patriarchs and prophets could perish. Augustine, in the Oration against the Jews, chapter 6.

units.la: Lapidem, &c. Sumta est metaphora ab ædificantibus, qui ædificio extruendo lapides aptos quærunt, & quos ineptos arbitrantur rejiciunt; quibus forte contigit, ut lapis primo rejectus, postea aptus inveniretur, qui collocaretur in angulo fundamenti. Igitur lapis ab ædificantibus rejectus & deinde factus anguli caput, seu ut Hebræi loquuntur, in caput anguli, Christus est, quem ædificantes, seu architecti, id est, Sacerdotes & Scribæ populi Judaici, quorum erat docere & gubernare populum, reprobaverunt dicentes Sap. 2. Quoniam inutilis est nobis: & adeo reprobaverunt, ut non solum Regem eum habere nollent, dicentes Luc. 19. Nolumus hunc regnare super nos. Joan. 19. Non habemus Regem, nisi Cæsarem: verùm etiam crucifigendum procurarent; idem tamen Christus, repentinâ factâ conversione, non modo receptus est in partem ædificii spiritualis, quod est Ecclesia, sed mirabili Dei consilio & dispositione (nam ut in Psalmo hic laudato sequitur: à Domino factum est istud & est mirabile in oculis nostris) etiam factus est lapis angularis, id est, totius Ecclesiæ unicum illud fundamentum, quod per se habet soliditatem, duos Ecclesiæ parietes, Judaicum scilicet populum & Gentilem in se ipso firmissimâ juncturâ connectens; & quia lapis angularis, ideò Rex est Christus, siquidem phrasi Hebraicâ Principes ac Primores in populis vocantur anguli populorum, quasi fundamenta eorum & sustentacula præcipua, ut videre est Judic. 20. v. 2. 1 Sam. seu Reg. 14. Esa. 19. Sophon. 1,&3. Hinc ipse Christus ait de se Psal. 2. Ego autem constitutus sum Rex ab eo super Sion montem sanctum ejus.
units.tr: The stone, etc. The metaphor is taken from builders, who seek fitting stones for the building they are erecting, and reject those they judge unfit. It may happen to them that a stone first rejected is afterwards found fit, and is placed at the corner of the foundation. So the stone rejected by the builders and afterwards made the head of the corner, or, as the Hebrews put it, the head of the corner, is Christ, whom the builders, that is the priests and scribes of the Jewish people, whose task it was to teach and govern the people, rejected, saying in Wisdom 2: For he is useless to us. And they rejected him so completely that they not only refused to have him as king, saying in Luke 19: We will not have this man reign over us, and in John 19: We have no king but Caesar, but they even arranged for him to be crucified. Yet the same Christ, after a sudden turn of events, was not only received into the part of the spiritual building which is the Church, but by the wonderful counsel and disposition of God (for, as the psalm cited here goes on: This was done by the Lord, and it is marvellous in our eyes), he was made the corner stone, that is, that single foundation of the whole Church which has solidity in itself, binding together the two walls of the Church, the Jewish people and the Gentile, in himself by a very firm joining. And because he is the corner stone, Christ is king. For in Hebrew idiom the princes and chief men among the peoples are called the corners of the peoples, as their foundations and chief supports; as may be seen in Judges 20.2, 1 Samuel (or 1 Kings) 14, Isaiah 19, Zephaniah 1 and 3. Hence Christ himself says of himself in Psalm 2: But I have been set up as king by him on Zion, his holy mountain.

units.la: Auferetur à vobis regnum Dei, &c. Q. d. Quia impleturi estis, quod in parabola de herede vineæ occidendo attuli, fiet ut amplius Deus in vobis non fit regnaturus, sed per gratuitam gratiam regnum hactenus à vobis possessum dabitur Gentibus edituris fructus Spiritûs, queis se comprobent regni cœlestis cives. Itaque prædicit hic Christus reprobationem Judæorum cum ablatione veri cultûs Dei, & Gentes occasione reprobationis eorum ad fidem & regnum Dei evocandas, ut clarè docet Paulus Act. 13. v. 46. & latiùs in Ep. ad Rom. c. 11. v. 25, & 26.
units.tr: The kingdom of God will be taken from you, etc. As if to say: because you are about to fulfil what I brought forward in the parable about killing the heir of the vineyard, it will come about that God will no longer reign among you. Rather, by free grace, the kingdom hitherto possessed by you will be given to the Gentiles, who will bring forth the fruits of the Spirit, by which they show themselves citizens of the heavenly kingdom. Thus Christ here foretells the rejection of the Jews, with the removal of the true worship of God, and that the Gentiles, through the occasion of their rejection, are to be called to faith and the kingdom of God, as Paul clearly teaches in Acts 13.46, and more fully in the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 11, verses 25 and 26.

units.la: Qui ceciderit, &c. De his dicit Christus quòd cadet super lapidem, qui illum modò contemnunt, vel injuriis afficiunt, ideò nondum penitùs intereunt, sed tamen confringuntur, ut non rarò ambulent. Super quos autem cadit, veniet illis desuper in judicio cum pœna perditionis, ideo dixit, Cónteret eos, ut sint impii tanquam pulvis quem projicit ventus à facie terræ. Aug. q. Evang. lib. 1. q. 30.
units.tr: Whoever falls, etc. Christ says of these that he who now despises or injures the stone will not indeed perish utterly at once, but will still be broken, so that he often walks about. But upon whom it falls, it will come down upon them from above in judgment with the punishment of destruction; therefore he said, It will grind them to powder, so that the wicked are like the dust which the wind drives from the face of the earth. Aug. q. Evang. lib. 1. q. 30.

units.la: CAPUT XXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXII.

units.la: I. Simile factum est, &c. Id est, simile quid accidit in colligenda ex hominibus Ecclesia, in qua Deus regnum suum inchoat, ut postea compleat, ac si Rex quispiam faceret nuptias filio suo. Sed quaerendum est an hæc apud Matthæum ipsa sit lectio, quæ apud Lucam appellatione cœnæ describitur? Et quidem sunt nonnulla quæ sibi dissona esse videntur, quia hic prandium, illic cœna memoratur, hic qui ad nuptias non dignis vestibus intravit, repulsus est: illic nullus qui intrasse dicitur, repulsus esse perhibetur. Qua ex re recte colligitur quod & hic per nuptias præsens Ecclesia, & illic per cœnam æternum & ultimum convivium designatur: quia & hanc nonnulli exituri intrant, & ad illud quisquis semel intraverit, ulterius non exibit. At, si quis forte contendat hanc eandem esse lectionem, ego melius puto, salva fide alieno intellectui cedere, quàm contentionibus deservire: quoniam & intelligi congruè forsitan potest, quia de projecto eo, qui cum nuptiali veste non venerat, quod Lucas tacuit, Matthæus dixit. Quod vero per illum cœna, per hunc autem prandium dicitur, nequaquam vel hoc nostræ intelligentiæ obsistit: quia cùm ad horam nonam apud antiquos quotidie prandium fieret, ipsum quoque prandium cœna vocabatur. Greg. Hom. 38. in Evang.
units.tr: I. The kingdom of heaven is like a king who made a marriage feast, etc. That is, something similar happens in the gathering of the Church from among men, in which God begins his kingdom so that he may later complete it, as if some king were to make a wedding for his son. But it must be asked whether this is the same passage that Luke describes under the name of a supper. Indeed there are some differences that seem to conflict: here a meal is mentioned, there a supper; here the man who came to the wedding without fitting clothes is cast out, there no one who is said to have entered is reported as cast out. From this it is rightly gathered that here the present Church is designated by the wedding, and there the eternal and final banquet by the supper: because some enter this one and will go out again, but whoever has once entered that one will never go out again. But if someone should insist that this is the same passage, I think it better, with the faith kept safe, to yield to another's understanding than to serve controversies; for it may perhaps be understood fittingly that Matthew mentions what Luke passed over, the casting out of the man who had not come in wedding clothes. And that the one calls it a supper and this one a meal does not in any way hinder our understanding, since among the ancients the principal daily meal was taken at the ninth hour, and that meal too was called a supper. Gregory, Homily 38 on the Gospels.

units.la: Fecit nuptias filio suo. Tunc Deus Pater Deo Filio suo nuptias fecit, quando hunc in utero Virginis humanæ naturæ conjunxit, quando Deum ante sæcula fieri voluit hominem in fine sæculorum. Sed quia ex duabus personis fieri solet ista nuptialis conjunctio, abest hoc ab intellectibus nostris, ut personam Dei & hominis, redemtoris nostri Jesu Christi, ex duabus personis credamus unitam. Ex duabus quippe atque in duabus hunc naturis existere dicimus, sed ex duabus personis compositum credi, ut nefas, vitamus. Apertius ergo atque securius dici potest, quia in hoc Pater Regi Filio nuptias fecit, quo ei per incarnationis mysterium sanctam Ecclesiam sociavit. Uterus autem genitricis Virginis, bujus sponsi thalamus fuit. Unde & Psalmista dicit: In sole posuit tabernaculum suum, & ipse tanquam sponsus procedens de thalamo suo. Tanquam sponsus, quippe de thalamo suo processit, qui ad conjungendam sibi Ecclesiam incarnatus Deus de incorrupto utero Virginis exivit. Greg. ibidem.
units.tr: He made a marriage feast for his son. Then God the Father made a marriage for his Son God, when he united him to human nature in the womb of a human virgin, when he willed the God who exists before the ages to become man at the end of the ages. But since such a nuptial union is usually made of two persons, it is hard for our minds to believe that the person of God and man, our Redeemer Jesus Christ, is united out of two persons. For we say that he exists from two natures and in two natures, but we avoid, as wrong, the belief that he is composed of two persons. It can therefore be said more plainly and more safely that in this the Father made a marriage for the King his Son, when by the mystery of the incarnation he joined the holy Church to him. The womb of the virgin mother was the bridal chamber of this Bridegroom. Hence the Psalmist also says: In the sun he has placed his tabernacle, and he himself as a bridegroom coming out of his chamber. As a bridegroom, indeed, he came out of his chamber, since God, incarnate to join the Church to himself, came out of the incorrupt womb of the Virgin. Gregory, ibid.

units.la: 3. Misit servos suos. Nempe, Prophetas.
units.tr: 3. He sent his servants. Namely, the Prophets.

units.la: 4. Misit alios servos. Scilicet, Apostolos. Bis itaque servos ad invitandum misit, quia incarnationem unigeniti & per Prophetas dixit futuram, & per Apostolos nunciavit factam. loco mox citato.
units.tr: 4. He sent other servants. That is, the Apostles. So he sent servants to invite twice, because through the Prophets he declared that the incarnation of the Only-begotten would take place, and through the Apostles he announced that it had taken place. Gregory, in the passage cited just above.

units.la: Tauri mei & altilia. Id est, tauri mei altiles per figuram ἐν σιτῷ ἀνοῖν; unde Arabs habet: Vituli mei sagináti occisi sunt.
units.tr: My oxen and fatted calves. That is, my fatted oxen, by a figure of speech [ἐν σιτῷ ἀνοῖν]; hence the Arabic has: My fattened calves have been slain.

units.la: 5. Abierunt, alius in villam suam, &c. In villam ire, est labori terreno immoderatè incumbere. In negotiationem verò ire, est actionum secularium lucris inhiare. Greg. ibidem.
units.tr: 5. They went away, one to his farm, etc. To go to the farm is to apply oneself immoderately to earthly labour. To go to business is to lust after the gains of worldly affairs. Gregory, ibid.

units.la: 6. Reliqui verò. Scilicet, longè magis impii & ingrati humanissimæ invitationi ad prandium jam paratum, vocantis gratiam non solùm respuunt, sed etiam persequuntur.
units.tr: 6. But the rest. That is, far more impious and ungrateful men, who not only reject the grace of the one calling them to the meal already prepared, but also persecute them.

units.la: 7. Missis exercitibus suis. Romanos intelligit sub Tito & Vespasiano.
units.tr: 7. He sent his armies. He means the Romans under Titus and Vespasian.

units.la: Perdidit homicidas illos. Gladio, fame, & peste usqueadeò, ut Josephus lib. 7. De bello Judaico c. 17. testetur periisse solâ ultimâ Jerosolymæ obsidione undecies centena millia praeter innumeras clades, quibus & ante & postea alibi affecti sunt Judæi, qui ad felicitatem prandii coelitus parati venire neglexerunt. Quamvis autem textus hoc factum dicat propter caesos servos Regis, non negat tamen praecipuam suisse causam illius occisionem, qui accepta forma servi non destitit esse æqualis Patri.
units.tr: He destroyed those murderers. By sword, famine and pestilence, to such an extent that Josephus, in book 7 of the Jewish War, chapter 17, testifies that during the last siege of Jerusalem alone eleven hundred thousand perished, besides the countless disasters with which the Jews were afflicted both before and afterwards elsewhere, who neglected to come to the happiness of the feast prepared from heaven. Although the text says this happened on account of the slaughter of the King's servants, it does not deny that the chief cause of his destruction was that he, who had taken the form of a servant, did not cease to be equal to the Father.

units.la: Civitatem illorum succendit. Hoc ad literam contigisse testatur Josephus loco citato.
units.tr: He burned their city. Josephus, in the passage cited, testifies that this happened literally.

units.la: 8. Tunc. Cùm scilicet pervicaciter Judæi ad nuptias venire detrectarent.
units.tr: 8. Then. That is, when the Jews obstinately refused to come to the wedding.

units.la: Non fuerunt digni. Plus significat quam dicit; id est, indignos se praestiterunt per suam pervicaciam, ingratam neglegentiam, & impium contemtum. Hinc ergo, ut ait Apostolus ad Rom. c. 11. v. 11. Judæorum delicto salus facta est Gentibus, quia cùm se judicassent indignos æternâ vitâ, & nuptiis istis, praedicatores ad Gentes conversi sunt, Act. 13. v. 46. ut qui nunquam invitati fuerant, in Christum credendo ad nuptias venirent, hoc est enim quod Christus dicit, Ite ergo ad exitus viarum, &c. Exitus autem viarum dicuntur compita, in quae plures vici exeunt, id est, definunt.
units.tr: They were not worthy. It means more than it says; that is, they showed themselves unworthy through their obstinacy, ungrateful negligence and impious contempt. Hence, as the Apostle says in Romans 11:11, salvation came to the Gentiles through the fall of the Jews; because when they judged themselves unworthy of eternal life and of these nuptials, the preachers were turned to the Gentiles (Acts 13:46), so that those who had never been invited might come to the wedding by believing in Christ. For this is what Christ says: Go therefore to the exits of the roads, etc. The exits of the roads are called the crossroads, into which several villages run out, that is, end.

units.la: 9. Quoscunque invenerítis. Nemine cujusquam conditionis quantumvis barbaro excluso.
units.tr: 9. Whomever you find. Excluding no one of any condition, however barbarous.

units.la: Io. Omnes. Id est, ex omni hominum genere, seu ex omni tribu, & lingua, & populo, & natione, & sexu, & professione.
units.tr: Io. All. That is, from every kind of men, or from every tribe, tongue, people, nation, sex and profession.

units.la: Malos & bonos. Non qui se malos perseveraturos prositerentur, sed malos, sive qui latherent, dum ingrediendo probitatem simularent: bonos autem qui seculo uti verbis, ita et factis renuntiabant.
units.tr: Both bad and good. Not those who professed that they would persevere in wickedness, but the bad, that is, those who lay hidden while pretending uprightness by entering; and the good, who renounced the world in words and also in deeds.

units.la: Impletæ sunt nuptiæ discumbentium. Id est, locus nuptialis impletus est discumbentibus.
units.tr: The wedding was filled with the guests reclining. That is, the wedding place was filled with those reclining.

units.la: II. Vidit ibi hominem non vestitum veste nuptiali. Quid exprimi per nuptialem vestem putamus? Si enim vestem nuptialem baptisma vel fidem dicimus, quis sine baptismate & fide has nuptias intravit? Eo enim ipso foris est, quo necdum credidit. Quid ergo debemus intelligere nuptialem vestem nisi charitatem? Intrat enim ad nuptias, sed cum nuptiali veste non intrat, qui in sancta Ecclesia assistens fidem (mortuam) habet, sed charitatem non habet. Recte enim charitas nuptialis vestis vocatur, quia hanc in se conditor noster habuit, dum ad associandas sibi Ecclesiæ nuptias venit. Sola quippe dilectione Dei actum est, ut ejus unigenitus mentes sibi electorum hominum uniret. Unde & Joannes dicit: Sic enim dilexit Deus mundum ut Filium suum unigenitum daret pro nobis. Qui ergo per charitatem venit ad homines, eandem charitatem innotuit (i. notum fecit) vestem esse nuptialem. Greg. loco supra citato.
units.tr: II. He saw there a man not clothed in a wedding garment. What do we think is expressed by the wedding garment? For if we say that the wedding garment is baptism or faith, who has entered these nuptials without baptism and faith? For by that very fact he is outside, that he has not yet believed. What then must we understand by the wedding garment except love? For he enters the wedding, but he does not enter with the wedding garment who, standing in the holy Church, has faith (dead) but does not have love.
