Love is rightly called the wedding garment, because our Creator himself had this love when he came to join the nuptials of the Church to himself. For it was by the love of God alone that his Only-begotten was brought to unite to himself the minds of the chosen men. Hence John also says: For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son for us. Therefore he who came to men through love made known that this same love is the wedding garment. Gregory, in the passage cited above.

units.la: 12. Amice. Amicum vocat, quia ad nuptias amico animo inviatus fuerat, inquit Hier. & ut zelo justitiæ, non autem odio se increpari intelligat.
units.tr: 12. Friend. He calls him friend, because he had been invited to the wedding in a friendly spirit, says Jerome, and so that he may understand that he is rebuked out of zeal for justice, not out of hatred.

units.la: Quomodo. Id est, quà fronte.
units.tr: How. That is, with what face.

units.la: Obmutuit. Quia quod dici sine gemitu non potest, in illa distinctione ultimæ increpationis omne argumentum cessat excusationis: quippe quia ille foris increpat, qui reflis conscientiæ intus animum accusat. Greg. ibidem.
units.tr: He was speechless. Because what cannot be said without groaning, in that distinction of the final rebuke, every argument of excuse ceases; for he who rebukes outwardly is the one whose conscience inwardly accuses his soul. Gregory, ibid.

units.la: 13. Ligatis manibus. Ligantur tunc pedes & manus per distinctionem sententiæ, qui modo à pravis operibus ligari noluerunt per meliorationem vitæ. Vel certè tunc ligat pœna, quos modo à bonis operibus ligavit culpa. Pedes enim qui visitare agrum negligunt, manus quæ nihil indigentibus tribuunt, à bono opere jam ex voluntate ligatæ sunt. Qui ergo nunc sponte ligantur in vitio, tunc in supplicio ligantur invite. Bene autem dicitur quod in exteriores tenebras projiciatur. Interiores quippe tenebras dicimus cæcitatem cordis, exteriores verò tenebras æternam noctem damnationis. Tunc ergo damnatus quisque, non in interiores, sed in exteriores tenebras mittitur, quia ille invitus projicitur in noctem damnationis, qui hîc sponte cecidit in cæcitatem cordis. Ubi fletus quoque & stridor dentium esse perhibetur, ut illic dentes strideant, qui hic de edacitate gaudebant, illic oculi defleant, qui hic per illicitas concupiscentias versabantur in mundo: quatenus singula quaeque membra supplicio subjaceant, quae hic singulis quibusque vitiis subjecta serviebant. Greg. ibidem.
units.tr: 13. With hands bound. By the distinction of the sentence, the feet and hands are bound of those who now would not be bound from evil works through the improvement of life. Or certainly then punishment binds those whom guilt has now bound from good works. For feet that neglect to visit the field, and hands that give nothing to the needy, are already bound by their own will from good work. Those therefore who are now bound willingly in vice are then bound unwillingly in punishment. It is rightly said that he is cast into outer darkness. For we call inner darkness the blindness of the heart, and outer darkness the eternal night of damnation. Therefore each damned person is sent not into inner but into outer darkness, because he who here fell willingly into blindness of heart is cast unwillingly into the night of damnation. There, it is said, there is weeping and gnashing of teeth: there the teeth gnash which here rejoiced in gluttony, there the eyes weep which here roamed in the world through unlawful desires; so that each member may undergo the punishment which here served each vice to which it was subjected. Gregory, ibid.

units.la: 14. Multi enim sunt vocati, pauci vero electi. Praeclare Aug. in Ep. 157. ad Optatum. Tam multos creando nasci voluit, quos ad suam gratiam non pertinere praescivit, ut multitudine incomparabili plures sint illis, quos in sui regni gloriam filios promissionis praedestinare dignatus est, ut etiam ipsa rejectorum multitudine ostenderetur, quam nullius momenti sit apud Deum justum quantalibet numerositas justissime damnatorum.
units.tr: 14. For many are called, but few are chosen. Augustine splendidly, in Letter 157 to Optatus: God wished so many to be born, whom He foreknew did not belong to His grace, so that by an incomparable multitude there would be more than those whom He deigned to predestine as sons of promise to the glory of His kingdom; and so that by the very multitude of the rejected it might be shown how little account with God is any number, however great, of those justly condemned.

units.la: 15. Tunc. Cum scilicet irritati essent Pharisaei tot parabolis.
units.tr: 15. Then. Namely, when the Pharisees had been provoked by so many parables.

units.la: 16. Cum Herodianis. Id est, ut Syrus vertit, cum iis qui erant de domo Herodis, vel ut ait Hieronymus hic, cum militibus Herodis, seu quos illudentes Pharisaei, quia Romanis tributa solvebant, Herodianos vocabant, & non divino cultui deditos. Quidam Latinorum ridiculè Herodianos putant, qui Herodem Christum esse credebant: quod nusquam omninò legimus. Hic tamen error Herodianis tribuitur ab ipso Hieronymo in dialogo adversus Luciferianos. Alii aiunt Herodianos fuisse corycaeos, qui quid à singulis diceretur sedulò expiscarentur, ut illud ad Herodem deferrent. Ab Herodianis Herodem habitum fuisse pro Christo, ait B. Epiphanius Haer. 7. Judaismi, Tertullianus lib. de praescript. adversus haereticos c. 45. S. Philastrius Haeresi ultima earum quae ante Christum.
units.tr: 16. With the Herodians. That is, as the Syriac version renders it, with those who were of the house of Herod, or, as Jerome says here, with the soldiers of Herod. Or the Pharisees, mocking them because they paid tribute to the Romans, called them Herodians, and considered them not devoted to divine worship. Some of the Latins foolishly think the Herodians were those who believed Herod to be the Christ, a thing we never read of anywhere at all. Yet this error is attributed to the Herodians by Jerome himself in his dialogue against the Luciferians. Others say the Herodians were flatterers, who carefully fished out what was said by each man so that they could report it to Herod. That the Herodians regarded Herod as the Christ is stated by St Epiphanius, Heresy 7 (Judaism), by Tertullian, On Prescription against Heretics, chapter 45, and by St Philastrius, in the last heresy of those before Christ.

units.la: Verax. Id est, veritatis amans.
units.tr: Truthful. That is, a lover of truth.

units.la: In veritate. Id est, sincerè & absque fuco.
units.tr: In truth. That is, sincerely and without guile.

units.la: Non enim respicit personam hominum. Q. d. Solius causae merita intueris, nihil curans quascunque extraneas personarum conditiones ad causam non pertinentes, puta divitias, honores, potentiam, & cetera hujusmodi. Hunc eundem sensum Marcus c. 12. v. 14. & Lucas c. 20. v. 21. expressere licèt aliis verbis.
units.tr: For you do not regard the person of men. That is to say: you look only at the merits of the cause, caring nothing for any extraneous circumstances of persons that do not pertain to the cause, such as wealth, honours, power and the like. Mark 12:14 and Luke 20:21 express the same sense, though in other words.

units.la: 17. Licet. Nempe, sine offensa Dei.
units.tr: 17. Is it lawful. Namely, without offence to God.

units.la: Censum. Id est, tributum, ut explicant Marcus & Lucas. Cùm enim census proprie diceretur descriptio agrorum & reliquarum fortunarum, ex quibus tributi pro sua virili cuique praestandi ratio constabat, obtinuit in provinciis, ut ipsum tributum appellaretur census, quae vox in ipso Evangelio Graeco Matthaei ter, & Marci semel legitur, etsi Latina distio sit; tamen census specialiter dicebatur nummus solvendæ capitationi apud Hesychium. Pensitatio ista census per capitationem, quæ coepit post Cæsarem Augustum in Judæa; ut ait Hieronymus in Matth. 17. professio erat apertissima & Judææ ad formulam provinciæ redactæ, & summi imperii, quo Cæsar potiebatur in Judæos, ex quo Archelaus Regis Herodis filius in exilium pulsus est, & bona ejus fisco sunt adjudicata.
units.tr: Tribute. That is, a tax, as Mark and Luke explain. For since census properly meant the register of fields and other property, from which the assessment of the tax each man was to pay according to his means was made, it came to be used in the provinces for the tax itself. This word is read three times in Matthew's Greek Gospel and once in Mark, although the Latin usage is different; still, according to Hesychius, census was specially used of the coin paid as a poll-tax. This assessment by poll-tax, which began in Judaea after Caesar Augustus, as Jerome says on Matthew 17, was a most open profession both that Judaea had been reduced to the form of a province and of the supreme power which Caesar held over the Jews, since Archelaus, son of King Herod, had been driven into exile and his goods had been adjudged to the fisc.

units.la: Cæsari. Scipionem Africanum priorem, primum Cæsarem vocatum tradidere, quod excisus utero matris fuerit. Sed hoc falsum est. Nam ante bellum Samniticum Claudius quidam Cæsar extitit. Falsa etiam nominis ratio. Nec enim Cæsar a cæso utero dictus; id de Cæsone potius verum esset. Sed ut ait Festus: Cæsar quod est cognomen Juliorum à cæsarie dictus est, quia scilicet cum cæsarie natus est. Ab occiso Elephanto, qui Cæsar Maurorum lingua appellatur, tanquam aciei perruptor [caffara enim Arabibus est perrumpere] deducere, nimis longè petitum est.
units.tr: Caesar. They have handed down that Scipio Africanus the Elder was the first to be called Caesar, because he was cut from his mother's womb. But this is false. For before the Samnite war there was a certain Claudius Caesar. The explanation of the name is also false: Caesar was not named from a womb that had been cut open; that would be truer of Caeso. But as Festus says: Caesar, which is a cognomen of the Julii, was named from caesaries (a head of hair), because he was born with thick hair. To derive it from the elephant that was killed, which in the Moorish tongue is called Caesar, as a breaker of the battle line (for caffara means to break through in Arabic), is far too remote.

units.la: 19. Ostendite mihi numisma census. Cùm vario & multiplici genere nummorum Judæi tum uterentur, propriorum scilicet gentis suæ, vicinarum regionum & Romanorum, nullum est dubium quin tributum, quod Cæsari pendebatur, in pecunia Romana exigeretur, non Judaica aut quavis alia; Dominus igitur numisma census appellat peculiare monetæ genus, quod ad census solutionem cuderetur.
units.tr: 19. Show me the coin of the tribute. Since the Jews used various and manifold kinds of money, namely their own, those of neighbouring regions, and Roman, there is no doubt that the tribute paid to Caesar was exacted in Roman money, and not in Jewish or any other. The Lord therefore calls it the coin of the tribute, a particular kind of money struck for the payment of the tax.

units.la: Obtulerunt ei denarium. Scilicet in exemplum pecuniæ Romanæ; neque enim denarius fuit peculiare aliquod monetæ genus ad tributi solutionem cusæ, verum omnes denarii erant pecunia Romana; & tam denarii, quàm alii nummi Romani dici poterant numisma census.
units.tr: They offered him a denarius. Namely, as an example of Roman money. For the denarius was not some particular kind of coin struck for the payment of tribute; rather, all denarii were Roman money, and both denarii and other Roman coins could be called the coin of the tribute.

units.la: 21. Quæ sunt Dei, Deo. Hoc est dicere, ô homo, sicut imaginem suam Cæsari reddis in nummo, sic redde Deo imaginem suam in te ipso. Redde, homo, creatori tuo imaginem suam; redde justam, non iniquam, redde humilem, non superbam; non avaritiæ turpem, non rapacitate deformem, non vitio iracundiæ levem, non terrenâ dilectione contritam, non livore sordidam, non fornicatione pollutam; sed prudentiâ pondere integram, fidei veritate mundam, & bonis moribus atque operibus splendidam. B. Fulg. Serm. de verbis Michææ, Indicabo tibi, ô homo, quid sit bonum, &c.
units.tr: 21. Render to God what is God's. That is to say: O man, as you render Caesar his image on the coin, so render to God His image in yourself. Render to your Creator, man, His image: render it just, not unjust; humble, not proud; not foul with avarice, not disfigured by rapacity, not made light by the vice of anger, not crushed by earthly love, not soiled by envy, not polluted by fornication; but whole in the weight of prudence, clean in the truth of faith, and bright with good morals and works. St Fulgentius, sermon on the words of Micah: I will show you, O man, what is good, and so on.

units.la: 22. Mirati sunt. Scilicet dexteritatem Christi, quâ tam caute respondit difficillimæ quæstioni, ut nihil reperiri posset, quo vel Cæsar, vel populus offenderetur.
units.tr: 22. They marvelled. Namely at the skill of Christ, by which He answered so cautiously so very difficult a question that nothing could be found by which either Caesar or the people might be offended.

units.la: 29. Erratis nescientes Scripturas, neque virtutem Dei. Id est, erratis negando resurrectionem, quia Scripturas non intelligitis, neque omnipotentiam Dei. Quibus autem Scripturæ indicabant resurrectionem mortuorum, iis etiam fuit nota vita æterna; quia vel ad vitam æternam, vel ad opprobrium æternum est resurrectio, ut patet ex Dan. 12. v. 2.
units.tr: 29. You err, not knowing the Scriptures, nor the power of God. That is: you err in denying the resurrection, because you do not understand the Scriptures, nor God's omnipotence. But to those to whom the Scriptures pointed to the resurrection of the dead, eternal life was also known, since the resurrection is either to eternal life or to eternal shame, as is clear from Daniel 12:2.

units.la: 30. In resurrectione. Id est, ut explicant Marcus & Lucas, cum à mortuis resurrexerint.
units.tr: 30. In the resurrection. That is, as Mark and Luke explain, when they have risen from the dead.

units.la: Neque nubent. Id est, non ducent uxores. Vera ergo carnis resurrectio, attamen sine carnis operibus erit. B. Ambr. in Symb. c. 24.
units.tr: Neither do they marry. That is, they will not take wives. The resurrection of the flesh is therefore true, yet it will be without the works of the flesh. St Ambrose on the Creed, chapter 24.

units.la: Neque nubentur. Id est, mulieres non ducentur. Rarum est autem apud Latinos verbum, nubo, de viris usurpatum, licet aliquando occurrat. Proprie autem uxori nubere dicitur, qui illi servit & ab ea quasi regitur. Hinc illud Martialis lib. 8. Epig. 10. ad Priscum, Uxorem quare locupletem ducere nolim Quaeritis? uxori nubere nolo meæ. Inferior matrona suo fit, Prisce, marito: Non aliter fiunt fœmina, virque pares.
units.tr: Neither are they given in marriage. That is, women will not be taken in marriage. The verb nubo, used of men, is rare among the Latins, although it does occasionally occur. Properly, however, a woman is said nubere to her husband, since she serves him and is as it were ruled by him. Hence that epigram of Martial, Book 8, Epigram 10, to Priscus: "Why do you ask why I do not wish to take a wealthy wife? I do not wish to marry my own wife. A lesser matron becomes her husband's, Priscus; not otherwise do woman and man become equals."

units.la: Sicut Angeli Dei in cælo. Id est, erunt sicut Angeli cœlestes, seu æquales Angelis beatis, immortalitate atque felicitate. Similitudo Angelica nobis promittitur, non carnis substantia negatur. Rectum ergo & catholicum est utrumque sexum in carnis resurrectione, sine sexus operibus resurrecturum confiteri: cum adhuc in hac vita positi nitamur cum Dei adjutorio, opera carnis, quæ contra spiritum concupiscit, non adimplere, probante hoc Apostolo ac dicente: Vos in carne non estis, sed in spiritu: Et iterum, Ergo fratres non sumus debitores carni, ut secundum carnem vivamus; negando vero eos in carne, quos in carne esse constabat, non carnis substantiam, sed peccata, id est, opera carnis damnavit; & iterum, Ut absorbeatur id quod mortale est à vita: quia licet exterior homo noster corrumpatur, interior tamen de die in diem renovatur, quod quidem non solum in regno cælorum & in baptismate, sed etiam in pœnitentibus quotidie fieri conspicimus, in quibus carnis interitus ad profectum cedit spiritualem. Ergo nec opera carnis erunt, nec augmenta membrorum, nec capillus crescet aut unguis, sed omnes in virum perfectum, qui Christus est, & in mensuram ætatis plenitudinis ejus resurgemus; nec mirum, nam si patribus in eremo constituti per quadraginta annos, non capilli, non ungues creverunt, aut calceamenta attrita sunt: in regno cælorum ubi aufugiet dolor, & gemitus & tristitia, hujusmodi modi quaeruntur? Hoc quàm impium sit, fidelis quisquè intelligit. Hæc Ambr. Tract. in Symbol. c. 24.
units.tr: As the angels of God in heaven. That is, they will be like the heavenly angels, or equal to the blessed angels in immortality and happiness. A likeness to the angels is promised us; the substance of the flesh is not denied. It is therefore right and catholic to confess that both sexes will rise in the resurrection of the flesh without the works of sex, since, while still placed in this life, we strive with God's help not to fulfil the works of the flesh, which lusts against the spirit; the Apostle proves this when he says: "You are not in the flesh, but in the spirit"; and again, "So then, brethren, we are not debtors to the flesh, to live according to the flesh." In denying that those were in the flesh who were known to be in the flesh, he condemned not the substance of the flesh but the sins, that is, the works of the flesh; and again: "that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life"; for although our outward man is corrupted, yet the inner man is renewed day by day. This we see happen not only in the kingdom of heaven and in baptism, but also daily in penitents, in whom the destruction of the flesh turns to spiritual progress. Therefore there will be no works of the flesh, nor growth of the limbs, nor hair or nails growing; but we shall all rise to the perfect man, who is Christ, and to the measure of the age of the fullness of Him. Nor is this surprising: for if the fathers who lived in the wilderness for forty years had neither hair nor nails grow, nor their shoes worn out, then in the kingdom of heaven, where sorrow and groaning and sadness flee away, why should such things be sought? How impious this is, every faithful person understands.* These are the words of Ambrose, Tractate on the Creed, chapter 24.

units.la: 32: Non est Deus mortuorum, sed viventium. Addit Lucas cap. 20. v. 38. Omnes enim viuunt ei, scilicet Deo, qui brevi eos excitaturus est à morte. Non probat Christus resurrectionem mortuorum, spem Christianorum, expressis Scripturæ verbis, sed argumentationem & consequentiam adhibet; idem contra hæreticos adhuc faciendum sæpissimè, dum evidentes S. Scripturæ phrases in alienum sensum detortas eripere nobis conantur: genuinus sensus collatione & argumentatione tunc eruendus atque affruendus est. Sapienter autem Christus ex dictis Mosis infert resurrectionem contra Saducæos, qui per Mosem conabantur dogma de Resurrectione destruere. Vis autem Dominicæ argumentationis in hoc consistit, quòd Abraham, Isaac, & Jacob non sunt nomina animarum, sed personarum seu suppositorum corpore & animâ constantium, ut observant Irenæus Chrysost. Theophylac. & Euthym. & viventes, cùm de hominibus sermo est, dicuntur qui corpore & animâ unitis vivunt. Itaque cùm dicatur Deus Abraham, Isaac, & Jacob, & Deus dicatur tantùm viventium, necesse est Abraham, Isaac, & Jacob vivere Deo, cui futura hominum resurrectio præsens est.
units.tr: 32: God is not the God of the dead, but of the living. Luke adds in chapter 20, verse 38: For all live unto him, that is, unto God, who will shortly raise them from death. Christ does not prove the resurrection of the dead, the hope of Christians, by the express words of Scripture, but by argument and inference. This should often be done against heretics too, when they try to snatch away from us the plain phrases of Holy Scripture and twist them to another sense. The genuine sense must then be drawn out and secured by comparison and argument. Christ wisely infers the resurrection from the words of Moses against the Sadducees, who tried to destroy the doctrine of the resurrection by means of Moses. The force of the Lord's argument lies in this: that Abraham, Isaac and Jacob are not names of souls but of persons, that is, of subjects consisting of body and soul. Irenaeus, Chrysostom, Theophylact and Euthymius observe this, and when we speak of men, those are called living who live with body and soul united. So since God is called the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and God is called the God only of the living, it follows that Abraham, Isaac and Jacob live to God, to whom the future resurrection of men is present.

units.la: 37. Diliges Dominum Deum tuum, &c. Dilectio est actus voluntatis, quæ hic significatur per cor: nam sicut cor corporale est principium omnium corporalium motuum; ita etiam voluntas (& maximè quantùm ad intentionem finis ultimi, quia est objectum charitatis) est principium omnium spiritualium motuum. Tria autem sunt principia actuum quæ moventur à voluntate; scilicet intellectus, qui significatur per mentem; vis appetitiva inferior, quæ significatur per animum; & vis executiva exterior, quæ significatur per fortitudinem, seu virtutem, sive vires. Præcipitur ergo nobis ut tota nostra intentio feratur in Deum, quod est ex toto corde; & quod intellectus noster subdatur Deo, quod est ex tota mente; & quod appetitus noster reguletur secundum Deum, quod est ex tota anima; & quod exterior actus noster obediat Deo, quod est ex tota fortitudine vel virtute, vel totis viribus Deum diligere. Auct. oper. imperf. Hom. 42. in Matth. Ex toto, inquit, corde ut cor tuum ad alterius dilectionem non magis inclinatum sit; in tota anima ut intellectus firmus in fide, nil boni alibi quærat quàm in Deo; in tota mente ut sensus omnes Deo vacent. Aug. 1. de Doctrina Christiana c. 22. refert cor ad cogitationes, animam ad vitam, mentem ad intellectum. Quidam etiam dicunt, ex toto corde, id est, intellectu; anima, id est, voluntate; mente, id est, memoriâ. Vel secundum Greg. Nyss. lib. de hominis opificio c. 8. per cor significat animam vegetabilem; per animam, sen̉sitivam; mentem, intellectivam; quia hoc quod nutrimur, sentỉmus & intelligimus, debemus ad Deum referre. D. Th. 22. q. 44. art. 5.
units.tr: 37. Thou shalt love the Lord thy God, etc. Love is an act of the will, which is signified here by the heart. For just as the bodily heart is the source of all bodily motions, so the will (especially as regards the intention of the final end, since it is the object of charity) is the source of all spiritual motions. There are three sources of the acts that are moved by the will: the intellect, signified by the mind; the lower appetitive power, signified by the soul; and the outward executive power, signified by strength, or power, or might. We are therefore commanded that our whole intention be directed toward God, which is "with the whole heart"; that our intellect be subject to God, which is "with the whole mind"; that our appetite be governed according to God, which is "with the whole soul"; and that our outward action obey God, which is "with all strength, or power, or might," to love God. The author of the unfinished work on Matthew, Homily 42: "With the whole heart," he says, so that your heart is not inclined more to the love of anything else; "with the whole soul," so that the intellect, firm in faith, seeks no good elsewhere than in God; "with the whole mind," so that all the senses are free for God. Augustine, On Christian Doctrine, book 1, chapter 22, refers the heart to thoughts, the soul to life, and the mind to understanding. Some also say: "with the whole heart," that is, with the understanding; "with the soul," that is, with the will; "with the mind," that is, with the memory. Or, according to Gregory of Nyssa, On the Making of Man, chapter 8, the heart signifies the vegetative soul; the soul, the sensitive soul; the mind, the intellective soul, because we ought to refer to God what we are nourished by, what we feel, and what we understand. Thomas Aquinas, Summa II-II, question 44, article 5.

units.la: 39. Secundum autem simile est huic. Officio, quia similiter dilectionem præcipit; amplitudine, quia universa secundæ tabulæ præcepta continet, sicut maximum & primum mandatum.
units.tr: 39. And the second is like unto it. It is like in its character, because it likewise commands love; and in its scope, because it contains all the precepts of the second table, just as the first and greatest commandment does.

units.la: Diliges proximum tuum sicut teipsum. Id est, sicut teipsum amare debes, quia justus es, aut ut justus sis, ita & proximum, id est, quosvis homines, aut quia justi sunt, aut ut justi sint, amare debes; & sicut teipsum non propter te debes diligere, sed propter illum ubi dilectionis tuæ rectissimus finis est, ita & proximum ut rectè diligas, hoc cumeo debes agere, ut etiam ipse toto corde diligat Deum, sicque ipsum propter Deum diliges. Vide Aug. 1. de Doctrina Christiana cap. 22. & 8. de Trinit. cap. 6. Apposite etiam in hanc rem Divus Bernardus Sermone 50. in Cantic. Qui te non diligit nisi quia diligit Deum, consequenter omnes qui similiter diligunt eum, diligit tanquam teipsum. Porro inimicum hominem, quoniam nihili est, pro eo quod non diligit Deum, non potes quidem diligere tanquam teipsum, qui Deum diligit: diliges tamen ut diligat. Non est autem idipsum diligere ut diligat, & diligere quia diligit. Proinde ut tibi & ipse sapiat prout est, sapiat tibi non quidem quod est, qui utique nihili est, sed quod si-turus forsitan est, quod est prope nihili, quippe quod adhuc perdet sub dubio. Etenim de quo constat quod ad amorem Dei non sit deinceps rediturus, sapiat tibi necesse est non prope jam nihil, sed nihil ex toto, utpote quod in æternum nihili est. Illo igitur excepto qui non modò jam non diligendus, insuper & odio habendus est, secundum illud: Nónne qui oderunt te Domine oderam, & super inimicos tuos tabescebam? de cetero nulli vel inimicissimo homini negari quantulumcunque affectum charitas sanè parte ambitiosa permittit.
units.tr: Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. That is, you ought to love yourself as one who is righteous, or so that you may be righteous, and in the same way you ought to love your neighbour, that is, any men whatever, either because they are righteous or so that they may be. And just as you ought to love yourself not for your own sake but for the sake of that most right end of your love, so, in order to love your neighbour rightly, you must act in such a way that he too loves God with his whole heart, and so you will love him for God's sake. See Augustine, On Christian Doctrine, chapter 22, and On the Trinity, book 8, chapter 6. Bernard also says aptly to this point, Sermon 50 on the Song of Songs: He who loves you only because he loves God, consequently loves all who likewise love him as himself. But an enemy, since he is nothing, because he does not love God, you cannot indeed love as yourself, since you love God; yet you will love him so that he may love God. Yet to love that he may love is not the same as to love because he loves. Therefore, that he may savour to you as he is, let him savour to you not as he is, for he is indeed nothing, but as he perhaps will be, which is nearly nothing, since he will still perish under doubt. For of one about whom it is certain that he will not return to the love of God from now on, it is necessary that he savour to you not nearly nothing, but wholly nothing, since he is nothing for ever. Therefore, excepting him who is not only no longer to be loved, but moreover to be hated, according to that: "Do I not hate them, O Lord, that hate thee? and am I not grieved with those that rise up against thee?" For the rest, charity, in its ambitious part, permits to no man, however much an enemy, however small an affection.

units.la: 40. Universa Lex pendet & Prophetæ. Id est, ad duo hæc præcepta, quæcunque in Lege & in Prophetis continentur, veluti ad finem referuntur; finis enim Legis dilectio est. Aureambanc Christi responsionem magnificè comprobavit Legis Doctor, qui primò ipsum interrogaverat tentandi animo, ut Marcus testatur cap. 12. v. 32, & 33.
units.tr: 40. On these two hang all the law and the prophets. That is, all the things contained in the Law and the Prophets are referred to these two precepts as to their end, for the end of the Law is love. The lawyer, who had first questioned him with the intent of testing him, greatly confirmed Christ's answer, as Mark records in chapter 12, verses 32 and 33.

units.la: 42. Quid vobis videtur, &c. Matthæus sic rem narrat quasi Christus ad Scribas aut Pharisæos sermonem direxerit. Marcus vero & Lucas quasi ad plebem. Res eadem est. Quis Evangelistarum verborum proprietatem tenuerit, Incertum; illud autem certum, quod Judæi Christum filium David tantummodò opinabantur, ignorantes excellentiam, quâ Dominus est ipsius Dávid, secundum id quod est Filius Dei, ut Aug. testatur in expositione inchoata in Ep. ad Rom initio, lib. 2. contra adversarium Legis & Prophetarum cap. 2. & in fine Psal. 9. Unde ut idem asserit lib. de Catechis. rud. cap. 21. non desiderabant Judæi Jesum qui salvaret populum suum à peccatis eorum, sed qui restitueret regnum ad exteros devolutum Israeli, eúmque à visibilibus hostibus tueretur. Ab hujusmodi opinione ac desiderio carnali tanquam reliquiis fictitiæ traditionis sibi cum lacte instillatæ necdum plene Apostoli erant liberati, quando paulo antequam acciperent virtutem Spiritûs Sancti in ipsos supervenientis sacratissimâ die Pentecostes à Christo, cujus jam Divinitas & immortalitas eis innotuerat, tamen interrogabant Act. 1. v. 6. Domine, si in tempore hoc restitues regnum Israël?
units.tr: 42. What think ye? etc. Matthew relates the matter as though Christ had addressed his speech to the scribes or Pharisees, while Mark and Luke relate it as though to the people. The matter is the same. Which of the evangelists kept the exact wording is uncertain, but this is certain: the Jews believed Christ to be only the son of David, ignorant of the excellence by which the Lord is David's Lord, according to what he is as the Son of God. Augustine attests this in his unfinished exposition of the Epistle to the Romans at the beginning, in book 2 against the adversary of the Law and the Prophets, chapter 2, and at the end of Psalm 9. Hence, as he also states in On the Catechising of the Uninstructed, chapter 21, the Jews did not desire a Jesus who would save his people from their sins, but one who would restore to Israel the kingdom that had passed to foreigners and would protect it from visible enemies. The Apostles were not yet fully freed from this opinion and carnal desire, as from the remnants of a fictitious tradition that had been poured into them with their milk, even when, shortly before receiving the power of the Holy Spirit that came upon them from Christ on the most sacred day of Pentecost, whose divinity and immortality were by then known to them, they still asked: Lord, wilt thou at this time restore again the kingdom to Israel? (Acts 1:6)

units.la: 44. Dixit Dominus Domino meo. Nempe Deus Pater, qui in textu Hebraeo exprimitur per nomen ineffabile, dixit Messiæ, quem David Dominum suum vocat, licèt sit ipsius filius, quia & ipsius Deus est, ac Salvator.
units.tr: 44. The Lord said unto my Lord. Namely, God the Father, who in the Hebrew text is expressed by the ineffable name, said to the Messiah, whom David calls his Lord, although he is David's son, because he is also God and Saviour of David.

units.la: Sede à dextris meis. A Regibus sumta est metaphora, quibus heres proximus dexter assidebat; is qui deinde sequebatur, sinister. Sic & heredis nomen Christo tribuitur. Paulus quod Psaltes dixit, Sedere à dextris meis, interpretatus est in Ep. 1. ad Cor. cap. 15. v. 25. per verbum, regnare. Igitur, sede à dextris meis, idem est ac, sis consors regni mei, gloriæ meæ & omnium bonorum meorum, & ut talis cognoscaris. Sic sponsa ad dextram Regis, ut consors regni ac potestatis collocatur Psal. 44. v. 12. Salomon Rex matrem honoris ergò ad dextram suam jussit sedere 3 Reg. 2. v. 19. Porro, inquit B. Joannes Damascenus lib. 4. Orth. fid. cap. 2. Christum corporeo modo ad Dei & Patris dexteram sedere dicimus, nec tamen proinde localem Patris dextram esse affirmamus. Quî enim fieri possit, ut is qui circumscriptionis expers est, certam ac loco definitam dextram habeat? Dextra enim & sinistra iis demum conveniunt, quæ circumscribuntur. Quocirca per Paternæ dextræ vocabulum nihil aliud significamus, quàm Divinitatis honorem atque gloriam, in qua cùm Dei Filius ut Deus, ejusdémque cum Patre substantiâ ante secula esset, ad extremum incarnatus, corporeóque modo considet, in eandem nimirùm gloriam ascitâ ipsius carne. Unâ etenim eâdémque cum sua carne adoratione ab omnibus rebus conditis afficitur. Donec ponam inimicos tuos. Id est, donec adversarios tuos omnes tibi subjiciam. Donec autem pro infinito sumitur, ut sit sensus, sede semper, & inimici tui in sempiternum subjicientur pedibus tuis.
units.tr: Sit thou at my right hand. The metaphor is taken from kings, at whose right hand sat the heir next in line, while the one who followed sat at the left. So too the name of heir is given to Christ. Paul, in 1 Corinthians chapter 15, verse 25, interpreted what the Psalmist said, to sit at my right hand, by the word to reign. Therefore sit at my right hand means the same as: be a partner in my kingdom, my glory and all my goods, and be recognised as such. So the bride is placed at the king's right hand as a partner in kingdom and power (Psalm 44:12). King Solomon ordered his mother to sit at his right hand as a mark of honour (1 Kings 2:19). Moreover, says St John Damascene in book 4 of the Orthodox Faith, chapter 2, we say that Christ sits at the right hand of God and the Father in a bodily manner, yet we do not therefore affirm that the Father's right hand is local. For how could he who is free from circumscription have a fixed right hand defined by place? For right and left belong only to things that are circumscribed. Accordingly, by the term the Father's right hand we signify nothing other than the honour and glory of the Godhead, in which the Son of God, who as God and of one substance with the Father was before the ages, and who was at last incarnate, sits in a bodily manner, having taken his flesh into that same glory. For he is honoured with one and the same worship, together with his flesh, by all created things. Until I make thine enemies thy footstool. That is, until I subject all your adversaries to you. Until, however, is taken as indefinite, so that the sense is: sit always, and your enemies will be placed under your feet for ever.

units.la: 45. Quomodo Filius est? Quomodo non est verbum negantis, sed quaerentis; non enim Christus se negat esse Filium David, sed eo collimat, ut ipsum etiam Filium Dei agnoscant, atque adeo Davidis Dominum.
units.tr: 45. "How is he the Son?" The word "How" is not a word of denial but of inquiry; for Christ does not deny that he is the Son of David, but aims at this, that they should also acknowledge him as the Son of God, and so the Lord of David.

units.la: 46. Nemo poterat ei respondere verbum. Quod Matthaeus hic observat, Marcus subjecit responsioni ad quaestionem Saducaeorum; de omnibus tamen in universum, & non de una sola responsione verisimiliter dicitur. Ceterum ex hoc loco Evangelii constat certum fuisse apud Judaeos illius temporis, quod ille Psalmus à Davide scriptus fuerit de Messia, ut etiam apud veteres Rabbinos legere est, contra cavillationes recentiorum Rabbinorum, qui fabulantur scriptum esse de Abrahamo à Melchisedech, vel ab Eliezer ipsius servo, vel de Davide à covis.
units.tr: 46. "No one was able to answer him a word." Matthew notes this here, and Mark added it after the answer to the question of the Sadducees; yet it is probably said of all of them in general, and not of a single answer. Moreover, from this passage of the Gospel it is clear that it was a certainty among the Jews of that time that this Psalm was written by David about the Messiah, as may also be read among the ancient rabbis, against the cavils of the more recent rabbis, who invent fables that it was written about Abraham by Melchizedek, or by Abraham's servant Eliezer, or about David by the Covites.

units.la: CAPUT
units.tr: CHAPTER

units.la: CAPUT XXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIII.

units.la: 2. Super Cathedram, &c. Id est, Pharisæi & Scribæ Legem Mosis publicè & privatim interpretantur.
units.tr: 2. Upon the seat, etc. That is, the Pharisees and scribes interpret the Law of Moses publicly and privately.

units.la: 3. Quæcunque. Supple, ad Mosis, seu Legis Mosaicæ mentem. Q. d. Quod utile pro vobis acceperunt, ab eis quasi vestrum tollite, & in eis quasi suum dimittite, quod non habent ad lucrum vestrum, sed ad interitum suum. Greg. lib. 4. in 1 Reg. Huic dicto non est oppositum quod Dominus dicit supra c. 7. Numquid colligunt de spinis uvas? Licet enim malefacientes spinæ sint, & bona doctrina sit uva, uva tamen illa non nascitur ex illis spinis malefactorum. Hoc egregiè explicat Aug. in lib. de Pastoribus c. 10. his verbis. Non est illa uva spinarum, sed aliquando increscens sarmentum implicat se in sepem, & pendet uva inter densa spinarum, sed non surgit de radice spinarum. Tu si esurieris, & aliud non habes unde sumas, caute manum mitte ne lacereris a spinis: id est, ne facta imiteris malorum, & lege uvam inter spinas pendentem, sed de vite nascentem. Ad te perveniat botri alimentum, spinis servetur ignis tormentum.
units.tr: 3. Whatsoever. Supply: according to the mind of Moses, or of the Mosaic Law. That is to say: what they have received as useful for you, take up as if it were yours, and leave in them as their own what does not serve your gain but their ruin. Gregory, Book 4 on 1 Kings. What the Lord says above in chapter 7 does not contradict this saying: Do men gather grapes from thorns? For although thorns are evil, and sound teaching is a grape, that grape does not grow from those thorns of evildoers. Augustine explains this well in his book on Pastors, chapter 10, in these words: That grape is not of the thorns, but sometimes a shoot that grows up entangles itself in the hedge, and the grape hangs among the dense thorns, yet it does not rise from the thorns' root. If you are hungry and have nothing else from which to take food, put your hand out carefully, lest you be torn by the thorns: that is, lest you imitate the deeds of the wicked; and pick the grape hanging among the thorns, but growing from the vine. Let the nourishment of the cluster reach you; let the fire of torment be kept for the thorns.

units.la: Secundum verò opera, &c. Vult hæc sententia præcepta præsidentium ad Cathedram pertinentia obedienter impleri, etiam si tales sint, quales erant Pharisæi, non eos factiosâ conspiratione à suis sedibus temoveri. Si verò ea præcipiant quæ sint contra doctrinam Evangelicam vel Apostolicam, ibi non esse eis obediendum, exemplo docemur Pauli Apostoli, qui Petro sibi pralato non recte incedenti ad veritatem Evangelii in faciem restitit, non tamen abjecit. Ivo Carnotensis Antistes. Ep. 233.
units.tr: But do not do according to their works, etc. This saying wants the precepts of those who preside in the seat to be obeyed dutifully, even if they are such as the Pharisees were; it does not want them to be removed from their seats by a factious conspiracy. But if they command things contrary to the Evangelical or Apostolic doctrine, we are taught by the example of the Apostle Paul, that one must not obey them. Paul withstood Peter to his face, when Peter, who was set above him, was not walking uprightly toward the truth of the Gospel; yet he did not cast him off. Ivo of Chartres, bishop, Letter 233.

units.la: 4. Alligant, &c. Metaphorâ à jumentis sumtâ Christus significat Pharisæos nolle facere, imò declinare quæ ceteris observanda præcipiunt.
units.tr: 4. They bind, etc. By a metaphor taken from beasts of burden, Christ signifies that the Pharisees were unwilling to do, indeed shrank from doing, what they ordered others to observe.

units.la: Importabilia. Id est, portatu difficilia, ut habet textus Græcus.
units.tr: Hard to bear. That is, difficult to carry, as the Greek text has it.

units.la: 5. Phylacteria. Germanus frater meus Ludovicus de Compiegne de Veil in eruditis notis ad tractatum Majemonidis de apparatu Templi cap. 10. Phylacteria, inquit, sunt membranacea schedulæ duæ; quæ inscriptæ certis Legis divinæ capitibus thecis ex atrato corio includuntur. Insertis autem oblongis ex aluta ligulis Judæi diebus profestis id temporis, quo manutinas Deo preces fundunt, ad frontem alligant earum unam, & alteram ad lacertum lævi brachii e regione cordis. Putant enim Lege sancitum, ut bis velut fasciis caput obligent, manúsque eâ mente, ut intelligant quomodo pueri ad voluntatem parentum sese totos accommodent, ita sibi singendum esse corpus & animum ad nutum Dei, cunctasque suas actiones, ac cogitationes ad Legis præceptionem esse dirigendas. Et enim scriptum videmus Exod. 13. v. 16. Et erit quasi signum in manu tua, & quasi frontalia inter oculos tuos. Et magis etiam aperte Deut. 6. v. 8. Et ligabis ea quasi signum in manu tua, & erunt quasi frontalia inter oculos tuos. Frontalia ista textus Hebr. טוטפות nuncupat, quam vocem hujus rei solius ita propriam, ut alias sufquam & nunquam occurrat, Paraphrastes Chaldaicus expressit תפילין, quod passim interpretantur oratoria, in quo verbo latina consuetudo de via deflexit, eóque deducta est ut monumenta ad preces pertinentia significet. Atqui hoc vocabulo Chaldaico cunƈti tum Talmudistæ, tum reliqui scriptores Hebræi utentes ad frontale simul & manuale significanda libros totos referserunt. Eadem hæc monumenta Matthæus Phylactéria nominat, utpote quæ Legis observandæ memoriam usque custodiunt. Atque ut Judæorum quisque maximè est pietatis studiosus, aut haberi cupit, ita religionis insignia maximè laxa ad preces adhibet. Quod cùm videret Christus à Pharisæis fieri verè virtutis expertibus, jure eorum ostentationem bis verbis increpat: Dilatant enim phylactéria sua. De simbriis egimus alias.
units.tr: 5. Phylacteries. My brother Louis de Compiègne de Veil, in his learned notes to Maimonides' treatise on the furnishings of the Temple, chapter 10, says: Phylacteries are two small membranous slips, inscribed with certain passages of the divine Law and enclosed in cases of black leather. Inserted into them are narrow strips of calfskin. On weekdays, at the time when they offer their morning prayers to God, the Jews fasten one of these to the forehead and the other to the upper left arm, opposite the heart. They believe that the Law ordains that they bind these on the head and hands, as with bands, so that they may understand how children should wholly conform themselves to the will of their parents. In the same way, they hold, they must shape their body and mind to the will of God and direct all their actions and thoughts by the precept of the Law. And indeed we read in Exodus 13:16: And it shall be as a sign upon your hand, and as frontlets between your eyes. And more plainly still in Deuteronomy 6:8: And you shall bind them as a sign upon your hand, and they shall be as frontlets between your eyes. The Hebrew text calls these frontlets [טוטפות]. The Chaldee paraphrast renders this word, which occurs nowhere else and is used only of this thing, by [תפילין], which is commonly rendered "prayer-objects". In Latin usage this word has drifted from its meaning and come to signify the monuments connected with prayer. Yet all the Talmudists and other Hebrew writers, using this Chaldee word to mean both the frontlet and the hand-band, applied it to the whole books. Matthew names these same monuments phylacteries [φυλακτήρια], since they keep the memory of the Law to be observed. And just as each Jew is most zealous for piety, or wishes to be thought so, so he makes the greatest display of the badges of religion in his prayers. When Christ saw that the Pharisees, who were utterly lacking in true virtue, did this, he rightly rebuked their ostentation in these words: For they enlarge their phylacteries. We have discussed the fringes elsewhere.

units.la: 6. Amant autem primos recubitus, &c. Q. d. Amant lenocinia superbiæ, & in eis ipsorum amor se sistit, & hæret, neque pergit ulterius. Itaque salutari ab hominibus & dignitatum titulis appellari, & primo sedere loco in consessibus non est malum, sed potius bonum; hoc ipsum tamen amare propter se, tanquam peccatum & animi ægritudo à Christo reprehenditur. Ut enim ait Aug. in lib. contra Secundinum Manichæum c. 16. potest amari res bona amore non bono.
units.tr: 6. But they love the first places at feasts, etc. That is to say: they love the flatteries of pride, and their love stops and sticks in these, and does not go further. Thus to be greeted by men and called by titles of dignity, and to sit in the first place at gatherings, is not an evil but rather a good; yet to love this for its own sake, as a sin and a sickness of the mind, is rebuked by Christ. As Augustine says in his book against Secundinus the Manichaean, chapter 16: a good thing can be loved with a love that is not good.

units.la: In Cœnis. Id est, in conviviis, ut patet ex Luc. 2o. v. 6. Cœnæ autem dicuntur convivia, quia antiquis magis esse solebant Cœnæ, quam prandia, ut liberius possent sine curarum interpellatione protrahi. Hinc illud Apostoli in Ep. 1. ad Thessal. c. 5. v. 7. Qui ebrii sunt, noƈte ebrii sunt.
units.tr: At suppers. That is, at banquets, as is clear from Luke 14:16. Banquets are called suppers because among the ancients suppers were more usual than dinners, so that they could be drawn out more freely, without the interruption of cares. Hence the saying of the Apostle in 1 Thessalonians 5:7: Those who are drunk, are drunk by night.

units.la: 7. Rabbi. Hoc nomen paulò ante Christi adventum tribui cœpit in Palestina eruditione præstantibus, qui per impositionem manuum in Doƈtores, seu Magistros inaugurabantur. Judæi verò Babylonii suos Doƈtores non Rabbi רבי, & רב appellaverunt.
units.tr: 7. Rabbi. This title began to be given, shortly before Christ's coming, to those in Palestine who excelled in learning, and who were installed as Doctors or Masters by the laying on of hands. The Babylonian Jews, however, did not call their teachers Rabbi [רבי] and Rab [רב].

units.la: §. Nolite. Id est, non ambiatis.
units.tr: §. Do not. That is, do not seek.

units.la: Unus enim est magister vester, &c. Nec magister, nec pater vocandus est alius, nisi Deus pater & Dominus noster Iesus Christus. Pater, quia ex ipso sunt omnia. Magister quia per ipsum omnia: vel quoniam per dispensationem carnis ejus omnes reconciliati sumus Deo. Quaeritur quare adversum hoc praeceptum, Doctorem Gentium Apostolus se esse dixerit: aut quomodo vulgato sermone, maxime, in Palaestina & Aegypti monasteriis se invicem patres vocent? Quod sic solvitur: Aliud esse natura patrem vel magistrum, aliud indulgentia. Nos si hominem patrem vocamus, honorem aetati deferimus, non autorem nostrae offendimus vitae. Magister quoque dicitur ex consortio veri magistri. Et ne infinita replicem: quomodo unus per naturam Deus & unus Filius, non praejudicat ceteris ne per adoptionem dii vocentur & filii: ita & unus pater & magister, non praejudicat aliis, ut abusive appellentur patres & magistri. B. Hier. sic & Chrysost. Hom. 73. in Matth. in haec verba: Principatus appetitio, & cathedrae docendi raptus ut malorum omnium causa diligenter ad eruditionem discipulorum in medium profertur. Quid enim ait? Nolite vocari Rabbi: Unus enim est magister vester: Nec alter altero praestantior, quia nihil scit a se ipso. Et rursus, Neque patrem vocate super terram. Non ut neminem patrem vocent, sed ne ignorent quem praecipue patrem vocare oporteat. Nam quemadmodum nemo principaliter magister est, sic neque pater, praeter illum, qui tam magistrorum, quam patrum omnium causa est.
units.tr: For one is your Master, etc. "Nor is anyone to be called master or father except God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ: Father, because all things are from him; Master, because all things are through him; or because through the dispensation of his flesh we have all been reconciled to God. It is asked why the Apostle said he was the Teacher of the Gentiles, contrary to this precept; or how, in common speech, especially in the monasteries of Palestine and Egypt, monks call one another fathers. This is resolved thus: being a father or master by nature is one thing, and by indulgence another. If we call a man father, we pay honour to his age; we do not usurp the author of our life. A master is also so called from fellowship with the true Master. And not to multiply words without end: just as the one God by nature and the one Son do not prevent others from being called gods and sons by adoption, so the one Father and Master does not prevent others from being wrongly called fathers and masters." So Blessed Jerome; Chrysostom also, Homily 73 on Matthew, in these words: "The desire for primacy and the seizing of the chair of teaching are brought forward as the cause of all evils, to be carefully weighed for the instruction of disciples. For what does he say? Do not be called Rabbi, for one is your Master: nor is one of you more excellent than another, because he knows nothing of himself. And again, Do not call anyone father upon the earth. Not that no one is to be called father, but that they should not be ignorant of whom they ought chiefly to call father. For just as no one is master in the principal sense, so neither is anyone father, except him who is the cause of all masters and all fathers."

units.la: Fratres estis. Scilicet natura & disciplinatu.
units.tr: You are brethren. That is, both by nature and by discipline.

units.la: 13. Vae autem vobis Scribae & Pharisaei. Ex Luca 11. v. 39.
units.tr: 13. Woe to you, Scribes and Pharisees. From Luke 11. v. 39.

units.la: apparet prius Christum solos increpasse Pharisaeos, Scribas vero, cum per consequentiam haec ad se trahi posse viderent, illi dixisse, ut habetur ibidem v. 45. Magister haec dicens etiam contumeliam nobis facis. Unde aliunde adjectum videtur, quod habent Graeci Codices ibidem v. 44. Vae vobis Scribae & Pharisaei hypocritae. Merito itaque ibi in Vulgat. haec voces Scribae & Pharisaei hypocritae omittuntur. Matthaeus tamen ubique Scribas & Pharisaeos conjungit, quia, ut ex responso Christi apud Lucam patet, in utrumque quadrabat, quod in alterutros dixerat; nihilominus intelligere est ex Luca priora vae, in Pharisaeos proprie dicta, posteriora in Legis-peritos sive Scribas. Porro necesse est, cum Lucas commemoret loco citato ista vae dicta a Domino inter prandendum apud quemdam Pharisaeum, quae Matthaeus hoc loco commemorat, ut vel Dominus haec saepius dixerit, vel Matthaeus more suo ea conjunxerit verbis Christi, quae etsi alio tempore dicta, habebant cum iis quae tum a Domino dicebantur affiniaffinitatem. Quod enim narrat Lucas occasionem dedisse huic Scribarum & Pharisaeorum increpationi, & quod habet in fine, cum haec ad illos diceret, coepisse illos graviter insistere, satis indicant Lucam illa suo loco retulisse.
units.tr: It appears that Christ first rebuked only the Pharisees. The Scribes, seeing that these words could by inference be applied to them too, said, as is recorded in the same place, v. 45: "Master, in saying these things you insult us also." Hence it seems that the words "Scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites," which the Greek codices have at Luke 11. v. 44, were added from elsewhere, and so in the Vulgate these words "Scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites" are rightly omitted there. Matthew, however, everywhere joins the Scribes and Pharisees, because, as Christ's answer in Luke makes clear, what he had said against one of them applied to the other as well. Nevertheless one may understand from Luke that the first woes were properly aimed at the Pharisees, and the later ones at the lawyers or Scribes. Further, since Luke records in the place cited that these woes were spoken by the Lord at a meal in the house of a certain Pharisee, it is necessary either that the Lord said these things more than once, or that Matthew, in his manner, joined them to Christ's words which, though spoken at another time, had affinity with what the Lord was then saying. For that Luke tells that the occasion gave rise to this rebuke of the Scribes and Pharisees, and that at the end, when he said these things to them, they began to press him hard, sufficiently indicates that Luke related them in their proper place.

units.la: Claudite regnum coelorum, &c. Quia scilicet oppugnatis praedicationem meam, quà aperitur regnum coelorum, & vos utpote Legis-peritos decebat quasi indagantes Legem Moysis & dicta Prophetarum referare quodammodo populo Iudaeorum januas notitiae Christi; at hoc non facitis, sed contra derogantes miraculis meis, & contra mea dogmata clamantes abstulistis clavem scientiae, sicque non permittentes ut in me credant homines, eos, qui alias erant in regnum coelorum intraturi, non finitis. Ceterum hoc va apud Lucam ordine est ultimum & quasi solis Legis-peritis dictum refertur.
units.tr: Shut up the kingdom of heaven, etc. Because, namely, you oppose my preaching, by which the kingdom of heaven is opened. You, as lawyers, ought to be searching the Law of Moses and the sayings of the prophets, and so in some measure unlock for the Jewish people the doors of the knowledge of Christ. But you do not do this; on the contrary, you disparage my miracles and cry out against my teaching, and so you have taken away the key of knowledge. By not allowing men to believe in me, you keep out those who otherwise would have entered the kingdom of heaven. Moreover, in Luke this woe stands last in order and is recorded as said to the lawyers alone.

units.la: 14. Comeditis domos viduarum. Id est, exhauritis ac devoratis facultates viduarum.
units.tr: 14. You devour the houses of widows. That is, you drain and devour the wealth of widows.

units.la: Orationes longas orantes. Id est, sub obtentu prolixae orationis.
units.tr: Making long prayers. That is, under the pretext of lengthy prayer.

units.la: Amplius accipietis judicium. Id est, graviorem condemnationem subibitis.
units.tr: You will receive greater judgment. That is, you will undergo a heavier condemnation.

units.la: 15. Circuitis mare & aridam. Hebraismus, id est, circuitis universum terrarum orbem, seu, ut Latini aiunt, omnem movetis lapidem.
units.tr: 15. You compass sea and land. A Hebraism: that is, you go round the whole circuit of the earth, or, as the Latins say, you turn over every stone.

units.la: Ut faciatis unum proselytum. Proselyti vocabantur Graece, qui ex aliis nationibus progeniti in fidem & conjortium populi Dei, acceptâ circumcisione, transierant, ut ait B. Eucherius in libros Regum p. 11.
units.tr: To make one proselyte. Those were called proselytes in Greek who, born of other nations, had passed over into the faith and fellowship of the people of God by receiving circumcision, as the blessed Eucherius says in his books on Kings, p. 11.

units.la: Facitis eum filium gehennae duplo quàm vos. Desideratur magis ut in illo Plauti, Mulier taeita bona est, quàm loquax: & Taciti, Claris majoribus, quàm vetustis. Ratio autem hujus Christi assertionis est, quia proselyti à Pharisaeis facti, eorumdem malà vita & hypocrisi offensi, vel etiam gravi onere Legis cum adjuncto onere traditionum Pharisaicarum refiliebant à proposito & redibant ad Paganismum & veterem idololatriam, sicque apostatae facti saltem in hoc Pharisaeis pejores fiebant, & proinde acerbiorum supplicium rei.
units.tr: You make him a son of gehenna twice as much as yourselves. The word magis ("more") is to be understood, as in Plautus: "A silent woman is better than a talkative one," and in Tacitus: "Distinguished by famous ancestors rather than ancient ones." The reason for this assertion of Christ is that proselytes made by the Pharisees, offended by their wicked lives and hypocrisy, or even by the heavy burden of the Law together with the added burden of Pharisaic traditions, would leap back from their purpose and return to paganism and their old idolatry. Thus they became apostates, and in this respect at least were worse than the Pharisees, and therefore guilty of a harsher punishment.

units.la: 16. In altari. Id est, per altare.
units.tr: 16. By the altar. That is, through the altar.

units.la: 18. Nihil est. Id est, non debet.
units.tr: 18. It is nothing. That is, it ought not to be (i.e. it is not binding).

units.la: In dono. Id est, per donum, quod super altare offertur, scilicet per victimam ovis, bovis, similae, &c. Hoc juramenti genus familiare Iudaeis, eísque solis, dicebatur juramentum corban, ut testis est Josephus lib. 1. contra Appionem cap. 8.
units.tr: By the gift. That is, through the gift offered upon the altar, namely through the victim of a sheep, an ox, fine flour, and so on. This kind of oath, familiar to the Jews and to them alone, was called the oath corban, as Josephus testifies in book 1 against Apion, chapter 8.

units.la: Debet. Id est, peccat. Purus putus Chaldaismus. Hinc debita peccata, & debitores peccatores dicuntur.
units.tr: Owes. That is, sins. Pure and simple Chaldaism. Hence sins are called debts and sinners debtors.

units.la: 23. Qui decimatis mentham, &c. Id est, qui decimas datis omnium etiam vilissimorum, quæ possidetis; ponitur enim res definita pro indefinita. Lucas hoc, væ, recitat quasi solis Pharisæis dictum.
units.tr: 23. You who tithe mint, etc. That is, you who give tithes of all the things you possess, even the most worthless; for a definite thing is put for an indefinite. Luke recounts this woe as said to the Pharisees alone.

units.la: Hæc. Supple, quæ ultimo dixi, hoc est, quæ graviora sunt Legis, judicium, id est, justitiam, quâ cuique suum tribuitur, & misericordiam, quâ ex benignitate, quantùm possumus, proximo succurrimus, & fidem, quâ constantia servatur in promissis, oportuit facere, & illa, supple, minora, quæ tam accuratè servatis, non omittere, supple, quanto ita vobis lubet Legem interpretari.
units.tr: These things. Supply: which I have just mentioned, that is, the weightier matters of the Law: judgment, that is, justice, by which each is given his due; mercy, by which out of kindness we help our neighbour as far as we can; and faith, by which constancy is kept in promises. You ought to have done these; and those, supply: the lesser things, which you observe so scrupulously, not to omit, supply: however much you like to interpret the Law in that way.

units.la: 24. Excolantes culicem. Vinum apud Judæos in colo, vel in sudario percolare moris erat, ne culex vel aliud animalculum per Legem prohibitum, tanquam immundum ab incautis absorberetur, unde Græci interpretantur Amos 6. v. 6. Qui bibunt vinum percolatum, quod textus Hebræus & Vulgatus dicunt, Bibentes vinum in phialis; sed forte ibi Græci interpretes pro Hebræo [Hebrew], in phialis, ut redditur à B. Justin. in dialogo cum Tryphone Judæo, legerunt [Hebrew], in colo, supple, [Hebrew], percolatum. Talmudici in Tractatu de Sabbato cap. 10. sol. 139. B. & Majemonides in Tractatu de cibis vetitis cap. 2. meminerunt percolationis vini; & culices, qui excolando ejiciuntur, appellant [Hebrew], à radice [Hebrew], miscere, quia illi culices vino immixti sunt, & à Latinis appellantur vinulæ, seu vinarii culices. Addito epitheto vocantur ab Hebræis, rubri.
units.tr: 24. Straining out the gnat. Among the Jews it was customary to strain wine through a cloth or linen cloth, lest a gnat or another small creature forbidden by the Law as unclean should be swallowed unawares. Hence the Greeks interpret Amos 6. v. 6, "Who drink wine strained," where the Hebrew text and the Vulgate say, "Drinking wine in bowls." But perhaps there the Greek translators, reading for the Hebrew [Hebrew] "in bowls," as is rendered by Blessed Justin in his Dialogue with Trypho the Jew, read [Hebrew] "in a strainer," supplying [Hebrew] "strained." The Talmudists, in the tractate on the Sabbath, chapter 10, page 139 B, and Maimonides, in the treatise on forbidden foods, chapter 2, mention the straining of wine. They call the gnats that are removed by straining [Hebrew], from the root [Hebrew], "to mix," because those gnats are mixed into the wine. By the Latins they are called vinulae, or vinarii culices. With an added epithet the Hebrews call them red.

units.la: Camelum autem glutientes. Christi mens non est camelum posse deglutiri, sed minutias illas Legis, in quibus erant tam accurati Pharisæi, gravioribus quæ negligebant, tantò minores fuisse, quantò camelo minor est culex. Simili locutione Christus dixit suprà cap. 7. v. 5. Vides festucam in oculo fratris tui, & trabem in oculo tuo non vides: quia Christus non significat trabem in oculo posse latere, sed vitia illa, quorum alios arguunt hypocritæ, iis criminibus, qui in seipsis securè prætereunt, tanto esse minora, quanto festuca minor est trabe.
units.tr: But swallowing a camel. Christ's meaning is not that a camel can be swallowed, but that those minute points of the Law, in which the Pharisees were so precise, were as much smaller than the weightier things they neglected as a gnat is smaller than a camel. In a similar way Christ said above, in chapter 7, v. 5, "You see the speck in your brother's eye, but do not see the beam in your own eye": because Christ does not mean that a beam can lie hidden in the eye, but that those faults which the hypocrites charge upon others are as much smaller than the crimes of those who pass over their own sins lightly as a speck is smaller than a beam.

units.la: 25. Mundatu quod deforis est, &c. Objurgat Christus Pharisæos, quòd exteriori munditiei studentes, interiorem negligant, atque ut intelligerent sermonem parabolicum, statim transit ad proprium, intùs, inquiens, id est, in anima & conscientia pleni estiù rapinâ, id est, injustitiis, pauperum & viduarum oppressionibus, & immunditiâ peccatorum. Græcè tamen perfiftitur in metaphora; habetur enim, plena sunt, scilicet calix & paropsis, rapina & injustitia. Et sic perpetua est Allegoria, significans eos in animo plenissimos esse fraudibus & injustitia, exterius innocentes & sanctos.
units.tr: 25. Cleanse what is outside, etc. Christ rebukes the Pharisees because, while they study outward cleanness, they neglect the inner. So that they might understand the parabolic speech, he at once passes to the plain sense, saying within, that is, in the soul and conscience, they are full of rapine, that is, of injustices, oppressions of the poor and widows, and the uncleanness of sins. In Greek, however, the metaphor is kept up, for it reads they are full, namely the cup and the dish, of rapine and injustice. And so the allegory is continuous, signifying that inwardly they are most full of fraud and injustice, while outwardly they are innocent and holy.

units.la: 26. Pharisæi cæcè. Cæcitas cordis, si peccatum non effet, injuste hîc & alia plurimis divinorum eloquiorum locis argueretur, inquit Aug. lib. 1. op. imp. n. 48.
units.tr: 26. Blind Pharisees. "Blindness of heart, if it were not a sin, would be unjustly charged here, and in many other places of the divine words," says Augustine, book 1 of the Opus imperfectum, n. 48.

units.la: 29. Qui ædificatis sepulchra Prophetarum, &c. Non opus vituperat Christus, sed intentionem, qua affectant placere hominibus, dum ædificant sepulchra Prophetarum, & ornant monumenta justorum, quasi detestantes patrum suorum facinus; cùm ipsi tamen satis testentur se consentire operibus patrum suorum, quoniam quos patres eorum occiderunt, eorum ipsi ædificant sepulchra ambitione humanæ gloriæ, sicque quasi trophæum victoriæ parentum erigere videntur, si non animi scopus, sed mores eorum spectentur.
units.tr: 29. You who build the tombs of the prophets, etc. Christ does not condemn the work but the intention, by which they seek to please men while they build the tombs of the prophets and adorn the monuments of the righteous, as if detesting their fathers' crime. Yet they themselves sufficiently testify that they agree with the works of their fathers, since they build the sepulchres of those whom their fathers killed, out of ambition for human glory. So they seem to raise a trophy to the victory of their parents, if one looks not to the purpose of their minds but to their conduct.

units.la: 32. Et vos implete, &c. Q. d. Itaque vos implete, seu absolvite mensuram impietatis a patribus vestris inchoatam. Ironiam hanc explicat Christus per id quod mox addit sine ironia. Ceterum Deus non finit impietatem ac scelera in immensum crescere, sed singulis non tantùm hominibus, verùm & nationibus certum limitem statuit, quem non excedat, & quo cùm perveniret, turbinem indignationis suæ vel excisionis effundit, ut palàm tollat ex Gen. 15. v. 16.
units.tr: 32. And you, fill up, etc. That is: therefore fill up, or complete, the measure of impiety begun by your fathers. Christ expresses this irony by what he immediately adds, without irony. Moreover, God does not allow impiety and crimes to grow without limit, but sets a fixed boundary not only for individual men but for nations, which they may not exceed; and when they reach it, he pours out the storm of his indignation, or destruction, so as to remove them openly, as in Gen. 15. v. 16.

units.la: 34. Ideò. Scilicet quia estis pessimi filii pessimorum parentum & ad summum gradum seu terminum malitiam patrum vestrorum impleturi.
units.tr: 34. Therefore. That is, because you are the wicked sons of wicked parents, and are about to fill up the malice of your fathers to its highest degree or limit.

units.la: Ecce ego mitto, &c. Energiam hujus locutionis explicat Lucas, quando dicit suis, non Christi verbis: Propterea & Sapientia Dei, nempe ipse Jesus, dixit: Mittam ad illos Prophetas, id est, prophetiæ donoillustres, & sapientes, quorum sapientiæ non poterunt resistere, & Scribas, hoc est, Doctores, & Scripturarum interpretes.
units.tr: Behold, I send, etc. Luke explains the force of this expression when he says, in his own words rather than Christ's: Therefore also the Wisdom of God, namely Jesus himself, said: I will send to them prophets, that is, men distinguished by the gift of prophecy and wise, whose wisdom they will not be able to withstand, and scribes, that is, teachers and interpreters of the Scriptures.

units.la: 35. Ut veniat, &c. Id est, ut ita juxta merita scelerum vestrorum redundet in caput vestrum omnis sanguis justorum injuste effusus ab Abel, qui primus propter justitiam celebris necatus fuit, usque ad sanguinem Zachariæ filii Barachiæ. Hunc Zachariam plerique Græci & Baronius putant esse patrem Joannis Baptistæ, quem aiunt inter Templum & altare occisum, quòd cùm pueros occideret Herodes, filium non prodidisset, vel quòd Beatam Virginem Mariam prædicasset. Sed hanc sententiam ex apocryphorum commentis manasse dicit Hieronymus. Alii hunc Zachariam volunt esse eum, qui in duodecim Prophetis minoribus undecimus est, sed nullibi proditur, nec fit verisimile hunc fuisse occisum inter Templum & altare, cùm temporibus ejus Templum nondum fuerit reparatum. Ipse Hieronymus intelligit Zachariam filium Joiadæ, quem occisum inter Templum & altare, id est, in atrio Templi, Scripturæ tradunt. Dicitur autem hujus Zachariæ pater Barachias, vel quia binomius fuit, vel quia ratione sanctitatis sic fuit cognominatus, q. d. Benedictus Domini; vel denique quia Joiadæ pater vocabatur Achias, ita ut Barachias sit idem ac filius Achiæ. Sunt denique qui hic intelligunt Zachariam filium Baruch, quod idem est ac Barachias, quem Josephus lib. 5. de bello Jud. cap. 1. paulò ante novissimam obsidionem Jerosolymitanam à Judæis Zelotis in atrio Templi occisum, cùm vir probus ille à LXX. Judicibus unanimiter fuisset absolutus. Hi autem autores suspicantur Christum prophetice id quod futurum erat, veluti præteritum narrasse. Ut ut est, tota natio ut unus populus consideratur, in quo facta majorum tribuuntur filiis, & contrà; sic enim Abrahæ dicitur promissa & data terra Chanaan, sed in posteris ejus; sic Judæis tempore Judith viventibus tribuitur habitatio in Mesopotamia, descensus in Ægyptum, transitus per mare Rubrum & desertum, quæ in majoribus contigerant. Ratione unitatis istius, quà unus est populus, in quo posteri sunt aliquid majorum, & majores aliquid posterorum, fieri solet, quando filii opera majorum imitantur, & ita complent mensuram ab illis inchoatam, ut facta majorum filiis imputentur, & in illis quoque tum à Deo, tum ab hominibus compensentur, sive in bonum, sive in malum. Hinc Amalecitæ exciduntur propter facta parentum à quadringentis annis perpetrata 1 Sam. seu Reg. 15. v. 2, & 3. Jam si consideres vindictam illam, apparebit esse quidem peccatorum à parentibus commissorum; cùm nisi illa præcessissent, non fuisset infilicta; multò minus tam acerba. Non excedit tamen vindicta magnitudinem sceleris à solis filiis perpetrati, ut patet in atrocissimis Judæorum facinoribus perpetratis in occisione Christi & Apostolorum, & Ecclesiæ persecutione.
units.tr: 35. That there may come, etc. That is, so that, in accordance with the deserts of your wicked deeds, all the innocent blood unjustly shed from Abel, who was the first to be killed for righteousness' sake and is famous for it, down to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, may fall back on your head. Many of the Greeks and Baronius think this Zechariah was the father of John the Baptist, whom they say was killed between the Temple and the altar because, when Herod was slaughtering the boys, he would not betray his son, or because he had preached concerning the Blessed Virgin Mary. But Jerome says this opinion flowed from the fictions of the apocryphal writings. Others want this Zechariah to be the one who is eleventh among the twelve Minor Prophets, but nowhere is this recorded, nor is it likely that this man was killed between the Temple and the altar, since in his time the Temple had not yet been rebuilt. Jerome himself understands Zechariah son of Jehoiada, whom the Scriptures record as killed between the Temple and the altar, that is, in the court of the Temple. Now this Zechariah's father is called Barachiah, either because he had two names, or because he was so surnamed on account of his holiness, as if to say "Blessed of the Lord"; or finally because the father of Jehoiada was called Achiah, so that Barachiah would be the same as the son of Achiah. There are also those who understand here Zechariah son of Baruch, which is the same as Barachiah, whom Josephus, in book 5 of the Jewish War, chapter 1, records as killed by the Zealots of the Jews in the court of the Temple shortly before the last siege of Jerusalem, although that upright man had been unanimously acquitted by the seventy judges. These authors suppose that Christ, speaking prophetically, narrated as past what was yet to happen. Be that as it may, the whole nation is regarded as one people, in which the deeds of the forefathers are attributed to the sons, and conversely. Thus the land of Canaan is said to have been promised and given to Abraham, but to his descendants; thus the dwelling in Mesopotamia, the descent into Egypt, and the passage through the Red Sea and the desert are attributed to the Jews living in the time of Judith, though these things had happened to their forefathers. Because of this unity, by which they are one people, in which the posterity has something of the forefathers and the forefathers something of the posterity, it commonly happens, when the sons imitate the works of their forefathers and so fill up the measure begun by them, that the deeds of the forefathers are imputed to the sons, and that in them they are repaid, both by God and by men, whether for good or for evil. Hence the Amalekites were destroyed for the deeds of their ancestors, committed four hundred years earlier (1 Sam., or 1 Kings, 15:2, 3). Now if you consider that vengeance, it will appear to be indeed on account of sins committed by the parents; for unless those had preceded, it would not have fallen, much less so severely. Yet the vengeance does not exceed the magnitude of the crime committed by the sons alone, as is evident in the most atrocious deeds of the Jews perpetrated in the killing of Christ and the Apostles, and in the persecution of the Church.

units.la: 37. Jerusalem, &c. Quod Matthæus hic refert quasi dictum post triumphalem Christi in Jerusalem ingressum, Lucas cap. 13. memorat à Christo dictum adversus Jerusalem, cùm adhuc esset in ditione Herodis, nempe in Peræa trans Jordanem; unde cùm verisimile non sit id à Christo bis pronuntiatum, vel Lucas anticipavit, vel Matthæus quod prius à Christo dictum fuerat, in seruit iis, quæ referebat à Christo dicta in Pharisæos propter argumenti similitudinem.
units.tr: 37. Jerusalem, etc. What Matthew here reports as said after Christ's triumphal entry into Jerusalem, Luke in chapter 13 records as said by Christ against Jerusalem while he was still under the rule of Herod, namely in Perea beyond the Jordan. Since it is not likely that Christ pronounced this twice, either Luke anticipated, or Matthew, because of the similarity of subject, inserted what Christ had said earlier into the words he was recording as said by Christ against the Pharisees.

units.la: Quoties volui, &c. Voluntas Dei ex Scripturis sacris recte distinguitur in voluntatem, signi & voluntatem beneplaciti. Voluntas signi seu voluntas metaphoricè de Deo dicitur, quando ea facit, quæ in nobis solent esse signa volendi, ut loquitur D. Th. I. p. q. 19. Art. 11. ad 2. licèt non sint signa quod Deus velit: sicut punitio non est signum quod in Deo sit ira, sed punitio eò ipso quod in nobis est signum ira, in Deo dicitur ira. Sic Marc. 6. dicitur de Christo vidente discipulos laborantes in remigando, quod volebat præterire eos, qui tamen non præterivit, sed voluisse dicitur voluntate signi, quia illud faciebat, quod signum esset in nobis voluntatis prætereundi, quia in diversum ibat, ut Aug. interpretatur lib. 2. de Conf. Evang. c. 47. Similiter Marc. 7. de Christo abeunte in fines Tyri & Sidonis dicitur: Et ingressus domum neminem voluit scire: quia domum latenter fuit ingressus, ac forte etiam jussit fores occludi, quod dum faciunt homines, signum esse solet quod latere velint. Sic Luc. 24. de Christo dicitur quod finxit se longius ire, quia nempe progressus fuit aliquantulum tanquam discessurus & longius iturus homo. Eodem modo dicitur Exod. 4. Dominus voluisse occidere Moysem, & alibi voluisse dispergere populum suum, quod videlicet fecisset quæ hujusmodi actionum præparationes esse solent. Hunc loquendi modum confirmat non modo frequens modus loquendi Scripturæ sacræ, sed etiam vulgaris vulgi sermocinatio; in qua frequenter occurrunt hujusmodi formulæ, hic homo vult perire, hæc domus vult cadere, cœlum vult pluere, quia nempe quæ in hominibus præparationes solent esse signa voluntatis, simpliciter aliquando voluntates dicuntur; sic passim signum nomine rei significatæ appellatur.
units.tr: As often as I wished, etc. The will of God is rightly distinguished in Scripture into the will of sign and the will of good pleasure. The will of sign is spoken of God metaphorically when he does those things which in us are wont to be signs of willing, as Thomas Aquinas says, Part I, question 19, article 11, reply 2: although they are not signs that God wills; just as punishment is not a sign that anger is in God, but punishment, by the very fact that in us it is a sign of anger, is said in God to be anger. So in Mark 6 it is said of Christ, seeing his disciples labouring at the rowing, that he wished to pass by them; yet he did not pass by, but is said to have wished it by the will of sign, because he was doing what in us would be a sign of the will to pass by, because he was going in the opposite direction, as Augustine interprets in book 2 of the Harmony of the Gospels, chapter 47. Similarly in Mark 7, of Christ departing into the regions of Tyre and Sidon, it is said: And when he had entered a house, he wished that no one should know; because he entered the house secretly, and perhaps even ordered the doors to be shut, which, when men do it, is usually a sign that they wish to be hidden. So in Luke 24 it is said of Christ that he pretended to go further, because he had indeed proceeded a little, as a man about to depart and go farther would do. In the same way it is said in Exodus 4 that the Lord wished to kill Moses, and elsewhere that he wished to scatter his people, that is, he did what the preparations for such actions are usually. This manner of speaking is confirmed not only by the frequent usage of holy Scripture but also by the common talk of the people, in which such formulas frequently occur: this man wants to perish, this house wants to fall, the sky wants to rain; because, namely, what in men are usually the preparations and signs of the will are sometimes simply called wills; so a sign is everywhere named by the name of the thing signified.

units.la: Voluntas beneplaciti seu voluntas proprie dicta, quæ est proprie & formaliter in Deo secundum D. Th. loco mox laudato & in quæst. difp. q. 23. de voluntate Dei art 2. per antecedentem & consequentem dividitur. Voluntas beneplaciti antecedens, sic dicta, quia præcedit considerationem rerum in particulari, nihil aliud est quàm velleitas quædam respiciens res in generali, ex qua nullus effectus sequitur. Voluntas beneplaciti consequens est vera & simpliciter dicta voluntas, quæ fertur in res ut sunt in se ipsis & secundum suas circumstantias particulares, & ex hac voluntate procedit omnis effectus justitiæ & misericordiæ divinæ. His observatis jam varias afferimus expositiones textûs Evangelici, quo de nunc agimus.
units.tr: The will of good pleasure, or the will properly so called, which is properly and formally in God according to the same Thomas in the place just cited and in the disputed questions, question 23, article 2, on the will of God, is divided into antecedent and consequent. The antecedent will of good pleasure is so called because it precedes the consideration of things in particular; it is nothing other than a certain mere inclination regarding things in general, from which no effect follows. The consequent will of good pleasure is the true will, and properly so called, which is directed to things as they are in themselves and according to their particular circumstances, and from this will proceeds every effect of divine justice and mercy. With these points noted, we now set out various expositions of the Gospel text with which we are now dealing.

units.la: Sunt
units.tr: Some.

units.la: Sunt qui velint Christum loqui de voluntate beneplaciti antecedenti. Sed haec expositio stare non potest, cum Christus dicat quoties volui, voluntas autem antecedens semper eadem perseveret. Deinde Christus significat effectum hujus voluntatis, qua voluit congregare filios Jerusalem, fuisse missionem Prophetarum; at ex voluntate antecedenti nullus effectus sequitur, sed sola voluntas consequens, quae est simpliciter voluntas, producit omnem effectum, ut pote quae sola considerat res ut sunt in se ipsis & secundum suas circumstantias particulares.
units.tr: Some wish Christ to speak of the antecedent will of good pleasure.
