But this exposition cannot stand, since Christ says as often as I wished, whereas the antecedent will always remains the same. Further, Christ signifies that the effect of this will, by which he wished to gather the children of Jerusalem, was the sending of the Prophets; but from the antecedent will no effect follows, only the consequent will, which is simply the will, produces every effect, since it alone considers things as they are in themselves and according to their particular circumstances.

units.la: Aug. in Enchir. c. 97. intelligit hunc locum de voluntate, quam D. Th. vocat consequentem, ita ut sensus Christi sit, quasi diceret se non obstante repugnantia impiae civitatis collegisse filios ejus absoluta voluntate, qua omnia quaecunque vult facit. Impios tamen cives puniendos, quod quantum in ipsis erat, relucta-ti fuerint Christo, ne, quos volebat, congregaret. Eandem expositionem tradit in Epist. 106. ad Paulinum & lib. 1. op. imperf. num. 19. Sed obstat quod Ezech. 24. Dominus simili exprobratione dixit ad eandem civitatem, Mundare te volui, & non es mundata a sordibus tuis; inde enim apparet etiam hoc loco Dominum significare non esse factum, quod se voluisse dicit.
units.tr: Augustine, in the Enchiridion, chapter 97, understands this passage of the will which Thomas calls consequent, so that the sense of Christ is as if he said that, notwithstanding the opposition of the impious city, he had gathered its children by an absolute will, by which he does whatever he wills. Yet the impious citizens were to be punished, because, as far as lay in them, they had resisted Christ, so that he might not gather those whom he wished to gather. He gives the same exposition in Epistle 106 to Paulinus and in book 1 of the Unfinished Work, number 19. But this is opposed by the fact that in Ezekiel 24 the Lord, with a similar reproach, said to the same city, "I wished to cleanse you" and "you were not cleansed from your filthiness"; from this it appears that here too the Lord signifies that what he says he wished did not happen.

units.la: Quidam sic exponunt, volui ex mea parte, sed noluistis ex vestra, qui sensus legitur in Hom. quadam Hieronymi titulo inter Homilias Patrum in festo B. Stephani; sed licet haec Homilia sumta sit ex Comment. Hier. in Matth. praefata tamen verba apud eum non habentur, licet tolerari possint, si intelligantur de vellejtate humanitatis Christi, & affectu naturali, quo sacro-sancta humanitas erat in filios Jerusalem misericorditer commota. Hunc sensum subindicat Hier. Esa. 1. & hanc naturalem voluntatem in Christo agnoscit sexta Synodus Oecumenica, & in ea lecta & approbata Ep. Agathonis Papae, in qua leguntur aliquae Scripturae huc pertinentes. Verum huic expositioni repugnat id quod Christus ait, quoties volui, quodque ante dixerat, quae occidis Prophetas & lapidas eos qui ad te missi sunt; per hoc enim, ut observat Hier. significat praedicatores omnium superiorum temporum a se fuisse missos, atque ita voluisse multoties congregare filios Jerusalem, non tantum eo tempore, quo in carne versabatur, sed jam olim tempore Prophetarum, atqui tunc non potuit Christus voluisse humana voluntate, quia naturam humanam nondum assumserat.
units.tr: Some explain it thus: "I was willing on my part, but you were unwilling on yours." This sense is read in a homily of Jerome under the title among the Homilies of the Fathers on the feast of St Stephen. But although this homily was taken from Jerome's commentary on Matthew, those words are not found in it there. They could nevertheless be tolerated, if they are understood of the wish of Christ's humanity and the natural affection by which his most holy humanity was mercifully moved towards the sons of Jerusalem. Jerome hints at this sense on Isaiah 1, and the Sixth Ecumenical Synod acknowledged this natural will in Christ, together with the letter of Pope Agatho which was read and approved there, in which some passages of Scripture pertaining to this are cited. Yet this explanation is contradicted by what Christ says, "how often I wished," and by what he had said before, "you who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you." For by this, as Jerome observes, he signifies that preachers of all the earlier times had been sent by him, and so that he had many times wished to gather the sons of Jerusalem, not only at the time when he was living in the flesh, but already long ago in the time of the Prophets. But Christ could not have wished this with a human will, since he had not yet assumed human nature.

units.la: SS. Hilarius & Hieronymus intelligunt de voluntate signi hunc locum, ita ut Christus velit loqui de praeceptis, exhortationibus, correptionibus, aliísque mediis ad salutem opportunis, quæ per Moysem aliósque Prophetas illi populo fuerunt à Deo subministrata, quæ tamen omnia populus ingratus & in peccatis obduratus rejecit atque contemsit.
units.tr: Saints Hilary and Jerome understand this passage of the will of the sign, so that Christ means to speak of the precepts, exhortations, corrections, and other means suited to salvation, which were supplied by God to that people through Moses and the other Prophets. Yet the ungrateful people, hardened in sins, rejected and despised all of these.

units.la: Omnium optima & ad literam accommodatissima est expositio D. Thomæ in opusculo de præscientia & prædestinatione, ut Christus dicatur voluisse congregare filios Jerusalem, quia Prophetis & sanctis à se missis pium hoc desiderium inspiraverat, sed impia civitas semper frustrata est pios eorum conatus. Hic sensus congruit & loco citato ex Ezech. ubi etiam proximè præcedunt hæc verba: Multo labore sudatum est, & non exivit de ea nimia rubigo ejus, neque per ignem: quæ verba satis indicant intelligi labores Propretarum voluntatem Dei annuntiantium & ignem tribulationis.
units.tr: The best of all, and the most suited to the letter, is the explanation of St Thomas in his little work on foreknowledge and predestination: that Christ is said to have wished to gather the sons of Jerusalem, because he had inspired this pious desire in the Prophets and saints whom he sent, but the impious city always frustrated their pious efforts. This sense also agrees with the passage of Ezekiel cited above, where the following words immediately precede: "The labour has been sweated through, and its great rust has not gone out of it, neither by fire." These words sufficiently indicate that the labours are to be understood as those of the Prophets announcing the will of God, and the fire as tribulation.

units.la: Gallina. Græcè ὄρνις, quæ vox Homero & Hesiodo cùm nihil sit aliud quam avis in genere, Platonis ævo cœpit usurpari pro gallinaceo in genere, & per aliquot secula tam de gallo, quàm de gallina dici, donec obtinuit usus, ut proprium esset gallinæ nomen. Unde apud Athenæum lib. 9. Myrtulus ait: Nunc quidem fert consuetudo, ut solæ gallorum fœminæ ὄρνιθες dicantur, & ὀρνίθια. Itaque meliùs hîc vertitur gallina, quàm avis ut vértit Arabs hîc & vulgatus cum ipso Luc. 13. v. 34. Gallinam constanter vertit Syrus in utroque loco. Ita etiam Cyprianus, Hilarius, Hieronymus, Augustinus & plerique veteres præter Ambrosium in Lucam, ubi hîc locus ita redditur: Quoties volui congregare filios tuos, quemadmodum avis nidum suum sub pennis? Sed gallinæ maximè proprium est, quod non solùm ovis incubat, quomodo reliquæ aves, sed & pullos jam editos sub alis congregat, ut materno calore foveantur & vegetentur; unde Arabice cognominatur mater congregationis. Hinc apud Euripidem in Hercule furente Megara de liberis, quos ex Hercule habuerat, maximè sollicita eos sub alis servare se dictitat, ut pullis gallina incubans. Verba sunt.
units.tr: Hen. In Greek ὄρνις. Although this word in Homer and Hesiod is nothing else than a bird in general, in Plato's age it began to be used for a fowl of the cock kind in general, and for several centuries it was said of both the cock and the hen, until custom prevailed so that the name became proper to the hen. Hence in Athenaeus, book 9, Myrtilus says: "Now custom bears that only the female cocks are called ὄρνιθες and ὀρνίθια." Therefore "hen" is translated here better than "bird," as the Arabic translates here and the Vulgate with the same passage in Luke 13.34. The Syriac consistently translates "hen" in both places. So also Cyprian, Hilary, Jerome, Augustine and most of the ancients, except Ambrose on Luke, where this passage is rendered thus: "How often I wished to gather your sons, as a bird gathers its nest under its wings?" But it is especially proper to the hen that she not only sits upon eggs, as other birds do, but also gathers her chicks already hatched under her wings, so that they may be cherished and nourished by maternal warmth; whence in Arabic she is called "mother of the gathering." Hence in Euripides' Hercules Furens, Megara, very anxious about the children she had by Hercules, says that she keeps them under her wings, as a hen sitting on her chicks. The words are these:

units.la: Ὀι δ' Ἡρακλέοι παῖδες, ὡς ὑποπτέρυγες ὄρνις ὡς ὑφ᾽ ἡμῖν. Et quos sub alis servo natos Herculis, Pullis ut incubare gallina assolet.
units.tr: "And the children of Hercules, whom I keep under my wings, as a hen broods over her chicks." (Greek: the sons of Heracles, who as a hen under her wings, under us.)

units.la: De gallinæ philostorgia Naturæ scriptores sæpè egerunt, sed ut prophanos omittamus, hujus passim meminit Aug. nam lib. 1. quæst. Evang. q. 36. Quod difficilius in ceteris animantibus invenies, alis filios suos protegens contra milvum pugnat. Ibidem. Hoc genus animantis magnum affectum in filios habet, ita ut eorum infirmitate affecta & ipsa infirmetur. Et in Pfal. 58. Infirmatus est Christus usque ad mortem, & assumsit infirmitatis carnem, ut pullos Jerusalem colligeret sub alas suas, tanquam gallina infirmatur cum parvulis...... Certè notam rem dico, quae in conspectu nostro quotidie versatur. Quomodo raucescit vox? quomodo hispidum fit totum corpus, dimittuntur alae, laxantur plumae? Et in Pfal. 90. Multae hic aves ante nos foveant, calefaciunt pullos suos: nulla sic avis infirmatur cum pullis suis, quomodo gallina. Attendat charitas vestra hirundines, passeres, & ciconias. Videmus extra nidos suos, nec cognoscimus, utrum foetum habeant. At vero gallinam cognoscimus in infirmitate vocis, & in relaxatione plumarum: tota mutatur affectu pullorum; quia illi infirmi sunt, infirmam se facit. Et de verbis Domini Serm. 29. Illa gallina Domini sapientiae est. Sed assumsit carnem, ut pullis congrueret. Videte gallinam hispidam plumis, dimissis alis, voce fracta, & quassa, ac lassa, & languida congrere pullis suis.
units.tr: Writers on nature have often treated of the hen's fondness for her young, but, to leave out the profane, Augustine often mentions it. For in book 1 of the Questions on the Gospels, question 36: "What you will find more rarely in other animals, she protects her sons with her wings, fighting against the kite." Also there: "This kind of animal has a great affection for its sons, so that when they are weakened, it too is weakened." And on Psalm 58: "Christ was weakened even unto death, and took on the weakness of the flesh, that he might gather the chicks of Jerusalem under his wings, as the hen is weakened with her little ones... Surely I speak of a known thing, which is before our eyes every day. How does the voice grow hoarse? How does the whole body become bristly, the wings droop, the feathers loosen?" And on Psalm 90: "Many birds here cherish and warm their young; no bird is so weakened with its young as the hen. Let your charity consider swallows, sparrows and storks. We see them outside their nests, and we do not know whether they have offspring. But we know the hen by the weakness of her voice and the loosening of her feathers; her whole state is changed by the affection for her chicks; because they are weak, she makes herself weak." And on the words of the Lord, Sermon 29: "That hen is the wisdom of the Lord. But she assumed flesh, that she might agree with the chicks. See the hen bristling with feathers, her wings drooping, her voice broken, shaken, weary and languid, gathering her chicks."

units.la: 38. Ecce. Jam in proximo in punitionem duritiae cordis veltri.
units.tr: 38. Behold. Now soon, in punishment for the hardness of your heart.

units.la: Relinquetur, &c. Id est, in vastitatem redigetur Templum & universa civitas per excidium urbis & gentis veltrae.
units.tr: It will be left, etc. That is, the Temple and the whole city will be reduced to desolation by the destruction of the city and of your nation.

units.la: 39. Dico enim vobis, &c. Causam illius vastitatis Christus esse dicit quod a praesentia & ipsius protectione fuerint deserti.
units.tr: 39. For I say to you, etc. Christ says the cause of that desolation is that they were forsaken by his presence and his protection.

units.la: Amodo. Id est, ab hoc tempore, seu post breve tempus.
units.tr: Henceforth. That is, from this time, or after a short time.

units.la: Donec dicatis. Scilicet ore filiorum, seu posterorum veltrorum.
units.tr: Until you say. Namely, with the mouth of your sons, or your posterity.

units.la: Benedictus. Id est, ab omnibus hominibus laudetur. Praedicit hic Christus futuram sub finem mundi Judaeorum conversionem, & tunc ipsum ab eis pro vero Messia in Lege & Prophetis promissο agnitum iri.
units.tr: Blessed. That is, let him be praised by all men. Here Christ foretells that at the end of the world the conversion of the Jews will take place, and that then he will be recognised by them as the true Messiah promised in the Law and the Prophets.

units.la: In nomine Domini. Id est, in autoritate & virtute Dei Patris sui.
units.tr: In the name of the Lord. That is, in the authority and power of God his Father.

units.la: CAPUT XXIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIV.

units.la: 1. EGressus Jesus de Templo ibat. E civitate versus montem Oliveti, ubi noctibus morari solebat.
units.tr: 1. Going out of the Temple, Jesus was on his way. He went out of the city towards the Mount of Olives, where he was accustomed to stay at night.

units.la: Ut offenderent ei ædificationes Templi. Non ignotas, sed tanquam admirandas, ut clarè exprimunt Marcus c. 13. & Lucas c. 21.
units.tr: That they might show him the buildings of the Temple. Not as things unknown to him, but as things to be admired, as Mark ch. 13 and Luke ch. 21 express clearly.

units.la: 2. Non relinquetur hic lapis super lapidem. Id est, lapidi adhærens, qui non dissolvatur. De mirando ædificio Templi videre est Josephum lib. 6. de bello Judaico c. 6. & de mirandis lapidibus quibus constabat, l. 15. antiq. c. ultimo; non enim sic excitatum erat Templum a Judæis è captivitate Babylonica redeuntibus, sed ab Herode Magno, ut latè describit Josephus locis citatis. Quod autem Matthæus hic dicit Christo ostensum a discipulis & ab eodem ipsis responsum, hoc Marcus c. 13. refert dictum ab uno ex discipulis & responsum eidem uni a Christo; unde vel Matthæus facit Enallagen numeri, vel forte unus ostendebat Christo ædificationes Templi reliquis discipulis præsentibus, aut alii discipuli ostendebant Christo ædificia Templi, & unus dicebat: Magister aspice quales lapides, & quales strucrturæ. Discimus autem à Scaligero can. ifagog. p. 304. etiam aratrum induetum fuisse imo Templo a quodam Turno Rufo, quem ipse Turranum vocat, de quo multa mentio in Talmud & apud alios scriptores Hebræos.
units.tr: 2. There shall not be left here one stone upon another. That is, a stone cleaving to a stone, which will not be dissolved. On the wonderful building of the Temple, see Josephus, Jewish War, bk. 6, ch. 6, and on the marvellous stones of which it was made, Antiquities, bk. 15, last ch. For the Temple was not built in this form by the Jews returning from the Babylonian captivity, but by Herod the Great, as Josephus describes at length in the places cited. As for Matthew's statement that the disciples showed these things to Christ and that he answered them all, Mark in ch. 13 reports that it was said by one of the disciples and answered by Christ to that one alone. Hence either Matthew uses an enallage of number, or perhaps one disciple showed Christ the buildings of the Temple while the other disciples were present, or other disciples showed Christ the buildings of the Temple and one said: Master, look what stones and what structures! We learn from Scaliger, Canon Isagogicus, p. 304, that the Temple was even ploughed under by a certain Turnus Rufus, whom he himself calls Turranus, of whom there is much mention in the Talmud and in other Hebrew writers.

units.la: 3. Accesserunt ad eum discipuli secretò. Id est, privatim, seu ut Marcus loquitur v. 13. separatim Petrus & Jacobus & Joannes & Andreas.
units.tr: 3. The disciples came to him privately. That is, in private, or, as Mark says in v. 13, separately, Peter and James and John and Andrew.

units.la: Quando hæc erunt? Id est, quando ædificium illud Templi, quod ad miraculum assurgit, ita ut dicis, destruetur?
units.tr: When will these things be? That is, when will that building of the Temple, which rises to a marvel, be destroyed, as you say?

units.la: Quod signum adventûs tui? Nempe secundi ad judicium.
units.tr: What is the sign of your coming? Namely, of the second coming to judgment.

units.la: Consummationis seculi. Id est, finis mundi, de quo sicut de adventu tuo gloriosò te alias audivimus.
units.tr: Of the end of the age. That is, the end of the world, concerning which we have heard you speak elsewhere, as of your glorious coming.

units.la: 4. Videte ne quis vos seducat. Q. d. Vos solliciti estis & anxii de Templo & novissimis mundi rebus, sed ante omnia de vobis ipsis sitis solliciti; ne inducamini in errorem. Multi enim venient. Post discessum meum corporalem à vobis.
units.tr: 4. See that no one leads you astray. That is: you are anxious and troubled about the Temple and the last things of the world, but above all be anxious about yourselves, lest you be led into error. For many will come, after my bodily departure from you.

units.la: In nomine meo. Id est, nomen meum sibi usurpantes.
units.tr: In my name. That is, claiming my name for themselves.

units.la: 6. Opiniones praeliorum. Id est, rumores praeliorum, qui saepe magis homines turbant, quàm ipsa praelia.
units.tr: 6. Reports of wars. That is, rumours of wars, which often disturb men more than the wars themselves.

units.la: Videte ne turbemini. Id est, cavete ne plus aequo in hujusmodi praeliis, vel praeliorum rumoribus audiendis turbemini.
units.tr: See that you are not troubled. That is, take care that you are not disturbed beyond measure by such wars or by hearing rumours of wars.

units.la: Nondum. Id est, non statim cùm ista fient.
units.tr: Not yet. That is, not immediately when these things happen.

units.la: Est finis. Sive Ierusalem, sive mundi; adhuc enim graviora & plura finem praecessura sunt, quorum ista tantùm sunt praeludia & praenuntia.
units.tr: It is the end. Whether of Jerusalem or of the world; for harder and more numerous things will go before the end, of which these are only the preludes and forerunners.

units.la: 7. Consurget enim gens in gentem. Id contigisse ante excidium Ierosolymitanum, luculentus testis est Iosephus, lib. 2. de Bello Judaico. c. II, 18, 19, 20, 21, & 25.
units.tr: 7. For nation will rise against nation. That this happened before the destruction of Jerusalem is clearly attested by Josephus, Jewish War, bk. 2, chs. 11, 18, 19, 20, 21 and 25.

units.la: Erunt pestilentia & fames. De ingenti fame ante vastatam Hierusalem fit mentio Act. 11. v. 28. de qua latius Iosephus, lib. 20. Antiq. c. 2, & 3.
units.tr: There will be pestilences and famines. Mention is made of a great famine before Jerusalem was laid waste in Acts 11:28, of which Josephus speaks more fully in Antiquities, bk. 20, chs. 2 and 3.

units.la: Terrae-motus per loca. Id est, in diversis locis. Testatur enim Eusebius in Chronico sub Nerone tres urbes terrae-motu in Asia concidisse. De alio terrae-motu loquitur Iosephus lib. 4. de Bello Judaico c. 7.
units.tr: Earthquakes in various places. That is, in different places. For Eusebius in his Chronicle testifies that under Nero three cities in Asia fell in an earthquake. Josephus, Jewish War, bk. 4, ch. 7, speaks of another earthquake.

units.la: 8. Haec autem omnia. Scilicet errores, seu seductiones, bella, rumores bellorum, pestes, fames, terrae-motus.
units.tr: 8. But all these things. Namely the errors or seductions, the wars, the rumours of wars, the plagues, the famines, the earthquakes.

units.la: Initia sunt dolorum. Qui scilicet mox Hierusalem & sub finem saeculi totum orbem invadent. Praecessisse autem Pseudo-christos ruinam Ierosolymae testantur Theodas, de quo Act. 5. v. 36. & Iosephus lib. 20. Antiq. c. 2. Simon Magus, qui se virtutem Dei magnam dixit Act. 8. v. 9. & se pro Christo venditavit, ut ait Aug. Haeresi. 1. Fuerunt alii multi quorum catalogum recensere longum esse & fortasse supervacaneum. Sed multò plures praecedent consummationem saeculi, cujus typus fuit excidium Ierosolymitanum.
units.tr: Are the beginnings of sorrows. These will soon attack Jerusalem and, towards the end of the age, the whole world. That false Christs went before the ruin of Jerusalem is attested by Theudas, of whom Acts 5:36 speaks, and by Josephus, Antiquities, bk. 20, ch. 2. Simon Magus, who said that he was the great power of God (Acts 8:9) and who passed himself off as Christ, as Augustine says in his Heresies, 1. There were many others, whose list would be long to recount and perhaps superfluous. But far more will precede the consummation of the age, of which the destruction of Jerusalem was a type.

units.la: Dolorum. Graece, parturitionum, id est, dolorum maximorum, quales sunt ii, quibus parturientes affliguntur.
units.tr: Of sorrows. In Greek, of birth-pangs [ὠδίνων], that is, of the greatest pains, such as those by which women in labour are afflicted.

units.la: 9. Tunc tradent vos. Luc. 21. v. 12 ante haec omnia. q. d. Nolite cogitare vos ab omnibus malis immunes futuros, dum ista affligentur improbi. Per Apostolos autem omnes fideles significari observat hîc Hieronymus.
units.tr: 9. Then they will deliver you up (Luke 21:12), before all these things. That is: do not suppose that you will be free from all evils while the wicked are troubled by these things. Jerome observes here that by the apostles all the faithful are meant.

units.la: 10. Scandalizabuntur. Id est, scandalum patientur.
units.tr: 10. Many will be offended. That is, they will suffer offence.

units.la: 11. Pseudo-Prophetae surgent. Id est, surgent homines, qui se Evangelicae veritatis doctores jactitabunt, ut sic in errorem inducant fideles. Hîc designantur omnes haeretici, qui partim ante excisam Hierusalem, ut Nicolaitae, Hymenaeus næus, Philetus & alii; partim ante mundi finem exorituri erant.
units.tr: 11. False prophets will arise. That is, men will arise who will boast that they are teachers of the evangelical truth, in order to lead the faithful into error. Here all heretics are designated, some of whom were to arise before Jerusalem was destroyed, such as the Nicolaitans, Hymenaeus, Philetus and others, and some before the end of the world.

units.la: 12. Iniquitas. Id est, crudelitas persequentium, scandalum deficientium, error male docentium.
units.tr: 12. Iniquity. That is, the cruelty of persecutors, the offence of those who fall away, the error of those who teach wrongly.

units.la: Refrigescet charitas multorum. Quâ antea orga Deum & proximum fervebant.
units.tr: The love of many will grow cold. By which they had formerly burned towards God and their neighbour.

units.la: 13. Perseveraverit. Græcè, sustinuerit, scilicet ista mala, persequutiones, scandala, odia, errores.
units.tr: 13. Endures. In Greek, endured [ὑπέμεινεν], namely these evils, persecutions, offences, hatreds, errors.

units.la: Usque in finem. Ita ut nullatenus dejiciatur.
units.tr: To the end. So that he is in no way cast down.

units.la: 14. Et prædicabitur. Q. d. Non obstantibus tot malis prædicabitur per vos & alios Evangelium, de regno cœlorum omnibus patefacto atque propositò, antequam finis veniat.
units.tr: 14. And this gospel will be preached. That is: notwithstanding so many evils, the gospel of the kingdom of heaven will be preached by you and others to all, set forth and offered, before the end comes.

units.la: In testimonium omnibus Gentibus. Id est, ut sit omnibus Gentibus loco testimonii, quo Deus testatur æternam salutem eis à se per Filium paratum, si ampleƈti velint: ita ut sint inexcusabiles, & nolint.
units.tr: As a testimony to all the nations. That is, so that it serves all nations as a testimony by which God attests the eternal salvation prepared for them by him through the Son, if they wish to embrace it; so that they are without excuse, and yet refuse.

units.la: Tunc veniet consummatio. Seculi, secundum Hieronymum; Jerosolymæ, secundum Hilarium & Chrysostomum; nam Paulus Rom. 1. v. 8, 10. & 18. Coloss. 1. v. 6. & 23. testatur suo jam tempore, ideoque ante eversam Jerusalem in universo orbe prædicatum fuisse Evangelium; nimirum quia in maxima orbis noti parte id factum fuerat, quamvis perfectius in fine mundi complendum. Nos quia nihil eorum, quæ hactenus dicta sunt, non contingerit juxta Scripturæ phrases etiam ante eversam Jerusalem, malumus omnia ad hunc usque versum indistincte de Jerosolymæ & seculi consummatione intelligere.
units.tr: Then the end will come. Of the age, according to Jerome; of Jerusalem, according to Hilary and Chrysostom. For Paul in Rom. 1:8, 10 and 18 and Col. 1:6 and 23 testifies that in his own time the gospel had already been preached throughout the whole world, and therefore before Jerusalem was overthrown; namely because it had been done in the greatest part of the known world, although it was to be completed more perfectly at the end of the world. But since none of the things said so far failed to happen, even before the overthrow of Jerusalem, according to the phrases of Scripture, we prefer to understand all of this up to this verse, without distinction, of the consummation both of Jerusalem and of the age.

units.la: 15. Cùm ergo, &c. Pòst monita generalia dilabitur Christus ad solutionem primæ Apostolorum quæstionis de excidio Jerusalem, eamque perducit usque ad versum 23. ut sentit Augustinus in Ep. 80. Qui igitur hunc & sequentes versus ad Antichristum referunt, allegoricum non literalem sequuntur sensum.
units.tr: 15. When therefore, etc. After the general warnings Christ passes on to answer the apostles' first question about the destruction of Jerusalem, and carries it on as far as verse 23, as Augustine holds in Ep. 80. Therefore those who refer this and the following verses to Antichrist follow an allegorical rather than a literal sense.

units.la: Abominationem desolationis. Id est, abominationem, quæ subsequutæ & à Daniele prædictæ desolationis vera causa suit. Hæc autem abominatio est sceleistissima illa prophanatio totius Templi per Zelotas seu per ingentem latronum manum, qui erumpentes in Jerosolymam pollutis pedibus, ut refert Josephus lib. 4. de Bel. Jud. c. 5. sanctum locum intrare cœperunt ac Templo uti, loco castri, ac domicilii tyrannidis adversus populum. Tot verò cædibus innocentium & nocentium toto illo tempore tum inter se pugnantes, tum cum populo, illud repleverunt, ut Josephus testetur lib. 6. c. 1. per atria divina diversorum sanguinem cadaverum fecisse stagnum, nec potuisse amplius manere Dei locum, qui domesticorum funerum erat sepulchrum. Hinc neque Judaeis, neque Romanis in tota obsidione Jerosolymitana intolerabilius, vel horribilius quicquam visum est, quàm illa immanis Templi prophanatio, quae facta est paulò post circumdatam ab exercitu Ceftii & liberatam Jerusalem; duravitque usque ad eversionem ejus per tres circiter annos cum dimidio. Hinc Josephus l. 6. c. ultimo, Puto, inquit, si Romani contra noxios venire tardassent, aut hiatu terrae devorandam fuisse civitatem, aut diluvio periturum, aut fulminum, aut Sodomae incendio passuram. Imo & Titus ipse seditiosos rogabat aliquoties ut à tanta prophanatione discederent, seque testabatur non esse causam ejus, ut videre est l. 7. c. 4. &c. Hinc idem Josephus l. 5. antiq. c. 2. testatur veterem fuisse sermonem tunc demum civitatem captum iri & sancta flammis exurenda, cùm seditio fuisset exorta, templúmque Dei propriae manus ante violatum; quibus, inquit, Zelota, nihil de eorum fide dubitantes se ministros praebuerunt. Hic autem sermo certè ex Danielis vaticinio, vel Christi praedictione ortum habuit. Ex dictis patet quòd cùm Lucas c. 21. v. 20. dicit, Cùm videritis circumdari ab exercitu Jerusalem, scilicet sub Ceftio (tunc enim erat fugae locus, non sub Tito) non desfigurat ipsam abominationem desolationis, sed potiùs tempus quo illa mox esset apparitura, & quo deberent de fuga cogitare ex Jerusalem & Judaea, eo quòd brevi inflaret ejus consummatio.
units.tr: The abomination of desolation. That is, the abomination which was the true cause of the desolation that followed and was foretold by Daniel. This abomination was that most wicked profanation of the whole Temple by the Zealots, or by the vast band of robbers, who, bursting into Jerusalem with polluted feet, as Josephus relates in Jewish War, bk. 4, ch. 5, began to enter the holy place and to use the Temple as a camp and a dwelling for their tyranny against the people. With the slaughter of innocent and guilty alike throughout that whole period, fighting both among themselves and against the people, they filled it so that, as Josephus testifies in bk. 6, ch. 1, the blood of the corpses in the divine courts made a pool, and God's place could no longer remain, since it had become the sepulchre of their family dead. Hence neither Jews nor Romans saw anything more intolerable or horrible in the whole siege of Jerusalem than that monstrous profanation of the Temple, which was done shortly after Cestius surrounded Jerusalem with his army and then lifted the siege; and it lasted until its overthrow, about three and a half years. Hence Josephus, bk. 6, last ch.: I think, he says, that if the Romans had delayed in coming against the guilty, either the city would have been devoured by a gaping of the earth, or would have perished by a flood, or would have suffered the fire of Sodom or lightning. Indeed Titus himself repeatedly begged the seditious to desist from so great a profanation, and declared that he was not the cause of it, as can be seen in bk. 7, ch. 4, etc. Hence the same Josephus, Antiquities, bk. 5, ch. 2, testifies that there was an old saying that the city would be taken and the holy places burned with fire when sedition had arisen and the Temple of God had first been violated by their own hands; to which, he says, the Zealots, not doubting at all about their faith, became ministers. This saying certainly arose from Daniel's prophecy or from Christ's prediction. From what has been said it is clear that when Luke 21:20 says, When you see Jerusalem surrounded by an army, namely under Cestius (for then there was a place of flight, not under Titus), he does not describe the abomination of desolation itself, but rather the time at which it was soon to appear, and at which they ought to think of fleeing from Jerusalem and Judaea, because its consummation was near at hand.

units.la: In loco sancto. Id est, in Templo.
units.tr: In the holy place. That is, in the Temple.

units.la: Qui legit intelligat. Si haec sunt verba Christi, ad Danielis locum referenda sunt; si Evangelistae, ad ipsamet Christi verba.
units.tr: Let him who reads understand. If these are the words of Christ, they are to be referred to the passage in Daniel; if they are the Evangelist's, they are to be referred to Christ's own words.

units.la: 16. Tunc, &c. His verbis & sequentibus intelligendum est festinationem fugae fuisse praeceptam, ut monet Aug. Ep. 80. Quare huic Christi monito parentes Christiani ex Jerusalem totaque regione migrarunt trans fluvium in urbem Pellam, quae parebat Regi Agrippae amico & coadjutori Romanorum, ut Eusebius testis est lib. 3. Hist c. 5. & Epiph. Haeref. 29. num. 7. & Josephus l. 2. c. 25. ait quòd post Ceftii casus adversos, nobilium Judaeorum multi, tanquam e navi pessum itura ex civitate enatarunt.
units.tr: 16. Then, etc. These words and those that follow must be understood to mean that haste in flight was commanded, as Augustine warns in Ep. 80. Accordingly, obeying this warning of Christ, Christian parents migrated from Jerusalem and the whole region across the river to the city of Pella, which was subject to King Agrippa, a friend and helper of the Romans, as Eusebius attests, book 3 of the History, ch. 5, and Epiphanius, Heresies 29, n. 7. Josephus, book 2, ch. 25, says that after the adverse fortunes of Cestius, many Jewish nobles swam out of the city, as though from a ship about to sink.

units.la: 20. Orate ut non fiat fuga vestra hieme vel Sabbato, Id est, ne impedimento aliquo detineamini, quia & hieme imbribus vel frigore, & Sabbato, in quo longiùs bis mille cubitis proficisci non licebat, impediebatur quis ab itinere. De spatio quod continebat iter Sabbati variae opiniones sunt, quamquam in numero duorum millium plerique omnes conveniunt, sed cubitos alii, & alii passus, Hieronymus pedes, Origenes ulnas memorat. Hebræi fere omnes iter Sabbati definiunt bis mille cubitis, quæ faciunt secundùm eosdem Hebræorum milliare unum, quantum distabat Tabernaculum ab extremis castris Hebræorum, cùm in deserto essent, unde hæc traditio de itinere Sabbati orta videtur.
units.tr: 20. Pray that your flight not be in winter or on the Sabbath. That is, that you not be held back by any hindrance, since in winter one was impeded from the journey by rain or cold, and on the Sabbath, when it was not lawful to travel further than two thousand cubits. There are various opinions about the distance that the Sabbath journey covered. Most agree on the number two thousand, but some say cubits, others paces; Jerome mentions feet, Origen ells. Almost all Hebrews define the Sabbath journey as two thousand cubits, which by the same Hebrews make one mile, the distance from the Tabernacle to the outermost camp of the Hebrews when they were in the desert. From this, the tradition about the Sabbath journey seems to have arisen.

units.la: 21. Erit enim, &c. Patet ex Luc. 21. v. 23. id de Judæorum vastatione intelligendum, ut notat Aug. Ep. 80. nam ibidem ait Josephus quòd talia mala illi populo tunc accidernt, ut vix credibilia videantur: intùs enim latrocinia, fames, pestis, foris ferrum & flamma.
units.tr: 21. For there will be, etc. It is clear from Luke 21:23 that this must be understood of the devastation of the Jews, as Augustine notes in Ep. 80. For there Josephus also says that such evils then befell that people as hardly seem credible: within, robberies, famine and pestilence; without, sword and flame.

units.la: Tribulatio. Græcè θλίψις, afflictio. Luc. 21. v. 13. pressura, Græcè ἀνάγκη, necessitas. Observat autem Aug. in Ps. 24. Heb. 25. v. 19. in illud De necessitatibus meis eripe me, afflictiones vocari necessitates, quòd necesse sit eas usque in finem tolerare ut salvemur. Hinc & ille lusus Senecæ in ambiguo vocis Ep. 12. Malum est in necessitate vivere, sed in necessitate vivere necessitas nulla est.
units.tr: Tribulation. In Greek θλίψις [thlipsis], affliction. In Luke 21:13 the word is pressure, in Greek ἀνάγκη [anankē], necessity. Augustine observes, on Ps. 24 (Hebrew 25:19), on the words "Deliver me from my necessities," that afflictions are called necessities, because it is necessary to bear them to the end if we are to be saved. Hence also that play of Seneca on the ambiguity of the word, Ep. 12: It is an evil to live in necessity, but to live in necessity is no necessity.

units.la: 22. Nisi breviati fuissent dies illi. Id est, nisi æterno Dei decreto dies illi ad parvum numerum redacti fuissent. Sic apud Augustinum Ep. 80. quæ est ad Hesychium, ex antiqua & certa traditione vel ex doctrina & sententia Patrum aiunt septuaginta hebdomadas Danielis ideò dici Dan. 9. abbreviatas, quòd propter lacrymas, preces & vota Prophetarum, citius venerit Christus, quàm aliàs venturus erat, juxta illud Psal. 11. Propter miseriam inopum & gemitum pauperum, nunc exsurgam dicit Dominus.
units.tr: 22. Unless those days had been shortened. That is, unless by the eternal decree of God those days had been reduced to a small number. So in Augustine's Ep. 80, addressed to Hesychius, they say, from ancient and certain tradition, or from the teaching and opinion of the Fathers, that the seventy weeks of Daniel are called abbreviated in Dan. 9 because, on account of the tears, prayers and vows of the prophets, Christ came sooner than he otherwise would have, according to Psal. 11: Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now will I arise, saith the Lord.

units.la: Non fieret salva omnis caro. Duplex Hebraismus, caro pro homine, non omnis pro nulla. Sensus igitur est, nullus Judæorum evasisset mortem temporalem.
units.tr: Not all flesh would be saved. This is a double Hebraism: flesh for man, and not all for none. The sense, then, is that not one of the Jews would have escaped temporal death.

units.la: Propter electos. Qui scilicet vel tum vivebant, vel ex Judæis usque ad finem mundi nascituri erant.
units.tr: For the sake of the elect. Namely, those who were then living, or who were to be born of the Jews until the end of the world.

units.la: Breviabuntur dies illi. Id est, scilicet, citius divina providentia bello & calamitatibus illis finem imponet.
units.tr: Those days will be shortened. That is, divine providence will more quickly bring that war and those calamities to an end.

units.la: 23. Tunc. Scilicet ab excidio Jerosolymitano usque ad finem mundi. Expedità enim quæstione de eversione Templi & civitatis Jerusalem, transit Christus ad secundam & tertiam quæstionem de regno Messiæ & de fine seculi.
units.tr: 23. Then. Namely, from the destruction of Jerusalem until the end of the world. For, having disposed of the question about the overthrow of the Temple and the city of Jerusalem, Christ passes to the second and third questions, concerning the kingdom of the Messiah and the end of the age.

units.la: 24. Surgent enim pseudo-Christi. Tales fuere non pauci, ut olim Barchochebas tempore Adriani Imperatoris, de quo præter Hebræos Eusebius l. 4. Hist. c. 6. Barchochebas, si Latinè interpreteris, valet filius stellæ: de quo exponebant locum illum, Orietur stella ex Iacob. Nam eum Messiam esse persuadere conabatur inter alios R. Aquiba, qui etiam ejus armiger fuit. Dicebat enim tempus adventus Messiæ præteriisse. Quod veriverbium utinam Judæi post tot annorum intervallum in aures admitterent. Fuerunt alii multi pseudo-Christi quorum catalogum recensere longum esset & fortasse supervacaneum.
units.tr: 24. For false Christs will arise. There were not a few such, for example Barchochebas in the time of the Emperor Hadrian. Concerning him, besides the Hebrews, Eusebius writes, book 4 of the History, ch. 6. Barchochebas, if translated into Latin, means son of a star, and with reference to him they explained that passage, A star shall come out of Jacob. Rabbi Akiba, who was also his armour-bearer, tried to persuade people, among others, that he was the Messiah, for he said the time of the Messiah's coming had passed. Would that the Jews, after so many years, would admit that true saying into their ears! There were many other false Christs; to list them all would be long and perhaps superfluous.

units.la: Pseudo-Prophetæ. Id est, falsitatis doctores, cujusmodi sunt hæretici pseudo-Prophetarum synagogæ in Ecclesia succesores.
units.tr: False prophets. That is, teachers of falsehood, such as the heretics, who are the successors in the Church of the false prophets of the synagogue.

units.la: Habent signa. Id est, edent miracula, quæ signa dicuntur ratione ejus propter quod manifestandum fiunt; dicuntur & virtutes, quia id quod fit in miraculis excedit facultatem naturæ; portenta vero à portendendo, id est, præostendendo; & prodigia quod porro dicant, id est, futura prædicant.
units.tr: They will show signs. That is, they will perform miracles. These are called signs because of the purpose for which they are displayed; they are also called powers, because what happens in miracles exceeds the faculty of nature; they are called portents, from portending, that is, foreshowing; and prodigies, because they say forth, that is, they foretell future things.

units.la: Magna. Sed mandacia, ut vocantur ab Apost. 2 Thess. c. 2. tum quia signa à pseudo-Christis & hæreticis edita in mendacium & errorem inducunt, tum quia eadem signa simpliciter miracula non sunt, sed tantum quoad nos; miraculum enim simpliciter dici solet, quod fit præter ordinem totius naturæ creatæ; sed quia non omnis virtus naturæ creatæ, nobis nota est, ideo cùm aliquid fit præter ordinem naturæ creatæ nobis notæ per virtutem creatam nobis ignotam, est miraculum quoad nos; horum autem aliud mendax est, quoniam in eo non vera res hominibus exhibetur, sed per phantasma mortales sensus à dæmonibus decipiuntur, ut quod magus, pseudo-Propheta, vel dæmones non faciunt, facere videantur. Aliud miraculum quoad nos dicitur verum, quia vera est res quæ exhibetur, sicut magi Pharaonis fecerunt veras ranas & veros serpentes, non tamen per verum miraculum, seu per virtutem excedentem vires naturæ creatæ, sed per virtutem naturalium causarum, seu per applicationem naturalium activorum passivis. Vide Aug. 3. de Trinitate c. 8.
units.tr: Great. But they are lies, as the Apostle calls them in 2 Thess. 2. This is both because the signs produced by false Christs and heretics lead into lie and error, and because these same signs are not miracles simply, but only with respect to us. A miracle simply is commonly taken to be what happens beyond the order of all created nature. But since not every power of created nature is known to us, when something happens beyond the order of the created nature known to us, through a created power unknown to us, it is a miracle with respect to us. Of these, one kind is false, because no real thing is exhibited to men in it; rather, through a phantasm, the mortal senses are deceived by demons, so that what a magician, a false prophet or demons do not really do seems to be done. Another kind of miracle, with respect to us, is called true, because the thing exhibited is real, as the magicians of Pharaoh made real frogs and real serpents. Yet this was not done by a true miracle, that is, by a power exceeding the strength of created nature, but by the power of natural causes, or by the application of active natural agents to passive ones. See Augustine, On the Trinity, book 3, ch. 8.

units.la: Ita ut in errorem inducantur. Sensus est: Ita ut absque magna Dei providentia & oppositione verorum miraculorum, tota plebs fidelium, atque adeo ipsi electi seducerentur, partim terrore Principum & persecutione, partim ambiguitate veritatis inter vera & falsa miracula vacillantis. Hinc B. Greg. lib. 1. in Ezech. Hom. 9. hunc locum explicans, Cur, inquit, hoc sub dubitatione dicitur, cùm quid futurum sit, à Domino præsciatur? unum verò ex duobus est, quia si electi sunt, fieri non potest, si autem fieri potest, electi non sunt. Ita Ista ergo dubitatio Dominici sermonis ex electorum cordibus, designatio tentationis fuit: quia qui electi sunt ad perficiendum, per signa prædicatorum Antichristi tentabuntur ad cadendum. Per hoc ergo quod dicitur, Si fieri potest, hoc exprimitur, quod electi in corde tentabuntur. Nutant enim, sed non cadunt; dicitur ergo, Si fieri potest: quia trepidabunt: & tamen dicuntur electi, qui non cadunt. Dubitatio itaque sermonis à Domino in electis excitat trepidationem mentis. Quos & electos nominat, quia certi sunt quòd in fide & bono opere perfistunt. Verissimè itaque Aug. in lib. de Corrept. & Grat. c.7. Electorum si quisquam perit fallitur Deus; sed nemo eorum perit, quia non fallitur Deus; horum si quisquam perit, vitio humano vincitur Deus, sed nemo eorum perit, quia nulla re vincitur Deus. Hinc Christus ipse de electis suis ovibus ait Joan. 10. v. 28. Non rapiet eas quisquam de manu mea.
units.tr: So that they are led into error. The sense is: so that, without the great providence of God and the opposition of true miracles, the whole body of the faithful, and indeed the elect themselves, would be seduced, partly by the terror and persecution of princes, partly by the ambiguity of truth wavering between true and false miracles. Hence blessed Gregory, explaining this passage in book 1 on Ezekiel, Homily 9: Why, he asks, is this said with doubt, when what is going to happen is foreknown by the Lord? One of two things is the case: if they are elect, it cannot happen; if it can happen, they are not elect. And again: This doubt in the Lord's words was a sign of temptation in the hearts of the elect, because those who are elect to be perfected will be tempted by the signs of the preachers of Antichrist to fall. Therefore, through what is said, "If it be possible," this is expressed: that the elect will be tempted in heart. For they waver, but they do not fall; therefore it is said, "If it be possible," because they will tremble; and yet they are called elect who do not fall. The doubt in the Lord's words therefore stirs trembling of mind in the elect. He also names them elect, because they are certain that they persevere in faith and good works. Most truly, therefore, Augustine, in the book On Rebuke and Grace, ch. 7: If any of the elect perishes, God is deceived; but none of them perishes, because God is not deceived. If any of them perishes, God is overcome by human vice; but none of them perishes, because God is overcome by nothing. Hence Christ himself says of his elect sheep, John 10:28: No one shall snatch them out of my hand.

units.la: 25. Ecce prædixi vobis. Periculi magnitudinem, ut illud sollicitè caveatis; non enim electio aut prædestinatio, etiam cognita, est aut esse debet causa socordiæ, sed sollicitudinis ac diligentiæ, ut per illam ipsam diligentiam, hoc est, sollicitam ardentémque voluntatem, id quod constitutum est, impleatur, & ex illa ipsa discant homines se ad prædestinationis divinæ gratiæ pertinere, ut præclarè tradit Aug. lib. de dono perseverantiæ c.22.
units.tr: 25. Behold, I have told you beforehand. He sets before them the magnitude of the danger, so that they may guard against it with care. For election or predestination, even when known, is not and must not be a cause of carelessness, but of anxious diligence, so that through that very diligence, that is, through an anxious and ardent will, what has been decreed may be fulfilled, and men may learn from that very diligence that they belong to the grace of divine predestination, as Augustine finely teaches in his book on the gift of perseverance, chapter 22.

units.la: 26. Si ergo, &c. Magis particulatim Christus explicat quod antè dixerat: Ecce hic est Christus, aut illic: ponítque loca determinata duo contraria pro quibusvis locis.
units.tr: 26. If therefore, etc. Christ explains more particularly what he had said before: Behold, here is Christ, or there, and he names two definite places, opposite to each other, in place of any places whatever.

units.la: 27. Sicut enim fulgur, &c. Q. d. Licet certò sciatis me secundò esse venturum, nolite tamen credere quibuscunque prædicantibus, Ecce hic est Christus aut illic, quia secundus meus adventus erit ita manifestus & evidens, & subitus, ut instar fulguris promicantis è nubibus in oriente positis & subitò non tantùm in meridie & aquilone, sed usque in occidentem, hoc est per universum undequaque orbem apparentis, omnibus innotescat sine præcone & nuntio in cunctis partibus orbis.
units.tr: 27. For as the lightning, etc. The sense is: Although you may know for certain that I shall come a second time, do not believe whoever preaches, Behold, here is Christ, or there, because my second coming will be so manifest, evident and sudden that, like lightning flashing from the clouds in the east, it will suddenly appear not only in the south and the north but even as far as the west, that is, visible throughout the whole world on every side, and will become known to all without any herald or messenger in every part of the world.

units.la: 28. Ubicunque fuerit corpus. Græcè, cadaver.
units.tr: 28. Wherever the body is. In Greek, the word is "corpse" [πτῶμα].

units.la: Illic congregabuntur & aquilæ. Sentiunt enim aquilæ naturaliter cadavera etiam transmarina ut hîc advertit Hier. Alludit Christus ad id quod dicitur Job 39. v. 30. Pulli ejus (aquilæ scilicet) lambent sanguinem, & ubicunque cadaver fuerit, statim adest, hoc autem pertinet ad percnopterum seu gypaetum degeneris aquilæ genus vulturinâ specie, quod solùm ex omnibus aquilæ generibus alitur cadaveribus, ut ex Aristotele lib. 9. hist. c. 32. habet Plinius lib. 10. c. 3. PerPerperàm autem Suidas id tribuit percnis, seu, qtod idem est, morphnis, qui non aluntur cadaveribus, sed venantur, ut cetera aquilarum genera. Jam sensus præsentis versiculi connectitur cum præcedente & versu 26. quasi diceretur: Siqui insusurraverint hic aut illic quasi latitantem Christum quærendum, ne credite. Palàm enim sese conspiciendum præbebit Christus, ut fulgur ab oriente ad occidentem emicans, & terrarum universum orbem irradians. Et sicut aquilæ ad cadaver statim advolant mirâ sagacitate: ita piis omnibus æquè demum erit concurrendum, ubi vivificum mortis Christi nidorem percipient. Nec frustra aquilæ vocantur, qui aggregantur Christo, cùm nemo cum illo uniatur, nisi qui ejus carne & sanguine vescitur. Proinde Chryf. Hom. 28. in 1 Cor. Christi corpus σῶμα, vocari dicit propter mortem. Et ad Eucharisticam Christi communionem hæc transferens, fideles addit aquilas appellari, ut ostendat ad alia eum oportere contendere, qui ad hoc corpus accedit, & nihil cum terra deberi ei esse commune, neque ad inferiora trahi, & repere; sed ad superiora semper volare, & in solem justitiæ intueri, mentisque oculum acutissimum habere. Ἀετοὶ γὰρ ὅπου ἂν ἡ τὸ σῶμα ἐκεῖ. Aquilarum enim, non graculorum est hæc mensa. Luc. 17. v. 37. idem Christi dictum repetens Evangelista pro τὸ πτῶμα habet τὸ σῶμα. Sed res eodem recidit. Nam τὸ σῶμα pro cadavere Græci passim usurpant.
units.tr: There the eagles also will be gathered. For eagles naturally perceive corpses even across the sea, as Jerome observes here. Christ alludes to what is said in Job 39:30, Her young ones (namely of the eagle) suck up blood, and wherever the carcass is, there she is. This, however, applies to the percnopterus or gypaetus, a degenerate kind of eagle with the appearance of a vulture, which alone of all the kinds of eagle feeds on carcasses, as Pliny reports in book 10, chapter 3, from Aristotle's History of Animals, book 9, chapter 32. Suidas wrongly attributes this to the percnis, or, which is the same thing, the morphnos, which do not feed on carcasses but hunt, like the other kinds of eagle. Now the sense of the present verse is connected with the preceding one and with verse 26, as if it were said: If anyone whispers that Christ is here or there, as if hiding and to be sought, do not believe them. For Christ will show himself openly to be seen, like lightning flashing from the east to the west and lighting up the whole orb of the earth. And just as eagles fly swiftly to a corpse with wonderful keenness, so all the godly will at last have to hasten together, when they perceive the life-giving odour of Christ's death. Nor are those rightly called eagles in vain who gather to Christ, since no one is united with him unless he feeds on his flesh and blood. Accordingly Chrysostom, in Homily 28 on 1 Corinthians, says that the body of Christ is called σῶμα because of his death. And applying this to the Eucharistic communion of Christ, he adds that the faithful are called eagles, to show that whoever approaches this body ought to strive toward other things, and that nothing in common with the earth should be owed to him, nor should he be drawn down to lower things and crawl, but should always fly upward and gaze upon the sun of righteousness, having the keenest eye of the mind. For "where the body is, there the eagles are" [Ἀετοὶ γὰρ ὅπου ἂν ἡ τὸ σῶμα ἐκεῖ]. For this table belongs to eagles, not to jackdaws. In Luke 17:37 the Evangelist, repeating the same saying of Christ, has σῶμα instead of πτῶμα. But the matter comes to the same thing, for the Greeks everywhere use τὸ σῶμα for a corpse.

units.la: 29. Post tribulationem dierum illorum. Quibus scilicet Pseudo Christi & Pseudo-Prophetæ dixerint, Ecce hic est Christus, &c.
units.tr: 29. After the tribulation of those days. That is, after the days in which the false Christs and false prophets will say, Behold, here is Christ, etc.

units.la: Sol obscurabitur. Id est, sanguineo colore trans innumeros vapores apparebit, & luna cum debiliorem sole lucem & actionem habeat, magis fusco, ideóque nigro aspectu demonstrabitur, quasi saccus cilicinus.
units.tr: The sun will be darkened. That is, it will appear through countless vapours with a blood-red colour, and the moon, having a weaker light and power than the sun, will be shown with a darker and therefore blacker appearance, like sackcloth of goats' hair.

units.la: Stellæ cadent de Cælo. Id elt, cadere videbuntur; stellæ enim cadere de cœlo videntur, dum luce privantur. Non desunt tamen qui hunc locum intelligant de exhalationibus ignitis, quæ stellis similes de cœlo, id est, de media aeris regione cadent, multò scilicet mirabilius, quàm nunc fit, ut ait Aug. c. 24. lib. 20. de civit. Dei.
units.tr: The stars will fall from heaven. That is, they will seem to fall: stars do seem to fall from heaven when they are deprived of light. Yet there are some who understand this place of fiery exhalations, which, like stars, will fall from heaven, that is, from the middle region of the air, far more wondrously than now happens, as Augustine says in book 20, chapter 24 of the City of God.

units.la: Et virtutes cælorum commovebuntur. Id est, omnes vires cœlorum removebuntur. Idem hic dici videtur, quod Epist.
units.tr: And the powers of the heavens will be shaken. That is, all the powers of the heavens will be removed. The same thing seems to be said here as in the Epistle.

units.la: 2 Pet. c. 3. v. 10. Cœli magno impetu transibunt, quod Aug. Greg. Mag. & alii de aeris regionibus intelligunt; licet, cùm præcipua cœli virtus fit in lumine, quo nobis illucescit, eo prohibito, atque, ut sic dicam, quoad nos extincto, moveri dici possint cœlorum virtutes, adeóque ipsi cœli; sicut moveri terra dicitur, cum homines terræ incolæ grávi metu, aut subitâ & improvisâ calamitate concutiuntur.
units.tr: 2 Pet. 3:10. The heavens will pass away with a great noise. Augustine, Gregory the Great and others understand this of the regions of the air. Yet since the chief power of the heaven lies in the light by which it shines on us, once that light is taken away, and, so to speak, extinguished as far as we are concerned, the powers of the heavens, and so the heavens themselves, may be said to be shaken, just as the earth is said to be shaken when its inhabitants are struck with great fear or with sudden and unforeseen calamity.

units.la: 30. Tunc. Sole obscurato, & luna non dante lumen.
units.tr: 30. Then: when the sun has been darkened and the moon gives no light.

units.la: Signum Filii hominis. Id est, vexillum, signumque majestatis ac potentiæ Filii hominis, in quo inhabitat plenitudo Divinitatis substantialiter, omnibus conspicuum apparebit, & tunc plangent omnes orbem terrarum inhabitantes à se offensum, quem adorant Angeli.
units.tr: The sign of the Son of Man. That is, the banner and sign of the majesty and power of the Son of Man, in whom the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily, will appear, and then all the inhabitants of the earth will mourn for the one offended by them, whom the angels adore.

units.la: Tunc. Illo scilicet spectaculo.
units.tr: Then: that is, at that sight.

units.la: Videbunt, Sensibiliter oculis corporis. Clarius explicat quod mox obscurius dixerat: Parebit signum Filii hominis in cœlo.
units.tr: They will see, with the bodily eyes. He explains more clearly what he had said somewhat obscurely a moment before: the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven.

units.la: 31. Cum tuba & voce magna. Hebraismus, q. d. cum tuba, id est, cum voce magna. Unde & Paulus cùm 1. ad Cor. 15. v. 25. dixisset, In novissima tuba, canet enim tuba; magis se declarasse videtur dicens 1 Thess. c. 4. v. 15. Ipse Dominus in jussu & in voce Archangeli & in tuba Dei descendit de cœlo. Ita ut omnia ista non aliud significent quàm motum concitatissimum non sine ingenti sonitu edendum ministerio Archangelorum, jussu Christi Domini, ad miscendum aërem cum ceteris elementis, & quasi spiritum reddendum mortuis necessarium, ut ex visione simili Ezechielis patere poterit. Hinc sonitus ille Joan. 3. v. 25. vocatur vox Filii Dei, quam mortui audient.
units.tr: 31. With a trumpet and a loud voice. A Hebraism, as if to say, with a trumpet, that is, with a loud voice. Hence Paul too, having said in 1 Cor. 15:25, at the last trump, for the trumpet will sound, seems to have made himself clearer when he says in 1 Thess. 4:15, The Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trumpet of God. So all these things mean nothing other than a most violent motion, which must come with a great sound through the ministry of the archangels, at the command of Christ the Lord, stirring the air together with the other elements, and as it were restoring the spirit needed by the dead, as may be seen from the similar vision of Ezekiel. Hence that sound in John 5:25 is called the voice of the Son of God, which the dead will hear.

units.la: Congregabunt. Angeli, & congregatos rapient nubes.
units.tr: They will gather. The angels, and the clouds will catch up those who have been gathered.

units.la: A quatuor ventis. Id est, à quatuor mundi plagis, unde spirant præcipui venti.
units.tr: From the four winds. That is, from the four quarters of the world, from which the chief winds blow.

units.la: A summis cœlorum usque ad terminos eorum. Id est, ab uno cœli extremo usque ad alterum. Per cœli autem extremum intelligitur locus cœli extremo subjectus, & ideo eandem rem expressit Marc. 13. v. 27. dicens: A summo terræ usque ad summum cœli.
units.tr: From one end of heaven to the other. That is, from one extremity of heaven to the other. By the extremity of heaven is meant the place lying under that extremity; so Mark 13:27 expresses the same thing, saying: from the end of the earth to the end of heaven.

units.la: 32. Discite parabolam. Id est, accipite similitudinem.
units.tr: 32. Learn the parable. That is, take the comparison.

units.la: Cùm jam ramus, &c. Explicat Matth. quod paulo obscurius dixit Lucas c. 21. v. 30. Cùm producunt jam ex se fructum arbores, fructum appellans quidquid arbores producunt, scilicet folia & gemmas, inchoamenta fructuum. Unde Græcè apud Luc. nulla fit mentio fructûs, sed habetur tantum verbum protrudunt sine addito, ut supplendum relinquatur lectori folia vel gemmas.
units.tr: When the branch now, etc. Matthew explains what Luke said somewhat more obscurely in chapter 21:30: when the trees now put forth their fruit, calling fruit whatever the trees produce, namely leaves and buds, the beginnings of fruit. Hence in the Greek of Luke there is no mention of fruit at all, but only the verb put forth without addition, so that the reader is left to supply leaves or buds.

units.la: 33. Prope est in januis. Adagialis locutio, id est, jam jam adest præ foribus regnum Dei, ut supplet Lucas c. 21. v. 31. illúdque plenum & pacatissimum, quod post judicium in sanctis revelabitur. Simili locutione Jacobus in Epistola sua catholica c. 5. v. 9. ait de tremendo Dei judicio, Ecce judex judex ante januam assistit. Et ut habetur in historia quadraginta Martyrum, mater ad filium Melithonem Martyrem dicebat: Fili paulisper sustine, ecce Christus ante ianuam stat adiuvans te. Apoc. 3. v. 20. Ecce, inquit Christus, sto ad ostium & pulso, id est, jam jam judicaturus & more Domini a negotio domum redeuntis cum servis suis rationem initurus, advenio. Hunc eundem sensum Christus ibidem expressit. v. 3. Veniam ad te tanquam fur & nescies quâ horâ veniam ad te. Et v. 11. Ecce venio cito. Sequitur autem, Siquis audierit vocem meam & aperuerit mihi januam, id est, si quis vigilaverit ad meum adventum, & confestim mihi ad judicium properanti aperuerit, seu gaudens & cum amore me exceperit judicem, de sua spe & operatione securus & de gloria retributionis hilarescens. Pergit Christus, Intrabo ad illum & cœnabo cum illo, & ipse mecum, id est, inquit doctissimus Estius, particeps erit gaudiorum atque honorum meorum. Atque ita nihil aliud significatur loco citato Apocal. nisi quod in præsenti capite sub finem & capite sequenti, Marc. 13. & Luc. 12. ubi ex similitudine servi vigilantis ad domini sui adventum, ut venienti confestim aperiat, Christus adhortatur omnes fideles ut semper vigilent in bonis operibus, ut, Domino ad judicium suris instar veniente, inveniantur læti sustinere judicem, & mereantur cum illo discumbere & cœnare, id est, æterni requie & gaudio fruì. Similis extat exhortatio 1 Thess. 5. & Apoc. 6.
units.tr: 33. It is near, at the doors. A proverbial expression: that is, the kingdom of God is now already at hand, now already before the doors, as Luke supplies in chapter 21:31, and that kingdom, full and most peaceful, which will be revealed in the saints after judgment. James, in chapter 5:9 of his catholic Epistle, speaks in a similar way of God's dreadful judgment: Behold, the judge judge stands before the door. And as is recorded in the history of the forty martyrs, the mother said to her son, the martyr Melito: Son, wait a little; behold, Christ stands before the door, helping you. Rev. 3:20: Behold, says Christ, I stand at the door and knock, that is, I come, about to judge at once, and, after the manner of a lord returning home from business, to settle accounts with his servants. Christ expresses the same sense in the same place, verse 3: I will come to you as a thief, and you will not know at what hour I will come to you. And verse 11: Behold, I come quickly. There follows: If anyone hears my voice and opens the door to me, that is, if anyone keeps watch for my coming, and at once opens to me as I hasten to judgment, or receives me gladly and lovingly as judge, secure in his hope and works and cheerful in the glory of reward. Christ goes on: I will enter to him and dine with him, and he with me, that is, as the most learned Estius says, he will share in my joys and honours. And thus nothing else is signified in the cited passage of Revelation, except what is signified in the present chapter at its end, and in the following chapter, in Mark 13 and Luke 12, where, from the likeness of a servant watching for his master's coming, so as to open at once when he comes, Christ exhorts all the faithful always to watch in good works, so that, when the Lord comes to judgment as a judge, they may be found glad to meet the judge, and may deserve to recline and dine with him, that is, to enjoy the rest and joy of eternity. A similar exhortation is found in 1 Thess. 5 and Rev. 6.

units.la: 34. Generatio hæc. Nempe Judæorum, quia pleraque ex prædictis in Judæis complenda erant.
units.tr: 34. Generatio hæc. That is, the generation of the Jews, since most of the things foretold were to be fulfilled in the Jews.

units.la: 35. Cœlum & terra transibunt. Immutatione, non aboliti one sui. Hier. lib. 4. in Matth. 24. Sic 2 Pet. 3. v. 5, & 6. aquâ inundatus periisse dictus est mundus, seu qui tunc erant cœli & terra; ubi cœli diserte usurpantur pro aeris regionibus.
units.tr: 35. Cœlum & terra transibunt. They will pass away by change, not by annihilation of their substance. Jerome, book 4 on Matthew 24. So 2 Peter 3:5-6 says that the world, that is, the heavens and earth of that time, perished when it was flooded with water; there "heavens" is plainly used for the regions of the air.

units.la: Verba autem mea. Id est, hactenus à me dicta.
units.tr: Verba autem mea. That is, the words I have spoken so far.

units.la: Non præteribunt. Id est, sortientur infallibiliter & immutabiliter quidquid significant, adeo ut nihil quidquam aliter sit eventurum, quàm ipsa sonant & significant.
units.tr: Non præteribunt. That is, they will infallibly and unchangeably come to pass in whatever they signify, so that nothing will happen otherwise than they sound and signify.

units.la: 36. De die autem illa & hora nemo scit, neque Angeli cœlorum. Additur Marc. 13. v. 32. neque Filius. Supple, quâ homo, cùm omnia sciat quâ Deus. Vide commentarium nostrum loco laudato Marci. Eandem distinctionem videre est apud S. Athanasium in fine Epistolæ ad Serapionem, & in oratione 4. contra Arianos, apud S. Hilarium Pictaviensem lib. 9. de Trinitate, S. Gregorium Nazianzenum oratione trigesimâ sextâ, quæ est quarta de Theologia, S. Ambrosium lib. 5. de fide cap. 7. Chrysostom. Ser. 117. Tom. 5. S. Cyrillum Alexandrinum lib. 9. Thesauri. cap. 4. & lib. 10. cap. 7. lib. 2. ad religiosissimas Reginas cap. 16, & 17. S. Proclum Constantinopolitanum in Epistola ad Armenios, Titum Boftrenfem in cap. fecundum Lucæ, Greg. Mag. lib. 8. Epist. 42. & πάντες οἱ Πατέρες propemodum universi patres, ut loquitur præclarissimus Scriptor Leontius Byzantinus in lib. de sectis Act. 10. Ab hac mente veterum Orthodoxorum Patrum longè aberant hæretici Agnoëtæ; non enim agnoscebant in Christo duas diversas naturas inconfuse unitas, salvâ proprietate utriusque naturæ, sed unam tantum putabant esse naturam compositam, atque adeò quod Christum dicebant ut hominem ignorare, illud Christum penitus ignorasse existimabant. Quicumque igitur duas in uno Christo agnoscit distinctas naturas contra Nestorium & Monophysitas, & agnoscit Christum secundum Deitatem neque esuriisse, neque sitivisse, neque mortem perpessum esse, neque quidquam ignorasse, quamvis dicat hæc omnia Christo secundum humanitatem contigisse, is ab hæresi Agnoëtarum immunis est cum SS. Patribus Athanasio, Cyrillo & ceteris supra laudatis. Agnoëtas autem sensisse quòd Christi Deitas ignoret futura, quæ sunt scripta de die & hora novissima, testatur Leontius loco supra laudato, S. Isidorus Hispalensis lib. 8. originum cap. 5. Rabanus Maurus lib. 2. de institutione clericorum cap. 58. Gratianus in decreto causa 24. q. 3. can. Quidam autem. Joannes Damascenus in lib. de Hæresibus, Joannes Maldonatus in cap. 24. Matth. Petrus Thyræus in tractatu de gloriosa Filii apparitione cap. 19. num. 26. Adamus Conzen in cap. 24. Matth. Ut fabula igitur rejicienda est narratio Nicephori Callisti, dum contra omnium Scriptorum veterum relationes ait Agnoëtas dixisse Deum quidem Verbum omnia nosse, humanitatem verò secundum substantiam ei unitam permulta ignorare. Sed fabulosam esse Nicephori relationem de Agnoëtis lib. 18. hist. Ecclef. c. 50. præter veterum autoritatem satis evincit primò quod ait Themistium Philosophum sub Valente Imperatore hæresis Agnoëtarum autorem extitisse, cùm Themistius ille Philosophus Ethnicus fuerit, & Themistius Agnoëtarum autor fuerit Diaconus Timothei Alexandrini Corrupticolæ circa annum Domini 531. Secundò quod Nicephorus ait Arianorum errorem ab Agnoëtis refumtum esse, & tamen soli humanitati ignorantiam secundum Agnoëtas tribuit, secum pugnat; neque enim Ariani concedebant Verbum omnia nosse, neque aliunde de Verbi & Patris inæqualitatem, quàm ex ipsius Verbi secundum Deitatem ignorantia, aliisque inferioris conditionis argumentis astruere satagebant. Tertiò Nicephorus ait Severum fuisse hæresis Agnoëtarum renovatorem, quem Diaconus Liberatus scribit præcipuè restitisse Themistio Agnoëtarum autori.
units.tr: 36. De die autem illa & hora nemo scit, neque Angeli cœlorum. Mark 13:32 adds neque Filius, "nor the Son". Supply: as man, since he knows all things as God. See our commentary on the passage of Mark cited above. This same distinction can be seen in St Athanasius at the end of his letter to Serapion and in his fourth oration against the Arians; in St Hilary of Poitiers, book 9 On the Trinity; in St Gregory Nazianzen, oration 36, which is the fourth on Theology; in St Ambrose, book 5 On the Faith, chapter 7; in Chrysostom, sermon 117, vol. 5; in St Cyril of Alexandria, Thesaurus book 9 chapter 4, book 10 chapter 7, and book 2 to the most religious queens, chapters 16 and 17; in St Proclus of Constantinople in his letter to the Armenians; in Titus of Bostra on the second chapter of Luke; in Gregory the Great, book 8 letter 42; and in propemodum universi patres [πάντες οἱ Πατέρες], almost all the Fathers, as the most distinguished writer Leontius of Byzantium puts it in his book On the Sects, Act. 10. The heretical Agnoetae were far from this mind of the ancient orthodox Fathers. For they did not acknowledge in Christ two distinct natures united without confusion, with the property of each nature preserved; they thought there was only one composite nature, and so, what they said of Christ as man, that he was ignorant, they thought was true of Christ entirely, that he had been wholly ignorant of it. Whoever therefore acknowledges two distinct natures in the one Christ, against Nestorius and the Monophysites, and acknowledges that Christ according to his Deity neither hungered, nor thirsted, nor suffered death, nor was ignorant of anything, although he says all these things happened to Christ according to his humanity, is free from the heresy of the Agnoetae, along with the holy Fathers Athanasius, Cyril and the others cited above. That the Agnoetae held that the Deity of Christ does not know the future things written about the last day and hour, Leontius testifies in the place cited above; so do St Isidore of Seville, book 8 of the Origins, chapter 5; Rabanus Maurus, book 2 On the Institution of Clerics, chapter 58; Gratian in the Decretum, causa 24, q. 3, can. Quidam autem; John of Damascus in his book On Heresies; John Maldonatus on Matthew 24; Peter Thyraeus in his tract On the Glorious Appearance of the Son, chapter 19, n. 26; and Adam Conzen on Matthew 24. Therefore the narrative of Nicephorus Callistus is to be rejected as a fable, when, against the reports of all the ancient writers, he says the Agnoetae taught that God the Word indeed knows all things, but the humanity united to him in substance knows very many things not. That Nicephorus's account of the Agnoetae is fabulous, apart from the authority of the ancients, is sufficiently proved, first, by his saying that the philosopher Themistius under the Emperor Valens was the author of the Agnoetae heresy, whereas that Themistius was a pagan philosopher, and the author of the Agnoetae was a deacon of Timothy the Corrupticola of Alexandria, around the year of the Lord 531. Secondly, Nicephorus says the error of the Arians was taken up again by the Agnoetae, and yet he attributes ignorance to the humanity alone according to the Agnoetae; this contradicts itself, for the Arians did not concede that the Word knows all things, nor did they try to establish the inequality of Word and Father from anything but the ignorance of the Word according to his Deity, and from other arguments of lower kind. Thirdly, Nicephorus says Severus was the renewer of the Agnoetae heresy, whereas the deacon Liberatus writes that Severus above all resisted Themistius, the author of the Agnoetae.

units.la: Nisi solus Pater. In Patre comprehendit & Filium, inquit Hier. tota quippe individua Trinitas unum est cognitionis, ut loquitur S. Ambr. in cap. 17. Lucæ. Itaque Christus scientiam, quam secundum humanitatem non habuit, ex qua cum Angelis creatura fuit, hanc se cum Angelis, qui creaturæ sunt, habere denegavit; sed quia secundum Deitatem consubstantialis est Patri, ejus Deitas seu natura, quæ est super Angelos, habet ut hoc sciat quod Angeli ignorant.
units.tr: Nisi solus Pater. In Patre comprehendit & Filium, says Jerome: for the whole undivided Trinity is unum est cognitionis, "of one knowledge", as St Ambrose puts it on the seventeenth chapter of Luke. Thus Christ denied that he has with the angels the knowledge which he did not have according to his humanity, by which he was a creature along with the angels; but because according to his Deity he is consubstantial with the Father, his Deity or nature, which is above the angels, has the knowledge that the angels do not have.

units.la: 37. Sicut autem in diebus Noë, &c. Non eodem loco & tempore id narrant à Christo dictum Matth. & Luc. vel quia bis idem à Christo dictum fuit, vel alteruter ordinem temporis non servat.
units.tr: 37. Sicut autem in diebus Noë, etc. Matthew and Luke do not relate that Christ said this in the same place and at the same time, either because Christ said the same thing twice, or because one of them does not keep the order of time.

units.la: Comedentes, &c. Id est, voluptatum illecebris æstuantes.
units.tr: Comedentes, etc. That is, burning with the allurements of pleasures.

units.la: 40. Tunc duo erunt in agro. Supple, hîc & versu sequenti, nihil minus quam de die judicii cogitantes. Expunxit Clemens VIII. ex præsenti versiculo has voces: duo in lecto, unum assumetur & unus relinquetur: existimans eas ex Luca hûc translatas, quæ tamen in Sixti V. editione & in multis codicibus tam Græcis, quàm Latinis hîc quoque habentur.
units.tr: 40. Tunc duo erunt in agro. Supply, here and in the following verse, thinking of nothing less than the day of judgment. Clement VIII struck from this verse the words duo in lecto, unum assumetur & unus relinquetur, "two in a bed, one will be taken and one left", thinking they had been carried over here from Luke; yet they are found here too in the edition of Sixtus V and in many manuscripts, both Greek and Latin.

units.la: Unum assumetur. Id est, sursum rapietur ad Filium hominis, ut indicat Lucas c. 17. v. 37. Per Christi conclusionem de quibusdam hominum generibus, quæ hîc & Luc. 17. per similitudines propositæ leguntur, discimus omnem professionem in Ecclesia habere fictos, & in quocunque genere vitæ, quod habet aliquam professionem, nec omnes inveniri probos, nec omnes inveniri reprobos, ut egregie suo more monet Aug. Conc. 1. in Psal. 36. in expos. Psal. 99. & in Psal. 132. Proinde ad quamcumque professionem te converteris, para te pati sitos: aliquin si te non paraveris, invenies quod non ferebas, & deficies, aut perturbaberis. Ita Aug. Conc. 1. in Psal. 36.
units.tr: Unum assumetur. That is, will be caught up on high to the Son of man, as Luke 17:37 indicates. From Christ's conclusion about certain kinds of men, set forth here and in Luke 17 by way of similitudes, we learn that every profession in the Church has its hypocrites, and that in whatever kind of life there is some profession, not all are found good nor all found reprobate, as Augustine admirably advises in his usual way: Sermon 1 on Psalm 36, the exposition of Psalm 99, and on Psalm 132. Therefore, to whatever profession you turn, prepare yourself to suffer; otherwise, if you have not prepared, you will find what you did not expect to bear, and you will fail or be thrown into confusion. Thus Augustine, Sermon 1 on Psalm 36.

units.la: Unus relinquetur. Id est, non rapietur.
units.tr: Unus relinquetur. That is, will not be taken.

units.la: 41. Duæ molentes, &c. Molere opus erat mulierum, ut patet passim ex Scriptura. Molendinum putat Aug. locis mox citatis dictum mundum istum, quia rota quædam temporum volvitur, & amatores suos conterit; molentes verò, qui devincti in sæculo, circuitu rerum temporalium, tanquam molî detinentur. 42. Vigilate ergo, &c. Jam dictum est in præcedentibus moris esse Matthæo simul conjungere quæ ad eandem doctrinam pertinent, licet alio loco & tempore dicta. Quare quæ inseruit de servo bono & malo præsenti sermoni Christi de judicio, videntur dicta eo loco & tempore, quo referuntur à Luca c. 12. v. 39.
units.tr: 41. Duæ molentes, etc. Grinding was the work of women, as is clear everywhere from Scripture. Augustine, in the places just cited, thinks this world is called a mill, because a certain wheel of times turns and grinds down its lovers; and those who grind are those who, bound fast in the age, are held as if by the round of temporal things, like millstones. 42. Vigilate ergo, etc. It has already been said in preceding passages that it is Matthew's custom to join together things pertaining to the same teaching, though spoken at another place and time. Hence what he has inserted about the good and bad servant in the present discourse of Christ on judgment seems to have been said at the place and time to which Luke refers in chapter 12, verse 39.

units.la: 44. Efiote parati. Explicat Christus quid intellexerit, dum nobis vigilandum esse dixit.
units.tr: 44. Estote parati. Christ explains what he meant when he told us that we must watch.

units.la: 45. Quis putas est fidelis servus. Græcè, quisnam est fidelis servus. Alludit Christus ad Patremfamilias, qui peregrè proficiscens, unum ex famulis toti familiæ præficit. Vox Dominica adeò rarum negotium esse demonstrat, ut quis bene Ecclesia Dei præsit, ut etiam Christus dubitabunda oratione usus fuerit, dicens, Quis est fidelis, &c. Isidor. Pelusiota lib. 3. Epist. 145.
units.tr: 45. Quis putas est fidelis servus. In Greek, "who then is the faithful servant". Christ alludes to a householder who, setting out on a journey abroad, places one of his servants over the whole household. "The Lord's voice shows this business to be so rare that, for one to preside well over the Church of God, Christ used a doubting form of speech, saying, 'Who is faithful?' etc." Isidore of Pelusium, book 3, letter 145.

units.la: Prudens. Id est, sapiens, qui, ut B. Hier. loquitur, non verit, quando debeat proferre sermonem.
units.tr: Prudens. That is, wise, who, as St Jerome puts it, does not err as to when he ought to bring out a word.

units.la: Ut det illis cibum in tempore. Non ut subditorum corda in sui amorem & propriam laudem convertat, sed ad utilitatem domesticorum præficitur unus e famulis toti familiæ, unicuique opportunè ministraturus pro modo capacitatis uniuscujusque, quod Lucas significat c. 12. v. 24. per tritici mensuram. Auctore Donato in Terentianum Phormionem Act. 1. sc. 1. v. 9. servi quolibet mense quaternos modios accipiebant, idque demensum est appellatum à demetiendo. Ad hanc consuetudinem alludere videntur & Lucæ & Matthæi locutiones præsentes.
units.tr: That he may give them food in due season. This does not mean that he is set over the household to turn the servants' hearts toward himself and his own praise. Rather, one of the servants is placed over the whole household for its benefit, to supply each person in good time according to the measure of each one's capacity. Luke expresses this in chapter 12, verse 24, by "the measure of wheat." According to Donatus, on Terence's Phormio, Act 1, scene 1, verse 9, slaves used to receive four measures each month, and this allowance was called demensum from demetiendo (measuring out). The words of both Luke and Matthew seem to allude to this custom.

units.la: 47. Super omnia bona sua constituet eum. Id est, non solum super famulitium, sed quia fidelitatem ejus expertus est, super omnes divitias suas penè parem sibi constituet eum.
