units.tr: 47. He will set him over all his goods. That is, not only over the servants' service, but because he has proved his faithfulness, he will set him over nearly all his riches, as an equal to himself.

units.la: 49. Manducet autem & bibat. Id est, comessationibus & voluptatibus vacet.
units.tr: 49. And he will eat and drink. That is, he will devote himself to feasting and pleasures.

units.la: 51. Dividet eum. Id est, separabit eum à corsortio ceterorum servorum, & ab officio ipsi credito amovebit.
units.tr: 51. He will cut him in pieces. That is, he will separate him from the company of the other servants and remove him from the office entrusted to him.

units.la: Partémque ejus ponet cum hypocritis. Id est, sortem ipsi dabit, qualem daturus est impiis, qui Hebraicâ proprietate hypocritæ vocari solent, ut patet Job 8. v. 13. Unde Luc. pro, cum hypocritis, habet, cum fidelibus.
units.tr: And he will appoint his portion with the hypocrites. That is, he will give him the lot he is going to give to the wicked, who in Hebrew idiom are usually called hypocrites, as is clear from Job 8, verse 13. Hence Luke, instead of with the hypocrites, has with the unbelievers.

units.la: CAPUT
units.tr: CHAPTER

units.la: CAPUT XXV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXV.

units.la: 1. Tunc. Scilicet, cùm advenero judicaturus vivos & mortuos.
units.tr: 1. Then. Namely, when I shall have come to judge the living and the dead.

units.la: Simile erit regnum cælorum. Id est, Ecclesia mea ex hoc mundo collecta similis erit decem virginibus. Hæc parabola sumta est ab antiquo ritu, quo sicut sponso juvenes, ut dicitur Judic. 14. v. 11. ita sponsæ honoris causà virgines addebantur, quæ ipsà nocte nuptiarum in sponsæ ædibus expectabant adventum sponsi; & accenso lumine prodibant obviàm sponso venienti in domum sponsæ, ut ipse eam inde cum virginibus lumen præferentibus in ædes suas vel aliam convivii domum duceret, ubi noctu pro more nuptiarum pompa celebrabatur. Hinc ortum habet Latina phrasis, ducere uxorem. Itaque ad rem significatam transeundo, virginum decem nomine significantur omnes profitentes catholicam fidem integram, nec aperte Ecclesiæ rebelles.
units.tr: The kingdom of heaven shall be like. That is, my Church, gathered out of this world, shall be like ten virgins. This parable is taken from an ancient custom. Just as young men were given to the bridegroom, as is said in Judges 14:11, so virgins were added to the bride as an honour. On the wedding night they waited in the bride's house for the coming of the bridegroom. Then, with their lamps lit, they went out to meet the bridegroom as he came to the bride's house, so that he might lead her from there, with the virgins carrying lamps before her, to his own home or to another house for the feast, where the wedding procession was held at night according to custom. From this comes the Latin phrase ducere uxorem (to lead a wife). So, passing to the thing signified, the ten virgins stand for all who profess the Catholic faith whole and entire, and are not openly rebellious against the Church.

units.la: Et sponsæ. Hæc verba desunt in textu Græco, & aptius quidem tum ad parabolam, ut ex mox dictis liquet, tum ad rem significatam; certum est enim per sponsum significari Christum. Eatenus tamen & sponsæ ibatur obviàm, quia illa per virgines ad ædes sponsi deducenda erat. Designatur autem per sponsam Ecclesia triumphans.
units.tr: And the bride. These words are missing from the Greek text, and they fit the parable less well, as is clear from what has just been said, and they fit the thing signified less well too. For it is certain that the bridegroom signifies Christ. Yet to that extent the bride was also met, because she was to be brought to the bridegroom's house by the virgins. The bride, moreover, signifies the Church triumphant.

units.la: 2. Quinque autem ex eis erant fatuæ. Fatuitas virginum in eo sita erat, quod in vasis suis, id est, in cordibus aut conscientia non sumserant oleum secum, id est, charitatem non erant amplexæ, quæ reliquis virtutibus supereminet, ut liquoribus supernatat oleum, fidémque quasi lampadem ardere facit, lætitiam in conscientia parit, & ad omne opus bonum instimulat.
units.tr: 2. Now five of them were foolish. The foolishness of the virgins lay in this: that they had not taken oil with them in their vessels, that is, in their hearts or consciences. That is, they had not embraced charity, which surpasses the other virtues as oil floats above liquids, which makes faith burn like a lamp, which brings joy to the conscience, and which spurs us on to every good work.

units.la: 5. Moram autem faciente sponso. Id est, Christo adventum suum ad judicium differente.
units.tr: 5. Now while the bridegroom delayed. That is, while Christ deferred his coming for judgement.

units.la: Dormitaverunt. Id est, ægrotaverunt. Ægritudo autem dicitur dormitatio, quia tendit ad mortem, quæ dicitur dormitio juxta illud 1 Thess. 4 De dormientibus autem nolo vos ignorare fratres: id est, de his, qui mortui sunt.
units.tr: They slept. That is, they fell ill. Sickness is called sleep, because it tends towards death, which is called falling asleep, as in 1 Thess. 4: But I would not have you ignorant, brethren, concerning those who are asleep; that is, concerning those who have died.

units.la: Dormierunt. Id est, occubuerunt. Ut enim ait Augustinus Sermone 23. de verbis Domini, ubi præsentem parabolam accuratè explicat, Fatua fit virgo, prudens fit virgo, somnum mortis omnes patiuntur.
units.tr: They all slept. That is, they died. For as Augustine says in Sermon 23 on the words of the Lord, where he explains this parable with care: The virgin becomes foolish, the virgin becomes wise; all suffer the sleep of death.

units.la: ¨6. Media autem nocte. Id est, hora inexpectata.
units.tr: 6. But at midnight. That is, at an unexpected hour.

units.la: Clamor factus est. Nempe vocis illius magnae, de qua diximus capite praecedente v. 31.
units.tr: There was a cry. Namely, of that great voice, of which we spoke in the previous chapter at verse 31.

units.la: 8. Lampades nostrae extinguuntur. Fatuae virgines, quae alias bona sunt operatae ut hominibus placerent, & ab his laudes haberent, jam laudibus humanis deficientibus, lampades earum extinguuntur, & quaerunt à prudentibus ut sibi accommodent oleum suum, seu ut sua charitate sibi subvenient.
units.tr: 8. Our lamps are going out. The foolish virgins, who had otherwise done good works in order to please men and to win praise from them, now that human praise is failing, see their lamps go out. They ask the wise to share their oil with them, that is, to help them with their charity.

units.la: 9. Ne forte non sufficiat nobis & vobis. Hac voce significant prudentes virgines quantus tremor fit futurus etiam in ipsis justis, quando judex est venturus cuncta strictè discussurus. Quis enim poterit dicere: Mundum est cor meum, purus sum à peccato? Prov. 20.
units.tr: 9. Lest perhaps there be not enough for us and for you. By these words the wise virgins signify how great the trembling will be, even in the righteous themselves, when the judge is about to come, who will examine all things strictly. For who can say: My heart is clean, I am pure from sin? Prov. 20.

units.la: Ite potius, &c. Haec est responsio non consulentium, sed subsannantium. Quasi dicerent, Olim tempus erat parandi olei, non modo; ite nunc ad eos, quorum vel gratiam vel laudem quaerebatis, ut lampades haberetis accensas.
units.tr: Go rather, etc. This is the answer not of people giving counsel but of people mocking. As if they were saying: there was a time for buying oil, but not now. Go now to those whose favour or praise you were seeking, so that you may have your lamps lit.

units.la: 10. Dum autem irent emere. Id est, dum anxii essent de remedio.
units.tr: 10. But while they went to buy. That is, while they were anxious about a remedy.

units.la: Venit sponsus. Scilicet ad domum sponsae.
units.tr: The bridegroom came. Namely, to the bride's house.

units.la: 14. Sicut enim homo peregrè proficiscens. Causalis particula enim indicat hanc parabolam eodem omnino spectare, quò parabola de decem virginibus, ut nimirum, dum horam ultimam praevidere non possumus, ad illam sine intermissione praeparemur, vigilantes tanquam rationem Deo reddituii. Est autem haec parabola talentorum valde similis parabolae minarum, quae refertur à Luca Capite 19. & eundem scopum habet, licet alio tempore & loco & occasione dicta, & in quibusdam circumstantiis narrationis diversa sit.
units.tr: 14. For it is as a man going abroad. The causal particle for shows that this parable looks to exactly the same end as the parable of the ten virgins: namely, that since we cannot foresee the last hour, we should prepare ourselves for it without pause, watching as those who must give an account to God. This parable of the talents is very like the parable of the pounds, which Luke reports in chapter 19. It has the same purpose, although it was spoken at another time, place and occasion, and it differs in some details of the narrative.

units.la: Unicuique secundum propriam virtutem, Graece, potestatem. Praeclare autem pro more suo Scholae Angelus Thomas 22. q. 24. art. 3. ad 1. Illa virtus secundum quam sua dona Deus dat unicuique, est dispositio vel praeparatio praecedens, sive conatus gratiam accipientis: sed hanc etiam dispositionem vel conatum praevenit Spiritus Sanctus movens mentem hominis, vel plus, vel minus, secundum suam voluntatem: unde & Apostolus dicit ad Coloss. 1. Qui dignos nos fecit in partem sortis Sanctorum in lumine.
units.tr: To each according to his own power. In Greek, power [δύναμιν]. The Angelic Thomas, in his usual excellent manner, writes in the Second Part of the Second Part, question 24, article 3, reply 1: That power according to which God gives his gifts to each person is a preceding disposition or preparation, or the effort of the one who receives grace. But the Holy Spirit, moving the mind of man, goes before even this disposition or effort, more or less according to his will. Hence also the Apostle says to the Colossians 1: He has made us fit to share in the inheritance of the saints in light.

units.la: 21. Euge serve bone. Sicut sunt duo timores, qui faciunt duo genera timentium, sic duae sunt servitutes, quae faciunt duo genera servientium. Est timor quem perfecta charitas foras mittit, & est alius timor castus permanens in seculum seculi. Illum timorem, qui non est in charitate, attendebat Apostolus cum dicebat: Non enim accepistis Spiritum seruitutis iterum in timore. Iterum autem timorem castum attendebat, cum dicebat: Noli altum sapere, sed time. In illo timore, quem foras charitas mittit, est etiam servitus simul foras cum ipso timore mittenda; utrumque enim junxit Apostolus, hoc est, servitutem & timorem, dicendo: Non enim accepistis Spiritum servitutis iterum in timore. Ad hanc servitutem servum pertinentem intuebatur & Dominus dicens: Jam non dicam vos servos, &c. Hic autem, ubi dicitur, Euge serve bone, &c. manifestum est illum significari servum pertinentem ad timorem castum, qui permanet in seculum seculi. Itaque miro quodam & ineffabili, sed tamen vero modo, servi non servi esse possumus; servi scilicet timore casto, ad quem pertinet servus intrans in gaudium Domini sui: non servi autem timorem foras mittendo, ad quem pertinet servus non manens in domo in æternum. Ut autem tales servi non servi simus, Dominum facere scimus; hoc autem servus ille nescit, qui nescit quid faciat Dominus ejus, & cum aliquid boni facit sic extollitur quasi hoc ipse faciat, non Dominus ejus, & in se, non in Domino gloriatur, cum se ipse deceperit, quia sic gloriatur, quasi non acceperit. Aug. Tract. 85, & 89. in Joan.
units.tr: 21. Well done, good servant. Just as there are two fears, which make two kinds of those who fear, so there are two servitudes, which make two kinds of those who serve. There is the fear which perfect love casts out, and there is another, chaste fear, which endures for ever and ever. The Apostle had in mind the fear that is not in love when he said: For you have not received the spirit of bondage again in fear. And again he had in mind chaste fear when he said: Do not be proud, but fear. In that fear which love casts out, servitude too is to be cast out together with the fear itself. For the Apostle joined the two, that is, servitude and fear, saying: For you have not received the spirit of servitude again in fear. The Lord also had in view the servant belonging to this servitude when he said: Now I will no longer call you servants, etc. But here, where it is said, Well done, good servant, etc., it is plain that the servant signified is the one who belongs to chaste fear, which endures for ever and ever. So, in a certain wonderful and ineffable but nonetheless true way, we can be servants and not servants: servants indeed by chaste fear, to which belongs the servant who enters into the joy of his lord; not servants by casting out fear, to which belongs the servant who does not remain in the house for ever. Now, that we may be such servants who are not servants, we know that the Lord makes us so. But that servant does not know this, who does not know what his lord does, and when he does some good he is so lifted up as if he himself did it, not his lord, and he glories in himself, not in the Lord, since he has deceived himself, for he glories as if he had not received it. Augustine, Tractates 85 and 89 on John.

units.la: Intra in gaudium Domini tui. Quia nimirum Deus major est corde creato, continens autem debet esse contento majus: idcirco in gaudium Dei nos intramus, non vero gaudium Dei in nos intrat, ut explicat autor commentarii sub nomine Divi Thomæ in Matthæum. Eandem expositionem amplectitur ipse Divus Thomas 22. q. 28. art. 3. in fine corporis articuli, quamvis intrare in gaudium Domini simpliciter explicet B. Hilar. Can. 27. in Matth. in honorem gloriæ Christi recipi. Et Chrysostomus Hom. 79. in Matth. universam beatitudinem assequi, & apud eumdem autor operis imperfecti Hom. 53. non spectatorem tantum beatitudinis esse, sed possessorem.
units.tr: Enter into the joy of your lord. Because, of course, God is greater than the created heart, and what contains must be greater than what is contained. Therefore we enter into God's joy; God's joy does not enter into us. So the author of the commentary published under the name of the Divine Thomas on Matthew explains it. The Divine Thomas himself embraces the same exposition in the Second Part of the Second Part, question 28, article 3, at the end of the body of the article, although Saint Hilary, on Matthew, canon 27, simply explains to enter into the joy of the Lord as to be received in the honour of Christ's glory. Chrysostom, Homily 79 on Matthew, explains it as to attain all blessedness; and in the same work, the author of the Opus Imperfectum, Homily 53, says that one is not merely a spectator of blessedness but its possessor.

units.la: 23. Quia super pauca fuisti fidelis, &c. Pauca bona sunt omnia præsentis vitæ, quamlibet multa esse videantur, comparatione retributionis æternæ. Sed tunc fidelis servus super multa constituitur, quando devistå omni corruptionis molestiå, de æternis gaudiis in cœlesti sede gloriatur. Tunc ad sui Domini gaudium perfectè intromittitur, quando in æternam illam patriam assumtus atque Angelorum cœtibus admixtus, sic interius gaudet de munere, ut non sit jam quod exterius doleat de corruptione. S. Greg. Mag. Hom. 9. in Evangelia.
units.tr: 23. Because you have been faithful over a few things, etc. All the good things of the present life are few, however many they may seem, when compared with the eternal reward. But the faithful servant is set over many things when, with every trouble of corruption cast off, he glories in eternal joys in the heavenly seat. He is then fully brought into his lord's joy when he is taken up into that eternal homeland and joined to the companies of the angels, and so rejoices inwardly in the gift that there is no longer anything outwardly to grieve over in corruption. Saint Gregory the Great, Homily 9 on the Gospels.

units.la: 24. Scio quia homo durus es, &c. Vere quod scriptum est: Ad excusandas excusationes in peccatis: etiam huic servo contigit, ut ad pigritiam & negligentiam, superbia quoque crimen accederet. Qui enim simpliciter debuit inertiam confiteri, & orare patremfamilias: e contrario calumniatur & dicit se prudenti fecisse consilio, ne dum lucra pecuniae quaereret, etiam de sorte periclitaretur. B. Hier. Nempe ut advertit Aug. Tract. 8. in cap. 4: Epist S. Joan. Perversi homines quod faciunt bene, volunt sibi tribuere: si male faciunt, Deum volunt accusare.
units.tr: 24. I know that you are a hard man, etc. Truly it is written: to make excuses for sins. This servant too was guilty of pride as well as laziness and negligence. For he ought simply to have confessed his idleness and begged the householder's pardon. Instead, on the contrary, he slanders him and says that he acted on prudent advice, lest, while seeking gain from money, he might also endanger the principal. St Jerome. Indeed, as Augustine observes in Tractate 8 on the Epistle of St John, chapter 4: Wicked men want to claim credit for whatever good they do; if they do evil, they want to accuse God.

units.la: 26. Respondens autem Dominus, &c. Retorquet Dominus in condemnationem servi, qui per pigritiam noluit duplicare talentum, quod attulit ipse in sui excusationem calumnians Domino per malitiam.
units.tr: 26. But the Lord answering, etc. The Lord turns it back on the servant for his condemnation. Through laziness he would not double the talent, and he brought it back in his own defence, maliciously accusing his Lord.

units.la: Meto ubi non semino, &c. Deus nihil requirit ab homine, nisi bonum quod ipse in nobis seminavit: Et ideo verbum illud vel intelligitur secundum pravam existimationem servi pigri, qui existimavit se non ab alio accepisse: Vel intelligitur quantum ad hoc quod Deus requirit a nobis fructus donorum, qui sunt & ab eo & a nobis: Quamvis ipsa dona a Deo sint sine nobis. D. Thom. 22. q. 62. art. 4. ad 3.
units.tr: I reap where I have not sown, etc. God requires nothing from a man except the good which he himself has sown in us. So this saying is understood either according to the lazy servant's wicked opinion, that he thought he had received nothing from another; or it is understood with regard to the fact that God requires from us the fruits of the gifts, which come both from him and from us, although the gifts themselves are from God without us. St Thomas, II-II, q. 62, art. 4, ad 3.

units.la: 27. Cum usura. Usura metaphorice accipitur pro superexcrescentio bonorum spiritualium, quam exigit Deus volens ut in bonis acceptis ab eo semper proficiamus, quod est ad utilitatem nostram, non ejus. D. Th. 22. q. 78. ar. 1. ad 1.
units.tr: 27. With usury. Usury is taken metaphorically for the surplus increase of spiritual goods, which God demands, wishing that we always make progress in the goods received from him, which is for our benefit, not for his. St Thomas, II-II, q. 78, art. 1, ad 1.

units.la: 28. Tollite, &c. Q. d. Servum, qui facere bona opera neglexerit, spoliate omnibus Spiritus-Sancti donis, & similia dona date ei, qui habet decem talenta, non ad fructificandum in aliis, sed ad gaudii, honoris, & gloriae cumulum.
units.tr: 28. Take, etc. That is to say: strip the servant who has neglected to do good works of all the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and give such gifts to him who has ten talents, not to bear fruit in others but to increase his joy, honour and glory.

units.la: Omni enim habenti. Scilicet Dei dona, eisque bene utenti.
units.tr: For to everyone who has. That is, God's gifts, and to one who uses them well.

units.la: Qui non habet. Scilicet bonum Dei donorum usum.
units.tr: From him who does not have. That is, the good use of God's gifts.

units.la: Quod videtur habere. Nempe sibi vel aliis.
units.tr: Even what he seems to have. That is, for himself or for others.

units.la: 30. In tenebras exteriores. Q. d. Extimas seu extremas, id est, profundissimas tanquam a regni coelestis luce remotissimas.
units.tr: 30. Into the outer darkness. That is to say, into the outermost or extreme darkness, that is, the deepest, as being most remote from the light of the heavenly kingdom.

units.la: 31. Cum autem. Jam describit Christus formam, qua rationem a praedictis servis fit exacturus.
units.tr: 31. But when. Now Christ describes the manner in which he will call these servants to account.

units.la: Sicut pastor segregat oves ab haedis. Alludit Christus ad illud Ezech. 34. v. 17. Ecce ego judico inter pecus & pecus arietum & bircorum, Hebraice, inter arietes & hircos. Electos igitur comparat Christus cum ovibus, reprobos vero cum hircis. Et licet ovibus & capris multae sint communes dotes, & non pauca communia vocabula; utrumque enim saepe Homerus nomine μυλᾶν complectitur, utrumque indifferenter significatur nomine collectivo ןִי, de singulis utriusque individuis dicitur nomen זכר, & utriusque pellis dicitur ναλ & μηλωτή, &c. tamen scribit probatissimè Theodoretus in Exod. q. 24. quòd cùm Lex dicit victimam Paschalem tollendam ex ovibus, vel ex capris, intendit ut qui ovem habet, eam immolet, & qui ove caret, hoedum. Unde cùm Christus nobis proponatur innumeris locis sub agni typo, & nominatim sub typo agni Paschalis, ne semel quidem illum hoedi nomine insigniri videas, quo in praesenti loco insigniuntur reprobi propter libidinem, quâ, si Chrysostomo credimus, fervet prae ceteris animalibus; propter rixas & gulam, ob quam non recta via sed per praecipitia solent incedere; adde in primis propter foetorem & immunditiam vitæ.
units.tr: As a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats. Christ alludes to Ezekiel 34:17: Behold, I judge between flock and flock, between the rams and the he-goats (in Hebrew, between the rams and the goats). Christ therefore compares the elect to sheep, but the reprobate to goats. And although sheep and goats have many common qualities and not a few common names (for Homer often embraces both under the Greek word for sheep [μηλῶν]; both are indifferently signified by the collective Hebrew word for flock [צֹאן]; of each individual of either kind the word for male [זָכָר] is used; and the skin of either is called nakos [νάκος] or sheepskin cloak [μηλωτή], etc.), still Theodoret writes most convincingly on Exodus, question 24, that when the Law says the Passover victim is to be taken from the sheep or from the goats, it intends that whoever has a sheep should sacrifice it, and whoever lacks a sheep should sacrifice a kid. Hence, although Christ is set before us in countless places under the type of the lamb, and especially under the type of the Passover lamb, you will not see even once that he is marked with the name of kid, which in the present place marks the reprobate on account of their lust, which, if we believe Chrysostom, burns more fiercely than in other animals; on account of their quarrels and gluttony, because of which they tend to walk not by the straight way but over precipices; and above all on account of the stench and filthiness of their lives.

units.la: 34. Tunc dicet. Nempe mentaliter, non vocaliter; totum enim judicium illud postremum, & quoad discussionem & quoad accusationem malorum & commendationem bonorum, & quoad sententiam de utrisque mentaliter perficietur; si enim vocaliter singulorum facta narrarentur, inestimabilis magnitudo temporis ad hoc exigeretur, sicut etiam Aug. dicit lib. 20. de Civ. Dei c. 14. Quod si liber, ex cujus scriptura omnes judicabuntur, carnaliter cogitetur, quis ejus magnitudinem, aut longitudinem valeat aestimare, aut quanto tempore legi poterit liber, in quo scripta sunt universæ vitæ universorum? Non autem minus tempus requiritur ad narrandum ore tenus singulorum facta, quàm ad legendum, si essent in libro materiali scripta. D. Th. in Supp. q. 88. ar. 2.
units.tr: 34. Then he will say. Namely in the mind, not aloud. For that whole final judgement, both as to the examination and accusation of evils and the commendation of goods, and as to the sentence on each, will be carried out mentally. For if the deeds of each were narrated aloud, an inestimable length of time would be needed for this, as Augustine also says in Book 20 of The City of God, chapter 14: But if the book by whose writing all shall be judged is thought of in a carnal way, who could estimate its size or length, or in how long a time could a book be read in which the whole lives of all are written? Yet no less time would be needed to recount the deeds of individuals by word of mouth than to read them, if they were written in a material book. St Thomas, Supplement, q. 88, art. 2.

units.la: Venite benedicti Patris mei, possidete paratum vobis regnum. Omnes corporales promissiones, quæ in præmium promittuntur Sanctis in sacra Scriptura, sunt metaphoricè intelligendæ, secundum quod in Scripturis solent spiritualia per corporalia designari, ut ex iis quæ novimus, ad desiderandum incognita consurgamus. Sic per cibum & potum Luc. 10. intelligitur delectatio beatitudinis; per divitias Matth. 6. sufficientia, quâ homini sufficiet. Denique per regnum, exaltatio hominis usque ad conjunctionem cum Deo. D. Th. 12. q. 4. art. 7. ad 1.
units.tr: Come, you blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you. All the bodily promises which are promised to the saints as reward in Holy Scripture are to be understood metaphorically, since in the Scriptures spiritual things are usually designated by bodily things, so that from what we know we may rise to desire what is unknown. Thus by food and drink (Luke 10) is understood the delight of blessedness; by riches (Matthew 6) sufficiency, by which a man will have enough; and finally by the kingdom, the exaltation of man up to union with God. St Thomas, II-II, q. 4, art. 7, ad 1.

units.la: 41. Discedite à me maledicti in ignem æternum. Quia ignis est maximè afflictivus, propter hoc, quod abundat in virtute activa, ideo nomine ignis omnis afflictio designatur, si sit vehemens. Unde hinc inferri non potest quod damnati inferno solâ poenâ ignis affligantur. D. Th. in Supp. q. 97. art. 1. ad 1.
units.tr: 41. Depart from me, accursed, into the eternal fire. Because fire is the most painful, since it abounds in active power, therefore by the name of fire every affliction is designated, if it be severe. Hence it cannot be inferred from this that the damned in hell are afflicted by the punishment of fire alone. St Thomas, Supplement, q. 97, art. 1, ad 1.

units.la: Qui paratus est diabolo. Ecce ad quod Dominus iniquos & impios praedestinavit, ad supplicium justum non ad opus injustum, ad poenam non ad culpam, ad punitionem non ad transgressionem; ad interitum, quem ira justi judicis peccantibus reddit, non ad interitum, quo in se iram Dei peccantium iniquitas provocavit. B. Fulg. lib. 1. ad Monimum c. 26.
units.tr: Who is prepared for the devil. Behold for what the Lord has predestined the wicked and impious: to a just punishment, not to an unjust work; to penalty, not to guilt; to chastisement, not to transgression; to the destruction which the anger of the just judge renders to sinners, not to the destruction by which the iniquity of sinners has provoked God's anger against themselves. St Fulgentius, Book 1 to Monimus, chapter 26.

units.la: 42. Esurivi, &c. Ponuntur definita opera misericordiæ pro indefinitis. Inculcat enim Christus quodvis misericordiæ opus seu corporale seu spirituale proximo exhibitum, quasi in se ipsum fuisset collatum, in judicio remuneratum iri, & è converso quodvis misericordiæ opus minimo ex suis discipulis denegatum in judicio non minoribus punitum iri suppliciis, ac si fuisset sibi ipsi denegatum.
units.tr: 42. I was hungry, etc. Particular works of mercy are put for indefinite ones. For Christ inculcates that any work of mercy, whether bodily or spiritual, shown to a neighbour, will be rewarded at judgement as if it had been done to himself; and conversely, that any work of mercy denied to the least of his disciples will be punished at judgement with no less severe penalties, as if it had been denied to himself.

units.la: Enim. Hæc particula causalis non refertur ad præparationem regni, sed ad possessionem; si enim ratio præparationis regni redderetur, Christus dixisset, Venite & possidete regnum vobis paratum à constitutione, id est, ante constitutionem mundi: eram enim esuriturus, & vos mihi daturi eratis ad manducandum. Quod ipsum etiam perspicuè probat altera sententia, quà reprobis dicitur, Discedite à me in ignem æternum, qui paratus est diabolo & angelis ejus: esurivi enim, & non dedistis mihi manducare, &c. Ubi certè particula causalis debet referri ad hæc verba, Discedite à me, non verò ad ista, Qui paratus est diabolo & angelis ejus, cùm diabolo, quem Scholastici Luciferum appellant, & angelis ejus ignis æternus non fuerit paratus, quòd homines reprobi non fecerint aut facturi essent opera misericordiæ. Præclarè itaque S. Greg. Mag. in Ps. 7. Pœnitentialem ait: Aliud est secundum opera reddere, & aliud propter ipsa opera reddere. In eo enim quod secundum opera dicitur, ipsa operum qualitas intelligitur, ut cujus apparuerint bona opera, ejus sit & retributio gloriosa. Illi namque beatæ vitæ in qua cum Deo, & de Deo vivitur, nullus potest æquari labor, nulla opera comparari, præsertim cùm Apostolus dicat: Non sunt condignæ passiones hujus temporis ad futuram gloriam quæ revelabitur in nobis. Quanquam & ex hoc quoque misericordiæ jure posset nominari sanctorum felicitas, quia pro illis operibus datur, quæ sine præveniente misericordiæ Dei nemo adsequitur. Unde in Psalmis dicitur: Deus meus, misericordia ejus prævéniet me. Nisi enim vasa iræ fecisset vasa misericordiæ, neminem ab illa perditionis massa conversatio sancta discerneret, neminem à pœna perpetuæ mortis, justitia propria liberaret. Constat ergo, quia quibus misericorditer tribuit, ut in hac vita bene operentur, eis misericordius largitur ut in æterna beatitudine centuplicato fructu remunerentur. Hæc est gratia quam pro gratia dandam Sanctis Dei Apostolus perhibet, ut quibus in hac vita divinitus datur gratia sanctificationis, eis et hæc quoque in futuro detur gratia æterna felicitatis. Hinc & Augustinus stinus in libro aureo de gratia & lib. arb. c. 8. Vita bona nostra nihil aliud est quam Dei gratia: sine dubio & vita æterna, quæ bona vitæ redditur, Dei gratia est: & ipsa enim gratis datur, quia gratis data est illa cui datur. Sed illa cui datur tantummodo gratia est. hæc autem quæ illi datur, quoniam præmium ejus est, gratia est pro gratia, tanquam merces pro justitia, ut verum sit quoniam verum est, quia reddet unicuique Deus secundum opera ejus. Ibidem c. 9. Dixit Apostolus, Gratia autem Dei vita æterna, in Christo Jesu Domino nostro: cùm priùs dixisset, Stipendium peccati mors. Meritò enim stipendium, quia militiæ diabolicæ mors æterna tanquam debitum redditur. Ubi cùm posset dicere, & rectè dicere, Stipendium autem justitiæ vita æterna: maluit dicere, Gratia autem Dei vita æterna: ut hinc intelligeremus non pro meritis nostris Deum nos ad æternam vitam, sed pro sua miseratione perducere. De quo in Psalmo dicit homo animæ suæ, Qui coronat te in miseratione & misericordia. Nunquid non corona bonis operibus redditur? sed quia ipsa bona opera ille in bonis operatur, de quo dictum est, Deus est enim qui operatur in vobis & velle & operari pro bona voluntate, ideò dixit Psalmus, Coronat te in miseratione & misericordia: quia ejus miseratione bona operamur, quibus corona reddetur. Unde idem Augustinus in libro de gratia Christi capite decimo sic loquitur de Pelagio: Gratiam istam aliquando fateatur, quâ futuræ gloriæ magnitudo, non solùm promittitur, verùm etiàm creditur & speratur, nec solùm revelatur sapientia, verùm etiam & amatur, nec suadetur solùm omne quod bonum est, verùm & persuadetur. Non enim omnium est fides, qui audiunt per Scripturas Dominum regnum cælorum pollicentem, aut omnibus persuadetur, quibuscumque suadetur, ut veniant ad eum qui dicit, Venite ad me omnes qui laboratis: Quorum autem sit fides, & quibus persuadetur ut ad eum veniant, satis ipse demonstravit, ubi ait, Nemo venit ad me, nisi Pater qui misit me, traxerit eum. Et paulò post, cùm de non credentibus loqueretur, Dixi, inquit, vobis, quia nemo potest venire ad me, nisi fuerit ei datum à Patre meo. Hanc debet Pelagius gratiam confiteri, si vult non solùm vocari, verùm etiam esse Christianus.
units.tr: For. This causal particle refers not to the preparation of the kingdom but to its possession. For if the reason for the preparation of the kingdom were being given, Christ would have said, "Come and possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world," since he was going to be hungry and you were going to give me food to eat. The other sentence, which is addressed to the reprobate, clearly proves the same point: Depart from me into eternal fire, which is prepared for the devil and his angels: for I was hungry, and you did not give me food to eat, etc. Here the causal particle must refer to the words "Depart from me," not to "which is prepared for the devil and his angels." Eternal fire was not prepared for the devil, whom the Schoolmen call Lucifer, and his angels because reprobate men did not do, or were not going to do, works of mercy. So St. Gregory the Great, in his commentary on Ps. 7 (the penitential psalm), rightly says: It is one thing to repay according to works, and another to repay on account of the works themselves. For in what is said "according to works," the quality of the works themselves is understood, so that whose good works have appeared, his glorious reward also belongs to him. For no labour can be equal to that blessed life in which one lives with God and from God, and no works can be compared with it, especially since the Apostle says: The sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that will be revealed in us. Yet the happiness of the saints may also be named from the right of mercy, because it is given for those works which no one attains without the prevenient mercy of God. Hence it is said in the Psalms: My God, his mercy will go before me. For unless he had made vessels of wrath into vessels of mercy, no holy conduct would distinguish anyone from that mass of perdition, and no one's own righteousness would free him from the punishment of eternal death. It is clear, then, that to those to whom he mercifully grants that they should do good in this life, he more mercifully grants that they be rewarded in eternal blessedness with a hundredfold fruit. This is the grace which the Apostle says is to be given in return for grace: that to those to whom the grace of sanctification is divinely given in this life, this also will be given in the future, the grace of eternal happiness. Hence also Augustine, in his golden book on grace and free will, chapter 8: Our good life is nothing other than the grace of God. Without doubt eternal life, which is rendered as the reward of a good life, is also the grace of God. For it is given freely, because it is given freely to the one to whom it is given. But the one to whom it is given is grace only. And this which is given to him, since it is his reward, is grace for grace, as wages are for righteousness, so that it is true because it is true that God will render to each according to his works. In the same book, chapter 9: The Apostle said: "But the grace of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord," when he had previously said, "The wages of sin is death." Rightly the wages is death, because eternal death is rendered as a debt to the service of the devil. Where he could have said, and rightly said, "But the wages of righteousness is eternal life," he preferred to say, "But the grace of God is eternal life," so that we might understand that God leads us to eternal life not for our merits but by his own compassion. Concerning this, a man says to his soul in the Psalm: "Who crowns you in compassion and mercy." Is not a crown rendered for good works? But because it is he who works those good works in the good, of whom it is said, "For it is God who works in you both to will and to work for his good pleasure," therefore the Psalm says, "He crowns you in compassion and mercy," because by his compassion we work good works, for which a crown is rendered. Hence the same Augustine, in his book on the grace of Christ, chapter 10, speaks thus about Pelagius: Let him at last confess that grace by which the greatness of future glory is not only promised but also believed and hoped for, and not only is wisdom revealed but also loved, and not only is all that is good urged upon us but also persuaded. For not all who hear through the Scriptures the Lord promising the kingdom of heaven have faith, nor are all persuaded, to whom it is urged, to come to him who says, "Come to me, all you who labour." Yet he himself has shown plainly whose faith it is and to whom it is persuaded to come to him, when he says: "No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him." And shortly after, when speaking of those who do not believe, he said: "I have told you that no one can come to me unless it has been given to him by my Father." Pelagius must confess this grace, if he wishes not only to be called but also to be a Christian.

units.la: In vitam æternam. Beatitudo Sanctorum dicitur vita æterna: quia per hoc quod Deo fruuntur, efficiuntur quodammodo participes æternitatis divinæ, quæ excedit omne tempus: Et ita continuatio beatitudinis non diversificatur per præsens, præteritum, & futurum: Et ideò beati non habent spem de continuatione beatitudinis, sed habent ipsam rem; quia non est ibi ratio futuri. D. Th. 22. q. 18. ar. 2. ad 2.
units.tr: Eternal life. The blessedness of the saints is called eternal life, because through enjoying God they become in some way participants in divine eternity, which exceeds all time. And so the continuance of blessedness is not diversified by present, past, and future. And therefore the blessed have no hope of the continuance of blessedness, but they have the thing itself, because there is no place for the future there. D. Th. 22. q. 18. ar. 2. ad 2.

units.la: CAPUT XXVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVI.

units.la: 2. Pascha fiet. Nempe à Judæis. Quâ ipsâ mente dicitur Marc. 14. v. 1. Erat autem Pascha & Azyma post biduum. Pascha nomen elt Chaldaicum, ut rectè notat Philo lib. 3. de vita Mosis. Sed Hebræis idem est ꝓᴐᴐ Pesach à radice Pasach, quod est διαβαίνειν transgredi, vel ὑπερβαίνειν praetergredi. Unde Hebræum Pesach Josephus πάσχα reddit, & Philo διαβατήρια. Ita etiam Origenes lib. 8. contra Celsum. Proinde Gregorius Nazianzenus hoc idem festum διαβατήριον vocat Oratione 43. & ἐορτὴν διαβατήριον Epistola 58. ad Helladium, voce Græcis non ignota. Lacedæmone enim τὰ διαβατήρια dicebantur sacrificia pro transitu, id est, pro felici expeditionis progressu; quibus si non esset litatum, expeditio in aliud tempus rejiciebatur. Hoc verbo utuntur non semel Xenophon & Thucydides. In Græca versione veteris Testamenti Hebræum Pesach ubique redditur Pascha, si excipias secundum Paralip. ubi ea vox decies occurrit & semper redditur Phasec: quod cum Theodotionis proprium esse dicatur, jure quidam suspicantur ipsum esse autorem versionis dicti libri 2 Paralip. Vulgatus interpres constanter; si unum aut alterum locum excipias vertit Phase. Ceterum Pascha dicitur primò Angeli percutientis primogenita Ægyptiorum transultus super Israelitarum ostia, cùm postes eorum videret sanguine agni tinctos, ut dicitur Exod. 12. v. 32. Secundò dicitur Pascha solemnitas Azymorum, in qua occidebatur agnus Paschalis in memoriam transfultûs Angelici mox dicti. Hinc Luc. 22. v. 1. Appropinquabat, inquit, dies festus Azymorum, qui dicitur Pascha. Hinc πασχάλιος nonnullis dicitur, qui festorum observationi maxime est addictus. Tertiò Pascha dicitur Agnus paschalis; sic Luc. 22. v. 7. Venit autem dies Azymorum in qua necesse erat occidi Pascha. Quartò Pascha dicuntur omnia sacrificia per septiduum solemnitatis Azymorum offerri solita. Sic Deut. 16. v. 2. Immolabisque Phase Domino Deo tuo de ovibus & de bobus. Qui certè locus non potest intelligi, quasi præciperetur ut Deo immolentur Agnus Paschalis & aliæ victimæ de ovibus & de bobus; alioqui Moses dixisset HeHebraicè, Immolabis Deo Pascha, oves & boves, vel immolabis Pascha oves & boves Domino Deo tuo, non verò, ut habetur in textu Hebræo, Immolabis Pascha Domino Deo tuo, oves & boves, ut Pascha sit veluti genus ad oves & boves, quomodo in simili locutione Exod. 20. v. 24. Holocausta & Pacifica sunt veluti genus ad oves & boves. Itaque in loco laudato Deuteronomii Pascha vocantur oves & boves, quæ Paschalibus feriis in pacifica sacrificia mactare moris erat; hancque expositionem confirmat, quod in veritate Hebraica post laudatum versum habetur, Septem diebus comedes azyma cum eo, id est, cum Pascha te; neque enim per septiduum cum agno comedebantur azyma, sed illa solùm horâ, quâ comedebatur agnus. Rabbi Moses Majemonides in tractatu de oblatione Paschatis cap. 10. per Pascha loco citato Deuteronomii vult intelligi דיי דיי diei decimæ quartæ, id est, victima vel pars victimæ unà cum Agno Paschali mensæ imponi solitæ, cujus esus poterat in posterum diem differri, ut pacificorum omnium Levit. 7. v. 16. & c. 19. v. 6. Quemadmodum autem in laudato Deuteronomii loco ex Rabbinis & ipsa inspectione loci constat, quòd quævis victima sive de ovibus sive de bobus per septiduum azymorum offerri solita dicitur phase sive Pascha sine addito, sic Joan. 18. v. 28. Judæi pollui timentes ne prohiberentur ab esu victimæ Paschalis pacificæ, quia res sanctas comedere iis non licebat, qui legali immunditiâ erant quoquomodo polluti, ut habetur Levitic. 7, & 21. &c. Judæi, inquam, illi dicuntur non introiisse Prætorium ne contaminarentur, ne comederent Pascha. Sunt qui ibi per Pascha intelligunt azyma, sed præter Scripturam & usum Hebræorum. Victimas verò omnes per septiduum azymorum offerri solitas dici Pascha sine addito, præter hactenus dicta confirmat Rabbinorum authoritas, & insuper siquis contentiosus non est, id colliget ex 2 Paralip. 3. v. 22. c. 35. v. 7, 8, & 9. & lib. 3. Esdræ 1. v. 8, & 9. atque hæc sint dicta de acceptione vocis Pascha, phase, pesach, phasec secundum usum Judæorum. Jam apud Christianos Paschæ vox nonnumquam sumitur pro quolibet festo in honorem Salvatoris instituto. Ita Lucas Patriarcha Constantinopolitanus sub Emmanuele Comneno, lib. Senten. Synod. Sent. 9. Cùm nobilis quidam Græcus, jurejurando vovisset, se unâquâque feriâ tertiâ, carnes non comesturum in honorem B. Joannis Baptistæ Præcursoris Christi, atque festus dies Nativitatis Christi incidisset in feriam tertiam, quæsivit Imperator Byzantinus an jusjurandum illud servandum esset, & Dominicum festum quod est Paschale, non lætè & jucundè ut par est celebrare. Respondet Lucas Patriarcha & Synodus quæ aderat, non esse jejunandum Paschali Christi festo. Illud ratione celebrationis Coenæ Dominicæ dictum videri debet, cum & B. Chrysostomus suos ad frequentiorem S. Eucharistiæ perceptionem cohortans, Pascha, id est, festum diem sacræ communioni idoneum sæpius occurrere dicat variis in locis, præsertim Homil. de jejunio primi Paschæ, scribit Pascha non esse jejunium, sed sacrificium (laudis scilicet) quod fit in unaquaque Synaxi. Pascha etiam vocatur ipsa Quadragesima beato Timotheo Patriarchæ Alexandrino interrogat. & Pelagio Pontifici Romano in Epist. ad Laurentium Episcopum Centumcellensem. Concil. Tollet. VIII. cap. 9. Quadragesimam appellavit festa Paschalia, vel quia per Quadragesimam disponuntur Christiani ad sanctè celebrandam Paschæ festivitatem, vel quia Pascha derivabant nonnulli a verbo πάσχειν, quod est pati, quasi Pascha significaret Passionem, cujus commemoratio celebratur tempore Quadragesimæ. Hæc dicta sint de nomine Paschæ. Verùm ut redeamus ad textum Evangelicum, utque seriem historiæ Passionis Christi accuratè teneamus, sciendum quòd secundum Legem dies decimus quartus primi mensis Agno Paschali immolando ita erat assignatus, ut qui illo die immundi erant, aut in locis ab urbe Hierosolymitana tam dissitis, ut ad eam maturè se conferre non possent, hoc est, secundum Rabbinorum expositionem, qui die decimâ quartâ mensis, orto jam sole distant ab urbe Jerusalem quindecim milliaribus, vel ampliùs, seu ut exponit Philo lib. 3. de vita Mosis, qui peregrinationis ergò sunt in regione à Judæa procul dissita, iis Num. 9. indicitur Pascha immolandum die decimâ quartâ secundi mensis inter, id est, intra duas vesperas, quas complectitur tempus, quod ab hora sesqui duodecima diurna fluit ad solis occasum, intra quod spatium etiam mactabatur juge sacrificium, accendebantur lampades & fiebat suffimentum, Exod. 29, & 30. Præstaret itaque à Paschatis celebratione ad tempus abstinere, quàm illud observare tempore non suo. Hinc & inter Jeroboami peccata hoc recensetur, quòd solemne festum celebravit mense, quem finxerat de corde suo, 3 Reg. 12. v. 32, & 33. id est, ut habet Chaldæus Paraphrastes, בְּרִעוּתֵיהּ, arbitrio suo. Hinc & tempore Ezechiæ Regis 4 Reg. c. 16. cùm non esset satis temporis à primo regni ipsius anno ineunte cum mense primo, ut Templum à patre suo Achaz prophanatum, Sacerdotes, Levitas & populum ipsum repurgaret, ante diem ejusdem primi mensis ירח decimum quartum; Templi enim consecratio absolvi non potuit ante diem decimum sextum ejusdem mensis 2 Paralip. 29. necdum sanctificati fuerant Sacerdotes ad sufficientem numerum, nec populus poterat Jerofolymam convocari 2 Paralip. 30. Paschatis celebratio universo populo differenda erat in decimum quartum diem secundi mensis. Unde qui volunt Christum celebrasse Pascha alio die, quàm ceteri Judæi, ansam ipsis præbent Christum redarguendi, quòd Legem transgressus Pascha celebraverit die quem finxerat ex corde, seu arbitrio suo, & proinde secundum Legem debuerit mori, quod ipsi Judæi, nec per falsos testes evincere poterant.
units.tr: 2. The Passover will take place. Namely, by the Jews. In this very sense it is said in Mark 14. v. 1, Now the Passover and the Unleavened Bread were after two days. "Pascha" is a Chaldean name, as Philo rightly notes in book 3 of the Life of Moses. But for the Hebrews the word is the same as Pesach [פֶּסַח], from the root Pasach, which means to cross over [διαβαίνειν, diabainein] or to pass over [ὑπερβαίνειν, hyperbainein]. Hence Josephus renders the Hebrew Pesach as pascha [πάσχα], and Philo as passings-over [διαβατήρια, diabatēria]. Origen also does so in book 8 against Celsus. Accordingly Gregory Nazianzen calls this same feast a passing-over [διαβατήριον, diabatērion] in Oration 43, and a passing-over feast [ἐορτὴν διαβατήριον, heortēn diabatērion] in Epistle 58 to Helladius, a word not unknown to the Greeks. For at Sparta the sacrifices for a crossing [τὰ διαβατήρια, ta diabatēria] were so called, that is, sacrifices for the successful progress of an expedition; if these were not favourable, the expedition was put off to another time. Xenophon and Thucydides use this word more than once. In the Greek version of the Old Testament, the Hebrew Pesach is everywhere rendered pascha, except in 2 Chronicles, where the word occurs ten times and is always rendered Phasec. Since this is said to be peculiar to Theodotion, some reasonably suspect that he himself is the author of the version of that book, 2 Chronicles. The Vulgate translator consistently renders it Phase, except in one or two places. Moreover, Pascha is first used of the angel who struck down the firstborn of the Egyptians and passed over [transultus] the doorposts of the Israelites, when he saw their doorposts stained with the blood of the lamb, as is said in Exodus 12. v. 32. Secondly, Pascha is used of the solemnity of the Unleavened Bread, in which the paschal lamb was killed in memory of the angelic passing-over just mentioned. Hence Luke 22. v. 1, The feast day of the Unleavened Bread, which is called the Pascha, was drawing near. Hence some call a person paschalios [πασχάλιος] who is especially devoted to the observance of the feasts. Thirdly, Pascha is used for the paschal lamb itself; so Luke 22. v. 7, Then came the day of the Unleavened Bread, on which the Pascha had to be killed. Fourthly, Pascha is the name for all the sacrifices customarily offered during the seven days of the solemnity of the Unleavened Bread. So Deuteronomy 16. v. 2, And you shall sacrifice the Phase to the Lord your God, from the sheep and from the oxen. This passage certainly cannot be understood as if it commanded that the paschal lamb and other victims of sheep and oxen be sacrificed to God. Otherwise Moses would have said in Hebrew, "You shall sacrifice the Pascha to God, sheep and oxen," or "You shall sacrifice the Pascha, sheep and oxen, to the Lord your God," not, as the Hebrew text has it, You shall sacrifice the Pascha to the Lord your God, sheep and oxen, so that Pascha is a general term over sheep and oxen, as in the similar phrase at Exodus 20. v. 24, where burnt offerings and peace offerings are a general term over sheep and oxen. Thus in the passage of Deuteronomy cited, the sheep and oxen that were customarily slaughtered as peace offerings on the paschal days are called Pascha. This interpretation is confirmed by the fact that in the Hebrew text, after the verse cited, it is written, For seven days you shall eat unleavened bread with it, that is, with the Pascha. For the unleavened bread was not eaten with the lamb for seven days, but only at the hour when the lamb was eaten. Rabbi Moses Maimonides, in his treatise on the offering of the Passover, chapter 10, wants the Pascha in the cited passage of Deuteronomy to be understood as the victim, or part of the victim, of the fourteenth day [דיי, diei] together with the paschal lamb, which was customarily placed on the table, and whose eating could be deferred to the following day, as with all peace offerings in Leviticus 7. v. 16 and chapter 19. v. 6. Just as in the cited passage of Deuteronomy it is clear from the Rabbis and from the inspection of the passage itself that any victim, whether of sheep or of oxen, customarily offered during the seven days of the Unleavened Bread, is called phase or Pascha without further qualification, so in John 18. v. 28 the Jews, fearing to be polluted and so prevented from eating the peace-offering of the paschal victim (since it was not lawful for those who were in some way polluted by legal uncleanness to eat holy things, as is found in Leviticus 7 and 21, etc.), are said not to have entered the Praetorium lest they be defiled, lest they eat the Pascha. I say, those Jews are said not to have entered. There are those who understand Pascha here to mean the unleavened bread, but this is against Scripture and the usage of the Hebrews. That all the victims customarily offered during the seven days of the Unleavened Bread are called Pascha without addition is confirmed, besides what has been said so far, by the authority of the Rabbis; and moreover, if anyone is not contentious, he will gather this from 2 Chronicles 3. v. 22, chapter 35. vv. 7, 8 and 9, and 3 Esdras 1. vv. 8 and 9. And let these things be said concerning the meaning of the words Pascha, phase, pesach, phasec according to the usage of the Jews. Now among Christians the word Pascha is sometimes taken for any feast instituted in honour of the Saviour. So Lucas, Patriarch of Constantinople, under Emmanuel Comnenus, in the book of the Synodal Sentences, Sentence 9: when a certain noble Greek had vowed under oath that on every Tuesday he would eat no meat in honour of St. John the Baptist, the forerunner of Christ, and the feast day of the Nativity of Christ fell on a Tuesday, the Byzantine Emperor asked whether that oath had to be kept, and whether the Lord's feast, which is the Paschal feast, should not be celebrated joyfully and cheerfully as it ought to be. Lucas the Patriarch and the Synod that was present replied that no fast was to be kept on the paschal feast of Christ. This ought to be understood with reference to the celebration of the Lord's Supper, since St. John Chrysostom, too, exhorting his people to more frequent reception of the holy Eucharist, says in various places that the Pascha, that is, the feast day suited to holy communion, comes round more often; especially in the homily on the fast before Easter he writes that the Pascha is not a fast but a sacrifice (namely of praise), which is offered in every synaxis. The Quadragesima itself is also called Pascha by the blessed Timothy, Patriarch of Alexandria, in his Answers, and by Pelagius, Roman Pontiff, in his Epistle to Laurentius, Bishop of Centumcellae. The Council of Toledo VIII, chapter 9, called the Quadragesima the Paschal feasts, either because Christians are prepared through the Quadragesima to celebrate the feast of Easter holily, or because some derive Pascha from the verb πάσχειν [paschein], to suffer, as if Pascha signified the Passion, whose remembrance is celebrated in the season of Quadragesima. Let these things be said about the name Pascha. But to return to the Gospel text, and to keep exactly to the order of the history of Christ's Passion, it must be known that according to the Law the fourteenth day of the first month was appointed for the sacrifice of the paschal lamb in such a way that those who were unclean on that day, or who lived in places so far from the city of Jerusalem that they could not betimes betake themselves to it (that is, according to the Rabbis' explanation, those who on the fourteenth day of the month, with the sun already risen, are fifteen miles or more distant from the city of Jerusalem; or, as Philo explains in book 3 of the Life of Moses, those who are away from Judea in a region far removed, on a journey) were directed, in Numbers 9, to keep the Passover on the fourteenth day of the second month, between the two evenings, that is, the time that runs from the hour of six and a half in the day to sunset; within this space too the continual sacrifice was slain, the lamps were lit, and incense was burned, Exodus 29 and 30. It is better, therefore, to abstain from celebrating the Passover at the proper time than to observe it at a time not its own. Hence also among the sins of Jeroboam this is numbered, that he celebrated a solemn feast in the month which he had devised from his own heart, 3 Kings 12. vv. 32 and 33, that is, as the Chaldee paraphrast has it, at his own will [בְּרִעוּתֵיהּ, berityehu]. Hence also in the time of King Hezekiah, 4 Kings chapter 16, since there was not enough time from the beginning of the first year of his reign, as the first month was beginning, for him to cleanse the Temple, which his father Ahaz had profaned, and the priests, Levites and people themselves, the Passover had to be put off until the fourteenth day of the second month, beyond the first day of that first month [ירח, yerach]; for the consecration of the Temple could not be completed before the sixteenth day of the same month, 2 Chronicles 29, nor had the priests yet been sanctified in sufficient number, nor could the people be gathered at Jerusalem, 2 Chronicles 30. So the celebration of the Passover had to be deferred for the whole people until the fourteenth day of the second month. Therefore those who want Christ to have celebrated the Pascha on a different day from the other Jews give them grounds for accusing Christ, that, having transgressed the Law, he celebrated the Pascha on a day which he had devised from his heart, or at his own will, and that accordingly, under the Law, he ought to have died; which the Jews themselves could not prove even by false witnesses.

units.la: 3. Tunc. Idest, sub idem tempus, quo Christus mortem suam prædixit, nempe ut ait Augustinus in Epist. 86. ad Catulanum Presbyterum, Quartâ Sabbati, quam vulgò quartam feriam vocant.
units.tr: 3. Then. That is, at about the same time as Christ foretold his death; namely, as Augustine says in Epistle 86 to Catulanus the presbyter, on the fourth day of the week, which is commonly called the fourth day.

units.la: 4. Ut Jesum dolo tenerent. Quia ut ait Lucas, timebant plebem, ne scilicet si apertà vi eum caperent, seditio populi Jesum amantis contra se oriretur.
units.tr: 4. That they might take Jesus by deceit. Because, as Luke says, they feared the people, namely lest, if they seized him by open force, a rebellion of the people who loved Jesus would arise against them.

units.la: 5. Non in die festo, ne forte tumultus fieret. Græcè fiat. Unde secundum textum Græcum verba sunt Judæorum, secundum textum Latinum verba sunt Evangelistæ reddentis rationem cur Judæi noluerint primò ipsum interficere in solemni Paschatis die. Sed nemo mirabitur eos, qui à Christo morti tradendo nunquam ipsâ festi religione, sed solo populi metu fuerant deterriti, poltea ab hoc consilio discessisse oblatâ per Judam occasione. Neque id sine Numine; ita enim factum est, ut Christi mors plures haberet testes, & in ipsum Paschæ festum incideret, ut vel hinc Christum sciremus per Paschalem Agnum fuisse adumbratum. Judæi ergo vesperâ Paschatis statim post eum Agni Paschalis violento impetu in Christum irruerunt, eodem spiritu acti, quo proditor Judas, qui Pascha jam modò cum Christo celebrato, tam scelerata cohortis se ducem & incentorem præstitit. Sic Cainum à fratricidio non prohibuit sacrificium solemni more nuper oblatum. Adultera mulier post consecratas victimas & vota sua Deo reddita, mox in libidines ruit, Proverb. 7. v. 14, & 15. Zachariam Joiadæ vel Barachiæ filium in ipso Templi atrio prope altare Judæi lapidibus obruerunt, idque, si Hebræis credimus, die propitiationum. Plebeius furor nullos habet limites, maxime cùm religionis velamine obtenditur; quo prætextu in Christum & ejus servos Judæi sæviebant. Unde illud Christi Joan. 16. v. 2. Venit hora, ut omnis qui interficit vos, arbitretur obsequium se præstare Deo: seu ut habent Syrus & Arabs, Venit miet tempus quo quisquis vos interfecerit, putabit se oblationem Deo offerre.
units.tr: 5. Not during the festival, lest perhaps a tumult arise. The Greek reads differently. So according to the Greek text these are the words of the Jews, but according to the Latin text they are the words of the Evangelist giving the reason why the Jews at first did not want to kill him on the solemn day of the Passover. But no one will be surprised that these men, who had never been deterred from handing Christ over to death by any religious scruple but only by fear of the people, afterwards abandoned this plan when Judas offered them an opportunity. Nor did this happen without the divine will; for it came about so that Christ's death would have more witnesses and would fall upon the Passover feast itself, so that from this alone we may know that Christ was foreshadowed by the Paschal Lamb. Therefore the Jews, on the evening of the Passover, immediately after the Paschal Lamb had been eaten, rushed upon Christ with violent assault, driven by the same spirit as the traitor Judas, who, though the Passover had just been celebrated with Christ, showed himself so wicked a leader and instigator of the band. Thus the sacrifice offered in the solemn manner did not keep Cain from fratricide. The adulterous woman, after the victims had been consecrated and her vows made to God, straightway rushed into lusts, Prov. 7. vv. 14 and 15. The Jews stoned Zechariah, son of Jehoiada or Berechiah, in the very court of the Temple near the altar, and this, if we believe the Hebrews, on the day of atonement. Popular fury has no limits, especially when it is veiled with the cloak of religion; under this pretext the Jews raged against Christ and his servants. Hence that saying of Christ, John 16. v. 2: The hour comes, that whoever kills you will think he is offering service to God; or as the Syriac and the Arabic have it: The time will come when whoever kills you will think he is offering a sacrifice to God.

units.la: 6. Cùm autem Jesus esset in Bethania, &c. Hæc historia per recapitulationem hîc narratur à Matthæo, ut diximus suprà c. 21. v. 1.
units.tr: 6. Now when Jesus was in Bethany, etc. Matthew here narrates this story by way of recapitulation, as we said above on chapter 21, verse 1.

units.la: In domo Simonis Leprosi. Sic cognominabatur, fortassis quia olim ipse vel aliquis ex majoribus leprâ laboraverat.
units.tr: In the house of Simon the Leper. He was so called, perhaps because at some time he himself or one of his ancestors had suffered from leprosy.

units.la: 7. Accessit ad eum mulier. Hanc Joannes c. 12. Mariam vocat, nempe Magdalenam, cujus soror Martha ministrabat & frater Lazarus unus erat ex discumbentibus cum Jesu.
units.tr: 7. A woman came to him. John, in chapter 12, calls her Mary, namely Magdalene, whose sister Martha served and whose brother Lazarus was one of those reclining at table with Jesus.

units.la: Habens alabastrum unguenti pretiosi. Supple ex Marc. 14. v. 13. Nardi spicati. Id est, unguenti ex spicis nardi, quod præstantissimum erat. Marcus tamen in textu Græco ut & Joannes habent, nardi pistici, quod quidam volunt esse idem ac nardi spicati, vel errore librariorum, vel latinâ voce à Syris aut à Græcis cum quadam literarum transpositione vurpatâ. Alabaster autem est pixis unguentaria ex alabastrite lapide, ut videre est apud Plinium lib. 36. c. 8. Unguentum autem dicitur mixtura ex liquoribus herbarum odoriseris.
units.tr: Having an alabaster flask of precious ointment. Supply from Mark 14. v. 3. Of spikenard. That is, ointment made from the spikes of nard, which was the most excellent kind. Mark, however, in the Greek text, as also John, has of pistic nard, which some think is the same as spikenard, either through an error of copyists or through a Latin word corrupted by the Syrians or the Greeks with some transposition of letters. An alabaster is a vessel for ointments made of alabaster stone, as can be seen in Pliny, book 36, chapter 8. Moreover, ointment is called a mixture of liquids from fragrant herbs.

units.la: Et effudit super caput ipsius recumbentis. Joannis addit: Et unxit pedes Jesu & extersit pedes ejus capillis: Id est, cùm extersisset pedes ejus, eos unxit; primò enim extersit, deinde unxit.
units.tr: And poured it upon the head of him who reclined. John adds: And anointed the feet of Jesus and wiped his feet with her hair. That is, when she had wiped his feet, she anointed them; for she first wiped them and then anointed them.

units.la: 8. Discipuli indignati sunt. Dici potest plures indignè tulisse, sed maximè Judam, qui altiori & acerbiori præ ceteris voce de hac unguenti effusione infremuit. Probabilius tamen est solum Judam hoc reprehendisse, ut Joannes notat; Matthæum verò & Marcum discipulis tribuere in genere, quod ab uno eorum factum est, per Enallagen numeri Scripturæ familiarem. Vide quæ diximus c. 2. v. 20. & c. 21. v. 7.
units.tr: 8. The disciples were indignant. It may be said that several took it badly, but especially Judas, who grumbled about this pouring out of ointment in a louder and harsher voice than the rest. It is more probable, however, that Judas alone made this complaint, as John notes; while Matthew and Mark attribute it to the disciples in general, because it was done by one of them, through an enallage of number familiar in Scripture. See what we said on chapter 2, verse 20, and chapter 21, verse 7.

units.la: 10. Quid molestî estis huic mulieri? Joan. 2. v. 7. Sinite illam ut in diem sepulturæ meæ servet illud. Q. d. Sinite illam, siquidem unguentum illud servavit, quomodo habetur in plerisque codicibus Græcis, ad funerandum me.
units.tr: 10. Why do you trouble this woman? John 2. v. 7 (?): Let her alone, that she may keep this for the day of my burial. That is: let her alone, since she has kept that ointment, as it is read in most Greek manuscripts, for my burial.

units.la: 12. Ad sepeliendum me fecit. Græcè ad verbum, ad funerandum me fecit. Hebraeis ṬJṆ est condire aromatibus corpora defunctorum. Hoc LXX. dicunt ἐνταφιάσαι, funerare, sepelire.
units.tr: 12. She did it for my burial. Literally in the Greek: she did it to prepare me for burial. In Hebrew, the word for to season with spices the bodies of the dead is ṬJṆ. The Seventy render this ἐνταφιάσαι, to prepare for burial, to bury.

units.la: 15. Constituerunt. Id est, promiserunt.
units.tr: 15. They agreed. That is, they promised.

units.la: Triginta argenteos. Supple, siclos, quanti caput servi æstimatur Exod. 21. v. 32.
units.tr: Thirty pieces of silver. Supply shekels, the sum at which the head of a slave is valued in Exod. 21. v. 32.

units.la: 17. Prima autem die azymorum. Matthæus Evangelista, inquit Aug. in Ep. 86. quintam Sabbati dicit fuisse primam diem azymorum, quia ejus vespera sequente futura erat cœna Paschæ, quâ cœnâ incipiebat azymum, & ovis immolatio manducari. Hinc diserte Marcus ait c. 14. v. 12. Prima die azymorum quando Pascha immolabant, scilicet, Judæi. Hoc igitur contigit die decima quartâ mensis ניסן[?], seu אייר[?], qui partim Martio, partim Aprili nostro respondet, inter duas vesperas, hoc est, horis pomeridianis, quæ, ut suprà diximus, in duas vesperas dividebantur, quarum unaquæque erat duarum sesquihorarum. Paschales autem agni, ut testatur Josephus lib. 7. de bello Judaico c. 17. mactabantur ab hora tertia nostra pomeridiana usque ad horam quintam vespertinam, quæ hora tertia ex Josephi sententia priorem vesperam a posteriori distinguebat. Hinc cœna Paschalis ad utrumque refertur diem, nempe ad decimum quartum & decimum quintum mensis, quia in utriusque diei confinio comedebatur agnus, & pars una cœnæ præcedebat, altera sequebatur solis occasum & in noctem usque producebatur. Hoc Christo Domino in ultima præsentis diei cœna accidisse colligas non solùm ex Apostolo, qui eum refert, quâ nocte traditus est, sanctissimum cœnæ Sacramentum instituisse, sed & ex Joannis c. 17. v. 30. ubi Judas accepta buccellâ statim exivit, cùm jam nox esset, & illum diem appellat idem Evangelista ante festum Pascha, quòd ita scilicet præcedat festum, ut tamen sit pars festi, uti prologus est pars orationis, & progressis pars linguæ; atque ita ante festum Paschæ apud Joannem c. 13. idem est ac, in ipso festi exordio. Nam ante occasum solis agnum Paschalem mactari & assari oportuit die mensis Nisan 14. ut diserte habetur in Misnâ Pesachim c. 5. & in Majemonide de Paschate c. 1. & comedi in ipso occasu solis ineunte festo diei 15. qui primus erat azymorum. Unde Matthæus, Marcus, & Lucas eandem cœnam Paschalem à Joanne relatam ad vigiliam Paschæ, referunt ad primum diem azymorum, id est, mensis diem 15. Ut enim rectè Gellius, licèt in argumento planè diverso, tempora duo, cùm inter se opposita sunt, atque ita coherentia, ut alterius finis cum alterius initio misceatur, non refert utrum per extremitatem prioris, an per initium sequentis locus ipse confinii demonstretur.
units.tr: 17. Now on the first day of unleavened bread. Matthew the Evangelist, says Augustine in Epistle 86, says that the fifth day of the week was the first day of unleavened bread, because the evening of the following day was to be the Passover supper, with which supper the unleavened bread began and the lamb sacrificed was to be eaten. Hence Mark says plainly in chapter 14, verse 12: On the first day of unleavened bread, when they sacrificed the Passover, namely the Jews. This therefore happened on the fourteenth day of the month Nisan [ניסן?] or Iyar [אייר?], which corresponds partly to our March and partly to April, between the two evenings, that is, in the afternoon hours, which, as we said above, were divided into two evenings, each of which was two and a half hours long. Moreover, the Paschal lambs, as Josephus testifies in book 7 of the Jewish War, chapter 17, were slain from our third hour in the afternoon until the fifth hour of the evening; and this third hour, in Josephus's opinion, divided the earlier evening from the later one. Hence the Paschal supper is referred to both days, namely to the fourteenth and the fifteenth of the month, because the lamb was eaten at the boundary of the two days, and one part of the supper preceded and the other followed sunset, and it was prolonged into the night. That this happened at the Lord Christ's last supper on this day you may gather not only from the Apostle, who relates that on the night in which he was betrayed he instituted the most holy Sacrament of the Supper, but also from John, chapter 13, verse 30, where Judas, having received the morsel, went out at once, when it was already night; and the same Evangelist calls that day before the feast of the Passover, because it so precedes the feast that it is nonetheless part of the feast, just as a prologue is part of a speech and the beginnings are part of a language; and thus before the feast of the Passover in John 13 is the same as at the very beginning of the feast. For the Paschal lamb had to be slain and roasted before sunset on the fourteenth day of the month Nisan, as is plainly stated in the Mishnah Pesachim, chapter 5, and in Maimonides on the Passover, chapter 1, and eaten at the very beginning of the feast at sunset of the fifteenth day, which was the first day of unleavened bread. Hence Matthew, Mark, and Luke refer the same Paschal supper, which John relates, to the vigil of the Passover, that is, to the first day of unleavened bread, the fifteenth day of the month. For as Gellius rightly says, though in a quite different context: two times, when they are opposed to each other and so join that the end of one is mingled with the beginning of the other, it makes no difference whether the place of the boundary is pointed out by the extremity of the first or by the beginning of the second.

units.la: Qui verò volunt à Christo anticipatum diem Paschæ, ita ut celebraverit die 13. contra præceptum Legis Deut. 16. v. 6. Judæis dant causam cur innocentes Christum ut prævaricatorem Legis cruci affixerint.
units.tr: But those who hold that the day of the Passover was anticipated by Christ, so that he celebrated it on the thirteenth day, contrary to the precept of the Law in Deut. 16. v. 6, give the Jews a reason for having crucified Christ, though innocent, as a transgressor of the Law.

units.la: Quidam aiunt Judæos illo anno rejecisse secundum traditionem suam Agni Paschalis immolationem in diem 15. Lunæ, ne solemnitas primi diei azymorum & Sabbatum immediatè se sequerentur; quia Judæi festis diebus ab omni opere tam scrupulose abstinebant, ut continua duo festa ab illis observari non potuerint absque gravi incommodo. Et verò hodie festum azymorum immediatè ante Sabbatum, vel continuo post nunquam servant. Nam in calendariis suis Neomenias ita disponunt, ut festi dies cum Sabbato nunquam continui sint. Atque ut vitent hoc incommodum, canones quosdam habent de suis festis, quos accuratè observant, puta de Pascha te, ut nunquam incidat in secundam, quartam aut sextam feriam voce <bl>מִנָה</bl> significatas.
units.tr: Some say that in that year the Jews, according to their tradition, deferred the immolation of the Paschal Lamb to the fifteenth day of the moon, so that the solemnity of the first day of unleavened bread and the Sabbath would not immediately follow one another; because the Jews abstained from all work on festal days so scrupulously that they could not observe two consecutive festivals without grave inconvenience. Indeed, even today they never keep the feast of unleavened bread immediately before or immediately after the Sabbath. For in their calendars they arrange the new moons so that the days of the feast are never continuous with the Sabbath. And to avoid this inconvenience they have certain rules about their feasts, which they observe carefully, for instance that the Passover may never fall on the second, fourth or sixth day of the week, signified by the word [מִנָה, minah].

units.la: Sed hi autores refelluntur primo quia Canones isti Christi tempore nondum erant in usu. Quin Talmudici libri, qui quinto demum post Christum seculo absoluti sunt, passim meminere festum, quæ Sabbato continua sunt. Unde Aben-Ezra in Levitic. 23. ait: Tam ex Mischna, quàm ex Talmude probatur Pascha in secundam, quartam & sextam feriam quandoque incidisse. Concinit S. Epiphanius in Ebionæis num. 32. & in Alogis num. 31. Ita Quartodecimanis, qui Paschà celebrabant iisdem diebus, quibus Judæi, Pascha in quamlibet hebdomadis diem incidebat, nulla excepta, ut videre est apud Eusebium l. 5. Hist. c. 23. Epiphanium Hær. 50. Augustinum de Hæresi c. 29. & expressius apud S. Philastrium in hæresi de festo Paschatis, & Theodoretum hæreticarum fabularum lib. 3. Itaque Judæi tempore Christi Neomenias nondum suo loco moverant, ne Paschale festum cum Sabbato continuum esset. Ut res sit compertior, sciendum est Judæos, quamdiu stetit eorum Respublica, non aliter Neomenias & festa sua constituisse, quàm juxta Lunæ apparitiones, ut Rabbinorum doctissimus Majemonides diserte verbis docet in tractatu de consecratione Neomeniæ c. 5. Sect. 2, & 3.
units.tr: But these authors are refuted first because those canons were not yet in use in Christ's time. Indeed the Talmudic books, which were not completed until the fifth century after Christ, mention everywhere festivals that fall on a Sabbath. Hence Aben-Ezra on Leviticus 23 says: It is proved from the Mishnah as well as from the Talmud that Passover sometimes fell on the second, fourth and sixth day of the week. St Epiphanius agrees, in the Ebionites, no. 32, and in the Alogi, no. 31. So too the Quartodecimans, who celebrated Passover on the same days as the Jews, had Passover fall on any day of the week without exception, as may be seen in Eusebius, Hist. bk 5, ch. 23; Epiphanius, Heresy 50; Augustine, On Heresies, ch. 29; and more plainly in St Philastrius, in his chapter on the heresy about the feast of Passover, and in Theodoret, Heretical Fables, bk 3. Therefore in Christ's time the Jews had not yet moved their new moons from their place, so that the Passover feast would not be continuous with the Sabbath. To make this plainer, it must be understood that while the Jewish commonwealth stood, the Jews fixed their new moons and feasts only according to the appearances of the moon, as the most learned of the rabbis, Maimonides, teaches expressly in his treatise on the sanctification of the new moon, ch. 5, sects. 2 and 3.

units.la: Refelluntur secundo quia dato non concesso, veteres illos Judæos, qui extiterunt tempore Christi stante Synedrio & eorum Republica, ferias Paschales ea ratione computasse, quâ Judæi posteriores, non licuisset tamen alio tempore Pascha celebrare, quàm quo celebrabat tota gens. Hic scilicet locum habere potuit Judaicus Canon: Cùm domus judicii seu Synedrium Neomeniam consecravit, sive erret aut in errorem inducat, illa tamen est consecrata: nec quisquam est, qui non teneatur observare secundum illam diem, licet errorem noverit. Nam in festivitatibus certo tempore celebrandis, non jube-
units.tr: They are refuted secondly because, even granting (which is not granted) that those ancient Jews who lived in Christ's time, while the Sanhedrin and their commonwealth stood, reckoned the Passover days by the same method as the later Jews, it would still not have been lawful to celebrate Passover at a different time from the one at which the whole nation celebrated it. Here the Jewish canon could indeed have applied: When the house of judgement, or the Sanhedrin, has consecrated the new moon, even if it is mistaken or leads others into error, it is nevertheless consecrated; and no one is bound to keep any day other than that one, even if he knows of the error. For in celebrating festivals at a fixed time, we are not commanded to follow

units.la: Hebraic words and marginal notes at the left and right edges are too faint to be read reliably. jubemur præcisè sequi rationes astronomicas, quæ vulgus plerumque latent; sed illorum sequi definitiones, quibus incumbit muneris, ut Calendariis præsint.
units.tr: Hebraic words and marginal notes at the left and right edges are too faint to be read reliably. We are commanded to follow precisely not the astronomical reasons, which for the most part lie hidden from the common people, but the definitions of those men whose duty it is to preside over the calendars.

units.la: Refelluntur tertio, quia si Pascha a Judæis anno Passionis Christi fuisset rejectum in Sabbatum, ne duo festa essent continua, in idem incommodum incidisset hebdomadâ sequenti, quia septimus azymorum, qui atque festus erat ac primus azymorum, incidisset in Veneris diem hebdomadæ sequentis.
units.tr: They are refuted thirdly, because if in the year of Christ's Passion the Jews had put Passover back to the Sabbath so that two feasts would not be continuous, the same inconvenience would have occurred in the following week, since the seventh day of Unleavened Bread, which was also a feast and the first day of unleavened bread, would have fallen on the Friday of the following week.

units.la: Quidam aiunt ideo à Christo & ceteris Judæis anno Passionis ejusdem Christi Pascha non fuisse celebratum eodem die, quia liberum erat singula festa per duos dies celebrare, cum de vero tempore, quo deberent celebrari, non esset satis certum. Recentiores enim Judæi propter dubium conjunctionis Lunæ cum Sole Pascha celebrant decimo quinto & decimo sexto Nisan. Veteres quoque, siqui erant à Judæa remotiores, binos dies observabant; quia latebat illos, quâ die Jerosolymitani decrevissent celebrare cujusque mensis Neomeniam, ex qua reliqua festa pendebant. Hoc videre est apud Majemonidem in libro de die festo c. 6. Sect. 14.
units.tr: Some say that for this reason Christ and the other Jews did not celebrate Passover on the same day in the year of Christ's Passion: it was permitted to celebrate each feast over two days, since the true time at which they ought to be celebrated was not sufficiently certain. For the more recent Jews celebrate Passover on the fifteenth and sixteenth of Nisan because of the uncertainty about the conjunction of the moon with the sun. The older Jews too, at least those who lived further from Judaea, observed two days, because they did not know on which day the Jerusalemites had decided to celebrate the new moon of each month, on which the other feasts depended. This may be seen in Maimonides, in his book on the festal day, ch. 6, sect. 14.

units.la: Refelluntur primo quia Christus Jerosolymis Pascha ultimum celebravit, Jerosolymis autem non potuit esse diffidium, quia quidquid decrevisset Domus judicii de Paschatis celebratione, seu de Neomeniæ consecratione, id omnes sequebantur, nec usquam legitur Jerosolymis aut in Judæa alios uno die, alios altero Pascha celebrasse. Hæc observatio iis quoque est opponenda, qui Judæorum alios putant Neomenias indixisse secundum apparitionem Lunæ, alios vero secundum Lunæ cum Sole conjunctionem, quæ ejusdem Lunæ apparitionem præcesserit integro ut minimum die, utrumque contendunt potuisse fieri legitime, cum Lex non definiat quando inchoanda sit Neomenia, an à conjunctione Lunæ cum Sole, an vero ab ipsius Lunæ apparitione. Christum igitur aiunt eos sequutum, qui à conjunctione Lunæ cum Sole Neomeniam inchoabant, & sic alios, quibus à Lunæ apparitione mensis initium erat, uno die antecessisse in celebratione Paschatis. Verum hæc omnia gratis dicuntur & sine ullo teste vetustatis. Doctores enim Talmudici, quorum nonnulli seculum Apostolicum proxime attingunt, nihil habent de Neomeniarum indictione à conjunctione Lunæ cum Sole; quæ tamen eos non potuit latere, si tum fuit in publico usu.
