Præterea si Novi-lunium secundum Legem à conjunctione Lunæ cum Sole fuisset inchoandum, necessaria fuisset Israelitis Astronomiæ peritia, ut Legi divinæ obsequerentur; at Astronomicæ scientiæ nullum apparet vestigium apud veteres IfraIsraëlitas, & diserte testantur Rabbini Neomenias statutas fuisse ab apparitione Lunæ, sive ad relationem idoneorum testium referentium ad Synedrium sibi Lunam nascentem apparuisse.
units.tr: They are refuted first because Christ celebrated his last Passover at Jerusalem, and at Jerusalem there cannot have been any disagreement, since whatever the House of Judgement had decided about the celebration of Passover, or about the consecration of the new moon, all followed, and nowhere is it read that at Jerusalem or in Judaea some celebrated Passover on one day and others on another. This observation must also be set against those who think that some Jews fixed the new moons according to the appearance of the moon, and others according to the conjunction of the moon with the sun, which precedes the moon's appearance by at least a whole day; they maintain that both could be done lawfully, since the Law does not define when the new moon should begin, whether from the conjunction of the moon with the sun or from the moon's first appearance. They say, then, that Christ followed those who began the new moon from the conjunction of the moon with the sun, and so that he anticipated by one day those others for whom the month began from the moon's appearance in the celebration of Passover. But all these things are asserted without cause and without any witness from antiquity. For the Talmudic teachers, some of whom come very near the apostolic age, have nothing about the fixing of new moons from the conjunction of the moon with the sun; yet this could not have escaped them if it had been in public use at that time. Moreover, if according to the Law the new moon had to begin from the conjunction of the moon with the sun, a knowledge of astronomy would have been necessary for the Israelites in order to obey the divine Law; but no trace of astronomical science appears among the ancient Israelites, and the rabbis expressly testify that the new moons were fixed from the moon's appearance, that is, on the report of suitable witnesses who reported to the Sanhedrin that they had seen the new moon rising.

units.la: 18. Apud te facio Pascha. Id est, secundum Legem per Moysem datam hodie apud te manducare Pascha decrevi. Nam agni Paschalis convivæ jubentur per domos convenire, Exod. 12. v. 3. numerus vero convivarum nec esse poterat infra decem, nec supra viginti excrescere, ut patet, ex Jonathanis Paraphrasi Exod. 12. & ex Josepho 1. 17. de bello judaico c. 7. nempe ut astantium unusquisque saltem haberet victimæ Paschalis offulam, vel ut Hebræi definiunt כזית, quantum olivam. Est autem Hebraismus Scripturæ familiaris, ut animi propositum per ipsam actionem propositam significet, quem admodum hic facio Pascha ponitur pro facere decrevi. Exod. 5. v. 10. Non do vobis paleas, id est, decrevi non amplius dare. Ezech. 2. v. 3. Fili hominis, mitto ego te ad filios Israël, id est, mittere destinavi. Luc. 1. v. 34. Quomodo fiet istud, quoniam virum non cognosco, id est, non cognoscere decrevi. Luc. 19. v. 8. Ecce dimidium bonorum do pauperibus, & si quid aliquem defraudavi, reddo quadruplum, id est, dare & reddere constitui.
units.tr: 18. I keep the Passover at your house. That is, I have decided to eat the Passover today at your house according to the Law given through Moses. For the guests at the Passover lamb are commanded to gather in houses, Exod. 12. 3; and the number of guests could be neither fewer than ten nor more than twenty, as is clear from Jonathan's Paraphrase on Exod. 12, and from Josephus, Jewish War 6, ch. 7; namely so that each of those present might have at least a morsel of the Passover victim, or, as the Hebrews define it, kezayit [כזית], as big as an olive. Now this is a Hebraism familiar in Scripture, by which the purpose of the mind is signified by the action itself proposed; thus here I keep the Passover is used for I have decided to keep. Exod. 5. 10: I will not give you straw, that is, I have decided no longer to give. Ezek. 2. 3: Son of man, I send you to the children of Israel, that is, I have resolved to send. Luke 1. 34: How shall this be, since I know not a man? that is, I have decided not to know. Luke 19. 8: Behold, I give half my goods to the poor, and if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold, that is, I have determined to give and to restore.

units.la: 19. Paraverunt Pascha. Id est, agnum Paschalem; ὁ Χριστὸς ... καὶ ἡ Ἐκκλησία, τὴν φησὶν αὐτὸν θύτην ἀπολύσαι τὸ νομικόν, περὶ τῆς μυστικῆς θυσίας, nam Chrysostomus & Ecclesia docent eopse anno, quo scilicet crucifixus est pro nobis; Legale pascha perfectisse Christum, antequam mysticam cœnam institueret, inquit Photius Bibliothecæ cap. 116. Unde idem Photius Romanæ Ecclesiæ infensissimus, nullam de azymis objectionem movit; quia nimirum agnovit azymi usum ex prima Eucharistiæ institutione habere autoritatem. Hanc enim ob causam saniores & doctiores quique ex Græcis graviter indignati sunt adversus suos, quod ea de re Latinis litem moverent, ut probat Allatius in lib. de perpetuo consensu utriusque Ecclesiæ. Hinc iterum invictum argumentum sumitur contra eos qui volunt a Christo fuisse anticipatum Paschæ Judæorum. Nam agnus Paschalis non potuit alibi maetari, quam in ipso Templi atrio, ubi reliquas victimas maetare moris erat, ut habetur Deut. 16. v. 5, & 6. & Majemonides docet in tractatu de Paschate c. 1. sect. 3. & diserte Exod. 12. v. 23, & 24. agnus Paschalis sacrificium appellatur, ut & alibi passim. Sacrificium autem proprie dictum animalis nullum erat sine effusione sanguinis per manus Sacerdotum ad altare circumcircà. Quis autem Sacerdotum id officii praestitisset Christo, si alio die celebrasset Pascha, quàm universus populus? Sacerdotes autem solitos spargere sanguinem agni Paschalis habetur diserte 2 Paralip. 30. v. 16. & c. 35. v. 11. Licet enim plebeiis agnos Paschales mactare per Legem fuerit liberum, modò ne immundities obstaret, ut patet ex 2 Paralip. 30. v. 17. non tamen inde sequitur, quod contendit Philo Judæus in libro de Decalog. & in libro tertio de vita Moßs, Oratorum more rem exaggerans, plebeios die Paschatis Sacerdotum egisse partes, cum per annum in quovis alio sacrificio idem fuerit concessum plebeiis hominibus, ut docent Talmudici in tractatu Zebachim capite quinto, & ibidem Bartenora, Majemonides in libro de ingressu Sacerdotis in sanctuarium sect. 6. quod patet de holocausto Levit. 1. v. 3, 4, & 5. & de sacrificio pacifico Levit. 3. v. 2. & de sacrificio pro peccato Levit. 4. v. 24. proinde Abrabanel in Leviticum res decem in sacrificio numerat, quarum quinque ad eos attinet, qui victimas offerunt, quinque ad solum Sacerdotem. Ad offerentes attinent impositio manuum in caput victimæ, mactatio, excoriatio, dissectio, extorum ablutio. Ad solum Sacerdotem pertinet Sanguinem in pelvi accipere, eundem aspergere, ignem super altare accendere, ligna digerere, & ordinare partes carnium adolendas. Ex quibus abunde patet in oblatione Paschatis nihil licuisse laicis, quod non eis æquè licuerit in quovis alio sacrificio. Nam ut in aliis sacrificiis, ita etiam in victima Paschali solus Sacerdos sanguinem vel à Levitis, vel à plebeiis acceptum in altare spargebat, ut patet ex 2 Paralip. 30. v. 16. & c. 35. v. 11. & Hebræi omnes etiam Karaitæ, qui nullam traditionem aut constitutionem præter Scripturam admittunt, constanter docent. Solus item Sacerdos extorum victimæ Paschatis adipes in altari adolebat, quod Hebræi omnes asserunt. Hinc Sacerdotes non latebat quot numero essent Paschata, & ut refert Josephus libro septimo de bello Judaico capite 17. sub Nerone Principe Sacerdotum ut Cestio satisfacerent Judæorum numerum ab iis sciscitanti, responderunt se Paschæ solemni die numerasse Hostiarum viginti quinque myriades & insuper quinque millia & sexcenta. 1 Reg. seu Samuelis, ut Hebræi vocant, cap. 15. v. 4. in Chaldæa paraphrasi Israelitas numerasse legitur Saul per agnos Paschales. Quod, licet fabulosum sit, cum ibi vox Hebræa Batelaim, pro qua Vulgatus vertens quasi agnos legit Catelaim, significet in loco ab agnis denominato Telaim, ut plerique interpretes agnoscunt, quomodo Græcis, Rhene, Arne, Polyrrhenium; hoc tamen probat ex Chaldaei Paraphraftis sententia, qui dicitur esse Jonathan, Israelitas sic potuisse numerari. Quod ne concipi quidem potest, si agnum Paschalem domi suae matatum quisque comedit.
units.tr: 19. They prepared the Passover. That is, the Paschal lamb; Christ ... and the Church [ὁ Χριστὸς ... καὶ ἡ Ἐκκλησία, τὴν φησὶν αὐτὸν θύτην ἀπολύσαι τὸ νομικόν, περὶ τῆς μυστικῆς θυσίας]: for Chrysostom and the Church teach that he did so in that year in which he was indeed crucified for us; that Christ had completed the legal Passover before he instituted the mystical supper, says Photius, Bibliotheca, ch. 116. Hence Photius himself, most hostile to the Roman Church, raised no objection about unleavened bread, because he clearly recognised that the use of unleavened bread had authority from the first institution of the Eucharist. For this reason the wiser and more learned Greeks were seriously indignant with their own people for stirring up a dispute with the Latins on this matter, as Allatius proves in his book on the perpetual agreement of both Churches. Here again an unanswerable argument is drawn against those who want Christ to have anticipated the Passover of the Jews. For the Paschal lamb could not be slaughtered anywhere but in the very court of the Temple, where it was customary to slaughter the other victims, as is found in Deut. 16. 5 and 6; and Maimonides teaches this in his treatise on the Passover, ch. 1, sect. 3; and Exod. 12. 23 and 24 expressly call the Paschal lamb a sacrifice, as it is also called elsewhere throughout. But a sacrifice properly so called, of an animal, was never without the shedding of blood by the hands of the priests at the altar, all around. Now which of the priests would have performed this office for Christ, if he had celebrated the Passover on a different day from the whole people? That the priests customarily sprinkled the blood of the Paschal lamb is stated plainly in 2 Chron. 30. 16 and ch. 35. 11. For although it was lawful under the Law for the common people to slaughter Paschal lambs, provided that uncleanness did not stand in the way, as is clear from 2 Chron. 30. 17, it does not follow from this, as the Jewish writer Philo maintains in his book on the Decalogue and in the third book of his Life of Moses, exaggerating the matter in the manner of orators, that the common people played the part of priests on the day of Passover; for throughout the year the same had been permitted to common people in any other sacrifice, as the Talmudists teach in the tractate Zebachim, ch. 5, and Bartenora there, and Maimonides in his book on the entry of the priest into the sanctuary, sect. 6. This is clear for the burnt offering, Lev. 1. 3, 4 and 5; for the peace offering, Lev. 3. 2; and for the sin offering, Lev. 4. 24. Accordingly Abarbanel, on Leviticus, counts ten things in a sacrifice, of which five pertain to those who offer the victims and five to the priest alone. To those who offer pertain the laying on of hands on the head of the victim, the slaughter, the flaying, the cutting up, and the washing of the entrails. To the priest alone pertains receiving the blood in a basin, sprinkling it, kindling the fire upon the altar, arranging the wood, and ordering the pieces of flesh to be burnt. From these things it is abundantly clear that in the offering of the Passover nothing was permitted to the laity that was not equally permitted to them in any other sacrifice. For as in other sacrifices, so also in the Paschal victim, only the priest sprinkled the blood on the altar, whether it had been received from the Levites or from the common people, as is clear from 2 Chron. 30. 16 and ch. 35. 11; and all Hebrews, even the Karaites, who admit no tradition or constitution apart from Scripture, consistently teach this. Likewise only the priest burnt the fat of the entrails of the Paschal victim upon the altar, which all Hebrews assert. Hence the priests were not ignorant of how many Passover lambs there were; and as Josephus reports in the seventh book of the Jewish War, ch. 17, under the emperor Nero, when the chief priests were questioned by Cestius about the number of Jews, in order to satisfy him they replied that on the solemn day of Passover they had counted twenty-five myriads of victims and in addition six hundred and five thousand. In 1 Kings, or as the Hebrews call it, 1 Samuel, ch. 15, verse 4, it is read in the Chaldee paraphrase that Saul numbered the Israelites by Paschal lambs. Although this is fabulous, since the Hebrew word Batelaim, for which the Vulgate translator, rendering "as lambs", read Catelaim, signifies in a place named from lambs, Telaim, as most interpreters acknowledge, just as the Greeks have Rhene, Arne, Polyrrhenium; nevertheless it proves, on the view of the Chaldee paraphrast, who is said to be Jonathan, that the Israelites could thus be numbered. This cannot even be conceived if each man ate the Paschal lamb slaughtered in his own house.

units.la: Temporis & loci angustia frustra nobis objicitur, quasi inter, seu intra duas vesperas, hoc est, ab hora sexta qui duodecima diurna ad solis occasum non potuerint tot agnorum millia ad unum altare suffi & offerri. Templi enim atrium latissime patuisse docent bovum viginti duo millia, & ovium centum viginti millia in Templi dedicatione à Rege Salomone ibi oblata 3 Reg. 8. v. 63. & à reliquo populo sacrificia sine numero 2 Paralip. 5. v. 6. Neque parvum fuit altare, quod in secundo Templo describit Josephus lib. 6. de bello Judaico cap. 6. quadratum, tam latum, quam longum cubitis quinquaginta, id est, pedibus septuaginta quinque. In illud autem altare non toti agni Paschales, sed solum extorum adipes imponebantur, & sanguis fundebatur ad basim; quibus offerendis, ut universi tradunt Hebraei, vacabant plurimi & expediti Sacerdotes per horas quatuor, si res ita postularet, & insuper Majemonides in tractatu de Paschate cap. 6. parag. 6. ex Exod. 23. v. 18. agni Paschalis adipes toti nocte potuisse adoleri docet.
units.tr: The narrowness of time and place is raised against us in vain, as if all those thousands of lambs could not have been burned and offered at one altar between the two evenings, that is, from the sixth hour, which is the twelfth of the day, until sunset. For they teach that the court of the Temple lay very wide open, where King Solomon offered at the dedication of the Temple twenty-two thousand oxen and a hundred and twenty thousand sheep (3 Kings 8:63), and the rest of the people offered sacrifices without number (2 Chron. 5:6). Nor was the altar small that Josephus describes in the second Temple (Jewish War, book 6, ch. 6): square, as broad as it was long, fifty cubits, that is, seventy-five feet. Moreover, the whole Passover lambs were not laid on that altar; only the fat of the entrails was placed there, and the blood was poured out at its base. As all the Hebrews report, many priests, who were free for the task, were occupied in offering these, for four hours if the matter required it. Besides, Maimonides, in his treatise on the Passover, ch. 6, par. 6, citing Exodus 23:18, teaches that the fat of the Passover lamb could be burned throughout the whole night.

units.la: Quod autem quidam ex illo Paschate, qui in Ægypto celebratum est, adstruunt plebeios posse immolare domi agnum Paschalem, gravis est allucinatio; nam in Ægypto in propria domo quisque Israelitarum mactavit, quia non licebat alibi, cum in Ægypto nullum fuerit altare, nec ullus locus, ad quem convenire illi populo fuerit liberum. At post excessum ex Ægypto res aliter se habuit; tum enim non potuit Pascha alibi mactari, ut dicitur Deut. 16. v. 6. quàm in loco sacro, quem Deus elegerat, & ad quem Deus jusserat toties Exod. 23. v. 17. & c. 34. v. 23. ut quotannis venirent mares omnes Paschatis festum celebraturi, ita ut etiam pollicitus sit se Israelitarum urbes ab invasione per miraculum servaturum, dum ad festa ter in anno celebranda in unum locum se conferrent, Exod. 34. v. 24. ut apparerent in conspectu Dei, sicque suas urbes vacuas relinquerent. Similiter cùm in Ægypto Sacerdotes ex populo nondum instituisset Deus, necesse erat laicos Sacerdotum implere locum, ita tamen ut hoc muneris cederet patrifamilias, vel ejus filio majori natu. Quod obtinuit maximè post exitum ex Ægypto; tum enim Deus Israelitarum primogenitos ex communi clade eximens, novum jus in eos sibi acquisivit, Exod. 13. v. 15. Num. 8. v. 17. Illos igitur vel redimi oportuit tuit Exod. 13. v. 13. pretio, nempe quinque siclorum. Num. 18. v. 16. vel Deo consecrari. Atque ut mundarum pecudum fœtus primogeniti victimæ fuere, ita hominum primogeniti Sacerdotum loco habiti sunt, donec iis in deserto recensitis & supra viginti duo millia numeratis, Levitæ, qui fere totidem reperti sunt, Deus in illorum locum sibi adscivit, & cultui suo dicavit, Num. 3. & 8. Itaque, cum Sacerdotes, qui ad Deum accedunt, jubentur se sanctificare Exod. 19. v. 22. plerique Sacerdotum nomine primogenitos intelligunt, quia tum nulli erant Sacerdotes proprie dicti. Neque aliter accipitur quod Exod. 24. v. 5. juvenes de filiis Israel Deo leguntur Holocausta obtulisse & pacificas Victimas immolavisse. Unde est quod pro juvenibus Onkelos & Jonathan Chaldæi, Saadias Arabs, & Tauvasius Persa habent primogenitos. Atque eosmetipsos intelligunt Rabbi Salomon Jarchi, & Rabbi Abraham Aben-Ezra. Quidni igitur pari ratione Pascha in Egypto fuerit administratum aut à patrefamilias aut à primogenitis? At in terra Chanaan non id fuisse juris laicis, ut Sacerdotum partes agerent, patet ex dictis.
units.tr: But that some maintain that ordinary people could sacrifice the Passover lamb at home, from the Passover that was celebrated in Egypt, is a serious error. For in Egypt each of the Israelites slaughtered it in his own house, because it was not permitted elsewhere, since there was no altar in Egypt and no place to which that people might freely gather. After the departure from Egypt, however, the matter stood otherwise. For then the Passover could not be slaughtered anywhere but in the holy place that God had chosen, as is said in Deut. 16:6, and to which God had so often commanded that all males should come to keep the feast of the Passover (Exod. 23:17; 34:23). He even promised that he would protect the cities of Israel from invasion by a miracle, while they went up to one place to celebrate the three feasts in the year, so that they might appear before the face of God and leave their cities empty (Exod. 34:24). Likewise, since God had not yet appointed priests from among the people in Egypt, it was necessary for laymen to fill the place of the priests, but in such a way that this duty fell to the head of the household or to his eldest son. This held especially after the exodus from Egypt. For then God, rescuing the firstborn of Israel from the common destruction, acquired for himself a new right over them (Exod. 13:15; Num. 8:17). It was therefore necessary either to redeem them (Exod. 13:13) for a price, namely five shekels (Num. 18:16), or to consecrate them to God. And just as the firstborn of clean beasts were victims, so the firstborn of men were regarded as priests, until, when they had been counted in the wilderness and numbered at more than twenty-two thousand, God took the Levites, who were found to be almost as many, in their place, and dedicated them to his worship (Num. 3 and 8). Accordingly, when priests who approach God are commanded to sanctify themselves (Exod. 19:22), most understand by "priests" the firstborn, because at that time there were no priests properly so called. Nor is what is read in Exod. 24:5, that young men of the sons of Israel offered burnt offerings to God and sacrificed peace offerings, to be understood otherwise. Hence it is that for young men Onkelos and Jonathan the Chaldeans, Saadias the Arab, and Tavus the Persian have firstborn; and Rabbi Solomon Jarchi and Rabbi Abraham Ibn Ezra understand the same. Why, then, should the Passover in Egypt not have been performed, by the same reasoning, either by the heads of households or by the firstborn? But that in the land of Canaan laymen had no right to act as priests is clear from what has been said.

units.la: 20. Vespere autem facto. Id clarius dicit Lucas 22. v. 14. Cum facta esset hora, scilicet esui Agni Paschalis præscripta, in vespera desinentis diei decimæ quartæ, seu inchoantis decimæ quintæ mensis Nisan, seu ut scribit Josephus lib. 3. antiq. c. 10. Nissan, ita ut mensi nomen fuerit à bellicis signis seu vexillis, quæ Hebraice dicuntur Nissim. Eadem de causa videtur à Romanis mensis, qui mensi Nisan seu Nissan partim respondet, fuisse dictus Martius; unde & Hebræi de hoc mense accipiunt quod dicitur 2 Reg seu Sam. II. v. 1. Factum est autem, vertente anno, eo tempore quo solent Reges ad bella procedere. Quod autem Evangelistæ loquantur de vespera, quà omnes Judæi eo anno Pascha celebrabant, patet vel ex ipsis verbis Christi ad Judam exeuntem è cœna inchoata ante diem festum Paschæ, ut loquitur Joannes c. 13. id est, vigilia Paschæ seu decimà quartà mensis Nisan, cum jam nox esset, hoc est, inchoaret dies decima quinta ejusdem mensis, quæ est prima solemnitatis azymorum, Quod facis, fac citius. Apostoli enim hæc verba sic acceperunt, quasi eis Christus emi jussisset quàm citissimè, quæ necessaria erant ad festum, quod certe Apostolis in mentem non veniisset, missum Judam scilicet intempestà nocte ad ea comparanda fuisse, tantâ festinatione, quæ facile comparare potuisset tota die sequenti, si festum azymorum non fuisset. Itaque ex ipso Joannis Evangelico textu argumentum sumitur invictum, ut probetur Christi Christum eidem die cum cæteris Judæis Pascha immolasse & manducasse ; quod qui negant, Christum reum faciunt transgressionis Legis de tempore, & loco Paschæ immolandi præscripto, & insuper Legis de ministris immolando Paschæ assignatis, quos probavimus fuisse solos Sacerdotes ; denique Legis de ritu immolandi Agni Paschalis, cum non potuerit immolari citra generalem populi consensum, juxta illud Exod. 12. v. 6. Immolabit eum universa multitudo filiorum Israël, quem consensum nunquam Christus obtinuisset, si festivitatem anticipasset. Has transgressiones si Christus fecisset, à Judæis ipsum ut Dominum Legis non agnoscentibus, vere & juste dici de Christo potuisset, Nos Legem habemus, & secundum Legem debet mori, maximè cùm Christus ipse professus sit se non venisse Legem solvere. Cùm itaque nemo Catholicus Judæos absolverit ut Christum damnet, merito venerabilis Beda in lib. De ratione temporum c. 47. ait: Quod dominus decimâ quintâ Lunâ feriâ sextâ crucem ascenderit, nulli licet dubitare Catholico.
units.tr: 20. When evening had come. Luke says this more clearly in 22:14: When the hour had come, namely the hour prescribed for eating the Passover lamb, at the evening ending the fourteenth day, or beginning the fifteenth day, of the month Nisan, or, as Josephus writes (Antiquities, book 3, ch. 10), Nissan, so that the month took its name from the military standards or banners, which in Hebrew are called Nissim. For the same reason the month that partly corresponds to Nisan or Nissan seems to have been called March by the Romans. Hence the Hebrews also apply to this month what is said in 2 Kings (2 Sam. 11:1): And it came to pass, when the year was expired, at the time when kings go out to battle. That the Evangelists speak of the evening on which all the Jews celebrated the Passover that year is clear even from the words of Christ to Judas going out from the supper that had begun, before the feast of the Passover, as John says in chapter 13, that is, on the eve of the Passover, or the fourteenth day of the month Nisan, when it was already night, that is, when the fifteenth day of the same month was beginning, which is the first day of the solemnity of unleavened bread: What you do, do quickly. For the apostles took these words as if Christ had bidden him buy, as quickly as possible, the things needed for the feast. Surely this would not have occurred to the apostles, if Judas had been sent in the dead of night to buy these things with such haste, when they could easily have been bought the whole of the following day, had it not been the feast of unleavened bread. Therefore an unanswerable argument is drawn from the very text of John's Gospel, to show that Christ on the same day as the other Jews sacrificed and ate the Passover. Those who deny this make Christ guilty of transgressing the Law concerning the time and place prescribed for sacrificing the Passover, and further of the Law concerning the ministers assigned to sacrifice the Passover, whom we have shown to be only the priests; and finally of the Law concerning the rite of sacrificing the Passover lamb, which could not be sacrificed without the general consent of the people, according to that word of Exod. 12:6: The whole multitude of the children of Israel shall kill it. Christ would never have obtained that consent if he had anticipated the festival. If Christ had committed these transgressions, then, the Jews, who did not acknowledge him as Lord of the Law, could truly and justly have said of him, We have a law, and by our law he ought to die, especially since Christ himself professed that he had not come to abolish the Law. Since, then, no Catholic has acquitted the Jews in order to condemn Christ, the venerable Bede rightly says in his book On the Reckoning of Time, ch. 47: That the Lord ascended the cross on the fifteenth moon, on the sixth day of the week, no Catholic may doubt.

units.la: 21. Unus vestrum me traditurus est. Proditorem designatum Matthæus & Marcus ante, Lucas post mysticæ cœnæ institutionem narrat. Lucæ narrationis seriei favere videtur Joannes.
units.tr: 21. One of you will betray me. Matthew and Mark narrate the designation of the betrayer before the institution of the mystical supper, Luke after it. John seems to favour the order of Luke's narrative.

units.la: 22. Nunquid ego sum. Supple, qui te prodet.
units.tr: 22. Surely it is not I? Supply: who will betray you.

units.la: 24. Bonum erat ei, si natus non fuisset homo ille. Non utique inquit Bernardus Serm. 35. in Cantica, si natus non fuisset omnino, sed si natus non fuisset homo, sed verbi gratiâ aut pecus, aut alia quæpiam creatura, quæ quoniam judicium non haberet, ad judicium non veniret, ac per hoc nec ad supplicium. B. Hier. simpliciter dictum existimat: Multò melius esse non subsistere quàm male subsistere.
units.tr: 24. It would have been good for that man if he had not been born. Not, to be sure, says Bernard, Sermon 35 on the Song of Songs, if he had not been born at all, but if he had not been born a man, but for example a beast or some other creature, which, since it had no judgment, would not come to judgment, and therefore not to punishment. Saint Jerome thinks it was said simply: It is far better not to exist than to exist badly.

units.la: 25. Tu dixisti. Id est, tu es ille traditor. Hic ergo Christus expressit traditorem, sed ita, ut Apostoli non adverterint, quia forte submisse loquebatur, ut ait Aug. lib. 3. de consensu Evang. c. 1. & ideo non est hic proprie notatio proditoris.
units.tr: 25. You have said so. That is, you are that betrayer. Christ thus indicated the betrayer, but so softly that the Apostles did not notice, perhaps because he was speaking in a low voice, as Augustine says (On the Harmony of the Gospels, book 3, ch. 1). For this reason the betrayer is not here properly named.

units.la: 26. Cænantibus autem eis. Id est, intra cœnam post lotionem pedum discipulorum & eum Agni Paschalis; tempus enim non actus cœnandi significatur.
units.tr: 26. Now while they were eating. That is, during the meal, after the washing of the disciples' feet and the eating of the Paschal Lamb. For the time is indicated here, not the act of eating.

units.la: Accepit Jesus panem. Azymum scilicet; nam intra septiduum azymorum, cujus initium erat vesperà diei decimi quarti finis verò vesperà diei vigesimi primi mensis Nisan, vetitum fuit non solùm fermentatum comedere, sed & domi habere, idque sub gravi poenâ, excisionis scilicet ex populo Dei. Refert autem Suidas in voce Ζύμη, ab hora sexta, hoc est, à meridie decimi quarti mensis Nisan, signo tubâ dato, omnem panem fermentatum, siquis apud Hebræos reliquus fuisset, igne cremari & penitùs absumi solitum. Hinc & Majemonidęs in tractatu de solemnitate Pafchatis c. 1. Parag. 8. illud Deuteronomii 16. præceptum de non comedendo pane fermentato cum Agno Paschali, sic dicit ex Traditione intelligi, ut prohibeatur esus panis fermentati ex illa hora, quæ sit ad Agni Paschalis immolationem idonea, hoc est, ex hora meridiana. Nec valet instantia Græcorum contra Latinos, ut probent Jesum accepisse panem fermentatum, quòd habeatur Græcè ἄζυμον, quæ vox derivatur ab ἀζύμω, fuftoller; nam Luc. 24. v. 30. ἄζυμος dicitur panis azymus, cùm ibi loquatur de pane, quo Judæi vescebantur in festis Paschalibus. Similiter Levitic. 21. panes propositionis, qui azymi erant, in textu Græco per nomen ἄζυμος designantur, sicut & ipsi panes azymi comedendi in solemnitate azymorum Exod. 12. Unde patet quod nomen ἄζυμος indifferenter accipitur pro pane fermentato & azymo. Licet verò Dominus Eucharistiam in Azymo pane omnino confecerit, nequaquam tamen hoc suum factum fixit nobis in legem. Reliquit hoc arbitrio suorum Apostolorum, & ipsis succedentium Episcoporum, inquit verè Christianus Lupus in erudita dissertatione de Leonis IX. R. P. Actis cap. 6. Plerique Theologi Scholastici post D. Thomam aiunt universam primitùs Ecclesiam azymo usam in mysteriis; at exortà hæresi Nazaræorum, seu, Ebionitarum, qui Legalium ceremoniarum jugum Christianis temerè imponebant, pro azymo in universa Ecclesia panem fermentatum coeptum adhiberi in Eucharistiæ usum. Hac hæresi extinctâ, ab Occidentalibus pristinam consuetudinem resumtam, ab Orientalibus morem in odium hæresis Ebionitarum inductum semper fuisse retentum. Sed nullus legitur apud Veteres, qui hujus mutationis meminerit. Laudant quidem Scholastici post D. Th. 4. Sent. distin. 11. q. 2. ar. 2. quæstiunc. 3. Leonem primum & Innocentium tertium RR. PP. Sed quod citant, nec in Leonis, nec in Innocentii operibus extat. Quod verò D. Th. 3. p. q. 74. ar. 4. laudat ex Gregorio, ut ratio reddatur tum consuetudinis Romanæ Ecclesiæ utentis azymo, tum Orientalis fermentatum panem adhibentis, non legitur in scriptis Gregorii Magni, sed quidpiam simile legitur in Registro Gregorii VII. R. P. lib. 8. Epist. 1.
units.tr: He took bread. Unleavened bread, of course. For during the seven days of unleavened bread, which began on the evening of the fourteenth day and ended on the evening of the twenty-first day of the month Nisan, it was forbidden not only to eat leavened bread but even to keep it in the house, and this under severe penalty, namely exclusion from the people of God. Suidas, in the entry Ζύμη [Zýmē], reports that from the sixth hour, that is from noon on the fourteenth day of the month Nisan, a signal was sounded with a trumpet, and any leavened bread that remained among the Hebrews was customarily burned in fire and entirely consumed. Hence also Maimonides, in his treatise on the solemnity of the Passover, ch. 1, par. 8, says that the precept of Deuteronomy 16 about not eating leavened bread with the Paschal Lamb is understood by tradition to mean that the eating of leavened bread is forbidden from that hour which is suitable for the sacrifice of the Paschal Lamb, that is, from the hour of noon. Nor does the argument of the Greeks against the Latins hold, that they prove Jesus took leavened bread because it is called in Greek ἄζυμον [ázymon], a word derived from ἀζύμω [azýmō], to remove. For at Luke 24:30 the word ἄζυμος [ázymos] is used of unleavened bread, although there it speaks of the bread which the Jews ate at the Paschal feasts. Similarly, in Leviticus 21 the showbread, which was unleavened, is designated in the Greek text by the name ἄζυμος, just as the unleavened loaves to be eaten at the feast of unleavened bread are called in Exodus 12. Whence it is clear that the name ἄζυμος is taken indifferently for leavened bread and for unleavened bread. Although the Lord indeed made the Eucharist entirely from unleavened bread, he did not by that act fix it for us as a law. He left this to the judgment of his Apostles and of the bishops who succeeded them, says the truly Christian Lupus in his learned dissertation on the Acts of the Reverend Father Leo IX, ch. 6. Many scholastic theologians after Aquinas say that at first the whole Church used unleavened bread in the mysteries; but when the heresy of the Nazarenes, or Ebionites, arose, who rashly imposed the yoke of the legal ceremonies on Christians, leavened bread began to be used in the Eucharist throughout the whole Church in place of unleavened bread. When that heresy was extinguished, the Westerners resumed the former custom, while the Easterners always kept the practice that had been introduced in hatred of the Ebionite heresy. But no one is read among the ancients who mentioned this change. The scholastics after Aquinas (4 Sent., dist. 11, q. 2, art. 2, quaestiunc. 3) indeed praise Leo I and Innocent III as reverend Fathers. But what they cite is found neither in the works of Leo nor in those of Innocent. What Aquinas (3 p., q. 74, art. 4) quotes from Gregory, to give the reason both for the custom of the Roman Church using unleavened bread and for the Eastern use of leavened bread, is not read in the writings of Gregory the Great; but something similar is read in the Register of Gregory VII, book 8, epistle 1.

units.la: Ut ut fit, certum est ante annum 867. seu ante medium nonum sæculum cœpisse in Occidente usum azymi ad Eucharistiæ confectionem. Hoc patet contra Sirmondum in Disquisitione de azymo ex Alcuini epistola 69. ad fratres Lugdunenses, in qua quosdam contendentes in materiam panis Eucharistici mittendum esse talem, hac ratione refellit; quòd panis qui in corpus Christi consecratur, absque fermento ullius alterius infectionis debet esse mundissimus, & aqua absque omni sordePurissima. Alcuinus autem obiit ex paralysi Turonibus die Pentecostes decimo nono Maii anno 804. id est, ante annos sexaginta, quàm Photius pulso Ignatio in sedem Byzantinam intruderetur. Idem patet ex cap. 31. libri primi Rabani Mauri de institutione Clericorum, quem conscripsit anno 819. & proinde plusquam quadraginta annos ante intrusionem Photii mox dictam, post cujus schisma Sirmondus collocat initium usus azymorum in Ecclesia Latina. Rabani verba sunt: Panem infermentatum, & vinum aquâ mixtum in Sacramentum corporis & sanguinis sanctificari oportet. Alienâ autem videtur cujusdam recentioris suspicio locum libri primi Rabani esse depravatum à modernis, quia liber tertius ejusdem operis de constitutione Clericorum editus quaedam diversa habet à manuscripto extante in bibliotheca Vaticana, ubi inscribitur Liber de officiis Ecclesiasticis; maximè cùm locus laudatus extet tum in editis, tum in manuscriptis codicibus, ut fidem faciunt duo exemplaria Bibliothecæ Regiæ Parisiis, quorum unum est annorum fere sexcentorum, alterum octingentorum. Idem etiam insinuat Paschasius Radbertus Abbas Corbeiensis, Rabani æqualis, sed quinque annis mortuus ante ipsum nimirum anno 851. septennio ante ambitum Photii. Dum enim Paschasius Missæ partes ad mores trahit, & azymum trahit in lib. de corpore & sanguine Domini c. 20. ubi & panem Eucharisticum vocat conspersionem, quæ definitur à Joanne Genuensi in Catholico farina per aquam conglutinata sine fermento. Unde & Haimo Halberstatensis Episcopus in 1 Cor. 5. scribit filios Israel egressos de Ægypto non detulisse inde fermentatam farinam, sed tantum modò conspersam.
units.tr: However that may be, it is certain that before the year 867, or before the middle of the ninth century, the use of unleavened bread for consecrating the Eucharist began in the West. This is clear, against Sirmond in his Disquisition on Unleavened Bread, from Alcuin's letter 69 to the brothers at Lyon, in which, refuting some who argued that such bread should be used as the matter of the Eucharist, he argues thus: the bread which is consecrated into the body of Christ, free of leaven or of any other contamination, ought to be most clean, and the water most pure, without any filth. Alcuin died of paralysis at Tours on the day of Pentecost, 19 May, in the year 804, that is, sixty years before Photius was set up in the Byzantine see after Ignatius was driven out. The same is clear from ch. 31 of the first book of Rabanus Maurus, On the Institution of Clerics, which he wrote in 819, and therefore more than forty years before the intrusion of Photius just mentioned, after whose schism Sirmond places the beginning of the use of unleavened bread in the Latin Church. Rabanus's words are: Unleavened bread and wine mixed with water ought to be sanctified into the sacrament of the body and blood. But the suspicion of a certain more recent writer seems unfounded, that the passage in the first book of Rabanus has been corrupted by modern editors, because the third book of the same work, On the Constitution of Clerics, as printed, contains some things different from the manuscript in the Vatican Library, where it is entitled On Ecclesiastical Offices. Especially since the passage cited is found both in the printed editions and in the manuscript codices, as two copies in the Royal Library at Paris attest, one of which is nearly six hundred years old and the other eight hundred. The same is also hinted at by Paschasius Radbertus, Abbot of Corbie, Rabanus's contemporary, who died five years before him, in 851, seven years before Photius's ambition. For while Paschasius draws the parts of the Mass into moral meanings and also draws unleavened bread into them in his book On the Body and Blood of the Lord, ch. 20, he also calls the Eucharistic bread a conspersio, which John of Genoa in the Catholicon defines as flour made into dough with water, without leaven. Whence also Haimo, Bishop of Halberstadt, writes on 1 Corinthians 5 that the sons of Israel, coming out of Egypt, did not carry away leavened flour from there, but only sprinkled flour.

units.la: Certum est secundò Sirmondum deceptum fuisse in eo quòd in Disquisitionis suæ capite tertio negat Leonem nonum & Humbertum Cardinalem, cùm azymorum causam agerent, se perpetui moris præscriptione defendisse. Nam Leo nonus in Epist. 6. ad Michaelem Patriarcham Constantinopolitanum cognomento Cerularium, illud, inquit, quis non stupeat, quòd post tot Sanctos & Orthodoxos Patres per mille & viginti à passione Salvatoris annos novus calumniator Ecclesiæ Latinorum emersisti, anathematizans omnes & publicam persecutionem excitans, quicumque participarentur Sacramentorum ex azymis? Idem in Ep. ad Michaelem eundem & Leonem Acridanum. Ecce Ecce jam post mille ac ferme viginti à passione Salvatoris nostri annos incipit per vos discere Romana Ecclesia, qualiter memoria passionis ejusdem sit recolenda, quasi nihil ei contulerit praesentia, conversatio, & diuturna institutio, seu quae clarificavit Deum, mors pretiosa illius venerabilis senis, cui specialiter Christus Filius Dei vivi dixit: Beatus es Simon Bar-Iona, quia caro & sanguis non revelavit tibi, sed Pater meus qui est in coelis. Non ergo perpenditis, quanta impudentia dicatur Pater, qui est in coelis, abscondisse à Principe Apostolorum Petro cultum, sive ritum visibilis sacrificii per dispensationem Unigeniti sui, cui per Iesum ipsum plenissime revelare dignatus est illud ineffabile arcanum invisibilis Divinitatis ejusdem Filii sui, &c. Humbertus vero licet non aperte dicat usum azymorum semper viguisse apud Latinos, non obscure tamen id tanquam indubitatum assumit.
units.tr: Secondly, it is certain that Sirmond was mistaken in that in chapter 3 of his Disquisition he denies that Leo IX and Cardinal Humbert, when they pleaded the cause of unleavened bread, defended it by appeal to the prescription of perpetual custom. For Leo IX, in epistle 6 to Michael, Patriarch of Constantinople, surnamed Cerularius, says: Who would not be astonished that, after so many holy and orthodox Fathers, through a thousand and twenty years from the passion of the Saviour, you have emerged as a new calumniator of the Latin Churches, anathematizing all and stirring up public persecution against whoever partake of the sacraments made of unleavened bread? In the same way, in his letter to Michael and Leo of Acrida: Behold, now after a thousand and nearly twenty years from the passion of our Lord, the Roman Church begins to learn from you how the memory of that passion is to be recalled, as though the presence, the conversation and the long instruction of the Lord had contributed nothing to it, nor the precious death of that venerable old man, to whom Christ the Son of the living God said especially: Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. Do you not weigh, then, how great an impudence it is to say that the Father who is in heaven hid from the Prince of the Apostles, Peter, the worship, or the rite, of the visible sacrifice, through the dispensation of his Only-begotten, to whom, through Jesus himself, he deigned to reveal fully that ineffable mystery of the invisible Divinity of the same Son of his, etc. Humbert, indeed, although he does not openly say that the use of unleavened bread has always flourished among the Latins, nevertheless does not obscurely take this as indubitable.

units.la: Certum est tertio Ebionaeos non in hoc ab Epiphanio fuisse haeresi notatos, quod panibus azymis mysteria celebrarent, cum Epiphanius nusquam azymorum usum, uti haereses solet, improbet; at improbat eos, qui in altera parte mysteriorum, ut Ebionaei, aquam solam adhibebant, in Haeresi 46. Editionis Petavianae, in qua haeresis Ebionitarum trigesima est. Praeterea Epiphanius referens Ebionaeos carnium usum repudiasse, eos confutat exemplo Christi, qui in ultima Paschatis celebratione carnes Agni manducavit & azyma. Qui ergo Epiphanio in mentem venire potuisset, ut haereseos insimularet Ebionaeos in eo, quod Christum Dominum exemplo suo docuisse ipse probat. Incertum est tamen an Ebionaei non reprehendantur ab Epiphanio, quod praeter morem Ecclesiae Orientalis, in qua vivebant, azymis utentur, non ut Christum imitarentur, sed ut Judaizarent. Certe Joannis Philoponi tempore, qui vivebat ineunte septimo Ecclesiae saeculo, Ecclesia Orientalis non nisi panem fermentatum ad Eucharistiam conficiendam adhibebat, unde ille male infert nec à Christo in prima Eucharistiae institutione adhibitum fuisse azymum. Οὐκ, inquit in Disputatione de Paschate, ἄζυμον ἄρτον κ.τ.λ. Hoc est, Balthasare Corderio Societatis Jesu Theologo interprete, Neque azymum proprii sui corporis antitypum fuisse dedit Christus; nam & hoc etiam mutum fieret. De pane Eucharistico hactenus, jam redeamus ad expositionem textus Evangelici.
units.tr: Thirdly, it is certain that Epiphanius did not charge the Ebionites with heresy for celebrating the mysteries with unleavened bread, since Epiphanius nowhere disapproves the use of unleavened bread, as heretics usually do. Rather, he disapproves those who, in the other part of the mysteries, used only water, as the Ebionites did, in Heresy 46 of the Petavian edition, where the heresy of the Ebionites is the thirtieth. Moreover, Epiphanius, reporting that the Ebionites rejected the eating of flesh, refutes them by the example of Christ, who ate the flesh of the Lamb and unleavened bread at the last celebration of the Passover. Who, then, could have come to Epiphanius's mind to accuse the Ebionites of heresy for that very thing which he himself proves Christ taught by his own example? It is uncertain, however, whether Epiphanius does not reprove the Ebionites for using unleavened bread contrary to the custom of the Eastern Church, in which they lived, not to imitate Christ but in order to Judaize. Certainly in the time of John Philoponus, who lived at the beginning of the seventh century of the Church, the Eastern Church used only leavened bread to consecrate the Eucharist, whence he wrongly infers that Christ did not use unleavened bread at the first institution of the Eucharist. Not, he says in his Disputation on the Passover, [οὐκ ἄζυμον ἄρτον] unleavened bread, etc. That is, in the translation of Balthasar Cordier, a theologian of the Society of Jesus: Christ did not give unleavened bread as the antitype of his own body, for this too would be mute. So much for the Eucharistic bread; now let us return to the exposition of the Gospel text.

units.la: Benedixit. Apud Hebraeos cibus & potus benedicebatur, seu sanctificabatur per gratiarum actionem Deo omnium bonorum conditori & largitori. Haec nisi praecessisset, cibus pro prophano habebatur: ea vero adhibita, sanctus, id est, quo vesci fas erat. Hic mos etiamnum apud Judæos perseverat. Hinc quod Matthæus hîc dicit Benedixit, Lucas c. 22. v. 19. dicit, Gratias egit. Hinc & sacra cœna dicta est Eucharistia & panis Eucharistizatus, seu, in quo gratiæ actæ sunt, apud B. Justinum.
units.tr: Blessed. Among the Hebrews food and drink were blessed, or sanctified, by giving thanks to God, the creator and giver of all good things. Unless this had come first, food was regarded as profane; once it had been done, it was holy, that is, fit to be eaten. This custom still continues among the Jews. Hence Matthew here says blessed, while Luke 22:19 says gave thanks. Hence too the Lord's Supper was called the Eucharist and eucharistized bread, or bread over which thanks have been given, according to St Justin.

units.la: Hoc. Scilicet, fructulum panis à me benedicti & fracti, quod unicuique veltrûm do sumendum manu, & edendum ore.
units.tr: This. That is, the morsel of bread which I have blessed and broken, which I give to each of you to take in the hand and eat with the mouth.

units.la: Est. Non per substantiam quidem, sed per significationem, seu, ut Scholastici loquuntur, sacramentaliter & symbolice; quomodo circumcisio est fœdus, Agnus est pháse, seu, pesach, & petra erat Christus.
units.tr: Is. Not indeed in substance, but by signification, or, as the Scholastics put it, sacramentally and symbolically; as circumcision is the covenant, the lamb is the Passover (pháse, or pesach), and the rock was Christ.

units.la: Corpus meum. Supple, datum, κλώμενον, ex Luc. 22. v. 19. & fractum κλώμενον ex 1 Cor. 11. v. 24. id est, morti traditum, & sanguine exhaustum pro expiandis hominum sceleribus. In priori hujus Commentarii editione tribus potissimum argumentis mihi præjudiciis errorum Romanæ Ecclesiæ præoccupato videbar invictissimè probare transubstantionis figmentum. Primum his verbis proponebam: Athanasius orat. 3. contra Arrianos sic eos increpat, quòd Christum pro vero ac proprio Dei Filio agnoscere detrectarent: Quis cùm Deo suo fidem habeat, loquenti ad eum modum non credat, Hic est Filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi complacui? At nos longè æquiùs Sacramentarios omnes increpamus: Quis cùm Christo suo fidem habeat, morienti & testamentum suum conficienti ac loquenti ad eum modum non credat, Hoc est corpus meum? Cai transubstantiatio hoc sophismate fuerit persuasum, idem credat necesse est calicem, in quo erat vinum à Christo benedictum, transubstantiari in sanguinem à Christo effusum, aut in novum testamentum, quia Christus jam jam moriturus testamentum suum conficiens accepto calice in quo erat vinum à se benedictum, dixit, Hic est sanguis meus, seu, ut habet Lucas, Hic est calix novum testamentum. Itaque Christo Filio Dei vivi credendum esse citra omnem hæsitationem profitemur Orthodoxi; at Christo verbis fictitium sensum subjicere horrendum arbitramur esse nefas. Credimus itaque Christo dicenti de pane à se benedicto, & fracto, Hoc est corpus meum, &c. Sed res ipsa clamat cum Augustino contra Adimantum cap. 12. quòd non dubitavit Dominus dicere, Hoc est corpus meum, cùm signum daret corporis sui. Sicut de ipso baptismo Apostolus, Consepulti, inquit, sumus Christo per baptismum in mortem. Non ait, sepulturam significamus: sed prorsus ait, Consepulti sumus. Sacramentum ergo tantæ rei, non nisi ejusdem rei vocabulo nuncupavit. Aug. Ep. 23. Secundum meum argumentum pro trantransubstantiatione sic procedebat: Hic est Filius, ait Tertul. lib. 4. contra Marcionem, sistit & repræsentat (id est, præsentem exhibet) eum, quem Deus antea per Prophetas promisit. Hoc est, corpus meum similiter verba sunt, quæ sistunt & repræsentant, seu præsentem exhibent carnem, de qua ante Christus dixerat, Joa. 6. Panis, quem ego dabo, caro mea est. Verum quemadmodum Tertullianus de resurrect. carnis cap. 37. Capernaitarum errori ascribit verba Christi Joa. 6. sic accipere, quasi vere, id est, corporali manducandi ratione, carnem suam edendam determinasset, sic idem lib. 4. adv. Marcionem, Christus professus, inquit, se concupiscentia concupivisse pascha suum edere, acceptum panem & distributum discipulis, corpus suum illum fecit, dicendo, Hoc est corpus meum, id est, figura corporis mei. Cum autem vox repræsentare semper opponatur rei actu præsentis exhibitioni, si adsit præter accusativum ablativus instrumentalis, ut si quis dicatur, vult repræsentare Cæsarem, merito Tertullianus lib. 1. contra Marcionem ait de Christo, Non recusavit panem, quo ipse corpus repræsentat. Tertium erat argumentum; Apostolus Gal. 3. v. 15. Testamentorum vult singulas syllabas numerari, ideoque infert, cum in testamento Abrahæ dictæ sint promissiones, & semini ejus, non vero, & feminibus, quamvis alias semen singulariter positum reperiatur pro nomine collectivo multitudinis filiorum, promissiones dictas esse soli Christo, qui pro nobis dignatus est esse Abrahæ semen, seu filius. Dicamus & nos scriptum esse in testamento Christi, Hoc est corpus meum, non vero, hoc est figura vacua, vel virtutis & efficacia plena corporis mei. Verum nullum potest proponi argumentum isto efficacius contra transubstantiationem. Cum enim in testamentis ex Apostolo verba secundum usitutissimam acceptionem intelligi debeant, qui fieri potest, ut transubstantiatio significetur his verbis, Hoc est corpus meum, cum nunquam & nusquam vox est usurpari soleat pro, transit, fit, transubstantiatur: Sed usitatissima est locutio Sacramentalis, qua signum dicatur esse quod significat, quemadmodum petra nuncupata est nomine Christi, quem significabat, ut loquitur Aug. lib. 2. de Trin. cap. 6. Præclare itaque Facundus Hermianensis Antistes lib. 9. pro defensione trium capitulorum cap. ult. Sacramentum corporis & sanguinis Christi, quod est in pane & poculo consecrato, corpus ejus, & sanguinem dicimus; non quod proprie corpus ejus sit panis, & poculum sanguis, sed quod in se mysterium corporis & sanguinis contineant. Hinc & Dominus benedictum panem & calicem quem discipulis suis tradidit, corpus suum, & sanguinem vocavit.
units.tr: My body. Supply given, broken [κλώμενον], from Luke 22:19, and broken [κλώμενον] from 1 Cor. 11:24, that is, handed over to death and drained of blood to expiate the sins of men. In the earlier edition of this commentary I seemed to myself, having been forestalled by the prejudices of the errors of the Roman Church, to prove most invincibly the fiction of transubstantiation by three main arguments. I first put forward these words: Athanasius, in his third oration against the Arians, rebukes them thus, because they refused to acknowledge Christ as the true and proper Son of God: Who, when he has faith in his God, would not believe him speaking in this way, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased"? But we far more justly rebuke all the Sacramentarians: Who, when he has faith in his Christ, would not believe him, dying and making his testament and speaking in this way, "This is my body"? If anyone was persuaded of transubstantiation by this sophism, he must likewise believe that the cup, in which was the wine blessed by Christ, was transubstantiated into the blood poured out by Christ, or into the new testament, because Christ, about to die and making his testament, took the cup in which was the wine he had blessed, and said, This is my blood, or, as Luke has it, This cup is the new testament. So we the orthodox profess without any hesitation that we must believe Christ the Son of the living God; but we think it a horrible sin to attach a fictitious sense to Christ's words. We therefore believe Christ saying of the bread he had blessed and broken, This is my body, etc. But the matter itself cries out with Augustine against Adimantus, ch. 12, that the Lord did not hesitate to say, "This is my body," when he gave the sign of his body. So also the Apostle says of baptism itself, "We are buried with Christ through baptism into death." He does not say, "we signify burial," but plainly says, "we are buried." Therefore he named the sacrament of so great a thing only by the name of the thing itself. Aug. Ep. 23. My second argument for transubstantiation ran thus: "This is the Son," says Tertullian, book 4 against Marcion, "presents and represents" (that is, exhibits in person) him whom God promised before through the prophets. "This is my body" are similarly words which present and represent, that is, exhibit in person, the flesh of which Christ spoke before, John 6: "The bread which I will give is my flesh." But as Tertullian, in his work On the Resurrection of the Flesh, ch. 37, ascribes to the error of the Capernaites the taking of Christ's words in John 6 as though truly, that is, in a corporeal manner of eating, so that he had determined his flesh to be eaten, so the same author in book 4 against Marcion says: Christ, professing that he had desired with desire to eat his passover, took the bread and distributed it to the disciples, and made it his body, saying, "This is my body," that is, the figure of my body. But since the word represent is always opposed to the actual exhibition of a thing present, if an instrumental ablative stands alongside the accusative, as when one says, he wishes to represent Caesar, Tertullian rightly says in book 1 against Marcion of Christ, He did not refuse bread, by which he himself represents his body. The third argument was this: the Apostle in Gal. 3:15 wishes the single syllables of testaments to be counted, and therefore infers that, since in Abraham's testament the promises were spoken to his seed and not to seeds, although elsewhere the singular "seed" is found for the collective name of the multitude of children, the promises were spoken to Christ alone, who for us deigned to be Abraham's seed, or son. Let us also say that it is written in Christ's testament, This is my body, not, this is an empty figure, or one full of the virtue and efficacy of my body. Yet no argument can be put forward more effective against transubstantiation than this. For since in testaments, according to the Apostle, words must be understood in their most usual sense, how can it happen that transubstantiation is signified by these words, This is my body, when the word is is never and nowhere customarily used for passes into, becomes, is transubstantiated? But the most usual expression is sacramental, by which the sign is said to be what it signifies, as the rock was named by the name of Christ, whom it signified, as Augustine speaks in book 2 On the Trinity, ch. 6. Therefore Facundus, bishop of Hermiane, rightly says in book 9 in defence of the Three Chapters, last chapter: We call the sacrament of the body and blood of Christ, which is in the consecrated bread and cup, his body and blood; not because the bread properly is his body, and the cup his blood, but because they contain within themselves the mystery of the body and blood. Hence also the Lord called the blessed bread and cup which he handed to his disciples his body and blood.

units.la: 27. Accipiens calicem. Cùm Christus id quod erat in calice à se consecrato vocaverit genimen vitis, infrà v. 29. & Marc. 14. v. 25. satis declaravit nullam nobis injungi necessitatem miscendi aquam cum vino in sacratissimæ coenæ celebratione, etsi in calice ab ipso Christo personaliter consecrato suerit vinum aquâ temperatum, ut vetustissima habet tradi-tio.
units.tr: 27. Taking the cup. Since Christ called what was in the cup he had consecrated the fruit of the vine, as below at v. 29 and in Mark 14:25, he sufficiently showed that no necessity is laid on us of mixing water with wine in the celebration of the most sacred Supper, even though in the cup which Christ himself personally consecrated there was wine tempered with water, as the most ancient tradition holds.

units.la: Bibite ex hoc omnes. Ergo non sine grandi sacrilegio fideles Laici arcentur à potione calicis.
units.tr: Drink from this, all of you. Therefore the lay faithful are kept from drinking from the cup not without great sacrilege.

units.la: 28. Hic est enim, &c. Q. d. Ideo volo omnes & singulos bibere ex hoc calice, quia vinum in eo contentum a me consecratum est symbolum sanguinis mei effusi, seu a corpore meo per mortem separati ad novum fœdus ineundum cum hominibus & vos, aliósque multos ex omni tribu, lingua, populo, & natione salvos faciendos à peccatis suis.
units.tr: 28. For this is, etc. That is: I want each and all of you to drink from this cup, because the wine contained in it, consecrated by me, is the symbol of my blood poured out, or of my body separated by death, for ratifying the new covenant with men, and for you and many others from every tribe, tongue, people and nation to be saved from your sins.

units.la: Novi Testamenti. Vox Testamentum & voces ipsi respondentes in Hebræa & Græca lingua quamlibet disposition em & pactionem significare possunt. Propriissimè tamen significant voluntatis decretum de eo, quod post obitum suum quis fieri velit, & consequenter continet promissionem hereditatis; unde & morte testatoris confirmatur Testamentum, ut Apostolus docet in Epist. ad Hebræos c. 9. In Scripturis autem duplicis Testamenti fit mentio, Veteris & Novi; Vetus dictum est, quod ante Novum revelatum fuit, nec proprie Testamentum est, sed potiùs pactum aut fœdus, utpote quod promissionem terrenorum bonorum non absolutam, sed sub conditione implendæ Legis continet, populo eam acceptante, ut videre est Exod. 24. Novum verò Testamentum continet id, quod vetus promittebat, & sicut vetus Testamentum habuit sanguinem vitulorum & ovium, ita novum habet sanguinem Dominicum, cujus effusione ipsum novum Testamentum in Lege & Prophetis promissum, à Christo revelatum & prædicatum sancitur.
units.tr: New Testament. The word testament, and the words corresponding to it in Hebrew and Greek, can signify any disposition or agreement. Most properly, however, they signify a decree of will concerning what someone wishes to be done after his death, and consequently it contains a promise of inheritance; whence a testament is also confirmed by the death of the testator, as the Apostle teaches in the Epistle to the Hebrews, ch. 9. In the Scriptures, however, mention is made of a twofold testament, Old and New. The Old was so called because it was revealed before the New; it is not properly a testament but rather a pact or covenant, since it contains a promise of earthly goods that is not absolute but conditional on the fulfilment of the Law, the people accepting it, as may be seen in Exod. 24. The New Testament, however, contains what the Old promised, and just as the Old Testament had the blood of calves and sheep, so the New has the blood of the Lord, by whose outpouring the New Testament itself, promised in the Law and the Prophets, revealed and proclaimed by Christ, is sanctioned.

units.la: 29. Cùm illud bibam, &c. Transit Christus à significatione vini propria ad metaphoricam, ut significet se in beatitudine cum Discipulis inebriandum ab ubertate domûs Dei, hoc est, communicaturum in beatitudine Discipulis suis fruitionem Dei clarè visi, quæ bonum est quod nullum sequëtur malum, & satietas quam nulla sequetur fames aut sitis, & deliciis copiosissimis nunquam cessaturis replet ani-mam.
units.tr: 29. "When I drink it," etc. Christ shifts from the proper sense of wine to the metaphorical, to signify that he will be made drunk with the diss of the house of God together with his disciples; that is, he will share with his disciples in blessedness the enjoyment of God clearly seen, which is a good followed by no evil, a satiety that no hunger or thirst will follow, and which fills the soul with most abundant delights that will never cease.

units.la: Novum. Id est, mirum, inauditum, non vulgare; hoc sensu Psaltes passim Canticum non vulgare, mirum, inauditum vocat Canticum novum. Eodem sensu ait Virgilius Eclogâ 3. Pollio & ipse fecit nova carmina.
units.tr: "New." That is, wonderful, unheard of, not ordinary. In this sense the Psalmist everywhere calls a song that is not ordinary, wonderful, unheard of, "a new song." In the same sense Virgil says in Eclogue 3: "Pollio himself also made new songs."

units.la: 30. Hymno dicto, id est, absoluto. Ut enim docet Rabbi Moses Majemonides tractatu de solemnitate Paschatis c. 7, & 8. singuli tum viri, tum mulieres ad coenam noctis Paschatis tenentur pocula vini potare quatuor ad minimum, quae ita oportet misceri ut sint potu jucunda, unde & vini & bibendis habenda est ratio, ita tamen ut non minus quarto rio meri cum poculis quatuor immisceatur. Quod si quis ista vini quatuor pocula ebibit mera, is etsi fecit officium, quod pocula ebibit quatuor, tamen hoc idem non praestitit, quia libere non potavit, sed servili ter. Horum autem quatuor poculorum suam quodque precem desiderat. Ad primum igitur dies festus consecratur. Incipitur ad alterum Hymnus, hoc est, series illa orationum, quibus explicatur cur illa nocte vescantur Agno Paschali, oleribus amaris & pane azymo. Super tertium poculum redditur Deo de cibo intra coenam capto gratiarum actio. Ad quartum absolvitur Hymnus & carmen illud canitur: Confiteantur tibi Domine omnia opera tua, & Sancti tui benedicant tibi, &c. Hoc epoto poculo nihil amplius libare per totam noctem licebat praeter aquam, nisi quis vellet super quintum poculum cantare Psalmum 136. Confitemini Domino quoniam bonus, &c. poculum enim hoc nequaquam est ita necessarium ut alia quatuor, atque licebat Hymnum Confitemini extra triclinium absolvere. Haec Rabbi Moses, ex quibus conjicimus in ultima coena vinum, quo usus est Christus, fuisse temperatum aqua, alioquin Judas ipsum ut Traditionum transgressorem insimulasset. Deinde colligimus Christum Hymno absoluto pro more surrexisse de mensa, quod Matthaeus significat per vocem, exierunt, id est, surrexerunt exituri. Verisimile enim sit ex illis, quae habentur Luc. 22. & Joan. 14. Christum cum Discipulis mansisse aliquandiu in Coenaculo, & forte etiam, ut fit, consedisse. Inter exeundum autem videtur Christus dixisse quae habentur Joan. 15, 16, & 17. Porro Christi exitus non erat contra Legem, quia non nisi in Aegypto Judaei tota Paschatis nocte ex aedibus egredi prohibiti sunt, ne scilicet incideret in Angelum a Deo missum ut Aegyptiorum primogenitos percuteret, qui quidem potuisset etiam extra aedes Israelitas dignoscere; sed ut doceret eorum salutem sitam in eo esse, ut se continerent veluti sub custodia sanguinis Agni, qui effusus fuerat, ne eorum sanguis effunderetur. Quod salutis suae Sacramentum si rejecissent, hoc ipso, gratia quoque illo signo significata indignos se reddidissent. Sic grassante diluvio Noë & suis nulla salus fuit, nisi in arca inclusis. Neque familiæ Rahab in Iericuntis excidio præterquam in domo ex qua pendebat funiculus coccineus, cui respondet Agni Paschalis sanguis, quo Exod. 12. in Egypto jussi erant Israelitæ ædium superliminaria & postes aspergere, ne, qui primitiva vastabat, tangeret eos; quod post exitum ex Ægypto factum non esse doctissimus Majemonides dicit; unde 2 Paralip. 30, & 35. docemur in Judæa Paschales Agnos in atrio Templi fuisse cæsos, ibique effusum eorum sanguinem, nec usquam apparet in privatas domos fuisse delatam ullam hujus sanguinis partem, quâ postes ædium aspergerentur. Fuit etiam Judæis in Ægypto peculiare, ut idem Majemonides dicit in fine libri de Pascha te, quod decimâ die primi mensis, id est, quatriduo ante tempus mactationis, Agnus Paschalis jussu Dei erat ipsis seponendus ne inter infensos populos, ut erant Ægyptii, Agnos non facile reperirent, si non nisi extremo tempore iis quærendis incumberent; at in Judæa non fuit cur id timeretur, cùm in id conspiraverit tota gens, ut huic sacrificio nihil deesset. Nec iis, qui è remotis Judææ partibus Jerosolymam se conferebant, facile fuisset tanto ante festum sibi de Agno prospicere. Plerisque enim Jerosolymam venire moris non erat, nisi biduum ante festum aut pridie festi. Itaque tum demum Agnos ab iis comparabant, qui boves, oves, & columbas in Templo venum exponebant, cùm Judæorum Pascha instabat, ut patet ex Joan. 2. v. 13, & 14. Proinde Josephus pro Lege Mosis, sui ævi morem respiciens, mirâ ἀℂλεψίᾳ scribit libro 2. antiquitatum cap. 5. Judæos in Ægypto decimâ tertiâ primi mensis præparasse Paschales victimas in diem decimam quartam ejusdem mensis. Denique Judæis in Ægypto videtur fuisse peculiare quod accincti & calceati cum baculis in manu & raptim Pascha comederunt, tanquam iter longum post paucas horas in hostili terra suscepturi. Quo emenso quietos, non jam accinctos sed discinctos, nec stantes sed sedentes, nec raptim sed lente & pacate comedisse verisimile est. Ita Christus non solùm sedens, sed & more Romano discumbens cum discipulis in triclinio grandi & strato Pascha ultimum celebravit. Hinc in illorum censu, quibus differt nox Paschatis à reliquis noctibus, hoc quoque Judæi observant, quòd cùm ceteris noctibus cœnaturi sedeant vel discumbent, nocte vero Paschali omnes prorsus discumbant. Proinde de primo Judæorum Pascha te in Ægypto celebrato loquitur Chrysosto-mus mus Hom. 23. in Epist. ad Ephes. & quidem tanquam de re praesenti, si versionem Latinam, non textum Graecum sequamur, dum dicit: Nunc (haec vocula abest à textu Graeco) praecincti & calceati vescuntur, ut rogati dicant, quoniam ad iter faciendum eramus parati. Ritus autem Paschatis, qui etiam in Judaea sunt observati, fuere Agni Paschalis integri, anniculi immolatio, assatio, manducatio cum oleribus amaris & azymis, absque ulla ossium fractione, &c.
units.tr: 30. "Having sung a hymn," that is, having finished it. For as Rabbi Moses Maimonides teaches in the treatise on the solemnity of the Passover, chapters 7 and 8, each man and each woman at the supper of the Passover night is bound to drink at least four cups of wine, which must be mixed so that they are pleasant to drink; hence account must be taken both of the wine and of those who drink it, yet so that not less than a third part of unmixed wine is mixed with the cups. If anyone drinks those four cups of unmixed wine, he has indeed performed the duty of drinking four cups, yet he has not done the same thing, because he has not drunk freely but as a slave. Each of these four cups has its own prayer. Over the first cup the festival is consecrated. At the second the hymn begins, that is, the series of prayers by which it is explained why on that night they eat the Paschal lamb, bitter herbs and unleavened bread. Over the third cup thanksgiving is rendered to God for the food taken during the supper. At the fourth the hymn is finished and that song is sung: "Let all your works praise you, O Lord, and let your saints bless you," etc. After this cup, it was not permitted to drink anything more through the whole night except water, unless someone wished to sing Psalm 136 over a fifth cup: "Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good," etc. For this cup is by no means as necessary as the other four, and it was permitted to finish the hymn "Give thanks" outside the dining room. So Rabbi Moses. From these words we conjecture that the wine Christ used at the last supper was mixed with water; otherwise Judas would have accused him of being a transgressor of the traditions. Next, we gather that Christ, having finished the hymn, rose from the table according to custom, which Matthew signifies by the word "they went out," that is, they rose in order to go out. For it is likely, from those things found in Luke 22 and John 14, that Christ remained with the disciples for some time in the upper room, and perhaps also, as happens, sat down. Moreover, while going out, Christ seems to have said the things found in John 15, 16 and 17. Further, Christ's going out was not against the Law, because the Jews were forbidden to go out of their houses during the whole night of the Passover only in Egypt, lest they should fall in with the angel sent by God to strike down the firstborn of the Egyptians, who indeed could have distinguished the Israelites even outside their houses; but so that he might teach that their salvation lay in this, that they should keep themselves as if under the guard of the blood of the Lamb, which had been poured out, lest their own blood should be poured out. If they had rejected this sacrament of their salvation, by that very fact they would have made themselves unworthy of the grace also signified by that sign. Thus, when the flood raged, Noah and his family had no salvation except those shut into the ark. Nor did the family of Rahab in the destruction of Jericho have salvation except in the house from which the scarlet cord hung, to which corresponds the blood of the Paschal Lamb, with which the Israelites were ordered in Exodus 12 in Egypt to sprinkle the lintels and doorposts of their houses, so that the destroyer of the firstborn would not touch them; which the most learned Maimonides says was not done after the exodus from Egypt. Hence 2 Chronicles 30 and 35 teach us that in Judea the Paschal lambs were slaughtered in the court of the Temple and their blood poured out there, and nowhere does it appear that any part of this blood was carried into private houses to sprinkle the doorposts. There was also something peculiar for the Jews in Egypt, as the same Maimonides says at the end of his book on the Passover, namely that on the tenth day of the first month, that is, four days before the time of slaughter, the Paschal lamb was by God's command to be set aside for them, lest among hostile peoples, such as the Egyptians were, they should not easily find lambs if they applied themselves to seeking them only at the last moment; but in Judea there was no reason to fear this, since the whole nation had combined so that nothing would be lacking for this sacrifice. Nor would it have been easy for those who came to Jerusalem from the remote parts of Judea to provide themselves with a lamb so long before the feast. For most people did not customarily come to Jerusalem except two days before the feast or the day before it. And so at that time they bought lambs from those who sold oxen, sheep and doves in the Temple, when the Passover of the Jews was approaching, as is clear from John 2:13 and 14. Accordingly Josephus, looking to the custom of his own age rather than to the Law of Moses, writes with remarkable carelessness in book 2 of the Antiquities, chapter 5, that the Jews in Egypt prepared the Paschal victims on the thirteenth day of the first month for the fourteenth day of the same month. Finally, it seems to have been peculiar to the Jews in Egypt that, girded and shod, with staves in hand, they ate the Passover hastily, as men about to undertake a long journey in hostile land within a few hours. Once that was over, it is likely they ate quietly and calmly, not now girded but ungirded, not standing but sitting, and not hastily but slowly and peacefully. So Christ celebrated his last Passover with the disciples not only sitting but also reclining in the Roman manner, in a large dining room with couches spread. Hence, among those things by which the night of the Passover differs from other nights, the Jews also observe this: that on other nights, when they are about to dine, they sit or recline, but on the Paschal night all without exception recline. Therefore Chrysostom speaks of the first Passover of the Jews celebrated in Egypt in his twenty-third homily on the Epistle to the Ephesians, and indeed as of a thing present, if we follow the Latin version and not the Greek text, when he says: "Now" (this little word is absent from the Greek text) "they eat girded and shod, so that, when asked, they may say that we were ready to make the journey." The rites of the Passover, which were also observed in Judea, were these: the sacrifice of an entire lamb of one year old, roasting, eating with bitter herbs and unleavened bread, without any breaking of the bones, etc.

units.la: 31. Omnes vos scandalum patiemini, Id est, ero vobis lapis offensionis & scandali hac nocte, quia ex his, quae circa me fient pro redemtione generis humani, occasionem ruinae & lapsus in peccatum accipietis.
units.tr: 31. "You will all be made to stumble because of me." That is, I will be a stone of stumbling and offence to you this night, because from the things that will be done around me for the redemption of the human race you will take occasion for ruin and for falling into sin.

units.la: Scriptum est enim. Q. d. Vera enim est illa Zachariae Prophetia cap. 13. v. 7.
units.tr: "For it is written." That is, the prophecy of Zechariah in chapter 13, verse 7, is true.

units.la: Percutiam. Apud Zachariam habetur percute, sed unus & idemque est sensus, percusso scilicet Pastore, dispergentur oves.
units.tr: "I will strike." In Zechariah it is "Strike," but the meaning is one and the same: namely, when the shepherd is struck down, the sheep will be scattered.

units.la: 34. Antequam gallus canet, &c. Id est, ante tempus, quod gallicinium vocatur, seu non cantabit gallus solemni illo cantu, à quo tempus, quo canit, gallicinium dicitur, priusquam ter me negaveris. Interim nullus dubito quin Marcus, qui Petri discipulus fuerat, ipsamet Christi verba retulerit, pro ut illa didicerat à Petro, scilicet: bodie in nocte hac, priusquam gallus vocem dederit, ter me es negaturus. Sed sufficit aliis Evangelistis id memorare, quod praecipuum suit, nempe Christum triplicem illam Petri negationem non solum praevidisse & praedixisse, sed & designasse tempus, & fore ut Christum Petrus ter negaret ante gallicinium, secundum scilicet, quod solum simpliciter gallicinium dicitur; tamen id diserte expressit Marcus, atque illud insuper, primam Petri negationem praecessisse primum gallicinium. At, inquies, inter primum & secundum gallicinium solet intercedere quarta pars noctis, quod spatium tum fuerit horarum prope trium; nam in Judaea, quo anni tempore Christus noctu traditus est, noctes horarum sunt plusquam undecim: porro inter primam Petri negationem vix potuit elabi media pars hujus spatii, ut patet ex Luc. 22. v. 56, 57, & 58. Ibi enim cum Petrus ancillae negasset se nosse Christum, quae prima fuit Petri negatio, post pusillum alius videns eum, dixit: Et tu de illis es, id est, ex discipulis Christi. Petrus vero ait: O homo, non sum, quae negatio secunda fuit. Et intervallo facto quasi horae unius, alius quidam affirmabat, dicens: Vere hic cum illo erat: nam & Galilaeus est. Tum Petrus tertio Christum negavit, & continuo adhuc Petro loquente cantavit gallus. Respondeo 1b. Evangelistas pleraque sum-
units.tr: 34. "Before the cock crows," etc. That is, before the time called the cockcrow, or before the cock sings that solemn song from which the time when it crows is called cockcrow, you will have denied me three times. Meanwhile I have no doubt that Mark, who had been a disciple of Peter, related the very words of Christ as he had learned them from Peter, namely: "Today, this night, before the cock has given its voice, you will deny me three times." But it is enough for the other Evangelists to mention what was chief, namely that Christ not only foresaw and foretold Peter's threefold denial, but also designated the time, and that Peter would deny Christ three times before the cockcrow, that is, the second cockcrow, since only the cockcrow is simply so called; nevertheless Mark expressed this clearly, and moreover that the first denial of Peter preceded the first cockcrow. But, you will say, between the first and second cockcrow there usually lies a quarter of the night, which space was then about three hours; for in Judea, at the time of year when Christ was betrayed by night, the nights are more than eleven hours long; moreover, between Peter's first denial scarcely half of this space could have elapsed, as is clear from Luke 22:56, 57 and 58. For there, when Peter had denied to a maidservant that he knew Christ, which was the first denial, after a little while another, seeing him, said: "You too are one of them," that is, one of Christ's disciples. But Peter said: "O man, I am not," which was the second denial. And after an interval of about one hour, another man affirmed, saying: "Surely this fellow was with him, for he is also a Galilean." Then Peter denied Christ the third time, and immediately, while Peter was still speaking, the cock crowed. I answer, first, that the Evangelists have related most things briefly, and while Peter, being accused, tried to clear himself, the matter could have been drawn out at greater length, and with many words exchanged back and forth, much time could have been spent in the very dispute itself. Next, from Luke's words "after a little while" it does not follow that between the first and second...

units.la: X summatim retulisse, & dum Petrus accusatus conatus est se purgare, potuisse rem in longius diduci, & pluribus verbis ultro citroque habitis, in ipsa disceptatione multùm insumi temporis. Deinde, ex Lucæ verbis post pusillum, non sequi inter primam & secundam Petri negationem nullum, aut brevissimum fuisse temporis intervallum; Joannes enim capite 18. à versu 17. usque ad 25. multa interserit, tanquam facta in illo intervallo. Et 3a. negatio, quam Lucas à secunda removet horæ, circiter, interstitio, tamen in Matthæo & Marco dicitur post pusillum contigisse. Itaque illud post pusillum potest extendi latius, quàm putatur. Tertio horæ Lucæ licet aliquid addere, cùm non dixerit præcisè horam unam intercessisse, sed intervallo facto, quasi horæ unius, quod idem est, ac si diceret, intercessisse horam, circiter, unam. Quarto, quamvis inter primum & secundum gallicinium quarta pars noctis soleat intercedere, tamen id perpetuum non est, nam sæpè accidit, ut galli temerè canant, nec statis horis. Quod se tam in excubiis olim, quàm postea in lucubrationibus expertum esse scribit Scaliger in Cardanum exercitatione 239. Potuit igitur gallus aliquis, post tertiam Petri negationem, solitum gallicinii tempus unâ horâ antecedere. At, inquiet aliquis, cùm Christum negavit Petrus, in Caïphæ domo fuere Scribæ, Sacerdotes & Seniores, ut in Christi vitam inquirerent, & Petrus interim in atrium ingressus expectavit, quo tandem res evaderet, & quid de Christo statueretur. Conventus autem ille usque in tam multam noctem durasse non videtur. Quis enim credat tot Judæorum Proceres noctem fore totam egisse insomnem, ut hanc litem decidèrent, cùm res potuisset æquè commodè in aliud tempus rejici?
units.tr: Briefly reported the event, and while Peter, when accused, tried to clear himself, the matter could have been drawn out at greater length, and with many words exchanged back and forth, a good deal of time could have been spent in the very dispute.
