Next, from Luke's words after a little while, it does not follow that there was no interval, or only a very short one, between Peter's first and second denial. For John, in chapter 18 from verse 17 to verse 25, inserts many events as though they happened in that interval. And the third denial, which Luke places about an hour after the second, is in Matthew and Mark said to have happened after a little while. So that phrase after a little while can be stretched further than is commonly thought. To Luke's an hour one may add something, since he did not say that exactly one hour had passed, but an interval having been made, as it were of one hour, which is the same as if he had said that about one hour had passed. Fourth, although a quarter of the night usually lies between the first and second cockcrow, this is not always so, for it often happens that cocks crow at random and not at fixed hours. Scaliger writes in his Exercitation 239 against Cardanus that he found this to be so both in his youth on watch and later when working late at night. So some cock may have crowed an hour before the usual time of cockcrow after Peter's third denial. But, someone will say, when Peter denied Christ, the scribes, chief priests and elders were in the house of Caiaphas, seeking to bring about Christ's death, and Peter meanwhile entered the courtyard to wait and see how the matter would turn out and what would be decided about Christ. That meeting, however, does not seem to have lasted into so late a night. For who would believe that so many leaders of the Jews spent the whole night awake in order to settle this suit, when the matter could just as conveniently have been put off to another time?

units.la: Sed hoc frustrà objicitur, certum enim est id ita factum. Quod patebit perpendentibus quàm multa fuerint gesta illa nocte ante tertiam Petri negationem. Nam secundum Evangelistas vespere facto, id est, in ipso Solis occasu Christus cum Apostolis Pascha celebravit, lavit eorum pedes, patr re nata longissimam concionem habuit, Sacro-sanctum Eucharistiæ Sacramentum instituit, ortam secundo inter discipulos de Primatu contentionem gravissimis verbis composuit Hymnum cecinit, qui ex pluribus psalmis constabat & orationibus, si Talmudicis creditur. Ivit in montem Oliveti & venit in villam nomine Gethsemani, secessit ut oraret & post horariam orationem rediit ad discipulos, quos, cùm dormientes reperisset, increpavit, quòd unam horam vigilare non potuissent. Idem secundò & tertiò factum. Interim tim cum Juda misši lictores Christum invadunt, & primùm ad Annam adducunt, atque inde ad Caipham, quo convenerunt Scribæ, Sacerdotes & Seniores. Et Petrus in atrium ægrè admissus & agnitus Christum negat. Deinde Christus à Caipha interrogatur. Quo facto, à Petro secundâ vice, & post horam, circiter, elapsâm, tertiâ vice negatur. Nemo erit æquus rerum æstimator, qui non statim agnoscat hæc omnia ante profundam & concubiam noctem fieri non potuisse. Atque id quidem fuit prorsus extraordinarium, ut horis illis de hominis capite ageretur. Sed, præter sensum proximè instans, ad id Judæorum Proceres impulit ferina in Christum rabies, & plusquam Vaticanum odium, quo in eum ferebantur. Ad nostram Evangelistarum collationem proximè accedit illa Theophylacti in Marcum: quod Matthæus obscurè dixit, priusquam gallus cantet, interpretatus est Marcus, quòd priusquam bis canet. Galli enim de more habent uno duntaxat sæpè canere, deinde tanquam dormire, & post aliquod tempus, iterum cantum incipere. Quod igitur dixit Matthæus, scilicet priusquam gallus cantet, id est, priusquam impleat clamorem prioris cantùs, ter me negabis.
units.tr: But this objection is made in vain, for it is certain that it happened as described. This will be clear to anyone who weighs how much was done on that night before Peter's third denial. For according to the Evangelists, when evening came, that is, at sunset itself, Christ celebrated the Passover with the apostles, washed their feet, gave a very long sermon as the occasion required, instituted the most holy sacrament of the Eucharist, settled with very weighty words the dispute among the disciples that had arisen a second time about primacy, and sang a hymn, which, if the Talmudists are to be believed, consisted of several psalms and prayers. He went to the Mount of Olives and came to a village named Gethsemane, withdrew to pray, and after an hour's prayer returned to the disciples, whom he found asleep and rebuked because they could not stay awake for one hour. This happened a second and a third time. Meanwhile, with Judas, officers were sent who seized Christ and first led him to Annas, and from there to Caiaphas, where the scribes, chief priests and elders had gathered. Peter, scarcely admitted into the courtyard and recognized, denies Christ. Then Christ is questioned by Caiaphas. After this, Peter denies him a second time, and, after about an hour had passed, a third time. No fair judge of events will fail to recognize at once that all this could not have happened before the deep and sleeping night. And indeed it was quite out of the ordinary that a man's life should be dealt with in those hours. But, besides the immediate purpose, the savage rage against Christ and a hatred more than Vatinian drove the leaders of the Jews to this. Closest to our comparison of the Evangelists is Theophylact's remark on Mark: what Matthew said obscurely, before the cock crows, Mark explained as before it crows twice. For cocks commonly crow only once, then as it were fall asleep, and after some time begin to crow again. So what Matthew said, namely before the cock crows, means before it finishes the crowing of its first call; you will deny me three times.

units.la: Ut hactenus dicta de gallicinio rectè intelligantur, superest notandum, quòd tempus proximum mediæ noctî (quâ Romani diem incipiebant & finiebant) dicitur media nox, seu gallicinium primum; gallus enim à media nocte canere incipit. Sequitur conticinium, id est, secundum veteres glossas, tempus, quod est inter gallicinium primum & secundum, quo scilicet intermissio, gallicantus cessat. Conticinio succedit secundum gallicinium, seu quarta vigilia noctis. Quia verò quartâ vigiliâ nocte gallicantus acriùs canunt, atque hominibus utilius, cùm hoc secundo cantu ad diurnos labores excitentur, & quia prioris gallicinii tempus alio designatur nomine, vocatur enim media nox, & mediocrium; secundum gallicinium, quod scilicet proximè auroram præcedit, intelligitur semper, cùm aliquid factum legitur gallicinii tempore, absque numeri adjectione. Hinc non solum hic Matthæus, Marcus c. 13. v. 35. Luc. 22. v. 34. Joan. 13. v. 38. sed & Censorinus cap. 19. Macrobius lib. 1. Saturnal. cap. 3. gallicinium ponunt inter mediam noctem, seu primum gallicinium & auroram. Hoc secundum, seu gallicinium simpliciter dictum significatur per pullorum cantum sine addito Tob. 5. v. 11.
units.tr: So that what has been said so far about cockcrow may be correctly understood, it remains to note that the time near midnight (at which the Romans began and ended the day) is called midnight or the first cockcrow, for the cock begins to crow from midnight. Next comes the conticinium, that is, according to the old glosses, the time between the first and second cockcrow, when the crowing of the cocks ceases. The conticinium is followed by the second cockcrow, or the fourth watch of the night. Because cocks crow more sharply in the fourth watch of the night, and because this second crowing is more useful to men, since by it they are roused to their daily labours, and because the time of the first cockcrow is designated by another name, for it is called midnight, or the middle of the night, the second cockcrow, which immediately precedes dawn, is always understood whenever something is read as having happened at cockcrow without any numeral added. Hence not only here in Matthew, and in Mark 13:35, Luke 22:34 and John 13:38, but also Censorinus in chapter 19 and Macrobius in Saturnalia 1, chapter 3, place the cockcrow between midnight, or the first cockcrow, and dawn. This second, or cockcrow simply so called, is indicated by the crowing of the young cocks without any addition, Tobit 5:11.

units.la: Ter me negabis. Ut magis probaretur libertum sibi unum nihil posse sine gratia, cui dictum fuerat: Confirma fratres tuos & roga ne intretis in tentationem: quique respondit, utique ex libero arbitrio: Domine tecum paratus sum & in carcerem, & in mor-tem ire, eidem prædicitur, quòd priusquam gallus cantet, ter Dominum negaturus sit. Quod quid est aliud, quàm quod in fide defecturus sit? Certè rogaverat pro eo Dominus, ne deficeret fides ipsius. Nec utique frustra rogaverat, cujus una erat cum eo, quem rogaverat, operatio. Sed ne libero arbitrio videretur fiare, qui de se magna promiserat, permittitur periclitari, ut conturbatum ac deficientem ille respiciat & reficiat, sine quo nemo perfiiit. Ab hac autem confessione gratia Dei, ideo quidam resiliunt, cùm eam talem confessi fuerint, qualis divino Eloquio prædicatur, & qualis opere sua potestatis agnoscitur, etiam hoc necesse habent confiteri, quòd ex omni numero hominum per secula cunctarum, certus apud Deum, definitiusque sit numerus prædestinati in vitam æternam populi, & secundum propositum Dei vocantis electi. Quod quidem tam impium est negare, quàm ipsi gratiæ contraire.
units.tr: You will deny me three times. To show more clearly that a free man cannot do anything without grace, Peter, to whom it had been said, "Strengthen your brethren, and pray that you do not enter into temptation" (Luke 22:32), and who answered, certainly out of his free will: "Lord, I am ready to go with you both into prison and into death", is here told that before the cock crows he will deny the Lord three times. What is this other than that he would fail in faith? Surely the Lord had prayed for him, that his faith might not fail. Nor had he prayed in vain, since the one for whom he prayed had a single work together with him. But so that he who had promised great things about himself should not seem to act by free will, he is allowed to be put in peril, so that the one who was troubled and failing might look back to him and be restored, since without him no one persists. Some men, however, shrink from this confession of the grace of God, though they have confessed it as it is proclaimed in the divine Word and recognized in its work of power; they must also confess that, out of the whole number of men through all ages, the number of those predestined to eternal life, and of the chosen people called according to God's purpose, is certain and fixed with God. To deny this is as impious as it is to oppose grace itself.

units.la: B. Prosper in Ep. ad Ruffin. c. 6.
units.tr: B. Prosper, in his Letter to Ruffinus, chapter 6.

units.la: 36. Tunc. Egressus scilicet ex urbe Jerosolymâ, & trajecto torrente Cedron, qui inter montem Oliveti ad Orientem situm, & inter Jerosolymam ad Occidentem fluit per mediam vallem Josaphat, quæ & vallis Hennon dicitur. Gethsemani. Hoc nomen sonat Latinè torcular olei, sic autem villa ista dicebatur, ob montem Oliveti, ad cujus radices sita erat.
units.tr: 36. Then. Namely, going out from the city of Jerusalem, and crossing the brook Kidron, which flows between the Mount of Olives to the east and Jerusalem to the west, through the middle of the valley of Jehoshaphat, which is also called the valley of Hinnom. Gethsemane. This name means in Latin oil press; the village was so called because of the Mount of Olives, at whose foot it lay.

units.la: 37. Cæpit contristari. Non ante contristabatur, quia Christus passionum dominus iis utebatur, cùm id expedire judicabat, doctrinæ & nostri exempli causâ.
units.tr: 37. He began to be sorrowful. He had not been sorrowful before, because Christ, as Lord of the sufferings, used them when he judged it expedient, for the sake of teaching and of our example.

units.la: 38. Tristis est anima mea usque ad mortem. Id est, tristitiâ tanti undique circumsepta est & obsessa anima mea, ut nisi aliunde sublevaretur, mortem ipsam inferre per se sola sufficeret. Nempe, ut ait Cyrillus lib. 4. in Joan. c. 1. Caro factus Christus permittit carni, ut sua patiatur.
units.tr: 38. My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death. That is, my soul is so surrounded and beset on every side with sorrow that, unless it were relieved from elsewhere, it would by itself be enough to bring on death itself. Indeed, as Cyril says in book 4 on John, chapter 1: Christ, made flesh, allows the flesh to suffer its own things.

units.la: 38. Progressus pusillum. Hoc clarius explicat Lucas c. 22. v. 41. & avulsus est ab eis (id est à tribus Discipulis) quantùm jactus est lapidis.
units.tr: 38. Going a little further. Luke explains this more clearly in chapter 22, verse 41: and he was withdrawn from them (that is, from the three disciples) about a stone's throw.

units.la: Procidit in faciem suam. Probabile est, primùm Christum quidem genua flexisse, quod notat Lucas; postea verò cùm intenderet vim precationis, quod idem Lucas significat his verbis, prolixius, Græcè intensius, orabat, toto corpore in terram procubuisse, quod notant Matth. & Marc. dum aiunt eum procidisse super terram, & in faciem suam.
units.tr: He fell on his face. It is probable that Christ at first indeed bent his knees, as Luke notes; but afterwards, when he intensified his prayer, which the same Luke signifies with the words more fully, in Greek more intensely, was praying, he lay prostrate on the ground with his whole body, as Matthew and Mark note when they say that he fell upon the ground and on his face.

units.la: - Pater mi. Hoc Marcus dicit, Abba Pater, quæ est formula Græcis notissima, quâ à pueruiis blandè appellari solet pater, & superiores, honoris & reverentiæ ergo, ab inferioribus. Fit autem Abba Græcè ab Appa, quod patrem, ut & Papa, Tata, Atta, Græcorum pueris sonuit. Meritò itaque que Aug. in Epist. 178. ait, Abba Graecum esse vocabulum; Syriace enim non dicitur Abba, sed Aba. Cum itaque Christus in hac precatione brevi & pathetica Patrem familiariter & reverenter lingua, qua loquebatur, Syriaca compellaverit, Marcus blandam & familiarem compellationem cum reverentia expressit formula blandae, familiaris itidem & honorificae compellationis, Graecis, quorum lingua ipse scripsit, usitatissima. Similiter cum Paulus dicit Spiritum Christi clamare in cordibus nostri, Abba, Pater, intelligit nobis tantam ingenerari per Spiritum-Sanctum fiduciam, ut Deum tam familiariter compellare possimus, quam a puerilis pater blande hac formula Graecis notissima Abba Pater, solet compellari.
units.tr: - My Father. Mark says Abba Father, which is a formula very well known to the Greeks, by which fathers are commonly addressed affectionately by small children, and by inferiors, out of honour and reverence, by their superiors. Abba is formed in Greek from Appa, which sounded to Greek children as Papa, Tata, Atta do. Rightly therefore Augustine says in Epistle 178 that Abba is a Greek word; for in Syriac it is not said Abba but Aba. Since Christ, then, in this brief and emotional prayer addressed the Father in the language he spoke, Syriac, in a familiar and reverent way, Mark rendered the affectionate and familiar address, together with its reverence, by a formula of the same affectionate, familiar and honorific kind, very common among the Greeks, in whose language he himself wrote. Similarly, when Paul says that the Spirit of Christ cries in our hearts, Abba, Father, he means that such confidence is engendered in us through the Holy Spirit that we can address God as familiarly as a small child addresses its father with the affectionate formula Abba Father, which is very well known among the Greeks.

units.la: Si possibile est. Id est, si vis, ut explicat Lucas.
units.tr: If it is possible. That is, if you will, as Luke explains.

units.la: Transeat a me calix iste. Non est factum, quod hic petiit Christus, quia ratio, quae petitionem propositit, nolebat ut hoc impleretur, sed ad instructionem nostram, volebat demonstrare nobis suam voluntatem naturalem, & magnum sensualitatis, quem sicut homo habebat. D. Th. 3. p. q. 21. art. 4. deinde ut ait Aug. Serm. 34. de verbis Apostoli mortem horret non opinio, sed natura.
units.tr: Let this cup pass from me. What Christ asked did not happen, because the reason which proposed the request was unwilling that this should be fulfilled, but for our instruction he wished to show us his natural will and the great reluctance of the senses, which he had as a man. Thomas, Summa 3, q. 21, art. 4. Then, as Augustine says in Sermon 34 on the words of the Apostle, it is not opinion but nature that shudders at death.

units.la: Non sicut ego volo. Hoc est, non juxta appetitum humanum naturalem assumtum.
units.tr: Not as I will. That is, not according to the natural human appetite that he had assumed.

units.la: 41. Vigilate & orate ne intretis in tentationem. Ergo unusquisque contra suam concupiscentiam dimicans oret, ne intret in tentationem: id est, ne sit ab illa abstractus & illectus. Non autem intrat in tentationem, si voluntate bona vincat concupiscentiam malam. Nec tamen sufficit arbitrium voluntatis humanae, nisi a Domino victoria concedatur oranti, ne intret in tentationem. Quid vero evidentius, quam Dei offenditur gratia, ubi quod oratur, accipitur? Si enim dixisset Salvator noster: Vigilate ne intretis in tentationem: admonuisse videretur tantummodo hominis voluntatem: cum vero addidit, Et orate, offendit Deum adjuvare, ne intretur in tentationem. Aug. de lib. arb. & gratia c. 4.
units.tr: 41. Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation. Therefore each person, struggling against his own concupiscence, should pray that he not enter into temptation, that is, that he not be drawn away and enticed by it. A person does not enter into temptation if by a good will he overcomes evil concupiscence. Yet the free choice of the human will is not sufficient, unless victory is granted by the Lord to the one who prays that he not enter into temptation. What is more evident than that the grace of God is offended, when what is prayed for is received? For if our Saviour had said only, Watch lest you enter into temptation, he would seem to have admonished the human will alone; but when he added, And pray, he showed that God helps us so that we do not enter into temptation. Augustine, On Free Will and Grace, ch. 4.

units.la: 42. Si non potest hic calix transfire. Id est, si non vis ut transeat.
units.tr: 42. If this cup cannot pass unless I drink it. That is, if you do not will that it pass.

units.la: 45. Dormite jam & requiescite. Exprobrat Christus Apostolis somnolentiam his verbis, quasi diceret, Periculum praesens jam vos satis excitabit, quos crebra monitio mea non excitaverat.
units.tr: 45. Sleep on now, and take your rest. Christ reproaches the Apostles for their drowsiness with these words, as if he said: The danger now present will rouse you enough, you whom my frequent warning did not rouse.

units.la: 49. Osculatus est eum. Recte Aug. lib. 3. de consensu Evangelistarum c. 3. existimat Judam post osculum Christo datum, recessisse versus turbas & tunc evenisse, quae Joannes narrat de turbis prostratis; si enim ante osculum ista contigissent, non opus fuisset osculi signo, cum bis dixisset ipsis Jesus, Ego sum.
units.tr: 49. He kissed him. Augustine rightly holds, in Book 3 of On the Harmony of the Evangelists, ch. 3, that Judas, after giving the kiss to Christ, withdrew toward the crowds, and that then there happened what John relates about the crowds being thrown to the ground; for if those things had happened before the kiss, there would have been no need of the sign of a kiss, since Jesus had twice said to them, I am he.

units.la: 50. Amice ad quid venisti? Luc. 22. v. 48. Osculo filium hominis tradis? Hoc est, amoris pignore scelus imples, & pacis instrumento odia seris, & charitatis officio mortem irrogas? B. Ambr. lib. 3. de Spiritu Sancto c. 18.
units.tr: 50. Friend, why have you come? Luke 22:48. Do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss? That is, do you fill up a crime with the pledge of love, sow hatreds with the instrument of peace, and inflict death by the service of charity? Saint Ambrose, Book 3, On the Holy Spirit, ch. 18.

units.la: Manus injecerunt in Jesum. Hoc dictum à Matthæo & Marco vel per anticipationem, vel ita ut nondum Christum ligarent, aut immotum detinerent, sed solum, quod in eum incurrerint & eum circumdederint.
units.tr: They laid hands on Jesus. This is said by Matthew and Mark either by anticipation, or in such a way that they had not yet bound Christ or held him fast, but only that they rushed upon him and surrounded him.

units.la: 52. Qui acceperint gladium. Ille accipit gladium, qui nulla superiori aut legitima potestate, vel jubente, vel concedente, in sanguinem alicujus armatur. B. Aug. lib. 22. contra Faustum. c. 70.
units.tr: 52. Those who take the sword. He takes up the sword who arms himself against another's blood without any higher or lawful authority, either commanding or permitting it. Saint Augustine, Book 22, Against Faustus, ch. 70.

units.la: Gladio peribunt. Id est, digni sunt qui pereant; non enim eventus, sed meritum homicidæ significatur, juxta legem Genef. 9. Sunt, qui non ad Petrum, sed ad Judæos referant. q. d. Noli Deo præripere ultionem, crudeles enim ili & sanguinarii, etiam te quiescente gravissimas Deo daturi sunt pœnas suo sanguine.
units.tr: Will perish by the sword. That is, they deserve to perish; for it is not the outcome but the guilt of the murderer that is signified, according to the law of Genesis 9. Some refer this not to Peter but to the Jews, as if to say: Do not snatch vengeance from God; for these cruel and bloodthirsty men, even if you keep still, will themselves pay the gravest penalties to God with their own blood.

units.la: 53. An putas, &c. Q. d. Tanta est mea dignitas, ut leve esset impetrare legiones Angelorum à Patre, si convenirent.
units.tr: 53. Do you think, etc. That is, my dignity is so great that it would be a small matter to obtain from the Father legions of angels, if I wished.

units.la: 55. In illa hora. Id est, in isto temporis articulo.
units.tr: 55. In that hour. That is, at that moment of time.

units.la: 57. Duxerunt ad Caiphām Principem Sacerdotum. Ductus est Jesus ad Annam primum, sed ostentationis tantum causâ, nec ibi quidquam actum; quæ enim referт Joannes gesta à Pontifice, non ad Annam referenda sunt, sed ad Caiphām, qui erat Pontifex anni illius, ut loquitur ipse Joannes. Unde cùm idem Joannes dicit c. 18. v. 24. Et misit eum Annas ligatum ad Caiphām, prætéritum perfectum misit ponitur pro præterito plusquam perfecto miserat. Sic supra cap. 14. v. 3. Herodes tenuit Joannem & alligavit eum, & posuit in carcerem, id est, tenuerat, alligaverat & posuerat.
units.tr: 57. They led him to Caiaphas the high priest. Jesus was first led to Annas, but only for show, and nothing was done there; for the things John relates as done by the high priest are not to be referred to Annas but to Caiaphas, who was high priest that year, as John himself says. Hence, when the same John says in chapter 18:24, And Annas sent him bound to Caiaphas, the perfect sent is used for the pluperfect had sent. So above, in chapter 14:3, Herod had seized John and bound him and put him in prison, that is, had seized, had bound and had put.

units.la: 58. Sequebatur eum à longè. Addit Joannes, & alius discipulus, quem verisimiliùs multi existimant fuisse civem Jerosolymitanum, ideòque Pontifici notum, fortasse in cujus domo Christus cœnaverat, quàm, vel Joannem, vel alium quempiam è duodecim Apostolis.
units.tr: 58. He followed him at a distance. John adds, and another disciple, whom many think, with more probability, was a citizen of Jerusalem, and therefore known to the high priest, perhaps in whose house Christ had eaten the supper, rather than John or some other of the twelve Apostles.

units.la: 61. Possum destruere, &c. Observat Marcus hoc testimonium non fuisse conveniens, id est, etsi fuisset verum, non tamen fuisse idoneum & sufficiens, ut Christus mortì adjudicaretur.
units.tr: 61. I am able to destroy, etc. Mark observes that this testimony was not suitable, that is, even if it had been true, it was not nevertheless fit and sufficient for Christ to be adjudged to death.

units.la: 62. Surgens Princeps Sacerdotum, &c. Unicum Caiphæ & Sacerdotum examen & judicium fuisse, non duplex, latis apparet, si conferantur cum Luca, quæ Marcus & Matthæus narrant. Unicum enim discrimen est, quòd Lucas à toto Concilio interrogatum refert Jesum, An esset Christus: Matthæus verò & Marcus, id tantùm à Caipha factum aiunt, quod leve est, cùm alii post Caiphăm à Christo idem postulasse potuerint, vel Lucas Concilio tribuisse, quod ab ejus capite factum fuerat, usitato tropo; quare, quod ait Lucas, & ut factus est dies, sic intelligendum est, cùm dies advenisset; quod verò ait Matthæus, mane facto consilium inisse Principes Sacerdotum, &c. adversus Jesum, non de examine & judicio accipiendum est, sed de judicii executione; quomodo nempe Jesum jàm morti adjudicatum morti traderent.
units.tr: 62. The high priest, standing up, etc. That the examination and judgement of Caiaphas and the priests was single, not double, appears plainly if what Mark and Matthew relate is compared with Luke. For the only difference is that Luke reports Jesus being questioned by the whole Council, whether he was the Christ; but Matthew and Mark say only that this was done by Caiaphas, which is a slight matter, since others after Caiaphas could have asked the same of Christ, or Luke may have attributed to the Council, by a common trope, what was done by its head. Therefore what Luke says, and when it was day, is to be understood as when day had come; and what Matthew says, that when morning had come the chief priests took counsel, etc., against Jesus, is not to be taken of the examination and judgement but of the execution of the judgement, namely how they might hand over Jesus, already adjudged to death, to death.

units.la: 64. A modò, &c. Q. d. Breve erit tempus insidiarum, quæ in me concitatæ sunt: parvo enim expleto tempore, superior omnibus meis inimicis efficiar.
units.tr: 64. From now on, etc. That is, the time of the plots that have been stirred up against me will be brief; for after a short time I shall be made superior to all my enemies.

units.la: 70. At ille negavit. Petrus primò est mentitus, secundò mendacio adjecit perjurium, tertiò præter mendacium & perjurium, diris se obligavit. Cæterum Marc. & Matth. tres negationes Petri simul narrant post judicium & illusiones; Lucas ante utrumque, Joannes verò primam negationem ante examen, reliquas post. Quis autem historiæ seriem diligentius hac in circumstantia servaverit incertum est.
units.tr: 70. But he denied it. Peter first lied, then added perjury to his lie, and thirdly, besides lying and perjury, bound himself with curses. Moreover, Mark and Matthew relate the three denials of Peter together, after the judgement and the mockeries; Luke relates them before both; but John relates the first denial before the examination and the rest after it. Who kept the order of the history more carefully in this circumstance is uncertain.

units.la: 71. Exeunte autem illo januam: Græcè, in vestibulum atrii. Petrus non domo exiit, sed tantùm ex atrio, quò etiam statim reversus est; cùm enim ex Marco constet Petrum ex atrio exiisse, ex Joanne verò, quòd ad ignem stans secundò negaverit; dicendum est, exeunte Petro, ancillam dixisse circumstantibus, sic ut Petrus audire posset: Et hic erat cum Jesu: cùm autem Petrus reversus esset, vel ne fugisse videretur, vel ut se purgaret, vel frigoris impatiens, vel scire studiosus, quid de Christo ageretur, alium quendam, ut Lucas notat, immò alios plures, ut Joannes observat, objecisse ei stanti, & se calefacienti idem, quod ancilla dixerat.
units.tr: 71. And when he had gone out to the porch: in Greek, into the vestibule of the court. Peter did not go out of the house, but only out of the court, to which he at once returned; for since Mark shows that Peter went out of the court, and John that he denied a second time while standing by the fire, it must be said that when Peter had gone out, the maidservant said to the bystanders, so that Peter could hear: This man also was with Jesus. When Peter had returned, either so as not to seem to have fled, or to clear himself, or unable to bear the cold, or eager to know what was being done about Christ, others, as Luke notes, or rather several more, as John observes, objected to him as he stood and warmed himself the same thing the maidservant had said.

units.la: 74. Tunc cæpit detestari. Id est, execrari, sibimet male precari, non verò Jesum detestari.
units.tr: 74. Then he began to curse. That is, to execrate, to call down evil upon himself; not that he detested Jesus.

units.la: Et continuò gallus cantavit. Addit Lucas c. 22. v. 61. Et conversus Dominus respexit Petrum. Non corporali facie, inquit Aug. Hom. 1. inter undecim è Carthusia majori deprompta, nam Dominus in interioribus (sursùm) judicabatur, Petrus foris (deorsùm) in atrio tentabatur, nec vacabat Christo ligato è loco superiori deorsùm respicere, ergo respexit eum Dominus, non corpore sed majestate, non oculorum carnis intuitu, sed mise-
units.tr: And immediately the cock crowed. Luke adds in chapter 22, verse 61: And the Lord turned and looked upon Peter. "Not with a bodily face," says Augustine, Homily 1 among the eleven taken from the Carthusian house at Major, "for the Lord was being judged in the inner place (above), while Peter was being tested outside in the courtyard (below). Christ, bound in the upper place, had no leisure to look down, so the Lord looked upon him, not with the body but with majesty, not with a glance of the carnal eyes but with mer-

units.la: X_4 miserericordia altissima. Respexit, ut ait idem Sanctus Doctor de gratia Christi c. 45. Petrum non corporalibus oculis, sed in mente & voluntate, quia latenter subvenit, cor tetigit, memoriam revocavit, interiore gratia sua visitavit Petrum, interioris hominis, usque ad exteriores lacrymas movit, & produxit assectum. Ecce quemadmodum Deus, adjuvando, adest voluntatibus & affectionibus nostris. Ecce quemadmodum & velle & operari operatur in nobis. Ergo, concludit Aug. Hom. mox citata, praesumtor periisset nisi Redemtor respexisset.
units.tr: cy most high. He looked upon him, as the same holy Doctor says in chapter 45 of his work on the grace of Christ: He looked upon Peter not with bodily eyes but in mind and will, because secretly he came to his aid, touched his heart, recalled his memory, visited Peter with his inner grace, and moved the inner man even to outward tears and produced affection. See how God, by helping, is present to our wills and affections. See how he himself works in us both to will and to work. Therefore, Augustine concludes in the homily just cited, the presumptuous man would have perished unless the Redeemer had looked upon him.

units.la: 75. Flevit. Quos Jesus respicit, plorant delicta. Negavit primo Petrus & non flevit, quia non respexerat Dominus. Negavit secundo & non flevit, quia adhuc non respexerat Dominus, Negavit & tertio, respexit Jesus, & amarissime flevit. B. Ambr. lib. 10. in Lucam.
units.tr: 75. He wept. Those whom Jesus looks upon, weep for their sins. Peter denied the first time and did not weep, because the Lord had not yet looked upon him. He denied the second time and did not weep, because the Lord had still not looked upon him. He denied a third time, Jesus looked upon him, and he wept most bitterly. Blessed Ambrose, book 10, on Luke.

units.la: Amare. Amara, erat negationis recordatio, ut dulcis effet gratia redemtionis, nisi desertus non negaret, nisi respectus non fleret. Odit Deus praesumtores de viribus suis, & tumorem istum in eis, quos diligit (tanquam medicus) secat, secando quidem infert dolorem, sed firmat postea sanitatem. Aug. Hom. 4. inter 11. in Carthusia majori repertas. Porro Hebraeis amara dicuntur, quaecumque animum graviter angunt.
units.tr: Bitterly. The recollection of the denial was bitter, so that the grace of redemption might be sweet; unless he had been abandoned he would not have denied, unless he had been looked upon he would not have wept. God hates those who presume on their own strength, and as a physician he cuts out the swelling of pride in those whom he loves; in cutting he indeed causes pain, but afterwards he restores health. Augustine, Homily 4 among the eleven found in the Carthusian house at Major. Moreover, among the Hebrews, whatever grievously distresses the soul is called bitter.

units.la: CAPUT XXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVII.

units.la: 1. Mane autem facto. Id est, statim atque illucescere coepit, ut colligitur ex Marco & Luca simul collatis.
units.tr: 1. Now when morning had come. That is, as soon as it began to grow light, as is gathered from Mark and Luke compared together.

units.la: Omnes Principes Sacerdotum. Ne quis causæ tanti momenti deesset.
units.tr: All the chief priests. So that no one of such weighty importance might be missing.

units.la: Ut morti traderent. Id est, ut qua via mortis sententiam jam latam exequerentur, determinarent.
units.tr: That they might put him to death. That is, that they might decide by what manner of death the sentence already passed should be carried out.

units.la: 2. Tradiderunt Pontio Pilato Praesidi. Adde ex Joan. 18. Et ipsi non introierunt in praetorium, ne scilicet ingressu Praetorii in capitali causa contaminarentur, sicque ab esu Paschae, id est, Pacificorum sacrificiorum in festo Paschae offerri solitorum, prohiberentur. Tradiderunt autem Judaei Christum Pilato, quia licet non fuerit Praeses proprie dictus, cum tantum Procuratorem ageret in Judaea & subesset Syriae Praesidi ex Josepho lib. 18. Antiq. tamen imperium merum, sed potespotestatem animadvertendi cum exercitu & copiis militari-bus acceperat à Tiberio Cæsare, ut Judæos sæpè tumultuantes & tributa dare Cæsari detrectantes compescëret, ut colligitur ex Joan. 19. v. 10. & Joseph 18. Antiq. cap. 4.
units.tr: 2. They delivered him to Pontius Pilate the governor. Add from John 18: And they themselves did not go into the praetorium, lest by entering the praetorium in a capital case they should be defiled, and so be prevented from eating the Passover, that is, from the peace offerings customarily offered at the feast of the Passover. The Jews delivered Christ to Pilate because, although he was not properly called governor, since he was only acting as procurator in Judaea and was subordinate to the governor of Syria (according to Josephus, Antiquities book 18), nevertheless he had received from Tiberius Caesar full authority, that is, the power of punishing with the army and military forces, so that he might restrain the Jews, who often rioted and refused to pay tribute to Caesar, as is gathered from John 19:10 and Josephus, Antiquities 18, chap. 4.

units.la: 3. Damnatus. Id est, determinato mortis generi adjudi-catus.
units.tr: 3. Condemned. That is, adjudged to a determined kind of death.

units.la: 4. Tradens sanguinem justum. Id est, hominem innoxium.
units.tr: 4. Betraying innocent blood. That is, an innocent man.

units.la: 6. In corbonam. Id est, in Thesaurum Sacrum, seu in ærarium Templi, quod sic dicitur à sacrificiis, quæ corbanim dicuntur Hebraicè, quibus emendis, ex ærario Templi sumtus petebantur.
units.tr: 6. Into the corban. That is, into the sacred treasury, or the treasury of the Temple, which is so called from the offerings, which in Hebrew are called corbanim, and for buying which money was drawn from the Temple treasury.

units.la: Pretium sanguinis est. Nempè, quo homo ad sanguinis effusionem est venditus. Magna Pharisæorum notatur hypocrisis, ut qui pecuniam immundam ducant, quia pretium sanguinis, securi sint interim de sua conscientia, quâ tamen mortem innocentis hoc sibi pretio traditi decreverunt. Sic verè Christus dixit eos Culicem colare, camelum verò deglutire; nec enim tam inanimis pecunia contrahit pollutionem, quàm mens. S. Ambrosius in Epistola ad Studium.
units.tr: It is the price of blood. Namely, the price for which a man has been sold to be shed. Here the great hypocrisy of the Pharisees is noted: they regard the money as unclean because it is the price of blood, and meanwhile they are untroubled about their conscience, though they had decided on the death of an innocent man who had been handed over for this price. So truly Christ said that they strain out the gnat but swallow the camel; for money, however lifeless, does not contract pollution as the mind does. St Ambrose, in his Letter to Studius.

units.la: 7. Emerunt ex illis agrum Figuli. Græcè, τὸ ἀγρὸν τοῦ κεραμέως, id est, Figuli illius; quasi diceret, Agrum illum emerunt, de quo olim prophetavit Jeremias, seu agrum illum, qui jam per prophetiam Jeremiæ factus est celebris.
units.tr: 7. With them they bought the potter's field. In Greek, τὸ ἀγρὸν τοῦ κεραμέως [the field of the potter], that is, of that potter; as if he were saying: they bought that field of which Jeremiah once prophesied, or that field which had already become famous through Jeremiah's prophecy.

units.la: In sepulturam peregrinorum. Hoc Providentiâ factum puto, ut pretium Salvatoris non peccatoribus sumtum prabeat, sed peregrinis requiem subministret, non sacrilegis Judæis sit ad lucrum, sed defunctis sit ad sepulchrum, ut jam exinde Christus & vivos passione sanguinis redimat, & mortuos pretiosâ passione suscipiat. P. Maximus Taurinensis Antistes.
units.tr: To bury strangers in. I think this was done by Providence, so that the price of the Saviour, taken not from sinners, should provide rest for strangers; it should not serve the gain of sacrilegious Jews, but should be a sepulchre for the dead; so that from then on Christ might redeem the living by the passion of his blood, and receive the dead by his precious passion. St Maximus of Turin, bishop.

units.la: 8. Haceldama. Est vox Syriaca significans agrum sanguinis.
units.tr: 8. Haceldama. It is a Syriac word meaning field of blood.

units.la: Usque in præsentem diem. Hoc aliis verbis dixit Lucas Act. I. v. 18. Et notum factum est omnibus habitantibus in Jerusalem, ità ut appellaretur ager ille linguâ eorum Haceldama, non enim aliud dicit notum esse factum, nisi pretio sanguinis Christi emtum fuisse agrum, quem ait à Juda possessum, vel quia Judas in eo fuit sepultus, vel quia possidere fecit; primum tamen magis arridet; quia ipse Judas nullo modo fuit particeps consilii de emendo illo agro, sed projectis argenteis desperatione se suspendit, & medius crepuit, & effusa sunt viscera ejus.
units.tr: Unto this day. Luke said this in other words, Acts 1:18: And it became known to all who lived in Jerusalem, so that that field was called in their language Haceldama; for he says nothing more than that it became known that the field had been bought with the price of Christ's blood, which he says was possessed by Judas, either because Judas was buried in it or because he caused it to be possessed. The first, however, pleases more, since Judas himself in no way took part in the counsel about buying that field, but, having cast down the silver pieces, he hanged himself in despair, burst asunder in the middle, and his bowels were poured out.

units.la: 9. Tunc impletum est, quod dictum est per Jeremiam Prophetam dicentem. Magna hic excitatur difficultas, cur prophetiâ, tia, quæ habetur apud Zachariam, dicta per Jeremiam dicitur. Nos omissis variis variorum solutionibus, ut minus probabilibus, advertimus non raro apud Evangelistas duorum Prophetarum sententias conhecti, & tamen sub unius nomine citari. Sic supra cap. 21. v. 4, & 5. dicitur dictum per Prophetam dicentem, Dicite Filiæ Sion, ecce Rex tuus venit tibi mansuetus, sedens super asinam, &c. ubi prima verba usque ad sedens super asinam, exclusive, habentur Esaiæ 62. v. 11. cetera apud Zachariam cap. 9. v. 1. Similiter eodem capite 21. quod dicitur apud Esaiam, Domus mea domus orationis vocabitur, connectitur cum his verbis, Vos autem fecistis illam speluncam latronum, quibus alluditur ad dicta Jeremiæ cap. 7. v. 11. quasi ab eodem Esaia dicta fuerint. Sic Marcus Evangelista duo testimonia, Malachiæ & Esaiæ sub uno Prophetæ nomine contexens, ita exorsus est: Initium Evangelii Filii Dei, sicut Scriptum est in Esaia Propheta, Ecce ego mitto Angelum meum ante faciem tuam, qui præparabit viam tuam ante te. Vox clamantis in deserto, parate viam Domini, rectas facite vias ejus. Hoc observato sic exponimus præsentem versiculum, ut sensus sit, tunc cum ager ille figuli emtus est pretio sanguinis, & inde dictus est ager sanguinis, impletum est, quod dictum est per Jeremiam cap. 19. & quod dictum est per Prophetam, scilicet Zachariam dicentem cap. 11. Et acceperunt triginta argenteos, &c. Atque ita virgulam interponimus inter Jeremiam & Prophetam, ut nimirum Prophetæ vox non intelligatur de Jeremia, sed de dicente, Et acceperunt triginta argenteos, &c. Ceterum locus Jeremiæ, ad quem alludit Matthæus, non est, ut quidam erroneè putant cap. 32. ubi Propheta dicitur vendidisse ex præscripto Domini agrum; quia ager, de quo ibi agitur, est benedictionis, & quæ ibi dicuntur, in benedictionem dicuntur, ut patet ibidem ex versu 15. nec satis solidè dicitur, quod ager ille à Jeremia venditus dicatur ager Figuli; quia Jeremias in vase fictili libros emtionis reponere jubetur, nec hoc quicquam facit ad agrum sanguinis, de quo agit Matthæus, & qui è Jeremia eruendus illi erat. Verum cum inter agros omnes olim maledictos nullum extitisse omnino certum est, quicum agro seu valle Ennon fit conferendus, utpote qui execrando & abominando Molochi sacro destinatus esset, qui ager situs erat ad portam Fictilem, seu Figuli ad radices montis Moriæ ad Austrum, ubi etiam ab Hieronymo in lib. de locis Hebraicis assignatur situs hujus agri Figuli, credimus per hunc agrum Figuli, vel assignari ipsum agrum Ennon, vel agrum ipsi quam proxime conjunctum, {tam}, & inde dictum fuisse olim agrum Figuli, nunc ob pretium sanguinis, quo emtus est, agrum Sanguinis; sicque impletum est, quod dicit Jeremias Propheta cap. 19. Haec dicit Dominus: Vade & accipe lagunculam figuli testeam a Senioribus populi & a Senioribus Sacerdotum, & egredere ad vallem filii Hinnom, quae est juxta introitum portae Fictilis, & praedicabis ibi verba, quae ego loquar ad te. Et dices, Audite verbum Domini Reges Juda & habitatores Jerusalem, &c. Ecce dies venient, dicit Dominus, & non vocabitur amplius locus hic, Topheth & vallis filii Hinnom, sed vallis Occisionis. Igitur Matthaeus per id, quod proxime dixit de agro Figuli qui dictus est ager Sanguinis, aic impletum, quod per Prophetam Jeremiam dictum est, locum Figuli olim nominatum ob confractam ibi jussu Domini testam a Jeremia, aliquando vocatum ibi locum Occisionis. Deinde addit Matthaeus impletum esse vaticinium Zachariae per id, quod prius dixerat de pretio Christi venditi. Hoc autem Zachariae vaticinium ita citat, ut simul illud exponat, verba aliquatenus variando, & quaedam de suo interserendo.
units.tr: 9. Then was fulfilled what was spoken through the prophet Jeremiah, saying. A great difficulty arises here, why what is found in Zechariah is said to have been spoken through Jeremiah. Setting aside the various solutions of various writers, as less probable, we observe that the Evangelists not infrequently join the sayings of two prophets and yet cite them under the name of one. Thus above, in chapter 21, verses 4 and 5, it is said to have been spoken through the prophet who says, Tell the daughter of Zion, behold your King comes to you meek, sitting upon an ass, etc., where the first words up to sitting upon an ass, not including it, are found in Isaiah 62:11, and the rest in Zechariah 9:9. Similarly in the same chapter 21, what is said in Isaiah, My house shall be called a house of prayer, is joined with the words, But you have made it a den of robbers, to which allusion is made to the words of Jeremiah 7:11, as if they had been spoken by the same Isaiah. So too the Evangelist Mark, weaving together two testimonies, of Malachi and Isaiah, under the name of one prophet, began thus: The beginning of the Gospel of the Son of God, as it is written in the prophet Isaiah, Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you. The voice of one crying in the wilderness, prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight. Having observed this, we explain the present verse thus: the sense is that when that potter's field was bought with the price of blood, and from that was called the field of blood, then was fulfilled what was spoken through Jeremiah in chapter 19, and what was spoken through the prophet, namely Zechariah, who says in chapter 11, And they took thirty pieces of silver, etc. And so we place a stop between Jeremiah and the prophet, so that the voice of the prophet is understood not as referring to Jeremiah, but to the one who says, And they took thirty pieces of silver, etc. Moreover, the passage of Jeremiah to which Matthew alludes is not, as some mistakenly think, chapter 32, where the prophet is said to have bought a field at the Lord's command; for the field there spoken of is one of blessing, and what is said there is said for a blessing, as is clear from verse 15 of the same chapter. Nor is it solidly said that the field sold by Jeremiah is called the potter's field, since Jeremiah is commanded to place the deed of purchase in an earthen vessel, and this has nothing to do with the field of blood of which Matthew speaks, and which was to be drawn out of Jeremiah. Yet since it is entirely certain that among all the fields once cursed there was none that can be compared with the field or valley of Ennom, which was set apart for the accursed and abominable sacrifice to Molech, a field situated at the Potsherd Gate, or the Potter's Gate, at the foot of Mount Moriah to the south, where Jerome in his book on Hebrew places also assigns the site of this potter's field, we believe that by this potter's field either the field of Ennom itself is meant, or a field very closely joined to it, and that from this it was once called the potter's field, and now, on account of the price of blood for which it was bought, the field of Blood. And so what the prophet Jeremiah says in chapter 19 was fulfilled: Thus says the Lord: Go and take a potter's earthen flask from the elders of the people and from the elders of the priests, and go out to the valley of the son of Hinnom, which lies by the entrance of the Potsherd Gate, and there you shall proclaim the words that I shall speak to you. And you shall say, Hear the word of the Lord, O kings of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem, etc. Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, when this place will no longer be called Topheth and the valley of the son of Hinnom, but the valley of Slaughter. Therefore Matthew, by what he has just said about the potter's field, which was called the field of Blood, says that what was spoken through the prophet Jeremiah was fulfilled, namely that the place once named the potter's place, because the vessel was broken there at the Lord's command by Jeremiah, was at some time called there the valley of Slaughter. Then Matthew adds that the prophecy of Zechariah was fulfilled by what he had said before about the price of the sold Christ. He cites this prophecy of Zechariah in such a way that he at the same time explains it, varying the words somewhat and inserting some things of his own.

units.la: Et acceperunt triginta argenteos. Graecum ἔλαβον, potest etiam verti accepi, seu tulì, ut vertitur a Vulgato interprete Zachariae II. v. 13. quod igitur Zacharias de se dixerat, quòd nimirum vile & abjectum pretium a Judaeis acceperat, nempe triginta argenteos, quibus ibi aestimatus Dominus dicitur, hoc Matthaeus citat, & applicat ei, qui agrum vendidit, qui eodem modo a Judaeis accepit triginta argenteos, quibus appretiatus erat Christus Dominus.
units.tr: And they took thirty pieces of silver. The Greek ἔλαβον [elabon] can also be rendered accepi or tuli, as the Vulgate translator renders it at Zechariah 11.13. Matthew therefore quotes what Zechariah said of himself, that he received from the Jews a base and despised price, namely thirty pieces of silver, by which the Lord is said to have been valued there. He applies this to the one who sold the field, who in the same way received from the Jews thirty pieces of silver, the price at which Christ the Lord was valued.

units.la: A filiis Israël. Hoc refertur ad verbum acceperunt; venditores enim agri a Judaeis dictum pretium, triginta siclicec argenteos, acceperunt.
units.tr: From the children of Israel. This refers to the verb they took, for the sellers of the field received from the Jews the price named, thirty shekels of silver.

units.la: 10. Et dederunt eos in agrum Figuli. Hebraismus; addit enim haec Matthaeus inter parenthesis, quasi diceret, Quos nimirum argenteos ad emendum agrum Figuli dederunt.
units.tr: 10. And they gave them for the potter's field. A Hebraism. Matthew adds these words in parentheses, as if he said: the silver which they gave in order to buy the potter's field.

units.la: Sicut constituit mihi Dominus. Sic reddit Matthaeus id, quod Zacharias dixerat paulò ante citatum versum, Dixit Dominus ad me.
units.tr: As the Lord appointed me. Matthew renders in this way what Zechariah said shortly before the verse quoted, The Lord said to me.

units.la: 11. Jesus autem stetit ante Praesidem. Nimirum priusquam primò exiisset Pilatus ad Judaeos foras, & voluisset Jesum ipsis tradere, ut secundum Legem suam judicarent eum, idque Judaei retusassent. Et cum accusassent ut Gentis subversorem & prohibentem tributa dari Caesari; introivit iterum in Praetorium Pilatus & vocavit Jesum, quem stantem ante se interrogavit, ut sequitur, & plenius narratur Luc. 23. & Joan. 18.
units.tr: 11. But Jesus stood before the governor. Namely, after Pilate had first gone out to the Jews and wished to hand Jesus over to them, so that they might judge him according to their own law, and the Jews had refused this. Then, when they had accused him as a subverter of the nation who forbade the payment of tribute to Caesar, Pilate went back into the praetorium, called Jesus, and questioned him while he stood before him, as follows. This is told more fully in Luke 23 and John 18.

units.la: Tu dicis. Hoc videtur legendum cum interrogatione, ut patet ex Joan. 18. v. 34.
units.tr: You say so. This seems to be read as a question, as is clear from John 18.34.

units.la: 15. Per diem autem solemnem. Supple Paschatis. Hinc novum emergit argumentum ad probationem communis sententiæ, quâ asseritur Christum fuisse crucifixum ipso die Paschatis Judæorum, qui hic vocatur dies Solemnis, quo solebat reus aliquis liber dimitti, & cujus mox præcedens dies designatur his verbis Joan. 13. Ante diem festum Paschæ. Omittit autem Matthæus missionem Christi ad Herodem, nam quæ hic habentur, contigerunt postquam Christus ab Herode remissus esset.
units.tr: 15. Now at the festival. Supply: of the Passover. Hence a new argument emerges for the common opinion, which asserts that Christ was crucified on the very day of the Passover of the Jews, which is here called the solemn day, on which some prisoner used to be released, and whose preceding day is indicated shortly afterwards in these words of John 13: Before the feast of the Passover. Matthew omits Christ's sending to Herod, for what is related here happened after Christ had been sent back by Herod.

units.la: 16. Habebat autem tunc vinctum insignem. Nempe, sceleribus, qui nimirum in seditione fectrat homicidium, ut dicitur Marc. 15.
units.tr: 16. And they had then a notorious prisoner. Namely, for crimes; he was one who, as Mark 15 says, had committed murder in the sedition.

units.la: 19. Sedente autem illo pro Tribunali. Postquam scilicet dixisset se nullam invenire in Christo causam, id est, novam, ut habetur Joan. 18. Non autem hic agitur de ultima cognitione, de qua Joannes post flagellationem Christi, sed de priori; aliquoties enim Pilatus sedit in Tribunali more judicum ad causam examinandam.
units.tr: 19. While he was sitting on the judgment seat. That is, after he had said that he found no cause in Christ, that is, no new one, as stated in John 18. But this does not refer to the final hearing, which John describes after Christ's scourging, but to the earlier one; for Pilate sat several times on the tribunal, in the manner of judges, to examine the case.

units.la: Uxor. Hanc Lucius Dexter in Chronico vocari vult Claudiam Proculam.
units.tr: His wife. Lucius Dexter in his Chronicle wishes her to be called Claudia Procula.

units.la: Nihil tibi & justo illi. Id est, nihil sit tibi negotii cum hoc viro justo.
units.tr: Have nothing to do with that just man. That is, let you have no business with this righteous man.

units.la: Multa enim passa sum hodie per visum. Græcè in somnis propter eum. Sunt qui volunt hoc somnium uxori Pilati immissum à diabolo, ut impediret passionem Christi, alii vero volunt immissum à Deo, ut uxor Pilatum moneret officii sui, utque Christus jam inciperet testimonium habere à Gentibus.
units.tr: For I have suffered much today in a dream because of him. In Greek, in dreams because of him. Some hold that this dream was sent to Pilate's wife by the devil, to hinder Christ's passion; others hold that it was sent by God, so that she might warn her husband of his duty, and so that Christ might now begin to have testimony from the Gentiles.

units.la: 22. Dicunt omnes: Crucifigatur. Sic nimirum impletum est in Agno vero per Agnum Paschalem olim adumbrato, quod de Agno eodem Paschali præcipiebatur Exod. 12. v. 6. Immolabitque eum universa multitudo; conspiraverant enim in Christum Sacerdotes, Scribæ, Pharisæi & universus populus, & omnes uno ore, & animo dixerunt: Crucifigatur. Nempe non solum Judæi Christum, ut blasphemum, & violatæ religionis reum accusabant; sed etiam ut seditiosum & turbas concitantem & prohibentem tributa dari Cæsari. At secundum leges Romanas pœna seditiosorum fuit Crux. Paul. lib. 5. Sent. tit. 22. Ita Quintilius Varus Syriæ Præses Judæos seditiosos cruci affixit. Josephus lib. 2. de bello Judaico c. 7. Ita & Florus Syriæ quoque Præses. Josephus ibidem c. 25.
units.tr: 22. They all say: Let him be crucified. Thus it was fulfilled in the true Lamb, which had been foreshadowed long before by the Paschal lamb, concerning which command was given in Exodus 12.6: The whole multitude shall kill it. For the priests, the scribes, the Pharisees and the whole people had conspired against Christ, and all with one mouth and one mind said: Let him be crucified. Indeed, the Jews accused Christ not only as a blasphemer and a violator of religion, but also as a seditious man who stirred up crowds and forbade the payment of tribute to Caesar. But according to Roman law the penalty for seditious men was the cross. Paulus, Sentences book 5, title 22. Thus Quintilius Varus, governor of Syria, crucified seditious Jews; Josephus, The Jewish War book 2, chapter 7. Florus, also governor of Syria, did likewise; Josephus, in the same place, chapter 25.

units.la: 24. Accepit aquâ lavit manus. Quò nimirum suam offenderet à Christi morte innocentiam; cœterum mos ille Judæorum maximè fuit, ut patet Deut. 21. & Psal. 72. expressè, Lavabo inter innocentes manus meas. Edmundus Merilius in suis notis ad passionem Christi annotavit, Pilatum, non tam Judæorum morem, cùm Romanus esset, quàm Gentium observasse. Mos enim erat antiquis, quando cædem hominis, vel alias mactationes fecerant, aquâ lavare manus, ad expiationem pollutionis, ait Scholiastes Sophoclis. Sic & Romani à Græcis acceptâ formâ, teste Dionysio Halicarn. lib. 7. Orig. Servio ad 12. Æneid. & Plin. Magistratus, & sacrificaturi togam Prætextam habent, & manus ablutas detergere lineis mantilibus curant. Quin & Clemens Romanus lib. 2. cap. 52. scribit Judices mortis sententiam laturos, manibus in Solem sublatis, testari solitos innocentiam suam, & tunc probabile est manus abluisse, ut puriores in coelum tollerent.
units.tr: 24. He took water and washed his hands. Plainly to show his innocence of Christ's death. The custom, however, was chiefly that of the Jews, as is clear from Deuteronomy 21 and from Psalm 26 (72 in some editions), where it is expressly said: I will wash my hands among the innocent. Edmund Merill, in his notes on the passion of Christ, observed that Pilate followed the custom not so much of the Jews as of the Gentiles, since he was a Roman. For it was the custom among the ancients, when they had committed a murder or other slaughter, to wash their hands with water, to cleanse the defilement, says the scholiast on Sophocles. So also the Romans, having received the practice from the Greeks, according to Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Roman Antiquities book 7, Servius on Aeneid 12, and Pliny: magistrates and those about to sacrifice wear the purple-bordered toga and take care to dry their washed hands with linen towels. Indeed Clement of Rome, book 2, chapter 52, writes that judges who were about to pronounce a sentence of death used to call the sun to witness their innocence, lifting their hands toward it; and then it is probable that they washed their hands, so as to lift them purer to heaven.

units.la: 25. Sanguis ejus super nos. Id est, poenâ, si quæ fit, ob hujus sanguinis effusionem, nos tenebimur. Cœterum hæc ablutio manuum Pilati & Judæorum responsio contigit, postquam Christus fuit flagellatus, spinis coronatus, à militibus illusus, & secundò à Pilato interrogatus)
units.tr: 25. His blood be on us. That is, we shall be bound to any punishment that may follow on account of the shedding of this blood. Moreover, this washing of Pilate's hands and the Jews' reply took place after Christ had been scourged, crowned with thorns, mocked by the soldiers, and questioned a second time by Pilate.

units.la: 26. Tunc. Victus Judæorum pervicaciâ Pilatus. Tradidit eum: Judæis scilicet, non ipsis militibus Gentili-bus per quorum manus crucifixus est. Non autem Pilatus tam citò de Christo supplicium sumens egit contra Senatus-consultum tempore Tiberii factum, quo poena damnatorum semper in decimum diem differri debuit, ut refert Sueto-nius in Tiberio cap. 75. Seneca de Tranq. vitæ cap. 14. vel in trigesimum diem, ut Sidon Apollin. retulit lib. 1. Epist. 7. quia hoc Senatus-consultum non pertinebat ad insignes latrones & seditiosos, quos damnatos statim puniri interest, ut ait Modestinus in L. Constitutiones 16. de appellationibus. Ut crucifigeretur, id est, ut crucifigendum curarent suâ quidem autoritate, non tamen sententiâ, quasi cruce dignum. Unde Luc. 23. ut indicaret Pilatum non tulisse sententiam in Jesum velut reum mortis, dixit: Et Pilatus adjudicavit fieri petitionem eorum. Quod autem congruum fuerit ut is qui pro omnium salute moriturus advenerat, & pro peccato primi hominis satisfacturus, non aliam, quam mortem crucis pateretur, patet primo, quia inde nullum genus mortis rectè viventi homini metuendum esse discimus, ut ait Aug. lib. 83. qq. q. 25. nihil enim erat inter omnia genera mortis, illo genere execrabilius & formidabilius. Secundò, qui in ligno vinvincebat, in ligno quoque victus est. Tertia, ita, veritas respondit figura; nam Agnus Paschalis, ut tradit Rabbi Moses in lib. de Paschate cap. 8. Sect. 10. ad ignem plene assandus ex Exod 12. non versabatur in veru ferreo, more nostro, sed veru ligneo transfixus a medio ore usque ad pudenda, subjecto igne, in medio furno suspendebatur, quod Christum in cruce pendentem, ira divina ardore (qui cum igne passim confertur, ut Jerem. 4. v. 4. Thren. 1. v. 3. c. 2. v. 4. &c.) in peccatores, quorum se Christus vadem praestiterat, merito accensae, torrendum utcunque referebat. Maxime & haec Justini vera sunt in Dialogo cum Tryphone Judaeo pag. 259. Agnus affixus, in figuram Crucis similem conformatus, ad ignem torretur; nam veru unum ab infimis partibus ad caput usque adactum perfigitur, & aliud rursus ad interscapillium, cui appenduntur manus Agni, seu pedes anteriores. Quidni vero hac in parte illi credamus viro, non solum Sancto, sed & rerum Judaicarum peritissimo, cum Sichemis natus fuerit ex patre Samaritano? Christi torrendi in Cruce sunt graves illae querelae, Fauces meae tanquam testa aruit, & lingua mea adhaeret faucibus meis. collegam Christus huic flagellatus, ... quorum non
units.tr: 26. Then. Pilate, overcome by the obstinacy of the Jews. He delivered him to the Jews, certainly, not to the Gentile soldiers through whose hands he was crucified. Pilate did not, however, act so hastily in taking up the punishment of Christ against the decree of the Senate made in the time of Tiberius, by which the punishment of condemned persons was always to be deferred until the tenth day, as Suetonius reports in Tiberius chapter 75, and Seneca, On Tranquillity of Mind chapter 14; or until the thirtieth day, as Sidonius Apollinaris reported in book 1, letter 7; because this decree did not apply to notorious robbers and seditious men, whom it is in the public interest to punish at once, as Modestinus says in the law Constitutiones 16, on appeals. That he be crucified: that is, that they should see to his crucifixion by their own authority, though not by a sentence, as if he were worthy of the cross. Hence Luke 23, to show that Pilate had not passed sentence on Jesus as a man guilty of death, says: And Pilate gave sentence that their request should be granted. That it was fitting that he who had come to die for the salvation of all, and to make satisfaction for the sin of the first man, should suffer no other death than that of the cross, is clear, first, because from this we learn that no kind of death is to be feared by a man who lives righteously, as Augustine says in Eighty-three Questions, question 25; for among all kinds of death there was none more accursed and more dreadful than that one. Second, he who conquered on the tree was also conquered on the tree. Third, thus the truth answered to the figure; for the Paschal lamb, as Rabbi Moses teaches in his book on the Passover, chapter 8, section 10, from Exodus 12, was to be roasted thoroughly over the fire; it was not turned on an iron spit after our manner, but was pierced by a wooden spit from the middle of the mouth to the private parts, and hung over the fire in the middle of the oven. This signified in some measure Christ hanging on the cross, roasted by the burning of divine wrath (which is often compared with fire, as in Jeremiah 4.4, Lamentations 1.3 and 2.4, etc.), kindled justly against sinners, for whom Christ had become surety. Justin's words in the Dialogue with the Jew Trypho, page 259, are also very true: the lamb is fixed, shaped into a figure like a cross, and roasted at the fire; for one spit is driven through from the lowest parts up to the head, and another across the shoulder-blades, to which the lamb's hands, or front feet, are hung. Why should we not believe that man on this point, who was not only holy but also most skilled in Jewish matters, since he was born at Shechem of a Samaritan father? Christ's complaints on the cross about roasting are grievous: My throat is dried up like a potsherd, and my tongue cleaves to my jaws.

units.la: 27. Tunc. Cum scilicet Jesus esset flagellandus, non cum tradendus esset ad crucem, per recapitulationem enim haec quae sequuntur dicit Matth. & similiter Marcus cap. 15.
units.tr: 27. Then: that is, when Jesus was to be scourged, not yet when he was to be handed over to the cross. Matthew, and likewise Mark in chapter 15, recounts by recapitulation what follows.

units.la: Suscipientes Jesum in Praetorium, id est, recipientes eum, duxerunt intus in atrium Praetorii, id est Marcus, locum scilicet habitationis Praetoris Romani, seu Praesidis. Caeterum flagellatio traditur ab Evangelistis facta jussu Pilati, non vero coronatio, quam Tertullianus ait fuisse Romanorum militum commentum; nam sicut cum esset a Caipha condemnatus, licentia Ministrorum exprobravit ei accerbissime quasi arrogatam prophetiam, ita flagellato licentia militaris arrogatam Regiam dignitatem, aliquo ludibrio crudelissimis, non jubente, sed permittente Pilato, ut ait S. Leo Serm. 8. de passione, patiens fidelitatem Judaeorum animos ita mitigandos.
units.tr: Taking Jesus into the Praetorium, that is, receiving him, they led him inside into the court of the Praetorium, that is, the residence of the Roman praetor or governor, as Mark has it. Moreover, the Evangelists report that the scourging was done at Pilate's command, but not the crowning, which Tertullian says was an invention of the Roman soldiers. For just as, when he had been condemned by Caiaphas, the attendants bitterly reproached him for his presumed prophecy, so when he had been scourged the soldiers, by license, mocked him with the cruellest jests for his presumed royal dignity. Pilate did not order this but permitted it, as St Leo says in Sermon 8 on the Passion, so that the minds of the Jews might be softened by the sufferer's patience.

units.la: Congregaverunt. Nimirum illi quatuor milites, qui secerunt Jesum in Praetorium; quatuor enim tantum fuisse infimatur Joan. 19. v. 23.
units.tr: They gathered together. Namely those four soldiers who took Jesus into the Praetorium, for John 19:23 hints that there were only four.

units.la: 28. Exuentes eum, propriis vestibus.
units.tr: 28. Stripping him, of his own clothes.

units.la: Chlamydem coccineam circumdederunt ei. Detritam scilicet alicujus militis, ut esset instar paludamenti, quo Reges & Imperatores in castris utebantur; Joannes vocat vestem purpuream, purpuram, & Marena purpurea, quæ Regibus & Principibus viris propria erat. Unde Ambr. & Hilar. putant purpuram fuisse distinctam à coccinea, colore, & vestis genere, sed Aug. vult eandem fuisse, eò quòd purpura quædam fit cocco similis, ut satis patet de Tyria purpura, quæ passim apud Poëtas maximè, & apud Plinium à rubro colore commendatur, & cum sanguine confertur. Unde Virgilius vel quidam alius ejus nomine, in Rosis, appellatur à S. Hieron. multæ rosæ rubræ populi, sed
units.tr: They put a scarlet cloak about him. That is, an old cloak of some soldier, serving as a military cloak such as kings and emperors used in camp. John calls it a purple robe, and Mark a purple garment, which belonged to kings and princely men. Hence Ambrose and Hilary think purple was distinct from scarlet in colour and kind of cloth. But Augustine holds they were the same, since some purple is like scarlet dye, as is clear of Tyrian purple, which the poets everywhere commend for its red colour, and Pliny too, comparing it with blood. Hence Virgil, or some other poet under his name, is called by St Jerome "many red roses of the people," but

units.la: Hanc tenui folio purpura rubra notat.
units.tr: The red purple marks this with its slender leaf.

units.la: Hinc & B. Justinus in Dialogo cum Tryphone Judæo vocat vestem hyacinthinam, vel purpuream, de qua Num. 15. v. 38.
units.tr: Hence also St Justin, in his Dialogue with Trypho the Jew, calls it a hyacinth or purple garment, about which see Numbers 15:38.

units.la: Dicerunt enim Marcus & Joan. Educerunt, nimirum extra Civitatem, ut juxta Apostolum ad Hebræos 13. Extra portam pateretur, cuti hostia pro peccato cremari solebat extra castra, sicque impleta est dicta olim à Christo parabola, quòd Judæi aliquando hereden esset ejecturi extra vineam.
units.tr: For Mark and John say "they led him out," namely outside the city, as the Apostle says in Hebrews 13, "he suffered outside the gate," just as the victim for sin used to be burned outside the camp. And so the parable Christ once spoke was fulfilled, that the Jews would one day cast the heir out of the vineyard.

units.la: Exeunte quia id est, in egressu portæ civitatis. Constat enim ex Joan. Christum exivisse ex Civitate bajulantem sibi Crucem ad instar Isaac ligna sui sacrificii bajulantis.
units.tr: Going out, that is, at the exit of the city gate. For it is clear from John that Christ went out of the city carrying his own cross, like Isaac carrying the wood for his sacrifice.

units.la: Cyrenæ urbs est Lybiæ in Africa, longéque à Judæa & trans Ægyptum, non illius Libyæ quæ proprié Africa est, sed quæ est Orientis pars contigua Africæ & omnino collimitanea, ita Aug. lib. de Pastoribus cap. 17. Sunt tamen, qui hunc Simonem non ex illa Cyrene, quæ ut Aug. loquitur loco citato, Libya est, Pentapolis est, (sic dicitur à Plinio Cyrenaica regio à quinque insignium urbium numero) quæ dicuntur Berenice, Arsinoë, Ptolemais, Apollonia, & ipsa Cyrene, unde regioni nomen, quæ à Cyrene Hypsei filia dicitur nomen summ accepisse, sed ab alia urbe ejusdem nominis à Cyro in Cypro insula condita oriundum, addunt Marc. & Luc. Vetiam. Quod autem Marcus addit ipsum Simonem Cyrenæum fuisse Patrem Alexandri & Rufi, vel distinctionis causâ hæc addit, vel quia hi viri erant tunc temporis quacunque tandem de causa valde noti. Et in lucrari alii crucitari ... multi dixerunt, si enim Iesus cum vino biberet.
units.tr: Cyrene is a city of Libya in Africa, far from Judaea and beyond Egypt. It is not that Libya which is properly Africa, but the eastern part bordering on Africa and wholly on its edge, as Augustine says in his book On the Shepherds, chapter 17. Some, however, deny that this Simon was from that Cyrene, which, as Augustine says in the passage cited, lies in Libya, the Pentapolis (so Pliny calls the Cyrenaic region, from its five notable cities), namely Berenice, Arsinoë, Ptolemais, Apollonia and Cyrene itself, from which the region takes its name, said to be named after Cyrene the daughter of Hypseus. They hold instead that he was from another city of the same name, founded by Cyrus in the island of Cyprus, as Mark and Luke add. As for Mark's addition that this Simon of Cyrene was the father of Alexander and Rufus, he adds it either to distinguish him, or because these men were then, for whatever reason, well known. And ... to be tormented ... many have said, for if Jesus were to drink with the wine ...

units.la: 33. Et venerunt in locum qui dicitur Golgotha. Omittit Matthæus historiam mulierum Christum sequentium, & in via plangentium, de qua Luc. c. 23. v. 27. Dicitur autem Golgotha Euphoniæ causâ pro Golgotha, quod Syriacè significat Calvariam; sic verò locus ille dicebatur propter occisorum crania, quæ ibi sparsa passim & neglecta videbantur, ut tradit Hieron. Veteres autem Patres aiunt sic dictum ob Proto-parentis Adami caput ibi repertum. Quæ etymologia appellatur à B. Hieron. mulseus aurem populi, nec tamen vera.
units.tr: 33. And they came to the place called Golgotha. Matthew omits the story of the women who followed Christ and lamented on the way, which is in Luke 23:27. Golgotha is so named, for the sake of euphony, in place of Golgotha, which in Syriac means "Calvary." That place was called so, as Jerome relates, because of the skulls of the slain which lay scattered and neglected there. The older Fathers, however, say it was so named because the head of the first parent Adam was found there. Jerome calls this etymology "honeying the ears of the people, but not true."

units.la: 34. Dederunt ei vinum bibere. Græcè ὄξος, quod plerumque est acetum. Marcus dicit: Et dabant ei bibere myrrhatum, id est, myrrhâ conditum, vel thure etiam, quia מר Hebraeis & Syris primò myrrham significat, deinde etiam aroma quodvis, unde Græcorum μύρον, quod ex Hebræo mor factum est, non solùm myrrhinum, sed & unguentum quodvis sonat. In Marco igitur ἐσμυρισμένον, idem est, quod μεμυρισμένον, vel etiam ἀσιλεσπανμένον, quâ voce utitur author Machabæorum lib. 3. ubi describit belluas vino thure condito terribiliter instructas. Extat in Talmude Tract. Sanhedrin cap. 6. sol. 43. hic Canon; Iis, qui exire neci tradendus, propinatur granum thuris in calice vini, ut mens ejus perturbetur: ubi Glossator addit, Ne mareat, atque ut stupidus fiat, cùm morti addicitur.
units.tr: 34. They gave him wine to drink. In Greek ὄξος [oxos], which is generally vinegar. Mark says: and they gave him myrrhed wine to drink, that is, wine seasoned with myrrh, or with frankincense too, because מר [mor] in Hebrew and Syriac first means myrrh, and then any aromatic. Hence the Greek μύρον [myron], which came from the Hebrew mor, means not only myrrh but any ointment. In Mark, then, ἐσμυρισμένον [esmyrismenon] is the same as μεμυρισμένον [memyrismenon], or even as the word the author of Maccabees uses in book 3, where he describes beasts terribly prepared with wine seasoned with frankincense. In the Talmud, tractate Sanhedrin, chapter 6, folio 43, there is this rule: To those who are to be led out to death, a grain of frankincense is given in a cup of wine so that their mind may be disturbed. The Glossator adds: So that he may not grieve, and be made stupid, when he is given over to death.

units.la: Cum felle mixtum. Si per vinum myrrhatum verè Marcus intelligit vinum thure conditum, ut diximus, fel potest esse positum à Matthæo pro amaritudine; eadem enim dictio מררה, quæ passim pro herba amarissima sumitur, à Vulgato interprete vertitur Psal. 68. v. 22. fel, & Osee 10. v. 4. amaritudo; si verò myrrhatum sumitur pro vino calido poculis myrrhæis infuso, quod inde odorem saporémque contrahit jucundissimum, vel pro vino myrrhâ condito, æquè jucundo & pretioso, ut constat ex Plinio lib. 14. hist. nat. cap. 13. & ex Athenæo lib. 11. cap. 30. tunc dicendum est vinum Christo porrectum fuisse conditum myrrhâ, ut vires adderet Christo, simúlque felle, seu aliquo aromate amarissimo, ut bibenti effet molestum; sed prior expositio magis placet ob Canonem ex Talmude citatum, & magis fit verisimile Matthæum denotasse amaritudinem potùs Christo porrecti, Marcum verò denotasse unde oriretur illa vini amaritudo, nimirùm ex myrrha, seu thure immixto. Si autem latrones cum Christo crucifixi biberunt ex illo vino myrrhato, ut se munirent & indurarent adversus cruciatus mox subeundos, non multùm biberunt; si enim largiùs cum vino bibatur myrrha, vel obumbrare mentem, vel accelerare fatum docet Galenus. Similiter thus si admisceatur vino largius, furorem excitat, ut testatur Dioscorides lib. 1. & Serapio, & Damir Arabs; latrones autem non fuisse mentis impotes dum crucifigerentur, patet ex iis quae locuti sunt.
units.tr: Mixed with gall. If by myrrhed wine Mark truly means wine seasoned with frankincense, as we have said, Matthew may have put gall for bitterness. For the same word מררה [mararah], which is everywhere taken for a very bitter herb, is rendered gall by the Vulgate translator in Psalm 68:22, and bitterness in Hosea 10:4. But if myrrhed is taken for warm wine infused with myrrh, which takes from it a most pleasant smell and taste, or for wine seasoned with myrrh, equally pleasant and precious, as is clear from Pliny, Natural History book 14, chapter 13, and Athenaeus book 11, chapter 30, then it must be said that the wine offered to Christ was seasoned with myrrh to give him strength, and at the same time with gall, or some very bitter aromatic, to make it unpleasant to drink. But the former explanation pleases more, because of the rule cited from the Talmud, and it is more likely that Matthew denoted the bitterness of the drink offered to Christ, while Mark denoted what caused that bitterness, namely the myrrh or frankincense mixed in. If, however, the thieves crucified with Christ drank of that myrrhed wine to fortify and harden themselves against the torments they were soon to undergo, they did not drink much. For Galen teaches that if myrrh is drunk in larger amounts with wine, it either clouds the mind or hastens death. Likewise, if frankincense is mixed into wine in larger quantity, it excites madness, as Dioscorides (book 1), Serapion and Damir the Arab testify. That the thieves were not out of their minds while being crucified is clear from what they said.

units.la: Cum gustasset. Ne scilicet traditionem contemnere videretur, quae nititur authoritate sacrae Scripturae per Salomonem dicentis cap. 31. Proverb. v. 6. Date siceram moerentibus & vinum his, qui amaro sunt animo, bibant & obliviscantur egestatis suae, & doloris sui non recordentur amplius. Hinc & calice consolationis recreabantur, qui suos sepelierant, de qua consuetudine Jerem. c. 16. v. 7.
units.tr: When he had tasted. Namely, so as not to seem to despise the tradition, which rests on the authority of Holy Scripture, as Solomon says in Proverbs 31:6: Give strong drink to those who are perishing, and wine to those of bitter mind; let them drink and forget their poverty, and remember their sorrow no more. Hence also those who had buried their own were refreshed with the cup of consolation, a custom referred to in Jeremiah 16:7.

units.la: Noluit bibere. Id est, transmittere, quod Marcus significat his verbis, non accepit; ut scilicet magis dolorem crucis perseentiret.
units.tr: He would not drink. That is, he did not take it to his lips, which Mark expresses in these words, he did not receive it; namely, so that he might feel the pain of the cross the more fully.

units.la: 35. Crucifixerunt eum. Nempe quatuor clavis, sic enim olim consueverant, ut patet apud Plautum in Mustella; Ea lege, inquit, crucifigatur, ut his affigantur pedes, bis brachia; idem sentit Gregorius Turonensis, cui antiquiores imagines suffragantur. Nonnus autem Metaphrastes Evangelii secundum Joannem, & Nazianzenus in carmine de Christo a cruce depósito aferunt communiorem sententiam, qua Christus asseritur fuisse crucifixus tribus clavis, uno videlicet duos pedes terebrante.
units.tr: 35. They crucified him. Namely with four nails, for so they used to do of old, as appears in Plautus in Mostellaria: "On this condition," he says, "let him be crucified, that his feet be fastened to these, and his arms ..."; Gregory of Tours holds the same view, and older images support it. But the Metaphrast Nonnus, on John's Gospel, and Gregory Nazianzen, in his poem on Christ taken down from the cross, give the more common opinion, by which Christ is said to have been crucified with three nails, one of which pierced both feet.

units.la: Diviserunt vestimenta ejus. Ergo nudus crucifixus est Christus, sicque secundum prophetiam Psaltis, operuit confusio faciem ejus. Ait autem Cyrillus damnatorum vestes quasi hereditatis lege ad se pertinentes sibi vindicasse milites, sicque partiti sunt in quatuor partes vestimenta Christi exteriora, sed tunica interior inconsutilis non fuit ab eis discissa, sed una cum reliquis quatuor partibus tota fuit sorti commissa, quis eam tolleret, ut patet ex Joan. 19. v. 24. & quid quis tolleret de vestimentis divisis, ut patet ex Marc. c. 15. v. 24.
units.tr: "They divided his garments." Therefore Christ was crucified naked, and so, according to the prophecy of the Psalm, shame covered his face. Cyril says that the soldiers claimed the clothes of the condemned for themselves, as if by the law of inheritance, and so they divided Christ's outer garments into four parts. But the inner tunic, being seamless, was not cut up by them; instead, together with the other four parts, it was committed entirely to the lot, to decide who should take it, as appears from John 19:24. What each man would take of the divided garments appears from Mark 15:24.

units.la: 36. Ut impleretur, &c. Haec in Sixti V. editione male omissa Clemens VIII. bene restituit ex Graec. Syr. & vetustis Codicibus.
units.tr: 36. "That it might be fulfilled," etc. Clement VIII rightly restored this, which had been wrongly omitted in the edition of Sixtus V, from the Greek, the Syriac and ancient manuscripts.
