units.la: Diviserunt sibi vestimenta mea, &c. Haec verba sumta sunt ex Psal. 21. qui totus est de Christo, quod satis indicat Christus, dum infra prima hujus Psalmi verba sibi applicat, dicens: Deus, Deus meus, ut quid dereliquisti me?
units.tr: "They divided my garments," etc. These words are taken from Psalm 21, which is wholly about Christ. Christ himself makes this sufficiently clear, since below he applies to himself the opening words of this Psalm, saying: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"

units.la: 36. Servabant eum. Scilicet carnifices & reliqui custodes cum Centurione suo, de quo infra.
units.tr: 36. "They kept watch over him." That is, the executioners and the other guards, together with their centurion, of whom more below.

units.la: 37. Hic est Jesus Rex Judæorum. Matth. Marc. & Luc. videntur expressisse sensum, non ipsa verba causæ supplicii, Joannes vero ipsa verba cruci affixa, ut confirmant communiter crucium inscriptiones.
units.tr: 37. "This is Jesus the King of the Jews." Matthew, Mark and Luke seem to have expressed the sense of the charge for his punishment, not the very words; John gives the very words affixed to the cross, as the inscriptions commonly found on crosses confirm.

units.la: 38. Duo latrones. In textu Græco apud Luc. c. 25. v. 33. appellantur κακούργοι, facinorosi, malefici.
units.tr: 38. "Two robbers." In the Greek text of Luke 25:33 they are called κακούργοι [kakourgoi], evildoers, criminals.

units.la: 42. Alios salvos fecit, seipsum non potest salvum facere. Christus erat Agnus e grege sumtus adinstar Agni Paschalis Exod. 12. v. 3. sumtus ex fratribus suis, ut dicitur Deut. 28. v. 15. Æque particeps carnis ac sanguinis, fratribus denique per omnia similis, excepto peccato, ut dicit Apostolus in Epist. ad Hebræos cap. 2. & 4. Quod ipsum Lex aperte innuit, cum Agnum jubet integrum eligi in victimam Paschalem Exod. 12. v. 5. pro quo Græci τέλειον, perfectum habent, aut, ἄμωμον immaculatum; quo patet Petrum in 1 Epist. c. 1. v. 19. alludere, cum redemtionem nostram tribuit sanguini, ἀμνὸς ἄμωμος καὶ ἄσπιλος Agni immaculati & incontaminati, id est, à peccato immunis; peccata enim sunt maculæ animæ. Ab iis autem Christum fuisse prorsus immunem in confesso est; quis enim eum arguit de peccato? Joan. 8. v. 46. non peccavit, neque inventus est dolus in ore ejus.
units.tr: 42. "He saved others; himself he cannot save." Christ was the lamb taken from the flock, like the Passover lamb of Exod. 12:3, taken from among his brothers, as Deut. 28:15 says. He was equally a partaker of flesh and blood, and in short like his brothers in all things except sin, as the Apostle says in the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapters 2 and 4. The Law openly hints at this as well, when it orders that a lamb be chosen whole for the Passover sacrifice (Exod. 12:5). For this the Greek has τέλειον [teleion], perfect, or ἄμωμον [amomon], unblemished. By this it is plain that Peter, in 1 Pet. 1:19, alludes to it when he ascribes our redemption to the blood of "a lamb without blemish and without spot" [ἀμνὸς ἄμωμος καὶ ἄσπιλος], that is, free from sin, for sins are stains of the soul. That Christ was utterly free of these is agreed by all; for who convicts him of sin? John 8:46: "He committed no sin, nor was any guile found in his mouth."

units.la: 1 Petri c. 2. v. 22. ille ipse Pilatus, qui Christum tanquam reum secundum petitionem Judæorum cruci adjudicavit, eumdem tanquam insontem suffragio suo absolvit, professus coram Judæis se nullam in eo noxam reperiisse. Talis enim decebat ut nobis esset Pontifex sanctus, innocens, impollutus, segregatus à peccatoribus, qui per Spiritum-Sanctum semetipsum offerret immaculatum Deo; neque enim pro nobis potuisset satisfacere, qui victimas offerre pro suis delictis necesse habuisset, ut Sacerdotes ceteri: neque immerito à Judæis id illi fuisset objectum: Alios salvos fecit, seipsum non potest salvum facere. Sed falluntur Judæi, ideo enim se non salvat, ut alios salvos faciat, qui apparuit ut peccata nostra tolleret, & peccatum in se non habet, ut dicitur 1 Joan. c. 3. v. 5.
units.tr: 1 Pet. 2:22. That same Pilate who, at the petition of the Jews, adjudged Christ to the cross as a guilty man, by his vote acquitted him as innocent, declaring before the Jews that he had found no fault in him. For such a one it was fitting to be our High Priest: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself without blemish to God. For he could not have made satisfaction for us if he had needed to offer sacrifices for his own offences, as the other priests did. Nor was it without reason that the Jews threw this at him: "He saved others; himself he cannot save." But the Jews are mistaken. He does not save himself so that he may save others; he who appeared to take away our sins has no sin in himself, as 1 John 3:5 says.

units.la: Descendat nunc de cruce. Non descendet, perfidi Judæi, quia tempus non est ostendendæ potentiæ, sed perfectæ patientiæ; ut advertit Aug. in Psal. 40. ne impatientiæ videatur cedere. Non descendet, ut majus divinitatis suæ præbeat testimonium, tantam patientiam exercendo, quantam nemo posset hominum, & post mortem gloriosè resurgendo.
units.tr: "Let him now come down from the cross." He will not come down, faithless Jews, because this is not the time to show power, but perfect patience, as Augustine observes on Psalm 40, lest he seem to yield to impatience. He will not come down, so that he may give greater witness to his divinity by exercising such patience as no man could, and by rising gloriously after death.

units.la: Et credimus ei. Græcè, credemus. Hæc non serio promittunt, sed propter conditionis, ut putant, impossibilitatem: ut enim ait Hieron. Quid est plus de cruce descendere adhuc viventem, an è fepulcbro mortuum resurgere? Resurrexit & non creditus, ergo si etiam de cruce descenderet similiter non credere-tis.
units.tr: "And we will believe him." In Greek it is "we will believe." These men do not promise this in earnest, but because of what they think is the impossibility of the condition. As Jerome says: "What is harder, to come down from the cross while still alive, or to rise from the tomb after death? He rose and was not believed; therefore, if he had come down from the cross, you would likewise not have believed."

units.la: 43. Confidit. Id est, jactavit se fiduciam habere.
units.tr: 43. "He trusts." That is, he boasted that he had confidence.

units.la: Si vult eum. Id est, si Deus Pater ei favet tanquam dilecto Filio suo.
units.tr: "If he wills him." That is, if God the Father favours him as his beloved Son.

units.la: 44. Latrones improperabant ei. Vide dicta supra c. 21, v. 7.
units.tr: 44. "The robbers reproached him." See what was said above, ch. 21, v. 7.

units.la: 45. A sexta autem hora. Scilicet, jam transacta, seu sig-no ejus dato, hoc est, ipso medio die, quo lumen solis est maximum. Hinc colligitur Christum fuisse crucifixum hora sexta, ut & insinuat Joan. dum dicit Christum hora quasi sexta fuisse adductum foras à Pilato sedente pro tribunali in loco qui dicitur Lithostrotos, ubi eum tradidit voluntati Judæorum, ut crucifigeretur. Verum opponitur quod Marcus dicit c. 15. v. 25. Erat autem hora tertia, & crucifixerunt eum. Hujus difficultatis duplex est solutio, ut improbabiles omittamus. Prima est communior, nimirùm ut dies dicatur partitus in quatuor partes, quarum unaquæque complectatur tres horas, ut patet ex Matth. 20. ubi paterfamilias dicitur exiisse conducere operarios primo mane, circa horam tertiam, sextam, & nonam, adeo ut unumquodque trium horarum spatium nomen habuerit à prima earum hora, sicque Marcus dixerit Jesum crucifixum hora tertiâ, quia nondum sexta erat data, totum autem spatium à tertia hora usque ad sextam horam datam tertia vocabatur. Quia verò mox datura erat sexta, ex Joan. colligitur Christum fuisse crucifixum hora quasi sextâ, seu ad exitum spatii trium horarum, quod tertia dicebatur; mox verò sextâ datâ factæ sunt tenebræ, de quibus loquitur Matth. Altera est solutio, ut sensus apud Marcum sit, erat autem tertia hora, seu tertia jam agebatur hora, ex quo actus fuerat Christus in crucem, dum facta est inter milites divisio vestimentorum Christi, de qua locutus est Marcus versu laudatum mox præcedenti, & ceteri Evangelistæ diserte testantur, quod contigerit post crucifixionem Christi, licet non determinent, quotâ præcisè hora post crucifixionem contigerit, adeo ut particula & sumatur pro, postquam, qui Hebraismus frequens est in Scripturis, ut videre est, Josue 7. v. 25. &c. sicque Marcus non assignat horam crucifixionis Christi an fuerit hora tertia vel sexta.
units.tr: 45. "Now from the sixth hour." That is, now already past, or at the sign given, that is, at midday itself, when the light of the sun is greatest. From this it is gathered that Christ was crucified at the sixth hour, as John also hints when he says that Christ, about the sixth hour, was brought out by Pilate, who was sitting on the judgment seat in the place called Lithostrotos, and that Pilate there handed him over to the will of the Jews to be crucified. But it is objected that Mark says (15:25): "Now it was the third hour, and they crucified him." There is a twofold solution to this difficulty, omitting the improbable ones. The first is the more common: the day is said to be divided into four parts, each containing three hours. This appears from Matt. 20, where the householder is said to have gone out early in the morning to hire workers, about the third, sixth and ninth hours. So each space of three hours took its name from its first hour, and Mark said that Jesus was crucified at the third hour because the sixth had not yet been reached; the whole span from the third hour up to the sixth was called the third. But since the sixth was soon to come, John's account implies that Christ was crucified about the sixth hour, that is, at the end of the span of three hours which was called the third. Soon after the sixth hour came, darkness fell, of which Matthew speaks. The other solution is that the sense in Mark is: "it was the third hour," or "the third hour was already being spent," from which time Christ had been put on the cross, while the division of Christ's garments among the soldiers was made. Mark spoke of this in the verse immediately preceding the one cited, and the other Evangelists plainly testify that it happened after Christ's crucifixion, though they do not say exactly how long after. So the particle "and" is taken to mean "after," a Hebraism frequent in Scripture, as may be seen in Joshua 7:25 etc. Thus Mark does not assign the hour of Christ's crucifixion as either the third or the sixth.

units.la: Tenebræ factæ sunt. Hujus eclypseos meminit pseudo-Dionysius Areopag. Epist. 7. ad Polycarpum, ubi notat factam illam contra rationem eclypsis solaris, cum non esset Synodi tempus. Harum tenebrarum etiam Phlegontem meminisse in Olympiadibus, testes sunt Tertullianus, Origenes, Africanus, Philoponus, & alii, qui & ipsa hujus prophani historici authoritate utuntur ad Gentilium obstinationem convincendam, & Christi mortem admirabilem persuadendam. Tertul. in Apolog. c. 21. Eodem, inquit, momento, quo Christus crucifixus est, dies, medium orbem signante Sole, subductâ est. Deliquium utique putaverunt, qui id quoque super Christo prædicatum non scierunt. Hanc eclypsim in Græcorum libris legi testatur Orofius lib. 7. c. 4. Ethnicis Romanis innotuisse, & ab ipsis in Annalibus scriptum, at evulgari vetitum invidia, ne cœlum doluisse Christi velut divini viri mortem putaretur, scribit B. Aug. Epist. 80. ad Hesychium. Hinc apud Ruffinum in Actis Sancti Luciani martyris illud solemne: Perquirite in Annalibus vestris, & invenietis temporibus Pilati fugato Sole interruptum tenebris diem.
units.tr: "Darkness came over." Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite mentions this eclipse in his seventh Epistle, to Polycarp, where he notes that it was contrary to nature, since it was not the time of a conjunction of the moon with the sun. Tertullian, Origen, Africanus, Philoponus and others are witnesses that Phlegon also mentioned these darknesses in his Olympiads. They use the authority of this secular historian both to confute the obstinacy of the Gentiles and to persuade them of the remarkable death of Christ. Tertullian, Apology ch. 21: "At the very moment that Christ was crucified, the day was taken away, the sun being in the middle of the sky. Those who did not know that this too had been foretold concerning Christ certainly thought it an eclipse." Orosius, book 7, ch. 4, testifies that this eclipse is read in Greek books. Augustine, in Letter 80 to Hesychius, writes that it was known to the Roman pagans and recorded by them in their annals, but that its publication was forbidden out of spite, lest it be thought that heaven grieved at the death of Christ as at the death of a divine man. Hence in Rufinus, in the Acts of St Lucian the martyr, that famous saying: "Search your annals, and you will find that in the time of Pilate, with the sun hidden, the day was interrupted by darkness."

units.la: 46. Sabachthani. Est dictio Syriaca pro Hebraeo Eli & Elohi ut habetur apud Marcum, idem sonant Hebraice.
units.tr: 46. Sabachthani. It is a Syriac word, standing for the Hebrew Eli & Elohi, as it is given in Mark; the two words mean the same thing in Hebrew.

units.la: Ut quid derelinquisti me? Hæc est vox dolentis, miserámque suam vicem deflentis ex præsenti sensu intolerabilis suæ desertionis. Quemadmodum autem sol in passione Christi à mundo non disjunctus, ad id tamen temporis mundum deseruit, subtrahendo ab ipso suum lumen; ita servata unione hypostatica, Christi divinitas humanitatem deseruit, ut eisdem teneretur angustiis, quibus illi qui cum maximis ægritudinum paroxysmis conflictantur. Unde Hieronymus, Ne mireris, inquit, verborum humilitatem, & querimonias derelicti, cùm formam servi sciens scandalum crucis videas. Porrò præsens hoc querimoniæ verbum est quartum à Christo in cruce prolatum. 10 enim pro crucifixoribus oravit, ut habetur Luc. 23. v. 34. 20 latroni se deprecanti Paradisum, id est, beatitatem voluptatis plenissimam promisit, ut habetur ibidem v. 43. Deinde Matri suæ Joannem commendavit, & Joanni Matrem suam, ut habetur apud Joannem c. 19. v. 26. Quarto postquam sol occidisset in meridie juxta prophetiam Amos cap. 8. & sic tenebræ factæ essent super universam terram usque ad horam nonam, quæ nobis tertia est pomeridiana, dereliction se questus est, non per desperationem, cùm in eodem Psalmo Christus Patrem suum vocet spem suam ab uberibus Matris, nec quisquam possit dicere, ut advertit Ambros. in Psal. 43. Deus meus, nisi qui Deo desert plenum pietatis affectum. B. Leo Serm. 17. 17. de Passione, vult hæc verba, ut quid dereliquisti me, esse inquirentis causam derelictionis, ut nobis daret occasionem quærendi causam mortis Christi & fructum ejus, scilicet peccatum hominum offendentium, & gratiam Dei offensi: nam utrumque tam magnum est, ut soli Deo plane perspectum fit. Cyrillus lib. 2. ad Reginas vult sensum esse, Memento Deus ut quid, seu in quem finem me derelinqueris, nimirum ut placatus ultionem humano generi imminentem avertas; & ita sunt verba Christi tanquam Sacerdotis Patrem placantis, & fructum sacrificii exorantis pro humano genere. Qui scire cupit quomodo factæ sint tenebræ supra universam terram, consulat Dionysium Areopagitam in Epist. ad Polycarpum, & Phlegontis testimonium, quod habetur apud Eusebium in Chronico anno Christi 33. quibus oppositum videre potest B. Ambrosium Epist. 83. & alibi, qui vult non per eclypsim, ut existimant authores præfati, sed per verum occasum solis in occidente trium horarum spatio super universam terram factas esse tenebras.
units.tr: Ut quid derelinquisti me? This is the cry of one who suffers and bewails his own wretched state, from the present feeling of his unbearable abandonment. Just as the sun in Christ's passion was not separated from the world, yet at that time forsook the world by withdrawing its light from it, so, while the hypostatic union was preserved, Christ's divinity forsook his humanity, so that the humanity was held in the same distress as those who struggle in the greatest paroxysms of sickness. Hence Jerome: "Do not wonder, he says, at the lowly words and the complaints of one forsaken, since you see the form of a servant, knowing the scandal of the cross." Moreover, this complaint is the fourth word spoken by Christ on the cross. For first he prayed for his crucifiers, as is found in Luke 23:34; second he promised Paradise, that is, the fullest blessedness, to the thief who begged him, as is found in the same place, v. 43; then he commended his mother to John, and John his mother, as is found in John 19:26. Fourth, after the sun had set at midday, according to the prophecy of Amos 8, and so darkness had come over the whole earth until the ninth hour, which for us is three in the afternoon, he complained of being forsaken. This was not from despair, since in the same Psalm Christ calls the Father his hope from his mother's breasts, and, as Ambrose observes on Psalm 43, no one could say "My God" unless he had a feeling of piety toward God. Blessed Leo, Sermon 17 on the Passion, holds that these words, "Why hast thou forsaken me?", are a question about the cause of the abandonment, so that he might give us an occasion to seek the cause of Christ's death and its fruit: namely the sin of men who offend, and the grace of God who is offended, for each of these is so great that it is plainly known to God alone. Cyril, in book 2 to the Queens, holds that the sense is: "Remember, O God, why, or to what end, thou hast forsaken me," that is, that being appeased thou mightest turn away the vengeance hanging over the human race; and so Christ's words are as of a priest appeasing the Father and begging for the fruit of the sacrifice on behalf of the human race. Whoever wishes to know how the darkness came over the whole earth, let him consult Dionysius the Areopagite in his letter to Polycarp, and the testimony of Phlegon, which is found in Eusebius's Chronicle under the year of Christ 33. He can see the opposite view in blessed Ambrose, Epistle 83 and elsewhere, who holds that the darkness was not caused by an eclipse, as the aforementioned authors think, but by the true setting of the sun in the west, and that the darkness came over the whole earth within a span of three hours.

units.la: 47. Eliam vocat iste. Id dictum verisimile est à Judæis Hellenifiis, qui cum Hebraica verba non intelligerent, Eliæ nomen sibi notum audire arbitrari sunt, nisi forte illudendi causa ex industria sacra Christi verba hi, de quibus loquitur Evangelista, perverterint.
units.tr: 47. Eliam vocat iste. It is likely that this was said by the Hellenist Jews, who, not understanding the Hebrew words, thought they heard the name of Elijah, which was familiar to them, unless perhaps those of whom the Evangelist speaks deliberately twisted the sacred words of Christ in order to mock him.

units.la: 48. Et continuo. Nimirum postquam verbum quintum, sitio, protulisset Christus, ut patet ex Joannis 19. v. 28, & 29.
units.tr: 48. Et continuo. Namely, immediately after Christ had uttered the fifth word, I thirst, as is plain from John 19:28–29.

units.la: Imposuit arundini. Ut nimirum posset porrigens spongiam aceto plenam pertingere ad os Christi in crucem à terra exaltati. Sunt qui existimant hanc arundinem fuisse hyssopi caulem, quòd Joan. cap. 19. ait, Illi autem (hîc Joannes quod ab uno milite factum esse constat ex Marc. & Matth. militibus indeterminatè tribuit, sicut Marc. & Matth. latronibus, quod ab uno latronum factum esse dicitur, Luc. 23. v. 39.) spongiam plenam aceto hyssopo circumponentes obtulerunt ori ejus. Sed falluntur, nam apud Marc. & Matth. in textu Græco habetur καλαμος. At καλαμω non pro sola quidem arundine capitur, sed proprie est, frumenti caulis, ut habetur in Hesychio, unde ad alia transfertur, & calamus dicta fistula ex calamis conflata, & stipula καλαμη; & proprie calamitatem rustici grandinem vocant, quòd comminuat calamum, hoc est, culmum & segetem. Ita Donatus ad Comicum. Et calamus scriptorius, quomodo cum Græci καλαμος nunquam sumserint, hujus tamen usus à Romanis ad Chaldæos, Arabes, Æthiopes & Persas est propagatus. pagátus. Nusquam tamen legitur pro herbæ caule, qui neque fit nodosus, neque concavus, qualis est hyssopi caulis. Secundò hyssopi caulis non potuit ad hoc sufficere, ut spongia ipsi defixa vel involuta potuerit ad Christi e terra in crucem exaltati os admoveri, cum hyssopi caulis etiam longissimus non sit cubitalis, ut testatur Isaacus Ben-Omram. Nec satis solida est eorum ratio, qui colligunt hyssopum in Judæa arborescere, ut sinapi, de quo Christus Matth. 13. v. 31. ex eo quod dicitur Salomon de omni arbore differuisse à cedro usque ad hyssopum, quasi hyssopus sit arbor; Hebraicè enim pro arboribus habetur אזוב, quod sonat ligni, quæ vox extenditur Josue 2. v. 6. usque ad stipulam lini. Nos itaque exiguimamus, neque idem dici à Joanne atque à Matthæo & Marco, neque sollicitandum textum Joannis citra fidem ullius exemplaris, sed hyssopo fumendum apud Joannem, non in Dativo, quasi spongia hyssopum circumdederit, ut communiter sumitur ob errorem olim inveteratum, Græcos carere Ablativo, sed in Ablativo, ut indicetur spongiam aceto plenam fuisse circumdatum hyssopo, seu herbâ hyssopi, ut existimat Augustus, seu hyssopi succo, ut existimat Nonnus; nempe ut aceti acore cum hyssopi amaritudine mixto fieret potus ingratior. Nemo autem mirabitur Evangelistam dixisse hyssopo circumponentes, supple, illam spongiam, obtulerunt ori ejus pro, hyssopo circumposito, qui legerit apud Matth. c. 26. v. 27. Accipiens calicem gratias egit & dedit illis, pro eo quod Marcus dicit c. 14. v. 23. Accepto calice gratias agens dedit eis, &c. atque ita Matth. & Marcus de aceti spongia egerant, & quomodo calamo alligata Christi ori fuisset admota; sed hoc unum præterierant, quod Joannes supplet, spongiam illam fuisse hyssopo circumdatam, ut non solùm acerbus, sed & amarus esset Christi potus, ut impleretur quod dictum est per David Psal. 68. Et dederunt in escam meam fel, in siti mea potaverunt me aceto: In quo Psalmi loco quod in Vulgata redditur fel, Hebraice est ראש, quod proprie est herbæ amaræ genus in segetibus nascens Oseæ 10. v. 4. ubi à Vulgata redditur amaritudo. Hæc autem herba cum absynthio sæpè jungitur, ut æque amara, ut videre est Deut. 29. v. 18. Jerem. 9. v. 15. Thren. 3. v. 19. & Amos 6. v. 12. Amaram autem in Judæa esse hyssopum testatur Isaacus Ben-Omram mox citatus.
units.tr: Imposuit arundini. So that the one who held out the sponge full of vinegar could reach the mouth of Christ, who had been lifted up from the earth on the cross. Some think that this reed was a stalk of hyssop, because John 19 says, "But they" (here John attributes indefinitely to soldiers what is known from Mark and Matthew to have been done by one soldier; just as Mark and Matthew attribute to the robbers what Luke 23:39 says was done by one of the robbers) "placing around a sponge full of vinegar on hyssop, offered it to his mouth." But they are mistaken, for in Mark and Matthew the Greek text has kalamos [κάλαμος]. Now kalamo [καλάμῳ] is not taken to mean a reed alone, but properly it is the stalk of grain, as is found in Hesychius, whence it is transferred to other things, and the pipe made from reeds is called calamus, and kalamē [καλάμη] is stubble; and country people properly call hail calamitas, because it batters the calamus, that is, the stalk and the crop. So Donatus on the Comic poet. And the writing reed: although the Greeks never took kalamos in this sense, the use of it spread from the Romans to the Chaldeans, Arabs, Ethiopians and Persians. Yet it is nowhere read as meaning the stalk of a herb, which is neither jointed nor hollow, as the stalk of hyssop is. Secondly, a stalk of hyssop could not have been enough for this purpose, so that a sponge fixed to it or wrapped round it could be brought to the mouth of Christ lifted up from the earth on the cross, since even the longest stalk of hyssop is not a cubit long, as Isaac Ben-Omram testifies. Nor is the reasoning of those solid who gather that hyssop grows as a tree in Judea, like the mustard of which Christ speaks in Matthew 13:31, from the fact that Solomon is said to have discoursed about every tree from the cedar to the hyssop, as if hyssop were a tree; for in Hebrew the word for trees is [אזוב], which means wood, and this word extends in Joshua 2:6 to the stalk of flax. We therefore think that John does not say the same as Matthew and Mark, and the text of John should not be disturbed without the authority of any manuscript; rather hyssopo is to be taken in John not as a dative, as if the sponge had put hyssop around it (which is commonly taken because of an old and long-standing error, that the Greeks lack an ablative), but in the ablative, to indicate that the sponge full of vinegar was wrapped about with hyssop, or with the herb hyssop, as Augustine thinks, or with the juice of hyssop, as Nonnus thinks; namely so that the sharpness of the vinegar mixed with the bitterness of hyssop would make the drink more unpleasant. No one will be surprised that the Evangelist said hyssopo circumponentes, with the sense "placing around it hyssop", and obtulerunt ori ejus, "they offered it to his mouth", for whoever has read in Matthew 26:27, "taking the cup he gave thanks and gave it to them," as against what Mark says in 14:23, "taking the cup, giving thanks, he gave it to them," etc., will see that Matthew and Mark had indeed spoken of the sponge of vinegar, and how it was brought to Christ's mouth fastened to a reed; but they had passed over this one thing, which John supplies: that the sponge had been wrapped round with hyssop, so that Christ's drink was not only sour but also bitter, that what was said through David in Psalm 68 might be fulfilled: "They gave me gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink." In that Psalm the word which the Vulgate renders gall is in Hebrew [ראש], which properly denotes a kind of bitter herb growing among the crops, Hosea 10:4, where the Vulgate renders it bitterness. This herb is often joined with wormwood, as equally bitter, as may be seen in Deuteronomy 29:18, Jeremiah 9:15, Lamentations 3:19 and Amos 6:12. That hyssop is bitter in Judea is attested by Isaac Ben-Omram, cited just above.

units.la: Dabat ei bibere, Supple ex Marco c. 15. v. 36. dicens, ceteris astantibus, Sinite videamus si veniet Elias ad deponendum eum.
units.tr: Dabat ei bibere, supply from Mark 15:36, saying, while the others stood by, Let us see whether Elias will come to take him down.

units.la: 49. Ceteri verò dicebant. Scilicet, porrigenti spongiam aceto plenam & hyssopo circumdatam.
units.tr: 49. Ceteri verò dicebant. That is, to the one holding out the sponge full of vinegar and wrapped round with hyssop.

units.la: 50. Iesus autem. Nempe cùm accepisset acetum, & dixisset consummatum est, ut habetur Joan. 19. v.30. clamans voce magnâ,clarè ac sonore emittens emortualia verba,Luc.23.v.46. Pater in manus tuas commendo spiritum meum, Græcè, commendabo, id est, jam jam deponam animam meam in manus tuas.
units.tr: 50. Iesus autem. Namely, when he had received the vinegar and said It is finished, as is found in John 19:30, crying out with a loud voice, uttering clearly and resonantly his last words, Luke 23:46: Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit; in the Greek, I shall commend, that is, I am now about to lay down my soul into thy hands.

units.la: Emisit spiritum. Supple, inclinato capite, ex Joan. 19. v.30. Verè tunc dici potuit illud Psalmi, Emittes spiritum & renovabis faciem terræ. Emisit Christus spiritum & novum induxit feculum & vetera abolevit, ut ea in melius mutaret & quasi recuderet; emisit spiritum & ecce nova fecit omnia, velum templi scissum est ad ostendendum reserationem mysteriorum Legis; aperta sunt monumenta ad ostendendum quod per ejus mortem vita mortuis daretur nova, terra mota est, & petræ scissæ sunt, ad ostendendum quod vetus cordium humanorum durities, per ejus passionem esset convertenda in novam compunctionem per quam emollirentur, novum instituit Testamentum, nomen novum victori pollicetur Apoc. 2. v.17. novam nobis viam per carnem suam consecravit Heb. 10. v.21. nos invitat ad novam Jerusalem Apoc. 3. v. 12. ex duobus populis condidit in semetipso unum novum hominem Ephes. 2. v. 15. Vult ut Deo serviamus in novitate spiritûs, non in vetustate literæ Rom. 7. v. 6. & hominem veterem crucifigamus ut novo induamur Ephes. 4. v. 24. Proinde si quis est in Christo, ut ait Apost. 2æ. ad Corinth. c. 5. v. 17. nova fit creatura, vetera enim trans-ierunt, & ecce facta sunt omnia nova. Est insuper animadvertendum quod Christus mortuus est & expiravit horâ nonâ, quæ nobis est tertia post meridiem, quâ horâ maclabatur olim Agnus Paschalis inter duas vesperas, quod est, Josepho interprete, ab hora nona usque ad undecimam. Et sicut à Davidis ævo Paschales Agnos mactari oportuit Jerosolymis, ita verus agnus ibi passus est, prout ipse prædixerat non contingere ut Propheta pereat extra Jerusalem Luc. 13. v. 33.
units.tr: Emisit spiritum. Supply with his head bowed, from John 19:30. Then truly that saying of the Psalm could be applied: You will send forth your spirit, and you will renew the face of the earth. Christ sent forth his spirit, introduced a new age and abolished the old, so as to change and, as it were, remake them for the better. He sent forth his spirit, and behold, he made all things new. The veil of the temple was torn to show the unlocking of the mysteries of the Law. The tombs were opened to show that through his death new life would be given to the dead. The earth quaked and the rocks were split, to show that the old hardness of human hearts was, through his passion, to be turned into a new compunction by which they would be softened. He instituted a New Testament. He promises the victor a new name (Rev. 2:17). He consecrated for us a new way through his flesh (Heb. 10:21). He invites us to the new Jerusalem (Rev. 3:12). Out of two peoples he made in himself one new man (Eph. 2:15). He wills that we serve God in the newness of the Spirit, not in the oldness of the letter (Rom. 7:6), and that we crucify the old man so that we may put on the new (Eph. 4:24). Therefore, as the Apostle says in 2 Corinthians 5:17, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creature; the old things have passed away, and behold, all things have become new. Moreover, it should be noted that Christ died and breathed his last at the ninth hour, which for us is the third hour after noon. At this hour the Paschal lamb was formerly slain, between the two evenings, which, according to Josephus' explanation, means from the ninth hour until the eleventh. And just as from the time of David the Paschal lambs had to be slain at Jerusalem, so the true Lamb suffered there, as he himself had foretold, that it could not happen that a prophet should perish outside Jerusalem (Luke 13:33).

units.la: 51. Et ecce. Hac loquendi connexione, ut observat Aug. lib. 3. de consensu Evang. c. 19. indicat Matthæus statim post expirationem Christi velum Templi scissum fuisse. An velum illud fuerit velum exterius, quod primis portis oppandebatur, ut existimant Origenes & Hieronymus, an verò velum interius, quod intra parietis separabat Sanctum Sanctorum à Sancto, ut existimant Cyrillus Alex. B. Leo & alii plerique veteres, definiri non potest. Duo autem fuisse vela in Templo, quod Herodes instauraverat, ex Josepho discimus belli Judaici lib. 5. c. 14. Unde non est urgendus articulus in textu Græco apud Matth. & Marc. dum dicunt τὸ καταπέτασμα quasi insinuarent unicum tunc in Templo velum fuisse; ut
units.tr: 51. Et ecce. By this connection of words, as Augustine observes (De consensu Evangelistarum, bk. 3, ch. 19), Matthew indicates that the veil of the temple was torn immediately after Christ's death. Whether that veil was the outer veil, which hung before the first gates, as Origen and Jerome think, or the inner veil, which separated the Holy of Holies from the Holy Place within, as Cyril of Alexandria, Leo the Great and many other ancient writers think, cannot be determined. We learn from Josephus (Jewish War, bk. 5, ch. 14) that there were two veils in the temple that Herod had restored. Hence the article in the Greek text of Matthew and Mark, τὸ καταπέτασμα [the veil], should not be pressed, as if they were implying that there was only one veil in the temple at that time. For, as Chrysostom notes more than once in his commentary on John, articles may be pressed only when neither theological reasons nor history stand in the way.

units.la: enim non semel in commentariis suis in Joannem monet B. Chrysostomus, tunc demum urgeri possunt articuli, cum neque rationes Theologicæ, neque Historia obstat.
units.tr: For, as Chrysostom notes more than once in his commentary on John, articles may be pressed only when neither theological reasons nor history stand in the way.

units.la: 53. Et exeuntes de monumentis post resurrectionem ejus. Hinc Tertul. hos vocat appendices Dominicæ Resurrectionis. Videtur autem illud post resurrectionem ejus referendum ad omnia precedentia, exeuntes, surrexerunt, aperta sunt; ratio enim sicut vetabat ne exirent de monumentis ante Christi resurrectionem; ita etiam ne ante resurgerent, vel ante monumenta aperirentur, quanquam hoc postremum fit incertius.
units.tr: 53. Et exeuntes de monumentis post resurrectionem ejus. Hence Tertullian calls these men appendices of the Lord's Resurrection. It seems that the phrase after his resurrection should be referred to everything that precedes: coming out, they rose, the tombs were opened. For the reason that forbade them to come out of the tombs before Christ's resurrection also forbade them to rise before it, or to have the tombs opened before it, although this last point is less certain.

units.la: Venerunt in sanctam civitatem. Id est, a monumentis, quæ erant extra civitatem, venerunt in civitatem Ierusalem, quæ sancta appellatur propter Templum et Sancta Sanctorum, et ob distinctionem aliarum urbium, in quibus idola colebantur. Quando vero dicitur, apparuerunt multis, offenditur non generaliter fuisse resurrectio, quæ omnibus appareret, sed specialiter ad plurimos, ut hi viderent, qui cernere merebantur. Hæc Hieron. Vide Aug. in Epist. 99. ad Evodium; ubi sentire videtur quod qui resurrexerunt cum Christo, iterum morituri resurrexerint, quam sententiam etiam D. Th. 3. p. q. 53. art. 3. ad 2. præfert alteri, qua dicuntur sic resurrexisse, ut non essent amplius morituri, licet hanc posteriorem opinionem idem S. Doctor junior 4 dist. 43. art. 3. quæstiunc. 1. & sub illius nomine autor commentarii in Matth. judicaverit probabiliorem. B. Hier. in hunc locum, & apud ipsum sub ejus nomine autor Sermonis de Assumtione utramque sententiam sub dubio reliquit.
units.tr: They came into the holy city. That is, from the tombs, which were outside the city, they came into the city of Jerusalem, which is called holy because of the Temple and the Holy of Holies, and to distinguish it from the other cities in which idols were worshipped. But when it is said that they appeared to many, it is not a difficulty that the resurrection was not general, so as to be seen by all, but particular, to many, so that those who deserved to see them might see them. Thus Jerome. See Augustine, Epistle 99 to Evodius, where he seems to hold that those who rose with Christ rose to die again. Thomas Aquinas (3 p., q. 53, art. 3, ad 2) also prefers this opinion to the other, by which they are said to have risen so as no longer to be mortal, although the same holy doctor, in his younger years (4 dist. 43, art. 3, quaestiuncula 1), and the author of the commentary on Matthew under his name, judged this later opinion more probable. Blessed Jerome, on this passage, and the author of the sermon On the Assumption under his name, left both opinions open as doubtful.

units.la: 54. Centurio autem. Supple ex Marc. 15. v. 39. Qui ex adverso stabat, hoc est, e regione Christi crucifixi.
units.tr: 54. Centurio autem. Supply from Mark 15:39: who stood over against, that is, opposite Christ crucified.

units.la: Et his quæ fiebant: Inter quæ potissimum comprehenditur, ut patet ex Marco, quod clamans Christus expirasset.
units.tr: And the things that were done: Among these is especially included, as is clear from Mark, that Christ had cried out with a loud voice and expired.

units.la: Dicentes. Hoc est, Deum glorificantes, ut patet ex Luc. c. 23. v. 47. Dicebant vere filius Dei erat ille. Cyrillus & Basilius existimant hic confessione Centurionem, & qui cum eo erant, agnovisse Christi divinitatem; sed magis verisimile videtur, eos tantum agnovisse innocentiam Christi, & justitiam. Unde apud Lucam, qui meminit tantum confessionis a Centurione factæ, non vero quæ ab iis, qui cum eo erant, facta est, hæc Centurioni Deum glorificanti tribuit verba; Vere hic homo justus erat. Aug. enim lib. 3. de cons. nsu Evang. c. 20. exis-timat Lucam non meminisse confessionis distinctæ ab ea, cujus meminit Matthæus. Addit autem Lucas omnem turbam adstantem ad spectaculum illud, visis his quæ fiebant, percutientes pectora sua esse reversos, ut indicetur qui facit mirabilia solus, fecisse ne in electis hominibus otiosa jam esset ea, quæ apud se erat copiosa reredemtio, ut impleretur istud Christi effatum, Si exaltatus fuero à terra, omnia trahám ad meipsum: Videlicet electa, inquit S. Greg. Magnus lib. 6. Ep. 179. ad Gregorium Presbyterum & Theodorum Diaconum.
units.tr: Saying. That is, glorifying God, as is clear from Luke 23:47: They said, Truly this was the Son of God. Cyril and Basil think that here the centurion and those with him acknowledged the divinity of Christ, but it seems more likely that they only recognised Christ's innocence and righteousness. Hence in Luke, who mentions only the confession made by the centurion and not that made by those with him, these words are given to the centurion glorifying God: Truly this man was righteous. For Augustine (De consensu Evangelistarum, bk. 3, ch. 20) thinks that Luke does not mention a confession distinct from the one Matthew records. Luke adds moreover that the whole crowd standing by at that spectacle, when they saw what was done, returned beating their breasts. This shows that he who alone does wonders did so, lest the redemption that was abundant in him should be idle among chosen men, so that the saying of Christ might be fulfilled: If I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself. That is, the elect, says St. Gregory the Great (Book 6, Epistle 179, to Gregory the presbyter and Theodore the deacon).

units.la: 55. Erant autem ibi mulieres, &c. Consuetudinis Judaicæ fuit (nec ducebatur in culpam more gentis antiquo) ut mulieres de substantia sua victum atque vestitum præceptoribus ministrarent. Hoc, quia scandalum facere poterat in Nationibus, Paulus abjecisse se memorat 1 Cor. 9. v. 5. dicit enim ipse, Numquid non habemus potestatem mulierem sororem circumducendi, sicut & ceteri Apostoli? ministrabant autem Domino de substantia sua, cujus illæ metebant spiritalia; non quòd indigeret cibis Dominus creaturarum, sed ut typum ostenderet magistrorum, quòd victu atque vestitu ex discipulis deberent esse contenti.
units.tr: 55. Now there were women there, etc. It was a Jewish custom (and it was not counted a fault, according to the ancient manner of the nation) for women to provide food and clothing for their teachers out of their own means. Paul records that he gave this up because it could cause offence among the Gentiles (1 Cor. 9:5). For he himself says: Do we not have the right to lead about a sister, a wife, as also the other Apostles do? These women ministered to the Lord out of their substance, and they reaped spiritual things from him in return. This was not because the Lord, the Creator of creatures, needed food, but to show a type for teachers, that they ought to be content with food and clothing from their disciples.

units.la: 56. Maria Jacobi, & Joseph Mater. Eadem hæc est, quæ vocatur à Joanne Maria Cleophæ, quod nomen patris ejus quidam esse volunt, ita ut fuerit filia Cleophæ, uxor Alphæi, & mater Jacobi fratris Domini, & Judæ, qui se ipse nominat fratrem Jacobi, & Joseph, sive Jose, Ἰωσῆ, ut habent Græca; idem enim nomen est, pronuntiatione diversa. Sunt qui exisłimant maritum hujus Mariæ, non patrem, fuisse Cleophram, qui fuerit cognominatus Alphæus.
units.tr: 56. Mary the mother of James and Joses. This is the same woman who is called by John Mary of Cleophas. Some think that Cleophas was the name of her father, so that she was the daughter of Cleophas, the wife of Alphaeus, and the mother of James the brother of the Lord, and of Jude, who calls himself the brother of James, and of Joseph, or Jose, Ἰωσῆ [Ioses], as the Greek has it. For it is the same name, pronounced differently. There are those who think that the husband of this Mary, not her father, was Cleophas, who was surnamed Alphaeus.

units.la: Et mater filiorum Zebedæi. Hanc existimat Origenes esse illam, quam Marcus 15. v. 40. vocat Salomen.
units.tr: And the mother of the sons of Zebedee. Origen thinks this is the woman whom Mark (15:40) calls Salome.

units.la: 57. Cùm autem sero factum esset. Supple ex Joan. 19. & Judæi, ut non remanerent in cruce corpora Sabbato, rogassent Pilatum, ut frangerentur crurifixorum crura, & unus militum transfixisset lancea latus Christi, & continuò exiisset sanguis & aqua, non fractis ejusdem Christi cruribus, quòd repertus esset jam mortuus. Nota obiter ad morem crucifixos è cruce eximendi, ut festi honori consulatur, insignia esse hæc Philonis, in Flaccum, ubi de festo Imperatoris natalitio; Quosdam jam novi crucifixos, instante tali festo, de cruce depositos, & cognatis reditos, ut sepulturam, & justa exequiarum exequerentur. Decebat enim vel ad mortuos redire aliquem fructum ex Imperatoris natalibus, simúlque solemnitatis factum servari honorem.
units.tr: 57. When therefore it was evening. Supply from John 19: and the Jews, so that the bodies should not remain on the cross on the Sabbath, asked Pilate that the legs of the crucified be broken, and one of the soldiers pierced Christ's side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out, since the legs of the same Christ were not broken, because he was found already dead. Note in passing the custom of taking the crucified down from the cross, so that the honour of the feast might be preserved. These are the words of Philo, Against Flaccus, where he speaks of the feast of the Emperor's birthday: I know that some already crucified, when such a feast was at hand, were taken down from the cross and given back to their relatives, so that they might perform burial and the due rites of the funeral. For it was fitting that some benefit should come back to the dead from the Emperor's birthday, and that the honour of the festival be kept at the same time.

units.la: Venit quidam homo dives, &c. Dives refertur non de jactantia scriptoris, quo virum nobilem atque ditissimum referrat Jesu fuisse discipulum, sed ut ostendat causam, quare à Pilato corpus Jesu potuerit impetrare. In alio Evangelista Joseph ißΔ βουλευτής appellatur, id est, Consiliarius, & de ipso quidam putant primum Psalmum esse compositum, Beatus vir qui non abiit in consilio impiorum, &c. ut refert Hieron. In Latina versione appellatur hic Joseph apud Marc. nobilis Decurio. Arimathæa. Civitas Judæ putatur esse propter Lyddam inter Jerusalem & Joppen; dicitur autem hic Joseph ab Arimathæa, quia inde erat oriundus, licet fuerit Jerosolymæ accola. Videat autem prudens lector, quid interfit inter illam locutionem, Venit Joseph ab Arimathæa, ut loquitur Marcus c. 15. v. 43. & illam quâ utitur Matthæus cap. 2. Magi venerunt ab Oriente, an non eodem modo dici posset Magos Orientales venisse, sicut hic dicitur Joseph Arimathæus? Vide dicta supra c. 2. v. 1.
units.tr: Venit quidam homo dives, &c. The word "rich" is not there to boast about the writer's own account, that a noble and very wealthy man was a disciple of Jesus. It is there to show the reason why Pilate could be persuaded to give up Jesus's body. In another Evangelist, Joseph is called councillor [βουλευτής], and some think that the first Psalm was composed about him, Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the wicked, &c., as Jerome reports. In the Latin version, Joseph is called noble decurion of Arimathaea in Mark. Arimathaea is thought to be a town of Judea near Lydda, between Jerusalem and Joppa. Joseph is called "of Arimathaea" because he was born there, though he lived in Jerusalem. Let the prudent reader consider how the expression Joseph came from Arimathaea, as Mark says in chapter 15, verse 43, differs from the expression Matthew uses in chapter 2, Magi came from the East. Could it not equally be said that the Eastern Magi came in the same way that Joseph of Arimathaea is here said to have come? See what was said above at chapter 2, verse 1.

units.la: 58. Tunc. Supple ex Marc. 15. v. 45. cùm cognovisset à Centurione Pilatus, quòd Iesus esset jam mortuus.
units.tr: 58. Tunc. Supply from Mark 15, verse 45: when Pilate had learned from the centurion that Jesus was already dead.

units.la: 59. Et accepto corpore Joseph involvit illud in sindone munda. Quam nimirum mercatus erat, ut dicit Marc. c. 15. v. 46. Involvit autem corpus Iesu postquam ad eum venisset Nicodemus, qui venerat ad Iesum noctè primùm, ferens mixturam myrrhæ & aloës, quasi libras centum. Est autem sindon pannus lineus subtilissimus, quæ hic dicitur munda, quia nova; non solùm autem Joseph involvit corpus Iesu centum libris aromatum conditum in sindone munda, sed etiam unà cum Nicodemo illigavit illud instítis, sicut mos est Judæis sepelire, faciem tegendo sudario. Conferatur v. 40. c. 19. Joan. cum v. 6, & 7. c. 21. patebit eâdem formâ Christum fuisse involutum, qui fuit Lazarus Joan. 11. v. 14. Monet autem Aug. super Joan. tract. 129, ideo ab Evangelista dici sepelierunt eum sicut mos est Judæis sepelire, ut admonerentur in hujusmodi officiis, quæ mortuis exhibentur, morem cujuslibet gentis esse servandum.
units.tr: 59. Et accepto corpore Joseph involvit illud in sindone munda. He had bought the linen, as Mark 15, verse 46 says. Joseph wrapped the body of Jesus after Nicodemus had come to him, the man who had first come to Jesus by night, bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds. The sindon is a very fine linen cloth, which is called clean here because it is new. Joseph did not wrap the body of Jesus, embalmed with a hundred pounds of spices, in a clean sindon only. Together with Nicodemus he also bound it in linen strips, as the Jews customarily bury, covering the face with a napkin. Compare John 19, verse 40 with John 11, verses 44 and 45, and it will be clear that Christ was wrapped in the same way as Lazarus was. Augustine, in his tractate 129 on John, observes that the Evangelist says they buried him as the Jews customarily bury so that people would be reminded that in such duties performed for the dead the custom of each nation must be observed.

units.la: 60. Et posuit illud in monumento novo. Ne post resurrectionem ceteris corporibus remanentibus, surrexisse alius fingeretur. Nemo autem miretur Christum Dominum à Josepho suisse sepultum ipso Paschatis die, siquidem & Tobias c. 2. v. 1, & 4. legitur in Textu Græco die Pentecostes mortuum extulisse, ut ejus sepulturæ prospiceret. Quidni autem de Christo idem licuisset, cùm res non posset differri, quia instabat Sabbatum, quo nullum prorsus opus facere licebat, ne cibum quidem parare, ut habetur Exod. 16. quod licebat facere die azymorum, ut habetur Exod. 12. Deinde etsi festa Judæorum duraverint noctem & diem, tamen nocturnis horis multò plura licebant, quàm diurnis, quibus populus convocandus, & cultui divino vacandum erat. Unde Evangelista observat Joseph um corpus Christi è cruce depositum pollinxisse & sepeliisse, cùm jam fero factum esset.
units.tr: 60. Et posuit illud in monumento novo. So that no one could pretend, after the resurrection, that another had risen while other bodies remained there. No one should wonder that Christ our Lord was buried by Joseph on the very day of the Passover, since in the Greek text of Tobit 2, verses 1 and 4, we read that he buried a dead man on the day of Pentecost, in order to provide for his burial. Why should the same not have been allowed in Christ's case, since the matter could not be deferred, because the Sabbath was at hand, on which no work at all was allowed, not even preparing food, as is found in Exodus 16? Preparing food was allowed on the day of unleavened bread, as is found in Exodus 12. Moreover, although the Jewish festivals lasted night and day, many more things were permitted in the night hours than in the daytime, when the people had to be called together and devoted to divine worship. Hence the Evangelist notes that Joseph took down the body of Christ from the cross, anointed and buried it when it was already evening.

units.la: 61. Erat autem ibi Maria Magdalene & altera Maria. Duas præcipuas nominant Matth. & Marc. hic ex mulieribus, quæ subsecutæ sunt Christum, & sederunt contra sepulchrum videntes ubi poneretur, & quemadmodum positum erat corpus ejus, & revertentes paraverunt aromata & unguenta, ut habetur Luc. 23. v. 55, & 56.
units.tr: 61. Erat autem ibi Maria Magdalene & altera Maria. Matthew and Mark name here the two chief women who followed Christ, who sat opposite the sepulchre, watching where he was laid and how his body was placed; and returning, they prepared spices and ointments, as Luke 23, verses 55 and 56 has it.

units.la: Sedentes contra sepulchrum. Id est, è regione sepulchri.
units.tr: Sedentes contra sepulchrum. That is, facing the sepulchre.

units.la: 62. Altera autem die, quae est post Parasceven. Hanc Parasceven vocat Joan. Parasceven Paschae, non quod fuerit vigilia festi Paschae, sed quod fuerit Veneris dies, quae Sabbati fuerit Parasceve, & inciderit in ipsum Paschatis festum; quomodo nos appellamus Dominicam Pentecostes, vel Paschatis, quae incidit in ipsum Paschatis festum, sic veris vel autumni aequinoxium, quod in ver vel autumnum incidit. Appellabatur autem ab Hebraeis dies Veneris ערב Erev, vel ערובתא Arowta, Parasceve, ut & ab ipsis Arabibus, qui Sabbatum non observabant; quia cum Sabbato ignem accendere, parare cibum non licuerit, necessaria fuit Parasceve, id est, horas aliquas ante Sabbati vesperam insumere in iis instruendis & adornandis, quae ad festum erant necessaria, ut praecipitur Exod. 16. v. 5, & 23. Hinc Marc. c. 15. v. 42. diserte dicit, Erat Parasceve, quod est AnteSabbatum. Et Luc. 23. v. 54. Et dies erat Parasceves & Sabbatum illucescebat, id est, imminebat. Et in Berefchith Rabba c.11. dies hebdomadis sic nominantur, prima hebdomadis, secunda, tertia, quarta, quinta, Parasceve, Sabbatum.
units.tr: 62. Altera autem die, quae est post Parasceven. John calls this day the Parasceve of the Passover. It was not the eve of the feast of the Passover, but the day of Friday, which was the Parasceve of the Sabbath, and it fell upon the very feast of the Passover. In the same way we call the Sunday of Pentecost, or of Easter, that which falls upon the feast of Easter itself; and so the equinox of spring or autumn is the one that falls in spring or autumn. The Hebrews called the day of Friday Erev [ערב] or Arowta [ערובתא], that is, Parasceve, and so did the Arabs themselves, who did not observe the Sabbath. Because it was not lawful to kindle a fire or prepare food on the Sabbath, the Parasceve was necessary, that is, to spend some hours before the evening of the Sabbath in arranging and preparing what was needed for the feast, as is commanded in Exodus 16, verses 5 and 23. Hence Mark 15, verse 42 plainly says: It was the Parasceve, that is, the day before the Sabbath. And Luke 23, verse 54: and it was the day of the Parasceve, and the Sabbath was dawning, that is, was at hand. And in Bereshith Rabba chapter 11, the days of the week are named thus: first day of the week, second, third, fourth, fifth, Parasceve, Sabbath.

units.la: 63. Post tres dies. Hebraismus, id est, intra tres dies, sic enim Hebraei loqui solent, ut dicant post tres dies fieri, quod fit tertio: Sic Deut. 31. v. 10. Annus remissionis dicitur esse post septem annos, cum tamen annus remissionis septimo quoque anno contingeret.
units.tr: 63. Post tres dies. This is a Hebraism, that is, within three days. For the Hebrews are accustomed to speak so that they say that something happens after three days when it happens on the third day. So in Deuteronomy 31, verse 10 the year of release is said to come after seven years, although the year of release fell every seventh year.

units.la: 64. Jube ergo custodiri sepulchrum, &c. Non sufficerat Principibus Sacerdotum, & Scribis, ac Pharisaeis crucifixisse Dominum Salvatorem, nisi sepulchrum custodirent, cohortem acciperent, signarent lapidem, & quantum in illis erat, manum opponeret resurgenti, ut diligentia eorum nostrae fidei proficeret. Quanto enim amplius reservatur, tanto magis resurrectionis virtus ostenditur. Unde & in monumento novo, quod excisum fuerat in petra, conditus est; ne si ex multis lapidibus aedificatum esset, suffossis tumuli fundamentis, ablatus furto diceretur. Quod autem in sepulchro ponendus esset, Prophetae testimonium est, nempe Esaiae dicentis c. 33. secundum LXX. Hic habitabit in excisa spelunca petrae fortissimae, statimque post duos versiculos sequitur, Regem cum gloria videbitis. Hieron.
units.tr: 64. Jube ergo custodiri sepulchrum, &c. It was not enough for the chief priests, scribes and Pharisees to have crucified the Lord and Saviour, unless they also guarded the sepulchre, took a cohort, sealed the stone, and, as far as lay in them, set their hand against the one who would rise, so that their diligence might serve our faith. For the more carefully the body is kept, the more clearly the power of the resurrection is shown. Hence also he was laid in a new tomb, which had been hewn out of the rock, so that it could not be said that, if it had been built of many stones, the foundations of the tomb had been dug under and he had been stolen away. That he was to be placed in a sepulchre is the testimony of the prophet, namely Isaiah, who says in chapter 33, according to the Seventy: He shall dwell in the hollow cave of a very strong rock, and immediately after two verses follows: you shall see the King in his glory. Jerome.

units.la: Novissimus error. Graece, novissima impostura.
units.tr: Novissimus error. In Greek: the last imposture.

units.la: 66. Munierunt. Graece, ἠσφαλίσαντο, quod verbum supra vertitur per custodiri: proprie autem significat, tutum reddere contra pericula & munire, sicut hic vertitur.
units.tr: 66. Munierunt. In Greek, ἠσφαλίσαντο, which above is rendered "guarded". Properly it means to make safe against dangers and to fortify, as it is rendered here.

units.la: Signantes lapidem cum custodibus. Q. d. Duobus modis sepulchrum munierunt. Primò sigillo publico contra omnem fraudem, sive corruptorum custodum, sive Discipulorum, obsignarunt lapidem, quo ostium sepulchri claudebatur; secundò adhibuerunt custodiam militum.
units.tr: Signantes lapidem cum custodibus. That is: they secured the sepulchre in two ways. First, with a public seal against all fraud, whether by corrupt guards or by disciples, they sealed the stone by which the door of the sepulchre was closed; second, they posted a guard of soldiers.

units.la: CAPUT XXVII- I.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVII- I.

units.la: 1. VEspere autem Sabbati, quæ lucescit in prima Sabbati. Hoc Gallicè diceretur, la nuit du Samedy au Dimanche; quia nimirùm nox seu vespera Sabbati dupliciter dici potest, scilicet vel quæ succedit feriæ sextæ, & secundum usum Judæorum à solis occasu diem inchoantium unà cum die Sabbati artificiali integrat diem naturalem; vel vespera seu nox, quæ succedit sabbato; hæc confusio ut tolleretur, & nulla esset ambiguitas, quì nocte surrexerit Christus, addit Evangelista quæ lucescit in prima Sabbati, ubi vesperam lucescentem dixit, noctem advenientem in prima Sabbati, quasi diceretur nox, quæ pertinet ad primam Sabbati. Sic Lucas c. 23. v. 54. narratis omnibus, quæ contigerant in sepultura Christi ait, Et dies erat Parasceves, & Sabbatum illucescebat, id est, adveniebat, seu imminebat. Hæc de tota phrasi Evangelistæ sunt scienda, nunc examinemus voces sigillatim.
units.tr: 1. And in the evening of the Sabbath, which dawns toward the first day of the week. This would be said in French as la nuit du Samedy au Dimanche, because the night or evening of the Sabbath can be understood in two ways. Either it is the evening that follows the sixth day, which by the Jewish custom, beginning the day at sunset, together with the artificial day of the Sabbath makes up one natural day; or it is the evening or night that follows the Sabbath. To remove this confusion, and so that there be no ambiguity about the night in which Christ rose, the Evangelist adds which dawns toward the first day of the week. Here he calls the evening "dawning," meaning the night that is passing away to make room for the coming dawn, as if he had said the night belonging to the first day of the week. So Luke, in chapter 23, verse 54, after relating everything that happened at Christ's burial, says: And it was the day of Preparation, and the Sabbath was dawning, that is, was approaching or impending. These points must be known about the whole phrase of the Evangelist. Now let us examine the words one by one.

units.la: Vespere. Vespera Hebræis & mane non sunt, sicut apud nos, extrema diei naturalis, à se invicem multùm dissita, sed integrantes naturalis diei partes, quæ totam conficiunt, ut videre est Genes. 1. Hinc totum ῥυχθήμερον, Dan. 8. v. 14. vocatur Hebraicè ערב בוקר vespera-mane. Et eadem vox ערב, ἑσπέρα vespere redditur Esaiæ 5. v. 1. & πρωΐ mane, Job 7. v. 4. Vocat igitur Matth. vesperam illucescentem, noctem jam recedentem ut illucescenti aurorae locum faciat, nisi malis illucescentem dici, quasi advenientem. Ceterùm indifferenter dici possunt mulieres fecisse vesperè, seu noctu, sive mane, seu diu, quod fecerunt valdè diluculo seu summo mane, cùm adhuc essent tenebræ; ut enim monet Gellius l. 7. c. 21. Tempora duo cùm inter se opposita sunt, atque ita cohærentia, ut alterius finis cum alterius initio misceatur, non refert utrum per extremitatem prioris, an per initium sequentis, locus ipse confinis demonstretur.
units.tr: Evening. For the Hebrews, evening and morning are not, as with us, the extremes of the natural day, far apart from each other, but parts of the natural day which together make up the whole, as can be seen in Genesis 1. Hence the whole ῥυχθήμερον (a day and a night), Daniel 8, verse 14, is called in Hebrew evening-morning [ערב בוקר]. The same word evening [ערב], rendered ἑσπέρα (evening), appears in Isaiah 5, verse 1, and πρωΐ (morning) in Job 7, verse 4. Matthew therefore calls the evening "dawning," the night already receding to make way for the rising dawn, unless you prefer to say "dawning" as meaning "approaching." Moreover, the women may be said to have gone out indifferently in the evening, at night, in the morning or by day; they went out very early, or at the very dawn of morning, while it was still dark. As Gellius observes, book 7, chapter 21: When two times are opposed to each other and so joined that the end of one blends with the beginning of the other, it does not matter whether the boundary itself is pointed out by the extremity of the first or by the beginning of the next.

units.la: Sabbati. Græcè, σαββάτων, est Enallage numeri familiaris Hellenistis, ut Hebræam vocem שבתון reddant, σάββατα, ut videre est Exod. 16. v. 10. & c. 20. v. 10. & alibi passim. Unde optimè Vulgatus interpres vertit τ σαββάτων per genitivum singularem bis in præsenti versiculo; neque raro in novo novo Testamento legimus τὰς σαββάτων evenisse, quod uno Sabbato evenit. Vocatur autem illud Sabbatum crucifixionem Christi mox subsequens Joan. 19. v. 31. Magna dies Sabbati, quia apud Judaeos nullum fuit festum, in quod non quadrafet hoc epitheton. Joan. 7. v. 37. Magna dies festi vocatur ultima Scenopegiae, quae tamen supra primam nihil habuit. Esa. 1. v. 13. ubi Hebraice habetur, Novilunium & Sabbatum & solemnem convocationem non feram. Graeci hab.nt: Neomenias veteras & Sabbata, & diem magnam non feram. Proinde ad hunc Esaiae locum Procopius asserit magnam diem appellari diem quamlibet in Lege Κλητὴ (à populi convocatione) dictam, ut azymorum prima & septima, & Pentecoste, & decima mensis (Tisri) & uno verbo, festa quaevis solemnia; itaque nulla est dies sacris coetibus convocandis destinata, quae non pro magna haberi debeat, ideoque omne Sabbatum magnum dici poterit, & in primis, si in aliquem azymorum diem incidat ad quorum celebrationem Jerosolymam undequaque confluebant Judaei omnes. Tamen hodie Judaei Sabbatum magnum vocant, non quod in Paschales dies incidit, sed quod illos proxime praecedit, cujus appellationis ratio fabulosa est in Synagoga Buxtorfii c. 12.
units.tr: Sabbath. In Greek σαββάτων (sabbaton, plural), [sabbaths], is a change of number familiar to the Hellenists, by which they render the Hebrew word שבתון, as σάββατα, as can be seen in Exodus 16, verse 10, and chapter 20, verse 10, and in many other places. Hence the Vulgate translator rightly renders τῶν σαββάτων by the genitive singular twice in the present verse. Nor is it rare in the New Testament to read that τὰς σαββάτων ("the Sabbaths") happened in one Sabbath. That Sabbath which immediately followed Christ's crucifixion is called in John 19, verse 31, a great day of the Sabbath, since among the Jews there was no festival to which this epithet did not fit. In John 7, verse 37, the last day of the Feast of Tabernacles is called the great day of the feast, though it had nothing greater than the first. Compare Isaiah 1, verse 13, where the Hebrew reads: New moon and Sabbath and the solemn assembly I will not bear. The Greeks have: The old new moons and Sabbaths, and the great day I will not bear. Accordingly, on this passage of Isaiah, Procopius asserts that "great day" is applied to any day called "convocation" (Κλητὴ, from the calling of the people) in the Law, such as the first and seventh of the unleavened bread, Pentecost, the tenth of the month (Tishri), and, in a word, any solemn festival. So there is no day appointed for holy assemblies that should not be held to be a great day; hence every Sabbath may be called a great one, and especially if it falls on one of the days of unleavened bread, for whose celebration all the Jews flocked to Jerusalem from every quarter. Yet today the Jews call the Sabbath great not because it falls on the Passover days but because it immediately precedes them; the reason for this name is a fable, as told in Buxtorf's Synagoga, chapter 12.

units.la: Qua luce scit. Id est, ut diximus, quae advenit, vel quae illucescenti aurorae locum facit.
units.tr: Which dawns. That is, as we have said, which arrives, or which makes room for the dawning day.

units.la: In prima. Graece, in unam, quod est Hebraismus; apud Hebraeos enim numerus Cardinalis passim ponitur pro numero ordinali. Sic Genes. 1. v. 5. dicitur, Factumque est vespere & mane dies unus; hic autem Hebraismus servatus est etiam in textu Latino apud ceteros tres Evangelistas.
units.tr: On the first. In Greek εἰς μίαν ("into one"), which is a Hebraism; for among the Hebrews the cardinal number is often used in place of the ordinal. So Genesis 1, verse 5 says: And there was evening and morning, one day. This Hebraism has been kept in the Latin text of the other three Evangelists too.

units.la: Sabbati. Id est, Hebdomadae; nam vox Sabbaton sumitur & pro die septima Hebdomadis, & pro Hebdomade; 1. modo sumitur principio praesentis versiculi. 2. sensu sumitur quoties praeceditur ab aliquo numero ordinali, & interdum etiam ubi non praeceditur ab hujusmodi numero; sicut in illo dicto Pharisaei apud Luc. c. 18. Jejuno bis in Sabbato. In veteri Calendario Romano à Doctissimo Academiae Parisiensis Cancellario Joanne Frontone in lucem edito & eruditissimis notis illustrato Hebdomada dicitur pro die Dominica; ita ut cum apud Hebraeos Hebdomada appelletur nomine Sabbati, apud Christianos è contra dies Dominica designata fuerit nomine Hebdomadae, quia Dominicae officium toti inservit Hebdomadae, uti observat idem Fronto. pag. 14. & 74. modo citati operis.
units.tr: Of the Sabbath. That is, of the week; for the word Sabbaton is taken both for the seventh day of the week and for the week. First, it is taken in this sense at the beginning of the present verse. Second, it is taken in the sense of week whenever it is preceded by an ordinal number, and sometimes even where it is not preceded by such a number, as in the saying of the Pharisee in Luke 18: I fast twice in the Sabbath. In the old Roman Calendar, published by the most learned Chancellor of the Paris Academy, John Fronto, and illustrated with very learned notes, week is used for the Lord's Day. So, while among the Hebrews the week is named by the name of Sabbath, among Christians, on the contrary, the Lord's Day has been designated by the name of week, because the office of the Lord's Day serves the whole week, as Fronto himself observes, pp. 14 and 74 of the work just cited.

units.la: Venit. Id est, secundum Dionysium Alexandrinum, ad veniendum se accinxit; secundum Augustum vero advenit. Nam Dionysius Alexand. in Epist. ad Basilidem vult mulieres nocte subsequente Sabbati diem valde diluculo suscepisse iter ad monumentum Christi, cùm scilicet adhuc essent tenebræ, sed ad sepulchrum non advenisse, nisi orto jam sole, ut habet Marcus. Secundum Aug. verò, cui libentius subscribimus, vespere seu nocte subsequente Sabbatum, jam illucescenti auroræ locum faciente, seu ut Marcus loquitur, valde mane, orto jam sole, id est, proximo adveniente in has partes sole, seu ortu suo jam cœlum illuminare incipiente (ad hunc enim sensum referri potest dictio Græca ἀνατολὴ, quasi dicat, cùm sol jam ad Orientem accessisset; est enim Græcis ἀνατολὴ Oriens) seu ut Lucas, valde diluculo, seu ut Joannes, cùm adhuc tenebræ essent, veniunt mulieres ad monumentum. Ut autem jam observavi ex Gellio, indifferenter dici potest accidisse diu vel noctu, quod accidit in illo temporis articulo, quo quàm proximè conjunguntur illæ duæ partes integrantes diei naturalis.
units.tr: Came. That is, according to Dionysius of Alexandria, they girded themselves to go; but according to Augustine they arrived. For Dionysius of Alexandria, in his Letter to Basilides, holds that the women, in the night following the Sabbath, set out very early on the way to Christ's tomb, while it was still dark, but did not arrive at the sepulchre until the sun had already risen, as Mark has it. According to Augustine, to whom we more willingly subscribe, they came in the evening or night following the Sabbath, which was making room for the dawn now breaking, or, as Mark puts it, very early in the morning, the sun having already risen, that is, the sun approaching these regions and already beginning to light the sky by its rising (for the Greek word ἀνατολή can be referred to this sense, as if to say that the sun had already come near the East; for ἀνατολή means the East to the Greeks); or, as Luke has it, at the break of day; or, as John has it, while it was still dark, the women come to the tomb. But as I have already observed from Gellius, it may indifferently be said to have happened by day or by night, since it happened at that point in time where the two parts that make up the natural day are most closely joined.

units.la: Maria Magdalene & altera Maria, Addit Marcus, & Salome.
units.tr: Mary Magdalene and the other Mary, Mark adds: and Salome.

units.la: Videre. An scilicet ingredi possent sepulchrum Christum unctúræ amoto lapide; nam de hoc fuisse sollicitas patet ex earum discursu apud Marcum c. 16. v. 3. Hunc versiculum Evangelistarum interpres Juvencus Presbyter sic expressit: Sydera jam noctis vicino cedere soli Incipiunt: tumuli matres tum visere septum.
units.tr: To see. Namely, whether they could enter the sepulchre to anoint Christ once the stone was moved; for that they were anxious about this is clear from their haste in Mark 16, verse 3. The Presbyter Juvencus, the poet who put the Evangelists into verse, expressed this verse thus: The stars of night begin to yield to the nearby sun; then the mothers come to see the closed tomb.

units.la: 2. Et ecce. Supple, cùm essent in itinere, & dicerent ad invicem, Quis nobis revolvet lapidem ob ostio monumenti, ut dicitur Marc. 16. v. 3. cùm enim ad monumentum advenissent, viderunt revolutum lapidem, ut dicitur ibidem versu 4.
units.tr: 2. And behold. Supply: while they were on the way and said to one another, Who will roll away the stone from the door of the tomb for us?, as is said in Mark 16, verse 3. For when they had arrived at the tomb, they saw the stone rolled away, as is said in the same place, verse 4.

units.la: Revolvit lapidem. Græce additur, ab ostio, scilicet monumenti.
units.tr: Rolled away the stone. The Greek adds from the door, namely of the tomb.

units.la: 5. Respondens. Id est, loqui incipiens, de quo Hebraismo alibi diximus.
units.tr: 5. Answering. That is, beginning to speak, a Hebraism of which we have spoken elsewhere.

units.la: 8. Exierunt. Hoc vocabulo significatur mulieres fuisse ingressas monumentum, ut dicitur Marc. 16. v. 5, contrarium tamen videtur indicare Matth. hîc v. 5. quasi Angelus super lapidem sederit extra monumentum, & invitaverit mulieres ut intrarent, cùm Marcus dicat mulieres ingressas in monumentum, & ibi Angelum vidisse. Vera solutio pendet à forma monumenti. Constat autem ex descriptione Brocardi, & eâ quam nuperrimè fecit Legatus Regis Franciæ, sepulchrum esse velut cubiculum fere quadratum ex petra excisum, septem plus minus pedum longitudine & altitudine. Ostium habet valde demissum ad Orientem. Ad dexteram, id est, ad latus boreale habet loculum instar mensæ valde demissum, cui Corpus Domini impositum fuit. Porrò antequàm speluncam seu cubiculum istud ingrediaris, occurrit alia crypta ejusdem figuræ, & magnitudinis, solo pariete ab illa altera separata, in quo pariete fuit ostium illud parvum, de quo dictum est. Sic ergo facile intelligitur lapidem ab ostio revolutum fuisse ab Angelo, ita quidem ut esset extra monumentum, in quo fuerat Corpus Domini; intra tamen prout complectitur etiam illam anteriorem cryptam, & in illo lapide ad dexteram revoluto sedit Angelus, quasi sepulchri interioris custos, tum demum conspicuus factus mulieribus, cum Petrus & Joannes rediissent ad semetipsos, ut plenius explicabimus Marc. 16. ubi & consonantiam Evangelistarum de Domini apparitionibus quinque primis, quae ipsa die resurrectionis evenerunt, fuse dicemus.
units.tr: 8. Went out. By this word it is signified that the women had gone into the tomb, as is said in Mark 16, verse 5. Matthew here, verse 5, seems however to indicate the opposite, as if the Angel had sat upon the stone outside the tomb and invited the women to enter; whereas Mark says that the women went into the tomb and there saw the Angel. The true solution depends on the form of the tomb. It is clear from the description of Brocardus, and from that which the Legate of the King of France lately made, that the sepulchre is like a chamber, nearly square, hewn out of rock, about seven feet more or less in length and height. Its door is set very low, facing East. On the right, that is, on the north side, it has a niche like a table, set very low, on which the Body of the Lord was laid. Moreover, before you enter this cave or chamber, you meet another crypt of the same shape and size, separated from the other only by a wall, in which wall was that small door of which we have spoken. So it is easily understood that the stone was rolled away from the door by the Angel, in such a way that it was outside the tomb in which the Body of the Lord had lain; yet inside, as it also enclosed that front crypt. And the Angel sat on that stone, rolled to the right, as a guardian of the inner sepulchre, and became visible to the women only when Peter and John had returned to themselves, as we shall explain more fully at Mark 16, where we shall also set out at length the agreement of the Evangelists about the first five appearances of the Lord, which took place on the very day of the resurrection.

units.la: 9. Jesus accurrit illis. Decies Christus apparuit post resurrectionem. 1o. Mariae Magdalenae sub specie Hortulani, Marc. 16. & Joan. 20. 2o. Reliquis mulieribus, de qua apparitione hic Matth. 3o. Petro, Luc. 24. 4o. Euntibus in Emaus, Marc. 16. & Luc. 24. 5o. Omnibus Apostolis simul, cum abesset Thomas, Marc. 16. Luc. 24. Joan. 20. haecque fuit ultima quae contigit ipsa die resurrectionis. 6o. Post dies octo undecim Apostolis simul, Joan. 20. 7o. Ad mare Tiberiadis Joan. 21. 8o. In Galilaeae monte plusquam quingentis fratribus simul, de qua apparitione hic Matth. v. 16. Apost.
units.tr: 9. Jesus ran to them. Christ appeared ten times after the resurrection: (1) to Mary Magdalene in the guise of a gardener, Mark 16 and John 20; (2) to the other women, concerning which appearance see here Matt. 3o.; (3) to Peter, Luke 24; (4) to the two going to Emmaus, Mark 16 and Luke 24; (5) to all the Apostles together, when Thomas was absent, Mark 16, Luke 24, John 20. This was the last appearance on the day of the resurrection itself; (6) after eight days, to the eleven Apostles together, John 20; (7) at the Sea of Tiberias, John 21; (8) on a mountain in Galilee, to more than five hundred brethren at once, concerning which appearance see here Matt. v. 16, Apost.

units.la: 1 Cor. 15. v. 6. 9o. Jacobo, Denique Apostolis omnibus in Jerusalem, 1 Cor. 15. v. 7.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 15. v. 6. (9) To James; finally, to all the Apostles in Jerusalem, 1 Cor. 15. v. 7.

units.la: 17. Dubitaverunt. Scilicet ante id tempus, est itaque dubitaverunt pro dubitaverant.
units.tr: 17. They doubted. That is, before that time. So dubitaverunt stands for dubitaverant, the pluperfect.

units.la: 18. Data est, &c. Q. d. Data est mihi ut homini authoritas quae ad universa se extendit, & ego non amplius secundum corporalem praesentiam cum hominibus conversaturus, vobis meam potestatem committo, ut non jam ad solas oves quae perierunt domus Israel, sed ad omnes totius mundi nationes eatis, eaque veltra doctrina mea ditioni subjiciatis, & deinde ubi fidei fuscperint veritatem, mundetis eas lavacro aquae in verbo vitae.
units.tr: 18. Authority has been given, etc. The sense is this: "Authority has been given to me as a man, and it extends over all things. Since I am no longer to live among men in bodily presence, I commit my power to you, so that you may go not only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel but to all the nations of the whole world, and bring them under my rule by your teaching; and then, when they have received the truth of the faith, you may cleanse them in the bath of water in the word of life."

units.la: 19. Docete omnes gentes. Non hic amplius secundum Legalis typicique cultus angustias audimus, Non intrabit Ammonita Ecclesiam Dei, aut Moabita: sed audimus, In omni gente, qui timet Deum, & operatur justitiam, acceptus est illi.
units.tr: 19. Make disciples of all nations. Here we no longer hear of the narrow limits of the legal and typical worship, "An Ammonite or a Moabite shall not enter the Church of God"; instead we hear, "In every nation, he who fears God and works righteousness is acceptable to him."

units.la: In nomine. Id est, in virtute, efficacia, authoritate, quae una est in Patre, Filio, & Spiritu-Sancto, licet Pater, & Filius, & Spiritus-Sanctus sint personaliter distincti. Vel potius baptizare in aliquem, seu aliquo, in nomen vel nomine alicujus est baptismo aliquem alteri auctorare, & devovere: unde Apostoli leguntur baptizasse in nomine Christi, Domini Jesu, Domini Jesu Christi; unde & illud Apost. Rom. 6. Quicunque baptizati sumus fumus in Christo Jesu, in morte ipsius baptizati sumus, id est, quicumque per baptismum Christo sumus auctorati, & devoti. Et idem, 1 Cor. 1. Nunquid in nomine Pauli baptizati estis? id est, nunquid Paulo per baptismum estis consecrati? Hinc possumus dici indifferenter baptizati in nomine Patris vel Filii, vel Spiritus Sancti, licet dum administratur baptismus soleat ex institutu Christi administrari in nomine Patris & Filii & Spiritus-Sancti. Secundum Hilarium lib. 2. de Trin. in nomine, id est, in confessione.
units.tr: In the name. That is, in the power, efficacy and authority which is one in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, although the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are personally distinct. Or rather, to baptize into or in the name of someone is, by baptism, to bind a person to another and devote him to him. Hence the Apostles are read to have baptized in the name of Christ, of the Lord Jesus, of the Lord Jesus Christ. Hence also that saying of the Apostle, Rom. 6: "As many of us as were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death," that is, as many as were bound and devoted to Christ by baptism. Likewise 1 Cor. 1: "Were you baptized in the name of Paul?" that is, were you consecrated to Paul by baptism? Hence we may be said indifferently to be baptized in the name of the Father, or of the Son, or of the Holy Spirit, although when baptism is administered it is customary, by the institution of Christ, to administer it in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. According to Hilary, book 2 On the Trinity, "in the name" means "in the confession."

units.la: Docentes eos, &c. Fidem ante baptismum, mores post baptismum jubentur docere, quem pulchrum ordinem hic observa B. Hieron. nam neque fides, neque baptisma satis ad salutem sunt, nisi digna Deo accesserit conversatio.
units.tr: Teaching them, etc. They are ordered to teach faith before baptism and morals after baptism. Observe this beautiful order here, as Blessed Jerome does; for neither faith nor baptism is enough for salvation unless a conduct worthy of God follows.

units.la: Omnia. Non haec, non illa, sed omnia, ut observat B. Basil. proœmio in Regul. fusius disputatas.
units.tr: All things. Not this, not that, but all things, as Blessed Basil observes in the preface to the Rules, where the matter is discussed more fully.

units.la: 20. Ecce ego vobiscum sum, &c. Omnibus Apostolis, eorumque successoribus in officio pastorali pariter facta est hic promissio perpetuae praesentiae Christi secundum providentiam, & secundum ineffabilem, & invisibilem gratiam. Neque ulla locorum, personarumque decedentium, vel succedentium diversitas discriminat potestatem ministerii ordinariam Apostolis datam, & ab eis ad successores pari autoritate transmissam. Hinc, ubicumque fuerit Episcopus, sive Romae, sive Eugubii, sive Constantinopoli, sive Rhegii, sive Alexandriae, sive Tanis, ejusdem meriti, ejusdem est sacerdotii. Potentia divitiarum, & pauperitatis humilitas vel sublimiorem, vel inferiorem Episcopum non facit. Ceterum omnes Apostolorum successores sunt, inquit Hier in Ep. ad Evagrium, quae incipit, Legimus in Esaia.
units.tr: 20. Behold, I am with you, etc. Here the promise of Christ's perpetual presence, according to his providence and his ineffable and invisible grace, is made equally to all the Apostles and to their successors in the pastoral office.
