Nor does any difference of places or persons, whether those who depart or those who succeed, diminish the ordinary ministerial power given to the Apostles and handed on by them to their successors with equal authority. Hence: "Wherever a bishop may be, whether at Rome, or at Gubbio, or at Constantinople, or at Reggio, or at Alexandria, or at Tanis, he is of the same worth and of the same priesthood. The power of wealth and the humility of poverty do not make a bishop higher or lower. Moreover, all are successors of the Apostles,"* says Jerome in the letter to Evagrius that begins "We read in Isaiah."

units.la: F I N I S. CHRISTO JESU AUTORI, ET CONSUMMATORI FIDEI SACRUM, ECCLESIÆ ANGLICANÆ ET CUJUSVIS ORTHODOXÆ JUDICIO, HOC QUICQUID EST OPERIS AUTHOR EX ANIMO SUBJICIT.
units.tr: THE END. Sacred to Christ Jesus, the author and finisher of faith; to the judgment of the English Church and of any orthodox reader, the author submits from his heart whatever this work is.

units.la: Semper agam grates Christo, dabo semper honores,Laus Domini semper vivet in ore meo.
units.tr: I will always give thanks to Christ, I will always give honour; the praise of the Lord will always live on my lips.

units.la: Explicatio Literalis EVANGELII SECUNDUM MARCUM.
units.tr: Literal Explanation of the Gospel according to Mark.

units.la: MARCI mentionem sæpè habent Actus Apostolorum & B. Pauli Epistolæ; sed quòd Evangelicæ historiæ scriptoris ea mentio sit Divo Hieronymo visum videtur, id tamen non apparet; Evangelii quippe scriptor is esse potiùs videtur, quem sub primæ suæ Epistolæ finem D. Petrus filium suum appellat. Is Alexandriæ Ecclesiam, secundam olim orbis Christiani Sedem, fundavit; ipsúmque Romæ, Christianis compellentibus, Evangelium scripsisse: communis est Sanctorum Patrum & Eusebii sententia. Quòd autem id, ut Lucas & Joannes, Græco idiomate conscripserit, testatur cum D. Hieronymo S. Augustinus, Patrúmque maxima pars. Matthæum in multis proximè secutus est, in pluribus solummodò contraxit, in quibusdam tamen Matthæo fusior est, & scitu dignissimas nonnunquam rerum circumstantias inter Evangelistas solus commemorat. Evangelii sui historiam, quâ à B. Petro audierat, eâdem ratione recensuit. Mortuus est autem, ut refert B. Hieronymus, octavo Neronis anno, & sepultus Alexandriæ, succedente ipsi Aniano. Circa annum à Christo nato DCCCXLI. hujus Evangelistæ corpus à Justiniano Duce Venetias translatum perhibetur.
units.tr: Mark is often mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles and in the Epistles of St Paul. That the mention refers to the writer of the Gospel history seemed so to Saint Jerome, though this does not clearly appear. The writer of the Gospel seems rather to be the one whom St Peter calls his son near the end of his first Epistle. He founded the congregation at Alexandria, once the second see of the Christian world, and it is the common opinion of the holy Fathers and of Eusebius that at the urging of the Christians he wrote his Gospel at Rome. That he wrote in Greek, as Luke and John did, is attested by Saint Augustine together with Saint Jerome, and by the greater part of the Fathers. He followed Matthew closely in most things, abridged him in many places, but in some is fuller than Matthew, and sometimes alone records circumstances of events most worthy of being known. He set down the history of his Gospel in the same manner in which he had heard it from St Peter. He died, as Saint Jerome reports, in the eighth year of Nero, and was buried at Alexandria, Anianus succeeding him. Around the year 841 after the birth of Christ, the body of this evangelist is said to have been translated to Venice by the Doge Justinian.

units.la: SANCTUM JESU CHRISTI EVANGELIUM SECUNDUM MARCUM.
units.tr: THE HOLY GOSPEL OF JESUS CHRIST ACCORDING TO MARK.

units.la: CAPUT I. VERS. I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I, VERSE 1.

units.la: INitium, &c. Sensus est, narraturus lætissimum illud nuntium de redemtione generis humani, quod in mundum attulit Jesus Christus consubstantialis Dei Filius, à prædicatione Joannis exordium duco, quem ut Evangelii Præcursorem, ita quasi initium fuisse futurum, jam olim à Prophetis erat scripto consignatum.
units.tr: Initium, etc. The sense is: intending to narrate that most joyful message concerning the redemption of mankind, which Jesus Christ, the Son of God consubstantial with the Father, brought into the world, I take the beginning from the preaching of John, whom, as the forerunner of the Gospel, it had already been written by the Prophets that he would be, as it were, its beginning.

units.la: 2. Sicut scriptum est. Vide dicta à nobis Matth. 27. v. 9.Mitto Angelum, &c. Vide Matth. 11. v. 10.
units.tr: 2. As it is written. See what we have said on Matt. 27:9. I send my messenger, etc. See Matt. 11:10.

units.la: 3. Vox clamantis, & cætera quæ sequuntur usque ad versum duodecimum, exposita sunt Matth. 3.
units.tr: 3. The voice of one crying, and the rest that follows, up to the twelfth verse, has been explained at Matt. 3.

units.la: 4. Baptizans, & prædicans. Hoc καθ' ὑσεγν τεῖτιεν dictum est; neque enim Joannes vocationem à baptismo ordiebatur: sed, uti Apostoli postea fecerunt, ita ipse etiam priùs prædicabat pœnitentiam, Mat. 3. v. 2. fidem in Christum pro peccatis totius mundi in cruce immolandum Joan. 1. v. 29. & studium bonorum operum, Luc. 3. v. 8. deinde in sigillum doctrinæ suæ de remissione peccatorum credentibus in Christum venturum & peccata mundi sublaturum, sincereque pœnitentibus, & dignos pœnitentiæ fructus facientibus certò concedendâ baptizabat in nomine, hoc est, confessione, atque invocatione Dei, qui unus est natura, & trinus personis, à quo jussus erat baptizare, ut dicitur Luc. 3. v. 2. & 3. Joan. 1. v. 33. Hinc ubi temporis ordo servatur, prædicatio quidem pœnitentiæ, hæc autem baptismo Joannis præponitur, ut videre est, Mat. 3. v. 1, 2, & 3. Luc. 3. v. 3, & 7.
units.tr: 4. Baptizing and preaching. This is said by way of an afterthought [καθ' ὕστερον]; for John did not begin his calling from baptism, but, as the Apostles afterwards did, he too first preached repentance (Matt. 3:2), faith in Christ, who was to be sacrificed on the cross for the sins of the whole world (John 1:29), and zeal for good works (Luke 3:8). Then, as a seal of his teaching concerning the remission of sins, he baptized in the name of the one who was to come and take away the sins of the world, those who believed in Christ and who sincerely repented and bore fruits worthy of repentance, to be granted with certainty; that is, in the confession and invocation of God, who is one in nature and three in persons, by whom he had been commanded to baptize, as is said in Luke 3:2–3 and John 1:33. Hence, where the order of time is observed, the preaching of repentance comes first and baptism with John's baptism follows, as can be seen in Matt. 3:1, 2, 3 and Luke 3:3, 7.

units.la: 5. Baptizabantur. Gregorius Hieromonachus Alexandrinæ Ecclesiæ Primicerius, ac Philothei Patriarchæ ad Florentinam Synodum Vicarius atque Legatus, in ejusdem Concilii historia apud Sylvestrum Sguropulum, Sect. 9. cap. 9. contendit baptisma dici mersionem, ad quam sequitur emersio; catabaptisma vero proprie dici demersionem, quâ quid pessum ire, scu, ad sui exitium fundum petere cogitur. Hinc adversus Parmenianum Carthaginensem Donatistarum Episcopum, qui Christi carnem dixerat Jordanis demersam diluvio, Scripsit E. Optatus Milevitanus Antistes: Satis inconsiderate hoc usus es verbo. Quod verbum soli Pharaoni & ejus populo debebatur, qui pondere delictorum, tanquam plumbum, ita mersus sit, ut ibi remanserit, Christi autem caro, dum in Jordanem descendit, & ascendit, demersa à te dici non debuit.
units.tr: 5. They were baptized. Gregory, a Hieromonk, Chief Cantor of the Alexandrian Church and Vicar and Legate of Patriarch Philotheus at the Council of Florence, in his history of that Council, quoted by Sylvester Syropoulos (Sect. 9, cap. 9), contends that baptisma means immersion, to which emersion follows; but katabaptisma properly means submersion, by which something is forced to sink to the bottom, or to seek the bottom to its own destruction. Hence, against Parmenianus, the Donatist Bishop of Carthage, who had said that the flesh of Christ was submerged by the flood of the Jordan, the Bishop Optatus of Milevis wrote: You used this word quite thoughtlessly. This word was owed only to Pharaoh and his people, who, weighed down by the burden of their sins like lead, were so submerged that they remained there; but the flesh of Christ, when it went down into the Jordan and came up again, ought not to have been called submerged by you.

units.la: 8. Ego baptizo, &c. Q. d. Ego quidem in remissionem peccatorum morte Christi impetrandam abluo vos aquâ naturali; at Christus aquâ spirituali extraordinariè vos abluet effusione visibili donorum, quæ Spiritûs nomine in Scripturis signantur.
units.tr: 8. I baptize, etc. That is: I indeed wash you with natural water for the remission of sins to be obtained by the death of Christ; but Christ will wash you extraordinarily with spiritual water, by the visible outpouring of those gifts which in the Scriptures are signified by the name of the Spirit.

units.la: Baptizabit. Apud Græcos autores ordinariè βαπτίζειν est mergere ac tingere. Sed quià aliquid mergi solet ac tingi, ut lavetur atque abluatur, βαπτίζειν pro abluere usurpatur Judith 12. v. 7. Ecclesiastici 34. v. 30. Luc. 11. v. 33. κατὰ μεταφορὰν· Ut autem ab ordinaria significatione fluxit metaphora quâ βαπτίζειν pro affligere usurpatur, quòd, qui affliguntur, quasi calamitatum gurgite mergantur & absorbeantur, ut videre est. Ps. 17. Heb. 18. v. 17. 31. Heb. 32. v. 6. 68. Heb. 69. v. 1. 15, & 16. Sic ab altera significatione, quâ βαπτίζειν abluere significat transfertur ad donationem Spiritus-Sancti, qui ut animam imbuat, & abluat, aquæ instar in eam effunditur, quomodo loquitur Joel c. 2. v. 28. Petrus Act. 11. v. 17. & Paulus Tit. 3. v. 6. Atque ita Christo interprete Act. 1. v. 5. & Petro Act 11. v. 16. Joannes metaphoricè dixit Christum baptizaturum SpirituSancto, prædicens visibilem ab ipso faciendam donorum effusionem, quæ facta narratur à Luca Act. 2. v. 3. Porro quemadmodum, teste B. Philastrio, quia Joannes dixerat Matth. 3. Christum igni baptizaturum, Hermius & Seleucus baptismo aquæ uti nolebant, Sic Pauliciani Manichæi, teste Euthymio Panopliæ parte 2 Tit. 21. quia Joannes dixit Christum baptizaturum Spiritu-sancto, res materiales in sacramentis aversabantur, & usum aquæ refugientes in baptismo, horum duntaxat verborum, Ego sum aqua viva, prolatione perficiebant baptismi sacramentum. Hos Paulicianos alios esse à Paulianis, seu Paulianistis, etsi Balsamo eos confundat, ex Cedreno, Matthæo Blastare, & Historia miscella evicit doctissimus Justellus notis in Codicem canonum Ecclesiæ universæ ad Can. 15.
units.tr: He will baptize. Among Greek authors, βαπτίζειν ordinarily means to dip [mergere] and to dye [tingere]. But because things are usually dipped and dyed in order to be washed and cleansed, βαπτίζειν is used for to wash [abluere] in Judith 12:7, Ecclesiasticus 34:30, and Luke 11:38, by metaphor. Moreover, from the ordinary meaning arose the metaphor by which βαπτίζειν is used for to afflict [affligere], because those who are afflicted are, as it were, plunged and swallowed up in a whirlpool of calamities, as can be seen in Ps. 17, Heb. 18:17, 31; Heb. 32:6; 68, Heb. 69:1, 15, 16. Likewise, from the other meaning, in which βαπτίζειν signifies to wash [abluere], it is transferred to the gift of the Holy Spirit, who is poured out upon the soul like water to imbue and cleanse it, as Joel says in chapter 2:28, Peter in Acts 11:17, and Paul in Titus 3:6. And so, with Christ as interpreter (Acts 1:5) and Peter (Acts 11:16), John spoke metaphorically of Christ baptizing with the Holy Spirit, foretelling the visible outpouring of gifts that Luke relates was done in Acts 2:3. Furthermore, just as, according to the blessed Philastrius, because John had said in Matt. 3 that Christ would baptize with fire, Hermius and Seleucus were unwilling to use the baptism of water, so too the Paulicians, the Manichaeans, according to Euthymius (Panoplia, part 2, title 21), because John said that Christ would baptize with the Holy Spirit, held material things in aversion in the sacraments, and, shunning the use of water in baptism, completed the sacrament of baptism merely by pronouncing these words: I am the living water. That these Paulicians are other than the Paulians, or Paulianists, although Balsamon confuses them, the most learned Justellus has proved from Cedrenus, Matthew Blastares, and the Historia miscella, in his notes on the Code of the canons of the universal Church, on Canon 15.

units.la: 9. Baptizatus est à Joanne in Jordane. Scilicet, nequis sub ullius sanctimoniæ, quam antebaptismum haberet, prætextu, aversetur baptismum aquæ veræ & naturalis, quali Joannes & Apostoli baptizasse tradunt Scripturæ. Non enim sola fides conversioque cordis ad salutem sufficit, nisi ubi articulus necessitatis aquam exclusit, non contemtus religionis, ut post Aug. loquitur Petrus Blesensis Ser. 24. in festo S. Jacobi. Quamvis autem, Tertullianus ait Lib. De baptismo, cap. 4. Nulla distinctio est, mari quis an flagno, flumine an fonte, lacu an alveo diluatur; neque quicquam refert inter eos, quos Joannes in Jordane, & Petrus in Tiberi tinxit, tamen, ut sanctimonia baptismi loco ipso, ubi baptizari voluit Christus, magis & efficacius Christi & baptismi ejus memoriam ob oculos poneret, multos in ipso Jordane baptizari voluisse in libro De locis Hebraicis ab Hieronymo translato testatur Eusebius, qui & id desideratum à Constantino in ejus vita lib. 4. cap 61. asserit. Hinc ab Episcopo Jerosolymitano fuisse Clerum præfectum baptizandis in Jordane advenis refert in Prato spirituali Joannes Moschus, qui sexto Ecclesiæ seculo vixit.
units.tr: 9. He was baptized by John in the Jordan. Namely, lest anyone, under the pretext of some holiness which they might have before baptism, should reject the baptism of true and natural water, with which Scripture tells us John and the Apostles baptized. For faith and conversion of heart alone do not suffice for salvation, except where the article of necessity has excluded water, not contempt of religion, as Peter of Blois says after Augustine (Sermon 24, on the feast of St James). Although Tertullian says in his book On Baptism, chapter 4: There is no difference whether one is washed in the sea or in a pool, in a river or in a spring, in a lake or in a channel; nor does it matter for those whom John dipped in the Jordan and Peter in the Tiber, yet Eusebius, in the book On the Hebrew Places translated by Jerome, testifies that many wished to be baptized in the Jordan itself, so that the holiness of the very place where Christ willed to be baptized might set before their eyes more vividly and effectively the memory of Christ and of his baptism; and Eusebius also asserts that Constantine desired this, in his Life (Book 4, chapter 61). Hence John Moschus, who lived in the sixth century of the Church, relates in the Spiritual Meadow that the Bishop of Jerusalem had appointed clergy to baptize newcomers in the Jordan.

units.la: 12. Statim expulit, & cætera quæ sequuntur usque ad versum vigesimum primum, exposita sunt Matth. 4.
units.tr: 12. Immediately he drove out, and the rest that follows, up to the twenty-first verse, has been explained at Matt. 4.

units.la: 21. Statim Sabbatis. Hellenismus, id est, Sabbato; non enim tamdiu Capharnai mansisse Christum, ut per plura Sabbata ibi docere potuisset, satis patet ex versu 38. & ex Luc. 4. v. 42. De similibus Hellenismis, vide Matth. 28. v. 1.
units.tr: 21. Immediately on the Sabbaths. A Hellenism, that is, on the Sabbath; for it is sufficiently clear from verse 38 and from Luke 4:42 that Christ did not remain at Capernaum long enough to teach there over several Sabbaths. On similar Hellenisms, see Matt. 28:1.

units.la: 22. Stupebant, &c. Vide Matth. 7. v.28. & 29.
units.tr: 22. They were astonished, etc. See Matt. 7:28–29.

units.la: 23. Erat in Synagoga eorum homo in spiritu immundo, &c. Id est, ut explicat Lucas. c. 4. v. 33. habens dæmonium immundum. Sic Galli eum esse in febre dicunt, qui febre tenetur seu laborat.
units.tr: 23. In their synagogue there was a man with an unclean spirit, etc. That is, as Luke explains (4:33), having an unclean demon. So the French say of one who is held by or suffers from a fever that he is in the fever.

units.la: 24. Quid nobis & tibi. Supple, rei. Luc. 4. v. 34. in textu Græco præponitur his verbis interjectio, Ε&, & in textu Latino sine, id est, permitte, supple, nobis torquere hunc hominem.
units.tr: 24. What have we to do with you? Supply: with the matter. In Luke 4:34, in the Greek text, these words are preceded by the interjection ea [ἔα], and in the Latin text by sine, that is, permit; supply: to torment this man for us.

units.la: Venisti perdere nos, &c. Exire ab homine perditionem suam vocant dæmones; sic nimirum se malum pati existimant crudeles, dum homines non torquent.
units.tr: You have come to destroy us, etc. Demons call going out of a man their destruction; for cruel spirits think they suffer harm when they do not torment men.

units.la: Scio. Hebraismus, id est, experior; nam experiebantur dæmones per effecta virtutis Christi ipsum esse fontem omnis sanctitatis, de cujus redundantia derivatur quidquid in hominibus est sanctitatis. Sic Paulus c. 3, ad Ephesios ait multiformem sapientiam Dei mediante suâ prædicatione per Ecclesiam esse manifestatam Principatibus & Potestatibus, id est, dæmoniis; quia per destructionem operum suorum experiebantur multiformem Dei sapientiam, excitatâ contra eos Ecclesiâ in Gentilitate ab ipsis tamdiu occupata & oppressa.
units.tr: I know. A Hebraism, that is, I experience; for the demons experienced, through the effects of Christ's power, that he himself is the fountain of all holiness, from whose overflow whatever holiness there is in men is derived. So Paul, in chapter 3 to the Ephesians, says that the manifold wisdom of God, through his preaching by the Church, has been made known to the Principalities and Powers, that is, to the demons; because through the destruction of their works they experienced the manifold wisdom of God, when the Church had been raised up among the Gentiles, which they had so long occupied and oppressed.

units.la: Sanctus Dei. Hebraismus, id est, infinitis & immensis intervallis superiorem quibusque creaturis habens sanctitatem, quæ definitur à B. Dionysio Areop. lib. de Divinis nominibus c. 12. ab omni scelere libera, perfecta & omnino immaculata puritas. Est autem, inquit Rabbi David Kimchi in illud Psal. 135. Justitia tua sicut montes Dei, ea lingua sanctæ consuetudo, cum rem aliquem eximiam vult demonstrare, ut illam cum Dei nomine conjungat. Idem in illud Psal. 79. Cedros Dei; Quam, inquit, rem vult Scriptura præ ceteris magnam, eam cum Dei nomine conjungit.
units.tr: Holy of God. A Hebraism, that is, one that has a holiness surpassing every creature by infinite and immeasurable distances. Blessed Dionysius the Areopagite defines it in the book On the Divine Names, chapter 12, as a perfect and wholly spotless purity, free from all wickedness. Rabbi David Kimchi, on Psalm 135, says: This is a holy custom of the language: when it wishes to show that something is outstanding, it joins it to the name of God. On Psalm 79, the cedars of God, he says: Whatever thing Scripture wishes to be great above others, it joins to the name of God.

units.la: 25 Comminatus est. Id est, minis adhibitis increpavit, unde Chrysost. Concion. 2. de Lazaro non longè à principio Christus, inquit, dicentes ipsi dæmones, Novimus te qui sis, increpavit multa cum acrimonia, nobis legem præscribens, ne quo pacto dæmoni credamus, licet veri aliquid dixerit; nam sana dogmata salutiferâque non à dæmonibus, sed ex divina Scriptura licet exactè discere.
units.tr: 25. He rebuked him. That is, he reproved him with threats. Hence Chrysostom, Sermon 2 on Lazarus, not far from the beginning: Christ, he says, rebuked the demons themselves, who said, "We know who you are," with great sharpness, laying down the law for us, that we should not believe the demon in any way, even though he said something true; for sound and saving doctrines may be learned exactly from divine Scripture, and not from demons.

units.la: Obmutesce. Immundum spiritum jubet Christus tacere, quia non est speciosa laus in ore peccatoris, &, ut ait B. Ambros. in Luc. 9. lib. 6. ne quis dum prædicantem audit, sequatur errantem; improbus enim magister est diabolus, qui salla veris sæpe permiscet, ut sub specie veritatis testimonium frau-dis dis obtexat. Hinc & Paulus dæmoniis tametsi vera dicentibus silentium imposuit Act. 16.
units.tr: Be silent. Christ commands the unclean spirit to be silent, because praise from the mouth of a sinner is not fitting, and, as Blessed Ambrose says in his commentary on Luke 9, book 6, lest anyone, while he hears the speaker, follow the one who errs; for the devil is a wicked teacher, who often mixes falsehoods with truths, so that under the appearance of truth he may cover the testimony of deceit. Hence Paul also imposed silence on demons, though they spoke true things (Acts 16).

units.la: 26. Discerpens. Id est, vehementi motu concutiens, quod forte Luc. c. 4. v. 35. expressit his verbis, cùm projecisset illum in medium.
units.tr: 26. Tearing. That is, shaking with violent motion, which Luke, chapter 4, verse 35, expresses in these words: when it had thrown him into the midst.

units.la: Exiit ab eo. Adde ex Luca, nihilque illum nocuit, ut loquitur Vulgatus interpres.
units.tr: Came out of him. Add from Luke: and it did him no harm, as the Vulgate translator puts it.

units.la: 27. Mirati. Nempe, admiratione religiosa, ut satis indicant quæ sequuntur, cujusmodi admiratio non solet esse sine timore.
units.tr: 27. Amazed. Namely, with a religious wonder, as what follows sufficiently indicates; a wonder of this kind is not usually without fear.

units.la: In potestate. Id est, cum potestate, seu tanquam potestatem habens.
units.tr: With authority. That is, with power, or as one having authority.

units.la: Quænam doctrina hæc nova. Quia Dominus ac Redemtor noster novus homo venit in mundum, nova præcepta dedit mundo. Vitæ etenim nostræ veteri in vitiis enutritæ contrarietatem opposuit novitatis suæ. Quid enim vetus, quid carnalis homo noverat, nisi ire post concupiscentias suas, neglectis æternis, ad temporales divitias & voluptates cor apponere, & abjectâ justitiæ servitute, diabolo & iniquitati servire? Sed his omnibus cœlestis medicus obviantia adhibet medicamenta, præcipiens pœnitentiam & fidem Evangelii, & miraculis suam doctrinam confirmans.
units.tr: What is this new doctrine? Because our Lord and Redeemer came into the world as a new man, he gave the world new precepts. For he set against our life, nourished in the vices of the old state, the contrariness of his own newness. For what did the old, carnal man know, except to go after his lusts, to set his heart on temporal riches and pleasures, neglecting the eternal, and, with the yoke of righteousness cast off, to serve the devil and iniquity? But the heavenly physician applies remedies against all these things, commanding repentance and faith in the Gospel, and confirming his teaching by miracles.

units.la: 38. Rumor. Id est, fama, ut habet Lucas. c. 4. v. 37.
units.tr: 28. Report. That is, fame, as Luke has it, chapter 4, verse 37.

units.la: 29. Et protinus, & cætera quæ sequuntur in præsenti capite exposita sunt à nobis Matth. 8.
units.tr: 29. And immediately, and the rest that follows in the present chapter has been explained by us on Matthew 8.

units.la: 34. Quoniam sciebant eum. Id est, experiebantur Christi potentiam, quam ipse dæmoniorum ministerio manifestari hominibus nolebat, ut suprà dictum est.
units.tr: 34. Because they knew him. That is, they experienced Christ's power, which he did not want to be made manifest to men through the ministry of demons, as was said above.

units.la: 43. Comminatus est ei. Id est, increpavit eum multa cum acrimonia, ut loquitur Chrysost. loco mox citato.
units.tr: 43. He rebuked him. That is, he reproved him with great sharpness, as Chrysostom says in the passage cited just above.

units.la: 44. Vide nemini dixeris. Non est prohibitio, sed humilitatis significatio, ad nostram instructionem; figuratus enim sermo est, quo significat se ex eo facto non quærerere suam gloriam; sicut alibi diserte dicit, Non quæro gloriam meam.
units.tr: 44. See that you say nothing to anyone. This is not a prohibition, but a sign of humility, for our instruction; for the saying is figurative, by which he signifies that he does not seek his own glory from that deed; as he says plainly elsewhere, I do not seek my own glory.

units.la: CAPUT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: I Post dies. Subauditur, aliquot. Ita Gr. & Syr. At Sixt. &c. Mf. habent post dies octo. Quæ habentur in præsenti capite, exposita sunt Matth. 9. & 12. capite.
units.tr: 1 After some days. Understand "some" (aliquot). So the Greek and Syriac; but Sixtus and other manuscripts read after eight days. What is contained in this chapter has been explained in Matthew 9 and 12.

units.la: 5. Vidisset. Supple, mfericorditer.
units.tr: 5 Had seen. Supply: out of mercy.

units.la: Fili dimittuntur, &c. Quemadmodum Christus hic rogatus ut paralysin sanaret, contulit & majus bonum remissionem videlcet peccatorum; ita Deus, quo spiritualem mundationem ac sanitatem faceret testatiorem interdum iis, qui baptizabantur, miraculose resituit corporis sanitatem. Sic ut cætera brevitatis causa omittam, Socrates narrat. lib. 8. Hist. cap. 4. Judæum, cum ab Attico Cp. baptizaretur, liberatum fuisse à paralysi.
units.tr: Son, your sins are forgiven, etc. Just as Christ, when asked here to heal the paralytic, also bestowed a greater good, namely the forgiveness of sins, so God, in order to make the spiritual cleansing and health more evident, sometimes restored bodily health miraculously to those who were being baptized. Thus, to omit the rest for the sake of brevity, Socrates relates (Hist. book 8, ch. 4) that a Jew, when he was baptized by an Attic bishop, was freed from paralysis.

units.la: 10. Filius hominis habet potestatem in terra dimittendi peccata. Non virtute humanæ naturæ, sed virtute naturæ Divinæ; in qua quidem natura Divina consistit potestas dimittendi peccata per autoritatem, in humana autem natura consistit instrumentaliter & per ministerium. D. Th. 3. p. q. 16. art. 11. ad 2um.
units.tr: 10 The Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins. Not by the power of human nature, but by the power of the divine nature; in which divine nature the power of forgiving sins by authority resides, while in the human nature it resides instrumentally and through ministry. Aquinas, Summa 3, q. 16, art. 11, ad 2.

units.la: 16. Vidéntes quia manducaret cum Publicanis. Convivere peccatoribus, infirmis quidem est vitandum propter periculum quod eis imminet, ne ab eis subvertantur. Perfectis autem, de quorum corruptione non timetur, laudabile est quod cum peccatoribus conversentur, ut eos convertant; sic enim Dominus cum peccatoribus manducabat & bibebat. Convictus tamen peccatorum, quantum ad consortium peccati, vitandum est omnibus. Et sic dicitur, 2 Cor. 6. Exite de medio eorum, & immundum ne tetigeritis; scilicet, secundum peccati consensum. D.Th. 2â 2æ.q.25. art. 6. ad 5um.
units.tr: 16 Seeing that he ate with the tax collectors. Living together with sinners ought indeed to be avoided by the weak, on account of the danger that threatens them, lest they be overthrown by them. But for the perfect, whose corruption is not feared, it is praiseworthy to associate with sinners in order to convert them; for so the Lord ate and drank with sinners. Nevertheless, the company of sinners is to be avoided by all, as far as fellowship in sin is concerned. And so it is said in 2 Corinthians 6: "Come out from among them, and touch no unclean thing"; that is, with respect to consent in sin. Aquinas, Summa 2-2, q. 25, art. 6, ad 5.

units.la: 19. Possunt. Id est, æquum est, rationique consentaneum, ut ait B. Greg. Nazianz. Or. 36. vel, possunt, id est, solent, quomodo Matth. 5. dicitur, Non potest civitas abscondi supra montem posita, id est, non solet. Ut enim advertit loco citato B. Greg. Nazianz. Fieri potest, ut civitas supra montem posita abscondatur, majori nimirum aliquo monte ipsius luminibus obstruente.
units.tr: 19 They can. That is, it is fitting and consonant with reason, as St. Gregory Nazianzen says (Or. 36); or they can, that is, they are accustomed to, as in Matthew 5: "A city set on a hill cannot be hidden," that is, it is not accustomed to be. For, as St. Gregory Nazianzen observes in the passage cited, "It can happen that a city set on a hill is hidden, namely when some greater mountain blocks its lights."

units.la: 22. Nemo mittit vinum novum. Id est, præcepta perfectæ vitæ. Vide supra c. 1. v. 27.
units.tr: 22 No one puts new wine. That is, the precepts of the perfect life. See above, ch. 1, v. 27.

units.la: In utres veteres. Id est, homines imperfectos.
units.tr: Into old wineskins. That is, imperfect men.

units.la: Alioquin dirumpet vinum utres, & vinum effundetur, & utres peribunt. Id est, praecepta perfectae vitae contemnentur, & homines imperfecti praecepta hujusmodi ferre non valentes in deteriora mala prorumpent, sicut dicitur Proverb. 3. Qui nimis emungit, elicit sangminem.
units.tr: Otherwise the wine will burst the skins, and the wine will be spilled, and the skins will perish. That is, the precepts of the perfect life will be despised, and imperfect men, not able to bear precepts of this kind, will break out into worse evils, as it is said in Proverbs 3: "He who wrings too hard brings out blood."

units.la: 23. Sabbatis. Enallage numeri, id est, Sabbato, quod a Luca dicitur secundo-primum; de hoc egimus Matth. 12. v. 20.
units.tr: 23 On the Sabbath. An enallage of number: that is, "on Sabbath," which Luke calls "on the second-first"; we have treated this at Matthew 12, v. 20.

units.la: 26. Abiathar. Hic & Abimeleh seu Achimelech dicitur. Vide quae diximus Matth. 12. v. 3. Fortassis tamen Marcus non appellat Abiathar Principem Sacerdotum, quod tunc temporis cum David manducarit panes propositionis, fuerit summus Pontifex, sed quia hoc nomen aliquando & de simplici Sacerdote dici potest, ut observavimus Matth. 8. v. 4.
units.tr: 26 Abiathar. Here he is also called Abimelech or Ahimelech. See what we said at Matthew 12, v. 3. Perhaps, however, Mark does not call Abiathar the chief priest because at the time when David ate the bread of the Presence with him he was high priest, but because this name can sometimes also be applied to an ordinary priest, as we observed at Matthew 8, v. 4.

units.la: CAPUT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: 1. Iterum. Supple ex Luc. 6. v. 6. in alio Sabbato. Manum. Supple ex Luc. 6. dexteram.
units.tr: 1. Again. Supply from Luke 6:6: on another Sabbath. A hand. Supply from Luke 6: the right hand.

units.la: 2. Observabant. Scilicet, Scribae & Pharisaei, ex Luc. 6. v. 7.
units.tr: 2. They watched. That is, the scribes and Pharisees, from Luke 6:7.

units.la: Si Sabbatis curaret. Enallage numeri, id est, si in Sabbato curaret, ut habet Lucas.
units.tr: If he healed on the Sabbaths. A change of number: that is, if he healed on the Sabbath, as Luke has it.

units.la: 3. Surge. Supple ex Luc. & sta.
units.tr: 3. Rise. Supply from Luke: and stand.

units.la: 4. Dicit eis. Scilicet Scribis & Pharisaeis ipsum interrogantibus utrum liceret Sabbatis curare, ut patet ex Matth. ubi praefens historia a nobis est expolita.
units.tr: 4. He said to them. That is, to the scribes and Pharisees, who asked him whether it was lawful to heal on the Sabbaths, as is clear from Matthew, where we have also explained the present story.

units.la: Cum ira. Nempe ad imperium rationis excitata, & secundum rationem moderata, nec mansuetudini opposita, quae, ut habet Philosophus 4. Ethic. c. 11. medium tenet in ira. Est autem in nobis duplex ira; prima dicitur a B. Greg. 5. mor. c. 33. ira per vitium, qua appetitur vindicta sine ordine rationis, & haec excaecat oculum mentis, & in Christo nullatenus esse potuit. Altera est, ira per zelum, quae moderata est secundum rationem, & ejus ductum sequitur, & haec licet sit laudabilis (satagit enim emendare, quae in domo Dei perversa videt, & si emendare non potest, tolerat & gemit) in nobis tamen haec ipsa ira utcumque turbat, & impedit oculum animae contemplantis; quia in nobis secundum ordinem naturalem potentiae animae mutuo se impediunt, ita scilicet, quod cum unius potentiae operatio fuerit intensa, alterius operatio debilitetur bilitetur; sed in Christo per moderationem Divinæ virtutis, unicuique potentiæ permittebatur agere quod erat ei proprium, ita quod una potentia ex alia non impediebatur. Et ideo sicut deletatio mentis contemplantis non impediebat tristitiam, vel dolorem inferioris partis, ita etiam è converso passiones inferioris partis in nullo impediebant actum rationis. D. Th. 3. parte q. 15. art. 9.
units.tr: With anger. Namely, anger aroused at the command of reason and moderated according to reason, and not opposed to gentleness; which, as the Philosopher says in Ethics 4, ch. 11, holds the mean in anger. There are two kinds of anger in us. The first is what St Gregory calls, in Moralia 5, ch. 33, anger through vice, by which vengeance is sought without the order of reason; this blinds the eye of the mind, and could in no way be in Christ. The other is anger through zeal, which is moderated according to reason and follows its guidance. Although this is praiseworthy (for it strives to correct what it sees perverse in the house of God, and if it cannot correct it, it endures and grieves), in us this very anger nonetheless disturbs somewhat and hinders the eye of the contemplating soul; because in us, according to the natural order, the powers of the soul mutually impede one another, so that when the operation of one power is intense, the operation of another is weakened; but in Christ, through the moderation of the divine virtue, each power was permitted to do what was proper to it, so that one power was not impeded by another. And therefore, just as the delight of the contemplating mind did not impede the sadness or pain of the lower part, so too, conversely, the passions of the lower part in no way impeded the act of reason. St Thomas, Summa 3, q. 15, art. 9.

units.la: 8. Idumæa. Regio Judææ vicina à meridie, Judæámque inter & Arabiam & Ægyptum, & aliquando Judæis erat subdita.
units.tr: 8. Idumaea. A region of Judea neighbouring it to the south, lying between Judea, Arabia and Egypt, and at times subject to the Jews.

units.la: Trans Jordanem. Vide quæ diximus Matth. 4. v. 25.
units.tr: Beyond the Jordan. See what we said at Matthew 4:25.

units.la: 13. Et ascendens. Vide dicta à nobis Matth. 5. v. 1.
units.tr: 13. And going up. See what we said at Matthew 5:1.

units.la: Vocavit ad se quos voluit ipse. Qui scilicet operatur omnia secundum consilium voluntatis suæ.
units.tr: He called to himself whom he himself wished. That is, he who works all things according to the counsel of his will.

units.la: 14. ut mitteret. Id est, ad missionem ordinaret, quæ postea contigit & describitur infrà cap. 6.
units.tr: 14. That he might send. That is, appointed for the mission, which happened later and is described below in chapter 6.

units.la: 15. Dedit illis potestatem, & cætera quæ sequuntur usque ad verf. 20. expósita sunt à nobis Matth. 10. à versu 1. ad 5.
units.tr: 15. He gave them power, and the rest that follows, up to verse 20, has been explained by us at Matthew 10, verses 1 to 5.

units.la: 16. Et imposuit. Fortassis est Hebraísmus pro imposuerat. Vide quæ diximus Matth. 4. v. 18.
units.tr: 16. And he imposed. Perhaps this is a Hebraism for had imposed. See what we said at Matthew 4:18.

units.la: 17. Boanerges. Corrupta dictio per infertionem o, pro banerges, ex בני bene, sive bane, filii, & רגש Regesch, strepitus, tumultus; quamvis alii, a, velint superfluere; aiunt enim, quòd Scheva, sæpe in o breve mutetur, ut patet in Sodoma & Gomorrha, & similibus.
units.tr: 17. Boanerges. A corrupted word, through the insertion of an o, for banerges, from [בני] bene (or bane), sons, and [רגש] regesch, noise, tumult. Others, however, wish the a to be superfluous; for they say that the sheva is often changed into a short o, as is clear in Sodoma and Gomorrha and similar words.

units.la: Filii tonitrui. Hebraísmus, id est, tonantis seu tonitoris; sic & pacifici dicuntur filii pacis. Hoc igitur nomine significavit Christus filios Zebedæi sublimitate prædicationis Evangelicæ & miraculis orbem commoturos. Unde primus Jacobus occisus, Joannes vero etiamnum per Apocalypsim suam, & ut ait Epiphan. hæref. 73. per propriam sui Evangelii grandiloquentiam, veluti ex quibusdam nubibus tonat.
units.tr: Sons of thunder. A Hebraism, that is, of the thundering or thunderer; so also the peacemakers are called sons of peace. By this name, therefore, Christ signified that the sons of Zebedee would shake the world by the sublimity of the Evangelical preaching and by miracles. Hence James was the first to be killed, while John, even now through his Apocalypse, and as Epiphanius says in heresy 73, thunders, as it were, out of certain clouds by the grandiloquence of his own Gospel.

units.la: 21. Cùm audiffent fui. Id est, ejus cognati & propinqui.
units.tr: 21. When they had heard of it. That is, his kinsmen and relatives.

units.la: In furorem versus est. Id est, extra se factus est. Prophetarum olim credebatur proprium, dum Spiritu corripe-rentur, extra se ac parùm sui compotes esse: unde & insanire, aut mitiori voce alienari dicebantur; sic Seneca lib. de constantia sapientis: Cùm, inquit, Sapientem negatis insanire, non negatis & alienari, & parum sana verba emittere. Hinc 4. Reg. cap. 9. v. 11. filius Prophetarum ab Elisæo missus à ceteris insanus vocatur, Sic & 1. Reg. cap. 9. v. 18. ubi habetur in textu Hebræo & Vulgato, invasit spiritus Dei malus Saul, Saul, & prophetabat, Chaldæus Paraphrastes vertit, & insaniebat; & ibidem cap. 19. dicitur de Saul, quod expoliavit ipse se vestimentis suis, & prophetavit cum cetiris coram Samuele, & cecidit nudus tota die illâ & nocte; quod satis indicat Saülem fuisse sui impotem, & in potestate Spiritûs. Hinc & Montanistæ, ut se Prophetas simularent, verba ambigua, & quæ nihil sani præ se ferrent, effundebant, ut testatur B. Epiphan. Atque ita etiam in præsenti loco amici, & cognati Christi ut furenti eum turbæ eriperent, ac sic (quod verisimile est) servarent, suæ eum potestatis esse negant.
units.tr: He had gone out of his mind. That is, he was beside himself. It was formerly thought to be characteristic of prophets, when they were seized by the Spirit, to be beside themselves and not quite in control of their wits; hence they were said to be mad, or, in a milder word, deranged. So Seneca, in the book on the constancy of the wise man: When you deny, he says, that the wise man is mad, you do not deny that he is deranged, and that he utters words not quite sound. Hence in 4 Kings ch. 9 v. 11, the son of the prophets sent by Elisha is called mad by the others. So too in 1 Kings ch. 9 v. 18, where the Hebrew text and the Vulgate have an evil spirit of God invaded Saul, and he prophesied; the Chaldee paraphrast renders it, and he raved. And in the same place, ch. 19, it is said of Saul that he stripped off his own clothes, and prophesied with the others before Samuel, and lay naked all that day and night; which sufficiently shows that Saul was beside himself and in the power of the Spirit. Hence also the Montanists, in order to pass themselves off as prophets, poured out ambiguous words containing nothing sound, as St Epiphanius bears witness. And so too in the present passage, Christ's friends and kinsmen, to snatch him from the raging crowd and so (as is likely) keep him safe, deny that he is in his own power.

units.la: 22. Beelzebub habet. Vide Matth. 9. v. 34, &c.
units.tr: 22. He has Beelzebub. See Matthew 9:34, etc.

units.la: 23. Omnia dimittentur, &c. Vide Matth. 12.
units.tr: 23. All things will be forgiven, etc. See Matthew 12.

units.la: CAPUT IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: 1. ENT iterum, &c. Quæ sequuntur usque ad vers. 21. exposita sunt Matth. 13.
units.tr: 1. And again, etc. What follows, up to verse 21, has been explained at Matthew 13.

units.la: 10. Qui cum eo erant duodecim. Noh diceret Marcus, duodecim, nisi, ante hic numerus Apostolorum fuisset constitutus, & essent hæ parabolæ dictæ post electionem Apostolorum; quare quod idem Marcus post parabolas narraturus sedatam maris tempestatem subdit: Et ait illis in illa die cum sero esset factum; id intelligi non potest de die dictarum parabolarum; hæc enim tempestas contigit ante vocationem Matthæi.
units.tr: 10. Those who were with him, the twelve. Why would Mark say "the twelve" unless this number of Apostles had already been appointed, and these parables had been spoken after the election of the Apostles? Hence, since Mark, about to relate after the parables the calming of the storm at sea, adds, "And he said to them on that day, when evening had come," this cannot be understood of the day of the said parables, for this storm happened before the calling of Matthew.

units.la: 22. Sed. Hebraismus Rabbinis usitatus, id est, nisi.
units.tr: 22. But. A Hebraism used by the rabbis, that is, "unless."

units.la: 24. Videte quid audiatis, &c. Id est, attendite istis quæ vobis dicuntur, quâ enim mensurâ metiemini attentionem, eâdem metietur vobis in cognitione.
units.tr: 24. Take heed what you hear, etc. That is, pay attention to what is said to you; for with whatever measure you measure your attention, the same will be measured to you in knowledge.

units.la: 26. Sic est regnum Dei, &c. Id est, perinde sancta Ecclesia aliquando cum Deo in cœlis regnatura perducitur per virtutis incrementa ad summa, atque sementis, quam jecerit agricola in terram, &c. Præclarè hanc parabolam explicat & applicat B. Greg. lib 2. in Ezechiel. Hom. 15. Semen inquit, homo jactat in terram, cum cordi suo bonam intentionem iuserit. Et postquam semen jactaverit, dormit, quia jam in spe boni operis quiescit. Nocte vero exsurgit ac die, quia inter adversa & prospera proficit. Et semen germinat & crescit, dum nescit ille: quia dum adhuc metiri incrementa sua non valet, semel concepta virtus ad perfectum ducitur. Et ultro terra fructificat; quia præveniente se gratiâ mens hominis spontanee ad profectum. sectum boni operis assurgit. Sed hæc eadem terra primùm herbam, deinde spicam, deinde plenum frumentum producit in spica. Herbam quippe producere, est inchoationis bonæ adhuc teneritudinem habere. Ad spicam verò herba pervenit, cùm si virtus animo concepta ad profectum boni operis pertrahit. Plenum verò frumentum in spica fructificat, quando jam in tantum virtus proficit, ut esse robusti & perfecti operis possit. Sed cùm ex se produxerit fructus, statim mittit falcem, quoniam deest tempus messis. Omnipotens enim Deus producto fructu falcem mittit, & messem suam desecat, quia cùm unumquemque ad opera perfecta perduxerit, ejus temporalem vitam per emissam sententiam incidit, ut granum suum ad cœlestia horrea perducat. Cùm igitur desideria bona concipimus, semen in terram mittimus; cùm verò operari recta incipimus, herba fumus; Cùmque in ejusdem operationis perfectione solidamur, jam plenum frumentum in spica proferimus.
units.tr: 26. So is the kingdom of God, etc. That is, in the same way the holy Church, sometimes destined to reign with God in heaven, is brought through the growth of virtue to its height, just as the seed which the farmer has cast into the earth, etc. Blessed Gregory explains and applies this parable admirably in his second book on Ezekiel, homily 15: "A man, he says, casts seed into the earth when he has sent a good intention into his heart. And after he has cast the seed, he sleeps, because now he rests in the hope of a good work. But he rises by night and by day, because he makes progress amid both adversity and prosperity. And the seed sprouts and grows while he does not know it, because while he cannot yet measure his growth, the virtue once conceived is brought to perfection. And the earth bears fruit of its own accord, because, with grace going before, the mind of man rises spontaneously to the advancement of a good work. But this same earth first produces the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. For to produce the blade is still to have the tenderness of a good beginning. The blade reaches the ear when the virtue conceived in the mind draws it on to the progress of a good work. The full grain bears fruit in the ear when virtue has advanced so far that it can be of a strong and perfect work. But when it has put forth its fruit, it at once sends the sickle, since the time of harvest has come. For almighty God, when the fruit is produced, sends the sickle and cuts down his harvest, because when he has brought each one to perfect works, he cuts off his temporal life by the sentence pronounced, so that he may bring his grain to the heavenly barns. Therefore, when we conceive good desires, we send the seed into the earth; when we begin to work uprightly, we become the blade; and when we are strengthened in the perfecting of the same work, we now bring forth full grain in the ear."

units.la: 25. Et ait illis, &c. Quæ sequuntur usque in finem capitis, expósita sunt à nobis Matth. 8. à v. 23. ad v. 28.
units.tr: 25. And he said to them, etc. What follows to the end of the chapter has been explained by us at Matthew 8, from verse 23 to verse 28.

units.la: CAPUT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: OMnia ferè, quæ in hoc capite habentur, enucleavimus Matth. 8. & 9.
units.tr: I have explained nearly everything contained in this chapter at Matthew 8 and 9.

units.la: 19. Vade, &c. Chrysoft. Hom. 33. in Matth. super illud Matth. 9. Videte ne quis sciat, ait non esse hoc contrarium ei, quod hic à dæmone liberato dicit, Vade in domum tuam ad tuos & annuntia illis quanta tibi Dominus fecerit. Erudit enim nos Christus, ut prohibeamus eos, qui volunt nos propter nos laudare; si verò ad Deum gloria referatur, injungamus nedum permittamus, ut hoc fiat.
units.tr: 19. Go, etc. Chrysostom, Homily 33 on Matthew, on the words of Matthew 9, See that no one knows it, says that this is not contrary to what Christ tells the man freed from the demon here, Go into your house to your own people and report to them how much the Lord has done for you. For Christ teaches us to forbid those who wish to praise us for our own sake; but if the glory is referred to God, we should enjoin, not merely permit, that this be done.

units.la: 20. In Decapoli. Id est, in omnibus Decapoleos civitatibus; quod Lucas c 8. v. 23. his verbis significat, per universam civitatem, supplendum relinquens Lectori ex Marco, Decapoleos. De Decapoli diximus Matth. 4. v. 25.
units.tr: 20. In the Decapolis. That is, in all the cities of the Decapolis. Luke expresses this in chapter 8, verse 23, with the words through the whole city, leaving the reader to supply "of the Decapolis" from Mark. I discussed the Decapolis at Matthew 4, verse 25.

units.la: 25. Mulier quæ erat in profluvio sanguinis. Id est, quæ laborabat nimio ac continuo per duodecim annos præter naturam sanguinis fluxu extra tempus menstruum. Unde à B. Optato Milevit. lib. 5. adversus Donatistas dicitur hæc mulier laborasse de secreta causa fœminarum.
units.tr: 25. A woman who had a flow of blood. That is, who for twelve years had suffered from a severe and continual flow of blood, unnatural and outside the time of menstruation. Hence blessed Optatus of Milevis, in book 5 against the Donatists, says this woman suffered from a hidden female complaint.

units.la: 27. Venit in turba. Ne scilicet agnosceretur, & ut immunda ex Lev. 15. ab accessu ad Christum prohiberetur. Hinc B. Petrus Chrysologus Ser. 1. De Hæmorroissa ait, quòd ipsa prima dedit formam, quomodo peccator tacita confessione deleat sine confusione peccatum: quomodo delinquens soli Deo cognitus, de reatu nudare apud homines verecunda conscientiæ non cogatur: quomodo homo possit venia judicium prævenire.
units.tr: 27. She came up in the crowd. Evidently so that she would not be recognised, and so that, being unclean according to Leviticus 15, she would not be kept from approaching Christ. Hence blessed Peter Chrysologus, in Sermon 1 on the woman with the issue of blood, says that she first gave the pattern of how a sinner may blot out sin by silent confession without shame, how one who has offended, known to God alone, need not be compelled to lay bare his guilt before men through modest conscience, and how a man may anticipate judgement by pardon.

units.la: Retrò. Pudor quippe, ut ait B. Optatus, impediebat ne causam suam coram masculis indicaret. Sic glossæ veteres αἰτίαν causam sumunt pro morbo.
units.tr: From behind. For shame, as blessed Optatus says, kept her from declaring her case before men. In this way the old glosses take the Greek aitian [αἰτίαν] ("cause") to mean the disease.

units.la: 28. Dicebat enim. Supple ex Matth. 9. v. 21. intra se, id est, cogitabat.
units.tr: 28. For she said. Supply from Matthew 9, verse 21: to herself, that is, she thought.

units.la: 29. Siccatus est fons sanguinis ejus. Eleganter & verecundè exprimit Evangelista mulierem ob continuum sanguinis fluxum per secretiores partes omni formâ privatam, & viribus exhaustam, ineptámque ad opus conjugale à Christo sic sanitati restitutam, ut non nisi tempore à natura constituto fluerent ipsi muliebria. Hoc phrasi Hebraicâ טהורה ממקור רמיה mundata est a fonte sanguinis sui dicitur Levit. 12. v. 7. Id est, fletit fluxus menstrui, seu, ut Celsus loquitur fluxus muliebrium sedatus est. Nempe sanguinis menstrui profluvium fontem מקור fine addito, aut מקור הרמים sanguinis fontem appellat Scriptura, ut videre est Levit. 12, & 20.
units.tr: 29. The fountain of her blood was dried up. The Evangelist expresses with elegance and modesty that the woman, deprived of all strength by the constant flow of blood from the more secret parts, exhausted in her powers and unfit for the marital act, was restored by Christ to health so that the female courses flowed again only at the time set by nature. In Hebrew this idiom, she is made clean from the fountain of her blood [טהורה ממקור רמיה], is used at Leviticus 12, verse 7; that is, the flow of the menstrual discharge has ceased, or, as Celsus puts it, the flow of the female discharges has been stopped. Scripture calls the menstrual flow the fountain [מקור] without addition, or the fountain of blood [מקור הדמים], as may be seen at Leviticus 12 and 20.

units.la: 30. Virtutem quæ exierat de illo. Id est, quæ operata erat Hæmorrhoissæ sanationem; virtus enim phrasi popülari dicitur exire ab agente, dum aliquem effectum extra se ipsum agens producit. Quid, inquit Fulgentius lib. 2. ad Thrasym. hæc virtus quæ de Domino exivit, nunquid exeundo discessit? an ad sanandum sic exiens potuit pervenire, ut à Salvatore localiter non posset exire? Quod si localiter ab eo, qui virtus dicitur, virtus exivit: dicatur qualiter virtus à virtute discessit? Si vero talis credulitas, fidei Christianæ videtur incongrua: non alium putemus illum de Christo virtutis exitum, nisi Divinæ curationis effectum. Tunc enim ad mulierem virtus Salvatoris exivit, quando in se virtutem Divinæ curationis agnovit.
units.tr: 30. The power that had gone out from him. That is, the power that had effected the healing of the woman with the issue of blood; in popular speech power is said to go out from an agent when the agent produces some effect outside itself. What, says Fulgentius in book 2 to Thrasymund, was this power that went out from the Lord? Did it depart by going out? Or, going out to heal, could it reach its goal, yet not be able to go out from the Saviour in place? If power went out locally from him who is called power, let it be said how power departed from power. But if such a belief seems incongruous with the Christian faith, let us think that the outflow of power from Christ was nothing other than the effect of divine healing. For the Saviour's power went out to the woman when she recognised in herself the power of the divine healing.

units.la: 31. Et dicebant ei. Supple ex Luc. 8 v.45. negantibus autem omnibus, scilicet, quàm proximè Christum circumdantibus.
units.tr: 31. And they said to him. Supply from Luke 8, verse 45: while all were denying it, that is, all those standing very close around Christ.

units.la: 32. Circumspicebat videre eam. Non quasi illam ignoraret cui fidem illam donaverat, quam interius ad se traxerat, quam exterius sanaverat, sed humano se habebat more, ut & interrogatione & circumspectione perculsa mulier se ipsa sponte proderet, & miraculum palàm profiteretur, ut sic effet commendatius.
units.tr: 32. He looked round to see her. Not as though he did not know her, to whom he had given that faith which he had drawn inwardly to himself, and whom he had healed outwardly; but he acted in the manner of men, so that the woman, startled by the question and by his looking around, would of her own accord reveal herself, and openly confess the miracle, and so it would be more commendable.

units.la: 33. Timens & tremens. Quòd nimirum immunda mundum tetigisset.
units.tr: 33. Fearing and trembling. Clearly because she, being unclean, had touched the clean one.

units.la: 34. Vade in pace. Hebraismus, id est, noli timere.
units.tr: 34. Go in peace. A Hebraism, that is, do not fear.

units.la: Esto sana à plaga tua. Quasi diceret, Sis secura profluvium sanguinis non amplius rediturum.
units.tr: Be healed of your affliction. As if he said, be assured that the flow of blood will not return again.

units.la: 35. Ab Archisynagogo. Id est, ab aedibus Archisynagogi; nam ipse Archisynagogus Jairus erat cum Jesu. Sic Terent. in Hecyra: Sed quid Bacchidem à nostro affine exeuntem video? id est, ab affinis domo.
units.tr: 35. From the house of the ruler of the synagogue. That is, from the dwelling of the ruler of the synagogue; for the ruler of the synagogue, Jairus, was himself with Jesus. So Terence in the Hecyra: But why do I see Bacchis coming out from our kinsman? that is, from the house of the kinsman.

units.la: 49. Ejectis omnibus. Scilicet, plangentibus, & lugentibus.
units.tr: 49. With all put out. Namely, those who were wailing and mourning.

units.la: 43. Et dixit dari illi manducare. Nimirum, inquit Chrysost. ut fidem resurrectionis faceret.
units.tr: 43. And he said that something should be given her to eat. Indeed, says Chrysostom, so that he might give proof of the faith of the resurrection.

units.la: CAPUT VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: 3. Nonne hic est faber. Vide dicta Matth. 13. v. 55.
units.tr: 3. Is not this the carpenter? See what was said at Matt. 13:55.

units.la: Joseph. Graece 'Ἰωσῆ[?] B. Hieron. hunc vocat Josetem, quis fuerit non constat.
units.tr: Joseph. In Greek [Ἰωσῆ?]. Blessed Jerome calls him Josetes; who he was is not established.

units.la: Simonis. Hic dicitur Jacobo fratri Domini successisse in Episcopatu Jerosolymitano, & esse diversus à Simone Cananaeo Apostolo in Perside post praedicatum Evangelium unà cum Juda Apostolo pro fide Christi occiso. Hegesippus tamen, & Eusebius Simonem Apostolum volunt post Jacobum rexisse Ecclesiam Jerosolymorum, & cùm esset 120. annorum martyrio affectum. Nonnulli volunt hos duos posteriores Judam & Simonem non fuisse germanos priorum, Jacobi scilicet, & Josephi, quòd Maria B. Virginis soror seu cognata, & ut ex collatione Matth. 23. Marc. 15. & Joan. 19. perspicuè deducit Hieron. contra Helvidium cap. 7. Cleophae uxor tantùm legitur Jacobi & Josephi mater Matth. 27. & Marc. 15.
units.tr: Simon. He is said to have succeeded James, the brother of the Lord, as bishop of Jerusalem, and to have been different from Simon the Cananaean Apostle, who was put to death for the faith of Christ in Persia after preaching the Gospel, together with the Apostle Jude. Hegesippus and Eusebius, however, hold that Simon the Apostle ruled the Church of Jerusalem after James, and that he suffered martyrdom when he was 120 years old. Some hold that these two later men, Judas and Simon, were not brothers of the earlier ones, namely James and Joseph. Blessed Jerome, in his book against Helvidius, chapter 7, clearly deduces this from a comparison of Matt. 23, Mark 15 and John 19, namely that they were sons of Mary, the sister or kinswoman of the Blessed Virgin. In Matt. 27 and Mark 15 only the wife of Cleophas is read of as the mother of James and Joseph.

units.la: 5. Non poterat. Id est, quasi non posset, se gerebat; impotentia enim, ignorantia, & hujusmodi attribuuntur Deo vel Christo secundum similitudinem effectûs, quia ea faciunt, quae dum ab hominibus fiunt, signa sunt impotentiae, ignorantiae, & hujusmodi. Vide Matth. 13. v. 53. ubi, quae in primis hujus capitis quinque versibus habentur, sunt expositá. Placet hic subjicere praeclaram B. Greg. Nazian. observationem de multiplici vocabulorum posse & non posse acceptione. Posse, inquit oratione 36. vel non posse, non uno modo dicitur: variam enim ac multiplicem significationem habet. Nonnunquam enim secundum virium defectum dicitur, & certi temporis ac personae ratione habita: ut quòd puer luctari non possit, aut catulus cernere, aut cum aliquo dimicare. Luctabitur enim fortasse aliquando, & cernet, & cum hoc dimicabit, etiamsi cum altera nequeat. Interdum de eo dicitur quod saepenumero contingit, ut illud, Non potest civitas abscondi supra montem posita. Fieri enim potest ut quaedam civitas abscondatur, majori nimirum aliquo monte ipsius luminibus obstruente. Impossibile etiam dicitur, quod minimè aequum est rationique consentaneum: cujus generis est illud, Non possunt filii sponsi jejunare, quamdiu praesens est sponsus, sive eum intelligas qui corporis oculis cernitur (neque enim aerumnae atque afflictionis tempus erat illud tempus, quo Christus nobiscum versabatur) sive eum ut Verbum spectes. Quid enim eos corporeo modo jejunare necesse est, qui sermone purgantur? Quartâ significatione hoc fieri non posse dicitur, à quo nostra voluntas abhorret: cujusmodi est illud, Non poterat illic signa facere propter incredulitatem eorum, qui ea excipiebant. Quoniam enim ad morborum depulsiones utrumque accedere necesse est, nempe ut & aegroti fidem, & medici vim & facultatem medendi afferant: idcirco alterum deficiente altero minimè contingebat. Quanquam haud scio, an hoc quoque genus tertio adjungendum sit, quo impossibile nihil aliud significat, quàm quod minimè rationi consentaneum est. Neque enim iis medicinam afferre conveniebat, quibus incredulitas detrimentum allatura erat. Quo etiam in ordine ponendum est illud, Non potest mundus non odisse vos: &, Quomodo potestis bona loqui, cùm sitis mali? Quo enim pacto quicquam horum impossibile est, nisi quia voluntas repugnat? Jam illud quoque impossibile dicitur, quod natura quidem impossibile est, Deo autem volenti possibile. Quo in genere est illud, eundem hominem bis nasci non posse, nec acu camelum admitti. Quid enim prohibeat quominus haec fiant, si Dei voluntas tulerit? Praeter bos omnes modos impossibile dicitur, quod nullâ omninò ratione fieri potest.
units.tr: 5. He could not. That is, he behaved as if he were not able. For inability, ignorance and the like are attributed to God or Christ by a likeness of effect, because they do things which, when done by men, are signs of inability, ignorance and the like. See Matt. 13:53, where what is found in the first five verses of this chapter is explained. It is well to add here the excellent observation of Blessed Gregory Nazianzen on the many senses of the words to be able and not to be able. To be able, he says in Oration 36, or not to be able, is not said in one way; for it has a varied and manifold meaning. Sometimes it is said with respect to a lack of strength, taking into account a certain time and person: as that a boy cannot wrestle, or a puppy see, or fight with someone. For he will perhaps wrestle at some time, and will see, and will fight with this one, even though he cannot with another. Sometimes it is said of what happens often, as that saying, A city set on a hill cannot be hidden. For it can happen that a certain city is hidden, namely when some larger mountain blocks its light. It is also said to be impossible when something is by no means fair and consistent with reason: of this kind is that, The sons of the bridegroom cannot fast while the bridegroom is present, whether you understand him as he who is seen with bodily eyes (for that time, when Christ dwelt among us, was not a time of hardship and affliction) or whether you regard him as the Word. For why must they fast in a bodily way who are cleansed by the word? In a fourth sense it is said that something cannot be done when our will shrinks from it: such as that, He could not do mighty works there because of the unbelief of those who received them. For since both things must come together for the driving off of diseases, namely that the sick man brings faith and the physician brings power and skill to heal, therefore when one was lacking the other did not happen. Yet I do not know whether this kind should not also be added as a third, in which impossible means nothing other than what is by no means consistent with reason. For it was not fitting to bring medicine to those for whom unbelief was going to bring harm. In this class too must be placed, The world cannot hate you; and, How can you speak good things, when you are evil? For in what way is any of these impossible, except because the will resists? Again, that is also called impossible which is indeed impossible by nature, but possible to God if he wills it. Of this kind is that a man cannot be born twice, nor a camel pass through the eye of a needle. For what would prevent these things from happening, if the will of God brought it about? Apart from all these ways, something is called impossible when it cannot be done by any means whatever.

units.la: 6. Mirabatur: Vide Matth. 8. v. 10.
units.tr: 6. He marvelled: See Matt. 8:10.

units.la: Castella. Non solum in civitatibus praedicabat Dominus, sed & in castellis, ut discamus pauca non spernere, neque magnas semper quaerere civitates, sed verbum Dei in vicis abjectis & vilibus seminare. Theophilus Antiochenus in Caten. aurea.
units.tr: Villages. The Lord preached not only in cities but also in villages, that we may learn not to despise small things, and not always to seek great cities, but to sow the word of God in humble and obscure villages. Theophilus of Antioch, in the Catena aurea.

units.la: 7. Et vocavit, &c. Vide Matth. 10. v. 1. &c. ex quo capite versus decimus quintus hic in textu Graeco inter versum 7. & 12. Vulgatae Editionis est forte-assis insertus.
units.tr: 7. And he called, etc. See Matt. 10:1 ff., from which chapter the fifteenth verse, perhaps, has been inserted here in the Greek text between verses 7 and 12 of the Vulgate edition.

units.la: 8. Ne quid tollerent. Quis hoc mandasset, nisi qui & corvos alit & flores agri vestit? Tert. lib. 4. cont. Marcionem cap. 21.
units.tr: 8. That they should take nothing. Who would have commanded this, except he who feeds the ravens and clothes the flowers of the field? Tertullian, book 4 against Marcion, chapter 21.

units.la: 13. ungebant oleo multos agros, & sanabant. Haec unctio non erat sacramentalis; dabatur enim etiam non baptizatis, inquit Balthasar Paës in suo Commentario in Epist. Jacobi cap. 5. v. 14. & 15.
units.tr: 13. They anointed with oil many that were sick, and healed them. This anointing was not sacramental; for it was given even to the unbaptized, says Balthasar Paës in his commentary on the Epistle of James, chapter 5, verses 14 and 15.

units.la: 14. Dicebat. Aug. lib. 2. de Conf. cap. 43. & antiqui Latini legunt hic pluraliter, dicebant, quod maxime congruit narrationi Lucae, qui videtur Marcum explicuisse; imo legendum pluraliter indicat ipse Marcus, cum subdat. v. 16. Quo audito Herodes ait, ubi perspicuum est non prius a Marco inductum esse Herodem loquentem, sed eos, qui Herodi narrabant.
units.tr: 14. He said. Augustine, book 2 of the Harmony of the Evangelists, chapter 43. And the older Latin authorities read here in the plural, they said, which agrees most closely with the narrative of Luke, who seems to have explained Mark. Indeed Mark himself indicates that the plural should be read, since he adds in verse 16, When Herod heard this, he said, where it is plain that Herod was not first introduced by Mark as speaking, but those who were telling it to Herod.

units.la: 15. Propheta est, quasi unus ex Prophetis. Id est, vel quasi unus ex Prophetis. Est autem supplenda disjunctio vel per virgulam, ut sensus sit Propheta ille est, qui sic Antonomastice dicitur, quique per Moysen Deuter. 18. est promissus, vel si non est hic ille Propheta, saltem nihil cedit aliis Prophetis. Hinc Euthymius, In quodam, inquit, exemplo dictio Propheta habet articulum ut sit, Propheta ille est, aut tanquam unus Prophetarum. Intelligebant autem illum Prophetam, de quo Moyses vaticinatus fuerat, is erat Christus.
units.tr: 15. He is a prophet, or as one of the prophets. That is, either as one of the prophets. The disjunction or must be supplied by a comma, so that the sense is: that is the prophet, who is called so by way of eminence, and who was promised through Moses in Deut. 18; or, if this is not that prophet, at least he is in no way inferior to the other prophets. Hence Euthymius: In a certain instance, he says, the word Prophet has the article, so that it means: That is the prophet, or as one of the prophets. But they understood that prophet, of whom Moses had prophesied, to be Christ.

units.la: 16. Herodes ait. Dubitans, non affirmans. Vide Matth. 14. ubi praesens narratio fuit a nobis expósita.
units.tr: 16. Herod said. Doubting, not affirming. See Matt. 14, where we have expounded the present narrative.

units.la: 21. Dies opportunus. Supple, Herodiadi.
units.tr: 21. A suitable day. Supply: for Herodias.

units.la: 27. Decollavit eum. Scilicet, spiculator, ut in textu Graeco clare exprimitur his verbis: Ille autem abiens decollavit eum in carcere. Quae sequuntur expósita sunt Matth. 14. ubi & Evangelistas inter se conciliavimus.
units.tr: 27. He beheaded him. Namely the executioner, as is clearly expressed in the Greek text in these words: And he went and beheaded him in the prison. What follows has been explained at Matt. 14, where we also reconciled the Evangelists with one another.

units.la: 38. Quot panes habetis. Interrogationes non semper ignorantiae signa esse, sed interdum ad utilitatem & instructionem illius, qui interrogatur, pertinere, etiam humanis & quotidianis exemplis doceri potest. Unde & Deus interrogat saepe numero, ut, Adam ubi es? ubi est frater tuus? &c.
units.tr: 38. How many loaves have you? Questions are not always signs of ignorance, but sometimes they serve the profit and instruction of the one who is asked; this can be taught even from human and everyday examples. Hence God also often asks questions, as Adam, where are you? Where is your brother? and so on.

units.la: 48. Volebat praeterire eos. Scilicet voluntate signi, quia ut ait Aug. lib. 2. de consensu Evangelii. cap. 47. in diversum ibat. Hoc autem erat indicium & praeparatio quaedam ad praetereundum, & in nobis signum esse solet nos velle praeterire. Revera itaque voluntate beneplaciti eos praeterire non volebat, sed magis, ut ait Bernardus, Serm. 74. in Cantic. probare fidem, & elicere precem. Vide Matth. 14.
units.tr: 48. He wished to pass by them. By an indication of the will, namely, as Augustine says in book 2 of the Harmony of the Gospels, chapter 47, he was going in the other direction. This, however, was a sign and a kind of preparation for passing by, and in us it is usually a sign that we wish to pass by. Indeed, therefore, he did not wish to pass them by in the will of good pleasure, but rather, as Bernard says, Sermon 74 on the Song of Songs, to test their faith and draw out their prayer. See Matt. 14.

units.la: 49. Putaverunt phantasma esse. Theodorus Pharanitanus Episcopus Cyri aflecta, ac monothelitarum ante ipsum Cyrum Alexandrinum patriarcham Antesignanus in Sexta Synodo damnatus scripsit, inquit venerabilis Beda, corporale pondus non habuisse secundum carnem Dominum, sed absque pondere & corcorpore super mare deambulasse. At contrà fides Catholica, & pondus secundum carnem eum habere prædicat, & onus corporeum & cum pondere, atque onere corporali incedere super aquas, non infusis pedibus. Nam Dionysius egregius inter Ecclesiasticos scriptores in opusculis de divinis nominibus hoc modo loquitur: Ignoranus qualiter de virgineis sanguinibus alia lege præter naturalem formabatur, & qualiter non infusis pedibus corporale pondus, & materiale onus habentibus deambulabat in humidam & instabilem substantiam. Hæc Beda in Marc. 6.
units.tr: 49. They thought it was a phantom. Theodore of Pharan, bishop of Cyrus, a supporter of the Monothelites and before Cyrus himself the patriarch of Alexandria, condemned in the Sixth Synod, wrote, says the venerable Bede, that the Lord according to the flesh had no bodily weight, but walked upon the sea without weight and without body. On the contrary, the Catholic faith teaches that he had weight according to the flesh, and that he walked upon the waters with a bodily burden and load and with bodily weight, not with feet that were infused. For Dionysius, that distinguished writer among the ecclesiastical authors, speaks in this way in his little works on the divine names: Not knowing how, by a law other than the natural one, he was formed from virginal blood, and how, not with infused feet, but with bodily weight and material load, he walked upon a moist and unstable substance. Thus Bede, on Mark 6.

units.la: Id est, multo magis.
units.tr: That is, much more so.

units.la: Hebraismus, id est, intellexerant, seu satis consideraverant miraculum mox in panum multiplicatione editum, ut inde ejus omnipotentissimam Divinitatem, cui nihil est impossibile, distincte perciperent.
units.tr: This is a Hebraism: they had understood, or had considered carefully enough, the miracle just performed in the multiplication of the loaves, so that from it they could clearly perceive his almighty Divinity, to which nothing is impossible.

units.la: Erat enim cor eorum obcæcatum. Q. d. Nondum ut non cæcis oculis mentis divina Christi opera viderent, quæ oculis carnis videbant, datum erat eis ab eo, qui operatur omnia secundum consilium voluntatis suæ. Vide Aug. 10. Conf. cap. 6.
units.tr: For their heart was blinded. As if to say: it had not yet been granted to them, by him who works all things according to the counsel of his will, that with the blind eyes of the mind they should see the divine works of Christ which they saw with the eyes of the flesh. See Aug. Conf. 10, cap. 6.

units.la: CAPUT. VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: Ad... Sasboldus scriptor pius & doctus in hunc Esaiæ locum ita commentatur: Sane qui & audit legunt certas preces & audiunt sacrum, & iis absolutis conferunt se ad pocula, aut his similia, illi quoque sunt, qui hic dicuntur labiis suis honorare Deum, cor autem eorum longè esse ab eo; quod valde est horribile in homine Christiano, & maximè in Sacerdote existimante omnia tunc recte se habere, quando lectæ sunt horæ, non cogitante interim, ut mens elevetur in Deum, & cor ei per amorem jungatur, ut sit humiliatum & contritum, & res fluxas atque mundanas contemnat. Sic ille, sed non est quod dicamus tantum contra eos hæc posita, qui in precibus evagationes mentis patiuntur, nam Judæi & Pharisæi veré de Deo cogitabant, quando Deum laudabant nominatim, ut ostendit Pharisæus dicens; Deus, gratias ago tibi, quia non sum sicut ceteri hominum: sed generaliter ponitur hæc sententia contra eos, qui verbis Deum honorant, factis autem contemnunt.
units.tr: To... Sasboldus, a pious and learned writer, comments thus on this passage of Isaiah: Certainly those who hear and read set prayers, and listen to the sacred office, and when these are finished turn to their cups or similar pursuits, are also those whom the text describes as honouring God with their lips while their heart is far from him. This is very horrible in a Christian man, and most of all in a priest who thinks that all is well when the hours have been read, without considering in the meantime that the mind should be raised up to God, that the heart should be joined to him through love, that it should be humbled and broken, and that it should despise fleeting and worldly things. So far Sasboldus. But we should not say that these words apply only to those who suffer wanderings of mind in their prayers. For the Jews and Pharisees truly thought of God when they praised him by name, as the Pharisee shows when he says: God, I thank you that I am not like other men. Rather, this saying is stated in general against those who honour God with words but despise him in deeds.

units.la: 31. Exiens de finibus Tyri venit per Sidonem ad mare, Gr. De finibus Tyri & Sidonis venit ad mare.
units.tr: 31. Leaving the borders of Tyre he came through Sidon to the sea. Greek: He came to the sea from the borders of Tyre and Sidon.

units.la: 32. Mutum. Id est. difficulter loquentem, seu balbutientem, ut textus Græcus sonat, & sequens versus 35. indicat.
units.tr: 32. Dumb. That is, one who speaks with difficulty, or stammers, as the Greek text has it, and as verse 35 indicates.

units.la: ut imponat illi manum. Quid, inquit Aug. lib. 3. de Baptismo adversus Donatistas cap. 16. est aliud manuum impositio, nisi oratio super hominem? Quibus verbis vult Aug. manus impositionem esse quandam ceremoniam externam, quâ, qui utitur, significat se orare, benedicere, bene precari, vel apud Deum intercedere pro eo, cui manum vel manus imponit. Est igitur oratio non vocalis, sed ut ita dicam ceremonialis cum vocali tamen, vel saltem mentali oratione conjuncta. Id autem significari per manuum impositionem patet ex Genef. 48. & 4. Reg. 5. v. 11.
units.tr: that he might lay his hand upon him. Augustine says in book 3 of On Baptism against the Donatists, chapter 16: What else is the laying on of hands than prayer over a man? By these words Augustine means that the laying on of hands is a certain external ceremony, by which the one who uses it signifies that he prays, blesses, invokes good upon, or intercedes with God for the one on whom he lays his hand or hands. Prayer is therefore not vocal only, but, so to speak, ceremonial, joined however with vocal or at least mental prayer. That this is signified by the laying on of hands is clear from Genesis 48 and 2 Kings 5:11.

units.la: 34. Apprehendens eum de turba seorsum misit. Id est, cùm apprehendisset eum seorsim, ut nos suo exemplo jactantiæ sugam doceret, misit, &c.
units.tr: 34. Taking him aside from the crowd, he sent him away. That is, when he had taken him aside privately, he sent him away, etc., teaching us by his example to flee from boasting.

units.la: Et expuens. Id est, cùm in digitos suos expuisset.
units.tr: And spitting. That is, when he had spat upon his fingers.

units.la: 33. Suspiciens in cælum ingemuit. Scilicet, ex commiseratione. Quærens autem à Patre auxilium ostendit se verum hominem, & Patre minorem secundum humanitatem, vel ut ait B. Greg. lib. 1 in Ezechiel. Homil. 10. Suspiciens in cælum ingemuit, non quòd ipse necessarium gemitum haberet, qui dabat quod postulabat, sed nos ad eum gemere, qui cælo præsidet, docuit, ut & aures nostræ per donum Spiritûs-Sancti, qui digitus Dei vocatur in Scripturis, & lingua per salivam, quæ ex capite in os defluit, id est, per sapientiam acceptam in divino eloquio solvi valeat ad verba prædicationis.
units.tr: 33. Looking up to heaven he sighed. Namely, out of compassion. Yet in seeking help from the Father he shows himself to be a true man, and less than the Father according to his humanity. Or, as Blessed Gregory says in book 1 on Ezekiel, homily 10: Looking up to heaven he sighed, not because he himself needed a sighing that gave what he asked, but he taught us to sigh to him who presides in heaven, so that our ears may be opened through the gift of the Holy Spirit, who in Scripture is called the finger of God, and our tongue loosed through the saliva which flows from the head into the mouth, that is, through the wisdom received in the divine utterance, for the words of preaching.

units.la: Ephpheta, quod est adaperire. Hoc est, aperitor, seu fis solutus tam à vinculis aurium, quàm à vinculis linguæ, ut audias & sine balbutie loquaris. Hoc autem se ostendit Deum coæqualem Patri, quòd uno verbulo, & solo imperio statim persectæ sanitati hominem restituit.
units.tr: Ephphatha, which means be opened. That is, be opened, or be loosed, both from the bonds of your ears and from the bonds of your tongue, so that you may hear and speak without stammering. In this he showed himself to be equal to the Father, since by one word and by his command alone he at once restored the man to perfect health.

units.la: 36. Præcepit, &c. Altissiod. lib. 3. tract. 7. dicit mandatum Christi mox à Spiritu-Sancto fuisse revocatum. Sed rectius dicemus non fuisse præceptum proprie dictum, sed quandam significationem modestiæ, quâ cupiebat non propalari miracula à se facta, nisi quatenus id spectaret ad gloriam Dei: juxta illud Joan. 8. Ego non quæro gloriam meam, etsi glorifico me ipsum, gloria mea nihil est; simul ut exemplum humilitatis, & vitandæ vanæ gloriæ nobis ostenderet. Vide D. Th. 3. p.q. 13. art. 4. ad. 2. & q. 44. art. 3. ad 4.
units.tr: 36. He commanded, etc. The author of book 3, tract 7 of Altissiodorensis says that Christ's command was soon revoked by the Holy Spirit. But we shall rather say that it was not a command properly so called, but a certain sign of modesty, by which he wished the miracles done by him not to be published abroad, except insofar as this concerned the glory of God; in accordance with John 8: I do not seek my own glory; though I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. At the same time he wished to show us an example of humility and of avoiding vainglory. See Aquinas, Summa 3, q. 13, art. 4, ad 2, and q. 44, art. 3, ad 4.

units.la: Tanto magis plus. Pleonasmus Scripturæ familiaris.
units.tr: So much the more. A pleonasm familiar to Scripture.

units.la: 37. Amplius admirabantur. Nimirum attoniti quòd Christus nollet laudari ab iis, quibus tot ac tanta bona opera erat operatus. Bene Bene omnia fecit. Hebraismus, id est, omnia beneficiorum genera in homines contulit. Hinc Act. 10. v. 38. dicitur Christus pertransiisse benefaciendo, & sanando omnes oppressos a diabolo.
units.tr: 37. They were astonished beyond measure. Clearly astonished that Christ should not wish to be praised by those for whom he had done so many and such great good works. He has done all things well. A Hebraism, that is, he conferred every kind of benefit upon men. Hence Acts 10:38 says that Christ went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil.

units.la: CAPUT VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: 6. Gratias agens. Vide quae diximus Matth. 15. v. 36.
units.tr: 6. Giving thanks. See what we have said at Matt. 15. v. 36.

units.la: 7. Piscículos. Vide dicta ibidem v. 34.
units.tr: 7. Small fish. See what was said there on v. 34.

units.la: 8. Sportas. Vide dicta ibidem v. 37.
