units.tr: 8. Baskets. See what was said there on v. 37.

units.la: 9. Quasi quatuor millia. Matth. 15. v. 38. quatuor millia extra parvulos & mulieres.
units.tr: 9. About four thousand. Matth. 15. v. 38. Four thousand, besides the little children and women.

units.la: Dalmanutha. Vide dicta ibidem v. 39.
units.tr: Dalmanutha. See what was said there on v. 39.

units.la: 12. Ingemiscens Spiritu. Vide dicta Matth. 16. v. 4.
units.tr: 12. Sighing deeply in spirit. See what was said on Matth. 16. v. 4.

units.la: Si dabitur, &c. Id est, non dabitur. Est autem, inquit Elias Cretensis in Orat. 1. Apol. B. Greg. Naz. multis in locis sacrae Scripturae hujusmodi quoddam loquendi genus, apertam negationem habens. Cujusmodi illud etiam est, quod a Propheta Elia ad Achab dictum est. 3 Reg. 17. Vivit Dominus Deus exercituum, si erit annis tribus ros & pluvia; hoc est, non erit. Ezechiel 14. Vivo ego dicit Dominus, si filii eorum aut filiae liberabuntur; id est, non liberabuntur.
units.tr: If a sign shall be given, etc. That is, none will be given. There is, however, says Elias Cretensis in his first Oration of the Apology for St Gregory Nazianzen, in many places of Holy Scripture a kind of speech of this sort, which has a plain negation. Such is also that which the prophet Elijah said to Ahab, 3 Kings 17: "As the Lord God of hosts lives, there shall be neither dew nor rain these three years"; that is, there will not be. Ezekiel 14: "As I live, says the Lord, if their sons or daughters shall be delivered"; that is, they shall not be delivered.

units.la: 15. Cavete, &c. Vide dicta ibidem v. 12.
units.tr: 15. Beware, etc. See what was said there on v. 12.

units.la: 16. Cogitabant. Vide dicta ibidem v. 7.
units.tr: 16. They reasoned. See what was said there on v. 7.

units.la: 17. Cogitatis Graece, disceptatis.
units.tr: 17. You consider; in the Greek, you dispute.

units.la: 22. Adducunt ei caecum. Scientes, inquit Beda, quod tactus Domini sicut leprosum mundare, etiam caecos illuminare valeret.
units.tr: 22. They bring him a blind man. Knowing, says Bede, that the touch of the Lord could cleanse a leper, it could also give sight to the blind.

units.la: 23. Extra vicum. Bethsaida; quae Joan. 1. v. 44. vocatur civitas, hic dicitur vicus, quia exigua, & forte neque moenibus cincta erat.
units.tr: 23. Outside the village. Bethsaida, which in John 1 v. 44 is called a city, is here called a village, because it was small and perhaps not walled.

units.la: 24. Video homines velut arbores ambulantes. Id est, homines ab arboribus non possum visu distinguere, nisi ex ambulatione; nondum quippe percipio lineamenta membrorum, quibus homines ab arboribus discernuntur. Idem contingere homines eminus, vel in nocturna luce spectantibus notat venerabilis Beda.
units.tr: 24. I see men like trees walking. That is, I cannot distinguish men from trees by sight except by their walking; for I do not yet perceive the outlines of the limbs by which men are told apart from trees. Venerable Bede notes that the same happens to people who look at men from a distance, or in nocturnal light.

units.la: 25. Deinde iterum, &c. Quem, inquit Beda, uno verbo totum simul curare poterat, paulatim curat, ut magnitudinem humanae caecitatis offendat, quae vix & quasi per gradus ad lucem redeat, atque gratiam suam nobis indicet, per quam singula perfectionis incrementa adjuvat. 27. Et egressus est, &c. Quæ sequuntur expósita manent ex dictis Matth. 16.
units.tr: 25. Then again, etc. He who could cure everything at once with one word, says Bede, cures him little by little, so as to show the greatness of human blindness, which returns to the light scarcely and, as it were, by degrees, and so makes known to us his grace, by which he helps each increase of perfection. 27. And he went out, etc. What follows remains explained from what was said on Matth. 16.

units.la: 28. Quasi. Hæc particula deest in textu Græco.
units.tr: 28. As it were. This particle is lacking in the Greek text.

units.la: 31. Post tres dies resurgere. Hebraismus, id est, tertio post die. Vide Matth. 27. v. 63.
units.tr: 31. To rise after three days. A Hebraism, that is, on the third day after. See Matth. 27. v. 63.

units.la: 33. Vade retro, &c. Cur, inquit S. Petrus Damiani Serm. 1. de Evangelista Marco, Marcum alloquens, à tot magistri praeconiis calamum reprimit? & sola, quæ infirmitatis sunt, ad posterorum memoriam stylo committis? Credendum est: quia cum unus utrumque Spiritus impleat, alter ab altero, ille in docendi, iste in scribendi studio non discordat. Sicut enim Petrus à propria sua laude abstinuit: ita veridicus illius interpres ab ea, quam in magistro non didicit, sua descriptionis articulum refrenavit. Ad magnum quippe est nostræ ædificationis exemplum, ut & ille de se non offerenda, reprehendenda proferret: & iste sic per veritatis lineam rectus incederet, ut ne ad magistri quidem favorem aliquatenus declinaret.
units.tr: 33. Get behind me, etc. Why, asks St Peter Damian, Sermon 1 on the Evangelist Mark, addressing Mark, does he restrain his pen from the many proclamations of his teacher? Why do you commit to the memory of posterity only those things which belong to weakness? It must be believed that, since one and the same Spirit fills both, the one does not differ from the other, the one in zeal for teaching, the other in zeal for writing. For just as Peter abstained from his own praise, so the truthful interpreter of him restrained his account from that praise which he had not learned in his master. Indeed it is a great example for our edification, that the one should bring forward about himself things neither to be offered nor to be censured, and the other should walk so straight along the line of truth that he did not in any way turn aside even for his master's favour.

units.la: CAPUT IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: Pleraque quæ habentur in præsenti capite expósita sunt Matth. 17. & 18.
units.tr: Most of what is contained in the present chapter has been explained at Matt. 17 and 18.

units.la: 1. Transfiguratus est. Transfiguratio, inquit Victor Antiochenus, de qua hic agitur, secundum quendam externum fulgorem facta est. Nam ut Matth. narrat, facies ejus resplenduit ut sol, vestimenta autem ejus facta sunt alba sicut nix; ut Lucas autem habet, species vultus ejus facta est altera, & vestitus ejus albus & refulgens. Hinc tamen inferre non licet aliquam naturalis formæ mutationem in cœlesti illo regno olim futuram. Ut enim Christi effigies secundum se non est immutata, sed tantum illustrata; ita nec justi quoque, qui corpori claritatis illius conformabuntur, secundum formam mutabuntur; sed illorum tantum corpora quamdam splendoris & lucis accessionem acceptura sunt, quem quidem splendorem, lucisve accessionem Apostolus Paulus mutationem, Evangelistæ autem transfigurationem vocant.
units.tr: 1. He was transfigured. Transfiguration, says Victor of Antioch, of which this passage speaks, took place through a certain outward radiance. For, as Matthew relates, his face shone like the sun and his garments became white as snow; but Luke has it that the appearance of his face was changed, and his clothing was white and gleaming. Yet it is not permissible to infer from this that some change of natural form will one day take place in that heavenly kingdom. For just as the image of Christ was not itself altered, but only made bright, so the bodies of the righteous, who will be conformed to that glorious body, will not be changed in their form; rather, their bodies will receive a certain added splendour and light. This splendour or addition of light the Apostle Paul calls a change, but the Evangelists call it a transfiguration.

units.la: 11. Quomodo scriptum est. Scilicet Esaiæ 53. de quo capite potissimum intelligendum est, quod dicit Hieron. in Epist. ad Paulinum, Esaias non Prophetiam mihi texere videtur, sed Evangelium. In illo enim capite non tam futura prædicere, quam præsentem Christi passionem propriis oculis conspectam narrare videtur.
units.tr: 11. As it is written. Namely, Isaiah 53, and it is chiefly to this chapter that what Jerome says in his letter to Paulinus applies: Isaiah seems to me to weave not a prophecy but a Gospel. For in that chapter he seems less to foretell future things than to narrate Christ's present passion as if seen with his own eyes.

units.la: 12. Sicut scriptum est de eo. Hoc refertur ad prima hujus versiculi verba, Elias venit, & alluditur ad Prophetiam Malachiæ cap.
units.tr: 12. As it is written of him. This refers to the opening words of this verse, Elijah has come, and alludes to the prophecy of Malachi, chapter [4].

units.la: 13. Conquirentes. Id est, disceptantes, seu altercantes.
units.tr: 13. Disputing. That is, arguing or quarrelling.

units.la: 16. Spiritum mutum. Id est, qui hominem mutum efficiebat.
units.tr: 16. A dumb spirit. That is, one that made the man dumb.

units.la: 17. Allidit illum. Supple, ad terram.
units.tr: 17. Threw him down. Supply: to the ground.

units.la: Spumat, &c. Haec omnia esse solent symptomata morbo comitiali, seu epilepsia laborantium. Hunc Matthaeus vocat simpliciter lunaticum.
units.tr: Foams, etc. These are all wont to be symptoms of the falling sickness, or epilepsy, from which those suffering it are afflicted. Matthew simply calls him a lunatic.

units.la: 18. Arescit. Id est, inquit Euthymius, sine sensu est.
units.tr: 18. Withers. That is, says Euthymius, is without feeling.

units.la: Respondens iis. Graece, ei. Nempe Christus patrem epileptici alloquendo arguit omnes, etiam suos ipsos discipulos de incredulitate.
units.tr: Answering them. In Greek, to them. Namely, by addressing the father of the epileptic, Christ rebukes all of them, even his own disciples, for unbelief.

units.la: Incredula. Supple ex Matth. & Luc. & perversa, seu ut habet textus Graecus, & distorta, quae scilicet videns non videt, & audiens non audit obcaecatum habens cor.
units.tr: Unbelieving. Supply from Matthew and Luke: and perverse, or, as the Greek text has it, and twisted; that is, those who, seeing, do not see, and, hearing, do not hear, having a hardened heart.

units.la: Quamdiu apud vos ero. Non taedio superatus hoc dicit Christus mansuetus, ac mitis, qui non aperuit, sicut Agnus coram tondente, os suum, sed loquitur Christus adinstar Medici, qui si aegrotum videat contra sua praecepta se gerere, dicit: usquequo artis perdam industriam, me aliud jubente & te aliud perpetrante? B. Hier. in Matth. 7.
units.tr: How long shall I be with you? Christ, who is gentle and meek, who did not open his mouth as a lamb before its shearer, does not say this, overcome with weariness; rather, Christ speaks like a physician who, seeing a patient act contrary to his instructions, says: How long shall I lose my skill, when I order one thing and you do another? Jerome on Matthew 7.

units.la: 19. Cum vidisset eum. Scilicet Jesus puerum epilepticum adhuc accedentem, ut patet ex textu Graeco Luc. 9. v. 24.
units.tr: 19. When he saw him. Namely, Jesus saw the epileptic boy still approaching, as is clear from the Greek text of Luke 9, verse 24.

units.la: 20. Interrogavit. Ut scilicet mali gravitas omnibus innotesceret.
units.tr: 20. He asked. So that, of course, the gravity of the evil might become known to all.

units.la: 22. Si potes credere. Vide quae diximus Matth. 13. v. 58.
units.tr: 22. If you can believe. See what we said at Matthew 13, verse 58.

units.la: Omnia sunt possibilia credenti. Vel accipere, vel facere in nomine meo.
units.tr: All things are possible to him who believes. Either: to receive, or to do, in my name.

units.la: 23. Credo Domine, &c. Adhuc, inquit B. Greg. lib. 22. Moral. c. 14. ascendebat ad fidem, quam jam perceperat, qui uno eodemque tempore clamabat se & jam credere, & adhuc se incredulitate dubitare. Hinc est etiam quod Redemtori nostro a discipulis dicitur, Auge nobis fidem, ut quae jam accepta per initium fuerat, quasi per augmenta graduum ad perfectionem veniret.
units.tr: 23. I believe, Lord, etc. Still, says Gregory the Great in book 22 of the Moralia, chapter 14, he who at one and the same time cried out that he already believed and that he was still troubled by unbelief was ascending toward the faith which he had already received. Hence it is also that the disciples say to our Redeemer, Increase our faith, so that what had been received at the beginning might, by degrees of growth, come to perfection.

units.la: 40. Quisquis enim, &c. Argumentatur Christus a minori ad majus. Q. d. Si qui minimum quid fecerit in nomine meo, mercedem pro beneficio est accepturus, quanto magis ille mercedem suam recipiet, qui nomini meo favens, in eo virtutis operatur? Vide dicta Matth. 10. v. 42.
units.tr: 40. For whoever, etc. Christ argues from the less to the greater. That is, if one who does the smallest thing in my name is to receive a reward for the kindness, how much more will he receive his reward who, favouring my name, works virtue in it? See what was said at Matthew 10, verse 42.

units.la: 41. Et quisquis, &c. Est antithesis opposita versui 36. eo enim redit Christus post quaestionem a Joan. interpositam de eo, qui in nomine Christi daemonem ejiciebat, qua ipse sermonem Christi abruperat. Vide dicta Matth. 5. v. 30. & 18. v. 6. & 7.
units.tr: 41. And whoever, etc. This is an antithesis opposed to verse 36. For Christ returns to this point after the question, interposed by John, about the man who cast out demons in Christ's name, which had interrupted Christ's discourse. See what was said at Matthew 5, verse 30, and 18, verses 6 and 7.

units.la: 43. ubi vermis eorum non moritur, & ignis non extinguitur. Sic Esai.66. v. 24. Vermis eorum non morietur, & ignis eorum non extinguetur. Eccli. 7. v. 19. Vindicta carnis impii ignis & vermis. Hinc Aug. lib. 21. de Civit Dei c. 9. Potuit, inquit, brevius dici, Vindicta impii, cur ergo dictum est, Carnis impii, nisi quia utrumque, id est, & ignis & vermis poena erit carnis. Verum cum neque in textu Graeco, neque in Syra & Arabica versione, sed in sola Latina loco citato Eccli. extet carnis mentio, melius Aug. tam vermem quam ignem ad corpus pertinere probasset ex Judith. 16. v. 21. Debit enim ignem & vermes in carnes eorum, ut urantur & sentiant usque in sempiternum. Tamen, ut testatur B. Hieron. in locum citatum Esaiae, vermis nomine a plerisque conscientia accipitur peccatorum, quae torqueat in supplicis constitutos, quare vitio suo atque peccato caruerint Electorum bono.
units.tr: 43. where their worm does not die, and the fire is not quenched. So Isaiah 66, verse 24: Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched. Ecclesiasticus 7, verse 19: The vengeance on the flesh of the ungodly is fire and worm. Hence Augustine, book 21 of The City of God, chapter 9: It could have been said more briefly, Vengeance on the ungodly; why then was it said, On the flesh of the ungodly, unless because both, that is, both fire and worm, will be a punishment of the flesh. But since mention of the flesh is found neither in the Greek text nor in the Syriac and Arabic versions, but only in the Latin version of the cited passage in Ecclesiasticus, Augustine would have done better to prove that the worm as well as the fire pertains to the body from Judith 16, verse 21: For he will give fire and worms into their flesh, that they may burn and feel it for ever. Yet, as Jerome bears witness on the cited passage of Isaiah, by the name of worm many understand the conscience of sins, which torments those placed in punishment, because they have lacked the good of the elect through their vice and sin.

units.la: 45. ubi vermis eorum non moritur. Cadavera dimittit vermis cum abfumfit usque ad offa, ita ut praeter solum ὀστέον nihil superfit. At in inferis alius est vermis, qui animas nunquam dimittit. Vermis ille, inquit Theophylact. uniuscujusque est conscientia & memoria eorum, quae in hac vita fede sunt acta, quae quasi vermis absumit. Idem forte significavit vetus illa fabula de vulturibus, qui in inferis Tityi jecur renascens, perpetuo lancinant. Idem videre est apud Procopium in Esaiam, & B. Bernardum de consideratione lib. 5. cap. 12.
units.tr: 45. where their worm does not die. The worm leaves corpses when it has consumed them down to the bones, so that nothing remains except the bone [ὀστέον]. But in Hades the worm is different: it never leaves the souls. That worm, says Theophylact, is the conscience of each person and the memory of those things which were done wickedly in this life, which, like a worm, consumes. Perhaps that old fable of the vultures, which in Hades, as the liver of Tityos grew back, tore it perpetually, signified the same thing. The same may be seen in Procopius on Isaiah and in Bernard, On Consideration, book 5, chapter 12.

units.la: 46. Si oculus tuus scandalizat te, &c. Hinc Julius in Epist. ad Orientales Episcopos relata apud Athanasium; In rebus, inquit, Ecclesiasticis non specimen eloquentiae, sed Canones Apostolici requiruntur, operaque dari solet, ne quis ex parvis in Ecclesia scandalizetur. Expedit enim secundum Evangelicum verbum molam asinariam suspendi a collo, atque ita demergi, quam unum ex pusillis scandalizari. Gravem hanc Julii monitionem ea conditione temperant Scriptores e Commentariis venerabilis Bedae in praefens caput, ut vitetur proximi scandalum, quantum fieri potest sine peccato.
units.tr: 46. If your eye causes you to stumble, etc. Hence Julius, in his letter to the bishops of the East, as reported by Athanasius: In ecclesiastical matters, he says, what is sought is not a display of eloquence but the apostolic canons, and care is usually taken that no one among the little ones be made to stumble in the Church. For it is better, according to the Gospel word, to have a millstone hung from the neck and so be drowned, than for one of the little ones to be made to stumble. The writers who draw on the commentaries of the venerable Bede on this chapter temper this grave admonition of Julius with the condition that the stumbling of a neighbour be avoided as far as possible without sin.

units.la: 47. ubi vermis eorum non moritur. En tertio eamdem sententiam repetit supremus Magister, ut altius impressa maneat. Omni, inquit Victor Antiochenus, supplicio gravius est immortalem illum vermem pertuo extra ullam prorsus intermissionem avidè vorantem, diréque corrodentem circumferre; designatur autem hoc vermis nomine impurata, scelerataque conscientia; siquidem una haec animam peccatricem, nulliusque boni sibi conscia, inutilis paenitentiae aculeis instar edacis vermis continuo pungit & rodit. Unusquisque ergo scelerum sui ipsius accusator erit: etenim dum secum perpendit, animoque jugiter revolvit, quae in mortali hac vita improbè gessit, vel invitus se reum confiteri compelletur, propriæ nimirum conscientiæ stimulis actus, ejusdemque contra se testimonio aperte convictus. Ad hunc itaque sensum peccatorum vermis immortalis dicitur; neque enim quæ de vermi hic disputantur, ad sensibilem aliquem vermem, qui impiorum corda apud inferos rodat, transferenda sunt. Hæc eleganter & doctissimè Victor Antiochenus.
units.tr: 47. where their worm does not die. Here the supreme Teacher repeats the same sentiment a third time, so that it may remain more deeply impressed. It is more grievous than any punishment, says Victor of Antioch, to carry that immortal worm about, which devours greedily and gnaws fiercely without any interruption at all; and by this worm is designated the defiled and wicked conscience. For this alone continually pricks and gnaws the sinful soul, which is conscious of no good and is useless, with the stings of unavailing repentance, like a devouring worm. Each one therefore will be the accuser of his own crimes. For while he weighs them within himself and constantly turns over in his mind the wicked things he did in this mortal life, he will be compelled, though unwilling, to confess himself guilty, driven by the goads of his own conscience and openly convicted by its testimony against himself. In this sense, therefore, the worm of sinners is called immortal; for what is discussed here about the worm must not be transferred to some sensible worm which gnaws the hearts of the wicked in the underworld. Thus elegantly and most learnedly Victor of Antioch.

units.la: Et ignis non extinguitur. ut ignis, inquit idem Victor Antiochenus, qui peccatores incendit, alibi æternus, ita hoc loco inextinguibilis appellatur. Sunt autem qui per inextinctum hunc ignem, pollutæ, improbæque conscientiæ judicium & æstimationem designatam putant. Quandoquidem judicium illud, per, & propter immortalem vermem, instar æstuantis ignis in impiis usque grassatur flammæque more viscera illorum perpetuò depascitur. B. Hieron. lib. 18. in Esaïam 66. Vermis inquit, qui non moritur, & ignis qui non extinguetur à plerisque conscientia accipitur peccatorum, quæ torqueat in supplicus constitutos, quia vitio atque peccato suo tanto caruerunt bono, juxta illud quod dicitur, Versatus sum in miseria, dum infigitur mihi spina. Psal. 31. & in Proverbiis cap. 25. Tinea ossium cor intelligens; & iterum sub obelo, Sicut tinea vestimentum & vermis lignum, sic mæror excruciat cor viri. Hoc ad verbum legitur Homil. 9. inter Homilias Origenis in diversos Matthæi locos. B. Ambro. lib. 7. in Luc. cap. 14. eamdem tuetur sententiam: Qui, inquit, pacem & charitatem non detulerit ad Christi altaria, tolletur pedibus & manibus & mittetur in tenebras exteriores: ibi erit fletus & stridor dentium. Quæ sunt tenebræ exteriores? Nunquid illic quoque carcer aliquis, latumiæque subeundæ sunt? Minimè, sed quicumque extra promissa sunt cœlestium mandatorum, in tenebris exterioribus sunt, quia mandata Dei lumen sunt; & quicumque sine Christo est, in tenebris est, quia lumen in tenebris est Christus. Ergo neque corporalium stridor aliquis dentium, neque ignis aliquis perpetuus flammarum corporalium, neque vermis est corporalis. Sed hæc ideo, quia sicut ex multa cruditate & febres nascuntur, & vermes: ita si quis non decoquat peccata sua velut quãdam interposita sobrietate abstinentiæ, sed miscendo peccata peccatis, tanquam cruditatem quamdam contrahat veterum & recentium delictorum, igne aduretur proprio, & suis vermibus consumetur; unde & Esaias ait: Ambulate in lumine ignis vestri, & flammæ, quam accenderistis. Ignis est, quem generat malitia delictorum. Vermis est, eo quod, irrationabilia animæ peccata meditem, sensumque compungant, & quædam exedant viscera conscientiæ: quæ tanquam vermes ex unoquoque nascuntur, tanquam ex corpore peccatoris. Denique Dominus id declaravit per Esaiam dicens, Et videbunt membra hominum praevaricantium in me, & vermis eorum non moritur, & ignis eorum non extinguetur. Sridor quoque dentium prodit indignantis affectum, eò quod fere unumquemque poenitet, fere ingemiscat, fere irascatur, quod tam pervicaci improbitate delinquerit. His favet, quod Aug. lib. 12. de Genesi ad literam cap. 34. ait duplici ratione inferos dici & credi sub terris, vel quia sicut carni mortuae locus sub terra deputatur, sic animae per carnis peccatum mortuae similitudine subterranei loci representantur, vel quia sicut in corporeis rebus inferiora dicuntur quae graviora sunt, ita in rebus spiritualibus inferiora dicantur quae triftiora sunt. Haec tamen verba retractans Aug. 2 Retractationum cap. 24. De inferis, inquit, magis mihi videor dicere debuisse, quod sub terris sint, quam rationem reddere, cur sub terris esse credantur, sive dicantur, quasi non ita sit. Philo Judaeus in lib. de congressu quaerendae eruditionis gratia, Deus, inquit, injustam, impiamque animam fugatam a se ipso longissime dissipat in locum concupiscentiarum ac facinorum, qui locus impiorum vocatur aptius, quam ille fabulosus apud inferos; revera enim infernus nihil aliud est, quam vita miseri, sceleratii, execrandique hominis. Philoni subscribit B. Greg. Nyff. in Dialogo de anima & resurrectione cum sorore Macrina, quem aureum librum vocat Baronius anno 378. num. 46. ubi solvit objectiones quae fieri solent ex Scripturis ad probandum esse quasdam subterraneas animarum receptacula, quae vulgo inferi & orci nomen obtinent. B. Joan. Damascenus librum 4. de fide orthodoxa concludit his verbis: Et tradentur diabolus, & daemones ejus, & homo ejus, id est, Antichristus, & impii, & peccatores in ignem aeternum, non materialem, qualis est apud nos, sed qualem novit Deus. B. Greg. Mag. lib. 15. Mor. cap. 14. Ignis, inquit, corporeus, ut esse valeat, corporeis indiget alimentis. Qui, cum necesse est ut fervetur, per congesta ligna procul dubio nutritur, nec valet nisi succensus esse, & nisi fotus subsistere. At contra gehennae ignis, cum sit incorporeus (D. Th. 4. Distinct. 44. q. 3. legit corporeus, ut habetur in Editione Lugdunensi Hugonis a Porta) & in se missos reprobos corporaliter exurat, nec studio humano succenditur, nec lignis nutritur, sed creatus semel durat inextinguibilis, & succensione non indiget, & ardore non caret. B. tamen. Hieron. in Epist. ad Avitum inter Origenis haereses recenset eam sententiam, qua ignis infernalis dicitur esse conscientia peccatorum. Origenes, inquit, lib. 2. Periarchon, ignem gehennae, & tormenta, quae Scriptura sancta peccatoribus comminatur, non ponit in suppliciis, sed in conscientia peccatorum, quando Dei virtute & potentia omnis memoria delictorum ante oculos nostros ponitur, & veluti ex quibusdam feminibus in anima derelictis, universa vitiorum sorges exoritur, & quidquid feceramus in vita vel turpe, vel impium, omnis eorum in conspectu nostro pictura describitur, ac praeteritae voluptates mens intuens conscientiae punitur ardore, & poenitudinis stimulis confoditur. Et lib. in Epist. ad Ephesios 3. exponens illud ex capite 5. Nemo vos decipiat inanibus verbis, &c. ait: Quia sunt plerique qui dicunt non futura pro peccatis esse supplicia, nec extrinsecus adhibenda tormenta: sed ipsum peccatum, & conscientiam delicti esse pro poena, dum vermis in corde non meritur, & animo ignis accenditur in similitudinem febris, quae non torquet extrinsecus aegrotantem, sed corpora ipsa corripiens punit sine cruciatuum forinsecus adhibitione, quod possidet. Haec itaque persuasiones, & decipulas fraudulentas Paulus verba inania appellavit & vacua, quae videntur florem quemdam habere sermonis, & blandiri peccantibus; sed dum fiduciam tribuunt, magis eos ferunt ad aeterna supplicia. D. quoque Greg. Magnus lib. 4. Dialog. cap. 29. post Augustinum lib. 21. de Civit. Dei cap. 9. & 10. cum D. Th. & ceteris Scholasticis docet ignem inferni esse corporeum; imo Haymo Halberstaten-sis in Esa. 66. Basilius in Psal. 33. Author de triplici habitaculo apud Aug. tom. 9, quem authorem B. Bonaventura Soliloq. cap. 4. citat nomine S. Fulgentii, alii nomine S. Patritii Hybernorum ac Scotorum Apostoli, Innocentius III. lib. de contemtu mundi cap. 1. & 2. Julianus Pomerius lib. 3. de vita contemplativa cap. 12. Hugo Victor. lib. 4. de anima cap. 13. Author Elucidarii B. Anselmo ascripti, Chrysostomus, Theophylactus, & inter recentiores Serrarius in Judith. 16. Greg. de Valentia 3. part de Beat. & Damnat. corporum Disput. 11. q. 5. puncto 3. existimant proprie dictos vermes fore in proprio dicto igne inferorum; hancque sententiam Aug. probabilem appellat lib. 12. de Civit. Dei, cap. 9. Verum nihil pro igne vel verme corporeo valide & irrefragabiliter colligi potest ex sacris Scripturis, quae passim assumta metaphora ex illis poenis, quas sentiunt homines, maximis, longe majores inferni poenas adumbrare solent. Dicamus itaque cum Damasceno ignem inferni esse qualem novit Deus, quia ut utar Aug. verbis lib. 20. de Civit. Dei cap. 16. Ignis inferni cujusmodi, & in qua rerum vel mundi parte futurus sit, hominem scire arbitror neminem, nisi forte cui Spiritus Divinus ostendit. Imo & ipse Greg. Magnus lib. 4. Dialog. cap. 4. ubi infernus sit definire non audet, licet nihil obstare dicat, quominus sub terra esse credatur. Ingeniosissimus Th. Anglus probat ignem inferni non esse corporeum, ex eo quod daemones quocumque pergant, suum secum infernum circumferre dicantur. Verùm jam plerique videntur non ambigere ignem gehennæ corporeum esse, in quo certum est corpora cruciari, ut loquitur B. Greg. Magnus lib. 4. Dialog. cap. 29. Facile autem conciliaveris fortassis inter se dicta Sanctorum Patrum allata & similia, si adverteris ex Aug. in Psal. 57.quòd futura post mortem peccatorum pœna duas species habet; aut inferorum est, ubi ardebat dives ille, qui volebat sibi stillam aquæ stillari in linguam de digito pauperis, quem ante januam suam contemserat, quando ait, Quoniam crucior in hac flamma; & altera est illa in fine, de qua audituri sunt, qui ad sinistram ponendi sunt, Ite in ignem æternum, qui paratus est diabolo & Angelis ejus. Itaque S. Doctor sentit ignem infernum, qui animas separatas cruciat, esse incorporeum; ignem verò, quem appellat ignem æternum, quo cruciabuntur corpora damnatorum, esse corporeum. Quamvis etiam, ut idem S. Doctor ait lib. 21. de Civit. Dei cap. 10. miris, veris tamen modis, etiam spiritus incorporei possint pœnâ corporalis ignis affligi, siquidem viventis hominis incorporeus spiritus tenetur in corpore, & ex ejusdem corporis variis affectionibus cruciatur.
units.tr: And the fire is not quenched. As the fire, says the same Victor of Antioch, who kindles sinners, is elsewhere called eternal, so in this place it is called unquenchable. Some, however, think that by this unquenched fire is meant the judgment and estimation of a polluted and wicked conscience. For that judgment, through and on account of the immortal worm, rages on in the wicked like a seething fire, and always feeds upon their entrails as a flame does. St. Jerome, book 18 on Isaiah 66: The worm, he says, that does not die, and the fire that is not quenched, are understood by most to be the conscience of sinners, which torments those who are placed in punishment, because they have been deprived of so great a good through their vice and sin, according to what is said: "I am turned into misery while the thorn is fixed in me" (Ps. 31), and in Proverbs chapter 25: "The moth in the bones is the understanding heart"; and again, under the obelus: "As the moth eats a garment and the worm wood, so grief torments a man's heart." This is read word for word in Homily 9 among the Homilies of Origen on various passages of Matthew. St. Ambrose, book 7 on Luke chapter 14, holds the same view: He who has not brought peace and charity to the altars of Christ, he says, will be taken by the feet and hands and cast into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. What are the outer darkness? Is there some prison there too, and chains to be endured? By no means, but whoever is outside the promises of the heavenly commandments is in the outer darkness, because the commandments of God are light, and whoever is without Christ is in darkness, because Christ is the light in darkness. Therefore there is neither any bodily gnashing of teeth, nor any perpetual fire of bodily flames, nor is the worm bodily. But these things are so because, just as fevers and worms are born from a great indigestion, so if someone does not digest his sins with a certain interposed sobriety of abstinence, but by mixing sins with sins, contracts a kind of indigestion of old and recent offences, he will be burned by his own fire and consumed by his own worms. Hence Isaiah also says: "Walk in the light of your fire and of the flame you have kindled." The fire is that which the malice of offences generates. The worm is that because the unreasonable sins of the soul plot and sting the mind, and eat away at certain entrails of conscience; these, like worms, are born from each person, as if from the body of the sinner. Finally, the Lord declared this through Isaiah, saying: "And they shall see the limbs of men who have transgressed against me, and their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched." The gnashing of teeth also reveals the feeling of one who is indignant, because nearly everyone repents, nearly groans, nearly is angry, that he sinned with such stubborn wickedness. Augustine's book 12 on the literal meaning of Genesis, chapter 34, favours these words, where he says that the underworld is said and believed to be under the earth for two reasons: either because, as a place under the earth is assigned to a dead body, so souls dead through the sin of the flesh are represented by a likeness to an underground place, or because, as in bodily things those things are called lower which are heavier, so in spiritual things those are called lower which are sadder. Yet Augustine, retracting these words in book 2 of the Retractations, chapter 24, says: "Concerning the underworld, I seem to myself to have had to say rather that they are under the earth than to give a reason why they are believed or said to be under the earth, as if it were not so." Philo the Jew, in his book on the search for learning by means of intercourse, says: "God drives far away from himself the unjust and impure soul, scattering it into a place of lusts and crimes, which is more fittingly called the place of the wicked than that fabulous one among the dead; for in truth hell is nothing other than the life of a wretched, wicked and accursed man." St. Gregory of Nyssa agrees with Philo, in his Dialogue on the soul and the resurrection with his sister Macrina, which Baronius calls a golden book, in the year 378, no. 46, where he answers the objections usually raised from the Scriptures to prove that there are certain underground receptacles of souls, which commonly bear the name of hell and Orcus. St. John Damascene concludes his fourth book on the orthodox faith with these words: And the devil, and his demons, and his man, that is, the Antichrist, and the impious and sinners, will be delivered into eternal fire, not material such as we have, but such as God knows. St. Gregory the Great, book 15 of the Morals, chapter 14: Corporeal fire, he says, in order to exist, needs corporeal food. Since it must be fed, it is undoubtedly nourished by heaped-up wood, and cannot be unless it is kindled and kept alive by fuel. But on the contrary, the fire of Gehenna, since it is incorporeal (Thomas Aquinas, book 4, distinction 44, question 3, reads "corporeal", as found in the Lyon edition of Hugo a Porta) and burns bodily the reprobate cast into it, is not kindled by human effort, nor fed by wood, but once created it endures unquenchable, needs no kindling, and lacks no heat. Nevertheless St. Jerome, in his letter to Avitus, counts among the heresies of Origen the view that the fire of hell is the conscience of sinners. Origen, he says, in book 2 of the Peri Archon, does not place the fire of Gehenna and the torments which holy Scripture threatens to sinners in punishments, but in the conscience of sinners, when by the power and might of God every memory of offences is set before our eyes, and as if from certain seeds left behind in the soul, the whole filth of vices arises, and whatever we have done in life that was shameful or impious is depicted in our sight, and the mind, looking upon past pleasures, is punished by the burning of conscience and pierced by the goads of remorse. And in his book on the Epistle to the Ephesians, book 3, explaining that verse of chapter 5, "Let no one deceive you with empty words," etc., he says: There are many who say that the punishments for sins are not to come, nor are torments to be applied from outside, but that sin itself and the consciousness of the offence are the punishment, while the worm does not die in the heart, and fire is kindled in the mind like a fever, which does not torment the sick man from outside, but seizing the body itself punishes it without any external application of torments, which it possesses. These persuasions and fraudulent snares, therefore, Paul called empty and vain words, which seem to have a certain flower of speech and flatter sinners; but while they grant confidence, they rather carry them on to eternal punishments. St. Gregory the Great also, book 4 of the Dialogues, chapter 29, after Augustine, book 21 of the City of God, chapters 9 and 10, teaches, with St. Thomas and the other Schoolmen, that the fire of hell is corporeal; indeed Haymo of Halberstadt on Isaiah 66, Basil on Psalm 33, the author of the work on the threefold dwelling-place among the works of Augustine, volume 9 (whom St. Bonaventure, in Soliloquies chapter 4, cites under the name of St. Fulgentius, others under the name of St. Patrick, Apostle of the Irish and Scots), Innocent III, book on the contempt of the world, chapters 1 and 2, Julian Pomerius, book 3 on the contemplative life, chapter 12, Hugh of St. Victor, book 4 on the soul, chapter 13, the author of the Elucidarium ascribed to St. Anselm, Chrysostom, Theophylact, and among more recent writers Serarius on Judith 16, and Gregory of Valencia, part 3 on the blessed and the damned, disputation 11, question 5, point 3, all think that worms properly so called will be in the proper fire of the underworld; and Augustine calls this opinion probable in book 12 of the City of God, chapter 9. Yet nothing can be validly and irrefutably inferred from the sacred Scriptures in favour of a bodily fire or worm, since the Scriptures, using metaphor drawn from those punishments which men feel as the greatest, commonly shadow forth far greater punishments of hell. Let us therefore say with Damascene that the fire of hell is such as God knows, for, to use Augustine's words in book 20 of the City of God, chapter 16: I think no one is able to know what sort of fire hell is, or in what part of the things of the world it will be, unless perhaps the Divine Spirit reveals it to someone. Indeed St. Gregory the Great himself, book 4 of the Dialogues, chapter 4, where he does not dare to define where hell is, though he says nothing hinders it from being believed to be under the earth. The most ingenious Thomas Anglus proves that the fire of hell is not corporeal, because the demons are said to carry their own hell with them wherever they go. But now most people seem to have no doubt that the fire of Gehenna is corporeal, in which it is certain that bodies are tormented, as St. Gregory the Great says in book 4 of the Dialogues, chapter 29. Perhaps you may easily reconcile the sayings of the holy Fathers cited and similar ones, if you notice, from Augustine on Psalm 57, that the punishment that sinners will face after death has two kinds: one belongs to the underworld, where that rich man burned, who wished a drop of water to be dripped onto his tongue from the finger of the poor man whom he had scorned at his gate, when he said: "Because I am tormented in this flame"; and the other is that at the end, which those who are to be placed at the left hand will hear of: "Depart into everlasting fire, which is prepared for the devil and his angels." Thus the holy Doctor holds that the infernal fire which torments separated souls is incorporeal, but that the fire which he calls eternal fire, in which the bodies of the damned will be tormented, is corporeal. Although also, as the same holy Doctor says in book 21 of the City of God, chapter 10, in wonderful yet true ways, even incorporeal spirits can be afflicted by the punishment of bodily fire, since the incorporeal spirit of a living man is held in the body and is tormented by the various affections of that same body.

units.la: 48. Omnis enim, &c. Præceptum Domini fuerat Levitici 2. v. 13. Quidquid obtuleris sacrificii, sale condies, nec auferes sal fœderis de sacrificio tuo. In omni oblatione offeres sal. Triplici præcepto, affirmativo, negativo, & universali obstringebat Deus Judæos ut quidquid offerrent, salirent. Perstat igitur Christus in eadem victimarum similitudine, q. d. Omnis enim, scilicet, qui in gehennam mittitur, instar victimæ, cuæ divinæ justitiæ immolatur, igne salietur, id est, ut crucietur semper, atque incorruptus maneat, igne, quasi sale, quod urendo, seu mordendo conservat, condietur, quemadmodum juxta Legem omne sacrificium sale condiri debet. Etiam in falsorum deorum sacrificiis solemne fuisse sale uti didicimus ex Plinio lib. 31. cap. 7. ubi de salis laudibus agens ait: Maximè autem in Sacris ejus commendatur autoritas, quando nulla conficiuntur sine mola salsa.
units.tr: 48. Omnis enim, &c. The Lord had given a command in Leviticus 2:13: "Whatever offering of meat you bring, you shall season with salt; neither shall you allow the salt of the covenant of your God to be lacking from your meat offering; with all your offerings you shall offer salt." God bound the Jews by a threefold command, affirmative, negative and universal, that whatever they offered they should salt. Christ therefore keeps to the same likeness of the victims, as if to say: for everyone, that is, everyone who is cast into Gehenna, being like a victim sacrificed to divine justice, will be salted with fire, that is, will be tormented always and remain undecayed. The fire, like salt, which preserves by burning or biting, will season him, just as by the Law every sacrifice had to be seasoned with salt. We have learned from Pliny, book 31, chapter 7, that it was also customary to use salt in the sacrifices of false gods, where, speaking of the praises of salt, he says: "Its authority is especially commended in their sacred rites, since none are performed without salted meal."

units.la: Et omnis victima. Particula, & non sumitur hic copulativè, sed comparativè pro, sicut. Quo sensu eadem particula usurpatur Proverb. 25. v. 3. 23. & 25.
units.tr: Et omnis victima. The particle et is not used here copulatively but comparatively, meaning just as. In this sense the same particle is used in Proverbs 25:3, 23 and 25.

units.la: 49. Bonum est sal, q.d. Obsoniorum obsonium & condimentum est sal, ut loquitur Plutarchus Sympos. lib. 5. Problem. 10. Hinc non immerito inter præcipua vitæ necessaria ponitur Eccli. 39. v. 31. Hinc & sal pro stipendio olim dabant Reges, ut testatur Plinius lib. 31. cap. 7. & patet ex textu Hebræo. 1. Esd. 4. v. 14. Unde & Salarii vocabulum manavit.
units.tr: 49. Bonum est sal: that is, salt is the seasoning and condiment of relishes, as Plutarch says in the Symposiacs, book 5, question 10. For this reason it is not without cause counted among the chief necessities of life in Ecclesiasticus 39:31. For this reason kings once gave salt as a stipend, as Pliny attests in book 31, chapter 7, and as is clear from the Hebrew text of 1 Esdras 4:14. Hence the word salarium (salary) also derives.

units.la: Quod si sal, &c. Idem hic intenditur atque Matth. 5. v. 13. Vide igitur quæ ibi diximus.
units.tr: Quod si sal, &c. The same thing is meant here as in Matthew 5:13. See therefore what we said there.

units.la: Habete in vobis sal, & pacem habete inter vos. Et, hic sumitur exegeticè, pro, id est, Hebraismo Scripturæ familiari ut alias observavimus in Matth. Quòd autem Salvator dicat habete in vobis sal, pro, pacem colite, seu pacem habete inter vos, inde est, quòd sal est unitivum, unde & in fœderibus, tanquam unionis tessera est Hebræis usitatum; unit enim, densat, & quasi coagulat. Hinc Num. 18. v. 19. dicitur, Pactum salis est sempiternum coram Domino. Quis autem miretur, pacis symbolum & vitæ, esse sal, quo etiam latrones ad societatem flectuntur, ut observat B. Isid. Pelusiota lib. Epist. 5. Miror, inquit, admodum quo pacto qui nudos vibrant gladios latrones, quíque etiam adversus eos, à quibus nulla afficiuntur injuriâ, armantur, sale communicato latrones esse desinant. Αἰαν Σαυμάζω, ὅτως οἱ μὲν λῃσταὶ ὀξίοφη γυμνὰ ὑποπλέ- τᾶς, ὃ κατὰ τ μηδὲν ἀδικούντων ὁπλιζόμενοι, ἀλλὰ καὶ- γυμνητὰς, ὃν ἔτι οἱ λῃσταί.
units.tr: Habete in vobis sal, et pacem habete inter vos. Here et is taken explicatively, meaning that is, a Hebraism familiar in Scripture, as we have noted elsewhere in Matthew. That the Saviour says have salt in yourselves to mean cultivate peace, or have peace among yourselves, is because salt is a uniting thing. Hence among the Hebrews it was customary to use it as a token of union in covenants; it unites, thickens and, as it were, binds together. Hence Numbers 18:19 says: "It is a covenant of salt for ever before the Lord." Who, then, would wonder that salt, by which even robbers are brought into fellowship, is the symbol of peace and of life, as Saint Isidore of Pelusium observes in book 5 of his Epistles? "I marvel," he says, "very greatly how it is that robbers who brandish bare swords, and who arm themselves even against those from whom they have suffered no injury, cease to be robbers when they have shared salt." [Θαυμάζω, ὅπως οἱ μὲν λῃσταὶ ξίφη γυμνὰ ἐπισείοντες, καὶ κατὰ μηδὲν ἀδικούντων ὁπλιζόμενοι, ἁλὸς κοινωνήσαντες λῃσταὶ οὐκέτι εἰσίν.]

units.la: CAPUT X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: PLeraque, quæ habentur in præsenti capite, exposuimus Matth. 19. & 20.
units.tr: Most of what is contained in the present chapter we have explained at Matthew 19 and 20.

units.la: 13. ut illos tangeret. Id est, ut juxta consuetudinem etiamnum Judæis usitatam manuum impositione illis benediceret, seu saufta precaretur. Hunc esse hujus loci sensum, patet ex Matth. 19. v. 13.
units.tr: 13. That he might touch them. That is, that according to the custom still in use among the Jews he might bless them by the laying on of hands, or pray for their welfare. That this is the sense of this passage is clear from Matthew 19:13.

units.la: 14. Talium est enim regnum Dei. Non, inquit venerabilis Beda, dicit Illorum, sed Talium, mores designans, non ætatem. Vide dicta Matth. 18. v. 3.
units.tr: 14. For of such is the kingdom of God. Not, says the venerable Bede, he says "of those," but "of such," designating their character, not their age. See what was said at Matthew 18:3.

units.la: 15. Quisquis non receperit regnum Dei velut parvulus. Id est, quisquis non habuerit æmulam puerilis simpliciatis bonitatem, quâ disponatur ad regni Dei intra se suscepionem, non intrabit in illud, seu non erit de regno Dei.
units.tr: 15. Whoever does not receive the kingdom of God as a little child. That is, whoever does not have the rival goodness of childlike simplicity, by which he is disposed to receive the kingdom of God within himself, will not enter into it, or will not be of the kingdom of God.

units.la: 21. Dilexit eum. Id est, signa dilectionis exhibuit ei, unde & ex textu Græco verti potest, osculatus est eum; oscula autem sunt signa exteriora dilectionis interioris.
units.tr: 21. Loved him. That is, he showed signs of love toward him; whence it can also be rendered from the Greek text, kissed him; kisses, however, are the outward signs of inward love.

units.la: unum tibi deest. Supple, ad perfectionem.
units.tr: One thing you lack. Supply: for perfection.

units.la: Sequere me. In textu Græco, & Syro additur; ferens crucem.
units.tr: Follow me. In the Greek and Syriac text the addition is: bearing the cross.

units.la: 29. Reliquerit. Scilicet, zelo Dei secundum scientiam, ut nempe mihi perfectius adhæreat, & expeditius Evangelica præcepta meditetur & exequatur.
units.tr: 29. Has left. Namely, out of zeal for God according to knowledge, so that he may cleave to me more perfectly and may more readily meditate upon and carry out the evangelical precepts.

units.la: Aut matrem. Græcè additur, aut uxorem.
units.tr: Or mother. In Greek the addition is: or wife.

units.la: 30. Nunc in tempore hoc. Vide dicta Matth. 19.
units.tr: 30. Now in this time. See what was said at Matthew 19.

units.la: 32. Præcedebat. Alacriter properans ad Crucem diu desideratam, & jam concupiscenti animo præparatam; Christus enim proposito sibi gaudio sustinuit Crucem confusione contemtâ. Vide reliqua, quæ habentur à præsenti versu usque in finem capitis exposita Matth. 20.
units.tr: 32. Was going before. Hastening eagerly toward the Cross long desired and already prepared in his mind's eager longing; for Christ, having the joy set before him, endured the Cross, despising the shame. For the rest, which is set out from the present verse to the end of the chapter, see Matthew 20.

units.la: 41. Erit omnium servus. Qui proximum, sicut oportet, diligit, non recusat servire ei submissius quolibet servo: propterea Apostolus Gal. 5. v. 13. non præcipit simpliciter Galatis, ut diligant se invicem, sed ut per charitatem serviant invicem, intensam significans amicitiam ἐπιθυμίαν φιλίας, inquit in laudatum Gal. 5. locum B. Chrysostomus.
units.tr: 41. Will be the servant of all. He who loves his neighbour as he ought does not refuse to serve him more humbly than any servant: therefore the Apostle in Galatians 5:13 does not simply enjoin the Galatians that they love one another, but that through love they serve one another, signifying an intense friendship [ἐπιθυμίαν φιλίας], as the venerable Chrysostom says in his comment on the cited passage of Galatians 5.

units.la: CAPUT XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: Cum appropinquarent Jerosolymæ, &c. Quæ sequuntur expósita sunt Matth. 21.
units.tr: When they drew near to Jerusalem, etc. What follows is explained at Matthew 21.

units.la: Vide quæ observavimus Matth. 21. v. 8, & 9. ad illustrandum morem præclarum obviàm eundi alicui honoris causâ, gestando ramos palmarum, aut aliarum arborum. Sed & ad exequias cum ramis veteres prodire solitos videre est apud Ammonium Monachum De Patribus Sinaitis & Rhaithenfibus p. 106, 128, & 129. Et in Historia Laufiaca cap. 39.
units.tr: See what we have noted at Matthew 21:8-9 to illustrate the splendid custom of going out to meet someone as an honour, carrying branches of palm or of other trees. That the ancients also used to go out with branches to funerals can be seen in Ammonius the Monk, On the Sinaite and Raithene Fathers, pp. 106, 128 and 129, and in the Lausiac History, chapter 39.

units.la: 10. Benedictum. Id est, felix fauflúmque fit. Quod venit. Id est, quod restauratum est.
units.tr: 10. Blessed. That is, let him be made happy and prosperous. That comes. That is, that which has been restored.

units.la: Hosanna in excelsis. Adventus Domini, ejusque incarnatio non solum hominum salus fuit in terra, sed etiam Angelorum in cælo: quia dum homines in terra salvantur, Angelorum numerus, qui, diabolo cadente, minoratus fuerat, integratur in cælo. Hosanna ergo in excelsis tantumdem est tanquam si dicatur, Salva nos, qui etiam es salus in cælis. D. Ambros. ferm. 45. in Dom. in Ramis.
units.tr: Hosanna in the highest. The coming of the Lord, and his incarnation, was the salvation not only of men on earth but also of the angels in heaven. For while men are saved on earth, the number of angels, which had been diminished when the devil fell, is made complete in heaven. So "Hosanna in the highest" amounts to the same as if it were said: Save us, you who are also the salvation in the heavens. St Ambrose, sermon 45, On the Lord's Day, on Palm Sunday.

units.la: 13. Cumque vidisset, &c. Qui dicit Christum propterea tantum fecisse miracula, ut non essent nisi miracula, potest illum etiam dicere nescisse quod non esset tempus pomorum, quando ficus quæsivit in arbore. Non enim erat illius pomi tempus, sicut Evangelista testatur, & tamen esuriens poma quæsivit in arbore. Christus nesciebat quod rusticus sciebat? Quod noverat arboris cultor, non noverat arboris Creator? Cum ergo esuriens poma quæsivit in arbore, significavit aliquid se esurire, & aliquid aliud quærere, & arborum illam sine fructu foliis plenam reperit, & maledixit, & aruit. Quid arbor fecerat fructum non afferendo? quæ culpa arboris infæcunditas? Sed sunt qui fructum voluntate dare possunt. Illorum est culpa sterilitas, quorum fœcunditas est voluntas. Erant ergo Judæi habentes verba Legis, & facta non habentes, pleni foliis, & fructus non ferentes. Hoc dixi ut persuaderem Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum ideo miracula fecisse, ut aliquid illis miraculis significaret, ut excepto eo, quod mira & magna & divina erant, aliquid inde etiam disceremus. B. Aug. Serm. 44. de verbis Domini.
units.tr: 13. And when he had seen, etc. Whoever says that Christ worked miracles only so that they would be nothing but miracles could also say that he did not know it was not the season for figs when he sought fruit on the tree. For it was not the season for that fruit, as the Evangelist testifies, and yet, being hungry, he sought fruit on the tree. Did Christ not know what the farmer knew? Did the Creator of the tree not know what the tree's cultivator knew? So when, being hungry, he sought fruit on the tree, he signified that he was hungry for something and was seeking something else; and finding the tree full of leaves but without fruit, he cursed it, and it withered. What fault had the tree committed in not bearing fruit? What is barrenness but the fault of a tree that could bear fruit by its will? The fault of sterility belongs to those whose fruitfulness lies in their will. So the Jews had the words of the Law but did not have the deeds, were full of leaves and did not bear fruit. I have said this to persuade you that our Lord Jesus Christ worked miracles so that they might signify something through them, so that, apart from the fact that they were wonderful and great and divine, we might also learn something from them. St Augustine, sermon 44, On the Words of the Lord.

units.la: 14. Jam non amplius, &c. Ficulneam Dominus haud sine causa execratione devinxit, verum ut ingratis Judæis illud ostenderet se eam vim habere, quæ inferendo quoque supplicio par esset; quoniam enim in omnibus miraculis nullam eum cuique molestiam intulisse perspexerant, idcirco eum prodesse tantum posse existimabant, ac non item eam vim habere, quæ improbos malo afficere posset, quamobrem à subsistentia animæ experti populum ingratum admonet, se ulcisci quidem ipsius scelera posse, sed pro sua bonitate nolle. Exaruit igitur arbor, ut hominibus terrorem injiciat. B. Ifid. Pel. lib. 1. Epist. 51.
units.tr: 14. Now no more, etc. The Lord did not bind the fig tree with a curse without cause, but so that he might show the ungrateful Jews that he had the power also to inflict punishment equal to the offence. For since they had seen that in all his miracles he had done no harm to anyone, they thought that he could only do good and did not have the power to afflict the wicked with evil. Therefore, from the experience of the soul's subsistence, he warns the ungrateful people that he can indeed avenge their wickedness, but that he is unwilling to do so, because of his goodness. The tree therefore withered, so that it might strike terror into men. St Isidore of Pelusium, book 1, letter 51.

units.la: 15. Cæpit ejicere, &c. Non frustra per semetipsum Dominus æs nummulariorum fudit, & cathedras vendentium columbas evertit, nimirum significans, quia per Magistros quidem vitam judicat plebium, sed per semetipsum falsa examinat Magistrorum. B. Greg. lib. 25. Mor. cap. 21.
units.tr: 15. He began to cast out, etc. It was not in vain that the Lord himself poured out the money of the moneychangers and overturned the seats of those who sold doves; clearly signifying that, while he judges the life of the people through the teachers, he himself examines the false teachers. St Gregory, Morals, book 25, chapter 21.

units.la: 16. Et non sinebat, ut quisquam transferret vas per Templum. Id est, & prohibebat ne quisquam nummulariorum, vel columbas vendentium sua utensilia transferens compendiosiorem per Templum viam captaret, sicque cogebantur omnes omnia per exteriorem viam asportare. Præclaré itaque Aug. in Regula. cap. 2. In Oratorio nemo aliquid agat, nisi ad quod factum est, unde & nomen accepit.
units.tr: 16. And he did not allow anyone to carry a vessel through the Temple. That is, he also forbade anyone, moneychanger or seller of doves, from carrying his utensils through the Temple to take a shorter route; so everyone was compelled to carry everything by the outer way. Augustine therefore rightly says in the Rule, chapter 2: In the oratory let no one do anything except that for which it was made, from which it also receives its name.

units.la: 17. Domus mea: Christus apud tres Evangelistas hunc Esaiæ locum allegat, dum de Templo materiali Judæorum ejicit ementes & vendentes. Et hic diserte etiam adjicit illud, omnibus Gentibus, cùm tamen Aug. ex his duabus potissimum particulis concludat in Præfat. Psal. 130. quòd hic locus non potuit de Templo materiali Judæorum intelligi, quia ad illud Templum jam olim destructum non possunt accurrere omnes Gentes orationis gratiâ; verùm secundum Prophetam, & interpretationem Christi etiam domus illa materialis prædicitur domus futura orationis omnibus Gentibus, quia post ejus restaurationem factam à reditu ex captivitate Babylonis futura erat ita gloriosa, ut passim etiam Gentes, sicut & in oratione Salomonis prædictum fuerat, orationis causa ad eam ascenderent. Ceterùm quòd dicitur domus orationis, simul sub oratione intelliguntur omnia, quæ ad externum Dei cultum pertinent, & in primis sacrificium; unde illud mulieris Samaritanæ ad Christum Joan. 4. Vos dicitis quia Jerosolymis est locus, ubi oportet adorare, id est, sacrificare, nam orationes & preces extra Jerosolymam quovis loco ad Deum fieri poterant, nec id negabant Judæi Samaritanorum adversarii. Cùm autem Templum materiale Judæorum figuraret verum illud Dei Templum, quod est Ecclesia, mirum non est, quòd hæc Esaiæ prophetia plenius fuerit impleta in ea, ad quam ex omnibus omninino Gentibus usque in hodiernum diem congregantur fideles.
units.tr: 17. My house: Christ, in three Evangelists, cites this passage of Isaiah when he drives out those who buy and sell from the material Temple of the Jews. And here he expressly adds the words for all the nations, although Augustine, in the Preface to Psalm 130, concludes chiefly from these two particles that this passage could not be understood of the material Temple of the Jews, because to that Temple, already long since destroyed, not all nations can run for the sake of prayer. Rather, according to the Prophet and Christ's interpretation, that material house too was foretold as a house of prayer for all nations, because after its restoration at the return from the Babylonian captivity it was to be so glorious that the nations also, as had been foretold in Solomon's prayer, would everywhere ascend to it for the sake of prayer. Moreover, when it is said house of prayer, everything that pertains to the external worship of God is understood together under prayer, and above all sacrifice; hence the words of the Samaritan woman to Christ in John 4: You say that in Jerusalem is the place where one must worship, that is, sacrifice, for prayers and supplications could be made to God at any place outside Jerusalem, and the Jews, the adversaries of the Samaritans, did not deny this. Since the material Temple of the Jews prefigured that true Temple of God, which is the Church, it is no wonder that this prophecy of Isaiah was more fully fulfilled in her, to whom the faithful are gathered from all the nations, up to the present day.

units.la: 22. Habete fidem Dei. Hebraismus, id est, fidem magnam seu plenissimam, quam alibi comparavit Christus grano sinapis.
units.tr: 22. Have the faith of God. A Hebraism, that is, great or most complete faith, which Christ elsewhere compared to a grain of mustard seed.

units.la: 23. Quicumque dixerit. Ponitur, unum determinatum pro quovis opere factu difficili, spēmque humanam superante.
units.tr: 23. Whoever shall say. One determinate thing is put for any work that is difficult to do and exceeds human hope.

units.la: Non hæsitaverit. Operis difficultate terrius.
units.tr: Shall not doubt. Lesser in degree, from the difficulty of the work.

units.la: CAPUT XI- I.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI- I.

units.la: I. Vneam passinavit, &c. Vide Matth. 21. v. 33. & sequent.
units.tr: I. He planted a vineyard, etc. See Matth. 21. v. 33 and following.

units.la: 6. Quia reverebuntur filium meum. Hoc itaque ideo arbitror positum ut quod de hominibus loquebatur, Pater humano locutus videatur affectu. Unde Luc. 20. v. 13. Idem Pater omnipotens & omniscius dixisse inducitur, Forsitan cum hunc viderint, verebuntur. Ambros. lib. 5. de fide cap. 7.
units.tr: 6. They will respect my son. I therefore think this was put in so that, since he was speaking of men, the Father seems to speak with human feeling. Hence Luke 20. v. 13, where the same Father, almighty and all-knowing, is introduced as saying, Perhaps when they see him they will respect him. Ambrose, book 5 On the Faith, ch. 7.

units.la: 13. Mittunt ad eum, &c. Vide Matth. 22. v. 15. & sequent.
units.tr: 13. They send to him, etc. See Matth. 22. v. 15 and following.

units.la: 15. Sciens versutiam. Græce. Hypocrisim.
units.tr: 15. Knowing their craftiness. Greek: hypocrisy [ὑπόκρισιν].

units.la: Denarium. Scilicet Romanum, sequitur enim denarium seu numisma illud, ut Matthæus loquitur, Cæsaris imagine & superscriptione percussum fuisse.
units.tr: The denarius. Namely the Roman one, for it follows that the denarius, or coin as Matthew calls it, bore Caesar's image and inscription.

units.la: 16. Cæsaris. Non putemus Cæsarem Augustum, sed Tiberium significari privignum ejus, qui in locum successit ipsius, sub quo passus est Dominus; omnes autem Reges Romani a primo Caio Cæsare, qui imperium arripuerat, Cæsares appellati sunt. E. Hieron. lib. 3. in Matth. 22.
units.tr: 16. Of Caesar. Let us not think Caesar Augustus is meant, but Tiberius, his stepson, who succeeded him, under whom the Lord suffered. All the Roman kings from the first Gaius Caesar, who had seized power, were called Caesars. Jerome, book 3 on Matthew 22.

units.la: 18. Venerunt, &c. Vide Matth. 22.
units.tr: 18. They came, etc. See Matth. 22.

units.la: 24. Erratis non scientes Scripturas. Id est, quia nescitis Scripturas.
units.tr: 24. You err, not knowing the Scriptures. That is, because you do not know the Scriptures.

units.la: 30. Ex toto, &c. Docemur, inquit Theodoret. q. 3. in Deuteron. dilectionem non scindere in dilectionem Dei, & dilectionem auri, sed totam dilectionis vim Creatori tribuere.
units.tr: 30. With all, etc. We are taught, says Theodoret, Q. 3 on Deuteronomy, not to divide love into love of God and love of gold, but to attribute the whole force of love to the Creator.

units.la: 34. Non es longè a regno Dei. Non longè abes a vera fide Evangelica, qui noveris quid sit, misericordiam volo, & non sacrificium, hoc est, plusquam sacrificium, sed adhuc tibi deest, ut credas in me, qui unus sum Deus cum Patre Cælesti, qui licet sim ex semine David secundum carnem, tamen ratione Divinitatis meæ sum ejus Dominus. In hunc ferè sensum hæc exponit B. Hilar. lib. 9. de Trinitate. Tacitè itaque Christus invitat Scribam ad agnitionem suæ Divinitatis.
units.tr: 34. You are not far from the kingdom of God. You are not far from the true Gospel faith, you who know what is meant by I desire mercy, and not sacrifice, that is, more than sacrifice; but you still lack to believe in me, who alone am God together with the Heavenly Father, and who, although I am of the seed of David according to the flesh, am nevertheless by reason of my Divinity his Lord. Blessed Hilary expounds this in roughly this sense in book 9 On the Trinity. Christ thus tacitly invites the scribe to acknowledge his Divinity.

units.la: 36. David dicit in Spiritu-sancto. Est quædam in hoc loquendi genere efficacia potentissima; significatur enim non tam Davidem locutum fuisse, quàm spiritum-sanctum, qui per os Davidis tanquam per organum locutus fuerit.
units.tr: 36. David said in the Holy Spirit. There is a most powerful force in this manner of speaking; for it signifies not so much that David spoke as that the Holy Spirit spoke through David's mouth, as through an instrument.

units.la: 38. In doctrina sua. Id est, inter docendum, cùm doctrinam suam traderet. Cavete, &c. Fastum, & avaritiam Scribarum fugiendam docet. Vide Matth. 23. v. 5. &c.
units.tr: 38. In his teaching. That is, while teaching, when he was delivering his doctrine. Beware, etc. He teaches that the pride and greed of the scribes must be shunned. See Matth. 23. v. 5 etc.

units.la: Volunt in stolis ambulare. Id est, affectant superbæ ostentationis insignia. Erat autem stola vestis talaris, & elegans, quâ Scribæ ad pompam ūtebantur.
units.tr: They want to walk in long robes. That is, they aim at the insignia of proud display. The stola was a long, elegant robe, which the scribes wore for show.

units.la: 40. Accipient prolixius judicium. Id est, gravius, durius, & acerbius. Usus autem est hac voce Dominus, ut alluderet ad prolixas orationes hypocritarum, qui, ut nummum tollant pauperi, in prece pernoctant; cum tamen porrecta manus pauperi preces juvare soleat, ut loquitur venerabilis Beda. Apud Lucam vertit Vulgatus interpres, damnationem majorem, apud Matthæum, amplius judicium.
units.tr: 40. They will receive a longer judgment. That is, a heavier, harsher and more bitter one. The Lord used this word alluding to the long prayers of hypocrites, who spend the night in prayer so that they may take a coin from a poor man; although an outstretched hand usually helps prayers for the poor, as the venerable Bede says. In Luke the Vulgate translator renders it "greater condemnation", in Matthew "more judgment."

units.la: 41. Contra Gazophylacium. Id est, juxta seu prope Gazophylacium, seu è regione Gazophylacii. Vox Gazophylacium est Semiperfica, & passim sumitur pro sacro ærario, cujus Præfectus dicitur à Nonno Gazophylax.
units.tr: 41. Opposite the treasury. That is, next to or near the treasury, or across from it. The word gazophylacium is Semitic, and is commonly used for the sacred treasury, whose prefect is called gazophylax by Nonnus.

units.la: 42. Minuta; Græcè Λεπτὰ. Juxta Suidam octo sunt minuta in chalco sive ære. Chalci in obolo sex. Minuta seu minutia, ut vocat Seneca, in obolo quadraginta octo. Oboli in drachma sex. Minuta in drachma 288. Sicque donum viduæ erat centesima quadragesima quarta drachmæ unius pars. Juxta Cleopatram in chalco minuta 8. Chalci in obolo 8. Minuta in obolo 64. In drachma oboli 6. & minuta 384. Atque ita donum viduæ esset centesima nonagesima secunda pars drachmæ.
units.tr: 42. Small coins; Greek: minuta [λεπτά]. According to Suidas, there are eight minuta in a chalcus, or copper coin; six chalci in an obol; forty-eight minuta, or minutia as Seneca calls them, in an obol; six obols in a drachma; 288 minuta in a drachma. Thus the widow's gift was the one hundred and forty-fourth part of one drachma. According to Cleopatra, there are eight minuta in a chalcus and eight chalci in an obol, so sixty-four minuta in an obol; six obols in a drachma make 384 minuta. And so the widow's gift would be the one hundred and ninety-second part of a drachma.

units.la: Quod est quadrans. Vide dicta. Matth. 5. v. 26.
units.tr: Which is a quadrans. See what was said at Matth. 5. v. 26.

units.la: 43. Plus omnibus misit. Ubertior est enim nummus è parvo, quàm thesaurus è maximo; quia non quantum datur, sed quantum residet expenditur: nemo plus tribuit, quàm qui sibi nihil relinquit. B. Ambros. lib. de Viduis.
units.tr: 43. She put in more than all. For a coin from a small sum is richer than a treasure from a very large one, because what counts is not how much is given but how much is left after spending; no one gives more than the one who keeps nothing back for himself. Blessed Ambrose, book On Widows.

units.la: 44. Omnes Hebraïsmus Scripturæ familiaris, id est, ceteri.
units.tr: 44. All. A Hebraism familiar in Scripture, that is, the rest.

units.la: Ex eo, &c. q.d. Omnes ex superfluo partem exiguam contulerunt, cum vidua ex eo quod parcissimè suppetebat illi ad victitandum, nihil prorsus sibi reservaverit, sed omnia, quæ habebat, obtulerit, ac si vitam propriam pro nihilo duceret.
units.tr: Out of their abundance, etc. That is to say: all of them gave a small part of their surplus, whereas the widow, out of what barely sufficed for her to live on, kept nothing at all for herself, but offered everything she had, as though she counted her own life as nothing.

units.la: C
units.tr: C

units.la: CAPUT XI- II.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI-II.

units.la: Cum egrederetur, &c. Vide Marth. 24. ubi pleraque, quæ in præsenti capite habentur difficilia, sunt exposita.
units.tr: When he went out, etc. See Matt. 24, where most of the difficult points in the present chapter are explained.

units.la: 3. Contra Templum. Id est, è regione Templi.
units.tr: 3. Against the Temple. That is, opposite the Temple.

units.la: 4. Incipient consummari. Græcè, sunt consummanda.
units.tr: 4. They will begin to be consummated. In Greek, "they are to be consummated."

units.la: 8. Et fames. Græcè additur, & turbationes.
units.tr: 8. And famines. The Greek adds "and troubles."

units.la: 9. Et in Synagogis vapulabitis. Supple, conciliorum iussu.
units.tr: 9. And in the synagogues you will be beaten. Supply: by the order of the councils.

units.la: Hyeme non fiant. Ad ambulandum quippe in hyemę corpore frigoris obsistit, & juxta præceptum Legis ambulare longius in Sabbato non licet. Quamvis enim præceptum illud in vitæ periculo cessaret, plerisque tamen Judæorum ea excep-tio non probabatur; & pauci fuere inter Christianos à Judaif-mo conversos, qui se ab obligatione Sabbati liberos esse intelligerent ante excidium Jerosolymitanum. Ceterum observantia diei Dominicæ in nova Lege successit observanti& Sabbati, non ex vi præcepti Legis, sed ex constitutione Ecclesiæ, & consuetudine populi Christiani, utait D. Th. 22. q. 122. a. 4. ad 4. Qua de re hæc habet Aug. serm. 151. de tempore, Dominicum ergo diem Apostoli, & Apostolici viri ideo religiosâ solemnitate habendum sanxerunt, quia in eodem redemtor noster à mortuis resurrexit. Quique ideo Dominicus appellatur, ut in eo à terrenis operibus vel mundi illecebris abstinentes, tantum divinis cultibus insistamus: dantes scilicet diei huic honorem & reverentiam propter ipsam resurrectionis nostræ, quam habemus in illa. Nam sicut ipse Dominus Iesus Christus & Salvator resurrexit à mortuis, ita & nos in novissima die resurrecturos speramus. Apparet autem hunc etiam in Scripturis sacris esse solemnem, ipse enim est primus dies seculi, in ipso formata sunt elementa mundi, in ipso creati sunt Angeli, in ipso quoque à mortuis resurrexit Christus, in ipso de cælis Spiritus Sanctus super Apostolos descendit, manna in eodem in eremo primum de cælo datum est. His enim speciebus, ac talibus indiciis Dominica dies extat insignis. Ac ideo sancti Doctores Ecclesiæ decreverunt omnem gloriam Iudaici Sabbatismi in illam transferre, ut quod ipsi in figura, nos celebraremus in veritate: quia tunc erit requies nostra vera, quando resurrectio fuerit perpetrata, & remuneratio in anima simul & corpore perfecta. Hæc Aug.
units.tr: Pray that it not be in winter. For walking in winter, the body is opposed by the cold, and by the precept of the Law it is not permitted to walk farther on the Sabbath. For although that precept lapses when life is in danger, most of the Jews did not approve this exception, and few among the Christians converted from Judaism understood themselves to be free from the obligation of the Sabbath before the destruction of Jerusalem. Moreover, the observance of the Lord's day in the new Law succeeded the observance of the Sabbath, not by the force of a precept of the Law, but by the constitution of the Church and the custom of the Christian people, as St. Thomas says, 22 q. 122 a. 4 ad 4. On this matter Augustine has the following in sermon 151 on the time: Therefore the Apostles and apostolic men ordained that the Lord's day be kept with religious solemnity, because on it our Redeemer rose from the dead. It is called the Lord's so that, abstaining on it from earthly works and worldly allurements, we may devote ourselves only to divine worship, giving this day honour and reverence on account of the resurrection of ourselves, which we have in it. For just as the Lord Jesus Christ himself, our Saviour, rose from the dead, so we too hope to rise on the last day. It appears moreover that this day is also solemn in the holy Scriptures: for it is the first day of the age; on it the elements of the world were formed; on it the Angels were created; on it too Christ rose from the dead; on it the Holy Spirit descended from heaven upon the Apostles; on the same day manna was first given from heaven in the desert. By these kinds of signs and such indications the Lord's day stands out. And so the holy Doctors of the Church decided to transfer all the glory of the Jewish Sabbath to that day, so that what they celebrated in figure, we might celebrate in truth: because our rest will be true then, when the resurrection has been accomplished and the reward perfected in soul and body together. Thus Augustine.

units.la: Neque Angeli. Voluit Christus discipulos docere, ne humanam naturam transcendentia discere annitantur; nam dum dicit ab Angelis ignorari diem Judicii, admonentur discipuli, quòd discere attentant id, quod Angeli ignorant; dum verò addit & à Filio ignorari, prohibentur non solùm discere, sed & ulterius quaerere. Ita Chrysostomus, & Theophylactus in cap. 24. Matthæi.
units.tr: Nor the Angels. Christ wished to teach the disciples not to strive to learn what transcends human nature. For when he says that the day of judgment is unknown to the Angels, the disciples are warned that they are trying to learn what the Angels do not know; but when he adds that it is unknown also to the Son, they are forbidden not only to learn but to inquire any further. So Chrysostom and Theophylact on Matthew 24.

units.la: Neque Filius. Quoad humanam naturam in statu exinanitionis; nam quoad divinam naturam, & in statu exaltationis, cùm sit constitutus judex, utique novit judicii diem & horam. Sic autor homiliarum in Marcum sub nomine Chrysostomi Hom. 14. Qui ante passionem nescit, post resurrectionem novit. Quod probat ex eo quod Act. 1. post resurrectionem ab Apostolis interrogatus quando restituturus esset regnum Israel, non respondit se nescire, sed, Non est vestrûm scire, non vobis prodest scire diem judicii.
units.tr: Nor the Son. With respect to human nature in the state of humiliation; for with respect to the divine nature and in the state of exaltation, since he has been constituted judge, he certainly knows the day and the hour of judgment. So the author of the homilies on Mark, under the name of Chrysostom, Hom. 14: He who before the passion does not know, after the resurrection knows. He proves this from the fact that in Acts 1, when after the resurrection he was asked by the Apostles when he would restore the kingdom to Israel, he did not reply that he did not know, but said, "It is not for you to know," "it is not profitable for you to know the day of judgment."

units.la: Nisi Pater. Hoc est, sed solus Pater habet scientiam illius diei & horæ, quâ mundus erit judicandus. Verùm omnia quæ habet Pater sunt Filii, [?πρὸ τῆς ἀγεννησίας], ut loquitur Nazianz. Orat. 44. seu, ut Oecumenius in cap. 1. epist. ad Hebræos [?πρὸ τῶν αἰώνων πατήρ]. Et omnia quæ habet Filius sunt SpiritûsSancti, [?πρὸ τῆς γεννήσεως], inquit Nazianzenus loco citato. Vide commentarium nostrum in Mat 24. v. 36 Præclarè itaque pro more B. Cyrillus Alexandrinus Thesauri lib.4. cap.4. Non oportet igitur propter hanc vocem (Neque Filius) ignorationem Dei Verbo inurere, sed potius misericordiam ejus admirari, quod non recusaverit propter nos ad tantam humilitatem descendere, ut omnia nostra, & ipsam etiam ignorantiam suscipceret--Filium etiam ignorare ait, de seipso ut homine loquens, nec sibi derogans ut Deo: scit enim ut Deus quod ut homo ignorat. Idcirco non addidit, quod Spiritus-Sanctus etiam ignoraret, Spiritus enim omnia scit, ipsa etiam profunda Dei, ut scribitur 1 Cor. 2. v. 10. Quod si Spiritus-Sanctus non ignorat, qui à Filio accipit, Ille namque inquit Joan. 16. v. 14. de meo accipiet, quomodo Filius ignorabit, qui omnia scientis Spiritus est largitor?--- Sed ignorat videlicet ut homo, quod ut Deus optimè novit--- Sicut ergo voluit tanquam homo fame ac siti, ceterisque hujusmodi laborare, sic etiam ut homo diem illum ignorat. Aliquando enim ut Deus, aliquando ut homo loquitur, ut & Deum & hominem verum se ostendat--Diem illum & horam & ignorat & scit, alterum ut homo, alterum ut Deus--- Igitur diem & horam adventûs sui, in quantum Verbum & Sapientia Dei est, non ignorat: Sed ne dolorem teneris adhuc discipulis faceret, desiderantibus illud scire, verè se dixit ut hominem ignorare; infirmitates enim nostras omnes accepit, hac de causa ignorâsse se dixit--- Cùm verè ab eo dicatur, ut ab homine, fratribus enim in omnibus similis fuit, secundum Paulum Heb. 2. v. 17.
units.tr: But the Father. That is, but the Father alone has knowledge of that day and hour on which the world is to be judged. Yet all that the Father has belongs to the Son, [before the unbegottenness], as Nazianzen puts it, Orat. 44; or, as Oecumenius says on chapter 1 of the Epistle to the Hebrews, [before the ages, the Father]. And all that the Son has belongs to the Holy Spirit, [before the begetting], says Nazianzen in the passage cited. See our commentary on Matt. 24:36. Excellently, therefore, and as is his custom, St. Cyril of Alexandria, Thesaurus book 4 chapter 4: It is not right, then, because of this word (Nor the Son) to brand the Word of God with ignorance, but rather to marvel at his mercy, that he did not refuse for our sake to descend to such humility as to take upon himself all our things, and even our very ignorance. ... He says that the Son too is ignorant, speaking of himself as man, and not disparaging himself as God: for as God he knows what he, as man, does not know. Therefore he did not add that the Holy Spirit too would be ignorant, for the Spirit knows all things, even the deep things of God, as it is written in 1 Cor. 2:10. If the Holy Spirit is not ignorant, who receives from the Son, for he, says John 16:14, will receive of mine, how can the Son be ignorant, who is the giver of the Spirit who knows all things? ... But he is ignorant, namely as man, of what as God he knows very well. ... Just as he chose, as a man, to suffer hunger and thirst and other such things, so also as man he does not know that day. For sometimes he speaks as God, sometimes as man, so that he may show himself to be both God and true man. ... That day and hour he both knows and does not know, the one as man, the other as God. ... Therefore the day and hour of his coming, insofar as he is the Word and Wisdom of God, he does not not know; but lest he cause grief to his disciples, who were still tender and desired to know it, he truly said that he was ignorant as man; for he took upon himself all our infirmities, and for this reason he said he was ignorant ... since it is truly said of him as of a man, for in all things he was like his brethren, according to Paul, Heb. 2:17.

units.la: Hæc Cyrillus ex versione Georgii Trapezuntii, textus Græcus non est mihi ad manum. Ignorat igitur secundum habitum humanitatis, qui omnia scit secundum potentiam deitatis, ἀγνοεῖ τοῦτο τὸ χρῆμα τῆς ἀνθρωπότητος, ὁ γινώσκων τὴν δύναμιν τῆς θεότητος, ut loquitur alicubi Chrysostomus.
units.tr: Thus Cyril, from the version of George of Trebizond; the Greek text is not at hand for me. He is ignorant, therefore, according to the habit of humanity, who knows all things according to the power of the deity, [ἀγνοεῖ τοῦτο τὸ χρῆμα τῆς ἀνθρωπότητος, ὁ γινώσκων τὴν δύναμιν τῆς θεότητος], as Chrysostom says somewhere.

units.la: 33. Nescitis enim quando tempus sit, ut pendulâ expectatione sollicitudo fidei probetur, semper diem observans dum semper ignorat; quotidie timens, quod quotidie sperat.
