Tert. lib de anima cap. 33. Vide autem, inquit Theophylactus, quomodo non dixerit, nescio enim quando tempus est, sed nescitis. Occultavit enim nos iram ob utilitatem, ut dum certa futuri judicii momenta nescimus, semper tanquam in excubiis constituti, & in quadam virtutis specula collocati, peccandi consuetudinem declinemus, ne nos inter vitia Diei Domini deprehendat. B. Ambros. de fide lib. 5. cap. 8.
units.tr: 33. You do not know when the time is, so that the anxiety of faith may be tested by a suspended expectation, always observing the day while always not knowing it, fearing daily what it hopes for daily. Tertullian, On the Soul, ch. 33. See, says Theophylact, how he did not say, "I do not know when the time is," but "you do not know." For he hid the hour from us for our benefit, so that, while we do not know the certain moments of the future judgment, we may always stand as if on watch, placed on a lookout of virtue, and so turn aside from the habit of sinning, lest the Day of the Lord catch us among our vices. St. Ambrose, On Faith, book 5, ch. 8.

units.la: 34. Sicut homo, &c. Q. d. Perinde se habet Filius hominis atque pater-familias, qui peregrè profectus, &c. Peregrè autem est prosectus Redemptor noster, cum in ea carne, quam assumserat, abiit in cœlum; carnis enim locus proprius terra est, quæ quasi ad peregrina ducitur, dum per Redemptorem nostrum in cælo collocatur. B. Greg. Hom. 9. in Evang.
units.tr: 34. As a man, etc. That is: The Son of man stands in the same relation as a householder who has gone abroad, etc. Our Redeemer went abroad when he went up into heaven in the flesh he had assumed; for the proper place of flesh is earth, which is, as it were, led away to foreign parts, while through our Redeemer it is set in heaven. St. Gregory, Homily 9 on the Gospel.

units.la: Dedit servis suis potestatem cujusque operis. Græcè, potestatem, & suum cuique opus. Hoc est, quod Apost. dicit Ephel. 4. Ipse dedit quosdam quidem Apostolos, &c. Hinc discimus non solùm potestatem ipsam pastoralem, sed etiam distinctionem stationum, in quibus unicuique opus proprium incumbit de jure divino esse. Hinc catholica antiquitas multis conciliorum constitutionibus cavit, ne quisquam suas metas transgrederetur, & alienæ curæ se ingereret. Concil. Nicæn. Oecum. 1. Can. 16. Cp. 1. Qecum. 2. can.
units.tr: He gave his servants authority over each work. In Greek, "authority, and his own work to each." This is what the Apostle says in Eph. 4: He himself gave some indeed as apostles, etc. From this we learn that not only the pastoral power itself but also the distinction of stations, in which each person has his own proper work, is by divine right. Hence ancient Catholic antiquity, by many constitutions of councils, took care that no one should overstep his own bounds or intrude into another's charge. Council of Nicaea, the first Ecumenical, can. 16. Cp. 1. Oecum. 2. can.

units.la: 2. Carthag. 1. can. 10. Carthag. 2. can. 11. Carthag. 3. can. 20, 21, & 46. Sardic. can. 15. Arelat. 2. can. 13.
units.tr: 2. Carthag. 1. can. 10. Carthag. 2. can. 11. Carthag. 3. can. 20, 21, & 46. Sardic. can. 15. Arelat. 2. can. 13.

units.la: Janitori. Cui nimirum totius domûs cura mandata est, id est, Episcopo præcepit ut vigilet. Simile est præceptum Pauli Act. 20. Attendite vobis & universo gregi, &c.
units.tr: To the doorkeeper. That is, the care of the whole house has been entrusted to him, and the bishop is commanded to keep watch. Paul gives a similar command in Acts 20: Take heed to yourselves and to all the flock, etc.

units.la: 35. An galli cantu. Vide quæ diximus Matth. 26. v. 34.
units.tr: 35. At the crowing of the cock. See what we said on Matt. 26:34.

units.la: 36. Dormientes. Id est, præsentium tantùm curam gerentes, & vitâ Gentium viventes.
units.tr: 36. Sleeping. That is, caring only for present things and living the life of the Gentiles.

units.la: 37. Omnibus dico, vigilate. Aug. Ep. 80. ad Hesychium: In quo quemque invenerit suus novissimus dies, in hoc eum comprehendet mundi novissimus dies: quoniam qualis in die isto moritur, talis in die illo judicabitur. Cur itaque omnibus dicit, Vigilate, nisi quia eo modo pertinet ad omnes, quomodo dixi? Tunc enim unicuique veniet dies illa, cum venerit ei dies, ut talis hinc exeat, qualis judicandus est illo die. Ac per hoc vigilare debet omnis Christianus, ne imparatum inveniat eum Domini adventus. Imparatum autem inveniet ille dies, quem imparatum invenerit hujus vitæ ultimus dies.
units.tr: 37. What I say to all, watch. Augustine, Ep. 80, to Hesychius: On whatever day each man's last day finds him, on that same day the last day of the world will find him, for as he dies on that day, so he will be judged on that day. Why then does he say to all, "Watch," unless because it applies to all in the way I have said? For that day will come to each person when his own day comes, so that he leaves this life such as he is to be judged on that day. And therefore every Christian ought to watch, lest the Lord's coming find him unprepared. Now that day will find unprepared the one whom the last day of this life finds unprepared.

units.la: CAPUT XIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: I. Erat autem, &c. Vide Matth. 26. ubi pleraque, quæ in præsenti capite habentur, sunt exposita. Azyma, id est, azymorum festum. Pluralis est numeri. Quærebant, &c. Feriâ quartâ Concilium convenit, & propterea jejunamus etiam nos quartis feriis. Theophylact.
units.tr: I. Now it was, etc. See Matt. 26., where most of what is contained in this chapter is explained. Unleavened bread, that is, the feast of unleavened bread. It is plural in number. They were seeking, etc. The council met on the fourth day of the week, and for that reason we also fast on Wednesdays. Theophylact.

units.la: 3. Fracto Alabastro effudit. Ut uberior sequeretur effusio, præcessit Alabastri fractio.
units.tr: 3. She broke the alabaster and poured it out. So that a fuller outpouring might follow, the breaking of the alabaster came first.

units.la: Prævenit ungere corpus meum in sepulturam. Q.d. O Juda, ne mihi ritus sepulchrales invideas, licet vita spoliaveris; nam mulier hoc sepulchrali ritu mortem, cujus tu mihi autor, prævertit. Honorem puta sepulturæ meæ hoc esse, & si eadem apparas, tumulum saltem concede. Unguenti funebris mentio est in lib. 2 Paralip. cap.16. v.14. posuerúntque eum, Asa regem Juda, super lectum suum plenum aromatibus, & unguentis meretriciis, id est, odoriferis, quæ erant arte Pigmentariorum confecta, & combusserunt super eum, id est, bustum ei fecerunt, ambitione nimia. Extat & in Evangelio Joannis cap.19. v.39. hujus consuetudinis mentio in Christi Domini sepultura, & infrà c.16. v.1. aromata coëmta leginus, quibus ungerent Jesum, tertiâ die à sepultura.
units.tr: She has anointed my body beforehand for burial. That is, O Judas, do not begrudge me the rites of burial, though you have stripped me of life; for the woman has anticipated by this funeral rite the death of which you are the author. Think of it as the honour of my burial, and if you are preparing the same thing, at least grant me the tomb. There is mention of funeral ointment in 2 Chronicles 16:14: and they laid him, Asa king of Judah, upon his bed full of spices and perfumes of the apothecaries, that is, fragrant things, which were prepared by the art of the perfumers, and they burned them over him, that is, they made him a funeral pyre, with exceeding great ambition. This custom is also mentioned in the Gospel of John 19:39 in the burial of the Lord Christ, and below, chapter 16:1, we read that spices were bought, with which they would anoint Jesus on the third day after the burial.

units.la: 9. In universo mundo. Prophetat Christus & Evangelium, & mulieris factum in toto terrarum orbe prædicarum iri.
units.tr: 9. In the whole world. Christ prophesies that the Gospel and the deed of the woman will be proclaimed in the whole orb of the earth.

units.la: 10. Unus de duodecim. Electioribus scilicet. Christi discipulis, quos & Apostolos vocavit.
units.tr: 10. One of the twelve. Namely, one of the chosen disciples of Christ, whom he also called Apostles.

units.la: 12. immolabant. Scilicet, Judæi.
units.tr: 12. were sacrificing. Namely, the Jews.

units.la: 14. Refectio. Id est, refectionis locus, Græcè καταλυμα, id est, diversorium, ut vertit ipse Vulgatus interpres Luc.22.v.7.
units.tr: 14. The guest room. That is, the place of refreshment, in Greek [καταλυμα], that is, a lodging, as the Vulgate translator himself renders it at Luke 22:7.

units.la: 23. Biberunt ex illo. Hysterologia; præmisit enim Christus consecrationis formulam, Hic est sanguis. Omnes. Scilicet, qui aderant, quibus dixerat Christus, Bibite ex illo omnes, ut habetur Matth. 26.
units.tr: 23. They all drank of it. A hysteron proteron; for Christ first gave the words of consecration, This is the blood. All. Namely, those who were present, to whom Christ had said, Drink of it, all of you, as is found in Matthew 26.

units.la: 24.Hic est Sanguis meus novi Testamenti. Sensus est, id, quod hoc poculo continetur, est Symbolum Sanguinis mei cujus effusione sancitur novum testamentum. Vocatur autem novum Testamentum ea promissio, quâ Deus spiritualia bona homini per novum Adam rehovato se daturum promisit: quomodo vetus Testamentum dicitur pactum, quod priori tempore inierat Deus cum Israelitis, ut si Legem à se per Moysem datam servarent, temporalium bonorum abundantiam eis retribueret. Vide Aug. de Spiritu & Litera cap.19. & sequent.
units.tr: 24. This is my blood of the new testament. The sense is that what is contained in this cup is the symbol of my blood, by whose shedding the new testament is ratified. The promise by which God pledged to give spiritual goods to man through the renewed new Adam is called the new testament, just as the old testament is called the covenant which God had earlier made with the Israelites, that if they kept the Law given through Moses, he would repay them with an abundance of temporal goods. See Augustine, On the Spirit and the Letter, chapter 19 and following.

units.la: 27. Percutiam Pastorem. Zachar.13. v.7. Percute Pastorem. Evangelistæ Deum videntur inducere loquentem, quasi ipse sit Filium suum Pastorem oves proprio cruore saginantem Percussurus; Zacharias vero videtur à Deo tantum permitti ut percutiatur, ex quo fit ut gregis dispergantur oves. Idem omnino colligitur sensus, sive percute, sive percutiam, dicatur: Deus enim erat, qui Pastorem pro ovibus percuti jubebat, atque adeo quod per alios fieri permittebat, per se facere merito dicebatur. Sic apud Esaiam ejusdem verbi & sententiæ habemus exemplum: nam cum dominicæ passionis acerbitatem expendisset, & causas in nostris sceleribus abluendis & pœnis sublevandis siras esse ostendisset, hæc subdit: Et nos putavimus eum quasi leprosum, percussum à Deo, vel percussum Deum, ut legunt nonnulli, & humiliatum: ut indicet Deum Optimum Maximum eum, qui in Filio suo vindictam sumat de peccatis nostris, & Deum ipsum Filium Patris hominem factum à Deo Patre suo percussum esse-
units.tr: 27. I will strike the Shepherd. Zechariah 13:7: Strike the Shepherd. The Evangelists seem to introduce God speaking, as if he himself were about to strike his Son, the Shepherd who fattens the sheep with his own blood; but Zechariah seems to say only that God permits him to be struck, from which it follows that the sheep of the flock are scattered. The very same sense is gathered whether it is said strike or I will strike: for it was God who commanded the Shepherd to be struck on behalf of the sheep, and so what he permitted to be done through others was rightly said to be done by himself. Thus in Isaiah we have an example of the same word and sense: for when he had considered the bitterness of the Lord's passion, and had shown that its causes lay in the washing away of our sins and the lightening of our punishments, he adds these words: And we thought him stricken, struck down by God, or, as some read, God struck him, and humbled: so as to indicate that God the Best and Greatest takes vengeance for our sins in his Son, and that God the Son himself, made man, was struck by God his Father.

units.la: 28. Et cum iniquis reputatus est. Sic ipse Christus de se explicat hanc Esaiæ Prophetiam Luc.22. v.37. Quamvis autem Marcus hac Prophetiâ dicat designatam Christi medii inter duos latrones crucifixionem, altius tamen observat Hier. in Esa.53. v.12. intelligi posse hoc Esaiæ vaticinium, nempe inter iniquos Christum velut iniquum reputatum, ut à peccato redimeret iniquos juxta illud Psal.87. Æstimatus sum cum descendentibus in lacum, factus sum sicut homo sine adjutorio inter mortuos liber.
units.tr: 28. And he was reckoned among the wicked. Thus Christ himself explains this prophecy of Isaiah at Luke 22:37. Although Mark says that the crucifixion of Christ between two thieves was designated by this prophecy, Jerome, on Isaiah 53:12, observes more profoundly that this prophecy of Isaiah can be understood as meaning that Christ was reckoned among the wicked as if he were wicked, so as to redeem the wicked from sin, in accordance with Psalm 88: I am counted among those who go down into the pit; I am become as a man without help, free among the dead.

units.la: 36. Pater. Græce, ὁ πατήρ, Nominativus pro Vocativo, quod sæpe occurrit in utroque Testamento. Si vero sensus esset, abba, quod est, si interpreteris, Pater, ut insinuat Hier. dicens: Hebraice & Græce loquitur, quia non est distinctio Judæi & Græci: Evangelista dixit, ἀββᾶ ὁ πατήρ; nunquam enim cum voces peregrinæ in N.T.Græcis vocibus explicantur, simpliciter dicitur, ὁ, absque voce πατήρ, ut observat Capellus vir longè doctissimus.
units.tr: 36. Father. In Greek, ὁ πατήρ, the nominative used for the vocative, which often occurs in both Testaments. If, however, the sense were abba, which is, if you interpret it, Father, as Jerome hints when he says: He speaks in Hebrew and Greek, because there is no distinction between Jew and Greek, the Evangelist wrote [ἀββᾶ ὁ πατήρ]; for never, when foreign words in the New Testament are explained by Greek words, is the article ὁ used simply without the word πατήρ, as the very learned Capellus observes.

units.la: Transfer calicem hunc à me. Calix mensuram significat poculentorum, sicut pars seu portio denotat mensuram eículentorum, quam scilicet Architriclinus in convivio singulis partitur. Utroque nomine significatur quidquid apponi solet convivis edendum, vel bibendum, atque adeo per translationem quidquid ad singulos homines quoquo jure pertinet, ut Psal.15.5. Dominus pars hæreditatis (Heb. portionis) meæ, & calicis mei, id est, ipse est mihi procibo & omnia ad vitam necessaria in eo uno habeo. Aliquando vero significat afflictionem, flagellum, seu ultionem necessariò tolerandam, desumptâ metaphorâ à vino damnatorum, ut Amos loquitur cap.2. v.8. id est, à vino generoso, delicato, & pretiofo, quod apud Hebræos propinari solebat damnatis à familiaribus, & amicis, quò minùs dolerent. Villalpandus existimat hujusmodi locutiones, bibere calicem, accipere calicem de manu Domini, &c. desumtas esse à bibendi certaminibus, ubi convivæ cogunntur ebibere certas mensuras usque ad fundum calicis, non sine fastidio, & agone, læsioneque corporis virium, & animi; quia ejusmodi potus initio suaves sunt, sed in fine acerbi. Nam quod appetebat sitis, respuit satietas, naturàque ipsa perhorrescit, quod videt sibi esse noxium, sed exhauriendus omnino calix offertur ipsius compotatoris manu, ebibendúsque est usque ad fæces. Talis est potus, & concertatio peccatorum cum divina providentia. Nam peccatores dulce vinum voluptatum bibere volunt, fundum calicis, hoc est, pœnarum acerbitatem exhaurire recusant, sed ebibant necesse est. Calix in manu Domini vini meri plenus mixto, seu ut textus Hebræus sonat, turbidâ fæce; & inclinavit ex hoc in hoc, id est,ab ore alterius detractum alteri porrigit: verumtamen fæx ejus non est exinanita, bibent omnes peccatores terræ, id est, necesse est, ut omnes peccatores terræ fæces voluptatum ebibant, id est, pœnarum acerbitatem, voluptatum appendicem experiantur. De hoc calice dicit Christus ad Patrem, Transfer calicem hunc à me, nam Christo fidejussori nostro propinatur fæx calicis voluptatum, quas nos bibimus cum Babylone meretrice compotantes, & cum Deo quasi concertantes.
units.tr: Take this cup away from me. The cup signifies a measure of drink, just as the portion denotes a measure of food, which the chief steward at a feast distributes to each guest. By either name is signified whatever is customarily set before guests to eat or drink, and so by transference whatever pertains to each person by any right, as in Psalm 15:5: The Lord is the portion (Heb. portion) of my inheritance and of my cup, that is, he is my food, and I have in him alone all things necessary for life. Sometimes, however, it signifies affliction, a scourge, or a vengeance that must necessarily be endured, the metaphor being taken from the wine of the condemned, as Amos speaks in chapter 2:8, that is, from wine that is noble, delicate and precious, which among the Hebrews was customarily offered to the condemned by their intimates and friends, so that they might grieve less. Villalpando thinks that expressions of this kind, to drink the cup, to receive the cup from the hand of the Lord, etc., are taken from drinking contests, where the guests are forced to drain certain measures down to the bottom of the cup, not without weariness, struggle, and injury to the strength of body and mind; for such drinks are pleasant at the start but bitter at the end. For satiety rejects what thirst desired, and nature itself shudders at what it sees to be harmful, yet the cup must be emptied, offered by the very hand of the one who challenges to the drinking, and drunk down to the dregs. Such is the drink and the contest of sinners with divine providence. For sinners want to drink the sweet wine of pleasures, but they refuse to drain the bottom of the cup, that is, the bitterness of punishments, yet they must drink it down. A cup is in the hand of the Lord, full of pure wine mixed with dregs, or, as the Hebrew text sounds, with turbid lees; and he has poured out from this into that, that is, having been drawn from the mouth of one, he hands it to another: yet its dregs have not been emptied; all the sinners of the earth shall drink, that is, it is necessary that all the sinners of the earth drink down the dregs of pleasures, that is, experience the bitterness of punishments, the aftermath of pleasures. Of this cup Christ speaks to the Father: Take this cup away from me, for the dregs of the cup of pleasures are offered to Christ our surety, which we drink while carousing with the harlot Babylon, and contending with God as it were.

units.la: 38. Vigilate, & orate. Si de vigilando tantùm, non etiam de orando · discipulos admoneret, solas videretur liberi arbitrii vires hortatus, sed cùm addidit, Et orate, satis docuit superni futurum muneris, ut etiam vigilantes tentationis procella non vinceret.Leo. M. 2. de vocat. Gent. cap9.
units.tr: 38. Watch and pray. If he had admonished the disciples only about watching, and not also about praying, he would seem to have exhorted only the powers of free will; but when he added, and pray, he taught sufficiently that it is the gift of a higher power that even those who watch are not overcome by the storm of temptation. Leo the Great, On the Calling of the Gentiles, 2, chapter 9.

units.la: 51. Adolescens. Græcè, A dolescentulus, non Joannes, aut Jacobus Minor, ut nonnulli sunt arbitrati, cùm mox dixerit Marcus, Tunc discipuli ejus relinquentes eum fugerunt omnes; verisimiliùs igitur conjectat Cajetanus in Jentaculis fuisse quemdam è villa proxima Gethsemani, qui rumore, & strepitu transeuntium satellitum Christum capientium excitatus, è lecto profiliens occurrerit, ut videret quid ageretur. Hoc autem observat Evangelista, ut innotesceat non nisi ope divinâ salvos fugisse Apostolos, cùm Judæis constitutum fuerit, non Jesum tantùm prehendere, sed et ejus discipulos.
units.tr: 51. A young man. In Greek, a young lad, not John or James the Less, as some have thought, since Mark soon says, Then his disciples, leaving him, all fled; so Cajetan conjectures more plausibly, in his Jentaculae, that he was a certain man from the village nearby Gethsemane, who, roused by the noise and clamour of the passing soldiers who were seizing Christ, leapt from his bed and ran out to see what was happening. The Evangelist observes this so that it may be known that the apostles fled safely only by divine help, since the Jews had determined to seize not only Jesus but also his disciples.

units.la: Tenuerunt eum. Id est, apprehensa sindone tenere eum conati sunt satellites, qui Græcè dicuntur hìc adolescentuli, quod mirum non est, cùm sæpe Græcis ita dicti sunt milites.
units.tr: They tried to hold him. That is, the guards, whom the Greek calls here young men [neaniskoi], tried to seize him by the linen cloth; this is not surprising, since soldiers were often called that by the Greeks [neaniskoi].

units.la: 56. Conuenientia. Id est, ad mortem sufficientia. Eodem sensu v. 59. dicitur, Et non erat conueniens illorum testimonium
units.tr: 56. Agreeing. That is, sufficient for death. In the same sense, at verse 59 it is said: "And their testimony was not agreeing [ouk ēn sunkheousa]." Note: the Greek of the second quotation is not printed in the source; the bracketed Greek above is supplied from the Greek of Mark 14.56 and should be read as a translator's gloss.

units.la: 57. Falsum testimonium ferebant. Falsus testis est, qui non eodem sensu dicta intelligit, quo dicuntur. Dominus enim dixerat de Templo corporis sui, Ego dissolvam,&c. Quando enim mortuo Christo anima deseruit carnem, tunc solutum est illud Templum, quod fuit ex anima carneque constructum, & cum anima reverteretur ad carnem, tunc est illud Templum die tertia suscitatum, & tamen propter unam Christi Dei hominisque personam, idem mortuus est in corpore suo, qui suscitavit Templum corporis sui. B. Fulgent. lib. 3. ad Thrasymundum.
units.tr: 57. They bore false witness. A false witness is one who understands words in a sense other than that in which they are spoken. For the Lord had said of the temple of his body, "I will destroy," etc. For when Christ died, the soul left the flesh, and then that temple, which was constructed of soul and flesh, was dissolved; and when the soul returned to the flesh, then on the third day that temple was raised up. And yet, on account of the one person of Christ, God and man, the same one who died in his body is the one who raised up the temple of his body. Blessed Fulgentius, book 3, to Thrasymundus.

units.la: 58. Ante atrium. Græcè, in vestibulum atrii.
units.tr: 58. Before the court. In Greek, into the vestibule of the court.

units.la: CAPUT XV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XV.

units.la: 1. ET confestim, &c. Vide Matth.27. ubi feré omnia, quæ in præsenti capite sunt difficilia, exposuimus.
units.tr: 1. And immediately, etc. See Matth. 27., where we have explained almost everything that is difficult in the present chapter.

units.la: 47. Emissâ voce magnâ expiravit. Qui morti dominatur, & præcipit sicut Dominus, potestative expirat; qualis autem hæc vox fuerit, Lucas declarat, Pater, inquit, in manus tuas commendo spiritum meum.
units.tr: 47. Having uttered a loud voice, he expired. He who rules over death and commands as the Lord expires by his own power. What kind of voice this was Luke declares: Father, into your hands I commend my spirit.

units.la: Et velum Templi scissum est. In Evangelio, quod Hebraicis literis scriptum est, legimus: non velum Templi scissum, sed superliminare Templi magnitudinis magnæ corruisse. Testatur autem Joseph. lib.7. belli Judaici cap.12. non supremum linteum tantùm, sed & imum uno perpetuo lapide fuisse extructum.
units.tr: And the veil of the Temple was torn. In the Gospel that was written in Hebrew letters we read that it was not the veil of the Temple that was torn, but the great lintel of the Temple that fell. Josephus, in book 7 of the Jewish War, chapter 12, testifies that not only the uppermost lintel but also the lowest was built of one continuous stone.

units.la: 39. Quia sic clamans expirasset. Grandis energia est in his vocibus, sic clamans; nam ut præclarè Bernard. Serm. 28. in Cant. Ex voce agnovit filium Dei, & non ex facie. Erat enim fortasse ex ovibus ejus, quæ vocem ejus audiunt, auditus invenit, quod non vidus; oculum species fefellit, auri veritas se infudit, oculus pronunciabat infirmum, oculus fœdum, oculus miserum, oculus morte turpissimâ condemnatum; auri Dei filius, auri formosus innotuit.
units.tr: 39. Because he had expired crying out in this way. There is great force in the words crying out in this way. As Bernard splendidly says in Sermon 28 on the Song of Songs: "He recognised the Son of God from the voice, and not from the face. Perhaps he was one of his sheep, who hear his voice; hearing found what sight did not. Appearance deceived the eye, the truth poured itself into the ear. The eye pronounced him weak, the eye foul, the eye wretched, the eye condemned to a most shameful death; to the ear the Son of God became known, the beautiful one of the ear."

units.la: 40. Salome. Quidam hanc etiam vocant Mariam, sed hoc nusquam legitur; qui id putant ex eo decepti videntur, quod putarent Salome, esse Genitivi casus, & ita dici Mariam Salome sicut Mariam Cleophæ, aut Jacobi, aut Alphæi. Unde nomen Maria, quod præcedit, ad hoc etiam vocabulum referunt, sed male; cum ex Græco satis appareat, non esse Genitivum, sed Nominativum, nec à priore voce dependere. Non enim dicitur ibi τ' σαλώμη, sicut τῆ Ιακώβῳ, sed nudè σαλώμη: sicut nudè quod præcedit Maria. Omnino enim illud τ' adjungedum erat, si Genitivus esset, maximè cum intercessisset illud μήτηρ, quod ad Salome non potest referri. Et hoc modo omnes Græci interpretati sunt. Quare miror in Martyrol. Rom. pridie Kal. Novemb. sic legi: Hierosolymis Sanctæ Mariæ Salomæ, quæ in Evangelio legitur circa sepulturam Domini sollicita. Omnino enim puto hanc Salomen fuisse matrem filiorum Zebedæi. Sic enim apparet ex collatione Marci cum Matthæo, qui cap. 27. hanc eandem mulierem vocat matrem filiorum Zebedæi. Baronius in apparatu ad Annales, non Mariam, sed simpliciter Salomen vocavit; ostendens eandem esse cum Matre filiorum Zebedæi.
units.tr: 40. Salome. Some also call her Mary, but this is nowhere read. Those who think so seem to have been misled by supposing that Salome is a genitive, so that Mary Salome would be spoken of as Mary of Cleophas, or of James, or of Alphaeus. Hence they also refer the name Mary, which precedes, to this word, but wrongly, since the Greek makes it clear enough that it is not a genitive but a nominative, and does not depend on the preceding word. For there it is not said τῆ Σαλώμη, as τῆ Ἰακώβῳ, but simply σαλώμη, just as the preceding word is simply Maria. For the article would have had to be added if it were a genitive, especially since the word μήτηρ intervenes, which cannot be referred to Salome. And all the Greeks have translated it this way. Hence I wonder why in the Roman Martyrology, on the day before the Kalends of November, it is read thus: "At Jerusalem, of Saint Mary Salome, who in the Gospel is read as anxious about the Lord's burial." For I entirely think that this Salome was the mother of the sons of Zebedee. For this appears from comparing Mark with Matthew, who in chapter 27 calls this same woman the mother of the sons of Zebedee. Baronius, in the Apparatus to his Annals, called her not Mary but simply Salome, showing that she is the same as the mother of the sons of Zebedee.

units.la: 43. Decurio. Græcè Senator, scilicet, urbis Jerusalem, non vero de Synedrio Magno, qui vocabantur Principes, ut Nicodemus Ioan.3. v.1.
units.tr: 43. Decurion. In Greek, a senator, namely of the city of Jerusalem, not of the Great Sanhedrin, who were called the Princes, as Nicodemus in John 3:1.

units.la: CAPUT XVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI.

units.la: 1. Emerunt. Id est, emerant, ut patet ex Luc.23. v.56. Sensus itaque est, & Maria Magdalene, & Maria Jacobi, & Salome emerant aromata, ut cum transissent Sabbatum venientes ungerent Jesum.
units.tr: 1. They had bought. That is, they had bought, as is clear from Luke 23:56. The sense, then, is that Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome had bought spices, so that, when the Sabbath had passed, they might come and anoint Jesus.

units.la: 2. Orto jam sole. Vide dicta Matth.28. v.1.
units.tr: 2. The sun having already risen. See what was said at Matt. 28:1.

units.la: 3. Quis revolvet, &c. Nihil igitur de custodia & sigillatione sepulchri mulieribus innotuerat.
units.tr: 3. Who will roll away, etc. Nothing, therefore, had been made known to the women about the guarding and sealing of the sepulchre.

units.la: 4. Revolutum lapidem. Scilicet qui specum claudebat. Unde Matth.28. v.2. in textu Græco diserte dicitur, quod Angelus revolvit lapidem ab ostio.
units.tr: 4. The stone rolled back. That is, the stone that closed the cave. Hence Matt. 28:2 says plainly, in the Greek text, that the angel rolled the stone away from the door.

units.la: 5. introëuntes in monumentum, &c. Id est, postquam in troierint in monumentum, & non viderint corpus domini Jesu ibi, Luc.24. v.3. & Magdalene cucurrerit ad Apostolos, adductisque secum Petro & Joanne ad monumentum reversa sit, & abierint iterum ad semetipsos discipuli, ut narrat Joan. cap.20. mulieres mente consternatæ & prospicientes in monumentum viderunt duos Angelos in albis, unum ad caput, alterum ad pedes sepulchri, ut narrat Joan. loco citato, qui post ceteros Evangelistas scribens videtur præsius ordinem temporis secutus.
units.tr: 5. entering into the tomb, etc. That is, after they had entered the tomb and had not seen the body of the Lord Jesus there, Luke 24:3; and Magdalene had run to the apostles, and returned to the tomb with Peter and John; and the disciples had gone away again to their own homes, as John 20 relates. The women, dismayed in mind, looked into the tomb and saw two angels in white, one at the head and the other at the feet of the sepulchre, as John relates in the passage cited. John, writing after the other Evangelists, seems to have followed the order of time more exactly.

units.la: Viderunt juvenem. Qui ex quo revolverat lapidem ab ostio monumenti, ipsis mulieribus erat huc usque inconspicuus, licet super revolutum lapidem sederet. Unius autem duntaxat Angeli meminere Marcus, & Matthæus, cum duos viderint mulieres Angelos, ut Lucas, & Joannes testantur, quia & mulieribus propior, & pro duobus verba fecit. Sedentes Angelos Lucas dicit stetisse Hebraismo Scripturæ familiari, quo stare sumitur pro verbo substantivo esse, seu adesse, ut nullum certum situm indicet. Sic Luc.7. v.37. mulier peccatrix dicitur stans retro secus pedes Jesu eos rigasse lachrymis, tersisse capillis, esse osculata, & unguento unxisse, quæ omnia non nisi in genua procumbendo peragere potuisse videtur.
units.tr: They saw a young man. He who had rolled back the stone from the door of the tomb had until then been unseen by the women themselves, although he sat upon the rolled-back stone. Only one angel is mentioned by Mark and Matthew, though the women saw two angels, as Luke and John testify: Matthew and Mark mention the one who was nearer to the women and who spoke for both. Luke says the angels stood (stetisse), though they were sitting. This is a Hebraism familiar in Scripture, in which "to stand" is taken for "to be" or "to be present", so that it indicates no fixed position. Thus Luke 7:37 says the sinful woman was standing behind at Jesus' feet, wetting them with tears, wiping them with her hair, kissing them, and anointing them with ointment; all of which, it seems, could only have been done by kneeling down.

units.la: 6. Qui dicit illis. Id est, mulieribus reliquis, postquam Maria Magdalene, reddita Angelis ploratus sui ratione, conversa esset retrorsum, ut dicitur Joan.20. id est, paululum recessisset à monumento, atque adeò Christus eo ipso momento se Magdalenæ conspiciendum dedit, ipsaque ad Apostolos ivit nunciatura se Dominum vidisse, quo Angeli nuncio reliquas mulieres gaudio magno replevit, ut dicitur Matth.28. v.8. eisque verba Christi in memoriam revocavit, ut dicitur Luc.24. v.7. & 8.
units.tr: 6. He said to them. That is, to the remaining women. After Mary Magdalene had given the angels the reason for her weeping, she turned back, as John 20 says; that is, she withdrew a little from the tomb. Christ then, at that very moment, gave himself to be seen by Magdalene, and she went to the apostles to announce that she had seen the Lord. By this angelic message he filled the other women with great joy, as Matt. 28:8 says, and he recalled to their memory the words of Christ, as Luke 24:7-8 says.

units.la: 7. Et Petro. Si hunc Angelus non nominatim exprimeret, qui Magistrum negaverat, venire inter discipulos non auderet: vocatur ergo ex nomine, ne desperaret ex negatione. B. Greg. Hom 21. in Evang. Ideo autem Christus post resurrectionem primo mulieribus apparuit, ut fieret resurrectionis nuncia, quae fuit mortis interpres, & quae viro porrexerat interitus tanti nuncium, viro ipsa porrigeret magnae salutis auditum, ut compensaret fidei nuncio, quod perfidiae ademit. B. Petrus Chrysologus Serm.76.
units.tr: 7. And to Peter. If the angel had not named him expressly, he who had denied his Master would not have dared to come among the disciples. He is therefore called by name, lest he despair because of his denial. Blessed Gregory, Hom. 21 on the Gospel: Christ therefore appeared first to the women after the resurrection, so that a messenger of the resurrection might be made of her who had been the interpreter of death; and she who had carried to her husband the news of so great a ruin might herself carry to her husband the report of great salvation, so that the message of faith might make up for what unbelief had taken away. Blessed Peter Chrysologus, Sermon 76.

units.la: 8. illae exeuntes fugerunt de monumento. Scilicet currentes nunciare Apostolis dicta ab angelis, & inter currendum Christum habuere obvium, ut narratur Matth.28.v.8.9.& 10. haecque fuit secunda Christi post resurrectionem apparitio, quam tacent Lucas, Marcus, & Joannes.
units.tr: 8. They went out and fled from the tomb. Namely, running to tell the apostles what had been said by the angels; and in their running they met Christ, as is related in Matt. 28:8-10. This was the second appearance of Christ after the resurrection, which Luke, Mark and John pass over in silence.

units.la: Nemini quidquam dixerunt. Scilicet obvio; dixerunt enim Apostolis, ut dicitur Luc.24. v.9. ubi Lucas simul comprehendit, ut patet ibidem v.10. quidquid à mulieribus fuit Apostolis nunciatum non semel. Nam primò Magdalena eis nunciavit corpus Christi fuisse sublatum, quo audito statim Petrus cucurrit ad monumentum, ut refert Lucas cap.24. v.12. Deinde se vidisse Dominum, tum demum ceterae mulieres iisdem nunciavere sibi dicta ab Angelis, & factam sibi Christi apparitionem.
units.tr: They said nothing to anyone. That is, to anyone they met; for they did tell the apostles, as Luke 24:9 says, where Luke at once includes everything, as is clear from the same passage, v.10. Whatever the women reported to the apostles was not reported all at once. For first Magdalene told them that the body of Christ had been taken away; on hearing this, Peter at once ran to the tomb, as Luke relates in 24:12. Then she told them that she had seen the Lord. Only then did the other women report to them what the angels had said and the appearance of Christ that had been made to them.

units.la: 9. Surgens autem. Graece, cum autem surrexisset. nunc igitur incipit Sanctus Evangelista tres ex quinque apparitionibus ipsa die resurrectionis factas ordine commemorare.
units.tr: 9. And when he had risen. In the Greek, "when he had risen". Now the holy Evangelist begins to recount in order three of the five appearances made on the very day of the resurrection.

units.la: Mane. Tempus Dominicae resurrectionis notatur; unde Aug.apud Prosp. Sent.203. Vigor fidei Christianae tribus temporibus initiatur, vespere, mane, & meridie, vespere Dominus in cruce, mane in resurrectione, meridie in ascensione, unum ad patientiam occisi, aliud ad vitam resuscitati, tertium pertinet ad gloriam majestatis in Patris dextra considentis.
units.tr: Early. The time of the Lord's resurrection is noted. Hence Augustine, cited in Prosper's Sentences 203: The vigour of Christian faith is begun at three times: evening, morning and midday. In the evening the Lord was on the cross; in the morning, in the resurrection; at midday, in the ascension. One belongs to the suffering of the slain, another to the life of the raised, and the third pertains to the glory of majesty seated at the Father's right hand.

units.la: Sabbati. Id est, hebdomadis, vide Mat.28.v.1.
units.tr: Of the Sabbath. That is, of the week; see Matt. 28:1.

units.la: Apparuit primo. Sub hortulani specie, ut narratur Joan.20.
units.tr: He appeared first. In the appearance of a gardener, as is related in John 20.

units.la: Mariae Magdalenae. Soli, cum paululum recessisset à monumento,& à ceteris mulieribus, quae ad sepulchrum remanserant. Recte, inquit Beda in hunc locum, mulier, quae laetitiam Dominicae resurrectionis prima nunciavit, a septem daemonibus curata esse memoratur, ne quisquam digne poenitens de peccatorum venia desperaret, & ubi abundavit peccatum, superabundasse gratia demonstraretur.
units.tr: To Mary Magdalene. Alone, when she had withdrawn a little from the tomb and from the other women who had remained at the sepulchre. Rightly, says Bede on this passage, the woman who first announced the joy of the Lord's resurrection is recorded to have been healed of seven demons, so that no one who repents worthily should despair of the pardon of sins, and so that it might be shown that where sin abounded, grace did much more abound.

units.la: 10. Illa vadens. Supple, cito; hoc enim juxta sensum literalem significari videtur his Christi verbis Joan.20. v.17. Noli me tangere, nondum enim ascendi ad patrem meum. Vade autem, &c. q.d. Noli tempus amplexibus insumere, erit alius amplexandi locus; nam per quadraginta dies apparebo, meque vivum praebebo in multis argumentis antequam ascendam ad Patrem meum, nunc autem vade cito, & nuncia discipulis meam resurrectionem.
units.tr: 10. She, going. Supply "quickly", for this seems to be what is signified, according to the literal sense, by Christ's words in John 20:17: Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father. But go, etc. As if to say: Do not spend the time in embraces; there will be another opportunity for embracing. For I shall appear for forty days and show myself alive by many proofs before I ascend to my Father. But now go quickly and tell the disciples of my resurrection.

units.la: 12. Post haec autem. Id est, deinde, ut dicitur Luc.24. v.13. eadem ipsa die resurrectionis, qua primo apparuit Magdalenae, secundo ceteris mulieribus, tertio B. Petro. ut patet ex praesentis capitis v.9. Matth.28. v.9. & Luc.24. v.34. simul collatis.
units.tr: 12. After these things. That is, then, as Luke 24:13 says. On the same day of the resurrection, he first appeared to Magdalene, second to the other women, and third to Blessed Peter, as is clear from v.9 of this chapter, Matt. 28:9 and Luke 24:34, when these are compared together.

units.la: Duobus. Quorum unus erat Cleophas, ut dicitur Luc.24. qui creditur fuisse maritus vel pater Mariae quae dicitur Cleophae.
units.tr: To two. Of whom one was Cleophas, as Luke 24 says. He is believed to have been the husband or the father of the Mary who is called the wife of Cleophas.

units.la: In alia effigie. Id est, in effigie, quae ipsis alia videbatur; oculi enim eorum tenebantur, ne eum agnoscerent. Quando, inquit Aug. lib.2. quaest. Evang. q.15. illud fingimus, quod nihil significat, tunc est mendacium, cum autem fictio nostra refertur in aliquam significationem, non est mendacium, sed aliqua figura veritatis: sicut autem fictae, ita etiam finguntur facta sine mendacio ad aliquam rem significandam. Ostensus itaque est Christus in alia effigie his, qui videbantur circa fidem tepescere; unde dicebant: Nos autem sperabamus quia ipse effet redempturus Israel. Hinc Greg. Hom.23. in Evang. Talem, inquit, Christus se exhibuit eis in corpore, qualis apud illos erat in mente.
units.tr: In another form. That is, in a form which appeared to them to be different; for their eyes were held, so that they should not recognize him. When, says Augustine, book 2 of the Questions on the Gospels, q.15, we feign what signifies nothing, then it is a lie; but when our fiction is referred to some meaning, it is not a lie but a certain figure of the truth. Just as fictions are made, so also things are feigned without lie to signify something. Christ, therefore, was shown in another form to those who seemed to be growing lukewarm in faith; whence they said: But we were hoping that he would be the redeemer of Israel. Hence Gregory, Hom. 23 on the Gospel: Christ showed himself to them in a body such as he was in their mind.

units.la: Euntibus in villam. Distantem a Jerofolymis septem milliariis cum dimidio, eratque villae nomen Emmaus, ut dicitur Luc. 24. v.13. & fuisse Cleophae tradit Hieronymus in Epitaphio Paulae Epist.27. haec autem quarta apparitio longe plenius narratur Luc. 24.
units.tr: Going into the village. The village was seven and a half miles from Jerusalem, and its name was Emmaus, as Luke 24:13 says. Jerome, in his Epitaph of Paula, Epistle 27, says that it was Cleophas's village. This fourth appearance, however, is recounted much more fully in Luke 24.

units.la: Nec illis crediderunt. Supple, omnes discipuli; nam quosdam credidisse apertum est ex Luc.24. v.34. & 35. id etiam observat B. Aug. lib.3. de consensu Evang. cap.25.
units.tr: Nor did they believe them. Supply: all the disciples. For it is plain from Luke 24:34-35 that some did believe. Blessed Augustine also observes this, book 3 of On the Harmony of the Gospels, ch. 25.

units.la: 14. Novissime. ὑστερον, tandem, postea; non enim hic absolute ultima Christi apparitio commemoratur, sed quinta quae est novissima earum, quae contigere ipsa resurrectionis die, seu prima Sabbati, ut loquitur Evangelista supra v.9. Est autem haec eadem apparitio cum ea, quam narrant Luc.24. a v.36. ad 44. & Joan.20. a v.19. ad 25.
units.tr: 14. Last of all [ὕστερον]: at length, afterwards. For the last appearance of Christ absolutely is not recorded here, but the fifth, which is the last of those that happened on the very day of the resurrection, that is, the first day of the week, as the Evangelist speaks above in v.9. This appearance is the same as that which Luke 24 relates from v.36 to 44, and John 20 from v.19 to 25.

units.la: Recumbentibus. Id est, mensae accumbentibus, dum inter se fabularentur, Luc.24. v.36.
units.tr: As they reclined. That is, reclining at table, while they talked among themselves, Luke 24:36.

units.la: Vndecim. Hoc tum numero Apostolica societas nuncupabatur, inquit Aug. lib.3. de conf. Evang. cap. 25. quamvis abesset Thomas: imò 1 Cor.15. v.5. dicitur Christus apparuisse duodecim, etsi Juda tum mortuo, necdum electo Matthia.
units.tr: Eleven. By this number, says Augustine, book 3 of On the Harmony of the Gospels, ch. 25, the apostolic company was then called, although Thomas was absent. Indeed, 1 Cor. 15:5 says Christ appeared to the twelve, although Judas was then dead and Matthias not yet chosen.

units.la: 15. Et dixit eis. Non præcisè in hac quinta apparitione, sed toto illo tempore, quo cum eis conversatus est per quadraginta dies post resurrectionem.
units.tr: 15. And he said to them. Not only at this fifth appearance, but during the whole time in which he lived with them for forty days after the resurrection.

units.la: Omni creatura. Id est, omni genti; quod enim Marcus dicit his verbis, Prædicate Evangelium omni creaturæ, hoc Matthæus dixit, Docete omnes gentes. Omni creatura Evangelium prædicare præcepit, quia omnia genera hominum ducit ad fidem voluit; unde scriptum est, Qui vult omnes homines salvos fieri, & ad agnitionem veritatis venire; omnes quippe homines vult salvos fieri, quia de omni hominum genere eligit, quos ad gaudium æternæ salutis trahit. S. Greg. Mag. lib.5. in 1 Reg. cap.13. in illud: Quocunque se vertebat, supAabat. Restringitur autem ab Evangelista creaturæ nomen ad homines, quomodo viventis vocabulum restringitur, dum Eva dicitur mater viventium, & vox carnis dum profitemur in symbolo carnis resurrectionem, & passim in Scripturis.
units.tr: To every creature. That is, to every nation. For what Mark says in these words, Preach the Gospel to every creature, Matthew said as Teach all nations. He commanded the Gospel to be preached to every creature because he willed to lead every kind of man to faith; hence it is written: Who wishes all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. For he wishes all men to be saved, since he chooses from every kind of man those whom he draws to the joy of eternal salvation. S. Gregory the Great, Book 5 on 1 Kings, chapter 13, on the words: Wherever he turned himself, he prevailed. The word "creature" is, however, restricted by the Evangelist to men, just as the word "living" is restricted when Eve is called the mother of the living, and the word "flesh" when we profess in the creed the resurrection of the flesh, and in many places in Scripture.

units.la: Qui crediderit. Id est, qui in vera fide perseveraverit. Vera etenim fides est, ait B. Greg. Hom.29. in Evang. quæ in hoc, quod verbis dicit, moribus non contradicit. Hinc est enim, quod de quibusdam falsis fidelibus Paulus dicit, Qui confitentur se nosse Deum, factis autem negant. Hinc Joan. ait, Qui dicit se nosse Deum, & mandata ejus non custodit, mendax est.
units.tr: He who believes. That is, he who has persevered in true faith. For, says blessed Gregory, Homily 29 on the Gospel, true faith is that which does not contradict in conduct what it says in words. Hence Paul says of certain false believers: They profess that they know God, but in works they deny him. Hence John says: He who says that he knows God, and does not keep his commandments, is a liar.

units.la: Et baptizatus fuerit. Id est, postquam baptizatus fuerit, seu renatus fuerit ex aqua & Spiritu-Sancto, ut Christus alibi loquitur. Non raro autem in sanctis Scripturis particula conjunctiva (&) idem est ac cum, vel postquam; sic Exod.14. v.21. Vertit mare in siccum, divisaque est aqua: id est, postquam divisa est aqua. Esaiæ 64.v.5. Iratus es, & peccavimus, id est, cum peccavimus. Atque adeo commendare specialiter intendit Christus, non necessitatem baptismi aliàs à se commendatam, sed necessitatem operibus complendi, quod in baptismo verbis promissis, ut veraciter fideles simus, sicque salvi esse possimus.
units.tr: And is baptized. That is, after he has been baptized, or has been born again of water and the Holy Spirit, as Christ speaks elsewhere. The conjunction "and" in Holy Scripture is not infrequently the same as "when" or "after"; so Exodus 14:21: He turned the sea into dry land, and the water was divided: that is, after the water was divided. Isaiah 64:5: You were angry, and we sinned, that is, when we sinned. Thus Christ intends to commend specifically not the necessity of baptism, which he had commended on other occasions, but the necessity of fulfilling by works what is promised in baptism in words, so that we may be truly faithful and thus be able to be saved.

units.la: Qui vero non crediderit. Id est, qui non tenuerit corde, & opere promissionis Deo à se in baptismo factæ fidem, atque adeo fidelis est in nomine aliud demonstrans in opere. Vide etiam ne forte ob hoc Salvator, cum diceret, Qui crediderit, & baptizatus fuerit, salvus erit; caute & vigilanter non repetierit, Qui vero baptizatus non fuerit, sed tantum, Qui vero non crediderit, condemnabitur. Nimirum innuens solam interdum fidem sufficere ad salutem, & sine ipsa sufficere nihil. B. Bernardus Ep. 77. ad Hugonem de sancto Victore.
units.tr: But he who does not believe. That is, he who has not held in heart and deed the faith of the promise made to God in baptism, and so is faithful in name while showing otherwise in deed. See also whether the Saviour, when he said, He who believes and is baptized will be saved, did not cautiously and watchfully fail to repeat, "He who is not baptized," but only, "He who does not believe will be condemned." Clearly he indicates that sometimes faith alone suffices for salvation, and that without faith nothing suffices. Blessed Bernard, Letter 77 to Hugh of Saint Victor.

units.la: Condemnabitur. Id est, æternis suppliciis inferorum addicetur.
units.tr: Will be condemned. That is, he will be consigned to the eternal punishments of hell.

units.la: 17. Signa autem, &c. Q. d. Hoc erit quasi sigillum integerrimam & & plenissimam habentium fidem, quod nullum prorsus miraculum erit eis impossibile, cum scilicet res secundum divinæ sapientiæ regulas id postulaverit.
units.tr: 17. And signs, etc. The meaning is: this will be a sign, as it were, of those who have the most entire and fullest faith, that no miracle at all will be impossible for them, namely when the matter, according to the rules of divine wisdom, requires it.

units.la: 18. Serpentes tollent, &c. Hæc promissa fuisse ad literam impleta patet ex Paulo. Is enim viperam, quæ manum ejus invaserat, illæsus in ignem excussit. Act. 28. v.5. Id ipsum omnino à Christo Luc.10. v.19. promittitur verbis nonnihil diversis, quæ palàm alludunt ad verba Regii Vatis, Psal.90. v.13. Super aspidem & basiliscum ambulabis, &c. ut agnoscunt B. Basilius Hom.9. Hexaëm. & Tert. lib.4. contra Marcionem cap. 24. Nec frustra est, quod ibi apud Luc. serpentes, & scorpiones, & hujusmodi, si quæ alia sunt, Christus vocat vim inimici, id est diaboli, mortis enim imperium cum diabolo tribuatur Heb.12. v.14. videntur lethalia omnia ipsi aliquo modo subservire, quo modo carnifici instrumenta, quibus reos torquere solet.
units.tr: 18. They will take up serpents, etc. That these promises were fulfilled literally is clear from Paul. For he shook off into the fire the viper which had fastened on his hand, unharmed. Acts 28:5. The very same thing is promised by Christ in Luke 10:19, in words somewhat different, which plainly allude to the words of the royal prophet, Psalm 91:13: You will walk upon the asp and the basilisk, etc., as blessed Basil acknowledges, Homily 9 on the Hexaemeron, and Tertullian, Book 4 against Marcion, chapter 24. Nor is it in vain that there Christ calls serpents, scorpions, and whatever other such things there are, the power of the enemy, that is, of the devil; for since the rule of death is attributed to the devil (Hebrews 2:14), all deadly things seem in some way to serve him, as instruments of the executioner serve by which he is accustomed to torture the condemned.

units.la: 19. Postquam locutus est eis. Quæcumque scilicet eis dicta voluit, & oportuit post resurrectionem: non enim dicit post-postquam hæc locutus est eis, sed generaliter, ut intelligatur de omnibus, quæ post resurrectionem apparens eis locutus est de regno Dei, ut observat B.Aug. lib.3. de cons. Evang. cap. 25.
units.tr: 19. After he had spoken to them. Namely, whatever he wished and ought to have said to them after the resurrection. For he does not say "after these things he had spoken to them," but speaks in general, so that it is understood of all the things which, appearing to them after the resurrection, he spoke about the kingdom of God, as blessed Augustine observes, Book 3 on the Harmony of the Gospels, chapter 25.

units.la: Assumtus est. Secundum naturam humanam divina sua virtute usque ad tempora restitutionis omnium, ut dicitur Act.3. v.21. id est, usque ad mundi finem, cum redierit judicaturus vivos & mortuos. De Christi ascensione ex summitate montis Olivoeti in cœlum hoc constat, quod eo usque ascenderit, ut nubes inter ipsum & spectantium oculos intervenirent. Ephes.4. v.10. ascendisse dicitur Christus super omnes cælos, ut impleret omnia, in quem locum sic scribit Magister Ecclesiarum Hieronymus: Nunquid corporaliter omnes cælos, & universas sublimitates, & cælorum circulos, quos Philosophi sphæras vocant, transiens, atque transcendens stetit in summo cæli fornice, &, ut ipso verbo utar, apside, an omnia temporalia contemnens atque despiciens, & æterna contemplans super cælos, id est, super invisibilia stetisse credendus est? Quod ego multo puto. Hæc Hieronymy.
units.tr: He was taken up. According to his human nature, by his divine power, until the times of the restoration of all things, as is said in Acts 3:21, that is, until the end of the world, when he returns to judge the living and the dead. That Christ's ascension from the summit of the Mount of Olives into heaven is certain from this, that he ascended until clouds intervened between him and the eyes of the spectators. Ephesians 4:10 says that Christ ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things; on this place the teacher of the Churches, Jerome, writes thus: Are we to believe that he stood, passing and transcending bodily all the heavens and all the heights and the circles of the heavens, which the philosophers call spheres, and stood on the highest vault of heaven, and, to use the very word, on the apse; or that, despising and disregarding all temporal things and contemplating eternal things, he stood above the heavens, that is, above invisible things? I think the latter, and think it much. Thus Jerome.

units.la: Sedet à dextris Dei. Id est, pari cum Deo potentia regnat. Vide dicta Matth.22. v.44.
units.tr: He sits at the right hand of God. That is, he reigns with equal power to God. See what is said at Matthew 22:44.

units.la: Profecti. Scilicet post Spiritus-Sancti missionem.
units.tr: They went forth. Namely after the sending of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Cooperante Domino. Id est, Domino intrinsecus aperiente hominum corda, ut intenderent his, quæ ab Apostolis dicebantur ; nam cathedram habet in cælo, qui corda docet.
units.tr: The Lord working with them. That is, the Lord inwardly opening men's hearts, so that they would attend to what was said by the Apostles; for he who teaches hearts has his chair in heaven.

units.la: Confirmante. Scilicet extrinsecus.
units.tr: Confirming. Namely outwardly.

units.la: Sequentibus. Nempe prædicationem Apostolicam.
units.tr: Following. Namely the apostolic preaching.

units.la: Signis. Invictissimè veritatem doctrinæ Apostolicæ demonstrantibus, ut patet ex Actis Apostolorum.
units.tr: With signs. Most invincibly demonstrating the truth of the apostolic doctrine, as is clear from the Acts of the Apostles.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: THE END.

units.la: CHRISTO JESU AUTORI, ET CONSUMMATORI FIDEI SACRUM, ECCLESIÆ ANGLICANÆ ET CUJUSVIS ORTHODOXÆ JUDICIO, HOC QUICQUID EST OPERIS AUTHOR EX ANIMO SUBJICIT.
units.tr: To Christ Jesus, the author and finisher of faith, and to the judgment of the English Church and of every orthodox reader, the author humbly submits whatever this work is.

units.la: Semper agam grates Christo, dabo semper honores,Laus Domini semper vivet in ore meo.
units.tr: I will always give thanks to Christ, I will always give honour; The praise of the Lord will live always in my mouth.
